explanation: The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius (marked as 2). The gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines. Insertion of the muscle is at the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve. Gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip joint. Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus: * When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in a slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position. * The actions of these muscles are affected when there is an injury to the superior gluteal nerve, neck of the femur, or loss of normal angulation of the shaft of the femur. This occurs in conditions like paralysis of the glutei, developmental dysplasia of the hip, etc. * When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb. This leads to a positive Trendelenburg's sign with a characteristic lurching gait - the patient lurches towards the affected side with contralateral pelvis drop. 206 > c pee = =< ot = ae Cercle SS SS oreo f aE — <> -- Other options 1Gluteus maximus - involved in the extension of flexed thigh, abduction (only upper fibres), and lateral rotation at the hip joint. explanation: 207 The given clinical scenario is suggestive of the involvement of 9th and 1oth cranial nerves due to occipitotemporal fracture and they are examined by testing the uvula which is marked as 2 in the given image. The jugular foramen is located between the lower border of the petrous part of the temporal bone and the condylar part of the occipital bone. As the investigations reveal fractures in the occipitotemporal region, along with the history of difficulty in swallowing and slurred speech, are suggestive of injury to the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve passing through the jugular foramen. Unilateral lesions of IX and X cranial nerves are commonly caused by skull-base fractures, strokes, or tumors. Glossopharyngeal and Vagus nerve examination include: * Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula(marked as 2 in the given image) at rest and with phonation (“aah”). + The pharyngeal (“gag”) reflex is evaluated by stimulating the posterior pharyngeal wall on each side with a sterile, blunt object (e.g., tongue blade) Patients with a proximal unilateral lesion of the vagus nerve complain of dysphagia. There will be a weakness of the soft palate muscles on the affected side. Attempts to voluntarily elevate the soft palate, like by asking the patient to say “aah” will reveal a weakness in elevation of the palate on the affected side. Along with this, there will be deviation of the uvula to the normal side, due to the unopposed action of palatal muscles on that side. The below image shows the base of the skull and its foramina:

explanation: The structure marked in the above image is mamillary body and the fibers from the mamillary body end in the anterior nucleus of the thalamus. The mammillary bodies are two small hemispherical, pea-sized eminences, lying side by side, forming the floor of the third ventricle. The fibres from medial mammillary nucleus project to the 208 anterior nucleus of the thalamus. The anterior thalamic nuclei have 3 subdivisions—anteroventral nucleus, anteromedial nucleus, and anterodorsal nucleus. * Major input: Mamillothalamic tract from the mammillary nuclei of the hypothalamus. * Major cortical output: Anterior limbic area, cingulate, and the parahippocampal gyrus * Major function: * Regulation of alertness and attention * Acquisition of memory

options: Vestibular nuclei Cc) Inferior olivary nucleus
explanation: The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. It is inhibitory to deep cerebellar nuclei. Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter. Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers. Pathological significance of Purkinje cells: + Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. + In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them. * Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

stem: The marked structure develops from which of the following structures? 184 ’ SS DZ, X x , r $ “Y
explanation: The structure marked in the given image is the azygos vein, which develops from the supracardinal vein. The azygos system of veins forms a connecting channel between the superior and inferior venae cavae. It occupies the upper part of the posterior abdominal wall and the posterior mediastinum. It also connects the portal, caval system, and vertebral venous systems.It drains the thoracic wall and the upper lumbar region. Development: The azygos venous system arises from the supra cardinal veins embryologically. The right supra cardinal vein becomes the azygos vein, while the left supra cardinal vein becomes 209 the hemiazygos vein. + The 4th to 11th right intercostal veins empty into the right supracardinal vein, which together with a portion of the posterior cardinal vein forms the azygos vein. * On the left, the 4th to 7th intercostal veins enter into the left supracardinal vein, and the left supracardinal vein, then known as the hemiazygos vein, which also empties into the azygos vein. Other options: Cardinal veins form the main venous drainage system of the embryo. It consists of, + Anterior cardinal veins, which drain the cephalic part of the embryo, and * Posterior cardinal veins, which drain the rest of the embryo. During the fifth to the seventh weeks, a number of additional veins are formed. It includes, ¢ Subcardinal veins, which mainly drain the kidneys; ¢ Sacrocardinal veins, which drain the lower extremities; * Supracardinal veins, which drain the body wall by way of the intercostal veins. stem: Inferior thyroid artery supplies which of the following structures?
explanation: All the given 4 structures are supplied by the Inferior thyroid artery. Inferior thyroid artery is a branch of the thyrocervical trunk, which in turn, is a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. The inferior thyroid artery loops upwards anterior to the medial border of the scalenus anterior, turns medially just below the sixth cervical transverse process, and then descends on longus colli to the lower border of the thyroid gland. Branches: + Pharyngeal branches: These supply the lower part of the pharynx. + Tracheal branches supply the trachea and anastomose with the bronchial arteries; 210 * Oesophageal branches supply the oesophagus and anastomose with the oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta; and + Inferior and ascending glandular branches supply the posterior and inferior regions of the thyroid gland, and anastomose with the contralateral inferior and ipsilateral superior thyroid arteries. + The ascending branch also supplies the parathyroid glands. * Ascending cervical artery * Inferior laryngeal * Muscular branches Note: Thymic branches originating from the internal thoracic, inferior thyroid artery, and sometimes superior thyroid arteries supply the thymus and the surrounding mediastinal connective tissue.

stem: Which part of this bone is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa? 185
explanation: The part of the scapula marked as 1 is the coracoid process and it is palpable in the infraclavicular fossa. The tip of the coracoid process lies approximately 2.5 cm below the clavicle, immediately lateral to the infraclavicular fossa (deltopectoral triangle). Hence, the coracoid process can be palpated below the clavicle. The coracoid process arises from the upper border of the neck of the scapula and it projects forwards and slightly laterally. Attachments at the coracoid process include * The conoid portion of the coracoclavicular ligament + Pectoralis minor * Medial end of coraco-acromial ligament * Coracohumeral ligament * Glenocorocoid ligament * Coracobrachialis muscle Other options Option B - Acromian process continues from the spine of the scapula. The acromion is subcutaneous over its dorsal surface, The attachments at the acromion are the coracoacromial ligament, the articular capsule of the acromioclavicular joint, and horizontal fibers of the trapezius. Option C - The glenoid fossa is present at the lateral angle of the scapula. It is articular with the humerus to form the shoulder joint. Option D - The inferior angle lies over the seventh rib. stem: Identify the pelvic diaphragm in the picture given below. 1 o—_ 6} Q = = es 4 MARROW
explanation: The structure marked "1" is the levator ani muscle which is part of the pelvic diaphragm. Other structures marked in the above image are 2: External anal sphincter 3: Internal anal sphincter 4: Pudendal canal Pelvic diaphragm The muscular part of the pelvic floor is the pelvic diaphragm. It is attached to the pelvic wall on either side between the greater and lesser sciatic foramen. Levator ani and coccygeus muscles form the pelvic diaphragm and delineate the lower limit of the true pelvis. Levator ani is formed by pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, and puborectalis. The muscles blend together posterior to the vagina in women and around the anus in both sexes. Posterior to the anal aperture, the form the anococcygeal body attaches to the coccyx. Urogenital hiatus is present anteriorly separating the muscles. This allows the urethra and vagina to pass through. Levator ani reinforces the external anal sphincter. In women, it functions as the vaginal sphincter. The coccygeus muscles, one on each side are triangular in shape and form the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm. The apices are attached to the tips of ischial spines. The bases are attached to the coccyx and sacrum.

stem: Third part of vertebral artery is related to which of the following ? 187
explanation: The third part of the vertebral artery (V3) is related to the area marked 2, which is the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra or the atlas. The given image shows the first cervical vertebra - atlas. + The area marked 1 is the posterior tubercle. + The area marked 2 is the posterior arch. The superior surface bears a groove for the of vertebral artery and venous plexus immediately behind. + The area marked 3 is the superior articular facet. ¢ The area marked 4 is the posterior surface of the anterior arch. It gives attachment to the apex of dens from the second cervical vertebra. The vertebral artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It passes through the foramina of transverse processes of C6 to C1 cervical vertebrae and enters the cranium through the foramen magnum. The vertebral arteries of both sides join to form the basilar artery. In its course, it is divided into four parts: The first part, V1, begins at its origin from the subclavian artery and ends at its entry into the transverse process of the C6 cervical vertebra. This part is crossed by the inferior thyroid artery on 213 both sides, and thoracic duct on the left side, and the right lymphatic duct on the right side. The second part, V2 is that part of the artery ascending through the foramina in the transverse process of the cervical vertebrae. The third part, V3 is curved backward behind the atlas. In this position, it lies in a groove on the posterior arch of the atlas. This part of the artery lies in the suboccipital triangle. The fourth part, V4 pierces the dura and arachnoid mater and unites with the contralateral vertebral artery to form the midline basilar artery at the lower border of pons. Parts of the Atlas mi OE >

stem: Identify the papillae from the given histological section. 218
explanation: The given histological image is a section of the tongue showing circumvallate papillae, the largest papillae of the tongue. Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures that are around 8-12 in number, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. They are arranged in a V-shaped row immediately in front of the sulcus terminalis (not on the sides of the tongue) on the dorsal surface of the tongue. It is narrower at its base than its apex. Numerous taste buds (around 250 taste buds for each of the 8-12 papillae) are present within the papillary walls and they contain chemosensory cells that synapse with the gustatory nerves. Serous glands of von Ebner empty via the ducts into the base of the sulcus. Identification: They can be identified by their characteristic dome-shaped structure lined by stratified squamous epithelium. Other options: 224 Option A - Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red in color and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve. Option CFiliform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. All except filiform papillae contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve. Option D - Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. explanation: The structure marked in the given sagittal section of the head and neck is the uvula. The sensory supply to the uvula is by the glossopharyngeal nerve and it is tested in this case. Nerve supply by glossopharyngeal nerve: * Sensory fibers to the uvula, tympanic cavity, pharyngotympanic tube, tonsils, fauces, nasopharynx, and posterior third of the tongue. * Motor fibers to the stylopharyngeus muscle + Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland * Gustatory fibers for the postsulcal part of the tongue. Pharyngeal plexus: The nerve supply of the pharynx is mainly from the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. It is formed by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion. The vagus nerve provides the motor supply and the glossopharyngeal nerve provides the sensory supply. Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve: + All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve) + All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve) Note: Previously cranial root of the spinal accessory nerve was thought to contribute to the motor functions of the pharyngeal plexus, but recent evidence suggests that it is not a major part of the motor drive to the pharyngeal plexus. Innervation of the soft palate: General sensation - It is mostly carried by the lesser palatine nerve which is a branch of maxillary nerve. The sensation from posterior part is carried by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and from the plexus around the tonsil which is formed by the tonsillar branches of the glossopharyngeal and lesser palatine nerves. 231 Taste sensation - There are taste buds in the oral surface of soft palate and sensation from them is carried by the lesser palatine nerve. Secretomotor supply - It is by the lesser palatine nerve via postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion. Motor supply - It is by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve except for tensor veli palatini which is supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. 232

stem: Arrange in sequence the structures involved in the direct pathway:
explanation: The sequence of structures involved in the direct pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus > substantia nigra > thalamus. There are five parallel circuits that connect the frontal cortex to the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and thalamus. These circuits have both direct and indirect pathways. The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibit it. The cerebral cortex projects into the striatum. The striatum is seen projected into the pallidum and substantia nigra pars reticularis. Fibres originate from different striatal cells according to their endings in the external and internal pallidum. In the direct pathway, striatal neurones project directly to the internal pallidum. Whereas some other fibres that arise from the neurons project to the external pallidum. This is called the indirect pathway. The sequence of structures involved in the indirect pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus externa > subthalamic nucleus > globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra >Thalamus The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. Putamen lies lateral and the internal capsule lies medial to the pallidum. It receives fibres from the striatum and subthalamic nuclei. It acts as the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus and superior colliculus. The substantia nigra is seen in each cerebral peduncle of the midbrain located deep to the crus cerebri. The levels of dopamine in the substantia nigra and striata are seen reduced in parkinsonism disease. 249 Anatomy of Basal Ganglia Y>> ~ Internal a Insula capsule _ oe Ww i Putamen Caudate IK Y pallidus MARROW , wo Ee 4 In parkinsonism disease, due to the death of neurons in substantia nigra activity of the direct pathway is reduced and the indirect pathway is increased. This results in bradykinesia in parkinsonism disease. Whereas in Huntington's disease, the activity of the indirect pathway is affected resulting in choreic involuntary movements. 250 Sydenham chorea XS

It arises from the hippocampus which wraps around the thalamus and ends in the mammillary body. It connects the hippocampus with distal brain sites. The fornix has two types of fibres: + Association fibres: They connect the various cortical regions within the same hemisphere + Commissural fibres: They connect the corresponding regions of two hemispheres. It is seen in the hippocampal commissure of the fornix. The blood supply of fornix is by the anterior communicating artery which arises from the anterior cerebral artery. The limbic system is a group of structures seen between the cerebral cortex and the hypothalamus. It is involved in emotional and motivation activity, learning, and memory. 255 Fornix: body Mammillothalamic tract Mammillary body Hippocampus F | x | ) Fan. By Ba - 4 Wha, = / \\ . : ~ Ys 4 . explanation: Sartorius is involved in lateral rotation, flexion, and abduction at the hip joint, and flexion at the knee. The structure marked '2' is sartorius. The sartorius muscle is known as the tailor muscle and is also the longest muscle in the body. The word "sartorius" is derived from the Latin word sartor, which translates to tailor, due to the way the individual will position one's leg while working. Origin: Anterior superior iliac spine and the upper half of the notch below it. Insertion: Into the superior aspect of the medial surface of the tibial shaft near the tibial tuberosity (joins aponeurosis of gracilis and semitendinosus to form pes anserinus). Action: Flexion, abduction, and lateral rotation of the thigh; and flexion of the leg. subject: Anatomy
stem: Which nerve is blocked when local anesthesia is given below the inguinal ligament during femoral vein catheterization? 240
explanation: Genitofemoral nerve is blocked when the local anesthetic is given below the inguinal ligament during femoral vein catheterization. The genitofemoral nerve originates from the L1 and L2 ventral rami. It divides into the genital and femoral branches after crossing behind the ureter. The genital branch enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring and accompanies the spermatic cord or round ligament. It exits the superficial inguinal ring and supplies the cremaster muscle and skin of the external genitalia. The femoral branch descends lateral to the external iliac artery to pass behind the inguinal ligament and enter the femoral sheath lateral to the femoral artery. It pierces the anterior wall of the femoral sheath and fascia lata and supplies them. 279 The genitofemoral nerve gives sensory supply to the anteromedial thigh via the femoral branch. The genital branch supplies skin of the scrotum in males and mons pubis and labium majus in females. The genitofemoral nerve also innervates the cremaster muscle via the genital branch and is responsible for the cremasteric reflex. It enters the femoral triangle by passing under the inguinal ligament. In the femoral triangle, it lies lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath. Later, it is divided into anterior and posterior branches by the lateral circumflex femoral artery. Option C: Lateral cutaneous nerve (a.k.a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) of the thigh is most commonly injured at the site where it leaves the pelvis. An injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh leads to pain and paresthesia over the anterolateral region of the thigh, a condition called meralgia paresthetica. Option D: Ilioinguinal nerve is most commonly injured within the inguinal canal in open hernia repair due to traction or thermal injury. Injury causes loss of sensation in the root of the penis and adjacent part of the scrotum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following statements are true about the internal capsule?
explanation: Statements 1, 2, and 4 are true about the internal capsule. The charcot’s artery of hemorrhage is a larger lenticulostriate or lateral striate artery. Lateral striate arteries supply the anterior limb, genu and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. These arteries are also commonly involved in ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes. The retrolentiform part of the internal capsule carries fibers mainly from optic radiation. A lesion here produces homonymous hemianopia, superior quadrantanopia, or inferior quadrantanopia. The anterior limb of the internal capsule carries fronto-pontine fibers. A lesion here produces confusion, impaired attention, agitation, and dysarthria. 284 The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries cortico-spinal motor fibers in the anterior part and the lesion here produces contralateral hemiparesis. The posterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule carries sensory fibers and lesions here may produce contralateral hemi-sensory deficits. The internal capsule predominantly contains projection fibers, not commissural fibers. Projection fibers are the fibers that project from higher to lower centers or vice versa in CNS. 2 >. subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following muscles form the pelvic diaphragm?
explanation: Iliococcygeus and pubococcygeus are parts of the pelvic diaphragm, which is also known as the levator ani. The levator ani muscle is a complex unit that consists of 3 muscle components: + Pubococcygeus + Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence + Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis + Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed + Puborectalis + Iliococcygeus Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constant state of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelvic contents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia from stretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, or rectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra. Other options: The obturator internus forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and is not a part of the levator ani. The deep transverse perineal muscle is the content of the deep perineal space and contributes to the formation of the perineal body. 289 Fe | Pubie a CS) 2 Rete are =2 >> mecca

stem: Fracture of the jugular canal can present as
options: Loss of taste sensation in anterioir 2/3rd of tongue
Loss of taste sensation in posterior 1/3rd of tongue
Loss of general sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue
Loss of motor sensation in anterior 2/3rd of tongue
explanation: Fracture of the jugular canal affects glossopharyngeal nerve and presents as loss of taste sensation in the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue. The lingual nerve which is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve gives general sensation, chorda tympani branch of facial nerve gives taste sensation for the anterior 2/3rd of tongue. Both taste and general sensation of the posterior 1/3rd is by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The muscles of the tongue, with the exception of palatoglossus, are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve. Palatoglossus is supplied via the pharyngeal plexus. The other nerves passing through the jugular foramen are glossopharyngeal(cranial nerve IX), vagus(cranial nerve X), and accessory nerve(cranial nerve XI). subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following lobes of the lung is affected when there is aspiration in supine position?
options: Upper part of right inferior lobe
explanation: The upper part of the right inferior lobe is prone to aspiration in the supine position. It is commonly seen in alcoholics. The posterior segment of the right superior lobe and the superior segment of the inferior lobes are the most commonly involved lung sites when aspiration occurs in a recumbent patient. The location of aspiration depends on the position of the patient since it is gravity-dependent. Aspiration while standing leads to infiltration of bilateral inferior lobes because of larger and more vertical corresponding bronchi, the middle lobes and the lingula. Aspiration of contents into foreign substances into the bronchial tree, usually oral or gastric contents, produces aspiration pneumonia. Chemical (gastric acid) injury or bacterial infection complicates the condition.

In the groove between the medulla and pons, abducens, facial, and vestibulocochlear nerves emerge arranged medially to laterally. The abducens nerve is the 6th cranial nerve that arises from the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, passes through Dorello's canal, and enters the cavernous sinus where it lies lateral to the internal carotid artery. It then enters the orbit through the common tendinous ring in the superior orbital fissure to supply the lateral rectus.

stem: Which of the following are a part of the limbic system?
explanation: The amygdala, hippocampus, and thalamus are all a part of the limbic system. The limbic system refers to the interconnected neuronal circuit in the basal part of the brain that controls emotional behavior and other vegetative functions such as body temperature, the osmolality of the body fluids, and the drives to eat and drink and to control body weight. The limbic system includes the following: + Subcallosal gyrus * Cingulate gyrus * Parahippocampal gyrus * Hippocampal formation ¢ Amygdaloid nucleus * Mammillary bodies 295 + Anterior thalamic nucleus + Hypothalamus The connecting pathways for this system comprise the alveus, the fimbria, the fornix, the mamumillothalamic tract, and the stria terminalis. explanation: The muscles marked in the above image are rhomboids minor and major. These muscles cause retraction and elevation of the scapula and they rotate the scapula tilting the glenoid cavity inferiorly. Rhomboids minor and major are innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve. They are supplied by the dorsal scapular artery or the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery. Muscles involved in movements of the scapula are: + Protraction (forward movement): Serratus anterior and pectoralis minor are prime movers. Rhomboid muscles control the rate and range of movements. explanation: The image above shows a patent ductus arteriosus due to a defect in the left side of the 6th aortic arch. Usually, in term infants, the ductus arteriosus closes within 72 hours of birth. Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close results in patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). PDA usually presents with a hyperdynamic precordium, bounding peripheral pulses, wide pulse pressure, a machine-like continuous or systolic murmur, cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, hepatomegaly, increasing oxygen dependence, carbon dioxide retention, and renal failure. In a majority of cases, PDA closes spontaneously. If spontaneous closure fails to occur, COX inhibitors like indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used. Surgical ligation is indicated in case of contraindications to medical management or failure of the same. Defects involving the 4th left aortic arch could cause a variety of aortic arch anomalies, such as interruption of the aortic arch, but not PDA. subject: Anatomy
stem: The spinal sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve has 2nd order neurons to carry which sensation?
explanation: The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing. Its sensory pathway involves three branches: the ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2), and mandibular (V3) divisions. The first-order neurons for each division originate from different sensory ganglia: 1.O0phthalmic Division (V1): First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion). 2. Maxillary Division (V2): First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion. 3. Mandibular Division (V3): First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion. 378 These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei: 1. Principal Sensory Nucleus (Main Sensory Nucleus): Receives input from all three divisions of the trigeminal nerve. Located in the pons. Second-order neurons here carry discriminative touch and proprioceptive information. 2. Spinal Trigeminal Nucleus (Spinal Nucleus of Trigeminal): Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions. Located in the medulla. Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations. After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.

stem: 366 Which of the following is not seen in the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle?
explanation: The tail of the caudate nucleus is not seen on the floor of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. It is present on the roof of the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle. The inferior horn is the largest compartment of the lateral ventricle and extends up to 2.5 cm from the temporal pole. The relations are: Roof - Tapetum of corpus callosum laterally and tail of caudate nucleus medially. Floor (lateral to medial) - Collateral eminence produced by collateral fissure, hippocampus. The floor of the temporal horn consists of the hippocampus medially and the collateral eminence, formed by the infolding of the collateral sulcus, laterally. subject: Anatomy
stem: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to which of the following nerves?
explanation: An absent gag reflex can result from injury to the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) and the vagus nerve (X). The afferent nerve for the gag reflex is the glossopharyngeal nerve, while the efferent nerve consists of both the glossopharyngeal (to the stylopharyngeus muscle) and vagus. Both these nerves pass through the jugular foramen and damage to them may be the cause for loss of gag reflex. Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion. Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are: + All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve) 405 + All the muscles of the pharynx(except the stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve). The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate, etc. Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc. The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include: * Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”). + By assessing the strength of the cough

The filiform papillae do not contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Other papillae of the tongue are: Circumvallate papillae are 8-12 in number which are large cylindrical structures. They form a V-shaped row just in front of the sulcus terminalis. Usually, the entire papillae are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Taste buds are present in the lateral wall of these papillae which surrounds the papillae circumferentially. Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. They are supplied by the facial nerve. Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. stem: What is the outer covering of the condition shown in the image? ~<a
explanation: The diagnosis based on the given image is omphalocele and is covered by the amnion. 410 Omphalocele is a midline abdominal wall defect where the bowel and other solid viscera protrude through the umbilicus. In this condition, the herniated organs are covered by both peritoneum and an amnion. The umbilical cord inserts directly into this sac, which helps in identifying the condition. The defect occurs due to the failure of the physiological hernia to return to the body cavity by the 11th week of gestation. The size of an omphalocele can vary significantly. It may be relatively small, containing only the gut, or it can be classified as a giant omphalocele if it measures 4 cm or more in diameter, encompassing the gut, liver, and other abdominal organs. The condition is often associated with other congenital anomalies such as trisomies 13, 15, 18, or 21, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, exstrophy of the bladder or cloaca, and pentalogy of Cantrell. Treatment for omphalocele involves covering the exposed organs to prevent fluid loss and protect them from infection. Prophylactic antibiotics may be administered in case of rupture. Surgical correction is usually performed once the baby is stable. In omphalocele, since the umbilicus is covered by a reflection of the amnion, this membrane also covers the omphalocele itself, differentiating it from other types of abdominal wall defects. explanation: Fluid resuscitation in burns: According to ATLS 10th edition, 2018, the resuscitation formula used in thermal burns is 2 mL/kg x % TBSA. First 8 hours: 1 mL/kg x % TBSA (lactated Ringer solution) Next 16 hours: 1 mL/kg x % TBSA (lactated Ringer solution) For a patient presenting 8 hours after sustaining thermal burns, the total volume using resuscitation formula should be given in the next 16 hours i.e; 2 mL/kg x % TBSA in the next 16 hours while maintaining target urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/hr for adults. Her eye opens to pain, moans, can localize limb towards the pain stimulus on the left hand and away from the pain stimulus on the right hand and both the legs in extended posture. Calculate her GCS.
explanation: The GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale) of this patient is E2V2M5, which comes to a total score of 9. E2-Eye opens to pain ‘V2-Moans M5-Localizes to pain on the left hand (the score represents the best performance elicited, which would be localizing towards the pain stimulus) Revised Glasgow coma scale for head injury: Minimum GCS is 3, maximum GCS is 15.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A patient who was on ventilator and being ventilated for past few days suddenly pulls out of the endotracheal tube. What is the next step of management?
options: Watch for spontaneous breaths and reintubate if needed
explanation: About half of self-extubated patients may not require re-intubation. Pre-extubation Fi02, PaO2/FiO2, and ventilator mode, as well as gender, may be useful in determining the likelihood that a self-extubated patient will require re-intubation and also watch for spontaneous breathing.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: 3407 The time required for preoxygenation before tracheal intubation?
explanation: Preoxygenation with tidal volume breathing of 3 mins is required before tracheal intubation. Preoxygenation or denitrogenation is the process of replacing nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen. This delays the onset of critical hypoxia during the period of apnea by 5-8 minutes. This lengthened apnea time provides an improved margin of safety while the anesthesiologist secures the airway and resumes ventilation.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which of the following is the correct sequence?
options: Assess the patient’s response, Activate ERS, check carotid pulse, Start CPR
Check carotid pulse, Start CPR, Call for help and activate ERS, Defibrillate
Defibrillate, Assess response, Check carotid pulse, Maintain airway
Start CPR, Activate ERS, Defibrillate, Check pulse Answer Key 3408 Question No. Correct Option a ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee a es Detailed Explanations
explanation: BLS sequence: First step — Assess safety of the surroundings. Second step - Assess for responsiveness Third step — Proceed if the patient is unresponsive. Shout for help. If the patient is unresponsive assess for breathing and carotid pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds. 3411

subject: Anesthesia
stem: At what level does the spinal cord end in adults?
explanation: The distal termination of the spinal cord is the lower border of L1 in adults. Because the spinal cord ends at L1, lower nerve roots course some distance before exiting the intervertebral foramina. These lower spinal nerves form the cauda equina. Note: In children, the spinal cord ends at L3 and moves up with age. 3413

subject: Anesthesia
stem: What is the mechanism of action of the curare group of muscle relaxants?
options: Competitively blocking the binding of ACh to its receptors
Repetitive stimulation of ACh receptors on muscle endplate
Inhibiting the calcium channels on presynaptic membrane
explanation: The curare group of drugs includes non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents that act by competitively blocking the binding of acetylcholine to its receptors. This leads to a decrease in the effect of acetylcholine and thus, neuronal transmission to the muscle does not occur.

stem: What alternative drug would you use for cardiac arrest if epinephrine is not effective? 3431
options: Adenosine Answer Key Question No. Correct Option a ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee Detailed Explanations
explanation: Epinephrine and amiodarone are the two main drugs approved by the AHA for the resuscitation of a cardiac arrest patient. The first dose of epinephrine 1 mg IV is administered after the 2nd defibrillator shock is delivered and it is continued every 3-5 minutes. If this is not effective, 300 mg IV bolus dose of amiodarone can be given and another dose of 150 mg given if necessary 3435

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which is not an obvious advantage of high pressure oxygen through nasal cannula:
explanation: High flow nasal cannula (HFNC), which delivers oxygen at high flow, and pressure through the nasal cannula. Advantages of high-flow nasal cannula: + Soft and pliable nasal prongs provide comfort to the patient. * Warming and humidification of secretions: The heating of air to core temperature and humidification of the inspired air is better at high-flow. The humidification causes increased water content in the secretions, which facilitates the removal of secretions. It also decreases the work of breathing and avoids airway dessication and epithelial injury. * Reduces dead space: The high flow of the oxygen delivered clears the upper airway of the expired air, which reduces dead space by a decrease of rebreathing and allows a higher fraction of minute ventilation to participate in alveolar gas exchange. 3417 * Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP): HFNC increases the positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and reduces the work of breathing. + High flow rate causes decreased entrainment of room air, allowing more accurate delivery of oxygen.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Identify the device shown in the image below. 3415
explanation: The device is an Automated External Defibrillator (AED). This is a special medical device that is commonly used for recognizing the absence/presence of rapid ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. With no need for intervention by an operator, it determines whether an electrical shock right to the heart must be performed (defibrillation). An automated external defibrillator can be used on those victims, who are unconscious and aren’t breathing in a normal way. As a rule, it is used together with CPR in cases of sudden cardiac arrest. It is forbidden to use it on patients who are less than eight years old or those weighing less than 25 kgs. 3418

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which among the following IV anaesthetics does not cause myocardial depression?
explanation: Etomidate, a short-acting I.V. anesthetic agent doesn’t cause myocardial depression. Etomidate is the most cardiac stable intravenous agent due to its lack of effect on the sympathetic nervous system and on the function of the baroreceptor. Hence, etomidate is the I.V. agent of choice in patients with coronary artery disease, cardiomyopathy, and cerebral vascular disease. Side effects of Etomidate: * The highest incidence of nausea and vomiting among inducing agents + Superficial thrombophlebitis and pain on injection * Adrenocortical suppression Note: Although Ketamine has an indirect sympathetic stimulatory effect, it possesses a direct negative inotropic effect on the myocardium. Hence, ketamine has to be used cautiously in critically ill patients with shock, as they are prone to have a depletion of endogenous catecholamines. Ketamine infusion in such patients can unmask its direct negative inotropic effects and further decrease the blood pressure and cardiac output. Hence, for this MCQ, Etomidate is the best answer.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which of the following is not used for induction of anaesthesia in pediatric patients?
explanation: 3438 Desflurane is a highly pungent gas and can produce laryngospasm if used for inhalational induction. Hence it is not used as an induction agent. The incidence of laryngospasm following desflurane induction is almost 50%. It is usually used for maintenance of anaesthesia only and is of particular value in obese patients, neurosurgical and spinal fusion procedures where rapid awakening is required for neurological function assessment. Option A: Halothane is hepatotoxic but can be used (Sevoflurane is preferred) Option B: Sevoflurane is the preferred inhalational agent for induction in the pediatric age group. Cardiovascular depression, bradycardia, and arrhythmias are less frequent with sevoflurane than with halothane and hence the former is preferred. Option D: Nitrous oxide has the highest minimum alveolar concentration and so it is the least potent. It is used in combination with other potent inhaled anaesthetics to reduce their dose. It can be used to hasten the induction of anaesthesia along with other induction agents.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which of the following agents does not elicit pain on injection?
explanation: Ketamine does not elicit pain on injection, instead produces profound analgesia. Propofol is formulated as a lipid emulsion, which causes pain on injection. A new aqueous prodrug, fospropofol is associated with less pain on injection. Etomidate, although it causes pain on injection, the lipid formulation of etomidate is associated with a much less frequent incidence of pain. Thiopentone at a concentration greater than 2.5% can produce pain on injection and venous thrombosis.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which among the following is most commonly used to monitor the depth of anaesthesia?
explanation: The bispectral index is the most commonly used method to monitor the depth of anesthesia. Note: Middle latency auditory evoked potential is the most sensitive indicator to evaluate the depth of anesthesia.

explanation: The given image depicts a pulse oximeter. Pulse oximetry is used for monitoring pulse rate and oxygen saturation of a patient. A small sensor is placed on the finger, toe, earlobe, or another convenient place. The relative absorption of light by oxyhemoglobin (HbO2) and deoxyhemoglobin is assessed by measuring the amount of red and infrared light emerging from tissues traversed by light rays and processed by the device, producing an oxygen saturation level. 3439 Pulse oximetry does not measure the absolute content or the partial pressures of oxygen or carbon dioxide. A pulse oximeter is not always reliable as it reads: + Falsely high - carboxyhemoglobinemia + Falsely low - severe anemia, low cardiac output states, hypovolemia, increased systemic vascular resistance * 80% to 85%, irrespective of the arterial oxygen saturation - methemoglobinemia 3440

stem: On your morning walk in the park, you notice an unconscious man lying on the ground. Which of the following options would be the next best step?
options: Check carotid pulse, start CPR, and call for help; Defibrillate if no pulse.
Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate if no pulse
explanation: The next best step is to Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate If no pulse. Steps in basic life support: First step — Assess safety of the surroundings. Second step - Assess for responsiveness Third step — Proceed if the patient is unresponsive. Shout for help. If the patient is unresponsive, assess for breathing and carotid pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds. In the given scenario, it is already mentioned that you are in a park (scene safety has been assessed), and that the person is unconscious (responsiveness has been assessed). So, the immediate next step is to call for help, and start CPR.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which of the following can be considered as effective CPR?
options: 1 and 2 only 3423 Answer Key Question No. Correct Option ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee Detailed Explanations
explanation: The ideal rescue breath rate for adults is 10 breaths/min, while in infants and children up to puberty it is 20-30 breaths/min. As the person's age group is not specified in the question, assuming an adult, statement 1 is incorrect, while 2, 3, and 4 are correct. Effective chest compression in adults: * Provide 100-120 compressions per minute (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec). 3428 + Place your arms, one over the other in the midline, on the lower 1/3rd of the patient's sternum, and lock your arms. * Use both arms to press the chest to a depth of 5-6 cm (2 - 2.4 inches) or more. * Press hard and fast + Allow for full chest recoil after every compression. Effective chest compressions in a child older than 1 year and up to puberty: + The compression rate is 100 - 120/min (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec). * One or both palms are placed in the midline. * The depth of compression is 2 inches. * Press hard and fast + Allow for full chest recoil after every compression. Effective chest compressions in infants (<1 year): * 100 to 120 compressions per minute (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec). * One provider: Place two fingers, one between the nipple line and the other 1 cm below. * Two providers: Encircle the infant's torso with both hands with both thumbs pointing cephalic positioned 1cm below the nipples over the sternum. * Depth of compressions should be at least 1.5 inches or 1/3 the depth of the infant’s chest. * Press hard and fast + Allow for full chest recoil after every compression. 3429

subject: Anesthesia
stem: Ventilatory support is required if SpO2 becomes less than 90% because
options: Tissues become vulnerable for hypoxia below 90%.
Peripheral chemoreceptors becomes insensitive to hypoxia below 90%.
Central chemoreceptors becomes insensitive to hypoxia below 90%.
Patient capacity to generate adequate tidal volume decreases below 90%.
explanation: Tissues become vulnerable to hypoxia when SpO2 falls below 90% and thus supplementary oxygen therapy is indicated below this oxygen saturation level. In adults, children, and infants (older than 1 month), When SpO2 falls below 90%, the PaO2 becomes less than 60 mmHg and hence to prevent tissues from hypoxia, supplemental oxygen therapy should be started. In neonates, when SpO2 falls below 88%, the PaO2 becomes less than 50 mmmHg and hence supplemental oxygen therapy should be initiated in these patients.

stem: In conventional oxygen therapy, which device will deliver highest Fi02?
explanation: Non rebreathing masks provide highest Fi02 during conventional oxygen therapy. The non-rebreather mask is a low flow device that can be used to deliver oxygen at higher concentrations (Fi02 80-95%). It uses a reservoir bag to let the oxygen get concentrated while a one-way valve doesn't allow to breathe in expired air. This type of masks are used in patients with significant hypoxia, with relatively normal ventilation, such as victims of trauma or carbon monoxide exposure. ; Lad ins i N \ Other options: Venturi mask: 3450 * Venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance oxygen delivery system and the highest oxygen concentration (FiO2) delivered is 60% at a flow rate of 15 L/min. * It is based on the Bernoulli Principle, which states that in order to maintain a constant flow, a fluid must increase its velocity as it flows through a constriction. * It is available in different colors, with the green valve venturi mask providing 60% FiO2. * This is useful with patients who require greater FiO2 such as COPD patients, where it is important to provide controlled oxygenation. subject: Anesthesia
stem: How long should elective surgery be deferred for a patient who had cough and fever, after he has recovered from COVID-19, and had not required any hospitalization?
explanation: A patient, who has recovered from COVID-19 and hadn’t required any hospitalization should be deferred from any elective surgery for a period of 6 weeks. The American Society of Anesthesiologists has suggested the following duration of intervals for patients recovered from COVID-19. The wait time is from the date of diagnosis of COVID-19 to the date of surgery as follows: + 4 weeks: for an asymptomatic patient or recovery from only mild, non-respiratory symptoms. * 6 weeks: for a symptomatic patient (e.g: cough, dyspnea) who did not require hospitalization * 8-10 weeks: for a symptomatic patient who is hospitalized or who has comorbidities such as diabetes or who is immunocompromised. * 12 weeks: for a patient who was admitted in intensive care unit due to COVID-19 infection.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A 42-year-old man who was under home isolation after testing positive for COVID-19, develops breathing difficulty and is brought to the ER. The patient is alert and responsive, but is breathing rapidly. SpO2 is measured to be 86%. He is administered oxygen via a face mask with a reservoir bag with a flow rate of 10 L/min. After a trial of one hour, his SpO2 is 88%. What is the next step in management?
explanation: This patient has persistent hypoxia after an adequate trial of standard oxygen therapy and should be started on high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy. When respiratory distress and/or hypoxemia of the patient cannot be alleviated after receiving standard oxygen therapy, high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy (HFNO), or non-invasive ventilation can be considered. Compared to standard oxygen therapy, HFNO reduces the need for intubation. Patients on HFNO should be closely monitored, and endotracheal intubation should be done if the patient acutely deteriorates or does not improve after a short trial (about 1 hr). 3454 Patients with hypercapnia (exacerbation of COPD), hemodynamic instability, multi-organ failure, or abnormal mental status should not receive HFNO. Note: If a high flow nasal cannula (HFNC) or simple nasal cannula is used to administer O02, an Ng5 mask should be applied over it. Some of the benefits of HFNC are ¢ It can deliver oxygen at 40L/min, 37°C, and 99.9% relative humidity. + The high-flow oxygen is delivered directly to the nasopharynx. This produces FiO2 equal to that delivered by traditional mask devices. * It also reduces the work of breathing, improves gas exchange by nasopharyngeal dead-space washout, and decreases energy required to humidify and heat respiratory gases. The HFNC equipment shown in the image below uses a heated humidifier (named PMH200), a nasal cannula (no. 2), and a ventilator (brand: vivo30). = 7a= ' Se 2 | a =” — i

subject: Anesthesia
stem: What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
explanation: Local anesthetics primarily act by blocking the sodium channels bound to the membrane. Sodium channels have one larger « subunit and one or two smaller B subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states : ¢ Resting (non conducting) * Open (conducting) and * Inactivated (non conducting) The local anesthetics bind to the « subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium. Local anesthetics have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in open and inactivated state than in the resting state. 3455 Local anesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibers are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations. Note: Local anesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors. But blocking of sodium channels is the best answer, of all the given options.

explanation: The reading marked as X in the monitor is the capnography. Waveform capnography is a continuous non-invasive measurement and graphical display of the EtCO2. It is a direct measure of lung ventilation and an indirect measure of circulation and metabolism. The normal capnograph displays the exhaled CO2 in both inspiratory and expiratory phases. The expiratory phase is divided into three distinct components: + Phase I: exhalation of dead space gas (i.e., partial pressure of CO2, pCO2 ~0). + Phase II: A sharp rise in pCO2 to a plateauindicates the sampling of transitional gas between the airways and alveoli. + Phase III: The plateau region of the capnograph, corresponds to the pCO2 in the alveolar compartment. + Following phase III, a sharp inspiratory downstroke occurs, which is referred to as the beginning of phase 0 or phase IV by some. subject: Anesthesia
stem: What is the most common cause for hospital admission after day care surgery?
explanation: 3456 Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the most common cause of unanticipated hospital admission following daycare surgery. The two most common complications of daycare surgery are PONV and postoperative pain. PONV refers to the presentation of symptoms in the postoperative care unit or within 24 hours of the procedure. Pain is usually managed preoperatively and postoperatively with the administration of analgesics. While it is a common complication, postoperative pain is not the most common cause of unanticipated hospital admission. Opioid medications which are commonly used to treat postoperative pain present with side effects such as nausea and vomiting which may aggravate PONV. The occurrence of PONV can be based on the following factors, patient, choice of anesthetic agent, and the procedure. The risk factors are: + Patient: Women (higher incidence in pregnancy), history of PONV or motion sickness, nonsmokers, younger age (incidence decreases as the age increases). ¢ Anesthetic agent: General anesthesia, inhalational agents (isoflurane, sevoflurane), nitrous oxide, longer duration of anesthesia, preoperative opioid administration. * Procedure: Laparoscopic procedures, lithotripsy, gynecologic procedures, adenotonsillectomy, strabismus surgery. The drugs used in the prophylaxis and treatment of PONV include ondansetron, dexamethasone, and transdermal scopolamine.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: What is the frequency of tetanic stimulation used in neuromuscular monitoring?
explanation: The commonly used frequency of tetanic stimulation in neuromuscular monitoring is 50 Hz. Tetanic stimulation is a method to evaluate residual neuromuscular blockade. Tetanic stimulation consists of a series of extremely rapid electrical stimuli typically applied over 5 seconds. The most commonly used frequency is 50 Hz stimulation given for 5 seconds. * During a depolarizing block, the muscle response to 50 Hz tetanic stimulation for 5 seconds is sustained. * In contrast, during a phase II block after the injection of succinylcholine, the response following tetanic stimulation is not sustained i.e., a fade occurs. Disadvantages of tetanic stimulation are: * This method has only 70% sensitivity to detect residual paralysis and its specificity is only about 50%. Hence, this test is of limited value for assessing neuromuscular recovery. * This method is very painful, which makes it difficult to use in unanesthetized patients. * During the late phase of neuromuscular recovery, tetanic stimulation can produce lasting antagonism of neuromuscular block in the stimulated muscle. This may change the response of the tested site such that it may no longer be representative of other muscle groups. Note: 3457 Other patterns of nerve stimulations, which are used to assess the patients for residual blockade are + Train of four stimulation: Here four supramaximal stimuli (2 Hz) are delivered every 0.5 seconds. ¢ Double-burst stimulation: Here two short bursts of 50 Hz tetanic stimuli is delivered, which are separated by 750 ms.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A 60-year-old male patient was undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. During the surgery, a sudden drop in EtCO2 to 8 mmHg was noted. His SpO2 became 90%, his blood pressure dropped to 80/50 mmHg, and peak airway pressure was 18 cm of H2O. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: A sudden fall in EtCO2 with hypotension (fall in BP to 80/50 mmHg) along with normal airway pressure (< 35 to 40 cm of H20) during surgery is suggestive of CO2 embolism. Intraoperative pulmonary embolism usually presents as sudden cardiovascular collapse and hypoxemia with a sudden fall in EtCO2. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the most sensitive device for detecting intracardiac air embolus. If air is identified in the right atrium, or if it is suspected, immediate central vein cannulation and aspiration of the air may be lifesaving. The placement of a vena cava filter should be considered postoperatively. The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography. Other options: Intraoperative bronchospasm is usually manifested as wheezing, increasing peak airway pressure, and a slowly rising waveform on the capnograph. Bronchospasm BN D> = E o Ps Fa 8 / f ao] 4 a wal / x wi Time> MARROW A pneumothorax may manifest as hypercapnia along with hypoxemia, hypotension, increased peak airway pressure, and decreasing tidal volumes. It may result in abrupt cardiovascular collapse unresponsive to fluid and vasopressor administration. Deep sulcus sign on a supine chest radiograph points towards pneumothorax. The costophrenic angle is abnormally deepened when the pleural air collects laterally, producing the deep sulcus 3458 sign. The below chest X-ray shows left pneumothorax. Notice the collapsed lung and absent lung markings on the left side. Also mediastinal shift towards the right side. * pa ‘ ; \ Endobronchial intubation shows increased peak expiratory pressure, hypoxemia, increased airway pressure, asymmetric chest expansion and the absence of breath sounds over one lung, generally the left. Note: Peak airway pressure is the amount of airway pressure delivered by the ventilator to overcome the resistance of the endotracheal tube, airway, and alveoli.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: The maximum oxygen flow rate which can be kept with a conventional oxygen mask is
explanation: The maximum oxygen flow rate which can be kept with a conventional oxygen mask is 10 L/min. A conventional oxygen mask is a simple face mask that is used routinely in hospitals. It covers the nose and mouth of the patient. There are 2 exhalation ports through which the patient exhales carbon dioxide. This mask is held in place with elastic around the back of the head and a metal piece that fits over the nose. It provides 40% to 60% of O2 concentration and delivers O02 at the rate of 6 to 10 L/min. 3459 Hudson mask Mf —— II (VOX | eS, é ) S=>> —vwa ©MARROW Conventional oxygen therapy includes all the devices that are used in routine practices. It includes nasal prongs, low-flow nasal cannula, or masks. It is the main supportive treatment administered to patients after planned extubation. Oxygen delivery devices can be broadly divided into low flow oxygen devices (eg: nasal cannula, simple face mask, non-rebreathing mask) and high flow oxygen devices (eg: venturi mask). Important noteIf the question is about the maximum flow rate with the conventional oxygen mask, it would be 10L/ min. Whereas if the question is asking about the maximum oxygen flow rate with conventional oxygen therapy, then it would include all the conventionally used devices. Therefore, the answer would be 15L/min. subject: Anesthesia
stem: Which of the following can be used for induction of anesthesia, maintenance and can be safely used in endotracheal intubation?
explanation: Among the given options, sevoflurane can be used for induction and maintenance of anesthesia. It can also be safely used in endotracheal intubation Inhalation agents such as sevoflurane and halothane are useful in the induction of anesthesia, But sevoflurane due to its nonpungency and rapid onset makes it an excellent choice for smooth and rapid inhalation inductions in pediatric and adult patients. Sevoflurane has low blood solubility and partition coefficients resulting in more rapid emergence. Sevoflurane also produces adequate muscle relaxation for intubation of children following an inhalation induction. Other options: Option A: Halothane can also be used for gaseous induction of anesthesia. Its disadvantage is long induction time owing to the high blood:gas partition coefficient. However, the incidence of halothane hepatitis and myocardial depression has reduced its use. Option B: Desflurane produces laryngospasm when used for inhalational anesthesia and hence it is not used for induction. Laryngospasm is because of the pungent nature of the gas. Option D: Isoflurane causes respiratory depression as well as upper respiratory irritation.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: 3448 During resuscitation, a patient received a 20% Intralipid injection. What could have been the most probable diagnosis?
explanation: Patients who are unresponsive due to local anesthesia toxicity require 20% Intralipid injection during resuscitation. Accidental intravascular injection of local anesthetic like bupivacaine results in bupivacaine-induced cardiotoxicity. 3462 Initial management includes immediate initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation as per the advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) algorithm. + Following CPR, Intralipid therapy is initiated. A rapid bolus of Intralipid 20% IV (1.5 mL/kg) is administered without delay, followed by an infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min. The infusion should be given continuously for at least 10 minutes after hemodynamic stability is achieved. + Intralipid decreases cardiac bupivacaine concentration by 11% within 3 minutes of administration, and cerebral bupivacaine concentration by 18% within 15 minutes. Bupivacaine is a long-acting local anesthetic that is the most cardiotoxic among the local anesthetics. It depresses the rapid phase of depolarization in Purkinje fibers and ventricular muscle due to a decreased availability of fast sodium channels in cardiac membranes. This reduced rate of depolarization depresses myocardial contractility. Hence, bupivacaine is a potent cardio-depressant. Note: Local anesthesia systemic toxicity (LAST) can also affect the central nervous system (CNS), which is more susceptible to local anesthetic action as compared to the cardiovascular system. Dizziness, tinnitus, and disorientation are the initial symptoms. Shivering, muscular twitching, and tremors follow. Tonic-clonic seizures occur. Finally, respiratory depression can lead to respiratory arrest.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A 50-year-old male patient has grade 3 ASA. Which of the following postbronchodilator PFT findings requires further evaluation of the lung function of the patient?
options: FEV1 < 0.8 and FEV1/FVC <0.75 Answer Key Question No. Correct Option a ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee ee 3449 Detailed Explanations
explanation: FEV1 <0.8 and FEV1/FVC <o.7 are classified as moderate COPD under GOLD classification and they require further evaluation of the lung function. Preoperative pulmonary function tests (PFTs) assess the severity of known pulmonary disease, diagnose causes of respiratory symptoms, and may help to identify patients who are at risk for postoperative pulmonary complications. The severity of COPD is assessed by using the Global Initiative for Lung Disease (GOLD) criteria. In pulmonary function testing, a postbronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of &1t;0.70 is considered diagnostic for COPD. The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) system categorizes airflow limitation into stages. In patients with FEV1/FVC <o0.70: * GOLD 1: mild: FEV1 >80% predicted * GOLD 2: moderate: 50% < FEV1 <80% predicted * GOLD 3: severe: 30% < FEV1 &I1t;50% predicted * GOLD 4: very severe: FEV1 &1t;30% predicted. This is important in the perioperative period as the diagnosis of COPD is an independent and significant risk factor in the development of postoperative pulmonary complications. Pre-operative FEV1 and DLCO of >80% imply a lower risk for a permanent postoperative pulmonary disability. Below these values, further risk-benefit assessment of the surgery needs to be examined and more information should obtained. 3463

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A patient undergoing surgery is maintained on anesthesia with halothane. During the procedure, the patient suddenly developed hyperthermia and muscle rigidity. Which of the following drugs is most likely implicated in this condition?
explanation: The given clinical scenario of a patient being operated under halothane, developing hyperthermia and muscle rigidity is suggestive of an episode of malignant hyperthermia. The drug most likely implicating/causing this condition is suxamethonium (succinylcholine). Suxamethonium is a peripherally acting depolarizing muscle relaxant, commonly administered during the induction of anesthesia to relax muscles of the jaw, neck, and airway and thereby facilitate laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation. Malignant hyperthermia is a rare genetic hypermetabolic muscle disease. It occurs due to mutation of the gene for the ryanodine receptor (Ryr 1), located on chromosome 19. Ryr 1 is an ion channel responsible for calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The symptoms develop when the patient is exposed to inhaled anesthetics (halothane in this case) or suxamethonium/succinylcholine. The mutated Ryr 1 leads to a sudden release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of the skeletal muscle. This uncontrolled increase in intracellular calcium removes the inhibition of troponin, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, which in turn, leads to an increase in adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) activity. This results in an uncontrolled hypermetabolic state with increased oxygen consumption and CO2 production, producing severe lactic acidosis and hyperthermia. The key clinical features are: * Succinylcholine-induced masseter muscle rigidity (causing trismus) or generalized muscle rigidity * Tachycardia 3466 * Hypercarbia ( increased CO2 production) and reduced oxygen saturation * Hyperthermia ( rise of 1° Celsius can occur every 5 minutes) ¢ Arrhythmia + Hypertension * Myoglobinuria and myoglobinemia indicating muscle damage * Metabolic derangements like hyperkalemia and mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis Treatment is to discontinue the triggering agents i.e; inhaled anesthetics and succinylcholine followed by administration of 100% oxygen. Metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia need to be corrected. Hyperthermia must be controlled by cooling the patient. Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice. It is given at a dose of 2.5 mg/ kg intravenously and can be repeated every 5-10 minutes till the attack subsides. Other options: D-curare or D-tubocurarine (option A), cis-atracurium (option C), and rocuronium (option D) are non-depolarizing muscle relaxants and are not implicated in malignant hyperthermia.

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A 30-year-old male patient was intubated for surgery by a final-year resident. Which of the following is the best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube?
explanation: The best method to confirm the position of the endotracheal tube is the end-tidal CO2 concentration assessed by capnography. Capnography is a non-invasive method of measurement and graphical display of partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) in exhaled breath or the end-tidal CO2. Capnograph is the device used for measurement and capnogram is the CO2 waveform that is displayed. It is the most reliable indicator of endotracheal tube placement. The proper placement of the endotracheal tube is indicated by a normal CO2 waveform for at least three breaths. Normal Capnography 50 Baz — O—*i |) M1 — End Tidal CO, 3 oO 0 wie El Time Expiration Phase 0 - Inspiratory downstroke Phase! - Inspiratory baseline: dead space Phase Il - Expiratory upstroke: mixture of dead space and alveolar gas Phase Ill - Alveolar gas plateau aangle - Transition from phase Il to phase III Bangle - Transition from phase Ill to 0 MARROW 3467 Other signs to confirm proper endotracheal intubation are: Symmetrical chest rise, presence of equal bilateral breath sounds, absent breath sounds over the epigastrium, visible condensation in the ETT, large exhaled tidal volume, and appropriate compliance of the reservoir bag during manual ventilation. Absent CO2 waveform tracing despite correct ETT intubation is seen in the following conditions: * Severe bronchospasm, * Equipment malfunction, * Cardiac arrest, or hemodynamic collapse Clinical relevance: * Capnography does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation. Signs of endobronchial intubation include increased peak expiratory pressure, hypoxemia, increased airway pressures, asymmetric chest expansion and the absence of breath sounds over one lung, generally the left. + In esophageal intubation, the capnograph can initially detect some CO2 in the stomach from swallowing expired air. But after a few breaths, this CO2 will be washed out and ETCO2 will become zero. * The most sensitive and earliest indicator of malignant hyperthermia is a persistent increase in ETCO2.

stem: What is the maneuver being performed in the given image? 3464 TSA >» ),
explanation: The maneuver being performed in the given image is that of head-tilt chin-lift. It is an important technique in emergency airway management to open up the airway. Basic life support involves early recognition and management of emergencies such as heart attack, stroke, and foreign body airway obstruction. The sequence of BLS is circulation (chest compression), airway, and then breathing. The airway is usually obstructed by posterior displacement of the tongue or epiglottis. One hand (palm) is placed on the patient’s forehead applying pressure to tilt the head back. Simultaneously, the chin is lifted with the forefinger and index finger of the opposite hand. This causes cervical flexion with an atlantooccipital extension (sniffing position). This lifts the tongue from the back of the throat. Head-tilt chin-lift should not be performed in a patient with suspected cervical injury. Other options: Option B: Jaw thrustBoth hands of the clinician are placed on either side of the patient’s head and the angles of the jaw are grasped and lifted. It can be performed in a patient with cervical injury but caution must be followed to not hyperextend the neck. 3468 J Jaw Thrust Option D: Manual inline stabilization is a maneuver that limits external head and neck movement in patients with cervical spine injuries. Fingers and palms of both hands are used to stabilize the patient's occiput and mastoid processes to ensure successful airway intervention. Manual in-line stabilization

subject: Anesthesia
stem: A patient presented with headache, vomiting, and fever. Meningitis was suspected. While performing a lumbar puncture, which is the last structure you will pierce just before entering the lumbar cistern?
explanation: The arachnoid membrane is the last structure you will pierce while performing a lumbar puncture, just before entering the lumbar cistern. Lumbar puncture is a diagnostic procedure done to obtain a sample of cerebrospinal fluid from the subarachnoid space. During the procedure, the following structures are pierced to reach the subarachnoid space, in the given order: + Skin 3469 + Subcutaneous tissue * Supraspinous ligament * Interspinous ligament * Ligamentum flavum ¢ Dura mater + Arachnoid membrane Indications: * Diagnosis of suspected meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage + Spinal anesthesia and intrathecal administration of antibiotics/chemotherapy + Therapeutic relief of pseudotumor cerebri, less frequently Contraindications for lumbar puncture include: * Thrombocytopenia or other bleeding diatheses (including anticoagulant therapy) * Raised intracranial pressure + Spinal epidural abscess + Infection over the site Site of the procedure: In adults, the spinal cord ends at the level of the lower border of the L1 vertebra. Lumbar puncture is usually performed at L3-L4 space (below L1 vertebra) to avoid potential needle trauma to the spinal cord. Technique: The patient is usually placed in the lateral recumbent position. An alternative position is the sitting position, useful in obese patients to determine the midline. L3-L4 space is located by palpating the right and left posterior superior iliac crests and moving the fingers medially toward the spine at the same level. A local anesthetic like 1% lidocaine is administered. A 22-gauge needle is advanced through the skin. In the lateral recumbent position, the bevel should face up, and in the sitting position, it should face to one side or the other, to avoid injury to the dural fibers. There is a loss of resistance as the needle enters the epidural space. Dura and then arachnoid are next pierced, to release CSF. Complications following lumbar puncture: Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a common post-procedure symptom. It occurs due to loss of CSF through the dura which causes traction on the pain-sensitive intracranial structures. The headache in PDPH is typically frontal or occipital. The smaller the needle used, the lesser the risk of PDPH. Other complications include infections, bleeding, cerebral herniation, and radicular pain.
