subject: Pathology
stem: Acute inflammatory response is not seen in:
explanation: An inflammatory response is not seen in apoptosis. In this process, the cell membrane remains intact. Hence, there is no leakage of cell contents and no surrounding inflammation. On the other hand, other forms of cell death including necrosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis involve the disintegration of the cell membrane. This causes the cell contents to leak out of the cell leading to an acute inflammatory response.

subject: Pathology
stem: 1868 An affected male does not have affected children but an affected female always has affected children. Type of inheritance?
explanation: In mitochondrial inheritance, if the mother is affected and the father is normal, then all their children (both male and female) will be affected. However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother will not be affected. The mitochondrial inheritance pattern is as shown in the image below: 1883 The unique feature of mitochondrial inheritance is maternal inheritance, as the disease is transmitted through the affected mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria. The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa has very few mitochondria if present. Hence, the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum. Therefore, affected mother transmits the disease to all the offsprings (both male and female), and only the daughters of the affected mother, will further transmit the disease. Characteristic features of mitochondrial inheritance: + The mitochondrial DNA encodes enzymes required for oxidative phosphorylation. Therefore, organs that are most dependent on the oxidative phosphorylation are the ones most affected in diseases due to mutations in mtDNA. These organs include central nervous system, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, liver, and kidneys. + There are several thousands of copies of mtDNA in each mitochondria, of which only a few copies are affected in case of mutation. Therefore, a diseased individual possesses copies of both wild type mtDNA and mutant mtDNA in each mitochondria This phenomenon is called heteroplasmy. + The disease manifests if a minimum number of copies of mutant mtDNA are present in the mitochondria that can lead to oxidative dysfunction, called the threshold effect. In most cases, this threshold effect is reached in the organs as mentioned above. + Also, during a cell division, the wild and mutant copies of the mtDNA are unequally distributed among the daughter cells. As a result, the expression of the disease varies even among different cells of an organ.

However, a platelet count >20,000 is ensured for safety purposes. Indications of bone marrow biopsy: + Evaluation of unexplained anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia + Evaluation of polycythemia, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis + Diagnosis and staging of lymphoma or solid tumors + Diagnosis and evaluation of plasma cell disorders and leukemias + Evaluation of suspected infiltrative and storage diseases 1892 + Evaluation of fever of unknown origin, suspected mycobacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections, or granulomatous diseases Contraindications of bone marrow biopsy: + Severe hemophilia + Severe disseminated intravascular coagulopathy + Severe bleeding disorders Procedure for bone marrow biopsy: Prone or lateral position is chosen for the procedure. subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following is true regarding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
options: Cells are spherical Cc) Cells don't lyse in hypotonic solution
explanation: G6PD deficiency has spherical red cells (Spherocytes). Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is an enzyme that helps in the synthesis of NADPH. NADPH helps in keeping glutathione in a reduced state (GSH). This reduced glutathione acts as a defense against oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are exposed to oxidants. These cross-linking of the reactive sulphydryl groups in the globin chain of hemoglobin. These are then deposited as inclusions in RBC membranes as Heinz bodies. When these RBCs pass-through spleen, macrophages pluck out these membrane inclusions. The remaining cells are seen as bite cells. Less severely damaged cells lose a part of their membrane, forming spherocytes. Spectrin is a part of the RBC membrane skeleton. It is commonly defective in hereditary spherocytosis. Normal biconcave RBCs have a bit of an ‘extra space’. They can accommodate a little fluid when exposed to a hypotonic solution. But spherocytes have already lost a part of its membrane, so are relatively full. Hence if they are placed in a hypotonic solution, they absorb more fluid and result in lysis of RBCs. This forms the basis of testing spherocytes in Hereditary spherocytosis or G6PD and is known as osmotic fragility testing. On the other hand, placing RBCs in a hypertonic solution may cause them to lose water and shrink in size. But hardly any hemolysis takes place. 1909

stem: 1897 A 24-year-old man met with an RTA and was brought to the casualty after 6 hours. His B.P. was 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate was 110/min, and SpO2 was 92%. A blood transfusion was done. After a few hours, the patient is febrile, tachypneic, and starts bleeding from the IV and NG tube sites. His SpO2 levels started falling. What could be the cause?
explanation: The symptoms of this patient (bleeding from the IV catheter and nasogastric tube sites) are suggestive of DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) within a few hours of blood transfusion. Hence, the most likely cause of this presentation is an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. These reactions are mediated by pre-existing IgM antibodies that act against the polysaccharide blood group antigens A or B. They bind to the red cells and cause complement-mediated lysis which further leads to intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Severe cases may present with DIC, which is a consumptive coagulopathy with bleeding manifestations. Other complications include shock, acute kidney injury, and sometimes, death. The various blood transfusion reactions according to their time of occurrence are as follows: « Anaphylactic reaction - Within a few seconds to minutes of the transfusion + Allergic/Urticarial reactions - Within 2-3 hours of transfusion * Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) - Within 24 hours of transfusion + Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) - Within 6 hours of transfusion * Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR) - After 24 hours of transfusion Other options: Option bAcute adrenal crisis usually presents as an unexplained shock that is refractory to fluids and vasopressors. Option cFat embolism is associated with fractures of the long bones. It develops within 2-3 days of fracture/trauma. Moreover, a history of petechial rash is characteristic of fat embolism. Option dHemorrhagic shock presents as tachypnea, tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, and oliguria. Cold extremities and delayed capillary refill time are other features. In this case, hemorrhagic shock might occur as a consequence of bleeding due to DIC, but the cause of this presentation is transfusion reaction. 1910

stem: All of the following are crosslinking fixatives except?
explanation: Methanol is not a crosslinking fixative. It is a dehydrant coagulant fixative. Fixation of tissues can be done by physical or chemical methods. Physical methods include heating, microwaving, and freeze-drying. Chemical methods: These methods are commonly used in the processing of tissue for various histopathological diagnoses. It includes the use of: 1911 * Cross-linking fixatives: These fixatives add covalent reactive groups which may induce cross-links between proteins, individual protein moieties within nucleic acids, and between nucleic acids and proteins. Eg: Formaldehyde and Glutaraldehyde. * Dehydrant coagulant fixatives: These fixatives remove free water from tissues and precipitate or coagulate the proteins. Eg: ethanol, methanol, and acetone. * Compound fixatives: Fixatives, which are the mixtures of reagents are referred to as compound fixatives. Eg: alcoholic formalin fixes tissues in two ways i.e firstly, by adding covalent hydroxymethyl groups and crosslinking proteins and secondly, by coagulation and dehydration. Note: Osmium tetraoxide causes additive cross-links and is used for ultrastructural visualization of membranes as an additive for post-fixation after glutaraldehyde.

stem: JAK2 mutation is most commonly associated with
explanation: Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90-95% of patients with polycythemia vera. It is characterized by : * Increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets (panmyelosis) + Low erythropoietin levels and elevated hematocrit * Blood viscosity and sludging lead to both thrombosis and bleeding. * Headache, dizziness, hypertension, dizziness, venous thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome due to hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, and stroke. + Intense pruritus especially aquagenic pruritus * Peptic ulceration, hyperuricemia * 15% to 20% of patients after an average period of 10 years ->Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis, 1913 * PCV transforms into AML in 2% of patients. Primary myelofibrosis * Marrow fibrosis associated with extramedullary hemopoiesis in the spleen. + Activating mutation in JAK2 (more commonly) or MPL. * Presence of neoplastic megakaryocytes, which are responsible for the release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) and TGF-B. * Bone marrow aspiration yields dry tap due to fibrosis of the bone marrow. * So, bone marrow biopsy is the investigation of choice, which shows the presence of hypocellularity with increased deposition of reticulin inside the marrow, abnormal megakaryocytes and the characteristic finding of dilated marrow sinusoids. * Blood shows mild leukocytosis, decreased Hb and hematocrit levels, and elevated LAP scores. + Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 5% to 20% of cases. Essential thrombocytosis (ET) may also be associated with JAK2, MPL, or CALR mutations. + Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is often associated with activating point mutations in JAK2 (50% of cases) or MPL (5% to 10% of cases), a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally activated by thrombopoietin. * In addition, recent DNA sequencing studies have revealed that most of the remaining cases have mutations in calreticulin (CALR), a protein with several functions in the endoplasmic reticulum and the cytoplasm. Since JAK2 and calreticulin mutations are mutually exclusive, it is hypothesized that the calreticulin mutations also increase JAK-STAT signaling through mechanisms that are currently unknown. CML is the consequence of the balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22]). PV, PMF, and ET are characterized by driver mutations that directly or indirectly constitutively activate JAK2, a tyrosine kinase essential for the function of the erythropoietin andthrombopoietin receptors and also utilized by granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor.

stem: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
explanation: A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing, which can remove lipids. explanation: Thromboelastography (TEG) tests the entire coagulation pathway. It measures coagulation cascade, platelet function, and fibrinolysis. subject: Pathology
stem: Identify the correct statement regarding immune surveillance.
options: Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers
Mutation of tumor supressor genes decreases antigen toxicity
PD1/ PDL1 activation leading to tumor supression
Binding of CD28 leads to immune tolerance
explanation: Anti-CTLA-4 antibody ipilimumab was the first drug to achieve a significant improvement in survival of advanced-stage melanoma. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) plays an important inhibitory role in the control of T-cell activation. Ipilimumab is a fully-humanized IgGi monoclonal antibody that inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4). It has been postulated that anti-CTLA-4 antibodies act by blocking inhibitory signals from effector T-cells, allowing costimulatory signaling and generation of antitumor T-cell responses. In vitro studies demonstrated also that the antitumor activity of CTLA-4 blockade is mediated by Fc gamma receptor-expressing macrophage and hypothesized a possible role of regulatory T-cell depletion in the tumor microenvironment. Option B - Mutation of tumor supressor genes is associated with increased risk of cancer. Antigen toxicity is when the immune response to an antigen is excessive or misdirected, causing damage to tissues or organs. Option C - PD1/PDL1 is an immune checkpoint whose activation inhibits T-cell function and helps with immune tolerance. Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction using immune checkpoint inhibitors reactivates T cells and enhances immune responses against tumors. Option D - CD28 is primarily involved in providing the second signal required for T cell activation. The first signal comes from the interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and the antigen presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Without CD28-mediated costimulation, T cells that only receive the TCR signal (without the second signal) can become anergic.

Germline 1927 heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 gene are present in approximately half of individuals with familial Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. It is also characterized by mucocutaneous dark blue to brown melanin pigmentation, which is particularly evident on the face, buccal mucosa, hands, feet, perianal and genital regions. This rare syndrome presents at a median age of 11 years. The hamartomatous polyps seen in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are characterized by a branching network of smooth muscle fibers continuous with the muscularis mucosa that supports the glandular epithelium of the polyp. Complications: * Peutz-Jeghers polyps can cause intussusception, which is occasionally fatal. + It is associated with a markedly increased risk of many malignant conditions. explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myxoid liposarcoma. The image shows abundant ground substance, with branching capillaries and a few immature adipocytes. Liposarcoma is the most common sarcoma in adults and is usually seen in the 5th to 6th decade of life. They commonly occur in the deep soft tissues of the proximal extremities and in the retroperitoneum. Histologically the liposarcomas are divided into three subtypes: * Well-differentiated liposarcoma: It consists of mature adipocytes and scattered spindle cells with hyperchromatic nuclei. It is associated with amplification of 12q13-q15. * Myxoid liposarcoma: It contains abundant basophilic extracellular matrix with branching capillaries. Few immature adipocytes are found scattered within the matrix. It is associated with t(12;16). * Pleomorphic liposarcoma: It consists of sheets of anaplastic cells with bizarre nuclei and few immature adipocytes. Among the three subtypes, the pleomorphic liposarcoma is the most malignant and often metastasizes, while the well-differentiated is least malignant. Myxoid liposarcoma has intermediate malignancy behaviour.

The typical presentation is painless rectal bleeding. Sometimes there may be a proliferating rectal mass. The disease may be sporadic or syndromic. * Sporadic juvenile polyp occurs as a single mass and is called retention polyp. + Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterized by multiple hamartomatous polyps, which may be premalignant. Morphologically, both of these types are indistinguishable. * Gross appearance: They appear as pedunculated, smooth reddish lesions, and with cystic spaces. * Microscopic appearance: The cysts appear as dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris. subject: Pathology
stem: What is the cell of origin of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia/Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma?
explanation: The cell of origin of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)/ Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) is either naive B cells or post-germinal centre memory B cell. The CLL and SLL differ only in the degree of peripheral blood lymphocytes. CLL is the most common leukemia of adults in the western world. The median age of diagnosis is 60 years. The most common genetic anomalies seen are deletions of 13q14.3, 11q, and 17p and trisomy 12q. Loss of tumor suppressor genes in chromosome 13 results in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2. The growth of CLL/SLL cells is confined to the proliferation centers (pathognomonic for CLL/SLL), where the tumor cells receive critical factors from the surrounding environments, such as NF-«B for cell survival, MYC for cell growth, Bruton Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) signaling pathway, etc., The tumor cells express CD19, CD20, CD23, and CD5. Smudge cells are also characteristic of CLL. Clinical features include easy fatiguability, weight loss, anorexia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, hemolytic anemia, etc. CLL/SLL has a tendency to transform to a more aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) - this is called Richter syndrome. Factors with a bad prognosis include: * Presence of deletions of 11q and 17p. * Lack of somatic hypermutation. * Expression of ZAP-70, a protein that augments signals produced by the Ig receptor. * Presence of NOTCH1 mutations BTK inhibitors and BCL2 inhibitors produce sustained therapeutic responses in a higher fractions of people with CLL/SLL.

RB gene exists in an active hypophosphorylated state in resting cells and in an inactive hyperphosphorylated state in cells undergoing G1/S transition. E7 protein from the high-risk types of HPV (such as HPV 16) binds to the hypophosphorylated RB through the same pocket that RB uses to bind and sequester the E2F transcription factors, thereby 2011 displacing the E2F which leads to the progression of the cell cycle and thus the proliferation of tumor cells. E7 proteins also inactivate the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27. E7 proteins from high-risk HPVs (types 16,18 and 31) also bind and presumably activates cyclins A and E. Oncogenic activities of protein E6: The E6 protein binds to and helps in the degradation of p53 and stimulates the expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which is the catalytic subunit of telomerase, thereby helping in the longevity of the cells. subject: Pathology
stem: Arrange the following cellular events of inflammation in the correct sequence:
explanation: The correct sequence of cellular events that occurs during inflammation is as follows: Rolling, Cytokine-mediated integrin activation, Adhesion, Migration. The recruitment of leucocytes to the site of inflammation is a multi-step process that is mediated by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines. This process can be divided into sequential phases: + In the lumen: margination, rolling and adhesion to the endothelium occurs. * Migration of the leucocytes across the endothelium and vessel wall * Migration in the tissues towards a chemotactic stimulus. The process of leucocyte recruitment is as follows: * Margination: Because of the dilation of the inflamed postcapillary venues, there is stasis of blood flow, and hence, more leucocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface; this process of leucocyte redistribution is called margination. + Rolling: The slowed down leucocytes then sense the signals from the endothelium and start rolling on the vessel wall. + Cytokine-mediated integrin activation: The attachment of leucocytes to the endothelial cells requires adhesion molecules that are activated by cytokines. The major families of proteins involved in adhesion and migration are selectins and integrins and their ligands. + Adhesions: The weak rolling interactions slow down the leucocytes and allow them to bind more firmly to the endothelium. Chemokines that were produced at the site of injury bind to the endothelial cell proteoglycans. These chemokines then bind to the rolling leucocytes and activate them. This, in turn, converts the ligands for B1 and 2 integrins, VLA-4, and LFA-1 present on the leucocytes to a high-affinity state. + This combination of cytokine-induced expression of integrin ligands on the endothelium and increased integrin affinity on the leucocytes leads to firm adhesion of leucocytes to the endothelium at the site of inflammation. * Leucocyte migration: This is the movement of leucocytes through the intact endothelium, called transmigration or diapedesis. This occurs in postcapillary venules. This migration occurs through the inter-endothelial gap towards the chemical concentration gradient created by the chemokines at the site of injury. This occurs with the help of adhesion molecules present in the intercellular junctions such as platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule (PECAM-1) or CD31. 2016 Leukocyte recruitment A \oe ‘ <a) microbes f ¥ ' nigh attinity oP tl < we Chemotinee adhesion } her Fionn ena “enrousn "(eoo) ——Nge gape = endothelium | Cara T — — BZ MARROW

stem: Which of the following is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anemia?
explanation: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anaemia. Pyridoxine 200mg per day for 2-3 months is administered routinely to all cases of sideroblastic anaemia. This cofactor is essential for ALA-synthase activity, and mutations in the pyridoxine binding site of the enzyme have been found in several responsive patients. Blood transfusion and other supportive therapy are also indicated. In cases of secondary sideroblastic anaemia, the primary focus is the removal of the offending agent. But no definitive treatment is available for hereditary and idiopathic types of sideroblastic anaemia. Sideroblasts are nucleated red cells (normoblasts) containing siderotic granules which stain positively with Prussian blue stain. Based on aetiology, sideroblastic anaemia are classified into hereditary and acquired types. Hereditary sideroblastic anaemia is an X-linked disorder caused due to a defect in the activity of aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase required for heme synthesis. Affected females act as carriers while males have moderate to marked anaemia and manifest in childhood or during early adulthood Acquired sideroblastic anaemia: I) Primary acquired: + Also called idiopathic or refractory acquired sideroblastic anaemia * Occurs in middle-aged and older individuals of both sexes * Due to the reduced activity of the enzyme ALA synthetase, there is disturbed growth and maturation of the erythroid precursors at the level of hematopoietic stem cell * Moderate to severe anaemia, which appears insidiously + Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia may also be seen 2017 * Regarded as a myelodysplastic disorder in the FAB classification and thus considered preleukaemic II) Secondary acquired: May appear secondary to * Drugs, chemicals and toxins: Isoniazid, Cycloserine, Chloramphenicol, Cyclophosphamide, Alcohol, Lead, etc., * Haematological disorders: myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, acute leukaemia, myeloma, lymphoma and hemolytic anaemia. * Miscellaneous: Carcinoma, myxoedema, rheumatoid arthritis and SLE. Laboratory findings: * Peripheral smear: Hypochromic, microcytic (sometimes normocytic) anaemia + Absolute values: MCV, MCH and MCHC are reduced except in acquired type, where MCV is raised. * Bone marrow: Erythroid hyperplasia with macronormoblastic erythropoiesis. Marrow iron stores are raised. Pathognomonic ring sideroblasts are present. * Serum ferritin: Raised + Serum iron: Raised * TIBC: Normal * Haemoglobin electrophoresis: Normal

subject: Pathology
stem: A 5-year-old child who presented with proptosis of one of the eyes was found to have a desmin positive tumour. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation: The clinical picture of a 5-year-old child with proptosis and a desmin positive tumor suggests a diagnosis of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with skeletal muscle differentiation. There are four subtypes: alveolar, embryonal, pleomorphic, and spindle cell/sclerosing. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood and adolescence and is usually of the alveolar and the embryonal variety. Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma is seen predominantly in adults. Spindle cell/sclerosing type affects all ages. The pediatric forms often arise in the sinuses, head and neck, and genitourinary tract. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma has sheets of both primitive round and spindled cells in a myxoid stroma. Rhabdomyoblasts with visible cross-striations may be present. Sarcoma botryoids is a variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma in the walls of hollow, mucosal-lined structures, such as the nasopharynx, common bile duct, bladder, and vagina with cambium layer. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma has a network of fibrous septae that divide the cells into clusters or aggregates, creating a crude resemblance to pulmonary alveoli. Clinically, the tumor is usually aggressive, with unilateral proptosis when the orbit is involved. Swelling and redness of the overlying skin, diplopia may be present. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin, myoglobin, myogenin, MyoD1, and vimentin 2018 Treatment involves surgical resection and chemotherapy, with or without radiotherapy. The best prognosis is for the botryoid variant while the pleomorphic has variant has the worst prognosis. Other options: Ewing's sarcoma: CD99 positive Leukaemia: CD45 positive

stem: 1999 Which of the following is true?
explanation: Of the given statements, 2 and 3 are true. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene and MYC is a proto-oncogene. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 17q21 and its function is to repair the double-stranded breaks in DNA. It is associated with familial breast and ovarian carcinoma. BRCA1-associated breast cancers are commonly poorly differentiated. All breast cancers are separated into 3 major groups based on the expression of two proteins, ER and HER2 (also known as ERBB2). HER2 cancers are defined as cancers overexpressing HER2 and can be either ER-positive or ER-negative. Thus HER2neu is expressed only in a fraction of people with breast cancer. EGF-receptor family has two proto-oncogenes: ERBB1 that codes for EGFR and ERBB2 that codes for HER. Mutation in EGFR results in adenocarcinoma of the lung, which is one of the main subtypes of non-small cell lung carcinoma. MYC is a proto-oncogene, that is expressed in all eukaryotic cells and belongs to the immediate-early response genes, which are rapidly induced by RAS/MAPK signaling following growth factor stimulation of quiescent cells. Normally, MYC protein concentration are tightly controlled at the level of transcription, translation and protein stability. The mechanisms by which MYC promotes neoplastic cell growth may be follows: * MYC activates the expression of many genes like D cyclins, that are involved in cell cycle progression + MYC regulates the expression of telomerase * MYC is one of the transcriptional factors that can act together to reprogram somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells MYC gene is deregulated in a number of cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, breast, colon, lung and other cancers. The functionally identical NMYC and LMYC genes are also amplified in 2021 neuroblastomas and small cell cancers of the lung, respectively.

stem: A 20-year-old athlete suddenly collapsed while playing football and was taken to the hospital where he was declared dead. His autopsy image is given below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of death? N” ZZ ne
options: Valvular heart disease due to RHD 2001
Sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia
Sudden cardiac death due to Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Sudden cardiac death due to atherosclerosis
explanation: The given image shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and along with the scenario, it is suggestive of sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have an increased risk of sudden cardiac death from ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In fact, arrhythmias are the most important/most common cause of death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the most common causes of sudden, otherwise unexplained death in young athletes. HCM is characterized by reduced stroke volume due to impaired diastolic filling, which is a consequence of the massively hypertrophic left ventricle. There is a dynamic obstruction to the left ventricular outflow as the anterior mitral leaflet moves towards the ventricular septum during systole. This compromised cardiac output in combination with a secondary increase in pulmonary venous pressure is the reason for exertional dyspnea at times of increased oxygen demand. Major clinical problems in HCM are atrial fibrillation, stroke, intractable cardiac failure, ventricular arrhythmias and also sudden death. There is a harsh systolic ejection murmur caused by the ventricular outflow obstruction. Mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) are most commonly seen in the genes encoding B-myosin heavy chain (MHC/MYH7) or myosin-binding protein C (MYBP-C). HCM is mostly an autosomal dominant disorder. The most important histologic features of HCM myocardium are as follows: + Massive myocyte hypertrophy particularly of transverse myocyte diameters ¢ Myofiber disarray including that of bundles of myocytes, individual myocytes, and contractile elements + Interstitial and replacement fibrosis 2030 Most of the patients can be treated with B blockers to decrease heart rate and contractility. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators are used in patients with increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Some patients can also be treated by surgical excision of the septal muscle or by carefully controlled septal infarction through a catheter-based infusion of alcohol. subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following can be prevented by transfusing irradiated RBCs?
explanation: Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevent the incidence of graft versus host disease (GVHD) associated with the transfusion. GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients and the transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may occur following transplantation of solid organs too. GVHD maybe of two types: acute and chronic. Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver( in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes. Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibodies production. Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation, before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its side effects such as recurrence of tumor in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the effect of Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase deficiency?
explanation: 2032 Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH. G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt. Defective enzyme function reduced the ability of red cells to protect themselves against oxidative injuries, thereby increasing lipid peroxidation and lead to hemolysis. * G6PD reduces NADP to NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate. * This NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione. * This reduced glutathione acts as a cofactor in reactions that neutralize compounds such as H202, thereby protecting against oxidant injury. + Exposure of G6PD deficient red cells to oxidative stress leads to crosslinking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains, which then becomes denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates called ‘Heinz bodies’, thereby producing membrane damage. * When these inclusion bearing RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these Heinz bodies. + The resultant cells are called ‘Bite cells’. Clinical features: + Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular * Hemolytic anaemia * Hemoglobinemia * Hemoglobinuria The episode of hemolysis is self-limiting, since only the older RBCs are at risk for lysis, leaving the G6PD-replete younger RBCs in circulation. The recovery phase is heralded by reticulocytosis.

subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following is not likely to be seen in a patient with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
explanation: Leukemia is least likely to be seen in patients with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH). Clinical manifestations of PNH include: * Hemolytic anemia * Pancytopenia + Intermittent hemoglobinuriaacute hemolytic episodes occur at night owing to a slight fall in pH during sleep + Haemosiderinuria * Venous thrombosis (a leading cause of death in PNH) * Patients diagnosed with PNH can later develop aplastic anemia and vice versa PNH is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of 2033 membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. PNH blood cells are abnormally susceptible to lysis or injury by complement since they are deficient in three GPIlinked proteins that regulate complement activity: * Decay-accelerating factor or CD55 * Membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis or CD59 (Inhibitor of C3 convertase) and * C8-binding protein Diagnosis: + Ham’s test: The abnormal sensitivity of red blood cells, leukocytes, and platelets to complement can be demonstrated in vitro using red cell lysis at acidic pH. + Flow cytometry detects the red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59. Treatment: Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody, that prevents the conversion of C5 to C5a has been proven effective in PNH. The definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

stem: What is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of myocarditis?
explanation: An endo-myocardial biopsy is the gold standard investigation for the diagnosis of myocarditis. Myocarditis can be due to * Infections: Coxsackie A and B, HIV, C.diphtheriae, Ricketssiae, Candida, Protozoa and helminths. + Immune-mediated reactions: Post-viral, post-streptococcal, drug hypersensitivity (e.g: methyl dopa, sulfinamides), transplant rejection, etc., 2035 * Unknown: Sarcoidosis, Giant cell myocarditis Active myocarditis is characterized by an interstitial inflammatory infiltrate associated with degenerating or apoptotic myocytes.

subject: Pathology
stem: A child presented with bilateral proptosis. From the peripheral smear, he was suspected to have chloroma. What is the next investigation of choice?
explanation: The next investigation of choice, in a child suspected to have a chloroma, is a bone marrow biopsy. Chloroma, also called myeloid sarcoma, granulocytic sarcoma, or myeloblastoma is an extramedullary tumor that occurs in 2% to 14% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Frequent sites of involvement are the skin, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, bone, soft tissue, testis, and peritoneum. Isolated orbital involvement of myeloid sarcoma is rare. Proptosis is the most common presentation. Other symptoms include lacrimal swelling, conjunctival mass lesion, retinal hemorrhages, ptosis, dystopia. Decreased visual acuity and ocular movement restriction have also been reported. Most cases of chloroma can be diagnosed on peripheral smear examination, which is easily available and is relatively inexpensive. Sometimes it may not be associated with any peripheral smear abnormality, and hence bone marrow aspirate and biopsy should be done to confirm AML. The diagnosis can also be made if Auer rods are detected. Myeloid sarcomas have immunophenotypic features that are identical to AML. Although myeloid sarcomas are radiosensitive, they are managed with systemic chemotherapy in most cases, even in the absence of bone marrow involvement. Surgery and/or radiation therapy may be indicated for symptomatic lesions or tumors causing local organ dysfunction or obstruction. Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells, and occasional plasma cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence, they are also called caterpillar cells. Chronic inflammation leads to diffuse thickening and fibrosis of the valve leaflets, often with calcific deposits. stem: A 60-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling and ataxia. Which among the following could likely be a cause?
explanation: The most likely cause in the following case is Non-Hodgkin lymphoma(NHL). Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a type of NHL is the most common lymphoma. NHL affects the elderly age group and extranodal presentation is common. DLBCL can involve CNS, and CNS involvement is particularly common if there is involvement of the testes, paranasal sinuses, or bone marrow as well. Primary testicular lymphoma is common in NHL when compared to Hodgkin lymphoma. Primary testicular lymphoma(PTL) is an aggressive and uncommon form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma(NHL) usually affecting the elderly age group(>60y). It typically presents as a painless, firm testicular mass. Constitutional symptoms are uncommon, and if present, warrant a systemic involvement. Metastasis involves the central nervous system (CNS), skin, contralateral testis, and pleura resulting in local complications. Even though ataxia is seen as a paraneoplastic symptom due to cerebellar degeneration in Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular involvement is very rare and so far only 5 cases have been reported. Hodgkin lymphoma arises in a single node or chain of nodes and spreads first to anatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. The extranodal presentation is rare. The extranodal disease can occur at any site like lung, liver, bone, and bone marrow is most common if it occurs. The central nervous system and the testis are exceptionally rare sites for Hodgkin's lymphoma. Thus Hodgkin's lymphoma can be ruled out. Other options: Glioblastoma multiforme is a highly malignant tumor, common in older adults in the fifth and sixth decades. The most common locations are the frontal and temporal lobes. The tumor may spread and invade the other hemisphere, resulting in a characteristic butterfly appearance. Extracranial metastases of malignant gliomas are extremely rare due to: + Absence of a lymphatic system in the brain and spinal cord for systemic dissemination + Dense dura around intracranial veins, preventing the penetration of the tumor 2044 + Lack of nurturing stroma in other organs prevents the proliferation of glioblastoma cells Therefore the tumor metastasizing to the testis is very much unlikely and glioblastoma can be ruled out. Germ cell tumors(GCT) account for 90%—95% of cases. Non-seminomatous form (NSGCT) metastasizes to the lungs, liver, central nervous system, and bone in order of frequency. The frequency of brain metastases is very low, not exceeding 1.2%. Note: This is a controversial question. stem: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites presented to you. The gross appearance of his liver is as shown below. Which among the following is true about it?
options: Dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver tissue
Dark areas represent viable liver tissue, white areas represent necrosis
explanation: The gross image of the liver shows a nutmeg appearance, seen in heart failure. The dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver tissue. Nutmeg liver refers to the mottled appearance of the liver which resembles the cut section of nutmeg. This occurs as a result of hepatic venous congestion following right heart failure. The dark centrilobular zones reflect sinusoidal congestion. Congestion is seen around the central veins usually from right-sided heart failure. The pale periportal zones reflect normal or fatty liver tissue. The liver derives its blood supply from the portal venous system and the hepatic artery. The portal triad constitutes: + Branches of the hepatic artery + Portal vein + Bile duct 2045 The blood from the portal vein and the hepatic artery flow through the intervening sinusoids and drains into the central vein. The central veins from adjacent lobules form interlobular veins, which then unite as hepatic veins and finally drain into the inferior vena cava. The hepatic lobule is divided into three zones: * Zone 1 is the periportal area + Zone 2 is the intermediate zone * Zone 3 is the area closest to the central vein Right-sided cardiac failure leads to passive congestion of the liver. Left-sided cardiac failure leads to hypoperfusion and hypoxia of hepatocytes around central veins. The combination of hypoperfusion and retrograde congestion causes centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, leading to this mottled appearance of the liver, known as nutmeg liver. stem: A person was brought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, and hypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase in which immunoglobulin?
explanation: The given clinical features suggest type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE). Immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity reactions refer to allergic reactions or allergies. It is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual. These reactions are 2049 induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals. Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils. IgE coats mast cells by binding to the FceRI receptor. Re-exposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FceRI which in turn causes activation of mast cells releasing powerful mediators. The principal mediators are: ¢ Histamine ¢ Proteases + Prostaglandins * Leukotrienes * Cytokines like TNF, IL-1, and chemokines. The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis. It occurs in two phases: ¢ The immediate phase is characterized by vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm (in asthma), or glandular secretions. These changes occur within minutes after exposure to an allergen and subside in a few hours. + Late-phase reaction is characterized by infiltration of tissues with eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, monocytes, and CD4+ T cells. Late-phase reaction sets in 2 to 24 hours later and may last for several days. stem: All of the following are associated with massive splenomegaly except :
explanation: 2050 All the above are associated with massive splenomegaly except aplastic anemia. Aplastic anemia is a syndrome of chronic primary hematopoietic failure. This results in pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia). Important causes include + Alkylating agents, antimetabolites ¢ Benzene + Whole-body irradiation + Viral infections: Hepatitis (unknown virus), Cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Herpes zoster + Fanconi anemia The patient will have + Decreased red blood cells leading to anemia * Decreased white blood cells leading to recurrent infections * Decreased platelets leading to petechiae and ecchymoses. Many other leukemias and lymphomas may have a similar presentation. However, splenomegaly is characteristically absent in these patients. The bone marrow is markedly hypocellular. It is largely devoid of hematopoietic cells. Marrow aspirates yield a dry tap having only fat cells, fibrous stroma, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Aplasia is best appreciated in marrow biopsies. subject: Pathology
stem: A 42-year-old female patient presents with cough, low-grade fever, and hemoptysis. Investigations reveal a cavitary lesion on her right lung apex, which on biopsy reveals caseous necrosis. The underlying pathophysiology is :
explanation: The clinical scenario with complaints of cough, low-grade fever, hemoptysis is suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis. The diagnosis is further supported by a cavitary lesion in the apex of the lung and a biopsy showing caseous necrosis. The pathophysiology is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction mediated by activated macrophages. Tuberculosis is a chronic pulmonary and systemic disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Granulomatous inflammation and tissue damage are by Th-1 mediated macrophage activation and killing of bacteria. Interferon-gamma (IFN-y) released by Th-1 cells is the critical mediator that activates the macrophages. This activation differentiates the macrophages into epithelioid cells that aggregate to form granuloma. This is a T-cell mediated (Type 4) hypersensitivity reaction. Pulmonary TB due to exogenous (new infection) or endogenous (reactivation of a dormant primary lesion) infection in a sensitized individual is called post-primary or reactivation or secondary or adult-type TB. The apical and posterior segments of the upper lobe and superior segments of the lower lobe are most commonly involved in post-primary TB due to increased ventilation in these segments than the lower zones. Patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss. Radiological findings include ill-defined opacification in the upper lobes, consolidation, collapse, and cavitation development. * Typically, the disease is parenchymal without nodal enlargement. * Cavitation is a distinguishing feature of postprimary TB. * Typical cavities are thick-walled and irregular. ¢ Air-fluid levels are uncommon in TB. The presence of air-fluid levels indicates superadded infections. * Upper-lobe involvement with cavitation and the absence of lymphadenopathy distinguishes postprimary TB from primary TB. It is seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels with deposition of fibrinoid material which is combination of immune complexes and plasma proteins. subject: Pathology
stem: A 45-year-old male patient was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is true about intracellular regulation of iron in the above condition?
options: Ferritin translation is increased by binding IRP to IRE
Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
Transferrin receptor 1 translation is unaffected by binding IRP to IRE
Transferrin receptor 1 translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE
explanation: In iron deficiency anemia, ferritin translation is decreased by binding iron regulatory protein to iron response elements. Dietary iron is carried in the blood by transferrin and enters cells via endocytosis, mediated by the transferrin receptor. Excess iron is stored by binding to ferritin. The levels of transferrin, transferrin receptor (TfR), and ferritin are therefore crucial to cellular iron homeostasis. The synthesis of these three proteins is regulated in response to iron availability and aconitase (enzyme in citric acid cycle). When a cell is depleted of iron, the aconitase enzyme is converted to apoaconitase. Apoaconitase is identical to iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP-1) and is closely related to IRP-2. It regulates iron metabolism. The iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) are two cytoplasmic RNA-binding proteins that control iron metabolism. They bind to regions in the mRNA containing the ferritin and transferrin receptor. These mRNA sequences are part of hairpin structures known as iron response elements (IREs). 2054 * When the IRPs bind to the 5' untranslated IRE sequence in the ferritin mRNA, IRPs block ferritin translation, thus decreasing ferritin. * When IRPs are bound to the 3' end of the untranslated IRE sequence, they stabilize the mRNA, prevent its degradation and increase the copies of transferrin receptor per mRNA molecule. Hence, in iron-deficient cells, iron storage (bound to ferritin) is reduced and iron uptake (via transferrin receptor) becomes more efficient.

subject: Pathology
stem: A 65-year-old male patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy presents to the outpatient department. His peripheral smear shows the presence of smudge cells. Which of the following additional investigations will you do to arrive at a diagnosis?
explanation: An elderly patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy, and a peripheral smear showing the presence of smudge cells suggest a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic feature of CLL is CD 19+, CD20+, CD 23+, CD5+. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients. The chromosomal defects in CLL include: * Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis) * Deletion of 11q * Trisomy 12q * Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis) The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells. On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates referred to as proliferation centers. These proliferation centers are pathognomic to CLL when present. Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab. Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). stem: Oil red O stain is used in which of the following?
explanation: Oil red O (ORO) stain is used in frozen section. Oil red O stains lipid/ fats and gives a characteristic orange/red appearance. It is used in the unfixed frozen sections as the fixation of fats with other routine processes may lose the lipid content. 10% Neutral buffer formaldehyde (NBF) is the preferred fixative in histopathological sections staining with Oil red O. Zenker's fixative and Helly's fixative are best avoided during staining with ORO. Oil red O stains the lipid in the vacuoles in the pulmonary vasculature. It can be useful in identifying fat emboli in lung tissue, diagnosing renal cell carcinoma, and sebaceous gland tumors of the skin. Other stains used for lipids or fats: + Nile blue sulfate. The preferred fixative is formal calcium. * Osmic acid is used in the frozen section. 10% NBF is the preferred fixative + Sudan black B is used in the frozen section. The preferred fixative is 10% NBF. Other Options: Option A: Formalin fixationFormalin as 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) is the most common fixative used in diagnostic pathology. stem: A boy presents with fever, night sweats, and neck swelling. The biopsy of swelling showed a starry sky appearance. What is the most likely genetic abnormality seen in this case?
explanation: The given clinical scenario and the classical histopathological finding of starry sky appearance suggest the diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma and the most likely genetic abnormality is the translocation of the MYC gene on chromosome 8. Burkitt's lymphoma arises from mature germinal center B-cells that express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6. It is divided into endemic and sporadic types, both of which occur mainly in children or young adults. 2057 + African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma often presents as a mass involving the mandible and may involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands. * Sporadic (non-endemic) Burkitt lymphoma most often appears as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum. « A subset of aggressive lymphomas occurs in individuals infected with HIV. All forms of Burkitt lymphoma are associated with translocations of the MYC gene on chromosome 8 that lead to increased MYC protein levels. Essentially all endemic Burkitt lymphomas are latently infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). The tumor shows a high mitotic index with numerous apoptotic cells. The nuclear remnants of these apoptotic cells are phagocytosed by interspersed benign macrophages. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic starry sky pattern. Burkitt lymphoma is very aggressive but responds well to intensive chemotherapy. The image below shows the starry sky appearance seen in Burkitt's lymphoma. subject: Pathology
stem: A 30-year-old male complained of fatigue for the past 1 year. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly. His blood workup shows the following findings. Which of the following is the most sensitive investigation in this case?
explanation: The clinical presentation with fatigue, splenomegaly, and the peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML). The BCR-ABL gene which is specific for CML is detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization(FISH) or polymerase chain reaction(PCR) based tests. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Clinical features: Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia. Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy. 2069 Peripheral blood: * Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. + Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells. * Platelet count is usually increased Bone Marrow: * Markedly hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils. * There is also an increase in megakaryocytes and usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is an increased reticulin deposition, but overt marrow fibrosis is rare early in the course. * Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-blue cytoplasm. Other options: Immunophenotyping and flow cytometry: Flow cytometry refers to the measurement of cellular antigens as they flow in a fluid stream. Immunophenotyping is employed using labeled antibodies against specific epitopes of cellular antigens. The technique that is usually used in immunophenotyping is flow cytometry. It has a limited role in the diagnosis of CML. It is mainly used in identifying CML blast transformation. LAP score: Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase(LAP) score is decreased in cases of CML. It is only a first-line test in the diagnosis of CML and the diagnosis needs to be confirmed by other tests including bone marrow biopsy, molecular diagnostics, and cytogenetic analysis.

explanation: True statements regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney are 1, 4. Clear cell carcinoma is the most common sporadic renal cell cancer and cells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen 2109 and fat. Clear cell cancer arises from the proximal tubular epithelium and usually occurs as solitary unilateral lesions. Most of the cases are sporadic, but can also occur either in familial forms or in association with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. They are associated with the loss of sequence of the short arm of chromosome 3. Those with VHL disease inherit a germline mutation of the VHL gene on chromosomal band 3p25 and lose the second allele by somatic mutation. The VHL protein causes the degradation of hypoxia-induced factors (HIFs), which are transcription factors that contribute to carcinogenesis by stimulating the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) that helps drive tumour cell growth. Histologically, the tumour cells have a rounded or polygonal shape and abundant clear or granular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids. Ewing sarcoma is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma in children. The majority of the patients affected are usually <20 years of age. It has a slight male predominance. It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus and flat bones of the pelvis. The majority of Ewing sarcomas have a balanced translocation between the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 and the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11. stem: Which of the following is a marker of natural killer cell?
explanation: The marker of the natural killer cells is CD94. It is expressed in natural killer cells and a small subset of T lymphocytes. Natural killer cells (NK cells) are essential cells of innate immunity. They act against malignant and virus-infected cells. NK cells are identified by CD16 and CD56 cell surface receptors. NK cells' activity is augmented by interferons and upon activation, they bind to glycoprotein receptors on the surface of target cells and release perforins. Perforins create pores in the membrane of the target cells. Through these pores, cytotoxic factors like tumor necrosis factor-beta (TNF-8) enter the cells and destroy them by apoptosis. NK cells express a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Here, NK cells have the capability of killing target cells that are coated by IgG antibodies. The image given below shows the actions of NK cells on cancer cells. 2122 Fc receptor Antibody \ x 4 \ \ Target cancer ¥ + - antigen \ Cancer cell e Perforin and Granzyme released Other options: Option A: CD68 is expressed on macrophages and monocytes. Option B: CD 3 is a T-cell receptor marker. They are involved in the transduction of signals to the T cells when an antigen binds to the T cell receptor. Option C: CD 25 is a component of the IL2 receptor and is important in T cell proliferation and activation.

subject: Pathology
stem: In a patient with bare lymphocytic disease, graft vs host reaction does not occur due to:
options: MHC class II deficiency on lymphocytes
MHC class I deficiency on lymphocytes
explanation: 2132 In a patient with bare lymphocytic disease, graft vs host reaction does not occur due to MHC class II deficiency on the lymphocytes. Bare lymphocyte disease occurs due to mutations in transcription factors required for class II MHC gene expression. This results in the lack of class II MHC molecules, leading to the impaired development of CD4+ T cells. As these CD 4+ T cells are required for both for cellular immunity and for assisting B cells, class II MHC deficiency results in a combined immunodeficiency.

stem: A child presents with multiple skin lesions over the inner thigh and genital areas. It initially started as macule and later developed to become nodules. Some nodules have central umbilication. The histology of the lesion is shown below. What would be found on biopsy? 2092 Rimi sae. | ie 2 ee ee Pe ee ee ee ee en oa
explanation: The given clinical scenario and histological image are diagnostic of molluscum contagiosum lesions, which show intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies, called Henderson—Patterson bodies or molluscum bodies. Infection is usually spread by direct contact, particularly among children and young adults. Multiple lesions occur on the skin and mucous membranes, with a predilection for the trunk and anogenital areas. Individual lesions are firm, pruritic, pink to skin-colored umbilicated papules. A curd-like material can be expressed from the central umbilication. Smearing this material onto a glass slide and Giemsa staining shows diagnostic molluscum bodies, which are ellipsoid, homogeneous, cytoplasmic inclusions that are found in the cells of the stratum granulosum and the stratum corneum and are up to 35 um in size. 2133 Molluscum contagiosum pee ee ee Enlarged keratinocytes of stratum malpighii with eosinophilic inclusion bodies - Henderson-Patterson bodies or molluscum bodies containing virus particles Other options: Option A: Multinucleate giant cells (called Tzanck cells) are seen in herpes simplex virus infections. They are formed when individual epidermal cells containing viral inclusions fuse to produce giant cells. These can be demonstrated by the diagnostic Tzanck test, which is based on the microscopic examination of the vesicle fluid. Option B: Donovan bodies are seen in donovanosis, caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies are minute, encapsulated coccobacilli in macrophages, which can be demonstrated in Giemsa-stained smears of the exudate. Option D: Koilocytes are characteristically seen in HPV infections, such as condylomata acuminata. Koilocytes are lining cells that have perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization.

subject: Pathology
stem: Investigations of a patient being evaluated for leukemia revealed a WBC count of 4,50,000/uL, with eosinophilia and basophilia. What is the likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation: A WBC count of 4,50,000/uL with eosinophilia and basophilia indicates a probable diagnosis of chronic myelogenous leukemia. CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. It is caused by the translocation of ABL gene on chromosome 9 onto BCR gene on chromosome 22, resulting in the formation of the BCR-ABL fusion gene. This chromosomal abnomality, called Philadelphia chromosome, is characteristic of CML. The resulting BCR-ABL translocation results in the activation of tyrosine kinase that signals pro-growth and pro-survival pathways like RAS and JAK/STAT pathways resulting in the proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells. Patients typically present with a dragging sensation abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. On peripheral smear there is leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm (neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils), blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells, the platelet count is usually increased. 2134 Basophils and eosinophils are often increased. Other options: Option D: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a hematopoietic progenitor malignancy that causes immature myeloblast accumulation in the bone marrow. Incidence increases with age and peaks after 60 years of age. The WBC count is about 15,000/uL. Few cases have either <5000 or >1,00,000/uUL WBC count. Squamous cell carcinoma is most commonly found in men and is strongly associated with smoking. Squamous cell carcinoma predominantly arises in the central segmental or subsegmental bronchi. The tumor may grow into the bronchial lumen and produce an intraluminal mass. In 2149 certain cases, the bronchial obstruction may lead to atelectasis or infection. The tumor may penetrate the wall of the bronchus and infiltrate the peribronchial tissue into the carina or the mediastinum. This tumor may be associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like hypercalcemia. The symptoms could include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, lethargy, polyuria, polydipsia, and dehydration. Squamous metaplasia and dysplasia often precede frank squamous cell carcinoma. Carcinoma in-situ persists for many years and this may often be recognized on cytologic smears or in BAL fluid or brushings. Gross appearance: The tissue is grey-white, firm, with areas of necrosis and hemorrhages. Red or yellow-white mottling and softening may be seen. The necrotic foci may cavitate. Keratinization occurs in the form of squamous pearls or individual cells with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm. It is positive for p4o and p63 markers. subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following statements are true about familial adenomatous polyposis? 2098
explanation: 2154 The true statements about familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) are statements 2 and 4 (option- . Familial adenomatous polyposis is an inherited autosomal dominant disorder presenting numerous colorectal adenomatous polyps. It is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a regulator in the Wnt signaling pathway. The diagnosis of FAP requires the presence of at least 100 polyps. Patients are usually teenagers and multiple polyps are visible in the colon during sigmoidoscopy. It is associated with a variety of extraintestinal manifestations including congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigmental epithelium. Colorectal adenocarcinoma occurs in almost all cases before the age of 50. Prophylactic colectomy is recommended in patients with APC gene mutations. The surgeries used are colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis (IRA), restorative proctocolectomy with an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (RPC), or total proctectomy and end ileostomy. The first 2 surgeries are preferred in young patients as it avoids a permanent stoma. Note - FAP along with brain tumors is called Turcot syndrome. FAP along with multiple osteomas, skin, and soft tissue tumors is called Gardner syndrome.

In addition, TH2 cells (as well as mast cells and epithelial cells) produce chemokines that attract more TH2 cells, as well as other leukocytes, to the reaction site. LCH occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is the BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation. It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system. When calvarium is affected, it results in otitis media and mastoiditis. Spinal involvement results in compression fractures and neurological involvement. Vertebral involvement results in a rapid flattening of the vertebral body (vertebra plana). Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. stem: 2102 Hereditary angioedema is due to a defect in which of the proteins mentioned below?
explanation: Hereditary angioedema is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by a deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitors. C1 esterase inhibitors usually target proteases like Cir and C1s, factor XII and the kallikrein system. Therefore, their deficiency leads to unregulated activation of kallikrein, leading to increased bradykinin. Clinical features include swelling of the skin and mucosal surfaces, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, which may be aggravated after minor trauma or emotional stress. The condition can be treated by giving C1 inhibitor concentrates from human plasma. The main inflammatory mediator responsible for these symptoms is bradykinin. Bradykinin is an inflammatory mediator formed by the cleavage of kininogen, in the presence of the enzyme kallikrein. Bradykinin has the following effects: * Increases the vascular permeability * Causes contraction of smooth muscle * Dilates the blood vessel * Mediates pain Other options: Options B and C: Decay-accelerating factor (DAF) and CD59 are two proteins that are linked by a glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor to the plasma membrane. DAF prevents the formation of C3 convertases and CD59 inhibits the formation of the MAC. An acquired deficiency of the enzyme that creates GPI anchors leads to a deficiency of these regulators and excessive complement activation and lysis of red cells resulting in Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria(PNH). During inflammation, C5a (Option D), C3a, and C4a, which are all cleavage products of their corresponding complement components, stimulate mast cells to release histamine. They have effects similar to those of mast cell mediators involved in anaphylactic reactions and therefore, are 2171 called anaphylatoxins. C5a is also chemotactic for neutrophils, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. Additionally, it activates the lipooxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism in neutrophils and monocytes, resulting in the further release of inflammatory mediators.

IDA is an example of microcytic hypochromic anemia. The causes of IDA can be inadequate diet, impaired reabsorption, increased requirement and increased blood loss. The manifestations of IDA depend upon the underlying cause. In general, IDA presents with koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic changes in the tongue, gastric mucosa, malabsorbtion and pica (craving for consumption of non-edible materials) Peripheral smears show small and pale red cells typically described as microcytic (reduced MCV) and hypochromic (enlarged zone of central pallor). Poikilocytosis can be seen in the form of elongated red cells, known as pencil cells. Target cells can be found in cases of severe IDA. Diagnosis is mainly by laboratory studies. The typical findings are: * Low hemoglobin and hematocrit * Low serum iron and ferretin + Increased Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) * Hepcidin is low (decreased stores of iron inhibit hepcidin synthesis) IDA is treated by giving oral and parenteral preparations if iron or packed cell transfusion depending upon the severity of the anemia. Option A: Megaloblastic anemia is defined by a high MCV Option C: Thalassemia presents much earlier in infancy, with reduced MCV and a normal/increased RBC count Option D: Essential thrombocytosis is characterized by isolated rise in platelet count (>450,000) along with normal hemoglobin, hematocrit and iron stores.

subject: Pathology
stem: Which of the following statements is true about interleukin-12?
explanation: The true statements are that interleukin-12 (IL-12) is produced by macrophages and increases the production of interferon-y (IFN-y). IL-12 is produced by dendritic cells and macrophages. Its principle actions are to promote the production of IFN-y, which drives TH1-type responses and further stimulates macrophage activation. It also promotes the differentiation of CD4+ T-cells to Thi cells. 2172

subject: Pathology
stem: A chronic smoker presents to the clinic with shortness of breath. A mass is noted at the lower lobe periphery of the lung. A diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma is made. The biopsy will be positive for:
explanation: The biopsy of adenocarcinoma of the lung will be positive for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) and napsin A. Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. It is associated with tobacco smoking, but less so than other histologic subtypes. It is the most common subtype in non-smokers and is associated with the loss of function of EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET or RET genes. The majority express TTF-1, which is a protein required for normal lung development. Napsin A is a new marker and is more sensitive and specific than TTF-1 in the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma. Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns: acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid. The lesions are small and are usually located in the periphery. At the periphery of the tumor there is often a lepidic pattern of spread, in which the tumor cells “crawl” along normal-appearing alveolar septa. Clinical features usually have an insidious onset. The incidence is usually at age 50 or more. The major presenting complaints are cough, weight loss, chest pain, and dyspnea. Other options: Option B: p4o, along with p63 is a marker for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. Option D: Chromogranin is a marker for small cell carcinoma of the lung.

In Sahli's method, oxyhemoglobin is converted to acid hematin with the action of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl). The brown color of the acid hematin is matched to its intensity with a standard brown glass comparator in a visual colorimeter called Sahli’s colorimeter. The reaction occurs within 24 hours of antibiotic treatment. Clinical features are fever, chills, nausea and vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension, flushing, myalgia, and exacerbation of skin lesions. Syphilis is the leading spirochetal infection associated with JHR. Other infections are Lyme disease, louse-borne relapsing fever, leptospirosis, and tick-borne relapsing fever. Antibiotics that have been most associated are penicillins, tetracyclines, and erythromycin. Mild reactions are self-limiting and often resolve spontaneously within 24 hours. Prevention of the JHR is by giving TNF-alpha antibodies and in some cases steroids. 2176

stem: A 56-year-old man was diagnosed with COVID-19 and was put on mechanical ventilation. He passed away after a week. What is the likely post-mortem change seen in the lungs?
options: Thick layer of fibrin lining the alveoli
Pulmonary artery hypertrophy with increased resistance 2179
explanation: The clinical scenario of a patient with COVID-19 pneumonia on mechanical ventilation is suggestive of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). A thick layer of fibrin or waxy hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls are characteristic of ARDS. COVID-19 is a respiratory disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. These are enveloped positive-sense RNA viruses. The spread of SARS-CoV-2 is believed to be primarily via respiratory droplets, direct contact, airborne, and fomites. The major complication in patients with severe COVID-19 is ARDS requiring oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation. ARDS is a clinical syndrome characterized by acute onset, severe dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure. Etiological factors can be divided into direct and indirect causes of lung injury as follows: Damage to the endothelial and alveolar epithelial cells, with inflammation, is the key initiating event and the basis of lung damage. Neutrophils play a significant role in tissue injury in this condition. There are three stages in the development of ARDS: + Exudative phaseoccurs for the first 7 days of the illness. This is associated with damage to alveolar-capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes. This results in a breach in the tight alveolar barrier. The release of proinflammatory cytokines leads to the recruitment of neutrophils and the development of a hyaline membrane in the alveoli. + Proliferative phaseoccurs from day 7-21. Recovery from mechanical ventilation is seen in most patients. + Fibrotic phaseis associated with increased mortality. Extensive alveolar duct and interstitial fibrosis are seen. The image given below shows hyaline membrane formation in the alveolar walls seen in ARDS. subject: Pathology
stem: Match the following disorders with their genetic abnormalities.
explanation: The correct match is: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant progressive brain disorder that causes uncontrolled movements, emotional problems, and loss of thinking ability. It occurs due to atrophy, with loss of neurons and gliosis in the caudate lobe, putamen, and globus pallidus. There is an abnormal expansion of the trinucleotide CAG in the Huntington gene on chromosome 4. Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome in which a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 is inherited as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker bottom feet. Patients have significant hypertonia including clenched hands with overlapping fingers. Cardiac anomalies (ventricular septal defects and patent ductus arteriosus) and gastrointestinal anomalies (Meckel’s diverticulum, malrotations) are common. Prenatal ultrasound reveals fetal growth restriction. 1. Trinucleotide repeat b. Huntington chore a 3. Trisomy 13 a. Patau syndrome 4. Hb beta chain Glu _| c. Phenotypic features include microcephaly, low-set ears, hypertelorism, and a broad nasal bridge. Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the B-globin gene, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS). Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis. Clinical features are moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice and painful bone crisis. The aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.
