Loss of taste on anterior 2/3 of tongue
explanation: LMN CN VII lesion (Bell's palsy): ALL ipsilateral facial muscles paralyzed including forehead (cannot wrinkle forehead, cannot close eye). UMN lesion (e.g., stroke): contralateral lower face paralyzed; forehead is SPARED because it has bilateral cortical representation.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies which muscles of the tongue?
options: All extrinsic and intrinsic muscles of tongue EXCEPT palatoglossus
explanation: CN XII supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus (supplied by CN X via pharyngeal plexus). In CN XII palsy, the tongue deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion when protruded (because the contralateral genioglossus is unopposed, pushing the tongue ipsilaterally).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which cranial nerve is the efferent limb of the carotid sinus reflex (baroreflex)?
options: CN IX (afferent) and CN X (efferent — vagus reduces heart rate)
explanation: Carotid sinus reflex: CN IX (Hering's nerve) carries baroreceptor afferents from the carotid sinus → nucleus tractus solitarius → vagal dorsal nucleus → CN X (efferent) slows heart rate. CN IX also carries chemoreceptor afferents from carotid body.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which cranial nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland?
options: CN VII (greater petrosal nerve → pterygopalatine ganglion)
explanation: CN VII → greater petrosal nerve → nerve of pterygoid canal → pterygopalatine ganglion → zygomatic nerve (V2) → lacrimal branch of V1 → lacrimal gland. Pterygopalatine ganglion also supplies nasal and palatal glands.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy causes inability to abduct the eye (lateral rectus paralysis). The eye deviates:
explanation: CN VI palsy: lateral rectus paralysis causes the eye to deviate medially (esotropia/convergent squint) due to unopposed medial rectus action. The patient cannot look laterally on the affected side. CN VI has the longest intracranial course and is vulnerable in raised ICP.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nucleus of CN IV (trochlear) is located in which part of the brainstem?
explanation: CN IV nucleus is in the caudal midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus (ventral to the cerebral aqueduct/periaqueductal grey). The nerve decussates in the superior medullary velum before exiting dorsally below the inferior colliculus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Horner's syndrome consists of which three features?
explanation: Horner's syndrome: ptosis (superior tarsal/Müller's muscle denervation), miosis (dilator pupillae denervation), anhidrosis (ipsilateral face), and apparent enophthalmos (due to lower lid elevation from inferior tarsal muscle denervation). Caused by interruption of sympathetic chain.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The fovea centralis of the retina is responsible for which visual function?
options: Highest visual acuity and color vision (packed with cones)
explanation: Fovea centralis (in the center of the macula) contains only cones (with densest packing) and provides maximum visual acuity and color vision. The optic disc (blind spot) is where the optic nerve exits the eye — no photoreceptors here.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Aqueous humor is produced by which structure?
explanation: Aqueous humor is produced by the ciliary body (non-pigmented ciliary epithelium) via active secretion (carbonic anhydrase) and diffusion. It flows from posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm → episcleral veins.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The most common cause of PAINLESS progressive visual loss in adults over 60 years is:
explanation: AMD is the leading cause of irreversible central visual loss in people over 60 years. Dry AMD (geographic atrophy) causes gradual loss; wet AMD (neovascular, choroidal neovascularisation) causes rapid central loss. Drusen are the earliest sign.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) in the thalamus receives input from which cranial nerve?
options: CN II (optic nerve, via optic radiation)
explanation: Visual pathway: retina → optic nerve (CN II) → optic chiasm (nasal fibers cross) → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus) → optic radiation (Meyer's loop for inferior, straight for superior fields) → primary visual cortex (V1) in occipital lobe.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Bitemporal hemianopia (loss of temporal fields in both eyes) is caused by a lesion at which location?
options: Optic chiasm (midline crossing fibers — e.g., pituitary adenoma)
explanation: Pituitary adenoma compresses the optic chiasm from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibers (which carry temporal visual field from each eye). Result: bitemporal hemianopia. A craniopharyngioma compresses from above, first affecting superior temporal fields.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing is caused by a lesion in which structure?
options: Primary visual cortex (V1) in occipital lobe — posterior cerebral artery territory
explanation: PCA territory infarction affecting occipital cortex causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia. Macular sparing (central vision preserved) occurs because the macula has dual blood supply (PCA and MCA) and a large cortical representation that may escape infarction.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Drusen in age-related macular degeneration are deposits of which material?
options: Extracellular debris between Bruch's membrane and RPE
explanation: Drusen are deposits of extracellular material (lipids, complement proteins, cellular debris) beneath the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) at Bruch's membrane level. Soft drusen and geographic atrophy are features of dry AMD; choroidal neovascularisation defines wet AMD.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The superior oblique tendon passes through which structure before inserting on the eye?
options: Trochlea (pulley) on the medial orbital wall
explanation: The superior oblique tendon passes through the trochlea (fibrocartilaginous pulley) on the anteromedial orbital wall, then turns posteriorly to insert on the posterior-lateral aspect of the globe. The trochlea acts as a redirect pulley, changing the direction of the muscle pull.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cherry red spot at the fovea is seen in which condition?
explanation: CRAO: pale, opaque edematous retina (ischemic) with a cherry red spot at the fovea (fovea retains its normal red color from the choroidal circulation beneath, contrasting with the surrounding pale ischemic retina). Also seen in Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick, Gaucher's.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle of the eye is responsible for elevation and intorsion when the eye looks toward the nose (adducted)?
explanation: Superior oblique (CN IV) depresses the adducted eye (when looking toward the nose/adducted, it depresses). It also intorts and abducts the eye. Best tested with patient looking medially (adducted): CN IV palsy shows failure to depress in adduction (subtle vertical diplopia).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The tympanic membrane has how many layers?
options: Three (outer squamous, middle fibrous, inner mucous)
explanation: Tympanic membrane has three layers: (1) outer squamous epithelium (continuous with external canal), (2) middle fibrous layer (2 parts: radial and circular collagen), (3) inner mucosal layer. The pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane) lacks the fibrous middle layer.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ossicles of the middle ear from the tympanic membrane inward are:
explanation: Middle ear ossicles (lateral to medial): Malleus (handle attached to TM) → Incus (bridge ossicle) → Stapes (footplate in oval window). The stapedius muscle attaches to stapes neck and is supplied by CN VII; it dampens sound and is the smallest skeletal muscle.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to which structure?
explanation: The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, equalizing middle ear pressure with atmospheric pressure. Children have a shorter, wider, more horizontal tube, predisposing to otitis media. Tube opens during swallowing/yawning.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Rinne's test differentiates which types of hearing loss?
explanation: Rinne test: air conduction (AC) vs bone conduction (BC) using a tuning fork. Normal/sensorineural: AC>BC (Rinne positive). Conductive: BC>AC (Rinne negative) because the cochlea is intact but sound cannot be conducted through the ossicles or external canal.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Weber's test: in a patient with left-sided sensorineural hearing loss, the sound lateralizes to which ear?
explanation: Weber test: in sensorineural hearing loss, sound lateralizes to the BETTER (unaffected) ear. In conductive hearing loss, sound lateralizes to the WORSE (affected) ear (because the affected ear is less distracted by background noise and perceives bone conduction better).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The mastoid antrum is connected to the middle ear via which structure?
options: Aditus ad antrum (aditus to the mastoid antrum)
explanation: The aditus ad antrum is the communicating channel between the epitympanum (attic/upper middle ear) and the mastoid antrum. Cholesteatoma typically starts in the pars flaccida, invades the epitympanum, and spreads through the aditus into the mastoid.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The facial nerve canal (Fallopian canal) passes through which bone?
explanation: CN VII courses through the facial (Fallopian) canal within the petrous temporal bone: internal acoustic meatus → geniculate ganglion (first genu) → horizontal part → second genu → vertical (mastoid) segment → stylomastoid foramen.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Kiesselbach's area (Little's area) in the nose is the most common site for nosebleeds. It is located:
options: Anteroinferior part of nasal septum (at junction of cartilaginous and bony septum)
explanation: Little's area/Kiesselbach's plexus: anteroinferior nasal septum where multiple arteries anastomose (anterior ethmoidal, superior labial, greater palatine, sphenopalatine). Most epistaxis (90%) is anterior from here. Posterior bleeds come from the sphenopalatine artery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nasolacrimal duct drains into which nasal structure?
explanation: Nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity under the inferior turbinate. The maxillary, anterior ethmoid, and frontal sinuses drain into the middle meatus (via the ostiomeatal complex). Posterior ethmoid and sphenoid drain into superior meatus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Waldeyer's ring is a circular arrangement of which lymphoid tissue?
options: Palatine tonsils, pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids), lingual tonsil, and tubal tonsils
explanation: Waldeyer's ring: subepithelial lymphoid tissue forming a ring at the nasopharynx and oropharynx: pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids, roof of nasopharynx), tubal tonsils (near Eustachian tube), palatine tonsils (most prominent, between pillars), lingual tonsil (base of tongue).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Broca's area (motor speech area), responsible for speech production, is located in which gyrus?
options: Inferior frontal gyrus (opercular and triangular parts, Brodmann areas 44,45)
explanation: Broca's area (areas 44,45) is in the inferior frontal gyrus, usually in the left (dominant) hemisphere. Broca's aphasia: non-fluent speech with intact comprehension. Patient knows what to say but cannot produce fluent words ('frustrating' aphasia).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Wernicke's area is located in which gyrus and is responsible for:
options: Posterior superior temporal gyrus (area 22) — speech comprehension
explanation: Wernicke's area (area 22, posterior superior temporal gyrus) is the speech comprehension center. Wernicke's aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech ('word salad'), poor comprehension. Patients are unaware of their deficit (unlike Broca's).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The primary motor cortex is located in which gyrus?
options: Precentral gyrus (anterior to central sulcus, Brodmann area 4)
explanation: Primary motor cortex (area 4) is in the precentral gyrus. The motor homunculus represents body parts somatotopically: feet/lower limbs on the medial surface (ACA territory); arm and hand on the lateral surface (MCA); face at the bottom lateral surface.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The sensory cortex (somatosensory area) is located in which gyrus?
options: Postcentral gyrus (areas 1,2,3 — receives thalamic input via VPL/VPM)
explanation: Primary somatosensory cortex (areas 1,2,3) is in the postcentral gyrus, posterior to the central sulcus. VPL nucleus of thalamus relays body sensation; VPM relays face sensation. Damage causes contralateral sensory loss, particularly fine touch and proprioception.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which lobe of the brain is responsible for primary visual processing?
options: Occipital lobe (primary visual cortex V1, area 17)
explanation: Primary visual cortex (V1, area 17/striate cortex) is in the occipital lobe, within the calcarine sulcus. It receives input from the LGN. V2,V3,V4,V5 (visual association areas) process color, depth, and motion in the occipital and parietal/temporal lobes.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The prefrontal cortex is involved in which higher functions?
options: Executive function, working memory, personality, and decision-making
explanation: Prefrontal cortex (areas 9,10,11,46,47) mediates executive functions: planning, working memory, decision-making, impulse control, and personality. Damage (as in Phineas Gage's case) causes personality changes, disinhibition, and impaired planning without motor or sensory deficits.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The hippocampus is involved primarily in which type of memory?
options: Declarative (explicit) — episodic and semantic — new memory formation
explanation: Hippocampus (in the medial temporal lobe, part of the limbic system) is critical for forming NEW declarative (explicit) memories: episodic (events) and semantic (facts). HM (Henry Molaison) after bilateral hippocampectomy had profound anterograde amnesia with preserved procedural memory.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Gerstmann's syndrome (finger agnosia, acalculia, agraphia, right-left disorientation) results from a lesion in which lobe?
options: Left parietal lobe (dominant hemisphere, angular gyrus region)
explanation: Gerstmann's syndrome: angular gyrus region of dominant (left) parietal lobe. The four features: finger agnosia, acalculia, agraphia (without alexia), and right-left disorientation. Associated with dominant parietal lobe lesions (stroke, tumor).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) is caused by occlusion of which artery?
options: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery
explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary infarct): PICA or vertebral artery occlusion. Features: ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss (V nucleus), contralateral body pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), vertigo/nausea (vestibular), dysphagia/hoarseness (CN IX,X), ipsilateral Horner's, ipsilateral cerebellar signs.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Medial medullary syndrome (Déjerine syndrome) is caused by occlusion of which artery?
options: Anterior spinal artery or paramedian branches of vertebral artery
explanation: Medial medullary infarct: anterior spinal artery or paramedian vertebral branches. Features: contralateral hemiplegia (pyramid), contralateral loss of position and vibration sense (medial lemniscus), ipsilateral tongue weakness/deviation (CN XII nucleus/fascicles).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Benedikt syndrome (ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral intention tremor/hemiataxia) is caused by a lesion in which part of the midbrain?
options: Tegmentum of midbrain (CN III fascicles + red nucleus)
explanation: Benedikt syndrome: midbrain tegmentum infarct involving CN III fascicles (ipsilateral oculomotor palsy + dilated pupil) and red nucleus/dentatorubrothalamic fibers (contralateral tremor, hemiataxia). Weber syndrome adds cerebral peduncle (contralateral hemiplegia) without ataxia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum) primarily carries which tract?
options: Dentatorubrothalamic tract (efferent — from dentate nucleus to contralateral red nucleus and thalamus)
explanation: Superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP) is primarily EFFERENT: dentate nucleus → crosses in decussation of SCPs at caudal midbrain → contralateral red nucleus and VL thalamus → motor cortex. Lesion causes ipsilateral tremor (decussation not yet occurred).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'locked-in syndrome' is caused by bilateral ventral pontine infarct damaging which tracts?
options: Corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts (with sparing of reticular formation and consciousness)
explanation: Locked-in syndrome: bilateral ventral pons infarct (usually basilar artery thrombosis) destroys corticospinal tracts (quadriplegia) and corticobulbar tracts (anarthria, dysphagia) while SPARING the reticular formation (patient is conscious and can move only eyes vertically/blink).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The cerebellum receives proprioceptive inputs via which peduncle?
options: Inferior cerebellar peduncle (dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts + vestibulocerebellar)
explanation: Inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body) carries mainly AFFERENTS: spinocerebellar tracts (proprioception from spinal cord), olivocerebellar fibers (from inferior olive), and vestibulocerebellar fibers. Middle peduncle carries pontocerebellar (cortical signals); superior carries efferents.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cerebellar hemispheres (neocerebellum) are primarily connected to which part of the cerebral cortex?
options: Motor and premotor cortex via dentatorubrothalamic loop
explanation: Lateral cerebellar hemispheres (pontocerebellum/neocerebellum) coordinate skilled voluntary movement via the dentatorubrothalamic loop: dentate nucleus → SCP → contralateral red nucleus/VL thalamus → motor cortex. Lesions cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection of spinal cord) produces which pattern of deficits?
options: Bilateral motor loss below the level
Ipsilateral motor + ipsilateral fine touch/vibration loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion
Ipsilateral motor loss and contralateral fine touch loss
explanation: Brown-Séquard: hemisection causes: (1) ipsilateral UMN signs (corticospinal tract, which crosses in medulla), (2) ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, proprioception (dorsal columns, which cross in medulla), (3) contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic, which crosses in cord 1–2 levels above entry).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The dorsal columns (posterior funiculus) carry which sensory modalities?
options: Fine touch, vibration, proprioception, and stereognosis
explanation: Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis — lower limb, and fasciculus cuneatus — upper limb): fine discriminative touch, vibration, conscious proprioception, and 2-point discrimination. These fibers ascend ipsilaterally and cross at the medullary decussation (sensory decussation).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The spinothalamic tract carries which sensory modalities and crosses where?
options: Pain, temperature, and crude touch; crosses in the spinal cord (within 1–2 segments of entry)
explanation: Anterior and lateral spinothalamic tracts carry pain, temperature (lateral), and crude touch (anterior). The first-order neurons synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order neurons cross in the anterior white commissure of the spinal cord (within 1–2 segments) and ascend to the VPL of the thalamus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis) primarily damages which spinal cord structure?
explanation: Tabes dorsalis: chronic syphilitic degeneration of dorsal roots and dorsal columns, causing loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch. Features: lightning pains, ataxia, Argyll Robertson pupils, absent deep tendon reflexes, positive Romberg sign.

subject: Anatomy
stem: In syringomyelia, the central cavity of the spinal cord first damages which fibers, producing which deficit?
options: Dorsal column fibers — loss of vibration
Corticospinal fibers — upper motor neuron signs
Anterior white commissure fibers — bilateral suspended loss of pain and temperature
explanation: Syringomyelia: the syrinx (fluid-filled cavity) expands centrally, first damaging the crossing pain/temperature fibers in the anterior white commissure (cape or shawl distribution bilateral suspended sensory loss for pain/temperature with preserved touch — dissociated sensory loss). Later, it affects anterior horn and corticospinal tracts.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The circle of Willis is formed by branches of which two major arteries?
explanation: Circle of Willis: ACA + anterior communicating artery (from ICA) + ICA + posterior communicating artery (connecting ICA to PCA) + PCA (from basilar artery, formed by two vertebral arteries). The circle equalizes blood pressure and provides collateral flow.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The most common site for berry (saccular) aneurysm in the circle of Willis is:
options: Junction of ACA and anterior communicating artery (ACoA)
explanation: Most common site: ACA/ACoA junction (~30–40%). Second: ICA/PCoA junction (~30%). Third: MCA bifurcation (~20%). Posterior circulation aneurysms occur at the basilar tip (10%). Rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage (sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies which surface of the brain?
options: Medial surface of frontal and parietal lobes + anterior corpus callosum
explanation: ACA supplies the medial surface of frontal and parietal lobes (motor and sensory homunculus for the leg and foot), anterior corpus callosum, and orbital frontal cortex. ACA territory infarction causes contralateral leg weakness (leg > arm in UMN pattern).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) supplies which area, and its occlusion causes which syndrome?
options: Lateral surface of frontal, parietal, temporal lobes — contralateral hemiplegia (arm/face > leg), hemianesthesia, homonymous hemianopia, aphasia (dominant)
explanation: MCA (largest branch of ICA) supplies the lateral cerebral surface: primary motor and sensory cortices (arm/face representation), Broca's/Wernicke's areas (dominant), and optic radiation. Occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia (arm/face > leg), hemisensory loss, hemianopia, and aphasia (if dominant side).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is produced by which structure and at what rate?
options: Choroid plexus (primarily in lateral ventricles) at ~500 mL/day; total volume ~150 mL
explanation: CSF is produced by the choroid plexus (~70% in lateral ventricles; remainder in 3rd and 4th ventricles) at ~20 mL/hour (500 mL/day). Total CSF volume is ~150 mL (50 mL ventricular, 100 mL subarachnoid space). It is absorbed by arachnoid granulations (Pacchionian bodies) into the dural venous sinuses.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which week of gestation does the neural tube close, and what are the consequences of failure?
options: Week 4 (days 22–28) — failure causes neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida)
explanation: Neural tube closure: days 22–28 (week 4). Anterior neuropore closes day 25 (failure → anencephaly); posterior neuropore closes day 28 (failure → spina bifida). Folic acid supplementation (400 mcg preconception) reduces NTD risk by 70%.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Neural crest cells are derived from which germ layer and contribute to which structures?
options: Neuroectoderm; melanocytes, peripheral ganglia, adrenal medulla, Schwann cells, craniofacial bones, conotruncal septum
explanation: Neural crest cells (neuroectoderm) are multipotent migratory cells. They form: melanocytes, DRG and autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, Schwann and glial cells, craniofacial cartilage and bone, conotruncal septum (cardiac outflow), thyroid C-cells, and cells of Meissner's and Auerbach's plexuses.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The dorsal pancreatic bud forms which parts of the pancreas?
options: Tail, body, and part of the head (superior head and uncinate process from ventral bud)
explanation: Pancreatic development: dorsal bud (from dorsal duodenum) forms the body, tail, and part of the head. Ventral bud (with CBD, rotates behind dorsal bud) forms the head and uncinate process. Failure of fusion causes pancreas divisum (most common pancreatic anomaly).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which branchial (pharyngeal) arch gives rise to the mandible and Meckel's cartilage?
explanation: 1st branchial arch (trigeminal V3): Meckel's cartilage → mandible, malleus, incus; muscles: mastication, tensor tympani, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor veli palatini. 2nd arch (Reichert's — CN VII): stapes, styloid, stylohyoid ligament; muscles: facial expression, stapedius, posterior digastric.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Branchial cleft cysts in adults are most commonly derived from which branchial cleft?
explanation: Second branchial cleft cysts (~95% of all branchial cleft anomalies): appear along the anterior border of SCM at the junction of upper and middle thirds. They present as fluctuant lateral neck swellings, may have a sinus tract opening to the tonsillar fossa internally.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ductus arteriosus normally closes within how many hours after birth, and what mediates its closure?
options: 10–15 hours; mediated by increased PO2 causing smooth muscle contraction
explanation: Functional closure of DA: within 10–15 hours of birth, triggered by increased arterial PO2 (causes vasoconstriction of ductal smooth muscle) and decreased prostaglandin E2. Anatomical closure (ligamentum arteriosum) takes 2–3 weeks. Indomethacin (PG inhibitor) closes a PDA; PGE1 keeps it open.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The foramen ovale closes at birth due to which mechanism?
options: Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance reduces right atrial pressure; flap is pushed closed by higher left atrial pressure
explanation: At birth, lung expansion reduces pulmonary vascular resistance → LA pressure rises above RA pressure → septum primum is pushed against septum secundum, closing the foramen ovale. Anatomical (permanent) closure occurs in ~75% of people; in 25% it remains patent (PFO) without significant shunting.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Abnormal rotation of the midgut loop (normal = 270° counterclockwise) leads to which condition?
explanation: Normal midgut (supplied by SMA) undergoes 270° counterclockwise rotation around the SMA during herniation and return to the abdomen (weeks 6–10). Malrotation (incomplete rotation) leaves the cecum high, with Ladd's bands causing duodenal obstruction, and predisposes to midgut volvulus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of which cells to migrate?
options: Neural crest cells (failure to migrate into the distal colon, absent myenteric/submucosal ganglia)
explanation: Hirschsprung's disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): neural crest cells fail to migrate caudally into the distal bowel, leaving it aganglionic (absent Meissner's and Auerbach's plexuses). The aganglionic segment cannot relax, causing functional obstruction proximal to it.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The urachus is the embryological remnant of which structure and, if patent, results in:
options: Allantois; urachal fistula draining urine through umbilicus
explanation: Urachus (allantois remnant): normally obliterates to form the median umbilical ligament. If patent: urachal fistula (urine at umbilicus), urachal cyst (midline), or urachal sinus. Patent urachus presents with umbilical wetness in a neonate.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure gives rise to the kidney (metanephros) and when?
options: Metanephros from ureteric bud + metanephric mesenchyme at 5th week
explanation: Kidney development: three sets of excretory organs. Pronephros (week 4): vestigial, disappears. Mesonephros: temporary, contributes to gonadal duct system. Metanephros (permanent kidney): from ureteric bud (gives collecting system, ureter, renal pelvis) + metanephric mesenchyme (gives nephrons). Starts week 5.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Posterior urethral valves are caused by anomalous development of which embryological structure?
options: Wolffian (mesonephric) duct — abnormal persistence of mucosal folds
explanation: Posterior urethral valves (PUV): abnormal fusion of the Wolffian duct remnants forming obstructing folds in the posterior urethra. Most common cause of severe obstructive uropathy in male infants. Diagnosed antenatally (bilateral hydronephrosis, dilated bladder, oligohydramnios).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterosuperior deviation of which embryological structure?
explanation: Anterosuperior deviation of the conotruncal/outlet septum causes TOF: (1) large perimembranous VSD, (2) overriding aorta, (3) RVOT obstruction (pulmonary stenosis — subvalvar/infundibular), (4) RVH (compensatory). Associated with DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion).

subject: Anatomy
stem: What is the fate of the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts in females?
options: Upper parts → fallopian tubes; lower parts fuse → uterus, cervix, upper vagina
explanation: In females (no testosterone, no AMH): Müllerian ducts persist and develop into: lateral portions → fallopian tubes; caudal portions fuse → uterus, cervix, upper 2/3 of vagina. In males: AMH (from Sertoli cells) causes regression.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which week does sex determination occur and what determines male phenotype?
options: Week 7; SRY gene on Y chromosome (testis-determining factor) activates Sertoli cells and Leydig cells
explanation: Gonadal sex determination occurs at week 7 when the SRY gene (on Y chromosome) activates Sertoli cells (secrete AMH to regress Müllerian ducts) and Leydig cells (secrete testosterone). Testosterone → Wolffian duct development + DHT (5α-reductase) → external male genitalia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The diaphragm is formed by fusion of which four structures?
options: Septum transversum, pleuroperitoneal membranes, dorsal mesentery of esophagus, body wall muscular ingrowth
Septum transversum and pleuropericardial membranes only
Pleuroperitoneal membranes and body wall only
explanation: Diaphragm = (1) septum transversum (central tendon), (2) pleuroperitoneal membranes (close the pleuroperitoneal canals — left side closes later, hence more left CDH), (3) dorsal mesentery of esophagus (crura), (4) body wall muscular ingrowth (peripheral muscular part). Failure of left pleuroperitoneal membrane closure → left CDH (Bochdalek hernia).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Situs inversus totalis is caused by defects in which developmental mechanism?
options: Left-right patterning (cilia-driven Nodal signaling) — normally leftward ciliary flow establishes left-right asymmetry
explanation: Left-right asymmetry is established in the node at gastrulation via leftward cilia-driven flow of Nodal morphogen, activating Nodal/Lefty/Pitx2 pathways on the left side. Kartagener's syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) — immotile cilia — randomizes L-R asymmetry, giving 50% situs inversus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The gubernaculum testis guides testicular descent to which structure in the fetus?
explanation: Gubernaculum (mesodermal band) connects the testis to the developing scrotum. During testicular descent, the gubernaculum shortens/expands, guiding the testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum (normally by 28–36 weeks). Androgen-insensitivity prevents this process.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Congenital hydrocele results from failure of obliteration of which structure?
explanation: Processus vaginalis: a peritoneal evagination that follows the gubernaculum through the inguinal canal and normally obliterates after testicular descent. Failure of obliteration: patent processus vaginalis → communicating hydrocele (fluid from peritoneal cavity) or indirect inguinal hernia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Esophageal atresia most commonly occurs at which level and is associated with which anomaly?
options: Upper thoracic, associated with TE fistula (most common type: proximal EA + distal TEF)
explanation: Most common EA type (85%): proximal esophageal atresia (blind-ending pouch) + distal tracheoesophageal fistula (air in stomach on X-ray, risk of aspiration). Associated with VACTERL (Vertebral, Anorectal, Cardiac, TE fistula, Esophageal atresia, Renal, Limb anomalies) and Down syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Duodenal atresia on AXR shows 'double bubble sign'. The two bubbles represent:
options: Stomach and proximal duodenum (stomach bubble + dilated duodenum)
explanation: Double bubble sign: one bubble = stomach, one bubble = distended proximal duodenum (both air-filled, separated by the pylorus). Duodenal atresia results from failure of recanalization of the solid cord stage of the duodenum (weeks 6–8). Associated with Down syndrome (30%) and annular pancreas.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which embryological structure, when persistent, forms the median umbilical ligament?
explanation: Median umbilical ligament = remnant of urachus (allantois). Medial umbilical ligaments (paired) = remnants of umbilical arteries. Lateral umbilical ligaments = inferior epigastric arteries. Round ligament of liver (ligamentum teres) = obliterated umbilical vein.

subject: Anatomy
stem: A baby born with ambiguous genitalia, 46XX karyotype, and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone has which condition?
explanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency): impaired cortisol and aldosterone synthesis → ACTH excess → androgen overproduction. 46XX female virilized (ambiguous genitalia), salt-wasting crisis in neonatal period, elevated 17-OHP (accumulates above the block), low sodium, high potassium.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The tracheoesophageal (TE) septum normally divides the foregut into trachea and esophagus during which week?
explanation: The laryngotracheal groove forms in the ventral wall of the foregut in week 4, and the tracheoesophageal septum progressively divides the foregut into the trachea (ventral) and esophagus (dorsal) by week 4–5. Incomplete septum formation causes TE fistula.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines which structures?
options: Urinary tract: renal pelvis, ureters, urinary bladder, and proximal urethra
explanation: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) lines the renal pelvis, ureters, urinary bladder, and proximal urethra. It is stratified, can stretch (relaxed: dome-shaped umbrella cells with scalloped apical membranes; distended: squamous-like), and is impermeable to urine due to uroplakins.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Type II pneumocytes are responsible for which function?
options: Gas exchange across the alveolar wall
explanation: Type II pneumocytes (granular pneumocytes, ~5% of alveolar cells): produce surfactant (DPPC/dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine, stored in lamellar bodies), proliferate and regenerate Type I pneumocytes after injury. Type I pneumocytes (~95%) are thin squamous cells for gas exchange.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Goblet cells are found in which epithelial locations and secrete which substance?
explanation: Goblet cells are unicellular mucous glands interspersed in simple columnar (intestine) and pseudostratified columnar ciliated (respiratory) epithelium. They secrete mucin glycoproteins; distended apical cytoplasm with mucin gives them the goblet shape.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Parietal (oxyntic) cells of the stomach secrete which substances?
options: HCl (via H+/K+ ATPase) and intrinsic factor
explanation: Parietal cells (in fundus/body): secrete HCl (proton pump H+/K+-ATPase inhibited by PPIs) and intrinsic factor (essential for vitamin B12 absorption in ileum). Their destruction in autoimmune gastritis causes achlorhydria and pernicious anemia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Kupffer cells of the liver are derived from which cell lineage?
explanation: Kupffer cells are resident liver macrophages located in the hepatic sinusoids (Disse space). They are derived from bone marrow monocytes. They phagocytose pathogens, aged red blood cells, cellular debris, and are involved in hepatic immune responses and liver injury.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Hepatic stellate cells (Ito cells) in the space of Disse normally store which vitamin?
explanation: Ito cells (perisinusoidal stellate cells) normally store 80% of the body's retinoids (Vitamin A) as fat droplets. When activated (by TGF-β, alcohol, viral injury), they transdifferentiate into myofibroblasts and produce collagen → hepatic fibrosis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex secretes which hormone?
explanation: Adrenal cortex zones (from capsule inward): GFR — Glomerulosa (aldosterone), Fasciculata (cortisol/glucocorticoids), Reticularis (androgens/DHEA). Mnemonic: 'The deeper you go, the sweeter it gets' (salt, sugar, sex). Medulla secretes catecholamines.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Juxtaglomerular cells (granular cells) are located in which part of the nephron?
explanation: Juxtaglomerular apparatus: JG cells (granular cells) in the wall of the afferent arteriole secrete renin. Macula densa cells (modified DCT cells) sense tubular sodium. Extraglomerular mesangial cells (Goormaghtigh cells) connect them. Together they regulate GFR and blood pressure.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Mesangial cells of the glomerulus have which functions?
options: Structural support of glomerulus, phagocytosis of immune deposits, and regulation of GFR by contractility
explanation: Mesangial cells (modified smooth muscle cells) reside between glomerular capillaries. Functions: structural support of glomerular tuft, phagocytosis of immune complexes, contraction (reducing GFR, e.g., in angiotensin II effect), and secretion of cytokines. Expanded in IgA nephropathy.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Sertoli cells of the testis perform all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Secretion of androgen-binding protein (ABP) and inhibin
explanation: Sertoli cells: form blood-testis barrier (tight junctions), secrete ABP (concentrates testosterone in seminiferous tubule), inhibin (negative feedback on FSH), and AMH (in fetal development). Testosterone is secreted by Leydig cells (interstitial cells), not Sertoli cells.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Endocrine cells of the islets of Langerhans: which cell type is most abundant?
explanation: Islet cell distribution: beta cells (70–75%, central — insulin), alpha cells (15–20%, peripheral — glucagon), delta cells (5–10%, somatostatin), F/PP cells (<5%, pancreatic polypeptide). Beta cell destruction → Type 1 DM; dysfunction + resistance → Type 2 DM.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Intercalated discs between cardiac myocytes serve which function?
options: Mechanical coupling (desmosomes/fascia adherens) and electrical coupling (gap junctions)
explanation: Intercalated discs: transverse and lateral portions contain: desmosomes (mechanical coupling, resist shear forces) + fascia adherens (attach actin to cell membrane) + gap junctions (nexus — allow rapid spread of action potentials). This makes the heart a functional syncytium.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Bone is remodeled by which two cell types working in opposition?
explanation: Osteoblasts (from mesenchymal stem cells): synthesize osteoid (type I collagen matrix), regulate mineralization, and become osteocytes when surrounded by matrix. Osteoclasts (from monocyte-macrophage lineage): resorb bone via acid and proteases in Howship's lacunae. Regulated by RANK-RANKL-OPG axis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The sinoatrial (SA) node cells have which histological feature?
options: Small, pale cells with sparse myofibrils, high spontaneous automaticity
explanation: SA node cells (in the right atrium, crista terminalis) are small, pale, irregular cells with sparse myofibrils and many gap junctions. They have the highest automaticity (60–100/min) due to a 'funny current' (If) of sodium/potassium and slow calcium-mediated action potentials.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Hyaline cartilage is characterized by which features on light microscopy?
options: Glassy, translucent matrix with collagen fibers not visible by LM; chondrocytes in lacunae
explanation: Hyaline cartilage: homogeneous glassy matrix (type II collagen, proteoglycans, water); chondrocytes in lacunae; avascular. Found on articular surfaces, costal cartilage, respiratory tract, and fetal skeleton. Type II collagen fibers are not visible by LM (similar refractive index to matrix — unlike fibrocartilage/elastic cartilage).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The substantia nigra neurons are dopaminergic and project where? Their degeneration causes which disease?
options: To striatum (caudate + putamen) via nigrostriatal pathway; degeneration causes Parkinson's disease
To cerebral cortex; causing Alzheimer's disease
explanation: Substantia nigra pars compacta neurons project to the striatum (nigrostriatal pathway) releasing dopamine, modulating movement. Degeneration of these neurons (Lewy bodies — alpha-synuclein inclusions) causes Parkinson's disease: bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, postural instability.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Mast cells are derived from which precursor and are found predominantly in which tissue?
options: Bone marrow mast cell precursors; found in connective tissue near blood vessels and epithelia
Plasma cells; found in bone marrow
explanation: Mast cells: derived from bone marrow progenitors (not circulating basophils, though similar), reside in connective tissue (especially near vessels and beneath epithelium of skin/mucosa). They release histamine, heparin, tryptase, and leukotrienes — mediators of Type I hypersensitivity.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The atlas (C1) is unique among cervical vertebrae because it lacks which structure?
explanation: The atlas (C1) has no body (it was transferred to C2 to form the dens/odontoid process) and no spinous process (only posterior tubercle). It consists of anterior and posterior arches and two lateral masses with superior articular facets for the occipital condyles.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The dens (odontoid process) is derived embryologically from the body of which vertebra?
explanation: The dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2) is derived from the body of the atlas (C1), which migrates and fuses with C2 during development. It articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas and is held by the transverse ligament of the atlas.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of which vertebra, and the mechanism is:
explanation: Jefferson fracture: C1 (atlas) burst fracture from axial compression (e.g., diving, top of head impact). The lateral masses are driven apart, often rupturing the transverse ligament. On open-mouth X-ray, lateral masses overhang the axis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Hangman's fracture is a traumatic spondylolisthesis of which vertebra?
explanation: Hangman's fracture: traumatic C2 bilateral pars interarticularis (pedicle) fracture + C2/C3 listhesis, from hyperextension + distraction (judicial hanging) or hyperextension compression (modern road traffic accidents). Paradoxically, often neurologically intact as the spinal canal expands.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The most common site for intervertebral disc herniation in the lumbar spine is:
explanation: L4-L5 and L5-S1 are the most common levels for lumbar disc herniation (90%). L4-L5 herniation compresses L5 root (foot drop, loss of great toe extension). L5-S1 herniation compresses S1 root (weak plantar flexion, reduced ankle reflex, lateral foot numbness).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lumbar spinal cord ends (conus medullaris) at which vertebral level in adults?
options: L1 (usually between L1 and L2 disc)
explanation: The conus medullaris (tapered end of spinal cord) ends at L1 in adults (can be up to L2; in neonates, it is lower at L3). Below this is the cauda equina (bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots in the thecal sac). LP is safely performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which ligament of the spine is most commonly involved in spinal stenosis causing ossification?
explanation: Ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and buckling (it buckles during extension) is the primary cause of lumbar spinal stenosis, contributing to compression of the cauda equina. Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) can cause cervical myelopathy.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on which surface of the vertebral body?
options: Anterior surface, in front of vertebral body
Posterior surface of vertebral body, inside spinal canal
explanation: Posterior longitudinal ligament runs on the posterior (inner) surface of vertebral bodies inside the spinal canal, attached to the intervertebral discs. It is narrower at the disc levels, which is why disc herniations tend to go posterolaterally (around the ligament) rather than directly posteriorly.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Lumbar puncture is performed at which interspace and what structure is accessed?
options: L3-L4 or L4-L5; subarachnoid space (below conus medullaris)
explanation: Lumbar puncture at L3-L4 or L4-L5 (Jacoby's line connects iliac crests at L4 level). Structures pierced from skin inward: skin → subcutaneous fat → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura mater → arachnoid mater → subarachnoid space (CSF).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The zygapophyseal (facet) joints of the cervical spine are oriented in which plane?
options: Approximately 45° to the horizontal plane — allows flexion, extension, and lateral flexion
explanation: Cervical facet joints are oriented at ~45° to horizontal, allowing significant flexion/extension, lateral flexion, and rotation. Lumbar facets are in the sagittal plane, limiting rotation but allowing flexion/extension. Thoracic facets in coronal plane limit flexion but allow rotation.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The perineum is divided into anterior (urogenital) and posterior (anal) triangles by which structure?
options: Transverse perineal line connecting ischial tuberosities
explanation: The perineum is divided by a transverse line connecting the anterior aspects of the ischial tuberosities. Anterior = urogenital triangle (contains external genitalia and urogenital openings). Posterior = anal triangle (contains anus, external anal sphincter, ischioanal/ischiorectal fossae).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The pudendal nerve (S2,3,4) innervates which structures?
options: All muscles of the pelvic floor
External urethral sphincter, external anal sphincter, perineal muscles, and skin of perineum
explanation: Pudendal nerve (S2,S3,S4 — 'the nerve that saves the grace'): supplies external urethral sphincter, external anal sphincter, bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, superficial and deep perineal muscles, and perineal skin. Blocked for pudendal nerve block during labor (needle at ischial spine).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle has the function of 'puborectalis' — maintaining the anorectal angle?
explanation: Puborectalis (part of levator ani, supplied by direct branches from S3,4 and inferior rectal nerve) forms a sling around the anorectal junction, maintaining the anorectal angle (~90°) that is critical for fecal continence. Relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens the angle (to ~135°).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa contains which structures?
options: Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels only
Fat, inferior rectal nerve and vessels, pudendal nerve (Alcock's canal on lateral wall)
explanation: Ischioanal fossa: wedge-shaped fat-filled space on each side of anal canal. Contents: fat (allows rectal distension during defecation), inferior rectal nerve and vessels (from pudendal), and the pudendal nerve + internal pudendal vessels in Alcock's canal on the lateral wall (obturator internus fascia).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The female pelvic floor muscles (levator ani) are supplied by which nerve?
options: Direct branches from S3,S4 from the sacral plexus (on pelvic surface) + inferior rectal/perineal branch of pudendal (on perineal surface)
explanation: Levator ani has dual innervation: upper (pelvic/endopelvic) surface from direct branches of S3,S4 nerve roots (perineal branches of sacral plexus); lower (perineal) surface from perineal branch of pudendal nerve. This dual supply is clinically relevant in childbirth-related pelvic floor injuries.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The internal pudendal artery enters the perineum through which foramen?
explanation: Internal pudendal artery (branch of internal iliac/anterior division): exits pelvis through greater sciatic foramen below piriformis → hooks around ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament → enters perineum through lesser sciatic foramen. Travels in Alcock's canal → divides into inferior rectal, perineal, and dorsal penile/clitoral arteries.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch) contains which muscle?
options: Deep transverse perineal muscle and sphincter urethrae
explanation: Deep perineal pouch (space deep to perineal membrane): contains deep transverse perineal muscle, external urethral sphincter (urethrovaginal sphincter in females), pudendal nerve, internal pudendal vessels, and (in males) bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Rupture of the male urethra at the bulbous urethra leads to extravasation of urine into which space?
options: Superficial perineal pouch → Colles' fascia → Buck's fascia → Scarpa's fascia
explanation: Bulbous urethral rupture (below urogenital diaphragm): urine extravasates into the superficial perineal pouch, then deep to Colles' fascia (superficial perineal fascia). It spreads to penis (deep to Buck's fascia), scrotum, and anterior abdominal wall deep to Scarpa's fascia — but NOT into the thigh (Colles' attaches to fascia lata) or ischioanal fossa.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The broad ligament of the uterus contains which structures?
options: Round ligament of uterus, uterine tube, ovarian ligament, parametrium
explanation: Broad ligament: a double peritoneal fold containing uterine tube (in mesosalpinx), round ligament of uterus, ovarian ligament, uterine vessels, nerves, lymphatics, and areolar tissue (parametrium). The ureter runs in the base (parametrium) and is at risk during hysterectomy when ligating the uterine artery ('water under the bridge').

subject: Anatomy
stem: The Allen test before radial artery harvest (for coronary bypass) evaluates which finding?
options: Adequate ulnar collateral circulation to the hand
explanation: Modified Allen test: both arteries compressed, patient exsanguinates hand, one artery released — hand should pink up in <7 sec (normal). Before radial artery harvest for CABG, Allen test confirms adequate ulnar circulation to prevent hand ischemia post-harvest.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Claw hand is most pronounced in which nerve injury?
explanation: Paradox of ulnar nerve: claw is MORE pronounced in low (wrist) ulnar lesion than high (elbow) lesion. High lesion also paralyses FDP to ring/little (denervated = more flaccid, less able to claw). Low lesion leaves FDP intact, pulling the fingers into flexion with unopposed intrinsics — more visible 'clawing' of ring and little.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Rotator interval is the triangular space between which two muscles?
explanation: Rotator interval: triangular gap between the superior edge of subscapularis and anterior edge of supraspinatus. It contains the biceps long head tendon, coracohumeral ligament, and glenohumeral ligament. Thickening causes restricted external rotation (seen in frozen shoulder).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Carpal tunnel syndrome is associated with which clinical conditions?
options: Hypothyroidism, pregnancy, acromegaly, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and obesity
explanation: CTS predisposing factors: pregnancy (fluid retention), hypothyroidism (myxoedema), acromegaly (GH excess causing tissue hypertrophy), diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis (synovial proliferation in carpal tunnel), obesity, and renal failure (dialysis-related amyloid deposition).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Phalen's test (wrist flexion test) is positive in which condition?
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome (tingling in median nerve distribution after 60 sec of wrist flexion)
explanation: Phalen's test: sustained wrist flexion (60 seconds) increases pressure in carpal tunnel, producing median nerve symptoms (tingling, numbness in thumb/index/middle fingers). Sensitivity 68%, specificity 73%. Tinel's test (percussion over carpal tunnel) is less sensitive but specific.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The pronator quadratus muscle at the wrist is the deepest muscle in the forearm. It is supplied by:
explanation: Pronator quadratus (proximal phalanx of ulna to distal radius, deepest forearm muscle): supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), branch of median nerve. AIN injury (pronator syndrome, supracondylar fracture) paralyses FPL, FDP of index/middle, and pronator quadratus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The brachial artery is best palpated where in the antecubital fossa?
explanation: Brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon in the antecubital fossa (relationships from lateral: Biceps Tendon, Brachial Artery, Median Nerve — TAN from lateral to medial). It is the site for blood pressure measurement and brachial artery cannulation.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve entrapment at elbow) most commonly causes:
options: Ring and little finger clawing, hypothenar wasting, and medial forearm paresthesia
explanation: Cubital tunnel syndrome: ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel (behind medial epicondyle). Causes: medial 1.5 finger paresthesia (ring and little), intrinsic hand wasting (hypothenar + interossei), clawing of ring and little fingers, and weakness of grip. FCU and medial FDP may also be affected.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which wrist flexor inserts into the pisiform bone?
explanation: FCU (ulnar nerve, C7,C8) inserts primarily into the pisiform (sesamoid bone within the FCU tendon), then indirectly to the hamate (pisohamate ligament) and 5th metacarpal (pisometacarpal ligament). FCR inserts into the base of 2nd (and 3rd) metacarpal.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscles form the 'anatomical snuff box' boundaries?
options: EPL and EPB posterior; APL and EPB anterior; scaphoid and radial styloid floor
FCR and ECR; radial artery crosses
explanation: Anatomical snuff box: posterior (ulnar) border = EPL (extensor pollicis longus); anterior (radial) border = EPB (extensor pollicis brevis) and APL (abductor pollicis longus); floor = scaphoid and trapezium (and radial artery crossing). Tenderness here after FOOSH suggests scaphoid fracture.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle prevents 'toe-off' failure and is the last muscle to leave the ground during walking?
explanation: Flexor hallucis longus (FHL, deep posterior compartment, tibial nerve) is the last muscle to push off the ground during gait (hallux push-off). It is also important for dancers (FHL tendinopathy is common in ballet). It inserts on the distal phalanx of the great toe.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The popliteal fossa contains which structures from superficial to deep?
options: Common peroneal nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery (deepest) — mnemonic: TAN (Tibial, Artery, Nerve) wrong — TNA from lateral to medial at thigh; in fossa = NAVEL equivalent
explanation: Popliteal fossa (from superficial to deep): tibial nerve (most superficial/posterior), common peroneal nerve (lateral), popliteal vein (intermediate), popliteal artery (deepest, against bone). The popliteal artery is closest to the posterior capsule of the knee joint and is at risk in posterior knee dislocation.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The great saphenous vein passes anterior to which malleolus?
explanation: Great saphenous vein passes 1 cm anterior to the medial malleolus (reliable landmark for cutdown/cannulation), then ascends medially. Small saphenous vein passes posterior to lateral malleolus (between Achilles tendon and lateral malleolus) and drains into popliteal vein.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle is tested by asking the patient to stand on tiptoe (rise on heels = testing anterior compartment)?
explanation: Standing on tiptoe (plantarflexion) tests gastrocnemius and soleus (triceps surae) via the Achilles tendon. Standing on heels (dorsiflexion) tests the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL). Single-leg heel rise test (Thompson single-leg stance) is positive if the patient cannot rise on one leg (indicates Achilles pathology or S1 root lesion).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The plantaris muscle is clinically important because:
options: It can be confused with Achilles tendon rupture (plantaris rupture causes medial calf pain) and is used as a tendon graft
It is the most powerful muscle in the leg
It is often absent and causes foot drop
explanation: Plantaris (vestigial muscle with a long thin tendon): a minor plantarflexor. Its rupture (sudden medial calf pain, 'tennis leg' when in the medial head of gastrocnemius) can mimic Achilles rupture. The plantaris tendon is absent in 10% and is used as a small tendon graft source.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The internal mammary (internal thoracic) artery arises from which vessel and is used clinically for:
options: Subclavian artery — used as coronary artery bypass graft (LIMA most commonly)
Axillary artery — used for breast reconstruction
Thyrocervical trunk — used as free flap
explanation: Internal thoracic artery (ITA): branch of first part of subclavian artery. Left ITA (LIMA) is the graft of choice for left anterior descending (LAD) coronary bypass (superior long-term patency vs. saphenous vein). It descends 1 cm lateral to the sternal edge, bifurcating at the 6th costal cartilage into superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which intercostal structures are at risk during pleural aspiration (thoracentesis)?
options: Intercostal nerve, artery, and vein at the upper border of the rib
Intercostal neurovascular bundle at the lower border of the rib (VAN = vein, artery, nerve from above downward)
explanation: Intercostal VAN (Vein, Artery, Nerve — from top to bottom) runs in the costal groove at the inferior margin of each rib. Thoracentesis needle should be inserted just ABOVE the upper border of the lower rib (to avoid the neurovascular bundle at the lower border of the upper rib).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The right vagus nerve passes anterior to the subclavian artery, giving off the right recurrent laryngeal nerve. The left vagus at which level gives off the left RLN?
options: At the level of the carotid bifurcation
At the aortic arch (hooks under the aortic arch at the ligamentum arteriosum)
explanation: Left RLN: branches from left vagus at the aortic arch level, hooking under the arch at the ligamentum arteriosum, then ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove to reach the larynx. Right RLN: branches from right vagus at the right subclavian artery level. Left RLN has a longer intrathoracic course and is vulnerable to mediastinal/aortic pathology.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The superior vena cava (SVC) is formed by union of which two veins?
options: Right brachiocephalic and right internal jugular
explanation: SVC = right + left brachiocephalic veins join behind the right 1st costal cartilage to form the SVC. SVC descends to open into the right atrium at T4 level. The azygos vein drains into the SVC at its arch. SVC syndrome (compression by tumor, nodes) causes facial swelling and dilated chest wall veins.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Pulmonary embolism most commonly lodges at which site?
options: Bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk (saddle embolus for massive PE) or lobar/segmental branches
explanation: Large PE: saddle embolus at main pulmonary trunk bifurcation → acute right heart strain, cardiovascular collapse. More commonly: smaller emboli in lobar and segmental pulmonary arteries (lower lobes more affected due to higher blood flow). Pleuritic chest pain + breathlessness + clinical risk factors (Virchow's triad).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure marks the posterior boundary of the aortic arch?
options: Trachea at T4, left recurrent laryngeal nerve
explanation: Aortic arch relations: superiorly — brachiocephalic, LCCA, LSCA (three branches); posteriorly — trachea/carina at T4, left RLN, esophagus, thoracic duct; anteriorly — sternum, thymus remnant, left phrenic nerve; inferiorly — bifurcation of pulmonary trunk, ligamentum arteriosum, left main bronchus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord?
explanation: Anterior spinal artery (single, midline): supplies anterior 2/3 of spinal cord (anterior horn, spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts). Forms from union of branches from each vertebral artery, supplemented by anterior radicular arteries (most important: artery of Adamkiewicz, T9-T12 level on the left). Posterior 1/3 supplied by paired posterior spinal arteries.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Anterior cord syndrome (flexion-compression injury) spares which sensory modality?
explanation: Anterior cord syndrome: damage to anterior 2/3 of cord (anterior spinal artery territory). Bilateral motor loss (corticospinal), bilateral pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic). Dorsal columns SPARED: vibration, proprioception, and fine touch are preserved.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Central cord syndrome (most common cervical injury in elderly) produces which pattern?
options: Greater motor loss in lower limbs
Greater motor loss in upper limbs than lower limbs ('burning hands' syndrome)
Isolated sensory loss below the level
explanation: Central cord syndrome: injury to the central gray matter and adjacent white matter of cervical cord. Upper limbs (represented more centrally in corticospinal/spinothalamic tracts) are weaker than lower limbs. Also: bladder dysfunction and variable sensory loss. Most common in hyperextension injuries in elderly patients with spondylosis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The dorsal root ganglia (DRG) contain which type of neurons?
explanation: DRG contain pseudounipolar (unipolar) sensory neurons with a T-shaped single process that divides into a peripheral branch (to the body) and a central branch (to the spinal cord dorsal horn). The cell bodies are in the DRG outside the spinal cord; they transmit sensory information (somatic afferents).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which type of collagen is most abundant in the body?
options: Type I collagen (skin, bone, tendon, cornea)
explanation: Type I collagen (~90% of total body collagen): found in skin, bone, tendon, ligaments, cornea, and organ capsules. Strongest tensile strength. Defective in osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) types I–IV (COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations). Type II = hyaline and elastic cartilage. Type III = reticular fibers of liver, spleen, lymph nodes. Type IV = basement membrane.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Elastic cartilage (in the ear, epiglottis, Eustachian tube) differs from hyaline cartilage by:
options: Presence of elastic fibers (elastin) visible on staining (orcein or Verhoeff)
Presence of a dense perichondrium but no lacunae
explanation: Elastic cartilage contains abundant elastic fibers (visible with orcein/Verhoeff stain), chondrocytes in lacunae, and type II collagen in matrix. Maintains shape while allowing flexibility. Found: auricle of ear, external auditory canal, Eustachian tube, epiglottis, cuneiform cartilage of larynx.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Fibrocartilage (in intervertebral discs, symphysis pubis, menisci) is unique in having:
options: Abundant type I collagen bundles (dense, parallel) with chondrocytes between them — no perichondrium
explanation: Fibrocartilage: dense type I collagen bundles arranged in parallel with chondrocytes in rows between them. No perichondrium. Found in IVD annulus fibrosus, articular discs (menisci, TMJ, wrist), symphysis pubis, and insertion zones of tendons. High compressive strength.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The liver lobule has which architecture, and which zone is most susceptible to ischemic injury?
options: Hexagonal with central vein at center; Zone 1 (periportal) most susceptible
Hexagonal with portal triad at center; Zone 1 most susceptible
Classic hexagonal lobule with central vein at center; Zone 3 (centrilobular — perivenous) most susceptible to ischemia and hepatotoxins
Triangular with bile duct at apex
explanation: Classic lobule: hexagonal, central vein at center, portal triads at 6 corners. Rappaport's acinus: zone 1 (periportal = best oxygenated, first affected in hepatitis A and Wilson's disease), zone 2 (intermediate), zone 3 (centrilobular/perivenous = last to receive O2, most susceptible to ischemia [right heart failure, shock], alcohol, and hepatotoxins [CCl4, acetaminophen]).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The renal corpuscle consists of which two structures?
options: Glomerulus (capillary tuft) enclosed within Bowman's (glomerular) capsule
explanation: Renal corpuscle = glomerulus (capillary tuft + mesangial cells) + Bowman's capsule. Filtration barrier (3 layers): fenestrated capillary endothelium (size barrier), glomerular basement membrane (GBM, charge and size barrier), and podocytes with filtration slits (size barrier). Damaged in nephrotic syndrome (podocyte foot process fusion).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have which distinctive histological feature?
options: Brush border (microvilli) — dense apical microvilli increasing surface area for reabsorption
explanation: PCT cells: tall columnar cells with a prominent brush border (dense apical microvilli), abundant mitochondria (for active transport), interdigitating basal processes, and eosinophilic cytoplasm on H&E. The PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered sodium, water, glucose, and amino acids.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells, and absorptive enterocytes differentiate from which intestinal stem cell?
options: Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells (crypt base columnar cells)
explanation: Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells in the crypt base (between Paneth cells) give rise to all intestinal epithelial lineages: absorptive enterocytes, goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells, and Paneth cells. Paneth cells are the niche cells that support stem cells with Wnt and EGF signals.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The three layers of the wall of the stomach (from inside to outside) are:
options: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria (muscularis externa), serosa — with muscularis having an extra oblique layer
Only two layers: mucosa and serosa
explanation: Stomach wall: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis propria (outer longitudinal + middle circular + inner oblique layers — unique oblique layer not in intestine), serosa. The extra oblique layer allows churning movements.

subject: Anatomy
stem: In the testis, the blood-testis barrier is formed by tight junctions between which cells?
explanation: Blood-testis barrier: Sertoli cell tight junctions (occluding junctions in the basal compartment of seminiferous tubule) divide it into basal (spermatogonia, early spermatocytes) and adluminal (later spermatocytes, spermatids, spermatozoa) compartments. Protects differentiating germ cells from immune attack.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Weibel-Palade bodies are specific organelles found in which cell type?
explanation: Weibel-Palade bodies: cigar-shaped secretory organelles unique to vascular endothelial cells. They store von Willebrand factor (vWF) and P-selectin. Released by thrombin, histamine, or shear stress → immediate vWF release (promotes platelet adhesion) and P-selectin expression (recruits leukocytes).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'terrible triad' of elbow (posterior elbow dislocation) involves which three structures?
options: Radial head fracture, coronoid fracture, and lateral collateral ligament (LCL) complex injury
MCL rupture, radial head, and olecranon
explanation: Terrible triad of elbow: posterior elbow dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid fracture. The LCL complex is also disrupted. This combination is unstable and often requires operative fixation of all components. Coronoid fracture destabilizes the elbow even more than the dislocations alone.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Colles' fracture of the distal radius typically shows what deformity?
explanation: Colles' fracture: fall on outstretched hand (FOOSH), distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation and displacement (+ radial shortening + supination). The dinner-fork (or bayonet) deformity is visible on lateral view. Smith's fracture = reverse Colles' (volar angulation, fall on flexed wrist or dorsum of hand).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Monteggia fracture-dislocation involves:
options: Fracture of radius + dislocation of ulnohumeral joint
Fracture of proximal ulna + anterior dislocation of radial head
Fracture of both radius and ulna
Fracture of distal radius + radial head dislocation
explanation: Monteggia lesion: fracture of proximal 1/3 of ulna (olecranon/proximal shaft) + dislocation of the radial head. Bado type 1 (most common, anterior radial head dislocation) is caused by forced hyperpronation. The posterior interosseous nerve (deep radial nerve) can be injured by the dislocating radial head.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Galeazzi fracture involves which structures?
options: Proximal ulna fracture + proximal radius dislocation
Fracture of distal 1/3 of radius + disruption of DRUJ (distal radioulnar joint)
Fracture of radius and ulna at same level
explanation: Galeazzi lesion: fracture of distal 1/3 of radius + disruption of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ). The distal ulna becomes prominent dorsally. 'GRUM' mnemonic: Galeazzi = Radius fracture, Ulna dislocates (at DRUJ). Unlike Monteggia (proximal), Galeazzi is at the distal forearm.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Nursemaid's elbow (pulled elbow) in young children involves slippage of which structure?
options: Radial head through the annular ligament (subluxation)
explanation: Nursemaid's elbow: sudden traction on an extended, pronated forearm (a child pulled by the hand) causes the radial head to subluxate (slip through/under) the annular ligament. The child holds the elbow slightly flexed and pronated, refuses to supinate. Treated by supination + flexion (palpable click indicates reduction).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which vascular anomaly predisposes to 'Bow hunter's stroke' (vertebral artery dissection)?
options: Dynamic compression of vertebral artery by C1-C2 rotation (Bow hunter's stroke)
explanation: Bow hunter's stroke (rotational vertebral artery occlusion): the contralateral vertebral artery is dynamically compressed by the lateral mass of C1 rotating on C2 during neck rotation (like an archer drawing a bow). Patients present with posterior circulation TIA/stroke with head turning. Treated with decompressive surgery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Lisfranc joint injury involves disruption of which tarsal-metatarsal joints?
options: Tarsometatarsal joints (Lisfranc joint complex between tarsal bones and bases of metatarsals)
explanation: Lisfranc joint: the tarsometatarsal articulations (1st–5th metatarsal bases and cuneiforms/cuboid). Injury (commonly missed): dorsal foot pain/swelling, widening between 1st and 2nd metatarsal bases on X-ray. Key ligament: Lisfranc ligament (2nd metatarsal base to medial cuneiform). Treated surgically — missed injuries cause severe flat foot deformity.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Flail chest (3+ consecutive rib fractures at 2 sites) causes paradoxical breathing because:
options: The flail segment moves inward on inspiration (paradoxically, opposite to normal rib movement) due to loss of structural integrity
explanation: Flail chest: segment moves paradoxically (in during inspiration when intrathoracic pressure is negative, out during expiration) due to loss of rib continuity. This reduces tidal volume and causes pain-splinting, leading to respiratory failure. Underlying pulmonary contusion (not just the mechanical flail) drives hypoxemia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'Bucket-handle' motion of ribs during inspiration refers to which movement?
options: Downward and inward movement of ribs
Upward and outward lateral movement of ribs, increasing the transverse diameter of the thorax
Anterior elevation of sternum increasing A-P diameter (pump-handle)
explanation: Bucket-handle movement: lateral portions of ribs (middle and lower ribs) swing upward and outward during inspiration, increasing the transverse diameter of the thorax — like a bucket handle lifting. Pump-handle movement (upper ribs): sternum moves anterosuperiorly, increasing the A-P diameter.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Intercostal drain (chest drain) for pleural effusion is inserted in which triangle?
options: Triangle of safety: bordered by anterior axillary line, lateral border of latissimus dorsi, and line of 5th ICS
Triangle of safety: 2nd ICS midclavicular line
At the posterior aspect of the chest
explanation: Triangle of safety for chest drain insertion: bounded anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major, posteriorly by lateral border of latissimus dorsi, and inferiorly by 5th ICS (approximately nipple level in men). This avoids the breast, underlying viscera, and neurovascular bundle.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle is used in the TRAM (transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous) flap for breast reconstruction?
options: Rectus abdominis (with the deep inferior epigastric vessels as pedicle)
explanation: TRAM flap: the rectus abdominis muscle with its overlying skin (based on the deep inferior epigastric perforators, DIEP artery) is rotated to reconstruct the breast. The free DIEP flap (perforator flap sparing the muscle) has become preferred to reduce donor site morbidity.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'danger space' in the neck where infection can spread rapidly to the posterior mediastinum is:
options: Retropharyngeal space (between alar and prevertebral fascia) — 'danger space 4'
explanation: Danger space (retropharyngeal/danger space 4): between the alar layer and prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia. Infection (e.g., from retropharyngeal abscess) can spread inferiorly through this space to the posterior mediastinum, causing descending necrotizing mediastinitis — a life-threatening complication.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The posterior triangle of the neck contains which of the following important structures?
options: Accessory nerve (CN XI), external jugular vein, cutaneous cervical branches (supraclavicular, lesser occipital nerves)
explanation: Posterior triangle contents: CN XI (accessory nerve) crosses its floor (at risk in node biopsy → shoulder drop from trapezius weakness), external jugular vein, supraclavicular nerves, occipital artery, cutaneous nerves (transverse cervical, supraclavicular, lesser occipital, great auricular), lower part of brachial plexus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Calot's triangle is bounded by which three structures?
options: Cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior edge of liver
Common bile duct, cystic artery, portal vein
Common hepatic duct, cystic duct, and portal vein
explanation: Calot's triangle (hepatocystic triangle): bounded by (1) cystic duct, (2) common hepatic duct, (3) inferior surface of liver. Contents: cystic artery (usually a branch of right hepatic artery). Critical during laparoscopic cholecystectomy — the 'critical view of safety' requires clearing this triangle.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Splenic artery courses along which structure before reaching the spleen?
explanation: Splenic artery (largest branch of celiac axis): tortuous, courses along the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail. At the splenic hilum, it divides into 5–6 segmental branches. The splenic vein runs along the posterior surface of the pancreatic body (important landmark during pancreatectomy).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which peritoneal fold connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
options: Falciform ligament (contains ligamentum teres hepatis — obliterated left umbilical vein)
explanation: Falciform ligament: double fold of peritoneum from diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall to the anterior surface of the liver. Its free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (obliterated left umbilical vein, L to RA in fetus). Used as a landmark for the left lobe of the liver.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) connects which two peritoneal spaces?
options: Greater sac and the space of Morrison
explanation: Epiploic foramen (Winslow): the only communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs. Bounded anteriorly by hepatoduodenal ligament (containing portal triad), posteriorly by IVC, superiorly by caudate lobe of liver, inferiorly by first part of duodenum. Pringle maneuver compresses the hepatoduodenal ligament here to control liver bleeding.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Meckel's diverticulum can cause GI bleeding when it contains which ectopic tissue?
options: Gastric mucosa (secretes HCl causing ileal ulceration)
explanation: Gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum (present in ~50% of symptomatic cases) secretes acid, causing peptic ulceration of the adjacent ileal mucosa. This presents as painless lower GI bleeding. Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan (Meckel's scan) detects ectopic gastric mucosa.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Hirschsprung's disease: the pathology is in the AGANGLIONIC segment. Where is the transition zone?
options: In the normal bowel (with ganglia) that is dilated
At the rectosigmoid junction most commonly (75%)
explanation: Hirschsprung's disease: aganglionic segment (fails to relax) is most commonly at the rectosigmoid (75%), rarely extending to total colonic aganglionosis. The proximal bowel (with normal ganglia) becomes dilated megacolon. The rectum is ALWAYS involved (internal sphincter region).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The appendix receives its blood supply from which artery, and what type of artery is it?
options: Appendicular artery (from ileocolic artery, SMA); end artery — no collateral supply
explanation: The appendicular artery is an end artery (terminal branch with no collateral circulation), arising from the ileocolic artery (branch of SMA). Thrombosis of the appendicular artery in untreated appendicitis causes gangrene and perforation. The meso-appendix carries the appendicular artery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which is the most common site for diverticulosis in the Western population?
explanation: Diverticulosis (acquired false diverticula — mucosa only, no muscularis propria) most commonly occurs in the sigmoid colon in Western populations (high-pressure, low-residue segment). In Asian populations, right-sided (cecal) diverticulosis is more common. Diverticulitis = inflammation, often with LIF pain.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Killian's dehiscence (Killian's triangle) is the site of origin of pharyngeal (Zenker's) diverticulum. It is found between which muscles?
options: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor and cricopharyngeus (Passavant's ridge)
Thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of inferior pharyngeal constrictor
explanation: Zenker's diverticulum (pharyngeal pulsion diverticulum): arises at Killian's dehiscence — the weak posterior wall between the thyropharyngeal (oblique) fibers and the cricopharyngeal (horizontal) fibers of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. Cricopharyngeal dysfunction creates high pressure forcing mucosa through this weak spot.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which triangle of the neck contains the carotid artery bifurcation?
options: Carotid (middle) triangle (part of anterior triangle of neck)
