explanation: Carotid triangle: bounded by superior belly of omohyoid, posterior belly of digastric, and SCM. Contains: common carotid artery (bifurcation at C3/C4 — upper border of thyroid cartilage), internal/external carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve, hypoglossal nerve, ansa cervicalis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by which cranial nerve?
explanation: Stylopharyngeus (from styloid process to pharyngeal wall) is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by CN IX (glossopharyngeal nerve). All other pharyngeal and palatal muscles (except tensor veli palatini — CN V3) are supplied by CN X via the pharyngeal plexus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of which artery?
explanation: Superior thyroid artery: first (and most anteriorly directed) branch of external carotid artery. It supplies the superior pole of the thyroid and the superior parathyroid glands. The superior laryngeal artery (branch of the superior thyroid) accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The palatine tonsil is located between which two pillars?
explanation: Palatine tonsil: lies in the tonsillar fossa (sinus) between the anterior palatoglossal arch (CN XII — hyoglossus depresses tongue; CN XI — palatoglossus from palate to tongue) and posterior palatopharyngeal arch. Blood supply: tonsillar branch of facial artery (main), with contributions from ascending palatine, ascending pharyngeal, lesser palatine, and lingual arteries.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Tornwaldt's cyst occurs at which location in the nasopharynx?
options: Midline posterior wall of nasopharynx (notochord remnant)
Inferior wall near the Eustachian tube orifice
explanation: Tornwaldt's cyst: a notochordal remnant forming a midline cyst in the posterior nasopharynx. It can become infected (Tornwaldt's bursitis) causing postnasal discharge, halitosis, and occipital headache. Distinguished from adenoids by its midline location and cystic nature on MRI.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The parotid duct (Stensen's duct) pierces which muscle to open into the mouth?
explanation: Stensen's duct: arises from the anterior margin of parotid gland, runs across the masseter (palpable when the muscle is contracted), turns medially to pierce the buccinator muscle, and opens on the buccal mucosa opposite the upper second molar tooth (parotid papilla).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The retropharyngeal space (between posterior pharyngeal wall and prevertebral fascia) extends inferiorly to which level?
explanation: Retropharyngeal space extends from the skull base to T2 (superior mediastinum), where the alar and prevertebral fasciae fuse. Retropharyngeal abscess (most common in children under 4 years, from adenoid/lymph node suppuration) in this space can dissect into the mediastinum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The facial vein drains into which vessel?
options: Internal jugular vein (via common facial vein)
explanation: Facial vein: descends along the face, crosses the mandible 2–3 cm anterior to the masseter, and joins the anterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the common facial vein, which drains into the internal jugular vein. The angular vein (superior facial vein) communicates with the cavernous sinus via the ophthalmic veins (dangerous area of face).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle is the most important depressor of the mandible (opens the mouth)?
explanation: Lateral pterygoid (CN V3): the primary muscle that depresses the mandible (opens mouth). Its inferior head pulls the mandibular condyle and disc forward in protrusion and the lower head depresses the mandible. Medial pterygoid, masseter, and temporalis all elevate the mandible (close mouth).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which foramen transmits the maxillary nerve (V2)?
explanation: V2 (maxillary nerve): exits through foramen rotundum → pterygopalatine fossa → infraorbital fissure/canal → infraorbital foramen. V1 (ophthalmic): superior orbital fissure. V3 (mandibular): foramen ovale. Middle meningeal artery: foramen spinosum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'cavernous sinus' receives venous drainage from which structures?
options: Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, cerebral veins, sphenoparietal sinus
explanation: Cavernous sinus: paired dural venous sinuses lateral to the pituitary and body of sphenoid. Receives: superior and inferior ophthalmic veins (dangerous face area communication), sphenoparietal sinus, middle cerebral veins. Drains via superior and inferior petrosal sinuses to sigmoid sinus/IJV.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Meckel's cartilage (first branchial arch) contributes to which adult structures?
options: Malleus (head and neck), incus (body and short process), sphenomandibular ligament, and anterior ligament of malleus
explanation: Meckel's cartilage (1st arch): gives rise to malleus and incus (auditory ossicles), sphenomandibular ligament, and anterior ligament of malleus. The mandible itself is formed by intramembranous ossification adjacent to (not from) Meckel's cartilage. The mandibular nerve (V3) accompanies this arch.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which bone is formed entirely by intramembranous ossification (no cartilage precursor)?
options: Clavicle and most flat bones of skull (parietal, frontal, temporal squama)
explanation: Intramembranous ossification (direct mesenchyme to bone, no cartilage model): flat bones of skull (frontal, parietal, temporal squama, occipital squama), mandible, clavicle (partly endochondral at medial end), and maxilla. Long bones form by endochondral ossification (cartilage → bone).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier syndrome) involves absence of which midline structures?
options: Septum pellucidum + hypoplasia of optic nerves ± pituitary abnormalities
explanation: Septo-optic dysplasia: triad of (1) absent septum pellucidum, (2) optic nerve hypoplasia (small optic discs), (3) pituitary hormone deficiency (hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus). Caused by mutations in HESX1, SOX2, or PAX6. Presents with nystagmus, visual impairment, and hypoglycemia in infancy.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Sacrococcygeal teratoma is the most common tumor in which age group and arises from:
options: Neonates and infants — from remnants of Hensen's node (primitive knot) or multipotent cells in the sacrococcygeal region
explanation: Sacrococcygeal teratoma (SCT): most common neonatal tumor. Arises from totipotent cells in the sacrococcygeal region, possibly from Hensen's node remnants. Contains all three germ layers (dermoid, neuroectodermal, endodermal elements). Mostly benign in neonates; malignancy increases after 6 months. Resection includes the coccyx.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cyclopia and holoprosencephaly are associated with failure of midline prosencephalon cleavage. Which gene is most commonly mutated?
explanation: Holoprosencephaly: failure of the prosencephalon to cleave into two cerebral hemispheres. Most commonly associated with mutations in SHH (sonic hedgehog) signaling, PTCH, ZIC2, SIX3. Also caused by chromosomal anomalies (trisomy 13 most common). Cyclopia is the most severe form.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The Wolffian (mesonephric) duct in males forms which structures?
options: Epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory duct
explanation: Under testosterone influence (from Leydig cells, beginning week 8), the Wolffian duct differentiates into: epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and ejaculatory duct. In females (no testosterone), the Wolffian duct regresses. The Müllerian duct is suppressed by AMH (from Sertoli cells).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (TAPVC) — pulmonary veins drain into which vessels?
options: Right atrium or systemic veins (SVC, IVC, coronary sinus) instead of left atrium
explanation: TAPVC: all 4 pulmonary veins drain anomalously into the right side of the heart (SVC, right atrium, coronary sinus, IVC) rather than the left atrium. Requires an ASD/PFO for survival. Obstructed TAPVC (infradiaphragmatic type) presents with severe cyanosis and pulmonary venous hypertension at birth — emergency surgery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Haversian system (osteon) in compact bone consists of which components?
options: Central Haversian canal (neurovascular) + concentric lamellae of bone + osteocytes in lacunae + canaliculi
explanation: Osteon (Haversian system): the structural unit of compact (cortical) bone. Central Haversian canal (contains blood vessels and nerves) surrounded by concentric lamellae of mineralized bone matrix. Osteocytes reside in lacunae between lamellae; they communicate via canaliculi (tiny channels filled with osteocyte processes).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Volkmann's canals in bone differ from Haversian canals in that they:
options: Run perpendicular to the long axis of bone (transversely), connecting Haversian canals and periosteum/endosteum
explanation: Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely/obliquely, connecting adjacent Haversian canals and connecting the periosteum to the endosteum. Haversian canals run parallel to the long axis of the bone. Both contain blood vessels; Volkmann's do NOT have concentric lamellae around them.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex is the thickest zone and secretes which hormones?
explanation: Zona fasciculata (middle, thickest zone ~75%): secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol) in response to ACTH. Cells are arranged in straight columns ('fascicles'); rich in lipid droplets (appear pale/vacuolated — 'clear cells'). Controlled by ACTH from anterior pituitary (which is controlled by CRH from hypothalamus).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cerebellar cortex has a characteristic three-layer architecture. The Purkinje cells are located in which layer?
options: Purkinje cell layer (single cell layer of large Purkinje neurons between molecular and granular layers)
explanation: Cerebellar cortex layers (from surface to deep): (1) Molecular layer (stellate cells, basket cells, Purkinje dendrites), (2) Purkinje cell layer (single row of large Purkinje cells — the ONLY output of the cerebellar cortex, GABAergic, project to deep cerebellar nuclei), (3) Granular layer (densely packed granule cells + Golgi cells).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The glomerular filtration barrier is formed by which three layers?
options: Endothelium, GBM, podocytes with filtration slits
explanation: Three-layer filtration barrier: (1) fenestrated capillary endothelium (pores 60–80 nm, blocks cells and large proteins), (2) GBM (charge-selective, negatively charged heparan sulfate proteoglycans repel negatively charged albumin), (3) podocyte filtration slits (~25 nm, size-selective, bridged by nephrin and podocin). All three disrupted in nephrotic syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Desmosomes (macula adherens) link adjacent cells mechanically via which proteins?
options: Desmogleins and desmocollins (cadherins) linked intracellularly to intermediate filaments (keratin in epithelium)
explanation: Desmosomes: macula adherens = desmoplakin + plakophilin anchoring transmembrane cadherins (desmogleins 1–4, desmocollins 1–3) to intermediate filaments (cytokeratin in epithelium, desmin in cardiac muscle). Pemphigus vulgaris = autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 → intraepidermal blistering.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which cells are responsible for myelination of CNS axons?
explanation: Oligodendrocytes (CNS): myelinate multiple CNS axons (each oligodendrocyte myelinates 40–60 internodes on different axons). Schwann cells (PNS): myelinate single PNS axons (one Schwann cell per internode). MS = demyelination of oligodendrocytes. Guillain-Barré = Schwann cell/PNS demyelination.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Satellite cells of skeletal muscle have which function?
options: Adult skeletal muscle stem cells — normally quiescent, activated by injury to regenerate muscle fibers
explanation: Muscle satellite cells: mononucleated stem cells located between the basal lamina and sarcolemma of muscle fibers. Normally quiescent; activated by injury/exercise → proliferate, differentiate into new muscle fibers (myogenesis), or self-renew. Essential for muscle repair but limited in muscular dystrophies.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Mucin is classified as which type of secretion based on the mechanism?
options: Merocrine (exocrine secretion with no loss of cell membrane or cytoplasm — exocytosis)
explanation: Merocrine secretion (exocytosis): secretory vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane to release contents without cell membrane loss. Most common glandular secretion type (mucus from goblet cells, serous from parotid acini, insulin from beta cells). Apocrine = apical cytoplasm shed (mammary glands, axillary sweat). Holocrine = entire cell disintegrates (sebaceous glands).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II) of the spinal cord is the first synapse for which sensory modality?
options: Pain and temperature (nociceptive signals from primary afferents)
explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II): the second-order neuron synapse for pain and temperature. First-order nociceptive (Aδ and C fibers) afferents synapse here, using substance P and glutamate. This is the target of opioid (μ-receptor) analgesia and the gate-control theory of pain modulation.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nucleus cuneatus and nucleus gracilis in the medulla are the first relay nuclei for which sensory pathway?
options: Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway (fine touch, vibration, proprioception)
explanation: Nucleus gracilis (lower limb, medial medulla) and nucleus cuneatus (upper limb, lateral medulla): relay nuclei for the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway. Second-order axons from these nuclei decussate (sensory decussation/medullary decussation) and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the VPL of the thalamus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'red nucleus' is located in which part of the brainstem and has which function?
options: Midbrain tegmentum — receives cerebellar and cortical inputs; contributes to rubrospinal tract
explanation: Red nucleus: in the midbrain tegmentum (caudal midbrain, at level of superior colliculi). Receives input from dentate nucleus (via SCP) and motor cortex. Gives rise to the rubrospinal tract (crosses and descends to facilitate flexor muscles of contralateral limb). Appears reddish due to high iron content and vascularity.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Periaqueductal grey (PAG) in the midbrain is involved in which function?
options: Endogenous pain modulation (release of endorphins, stimulation inhibits pain)
explanation: PAG (periaqueductal grey): surrounds the cerebral aqueduct in the midbrain. Activated by opioids and electrical stimulation → releases endogenous opioids (enkephalins) → activates descending inhibitory pathways (raphe nuclei, locus coeruleus) → inhibits dorsal horn pain neurons. Key target of opioid analgesia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The internal capsule carries which motor and sensory fibers in its posterior limb?
options: Corticospinal + corticobulbar fibers in the genu; sensory fibers in the posterior limb
Corticospinal fibers (leg anterior, arm posterior) and thalamocortical sensory fibers — in the posterior limb
explanation: Internal capsule posterior limb: corticospinal fibers (UMN tract), corticorubral, and thalamocortical (sensory relay) fibers. The genu contains corticobulbar fibers (to cranial nerve motor nuclei — face/speech). A small lacunar infarct in the posterior limb causes contralateral pure motor hemiplegia (without cortical signs).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which nerve is most commonly injured during thyroid surgery (thyroidectomy)?
explanation: RLN is most commonly injured during thyroidectomy (incidence 1–2%): the RLN enters the larynx posterior to the cricothyroid joint, near the inferior thyroid artery. Unilateral RLN injury → hoarse voice (paralysis of all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid). Bilateral injury → respiratory distress (bilateral vocal cord paralysis).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts for choking) creates pressure to expel foreign bodies. The thrusts are directed:
options: Upward and posteriorly (diaphragm is pushed up, increasing intrathoracic pressure)
explanation: Heimlich maneuver: fists placed below the sternum (epigastric area), sharp upward and posterior thrusts push the diaphragm superiorly, increasing intrathoracic pressure to expel a foreign body obstructing the airway. Can injure the liver or spleen if performed incorrectly.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'safe triangle' for chest drain insertion is in which intercostal space?
options: 4th or 5th ICS anterior axillary line (within the triangle of safety)
explanation: Chest drain in the safe triangle (4th–5th ICS, anterior axillary line): avoids the breast, pectorals, and neurovascular bundles. Insert just above the upper border of the lower rib (to avoid intercostal VAN at lower border). The needle passes: skin → subcutaneous tissue → intercostal muscles → parietal pleura.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Intercostal nerve block should be performed at which point along the rib?
options: At the costovertebral angle (posterior angle of rib, where neurovascular bundle exits from beneath the rib)
explanation: Intercostal nerve block: most effective at or just posterior to the angle of the rib (posterior to the posterior axillary line). At this point, the neurovascular bundle (VAN — from above downward: vein, artery, nerve) lies in the costal groove, and local anesthetic can block the nerve before it gives its lateral cutaneous branch.

subject: Anatomy
stem: During a lumbar puncture, the dural sac ends at which sacral level?
explanation: The dural sac (thecal sac) ends at S2 sacral level (2nd sacral vertebra). Below S2, only the filum terminale (pia mater) continues to the coccyx. The epidural space is continuous throughout the spinal canal. Caudal epidural block uses the sacral hiatus (between sacral cornua at S4/S5) to access the sacral epidural space.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The splenic flexure of the colon is supported by which ligament?
options: Phrenocolic ligament (suspends the splenic flexure from the left diaphragm)
explanation: Phrenocolic ligament: connects the splenic flexure of the colon to the left hemidiaphragm. It 'cradles' the spleen inferiorly. When the spleen is enlarged, the splenic flexure is displaced inferiorly. Division of this ligament is necessary during left hemicolectomy and splenectomy.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle is tested by the 'Ober test' (patient in lateral decubitus, examiner abducts and extends the hip, then releases)?
explanation: Ober test: patient in lateral position, hip extended, knee flexed 90°. If the hip does not adduct (fails to fall to table), this indicates iliotibial band (ITB) tightness. ITB (from TFL and gluteus maximus via iliac crest to Gerdy's tubercle of tibia) is commonly tight in runners causing ITBS (IT band syndrome).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'drawer sign' positive at 90° hip flexion in hip dislocation refers to which test?
options: Anterior drawer at hip (Ortolani/Barlow neonatal test for DDH)
Telescoping sign (pistoning of femoral head in hip)
explanation: Telescoping sign (also called pistoning or piston sign): in hip dislocation (DDH or acute dislocation), the femoral head can be pushed up and down (telescoped) along the axis of the femur while the hip is flexed at 90°. Different from the knee drawer sign — this tests hip stability.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Kehr's sign (left shoulder pain with splenic injury) is due to which anatomical principle?
options: Direct nerve connection between spleen and shoulder
Blood or fluid irritating the diaphragm, causing referred pain via phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) to the shoulder tip (dermatomes C3,4,5)
Direct compression of the brachial plexus
explanation: Kehr's sign: left shoulder tip pain (C4 dermatome) in splenic trauma/rupture. Blood or fluid from the ruptured spleen pools under the left hemidiaphragm, irritating its peritoneal surface. This irritates the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5), causing referred pain to the shoulder tip (dermatome C3,4,5 overlap). Same principle applies to right shoulder pain in liver laceration or ruptured right ectopic.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nerve of Kuntz is a communicating branch between which two nerves?
options: Upper thoracic sympathetic trunk (T1-T2) to brachial plexus, bypassing the stellate ganglion
explanation: Nerve of Kuntz: an inconstant communicating ramus between the second (sometimes third) thoracic sympathetic rami and the first thoracic root of the brachial plexus, bypassing the stellate ganglion. It can be responsible for incomplete Horner's syndrome after stellate ganglion block or incomplete sympathectomy for hyperhidrosis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Thoracic outlet syndrome (neurogenic type) compresses which nerve roots, and the 'costoclavicular test' positions the arm how?
options: C8,T1 (lower trunk); arm extended and shoulder depressed with neck rotated contralaterally
explanation: Neurogenic TOS: C8,T1 lower trunk compression → medial forearm and hand paresthesia, hypothenar wasting. Costoclavicular test: shoulder depressed and retracted + arm slightly abducted (costoclavicular position) → reproduces symptoms by narrowing the space between the first rib and clavicle.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Wartenberg's syndrome (cheiralgia paresthetica) involves compression of which nerve?
options: Superficial radial nerve at the wrist between brachioradialis and ECRL tendons
explanation: Wartenberg's syndrome: entrapment of the superficial radial nerve (purely sensory — superficial branch of radial nerve) between the tendons of brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus at the wrist. Causes dorsal radial hand paresthesia/pain (over the anatomical snuff box and dorsum of thumb). Mimics de Quervain's tenosynovitis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'ring avulsion injury' classification by Urbaniak categorizes based on:
options: Degree of vascular and soft tissue injury (Class I: adequate circulation; Class II: inadequate; Class III: complete degloving)
explanation: Ring avulsion injury: caused by a ring catching on a fixed object while the finger continues forward. Urbaniak classification: Class I (adequate circulation — treat conservatively), Class II (inadequate circulation — vascular repair needed), Class III (complete degloving or amputation — consider replantation vs. completion amputation).

subject: Anatomy
stem: In lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), which specific pathological change occurs in the tendon?
options: Angiofibroblastic tendinosis (degenerative non-inflammatory change with fibroblast proliferation and immature vasculature)
explanation: Tennis elbow pathology: angiofibroblastic tendinosis (Nirschl pathology) — NOT acute inflammation. Features: fibroblast proliferation, disorganized immature collagen, immature vascular elements (neovascularization), absence of acute inflammatory cells. Hence, corticosteroid injections provide only short-term relief, and the condition is better termed 'tendinopathy' not 'tendinitis.'

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle is the primary hip abductor and, when weak, causes the Trendelenburg lurch (trunk shift)?
options: Gluteus medius (with tensor fasciae latae as secondary abductor)
explanation: Gluteus medius (superior gluteal nerve L4,L5,S1): primary hip abductor. Weakness causes Trendelenburg sign (pelvis drops on opposite side when weight-bearing). To compensate, patients laterally flex the trunk toward the affected side (Trendelenburg lurch/gait), shifting center of gravity over the hip. Key in total hip arthroplasty — preserving the superior gluteal nerve prevents persistent lurch.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The medial compartment of the thigh is supplied by the obturator nerve EXCEPT for which muscle?
options: Adductor magnus (posterior/hamstring part — supplied by sciatic nerve)
explanation: Adductor magnus has dual innervation: anterior (adductor) part by obturator nerve (L2,L3,L4); posterior (hamstring/ischiocondylar) part by the tibial division of sciatic nerve (L4). The hamstring part also contributes to hip extension. This is why adductor magnus maintains some function in isolated obturator nerve palsy.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The saphenous nerve (terminal branch of femoral nerve) supplies sensation to which area?
options: Medial side of leg and foot down to the medial malleolus
explanation: Saphenous nerve (purely sensory — the only part of femoral nerve that descends below the knee): supplies medial side of the leg from below the knee to medial malleolus and medial foot (variable). It travels with the great saphenous vein. Injured in knee surgery (medial portal placement, medial meniscus surgery) causing medial leg numbness.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Sural nerve grafting is commonly used because this nerve is expendable. What sensation does it provide, and what does its sacrifice affect?
options: Dorsal foot sensation; graft creates complete foot numbness
Lateral foot and heel sensation; sacrifice causes only mild lateral foot sensory loss (minimal functional deficit)
explanation: Sural nerve (mixed branch from tibial and common peroneal): provides sensation to lateral heel, lateral foot, and 5th toe. Sacrifice causes a small area of numbness on the lateral foot, which is generally well-tolerated. The sural nerve is commonly harvested for nerve graft due to its accessibility and acceptable donor deficit.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery) arises from the femoral artery at which level?
options: 2–5 cm below the inguinal ligament in the femoral triangle
explanation: Profunda femoris (deep femoral artery): the largest branch of femoral artery, arising from its lateral (or posterolateral) side 2–5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It gives medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and 4 perforating branches to supply posterior and medial thigh. It is preserved during femoral artery catheterization.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The pericardium is attached to the sternum by which ligaments?
options: It has no attachments — free floating
explanation: The fibrous pericardium is attached to: (1) diaphragm (inferiorly — phrenopericardial ligaments/central tendon), (2) sternum (superior and inferior sternopericardial ligaments — helps anchor the pericardium), (3) great vessel adventitia (superiorly). These attachments help maintain mediastinal position and prevent cardiac displacement.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which chest wall muscle has innervation from the same nerve root as the serratus anterior?
explanation: Serratus anterior: long thoracic nerve C5,C6,C7 (C5 to C7 'keep the wing by your side'). The intercostal muscles (T1–T11) are innervated by the respective intercostal nerves. Trapezius is supplied by CN XI + C3,C4. However, upper slips of serratus anterior share C5 supply with portions of rhomboids and suprascapular nerve distribution.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The thymic remnant in adults is located in which mediastinal compartment?
explanation: Thymus: large gland behind the sternum in the anterior and superior mediastinum in children. After puberty it involutes (replaced by fat). Thymoma (tumor of thymus epithelial cells) occurs in the anterior mediastinum and is the most common anterior mediastinal mass in adults; associated with myasthenia gravis (in 15% of thymomas) and pure red cell aplasia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm?
options: Esophagus, left and right vagus nerves, and esophageal branches of left gastric vessels
explanation: Diaphragmatic openings: (1) Aortic hiatus (T12): aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein — posterior to diaphragm, doesn't compress on respiration. (2) Esophageal hiatus (T10): esophagus, left and right vagi, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels — in the muscular part. (3) IVC foramen (T8): IVC and right phrenic nerve — in central tendon.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Pectus excavatum (funnel chest) most severely compresses which structure?
options: Right ventricle (RV compression against the sternum impairs RV filling)
explanation: Pectus excavatum: depression deformity of the anterior chest wall (sternum depressed). Severe forms compress the right ventricle against the spine, impairing RV diastolic filling and reducing cardiac output. The heart shifts to the left, causing cardiac murmurs and symptoms on exertion. Treated by Nuss procedure (metal bar placed to correct sternum).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The transpyloric plane (of Addison) at L1 passes through which anatomical structures?
options: Pylorus of stomach, neck of pancreas, duodenal-jejunal flexure, fundus of gallbladder, hila of kidneys, SMA origin, and L1
explanation: Transpyloric plane (halfway between suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis, at L1): passes through pylorus, fundus of gallbladder, neck of pancreas, duodenal-jejunal flexure (Treitz), tips of 9th costal cartilages, hila of kidneys, and origin of SMA. Useful anatomical reference for abdominal surgery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which branch of the celiac axis supplies the spleen?
options: Splenic artery (largest branch of celiac axis)
explanation: Celiac axis (celiac trunk, T12/L1): three branches — left gastric artery (smallest), splenic artery (largest — tortuous, along superior pancreatic border), and common hepatic artery. Splenic artery also gives off short gastric arteries (to gastric fundus) and left gastroepiploic artery (to greater curve).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The portal triad (portal tract) of the liver contains all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation: Portal triad (in the corners of liver lobules): portal venule (branch of portal vein), hepatic arteriole (branch of hepatic artery), and bile ductule (duct of Hering, draining bile centrifugally). The central vein (hepatic venule) is at the CENTER of the lobule, NOT in the portal triad.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The peritoneum covering the posterior surface of the liver forms which ligament?
options: Coronary ligament (and bare area of liver)
explanation: Coronary ligament: peritoneal reflections from the posterior liver surface to the diaphragm, forming an upper and lower layer enclosing the 'bare area' of the liver (a triangular area directly adherent to the diaphragm without peritoneal covering). The right triangular ligament joins the two layers.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Auerbach's plexus (myenteric plexus) is located between which layers of the gut wall?
options: Circular and longitudinal layers of muscularis propria (muscularis externa)
explanation: Auerbach's myenteric plexus: between inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers of the muscularis propria. Controls peristaltic movements. Meissner's submucosal plexus: in the submucosa, controls secretion and local blood flow. Both are lost in Hirschsprung's disease (aganglionic segment) and Chagas disease.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nasal cavity receives arterial supply from which arteries?
options: Sphenopalatine artery (from maxillary artery ECA — main supply), anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from ophthalmic artery ICA), and superior labial artery (from facial artery ECA)
explanation: Nasal blood supply: (1) sphenopalatine artery (terminal branch of maxillary artery from ECA) — most important for posterior bleeds; (2) anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from ophthalmic artery, ICA branch) — supply upper nasal septum; (3) superior labial artery (ECA) and greater palatine artery (ECA) — supply anterior septum (Kiesselbach's area).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ophthalmic artery is the first intracranial branch of which artery?
options: Internal carotid artery (enters orbit through optic canal)
explanation: Ophthalmic artery: first branch of the ICA after it exits the cavernous sinus and passes through the dural ring. It enters the orbit through the optic canal (with the optic nerve). It gives: central retinal artery, posterior ciliary arteries, lacrimal artery, and ethmoidal arteries. Central retinal artery occlusion → sudden painless monocular visual loss.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscles are responsible for movements of the larynx — specifically what does the lateral cricoarytenoid do?
options: Closes the glottis — adducts (medializes) the vocal cords
explanation: Laryngeal muscles: posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) — ONLY abductor of vocal cords (opens glottis); lateral cricoarytenoid (LCA) — adducts cords (closes glottis); transverse arytenoid — closes posterior glottis; cricothyroid (external SLN) — tenses cords (elevates pitch); thyroarytenoid — relaxes cords. All supplied by RLN except cricothyroid (external SLN).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Subglottic stenosis after prolonged endotracheal intubation affects which tracheal rings?
options: At the cricoid level (below the vocal cords — the subglottis, the narrowest part of the pediatric airway)
explanation: Subglottic stenosis: the subglottis (below the vocal cords, at the level of the cricoid cartilage) is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway. Prolonged intubation → pressure necrosis → granulation tissue → stenosis. Presents as biphasic stridor. The cricoid is the only complete tracheal ring, limiting expandability.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The basal ganglia 'direct pathway' is initiated by which dopamine receptor stimulation?
options: D1 receptor activation (direct pathway) — facilitates movement
explanation: Direct pathway (facilitates movement): cortex → striatum (D1 receptor dopamine facilitates) → inhibits GPi/SNr → disinhibits thalamus → facilitates cortex. Indirect pathway (inhibits movement): cortex → striatum (D2 receptor dopamine inhibits the indirect pathway) → GPe → STN → GPi/SNr → inhibits thalamus. Loss of dopamine (Parkinson's) → overactive GPi → decreased thalamic activity → bradykinesia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Hypothalamic nuclei — which nucleus controls the circadian rhythm?
options: Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) — the master circadian pacemaker
explanation: Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN): bilateral nuclei in the anterior hypothalamus above the optic chiasm. The master circadian pacemaker — receives direct light input via the retinohypothalamic tract. Controls sleep-wake cycles, hormone secretion rhythms (cortisol, melatonin), and autonomic functions through rhythmic gene expression (CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, CRY genes).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The limbic system includes which structures (memory the CHAMPP mnemonic)?
options: Cingulate gyrus, Hippocampus, Amygdala, Mammillary bodies, Parahippocampal gyrus, and the fornix connections (plus hypothalamus and thalamic nuclei)
explanation: Limbic system (Papez circuit): cingulate gyrus → hippocampus (memory) → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nucleus → cingulate cortex. Plus: amygdala (fear/emotional memory), parahippocampal gyrus, and connections to hypothalamus. Controls emotion, memory, and olfaction.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is maintained by which cells at the cellular level?
options: Brain capillary endothelial cells with tight junctions + astrocyte end-feet + pericytes
explanation: BBB components: (1) brain capillary endothelial cells with extremely tight junctions (occludin, claudin-5, ZO-1) — no fenestrations unlike systemic capillaries, (2) astrocyte end-feet ensheathing the capillary (induce and maintain BBB properties), (3) pericytes (regulate permeability). Brain capillaries also lack pinocytotic vesicles. Disrupted in meningitis, tumors, stroke.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Failure of fusion of the labioscrotal folds in a genetic male (46XY) results in:
options: Bifid scrotum (with or without perineal hypospadias)
explanation: Labioscrotal swellings (from genital swellings): in males they fuse in the midline to form the scrotum; in females they remain separate as labia majora. Failure of fusion in males → bifid scrotum. Combined with failure of urethral fold fusion (hypospadias) → perineal hypospadias with bifid scrotum, resembling female genitalia.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The processus vaginalis is an outpouching of which layer of the peritoneum?
options: Parietal peritoneum following the gubernaculum through the inguinal canal
explanation: Processus vaginalis: an evagination of parietal peritoneum that follows the gubernaculum testis through the inguinal canal into the scrotum in males (or labia majora in females as canal of Nuck). In males, the lower part forms the tunica vaginalis around the testis; the rest obliterates. Patent processus vaginalis → communicating hydrocele (fluid) or indirect inguinal hernia (bowel or omentum).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which embryological structure separates the primitive atria into right and left atria?
options: Septum primum grows from the roof (crista dividens), then septum secundum forms to the right with foramen ovale
explanation: Atrial septation: (1) septum primum grows from the atrial roof toward endocardial cushions — the gap (ostium primum) closes as they fuse; then fenestrations form (ostium secundum). (2) Septum secundum grows from the right, leaving a gap (foramen ovale). In fetal life, blood flows right → left through foramen ovale. ASD: ostium secundum ASD (most common) is failure of septum secundum to close the fenestrations.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Meissner's corpuscles are found in which tissue and detect which stimuli?
options: Dermal papillae of glabrous (hairless) skin — light discriminative touch, texture, low-frequency vibration (0–50 Hz)
explanation: Meissner's corpuscles: encapsulated rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors in the dermal papillae of glabrous skin (fingertips, lips, genitalia). They detect fine touch, slipping of objects, and low-frequency flutter (10–50 Hz). Most dense at fingertips — key for reading Braille. Diminish with age.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Pacinian corpuscles are located where and detect which stimuli?
options: Deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue, viscera, joint capsules — high-frequency vibration (200–300 Hz) and pressure
explanation: Pacinian corpuscles: large encapsulated rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors in deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, periosteum, mesenteries, and joint capsules. Detect high-frequency vibration (200–300 Hz) and deep pressure. The onion-like lamellar capsule is the diagnostic histological feature.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Ruffini endings are found in skin and detect which sensory modality?
options: Skin stretch, sustained pressure, and joint position (slowly adapting)
explanation: Ruffini endings (Ruffini corpuscles): slowly adapting mechanoreceptors in deep dermis, joint capsules, and ligaments. Detect sustained skin stretch, directional shear force, and joint rotation/position. They do NOT adapt rapidly — remain active throughout sustained deformation.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The thyroid follicles are lined by which epithelium, and follicular cells do what?
options: Simple cuboidal (low columnar when active) follicular cells surrounding colloid — secrete thyroglobulin and convert it to T3/T4
explanation: Thyroid follicle: spherical units filled with colloid (mainly thyroglobulin). Lined by follicular cells (principal cells): simple squamous-to-low cuboidal at rest, tall columnar when highly active (hypothyroidism/TSH stimulation). They synthesize thyroglobulin, iodinate it (thyroid peroxidase), and endocytose it back to cleave T3/T4.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid secrete which hormone, and they are derived from:
options: Calcitonin — neural crest cells (ultimobranchial body, 5th pharyngeal pouch)
explanation: C-cells (parafollicular cells): located between follicles and in the interfollicular stroma of the thyroid. Derived from neural crest cells (5th branchial pouch/ultimobranchial body). Secrete calcitonin (lowers serum calcium, inhibits osteoclast activity). C-cell hyperplasia/medullary thyroid carcinoma produces calcitonin (tumor marker, part of MEN 2A/2B).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Osteoclasts are multinucleated giant cells derived from which cell lineage and found in which location?
options: Monocyte-macrophage lineage (hematopoietic stem cells) — in Howship's lacunae on bone surfaces
explanation: Osteoclasts: multinucleated (10–20 nuclei), bone-resorbing cells derived from monocyte-macrophage lineage (hematopoietic stem cells, fuse after differentiation). Reside in resorption pits (Howship's lacunae) on bone surfaces. They pump H+ (via vacuolar H+-ATPase) and proteases (cathepsin K, MMP-9) into a sealed zone to dissolve mineral and matrix.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture follows compartment syndrome of which compartment?
options: Anterior (flexor) compartment of forearm — due to raised pressure compressing FDP, FDS, FPL
explanation: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture: late sequela of forearm compartment syndrome (e.g., after supracondylar fracture in children, tight cast). Ischaemia of the deep anterior compartment (FDP, FDS, FPL, pronator quadratus) → fibrosis → wrist flexion contracture + finger clawing (PIP and DIP flexed). Prevent with fasciotomy within 6 hours.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Langer's lines (tension lines of skin) are important in surgery because incisions parallel to them:
options: Produce minimal scarring (less wound tension, less scar hypertrophy)
explanation: Langer's lines (cleavage lines, skin tension lines): reflect the predominant orientation of collagen fibers in the dermis. Surgical incisions parallel to Langer's lines produce less tension during healing → finer scars, less hypertrophic scarring. Transverse laparotomy scars generally heal better than vertical midline scars.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which sign is present in a patient with L4-L5 disc herniation compressing the L5 nerve root?
options: Weakness of great toe extension (EHL) and foot dorsiflexion
explanation: L5 nerve root (L4-L5 disc herniation): foot drop (tibialis anterior dorsiflexion weak), great toe extension weak (extensor hallucis longus), foot inversion weak (tibialis posterior). Sensory loss: medial dorsum of foot and big toe. Reflexes: no specific reflex (no L5 reflex test — note: ankle reflex = S1, knee = L3-4).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The spiral groove of the humerus transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery. Midshaft humeral fracture can damage the radial nerve here. What sign is seen?
options: Wrist drop + loss of finger extension + sensory loss over dorsal hand
Wrist drop + loss of elbow extension (triceps) + sensory loss
explanation: Midshaft humeral fracture + radial nerve injury at spiral groove: wrist drop (loss of wrist extension), finger and thumb drop (loss of MCP extension), loss of thumb abduction. Sensory loss: dorsal thumb-index webspace (anatomical snuff box area). Triceps and brachioradialis may be partially spared if injury is at the mid-groove level.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lymphatics of the breast drain primarily to which lymph nodes?
options: Axillary nodes (75% drainage — especially anterior/pectoral group)
explanation: Breast lymphatics: ~75% drains to axillary nodes (lateral, pectoral/anterior, central, subscapular/posterior, apical). ~25% drains to internal mammary (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels. The sentinel node (first node in chain) is identified in breast cancer staging.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Sentinel lymph node biopsy maps lymphatics in which cancers?
explanation: Sentinel node biopsy (technetium-99m colloid or blue dye): maps the first draining lymph node in breast cancer (usually axillary) and melanoma (regional). If the sentinel node is negative for cancer, formal lymph node dissection (with its morbidity — lymphedema) is avoided. Now standard of care for clinically node-negative breast cancer.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Virchow's node (Troisier's sign) is an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node indicating:
options: Abdominal/pelvic malignancy (left supraclavicular node is the terminal node of the thoracic duct)
explanation: Virchow's node: the left supraclavicular lymph node (located above the clavicle near the thoracic duct entry into the left venous angle). Enlargement = Troisier's sign, indicating metastasis from abdominal or pelvic malignancy (gastric, pancreatic, colon, ovarian, testicular cancer) spreading via the thoracic duct.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which structure passes through the muscular portion of the diaphragm?
explanation: Diaphragm openings: (1) Caval foramen T8 — IVC and right phrenic nerve (in central tendon — a membranous part). (2) Esophageal hiatus T10 — esophagus + left and right vagi (in MUSCULAR part — that's why hiatus hernias can compress the esophagus but not the IVC). (3) Aortic hiatus T12 — aorta, thoracic duct, azygos vein (posterior to diaphragm, so not compressed).

subject: Anatomy
stem: An 'Inguinal hernia': what is the relationship to the inferior epigastric artery?
options: Indirect hernia: medial to inferior epigastric; direct: lateral
Indirect hernia: lateral to inferior epigastric (enters deep inguinal ring lateral to the artery); Direct: medial (through Hesselbach's triangle)
explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (site of direct inguinal hernia): bounded laterally by inferior epigastric vessels, medially by lateral edge of rectus abdominis, inferiorly by inguinal ligament. Direct hernia passes MEDIAL to the inferior epigastric artery through the posterior wall. Indirect hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring LATERAL to the inferior epigastric artery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The inguinal canal runs obliquely and is bounded by which structures?
options: Floor: inguinal ligament + lacunar ligament; Roof: internal oblique + transversus arches; Anterior: EO aponeurosis (throughout) + IO (lateral 1/3); Posterior: transversalis fascia (lateral) + conjoint tendon (medial)
Only two walls — anterior and posterior
Floor: pubic bone; Roof: inguinal ligament
explanation: Inguinal canal (4 cm long in adults, oblique): Anterior wall = EO aponeurosis throughout + IO muscle laterally; Posterior wall = transversalis fascia laterally + conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) medially; Roof = arching fibers of IO and TA; Floor = inguinal ligament + lacunar ligament medially. Deep inguinal ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels) → superficial ring (in EO aponeurosis, above pubic tubercle).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Contents of the inguinal canal in males vs. females:
options: Males: spermatic cord; Females: round ligament of uterus + ilioinguinal nerve (in both)
Males: round ligament; Females: spermatic cord
explanation: Inguinal canal contents: in males = spermatic cord (ductus deferens, testicular artery, pampiniform plexus, cremasteric vessels, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve, sympathetic nerves) + ilioinguinal nerve. In females = round ligament of uterus + ilioinguinal nerve. The ilioinguinal nerve traverses the canal in both sexes.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Femoral vein lies in which position relative to the femoral artery in the femoral sheath?
explanation: In the femoral triangle, from lateral to medial: femoral Nerve (outside the sheath), femoral Artery, femoral Vein, femoral Canal (with lymphatics) — mnemonic NAVAL (N=nerve outside sheath, A=artery, V=vein, A=empty/lymph canal, L=lymphatics). The femoral vein lies MEDIAL to the femoral artery within the femoral sheath.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Spermatic cord passes through the inguinal canal. The vas deferens within it crosses which structure at the pelvic brim?
options: Ureter — the vas deferens crosses OVER the ureter ('water under the bridge')
explanation: Vas deferens (ductus deferens) descends in the pelvis, hooks around the inferior epigastric vessels at the deep ring, loops over the external iliac vessels, and crosses OVER the ureter near the bladder ('water under the bridge' — ureter is the water, vas is the bridge). Relevant in pelvic surgery (vasectomy reversal, renal transplant, ureter identification).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The cremasteric reflex is mediated by which nerve roots?
options: L1,L2 (genitofemoral nerve: afferent from L1; efferent via genital branch)
explanation: Cremasteric reflex: stroking the medial thigh skin (genitofemoral nerve, L1,L2 — femoral branch, afferent) → contraction of cremaster muscle (genitofemoral nerve, L1,L2 — genital branch, efferent) → testis retracts. Lost in UMN lesions above L1 or in genitofemoral nerve injury. Useful for assessing L1,L2 cord level.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen BELOW the piriformis muscle. What percentage of people have an anomalous split sciatic nerve passing through or above piriformis?
explanation: In ~10–12% of people, the sciatic nerve (or common peroneal division) passes through or above the piriformis muscle rather than entirely below it. This anatomical variant predisposes to piriformis syndrome — compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis muscle, causing buttock pain radiating down the leg (mimicking disc herniation but without lumbar disc pathology).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lumbosacral trunk (L4,L5) joins the sacral plexus at which level?
options: Junction with S1 over the ala of sacrum
explanation: Lumbosacral trunk: a branch of the L4,L5 ventral rami descends over the ala of sacrum to join the sacral plexus, combining with S1 to contribute to the sciatic nerve (L4,L5,S1,S2,S3). It is vulnerable to compression by the fetal head during labor, causing foot drop post-partum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The saphenous vein is used for coronary artery bypass because it is:
options: An artery, providing better long-term patency
A large accessible superficial vein with suitable diameter for bypass; 10-year patency ~50-60% (vs. LIMA ~90%)
explanation: Great saphenous vein: used as a conduit for CABG. Advantages: length, accessibility, diameter match. Disadvantages: vein graft undergoes intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis (50–60% patency at 10 years vs. LIMA >90%). Endoscopic harvesting reduces leg wound complications.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The medial canthus drains tears via the lacrimal canaliculi into the lacrimal sac, which then drains into:
options: The middle meatus of the nose
The inferior meatus of the nose via the nasolacrimal duct
explanation: Tear drainage: lacrimal gland → conjunctival sac → lacrimal puncta (upper and lower eyelids, at the medial canthus) → lacrimal canaliculi → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus of nose (under the inferior turbinate). Nasolacrimal duct obstruction (dacryostenosis) causes watering eye (epiphora) and neonatal mucopurulent discharge.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The facial artery crosses the mandible at which point where it is palpable?
options: At the angle of the mandible
At the anterior border of masseter muscle (notch of mandible)
explanation: Facial artery: passes deep to the digastric (posterior belly) and stylohyoid muscles, loops around the submandibular gland, then crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anterior border of masseter muscle (where its pulse can be palpated). It then winds up the face toward the medial canthus (becoming angular artery).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The zygomatic arch is formed by which two bones?
options: Zygomatic process of temporal bone + temporal process of zygomatic bone
explanation: Zygomatic arch: formed by the zygomatic process of temporal bone (posteriorly) + temporal process of zygomatic (malar) bone (anteriorly). The masseter muscle originates from its lower border. Depression fractures of the arch affect masticatory movement.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The submandibular triangle contains which gland, and its duct (Wharton's duct) opens where?
options: Parotid gland; opposite the upper 2nd molar
Submandibular gland; at the sublingual papilla (floor of mouth, lateral to frenulum)
Sublingual gland; at the sublingual fold
explanation: Submandibular triangle (part of anterior neck triangle): bounded by anterior and posterior bellies of digastric and mandible. Contains: submandibular gland (superficial part + deep part hooking around mylohyoid), facial artery/vein, and 12th CN. Wharton's duct (5 cm) opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'safe area' for parotid surgery to avoid facial nerve branches is which region?
options: At the anterior border of parotid gland (where terminal branches are more superficial and identifiable)
explanation: The facial nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen and enters the parotid gland, dividing into 5 branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical). The safest approach in parotidectomy is to identify the main trunk of CN VII (posterior to parotid, at the tragal pointer landmark just deep to the tympanomastoid suture), then dissect forward. The marginal mandibular branch is the most vulnerable during lower parotid/submandibular surgery.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The infraorbital foramen transmits which nerve and is at risk during which surgical procedure?
options: Infraorbital nerve (V2) and vessels — Caldwell-Luc procedure (maxillary sinus surgery) or Le Fort I osteotomy
explanation: Infraorbital foramen: ~1 cm below the infraorbital rim in the midpupillary line. Transmits the infraorbital nerve (branch of V2) and vessels. Anesthetized for dental procedures and infraorbital nerve blocks. At risk during Caldwell-Luc (radical maxillary antrostomy), Le Fort I osteotomy, and repair of maxillary fractures.

subject: Anatomy
stem: A cavernous sinus thrombosis from facial infection (e.g., furuncle of upper lip/nose) spreads via which venous route?
options: Angular vein → ophthalmic veins → cavernous sinus (danger area of face)
explanation: Danger area of face (upper lip to nasolabial fold to nose): facial vein communicates with cavernous sinus via angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein. Infection in this area can spread to the cavernous sinus → cavernous sinus thrombosis (proptosis, chemosis, external ophthalmoplegia, sepsis). The danger area has no valves in its veins.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Glabellar (corrugator) frown lines treated with botulinum toxin involve which muscle?
options: Corrugator supercilii (draws the brow medially and downward, creating vertical frown lines — innervated by temporal branch of CN VII)
explanation: Corrugator supercilii: originates from medial supraorbital ridge, inserts into skin above the brow. Pulls brow medially and downward (creates vertical glabellar lines/11s). Innervated by the temporal branch of CN VII. BoNT-A injection here (plus procerus and frontalis) treats glabellar lines.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The optic chiasm lies just above the pituitary gland. Which visual field defect is caused by a superior midline chiasmal lesion (craniopharyngioma pressing from above)?
options: Bitemporal upper quadrantanopia (superior nasal retinal fibers are affected first)
explanation: Craniopharyngioma: a suprasellar calcified cystic tumor compressing the chiasm from ABOVE. It first damages the superior nasal retinal fibers (which carry inferior temporal visual field). Initially: bitemporal superior quadrantanopia; progresses to complete bitemporal hemianopia. A pituitary adenoma pressing from below first causes inferior temporal field loss.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which cranial nerve is the afferent limb of the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia during eye compression)?
options: CN V (ophthalmic division, V1 — afferent via nasociliary nerve to trigeminal nucleus → vagal dorsal nucleus → CN X efferent)
explanation: Oculocardiac reflex (Aschner reflex): pressure on the eyeball → nasociliary nerve (V1) afferent → trigeminal brainstem nucleus → vagal motor nucleus → CN X efferent → heart slows (bradycardia). Important during strabismus surgery and enucleation. Treated by retrobulbar block or atropine.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The optic nerve is surrounded by meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia), so raised intracranial pressure can cause:
options: Papilloedema (disc swelling due to impaired axoplasmic flow in the raised ICP compressing the optic nerve sheath)
explanation: Papilloedema: the optic nerve is covered by all three meninges with a subarachnoid space continuous with the cranial subarachnoid space. Raised ICP transmits to the optic nerve sheath → impairs axoplasmic flow → optic disc swelling. Features: blurred disc margins, venous engorgement, hemorrhages. Visual acuity preserved until late.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle elevates the upper eyelid, and which nerve innervates each component?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris (LPS — CN III) and superior tarsal muscle (Müller's muscle — sympathetic)
Orbicularis oculi and levator palpebrae; CN III only
explanation: Upper eyelid elevation: levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) = CN III (oculomotor). Superior tarsal muscle (Müller's muscle) = sympathetic innervation (T1 from superior cervical ganglion). CN III palsy → ptosis (complete). Horner's syndrome (sympathetic loss) → partial ptosis (2–3 mm, drooping of the upper lid) + lower lid elevation (inferior tarsal muscle denervation).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The tympanic plexus (Jacobson's plexus) on the medial wall of the middle ear is formed by branches of which nerves?
options: CN IX (tympanic nerve, Jacobson's nerve) + sympathetic fibers from carotid plexus + CN VII (chorda tympani nearby)
explanation: Tympanic plexus: located on the promontory (medial wall of middle ear). Formed by Jacobson's nerve (tympanic branch of CN IX) + sympathetic fibers from carotid plexus. Gives rise to the lesser petrosal nerve (parasympathetic → otic ganglion → parotid). Also gives sensory branches to middle ear mucosa (why middle ear infections are painful — CN IX mediates).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'nerve to stapedius' is a branch of which cranial nerve, and its clinical test is:
options: CN VII — stapedius reflex (hyperacusis on same side when CN VII lesion is proximal to stapedius branch)
explanation: Nerve to stapedius: a branch of CN VII (given off in the vertical/mastoid segment of the facial canal). Stapedius reflexly contracts to dampen loud sounds. CN VII lesion proximal to stapedius branch → hyperacusis (sounds seem abnormally loud on the affected side). The stapedius reflex (measured by tympanometry) tests the integrity of the CN VII proximal to this branch.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which is the most common congenital hearing loss, and what is its etiology?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss due to genetic causes (connexin 26 / GJB2 mutation — ~50% of hereditary congenital deafness)
Conductive hearing loss due to ossicular malformation
Conductive from atresia of external auditory canal
explanation: Connexin 26 (gap junction protein beta 2, GJB2 gene) mutations are the most common cause of non-syndromic autosomal recessive congenital sensorineural hearing loss, accounting for ~50% of hereditary cases in some populations. Connexin 26 is critical for potassium recycling in the cochlea.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The palatine tonsil arterial supply: which is the dominant artery?
options: Tonsillar branch of facial artery (most important) + ascending pharyngeal, lesser palatine, lingual (dorsal lingual), and ascending palatine branches
explanation: Tonsillar blood supply: tonsillar branch of facial artery is the dominant supply (bleeding during tonsillectomy). Also: ascending pharyngeal, lesser palatine (from maxillary artery), dorsal lingual (from lingual artery), and ascending palatine. External palatine (paratonsillar) vein runs over the tonsil — its injury causes significant bleeding.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The internal carotid artery (ICA) enters the temporal bone through which foramen?
options: Carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone
Foramen lacerum (traverses it after exiting the carotid canal)
explanation: ICA enters the temporal bone through the carotid canal (in the petrous temporal bone), then curves anteriorly to exit at the foramen lacerum (a cartilaginous-filled opening it traverses but does not exit through), then enters the cavernous sinus. The carotid siphon (S-shaped ICA in the cavernous sinus) is a common site for aneurysms.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The mastoid process begins to develop at which age?
options: 2 years of age (before this, the facial nerve is superficial and at risk in surgeries)
explanation: The mastoid process develops after birth, becoming prominent by age 2. Before this (in neonates and infants), the stylomastoid foramen (and thus the facial nerve) is relatively superficial (without mastoid process to protect it). This is why otological surgery in young infants carries higher risk of CN VII injury.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The maxillary sinus is the largest paranasal sinus. It drains into which nasal structure?
options: Middle meatus (via the hiatus semilunaris in the ostiomeatal complex)
explanation: Maxillary sinus drainage: ostium opens into the hiatus semilunaris in the middle meatus via the ostiomeatal complex (also drains frontal sinus and anterior ethmoidal cells). The drainage opening is on the UPPER MEDIAL WALL of the sinus — therefore not dependent on gravity — explaining poor drainage and sinusitis susceptibility.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which paranasal sinus is present at birth?
options: Maxillary sinus and ethmoid cells (rudimentary at birth, maxillary reaches full size by 12 years)
All sinuses are present at birth
explanation: Paranasal sinus development: maxillary sinus and anterior ethmoidal cells are present at birth (rudimentary). Sphenoid sinus visible radiologically by 4–5 years. Frontal sinus not present until 5–6 years (fully formed by 20 years). This explains why frontal sinusitis is rare in young children.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The nasolacrimal duct is sometimes blocked in neonates. This is because:
options: The lower end (opening into inferior meatus) fails to canalize — Hasner's membrane fails to rupture
The lacrimal gland is not functional
There is no inferior meatus at birth
explanation: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (CNLDO): the most common cause is failure of canalization of the membrane of Hasner (at the inferior end of the nasolacrimal duct where it opens into the inferior meatus). Presents with persistent epiphora and mucopurulent discharge from birth. Resolves spontaneously in 90% by age 1; persistent cases need probing.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which sinusitis most commonly causes orbital cellulitis in children?
options: Ethmoidal sinusitis (direct extension through the thin lamina papyracea into the orbit)
explanation: Ethmoidal sinusitis → orbital cellulitis: the ethmoid sinuses are separated from the orbit by the lamina papyracea (extremely thin paper-like bone). This is the most common route of orbital infection (subperiosteal abscess) in children. Frontal sinusitis in adults can cause Pott's puffy tumor (subperiosteal abscess of the frontal bone).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The motor nucleus of CN VII (facial nucleus) is located in the pons. Which part of the facial nucleus supplies the upper face?
options: Dorsal division (receives bilateral cortical input — explains sparing of forehead in UMN lesions)
All facial nucleus receives only contralateral cortical input
explanation: Facial nucleus: the dorsal (superior) division supplies the forehead/eye muscles and receives bilateral cortical projections (both hemispheres). The ventral (inferior) division supplies the lower face and receives only contralateral cortical input. This explains why UMN (cortical/internal capsule) lesions spare the forehead but paralyse the contralateral lower face.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The chorda tympani nerve is a branch of CN VII. Where does it enter the infratemporal fossa?
options: Between the sphenomandibular ligament and the neck of mandible (petrotympanic fissure → medial to lateral pterygoid → joins lingual nerve)
explanation: Chorda tympani: exits the temporal bone via petrotympanic fissure (anterior to the eardrum), enters the infratemporal fossa between the sphenomandibular ligament and the neck of mandible (just medial to the lateral pterygoid), and joins the lingual nerve (V3). Carries taste from anterior 2/3 tongue and parasympathetic to submandibular ganglion.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) is innervated by which nerve?
options: CN XI (spinal accessory nerve — motor) + C2,C3 (proprioception/sensory)
explanation: SCM: supplied by CN XI (spinal accessory nerve — motor function). CN XI exits the skull via the jugular foramen, enters the SCM deeply, exits at its posterior border to cross the posterior triangle to reach trapezius. C2,C3 cervical branches provide proprioceptive (not motor) input to SCM. CN XI damage during posterior triangle lymph node biopsy → shoulder drop (trapezius) + SCM weakness.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Trapezius muscle receives motor innervation from which nerve?
options: CN XI (spinal accessory nerve) + proprioception from C3,C4
explanation: Trapezius: motor supply from CN XI (spinal accessory nerve — both SCM and trapezius). CN XI injury in posterior triangle surgery (node biopsy) → trapezius weakness → shoulder drop, difficulty abducting arm above 90°, winging of lateral scapula, chronic shoulder pain. C3,C4 provide proprioception.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Craniocervical junction instability in Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) is due to laxity of which ligament?
options: Transverse ligament of the atlas (which normally holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas)
explanation: Atlanto-axial instability (AAI) in Down syndrome: laxity of the transverse ligament of the atlas (which normally restrains the dens of the axis against the anterior arch of C1). Atlanto-dens interval >5 mm (children) or >3 mm (adults) on lateral flexion-extension X-ray is diagnostic. Screen all Down syndrome children before contact sports or anesthesia (neck extension risk).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'ring of LaCroix' in the long bone growth plate refers to which structure?
options: A fibrous and periosteal ring at the periphery of the physis (growth plate) that provides mechanical stability and contributes cells to the zone of Ranvier
explanation: Ring of LaCroix (ring apophysis): periosteal fibrocartilaginous ring surrounding the periphery of the growth plate (physis). It anchors the epiphysis to the metaphysis and provides mechanical stability during growth. The zone of Ranvier adjacent to it provides reserve/proliferating chondrocytes. Important in physeal injuries — Salter-Harris fractures.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The flexor retinaculum of the wrist has how many compartments (dorsal retinaculum of the extensor tendons)?
options: Six extensor compartments (1: APL+EPB; 2: ECRL+ECRB; 3: EPL; 4: EDC+EIP; 5: EDM; 6: ECU)
explanation: The extensor retinaculum (posterior retinaculum) at the wrist creates 6 synovial compartments containing the 12 extensor tendons: 1st=APL+EPB; 2nd=ECRL+ECRB; 3rd=EPL; 4th=EDC+EIP (or EI); 5th=EDM; 6th=ECU. De Quervain's affects the 1st compartment; intersection syndrome the 1st and 2nd junction.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The patella (largest sesamoid bone) is functionally important because:
options: It increases the mechanical advantage (lever arm) of the quadriceps by increasing the distance between the patellar tendon and the knee joint axis by ~50%
It stabilizes the knee against valgus forces
explanation: The patella increases the mechanical advantage of the quadriceps femoris by acting as a lever that keeps the patellar tendon away from the axis of rotation of the knee joint, increasing the angle of pull and amplifying the extensor torque by approximately 50%. Patellectomy significantly weakens knee extension.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'Schober test' is used to measure mobility of which part of the spine?
explanation: Schober test (modified Schober test): marks at L5 sacral junction and 10 cm above (standing). Normal lumbar flexion increases this distance by >5 cm (to >15 cm). Reduced in ankylosing spondylitis (lumbar flexion limited due to sacroiliac and lumbar facet joint fusion) and lumbar disc disease.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Kyphosis (posterior thoracic curvature) and lordosis (anterior lumbar curvature) are normal spinal curves. Which is the primary curve?
options: Lumbar lordosis (secondary curve — develops with walking)
Thoracic kyphosis and sacral kyphosis (primary — present at birth, persist from fetal C-shape)
explanation: Primary spinal curves: thoracic kyphosis and sacral/pelvic kyphosis — present at birth (concave anteriorly, 'C'-shaped fetal spine). Secondary (compensatory) curves: cervical lordosis (develops with head raising, ~3 months) and lumbar lordosis (develops with walking, ~1 year). Primary curves have thicker posterior vertebral bodies; secondary have thicker anterior vertebral bodies.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The ossification of the femoral head epiphysis begins at what age?
explanation: Femoral head ossification centre: appears between 3–6 months of age. At birth, the femoral head is entirely cartilaginous. Absence of the ossification centre on X-ray in infants >6 months may suggest DDH (developmental dysplasia of hip), avascular necrosis, or multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. Ultrasound is used for DDH in infants <3–4 months (before ossification).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'danger zone' for the brachial artery during antecubital venous access (PICC line) is:
options: The artery is safe in this location
The brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon; inadvertent puncture can cause hematoma or pseudoaneurysm
The cephalic vein is lateral and the artery is nowhere near
Only the median nerve is at risk
explanation: Antecubital fossa relationships (lateral to medial): biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve. The brachial artery (2–3 cm wide) lies just medial to the bicipital tendon, so medially placed cannulas or PICC lines are at risk of arterial injury. Basilic vein (more medial, ideal PICC vein) passes close to the median nerve and brachial artery at the elbow.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The dorsal venous arch of the foot drains into which two superficial veins?
options: Medially into great saphenous vein (medial marginal vein) and laterally into small saphenous vein (lateral marginal vein)
Both into the great saphenous vein
explanation: Dorsal venous arch of foot: the superficial venous network on the dorsum of the foot. Medial marginal vein → great saphenous vein (passes anterior to medial malleolus, up the medial leg). Lateral marginal vein → small saphenous vein (passes posterior to lateral malleolus, up the posterior calf to popliteal vein).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Compartment syndrome of the leg can occur in which four compartments?
options: Anterior (muscles for dorsiflexion), lateral (peroneal), deep posterior (toe flexors, tibialis posterior), and superficial posterior (gastrocnemius, soleus)
explanation: Four leg compartments: (1) Anterior: TA, EDL, EHL, peroneus tertius (deep peroneal nerve); (2) Lateral: peroneus longus and brevis (superficial peroneal nerve); (3) Deep posterior: TP, FDL, FHL, popliteus (tibial nerve); (4) Superficial posterior: gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris (sural nerve). All four can be affected in compartment syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'unhappy triad' sports injury: which mechanism produces it?
options: Valgus stress (lateral blow to the knee) + external rotation + flexion — ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus are torn
explanation: Unhappy triad mechanism: a valgus force applied to the lateral aspect of a planted, flexed, and externally rotated knee (e.g., a tackle from the side in contact sports) simultaneously tears the ACL, MCL, and medial meniscus. The lateral meniscus is now recognized as the more commonly injured in the acute setting (but medial is classically quoted).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The plantarfascial insertion is on the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity. Plantar fasciitis is diagnosed by:
options: Localized tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle (origin of plantar fascia), worse with first steps in the morning
X-ray showing a calcaneal spur (though spurs are often incidental)
explanation: Plantar fasciitis: inflammation at the proximal attachment of the plantar fascia (medial process of calcaneal tuberosity). Classic history: first-step pain in the morning (postinactivity pain), tenderness at the heel medially. Treated with stretching (plantar fascia + Achilles), orthotics, and NSAIDs. Calcaneal spurs are seen in ~50% of plantar fasciitis patients but are not diagnostic.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'critical zone' of the supraspinatus tendon (site of most tears) is located approximately:
options: 1 cm proximal to the insertion on the greater tuberosity (relatively avascular zone)
explanation: The critical zone of the supraspinatus: a relatively avascular zone approximately 1 cm proximal to the bone insertion on the greater tuberosity, where the tendon is most prone to degenerative tears. This zone is the watershed between the osseous insertion blood supply and the muscular blood supply, explaining its vulnerability to degeneration and rupture.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'bicipital groove' (intertubercular sulcus) of the humerus lodges which tendon?
options: Long head of biceps tendon (retained by transverse humeral ligament)
explanation: The bicipital (intertubercular) groove on the anterior humerus: bounded by lesser tuberosity (medially, subscapularis attached) and greater tuberosity (laterally, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor). The long head of biceps tendon runs in this groove, held by the transverse humeral ligament. Bicipital groove tenderness indicates biceps tendinopathy (Yergason's test, Speed's test).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The trochlea of the humerus articulates with which forearm bone?
explanation: Humeroulnar joint: trochlea of humerus (pulley-shaped medial condyle) articulates with the trochlear notch (semilunar notch) of the ulna, forming the primary hinge of the elbow. The humeroradial joint: capitulum of humerus articulates with the radial head (allows flexion and rotation). Together they form the elbow joint.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve' is the continuation of which nerve?
options: Musculocutaneous nerve (after piercing the brachial fascia at the elbow)
explanation: Lateral antebrachial (cutaneous) nerve of forearm: the terminal sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve. After supplying coracobrachialis, biceps, and brachialis (motor), the musculocutaneous nerve pierces the brachial fascia lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow, continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (sensation to lateral forearm).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which cranial nerve is responsible for the sensation of pain from the nasal septum?
options: Ophthalmic (V1) via anterior ethmoidal nerve (anterior/superior septum) and maxillary (V2) via nasopalatine nerve (posterior/inferior septum)
explanation: Nasal septum sensation: (1) Anterior superior part: anterior ethmoidal nerve (branch of nasociliary nerve → ophthalmic V1). (2) Posterior inferior part: nasopalatine nerve (branch of pterygopalatine nerve → maxillary V2). Nasal septal hematoma (after nasal trauma) deprives the septal cartilage of perichondrial blood supply → avascular necrosis → saddle nose deformity.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The auditory cortex is located in which gyrus?
options: Heschl's gyri (transverse temporal gyri) — in the superior temporal plane (planum temporale) within the lateral sulcus
explanation: Primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyri, Brodmann areas 41,42): located on the superior surface of the superior temporal gyrus, within the lateral (Sylvian) fissure. The left Heschl's gyrus is typically dominant (larger planum temporale on the left). Adjacent auditory association cortex (area 22) is part of Wernicke's area.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Calcaneal fractures most commonly occur from which mechanism?
options: Axial compressive load (fall from height, landing on heels) — Böhler's angle is reduced (<20°)
explanation: Calcaneal fractures: most common tarsal bone fracture. Mechanism: axial compression (fall from height). Böhler's tuber-joint angle (normal 20–40°) is reduced to <20° in fractures. They are associated with spinal compression fractures (10–15% — same axial loading mechanism) and bilateral in 10%. Often intraarticular, involve the subtalar joint.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The anatomical position of the vermiform appendix most likely to cause pain at McBurney's point is:
explanation: Retrocecal position (~74%) is most common for the appendix and still produces McBurney's point tenderness because the cecum is in the RIF. Pelvic appendix may cause pelvic/suprapubic pain. Retrocecal appendix may cause right flank pain and less anterior guarding.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lesser omentum (gastrohepatic and hepatoduodenal ligaments) connects which structures?
options: Liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach + first part of duodenum
explanation: Lesser omentum (peritoneal fold from the porta hepatis): (1) gastrohepatic ligament — connects liver to lesser curvature of stomach; (2) hepatoduodenal ligament (free right edge) — connects liver to first part of duodenum; contains portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, CBD).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'bare area' of the liver is located on which surface and lacks which covering?
options: Posterior-superior surface; lacks peritoneal covering (directly adherent to diaphragm)
explanation: Bare area of liver: posterior-superior surface of the right lobe, bounded by the upper and lower layers of the coronary ligament (and right triangular ligament). This area has no peritoneal (serosal) covering and is directly adherent to the diaphragm. Clinically relevant in hydatid disease (can rupture into pleurae) and hepatocellular carcinoma staging.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) descends through the superior mediastinum on which surface of the heart?
explanation: Phrenic nerves (C3,C4,C5 — 'keep the diaphragm alive'): each phrenic nerve runs anterior to the hilum of the lung, between the pericardium and mediastinal pleura. Right phrenic: runs along right side of SVC, right atrium, IVC. Left phrenic: crosses over the aortic arch, runs over left ventricle. Their course is relevant in cardiac surgery and pericardiocentesis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The subphrenic space is the compartment between the liver and diaphragm. A right subphrenic abscess can cause referred pain to:
options: Right shoulder (via right phrenic nerve C3,4,5)
explanation: Right subphrenic abscess: pus collects between the right lobe of liver and the right hemidiaphragm. Irritation of the right diaphragm → right phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) stimulation → referred pain to the right shoulder tip (same dermatomes as the neck/shoulder, C3,4,5). Left subphrenic → left shoulder pain (e.g., splenic abscess/rupture = Kehr's sign).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The sigmoid colon is unique in having a mesentery (sigmoid mesocolon). Why is it prone to volvulus?
options: The long redundant sigmoid mesocolon with a narrow base predisposes to twisting (volvulus)
Its wall is thinner than other colon segments
explanation: Sigmoid volvulus: the sigmoid colon (having a mesentery — sigmoid mesocolon) can twist on itself, especially when the mesocolon has a long redundant loop with a narrow attachment base (common in elderly, institutionalized patients, high-fiber diet countries). Causes large bowel obstruction with a 'coffee bean' sign on X-ray.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which is the only intrinsic muscle of the larynx that abducts the vocal cords?
