explanation: Posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA): the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords (bilateral contraction opens the glottis for breathing). 'PCA = precious and cannot afford to lose.' Bilateral RLN palsy paralyses all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, leaving the PCA paralysed → adducted vocal cords → stridor and respiratory obstruction.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The bony orbit is formed by how many bones?
options: 7 bones (frontal, zygomatic, maxilla, palatine, ethmoid, sphenoid, lacrimal)
explanation: Seven bones form the bony orbit: (1) Frontal (roof mainly), (2) Zygomatic (lateral wall partly), (3) Maxilla (floor mainly), (4) Palatine (posterior floor), (5) Ethmoid (medial wall, lamina papyracea), (6) Sphenoid (posterior apex, lesser and greater wings), (7) Lacrimal (medial wall, lacrimal groove). Mnemonic: 'Few Zebras Make People Elope Seriously Late.'

subject: Anatomy
stem: The lacrimal gland is divided into orbital and palpebral parts by which muscle?
options: Levator palpebrae superioris (aponeurosis divides the gland)
explanation: Lacrimal gland: located in the lacrimal fossa (superolateral orbit). The aponeurosis of LPS (levator palpebrae superioris) divides it into a larger orbital lobe (in the lacrimal fossa) and a smaller palpebral lobe (in the upper lid). Dacryoadenitis (inflammation) causes S-shaped ptosis (drooping of the lateral upper lid).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which embryological structure forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands?
options: 3rd branchial pouch (dorsal wing = inferior parathyroids; ventral wing = thymus)
explanation: 3rd branchial pouch: dorsal wing → inferior parathyroid glands (migrate inferiorly with the thymus to their final position, ending up inferior to superior parathyroids — hence the 'crossed' naming). Ventral wing → thymus (migrates into the anterior mediastinum). 4th branchial pouch: superior parathyroid glands and C-cells of ultimobranchial body.

subject: Anatomy
stem: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) results from absence of derivatives of which branchial pouches?
options: 3rd and 4th branchial pouches (thymic aplasia + absent/hypoplastic parathyroids + aortic arch anomalies)
explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, velocardiofacial syndrome): neural crest cell migration failure affects 3rd and 4th branchial pouches. Results in: thymic aplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, tetany), conotruncal heart defects (Tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus), and palatal/facial anomalies.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Which vascular characteristic makes it prone to avascular necrosis?
options: Retrograde (distal to proximal) blood supply from dorsal carpal branches; proximal pole is at risk when waist fractures disrupt this supply
Blood supply only from the ulnar artery
explanation: Scaphoid blood supply: dorsal (intercarpal) branches of radial artery enter the dorsal surface and supply the scaphoid in a distal-to-proximal (retrograde) direction. Fracture at the waist interrupts this supply to the proximal pole → avascular necrosis of the proximal pole in 15–30% of waist fractures and 100% of proximal pole fractures.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The palmar aponeurosis (palmar fascia) is the thickened deep fascia of the palm. In Dupuytren's contracture, which rays are most commonly affected?
options: Ring finger (4th ray) most commonly, followed by little finger (5th ray) and middle finger (3rd ray)
explanation: Dupuytren's contracture: fibroproliferative disorder of palmar fascia. Ring finger most commonly affected, then little finger, middle finger. Thumb and index rarely affected. Progressive MCP and PIP contracture. Risk factors: diabetes, alcohol, epilepsy (phenytoin), liver disease, northern European ancestry. Treatment: needle aponeurotomy or fasciectomy.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The palmaris longus tendon is absent in approximately what percentage of the population?
explanation: Palmaris longus (PL) is absent in 10–20% of people (estimates vary by study), most commonly unilaterally. It is the most common anatomical variant in the forearm. Clinically: its absence causes no functional deficit, and the tendon is often used as a graft for reconstructive procedures (flexor tendon repair, palmar fascia, ligament reconstruction).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) blood most commonly collects in which cisterns?
options: Perimesencephalic cisterns, sylvian fissures, and basal cisterns (sylvian/chiasmatic/interpeduncular cisterns)
explanation: SAH (most commonly from berry aneurysm rupture): blood fills the subarachnoid space preferentially in the basal cisterns (interpeduncular, chiasmatic, sylvian fissures). On CT, hyperdense blood appears in these locations. The pattern can suggest aneurysm location: perimesencephalic = basilar tip; sylvian = MCA; interhemispheric = ACA/ACoA.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The anterior communicating artery (ACoA) connects which vessels?
options: Left and right posterior cerebral arteries
Left and right anterior cerebral arteries (ACAs)
explanation: ACoA: connects the left and right A1 segments of the anterior cerebral arteries, completing the anterior part of the circle of Willis. It is the most common site for intracranial aneurysm (~30–35%). ACoA aneurysm rupture causes SAH and can cause infarction of the anterior hypothalamus (diabetes insipidus), frontal lobe, and corpus callosum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: A Duret haemorrhage (brainstem haemorrhage secondary to herniation) occurs in which part of the brainstem?
options: Midbrain and upper pons (midline/paramedian perforating vessels torn during downward displacement of the brainstem)
explanation: Duret haemorrhage: linear midline/paramedian haemorrhages in the midbrain and upper pons, caused by downward transtentorial herniation (cingulate or uncal herniation). As the brainstem is displaced downward, basilar artery perforators are stretched and torn. Duret haemorrhages are secondary (herniation) not primary brain injuries.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which hormone, if given to the mother before birth, accelerates fetal lung maturity by stimulating surfactant production?
options: Corticosteroids (betamethasone/dexamethasone) — stimulate Type II pneumocyte maturation and surfactant synthesis
explanation: Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM × 2 doses, or dexamethasone): given to mothers at risk of preterm delivery (24–34 weeks) to accelerate fetal lung maturity. They stimulate Type II pneumocyte differentiation and surfactant (DPPC) production, reducing the incidence and severity of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS/HMD) by 50%.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The pronephros (first excretory organ in embryology) is functional in which species?
options: Fish and amphibians; in humans it is vestigial and degenerates by 5th week
explanation: Pronephros: forms at 3rd–4th week in humans as a vestigial, non-functional structure, degenerating by the 5th week. It is the functional larval kidney in fish and amphibians. Its duct (pronephric duct, which becomes the mesonephric/Wolffian duct) is important for subsequent development of the mesonephros and metanephros.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The fetal circulation bypasses the lungs via which two structures?
options: Foramen ovale and ductus venosus and ductus arteriosus (three bypasses)
explanation: Fetal circulation has THREE bypasses: (1) Foramen ovale (right atrium → left atrium, bypassing lung); (2) Ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk → aortic arch, bypassing lung); (3) Ductus venosus (umbilical vein → IVC, bypassing liver). At birth, all three close: FO → fossa ovalis; DA → ligamentum arteriosum; DV → ligamentum venosum.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Cri du chat syndrome is caused by deletion of which chromosome and which characteristic feature gives it its name?
options: Deletion of short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-); high-pitched cat-like cry due to laryngeal maldevelopment
explanation: Cri du chat (cry of the cat) syndrome: deletion of chromosome 5p (5p-). Cardinal features: cat-like cry (laryngeal underdevelopment/small larynx), intellectual disability, microcephaly, low birth weight, widely spaced eyes (hypertelorism), round face, and simian crease. No single-gene therapy available; supportive care.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'anatomical dead space' in the respiratory tract is approximately:
options: 150 mL (conducting airways — trachea, bronchi, bronchioles — that participate in bulk air movement but not gas exchange)
explanation: Anatomical dead space: ~150 mL (approximately 2 mL/kg body weight). This is the volume of the conducting airways (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles down to terminal bronchioles) that is ventilated but does not participate in gas exchange. Normal tidal volume ~500 mL; alveolar ventilation = (TV - dead space) × respiratory rate.

subject: Anatomy
stem: What type of joint is the sternoclavicular joint and what movements does it allow?
options: Hinge joint; only flexion and extension
Saddle joint (sellar) — synovial joint with an articular disc; allows elevation/depression, protraction/retraction, and limited rotation of the clavicle
explanation: Sternoclavicular joint: the only true synovial joint connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton. Saddle (sellar) joint with an intraarticular fibrocartilaginous disc. Allows: elevation/depression (shoulder shrug), protraction/retraction, and axial rotation of the clavicle. Dislocation is usually anterior (posterior dislocation is dangerous — compresses trachea/great vessels).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which of the following is NOT a content of the cavernous sinus?
options: CN VI (abducens) — runs freely in the sinus
explanation: Cavernous sinus contents: CN III (in the lateral wall), CN IV (lateral wall), CN VI (runs freely within the sinus — not in the lateral wall, hence most commonly affected), V1 ophthalmic (lateral wall), V2 maxillary (lateral wall), and the internal carotid artery (ICA siphon) with surrounding sympathetic plexus. V2 maxillary is in the lateral wall; V3 is NOT in the cavernous sinus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The muscle responsible for 'scapular elevation' (shrugging the shoulder) is:
explanation: Shoulder shrug/scapular elevation: upper trapezius (CN XI) and levator scapulae (dorsal scapular nerve, C3,C4,C5). CN XI lesion → inability to shrug the shoulder on the affected side, drooping of the shoulder, and difficulty abducting the arm above 90° (trapezius cannot upwardly rotate the scapula).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The angle of Louis (sternal angle) is a palpable landmark used to identify:
options: 2nd rib/costal cartilage (for counting ribs) and T4/T5 vertebral level
explanation: Sternal angle (angle of Louis, manubriosternal junction): where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. At T4/T5 level. Key landmark: (1) 2nd rib articulates here — starting point for counting ribs and intercostal spaces; (2) tracheal bifurcation (carina); (3) aortic arch begins/ends; (4) superior/inferior mediastinum division.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
explanation: Femoral triangle boundaries: superiorly = inguinal ligament; laterally = sartorius; medially = adductor longus. Floor = iliopsoas (lateral) and pectineus (medial). Roof = fascia lata with saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Contents: femoral nerve (lateral), femoral artery, femoral vein, femoral canal (medial).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The longest nerve in the body is:
options: Vagus nerve (CN X) — from brainstem to the pelvic viscera
explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) is the longest cranial nerve and the longest nerve in the body, extending from the medulla oblongata through the neck, chest, and abdomen to the splenic flexure of the colon. The sciatic nerve is the thickest (widest diameter) peripheral nerve.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The floor of the fourth ventricle contains which structures related to cranial nerve nuclei?
options: Facial colliculus (CN VI nucleus + CN VII genu), hypoglossal triangle (CN XII), vagal triangle (CN X DMN), area postrema (vomiting center)
explanation: The rhomboid fossa (floor of 4th ventricle): facial colliculus = CN VI nucleus wrapped by CN VII internal genu (raised prominence), hypoglossal triangle (CN XII), vagal triangle (dorsal motor nucleus of CN X), locus coeruleus (noradrenergic), striae medullares. Area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone, vomiting) is at the caudal end.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The left vagus nerve in the chest gives which important branch?
options: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hooks under aortic arch at ligamentum arteriosum)
explanation: Left vagus nerve descends in the left carotid sheath, crosses the left subclavian artery, and enters the chest anterior to the aortic arch. In the chest, it gives off the left RLN (hooks under the aortic arch at the level of the ligamentum arteriosum) and continues as the posterior vagal trunk (part of the esophageal plexus) through the esophageal hiatus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The pterygoid plexus of veins communicates with the cavernous sinus via which route?
options: Emissary veins through the foramen ovale and foramen of Vesalius
explanation: Pterygoid plexus (in the infratemporal fossa, around the lateral pterygoid muscle) communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins passing through foramen ovale and foramen of Vesalius (emissary sphenoidal foramen). Also communicates with facial vein via deep facial vein. Dental infection → pterygoid plexus → cavernous sinus.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which nerve is specifically tested by the 'Tinel's test at the cubital tunnel' and where is the test performed?
options: Radial nerve at the radial groove
Ulnar nerve — tapping the ulnar nerve posterior to the medial epicondyle produces tingling in the ring and little fingers
explanation: Tinel's test at cubital tunnel: tapping over the ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel (groove posterior to medial epicondyle) reproduces paresthesia in the ulnar nerve distribution (ring and little fingers, medial forearm). Positive test indicates cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'tympanic membrane' (eardrum) has its anterior portion supplied by which nerve for sensation?
options: Auriculotemporal nerve (V3) anterosuperiorly + auricular branch of vagus (CN X, Arnold's nerve) posteroinferiorly
explanation: Tympanic membrane sensation: anterior-superior = auriculotemporal nerve (V3); anterior-inferior = auricular branch of vagus (Arnold's nerve, CN X); posterior = auricular branch of vagus. Stimulation of Arnold's nerve (CN X) during ear syringing/otoscopy can trigger a cough reflex (auricular-vagal cough reflex).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Injury to which thoracic sympathetic fibers causes loss of sweating on the ipsilateral face?
options: T1 preganglionic fibers (synapse in superior cervical ganglion; postganglionic fibers travel via the plexus on the ICA to reach the head/face)
explanation: Facial sweating is controlled by T1 sympathetic preganglionic fibers → superior cervical ganglion (at C2-C3) → postganglionic fibers travel along the external carotid artery and internal carotid artery to reach the face and head. Horner's syndrome (T1 disruption) causes ipsilateral facial anhidrosis (depending on the level of injury — preganglionic vs. postganglionic).

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which cell type in the epidermis provides immunological surveillance?
options: Langerhans cells (dendritic cells, bone marrow derived, MHC II positive)
explanation: Langerhans cells: antigen-presenting dendritic cells of the epidermis (suprabasal layers), derived from bone marrow monocyte precursors. They express MHC class II (HLA-DR) and CD1a. Birbeck granules (tennis racket-shaped on EM) are characteristic. They capture antigens and migrate to lymph nodes to present to T-helper cells. Pathologically: Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'zone of polarizing activity' (ZPA) in the developing limb bud controls which aspect of limb development?
options: Anteroposterior axis (radial-ulnar or thumb-little finger axis) via SHH signaling
explanation: ZPA (zone of polarizing activity): a region of posterior limb bud mesenchyme that secretes Sonic Hedgehog (SHH), controlling anteroposterior (AP) patterning of the limb (deciding which side becomes thumb/radial vs. little finger/ulnar). High SHH → posterior digits (4th, 5th); low SHH → anterior digits (1st, 2nd). ZPA transplantation to the anterior limb bud induces mirror-image digit duplication.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) is required for which aspect of limb development?
options: Proximodistal outgrowth and patterning of limb bud (from shoulder to fingertips)
explanation: Apical ectodermal ridge (AER): thickened ectodermal ridge at the tip of the limb bud. Maintains the underlying progress zone (mesenchyme) in a proliferative, undifferentiated state, driving proximal-to-distal limb outgrowth. AER secretes FGF (FGF4, FGF8); removal causes truncation of distal limb elements. Thalidomide disrupts FGF signaling → phocomelia (very short limbs, hands near shoulder).

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'carpal tunnel' contains how many tendons?
explanation: Carpal tunnel contents: median nerve + 4 FDS tendons (for index, middle, ring, little) + 4 FDP tendons (for same fingers) + 1 FPL tendon = 1 nerve + 9 tendons (10 total structures). The flexor carpi radialis runs in a separate groove in the trapezium outside the carpal tunnel, and FCU/pisiform are superficial.

subject: Anatomy
stem: Which ligament is the primary stabilizer of the ankle against excessive inversion?
options: ATFL (anterior talofibular ligament) in plantarflexion, but the CFL (calcaneofibular ligament) provides primary lateral ankle stability in neutral position
explanation: Lateral ankle ligament complex: ATFL (weakest, most commonly torn), CFL, PTFL (strongest). ATFL is primary restraint to inversion in plantarflexion; CFL is primary restraint in neutral and dorsiflexion. Grading ankle sprains: Grade I = ATFL sprain; Grade II = ATFL + CFL; Grade III = ATFL + CFL + PTFL rupture.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'Salter-Harris classification' of physeal (growth plate) fractures: which type has the WORST prognosis?
options: Type V (C — crush/compression of the physis — worst prognosis for growth arrest)
explanation: Salter-Harris classification (SALTR): Type I = physis only; II = physis + metaphysis (most common, best prognosis); III = physis + epiphysis (intraarticular); IV = epiphysis + physis + metaphysis; V = crush/compression of physis (worst prognosis — damages the germinal zone, causes growth arrest/angular deformity). SALTR mnemonic: Slip, Above, Lower, Through, Rammed.

subject: Anatomy
stem: The 'arch of the aorta' has three branches in which order from proximal to distal?
options: Left common carotid, right common carotid, subclavian
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery
Left subclavian, brachiocephalic, left common carotid
Right and left common carotid arteries, then subclavian
explanation: Aortic arch branches (right to left/proximal to distal): (1) brachiocephalic trunk (innominate artery) — divides into right common carotid + right subclavian; (2) left common carotid artery; (3) left subclavian artery. A cervical aortic arch or aberrant right subclavian (arteria lusoria) are common variants. The left vertebral artery arises directly from the aortic arch in ~5% as a fourth branch.

subject: Physiology
stem: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is approximately:
explanation: Resting membrane potential (RMP) of a typical neuron is approximately -70 mV (more negative inside). It is determined mainly by the K+ equilibrium potential (K+ leaks out via leak channels), the Na+/K+ ATPase pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in — electrogenic, contributes -4 mV), and selective membrane permeability to K+ > Na+ at rest.

subject: Physiology
stem: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a single ion. For K+ in a neuron, the equilibrium potential (EK) is approximately:
explanation: Nernst equation: E = (RT/zF) × ln([ion]o/[ion]i). For K+ (z=-1): EK ≈ -90 mV (because intracellular K+ is ~140 mM, extracellular ~4 mM). For Na+: ENa ≈ +60 mV. The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation gives RMP by combining permeabilities of all ions.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which transport mechanism moves glucose into intestinal epithelial cells from the lumen?
explanation: Intestinal glucose absorption: luminal side uses SGLT1 (sodium-glucose linked transporter 1) — secondary active transport that couples glucose uptake to Na+ entry down its electrochemical gradient. The Na+/K+ ATPase on the basolateral side maintains the Na+ gradient. Glucose exits the basolateral side via GLUT2 (facilitated diffusion).

subject: Physiology
stem: Osmolarity of normal plasma is approximately:
explanation: Normal plasma osmolarity is 285–295 mOsm/L (often estimated as 290 mOsm/L). Calculated: 2×[Na+] + [glucose]/18 + [BUN]/2.8. Sodium is the dominant determinant. Osmolality (mOsm/kg water) ≈ osmolarity in plasma. Regulated by hypothalamic osmoreceptors → ADH release → renal water reabsorption.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which law governs the relationship between the volume, pressure, and flow in the cardiovascular and respiratory systems?
options: Poiseuille's law (flow = π×r4×ΔP / 8×η×L) — flow is proportional to radius to the 4th power
explanation: Poiseuille's law: flow (Q) = (ΔP × π × r⁴) / (8 × η × L). Flow is proportional to the FOURTH POWER of radius — halving the radius reduces flow 16-fold. Resistance (R) = 8ηL/πr⁴. This is the basis for the profound effect of vessel radius on resistance (arteriole constriction dramatically increases peripheral resistance).

subject: Physiology
stem: Fick's principle for measuring cardiac output requires measurement of:
options: Heart rate and stroke volume only
Oxygen consumption (VO2) divided by arteriovenous oxygen difference [VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2)]
explanation: Fick's principle: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2). If VO2 = 250 mL/min and A-V O2 difference = 50 mL/L (5 mL/dL), then CO = 250/50 = 5 L/min. This principle underlies thermodilution cardiac output measurement and dye dilution methods.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which ion is primarily responsible for the upstroke (phase 0) of the ventricular action potential?
options: Na+ rapid inflow (through fast voltage-gated Na+ channels)
explanation: Ventricular AP phases: Phase 0 (upstroke) = fast Na+ influx (INa) through voltage-gated Na+ channels (threshold ~-65 mV → peak +30 mV). Phase 1 = transient K+ efflux (Ito). Phase 2 (plateau) = Ca2+ influx (ICa-L) balancing K+ efflux. Phase 3 = delayed rectifier K+ efflux. Phase 4 = RMP maintained by IK1.

subject: Physiology
stem: The action potential in pacemaker cells (SA node) lacks which phase compared to ventricular myocytes?
options: Phase 2 (plateau) and the rapid Na+ phase 0 — pacemaker cells have a slow Ca2+-dependent upstroke
explanation: SA node action potential: NO fast Na+ channel (TTX-resistant because RMP is -60 mV — too depolarized for fast Na+ channels). Phase 0: slow upstroke via L-type Ca2+ channels (ICa-L). Phase 3: K+ efflux. Phase 4: spontaneous diastolic depolarization via If (funny current — Na+/K+ inward current), IK decay, and ICa-T. No true plateau (phase 2).

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal cardiac output (CO) at rest is approximately:
options: 5 L/min (stroke volume ~70 mL × heart rate ~70 bpm)
explanation: Normal resting CO: ~5 L/min (range 4–8 L/min). CO = Stroke volume (SV) × Heart rate (HR). SV ≈ 70 mL; HR ≈ 70 bpm; CO = 70 × 70 = 4,900 mL/min ≈ 5 L/min. Cardiac index (CI) = CO/BSA = 2.5–4 L/min/m².

subject: Physiology
stem: Frank-Starling law of the heart states that:
options: Contractility is inversely proportional to preload
Stroke volume increases as end-diastolic volume increases (within physiological limits) — greater preload → greater force
explanation: Frank-Starling mechanism: as end-diastolic volume (EDV) increases, the sarcomeres are stretched to a more optimal overlap, increasing the force of contraction and thus stroke volume. The ventricular function curve (Starling curve) shifts up with positive inotropes and down with heart failure. Preload = EDV (related to venous return).

subject: Physiology
stem: The absolute refractory period of a nerve corresponds to which phase of the action potential?
options: Phase 0 to phase 3 (upstroke through repolarization) — Na+ channels are inactivated, no new AP possible
explanation: Absolute refractory period: occurs during Phase 0-3 of the action potential (from depolarization to repolarization). The fast Na+ channels are in an 'inactivated' state (the inactivation gate is closed) and cannot be reopened by any stimulus, no matter how strong. This prevents re-excitation and ensures unidirectional AP propagation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Myelin sheath accelerates nerve conduction by which mechanism?
options: Increasing the capacitance of the nerve membrane
Saltatory conduction — the AP jumps between Nodes of Ranvier (where membrane is unmyelinated), dramatically increasing conduction velocity
Preventing K+ loss from the axon
explanation: Saltatory conduction (Latin: saltare = to jump): myelin insulates the axon between Nodes of Ranvier (where voltage-gated Na+ channels are densely concentrated). The AP 'jumps' from node to node, greatly increasing conduction velocity (up to 70–120 m/s in large myelinated A-alpha fibers) with less energy consumption.

subject: Physiology
stem: Classification of nerve fibers by diameter and myelination: which fiber type carries pain and temperature?
options: A-delta fibers (myelinated — sharp, well-localized pain, cold) and C fibers (unmyelinated — dull, burning pain, warmth)
explanation: Pain fiber classification: Aδ (A-delta) fibers — myelinated, 2–5 μm, 5–30 m/s — fast pain (sharp, pricking, well-localized). C fibers — unmyelinated, <1 μm, 0.5–2 m/s — slow pain (burning, aching, poorly localized), also warm temperature, itch. A-alpha (Ia, Ib): proprioception, motor. A-beta: light touch, pressure.

subject: Physiology
stem: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) transmitter is acetylcholine (ACh). After release, ACh is degraded by which enzyme?
explanation: ACh released at the NMJ binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, causing depolarization (end plate potential). AChE rapidly degrades ACh into choline (recycled) and acetate, terminating the signal. AChE inhibitors (neostigmine, edrophonium) are used to treat myasthenia gravis. Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) synthesizes ACh.

subject: Physiology
stem: Myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against which receptor?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ
Nicotinic ACh receptor (nAChR) on the post-synaptic motor end plate — reduces functional receptors
explanation: Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune destruction/blockade of nicotinic ACh receptors (nAChR, Nm subtype) at the NMJ by IgG antibodies. This reduces the number of functional receptors → decremental end plate potentials → fatigable muscle weakness. Anti-MuSK antibodies are found in 5% of seronegative cases. Treated with AChE inhibitors + immunosuppression.

subject: Physiology
stem: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) targets which structure at the NMJ?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) on the pre-synaptic motor nerve terminal — reduces ACh release
explanation: LEMS: autoimmune attack on P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) on the pre-synaptic terminal. Reduced Ca2+ influx → reduced ACh vesicle fusion and release → reduced end plate potential. Paradoxically, repeated stimulation causes INCREMENTAL response (unlike MG's decremental). Associated with small-cell lung carcinoma.

subject: Physiology
stem: The threshold for an action potential to fire is typically:
options: Equal to the resting membrane potential
~15–20 mV more positive than RMP (approximately -55 to -50 mV in a neuron with RMP of -70 mV)
explanation: Threshold potential is the membrane potential at which enough voltage-gated Na+ channels open to produce an all-or-nothing AP. For a neuron with RMP -70 mV, threshold is approximately -55 mV (15 mV depolarization needed). Below threshold = subthreshold response (no AP). At or above threshold = full AP regardless of stimulus strength (all-or-none law).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'all-or-none' law of action potentials states that:
options: All neurons fire at the same amplitude
Once threshold is reached, the AP amplitude is maximal and does not vary with stimulus strength; graded below threshold, all-or-none at/above threshold
Stronger stimuli produce higher-frequency APs of the same amplitude
No AP occurs below threshold and multiple APs above
explanation: All-or-none law: the amplitude and duration of the AP are constant (fixed) once triggered — they do not increase with stronger stimuli. The AP is either produced at full amplitude or not at all. Stimulus intensity is coded by the FREQUENCY of APs (rate coding), not by AP amplitude.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which type of summation occurs when multiple stimuli arrive simultaneously at different synapses on a neuron?
options: Spatial summation (simultaneous activation of multiple input synapses adds up at the axon hillock)
explanation: Spatial summation: multiple excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) from different synaptic inputs arriving simultaneously add up at the axon hillock. If their combined depolarization exceeds threshold, an AP fires. Temporal summation: rapid successive stimuli from the SAME synapse add up before the EPSP decays.

subject: Physiology
stem: The inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) is produced by which ion changes?
options: K+ efflux and/or Cl- influx (hyperpolarizing the membrane away from threshold)
explanation: IPSP: activation of inhibitory synapses (GABA-A, glycine) opens Cl- channels (Cl- flows in → hyperpolarization) and/or K+ channels (K+ flows out → hyperpolarization). The membrane is driven away from threshold, making it harder to fire an AP. GABA-A is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain; glycine in the spinal cord.

subject: Physiology
stem: GABA-A receptor is which type of receptor?
explanation: GABA-A: ionotropic GABA receptor — a ligand-gated Cl- ion channel. GABA binding → Cl- influx → hyperpolarization (IPSP). Benzodiazepines bind at the α-γ subunit interface → increase Cl- channel FREQUENCY (allosteric potentiation). Barbiturates increase Cl- channel DURATION. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist.

subject: Physiology
stem: The conduction velocity of nerve fibers increases with:
options: Increased temperature (up to a point) and larger fiber diameter
explanation: Conduction velocity is positively correlated with: (1) larger axon diameter (less internal resistance to current flow), (2) myelination (saltatory conduction), (3) temperature (up to ~40°C — beyond which proteins denature). Multiple sclerosis (demyelination) dramatically slows conduction velocity.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'H reflex' is the electrical equivalent of which clinical reflex?
options: Deep tendon (monosynaptic stretch) reflex — Ia afferent → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle contraction
explanation: H reflex (Hoffmann reflex): elicited by electrical stimulation of the Ia afferent fibers in a peripheral nerve, bypassing the muscle spindle. It tests the monosynaptic reflex arc (Ia afferent → spinal cord → alpha motor neuron → muscle). The clinical equivalent is the deep tendon reflex (e.g., ankle jerk = S1 reflex).

subject: Physiology
stem: The autonomic nervous system neurotransmitter at the target organ of the sympathetic nervous system is primarily:
options: Norepinephrine (most sympathetic postganglionic endings) — exception: sweat glands (ACh), some vessels (ACh)
explanation: Sympathetic neurotransmitters: preganglionic = ACh (nicotinic) at the sympathetic ganglion. Postganglionic = norepinephrine (NE) at most target organs (adrenergic). Exceptions: (1) Eccrine sweat glands — ACh (muscarinic), (2) some blood vessels causing vasodilation — ACh, (3) adrenal medulla — ACh stimulates direct epinephrine release.

subject: Physiology
stem: Parasympathetic neurotransmitter at the target organ is:
options: Acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors on target organs
explanation: Parasympathetic: both preganglionic (at ganglia, nicotinic nAChR) and postganglionic (at target organs, muscarinic mAChR) use ACh. Muscarinic receptors: M1 (CNS, gastric parietal — GIP), M2 (heart — slows HR, reduces contractility), M3 (smooth muscle — bronchoconstriction, increased GI motility, pupil constriction, gland secretion, bladder contraction), M4, M5.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'fight or flight' response is mediated by which neurotransmitter and receptors?
options: Norepinephrine and epinephrine via α and β adrenoreceptors
explanation: Sympathetic fight-or-flight: NE (from sympathetic postganglionic neurons) and epinephrine (from adrenal medulla) act on: α1 (vasoconstriction, pupil dilation, GI relaxation), α2 (presynaptic — reduces NE release), β1 (heart — increases HR and contractility), β2 (bronchodilation, vasodilation of skeletal muscle vessels, gluconeogenesis), β3 (lipolysis).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cholinergic crisis vs. myasthenic crisis: which drug helps differentiate them?
options: Edrophonium (Tensilon test): improves symptoms in myasthenic crisis (more ACh needed), worsens in cholinergic crisis (already too much ACh)
explanation: Edrophonium (short-acting AChE inhibitor, Tensilon test): in myasthenic crisis (inadequate ACh at NMJ), edrophonium transiently improves muscle strength. In cholinergic crisis (excess ACh from AChE inhibitor overdose), edrophonium worsens weakness + adds SLUDGE signs (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis) + bradycardia.

subject: Physiology
stem: The blood-brain barrier is most permeable to which substances?
options: Lipid-soluble, uncharged, small molecules (e.g., O2, CO2, alcohol, steroids, most anesthetic agents)
explanation: BBB permeability: lipid-soluble molecules (O2, CO2, ethanol, heroin, chloramphenicol, most anesthetics, steroids) cross freely. Water and glucose cross via specific carriers (GLUT1 for glucose). Large proteins, most antibiotics (aminoglycosides, penicillin in normal BBB), and ionized molecules are excluded. Inflammation (meningitis) disrupts the BBB, allowing normally excluded drugs to enter.

subject: Physiology
stem: Referred pain from the heart (angina pectoris) is most commonly felt in:
options: Left chest, left arm (ulnar border), left jaw — via convergence of cardiac afferents onto T1-T5 spinal cord segments
explanation: Cardiac referred pain: visceral pain afferents from the heart travel with sympathetic nerves (T1-T5). They converge onto the same spinal segments as somatic afferents from the left chest wall, inner left arm (ulnar, T1-2), and left jaw (T1-2). The brain misattributes the pain to the somatic area — this is the basis of referred pain (Roux's theory of convergence).

subject: Physiology
stem: The gate control theory of pain (Melzack and Wall) proposes that pain is modulated in which location?
options: Dorsal horn of spinal cord (substantia gelatinosa) — large-fiber activation 'closes the gate'
explanation: Gate control theory: the dorsal horn substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II) acts as a 'gate.' Large-fiber (A-beta — touch, vibration) activation excites inhibitory interneurons that 'close the gate' to pain (C-fiber) signals. Small-fiber (C-fiber) activation 'opens the gate.' This explains why rubbing a sore area reduces pain and is the basis for TENS therapy.

subject: Physiology
stem: Phantom limb pain is best explained by which neural mechanism?
options: Central sensitization and cortical reorganization — the somatosensory cortex reorganizes after limb loss, with neighboring cortical representations invading the deafferented area
explanation: Phantom limb pain: combines peripheral (stump neuromas) and central mechanisms. Cortical reorganization (neuroplasticity): neighboring somatosensory cortical areas invade the deafferented limb representation. These reorganized areas generate spontaneous activity perceived as pain in the missing limb. Mirror therapy exploits this neuroplasticity for treatment.

subject: Physiology
stem: Endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins are endogenous opioids that act on which receptors?
options: Opioid receptors (μ, δ, κ) — inhibit pain transmission by reducing cAMP, increasing K+ conductance (hyperpolarization), and reducing Ca2+ influx at presynaptic terminals
explanation: Endogenous opioids (β-endorphin from POMC, met/leu-enkephalin from proenkephalin, dynorphin from prodynorphin) act on: μ (morphine-like analgesia + euphoria), δ (analgesia + mood), κ (analgesia + sedation + dysphoria). Mechanism: inhibit adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP), open K+ channels (hyperpolarization), close voltage-gated Ca2+ channels → reduced neurotransmitter release.

subject: Physiology
stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart primarily acts via which receptor, and what is the effect?
options: β1-adrenergic — positive chronotropy (HR↑), positive inotropy (contractility↑), positive dromotropy (AV conduction↑), lusitropy (relaxation↑)
explanation: Cardiac sympathetic effects via β1 receptors: chronotropy (HR↑ — accelerates SA node phase 4), inotropy (contractility↑ — phosphorylates troponin I and RyR2), dromotropy (AV conduction speed↑), and lusitropy (faster relaxation). Mechanism: β1 → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of L-type Ca2+ channels and SERCA2.

subject: Physiology
stem: Parasympathetic stimulation of the heart (vagal tone) slows the heart by acting on:
options: Muscarinic M2 receptors on SA and AV nodes → increased K+ conductance (IKACh) → hyperpolarization → slowed diastolic depolarization → decreased HR
explanation: Vagal stimulation → ACh → M2 muscarinic receptors → Gi → inhibits adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP) AND directly opens GIRK channels (IKACh) → K+ efflux → hyperpolarization of SA node → slower phase 4 depolarization → lower heart rate (negative chronotropy). Extreme vagal stimulation can cause asystole.

subject: Physiology
stem: Dopamine at low doses acts primarily on which receptors, causing which effect?
options: Dopaminergic D1 receptors (renal and mesenteric vasodilation) and β1 at slightly higher doses
explanation: Dopamine dose-dependent effects: LOW dose (1–5 mcg/kg/min) → D1/D2 dopaminergic → renal and mesenteric vasodilation, natriuresis. MEDIUM dose (5–10 mcg/kg/min) → β1 → ↑HR, ↑contractility. HIGH dose (>10 mcg/kg/min) → α1 → vasoconstriction (↑SVR). Used in cardiogenic shock and renal perfusion support.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'QRS complex' on the ECG represents which cardiac event?
options: Ventricular depolarization (the electrical activation spreading through the ventricular myocardium)
explanation: ECG waves: P wave = atrial depolarization (SA node → atrial muscle). PR interval = AV nodal delay (0.12–0.20 sec). QRS complex = ventricular depolarization (0.06–0.10 sec, wide QRS if bundle branch block). ST segment + T wave = ventricular repolarization. QT interval = total ventricular electrical systole. Atrial repolarization is hidden within the QRS.

subject: Physiology
stem: The PR interval on the ECG represents:
options: AV nodal conduction time (from atrial depolarization beginning to start of ventricular depolarization) — normally 0.12–0.20 sec
Time for SA node to fire
explanation: PR interval: from beginning of P wave to beginning of QRS. Represents: atrial depolarization + AV nodal delay (AV node slow conduction via gap junctions) + His-Purkinje conduction to ventricular myocardium. Normal: 0.12–0.20 sec. Prolonged: 1st degree AV block (>0.20 sec). AV node delay is the pacemaker protection — filters rapid atrial rates.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which drug blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels and is used to treat ventricular arrhythmias?
options: Lidocaine / mexiletine (Class IB Na+ channel blockers — fast on/off kinetics, prefer depolarized/ischemic tissue)
explanation: Vaughan Williams Classification: Class I = Na+ channel blockers (A: quinidine, procainamide; B: lidocaine, mexiletine — prefer ischemic/depolarized tissue; C: flecainide, propafenone — marked use-dependence). Class II = β-blockers. Class III = K+ channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol). Class IV = Ca2+ channel blockers.

subject: Physiology
stem: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is calculated as:
options: Diastolic BP + 1/3 (Pulse Pressure), OR 1/3 Systolic + 2/3 Diastolic
explanation: MAP = Diastolic BP + 1/3 (Pulse Pressure). Since diastole occupies ~2/3 of the cardiac cycle, MAP is closer to diastolic pressure. Alternatively: MAP = (Systolic + 2×Diastolic) / 3. Normal MAP: ~93 mmHg (from 120/80 mmHg BP: 80 + 1/3 × 40 = 80+13 = 93 mmHg). MAP is the driving force for organ perfusion.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which component of the blood pressure is determined primarily by peripheral vascular resistance?
options: Diastolic BP (maintained by arteriolar tone — peripheral vascular resistance while the aortic valve is closed)
explanation: Diastolic BP: maintained during ventricular diastole by peripheral vascular resistance (PVR/SVR) and Windkessel effect of the aorta. Elevated by: α-adrenergic tone (vasoconstriction), sympathetic activity. Systolic BP is primarily determined by cardiac output and arterial stiffness. Pulse pressure = SBP - DBP; reflects stroke volume and arterial compliance.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which vessels account for the largest portion of total peripheral resistance?
options: Arterioles (the resistance vessels — small radius, large total resistance)
explanation: Arterioles (small arteries and arterioles, 20–100 μm) are the major determinants of peripheral vascular resistance. Their small radius (Poiseuille's: R = 8ηL/πr⁴) and rich smooth muscle innervation allow precise regulation of blood flow to different organs. They are the 'resistance vessels.' Capillaries have highest total cross-sectional area and lowest velocity.

subject: Physiology
stem: Venous return to the heart is enhanced by which mechanisms?
options: Skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pump (intrathoracic pressure drop during inspiration), venous valves, sympathetic venous tone, and position (leg elevation)
explanation: Venous return (Guyton's ventricular filling): (1) Skeletal muscle pump — contracting muscles compress veins → propel blood toward heart (unidirectional due to venous valves). (2) Respiratory pump — inspiration → ↓intrathoracic pressure → expands IVC and right atrium → venous return ↑. (3) Venous valves prevent retrograde flow. (4) Sympathetic venoconstriction — mobilizes venous reservoir.

subject: Physiology
stem: Autoregulation of blood flow ensures constant organ perfusion over a range of pressures. This is most important in which organs?
options: Brain, kidney, and heart (autoregulate flow from MAP 60–150 mmHg)
explanation: Autoregulation: brain maintains constant blood flow from MAP 60–150 mmHg via myogenic mechanism (stretching → smooth muscle contraction) and metabolic mechanism (CO2, O2, adenosine, K+ ion regulation). Kidney also autoregulates (protects glomeruli). Lost in malignant hypertension or severe hypotension, causing breakthrough hyperperfusion or ischemia.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'Bainbridge reflex' (atrial reflex) states that:
options: Increased atrial pressure decreases heart rate
Increased atrial pressure (stretch of right atrial baroreceptors) reflexly increases heart rate via sympathetic stimulation
explanation: Bainbridge reflex: stretch of the right atrium (increased venous return/CVP) → stimulates volume receptors in the right atrial wall → vagal afferents → medullary center → sympathetic HR increase. This acts as a protective mechanism to clear venous congestion. It counterbalances the baroreflex during exercise to maintain adequate CO.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'carotid sinus baroreceptor reflex': carotid sinus stretch causes which sequence?
options: Increased afferent firing (CN IX) → medullary NTS → increased vagal output → HR↓ + decreased sympathetic tone → BP↓ (buffering hypertension)
explanation: Carotid sinus baroreflex: increased BP → stretches carotid sinus (at ICA bifurcation) → increased firing of CN IX (Hering's nerve) → nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in medulla → increased vagal output to heart (HR↓, contractility↓) + decreased sympathetic → vasodilation → BP↓. Activated by carotid massage (for SVT treatment). Carotid sinus hypersensitivity → syncope.

subject: Physiology
stem: Starling's law of the capillary (Starling forces): net filtration depends on which pressures?
options: Net ultrafiltration pressure = (Pc - Pi) - (πc - πi): capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) and plasma oncotic pressure (πc) are the main determinants
explanation: Starling forces: net filtration = Kf [(Pc - Pi) - σ(πc - πi)]. Pc = capillary hydrostatic (pushes fluid out); Pi = interstitial hydrostatic (pushes fluid in); πc = plasma oncotic (~25 mmHg, mainly albumin — holds fluid in); πi = interstitial oncotic (draws fluid out). Edema: when filtration > lymphatic return (↑Pc in heart failure, ↓πc in hypoalbuminemia, lymphatic obstruction, ↑capillary permeability).

subject: Physiology
stem: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) estimates which pressure?
options: Left atrial pressure (and thus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure — LVEDP) — reflecting left heart filling pressure
explanation: PCWP (Swan-Ganz catheter with balloon wedged in small pulmonary artery): measures pressure distal to the balloon, which is transmitted retrograde through the pulmonary capillaries from the left atrium. Normal PCWP = 6–12 mmHg. Elevated (>18 mmHg) in left heart failure (cardiogenic pulmonary edema). <18 mmHg with pulmonary edema suggests ARDS (non-cardiogenic).

subject: Physiology
stem: Coronary blood flow occurs predominantly during which phase of the cardiac cycle?
options: Diastole (when ventricular compression is released, allowing coronary flow to increase — especially for the left ventricle)
explanation: Coronary blood flow: left ventricular coronary flow occurs mainly during diastole (systolic compression nearly stops LCA flow). The right ventricle (lower pressure) maintains some systolic flow. Factors determining coronary flow: aortic diastolic pressure, coronary resistance (autoregulated by adenosine, O2, NO), heart rate (longer diastole at slower HR = more coronary filling time).

subject: Physiology
stem: The Valsalva maneuver has four phases. During phase 2 (straining against closed glottis), what happens to blood pressure?
options: BP rises then falls due to reduced venous return
BP initially rises (phase 1), then falls progressively as venous return decreases → ↓CO → ↓BP (phase 2)
explanation: Valsalva maneuver phases: Phase 1 (straining onset) — aortic pressure briefly rises (mechanical compression). Phase 2 — sustained raised intrathoracic pressure → ↓venous return → ↓CO → BP falls → reflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction. Phase 3 (release) — intrathoracic pressure drops → aorta re-expands → transient BP fall. Phase 4 — BP overshoot (reflex vasoconstriction still active + venous return restored) → reflex bradycardia.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cardiac tamponade produces pulsus paradoxus. This is defined as:
options: Pulsus alternans — alternating strong and weak beats
Fall in systolic BP of >10 mmHg during inspiration (exaggerated normal inspiratory fall)
explanation: Pulsus paradoxus: >10 mmHg fall in systolic BP during inspiration (normal is <10 mmHg). In tamponade, pericardial pressure is elevated. During inspiration: RV fills more → IVS shifts leftward (ventricular interdependence) → LV filling decreases → LV SV falls → SBP drops. Also seen in severe asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which ion is primarily responsible for the plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential?
options: Ca2+ inflow via L-type Ca2+ channels (ICa-L) balanced by K+ outflow — prolongs repolarization
explanation: Phase 2 (plateau) of ventricular AP: lasts ~200 ms. Ca2+ influx via L-type channels (ICa-L, slow inward Ca2+ current) is balanced by K+ efflux via various K+ channels. This plateau is responsible for calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) from the SR, causing muscle contraction. The prolonged plateau prevents premature re-excitation (no sustained tetanus possible in cardiac muscle).

subject: Physiology
stem: Stroke volume (SV) is determined by which three factors?
options: Heart rate, blood pressure, and vascular resistance
Cardiac output and heart rate only
explanation: Stroke volume determinants: (1) Preload (Frank-Starling: ↑EDV → ↑SV). (2) Afterload (↑SVR → ↓SV — harder to eject against high resistance). (3) Contractility (positive inotropes — catecholamines, digoxin → ↑SV at any preload; negative inotropes — β-blockers, Ca2+ channel blockers → ↓SV). SV = EDV - ESV; EF = SV/EDV (normal ≥55%).

subject: Physiology
stem: The QT interval on the ECG is prolonged by which conditions or drugs?
options: Hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia; drugs: class IA/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics (haloperidol, droperidol)
explanation: Long QT syndrome (LQTS): QTc >440 ms (men) or >460 ms (women). Causes: congenital (channelopathies — LQT1 KCNQ1 K+ channel; LQT2 hERG K+ channel; LQT3 SCN5A Na+ channel), electrolytes (↓Ca2+, ↓K+, ↓Mg2+), drugs (class IA: quinidine; class III: amiodarone, sotalol; macrolides, quinolones, antipsychotics, antihistamines). Risk of Torsades de Pointes (TdP) → VF.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypokalemia (low serum K+) produces which ECG changes?
options: Peaked T waves and widened QRS
Flattened or inverted T waves, prominent U waves, ST depression — overall appearance of 'prolonged QT' due to U wave
explanation: Hypokalemia ECG: decreased K+ → increased resting potential → prolonged repolarization. Features: flattened/inverted T waves, prominent U waves (best seen in V2-V3), ST depression, PR prolongation. Appearance of 'long QT' (actually QU prolongation). Predisposes to ectopic beats, TdP, AF, VF. U wave: positive deflection after T wave, best seen in V2-V3.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hyperkalemia (elevated serum K+) produces which ECG changes?
options: Flat T waves and U waves
Progressive changes: peaked/tall tented T waves (first) → widened QRS → loss of P wave → sine wave → VF/asystole
explanation: Hyperkalemia ECG progression: K+ 5.5–6 mEq/L → peaked (tent-shaped) T waves. 6–7 → PR prolongation, widened QRS. 7–8 → loss of P wave (atrial standstill). >8 → 'sine wave' pattern (wide QRS merging with T wave). >10 → VF/asystole. Treatment: Ca2+ gluconate (membrane stabilization), Na+-HCO3-/insulin-glucose (shift K+ intracellularly), Kayexalate/dialysis (remove K+).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'jugular venous pulse' (JVP): the 'a' wave represents:
options: Atrial systole (contraction of the right atrium)
Ventricular systole causing tricuspid valve closure
explanation: JVP waveforms: 'a' wave = atrial systole (right atrial contraction). 'c' wave = tricuspid valve closure (bulging into right atrium). 'x' descent = atrial relaxation + tricuspid valve pulled down by ventricular contraction. 'v' wave = venous filling of right atrium while tricuspid is closed (ventricular systole). 'y' descent = tricuspid opens, blood flows into RV.

subject: Physiology
stem: Giant 'a' waves in the JVP are seen in which condition?
options: Tricuspid stenosis or pulmonary hypertension (increased resistance to right atrial emptying → forceful atrial contraction)
explanation: Giant 'a' waves: exaggerated atrial systole contracting against increased resistance. Causes: tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, complete heart block (cannon 'a' waves — when P occurs during closed tricuspid valve in ventricular systole). In AF, 'a' waves are absent (no organized atrial systole). Cannon waves = giant 'a' waves in AV dissociation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal tidal volume (TV) at rest is approximately:
explanation: Tidal volume (TV): volume of air breathed in/out in one breath at rest = ~500 mL. Other lung volumes: IRV (inspiratory reserve) ~3000 mL; ERV (expiratory reserve) ~1200 mL; RV (residual volume) ~1200 mL (cannot be exhaled). Total lung capacity = TV + IRV + ERV + RV = 6000 mL. Functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV = 2400 mL.

subject: Physiology
stem: The alveolar ventilation rate differs from total ventilation because of:
options: Dead space volume: alveolar ventilation (VA) = (TV - VD) × RR, where VD ≈ 150 mL (anatomical dead space)
explanation: Alveolar ventilation (VA): VA = (TV - VD) × RR = (500 - 150) × 12 = 4200 mL/min. VD (anatomical dead space = 150 mL) is the volume of conducting airways that does not participate in gas exchange. Physiological dead space = anatomical dead space + alveolar dead space (ventilated but poorly perfused alveoli). Increasing TV is more efficient than increasing RR for improving VA.

subject: Physiology
stem: The alveolar gas equation estimates alveolar PO2 (PAO2):
options: PAO2 = PiO2 - PaCO2/R (where R = respiratory quotient ~0.8)
explanation: Alveolar gas equation: PAO2 = PiO2 - (PaCO2/R). PiO2 = FiO2 × (PB - PH2O) = 0.21 × (760 - 47) ≈ 150 mmHg at sea level breathing air. PaCO2 ≈ 40 mmHg. R (RQ) ≈ 0.8. PAO2 = 150 - (40/0.8) = 150 - 50 = 100 mmHg. A-a gradient (PAO2 - PaO2) is normally <10 mmHg; widens in V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion impairment.

subject: Physiology
stem: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension. The main component of surfactant is:
explanation: Surfactant: ~70% phospholipids (mainly DPPC — dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine/lecithin), 10% protein (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D), 10% neutral lipids. DPPC reduces surface tension at the air-liquid interface in alveoli, preventing collapse. L:S ratio (lecithin:sphingomyelin) >2:1 in amniotic fluid indicates fetal lung maturity. RDS (NRDS) = surfactant deficiency in premature infants.

subject: Physiology
stem: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the RIGHT (Bohr effect) in which conditions?
options: Increased pCO2, acidosis (↓pH), increased temperature, increased 2,3-DPG — right shift = decreased O2 affinity = increased O2 delivery to tissues
explanation: Right shift of ODC (decreased O2 affinity, P50 increases): ↑PCO2 (Bohr effect), ↓pH (acidosis), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-DPG (high altitude, chronic anemia, exercise). This is physiologically appropriate: tissues with high CO2/acid/heat get better O2 delivery. Left shift (increased affinity): fetal Hb (HbF), CO poisoning (CO-Hb left shifts residual Hb), alkalosis, ↓temperature, ↓2,3-DPG, methemoglobinemia.

subject: Physiology
stem: Haldane effect describes which relationship?
options: CO2 transport is enhanced when O2 unloads from hemoglobin in tissues
CO2 and O2 compete for hemoglobin binding: oxygenated Hb has lower affinity for CO2 (deoxygenated Hb is a better CO2 carrier)
O2 transport improves with increased pH
explanation: Haldane effect: deoxygenated Hb (in tissues) has higher affinity for CO2 than oxygenated Hb. As O2 unloads in tissues, Hb can bind more CO2 (as carbaminohemoglobin). In the lungs, O2 loading displaces CO2 from Hb, facilitating CO2 exhalation. This complementary mechanism enhances both O2 delivery and CO2 removal.

subject: Physiology
stem: Control of breathing: what is the primary stimulus for the central chemoreceptors in the medulla?
options: PaCO2 / H+ (pH) in the brain extracellular fluid — CO2 crosses BBB, forms H+ which stimulates central chemoreceptors
explanation: Central chemoreceptors (in the ventral medulla): respond to CO2/pH of the interstitial fluid of the medulla (not blood directly). CO2 diffuses across the BBB → H2CO3 → H+ → stimulates chemoreceptors → increased ventilation. CO2 is the primary moment-to-moment drive to breathe. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond to hypoxia (PaO2 <60 mmHg), hypercapnia, and acidosis.

subject: Physiology
stem: In 'hypercapnic respiratory failure' (Type II), PaCO2 is elevated. The body compensates by:
options: Renal retention of bicarbonate (HCO3-) over days — metabolic alkalosis compensates the respiratory acidosis
explanation: Chronic hypercapnia (Type II RF, e.g., COPD): raised PaCO2 → respiratory acidosis → kidneys compensate by retaining HCO3- (increased reabsorption, increased NH4+ excretion) over 3–5 days → metabolic alkalosis partly normalizes pH. Chronic CO2 retainers lose their hypercapnic drive and depend on hypoxic drive (carotid bodies) — hence oxygen should be titrated carefully in COPD.

subject: Physiology
stem: V/Q mismatch: in a lung region with low V/Q ratio (perfusion > ventilation), the gas exchange result is:
options: Low PAO2 and high PACO2 in that alveolus (mimics shunt physiology), contributing to hypoxemia
explanation: Low V/Q regions (poor ventilation, normal perfusion — e.g., consolidation, secretion): alveolar gas equilibrates with venous blood → low PAO2, high PACO2. This contributes to systemic hypoxemia. High V/Q (dead space — e.g., PE): well-ventilated but poorly perfused → high PAO2, low PACO2. Normal V/Q = 0.8 (overall). Supplemental O2 can correct V/Q mismatch but NOT true shunt.

subject: Physiology
stem: The work of breathing is increased by which conditions?
options: Increased airway resistance (asthma, COPD) and decreased lung compliance (fibrosis, pulmonary edema, RDS)
explanation: Work of breathing (WOB): WOB = volume × pressure. Increased by: (1) Increased resistance (narrowed airways — asthma, COPD, obstruction → more pressure needed per breath); (2) Decreased compliance (stiff lungs — fibrosis, RDS, pulmonary edema → more pressure needed to inflate). High WOB → respiratory muscle fatigue → ventilatory failure. CPAP/BiPAP reduces WOB.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) redirects blood from hypoxic lung segments. Its mechanism involves:
options: Increased nitric oxide in hypoxic areas
Smooth muscle contraction due to direct local O2 sensing (inhibition of K+ channels, depolarization, Ca2+ influx) in pulmonary arterioles responding to low alveolar PO2
explanation: HPV (Euler-Liljestrand mechanism): low alveolar PO2 directly triggers smooth muscle contraction in pulmonary arterioles (opposite to systemic circulation). Mechanism: hypoxia inhibits voltage-gated K+ channels → depolarization → L-type Ca2+ channel opening → vasoconstriction → diverts blood to better-ventilated alveoli. Useful locally; when generalized (COPD, high altitude) → pulmonary hypertension.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'Hering-Breuer reflex' prevents over-inflation of the lungs. It is mediated by:
options: Stretch receptors in bronchial smooth muscle sending afferent signals via vagal nerve (CN X) to inhibit inspiration when lungs are over-inflated
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid body
explanation: Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: pulmonary stretch receptors (slowly adapting, in airway smooth muscle) detect lung inflation → afferents via vagus → pontine pneumotaxic center and medullary inspiratory center → inspiration is switched off (prevents over-inflation). Mainly active at large tidal volumes (>800 mL in adults). More important in neonates.

subject: Physiology
stem: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and FEV1/FVC ratio: in obstructive lung disease (asthma, COPD), these values are:
options: FEV1 decreased, FEV1/FVC ratio <70% (obstructive pattern); FVC may be normal or slightly decreased
Both normal but RV is increased
explanation: Spirometry patterns: Obstructive (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis): FEV1 ↓, FVC normal or ↓, FEV1/FVC <70%. Restrictive (fibrosis, obesity, neuromuscular disease): FEV1 ↓, FVC ↓ (proportionally), FEV1/FVC ≥70% (or normal), TLC ↓. RV is increased in obstructive (air trapping) and decreased in restrictive disease.

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is approximately:
options: 125 mL/min (180 L/day total filtration; ~99% is reabsorbed, 1.5 L/day excreted)
explanation: GFR: ~125 mL/min (180 L/day filtered). Only ~1.5 L/day is excreted as urine (~99% reabsorbed). GFR is the best single measure of kidney function. Estimated by serum creatinine (eGFR using CKD-EPI or MDRD formula). Inulin clearance = true GFR (filtered but not secreted or reabsorbed). Creatinine clearance slightly overestimates GFR (some tubular secretion).

subject: Physiology
stem: The filtration fraction (FF) in the glomerulus is normally:
explanation: Filtration fraction (FF) = GFR/RPF. GFR = 125 mL/min; RPF (renal plasma flow) ≈ 600 mL/min (RBF ≈ 1200 mL/min; RBF = RPF/(1-hematocrit)). FF = 125/600 ≈ 20%. After filtration, the remaining plasma in efferent arterioles has higher oncotic pressure and lower hydrostatic pressure — this drives tubular reabsorption in peritubular capillaries.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which segment of the nephron reabsorbs the largest fraction (~65%) of filtered sodium?
options: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) — isosmotic reabsorption via Na+/H+ exchanger, Na+/glucose, Na+/phosphate cotransporters + Na+/K+ ATPase
explanation: PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na+, water (obligatory — follows Na+ osmotically), glucose (100%), amino acids (100%), HCO3- (~80%), and uric acid. Transport mechanisms: Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) on luminal side; Na+/K+ ATPase on basolateral side. Reabsorption is isosmotic (luminal fluid remains ~300 mOsm throughout PCT).

subject: Physiology
stem: Aldosterone acts primarily on which part of the nephron?
options: Distal convoluted tubule (DCT) and collecting duct — increases ENaC (Na+ channels) and Na+/K+ ATPase expression → Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion
explanation: Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid from zona glomerulosa): binds intracellular MR (mineralocorticoid receptor) in principal cells of the DCT and CCD. Increases: (1) ENaC (epithelial Na+ channels) on the luminal surface → Na+ reabsorption → water follows; (2) Na+/K+ ATPase on basolateral side; (3) K+ secretion (ROMK channels) → hypokalemia. Also secretes H+ (intercalated cells).

subject: Physiology
stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) acts on which part of the nephron and via which receptor?
options: Collecting duct principal cells via V2 receptors (Gs) → cAMP → PKA → inserts aquaporin-2 (AQP2) into luminal membrane → water reabsorption
explanation: ADH (from posterior pituitary, released in response to ↑osmolarity or ↓blood volume): V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells → Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA phosphorylates AQP2 vesicles → exocytosis of AQP2 into the luminal membrane → water reabsorption (concentrated urine). Absent in central DI (no ADH); AQP2 not responding in nephrogenic DI.

subject: Physiology
stem: The tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) mechanism at the juxtaglomerular apparatus regulates GFR by:
options: Increasing renin release when Na+ is high
Macula densa sensing increased NaCl delivery → releases adenosine/TXA2 → constricts afferent arteriole → ↓GFR (negative feedback to reduce NaCl delivery)
explanation: Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF): when GFR increases → more NaCl delivered to macula densa → NKCC2 transport in macula densa → signals to afferent arteriole via adenosine (and ATP) → vasoconstriction → ↓GFR → negative feedback to maintain constant GFR. Conversely: ↓NaCl delivery → afferent dilation → ↑GFR + renin release.

subject: Physiology
stem: Acidification of urine in the collecting duct: proton secretion is primarily carried out by which cells?
options: Alpha intercalated cells (type A) — H+/K+ ATPase and H+ ATPase secrete H+ into lumen, HCO3- is reabsorbed via AE1 (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger) on basolateral side
explanation: Urinary acidification: alpha-type intercalated cells in CCD/OMC/IMCD secrete H+ via H+-ATPase (V-type) and H+/K+-ATPase into the lumen → luminal H+ combines with NH3 (from glutamine) → NH4+ (trapped, excreted), or with HPO4²- → H2PO4- (titratable acid). HCO3- is reabsorbed via AE1 basolaterally. Net result: acidic urine, new HCO3- generation.

subject: Physiology
stem: The RAAS (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) is activated by which stimuli?
options: Decreased renal perfusion pressure, decreased Na+ at macula densa, and sympathetic stimulation (β1 receptors) → renin release from JG cells → angiotensinogen → Ang I → ACE (lungs) → Ang II → aldosterone
explanation: RAAS activation: stimuli for renin release from juxtaglomerular (granular) cells: (1) ↓renal perfusion pressure (stretch/baroreceptor), (2) ↓NaCl at macula densa (TGF), (3) β1 adrenergic stimulation (sympathetic). Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (liver) → Ang I → ACE (lung) → Ang II → (1) vasoconstriction, (2) aldosterone (zona glomerulosa), (3) ADH release, (4) thirst. Net: ↑BP, ↑Na+ and water retention.

subject: Physiology
stem: Gastrin is secreted by which cells and stimulates which secretion?
options: G cells (antrum of stomach) — gastrin stimulates parietal cells to secrete HCl, and chief cells to secrete pepsinogen; also stimulates gastric motility
explanation: Gastrin: secreted by G cells (antrum and duodenum). Stimulates: HCl secretion (parietal cells via CCK-B/gastrin receptor), pepsinogen secretion (chief cells), gastric motility, lower esophageal sphincter contraction. Stimulated by: protein digestion products, gastric distension, vagal stimulation (ACh). Inhibited by: low luminal pH (<2.5), somatostatin.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released from which cells and has which primary functions?
options: S cells of duodenum — stimulates pancreatic HCO3- secretion
I cells of duodenum and jejunum — stimulates gallbladder contraction, pancreatic enzyme secretion, and inhibits gastric emptying
explanation: CCK (from I cells of duodenum and proximal jejunum): released in response to fats and proteins in the duodenum. Actions: (1) gallbladder contraction + relaxation of sphincter of Oddi → bile release, (2) pancreatic enzyme secretion (proteases, lipase, amylase), (3) inhibits gastric emptying (protects the duodenum from acid overload), (4) satiety signal. Acts on CCK-A receptors.

subject: Physiology
stem: Secretin (from S cells of duodenum) is the primary stimulus for which pancreatic secretion?
options: Bicarbonate (HCO3-) secretion from pancreatic ductal cells (to neutralize duodenal acid) — stimulated by luminal pH <4.5
explanation: Secretin (from S cells of duodenum and jejunum, released by low luminal pH <4.5): stimulates pancreatic ductal cells to secrete HCO3--rich juice (via CFTR and AE2 exchanger), neutralizing the acid chyme. Also inhibits gastrin, reduces gastric acid, and stimulates biliary HCO3- secretion. Acts via cAMP. Secretin test: used to diagnose Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which is the most potent stimulus for insulin secretion?
options: Glucose (glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, GSIS) — glucose enters β-cells via GLUT2 → glycolysis → ↑ATP/ADP → closes KATP channels → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → exocytosis of insulin granules
explanation: Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS): Glucose → GLUT2 → glycolysis → ↑ATP/ADP ratio → KATP channel closure → membrane depolarization → voltage-gated Ca2+ channel (VGCC) opens → Ca2+ influx → insulin granule exocytosis. This is the main mechanism. Sulfonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide) close KATP channels → stimulate insulin secretion independently of blood glucose.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'gastrocolic reflex' causes defecation urge after eating. Which neural mechanism mediates it?
options: Local myenteric reflex (peristaltic rush) triggered by gastric filling + long reflex via vago-vagal pathways
explanation: Gastrocolic reflex: food entering the stomach triggers increased propulsive colonic motor activity (colonic mass movements) via: (1) long vagovagal reflex (vagal afferents from stomach → brainstem → vagal efferents to colon), (2) gastrin and CCK release. This explains the urge to defecate after meals. The intrinsic myenteric plexus mediates local propulsion.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cortisol (glucocorticoid) secretion follows which pattern and is regulated by:
options: Circadian rhythm (peak at ~8 AM — waking; nadir at midnight) regulated by the HPA axis: CRH (hypothalamus) → ACTH (anterior pituitary) → cortisol (adrenal cortex, zona fasciculata)
Pulsatile throughout the day with no circadian pattern
Regulated by sympathetic nervous system only
explanation: Cortisol: diurnal (circadian) secretion, highest in early morning (~8 AM), lowest at midnight. Regulated by HPA axis: stress/CRH → ACTH release → cortisol. Negative feedback: cortisol → inhibits both CRH and ACTH. Cortisol actions: gluconeogenesis, proteolysis, lipolysis, anti-inflammatory (reduces PLA2, IL-1,2, TNF), immunosuppression, Na+ retention.

subject: Physiology
stem: Thyroid hormone synthesis requires which mineral, and which enzyme is key?
options: Iodine — thyroid peroxidase (TPO) incorporates I2 into tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin (organification)
explanation: Thyroid hormone synthesis: Iodide (I-) trapped by NIS (Na/I symporter, TSH-stimulated) → oxidized to I2 by thyroid peroxidase (TPO) + H2O2 → organification (addition to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin: MIT and DIT) → coupling (DIT+DIT=T4; MIT+DIT=T3) → pinocytosis + lysosomal proteolysis → T3/T4 release. TPO is blocked by thionamides (PTU, methimazole).

subject: Physiology
stem: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) increases serum calcium by which mechanisms?
options: Increases bone resorption (osteoclast activation), increases renal Ca2+ reabsorption (DCT), increases 1α-hydroxylase (activates 25-OH vitamin D to 1,25-(OH)2 D3/calcitriol which enhances intestinal Ca2+ absorption)
explanation: PTH (from parathyroid glands, released by ↓Ca2+): (1) Bone: activates osteoclasts (via RANKL on osteoblasts) → bone resorption → ↑Ca2+ and PO4³-. (2) Kidney: ↑Ca2+ reabsorption (DCT), ↓PO4 reabsorption (PCT — phosphaturia), activates 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol synthesis. (3) Gut: indirect via calcitriol → ↑Ca2+ and PO4 absorption. Net: ↑Ca2+, ↓PO4.

subject: Physiology
stem: Growth hormone (GH) is secreted from which pituitary cells and its main effects are mediated by:
options: Somatotrophs (acidophils) of anterior pituitary — many effects mediated via IGF-1 (somatomedin C) produced by the liver
explanation: GH (somatotropin): secreted by somatotrophs (acidophils) of anterior pituitary, stimulated by GHRH (growth hormone releasing hormone) from hypothalamus and inhibited by somatostatin. Direct effects: lipolysis, insulin resistance (diabetogenic). Indirect (via IGF-1, mainly from liver): bone growth (epiphyseal plates), muscle protein synthesis, organ growth.

subject: Physiology
stem: Prolactin: what is its primary inhibitory control?
options: Dopamine (from hypothalamic tuberoinfundibular neurons) tonically inhibits prolactin; TRH and VIP stimulate prolactin
explanation: Prolactin (from lactotrophs of anterior pituitary): unique in being tonically inhibited. Dopamine (PIH — prolactin-inhibiting hormone) from the hypothalamic tuberoinfundibular pathway is the main inhibitor. Stimulators: TRH, VIP, suckling (neurogenic reflex). Dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) → hyperprolactinemia → galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia.

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal hemoglobin (Hb) concentration in adult males is:
explanation: Normal Hb: males 13.5–17.5 g/dL, females 12–15.5 g/dL. Each gram of Hb carries 1.34 mL O2 when fully saturated. Total O2 carrying capacity = Hb × 1.34 × SpO2. Anemia defined as Hb <13 g/dL (males) or <12 g/dL (females). Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) = 80–100 fL; MCH = 27–32 pg; MCHC = 32–36 g/dL.

subject: Physiology
stem: The oxygen carrying capacity of blood is calculated as:
options: Hb × 1.34 × SpO2/100 + (PaO2 × 0.003) — Hb-bound O2 dominates over dissolved O2
explanation: O2 content (CaO2) = [Hb × 1.34 × SaO2] + [PaO2 × 0.003]. At normal Hb (15 g/dL) and SaO2 100%: Hb-bound O2 = 15 × 1.34 × 1.0 = 20.1 mL/dL. Dissolved O2 = 100 × 0.003 = 0.3 mL/dL. Total ≈ 20.4 mL/dL. In carbon monoxide poisoning, SaO2 measured by pulse oximetry is falsely normal (CO-Hb absorbs light at similar wavelength to Oxy-Hb).

subject: Physiology
stem: Erythropoiesis is regulated primarily by:
options: Erythropoietin (EPO) secreted by peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia
explanation: Erythropoietin (EPO): secreted by peritubular interstitial cells (fibroblast-like cells) of the renal cortex in response to hypoxia. EPO → stimulates BFU-E and CFU-E in bone marrow → increased red cell production. Chronic kidney disease → reduced EPO → normocytic anemia. Exogenous rEPO used in CKD anemia and by athletes (doping).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which protein is deficient in hereditary spherocytosis?
options: Spectrin (or ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2) — cytoskeletal proteins of the RBC membrane
explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis: autosomal dominant (most common) or recessive. Deficiency of spectrin (most common), ankyrin, band 3, or protein 4.2 → unstable RBC membrane → spherical RBCs → destroyed in the spleen → extravascular hemolytic anemia. Features: anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones. Osmotic fragility test positive.

subject: Physiology
stem: G6PD deficiency causes which type of anemia and is triggered by:
options: Episodic hemolytic anemia (intravascular) triggered by oxidative stress: primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, fava beans, infection
explanation: G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive, most common enzyme deficiency causing hemolytic anemia): G6PD is essential for the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH → maintains glutathione in reduced form (protects RBCs from oxidative damage). Oxidative stress → Heinz bodies (denatured Hb) → intravascular hemolysis → hemoglobinuria (dark urine). Triggers: primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, fava beans, infections (typhoid).

subject: Physiology
stem: ABO blood group system: type O blood has which antigens on RBCs and which antibodies in plasma?
options: A and B antigens; no antibodies
No A or B antigens; anti-A and anti-B antibodies (natural IgM antibodies)
explanation: ABO groups: Type O = no A or B surface antigens on RBCs; plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B (IgM, naturally occurring, called 'pre-formed'). Type A = A antigen + anti-B. Type B = B antigen + anti-A. Type AB = A and B antigens + no antibodies (universal recipient). Type O = universal donor (but only packed RBCs — plasma has both antibodies). Cross-matching essential before transfusion.

subject: Physiology
stem: The rhesus (Rh) blood group: Rh-negative individuals:
options: Have Rh antigens but no antibodies
Do not have the RhD antigen; anti-D antibodies develop only after exposure to RhD+ blood (immune IgG — not pre-formed)
Are unable to receive any blood transfusion
explanation: Rh system: 85% of people are Rh+ (have the D antigen). Rh- individuals do not naturally have anti-D antibodies; they develop them (IgG) after exposure to Rh+ blood (transfusion or pregnancy). Anti-D IgG can cross the placenta → hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN/erythroblastosis fetalis) in subsequent Rh+ pregnancies of an Rh- sensitized mother. Prevented by anti-D (Rhogam) prophylaxis.

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal platelet count and platelet lifespan:
options: 150,000–400,000/μL; 7–10 days (produced from megakaryocytes, destroyed in spleen/liver)
explanation: Platelets (thrombocytes): normal count 150,000–400,000/μL. Lifespan 7–10 days. Derived from megakaryocytes in bone marrow (thrombopoietin-regulated). Thrombocytopenia: <150,000 (bleeding risk ↑ <50,000; severe <20,000). Thrombocytosis: reactive (infection, iron deficiency, splenectomy) or primary (essential thrombocythemia).

subject: Physiology
stem: Hemostasis: primary vs. secondary hemostasis — what is primary hemostasis?
options: Formation of the platelet plug: vascular injury → von Willebrand factor (vWF) bridges collagen and GPIb on platelets → platelet adhesion → platelet activation → ADP, TXA2 amplify → platelet aggregation (GPIIb/IIIa-fibrinogen bridges)
explanation: Primary hemostasis (platelet plug): vascular injury → subendothelial collagen exposure + vWF release → platelet adhesion (GPIb-IX-V binds vWF on collagen at high shear rates) → platelet activation → ADP (P2Y12/P2Y1 receptors) and TXA2 (TP receptor) amplify → shape change → GPIIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) activated → fibrinogen bridges → platelet aggregation. Tested by bleeding time or PFA-100.

subject: Physiology
stem: The intrinsic coagulation pathway is initiated by:
options: Tissue factor (TF) exposed to factor VII
Contact activation: Factor XII (Hageman factor) activated by contact with negatively charged surfaces (e.g., glass, collagen) → XIIa → XI → IXa
explanation: Intrinsic pathway (contact activation): FXII → FXIIa (contact with negatively charged surface, kallikrein, HMWK) → FXI → FXIa → FIX → FIXa (with FVIII cofactor) → FX. Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor (TF) + FVIIa → FX. Both pathways converge at FX → FXa → prothrombin → thrombin → fibrinogen → fibrin. PTT tests intrinsic pathway; PT/INR tests extrinsic.

subject: Physiology
stem: Factor VIII deficiency causes which coagulation disorder?
options: Hemophilia A (X-linked recessive, affects males predominantly) — elevated PTT, normal PT, normal bleeding time
explanation: Hemophilia A: X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII. Presents with hemarthroses (joint bleeds), deep muscle hematomas, prolonged bleeding after trauma. Lab: ↑PTT (intrinsic pathway), normal PT (extrinsic), normal bleeding time (primary hemostasis normal, platelet count normal). Treatment: recombinant FVIII concentrate.

subject: Physiology
stem: Vitamin K is required for the activation of which coagulation factors?
options: Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X (and protein C, protein S, protein Z) — the 'PIVKA' factors
explanation: Vitamin K (fat-soluble)-dependent factors: II, VII, IX, X (coagulation), Protein C, Protein S, Protein Z (anticoagulant). Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues (by γ-glutamyl carboxylase), enabling Ca2+-mediated binding to phospholipid surfaces. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase → depletes active vitamin K → prolongs PT/INR (mainly extrinsic VII, shortest half-life).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which protein inhibits ADP-induced platelet aggregation?
options: Prostacyclin (PGI2) produced by endothelial cells — via cAMP elevation → inhibits platelet activation, and causes vasodilation
explanation: Prostacyclin (PGI2, prostacyclin synthase in endothelium): potent inhibitor of platelet aggregation (↑cAMP → reduces Ca2+ → inhibits GPIIb/IIIa activation) and vasodilator. In balance with platelet TXA2 (stimulates aggregation and vasoconstriction). Aspirin inhibits COX-1 → reduces both TXA2 (platelets, desired) and PGI2 (endothelium). Low-dose aspirin preferentially reduces TXA2.

subject: Physiology
stem: 'Virchow's triad' for thrombosis includes:
options: Endothelial injury, stasis of blood flow, and hypercoagulability
explanation: Virchow's triad (1856): three factors predisposing to thrombosis: (1) Endothelial injury/dysfunction (e.g., atherosclerosis, hypertension, inflammation — exposes subendothelial matrix), (2) Stasis (e.g., atrial fibrillation, prolonged immobility, DVT), (3) Hypercoagulability (e.g., factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid syndrome, OCP, cancer). Most clinical thrombi involve ≥2 factors.

subject: Physiology
stem: Iron is absorbed in which part of the intestine and in which form?
