options: Duodenum and upper jejunum as Fe2+ (ferrous form) via DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1)
explanation: Iron absorption: predominantly in the duodenum and upper jejunum. Non-heme iron: Fe3+ (ferric) reduced to Fe2+ (ferrous) by duodenal cytochrome b (DcytB, ferrireductase) on the brush border → transported into enterocytes via DMT1. Heme iron: absorbed via heme carrier protein (HCP1), then Fe2+ released intracellularly by heme oxygenase. Fe2+ exits the enterocyte via ferroportin (regulated by hepcidin — hepcidin ↑ → ferroportin ↓ → less Fe export).

subject: Physiology
stem: The sliding filament theory of muscle contraction: what is the role of calcium?
options: Ca2+ binds troponin C (TnC) → conformational change in the troponin-tropomyosin complex → uncovers myosin-binding sites on actin → cross-bridge cycling
explanation: Excitation-contraction coupling: AP → T-tubule → voltage-sensing DHPR (L-type Ca2+ channel) → activates RyR1 (ryanodine receptor) → Ca2+ release from SR. Ca2+ binds TnC (troponin C) → troponin complex rotates → tropomyosin moves aside → exposes actin binding sites for myosin S1 heads → cross-bridge formation → power stroke (ADP + Pi released) → ATP binding → cross-bridge detachment → relaxation when Ca2+ is re-sequestered by SERCA.

subject: Physiology
stem: The A band, I band, and H zone in striated muscle sarcomere: what disappears during contraction?
options: H zone (central part of A band — only thick myosin filaments) and I band (only thin actin filaments) shorten; A band remains constant
explanation: Sarcomere changes during contraction: A band (thick filaments = constant length) does NOT change. I band (only thin filaments outside the A band) shortens as actin slides in. H zone (only thick filaments in the A band where no actin overlaps) shortens. Z lines come closer together. The sarcomere shortens but the filament lengths remain constant — supporting the sliding filament model.

subject: Physiology
stem: Rigor mortis (post-mortem muscle stiffness) is due to:
options: ATP depletion after death → cross-bridges cannot detach (need ATP to separate myosin from actin) → permanent actin-myosin linkage → muscle stiffness
explanation: Rigor mortis: after death, cellular metabolism ceases → ATP depleted → SERCA pump fails (Ca2+ remains elevated → actin-myosin bonds form) + ATP needed for cross-bridge detachment is unavailable → permanent actomyosin cross-bridges → stiffness. Begins 2–6 hours after death, maximum 12 hours, resolves in 24–48 hours (autolysis of proteins).

subject: Physiology
stem: The maximum velocity of muscle shortening (Vmax) occurs when:
options: Load on the muscle is maximum
Load on the muscle is zero (no load — maximal shortening velocity when there is no external resistance)
explanation: Force-velocity relationship (Hill's equation): at maximum load (isometric) = maximum force, zero velocity. As load decreases → shortening velocity increases. At zero load (zero external resistance) = maximum velocity (Vmax). Vmax reflects the maximum rate of cross-bridge cycling (determined by myosin ATPase activity). Fast-twitch fibers have higher Vmax and myosin ATPase activity than slow-twitch.

subject: Physiology
stem: Type I muscle fibers (slow-twitch, oxidative) are characterized by:
options: High glycolytic capacity, low myoglobin, white fibers
High oxidative capacity, high myoglobin content (red fibers), many mitochondria, fatigue-resistant, suited for sustained aerobic activity
High glycogen content and fast fatigue
explanation: Type I fibers (slow-twitch, red, oxidative/SO): low myosin ATPase (slow twitch), high mitochondria and myoglobin (red), resistant to fatigue, ideal for endurance activities (marathon running, postural muscles). Type IIA (fast-twitch, oxidative-glycolytic, intermediate). Type IIB/IIX (fast-twitch, white, glycolytic, fast fatigue, high power, sprinting).

subject: Physiology
stem: Tetanus in skeletal muscle occurs when:
options: A single twitch reaches maximum tension
Action potentials arrive at a rate faster than the relaxation time between twitches (fused tetanus: >60–100 Hz in human skeletal muscle) — tension summation leads to sustained maximum tension
The muscle is stimulated only once
explanation: Twitch summation → tetanus: if a second AP arrives before the first twitch is complete (and Ca2+ is still elevated), the tensions add up (temporal summation). At sufficiently high stimulation frequency → fused tetanus (constant maximal tension). In vivo, motor units are asynchronously recruited at different rates to produce smooth graded muscle force.

subject: Physiology
stem: Smooth muscle contraction differs from skeletal muscle in that it is regulated by:
options: Calmodulin-myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) pathway: Ca2+ binds calmodulin → activates MLCK → phosphorylates myosin light chain (MLC) → actin-myosin crossbridge cycling
explanation: Smooth muscle regulation: lacks troponin. Ca2+ binds calmodulin → Ca2+/calmodulin complex activates MLCK (myosin light chain kinase) → phosphorylates the 20-kD myosin light chain → myosin ATPase activated → crossbridge cycling. Relaxation: MLCP (myosin light chain phosphatase) dephosphorylates MLC. NO → ↑cGMP → protein kinase G → activates MLCP → relaxation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which ion is essential for cardiac muscle contraction but is provided by extracellular Ca2+ influx rather than only SR release?
options: Ca2+ — cardiac muscle uses both L-type Ca2+ channel (ICa-L) influx (trigger) and ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) SR release (CICR — calcium-induced calcium release)
explanation: Cardiac CICR (calcium-induced calcium release): the L-type Ca2+ channel (ICa-L) in the T-tubule admits a small amount of Ca2+ → triggers RyR2 to release a large amount of Ca2+ from the SR (CICR) → binds TnC → contraction. Unlike skeletal muscle (where DHPR-RyR1 is a direct mechanical coupling), cardiac muscle depends on Ca2+ entry for each beat (making it sensitive to extracellular Ca2+).

subject: Physiology
stem: The menstrual cycle: which hormone peaks just before ovulation (LH surge), triggering ovulation?
options: LH surge (~36 hours before ovulation) triggered by peak estrogen from the dominant follicle (positive feedback at LH >200 IU/L)
explanation: Ovulation trigger: sustained high estrogen from the dominant follicle (>200 pg/mL for >48 hours) → switches from negative to POSITIVE feedback on the anterior pituitary → massive LH surge (GnRH dependent) → final maturation of oocyte → ovulation ~36 hours after the LH surge peak (~day 14 of a 28-day cycle). FSH also surges but is less significant.

subject: Physiology
stem: Progesterone secreted during the luteal phase has which main effects?
options: Thins cervical mucus and promotes ovulation
Thickens the endometrium (secretory phase), thickens cervical mucus (hostile to sperm), raises basal body temperature (~0.5°C), and inhibits further LH/FSH release (negative feedback)
explanation: Progesterone (from corpus luteum, days 14–28): (1) Endometrium → secretory phase (glycogen, spiral arteries) for implantation, (2) Cervical mucus → thick, hostile to sperm, (3) BBT ↑0.5°C (thermogenic via hypothalamus) — used to detect ovulation retrospectively, (4) Negative feedback on hypothalamus/pituitary → ↓LH/FSH, (5) Relaxes uterine smooth muscle (tocolytic).

subject: Physiology
stem: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is secreted by which structure and maintains what?
options: Syncytiotrophoblast of the developing placenta — maintains the corpus luteum (preventing luteolysis) and thereby maintains progesterone secretion in early pregnancy
explanation: hCG: produced by the syncytiotrophoblast from ~8 days post-fertilization (detectable in urine/blood basis of pregnancy tests). Acts like LH on corpus luteum LH receptors → maintains corpus luteum → corpus luteum continues secreting progesterone → endometrium not shed (no menstruation). hCG peaks at 8–10 weeks gestation, then decreases as placenta takes over progesterone production.

subject: Physiology
stem: The placenta produces which hormones in late pregnancy?
options: Progesterone, estrogen (estriol), hPL (human placental lactogen), hCG; and cortisol in some species
explanation: Placental hormones: (1) Progesterone (takes over from corpus luteum by 8–10 weeks), (2) Estrogens (primarily estriol, requires fetal adrenal DHEAS → placental aromatase), (3) hCG (peaks 10 weeks), (4) hPL (human placental lactogen/choriomammotropin — GH-like, stimulates lipolysis and insulin resistance in mother, spares glucose for fetus), (5) CRH (drives fetal cortisol for lung maturation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Spermatogenesis occurs in which structure, and the process takes how long?
options: Seminiferous tubules — approximately 64–74 days (spermatogonia → primary spermatocyte → secondary spermatocyte → spermatid → spermatozoa, via mitosis then meiosis)
explanation: Spermatogenesis in seminiferous tubules: begins at puberty, continuous throughout life. Process: spermatogonia (2n) → primary spermatocytes (meiosis I) → secondary spermatocytes → spermatids (1n) → spermatozoa (via spermiogenesis: head, midpiece, flagellum formation). Total ~74 days. Sperm then mature in the epididymis (12–21 days). FSH acts on Sertoli cells; LH on Leydig cells (testosterone).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which hormone drives testosterone secretion from Leydig cells?
options: LH (luteinizing hormone) acts on Leydig cell LH receptors → Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA → steroidogenesis → testosterone
explanation: LH → Leydig cells → testosterone. Testosterone: (1) stimulates spermatogenesis (local high concentration in testis via Sertoli cell ABP/androgen-binding protein), (2) male secondary sexual characteristics, (3) anabolic effects (muscle, bone), (4) negative feedback on HPG axis (hypothalamus/pituitary). FSH → Sertoli cells → ABP secretion + inhibin (negative feedback on FSH).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'morning after pill' (emergency contraception) mechanism includes:
options: Prevention or delay of ovulation (mainly), possibly alteration of endometrium or cervical mucus — does NOT work if implantation has already occurred
Inhibition of fertilization by blocking acrosome reaction
explanation: Emergency contraception (levonorgestrel/Plan B): primarily delays or inhibits ovulation (by preventing the LH surge) when taken before ovulation. May also affect cervical mucus and endometrium to reduce fertilization/implantation. It is NOT an abortifacient — does not terminate an established pregnancy (i.e., after implantation). Ulipristal acetate (ella) works similarly but 5-day window.

subject: Physiology
stem: Photoreceptor transduction: how does light activate a photoreceptor?
options: Light converts 11-cis retinal → all-trans retinal → activates opsin → activates transducin (Gt) → activates PDE → ↓cGMP → closes cGMP-gated channels → hyperpolarization
explanation: Phototransduction: dark: high cGMP → cGMP-gated channels open → Na+/Ca2+ influx → depolarized (release glutamate continuously). Light: rhodopsin (11-cis retinal + opsin) absorbs photon → 11-cis retinal → all-trans retinal → activates transducin (Gαt) → activates PDE6 → cGMP hydrolysis → ↓cGMP → channels close → hyperpolarization → reduced glutamate release → OFF bipolar cells depolarize (sign-reversing synapse).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which photopigment is responsible for night (scotopic) vision?
options: Rhodopsin (rod pigment) — a combination of opsin (a membrane protein) and 11-cis retinal (a Vitamin A derivative)
explanation: Rhodopsin: found in rods (120 million in the human retina), contains 11-cis retinal (from Vitamin A) as chromophore. Sensitive to low light (single-photon detection). Peak sensitivity ~500 nm. After bleaching by light, rhodopsin must be regenerated from all-trans retinal via retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), requiring vitamin A. Night blindness (nyctalopia) = vitamin A deficiency.

subject: Physiology
stem: The three types of cone photopigments (opsins) are sensitive to which wavelengths?
options: Blue/short (~420 nm), green/medium (~530 nm), red/long (~560 nm) — this allows color vision via opponent process
explanation: Three cone types (L, M, S = Long, Medium, Short wavelength): S cones (short/blue, ~420 nm, ~3% of cones), M cones (medium/green, ~530 nm), L cones (long/red, ~560 nm). Color discrimination by opponent processes: L−M (red-green), L+M−S (blue-yellow), and luminance (L+M). Red-green color blindness: protanopia (absent L cones) or deuteranopia (absent M cones).

subject: Physiology
stem: The visual pathway: where do nasal retinal fibers cross?
options: Optic chiasm (the nasal half of each retina carries temporal visual field information and crosses to the contralateral optic tract)
explanation: Visual pathway: retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm (nasal fibers cross, temporal fibers stay ipsilateral) → optic tract (carries contralateral visual field information) → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus, 6 layers — 1,2 = M layers from M-ganglion cells; 3-6 = P layers) → optic radiation → primary visual cortex V1 (Brodmann area 17, calcarine sulcus). Right optic tract carries left visual field from both eyes.

subject: Physiology
stem: Presbyopia (age-related loss of near vision) is due to:
options: Increased axial length of the eye
Loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens (and reduced ciliary muscle strength) — the lens cannot increase its curvature sufficiently for near focus (accommodation fails)
explanation: Accommodation (near focus): ciliary muscle contracts → zonules relax → crystalline lens rounds up (increases curvature) → increases refractive power. Presbyopia: lens becomes less elastic with age (increased cross-linking of crystallin proteins) → cannot become convex enough for near vision. Apparent by ~40–45 years, complete by ~65 years. Corrected with reading glasses (+lenses).

subject: Physiology
stem: Sound transduction in the cochlea: how does sound wave movement generate an electrical signal?
options: Sound waves directly open ion channels in the auditory nerve

Basilar membrane vibration → stereocilia of IHC (inner hair cells) deflected → K+ influx via MET (mechanoelectrical transduction) channels → depolarization → Ca2+-dependent glutamate release → activates auditory nerve (CN VIII)
Sound waves compress the endolymph, which directly excites the auditory nerve
Sound is converted to electrical energy at the tympanic membrane
explanation: Cochlear transduction: sound → oval window vibration → perilymph waves → basilar membrane vibration (place coding: high frequency at base, low frequency at apex) → stereocilia of inner hair cells (IHC) deflect toward the tallest stereocilium → tension-gated K+ channels (MET channels) open → K+ and Ca2+ influx (from endolymph, high K+, +80 mV endocochlear potential) → depolarization → basolateral Ca2+ channels → glutamate release → activates afferent CN VIII fibers.

subject: Physiology
stem: The cochlea is divided into three fluid-filled compartments. The endolymph is found in which compartment?
options: Scala media (cochlear duct) — rich in K+ (145 mM), low Na+, positive endocochlear potential (+80 mV)
explanation: Cochlear compartments: Scala vestibuli (above basilar membrane) and Scala tympani (below) both contain perilymph (high Na+, similar to ECF). Scala media (between them) contains endolymph (high K+, low Na+ — like ICF) maintained by stria vascularis. Endocochlear potential (+80 mV) is the high positive potential of endolymph, providing a ~150 mV driving force for K+ into IHCs through MET channels.

subject: Physiology
stem: Sensorineural hearing loss vs. conductive hearing loss: in sensorineural HL, which test is positive?
options: Weber lateralizes to better ear; Rinne positive in affected ear (AC>BC, but both reduced)
Tuning fork not audible at all
Only Weber test matters, not Rinne
explanation: Sensorineural HL (SNHL — cochlear/neural lesion): Rinne positive in both ears (AC>BC normally, even in affected ear — both are reduced equally). Weber lateralizes to the BETTER (normal) ear. Conductive HL: Rinne negative in affected ear (BC>AC because bone conduction bypasses the mechanical problem). Weber lateralizes to the WORSE (affected) ear.

subject: Physiology
stem: Otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) reflect function of which cell type in the cochlea?
options: Outer hair cells (OHCs — active amplifiers of basilar membrane movement; motility driven by prestin protein in their lateral walls)
explanation: Outer hair cells (OHCs): electromotile cells that amplify basilar membrane motion (active cochlear amplifier). Prestin (a motor protein in OHC lateral membrane) contracts/elongates in response to voltage changes → amplifies BM vibration ~50-fold → sharpens frequency tuning. OHC integrity is measured by otoacoustic emissions (OAEs: sounds emitted by the cochlea). Absent OAEs → OHC dysfunction (ototoxicity, noise damage).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'tonotopic organization' of the cochlea refers to:
options: Different frequencies being processed at different locations: high frequencies at the base (near oval window), low frequencies at the apex
Color coding of different hair cells
explanation: Tonotopy (place coding) in the cochlea: basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base (responds to high frequencies, 20,000 Hz) and wide and floppy at the apex (responds to low frequencies, 20 Hz). This spatial frequency mapping is maintained throughout the auditory pathway (CN VIII, cochlear nuclei, inferior colliculus, MGN of thalamus, primary auditory cortex in Heschl's gyrus).

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal blood pH, PaCO2, and HCO3- values:
explanation: Normal ABG values: pH 7.35–7.45 (mean 7.40), PaCO2 35–45 mmHg (mean 40 mmHg), PaO2 75–100 mmHg, HCO3- 22–26 mEq/L (mean 24 mEq/L), SpO2 >95%, BE (base excess) -2 to +2 mEq/L. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = 6.1 + log [HCO3-] / (0.03 × PaCO2).

subject: Physiology
stem: Metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap is caused by which conditions?
options: Diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis (normal AG)
MUDPILES: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Isoniazid/Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates
explanation: High anion gap metabolic acidosis: AG = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-), normal 8–12 mEq/L. High AG = unmeasured anions added to the blood. MUDPILES mnemonic: Methanol (formate), Uremia (sulfates, phosphates), DKA (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate), Propylene glycol, Isoniazid/Iron, Lactic acidosis (L-lactate), Ethylene glycol (oxalate/glycolate), Salicylates.

subject: Physiology
stem: Respiratory alkalosis (↓PaCO2) causes which compensatory response?
options: Renal compensation: decreased HCO3- reabsorption (↓HCO3- to lower pH toward normal) — takes 2–3 days
explanation: Respiratory alkalosis: ↓PaCO2 (hyperventilation → causes: anxiety, early ASA toxicity, hypoxia at altitude, PE, liver failure, pregnancy). Acute: pH ↑, compensation = cells exchange H+ for K+ (↓K+). Chronic (>3–5 days): renal compensation = ↓HCO3- reabsorption (↓secretion of H+, ↑HCO3- excretion) → HCO3- falls, normalizes pH. Expected HCO3- compensation: 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓PaCO2 (chronic).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'anion gap' is calculated as:
options: Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) — normally 8–12 mEq/L (reflects unmeasured anions like albumin, phosphate, sulfate)
explanation: Anion gap (AG) = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 8–12 mEq/L. The gap is due to unmeasured anions (mainly albumin, ~2.5 mEq/dL per g/dL albumin, plus phosphate, sulfate). Corrected AG (for hypoalbuminemia) = measured AG + 2.5 × (4 - albumin in g/dL). Useful to classify metabolic acidosis as high AG (added unmeasured anions) or normal AG (loss of HCO3-/addition of Cl-).

subject: Physiology
stem: During exercise, cardiac output can increase to what maximum?
options: 20–25 L/min in trained athletes (SV ↑ + HR ↑ maximally)
explanation: Cardiac output during maximal exercise: CO = SV × HR. Trained athlete: SV may increase from 70 to 150–200 mL; HR from 70 to 180–200 bpm. Max CO: 150 × 200/1000 = 30 L/min in elite athletes vs. ~20 L/min in fit untrained individuals. Frank-Starling (increased EDV) increases SV initially; sympathetic drive increases HR and contractility.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'anaerobic threshold' (lactate threshold) in exercise represents:
options: The point at which O2 consumption begins
The exercise intensity above which lactic acid production exceeds clearance → blood lactate rises → metabolic acidosis begins
The point at which glycolysis begins
explanation: Lactate/anaerobic threshold: at low intensity exercise, oxidative phosphorylation meets all energy needs (no lactate accumulation). Above a critical intensity, fast-twitch fibers recruited → pyruvate production exceeds TCA cycle capacity → pyruvate → lactate (LDH). Lactate rises above 2 mmol/L (OBLA = 4 mmol/L). This threshold (AT) is a key predictor of endurance performance.

subject: Physiology
stem: Oxygen debt (EPOC — excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) after exercise is due to:
options: Repayment of O2 deficit: restoration of myoglobin/Hb O2 stores, resynthesis of creatine phosphate, conversion of lactate → glucose (Cori cycle) in liver, elevated body temperature, and catecholamine effects
explanation: EPOC (oxygen debt): after exercise stops, O2 consumption remains elevated for minutes to hours. Alactacid component (fast): restores O2 to myoglobin/blood, resynthesizes phosphocreatine (PC). Lactacid component (slow): lactate → glucose (Cori cycle in liver, ~20% of lactate), gluconeogenesis, elevated temperature (Q10 effect), hormonal effects (catecholamines persist). Total EPOC may be 2× the original O2 deficit.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which substrate provides the primary energy source during prolonged low-intensity exercise (>30 minutes)?
options: Fat (free fatty acids from triglycerides via lipolysis) — at low intensity, fat oxidation dominates; at high intensity, carbohydrate predominates
explanation: Energy substrate during exercise: 0–10 sec: creatine phosphate (PCr) → rapid ATP. 10 sec–2 min: anaerobic glycolysis. 2–30 min: aerobic glycolysis (glucose). >30 min: fat oxidation (triglyceride lipolysis → FFA → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA → TCA) increasingly predominates. Fat provides ~9 kcal/g vs. carbohydrate 4 kcal/g — nearly unlimited supply in adipose tissue.

subject: Physiology
stem: The hypothalamus acts as the 'thermostat' of the body. Which nucleus is the primary thermoregulatory center?
options: Anterior hypothalamus / preoptic area (POAH) — contains thermosensitive neurons; set point; stimulates sweating when overheated; POAH lesion → hyperthermia
explanation: Thermoregulation: POAH (anterior hypothalamic preoptic area) is the primary thermoregulatory center. It receives inputs from peripheral and central thermoreceptors and compares to the set point (~37°C). Response to heat: ↑sweating (cholinergic sympathetic), cutaneous vasodilation, behavioral change. Response to cold: shivering (posterior hypothalamus), vasoconstriction, piloerection, non-shivering thermogenesis (BAT, thyroid hormones, catecholamines).

subject: Physiology
stem: Fever is mediated by which prostaglandin acting on which hypothalamic structure?
options: PGE2 (prostaglandin E2) acts on EP3 receptors in the POAH → raises the thermoregulatory set point → initiates heat-conserving responses (shivering, vasoconstriction) until the new temperature is reached
explanation: Fever: Pyrogens (bacterial LPS, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) → stimulate macrophages → increase COX-2 → ↑PGE2 in the blood-brain barrier/endothelium of hypothalamic vessels → PGE2 crosses to POAH → EP3 receptors → ↑cAMP → raises set point. Result: shivering, vasoconstriction → core temperature rises. NSAIDs/aspirin inhibit COX → reduce PGE2 → antipyretic.

subject: Physiology
stem: The electroencephalogram (EEG) shows alpha waves in which state?
options: Relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed (8–13 Hz, posterior dominant — 'alpha rhythm')
Focused mental activity or eyes open
explanation: EEG rhythms: Alpha (8–13 Hz) — relaxed wakefulness, eyes closed, posterior regions. Beta (13–30 Hz) — active thinking, focused attention, eyes open. Theta (4–8 Hz) — drowsiness, early sleep, children. Delta (<4 Hz) — deep sleep (N3), anesthesia. Gamma (>30 Hz) — high cognitive binding. In REM sleep: low-voltage mixed-frequency (desynchronized, similar to wakefulness).

subject: Physiology
stem: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is characterized by:
options: Delta waves and muscle atonia only
Paradoxical sleep: EEG resembles wakefulness (desynchronized), skeletal muscle atonia (prevent acting out dreams), vivid dreams, REMs, fluctuating autonomic activity (↑HR, ↑RR, penile erections)
explanation: REM sleep: desynchronized EEG (β-like), complete skeletal muscle atonia (except respiratory and extraocular muscles — brainstem glycine/GABA neurons inhibit motor neurons), vivid, emotional dreams. Physiological REM: ↑HR, ↑BP variability, irregular breathing. REM occurs every ~90 min (4–5 cycles/night); increases toward morning. Growth hormone secreted during N3 (deep NREM, stage 3/4).

subject: Physiology
stem: Sleep apnea: obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is caused by:
options: Failure of central respiratory drive (central apnea)

Upper airway collapse during sleep (pharyngeal muscle atonia + obstruction) → apnea → arousal → repeat hundreds of times per night → non-restorative sleep, daytime sleepiness, ↑risk of hypertension, arrhythmia, stroke
explanation: OSA: repetitive upper airway collapse during sleep (pharyngeal muscles relax → negative pressure of inspiration → pharynx collapses at soft palate/base of tongue → airflow obstruction). Each apnea → hypoxemia + hypercapnia → arousal → airway opens → breathing resumes → re-sleep → cycle repeats. Risk factors: obesity, large neck, retrognathia. Treatment: CPAP (splints airway open), weight loss.

subject: Physiology
stem: Diabetes insipidus (DI): how is central DI differentiated from nephrogenic DI?
options: Water deprivation test: both give high urine osmolarity after desmopressin (DDAVP) in central DI (ADH-deficient); urine remains dilute in nephrogenic DI (ADH-insensitive)
explanation: Water deprivation test: both central and nephrogenic DI → concentrated urine during deprivation as much as possible, but serum osmolarity rises and urine stays dilute. After DDAVP (synthetic ADH): central DI → urine concentrates (kidneys respond normally, just lacked ADH). Nephrogenic DI → urine remains dilute despite DDAVP (kidneys are resistant). Plasma ADH is low in central, high in nephrogenic DI.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which drug class increases renal glucose excretion by blocking glucose reabsorption in the PCT?
options: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) — block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule → glycosuria → lower blood glucose + slight osmotic diuresis + weight loss
explanation: SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2): handles ~90% of glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule. SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins): block SGLT2 → glucose spills into urine → reduce blood glucose (insulin-independent). Also cause: BP reduction (natriuresis), weight loss, HbA1c reduction, and cardiovascular/renal protection in T2DM (reduced hospitalizations for heart failure, slowed CKD progression).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'threshold' for glucosuria (glucose appearing in urine) is normally:
options: Serum glucose ~180 mg/dL (the transport maximum [Tm] for glucose reabsorption in PCT is exceeded)
explanation: Renal glucose threshold: at normal blood glucose (80–100 mg/dL), all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT (SGLT1 + SGLT2). Tm for glucose = 320 mg/min (~renal threshold ≈ 180 mg/dL blood glucose). Above this, transport capacity is saturated → glucose appears in urine (glycosuria). In DM, blood glucose often exceeds 180 mg/dL → classical glycosuria (+ polyuria from osmotic diuresis, polydipsia, polyphagia).

subject: Physiology
stem: Loop diuretics (furosemide) block which transporter in the nephron?
options: NKCC2 (Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter) in the thick ascending limb of Henle — blocks solute reabsorption that drives the countercurrent concentration of the medullary interstitium → impairs maximal urine concentration
explanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid): block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb of Henle (TALH). The TALH is the diluting segment (impermeable to water, reabsorbs NaCl) and the main contributor to medullary hyperosmolarity (countercurrent multiplication). Blocking NKCC2 → large NaCl, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ excretion → profound diuresis (ceiling dose gives maximal effect). Most powerful diuretics.

subject: Physiology
stem: Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) act on which segment of the nephron?
options: Early distal convoluted tubule (DCT1) — block NCC (Na+/Cl- cotransporter) → reduces Na+ and Cl- reabsorption
explanation: Thiazide diuretics: block NCC (electroneutral Na-Cl cotransporter) in the early DCT. Effects: moderate Na+ and water diuresis, ↓K+ (alkalosis from increased aldosterone), ↑Ca2+ reabsorption (paradoxical: used in hypercalciuria/nephrolithiasis), ↑uric acid retention (used cautiously in gout). Unique: antihypertensive independent of diuresis (vasodilation of resistance vessels). First-line antihypertensive.

subject: Physiology
stem: Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, amiloride): how do they work?
options: Spironolactone: competes with aldosterone at MR (aldosterone antagonist) in collecting duct. Amiloride/triamterene: directly block ENaC (luminal Na+ channel) in CCD — both reduce Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion → K+ retention
explanation: Potassium-sparing diuretics: (1) Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone): competitively block MR (mineralocorticoid receptor) in principal cells of CCD → reduced ENaC and ROMK expression → ↓Na+ reabsorption + ↓K+ secretion → K+ retention. Used in heart failure (survival benefit from anti-fibrotic effects), hyperaldosteronism, and hypokalemia. (2) Direct ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene): block ENaC directly (K+-sparing without antialdosterone effects).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'cardiac cycle' — during isovolumetric contraction, which statement is correct?
options: All valves are CLOSED (both mitral/tricuspid and aortic/pulmonary valves) — ventricular pressure rises but no volume change; ends when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure and semilunar valves open
Only the aortic valve is open
Only the mitral valve is open
explanation: Phases of the cardiac cycle (Wiggers diagram): (1) Isovolumetric contraction (IVC): MV + TV closed, AV + PV closed. Pressure rises. (2) Rapid ejection: AV + PV open. (3) Reduced ejection. (4) Isovolumetric relaxation (IVR): all valves closed, pressure falls. (5) Rapid filling: MV + TV open. (6) Slow filling (diastasis). (7) Atrial systole (20% extra fill). EDV = 130 mL, ESV = 50 mL, SV = 80 mL, EF = 62%.

subject: Physiology
stem: Heart sounds: what causes the first heart sound (S1)?
options: Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves (AV valves) at the start of ventricular systole
explanation: Heart sounds: S1 = closure of AV valves (mitral M1 + tricuspid T1, M1 slightly earlier) at the end of diastole/start of systole. Best heard at apex. Loud S1 in MS (rigid valves), tachycardia, high CO. Soft S1 in MR, PR prolongation, cardiomyopathy. S2 = closure of semilunar valves (A2 + P2) at end of systole. Physiological splitting: A2 before P2, widens on inspiration (increased RV filling → delayed P2).

subject: Physiology
stem: The third heart sound (S3) is associated with:
options: Rapid filling of the LV in early diastole — heard as a low-pitched sound at the apex; normal in children and athletes; pathological in heart failure (↑LVEDP, ↓compliance)
explanation: S3 (ventricular gallop): occurs during the rapid filling phase of diastole (passive filling). Pathological in adults >40 years — suggests volume overload, dilated cardiomyopathy, or heart failure (↑EDV, ↓LV compliance). Heard at apex with bell of stethoscope. S4 (atrial gallop): occurs during atrial systole — suggests stiff LV (hypertrophy, ischemia, HTN), normal in trained athletes. Both form 'gallop rhythm' when heart rate is fast.

subject: Physiology
stem: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) — what formula is used clinically?
options: MAP = DBP + (SBP - DBP)/3 [= DBP + Pulse Pressure/3] — because diastole occupies ~2/3 of the cardiac cycle at rest
explanation: MAP = DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) = DBP + 1/3(PP). At HR 60 bpm, diastole is twice as long as systole. Normal MAP ~70–100 mmHg. At SBP/DBP 120/80: MAP = 80 + (120-80)/3 = 80 + 13.3 = 93.3 mmHg. MAP is the best indicator of organ perfusion pressure (cerebral, renal, coronary autoregulate around MAP).

subject: Physiology
stem: The P-wave in the ECG represents:
options: Atrial depolarization — normally <0.12 sec (3 small squares), <0.25 mV amplitude
explanation: ECG intervals: P-wave = atrial depolarization (SA node → both atria). Normal P: duration <120 ms, amplitude <2.5 mm in limb leads. Tall P (>2.5 mm in II) = right atrial enlargement ('P pulmonale'). Broad bifid P (>120 ms in II) = left atrial enlargement ('P mitrale'). PR interval = P start to QRS start = 120–200 ms (represents AV nodal conduction delay, physiological). QRS = ventricular depolarization (<120 ms normal).

subject: Physiology
stem: In the ECG, T-wave inversion in precordial leads V1-V4 indicates:
options: Anterior myocardial ischemia (reduced oxygen supply to the anterior wall — left anterior descending artery territory)
explanation: T-wave changes in ECG: T-wave inversion in V1-V4 → anterior myocardial ischemia or non-ST elevation MI (NSTEMI). T-wave inversion in V4-V6 → lateral ischemia (LCX territory). Hyperacute T waves (tall peaked) → very early STEMI. Symmetric deep T-wave inversion in V1-V4 ('Wellens' T-waves') = critical LAD stenosis before infarction.

subject: Physiology
stem: The PR interval is prolonged in:
options: First-degree AV block (PR >200 ms, 5 small squares) — all beats conducted but with increased AV nodal delay
explanation: AV block degrees: First-degree = PR >200 ms, all P waves conduct (1:1). Second-degree, Mobitz I (Wenckebach) = progressive PR lengthening → dropped QRS → cycle repeats. Second-degree, Mobitz II = fixed PR, sudden dropped QRS (more serious). Third-degree (complete) = P waves and QRS independent (complete dissociation). WPW = SHORT PR (<120 ms), delta wave (slurred upstroke of QRS), tachyarrhythmias.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which ion causes the plateau phase of the cardiac action potential?
options: Ca2+ influx through L-type Ca2+ channels (ICa-L) — the plateau (phase 2) lasts ~200–250 ms in ventricular myocytes, allowing time for ventricular contraction
explanation: Ventricular AP phases: Phase 0 (rapid depolarization, Na+ INa), Phase 1 (early repolarization, Ito — transient outward K+ current), Phase 2 (plateau, ICa-L inward balances IKr/IKs outward), Phase 3 (repolarization, IKr/IKs dominate), Phase 4 (resting, -90 mV, IK1). The long plateau prevents tetanic contraction of the heart (absolute refractory period spans most of phase 2–3).

subject: Physiology
stem: QT interval prolongation increases the risk of which arrhythmia?
options: Torsades de pointes (TdP) — a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate to VF
explanation: QT prolongation: QTc (Bazett: QT/√RR) normal <440 ms males, <460 ms females. Prolonged → early afterdepolarizations (EADs) → TdP → VF → sudden cardiac death. Causes: Congenital LQTS (KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A mutations), drugs (quinidine, sotalol, amiodarone, antipsychotics, macrolides, azoles), electrolytes (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia).

subject: Physiology
stem: The coronary arteries fill primarily during which phase of the cardiac cycle?
options: Diastole — during systole, intramyocardial pressure compresses intramural coronary vessels (especially the left coronary, which supplies the left ventricle)
explanation: Coronary circulation: left coronary artery (LAD + LCX) → supplies most of the LV. During systole, high intraventricular pressure compresses intramural vessels → minimal LCA flow. During diastole, LV relaxes → intramural pressure falls → LCA fills. This is why tachycardia (shortened diastole) increases risk of ischemia. Right coronary fills throughout the cycle (thin RV wall → lower intramural pressure during systole).

subject: Physiology
stem: In hemorrhagic shock, which compensatory mechanism is FIRST activated?
options: Baroreceptor reflex: ↓BP → ↓stretch in carotid sinus/aortic arch baroreceptors → ↓afferent inhibition → ↑sympathetic outflow → tachycardia + vasoconstriction (to maintain BP and redirect blood to vital organs)
ADH release (takes minutes but slower than baroreceptors)
explanation: Hemorrhagic shock compensation: Immediate (seconds): baroreceptor reflex → ↑SNS → tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, ↑contractility. Minutes: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation → Na+/water retention. Hours: ADH (vasopressin) release → water reabsorption. Blood glucose ↑ (catecholamines → glycogenolysis). Classification: Class I (<15% blood loss, no compensation needed), II (15-30%, tachycardia), III (30-40%, BP drops), IV (>40%, life-threatening).

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the 'Fick principle' used to calculate?
options: Cardiac output: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2) — oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous O2 difference
explanation: Fick principle: CO = O2 consumption (VO2) / (arterial O2 content - venous O2 content). E.g.: VO2 = 250 mL/min, CaO2 = 20 mL/dL, CvO2 = 15 mL/dL → CO = 250/[(20-15)×10] = 250/50 = 5 L/min. Thermodilution (cold saline via Swan-Ganz) is the clinical gold standard. Echocardiography measures SV × HR for CO. Fick method is gold standard for oxygen consumption calculations.

subject: Physiology
stem: Jugular venous pressure (JVP): the 'c' wave represents:
options: Tricuspid valve bulging into the right atrium during early ventricular systole (isovolumetric contraction)
Venous filling of the right atrium
Fall of atrial pressure during ventricular systole
explanation: JVP waveform: 'a' wave = atrial contraction (absent in AF, prominent in tricuspid stenosis, pulmonary hypertension). 'c' wave = tricuspid valve bulging back toward RA during IVC (often not visible clinically). 'x' descent = atrial relaxation + tricuspid valve descent during ventricular ejection. 'v' wave = venous filling of RA while TV is closed (large in tricuspid regurgitation). 'y' descent = opening of TV → ventricular filling.

subject: Physiology
stem: Blood flow in a vessel: if the radius is halved, resistance changes by how much? (Poiseuille's law)
options: Increases 16-fold (resistance ∝ 1/r4 — so halving radius → 24 = 16× increase in resistance)
explanation: Poiseuille's law: Flow (Q) = ΔP × π × r4 / (8 × η × L). Resistance (R) = 8ηL / πr4 ∝ 1/r4. If radius halved: R ∝ 1/(r/2)4 = 1/(r4/16) = 16/r4 → 16× increase in resistance. This is why small arteries/arterioles are the major site of vascular resistance — small radius changes dramatically affect flow. Arterioles: 'resistance vessels', major regulators of blood pressure and organ blood flow distribution.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cardiac output is reduced in which physiological condition?
options: Recumbent position (lying down) vs. standing → actually increases CO; but CO is LOWEST during sleep and reduced in upright posture compared to supine (due to venous pooling)
explanation: CO is increased by: exercise (5 L → 20-25 L/min), pregnancy (30-50% increase by 24 weeks), fever, anemia, AV fistula, hyperthyroidism. CO is decreased by: hypovolemia, cardiomyopathy, severe valvular disease, cardiac tamponade, extreme bradycardia. Normal CO at rest ~5 L/min; cardiac index (CI) = CO/BSA = 2.4–4.0 L/min/m2; reduced CI <2.2 = cardiogenic shock.

subject: Physiology
stem: Ventricular preload is best represented by:
options: End-diastolic volume (EDV) or end-diastolic pressure (EDP) — reflects the degree of ventricular stretch before contraction (Frank-Starling mechanism)
explanation: Preload = EDV = degree of stretch of ventricular myocardium before systole. Increased by: hypervolemia, venous return increase, bradycardia, mitral/tricuspid regurgitation (↑volume load). Decreased by: hypovolemia, diuretics, venodilators (nitroglycerin, morphine). Frank-Starling: ↑preload → ↑sarcomere stretch → ↑cross-bridge overlap → ↑force. Clinically: PCWP approximates LVEDP (preload indicator).

subject: Physiology
stem: Afterload on the left ventricle is primarily determined by:
options: Systemic vascular resistance (SVR/TPR) and aortic compliance — the pressure the LV must generate to eject blood
explanation: Afterload = systolic wall stress = the resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Laplace: wall stress = (P × r) / (2h) [P=pressure, r=radius, h=wall thickness]. Increased afterload: aortic stenosis, hypertension (↑SVR). ↑afterload → ↑O2 demand. Heart failure with ↑afterload: give ACE inhibitors/ARBs/hydralazine (arterial vasodilators → reduce SVR → reduce afterload). IABP (balloon counterpulsation) inflates in diastole (↑coronary flow) and deflates in systole (↓afterload).

subject: Physiology
stem: Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg fall in SBP during inspiration) is a sign of:
options: Cardiac tamponade (and severe constrictive pericarditis, tension pneumothorax, severe asthma/COPD) — inspiration → ↑venous return to RV → RV expands → interventricular septum shifts left → ↓LV filling → ↓CO → ↓SBP
explanation: Cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds): pericardial fluid compresses all cardiac chambers. On inspiration, ↑RV filling (exaggerated) → septal shift → ↓LV filling → ↓SV → ↓SBP >10 mmHg (pulsus paradoxus). ECG: electrical alternans (QRS alternating in size/axis — swinging heart). Kussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration) is seen in constrictive pericarditis, NOT tamponade (differentiation from constrictive).

subject: Physiology
stem: Lung compliance is defined as:
options: Change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure (C = ΔV/ΔP) — normally 200 mL/cmH2O for the lungs; reduced in restrictive diseases, fibrosis; increased in emphysema
The pressure needed to overcome airway resistance
explanation: Lung compliance = ΔV/ΔP (mL/cmH2O). Normal total respiratory system compliance ~100 mL/cmH2O (lung + chest wall). Decreased compliance (stiff lungs): pulmonary fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary edema, atelectasis. Increased compliance (floppy lungs): emphysema (loss of elastic recoil). Chest wall compliance decreased by: obesity, kyphoscoliosis, pregnancy.

subject: Physiology
stem: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is:
options: Maximum volume exhaled after maximum inspiration
Volume remaining in lungs after a NORMAL tidal exhalation — the equilibrium point where outward chest wall recoil balances inward lung recoil (~2500 mL in adults)
explanation: Lung volumes: TLC = TV + IRV + ERV + RV (total ~6L). FRC = ERV + RV (~2500 mL) = equilibrium point. FRC is measured by helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography (can measure RV which spirometry cannot). FRC reduced by: obesity, supine position, pregnancy, atelectasis. FRC increased by: emphysema, asthma, COPD (air trapping, lung hyperinflation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Closing capacity and its significance in clinical anesthesia:
options: The volume at which pulmonary surfactant depletes

The lung volume at which small airways begin to close during expiration — when FRC falls below closing capacity (as in obesity, supine position, old age), airway closure during normal breathing → V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia
The tidal volume minus dead space
explanation: Closing capacity (CC) = closing volume + RV. In young healthy adults, CC < FRC. With age, obesity, or supine position, FRC decreases while CC increases → when CC > FRC, small airways close during tidal breathing → gas trapping → V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia. This is why elderly patients and obese patients (and those lying supine under anesthesia) are prone to atelectasis and hypoxemia.

subject: Physiology
stem: Dead space: which formula calculates physiological dead space?
options: Bohr's equation: VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2 — compares alveolar CO2 to expired CO2 to calculate the fraction of wasted ventilation
explanation: Bohr's equation for physiological dead space: VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PēCO2) / PaCO2. Where PēCO2 is mixed expired CO2. Normal VD ≈ 150 mL (anatomical) out of VT 500 mL → VD/VT = 0.30. Increased dead space in: PE (ventilated but non-perfused alveoli), emphysema (destroyed alveoli), high positive pressure ventilation. Increased VD/VT requires greater minute ventilation to maintain normal PaCO2.

subject: Physiology
stem: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve: a right shift (↑P50) means:
options: Hb binds O2 more tightly (less O2 released to tissues)
Hb releases O2 more readily to tissues (↓O2 affinity); causes: ↑temperature, ↑PaCO2/↑H+ (Bohr effect), ↑2,3-DPG, ↑blood pH going left
explanation: Right shift of ODC (↑P50, P50 normally ~27 mmHg): Bohr effect — ↑CO2 or ↑H+ (acidosis) → Hb releases O2 more readily → beneficial in exercising tissue. Also: ↑temperature, ↑2,3-DPG (chronic hypoxia, anemia). Left shift (↓P50, ↑affinity): ↓temperature, ↓CO2/↓H+ (alkalosis), ↓2,3-DPG (stored blood), fetal Hb (HbF — binds 2,3-DPG poorly), COHb (carboxyhemoglobin, from CO poisoning).

subject: Physiology
stem: 2,3-Diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) in RBCs: its role and what increases it?
options: 2,3-DPG binds to the β-chains of deoxyHb → stabilizes deoxy conformation → right shifts ODC → ↓O2 affinity → ↑O2 release to tissues; 2,3-DPG increases in chronic hypoxia, anemia, high altitude
2,3-DPG has no effect on oxygen transport
explanation: 2,3-DPG (bisphosphoglycerate, BPG): synthesized in RBC glycolysis (Rapoport-Luebering shunt). Binds exclusively to deoxyHb (β-chains) → stabilizes T-state → right shifts ODC → ↓Hb-O2 affinity → ↑O2 release. Increased by: altitude acclimatization, chronic anemia, chronic hypoxia, thyroid hormones. Decreased in: stored blood (falls after 24h), fetal blood (HbF doesn't bind 2,3-DPG well — allows fetal Hb to bind O2 from maternal Hb).

subject: Physiology
stem: Surfactant deficiency in premature infants causes:
options: Infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS/NRDS): ↑alveolar surface tension (surfactant normally reduces surface tension → reduces work of breathing and prevents alveolar collapse) → alveolar collapse (atelectasis) → ↓V/Q → hypoxemia → acidosis
explanation: Pulmonary surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, DPPC + phosphatidylglycerol + SP-A/B/C/D): produced by Type II pneumocytes after 34 weeks. Reduces alveolar surface tension (Laplace: P = 2T/r — surfactant lowers T → reduces pressure needed to inflate small alveoli → prevents collapse). IRDS in premature (<34 weeks) babies → atelectasis, 'ground glass' CXR, respiratory grunting, intercostal retraction. Treatment: antenatal corticosteroids (mothers) → accelerates surfactant; exogenous surfactant for neonate.

subject: Physiology
stem: The alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient) is normally:
options: <10–15 mmHg in young adults (increases with age up to ~25 mmHg); calculated as: A-a O2 gradient = PAO2 - PaO2 — reflects efficiency of O2 transfer from alveoli to blood
explanation: A-a gradient: PAO2 (from alveolar gas equation: FiO2 × [Patm - PH2O] - PaCO2/R) minus PaO2 (measured ABG). Normal ~10 mmHg (increases with age due to V/Q mismatch from airway closure). Increased in: V/Q mismatch, diffusion impairment, intracardiac shunt, pulmonary embolism. In pure hypoventilation (e.g., opioid overdose): A-a gradient is NORMAL (hypoxemia from ↑PaCO2  'displacing' O2 in alveolus, but V/Q matching is normal).

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypercapnia (↑PaCO2) as a respiratory drive: what are the central chemoreceptors' primary stimulus?
options: [H+] in CSF (determined mainly by CO2 — CO2 crosses BBB, is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-; the H+ stimulates central chemoreceptors in the medulla)
explanation: Central chemoreceptors (ventral medullary surface): respond to CO2/pH of CSF. CO2 crosses BBB freely → CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3- (catalyzed by CA). ↑H+ in CSF → stimulates central chemoreceptors → ↑ventilation. BBB is relatively impermeable to H+ and HCO3-. In chronic hypercapnia (COPD), CSF HCO3- rises (compensates) → pH normalizes → reduced CO2 drive → 'hypoxic drive' from peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid/aortic bodies, PaO2<60 mmHg) takes over.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which condition causes hypoxemia with a NORMAL alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient?
options: Hypoventilation (e.g., sedative overdose, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation) — ↑PaCO2 → displaced O2 in alveolus (per alveolar gas equation), but V/Q matching is intact → A-a gradient is normal
explanation: A-a gradient interpretation: Normal A-a gradient with hypoxemia → pure hypoventilation (↑PaCO2, ↑PaCO2/R reduces PAO2). Elevated A-a gradient → impaired O2 transfer due to: (1) V/Q mismatch (most common — COPD, PE, pulmonary edema), (2) Diffusion impairment (pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial disease — PaO2 improves with 100% O2), (3) Shunt (ASD, PDA, hepatopulmonary syndrome, intracardiac — does NOT improve with 100% O2, as shunted blood bypasses alveoli).

subject: Physiology
stem: The hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) response diverts blood from:
options: Poorly-ventilated (low V/Q, hypoxic) areas to better-ventilated alveoli — reduces V/Q mismatch and maintains arterial oxygenation
High-pressure pulmonary arteries to pulmonary veins
explanation: HPV (Euler-Liljestrand reflex): local alveolar hypoxia → local pulmonary arteriole constriction → diverts blood to better-ventilated areas → maintains V/Q matching. Mechanism: alveolar hypoxia → smooth muscle Ca2+ ↑ (via inhibition of K+ channels → membrane depolarization → L-type Ca2+ channel opening) → vasoconstriction. Clinically: chronic global hypoxia (high altitude, COPD) → widespread HPV → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure (cor pulmonale).

subject: Physiology
stem: Spirometry: FEV1/FVC ratio distinguishes obstructive from restrictive disease. In obstructive lung disease (COPD/asthma):
options: FEV1/FVC is <0.70 (reduced); FVC is typically normal or only mildly reduced — airway resistance prevents fast exhalation
FEV1 and FVC are proportionally reduced
explanation: Spirometry patterns: Obstructive (COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis): ↓FEV1, normal/↓FVC → FEV1/FVC <0.70. ↑TLC (air trapping in COPD). ↑RV. ↑FRC. Restrictive (fibrosis, obesity, neuromuscular): FEV1 and FVC proportionally reduced → FEV1/FVC ≥0.70 (may be elevated). ↓TLC. ↓FRC. ↓RV. In asthma: FEV1/FVC <0.70, but may improve after bronchodilator (reversibility ≥12% + ≥200 mL = asthma, vs COPD where it is irreversible).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cyanosis becomes clinically apparent when:
options: ≥5 g/dL of deoxygenated hemoglobin is present in capillary blood — appears as blue discoloration of skin and mucous membranes
explanation: Cyanosis: requires ≥5 g/dL of deoxyHb in capillaries (absolute amount, not percentage). Central cyanosis: low SaO2 (lung disease, cardiac shunts). Peripheral cyanosis: normal SaO2 but poor peripheral circulation (cold, heart failure — ↑O2 extraction by slowed peripheral blood). Important: anemia — may be severely hypoxic (low SaO2) without cyanosis (Hb total too low to provide 5 g/dL deoxyHb). Polycythemia — cyanosis at relatively mild hypoxia.

subject: Physiology
stem: The hypothalamic-pituitary axis: what is the mechanism of negative feedback in thyroid regulation?
options: High levels of free T3/T4 suppress TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary — feedback primarily at the pituitary level (T4 → T3 conversion by deiodinase in thyrotrophs)
explanation: HPT axis: TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (anterior pituitary) → T3/T4 (thyroid). T3/T4 (especially T3 — intracellular conversion by type 2 deiodinase in pituitary thyrotrophs) → suppresses TSH (inhibits TRH receptor expression, reduces TSH synthesis/secretion). Primary hypothyroidism: ↓T4 → ↑TSH (most sensitive marker). Secondary hypothyroidism: ↓TSH → ↓T4 (pituitary disease). Subclinical hypothyroidism: ↑TSH, normal T4.

subject: Physiology
stem: Glucocorticoids (cortisol): effects on glucose metabolism?
options: Raises blood glucose via multiple mechanisms: promotes gluconeogenesis (liver), inhibits glucose uptake (peripheral tissues), stimulates protein catabolism → amino acids for gluconeogenesis, stimulates lipolysis → glycerol for gluconeogenesis
explanation: Cortisol (counter-regulatory hormone for insulin): (1) ↑gluconeogenesis in liver (via PEPCK, G6Pase upregulation), (2) ↑proteolysis in muscle → ↑gluconeogenic amino acids (alanine, glutamine), (3) ↑lipolysis → FFA + glycerol (glycerol → gluconeogenesis), (4) ↓GLUT4 expression → insulin resistance in peripheral tissues. Net: hyperglycemia. Cushing's syndrome → 'steroid diabetes.' Addison's disease → hypoglycemia, especially under stress.

subject: Physiology
stem: Aldosterone synthesis is stimulated by which THREE primary stimuli?
options: Angiotensin II (via AT1 receptors), hyperkalemia (↑K+ directly depolarizes zona glomerulosa cells → ↑Ca2+ influx → ↑aldosterone), and ACTH (minor, permissive role)
explanation: Aldosterone (zona glomerulosa of adrenal cortex): synthesis stimulated by (1) Angiotensin II (via RAAS — ↓Na+/↓blood volume → renin → angiotensin I → ACE → Ang II), (2) Hyperkalemia (↑K+ → depolarizes zona glomerulosa → ↑Ca2+ → aldosterone synthase), (3) ACTH (weak, becomes significant only in states of high ACTH). Aldosterone → principal cells of CCD → ↑ENaC + ↑ROMK + ↑Na+/K+-ATPase → Na+ retention + K+/H+ secretion.

subject: Physiology
stem: The zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex produces:
options: Glucocorticoids (cortisol — regulated by ACTH; cortisol synthesis requires CYP17A1 hydroxylation at 17-alpha, then CYP21A2 at 21, then CYP11B1 at 11-beta)
explanation: Adrenal cortex zones: 'GFR = salt, sugar, sex': Zona Glomerulosa (outermost) → mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). Zona Fasciculata (largest, middle) → glucocorticoids (cortisol, corticosterone). Zona Reticularis (innermost) → sex steroids (DHEA, androstenedione). Adrenal medulla → catecholamines (epinephrine 80%, norepinephrine 20%). Regulated by: aldosterone → renin-Ang II + K+; cortisol → ACTH; DHEA → ACTH; epinephrine → preganglionic sympathetic cholinergic neurons.

subject: Physiology
stem: Insulin: which intracellular signaling pathway does its receptor use?
options: Tyrosine kinase receptor (RTK): insulin → dimerized receptor → autophosphorylation → IRS-1/2 (insulin receptor substrates) → PI3K → PIP3 → PDK1 → Akt (PKB) → GLUT4 translocation + glycogen synthesis + lipogenesis + protein synthesis
explanation: Insulin receptor: transmembrane RTK. Insulin binds α-subunits → conformational change → autophosphorylation of β-subunits (tyrosine kinase) → phosphorylates IRS-1/2 → activates PI3K → PIP2 → PIP3 → PDK1 → Akt phosphorylation → (1) GLUT4-containing vesicles translocate to plasma membrane (muscle, fat), (2) Glycogen synthase activation (glycogenesis), (3) Protein synthesis (mTOR), (4) Lipogenesis. Also: MAPK pathway → cell growth/differentiation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Growth hormone: what is the 'somatogenic effect' mediated by IGF-1?
options: GH from pituitary → acts on liver + peripheral tissues → IGF-1 (somatomedins) secretion → IGF-1 binds IGF-1R (similar to insulin receptor, RTK) → stimulates chondrocyte proliferation at epiphyseal plate → linear bone growth (height)
explanation: GH actions: Direct effects: anti-insulin (↑lipolysis, ↑blood glucose, ↑gluconeogenesis — 'diabetogenic'). Indirect (via IGF-1, somatomedin C): ↑protein synthesis, ↑lean mass, ↑bone growth (epiphyseal plate). IGF-1 is produced by the liver and locally by chondrocytes. GH excess: acromegaly (adults, after epiphyseal fusion) → enlarged hands, feet, jaw; gigantism (children, before fusion) → tall stature. GH deficiency in children → short stature.

subject: Physiology
stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin): what are its two main receptors and their actions?
options: V1 (kidney — aquaporins) and V2 (vascular smooth muscle — vasoconstriction)

V1 (vascular smooth muscle, platelet aggregation, hepatic glycogenolysis) and V2 (principal cells of collecting duct — AQP2 insertion → water reabsorption); V2 also on inner medullary collecting duct → urea reabsorption → medullary hyperosmolarity
V1 in the kidney and V2 in the lungs
explanation: ADH/vasopressin receptors: V1R (Gq → IP3/DAG → Ca2+): vascular smooth muscle (vasoconstriction at high doses), platelet aggregation, liver glycogenolysis. V2R (Gs → cAMP → PKA): renal principal cells → AQP2 channel trafficking to apical membrane → ↑water permeability → water reabsorption. V2R also → ↑urea transporters (UT-A1/A3) in IMCD → urea recycling → medullary interstitial osmolarity. DDAVP (desmopressin) = selective V2 agonist (used in central DI, von Willebrand disease — ↑vWF from endothelium via V2).

subject: Physiology
stem: Parathyroid hormone (PTH): which enzyme does it stimulate in the kidney?
options: 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) in the proximal tubule — converts 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (25-OH-D3) to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol/active vitamin D) — the most active form
explanation: PTH actions: (1) Bone: ↑osteoclast activity via RANK-L → ↑Ca2+ and ↑phosphate release (net hypercalcemia). (2) Kidney: ↑Ca2+ reabsorption (DCT), ↓phosphate reabsorption (PCT → phosphaturia, hypophosphatemia), stimulates 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol. (3) Gut (indirect via calcitriol): ↑Ca2+ and phosphate absorption. Net: ↑serum Ca2+, ↓serum phosphate. Hyperparathyroidism: ↑Ca2+, ↓PO4, ↑ALP, ↑PTH.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which hormones oppose insulin action (counter-regulatory hormones)?
options: Glucagon, epinephrine (most potent, acts within seconds), cortisol, and growth hormone — all raise blood glucose by various mechanisms
Insulin and glucagon cancel each other out
explanation: Counter-regulatory hormones (stress hormones): Glucagon (from α-cells) → ↑glycogenolysis, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑ketogenesis. Epinephrine → ↑glycogenolysis (liver + muscle via β2), ↑lipolysis, ↑glucagon release, ↓insulin release (α2). Cortisol → ↑gluconeogenesis, ↑proteolysis, insulin resistance. GH → ↑lipolysis, insulin resistance. In hypoglycemia, glucagon and epinephrine are the PRIMARY acute defenders (fastest); cortisol and GH are important for prolonged (>4h) fasting.

subject: Physiology
stem: Testosterone: which enzyme converts it to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in peripheral tissues?
options: 5α-reductase (in skin, hair follicles, prostate, liver) — DHT is more potent than T at androgen receptors; responsible for male pattern baldness, prostate growth, external genitalia virilization in utero
explanation: Testosterone → DHT via 5α-reductase type 2 (gonads, prostate) and type 1 (skin, liver, scalp). DHT: 3× more potent than T at AR. DHT responsible for: external genitalia masculinization (intrauterine), prostate growth, benign prostatic hyperplasia, male pattern baldness (androgenic alopecia). Finasteride (5α-reductase inhibitor) → used for BPH and male pattern baldness. Testosterone → estradiol via aromatase (CYP19A1) in adipose tissue, testes, brain.

subject: Physiology
stem: Gastric acid secretion: which cells produce HCl and what stimulates them?
options: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the fundus/body — stimulated by (1) Gastrin (CCK-B/gastrin receptor), (2) Histamine (H2 receptor → cAMP → PKA → ↑H+/K+-ATPase), (3) Acetylcholine (M3 receptor → IP3/Ca2+) — all converge on H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump)
explanation: Parietal cells: produce HCl (via H+/K+-ATPase on canalicular membrane) and intrinsic factor (IF). Three stimulatory pathways converging on H+/K+-ATPase: (1) Gastrin (from antral G cells, activated by protein/peptides, distension) via CCK-B → IP3/Ca2+ + cAMP, (2) Histamine (from ECL cells, paracrine) via H2R → ↑cAMP → PKA, (3) ACh (vagal, stimulates via M3 → IP3/Ca2+). PPIs (omeprazole, pantoprazole) irreversibly inhibit H+/K+-ATPase.

subject: Physiology
stem: Intrinsic factor: where is it produced and what is its role?
options: Produced by chief cells — digests fats
Produced by parietal cells — binds vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the stomach, forming the IF-B12 complex, which is absorbed by specific receptors in the terminal ileum (cubam receptor)
Produced by goblet cells — mucus production
Produced by S cells in duodenum
explanation: Intrinsic factor (IF): produced exclusively by gastric parietal cells (fundus/body). Secreted in response to the same stimuli as HCl (gastrin, histamine, ACh). Binds vitamin B12 (released from food by pepsin/acid, then binds R-binders in stomach, then IF from pancreatic trypsin digestion of R-binders). IF-B12 complex → absorbed at terminal ileum by cubam (cubilin/amnionless) receptor. Total gastrectomy → no IF → B12 malabsorption → pernicious anemia (or post-gastrectomy megaloblastic anemia).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cholecystokinin (CCK): where is it produced and what are its functions?
options: I cells of the duodenum and jejunum — stimulated by peptides and fatty acids in the duodenum; causes gallbladder contraction, pancreatic enzyme secretion, slows gastric emptying, increases lower esophageal sphincter tone
explanation: CCK: I cells (duodenum/jejunum), stimulated by fatty acids and partially digested proteins (peptides, amino acids). Actions: (1) Gallbladder contraction + relaxes sphincter of Oddi → bile release, (2) Pancreatic acinar cells → enzyme secretion (lipase, amylase, proteases), (3) Delays gastric emptying (appropriate time for digestion), (4) Stimulates pancreatic growth (trophic), (5) Satiety signaling to brain. CCK-A receptor in periphery; CCK-B in CNS.

subject: Physiology
stem: Secretin: stimulus and primary action?
options: Acid (low duodenal pH <4.5) → secretin from S cells → stimulates pancreatic ductal cells (via cAMP → CFTR) to secrete HCO3-rich fluid to neutralize acid → also inhibits gastric acid and gastric emptying
explanation: Secretin (S cells, duodenum): released by acid chyme entering duodenum (pH <4.5). Actions: (1) Pancreatic ductal cells → ↑HCO3- secretion (via cAMP → CFTR Cl- channel → Cl-/HCO3- exchanger) → neutralizes duodenal acid. (2) ↓Gastric acid secretion (inhibits parietal cells). (3) ↓Gastric motility. (4) Stimulates bile HCO3- secretion. Secretin test: used to diagnose Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (secretin paradoxically increases gastrin in ZES).

subject: Physiology
stem: The small intestine absorbs fat as:
options: Free fatty acids directly into portal blood

Micelles (mixed with bile salts) → passive diffusion of fatty acids and monoglycerides into enterocytes → reassembled into triglycerides in the ER → packaged into chylomicrons (with apoB-48) → exocytosed into lacteals (lymphatics) → thoracic duct → subclavian vein
All fat absorbed in the colon
explanation: Fat digestion and absorption: triglycerides → pancreatic lipase (with colipase) → 2-monoglycerides + 2 fatty acids. Bile salts + monoglycerides + FFA → mixed micelles → passively diffuse through apical membrane of enterocytes (not Na+-dependent). Inside enterocyte: FFA + monoglycerides → triglycerides (SER) → packaged with apoB-48, cholesterol, phospholipids → chylomicrons (large, apoB-48). Exocytosis into lacteals → lymph → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein. Chylomicronemia after fatty meals.

subject: Physiology
stem: Bile salt enterohepatic circulation: where are bile salts reabsorbed?
options: Terminal ileum — active reabsorption of conjugated bile salts by the ASBT (apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter), then via portal blood back to the liver (95% recirculated)
explanation: Bile salt enterohepatic circulation: liver → bile → gallbladder → duodenum (emulsification) → along small intestine (micellar fat absorption). Primary bile acids (cholic acid, chenodeoxycholic acid) conjugated with glycine/taurine → bile salts. Actively reabsorbed in terminal ileum (ASBT on enterocytes) → portal vein → liver (Na+-dependent cotransport on hepatocyte basolateral). 95% recirculated; 5% lost in feces and replaced by hepatic synthesis from cholesterol. Ileal resection → bile salt malabsorption → steatorrhea + bile-acid diarrhea.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cells of the stomach produce pepsinogen?
options: Chief (zymogenic) cells in the fundus/body — stimulated by ACh and acid; pepsinogen is converted to pepsin (active protease) at pH <2
explanation: Gastric cells: Chief cells (fundus/body) → pepsinogen (zymogen) + gastric lipase. Parietal cells → HCl + intrinsic factor. G cells (antrum) → gastrin. D cells (antrum/pancreas) → somatostatin. ECL (enterochromaffin-like) cells (fundus) → histamine. Pepsinogen is inactive until activated by HCl at pH <2 (autocatalytic at very low pH). Pepsin is an endopeptidase, cleaves aromatic amino acid bonds. Optimum pH 2–3; inactivated at pH >5.

subject: Physiology
stem: The migrating motor complex (MMC) occurs:
options: During active digestion of a meal

Between meals (interdigestive period) — cyclic sweeping motor activity that moves residual contents from stomach → small intestine → prevents bacterial overgrowth; motilin (from M cells of duodenum/jejunum) is the hormone that initiates phase III of MMC
explanation: MMC (interdigestive housekeeper): occurs every 90 minutes between meals. Three phases: I (quiescence), II (irregular contractions), III (intense peristaltic waves, motilin-driven — sweeps undigested material and bacteria aborally). Disrupted by feeding (gastrin, CCK inhibit MMC). Disruption of MMC → small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist → used as prokinetic.

subject: Physiology
stem: Acetylcholine is released at which synapses?
options: ALL preganglionic autonomic synapses (both sympathetic and parasympathetic preganglionic → ganglionic neurons), ALL parasympathetic postganglionic synapses, sympathetic postganglionic to sweat glands and some blood vessels, and the NMJ (skeletal muscle)
explanation: ACh release: (1) All preganglionic fibers (sympathetic + parasympathetic) → ganglionic nicotinic receptors (nAChR — Nm type in ganglia). (2) Parasympathetic postganglionic → effector organs (muscarinic receptors). (3) Sympathetic postganglionic → sweat glands (muscarinic), some blood vessels (muscarinic vasodilation). (4) NMJ: Nm (nicotinic muscle subtype). The rest of sympathetic postganglionic (smooth muscle, heart) → norepinephrine.

subject: Physiology
stem: Dopamine pathways in the brain: which pathway is impaired in Parkinson's disease?
options: Nigrostriatal pathway: dopaminergic neurons from substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) → striatum (caudate + putamen); loss of >80% of SNc neurons → reduced inhibition of the indirect pathway → ↑inhibition of thalamus → ↓motor initiation → bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor
explanation: Dopamine pathways: (1) Nigrostriatal (SNc → striatum): movement; Parkinson's disease = loss of neurons here. (2) Mesolimbic (VTA → limbic system/NAc): reward, motivation; excess → positive symptoms of schizophrenia. (3) Mesocortical (VTA → PFC): cognition; deficit → negative symptoms of schizophrenia. (4) Tuberoinfundibular (hypothalamus → pituitary): tonic inhibition of prolactin; antipsychotics block D2 here → ↑prolactin → galactorrhea/amenorrhea.

subject: Physiology
stem: The stretch reflex (deep tendon reflex): which neurons are involved?
options: Muscle spindle (Ia afferents, 1a fibers from annulospiral endings) → monosynaptic → alpha motor neuron → muscle contraction (and simultaneous inhibition of antagonist via Ia inhibitory interneuron — reciprocal inhibition)
explanation: Stretch reflex (myotatic reflex): monosynaptic (fastest reflex). Stimulus: muscle stretch → activates muscle spindle Ia (and II) afferents → directly synapse on α-motor neurons of the SAME muscle (Sc. 'autogenic facilitation') → contraction (resists stretch). Simultaneously: Ia fibers collateralize → inhibitory interneurons (Ia inhibitory neurons) → inhibit antagonist α-motor neurons (reciprocal inhibition). DTR depends on: intact Ia afferent, α-motor neuron, intact muscle spindle, synaptic transmission.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which inhibitory neurotransmitter is released by Renshaw cells in the spinal cord?
options: Glycine — Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons activated by α-motor neuron collaterals → release glycine → inhibit the same α-motor neuron (recurrent inhibition) and Ia inhibitory interneurons (allowing antagonist co-contraction if needed for stabilization)
explanation: Renshaw cells: spinal interneurons activated by axon collaterals of α-motor neurons. Release glycine → (1) inhibit the same α-motor neuron (recurrent/autogenic inhibition — prevents runaway excitation), (2) inhibit Ia inhibitory interneurons (allowing co-contraction of antagonists during fine movements). Strychnine: blocks glycine receptors → loss of recurrent inhibition → uncontrolled motor neuron firing → spastic paralysis/convulsions.

subject: Physiology
stem: Golgi tendon organ (GTO): what is its function?
options: Detects muscle tension/force (located in tendons, in series with muscle fibers) → Ib afferents → Ib inhibitory interneurons → inhibit agonist α-motor neurons (autogenic inhibition/inverse myotatic reflex) — protects against excessive force → tendon/muscle injury prevention
explanation: GTO: encapsulated mechanoreceptors at musculotendinous junction, sensitive to active muscle contraction (not passive stretch like spindle). Ib afferent fibers → spinal cord → Ib inhibitory interneurons → inhibit agonist α-motor neurons and excite antagonist. Clasp-knife reflex: initial resistance to passive stretch (stretch reflex) followed by sudden give-in (GTO firing as tension mounts → autogenic inhibition). Ib afferents also project to cerebellum and cortex.

subject: Physiology
stem: The countercurrent multiplier system of the loop of Henle creates the medullary osmotic gradient for which purpose?
options: To concentrate urine: creates a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium (up to 1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla) → when ADH is present, water is reabsorbed in the collecting duct into this hyperosmotic interstitium → concentrated urine
explanation: Countercurrent multiplication: Descending limb of Henle (DLH): water-permeable, impermeable to solutes → water exits → filtrate becomes hyperosmotic as it descends. Ascending limb (TALH): impermeable to water, actively transports NaCl (NKCC2) → solute leaves without water → filtrate becomes hypoosmotic. This creates medullary interstitial gradient (300 → 1200 mOsm/kg from cortex → papilla). Urea also contributes (UT-A1/A3 in IMCD, regulated by ADH).

subject: Physiology
stem: Tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF): what is the mechanism?
options: Increased GFR → increased tubular pressure directly dilates afferent arterioles

↑NaCl delivery to macula densa → macula densa cells release adenosine (and TXA2/prostaglandins) → afferent arteriole constriction → ↓GFR → restores NaCl delivery to macula densa (negative feedback to maintain constant GFR)
Aldosterone directly constricts the afferent arteriole
High tubular flow stimulates renin release
explanation: TGF: NaCl sensed by macula densa (thick ascending limb/DCT junction). ↑NaCl → macula densa → (1) ↑adenosine release → constricts afferent arteriole (A1 receptor) → ↓GFR (negative feedback). (2) ↓renin release. ↓NaCl delivery → ↓adenosine → afferent dilation → ↑GFR. Also ↑renin release. This is why ACE inhibitors can worsen GFR in RAS (afferent constriction from Ang II on efferent → corrected by ACEi → but in low perfusion, this can drop GFR).

subject: Physiology
stem: Renin is secreted by which cells?
options: Principal cells of the collecting duct
Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the afferent arteriole — stimulated by ↓renal perfusion pressure (baroreceptor mechanism), ↓NaCl at macula densa, and ↑sympathetic activity (β1-adrenergic receptors)
explanation: Renin: aspartyl protease secreted by juxtaglomerular cells (granular cells) in the wall of afferent arteriole. Stimuli: (1) ↓stretch of afferent arteriole (↓perfusion pressure → intrarenal baroreceptor), (2) ↓NaCl delivery to macula densa → paracrine signal → JG cells, (3) ↑sympathetic stimulation (β1 receptors on JG cells → ↑cAMP → renin release). Renin → cleaves angiotensinogen → Ang I → ACE (lung endothelium) → Ang II. Inhibited by: high BP, ↑NaCl, ANP/BNP, AT1 receptor blockers.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the normal filtration fraction (FF) and its significance?
options: ~20% (FF = GFR/RPF = 125/625 mL/min); increased FF → ↑tubular oncotic pressure → ↑Na+ and water reabsorption in PCT; FF increases in heart failure and renal artery stenosis
explanation: Filtration fraction (FF) = GFR / RPF = 125/625 = 0.20 (20%). As filtrate is produced, plasma proteins become concentrated in the post-glomerular (peritubular) capillary blood → ↑oncotic pressure → drives PCT reabsorption. ↑FF (in CHF: efferent constriction > afferent, or renal artery stenosis) → ↑peritubular oncotic pressure → ↑Na+/H2O reabsorption (avid salt/water retention). ANP → dilates afferent + constricts efferent → ↑FF → slight natriuresis (not a primary effect).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which segment of the nephron is the major site of phosphate reabsorption and is inhibited by PTH?
options: Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) — NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc cotransporters on the brush border; PTH → phosphaturia by internalization of NaPi cotransporters
explanation: Phosphate handling: ~80–90% filtered phosphate is reabsorbed in the PCT via NaPi-IIa/IIc (sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporters). PTH → activates PTH1R on PCT → Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA → internalizes NaPi-IIa/IIc → phosphate excretion ↑ (phosphaturia) → lowers serum phosphate. FGF-23 (fibroblast growth factor 23, from osteocytes) also inhibits NaPi → phosphaturia + ↓1α-hydroxylase → ↓calcitriol → ↓phosphate absorption (all to lower serum PO4).

subject: Physiology
stem: Total body water (TBW) is approximately what percentage of body weight in a 70 kg adult male?
options: 60% (approximately 42 L in a 70 kg male); distributed: 2/3 intracellular (28 L) and 1/3 extracellular (14 L); females slightly less (~55%) due to higher fat percentage
explanation: TBW = 60% of body weight (Edelman). Distribution: ICF = 2/3 of TBW = ~28 L. ECF = 1/3 of TBW = ~14 L, which is divided into: interstitial fluid (~10.5 L, 75% of ECF) and plasma volume (~3.5 L, 25% of ECF). Bone and transcellular fluids (CSF, synovial, GI fluids) make up the remaining ECF. Lean body mass contains more water than fat.

subject: Physiology
stem: Plasma osmolarity is primarily maintained by:
options: Sodium (and its accompanying anions — mainly Cl- and HCO3-) — accounts for >90% of plasma osmolarity; calculated as 2×Na+ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (normal 285–295 mOsm/kg)
explanation: Plasma osmolarity formula: 2×[Na+] + [glucose (mg/dL)]/18 + [BUN (mg/dL)]/2.8 = ~290 mOsm/kg. Na+ contributes ~2×140 = 280 mOsm/kg. Glucose contributes ~5 mOsm/kg normally. Osmolar gap = measured (by freezing point depression) - calculated. Elevated gap (>10) = unmeasured osmoles: ethanol, methanol, isopropyl alcohol, mannitol. Effective osmolarity excludes urea (freely penetrates membranes).

subject: Physiology
stem: The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a neuron is approximately -70 mV. This is mainly determined by:
options: The relative permeability of the membrane to K+ (high PK via K+ leak channels) → K+ equilibrium potential (EK ≈ -90 mV) dominates, and the Na+/K+ ATPase maintains the concentration gradients
explanation: RMP determined by the Goldman equation. At rest, membrane is most permeable to K+ (via Kir leak channels, GIRK channels). K+ tends to diffuse out (concentration gradient outward) → inside becomes negative → electrical gradient restrains further K+ efflux → equilibrium at EK ≈ -90 mV. Na+ permeability at rest is much lower → pulls RMP toward ENa (+60 mV) slightly → RMP ≈ -70 mV. The Na+/K+-ATPase maintains concentration gradients.

subject: Physiology
stem: Donnan equilibrium: in the presence of non-diffusible proteins on one side of a membrane:
options: Concentrations of diffusible ions are equal on both sides
Diffusible cations (Na+, K+) are higher on the side with non-diffusible anions (proteins), and diffusible anions (Cl-) are lower on that side
explanation: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium: intracellular proteins (negative charge) cannot cross the cell membrane → attract and retain diffusible cations → [Na+]i and [K+]i are higher than predicted by diffusion alone → [Cl-]i is lower than [Cl-]o. This creates an osmotic imbalance that would cause cells to swell (Donnan osmotic effect) → prevented by Na+/K+-ATPase (pumps Na+ out, maintains osmotic balance).

subject: Physiology
stem: The sodium-potassium ATPase pump maintains:
options: High intracellular Na+, high extracellular K+

High intracellular K+ (~140 mEq/L ICF) and high extracellular Na+ (~142 mEq/L ECF); it uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per cycle (electrogenic — net outward positive current → hyperpolarizes membrane slightly)
explanation: Na+/K+-ATPase (ubiquitous plasma membrane pump): pumps 3 Na+ OUT for every 2 K+ IN (uses 1 ATP) → net electrogenic effect (positive charge moved out → hyperpolarizes by ~3–4 mV). Maintains ICF: [K+] ~140 mEq/L, [Na+] ~10 mEq/L; ECF: [K+] ~4 mEq/L, [Na+] ~142 mEq/L. Inhibited by cardiac glycosides (digitalis) → ↑[Na+]i → reduces Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) activity → ↑[Ca2+]i → ↑cardiac contractility.

subject: Physiology
stem: The semicircular canals detect which type of motion?
options: Angular (rotational) acceleration — the three canals (anterior, posterior, lateral) are oriented in mutually perpendicular planes; movement → endolymph deflects the cupula (a gelatinous structure) → deflects stereocilia of hair cells
explanation: Vestibular labyrinth: (1) Semicircular canals (3 paired, each canal = 1 ampulla with crista ampullaris) → detect rotational/angular acceleration; ampullary crest contains hair cells embedded in the cupula (endolymph drag deflects cupula). (2) Otolith organs (saccule + utricle) → detect linear acceleration and gravity (static head position); macula contains hair cells embedded in otolithic membrane with otoliths (calcium carbonate crystals).

subject: Physiology
stem: The utricle and saccule (otolith organs) detect:
options: Linear acceleration and gravity: otoliths (calcium carbonate crystals) shift under gravity or linear acceleration → deflect hair cells → detect head tilt and linear motion; utricle = horizontal plane; saccule = vertical plane
explanation: Otolith organs: Utricle: macula is horizontal → primarily detects horizontal linear acceleration and forward tilt of head. Saccule: macula is vertical → primarily detects vertical linear acceleration (up/down). Both respond to static gravity. Hair cell deflection toward kinocilium → depolarization (excitation). Away from kinocilium → hyperpolarization (inhibition). Signal from vestibular nerve (CN VIII, inferior division for saccule) → vestibular nuclei → cerebellum, ocular nuclei (VOR), spinal cord.

subject: Physiology
stem: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is caused by:
options: Viral infection of the vestibular nerve

Canalolithiasis: calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia/otoliths) detached from the utricle → enter the posterior semicircular canal → with head movement, crystals move → abnormal endolymph currents → pathological hair cell stimulation → vertigo + nystagmus
