explanation: BPPV (most common cause of vertigo): otoconia dislodged from utricle → float into semicircular canals (posterior canal in 85%). Positional change (e.g., lying down, turning in bed) → otoconia move → stimulate canal incorrectly → brief (seconds) vertigo + torsional geotropic nystagmus. Dix-Hallpike test: positive. Treatment: Epley canalith repositioning maneuver (moves otoconia back to utricle).

subject: Physiology
stem: C fibers (nociceptors): which type of pain do they transmit?
options: Slow, burning, dull, poorly localized pain (second pain) — unmyelinated C fibers (0.5–2 m/s conduction velocity) carry information about burning/aching pain and temperature; first pain (sharp, fast) is Aδ fibers (5–30 m/s)
explanation: Pain fibers: Aδ fibers (thinly myelinated, 5–30 m/s): first pain — sharp, well-localized, immediate. C fibers (unmyelinated, 0.5–2 m/s): second pain — burning, aching, poorly localized, prolonged. Both use glutamate (AMPA/NMDA receptors for fast pain) and substance P (NK1 receptor for slow pain) as neurotransmitters at the dorsal horn. Hyperalgesia: sensitization of peripheral nociceptors (COX-2, PGE2, bradykinin) or central sensitization (wind-up, NMDA receptors).

subject: Physiology
stem: Gate control theory of pain (Melzack and Wall, 1965):
options: Pain is purely a peripheral nervous system phenomenon

Activation of large-diameter Aβ touch fibers (by rubbing/massage/TENS) activates inhibitory interneurons (substantia gelatinosa, lamina II) → close the 'gate' → inhibit pain transmission from Aδ and C fibers to projection neurons in dorsal horn — explains why rubbing an injury relieves pain
Pain is produced only in the spinal cord
Opioids work at peripheral receptors only
explanation: Gate theory: substantia gelatinosa (lamina II of dorsal horn) contains interneurons that can inhibit or facilitate transmission from nociceptive (C, Aδ) fibers to second-order (projection, T-cell) neurons. Aβ fibers (touch, vibration) → activate inhibitory SG interneurons → 'close gate' → less pain signal transmitted. Descending inhibition (from PAG, raphe nuclei — serotonin; locus coeruleus — NE) also closes the gate.

subject: Physiology
stem: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) area is important for:
options: Descending pain modulation: stimulation of PAG → activates raphe nuclei (5-HT) and locus coeruleus (NE) → descending inhibitory pathways → release of enkephalins in dorsal horn → inhibit pain transmission (endogenous opioid-mediated analgesia)
explanation: PAG (midbrain): central site for endogenous opioid analgesia. PAG has high density of μ-opioid receptors. Activation: stimulation (via brain stimulation analgesia), systemic opioids, stress → ↑endogenous opioids (enkephalins, endorphins, dynorphins) → inhibit interneurons in PAG → release descending inhibitory pathways → raphe (serotonin) and locus coeruleus (NE) → dorsal horn → inhibit C/Aδ transmission.

subject: Physiology
stem: The cerebellum: which cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex?
options: Purkinje cells — they project to the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, interposed, fastigial) and the vestibular nuclei; they are the only cortical efferents and use GABA (inhibitory)
explanation: Cerebellar cortex layers: Molecular layer (outer) — basket and stellate cells (inhibitory interneurons). Purkinje cell layer — Purkinje cells (large, distinctive, GABA-ergic → inhibit deep cerebellar nuclei). Granular layer — granule cells (excitatory, use glutamate; most numerous neurons in the CNS; receive mossy fiber inputs → parallel fibers → Purkinje cells). Deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) → provide excitatory output (glutamate) via VL thalamus → motor cortex.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cerebellar damage causes which characteristic signs?
options: Contralateral spastic paralysis and hyperreflexia (UMN signs)

Ipsilateral ataxia (uncoordinated movement), intention tremor (worsens as limb reaches target), past-pointing (dysmetria), dysdiadochokinesia (inability to rapidly alternate movements), nystagmus, dysarthria (scanning speech), hypotonia — all ipsilateral because cerebellum connects ipsilateral via double-crossing pathways
explanation: Cerebellar lesions: Ipsilateral signs (cerebellar pathways cross twice → back to same side). Hemispheric lesion → limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia. Vermian lesion → truncal ataxia, gait ataxia. Flocculonodular lesion → nystagmus, vertigo, vomiting (connections with vestibular system). Important: cerebellar tremor = ACTION/INTENTION tremor (absent at rest, worsens near target) vs. Parkinson's = resting tremor ('pill-rolling').

subject: Physiology
stem: In the basal ganglia circuit: what happens in Parkinson's disease to the activity of the internal globus pallidus (GPi)?
options: GPi activity decreases → less inhibition of thalamus → more movement
GPi activity increases (due to loss of striatal dopamine → ↑indirect pathway activity → ↓GPe → ↑STN → ↑GPi) → ↑inhibition of VL thalamus → ↓thalamocortical drive → bradykinesia, akinesia
GPi is not involved in Parkinson's disease
GPi activity decreases because STN is inhibited
explanation: Basal ganglia circuits: Direct pathway: Cortex → striatum (D1 receptors, excited by dopamine) → GPi/SNr (inhibit) → thalamus disinhibited → ↑movement. Indirect pathway: Cortex → striatum (D2 receptors, inhibited by dopamine) → GPe → STN → GPi/SNr → ↑inhibition → ↓movement. Parkinson's: ↓dopamine from SNc → D1 understimulation (less direct) + D2 disinhibition (more indirect) → ↑GPi → ↓thalamus → bradykinesia. L-DOPA → replenishes striatal dopamine → restores balance.

subject: Physiology
stem: Huntington's disease: which neurons are primarily lost?
options: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra

Striatal GABAergic neurons (mainly medium spiny neurons) — particularly those of the indirect pathway (D2 receptors + enkephalin) → GPe disinhibited → inhibits STN → reduces GPi activity → reduced inhibition of thalamus → excessive, involuntary movements (chorea)
explanation: Huntington's disease: autosomal dominant, expanded CAG repeats in huntingtin gene (>36 on chromosome 4). Loss of striatal MSNs (medium spiny neurons), especially those of the indirect pathway → ↓GPe activity → ↑disinhibition of thalamus → uncontrolled movements (chorea). Clinical: choreiform movements, personality change, dementia, psychiatric features. Caudate atrophy → 'boxcar' ventricles on CT/MRI.

subject: Physiology
stem: The lateral hypothalamus (LH) is considered the 'hunger center.' Lesion of the lateral hypothalamus causes:
options: Hypophagia (decreased eating) → starvation; animals with LH lesions refuse to eat (aphagia); stimulation → increased feeding
explanation: Hypothalamic feeding regulation: Lateral hypothalamus (hunger center): lesion → aphagia, starvation. Stimulated by ghrelin (from stomach, stimulates hunger), hypoglycemia. Ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH, satiety center): lesion → hyperphagia, obesity. Stimulated by leptin (from adipose, signals satiety → ↓NPY/AgRP + ↑POMC → ↓appetite). These interact with the arcuate nucleus (orexigenic: NPY/AgRP neurons; anorexigenic: POMC/CART neurons).

subject: Physiology
stem: ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary is increased by:
options: Low plasma osmolarity and high blood volume

High plasma osmolarity (>290 mOsm/kg) sensed by osmoreceptors in the OVLT/anterior hypothalamus, AND low blood volume/BP (hypovolemia, ≥8% blood volume loss) sensed by cardiopulmonary/aortic baroreceptors — both stimulate ADH secretion; pain, nausea, opioids, nicotine also stimulate
explanation: ADH (vasopressin) release: synthesized in paraventricular (PVN) and supraoptic nuclei (SON) of the hypothalamus → transported down axons → stored in posterior pituitary. Released by: ↑plasma osmolarity (primary stimulus, most sensitive — threshold ↑1–2% in osmolarity), ↓blood volume (less sensitive, requires ≥8% volume loss), nausea, pain, opioids, nicotine, carbamazepine, chlorpropamide. Inhibited by: alcohol (ethanol), cold, ANP, ↓osmolarity.

subject: Physiology
stem: Broca's area: location and function?
options: Posterior superior temporal gyrus — language comprehension

Inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann areas 44 and 45) of the dominant (left in most) hemisphere — PRODUCTION of speech (motor speech area); Broca's aphasia = non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension but impaired speech production, with good naming (expressive aphasia)
explanation: Broca's area (area 44/45, dominant inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis and pars opercularis): motor programming of speech. Broca's aphasia: non-fluent (few words, telegraphic, effortful speech), comprehension INTACT, repetition impaired. Patient is aware of the deficit (frustrated). Connected to Wernicke's area by the arcuate fasciculus. Damage: left MCA superior division territory.

subject: Physiology
stem: Wernicke's area: location and function?
options: Posterior superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 22) of the dominant hemisphere — language COMPREHENSION; Wernicke's aphasia = fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension, jargon speech (paraphasias), impaired repetition
explanation: Wernicke's area (area 22, posterior STG, dominant hemisphere): language comprehension. Wernicke's aphasia: fluent speech (often excessive, jargon-filled with paraphasias — wrong words/sounds), severely impaired comprehension, impaired repetition. Patient is unaware of errors (anosognosia). Supplied by left MCA inferior division. Conduction aphasia: arcuate fasciculus damage → fluent, comprehension intact, repetition severely impaired.

subject: Physiology
stem: The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is located in which gyrus?
options: Postcentral gyrus (parietal lobe, Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2) — receives discriminative touch, pain, temperature, proprioception from the contralateral body via the thalamus (VPL nucleus); organized somatotopically (homunculus, with large representation for lips and hands)
explanation: Somatosensory cortex (S1): postcentral gyrus. Receives: discriminative touch (fine tactile, 2-point discrimination) via dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway → VPL thalamus → S1. Somatotopic organization (Penfield's homunculus): large areas for face, lips, tongue, hands (high receptor density = fine discrimination). Lesion → contralateral hemianesthesia, astereognosis, agraphesthesia, impaired two-point discrimination.

subject: Physiology
stem: 'Neglect syndrome' (hemispatial neglect) occurs after damage to which area?
options: Non-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe — specifically the inferior parietal lobule (supramarginal + angular gyri); patient ignores contralateral (left) side of space and body; does not draw the left side of clocks/flowers; may deny left-sided paralysis (anosognosia)
explanation: Hemispatial neglect: most common and severe after right parietal (inferior parietal lobule) damage. Patient: ignores left side (fails to draw left side of clock face, doesn't shave left side of face, ignores left food on plate), may deny left hemiplegia (Anton/anosognosia), may deny ownership of left limb (somatoparaphrenia). Right hemisphere mediates attention to BOTH hemispheres (left hemisphere only to right). Therefore, right parietal lesions cause severe neglect; left parietal lesions less so.

subject: Physiology
stem: Neutrophils: which is their primary killing mechanism after phagocytosis?
options: Oxidative burst (respiratory burst): NADPH oxidase generates superoxide (O2-) → H2O2, HOCl (myeloperoxidase + Cl-) — powerful oxidants that kill bacteria; also azurophilic granules contain elastase, cathepsin G, defensins
explanation: Neutrophil killing: (1) Oxidative: NADPH oxidase → O2- (superoxide) → H2O2 + OH- (Fenton reaction) + HOCl (MPO + Cl-) → kills bacteria. CGD (chronic granulomatous disease): NADPH oxidase defect → catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Aspergillus, Klebsiella, Serratia, Pseudomonas — mnemonic: SACKS P) survive → recurrent infections. (2) Non-oxidative: granule contents (lysozyme, elastase, cathepsin G, lactoferrin, defensins).

subject: Physiology
stem: Natural killer (NK) cells kill target cells by which mechanism?
options: Perforin and granzyme pathway: NK cells recognize 'missing self' (cells lacking MHC class I — e.g., virally infected cells, tumor cells) → perforin forms pores in target cell membrane → granzymes (serine proteases) enter → caspase activation → apoptosis; also ADCC via Fc receptors (CD16)
explanation: NK cells (CD56+, CD16+, CD3-): innate lymphoid cells that kill without prior sensitization. 'Missing self' surveillance: MHC I on healthy cells → inhibitory signals via KIR receptors → NK cells do NOT kill. Virus-infected/tumor cells → down-regulate MHC I → lose inhibitory signals + gain activating signals (e.g., MICA/MICB ligands for NKG2D) → NK cells kill. ADCC: CD16 (FcγRIII) binds Fc of IgG coating target → triggers NK killing. KIR (killer inhibitory receptor).

subject: Physiology
stem: T lymphocyte activation requires:
options: Two signals: Signal 1 = TCR binds peptide-MHC (CD4+ T helper → MHC II; CD8+ cytotoxic T → MHC I) via CD3/TCR complex. Signal 2 = co-stimulatory signal: CD28 on T cell + B7-1 (CD80)/B7-2 (CD86) on APC; without signal 2 → T cell anergy
Antibody binding to T cell surface
explanation: T cell activation (two-signal model): Signal 1 (TCR): CD4+ T cells recognize antigen (8-15 amino acids) in MHC II groove; CD8+ T cells recognize antigen (8-10 aa) in MHC I groove. TCR + CD3 (signal transduction) + CD4/CD8 (coreceptor). Signal 2 (costimulation): CD28-B7 interaction (most important). Without signal 2 → anergy. Once activated: ZAP-70 → NFAT, NF-κB, AP-1 → IL-2 (autocrine growth factor) → clonal expansion. Signal 3: cytokines determine differentiation (Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg).

subject: Physiology
stem: MHC class I molecules present antigen to which T cells?
options: CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) — MHC I is expressed on virtually ALL nucleated cells; it presents intracellular antigens (viral peptides, tumor antigens) via TAP transporter → rough ER → peptide loading → cell surface
explanation: MHC I (HLA-A, B, C): on all nucleated cells + platelets. Presents endogenous antigens (intracellular proteins degraded by proteasome → peptides → TAP → ER → peptide loading on β2m/α-chain → cell surface). CD8+ T cell (CTL) recognizes peptide-MHC I → kills target cell. MHC II (HLA-DR, DQ, DP): on professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells). Presents exogenous antigens (phagocytosed → endosome → lysosome → peptide loading → MHC II). CD4+ T cells recognize peptide-MHC II.

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal white blood cell (WBC) count and differential in adults:
options: 4,000–11,000 cells/μL; with neutrophils 50–70% (most abundant), lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 1–4%, basophils 0.5–1%
explanation: WBC differential: Neutrophils 50–70% (most abundant — first responders in bacterial infection). Lymphocytes 20–40% (second most abundant). Monocytes 3–8% (precursors of tissue macrophages, DCs). Eosinophils 1–4% (allergic diseases, helminthic infections). Basophils 0.5–1% (IgE-mediated reactions, similar to mast cells). Leukocytosis (>11,000): infection (bacterial → neutrophilia, viral → lymphocytosis), inflammation, leukemia. Leukopenia (<4,000): viral infections, bone marrow suppression.

subject: Physiology
stem: Neutrophil response to bacterial infection: which process allows them to exit blood vessels?
options: Diapedesis (extravasation): selectin-mediated rolling → integrin-mediated adhesion (LFA-1:ICAM-1, Mac-1:ICAM-1) → chemotaxis (IL-8/CXCL8, C5a, fMLP, LTB4) → diapedesis through endothelial gaps → migration to infection site
explanation: Leukocyte extravasation: (1) Rolling: selectins (E-selectin, P-selectin on endothelium; L-selectin on neutrophils) bind sialyl-Lewis X on neutrophils (E- and P-selectin) — low affinity, reversible. (2) Activation: IL-8, C5a, fMLP → activate β2 integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) on neutrophil → high-affinity state. (3) Adhesion: LFA-1/ICAM-1, Mac-1/ICAM-1 — firm. (4) Diapedesis: migration between/through endothelial cells (PECAM-CD31 helps). (5) Chemotaxis along gradient.

subject: Physiology
stem: Coagulation factor XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor) function:
options: Crosslinks fibrin monomers (covalently) to form a stable fibrin clot resistant to fibrinolysis; activated by thrombin (requires Ca2+); transglutaminase that forms isopeptide bonds between γ and α chains of adjacent fibrin molecules
explanation: Coagulation cascade summary: XIIa→XI→IXa; VIIa+TF→Xa (extrinsic); both → Xa (common pathway). Xa+Va+Ca2++PL → prothrombin → thrombin. Thrombin: (1) cleaves fibrinogen → fibrin monomers → polymerize (H-bonds) → loose clot. (2) Activates FXIII → FXIIIa → crosslinks fibrin (covalent, stable clot). (3) Activates FV, FVIII, FXI (positive feedback). (4) Activates protein C (anticoagulant pathway). Clot dissolution: plasmin (from tPA/urokinase + plasminogen) → fibrinolysis → fibrin degradation products (D-dimer from crosslinked fibrin).

subject: Physiology
stem: Heparin mechanism of action:
options: Binds and activates antithrombin III (AT III) → AT III inhibits thrombin (IIa), Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa; UFH (unfractionated heparin) inactivates both thrombin and Xa; LMWH (enoxaparin) preferentially inhibits Xa
explanation: Heparin (UFH and LMWH): binds antithrombin III → conformational change → AT III becomes a rapid inhibitor of serine proteases. UFH (large, 5000-30,000 Da): inhibits thrombin (IIa) AND Xa (requires pentasaccharide + 13-sugar chain to bridge AT III to thrombin). LMWH (3000-6000 Da): inhibits Xa predominantly (short chain cannot bridge to thrombin). UFH: IV, monitored by aPTT, reversible with protamine sulfate. LMWH: SC, predictable, monitored by anti-Xa activity (not routine).

subject: Physiology
stem: Fibrinolysis: what activates plasminogen to plasmin?
options: Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, secreted by endothelial cells in response to clot formation) and urokinase (uPA) convert plasminogen → plasmin; plasmin cleaves fibrin → FDPs (D-dimer from crosslinked fibrin); controlled by PAI-1 (inhibits tPA/uPA) and α2-antiplasmin (inactivates free plasmin)
explanation: Fibrinolysis: tPA (endogenous) or thrombolytics (streptokinase, alteplase, tenecteplase) → activate plasminogen (bound to fibrin) → plasmin → degrades fibrin → fragments (D-dimer specific for crosslinked fibrin, measured in DVT/PE diagnosis). Controlled by: PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, from endothelial cells and platelets) + α2-antiplasmin (rapidly inactivates free plasmin). D-dimer elevated in: DVT, PE, DIC, pregnancy, post-surgical.

subject: Physiology
stem: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): mechanism?
options: Systemic activation of coagulation → consumption of coagulation factors and platelets → simultaneous microvascular thrombosis AND bleeding; caused by sepsis, trauma, obstetric complications, malignancy, snake bites
explanation: DIC: dysregulated, systemic coagulation → consumptive coagulopathy. Causes: sepsis (LPS → TF expression), trauma, amniotic fluid embolism, placental abruption, malignancy (especially AML-M3, mucin-secreting tumors), transfusion reactions. Labs: ↑PT, ↑aPTT, ↑D-dimer, ↑fibrin degradation products (FDPs), ↓fibrinogen, ↓platelets. Mixed picture: thrombosis (microthrombi → organ failure) + bleeding (consumptive coagulopathy).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cyclic AMP (cAMP) is the second messenger for which receptor types?
options: Gs-coupled GPCRs: ligand → Gs → adenylate cyclase (AC) → ATP → cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA) → phosphorylates serine/threonine residues on target proteins; examples: β-adrenergic receptors, glucagon receptor, D1 dopamine receptor, calcitonin, FSH, LH, TSH, ACTH, PTH receptors
explanation: cAMP second messenger: Gs-GPCR → Gαs subunit → activates AC → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation. Gi-GPCR → Gαi → inhibits AC → ↓cAMP. Examples of Gs: β1 (heart, ↑HR + contractility), β2 (bronchodilation), glucagon (glycogenolysis), TSH, FSH, LH, PTH, ACTH, D1, H2 (parietal cells). Examples of Gi: α2 (NE autoreceptors, ↓NE release), M2 (vagal, ↓HR), D2 (striatum), GABAB, opioid receptors.

subject: Physiology
stem: Phospholipase C (PLC) pathway: which second messengers are produced?
options: Inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG): Gq → PLCβ → cleaves PIP2 → IP3 (→ releases Ca2+ from ER) + DAG (→ activates PKC → phosphorylates targets; DAG remains in membrane)
explanation: Gq-GPCR pathway: Gαq → activates PLCβ → PIP2 → IP3 + DAG. IP3 → binds IP3R on ER/SR → Ca2+ release from intracellular store → ↑[Ca2+]i. DAG → activates PKC (protein kinase C, Ca2+-dependent) → phosphorylates Ser/Thr residues. Examples: M1, M3 (ACh), α1 (NE/E), H1 (histamine), AT1 (angiotensin II), oxytocin, vasopressin V1, TRH, GnRH receptors, thromboxane A2, endothelin.

subject: Physiology
stem: Nitric oxide (NO): mechanism of smooth muscle relaxation?
options: NO → activates soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) → ↑cGMP → protein kinase G (PKG) → phosphorylates MLCP (activates) and phospholamban/BKCa → ↓[Ca2+]i + ↓MLCK activity → smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation
explanation: NO signaling: synthesized by NOS (eNOS in endothelium = constitutive, activated by Ca2+-calmodulin; iNOS in macrophages = inducible by cytokines; nNOS in neurons). NO diffuses into smooth muscle → activates soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC, unlike particulate/receptor GC) → cGMP → PKG → (1) phosphorylates MLCP → dephosphorylates MLC → relaxation, (2) phosphorylates SERCA → ↑Ca2+ reuptake into SR, (3) activates BKCa → hyperpolarization. Sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor) → ↑cGMP → maintains NO-mediated vasodilation.

subject: Physiology
stem: The macula densa cells are located in which part of the nephron?
options: The thick ascending limb/early distal tubule junction (actually the early DCT where it passes between afferent and efferent arterioles of its own glomerulus) — these specialized cells sense NaCl concentration and regulate TGF and renin release
explanation: JGA (juxtaglomerular apparatus): consists of (1) JG cells (granular cells) in the wall of the afferent arteriole — contain renin-filled granules, respond to reduced stretch (↓perfusion pressure) and β1 stimulation. (2) Macula densa cells — in the thick ascending limb/early DCT, sense [NaCl] in tubular fluid → ↑NaCl → adenosine release → constrict afferent arteriole (TGF) + ↓renin. ↓NaCl → ↑renin release + paracrine dilator PGE2 → dilates afferent arteriole. (3) Extraglomerular mesangial cells.

subject: Physiology
stem: Metabolic alkalosis occurs in which clinical situation?
options: Prolonged vomiting — loses HCl (H+ + Cl-) → ↑plasma HCO3-, ↑pH, ↑PaCO2 (respiratory compensation, hypoventilation), hypokalemia (H+ shifts out of cells → H+ replaces K+ in ECF), ↓Cl- (hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis)
explanation: Metabolic alkalosis: ↑HCO3-, ↑pH, respiratory compensation = hypoventilation (↑PaCO2 by ~0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in HCO3-). Causes: (1) H+ loss: vomiting, NG suction (lose HCl), loop/thiazide diuretics (↑H+ secretion in CCD), (2) HCO3- gain: bicarb ingestion, blood transfusion (citrate→HCO3-), Milk-alkali syndrome. (3) Contraction alkalosis: loop diuretics → ECF volume contracts around fixed HCO3- → ↑HCO3- concentration. Saline-responsive (lose Cl-, ECF contracted) vs. saline-resistant (hyperaldosteronism).

subject: Physiology
stem: Anion gap metabolic acidosis with NORMAL anion gap (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis) is caused by:
options: Diarrhea (loss of HCO3- → ↑Cl- to maintain electroneutrality → NAGMA), renal tubular acidosis (RTA — kidneys fail to excrete H+ or fail to reabsorb HCO3-), ureterosigmoidostomy, pancreatic fistula — all involve HCO3- loss, replaced by Cl-
explanation: Normal anion gap (NAGMA, hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis: HCO3- is lost or H+ is added but Cl- rises proportionately (so AG unchanged). Mnemonic: USED CARP. Ureteral diversion, Saline infusion (excess NaCl → dilution + ↑Cl-), Endocrine (Addison's, hypoaldosteronism), Diarrhea (most common cause, HCO3- rich stool), Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide), Ammonium chloride, RTA, Post-hypocapnia. Urine AG (Na+ + K+ - Cl-) used to differentiate: negative (extra-renal, e.g., diarrhea) vs. positive (renal, RTA).

subject: Physiology
stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP): what stimulates its release and what does it do?
options: Increased atrial stretch (↑blood volume or ↑atrial pressure) → ANP from atrial myocytes; ANP → dilates afferent arteriole + constricts efferent arteriole → ↑GFR; inhibits renin, aldosterone, ADH → promotes natriuresis and diuresis to reduce blood volume
explanation: ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide): 28-amino acid peptide from atrial cardiomyocytes. Released by: ↑atrial stretch (↑filling pressure, ↑blood volume, CHF). Actions (via particulate guanylate cyclase → ↑cGMP): (1) Renal: vasodilates afferent, constricts efferent → ↑GFR, ↑Na+ filtration + blocks Na+ reabsorption in medullary collecting duct → natriuresis. (2) Inhibits renin, inhibits aldosterone, inhibits ADH release. (3) Vasodilates (reduces PVR). Net: ↓blood volume and ↓BP. BNP (brain/B-type): from ventricles, similar effects; diagnostic marker of CHF.

subject: Physiology
stem: The Nernst equation calculates:
options: The equilibrium potential for a single ion species (Ex) based on the concentration gradient across the membrane: Ex = (RT/zF) × ln([X]o/[X]i); for K+ at 37°C, EK ≈ -90 mV; for Na+, ENa ≈ +60 mV; for Cl-, ECl ≈ -70 mV
explanation: Nernst equation: Ex = (61/z) × log([X]o/[X]i) at 37°C. For K+ (z=+1): EK = 61 × log(4/140) = 61 × (-1.54) ≈ -94 mV. For Na+ (z=+1): ENa = 61 × log(142/10) ≈ +70 mV. For Ca2+ (z=+2): ECa = 30.5 × log(2.5/0.0001) ≈ +130 mV. For Cl- (z=-1): ECl = -61 × log([Cl-]o/[Cl-]i) ≈ -70 mV. Goldmann equation includes all ions weighted by their permeabilities → gives RMP.

subject: Physiology
stem: Einthoven's triangle: limb leads I, II, III in ECG measure:
options: Potential differences between limb electrodes: Lead I = LA - RA; Lead II = LL - RA; Lead III = LL - LA (Einthoven's law: I + III = II); augmented leads: aVR = -(I+II)/2; aVL = (I-III)/2; aVF = (II+III)/2 — all 6 measure in the frontal plane
explanation: Standard limb leads: bipolar (measure between two electrodes). Lead I: positive electrode at LA, negative at RA (0° angle). Lead II: positive at LL, negative at RA (+60°). Lead III: positive at LL, negative at LA (+120°). Augmented limb leads (Wilson central terminal as reference): aVR (+210°), aVL (-30°), aVF (+90°). Cardiac axis: normal -30° to +90°. Right axis deviation (RAD) >+90°: RVH, posterior fascicular block. Left axis deviation (LAD) <-30°: LBBB, anterior fascicular block.

subject: Physiology
stem: Action potential in the SA node is different from the ventricular myocyte because:
options: SA node has a fast phase 0 (Na+ INa like ventricular cells)

SA node has NO stable resting potential (slow spontaneous depolarization due to 'funny current' If — nonselective cation channel) and phase 0 (upstroke) is due to Ca2+ via L-type Ca2+ channel (ICa-L), not fast Na+ INa; hence SA node AP is slow and smaller in amplitude
SA node has a plateau phase
SA node repolarizes faster than ventricular cells
explanation: SA node AP features: (1) No true resting potential (maximum diastolic potential ~-60 mV); (2) Spontaneous depolarization (pacemaker potential) driven by: ↓IK (K+ conductance ↓), ↑If (funny current, nonselective cation channel, activated at -60 mV, inward Na+/K+), ↑ICa-T (T-type Ca2+ current). (3) Phase 0 upstroke: L-type Ca2+ channel (NOT Na+ INa — hence no fast upstroke, blocked by Ca2+ blockers verapamil, diltiazem, not Na+-channel blockers like lidocaine). (4) Automaticity: intrinsic rate ~60–100 bpm.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the physiological significance of the 'all-or-none principle' of action potentials?
options: Action potentials vary in amplitude with stimulus strength

Once the threshold is reached, the action potential is always the same size and shape regardless of the strength of the stimulus — coding of stimulus intensity is by frequency of APs (rate coding) and the number of fibers recruited (spatial coding), NOT by AP amplitude
APs can be graded like EPSPs
APs of smaller amplitude occur at lower temperatures
explanation: All-or-none law: if a stimulus reaches threshold (typically -55 mV for neurons), a full-sized AP is generated; below threshold, no AP (just EPSP). AP amplitude is constant and maximal regardless of stimulus intensity (as long as threshold is reached). Intensity coding: (1) Rate coding — stronger stimulus → higher frequency of APs. (2) Spatial/population coding — stronger stimulus → more sensory fibers recruited. This is different from graded potentials (EPSPs, receptor potentials) which are proportional to stimulus strength.

subject: Physiology
stem: Local anesthetics (lidocaine, bupivacaine) work by:
options: Blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels in the inactivated state — enter the channel from the intracellular side in the ionized (protonated) form → prevent Na+ influx → prevent depolarization → block AP propagation; preferentially block small-diameter, myelinated fibers first (C > Aδ > Aβ > Aα = pain first, touch later, motor last)
explanation: Local anesthetics: weak bases (pKa ~7.8–8.5). At physiological pH, exist as both charged (ionized) and uncharged forms. Uncharged form crosses neuronal membrane → intracellular → protonated → enters Na+ channel from inside → blocks channel (state-dependent: preferentially binds inactivated/open state). Cannot work in acidic environments (e.g., pus/infection — ionized → cannot penetrate). Order of blockade: B>A>C (smallest unmyelinated fibers most sensitive → pain blocked first, then touch, then motor last).

subject: Physiology
stem: Inhalation anesthetics: which property determines speed of induction?
options: High blood-gas solubility coefficient (means fast induction)

LOW blood-gas partition coefficient (poorly soluble in blood → blood equilibrates quickly with alveolar gas → fast rise in brain partial pressure → fast onset); e.g., desflurane and N2O have low solubility → rapid onset/offset; halothane has high solubility → slow onset
High oil-gas coefficient (determines potency, not speed)
explanation: Inhalation anesthetic pharmacokinetics: Blood-gas partition coefficient (λ): ratio of anesthetic concentration in blood/alveolar gas at equilibrium. Low λ: poorly blood-soluble → blood quickly reaches equilibrium with inspired gas → fast rise in PAgas = fast rise in brain partial pressure → rapid onset AND rapid offset. High λ: highly blood-soluble → blood acts as reservoir, slow equilibration → slow onset/offset. Desflurane (λ=0.42, fastest) < N2O (0.47) < Isoflurane (1.4) < Halothane (2.4, slowest).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'minimal alveolar concentration' (MAC) of an inhalation anesthetic represents:
options: The alveolar concentration (at 1 atmosphere) that prevents movement in 50% of subjects in response to a standard surgical stimulus (skin incision) — it measures potency; MAC is inversely related to the oil-gas partition coefficient (Meyer-Overton correlation: higher lipid solubility → more potent → lower MAC)
The concentration at which apnea occurs
The concentration needed for induction only
explanation: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration): ED50 for immobility (50% of patients don't move). More potent = lower MAC. Meyer-Overton correlation: MAC ∝ 1/oil-gas partition coefficient → higher lipid solubility = greater potency = lower MAC. Examples: Halothane MAC 0.75% (most potent), Isoflurane 1.15%, Sevoflurane 2.0%, Desflurane 6.0%, N2O 104% (cannot achieve MAC in 100% O2 atmosphere at sea level → used as adjuvant).

subject: Physiology
stem: What determines stroke volume of the heart?
options: Preload (EDV — Frank-Starling), afterload (SVR — inversely), and contractility (inotropy); SV = EDV - ESV, normally 70 mL at rest
explanation: Determinants of SV: (1) Preload (EDV): ↑EDV → ↑SV (Frank-Starling mechanism; more stretch → more crossbridge overlap → stronger contraction). (2) Afterload (resistance to ejection, mainly SVR): ↑afterload → ↓SV (pump has to work against higher pressure). (3) Contractility (inotropy): ↑contractility → ↑SV at any given preload/afterload (upward/leftward shift of Frank-Starling curve). Positive inotropes: catecholamines, digoxin, Ca2+, warm temperature. Negative inotropes: β-blockers, CCBs, acidosis, hypoxia.

subject: Physiology
stem: The pulmonary circulation has which haemodynamic features compared to systemic?
options: Low resistance (pulmonary vascular resistance = 60–120 dynes·s·cm-5 vs. systemic 900–1200 dynes·s·cm-5), low pressure (PAP 25/8 mmHg, mean 15 mmHg), high compliance — allows the RV to pump the same CO as the LV at much lower pressures
explanation: Pulmonary circulation: Mean PAP ~15 mmHg (normal <25 mmHg; pulmonary hypertension ≥25 mmHg at rest). PVR = (mean PAP - PCWP)/CO = (15-8)/5 = 1.4 Wood units (~112 dynes·s·cm-5). SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO = (93-2)/5 = 18.2 Wood units (~1456 dynes·s·cm-5). RV: thin-walled (handles low pressure), less tolerant of acute pressure increase (acute cor pulmonale from massive PE). PVR decreases with increasing CO (recruitment + distension of pulmonary vessels).

subject: Physiology
stem: During inspiration, what happens to venous return and cardiac output?
options: Both decrease due to intrathoracic pressure change

Intrathoracic pressure falls → ↑venous return to the right heart (↑RV preload) → ↑RVCO; simultaneously, pulmonary vascular bed expands → ↑pulmonary blood volume → transiently ↓pulmonary venous return → ↓LV filling → ↓LVCO. LV output increases after a few beats as the increased RV output reaches the lungs.
Heart rate is the only change
explanation: Respiratory influence on cardiac output: Inspiration (↓intrathoracic pressure): ↑venous return → ↑RV preload → ↑RVCO. But pulmonary veins (intrathoracic) expand → holds more blood → transient ↓LV preload → ↓LVCO → explains why SBP falls slightly on inspiration (~5 mmHg normal). Abnormal: pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg fall) in tamponade/constrictive pericarditis/tension pneumothorax/severe asthma.

subject: Physiology
stem: The electrocardiogram: what does the ST segment represent?
options: The period between the end of ventricular depolarization and the beginning of repolarization (phase 2 plateau of the ventricular AP — all myocardium is depolarized, no net current, normally isoelectric)
explanation: ECG intervals: ST segment: from end of QRS (J point) to start of T wave. Isoelectric normally (all ventricular cells depolarized simultaneously → no current flow → no ECG deflection). ST elevation (>1 mm in limb leads, >2 mm in precordial): transmural ischemia/STEMI (current of injury), pericarditis (widespread elevation with concave shape, no reciprocal changes), ventricular aneurysm, Brugada (V1-V2 saddle/coved). ST depression: subendocardial ischemia, NSTEMI, digoxin (reverse tick), LVH (strain pattern).

subject: Physiology
stem: During atrial fibrillation (AF), the ECG shows:
options: Regular P waves and normal QRS

No distinct P waves (replaced by irregular 'fibrillatory' baseline, 350–600 atrial impulses/minute), irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm (QRS irregular in timing and often rapid at 100–160 bpm if untreated)
explanation: AF: most common sustained arrhythmia. Multiple re-entrant wavelets in atria → chaotic rapid atrial depolarizations. AV node receives 350-600 impulses/min but conducts only a fraction (decremental conduction) → irregular ventricular rate. ECG: absence of distinct P waves, irregular baseline (fibrillatory waves f, especially V1), irregularly irregular QRS. Risks: ↑stroke (LA thrombus, no coordinated atrial contraction → CHA2DS2-VASc score). Rate control: β-blockers, CCBs, digoxin. Rhythm control: amiodarone, cardioversion.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cardiac hypertrophy: concentric hypertrophy vs. eccentric hypertrophy?
options: Concentric: ↑wall thickness, ↑r/h ratio improves (decreased wall stress); due to ↑afterload (pressure overload — hypertension, aortic stenosis; sarcomeres added in PARALLEL → thicker wall, relatively smaller cavity). Eccentric: ↑chamber volume, ↑wall thickness (sarcomeres added in SERIES → longer fibers, larger cavity); due to ↑preload (volume overload — MR, AR, dilated CMP)
explanation: Laplace (wall stress = Pr/2h): concentric hypertrophy reduces r and increases h → normalizes wall stress (compensated). Eccentric: r increases (volume overload) → ↑wall stress → stimulus for h increase as compensation. Eventually both may decompensate → dilated cardiomyopathy. Key: concentric = pressure overload (HTN, AS, PS); eccentric = volume overload (AR, MR, VSD). Diastolic dysfunction: mainly concentric (stiff ventricle). Systolic dysfunction: mainly eccentric (reduced EF).

subject: Physiology
stem: Osmoregulation of blood volume: when blood volume is reduced, the first compensatory response is:
options: Vasoconstriction and tachycardia mediated by the sympathetic nervous system (immediate, within seconds) via baroreceptor reflex
Release of aldosterone (takes minutes to hours)
explanation: Acute blood volume reduction: Immediate (seconds): baroreceptor reflex (↓stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch → ↓afferent inhibition on CNS → ↑SNS → ↑HR, ↑vasoconstriction, ↑cardiac contractility → maintain BP). Minutes: RAAS activation (renin → Ang II → aldosterone, thirst). Hours: ADH → water retention. Days: erythropoietin → ↑RBC production. The baroreceptor reflex is FASTEST — essential in orthostatic hypotension, hemorrhage.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which receptor mediates the Bezold-Jarisch reflex (vasovagal syncope)?
options: Cardiac mechanoreceptors (C fibers/unmyelinated afferents) in the inferoposterior wall of the LV → vigorous stimulation (ischemia, chemical, vigorous contraction with low volume) → vagal afferents → medullary centers → paradoxical bradycardia + vasodilation → syncope (vasovagal)
explanation: Bezold-Jarisch reflex: LV mechanoreceptors/chemoreceptors (type C fibers, unmyelinated vagal afferents) in the inferior wall → activated by vigorous contraction of a relatively empty heart (e.g., hypovolemia, upright posture), ischemia (inferior MI, causing bradycardia in 30% of inferior MI → inferior MI = 'Bezold-Jarisch' response), chemical stimuli. Response: ↓HR (vagal), ↓SVR (vasodilation) → hypotension → syncope. Treatment: atropine (in inferior MI bradycardia).

subject: Physiology
stem: In mechanical ventilation, which ventilatory mode delivers a set tidal volume regardless of lung compliance?
options: Volume-controlled ventilation (VCV) — delivers a preset tidal volume; as lung compliance decreases (ARDS, pneumothorax), airway pressure rises; risk of barotrauma if pressure too high
explanation: Mechanical ventilation modes: VCV: set TV → consistent minute ventilation; but peak pressure rises if compliance ↓ or resistance ↑ → risk of volutrauma/barotrauma. PCV: set inspiratory pressure → consistent peak pressure but TV varies with compliance (↓compliance → ↓TV → ↓minute ventilation). ARDS Protocol: lung-protective ventilation — low TV (6 mL/kg IBW), plateau pressure <30 cmH2O, PEEP to keep alveoli open, permissive hypercapnia if needed.

subject: Physiology
stem: The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: which receptors are involved?
options: Slowly adapting stretch receptors (SARs) in airway smooth muscle → sense lung inflation → via vagal afferents → inhibit the inspiratory center (apneustic center) → terminate inspiration → protect against overinflation; more prominent in infants, less in awake adults
explanation: Pulmonary mechanoreceptors: (1) Slowly adapting stretch receptors (SARs): in smooth muscle of bronchi/bronchioles. Respond to lung distension → inhibit inspiration (Hering-Breuer reflex) → important in animals and infants; in adults active mainly at high TV (>1L). (2) Rapidly adapting receptors (RARs, irritant receptors): in airway epithelium → respond to irritants, rapidly changing lung volume → cough, bronchoconstriction. (3) C fibers (J receptors): alveolar walls → respond to stretch, pulmonary edema, irritants → tachypnea, apnea.

subject: Physiology
stem: PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is used in ARDS to:
options: Prevent alveolar collapse at end-expiration → increase FRC → improve V/Q matching → improve oxygenation; also reduce atelectrauma (repetitive opening/closing of alveoli); optimal PEEP recruits atelectatic alveoli without overdistending others
explanation: ARDS (diffuse alveolar damage, surfactant dysfunction, ↓compliance, ↑shunt): PEEP maintains positive airway pressure at end-expiration → prevents alveolar collapse (atelectasis) → improves FRC → reopens collapsed alveoli (recruitment) → ↑V/Q matching → ↑oxygenation. Lung-protective strategy: TV 6 mL/kg IBW, plateau pressure <30 cmH2O, PEEP (individualized, often 8-15 cmH2O), permissive hypercapnia, prone positioning (improves V/Q by redistributing blood to better-ventilated dorsal lung).

subject: Physiology
stem: Regarding pulmonary blood flow distribution in an upright lung — which zone has the lowest blood flow?
options: Zone 1 (apex) — where Palveolar > Parterial > Pvenous — alveolar pressure exceeds arteriolar pressure → capillary compression → no flow; in a healthy person, Zone 1 is small or absent (pulmonary arterial pressure sufficient to perfuse apex). In hemorrhagic shock or high PEEP, Zone 1 expands → increased dead space
explanation: West's zones of the lung (gravity-dependent flow): Zone 1 (apex): Palv > Pa > Pv → capillaries compressed → dead space (normally absent in healthy standing person). Zone 2 (middle): Pa > Palv > Pv → flow determined by Pa-Palv difference → 'starling resistor'. Zone 3 (base): Pa > Pv > Palv → flow determined by Pa-Pv difference (maximum flow). Overall: blood flow increases from apex to base. V/Q ratio: highest at apex (well-ventilated relative to flow), lowest at base.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypoxemia correction by 100% O2 administration helps in which condition but NOT in which?
options: Helps in shunt; doesn't help in V/Q mismatch

Helps in V/Q mismatch (can raise PAO2 in low V/Q units, corrects hypoxemia) but does NOT correct right-to-left shunt (bypassed blood never contacts alveolar gas → 100% O2 cannot increase SaO2 of shunted blood; PaO2 does not reach expected levels)
explanation: Response to 100% O2: V/Q mismatch → 100% O2 raises PAO2 in hypoventilated units → O2 diffuses in → improved oxygenation. Diffusion impairment → extra O2 driving pressure → often improves. True shunt (anatomic — ASD, PDA, hepatopulmonary syndrome, or physiological — atelectasis, pneumonia consolidation) → shunted blood never contacts O2 → 100% O2 gives less than expected improvement. If PaO2 fails to reach >500 mmHg on FiO2 1.0 → intracardiac shunt or significant atelectatic shunt.

subject: Physiology
stem: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): physiological basis of airway obstruction?
options: Emphysema: loss of elastic recoil → air trapping, ↑compliance → dynamic airway collapse during expiration (loss of tethering of small airways by alveolar elastin). Chronic bronchitis: mucous gland hypertrophy, excess mucus, airway wall inflammation → obstruction. Both cause: ↑TLC, ↑FRC, ↑RV, ↓FEV1, ↓FEV1/FVC (<0.7), ↓DLCO (emphysema)
explanation: COPD mechanisms: Emphysema (usually smoking → neutrophil elastase > anti-elastase): destruction of alveolar walls → ↑compliance, ↓elastic recoil → loss of radial traction on airways → dynamic expiratory collapse → airflow obstruction + air trapping. Chronic bronchitis: Reid index (mucous gland thickness/wall thickness) >0.4 → excessive mucus production (>3 months/year for 2 consecutive years). Both → ↑RV, ↑TLC, barrel chest. DLCO: reduced in emphysema (lost alveolar surface area + capillaries); normal or increased in asthma.

subject: Physiology
stem: The diffusing capacity (DLCO) measures:
options: The rate of CO transfer from alveolar gas to pulmonary capillary blood, reflecting the surface area, membrane thickness, and V/Q matching; DLCO = VCO / (PAco - PcCO); CO used because Hb has very high affinity → Pc remains ~0; abnormal if <75% predicted
explanation: DLCO (diffusing capacity of lung for CO): measures gas transfer efficiency. Reduced in: emphysema (↓surface area), pulmonary fibrosis/ILD (↑membrane thickness), pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary vascular disease, anemia (↓Hb to carry CO). Increased in: polycythemia, exercise, supine position (↑pulmonary blood volume), left-to-right intracardiac shunt, early left heart failure (↑pulmonary vascular congestion). Normal: >75% predicted. Carbon monoxide chosen because Hb affinity ≈240× O2 → Pc never limiting.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'response to exercise' in a healthy person includes all EXCEPT:
options: Increased cardiac output and heart rate

Increased dead space-to-tidal volume (VD/VT) ratio — actually VD/VT DECREASES during exercise as VT increases substantially while anatomical dead space remains constant and physiological dead space may decrease (improved V/Q matching); the false answer is 'increased VD/VT'
Increased O2 consumption and CO2 production
explanation: Exercise physiology: ↑VO2 and ↑VCO2 → ↑minute ventilation. ↑CO (primarily ↑HR, also ↑SV). ↑C(a-v)O2 (more O2 extraction by working muscle). VD/VT: anatomical VD (~150 mL) is fixed; VT increases to 2-3L → VD/VT falls. Redistribution of pulmonary blood flow: even apical perfusion → ↓V/Q mismatch → ↑DLCO (with exercise). Arterial PaO2 maintained near normal (only drops in elite athletes — 'exercise-induced hypoxemia' due to diffusion limitation from very fast transit).

subject: Physiology
stem: Swallowing (deglutition): what phase is completely involuntary?
options: Pharyngeal phase — once the bolus reaches the posterior pharynx, the pharyngeal phase is entirely involuntary (reflexive, controlled by the swallowing center in the medulla): elevation of soft palate, closure of glottis (epiglottis tips back, true vocal cords adduct), relaxation of upper esophageal sphincter (UES)
explanation: Swallowing phases: (1) Oral (voluntary): tongue pushes bolus to oropharynx. (2) Pharyngeal (involuntary): triggered by bolus contact with posterior pharynx; medullary swallowing center; closure of nasopharynx (soft palate elevation), glottic closure (epiglottis + arytenoids + adduction of VCs), UES relaxation — apnea during this phase. (3) Esophageal phase: primary peristalsis carries bolus down; LES relaxes to receive bolus. Achalasia: failure of LES to relax (degenerating myenteric plexus neurons).

subject: Physiology
stem: The ileocecal valve: what regulates its opening and closure?
options: Distension of the ileum (↑peristalsis → relaxes ileocecal sphincter) and distension of the cecum (↑tone of ileocecal sphincter — prevents backflow); gastroileal reflex (meal → gastric distension → ileal peristalsis → opens ileocecal valve)
explanation: Ileocecal valve (Bauhin's valve): functional sphincter between terminal ileum and cecum. Prevents reflux of colonic bacteria into small intestine (→ SIBO if incompetent). Opens when ileal pressure rises (peristaltic wave arrives). Closes when cecal pressure rises (prevents retrograde flow). Gastroileal reflex: eating → gastric distension → stimulates ileal motility → ileocecal valve opening → mass movement in colon (also triggers gastrocolic reflex → urge to defecate postprandially).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cells of the gastric mucosa produce mucus and bicarbonate?
options: Mucous neck cells (in the neck of gastric glands) and surface mucous cells (on the luminal surface) — both secrete mucus (glycoproteins that form a gel layer ~0.5 mm thick) and HCO3- (alkaline, traps HCO3- in mucus layer → pH gradient: ~7 at mucosal surface vs. ~2 in lumen — gastric mucosal barrier)
explanation: Gastric mucosal barrier: mucus (gel layer) secreted by surface epithelial cells and mucous neck cells → traps HCO3- → protects against acid/pepsin. Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) stimulate mucus and HCO3- secretion + promote epithelial cell renewal + maintain mucosal blood flow (cytoprotective). NSAIDs inhibit COX → reduce prostaglandins → impair mucosal barrier → peptic ulcers. Misoprostol (PGE1 analog) used to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers.

subject: Physiology
stem: Small intestinal motility: what are segmentation contractions?
options: Rhythmic, non-propulsive contractions of the circular muscle at multiple points simultaneously → churn and mix (but don't propel) chyme with digestive secretions → ↑contact with absorptive surface → ↑absorption efficiency; driven by slow waves (basal electrical rhythm, BER) — 12/min in duodenum, 8–9/min in ileum
Power propulsive contractions from the colon
explanation: Small intestinal motility: (1) Segmentation: ring-like contractions (circular muscle) at multiple points → mixing without net propulsion. (2) Peristalsis: coordinated contraction behind and relaxation ahead of bolus (ascending excitation via SP, CGRP; descending inhibition via NO, VIP) → net propulsion. Migrating motor complex (MMC): between meals, cyclic phase III contractions sweep residual contents toward colon. Intestinal transit time: 2–5 hours from duodenum to ileocecal valve.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which hormone is responsible for the 'insulin-independent' incretin effect?
options: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1, from L cells of the ileum and colon) and GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, from K cells of the duodenum/jejunum) — both are released by nutrient ingestion → augment glucose-stimulated insulin secretion ('incretin effect' — up to 70% of meal-related insulin secretion); also suppress glucagon
explanation: Incretins: GLP-1 and GIP released in response to meals → act on pancreatic β-cells to ↑insulin secretion (glucose-dependent → no hypoglycemia if glucose normal). GLP-1 also: suppresses glucagon, delays gastric emptying (↓postprandial glucose spike), central satiety (↓appetite). DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins) block GLP-1/GIP degradation → longer action. GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) → used in T2DM + weight loss. Incretin effect lost in T2DM.

subject: Physiology
stem: The liver receives blood from two sources. Which provides the majority of the oxygen supply?
options: Portal vein (60–80% of blood, but only 40–50% of oxygen supply; deoxygenated from gut)
Hepatic artery (only 30–40% of blood volume but provides 40–60% of oxygen supply, as it is fully oxygenated); both eventually drain into hepatic sinusoids and then hepatic veins → IVC
explanation: Hepatic blood supply: Portal vein (75% of blood flow, 50% of oxygen) — carries nutrient-rich but partially deoxygenated blood from the gut, spleen, and pancreas. Hepatic artery (25% of blood flow, 50% of oxygen) — fully oxygenated. Both supply hepatic sinusoids (lined by fenestrated Kupffer cells). Acinar zones: Zone 1 (periportal) = well-oxygenated, first to receive nutrients, first to be damaged in viral hepatitis. Zone 3 (centrilobular) = most hypoxic, first damaged by ischemia/heart failure, halothane/acetaminophen toxicity.

subject: Physiology
stem: Bile production: what stimulates secretion of bile from the gallbladder?
options: CCK (cholecystokinin): released by fat and protein in the duodenum → acts on CCK-A receptors on gallbladder smooth muscle → contraction of gallbladder + relaxation of sphincter of Oddi → bile ejected into duodenum; also stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion
explanation: Gallbladder physiology: stores and concentrates bile (up to 10×). Fasting: Sphincter of Oddi (SoO) closed → bile accumulates in gallbladder. During a meal: fat/protein → duodenum → I cells → CCK → (1) Gallbladder muscle contracts (CCK-A receptor, Gq → IP3/Ca2+), (2) SoO relaxes → bile enters duodenum → emulsification of fat. CCK also stimulates pancreatic enzymes via CCK-A on acinar cells. SoO is under sphincteric (myogenic + cholinergic) tone between meals.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the primary function of the large intestine?
options: Water and electrolyte absorption (primarily Na+ via electroneutral NaCl absorption and aldosterone-sensitive Na+ absorption; turns liquid chyme into solid feces); also houses colonic microbiota (1012-1014 bacteria/g), produces short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate) from fermentation
explanation: Colon functions: (1) Water absorption: ~1.5 L of the 1.5-2 L of ileal effluent absorbed → ~150 mL in feces. Na+ absorbed via NHE3 (luminal Na+/H+ exchanger), ENaC (aldosterone-regulated, in distal colon), CFTR secretes Cl-. (2) Colonic microbiota (gut microbiome): Bacteroides, Firmicutes, anaerobes → ferment dietary fiber → short-chain FAs (SCFA, especially butyrate — major fuel for colonocytes). (3) Mucus secretion (goblet cells, protect from bacteria). (4) Defecation reflex (internal and external anal sphincters).

subject: Physiology
stem: Pancreatic exocrine secretion: what does the acinar cell secrete?
options: Digestive enzyme zymogens: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase (proteases), prophospholipase A2, procarboxy­peptidases (peptidases), proamylase, lipase, colipase (fat digestion); stimulated by CCK (via CCK-A receptor) and ACh (vagal M1 receptor)
explanation: Pancreatic secretion: Two cell types: (1) Acinar cells: enzyme zymogens (inactive forms) secreted in response to CCK and ACh → activated in duodenum by enterokinase (enteropeptidase, from brush border) → trypsin → activates all other proteases; also active forms: amylase, lipase. (2) Ductal cells: HCO3--rich fluid (secretin → cAMP → CFTR → Cl-/HCO3- exchanger) neutralizes duodenal acid. Pancreatitis: premature trypsinogen activation → autodigestion.

subject: Physiology
stem: Vitamin D absorption: which form is absorbed from the intestine?
options: Both D2 (ergocalciferol, plant-derived) and D3 (cholecalciferol, animal-derived, also synthesized in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol + UVB radiation) are absorbed in the small intestine as fat-soluble vitamins (micelle-dependent) → liver 25-hydroxylation → 25-OH-D (storage form, measured clinically) → kidney 1α-hydroxylation (PTH ↑, hypophosphatemia ↑) → 1,25-OH2-D3 (calcitriol, active form)
Vitamin D is not absorbed from the gut
Only vitamin D3 is absorbed, not D2
explanation: Vitamin D metabolism: Skin: 7-dehydrocholesterol + UVB → cholecalciferol (D3). Dietary: D2 or D3 from foods/supplements → absorbed in small intestine (fat-soluble, chylomicron transport). Liver: 25-hydroxylase → 25-OH-D3 (calcidiol, measured for deficiency status; t½ ~3 weeks). Kidney: 1α-hydroxylase → 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol, active; t½ 4-6 hours). Calcitriol: ↑intestinal Ca2+ absorption (TRPV6 channel, calbindin), ↑renal Ca2+ reabsorption, ↑bone mineralization.

subject: Physiology
stem: SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion): what are the typical lab findings?
options: Hyponatremia (↓serum Na+ and osmolarity), inappropriately high urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg, often >300), high urine Na+ (>20 mEq/L — because the kidneys are appropriately responding to ADH, not to hypovolemia), euvolemia or mild hypervolemia
High serum osmolarity with low urine sodium
explanation: SIADH: ADH secreted inappropriately (not due to high osmolarity or low volume). Causes: CNS (stroke, SAH, meningitis, trauma), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, small cell lung cancer — ectopic ADH), drugs (carbamazepine, SSRIs, cyclophosphamide, chlorpropamide, NSAIDs), surgery/pain/nausea (physiological ADH release). Lab: ↓serum Na+ (<135), ↓plasma osmolarity (<280), urine osm >serum osm (>100), urine Na+ >20 mEq/L, euvolemic. Treat: fluid restriction, salt tablets, vasopressin receptor antagonists (vaptans).

subject: Physiology
stem: Thyroid storm: mechanism and triggers?
options: Life-threatening complication of severe hyperthyroidism (↑↑↑T3/T4 → ↑↑sympathetic activation + metabolic activation): fever (>38.5°C), tachyarrhythmias, altered mental status, GI symptoms; precipitated by infection, surgery, iodine load (Jodbasedow effect), radioiodine in severely hyperthyroid patient, trauma, childbirth
explanation: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis): usually in undiagnosed or undertreated hyperthyroidism. Precipitants: infection (most common), surgery, trauma, iodine contrast (Jodbasedow), radioiodine, abrupt discontinuation of antithyroid drugs, eclampsia, acute MI. Features: fever, extreme tachycardia, AF, hypertension, anxiety/agitation/psychosis/coma, GI (N/V/D, jaundice). Burch-Wartofsky score. Treatment: PTU (blocks synthesis AND T4→T3 conversion), β-blockers (symptomatic), hydrocortisone (blocks T4→T3 peripherally), iodine (Wolf-Chaikoff effect — AFTER PTU given).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cushing's syndrome: which finding differentiates Cushing's disease (pituitary) from ectopic ACTH secretion?
options: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test (8 mg overnight): in Cushing's disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma), cortisol suppresses ≥50% (negative feedback still partially functional at high-dose). In ectopic ACTH (e.g., small cell lung carcinoma, carcinoid), cortisol does NOT suppress (autonomous ACTH secretion independent of cortisol feedback)
explanation: Cushing's syndrome differential: ACTH-dependent: Cushing's disease (pituitary, 68%) or ectopic ACTH (bronchial carcinoid, SCLC, 12%). ACTH-independent: adrenal adenoma/carcinoma (20%). Diagnosis: 1mg overnight DST (screen, low-dose); 24h UFC; midnight salivary cortisol. Differentiation: CRH stimulation test (Cushing's disease: exaggerated ACTH response; ectopic: blunted). IPSS (inferior petrosal sinus sampling) = gold standard for distinguishing pituitary vs. ectopic source.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the main stimulus for insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells?
options: Amino acids and fat ingestion only

Elevated blood glucose (via KATP channel mechanism: glucose uptake → glycolysis → ↑ATP/ADP ratio → closes KATP channels → membrane depolarization → opens L-type Ca2+ channels → Ca2+ influx → exocytosis of insulin granules)
explanation: GSIS (glucose-stimulated insulin secretion): ↑blood glucose → GLUT2 in beta cells (high Km, non-saturable at physiological glucose concentrations) → glucose enters → glucokinase (hexokinase IV, glucose sensor, low affinity + non-inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate) → glucose-6-phosphate → glycolysis → ↑ATP → KATP channel (Kir6.2/SUR1) closes → membrane depolarization → L-type Ca2+ channel opens → ↑[Ca2+]i → insulin exocytosis. Sulfonylureas close KATP directly → insulin release regardless of glucose.

subject: Physiology
stem: What causes the Somogyi effect (rebound hyperglycemia)?
options: Nocturnal hypoglycemia (due to too much evening insulin) → counter-regulatory hormone release (glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, GH) → rebound hyperglycemia in the morning; distinct from dawn phenomenon (physiological morning rise in cortisol and GH → reduced insulin sensitivity at 6–8 AM → hyperglycemia without preceding hypoglycemia)
Dawn phenomenon is the same as Somogyi
explanation: Somogyi effect: evening insulin overdose → nocturnal hypoglycemia → counterregulatory hormone surge → rebound hyperglycemia (fasting morning hyperglycemia with high ketones, sweating during sleep, nightmares). Distinguished from dawn phenomenon (normal circadian rise in GH/cortisol → AM hyperglycemia, no preceding hypoglycemia, no ketones). Management of Somogyi: reduce evening insulin dose; confirm with 3 AM glucose check or CGM.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the most abundant circulating thyroid hormone and how is it converted to the active form?
options: T3 is the most abundant (and active form)

T4 (thyroxine) is the most abundant (90% of thyroid output); T3 (triiodothyronine, ~3–4× more potent) constitutes only 10% of thyroid output but ~80% of circulating T3 comes from peripheral deiodination of T4 by type 1 and type 2 deiodinase (removes one iodine from the outer ring)
Reverse T3 is the most abundant
explanation: Thyroid hormones: T4/T3 produced by thyroid follicular cells. T4 is secreted 10× more than T3. In peripheral tissues (liver, kidney, muscle) type 1 deiodinase (5'-deiodinase, inhibited by propylthiouracil) converts T4 → T3 (active, higher affinity for nuclear TR receptors). Type 3 deiodinase: T4 → reverse T3 (rT3, inactive, by inner ring deiodination). rT3 elevated in: sick euthyroid syndrome (non-thyroidal illness syndrome), low-carbohydrate diets, starvation, amiodarone (iodine-rich, inhibits T4→T3).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which pituitary hormone controls the adrenal cortex?
options: ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) from the anterior pituitary corticotrophs; ACTH acts on MC2R (melanocortin-2 receptor, Gs → cAMP → PKA) on adrenocortical cells → stimulates all three zones (primarily zona fasciculata → cortisol synthesis) → also stimulates pigmentation (via MC1R on melanocytes — explains hyperpigmentation in Addison's and Nelson's syndrome)
explanation: HPA axis: CRH (hypothalamus, PVN) → ACTH (anterior pituitary, corticotrophs; POMC precursor cleaved into ACTH + α-MSH + β-endorphin) → cortisol + DHEA (adrenal zona fasciculata + reticularis). ACTH also → aldosterone (weak effect). Cortisol: long-loop negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary. Circadian rhythm: ACTH and cortisol peak at 6–8 AM, trough at midnight. ACTH stimulation test ('Synacthen test') used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency.

subject: Physiology
stem: Prolactin: which hypothalamic factor INHIBITS its secretion?
options: Dopamine (from tuberoinfundibular neurons of the hypothalamus; normally tonically inhibits prolactin via D2 receptors on lactotrophs — so dopamine antagonists like metoclopramide, haloperidol, risperidone cause hyperprolactinemia → galactorrhea, amenorrhea)
explanation: Prolactin regulation: only anterior pituitary hormone with predominantly INHIBITORY hypothalamic control (dopamine via D2R → inhibits prolactin secretion). Stimulated by: TRH, estrogen (explains ↑prolactin in pregnancy), VIP, stress, suckling (nipple stimulation → inhibits dopamine pulsatility → ↑prolactin), metoclopramide, domperidone. Hyperprolactinemia: dopamine antagonists, pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma, most common pituitary tumor), stalk compression (↓dopamine reaches pituitary). Treat prolactinoma: cabergoline/bromocriptine (D2 agonists).

subject: Physiology
stem: The adrenal medulla secretes which ratio of catecholamines?
options: Epinephrine (adrenaline) ~80%, Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) ~20%; phenylalanine → tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine → NE → Epi (via PNMT, which requires cortisol for induction — glucocorticoid-containing adrenal blood flows centripetally → high local cortisol induces PNMT in medulla)
explanation: Catecholamine biosynthesis: Tyrosine → DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting step) → Dopamine (DOPA decarboxylase/AAAD) → NE (dopamine β-hydroxylase, DBH, in secretory vesicles) → Epi (PNMT, in cytosol of adrenal chromaffin cells, requires high local cortisol from portal adrenal blood for induction). Adrenal medulla: ~80% Epi, ~20% NE. Sympathetic nerve terminals release primarily NE (no PNMT). Pheochromocytoma: excess catecholamines → hypertensive crisis, headache, palpitations, diaphoresis. Diagnosed by 24h urine metanephrines/catecholamines.

subject: Physiology
stem: Acetylcholine receptors: muscarinic M2 and M3 differ in location and second messenger?
options: M2 (heart, Gi → ↓cAMP → opens KATP → hyperpolarizes SA node → ↓HR; and opens IKACh → slows AV conduction — vagal bradycardia); M3 (smooth muscle, exocrine glands, Gq → IP3/Ca2+ → contraction, secretion, vasodilation via NO release from endothelium)
M2 in salivary glands, M3 in heart
explanation: Muscarinic receptors: M1 (neurons, gastric parietal cells, Gq → IP3/Ca2+). M2 (heart, Gi → ↓cAMP + IKACh → bradycardia, ↓AV conduction; also presynaptic autoreceptors). M3 (smooth muscle everywhere except heart, exocrine glands, vascular endothelium [→ NO → vasodilation], Gq). M4 (CNS, Gi). M5 (CNS, Gq). Atropine blocks all muscarinic receptors → ↑HR, ↓secretions, mydriasis, ↑GI tone. Organophosphate poisoning (SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis) + miosis, bradycardia → treat with atropine + pralidoxime.

subject: Physiology
stem: The sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' response is mediated primarily by:
options: Norepinephrine (NE) from postganglionic sympathetic neurons acting on α1 (vasoconstriction, ↑BP), β1 (↑HR, ↑contractility), β2 (bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle); and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla (acts on all α and β — systemic effects)
explanation: Sympathetic activation: Preganglionic neurons (myelinated, short) → ACh → nicotinic ganglionic receptors → postganglionic neurons (unmyelinated) → NE (most organs). NE receptors: α1 (vascular SM contraction, pupil dilation, ↑glycogenolysis, ↑urethral sphincter), α2 (presynaptic autoreceptors ↓NE release, ↓insulin), β1 (↑HR, ↑contractility, ↑renin), β2 (bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle and coronary vessels, ↑glucagon, ↑glycogenolysis/lipolysis), β3 (lipolysis, thermogenesis in BAT).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which neurotransmitter is deficient in Alzheimer's disease?
options: Acetylcholine (ACh) — cholinergic neurons of the nucleus basalis of Meynert (basal forebrain) degenerate → ↓ACh in the cortex → memory impairment; also loss of cholinergic input from the medial septal nucleus to the hippocampus
explanation: Alzheimer's disease: pathology = amyloid plaques (extracellular β-amyloid from APP processing → Aβ42) + neurofibrillary tangles (intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau). Neurotransmitter: ↓ACh (nucleus basalis of Meynert cholinergic neurons degenerate → cholinergic hypothesis). Treatment: AChE inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) → ↑ACh at synapses. Memantine (NMDA antagonist → reduces excitotoxicity). Note: serotonin (5-HT) reduced in depression; dopamine in Parkinson's; NE in depression + anxiety.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the function of the spinothalamic tract (anterolateral system)?
options: Carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception

Carries pain, temperature, and crude touch from the contralateral body; primary afferent → dorsal horn (synapse in lamina I, IV, V, X) → decussates in the SAME spinal cord level (within a few segments) through the anterior commissure → ascends in the anterolateral columns → VPL thalamus → somatosensory cortex
Carries motor commands from cortex to spinal cord
explanation: Anterolateral (spinothalamic) system: carries pain (Aδ and C fibers, spinothalamic), temperature, crude touch. First-order neuron: enters dorsal horn → ascends or descends 1-2 levels in Lissauer's tract → synapses in dorsal horn (lamina I = pain/temp; V = wide dynamic range neurons). Second-order: crosses in anterior commissure at same level → ascends anterolateral column → VPL of thalamus. Third-order: VPL → somatosensory cortex. Lesion: contralateral pain + temperature loss BELOW the level, ipsilateral fine touch intact.

subject: Physiology
stem: The dorsal column-medial lemniscal (DCML) pathway carries:
options: Fine touch (discriminative), vibration, conscious proprioception, 2-point discrimination, stereognosis; ipsilateral ascending in dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis-below T6, fasciculus cuneatus-above T6) → first synapse at medullary level (gracile and cuneate nuclei) → decussates (internal arcuate fibers) → ascends as medial lemniscus → VPL thalamus → somatosensory cortex
explanation: DCML: first-order neurons enter dorsal horn but pass directly up in ipsilateral dorsal column → nucleus gracilis (lower limb, medial) and nucleus cuneatus (upper limb, lateral) in the medulla → second-order neurons decussate (internal arcuate fibers) → medial lemniscus → VPL thalamus → S1 cortex. Lesion (e.g., B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis): ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, proprioception below the lesion. Note: decussation is in the MEDULLA (not spinal cord) — unlike spinothalamic (decussates at spinal level).

subject: Physiology
stem: Corticospinal tract (pyramidal tract): where does it decussate?
options: In the spinal cord at each level

In the medulla (pyramidal decussation, ~85-90% of fibers decussate at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord) → forms the lateral corticospinal tract (LCST) in the dorsolateral column → innervates ipsilateral LMNs (opposite from where the UMN originated in the motor cortex — contralateral motor cortex controls ipsilateral body after decussation)
explanation: Corticospinal (pyramidal) tract: UMNs from motor cortex (Brodmann 4, 6) + sensory cortex → converge in posterior limb of internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pons (dispersed) → medullary pyramids (concentrated) → 85-90% decussate (pyramidal decussation) → LCST (contralateral) → synapses on alpha-LMNs in ventral horn. 10-15% stay ipsilateral → ventral (anterior) CST → eventually crosses near target. UMN lesion: contralateral spastic hemiplegia, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive, ↑tone.

subject: Physiology
stem: Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) is a sign of:
options: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion above the level of L4-S2 spinal cord — stroking the lateral sole → great toe dorsiflexes (extends upward) + fanning of other toes; normal in infants (<18 months, before CST myelination) but abnormal in adults (indicates UMN dysfunction)
explanation: Babinski response: normal in infants <18 months (descending inhibition from UMN incomplete). In adults = pathological UMN sign. Elicited by stroking lateral plantar surface → big toe extends + others fan out (positive Babinski). UMN lesion signs: Babinski positive, hyperreflexia, spasticity (velocity-dependent ↑tone, clasp-knife quality), clonus, ↑DTRs. LMN lesion signs: flaccidity, ↓DTRs, fasciculations, atrophy (denervation), Babinski absent/down.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which neurotransmitter is primarily released from the locus coeruleus?
options: Norepinephrine (NE) — the locus coeruleus (LC) in the pontine tegmentum is the primary source of noradrenergic projections to the entire CNS (cortex, limbic system, cerebellum, spinal cord); involved in arousal, attention, fear/anxiety, stress response, and the sleep-wake cycle
explanation: Locus coeruleus (LC): largest NE nucleus in the brain. Projects to: cortex (arousal, attention), hippocampus (memory consolidation), amygdala (fear/anxiety), cerebellum (motor coordination), spinal cord (modulates pain, motor activity). LC fires rapidly during wakefulness/stress/arousal, slowly during sleep, silent during REM sleep. NE reuptake blockers (NRIs, SNRIs) enhance NE signaling → antidepressant, anxiolytic effects. LC hyperactivity → panic disorder, PTSD.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cystatin C vs. creatinine: which is a better marker of GFR in early CKD?
options: Cystatin C — a cysteine protease inhibitor produced by all nucleated cells at a constant rate; freely filtered and completely reabsorbed and catabolized by the proximal tubule (not secreted) → serum cystatin C rises earlier as GFR falls; not affected by muscle mass (creatinine is), making it better in elderly, malnutrition, obesity
explanation: GFR estimation: Creatinine: produced by muscle metabolism (creatine → creatinine, constant rate). Freely filtered + ~10-15% actively secreted (overestimates GFR). Serum Cr doesn't rise above normal until GFR falls ~50%. Affected by muscle mass (low Cr in elderly/malnutrition; high in bodybuilders). Cystatin C: constant production (not affected by muscle mass or diet) → better in patients where creatinine is unreliable. eGFR equations: MDRD or CKD-EPI (creatinine based); also CKD-EPI combined cystatin C for better accuracy.

subject: Physiology
stem: The syndrome of type 4 renal tubular acidosis (RTA) is due to:
options: Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance → hyperkalemia → ↓NH3 synthesis in PCT (hyperkalemia inhibits ammoniagenesis) → ↓urinary NH4+ excretion → ↓net acid excretion → normal AG metabolic acidosis; common in diabetes (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, heparin, TMP/SMX
Proton pump failure in distal tubule
explanation: RTA types: Type 1 (Distal RTA): urine pH >5.5 despite acidosis; failure of distal H+ secretion; causes: Sjögren's, SLE, amphotericin B → nephrolithiasis (calcium phosphate stones). Type 2 (Proximal RTA): failure of HCO3- reabsorption in PCT; urine pH <5.5 during severe acidosis; causes: Fanconi syndrome, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Type 4 (Hypoaldosteronism/resistance): most common type; hyperkalemia, normal anion gap acidosis. Type 3 (rare) = carbonic anhydrase II deficiency.

subject: Physiology
stem: In the kidney, aquaporin-2 (AQP2) is found in which location?
options: Collecting duct principal cell apical membrane — ADH (V2 receptor → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates AQP2) → AQP2-containing vesicles traffic to apical membrane → ↑water permeability → water reabsorption (osmotic gradient into hyperosmotic medullary interstitium)
explanation: Aquaporins in the kidney: AQP1: PCT (apical + basolateral) and descending thin limb — constitutively expressed, ~60-65% of filtered water reabsorbed here. AQP2: collecting duct principal cell apical membrane — ADH-regulated (insertion from intracellular vesicles). AQP3 and AQP4: collecting duct principal cell basolateral membrane — constitutive, allow water exit into peritubular capillaries. Nephrogenic DI: AQP2 gene mutation or downregulation (from lithium, which enters via ENaC → accumulates in principal cells → inhibits AQP2 expression).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which molecule mediates the renal vasodilation response to renal ischemia (autoregulation)?
options: Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) and adenosine at low concentrations — vasodilate afferent arterioles to maintain GFR; NSAIDs block prostaglandin synthesis → lose renal vasodilatory prostaglandins → afferent arteriole constricts → ↓GFR → acute kidney injury (especially in already-compromised renal perfusion: heart failure, cirrhosis, CKD, elderly, dehydration)
explanation: Renal prostaglandins: vasodilatory prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) are produced locally in the kidney in response to ↓perfusion (low flow → activate COX-2 in macula densa, mesangium). They dilate afferent arterioles to maintain GFR under conditions of ↓renal blood flow. In healthy kidneys at rest, prostaglandins have little effect. But in states of ↓perfusion (CHF, cirrhosis, hypovolemia, CKD), prostaglandins become critical → NSAIDs → acute kidney injury. Selective COX-2 inhibitors carry same renal risk.

subject: Physiology
stem: The plasma glucose concentration at which glycosuria begins is approximately:
options: 180 mg/dL — this is the approximate renal threshold for glucose (Tm for glucose in the proximal tubule = ~320 mg/min, plasma Tm ≈ 180–200 mg/dL); above this, filtered load exceeds reabsorptive capacity → glucose appears in urine
explanation: Renal glucose handling: Filtered load (FL) = GFR × plasma [glucose] = 125 mL/min × 1 mg/mL = 125 mg/min (at normal glucose). Reabsorptive Tm = 320 mg/min (but splay occurs due to heterogeneity → threshold appears ~180 mg/dL). Above 180 mg/dL: FL exceeds Tm → glycosuria. In DM: blood glucose 200-300+ mg/dL → significant glycosuria → osmotic diuresis (polyuria, polydipsia). SGLT2 inhibitors lower the renal threshold to ~45-60 mg/dL → increase glycosuria even at lower blood glucose.

subject: Physiology
stem: The normal lifespan of a red blood cell is approximately:
options: 120 days (approximately 3–4 months) — RBCs are then phagocytosed by macrophages in the spleen, liver (Kupffer cells), and bone marrow (extravascular hemolysis); hemoglobin → heme + globin → heme → biliverdin (biliverdin reductase) → unconjugated bilirubin → liver → conjugated → bile
30 days (WBC lifespan varies greatly by type)
explanation: RBC lifespan 120 days: RBCs lack nucleus/mitochondria/ribosomes → cannot synthesize new proteins → accumulate oxidative damage → membrane stiffen → cleared in spleen. Normal RBC destruction: ~2 mL packed RBCs/hour destroyed = ~0.8% of total RBC mass/day. Hemoglobin catabolism: Hb → globin (amino acid recycled) + heme → biliverdin (biliverdin reductase) → unconjugated bilirubin (UCB, fat-soluble, bound to albumin in blood) → liver conjugation (UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, UGT1A1) → conjugated bilirubin → bile → urobilinogen → stercobilin (stool color) + urobilin (urine color).

subject: Physiology
stem: Sickle cell anemia: pathophysiology of vascular occlusion?
options: Osmotic fragility of RBCs causes lysis

HbS (β6 glutamic acid → valine) polymerizes when deoxygenated → distorts RBC into sickle shape → ↑viscosity, ↓deformability → vascular occlusion (vaso-occlusive crisis), hemolysis; HbS can be prevented from sickling by HbF (fetal hemoglobin) — hence hydroxyurea (↑HbF production) is used therapeutically
The RBCs clot within blood vessels via platelet aggregation
explanation: Sickle cell disease (SCD, HbSS): autosomal recessive. HbS: β6 Glu→Val mutation → hydrophobic valine on surface → deoxyHbS polymerizes (not oxy-HbS) → sickling. Vaso-occlusive crisis: pain (bones, abdomen), acute chest syndrome, stroke. Hemolytic anemia: ↑unconjugated bilirubin, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, Howell-Jolly bodies (functional asplenia from repeated splenic infarcts). HbF inhibits HbS polymerization. Hydroxyurea → ↑HbF + ↓WBC (anti-inflammatory). Stroke risk: hydroxyurea + chronic transfusion.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hepcidin: what is its role in iron homeostasis?
options: Stimulates iron absorption from the gut

Hepcidin (liver-derived antimicrobial peptide) binds ferroportin (the only iron exporter on enterocytes, macrophages, hepatocytes) → causes its internalization and degradation → ↓iron export → ↓serum iron; ↑hepcidin in: inflammation (IL-6 → hepcidin → anemia of chronic disease), iron overload; ↓hepcidin in: iron deficiency, anemia, hypoxia, erythropoiesis↑ (erythroferrone from erythroblasts suppresses hepcidin)
explanation: Hepcidin-ferroportin axis: key regulator of systemic iron homeostasis. High hepcidin → ferroportin internalized → iron trapped in enterocytes (excreted in stool as cells turn over), macrophages (can't recycle iron from RBC hemolysis), hepatocytes → ↓serum iron → ↓transferrin saturation. Anemia of chronic disease: ↑IL-6 (inflammation) → ↑hepcidin → iron sequestration in macrophages → low serum iron but normal/↑ferritin. Iron-deficiency anemia: ↑erythroferrone → ↓hepcidin → ↑ferroportin → ↑iron absorption.

subject: Physiology
stem: Polycythemia vera: what is the primary defect?
options: A myeloproliferative neoplasm caused by JAK2 V617F mutation (>95%) in a hematopoietic stem cell → constitutive (EPO-independent) activation of JAK2/STAT5 → unregulated proliferation of RBCs (and WBCs + platelets); serum EPO is LOW (distinguishes from secondary polycythemia where EPO is high)
explanation: Polycythemia vera (PV): JAK2 V617F gain-of-function mutation → JAK-STAT pathway constitutively activated → EPO-independent erythroid proliferation (also ↑WBC, ↑platelets — panmyelosis). Features: hyperviscosity (headache, plethora, pruritus after hot shower — histamine from basophils), thrombosis risk (Budd-Chiari, DVT, stroke), erythromelalgia (burning pain + warmth of feet — platelet-mediated). Low EPO. Treatment: phlebotomy, hydroxyurea, ruxolitinib (JAK2 inhibitor).

subject: Physiology
stem: Splenomegaly and hypersplenism: what are the typical blood count findings?
options: Pancytopenia (↓RBC — hemolytic anemia, ↓WBC, ↓platelets — thrombocytopenia) due to sequestration and destruction of blood cells by the enlarged spleen; reticulocytes are elevated (bone marrow compensates); requires correcting the underlying cause or splenectomy
