explanation: Hypersplenism: ↑splenic blood pooling and phagocytosis → traps 30-40% of circulating platelets (vs. normal 30%), destroys RBCs prematurely, sequesters WBCs. Pancytopenia with hyperplastic marrow. Causes of splenomegaly: portal hypertension (most common in India — cirrhosis, schistosomiasis), hematological (lymphoma, leukemia, myelofibrosis, hemolytic anemias), infections (EBV, malaria, leishmaniasis), storage disorders (Gaucher's disease). Splenectomy: removes hypersplenism but increases risk of encapsulated bacteria (Pneumococcus, H. influenzae, Meningococcus).

subject: Physiology
stem: During pregnancy, maternal cardiac output increases by approximately:
options: 30–50% by week 24 (SV ↑ ~25% and HR ↑ ~15–20 bpm; due to ↓SVR from progesterone + estrogen-induced vasodilation, and ↑blood volume → ↑venous return → ↑SV via Frank-Starling)
explanation: Cardiovascular changes in pregnancy: CO ↑30-50% (peaks at 24-28 weeks). HR ↑15-20 bpm. SV ↑25%. SVR ↓ (estrogen/progesterone → relaxin → vasodilation + uteroplacental circulation = low resistance). BP falls mid-pregnancy (↓SVR > ↑CO). Blood volume ↑40-50% (plasma 50% > RBC 30% → physiological hemodilution/dilutional anemia: Hb may fall to 11 g/dL). Aortocaval compression in supine position → ↓venous return → ↓CO (treat by left lateral decubitus position).

subject: Physiology
stem: The corpus luteum is maintained in early pregnancy by:
options: FSH and LH from the pituitary

hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the implanting blastocyst — acts on LH receptors of the corpus luteum → continues progesterone production → maintains the decidua (uterine lining) until the placenta can produce sufficient progesterone (placental rescue of the corpus luteum; luteoplacental shift at ~8–10 weeks gestation)
explanation: hCG timeline: detectable in maternal blood ~8 days after fertilization (implantation occurs ~6-7 days). hCG doubles every 48-72 hours in early pregnancy (used to monitor early pregnancy viability). Peaks at 8-10 weeks (~100,000 mIU/mL), then falls (as placenta takes over progesterone production → corpus luteum can regress). hCG also: (1) stimulates fetal testicular testosterone (masculinization), (2) may cause thyroid stimulation (structural similarity to TSH → gestational thyrotoxicosis in hyperemesis gravidarum).

subject: Physiology
stem: Puberty: the first sign in females is usually:
options: Breast development (thelarche) — typically at 8–13 years; sequence in females: thelarche → pubic hair (pubarche/adrenarche) → peak height velocity → menarche (last, ~2–3 years after thelarche, typically 10–16 years); due to increasing GnRH pulsatility → ↑FSH/LH → estrogen from developing follicles
explanation: Puberty onset: triggered by ↑hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility (kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate nucleus increase pulsatile GnRH). Tanner stages 1→5. Females (puberty: 8-13 years): Thelarche (breast) → Pubarche (pubic hair) → Peak height velocity → Menarche. Males (puberty: 9-14 years): Testicular enlargement (first sign, >4 mL volume or >2.5 cm) → Pubic hair → Growth spurt → Axillary hair → Voice change. Precocious puberty: <8 years in girls, <9 years in boys. Delayed: >13 girls, >14 boys.

subject: Physiology
stem: The LH surge in the menstrual cycle occurs at approximately which cycle day (in a 28-day cycle)?
options: Day 12–13, triggering ovulation approximately 36–40 hours later (Day 14); positive feedback from peak estrogen (≥200 pg/mL for ≥50 hours) on pituitary → massive LH surge
explanation: Menstrual cycle (28 days): Follicular phase (Days 1-14): FSH → recruits follicles → dominant follicle → increasing estrogen → negative feedback on FSH (remaining follicles atretic) → on day 12-13, sustained high estrogen → POSITIVE feedback on LH → LH surge → ovulation day 14. Luteal phase (Days 14-28): corpus luteum forms → progesterone + estrogen peak → negative feedback → FSH/LH suppressed → if no implantation → corpus luteum involutes (days 23-24) → P4/E2 fall → endometrial sloughing → menstruation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Oxytocin: which cells produce it and what are its physiological functions?
options: Adenohypophysis — stimulates labor and milk ejection

Paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and supraoptic nucleus (SON) of the hypothalamus — synthesized and transported to posterior pituitary → released by suckling (neuroendocrine reflex) and cervical distension (Ferguson reflex) → stimulates uterine contraction (during labor + postpartum) and milk ejection (myoepithelial cells of breast)
explanation: Oxytocin (OT): peptide hormone (9 aa) from hypothalamic PVN/SON neurons, stored and released from posterior pituitary. Functions: (1) Uterine contraction: ↑uterine OT receptors at term (estrogen induces); positive feedback during labor (cervical stretch → more OT → more contractions → Ferguson reflex); used clinically to induce/augment labor. (2) Milk ejection (let-down reflex): suckling → afferent to hypothalamus → OT release → myoepithelial cells of mammary alveoli contract → milk ejection. (3) CNS: social bonding, trust, pair bonding.

subject: Physiology
stem: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation applied to the bicarbonate buffer system is:
options: pH = 6.1 + log ([HCO3-] / 0.03 × PaCO2); where pKa of H2CO3/HCO3- = 6.1, and dissolved CO2 = 0.03 × PaCO2; shows that pH depends on the ratio of base (HCO3-) to acid (H2CO3 = 0.03 × PaCO2)
explanation: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log ([A-]/[HA]) = 6.1 + log ([HCO3-] / [H2CO3]). [H2CO3] = 0.03 × PaCO2 (CO2 solubility coefficient × PaCO2 in mmHg = ~1.2 mEq/L at PaCO2 40 mmHg). At pH 7.4: log([HCO3-]/1.2) = 7.4 - 6.1 = 1.3 → [HCO3-]/1.2 = 20 → [HCO3-] = 24 mEq/L. This 20:1 ratio of HCO3-:H2CO3 is the key (20:1 → pH 7.4). Regulation: kidneys adjust HCO3- (metabolic component); lungs adjust PaCO2 (respiratory component).

subject: Physiology
stem: Base excess (BE): what does it represent clinically?
options: The amount of strong acid or base needed to restore 1 liter of blood to pH 7.4 at 37°C and PaCO2 40 mmHg; BE = 0 ± 2 mEq/L (normal); negative BE (base deficit) = metabolic acidosis; positive BE = metabolic alkalosis; independent of respiratory component
explanation: Base excess (BE): derived parameter in ABG analysis. BE > +2 → metabolic alkalosis (excess base/HCO3-). BE < -2 (base deficit) → metabolic acidosis (e.g., BE = -10 = significant metabolic acidosis). Calculated by the Siggaard-Andersen equation from pH, PaCO2, and Hb. In severe metabolic acidosis (e.g., DKA), gives an idea of the degree of acid load. NOT affected by acute respiratory changes (unlike pH or HCO3-) → useful to identify pure metabolic component.

subject: Physiology
stem: Compensation in respiratory acidosis (chronic): what is the expected HCO3- rise?
options: 0.1 mEq/L per mmHg rise in PaCO2

For chronic respiratory acidosis: HCO3- rises ~3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2 (renal compensation, takes 3–5 days: increased H+ secretion → increased HCO3- reabsorption + new HCO3- generation); for acute respiratory acidosis: HCO3- rises only ~1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg (immediate buffering by ICF proteins)
HCO3- does not change in respiratory acidosis
explanation: Acid-base compensation rules: (1) Metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × [HCO3-] + 8 ± 2 (Winter's formula). (2) Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 rise = 0.7 × ΔHCO3- + 5 ± 2. (3) Acute respiratory acidosis: HCO3- rises 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑PaCO2. (4) Chronic respiratory acidosis: HCO3- rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑PaCO2. (5) Acute respiratory alkalosis: HCO3- falls 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓PaCO2. (6) Chronic respiratory alkalosis: HCO3- falls 5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓PaCO2. If measured HCO3- ≠ expected → mixed disorder.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the myogenic theory of autoregulation?
options: Intrinsic property of vascular smooth muscle to contract in response to increased intraluminal pressure (↑stretch → opens mechanosensitive channels → ↑[Ca2+]i → vasoconstriction) and relax in response to decreased pressure → keeps blood flow constant over a range of perfusion pressures (60–160 mmHg for the brain, 70–180 mmHg for the kidney)
explanation: Autoregulation mechanisms: (1) Myogenic (primary in brain, kidney, skeletal muscle): pressure-induced stretch → SM contraction → maintains constant flow. (2) Metabolic (primary in skeletal muscle, heart during exercise): ↑metabolic activity → ↑adenosine, CO2, K+, H+, ↓O2 → vasodilation. (3) Flow-induced dilation (endothelium-dependent): shear stress → eNOS → NO → vasodilation. Brain autoregulates between MAP 60-160 mmHg; kidneys 70-180 mmHg. Autoregulation lost in acute hypertension → hypertensive encephalopathy (breakthrough of autoregulation at MAP >160 mmHg).

subject: Physiology
stem: The P-wave duration is longer in left atrial enlargement. What condition causes this?
options: Mitral stenosis (MS) — impaired blood flow from LA to LV → pressure overload of the LA → left atrial hypertrophy/dilatation → ↑left atrial depolarization time → P wave broad and notched (bifid P, 'P mitrale', >120 ms in lead II, also positive-then-negative in V1); right atrial enlargement: 'P pulmonale' — tall peaked P >2.5 mm in lead II
explanation: LA enlargement ECG: P mitrale (broad, bifid/notched P wave in lead II, >120 ms; biphasic P in V1 with terminal negative portion >40 ms and >1 mm deep). Causes: MS (most common), mitral regurgitation, cardiomyopathy, hypertension. RA enlargement: P pulmonale (tall peaked P in II >2.5 mm, upright in V1). Causes: pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid stenosis, COPD. AF: no distinct P waves.

subject: Physiology
stem: Cardiac tamponade: which finding on echocardiography is diagnostic?
options: Right atrial collapse in late diastole and right ventricular collapse in early diastole (respiratory variation in filling — Doppler shows >25% respiratory variation in tricuspid inflow and >30% in mitral inflow); also swinging heart, dilated IVC with no respiratory collapse
explanation: Cardiac tamponade echo findings: (1) RA systolic collapse (late diastolic), (2) RV diastolic collapse (early diastole — due to high pericardial pressure exceeding low RV diastolic pressure), (3) IVC dilatation with <50% inspiratory collapse (elevated RA pressure), (4) Respiratory variation in valve inflow (Doppler): ↑tricuspid/↓mitral on inspiration (septum shifts left → ↓LV filling → ↓mitral inflow). Treatment: pericardiocentesis (needle aspiration, subxiphoid approach).

subject: Physiology
stem: Starling's law of the heart: the Frank-Starling mechanism is due to:
options: Increased sarcomere length (up to optimal ~2.2 μm) → optimal myosin-actin overlap → increased force of contraction; the mechanism relates to length-dependent activation of myofilaments (Ca2+ sensitivity of troponin C increases with stretch) rather than actual change in crossbridge number
explanation: Frank-Starling mechanism: within physiological range (EDV 130-170 mL), increasing preload (↑EDV → ↑sarcomere length) → ↑force development. Mechanism: NOT increased crossbridge formation (actin-myosin overlap). Rather: sarcomere stretch → ↑myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity (length-dependent activation) → stronger contraction at same [Ca2+]. Also: reduction in interfilament lattice spacing → ↑cross-bridge interaction probability. Clinical: ↑venous return (e.g., exercise, fluid bolus) → ↑EDV → ↑CO.

subject: Physiology
stem: The central venous pressure (CVP) is an estimate of:
options: Right atrial pressure (or right ventricular end-diastolic pressure when tricuspid valve is open) — measured via a catheter in the superior vena cava or right atrium; normal CVP = 0–8 cmH2O (0–6 mmHg); elevated in: right heart failure, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, fluid overload; low in: hypovolemia, vasodilation
explanation: CVP measurement: tip of central venous catheter in SVC/RA junction. Reflects RV preload. Limitations: does not reliably predict fluid responsiveness (especially in patients with poor cardiac function). PCWP (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure via Swan-Ganz, distal occlusion of PA branch) = estimates LVEDP (LA pressure). PCWP normal = 8-12 mmHg. Elevated PCWP (>18 mmHg) = cardiogenic pulmonary edema; normal PCWP + pulmonary edema = ARDS (noncardiogenic).

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the role of the 'cardiovascular center' in the medulla?
options: Contains the vasomotor center (cardiovascular regulatory center): rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) — tonic sympathetic activity to the heart and blood vessels; and cardioinhibitory center (nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor nucleus — vagal) — inhibitory to the heart; receives inputs from baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, hypothalamus, cortex
Only generates the heart's intrinsic rate
explanation: Medullary cardiovascular centers: (1) Vasomotor center (VMC, RVLM): tonic excitatory output to sympathetic preganglionic neurons (intermediolateral column of spinal cord) → ↑HR, ↑contractility, vasoconstriction. (2) Cardioinhibitory center (CIC, dorsal vagal nucleus + nucleus ambiguus): parasympathetic (vagal) output → ↓HR, ↓AV conduction. Baroreceptor reflex: ↑BP → ↑afferent from NTS → ↑CIC + ↓VMC → ↓HR + vasodilation. Chemoreceptor reflex: hypoxia → ↑SN (vasoconstriction) but also vagal bradycardia (diving reflex).

subject: Physiology
stem: Arterial pulse: what gives rise to the dicrotic notch?
options: Aortic valve closure — when ventricle relaxes, aortic pressure transiently exceeds aortic root pressure → aortic valve snaps shut → creates a secondary pressure wave seen as a notch on the descending limb of the arterial pressure tracing
explanation: Arterial pressure waveform: Upstroke = ejection of blood from LV. Peak = systolic BP. Downstroke = elastic recoil of aorta as blood flows peripherally. Dicrotic notch (incisura) = aortic valve closure (corresponds to S2); the notch marks the transition from systole to diastole. After the notch: diastolic pressure run-off as blood flows to peripheral circulation. Augmentation index (AI): ratio of reflected wave to pulse pressure — increased in arterial stiffness (aging, hypertension).

subject: Physiology
stem: If a patient's jugular venous pulse (JVP) shows abolition of the 'a' wave — what is the diagnosis?
options: Atrial fibrillation — no coordinated atrial contraction → no 'a' wave in JVP; also loss of 'P' waves on ECG
explanation: JVP 'a' wave: atrial contraction filling the RV just before tricuspid valve closes. Absent 'a' wave → no coordinated atrial contraction → atrial fibrillation. Giant 'a' waves: tricuspid stenosis (resistance to filling), pulmonary hypertension (↑RV pressure → ↑resistance to filling → forceful atrial contraction). Cannon 'a' waves: atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (as in complete heart block, VT with ventriculoatrial dissociation, nodal/junctional rhythm).

subject: Physiology
stem: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD): which physiological parameter is measured by the ankle-brachial index (ABI)?
options: Venous pressure at the ankle vs. arm

Systolic BP at the ankle divided by systolic BP in the arm (brachial artery); normal ABI ≥1.0; ABI 0.91–0.99 borderline; ABI ≤0.90 = PAD; ABI <0.40 = critical limb ischemia; reduced because atherosclerosis → stenosis → pressure drops distally
explanation: ABI = Ankle SBP / Brachial SBP. Normal: 1.0–1.3 (>1.3 = possibly calcified, non-compressible vessels → diabetics). Mild PAD: 0.70–0.90. Moderate: 0.40–0.70. Severe: <0.40 (critical limb ischemia, rest pain, ulcers, gangrene). Symptoms: intermittent claudication (calf pain with walking, relieved by rest → PAD of superficial femoral/popliteal artery). Risk factors: smoking, DM, dyslipidemia, hypertension. Measured with a Doppler probe.

subject: Physiology
stem: Control of breathing: which receptors respond to decreased PaO2 (hypoxia)?
options: Central chemoreceptors (medulla) — respond to CO2/H+ not hypoxia

Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid bodies (glomus cells, CN IX afferents) and aortic bodies (CN X afferents); they respond to ↓PaO2 (<60 mmHg), ↑PaCO2, ↑H+ (↓pH), and ↓blood flow; carotid bodies are the primary O2 sensors
explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies): Type I glomus cells (O2 sensors): ↓PO2 → inhibits K+ channels → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → dopamine/ACh release → afferent firing. Carotid body (primary in humans): responds to: ↓PaO2 (K channels, very sensitive below 60 mmHg), ↑PaCO2 (direct), ↑H+ (metabolic acidosis). Aortic body: less important for ventilatory drive. Both respond to ↓blood flow (e.g., CO poisoning, severe anemia — low O2 delivery even with normal PaO2 → sensors ↑firing).

subject: Physiology
stem: Apneustic breathing and Biot's breathing: which is associated with pontine damage?
options: Apneustic breathing (prolonged inspiration with brief expiration) — due to damage to the pneumotaxic center in the upper pons (parabrachial nucleus, Kölliker-Fuse nucleus) → apneustic center (lower pons) activity unopposed → sustained inspiratory apnea; seen in pontine strokes/infarcts and brainstem herniation
explanation: Respiratory pattern abnormalities: Cheyne-Stokes (waxing-waning crescendo-decrescendo): bilateral supratentorial lesions (stroke, CHF) or high altitude. Biot's/ataxic breathing: irregular, random breath size with apneic pauses → medullary damage (medullary injury, severe pontine damage). Apneustic: prolonged inspiratory hold → pneumotaxic center lesion. Kussmaul: deep, rapid (acidotic breathing — response to metabolic acidosis → try to blow off CO2). Central neurogenic hyperventilation: rapid deep breaths → midbrain-upper pons damage.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cells produce pulmonary surfactant and what is the marker of surfactant production?
options: Type I pneumocytes (flat, alveolar gas exchange cells)

Type II pneumocytes (cuboidal, produce and store surfactant in lamellar bodies; also progenitor cells that can regenerate Type I pneumocytes after injury); lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio (L/S ratio) >2.0 in amniotic fluid = fetal lung maturity
explanation: Type II pneumocytes: cuboidal cells at alveolar corners. Functions: (1) Produce surfactant (DPPC = dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylglycerol, SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D) stored in lamellar bodies → exocytosed into alveolar fluid. (2) Progenitor for Type I cells. L/S ratio: reaches 2.0 at ~34-36 weeks gestation → lung maturity marker. SP-B deficiency → fatal surfactant deficiency. Surfactant composition: ~40% DPPC (most surface-active), 25% PG, 10% other phospholipids, 5-10% surfactant proteins.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'work of breathing' is increased by all EXCEPT:
options: Reduced compliance (stiff lungs, as in pulmonary fibrosis)
Increased compliance (emphysema, actually reduces elastic work but may increase resistive work due to dynamic airway collapse)
Rapid breathing reducing anatomical dead space
explanation: Work of breathing: (1) Resistive work: overcome airway resistance (↑in COPD, asthma, bronchospasm). (2) Elastic work: overcome lung compliance (↑in fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary edema — stiff lungs require more pressure to inflate). In emphysema: ↑compliance (↓elastic work) but dynamic airway collapse (pursed-lip breathing to maintain positive airway pressure) → ↑resistive work. Rapid breathing: ↑resistive work; slow deep breathing: ↑elastic work. Patients choose a respiratory rate that minimizes total work of breathing.

subject: Physiology
stem: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is transported in blood primarily as:
options: Bicarbonate (HCO3-): ~70–80% of CO2 is converted to HCO3- in RBCs (carbonic anhydrase: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-; HCO3- exits into plasma via Cl-/HCO3- exchanger/Band 3 — 'chloride shift'); also ~20% as carbamino compounds (bound to Hb as HbCO2); ~7% dissolved
explanation: CO2 transport: (1) Dissolved (7%): minor. (2) Bicarbonate (70-80%): CO2 enters RBC → CA (carbonic anhydrase II) → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-. H+ buffered by Hb (deoxyHb better buffer — Haldane effect: deoxyHb has more buffering capacity). HCO3- leaves RBC via Band 3 (AE1) antiporter (in exchange for Cl- entering — chloride shift). (3) Carbamino (20%): CO2 binds N-terminal amino groups of Hb → carbamates (preferentially to deoxyHb — also Haldane effect → deoxygenation at tissues promotes CO2 loading). All three release CO2 in the lung.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypoxic vasoconstriction in the pulmonary circulation is mediated at the cellular level by:
options: Inhibition of voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels in pulmonary arterial smooth muscle → membrane depolarization → opening of L-type Ca2+ channels → ↑[Ca2+]i → pulmonary vasoconstriction; triggered by alveolar hypoxia (O2 tension sensed by Kv channels in pulmonary VSMC, mechanism may also involve mitochondrial ROS)
explanation: HPV mechanism: unique to pulmonary circulation (systemic circulation vasodilates in hypoxia). Pulmonary VSMC: ↓PO2 → inhibits Kv channels (and possibly mitochondrial ETC changes) → ↑[K+]i → membrane depolarization → opens L-type Ca2+ channels → ↑[Ca2+]i → smooth muscle contraction → HPV. Also: ↓K+ channel activity → ↑ROS (from mitochondria) → Rho-kinase → ↑MLCK/↓MLCP → vasoconstriction. Drugs that inhibit HPV: inhaled anesthetics (halothane, isoflurane), calcium channel blockers, nitrates.

subject: Physiology
stem: Motor unit: what is the 'size principle' (Henneman's size principle)?
options: Larger motor units are always recruited first

Smaller motor units (slow-twitch, Type I, with small soma and slow-firing motoneurons) are recruited first at low force levels; as force requirement increases, larger motor units (fast-twitch, Type IIA, then IIB/IIX) are recruited progressively — because larger alpha-motoneurons have a higher recruitment threshold
Fast-twitch fibers are always recruited first for any movement
explanation: Henneman's size principle (1957): motor units recruited in order of motoneuron size (smallest → largest as force needed increases). Small motoneurons (low threshold, slow-firing) → innervate slow-twitch (Type I) fibers → fatigue-resistant → recruited for low-intensity sustained activities (posture). Larger motoneurons (high threshold, fast-firing) → innervate fast-twitch (Type II) fibers → powerful, fast, easily fatigued → recruited for high-intensity activities (jumping, sprinting). Exceptions: fast voluntary ballistic movements may circumvent strict size principle.

subject: Physiology
stem: Muscle fasciculation vs. fibrillation: what is the key clinical difference?
options: Both are only visible on EMG, not clinically

Fasciculations are visible under the skin (spontaneous discharges of WHOLE motor units → brief visible twitches) — seen in LMN disease, ALS, benign fasciculations. Fibrillations are NOT visible to the naked eye (spontaneous discharges of individual muscle fibers after denervation → too small to see, only on EMG — fine twitching of denervated fibers)
Fasciculations occur only in UMN disease
Fibrillations are visible as large contractions
explanation: EMG findings: Fibrillation potentials: spontaneous discharges of single denervated muscle fibers (2–3 weeks after nerve damage → fibers lose motor contact → ↑ACh receptor sensitivity → spontaneous activity). Not visible clinically. Positive sharp waves: similar to fibrillations. Fasciculation potentials: spontaneous discharge of entire motor units (visible as skin twitches). Seen in: ALS (both UMN + LMN signs + fasciculations), benign fasciculation syndrome, electrolyte abnormalities.

subject: Physiology
stem: Duchenne muscular dystrophy: which protein is absent?
options: Dystrophin — a cytoskeletal protein linking F-actin inside the muscle cell to laminin in the extracellular matrix via the dystrophin-associated protein complex (DAPC); absence → membranes fragile → Ca2+ influx → muscle fiber necrosis → progressive weakness, pseudohypertrophy of calves (fat + fibrosis), Gowers' sign
explanation: Duchenne MD: X-linked recessive, DMD gene (Xp21, largest gene in the human genome). Dystrophin protein: sub-sarcolemmal, N-terminal binds F-actin, C-terminal binds β-dystroglycan → extracellular via α-dystroglycan → laminin in BM. Without dystrophin → mechanical instability of sarcolemma → repeated contraction-induced injury → Ca2+ overload → proteolysis → necrosis. CK massively elevated (10,000-50,000 IU/L). Becker MD: truncated but partially functional dystrophin → milder, later onset.

subject: Physiology
stem: The thalamus is called the 'gateway to the cortex.' Which thalamic nucleus relays sensory information from the body?
options: Ventroposterolateral (VPL) nucleus — relays somatosensory information from the body (DCML: touch/proprioception, spinothalamic: pain/temperature); the VPM (ventroposteromedial) nucleus relays sensory information from the face (CN V and taste)
explanation: Thalamic nuclei and projections: VPL → body somatosensation (S1, S2). VPM → face sensation + taste (S1, insula). LGN (lateral geniculate nucleus) → primary visual cortex (V1, calcarine sulcus). MGN (medial geniculate nucleus) → primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus, A1). VA/VL (ventral anterior/lateral) → motor (receives from BG and cerebellum → motor cortex). Mediodorsal → prefrontal cortex (cognition, emotion). Anterior → cingulate gyrus (Papez circuit). Pulvinar → parietal/temporal/occipital association (higher visual/multisensory).

subject: Physiology
stem: Long-term potentiation (LTP): which receptor is crucial?
options: NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor — at rest, Mg2+ blocks the NMDA channel (even when glutamate is bound); strong synaptic activation activates AMPA receptors → depolarization → relieves Mg2+ block → NMDA channel opens → Ca2+ influx → activates kinases (CaMKII, PKA, PKC) → AMPA receptor phosphorylation + more AMPA receptors trafficked to synapse → ↑synaptic strength (LTP)
explanation: LTP at hippocampal Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapse (Bliss and Lømo, 1973): repeated high-frequency stimulation → glutamate release → AMPA receptor activation → membrane depolarization → removes Mg2+ block from NMDA receptor (voltage AND ligand gated) → Ca2+ + Na+ influx → Ca2+ activates CaMKII → (1) phosphorylates existing AMPA receptors → ↑conductance, (2) promotes AMPA receptor insertion → ↑synaptic AMPARs. Early LTP (E-LTP): hours, no new protein. Late LTP (L-LTP): days/weeks, requires protein synthesis, CREB, BDNF. LTP = cellular basis of memory.

subject: Physiology
stem: The limbic system: which structure is critical for the formation of new declarative memories?
options: Hippocampus — specifically the CA1-CA3 regions and the dentate gyrus; essential for forming new episodic and semantic (declarative/explicit) memories; damage → anterograde amnesia (inability to form NEW memories, retrograde usually spared for older memories)
explanation: Hippocampus and memory: Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate gyrus → entorhinal cortex → hippocampus. Bilateral hippocampal damage (e.g., H.M. — bilateral temporal lobectomy): profound anterograde amnesia (cannot form new declarative memories), relatively preserved procedural (implicit) memory (basal ganglia/cerebellum, not hippocampus-dependent). Korsakoff's syndrome (thiamine deficiency): bilateral mammillary body lesions → anterograde + retrograde amnesia + confabulation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Phantom limb pain is thought to arise from:
options: Pain signals from peripheral nerves in the stump only

Cortical reorganization: after limb amputation, the somatotopic representation in S1 is invaded by adjacent body areas → abnormal neural activity in the cortical area previously representing the lost limb → perceived as pain or sensation from the absent limb; may also involve central sensitization in the spinal dorsal horn
Ectopic discharge in the stump neuromas only
explanation: Phantom limb: after amputation, the deafferented cortical area is taken over by surrounding regions (cortical plasticity/reorganization), particularly face and shoulder representations invading the arm/hand area. This reorganization correlates with phantom limb pain intensity. Treatment: mirror therapy (visual feedback of intact limb → desensitizes cortical reorganization), graded motor imagery, TENS, ketamine (NMDA antagonist, reduces central sensitization), gabapentin/pregabalin (reduces wind-up).

subject: Physiology
stem: Spinal cord injury: at which spinal level would injury produce quadriplegia (all four limbs)?
options: T10 — below the level for limb control

C4 or above — the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 — keeps the diaphragm alive) is affected at C3/C4 → ventilator dependence; all upper and lower limb function lost; injury at C5 = limited shoulder and elbow flexion; C7 = triceps, wrist extension; T1 = intrinsic hand muscles
S1 — affects only ankle plantar flexion
explanation: Spinal cord injury levels: C1-C3: complete ventilator dependence, quadriplegia. C3-C4: may breathe (diaphragm via phrenic), no arm function. C5: shoulder abduction, elbow flexion (biceps). C6: wrist extension (able to use tenodesis grip). C7: elbow extension (triceps, key for transfers). C8-T1: intrinsic hand muscles. Below T1: paraplegia (legs only). Dermatome landmarks: T4 = nipple, T10 = umbilicus, L4 = medial malleolus, S1 = lateral foot.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which enzyme converts androstenedione to testosterone and estrone to estradiol?
options: 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (17β-HSD) — reduces C17 ketone to C17 hydroxyl; androstenedione → testosterone (17β-HSD type 3 in testes); estrone → estradiol (17β-HSD type 1 in granulosa cells)
explanation: Steroid biosynthesis key enzymes: (1) CYP11A1 (P450scc): cholesterol → pregnenolone (rate-limiting, mitochondria, stimulated by ACTH/LH). (2) CYP17A1: 17α-hydroxylation (pregnenolone → 17-OH-pregnenolone, progesterone → 17-OH-progesterone) AND 17,20-lyase (17-OH-pregnenolone → DHEA; 17-OH-progesterone → androstenedione). (3) CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase): 17-OH-progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol; progesterone → 11-deoxycorticosterone. (4) CYP11B1: 11-deoxycortisol → cortisol. (5) CYP19A1 (aromatase): androstenedione/testosterone → estrone/estradiol.

subject: Physiology
stem: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH): the most common form is due to deficiency of which enzyme?
options: 21-hydroxylase (CYP21A2) — accounts for >90% of CAH cases; leads to: ↓cortisol (→ ↑ACTH → adrenal hyperplasia) + ↓aldosterone (severe/classic form: salt-wasting crisis in neonates) + ↑androgen precursors (17-OH-progesterone → shunted to androgen pathway → virilization of females, early puberty in males); 17-OH-progesterone is the diagnostic marker
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH: most common IEM of the adrenal. Autosomal recessive, CYP21A2 gene. Classic salt-wasting form (75%): ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone → hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, metabolic acidosis in neonate (adrenal crisis). ↑ACTH → adrenal hyperplasia. ↑androgen precursors → females: virilization (ambiguous genitalia at birth), males: early puberty. Newborn screen: 17-OH-progesterone. Treatment: hydrocortisone (replaces cortisol + suppresses ACTH) + fludrocortisone (for salt-wasting).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'secondary hypothyroidism' is distinguished from primary hypothyroidism by:
options: Low TSH (insufficient pituitary TSH despite low T4) in secondary hypothyroidism vs. high TSH (normal pituitary response to low T4) in primary hypothyroidism; secondary: pituitary or hypothalamic disease (TRH deficiency) → ↓TSH → ↓T4
explanation: Hypothyroidism: Primary (thyroid failure): ↓T4, ↑TSH (pituitary compensates by ↑TSH → sensitive early marker). Causes: Hashimoto's (anti-TPO + anti-Tg antibodies, most common), iodine deficiency, post-radioiodine, thyroidectomy. Secondary (pituitary failure): ↓T4, low or inappropriately normal TSH. Tertiary (hypothalamic): ↓TRH → ↓TSH → ↓T4. Subclinical hypothyroidism: ↑TSH, normal T4/T3.

subject: Physiology
stem: Growth hormone deficiency in adults: what are the cardinal features?
options: Reduced lean muscle mass, ↑fat mass (especially visceral adiposity), ↓bone mineral density, fatigue, impaired quality of life, impaired lipid profile (↑LDL, ↓HDL) — GH deficiency in adults is an underrecognized condition treated with recombinant GH
explanation: Adult GHD (acquired — pituitary tumors, radiation, TBI): ↓GH → ↓IGF-1 → loss of anabolic, lipolytic, and metabolic effects of GH/IGF-1. Features: ↑fat mass (truncal obesity), ↓lean mass, ↓bone density (↑fracture risk), dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, reduced exercise capacity, depression. Diagnosis: GH stimulation test (insulin tolerance test or GHRH-arginine → inadequate GH rise confirms GHD). Treatment: recombinant GH (improves body composition, bone density, quality of life, but NOT mortality if secondary malignancy risk managed).

subject: Physiology
stem: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS): at which step does ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) act?
options: Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II (ACE removes two C-terminal amino acids — 'dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase' — from Ang I [10 aa] → Ang II [8 aa]); ACE also degrades bradykinin (a vasodilator) → blocking ACE with ACE inhibitors → ↑bradykinin → cough (dry, nonproductive, side effect of ACEi)
explanation: RAAS steps: Liver → angiotensinogen (α2-globulin). Kidney JG cells → renin (secreted when ↓BP/↓NaCl/↑SNS). Renin cleaves angiotensinogen → Angiotensin I (10 aa, biologically inactive). Lung/endothelium: ACE (kininase II) removes 2 C-terminal amino acids → Ang II (8 aa, biologically active). Ang II: AT1R (Gq): vasoconstriction, ↑aldosterone (adrenal zona glomerulosa), ↑ADH release, ↑thirst, ↑SNS, ↑Na+/H+ exchanger (PCT), ↑ACTH, cardiac/vascular hypertrophy. AT2R: vasodilation, antiproliferative (largely counterbalances AT1R).

subject: Physiology
stem: What is 'oncotic pressure' and how does it affect fluid distribution?
options: The osmotic pressure exerted by proteins (mainly albumin in the plasma — ~28 mmHg COP; capillary oncotic pressure pulls fluid into capillaries) vs. interstitial fluid proteins (~3 mmHg); according to Starling forces: net filtration = Pc - Pi - πc + πi [capillary hydrostatic pressure - interstitial hydrostatic pressure - plasma oncotic + interstitial oncotic]
explanation: Starling equation for capillary fluid exchange: Jv = Lp × [(Pc − Pi) − σ(πc − πi)]. Pc = capillary hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid OUT). Pi = interstitial hydrostatic pressure (resists filtration, usually slightly negative). πc = plasma colloid osmotic pressure (pulls fluid IN, ~28 mmHg). πi = interstitial oncotic pressure (pulls fluid out, ~3 mmHg). At arteriolar end: Pc (32) > πc (28) → net filtration (outward). At venular end: Pc (17) < πc (28) → net reabsorption. Edema: ↑Pc (CHF), ↓πc (hypoalbuminemia), ↑capillary permeability (inflammation), blocked lymphatics.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which diuretic is used to treat nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (NDI)?
options: Thiazide diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide) — paradoxically reduce urine volume in NDI; mechanism: block NCC in early DCT → Na+ depletion → ↑PCT Na+ reabsorption → ↓fluid delivery to collecting duct → ↓urine volume despite lack of ADH response; amiloride also used (blocks ENaC in CCD — especially for lithium-induced NDI since Li+ enters through ENaC)
ADH (DDAVP) — ineffective since receptors are resistant
explanation: NDI treatment: (1) Remove precipitant (e.g., lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia). (2) Low salt + low protein diet (↓solute load → ↓osmotic diuresis). (3) Thiazide diuretic: ↓ECF volume (Na+ depletion) → ↑PCT reabsorption (SGLT-1, NHE-3) → ↓water delivery to collecting duct → ↓urinary output by ~50%. (4) Amiloride (for lithium-induced NDI): Li+ enters principal cells through ENaC → blocks KATP and inhibits AQP2; amiloride blocks ENaC → reduces Li+ uptake into cells → restores AQP2 regulation. (5) NSAIDs (indomethacin): reduce prostaglandin-mediated inhibition of collecting duct AQP2.

subject: Physiology
stem: Normal urinalysis: what does the presence of nitrites in urine indicate?
options: Gram-negative bacteriuria (most E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus) — these bacteria contain nitrate reductase → convert urinary nitrates to nitrites; a positive dipstick nitrite + positive leukocyte esterase (from WBCs) = highly suggestive of UTI; false-negative: short dwell time (<4h), low dietary nitrate, Gram-positive organisms, Pseudomonas
explanation: Urinalysis dipstick: Nitrites: reduced from dietary nitrates by Gram-negative bacteria → suggests bacteriuria. Leukocyte esterase: from WBCs (pyuria) → suggests inflammation/infection. Both positive → sensitivity ~75%, specificity ~80% for UTI. Protein: detects albumin (not Bence Jones protein, which is detected by urine protein electrophoresis). Glucose: appears when plasma glucose >180 mg/dL. Blood: detects Hb and myoglobin (can be hematuria or hemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria). Ketones: acetoacetate detected (not β-hydroxybutyrate — the predominant ketone in DKA).

subject: Physiology
stem: B lymphocyte activation: which co-stimulatory molecule is essential?
options: CD40-CD40L (CD154) interaction between B cells (CD40) and T helper cells (CD40L/CD154) — essential for isotype class switching, germinal center formation, somatic hypermutation (affinity maturation), and memory B cell generation; blocking CD40L (lupus, transplant rejection)
BCR alone is sufficient for full activation
explanation: B cell activation: T-dependent antigen: (1) BCR binds antigen (signal 1) + CD19/CD21 co-receptor → activates B cell. (2) B cell presents antigen (MHC II) to Th2 cell → Th2 activates → upregulates CD40L → binds B cell CD40 (signal 2) + cytokines (IL-4, IL-21). CD40-CD40L: essential for class switch recombination (IgM → IgG, IgA, IgE), somatic hypermutation (V-region mutations → ↑affinity), memory formation. T-independent antigens (e.g., polysaccharides): activate B cells without T help → only IgM, no memory → reason why capsular vaccines are conjugated to protein carriers.

subject: Physiology
stem: The complement system: which pathway is activated by C-reactive protein (CRP)?
options: Lectin pathway — not CRP. CRP activates the CLASSICAL pathway (not CRP-specific lectin). CRP (acute phase reactant, binds phosphocholine on bacterial surfaces) → binds C1q → activates classical pathway → C1r → C1s → C4 → C2 → C3 convertase (C4b2a) → C3b opsonization + MAC
Classical pathway — antibody complex activates C1q; CRP also activates C1q
explanation: Complement pathways: (1) Classical: IgG/IgM-Ag complex → C1q binding → C1r → C1s → C4 + C2 → C3 convertase (C4b2a) → C3b. Also: CRP/serum amyloid P → C1q → classical pathway. (2) Lectin: MBL/ficolins (pattern recognition, bind mannose/fucose on pathogens) → MASP1/2 → cleave C4/C2 → C3 convertase. (3) Alternative: constitutively active C3 hydrolysis → C3b binds surface → Factor B + D → C3bBb (C3 convertase) → amplification loop. All converge at C3 → C3b (opsonization) → C5 → C5a (anaphylatoxin, chemotaxis) → MAC (C5b-9).

subject: Physiology
stem: Anaphylaxis: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releases which mediators?
options: Preformed (immediate): histamine (H1R → vasodilation + ↑vascular permeability; H1R bronchoconstriction), tryptase (marker of mast cell activation), heparin. Newly synthesized (minutes): leukotrienes (LTC4/D4/E4, SRS-A — slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis, potent bronchospasm + mucus), prostaglandin D2, PAF. Late phase (cytokines, IL-4, TNF-α)
explanation: Anaphylaxis mechanism: First exposure: antigen → IgE production → IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells/basophils (sensitization, no symptoms). Second exposure: antigen crosslinks IgE-FcεRI → mast cell degranulation → preformed granule contents (histamine, heparin, tryptase, chymase) → and newly synthesized (leukotrienes, PGD2, PAF). Systemic effects: urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension (vasodilation + ↑permeability → distributive shock). Treatment: epinephrine (IM, alpha1 → vasoconstriction + beta2 → bronchodilation, first-line).

subject: Physiology
stem: Glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis) occurs mainly in which tissues?
options: Liver (stores ~100 g, regulated by glucagon/insulin) and skeletal muscle (stores ~400 g, regulated by insulin/exercise) — both use glycogen synthase (GS, activated by insulin via PP1, inhibited by glucagon/epinephrine via cAMP/PKA-mediated phosphorylation) to synthesize glycogen from UDP-glucose
explanation: Glycogen metabolism: Synthesis (glycogenesis): glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase/glucokinase) → glucose-1-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase) → UDP-glucose (UGP) → added to glycogen chain by glycogen synthase (α-1,4-glycosidic bonds; branching enzyme makes α-1,6 branches). Liver glycogen: released as glucose to the blood (glucose-6-phosphatase present). Muscle glycogen: cannot release glucose to blood (no G6Pase) → provides local energy only. Glycogen storage diseases: Pompe (GSD II, acid maltase/GAA deficiency → lysosomal accumulation → cardiomegaly + myopathy).

subject: Physiology
stem: Lipid metabolism: which enzyme is rate-limiting for de novo fatty acid synthesis?
options: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) — converts acetyl-CoA + CO2 → malonyl-CoA (the first committed step in FA synthesis); requires biotin; activated by insulin (dephosphorylation by PP2A) and citrate; inhibited by glucagon/epinephrine (via AMPK phosphorylation) and by long-chain fatty acyl-CoA (feedback inhibition)
explanation: De novo lipogenesis: occurs mainly in liver and adipose tissue. Requires NADPH (from PPP + malic enzyme). Malonyl-CoA (from ACC) + acetyl-CoA → FAS complex → palmitate (C16:0) → extended. Insulin → activates ACC (dephosphorylation) + FAS → ↑lipogenesis. AMPK (energy sensor, activated by ↓ATP) → phosphorylates ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓FA synthesis + ↓inhibition of CPT-1 → ↑FA oxidation. Malonyl-CoA also inhibits CPT-1 (carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1) → prevents FA from entering mitochondria for β-oxidation (coordinate regulation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the first step of glycolysis (glucose phosphorylation)?
options: Hexokinase (all tissues, high affinity, low Km, saturated at normal blood glucose, inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate) or glucokinase (liver and pancreatic β-cells, low affinity, high Km ~10 mM, NOT inhibited by G6P, acts proportionally to blood glucose — 'glucose sensor')
explanation: Glucose phosphorylation: Hexokinase (I-III): Km = 0.1 mM, ubiquitous, product-inhibited by G6P, always active. Glucokinase (hexokinase IV): Km = 10 mM, liver and pancreatic β-cells, NOT product-inhibited, sigmoidal kinetics, GKRP (regulatory protein) sequesters in nucleus when fasting → cytosol during high glucose. Glucokinase maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY2): heterozygous glucokinase mutation → mild hyperglycemia (higher glucose threshold to trigger insulin secretion and hepatic glycogen storage).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which enzyme is rate-limiting for cholesterol synthesis?
options: HMG-CoA reductase — converts HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA) to mevalonate; this is the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis; statins (lovastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin) competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓hepatic cholesterol synthesis → ↑LDL receptor expression → ↑LDL clearance from blood → ↓LDL cholesterol
explanation: Cholesterol synthesis (mevalonate pathway): Acetyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase) → mevalonate (HMG-CoA reductase, rate-limiting, statin target) → IPP → geranyl-PP → farnesyl-PP (also used for: dolichol, ubiquinone, farnesylation of Ras/Ras-related GTPases — statins may affect these too) → squalene → lanosterol → cholesterol. HMG-CoA reductase regulated by: ↓cholesterol → ↑SREBP → ↑HMG-CoA reductase expression; insulin → ↑; glucagon → ↓.

subject: Physiology
stem: Olfaction: the olfactory receptor neurons project where?
options: Olfactory bulb (mitral cells → lateral olfactory stria) → primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex, anterior olfactory nucleus, amygdala, entorhinal cortex) WITHOUT passing through the thalamus first (unique among senses — all other sensory modalities relay through the thalamus)
explanation: Olfactory pathway: Bipolar olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) in the nasal olfactory epithelium → fila olfactoria (axons pass through cribriform plate of ethmoid bone — fractures here → anosmia + CSF rhinorrhoea) → olfactory bulb (glomeruli, mitral cells) → lateral olfactory tract → primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex, periamygdaloid area, entorhinal cortex). UNIQUE: no thalamic relay for conscious olfactory perception (some fibers reach thalamus → orbitofrontal cortex for consciously processed olfaction). Anosmia: COVID-19 (olfactory epithelium/bulb), cribriform plate fracture, olfactory groove meningioma, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's (early sign).

subject: Physiology
stem: Taste (gustation): which ion channel mechanism mediates the perception of salty taste?
options: Direct Na+ entry through apical amiloride-sensitive epithelial Na+ channels (ENaC) in taste receptor cells → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → neurotransmitter release → salty taste; blocked by amiloride (diuretic that blocks ENaC)
All tastes use the same mechanism
explanation: Taste transduction mechanisms: Salty: Na+ → ENaC → depolarizes taste cell. Sour: H+ → blocks K+ channels (or enters through HCN channels) → depolarization; also H+-gated ion channels (PKD2L1). Sweet, Bitter, Umami: GPCRs (T1R family for sweet/umami; T2R family for bitter) → Gαq or Gα-gustducin → PLC → IP3 → Ca2+ from ER → depolarization → ATP release → purinergic receptors on afferent nerves. Cranial nerves: anterior 2/3 tongue → chorda tympani (CN VII); posterior 1/3 → CN IX; epiglottis/pharynx → CN X.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which receptor adapts rapidly (within milliseconds) and codes for vibration and texture?
options: Meissner's corpuscles (in the dermal papillae, rapid adaptation, vibration 20–50 Hz, flutter, light touch) and Pacinian corpuscles (deep in dermis/subcutis, extremely rapid adaptation, vibration 200–300 Hz, pressure change, texture)
explanation: Cutaneous mechanoreceptors: Rapidly adapting (RA): Meissner's corpuscles (RA-1, fingertips, dermis, 20-50 Hz vibration, light touch, object slip detection) and Pacinian corpuscles (RA-2, 200-300 Hz vibration, deep pressure, texture via tools). Slowly adapting (SA): Merkel's discs (SA-1, fine spatial discrimination, 2-point discrimination, sustained pressure) and Ruffini endings (SA-2, skin stretch, finger position). Fingertip: highest density of Merkel + Meissner → finest discrimination.

subject: Physiology
stem: Estrogen: which tissues are affected by the loss of estrogen at menopause?
options: Multiple target tissues: bone (↓estrogen → ↑osteoclast activity → ↓bone density → osteoporosis), cardiovascular (↑LDL, ↓HDL, loss of vasculoprotective NO effect), urogenital (vaginal atrophy, stress urinary incontinence, ↑UTI), CNS (hot flushes/vasomotor symptoms — mediated by hypothalamic GnRH/NK neurons reacting to withdrawn estrogen-mediated inhibition)
explanation: Menopause (average age 51 years): FSH >40 IU/L (most sensitive marker). Loss of follicles → ↓inhibin → ↑FSH; ↓estrogen → ↑LH/FSH (loss of negative feedback). Vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes): ↑GnRH pulse frequency from KNDy neurons (kisspeptin/NKB/dynorphin) → NKB acts on nucleus in preoptic area → dysregulation of thermoregulatory set point → ↑cutaneous vasodilation and sweating. Osteoporosis: most rapid bone loss in first 5 years post-menopause. HRT: effective for symptoms; risk-benefit depends on type, route, duration, and individual risk.

subject: Physiology
stem: Testicular torsion: why does the testis become ischemic?
options: The spermatic cord twists → obstructs venous drainage first (low pressure veins more susceptible to compression) → venous congestion → edema → then arterial occlusion → testicular ischemia → necrosis; time-sensitive: salvage rate ~100% <6h, ~50% at 12h, <10% at 24h
explanation: Testicular torsion: twisting of the spermatic cord. Most common in adolescents (bell-clapper deformity = high insertion of tunica vaginalis → testis swings freely). Sudden onset severe scrotal pain, nausea/vomiting, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex. Venous congestion precedes arterial occlusion. Radiology: Doppler ultrasound (↓blood flow); don't delay imaging if diagnosis certain → surgery. Treatment: manual detorsion (rotate like opening a book) + urgent surgical fixation of both testes (bilateral orchidopexy since contralateral may have same deformity).

subject: Physiology
stem: The ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) is elevated in inflammation because:
options: Acute phase proteins (fibrinogen, immunoglobulins) cause RBCs to form 'rouleaux' (stacked-coin aggregates) → increased settling rate; ESR normal: males <15 mm/hr, females <20 mm/hr (higher with age); highly non-specific; elevated in: pregnancy, anemia, infections, autoimmune, malignancy
explanation: ESR (Westergren method): RBCs normally have a net negative charge (zeta potential) → repel each other → slow settling. Inflammation → ↑fibrinogen (acute phase protein) → neutralizes zeta potential → rouleaux → ↑sedimentation rate. ESR elevated in: chronic infections (TB), inflammatory arthritis (RA, GCA — giant cell arteritis, very high ESR >100), multiple myeloma (abnormal proteins), malignancy, pregnancy. NOT a useful test in acute illness (slow to rise and fall). CRP rises and falls faster → preferred for acute monitoring.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hemolytic anemia: which finding distinguishes intravascular from extravascular hemolysis?
options: Jaundice — both types have elevated bilirubin

Hemoglobinuria (dark urine, positive dipstick blood without RBCs) is specific for INTRAVASCULAR hemolysis (RBCs lysed within blood vessels → free Hb in plasma → exceeds haptoglobin binding capacity → free Hb filtered by kidney → Hb in urine); extravascular hemolysis (in macrophages): jaundice (unconjugated bilirubin) without hemoglobinuria; both: ↓haptoglobin, ↑LDH, ↑unconjugated bilirubin
explanation: Intravascular hemolysis: mechanical (TTP-HUS, MAHA — microangiopathic HA, prosthetic valve), immune (transfusion reaction, PNH, ABO incompatibility), osmotic, toxins. Free Hb in plasma → binds haptoglobin (saturated, ↓haptoglobin → ↑Hb → hemoglobinemia) → filtered by kidney → hemoglobinuria (dipstick positive for blood, no RBCs on microscopy) → Hb absorbed by tubular cells → hemosiderin in urine (Rous test positive). Also: methemalbuminemia, ↑LDH. Extravascular: spleen/liver macrophages. Jaundice prominent. No hemoglobinuria.

subject: Physiology
stem: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): which type of anemia has a HIGH MCV (macrocytic)?
options: Megaloblastic anemia (vitamin B12 or folate deficiency) and non-megaloblastic macrocytosis (liver disease, hypothyroidism, alcoholism, hemolytic anemia with reticulocytosis, drugs: methotrexate, hydroxyurea, zidovudine); MCV >100 fL = macrocytic
explanation: MCV classification: Microcytic (<80 fL): iron deficiency (most common worldwide), thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia, lead poisoning ('TAILS'). Normocytic (80-100 fL): acute blood loss, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, anemia of chronic disease, CKD/EPO deficiency, hypothyroidism (can be either). Macrocytic (>100 fL): megaloblastic (B12/folate deficiency — hypersegmented neutrophils, oval macrocytes), non-megaloblastic (liver disease, alcohol, drugs, reticulocytosis). B12 deficiency also: subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (dorsal columns + lateral CSTs).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'sympathetic chain' ganglia: where are they located?
options: Paravertebral chain ganglia (bilateral chains adjacent to the vertebral column, T1 to L2/L3 level — 'lateral chain ganglia'); preganglionic fibers from thoracolumbar (T1-L2) outflow synapse here; postsynaptic fibers travel to body wall, limbs, head and neck via the rami communicantes + peripheral nerves; also prevertebral ganglia (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, aorticorenal — for abdominal viscera)
explanation: Autonomic ganglion locations: Sympathetic: (1) Paravertebral ganglia (sympathetic chain): bilateral, T1-L2 → 22 pairs. Superior cervical ganglion (SCG): supplies head, neck (pupil dilation, salivary glands, vasomotor). (2) Prevertebral (collateral) ganglia: celiac ganglion (T5-T12 preganglionic → gut, liver, pancreas, spleen), superior mesenteric (T5-T12 → small intestine, right colon), inferior mesenteric (L1-L2 → left colon, rectum, bladder, genitalia). Parasympathetic ganglia: near or within the target organs (ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular, otic, intramural ganglia in gut/heart/lungs).

subject: Physiology
stem: The pain of angina pectoris is typically felt in the chest and left arm. This is an example of:
options: Referred pain: cardiac pain afferents (C fibers from the heart, visceral) travel with sympathetic fibers (upper 4 thoracic sympathetic segments, T1-T4) → enter the same spinal cord levels as somatic afferents from the left chest wall and left arm → brain misinterprets the source as coming from the body wall (convergence-projection theory of referred pain)
explanation: Referred pain (Roth's convergence-projection theory): visceral afferents converge onto the same dorsal horn neurons as somatic afferents from dermatomal skin areas → brain attributes the pain to the skin/body wall (where it is accustomed to receiving signals from that spinal segment). Other examples: appendicitis → periumbilical then RIF; renal colic → flank to groin (L1 dermatome); diaphragm irritation (pericarditis, ruptured spleen, subphrenic abscess) → C3-C5 dermatome → shoulder tip pain. Heart: T1-T4 → left chest + left arm + jaw.

subject: Physiology
stem: Functional residual capacity (FRC) decreases when:
options: Supine position, obesity, pregnancy, anesthesia (general) — these increase abdominal pressure or reduce chest wall outward recoil → shift the equilibrium point inward → ↓FRC; also reduced in pulmonary fibrosis (↓lung compliance → shifts equilibrium inward), ARDS, atelectasis, pneumothorax
explanation: FRC = equilibrium lung volume where lung elastic inward recoil = chest wall elastic outward recoil. Reduced FRC: (1) Supine → abdomen pushes diaphragm cephalad → ↓FRC by ~15-20%. (2) Obesity → ↑abdominal pressure. (3) Pregnancy → ↑uterus → ↑abdominal pressure. (4) General anesthesia (supine + muscle relaxants) → loss of chest wall muscle tone → ↓FRC → atelectasis risk. (5) Pulmonary fibrosis → stiff lungs → reduced inward recoil balance point. Increased FRC: COPD/emphysema (air trapping), asthma (bronchospasm + air trapping).

subject: Physiology
stem: What is physiological dead space in the context of mechanical ventilation?
options: VD (dead space) = anatomical dead space (conducting airways, ~150 mL) + alveolar dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli); during mechanical ventilation with high PEEP and/or hemodynamic compromise → ↑alveolar dead space (West's Zone 1 increases) → need to increase minute ventilation to maintain normocarbia; VD/VT ratio normally 0.3; >0.5 suggests significant dead space pathology
The volume of gas between the ETT and the carina
explanation: Dead space in ventilated patients: Total VD/VT measured by Bohr equation (using PaCO2 and PETCO2). In ARDS: ↑physiological dead space (damaged capillaries → ventilated alveoli unperfused → ↑alveolar dead space). High VD/VT (>0.6) → patient needs ↑RR or ↑TV to maintain PaCO2 (more difficult to wean from ventilator). PE: classic cause of acute ↑dead space (↑VD/VT → ↑PETCO2/PaCO2 gradient, hypoxemia with low EtCO2). Normal spontaneous breathing VD/VT ≈ 0.3 (150/500 mL).

subject: Physiology
stem: The maximal oxygen consumption (VO2 max) is the best measure of:
options: Cardiorespiratory fitness — it reflects the maximum rate at which the heart, lungs, and muscles can take up and utilize oxygen during exercise; VO2 max = CO × C(a-v)O2; limited by: maximal CO (cardiac limitation in most people) + O2 extraction; trained athletes: VO2 max up to 70-85 mL/kg/min; sedentary: 30-40 mL/kg/min; declines with age (~1%/year from age 30)
explanation: VO2 max: gold standard for cardiorespiratory fitness. Fick: VO2 max = CO max × C(a-v)O2 max. Trained athletes: ↑CO max (↑SV primarily, max SV 150-200 mL vs. 70-90 mL sedentary), ↑skeletal muscle O2 extraction (↑mitochondrial density + capillary density + myoglobin → ↑C(a-v)O2). At VO2 max, O2 delivery is the limiting factor (in healthy subjects). Training adaptations: ↑SV (eccentric LVH, ↑EDV), ↑mitochondria density (aerobic), ↑lactate threshold. Predictors of survival in heart failure: VO2 max <10-12 mL/kg/min = poor prognosis.

subject: Physiology
stem: Blood pressure regulation — short-term vs. long-term: which is the most important long-term regulator?
options: The kidney — through pressure natriuresis/diuresis (Guyton's theory): ↑BP → ↑renal blood flow → ↑urinary Na+ and water excretion → ↓blood volume → ↓CO → restores BP; this feedback loop has infinite gain for Na+ balance and is the ULTIMATE BP regulator
explanation: Guyton's pressure-natriuresis: the kidney resets blood volume in response to BP. At normal BP (MAP ~93 mmHg), urine output = intake. ↑BP → ↑renal perfusion → ↑GFR + ↓tubular reabsorption (pressure natriuresis, pressure diuresis) → ↑Na+ excretion → ↓ECF volume → ↓venous return → ↓CO → ↓BP back to set point. This is why only the kidney can produce sustained hypertension (shifting the pressure-natriuresis curve requires renal mechanisms — primary hyperaldosteronism, RAS, CKD all shift this curve right).

subject: Physiology
stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP): at which receptor does it act?
options: Guanylyl cyclase A (GC-A/NPRA receptor) — a transmembrane receptor with intrinsic guanylyl cyclase activity → ↑cGMP → PKG → smooth muscle relaxation (vasodilation) + inhibits ENaC in collecting duct + inhibits renin + inhibits aldosterone
explanation: ANP receptor (NPR-A/GC-A): natriuretic peptide receptor with intracellular guanylyl cyclase domain. Binding → intracellular domain dimerizes → ↑cGMP → PKG → (1) vasodilation (relaxes VSM), (2) inhibits ENaC-mediated Na+ reabsorption (distal nephron), (3) ↑GFR (afferent dilation + efferent constriction), (4) inhibits renin and aldosterone, (5) ↑capillary permeability → shifts fluid to interstitium → ↓plasma volume. BNP (from ventricles) acts on same receptor. cGMP also degraded by PDE5 (sildenafil blocks PDE5 → ↑cGMP → pulmonary vasodilation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Vasovagal syncope: what is the sequence of events?
options: Prolonged standing/emotional trigger → blood pooling in legs → ↓venous return → vigorous LV contraction on nearly empty ventricle → Bezold-Jarisch reflex → ↑vagal output → bradycardia + vasodilation → ↓BP → cerebral hypoperfusion → syncope (loss of consciousness for seconds)
explanation: Vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) syncope: most common cause of syncope. Triggers: prolonged standing, pain, emotion, medical procedures. Prodrome: nausea, diaphoresis, pallor, visual dimming. Mechanism: ↓venous return → Bezold-Jarisch activation → paradoxical vagotonia → bradycardia + vasodilation → ↓BP → loss of consciousness → usually self-resolving when supine (↑venous return). Tilt-table test: positive if reproduces syncope with HR drop and BP drop at 60–70° tilt. Treatment: sit/lie down, increase salt/fluid, fludrocortisone, β-blockers in some.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which part of the cardiac conduction system has the slowest conduction velocity?
options: The AV node (~0.05 m/s — slowest in the conduction system; provides the critical delay of ~0.1 second between atrial and ventricular contraction to ensure atria empty before ventricles contract)
explanation: Conduction velocities: SA node ~0.05 m/s → Atrial muscle ~0.3–1 m/s → AV node ~0.05 m/s (slowest, safety block, allows atria to complete contraction before ventricles contract) → Bundle of His ~1 m/s → Bundle branches ~2 m/s → Purkinje fibers ~2–4 m/s (fastest, ensures simultaneous ventricular activation from apex to base) → Ventricular muscle ~0.3–0.5 m/s. AV nodal delay is essential — it separates atrial and ventricular systole. Degree of AV block reflects AV node disease.

subject: Physiology
stem: Ventricular tachycardia (VT): what is the key ECG feature?
options: Wide complex (>120 ms, monomorphic or polymorphic QRS), rate >100 bpm (usually 100–250 bpm), AV dissociation (P waves dissociated from QRS — at a slower rate), and capture beats or fusion beats (pathognomonic of VT — proves the QRS is of ventricular origin)
explanation: VT criteria (Brugada algorithm helps differentiate from SVT with aberrancy): AV dissociation (P independent of QRS) = most specific for VT. Capture beats (normal narrow QRS when SA node 'captures' ventricle) and fusion beats (hybrid of sinus + ectopic = partial capture). QRS morphology: concordance (all positive or all negative in precordials), NW axis (no man's land: -90 to ±180°), QRS >160 ms. In clinical practice: any wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as VT unless proven otherwise. Pulseless VT: immediate defibrillation.

subject: Physiology
stem: The concept of 'receptive field': what is it?
options: The total area of the cerebral cortex dedicated to a sensory modality

The area of sensory space (e.g., skin area) within which a stimulus activates a given sensory neuron; smaller receptive fields (fingertips) allow fine spatial discrimination; lateral inhibition (surround inhibition) sharpens spatial contrast by inhibiting adjacent neurons via interneurons (center-excitation + surround-inhibition = 'Mexican hat' configuration in retina, somatosensory cortex)
The threshold intensity of a stimulus
explanation: Receptive fields: All sensory systems have neurons with specific receptive fields. Size: retinal ganglion cells at the fovea have tiny RFs (high acuity); peripheral retina = large RFs (low acuity). Two-point discrimination test: minimum distance at which 2 touch points are perceived as separate. Fingertips: 2–3 mm (small RFs, dense innervation). Back: 40–70 mm (large RFs). Two-point discrimination requires cortical magnification factor + small overlapping RFs. Lateral inhibition (through Renshaw cells, stellate cells) sharpens contrast.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the difference between Aα, Aβ, Aδ, and C nerve fibers?
options: Only Aα fibers carry sensory information

Aα (Ia/Ib, 70–120 m/s, large diameter, heavily myelinated): primary afferents from muscle spindles (Ia) and GTOs (Ib). Aβ (II, 30–70 m/s): touch, pressure, vibration. Aδ (III, 5–30 m/s): fast pain (sharp, localized), cold temperature. C fibers (IV, 0.5–2 m/s, unmyelinated): slow pain (burning, dull), warmth, itch
B fibers are the primary sensory fibers
explanation: Nerve fiber classification: A fibers (myelinated): Aα largest (motor + proprioception: Ia spindle, Ib GTO, alpha-motor neurons). Aβ: touch, vibration, pressure. Aγ: gamma motor neurons (spindle intrafusal fibers). Aδ: fast pain (well-localized, sharp — 'first pain'), cool temperature. B fibers: preganglionic autonomic. C fibers (unmyelinated): slow pain ('second pain', burning, aching), warmth, itch (pruritoceptors, specific C fibers expressing MrgprA3 activated by histamine, chloroquine). Local anesthetics: block Aδ and C first (pain) → Aβ (touch) → Aα (motor/proprioception) last.

subject: Physiology
stem: Synaptic transmission: what is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)?
options: Increased Cl- conductance → hyperpolarization → reduced firing

A graded depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane produced by a neurotransmitter (e.g., glutamate opening AMPA or NMDA receptors → Na+/K+ influx → net inward current → depolarizes membrane toward threshold); EPSPs from multiple synapses can summate spatially and temporally to reach threshold and trigger an AP
Removal of neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft
explanation: Synaptic integration: EPSPs (excitatory): glutamate → AMPA (Na+/K+), NMDA (Na+/K+/Ca2+), kainate → inward current → depolarization. IPSPs (inhibitory): GABA-A → Cl- inflow (hyperpolarization) or GABA-B → K+ outflow/↓Ca2+ (hyperpolarization). Temporal summation: rapid successive EPSPs from same synapse add up. Spatial summation: simultaneous EPSPs from different synapses add up. If EPSP + summation reaches threshold (~-55 mV at axon initial segment) → action potential is generated. IPSPs raise the threshold (harder to depolarize to -55 mV).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which neurotransmitter mediates the final common inhibitory pathway for sleep (GABAergic sleep-promoting neurons)?
options: GABA: sleep-promoting neurons in the ventrolateral preoptic area (VLPO) release GABA (and galanin) → inhibit wake-promoting neurons (tuberomammillary nucleus-histamine, locus coeruleus-NE, raphe-5HT, basal forebrain-ACh) → promote NREM sleep; 'flip-flop switch' model (Saper): VLPO and arousal systems mutually inhibit each other
explanation: Sleep regulation (flip-flop switch, Saper): Arousal side: tuberomammillary nucleus (TMN, histamine), locus coeruleus (NE), dorsal raphe (5-HT), basal forebrain (ACh) → activate cortex → wakefulness. Sleep side: VLPO neurons (GABA + galanin) → inhibit arousal nuclei. Each side inhibits the other (bistable switch). Orexin/Hypocretin (lateral hypothalamus): stabilizes the switch on the wake side → prevents inappropriate transitions to sleep. Narcolepsy: orexin deficiency → unstable wake/sleep switch → sudden sleep attacks, cataplexy.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the knee-jerk reflex and its spinal cord level?
options: L3-L4: tapping the patellar tendon → stretches the quadriceps muscle → activates Ia afferents from muscle spindles → synapses directly on L2-L4 alpha-motor neurons → quadriceps contracts → knee extension; an example of a monosynaptic stretch reflex; diminished = LMN lesion at L3-L4 or peripheral neuropathy; exaggerated = UMN lesion
explanation: Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) and spinal levels: Biceps: C5-C6. Brachioradialis: C5-C6. Triceps: C7-C8. Knee (patellar): L3-L4. Ankle (Achilles): S1-S2. Diminished DTR: LMN lesion at that level, peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy, tabes dorsalis (dorsal root ganglion disease), Holmes-Adie pupil (peripheral autonomic). Exaggerated (hyperreflexia): UMN lesion anywhere above the spinal cord segment (releases DTR from cortical inhibition), hyperthyroidism, anxiety.

subject: Physiology
stem: The oculomotor nerve (CN III): a complete CN III palsy causes which eye signs?
options: Ptosis (levator palpebrae superioris), dilated pupil (loss of parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor from Edinger-Westphal nucleus), 'down-and-out' eye position (unopposed CN IV/trochlear and CN VI/abducens action → depression + abduction)
Miosis and anhidrosis (Horner's syndrome — CN not involved)
explanation: CN III (oculomotor): exits mesencephalon → runs along the tentorial edge → cavernous sinus → superior orbital fissure → innervates: superior rectus (eye up), medial rectus (eye in/adduction), inferior rectus (eye down), inferior oblique (eye up and out), levator palpebrae (eye opening), and parasympathetics to pupil (Edinger-Westphal → ciliary ganglion → pupilloconstrictor + ciliary muscle). CN III palsy: posterior communicating artery aneurysm (surgical CN III = pupil involved, PCoA aneurysm), diabetic CN III (vasa nervorum ischemia = pupil SPARED, as parasympathetics in outer perimeter).

subject: Physiology
stem: Urea recycling in the kidney: what is its importance?
options: Urea is toxic and must be eliminated completely

Urea recycling via UT-A transporters in the inner medullary collecting duct (IMCD) and UT-A3 on the basolateral side + UT-B in descending vasa recta → contributes to the osmotic gradient of the medullary interstitium (up to 50% of the papillary osmolarity is due to urea); ADH upregulates UT-A1/A3 → ↑urea reabsorption in IMCD → ↑medullary urea → ↑osmotic gradient → allows more water reabsorption
Urea is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule only
explanation: Urea as an osmotic scaffold: medullary interstitium: NaCl (from TALH) + urea (from IMCD via UT-A1/A3) together generate ~1200 mOsm/kg at the papilla. Urea enters the tubular lumen from the DLH (passive) → is concentrated in the IMCD → UT-A1/A3 (ADH-upregulated) → exits into medullary interstitium → circulates in vasa recta (UT-B) → re-enters DLH. This 'urea recycling' is essential for maximal urinary concentration. Low protein diet → ↓urea → ↓concentrating ability (less gradient). Protein-calorie malnutrition → inability to concentrate urine maximally.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the effect of ACE inhibitors on the kidney in the setting of bilateral renal artery stenosis?
options: Dangerous — ↓GFR sharply: bilateral RAS → ↓renal perfusion → RAAS activated → Ang II constricts the efferent arteriole → maintains GFR despite low perfusion. ACE inhibitor → removes Ang II → efferent arteriole dilates → GFR drops precipitously → acute kidney injury (AKI)
Only lowers blood pressure, no renal effect
explanation: Renal artery stenosis (RAS) and ACE inhibitors: In bilateral RAS (or in a solitary kidney with RAS), the kidney compensates by activating RAAS → Ang II constricts efferent arteriole → maintains glomerular hydrostatic pressure → maintains GFR. Give ACE inhibitor (or ARB) → blocks Ang II → efferent arteriole dilates → GFR falls → acute kidney injury. This is a contraindication to ACE inhibitors/ARBs. Also contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic), hyperkalemia, angioedema. Unilateral RAS + contralateral normal kidney: ACE inhibitor may actually be beneficial (reduce Ang II effects in hypertension).

subject: Physiology
stem: Urine specific gravity reflects which parameter?
options: The total dissolved solute concentration in urine (osmolarity); SG 1.001–1.035; each 30 mOsm/kg ≈ SG increase of 0.001; SG 1.010 ≈ 300 mOsm/kg (isotonic to plasma); SG <1.003 = dilute (diabetes insipidus, polydipsia); SG >1.025 = concentrated (ADH effect, dehydration)
Glucose content (negligible effect on SG normally)
explanation: Urine SG: measures weight of urine relative to water. Normal range 1.001–1.035 (varies with hydration). SG affected by any solute: Na+, urea, glucose, protein, contrast media. NOT a perfect measure of osmolarity when large solutes present (e.g., proteinuria → falsely elevates SG, mannitol, contrast dye → SG very high with normal/low osmolarity). Urine osmolarity more accurate. Isosthenuria (fixed SG ~1.010): chronic kidney disease → inability to dilute or concentrate → fixed SG.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'Henderson' simplified equation for acid-base: [H+] in nmol/L from pH
options: [H+] (nmol/L) ≈ 24 × PaCO2 / [HCO3-] (from Henderson equation: [H+] = 24 × PaCO2 / [HCO3-] where [H+] is in nmol/L, PaCO2 in mmHg, HCO3- in mEq/L); at pH 7.4: [H+] = 24 × 40/24 = 40 nmol/L
explanation: Henderson equation (non-log form): [H+] = 24 × PaCO2 / [HCO3-]. At pH 7.4: [H+] = 40 nmol/L. pH-to-[H+] conversion shortcut: pH 7.0 = 100 nmol/L, 7.1 = 80, 7.2 = 63, 7.3 = 50, 7.4 = 40, 7.5 = 32, 7.6 = 25 (roughly: each 0.3 pH unit change = doubling/halving [H+]). Clinical use: quickly check internal consistency of ABG: [H+] = 24 × PaCO2 / [HCO3-] should match pH (if not, ABG error). Example: pH 7.1, PaCO2 20, HCO3- 6: [H+] = 24 × 20/6 = 80 → matches pH 7.1 (80 nmol/L). Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Carcinoid syndrome: which mediator is responsible for diarrhea and flushing?
options: Serotonin (5-HT, from ECL/enterochromaffin cells of the midgut carcinoid tumor, now called neuroendocrine tumors) → diarrhea, secretory (watery, voluminous). Flushing: bradykinin + histamine + tachykinins. Cardiac: tricuspid regurgitation + pulmonic stenosis (right heart, as serotonin is inactivated in the lungs by MAO — liver metastases allow access to systemic circulation bypassing pulmonary metabolism). Diagnosed: 24h urine 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, serotonin metabolite)
Glucagon (causes necrolytic migratory erythema, not flushing)
explanation: Carcinoid tumors: NETs from enterochromaffin cells. Appendix most common location, usually non-functional. Midgut (ileum): serotonin-secreting, carcinoid syndrome only when liver metastases present (bypasses first-pass liver metabolism). Carcinoid syndrome: FADS — Flushing (serotonin + histamine + bradykinin), Abdominal cramps, Diarrhea (secretory, serotonin), Skin (pellagra-like skin due to diversion of tryptophan to serotonin instead of niacin). Diagnosis: ↑urine 5-HIAA (serotonin metabolite), chromogranin A. Octreotide (somatostatin analog) → inhibits secretion.

subject: Physiology
stem: Diabetes mellitus type 1: which HLA antigens are most strongly associated?
options: HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 (encoded by HLA class II MHC genes on chromosome 6p21); homozygous DR3/DR4 = highest risk (>30× vs. general population); the DQ8 (DQB1*0302) and DQ2 haplotypes linked with DR4 and DR3 respectively are the actual susceptibility determinants
HLA-DR2 (associated with MS and narcolepsy, NOT T1DM — actually DR2 is PROTECTIVE for T1DM)
explanation: T1DM genetics: HLA-DR3 (DQ2) and HLA-DR4 (DQ8) strongly predispose. HLA-DR2 (DQ6) is PROTECTIVE. Other genes: INS (insulin gene VNTR), PTPN22 (protein tyrosine phosphatase — involved in T cell activation), CTLA4 (negative T cell regulator). Pathology: T1DM = autoimmune destruction of β-cells by CD4+ and CD8+ T cells → insulitis → gradual β-cell loss. Anti-GAD65, anti-IA-2, anti-ZnT8 antibodies (diagnostic markers). 90% β-cell destruction before clinical symptoms (honeymoon period from remaining β-cells).

subject: Physiology
stem: Pheochromocytoma: which neurotransmitter is typically elevated?
options: Catecholamines (epinephrine and/or norepinephrine, in a ratio depending on location — adrenal medulla produces mostly Epi; extra-adrenal paragangliomas produce mostly NE since no PNMT); urine metanephrines (normetanephrine + metanephrine) = best screening test
explanation: Pheo triad: episodic headache, palpitations, sweating + hypertension (episodic or sustained). 'Rule of 10s': 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% malignant, 10% familial, 10% in children. Biochemistry: epinephrine (from adrenal, acts on β2 → vasodilation + tachycardia + hyperglycemia) or NE (extra-adrenal, α1 + α2 → vasoconstriction + severe hypertension). Diagnosis: 24h urine metanephrines (catecholamine metabolites; most sensitive). Plasma metanephrines (highest sensitivity, useful for MEN2, VHL, SDH mutations). Treatment: α-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine) THEN β-blockade → surgery.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypothyroidism: which enzyme activity is decreased leading to hyperlipidemia?
options: LDL receptor downregulation (thyroid hormone normally upregulates LDL receptors in the liver → facilitates LDL clearance → ↓LDL; hypothyroidism → ↓LDL receptor → ↑LDL); also ↓lipoprotein lipase activity → ↑triglycerides
explanation: Hypothyroidism and lipids: T3/T4 upregulates hepatic LDL receptor expression → ↑LDL clearance. In hypothyroidism: ↓LDL receptor → ↑serum LDL. Also: ↓LPL activity → ↑triglycerides; ↑cholesterol (reduced bile acid synthesis and ↑cholesterol content in cell membranes). Features: ↑total cholesterol, ↑LDL, ↑TG. Treat hypothyroidism → normalizes lipids (often no need for statins after euthyroid). Secondary cause of dyslipidemia: always check TSH.

subject: Physiology
stem: Aldosteronism: primary vs. secondary — how to differentiate?
options: Plasma renin activity (PRA): Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's — adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia): ↑aldosterone, SUPPRESSED renin (aldosterone production is autonomous, not driven by RAAS, and high aldosterone causes salt/water retention → ↑BP → ↓renin). Secondary hyperaldosteronism (renal artery stenosis, heart failure, cirrhosis, diuretic use): ↑renin (stimulus to aldosterone) → ↑aldosterone
explanation: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR): elevated (>30 ng/dL per ng/mL/hr, or >30 if aldo in ng/dL) → suggests primary aldosteronism. Confirmed by: salt loading test (saline infusion → normally suppresses aldo; in primary aldosteronism, aldo remains >10 ng/dL). Subtype differentiation: adrenal CT (adenoma vs. bilateral hyperplasia) + adrenal vein sampling (gold standard). Treatment: unilateral adrenal adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone/eplerenone.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which hormone stimulates the growth of pubic and axillary hair (adrenarche)?
options: Adrenal androgens (DHEA, DHEAS, androstenedione) from zona reticularis — adrenarche (6–8 years, before gonadarche) stimulates pubic/axillary hair, body odor, mild acne; mediated by rising ACTH sensitivity of zona reticularis and ↑DHEA; does not depend on sex steroids from the gonads (premature adrenarche = benign early pubic hair, not true precocious puberty)
explanation: Adrenarche: increase in adrenal androgen secretion (mainly DHEAS) that begins at 6-8 years (precedes gonadal activation by 2 years). Mechanism: selective ↑17,20-lyase (CYP17A1) activity in zona reticularis → ↑DHEA/DHEAS. Stimulated by ACTH but ACTH does NOT increase significantly (the change is in zona reticularis sensitivity/maturation). Effects: pubic/axillary hair (pubarche), body odor, oily skin (sebaceous gland stimulation). DHEA/DHEAS = substrate for peripheral conversion to testosterone and estradiol.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hemoglobin types in an adult: which is the most abundant?
options: Hemoglobin A (HbA, α2β2) — comprises ~96–98% of adult hemoglobin; HbA2 (α2δ2) = 2–3%; HbF (α2γ2) = <1% in adults (persists in higher amounts in sickle cell disease and thalassemia)
Hemoglobin S (HbS, α2βS2) in normal adults
explanation: Hemoglobin structure: tetramer of 4 globin chains, each with an iron-containing heme group. HbA (α2β2): 96-98%. HbA2 (α2δ2): 2-3% (elevated in β-thalassemia trait >3.5%). HbF (α2γ2): <1% adults (elevated in HPFH, β-thalassemia). HbS (α2βS2): present in sickle cell disease (βS = β6 Glu→Val). HbC (α2βC2): βC = β6 Glu→Lys. Switching: HbF → HbA during the first 6 months of life (γ-globin gene silenced → β-globin gene expressed). HbF persistence (HPFH): β-globin cluster deletion → γ-genes remain active → ↑HbF, benign.

subject: Physiology
stem: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: which cells are primarily affected?
options: Platelets (thrombocytopenia with small dysfunctional platelets) + T cells (T cell dysfunction, reduced IgM); X-linked recessive, mutation in WASp (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein) — actin cytoskeletal regulator; triad: thrombocytopenia (bloody diarrhea as first sign), eczema, recurrent infections (encapsulated bacteria from poor IgM/opsonization, opportunistic from T cell dysfunction)
explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS): WASp gene (Xp11.23) → WASp protein in hematopoietic cells → regulates actin polymerization (important for immune cell migration, signaling, cytotoxicity). Classic triad: WATER (Wiskott-Aldrich: Thrombocytopenia, Eczema, Recurrent infections). Immunology: IgM ↓, IgA ↑, IgE ↑, IgG normal or low; poor antibody response to polysaccharides (↑susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria). Lymphopenia (T cell loss over time). Risk: lymphoma. Treatment: HSCT (curative).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which clotting factor is inhibited by aspirin?
options: Aspirin does not directly inhibit a clotting factor — it irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1) and COX-2 (acetylation of serine residue) → reduces thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis in platelets (COX-1 → TXA2 → platelet aggregation) and prostacyclin (PGI2) in endothelium (COX-2 → PGI2 → anti-aggregation); the NET effect at low dose is predominantly anti-platelet (platelets cannot regenerate COX → effect lasts platelet lifetime ~7-10 days)
