explanation: Aspirin mechanism: Irreversible acetylation of COX-1 (and COX-2) at Ser530 (COX-1) → blocks the channel where arachidonic acid binds → no PGH2 produced → no TXA2 (in platelets, via COX-1) or PGI2 (endothelium, via COX-2). Platelets cannot synthesize new COX (no nucleus) → effect lasts entire platelet lifespan (7-10 days). Endothelial cells regenerate COX within hours → PGI2 resumes. Low-dose aspirin (75-150 mg/day): predominantly blocks platelet COX-1 → anti-thrombotic. High dose: also blocks endothelial PGI2 → may ↓protective effect.

subject: Physiology
stem: Aplastic anemia: pathophysiology?
options: Destruction or suppression of hematopoietic stem cells → hypocellular bone marrow → pancytopenia; most often autoimmune (CD8+ T cells attack HSCs via IFN-γ/TNF-α) — hence immunosuppressive therapy (ATG + cyclosporine) is effective; also: radiation, benzene, chloramphenicol, viruses (hepatitis, parvovirus B19 — pure red cell aplasia)
explanation: Aplastic anemia (AA): acquired (80%) vs. inherited (Fanconi anemia, Diamond-Blackfan). Pancytopenia: anemia, thrombocytopenia (bleeding), neutropenia (infections). BM biopsy: hypocellular marrow, fat replacement. Cause: often idiopathic autoimmune (T cells → HSC destruction), or after hepatitis (non-A-non-B seronegative hepatitis most strongly associated, not viral hepatitis A/B/C). Drugs: benzene, chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, phenytoin, gold. Diagnosis: BM biopsy (cellularity <25%). Treatment: HSC transplantation (young, matched donor) or ATG + cyclosporine (immunosuppression).

subject: Physiology
stem: The visual field defect in homonymous hemianopia means the patient has lost vision:
options: In the same side of the visual field in BOTH eyes (e.g., right homonymous hemianopia = loss of right visual field in both eyes = left optic tract/radiation/cortex lesion because right visual field → left optic tract/cortex after chiasmal crossing)
Only the upper half of vision (altitudinal)
explanation: Visual field defects: Complete optic nerve lesion: monocular blindness (ipsilateral). Optic chiasm (bitemporal): bitemporal hemianopia (outer temporal visual fields lost from both eyes) — nasal retinal fibers cross at chiasm. Optic tract: contralateral homonymous hemianopia (macula often spared in cortical lesions — 'macular sparing' due to dual blood supply of macular cortex). Optic radiation lesion: homonymous quadrantanopia: upper fibers (parietal lobe) → inferior quadrant, lower fibers (temporal lobe, Meyer's loop) → superior quadrant. Primary visual cortex (V1): contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (posterior circulation supplies macular cortex area).

subject: Physiology
stem: The accommodation reflex: what three changes occur when the eye focuses on a near object?
options: Pupil dilation, lens flattening, divergence of eyes

Convergence of eyes (medial rectus contraction, CN III), pupil constriction (miosis — iris sphincter, parasympathetic, CN III), and increase in lens curvature (ciliary muscle contracts → zonule relaxation → lens rounds up = accommodation); all three = 'near triad' mediated by CN III and EW nucleus
explanation: Near response (accommodation triad): stimulus: approaching object seen as blurred on retina → parietal/occipital cortex → vergence neurons in midbrain → CN III (Edinger-Westphal nucleus → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves): (1) Ciliary muscle contraction → zonule relaxation → lens spherical (↑power → +12D). (2) Pupil constriction (iris sphincter). (3) Vergence neurons → medial rectus (CN III) → convergence of eyes. Presbyopia: lens loses elasticity → accommodation fails. Argyll Robertson pupil (tabes dorsalis): accommodates but does not react to light (dissociation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Lactulose therapy for hepatic encephalopathy: mechanism?
options: Directly detoxifies ammonia in the colon

Non-absorbable disaccharide metabolized by colonic bacteria to lactic and acetic acids → acidifies colon → NH3 (volatile, absorbable) is converted to NH4+ (ionized, non-absorbable) → traps ammonia in the colon → reduces absorption; also acts as an osmotic laxative → ↑bowel frequency → ↓transit time → ↓bacterial ammonia production
Only laxative effect — no direct ammonia reduction
explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy: impaired hepatic clearance of ammonia (and other gut-derived toxins) → cerebral ammonia toxicity → astrocyte swelling (Alzheimer type II astrocytes) → brain dysfunction. Treatment: (1) Lactulose (1st line): acidifies colon → NH3 → NH4+, osmotic laxative. (2) Rifaximin (non-absorbed antibiotic): ↓ammonia-producing bacteria. (3) Low-protein diet? (controversial, avoid excess protein but don't restrict — muscle mass maintains ammonia metabolism). Precipitants: GI bleed (blood = protein load → ↑NH3), constipation, infection, sedatives, hypokalemia (K+ competes with H+ in exchangers → alkalosis → ↑NH3).

subject: Physiology
stem: Helicobacter pylori: which enzyme does it produce to survive the acidic gastric environment?
options: Catalase (protects from oxidative burst — secondary enzyme)

Urease — hydrolyzes urea → ammonia + CO2; ammonia raises the local pH around the bacterium → protection from gastric acid; urease is also the basis of the urea breath test (UBT): ingested 13C- or 14C-labeled urea → H. pylori urease → labeled CO2 → detected in exhaled breath (non-invasive diagnostic test for H. pylori)
explanation: H. pylori virulence factors: Urease (essential for survival): urea → NH3 + CO2 → ↑local pH. Cag pathogenicity island (CagA): type IV secretion system → injects CagA into gastric epithelium → oncogenic (↑gastric cancer risk). VacA (vacuolating cytotoxin): creates vacuoles in epithelial cells → apoptosis → mucosal damage. OipA (outer inflammatory protein): stimulates IL-8 → inflammation. H. pylori associated: peptic ulcer disease (90% of duodenal ulcers), chronic active gastritis, MALT lymphoma, ↑risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cells in the duodenal mucosa produce intrinsic factor?
options: Parietal cells of the GASTRIC fundus and body produce intrinsic factor (not the duodenum); the duodenum has I cells (CCK), S cells (secretin), K cells (GIP), M cells (motilin); total gastrectomy (removing parietal cells) leads to B12 deficiency in a few years as body B12 stores (liver) are gradually depleted
explanation: Gastric cell types and their secretions: Parietal (oxyntic) cells (body/fundus): HCl + intrinsic factor. Chief (zymogenic) cells (body/fundus): pepsinogen + gastric lipase. G cells (antrum): gastrin. D cells (antrum + body): somatostatin. ECL cells (body): histamine (paracrine → parietal cells). Surface mucous cells (all regions): mucus + HCO3-. Mucous neck cells (gland necks): mucus + stem cells for gland renewal. Duodenal Brunner's glands (submucosa): mucus + HCO3- (protect duodenal mucosa from acid).

subject: Physiology
stem: The Fick's first law of diffusion: what does it state?
options: Diffusion rate is inversely proportional to concentration gradient

Rate of diffusion (J) = -D × A × (ΔC/Δx) — proportional to: diffusion coefficient (D, which depends on temperature + inversely on molecular weight and viscosity), surface area (A), and concentration gradient (ΔC/Δx); inversely proportional to membrane thickness; as applied to pulmonary gas exchange (Fick's law): CO2 diffuses 20× faster than O2 (despite same A, similar Δx) because of 20× higher solubility (compensates for molecular weight)
Diffusion only applies to gases, not ions
Gases only diffuse by active transport
explanation: Fick's law applied to alveolar gas exchange: V̇gas = D × A × (P1-P2) / T, where D ∝ solubility / √MW. CO2: solubility 20× > O2, MW 44 vs. 32 → CO2 diffuses 20× faster → CO2 never diffusion-limited (equilibrates instantly). O2: may be diffusion-limited in extreme exercise or ILD (insufficient time for O2 to equilibrate across thickened/fibrotic membrane). N2O diffuses rapidly (high solubility × adequate AP) → not limited by diffusion. DLco measures overall diffusing capacity for CO.

subject: Physiology
stem: Countercurrent heat exchange in the testis: why is testicular temperature lower than body temperature?
options: Sweat glands in the scrotum cool the testes

The pampiniform plexus (network of veins surrounding the testicular artery in the spermatic cord) acts as a countercurrent heat exchanger: venous blood returning from the testis (cooler) cools the incoming arterial blood → testicular temperature is 2–4°C below core temperature (32–34°C vs. 37°C) — optimal temperature for spermatogenesis
The testis has no blood supply between cell divisions
Testicular temperature equals body temperature normally
explanation: Testicular thermoregulation: Spermatogenesis requires temperature below 37°C (32–35°C optimal for spermatogonial division). Countercurrent heat exchange: testicular artery runs alongside the pampiniform plexus (a convoluted venous network) → venous blood (cooled by scrotal skin radiation) → cools arterial blood before it enters the testis. Cryptorchidism (undescended testis): remains at 37°C → impaired spermatogenesis → infertility; also ↑seminoma risk (even after orchidopexy). Varicocele: abnormally dilated pampiniform plexus → impaired cooling → ↑testicular temperature → ↓spermatogenesis.

subject: Physiology
stem: Fick's principle for oxygen consumption: if the A-V O2 difference increases while cardiac output decreases, O2 consumption:
options: May remain constant: VO2 = CO × C(a-v)O2; if CO halves and C(a-v)O2 doubles, VO2 is unchanged (muscles extract proportionally more O2 from each unit of blood, maintaining O2 delivery to tissues at the expense of lower mixed venous O2 saturation)
explanation: O2 delivery and consumption: DO2 = CO × CaO2 (O2 delivery). VO2 = CO × [CaO2 - CvO2] = CO × C(a-v)O2 (Fick). When CO ↓: compensatory ↑O2 extraction (tissues extract more O2 from reduced blood flow) → ↑C(a-v)O2 → ↓SvO2. VO2 can remain constant until DO2 falls below the critical DO2 threshold (VO2-DO2 relationship: at first, VO2 is supply-independent as extraction increases; when extraction is maximal and DO2 still falls, VO2 becomes supply-dependent → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acidosis). Normal SvO2 ~75%; in severe cardiac failure, SvO2 may fall to 50-60%.

subject: Physiology
stem: Specific dynamic action (SDA) or thermic effect of food: which macronutrient has the highest SDA?
options: Protein (4 kcal/g): SDA = 20–30% of energy content (i.e., 20–30% of protein calories are used for digestion, absorption, and metabolism of protein); carbohydrate SDA = 5–10%; fat SDA = 2–5%; protein ingestion increases metabolic rate most (useful for weight management)
explanation: Thermic effect of food (TEF/SDA): energy cost of digesting, absorbing, and metabolizing nutrients. Protein: ~20–30% of protein calories consumed in processing (deamination, transamination, urea synthesis, GNG). Carbohydrate: ~5–10% (glycolysis, glycogenesis). Fat: ~2–5% (re-esterification, lipogenesis). Mixed diet: ~10% of total caloric intake. High-protein diets → ↑TEF → more of calories 'burned' in metabolism → effective for weight loss. TEF accounts for about 10% of total energy expenditure (alongside basal metabolic rate [60-75%] and activity [15-30%]).

subject: Physiology
stem: The Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC) in the body: where else is it important besides the kidney?
options: In the inner ear: NKCC1 in the stria vascularis (basolateral membrane) pumps K+ into endolymph → generates the high-K+ endolymph and the +80 mV endocochlear potential (essential for hair cell mechanotransduction); also: NKCC1 in neurons (important in early development — neonatal neurons have higher [Cl-]i via NKCC1 → GABA is depolarizing in early development, only becomes inhibitory after KCC2 [K+/Cl- cotransporter, export Cl-] is expressed postnatally)
explanation: NKCC isoforms: NKCC2 (kidney-specific): TALH → targeted by loop diuretics. NKCC1 (ubiquitous): inner ear (stria vascularis → endolymph K+ secretion → endocochlear potential), neurons (early development, Cl- import → Cl-i high → GABA depolarizes neonatal neurons), salivary glands (Cl-/fluid secretion), blood-brain barrier. Neonatal GABA depolarization: before KCC2 (K+-Cl- cotransporter) is expressed (~2 weeks postnatal in rats, ~1 year in humans), GABA-A → Cl- efflux → depolarization. Explains why benzodiazepines can paradoxically excite neonates.

subject: Physiology
stem: The atrioventricular (AV) node is located in:
options: The Koch's triangle (bounded by the tendon of Todaro superiorly, the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve anteriorly, and the coronary sinus ostium posteriorly), in the interatrial septum near the tricuspid valve annulus
explanation: AV node anatomy: situated in the floor of the right atrium, in the Koch's triangle. Blood supply: right coronary artery (90%) in right-dominant hearts. AV nodal artery = also from RCA. This is why inferior MI (RCA occlusion) → AV block (bradycardia, heart block). P-R interval prolongation reflects AV nodal conduction delay. Junctional rhythm (escape) = AV node fires at 40-60 bpm if SA node fails.

subject: Physiology
stem: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor stimulation in the heart produces:
options: Positive chronotropy (↑HR), positive inotropy (↑contractility), positive dromotropy (↑AV conduction velocity), and positive lusitropy (↑relaxation rate) — all via Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban (↑SERCA2a activity → faster relaxation), troponin I (↓Ca2+ sensitivity → faster relaxation)
explanation: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor (cardiac): Gs → adenylate cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA → (1) Chronotropy: phosphorylates HCN channel (If) → ↑funny current → ↑slope of pacemaker potential → ↑SA node rate. (2) Inotropy: phosphorylates L-type Ca2+ channel → ↑Ca2+ influx → CICR → ↑[Ca2+]i → ↑force. (3) Lusitropy: phosphorylates phospholamban (removes inhibition on SERCA2a → faster Ca2+ reuptake → faster relaxation) and troponin I (↓myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity → faster detachment). Beta-1 blockers (metoprolol, atenolol) → ↓HR, ↓contractility, ↓O2 demand.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which clinical test is used to evaluate conduction velocity of peripheral nerves?
options: Nerve conduction studies (NCS): apply an electrical stimulus at one point on a peripheral nerve → record the evoked potential downstream; conduction velocity (m/s) = distance/latency; abnormal in: demyelinating neuropathy (↓velocity, ↑latency) vs. axonal neuropathy (↓amplitude of CMAP/SNAP but normal velocity)
Evoked potentials from the brain only
explanation: Nerve conduction studies (NCS): motor NCS measures CMAP (compound muscle action potential) — amplitude reflects axon numbers. Sensory NCS measures SNAP (sensory nerve action potential). Demyelinating neuropathy (Guillain-Barré, CIDP, CMT type 1): ↓velocity (can be <38 m/s; normal >45 m/s for median nerve), ↑distal latency, temporal dispersion, conduction block. Axonal neuropathy (diabetes, B12 deficiency, toxic): ↓CMAP/SNAP amplitude (axon loss), relatively normal velocity. Carpal tunnel syndrome: ↑distal latency of median nerve across the wrist (focal slowing).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which statement about the baroreceptor reflex is correct?
options: Baroreceptors are in the aortic arch and carotid body (chemoreceptors)

Carotid sinus baroreceptors (CN IX, Hering's nerve) and aortic arch baroreceptors (CN X) are stretch receptors (Aδ and C fibers in the adventitia); ↑BP → ↑afferent discharge → nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) → ↑vagal output (↓HR) + ↓sympathetic outflow (↓HR, ↓contractility, vasodilation) → ↓BP (restores set point); reset with sustained hypertension (explain why long-term HTN doesn't trigger constant reflex)
explanation: Baroreceptors: mechanosensory nerve endings in the adventitia of the carotid sinus (at the bifurcation, most sensitive) and aortic arch. They fire in proportion to the stretch of the vessel wall (systolic pressure, pulse pressure, rate of pressure change). Afferents: CN IX (carotid sinus → Hering's nerve → NTS) and CN X (aortic → NTS). NTS → activates cardioinhibitory center + inhibits vasomotor center → ↓HR + ↓TPR → ↓BP. Baroreceptor resetting: in chronic hypertension, baroreceptors reset to operate at a higher pressure set point (adaptation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Myocardial ischemia: which ion accumulates intracellularly and is responsible for arrhythmias?
options: Calcium (Ca2+ overload): ischemia → ATP depletion → Na+/K+ ATPase fails → ↑[Na+]i → NCX (Na+/Ca2+ exchanger) reverses → extrudes Na+ but imports Ca2+ → ↑[Ca2+]i → triggered afterdepolarizations → arrhythmias; also: ↑[Ca2+]i → activates phospholipases, proteases → irreversible cell injury
explanation: Ischemia → reperfusion injury (paradoxical worsening when blood flow restores): (1) Ca2+ overload: Na+/H+ exchanger activation (acidosis → ↑[H+]i → NHE-1 exports H+, imports Na+) → ↑[Na+]i → NCX reverses → ↑[Ca2+]i; reperfusion washes out H+ → NHE-1 pumps hard → Na+ → more NCX reversal → Ca2+ overload. (2) ROS (reactive oxygen species) from reperfusion: mitochondrial electron chain → ↑superoxide → oxidative stress. (3) mPTP (mitochondrial permeability transition pore) opening → cell death. Reperfusion injury paradox: 'second wave' of injury despite restoring flow.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which ECG finding is pathognomonic of hyperkalemia (severe, serum K+ >7 mEq/L)?
options: Sine-wave pattern (QRS and T merge into a continuous undulation, preceding ventricular fibrillation); earlier findings: peaked T waves (first sign, at K+ 5.5-6.5), wide QRS, flat P waves, PR prolongation; treatment: Ca gluconate (membrane stabilization, immediate) → insulin+glucose → sodium bicarbonate → kayexalate or dialysis
explanation: Hyperkalemia ECG changes (sequential with rising K+): K+ 5.5-6.5: peaked tall T waves (narrow base, tent-shaped). K+ 6.5-7: PR prolongation, flat P waves. K+ 7-8: wide QRS (bundle branch block pattern). K+ >8: sine wave (QRS merges with T) → ventricular fibrillation/asystole. Calcium gluconate 10% IV: stabilizes cardiac membranes (immediately, minutes) → window to lower K+. Insulin+dextrose: drives K+ into cells. Salbutamol (IV): β2 → drives K+ intracellularly. NaHCO3 (if acidosis). Kayexalate or patiromer (GI exchange resins). Dialysis (most effective for severe/refractory).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'diving reflex': which two components define it?
options: Bradycardia (vagal, triggered by facial immersion in cold water → trigeminal afferents → medulla → ↑vagal outflow → bradycardia) AND peripheral vasoconstriction (sympathetic → diverts blood to heart and brain) — reduces O2 consumption, extends breath-hold time; most pronounced in marine mammals; in humans: HR may drop 10-25% during cold-water facial immersion
explanation: Diving reflex (trigeminocardiac reflex): facial immersion in cold water → trigeminal afferents (CN V, particularly ophthalmic branch) → NTS → (1) ↑vagal outflow → bradycardia, ↓AV conduction; (2) ↑sympathetic → peripheral vasoconstriction (splanchnic, muscles) → blood redistributed to vital organs. Evolved apneic oxygen conservation. In neonates: well-developed diving reflex (protective during difficult delivery/cord compression). Triggered in clinical practice during ocular procedures (oculocardiac reflex) or carotid sinus massage (clinical application in SVT).

subject: Physiology
stem: Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP): how does it reduce afterload?
options: It inflates during systole to help pump blood

It deflates rapidly at the onset of systole (just before LV ejection) → creates a vacuum effect → reduces resistance for LV ejection (↓afterload); then inflates during diastole → augments diastolic BP → increases coronary perfusion pressure; net effect: ↓myocardial O2 demand (↓afterload) + ↑O2 supply (↑coronary perfusion)
It inflates during diastole and deflates randomly
explanation: IABP (counter-pulsation): helium-filled balloon in the descending aorta (just distal to left subclavian artery). Timed to ECG: inflates at the start of diastole (dicrotic notch = aortic valve closure) → augments diastolic pressure → ↑coronary and cerebral perfusion. Deflates at the onset of systole (just before aortic valve opens) → creates suction effect → ↓impedance to LV ejection → ↓afterload → ↓O2 demand. Indications: cardiogenic shock, unstable angina/NSTEMI refractory to medical therapy, mechanical complications of MI (VSD, MR). Contraindicated in: aortic regurgitation (inflates in diastole → forces blood backward), aortic dissection.

subject: Physiology
stem: Insulin resistance: what is the primary molecular defect?
options: Post-receptor signaling defect: IRS-1 phosphorylation is impaired (by serine/threonine kinases activated by FFA, ceramide, inflammatory cytokines like TNF-α, IL-6) → ↓PI3K/Akt activation → ↓GLUT4 translocation → reduced cellular glucose uptake; in the liver: ↓glycogen synthesis + ↑gluconeogenesis (paradoxical retained hepatic Akt activation via alternate pathways → SREBP1c → ↑lipogenesis)
Reduced number of insulin receptors only
explanation: Insulin resistance (T2DM, metabolic syndrome): molecular: FFA → activates PKC (serine phosphorylation of IRS-1) + inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6 → JNK/IKK → serine phosphorylation of IRS-1) → blocks tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS-1 → ↓PI3K → ↓Akt → ↓GLUT4 translocation (muscle, fat) + ↓glycogen synthesis + ↓protein synthesis. Liver: gluconeogenesis continues (Foxo1 → PEPCK/G6Pase) + ↑de novo lipogenesis (Akt still activates TORC2/SREBP1c). β-cell compensates by ↑insulin secretion → hyperinsulinemia → eventually β-cell fails → T2DM.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'zone of polarizing activity' (ZPA) in limb development was already addressed in anatomy. In reproductive physiology, what is the role of inhibin?
options: Inhibin (A and B, dimers of α and β subunits, produced by ovarian granulosa cells and testicular Sertoli cells) → selectively suppresses FSH secretion from the anterior pituitary (negative feedback), while NOT suppressing LH; this allows fine regulation of follicular recruitment (↑inhibin from growing follicles → ↓FSH → remaining small follicles become atretic → dominant follicle selection)
explanation: Inhibin: member of the TGF-β superfamily. Inhibin A (α-βA): from corpus luteum (luteal phase). Inhibin B (α-βB): from developing follicles (follicular phase, early phase). Both inhibit FSH release selectively. Role in FSH regulation: as a growing follicle increases inhibin B secretion → ↓FSH → smaller follicles (less FSH-responsive, lower FSH threshold already crossed) → become atretic → dominant follicle (highest FSH sensitivity, most granulosa cells) survives. Inhibin A elevated in Down syndrome (maternal triple/quad screen marker — ↑hCG + ↑inhibin A + ↓AFP + ↓estriol).

subject: Physiology
stem: During pregnancy: which changes occur in thyroid function?
options: TSH is markedly elevated throughout pregnancy

↑Thyroid-binding globulin (TBG, due to estrogen-induced ↑hepatic synthesis) → ↑total T4 (protein-bound) but FREE T4 remains normal; hCG (peak at 10 weeks) has weak TSH-like activity → may transiently suppress TSH in first trimester (physiological TSH ↓); iodine requirements ↑ (fetal needs)
explanation: Thyroid changes in pregnancy: (1) ↑TBG (due to high estrogen → ↑hepatic TBG synthesis + ↓TBG clearance) → ↑total T4 and T3 (protein-bound) but FREE T4 and FREE T3 NORMAL. (2) hCG (structural similarity to TSH, shares α-subunit) → mild thyroid stimulation → slight ↑T4, slight ↓TSH (first trimester gestational TSH suppression is normal). (3) ↑Iodine clearance (↑GFR) + fetal iodine demand → ↑iodine requirements (220 μg/day in pregnancy). Hypothyroidism in pregnancy: ↑risk of miscarriage, preterm birth, low IQ in offspring (critical for fetal brain development, especially first trimester).

subject: Physiology
stem: The fetal circulation: which structure allows blood to bypass the lungs?
options: The ductus arteriosus (connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta, fetal → high pulmonary vascular resistance → blood shunts from PA to aorta, right-to-left) AND the foramen ovale (interatrial communication → oxygenated blood from IVC preferentially crosses to left atrium); ductus venosus (umbilical vein → IVC, bypasses liver)
explanation: Fetal circulation: Umbilical vein (oxygenated blood from placenta) → ductus venosus → IVC → right atrium → foramen ovale (patent in fetus → preferential flow to LA, via Eustachian valve directing blood from IVC across FO) → LV → aorta → brain + coronary. Deoxygenated blood from SVC → RV → PA → ductus arteriosus → descending aorta (bypasses high-resistance lungs). At birth: ↑PaO2 → ↓prostaglandins → DA closes (functional in hours, permanent within weeks). ↑LA pressure → FO closes functionally (permanent in ~1 year). Failure to close: PDA, ASD.

subject: Physiology
stem: Erythropoiesis: the progenitor cell for red cells that can be identified morphologically is:
options: Pronormoblast (proerythroblast) — the earliest recognizable erythroid precursor in the bone marrow; maturation: pronormoblast → basophilic normoblast (↑Hb, ↑RNA) → polychromatophilic normoblast → orthochromatic normoblast (ejects nucleus) → reticulocyte (still has ribosomes → RNA stains blue-gray polychromasia on Wright-Giemsa, or stains with new methylene blue) → mature RBC (loses ribosomes, ~3 months in circulation)
explanation: Erythroid maturation (bone marrow → blood): Proerythroblast (large, 12-20 μm, scant blue cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli) → Basophilic normoblast (more condensed nucleus, deep blue cytoplasm with hemoglobin synthesis starting) → Polychromatophilic normoblast (gray-pink cytoplasm from Hb + RNA mix) → Orthochromatic normoblast (pink cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus → expelled in marrow → becomes reticulocyte) → Reticulocyte (no nucleus, polychromatophilia, released into blood, matures in 1-2 days in blood → lost ribosomes = mature RBC). Reticulocyte count 1-2% normally; ↑in hemolytic anemia, bleeding.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the mechanism of megaloblastic changes in vitamin B12/folate deficiency?
options: Impaired DNA synthesis (↓thymidine synthesis): B12 is required for methionine synthase (homocysteine + methyl-THF → methionine + THF); without B12, folate is 'trapped' as methyl-THF (unable to enter the folate cycle for thymidine synthesis → ↓dTMP synthesis → impaired DNA replication → cells enlarge but don't divide → megaloblastic changes (large nuclei, immature nuclei, hypersegmented neutrophils)
explanation: Megaloblastic anemia: B12 deficiency → methyl-THF trap (B12 needed to convert methyl-THF → THF, which enters folate cycle) → ↓THF → ↓5,10-methylene-THF → ↓thymidylate synthase (dUMP → dTMP) → ↓DNA synthesis → S-phase arrested nuclei → asynchronous nuclear-cytoplasmic maturation → megaloblasts. Same with folate deficiency (↓folate → ↓THF). Both: ↑MCV, ↑homocysteine. B12 deficiency ALSO: ↑methylmalonic acid (MMA) — unique to B12 (succinyl-CoA synthesis requires B12, not folate). Neurological: B12 deficiency → subacute combined degeneration (SCD) — dorsal columns + lateral CST.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which surface marker is used to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: Absent CD55 (DAF, decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (MIRL, membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) on red blood cells — PNH: acquired mutation in PIG-A gene (X-linked) in a hematopoietic stem cell → deficiency of GPI anchor (glycosylphosphatidylinositol) → all GPI-anchored proteins absent from cell surface → CD55 and CD59 absent → complement activation goes unchecked → complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis
explanation: PNH: acquired clonal disorder of hematopoiesis. PIGA gene mutation → no GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59, CD14, CD16, CD24, CD66b, etc.) on RBCs and other blood cells. CD55 (DAF): accelerates decay of C3/C5 convertases. CD59 (MIRL): blocks MAC (C5b-9) formation. Absence → spontaneous complement activation → intravascular hemolysis (hemoglobinuria classically in the morning from complement activation overnight — now known not to be specific for morning). Also: thrombosis (Budd-Chiari, hepatic, cerebral, mesenteric veins — high risk). Diagnosis: flow cytometry (CD55/CD59 absent on RBCs and WBCs). Treatment: eculizumab (anti-C5 antibody).

subject: Physiology
stem: Neutrophil count: absolute neutropenia is defined as ANC below:
options: <1500/μL (mild neutropenia: 1000-1500; moderate: 500-1000; severe: <500 = agranulocytosis, severe infection risk); ANC = WBC × % neutrophils (segs + bands)
explanation: Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) = WBC × (% segs + % bands). Normal ANC: 2500-7500/μL. Neutropenia: <1500/μL. Mild (1000-1500): small risk. Moderate (500-1000): moderate risk. Severe (<500): high risk of life-threatening bacterial/fungal infections. Causes: congenital (severe congenital neutropenia/Kostmann syndrome: ELANE mutation, G-CSF receptor), acquired (drugs: carbamazepine, clozapine, methimazole, rituximab; viral infections; autoimmune; bone marrow failure). Febrile neutropenia (ANC <500 + temp >38.3°C or >38°C sustained): empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately (within 1 hour).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which enzyme deficiency causes phenylketonuria (PKU) and what is the key substrate that accumulates?
options: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH, converts phenylalanine → tyrosine, requires BH4 cofactor); deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → converted to phenylketones (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate) → excreted in urine ('mousy'/'musty' odor); ↑Phe inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase (↓dopamine, NE) + Phe competes with neutral amino acid transporters in the BBB → ↓large neutral amino acids → ↓myelin synthesis → intellectual disability
explanation: PKU: autosomal recessive, most common amino acid disorder. Incidence: 1/10,000. Phe → Tyr blocked → ↑Phe. Newborn screen (Guthrie test, now MS/MS). Untreated: progressive intellectual disability, seizures, fair skin and hair (↓melanin = ↓tyrosine → ↓DOPA → ↓melanin), microcephaly, musty odor. Maternal PKU: uncontrolled Phe in pregnant woman → fetal brain damage (even if fetus heterozygous). Treatment: phenylalanine-restricted diet (low-Phe, tyrosine supplemented); sapropterin (BH4, for BH4-responsive PAH mutations); pegvaliase (enzyme substitution therapy, for adults).

subject: Physiology
stem: Myasthenia gravis (MG): the target antigen in most cases is:
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC) — that is Lambert-Eaton

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) at the neuromuscular junction — IgG autoantibodies (anti-AChR, 85% of patients) bind the alpha-subunit → complement activation → degradation of receptors → simplified postsynaptic folds → reduced amplitude of end-plate potentials → fatigable muscle weakness
explanation: MG vs. LEMS: MG: anti-AChR (85%) or anti-MuSK (10-15% seronegative), postsynaptic NMJ. Features: ocular (ptosis, diplopia first), bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria), fatigable proximal limb weakness, ↑with use, ↓with rest. Edrophonium (Tensilon) test: ↑AChE inhibition → transient improvement. EMG: decremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation (>10%). CT chest: thymoma (10-15%), thymic hyperplasia. LEMS (Lambert-Eaton): anti-VGCC, presynaptic, paraneoplastic (SCLC). Incremental response on high-frequency repetitive NCS. Treat MG: pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy, IVIG, plasma exchange.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the mechanism of action of succinylcholine (suxamethonium)?
options: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent: binds nAChR → prolonged depolarization of the motor end-plate → initial fasciculations (Phase I block — persistent depolarization → muscle relaxation) → further exposure or in certain conditions → Phase II block (desensitization, behaves like non-depolarizing); metabolized rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase
explanation: Succinylcholine: two ACh molecules joined end-to-end. Binds nAChR (Nm subtype) → prolonged receptor opening → persistent end-plate depolarization → inactivation of surrounding NaV channels → muscle paralysis. NOT reversed by neostigmine (AChEI → increases ACh → worsens depolarizing block). Ultra-short duration (~10-15 minutes) → hydrolyzed by plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase). Contraindications: hyperkalemia (burns, crush injury, rhabdomyolysis — succinylcholine → K+ efflux → ↑serum K+ → cardiac arrest), malignant hyperthermia susceptibility (triggers MH in genetically susceptible).

subject: Physiology
stem: What is malignant hyperthermia (MH) and its mechanism?
options: A pharmacogenetic disorder: trigger agents (volatile anesthetics + succinylcholine) → uncontrolled Ca2+ release from skeletal muscle SR (via mutant RyR1 — Ryanodine Receptor 1, gain-of-function mutation) → sustained muscle contraction + hypermetabolism → hyperthermia (>40°C), rigidity, metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuria, ↑CO2; treated with dantrolene (blocks RyR1, reduces Ca2+ release)
Normal response to high doses of anesthetic
explanation: Malignant hyperthermia (MH): autosomal dominant mutation in RYR1 (most common, 70%) or CACNA1S (DHPR/L-type Ca2+ channel). Triggers: all volatile halogenated anesthetics (halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) + succinylcholine. Activation: mutant RyR1 → excessive SR Ca2+ release → sustained muscle contraction + ↑oxidative phosphorylation → ↑heat, ↑CO2, ↑lactate. First sign: ↑EtCO2 (rise in end-tidal CO2), muscle rigidity (especially masseter). Treatment: STOP trigger → 100% O2 → dantrolene (IV, blocks RyR1) → cooling, correct metabolic acidosis, monitor renal function. MH susceptibility test: caffeine-halothane contracture test (CHCT, muscle biopsy).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'omega-3 fatty acids' (EPA, DHA) exert cardiovascular protection by:
options: Reducing triglycerides (via ↓VLDL synthesis and ↑clearance), anti-inflammatory effects (compete with arachidonic acid as COX/LOX substrate → produce less potent prostaglandins and leukotrienes and more resolvins/protectins/maresins), ↓platelet aggregation, ↓blood pressure, anti-arrhythmic (stabilize cardiomyocyte membranes via ion channel modulation)
explanation: Omega-3 FAs (EPA: eicosapentaenoic acid, DHA: docosahexaenoic acid): from fish oil/algae. Key actions: (1) ↓TG (FDA-approved: icosapentaenoic acid [Vascepa] → ↓TG 45% + ↓cardiovascular events in REDUCE-IT trial). (2) Anti-inflammatory: competitively inhibit arachidonic acid metabolism → prostaglandins/leukotrienes from omega-3 series (e.g., PGI3, TXA3) are less potent; promote resolution via resolvins, protectins. (3) Anti-platelet. (4) Membrane effects: ↑membrane fluidity, ↓ion channel excitability (Na+/Ca2+ channels). (5) ↓Adipose inflammation (↑adiponectin).

subject: Physiology
stem: The protein responsible for iron storage in the liver is:
options: Ferritin — the primary intracellular iron storage protein in all cells, especially liver (hepatocytes), spleen (macrophages), bone marrow, intestine; each ferritin molecule stores up to 4500 Fe3+ atoms in its mineral core; serum ferritin reflects body iron stores (1 μg/L ≈ 8 mg stored Fe); low serum ferritin (<12 μg/L) = iron deficiency (most specific); elevated in inflammation, liver disease, malignancy (acute phase reactant)
explanation: Iron storage and transport: Ferritin: soluble, 24-subunit shell (H and L chains), apoferritin + Fe3+ = ferritin. Intracellular iron buffer. Serum ferritin = small amount released → reflects stores. Low ferritin: specific for iron deficiency (even before anemia). High ferritin: iron overload, but also acute phase reactant (infection, inflammation, malignancy → ferritin ↑ despite potentially low iron stores). Hemosiderin: insoluble iron storage (degraded ferritin aggregates in lysosomes) → stains blue with Prussian blue/Perls' stain in bone marrow macrophages, tissue (hemochromatosis → hemosiderin deposits in liver, heart, pancreas, skin, gonads).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which type of collagen is most abundant in the skin?
options: Type I — the most abundant protein in the human body (~90% of body collagen); found in skin, bone, tendon, ligament, cornea, dentin; fibrillar collagen; synthesized from procollagen (triple helix of α1[I]2α2[I]) in fibroblasts → extracellular cleavage by procollagen peptidases → tropocollagen → self-assembles into fibrils → cross-linked by lysyl oxidase
Type III (reticulin — fetal skin, blood vessels)
explanation: Collagen types (mnemonic for boards): Type I (Be FiBrous): Bone, skin, Fibrous tissue, tendons, dentin — most abundant in body. Type II: Cartilage (only). Type III: Reticulin (fetal skin, BV walls, reticular fibers of lymphoid organs). Type IV: Basement membranes (basal lamina → Alport syndrome: COL4A3/A4/A5 mutation → nephritis, deafness, eye abnormalities; Goodpasture: anti-GBM antibodies against α3[IV] collagen). Type VII: Epidermolysis bullosa. Osteogenesis imperfecta: type I collagen defects.

subject: Physiology
stem: Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is influenced most significantly by:
options: Lean body mass (fat-free mass, skeletal muscle) — muscle is the most metabolically active tissue at rest (accounts for ~40% of RMR despite not being the highest per-kg rate); also: thyroid status (T3 directly regulates UCP and mitochondrial activity → hypothyroidism ↓RMR, hyperthyroidism ↑RMR), catecholamines, body surface area
explanation: Basal/resting metabolic rate (BMR/RMR): energy expenditure at rest to maintain basic physiological functions. Normal adult: ~1600-2000 kcal/day. Determinants: Lean body mass (LBM) — greatest absolute contributor to RMR (more muscle → higher RMR). Thyroid hormones (T3 → ↑Na+/K+ ATPase expression, ↑mitochondrial uncoupling, ↑oxidative metabolism). Body size and surface area. Age (decreases ~2% per decade after 30 due to ↓LBM). Sex (males have higher RMR due to ↑LBM). Fever: ↑10% per 1°C rise in temperature.

subject: Physiology
stem: Nitric oxide (NO): which cells produce the endothelial NOS (eNOS)?
options: Vascular endothelial cells — eNOS (NOS3, constitutive, Ca2+-calmodulin activated): activated by fluid shear stress (most physiological stimulus), ACh (M3 receptors on endothelium → Ca2+ → eNOS), bradykinin, VEGF, estrogen; produces NO in pulsatile fashion → relaxes vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation; essential for normal vascular tone
explanation: NOS isoforms: (1) nNOS (NOS1): neurons, skeletal muscle, macula densa; constitutive, Ca2+-dependent; role in synaptic plasticity, penile erection (also neurogenic NO), TGF. (2) eNOS (NOS3): endothelium; constitutive, Ca2+-dependent; activated by shear stress (most important physiological stimulus), bradykinin, ACh, VEGF, estrogen, insulin; tonically produced NO → vasodilation, inhibits platelet aggregation and adhesion, inhibits VSMC proliferation. (3) iNOS (NOS2): macrophages, hepatocytes, smooth muscle; inducible by LPS + cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IFN-γ); produces large amounts of NO → cytotoxic (kills bacteria/tumors) but also mediates septic shock vasodilation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cytokine is most responsible for the fever response in infection?
options: IL-1β and IL-6 (and TNF-α) — produced by activated macrophages/monocytes in response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) → reach the hypothalamus → COX-2 → PGE2 → EP3 receptors on POAH → ↑set point → fever; IL-6 is also the major inducer of acute phase proteins (CRP, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, serum amyloid A) from the liver
explanation: Pyrogenic cytokines: IL-1β (macrophage-derived, acts on POAH), TNF-α (endogenous pyrogen), IL-6 (most potent inducer of hepatic acute phase proteins: CRP, fibrinogen, haptoglobin, SAA, ferritin ↑; albumin, transferrin ↓ = 'negative acute phase proteins'). Fever is adaptive: ↑temperature inhibits bacterial growth, ↑phagocytic activity, ↑antibody synthesis, ↑IFN efficacy. IL-1 also: activates T cells (co-stimulatory with antigen), promotes B cell growth, causes muscle catabolism, ↑ACTH (stress response). Antipyretics: NSAIDs, acetaminophen (inhibit COX → ↓PGE2 → lower set point).

subject: Physiology
stem: Lipid-soluble vs. water-soluble vitamins: which vitamins are NOT stored in the body for long periods?
options: Water-soluble vitamins (B complex vitamins and vitamin C) — these are not stored in large amounts and need regular dietary intake; excess is excreted in urine; exceptions: B12 is stored in the liver for 3-5 years; folic acid stored for 3-4 months
explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K): stored in fat and liver; toxicity from excess accumulation; do not require daily intake. Water-soluble (B vitamins + C): minimal storage (exception: B12 stored in liver 3-5 years). Deficiency: B1 (thiamine → Wernicke's encephalopathy, wet beriberi), B2 (riboflavin → corneal vascularization, angular stomatitis), B3 (niacin → pellagra: 3 Ds — Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia), B6 (pyridoxine → sideroblastic anemia, peripheral neuropathy), B12 (cobalamin → megaloblastic anemia + SCD), folate (megaloblastic, NTDs), C (ascorbic acid → scurvy).

subject: Physiology
stem: The role of the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) in hepatocytes:
options: Drug and toxin detoxification via cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYPs, e.g., CYP3A4 → oxidation, hydroxylation of hydrophobic drugs); also: steroid hormone synthesis, fatty acid metabolism, bile acid synthesis, glycogen metabolism (G6Pase is in SER membrane), glucuronidation
explanation: SER functions (cell type dependent): Hepatocytes: drug metabolism (Phase I: CYP450 oxidation; Phase II: conjugation — glucuronidation, sulfation, glutathione). Steroid hormone-producing cells (adrenal, gonads): steroid synthesis (CYP enzymes). Muscle cells: SR (sarcoplasmic reticulum) = Ca2+ storage and release for contraction. Intestinal cells: lipid absorption and processing. B cells: RER (rough ER) → antibody synthesis. RER: protein synthesis, co-translational modification, protein folding (chaperones: BiP/GRP78), disulfide bond formation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cells produce type I interferon (IFN-α/β) in the innate immune response to viral infection?
options: Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs, formerly known as natural IFN-producing cells) are the most potent producers of type I IFN; ALL nucleated cells can produce IFN-β when infected by virus (dsRNA activates TLR3 in endosomes, or RIG-I/MDA5 in cytosol → IRF3/7 → IFN-β gene)
explanation: Type I interferons (IFN-α/β): produced by all nucleated cells (especially pDCs) in response to viral infection. Mechanism: viral dsRNA → TLR3 (endosomal, adaptor TRIF) or RIG-I/MDA5 (cytosolic RNA helicases, adaptor MAVS/IPS-1) → TBK1 → IRF3/7 phosphorylation → IFN-α/β gene transcription. IFN-α/β actions: (1) Autocrine/paracrine: JAK1/TYK2 → STAT1/STAT2 → ISGs (interferon-stimulated genes) → antiviral state (↑PKR, ↑OAS-RNase L, ↑Mx proteins → degrade viral RNA, inhibit viral translation). (2) Activate NK cells. (3) Upregulate MHC I on infected cells → better CTL recognition.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'second wind' phenomenon in exercise is due to:
options: Enhanced fat utilization: after the initial depletion of glycogen from fast-twitch fibers (and associated fatigue, anaerobic lactate accumulation), the cardiovascular system adapts → ↑O2 delivery → slow-twitch fibers switch to beta-oxidation of fatty acids → more sustainable energy → relief of symptoms ('second wind') after approximately 10-20 minutes of sustained aerobic exercise
Increased muscle glycogen synthesis during exercise
explanation: Second wind: after initial exercise onset (oxygen deficit, transient reliance on anaerobic glycolysis → lactate, fatigue), the cardiorespiratory system catches up: ↑CO, ↑O2 delivery, shift to aerobic metabolism (↑fat oxidation in slow-twitch fibers, ↑mitochondrial respiration), ↑endorphin release (reduces pain perception). In patients with metabolic myopathies (McArdle disease: myophosphorylase deficiency → cannot break down glycogen → early muscle cramps → second wind after 10-15 min when FFA mobilization compensates): 'ischemic' forearm exercise test → no lactate rise (cannot break down glycogen → no pyruvate → no lactate).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cerebral autoregulation: at what blood pressure range is it intact?
options: MAP 60–150 mmHg (approximately): cerebral blood flow is kept constant despite changes in MAP within this range (myogenic autoregulation + metabolic); below 60 mmHg: CBF falls (ischemia); above 150-160 mmHg: breakthrough → acute hypertensive encephalopathy, PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome)
explanation: Cerebral autoregulation: CBF maintained at ~50 mL/100g/min (normal). MAP range: 60-150 mmHg. Loss of autoregulation: chronic hypertension shifts the curve rightward (autoregulates at higher MAPs but more vulnerable to hypotension); acute severe hypertension → breakthrough → PRES. CO2 is a powerful regulator: ↑PaCO2 → cerebral vasodilation (↑CBF); ↓PaCO2 → vasoconstriction (↓CBF). Used clinically: therapeutic hyperventilation in acute ↑ICP (↓CO2 → vasoconstriction → ↓cerebral blood volume → ↓ICP), but only temporary (metabolic compensation reduces HCO3- → resets pH).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis' (SRS-A) is now known to be:
options: Cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) — produced from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway (5-LOX + FLAP → LTA4 → conjugated with glutathione → LTC4 → cleaved → LTD4 → LTE4); most potent bronchoconstrictors (1000× more potent than histamine), cause mucus hypersecretion, ↑vascular permeability, mucosal edema; blocked by cysteinyl leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast)
explanation: Cysteinyl leukotrienes (CysLTs): LTC4/LTD4/LTE4, produced by mast cells, eosinophils, basophils via 5-LOX pathway. Arachidonic acid → 5-HPETE → LTA4 → LTC4 (+ glutathione via LTC4S) → LTD4 (remove Glu) → LTE4 (remove Gly). CysLT1 receptor: on bronchial smooth muscle → powerful bronchospasm (>>histamine), mucus, mucosal edema. LTB4 (dihydroxyacid, not cysteinyl): potent neutrophil chemoattractant. Montelukast (Singulair): CysLT1 receptor antagonist → used in asthma and allergic rhinitis. Zileuton: 5-LOX inhibitor (reduces all leukotrienes).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which vitamin acts as a coenzyme in transamination reactions?
options: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) — in its active form pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), acts as coenzyme for: aminotransferases (transaminases: AST, ALT → transfers amino groups), amino acid decarboxylases (histidine → histamine; DOPA → dopamine; tryptophan → serotonin → melatonin; glutamate → GABA), delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase (heme synthesis), glycogen phosphorylase
explanation: PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, active B6): most versatile enzyme cofactor in amino acid metabolism. Reactions: (1) Transamination: amino acid + α-ketoglutarate → α-keto acid + glutamate (ALT: alanine + αKG → pyruvate + Glu; AST: aspartate + αKG → OAA + Glu). (2) Decarboxylation: aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DOPA → dopamine; 5-HTP → serotonin; histidine → histamine; GABA synthesis). (3) ALA synthase (glycine + succinyl-CoA → ALA, first step of heme synthesis in mitochondria — inhibited by heme, induced by steroids). B6 deficiency: peripheral neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia (impaired heme synthesis), glossitis, stomatitis, seborrheic dermatitis. Isoniazid → B6 deficiency (via competitive antagonism).

subject: Physiology
stem: The carotid body chemoreceptors respond primarily to:
options: ↓PaO2 below 60 mmHg (steep response below 60), ↑PaCO2, ↑[H+] (↓pH), and ↓blood flow (from any cause — anemia, CO poisoning, cyanide poisoning — the sensor detects low O2 delivery, not just low PaO2)
explanation: Carotid body (glomus type I cells, neural crest-derived): O2 sensing via K+ channel inhibition (Kv3.3, TASK-type K+ channels: ↓PO2 → channels close → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → vesicle release of dopamine, ATP, ACh → sinus nerve [CN IX] afferents). High-sensitivity to PO2 below 60 mmHg (sigmoid relationship). Also responds to: ↑PaCO2 (carbonic anhydrase in glomus cells), ↑[H+], ↓flow (low O2 delivery). CO poisoning: PaO2 normal, SpO2 falsely normal (pulse ox reads CO-Hb as Oxy-Hb) → no peripheral chemoreceptor response → treatment: 100% O2 or hyperbaric O2.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'Bohr effect': how does an increase in CO2 affect oxygen-hemoglobin binding?
options: ↑CO2 (or ↑H+ from carbonic acid) → stabilizes the deoxy conformation (T-state) of hemoglobin → ↓O2 affinity → right shift of ODC → ↑P50 → Hb releases more O2 to metabolically active tissues (where CO2 is high); reverse: in lungs, CO2 is low → ↑O2 affinity → ↑O2 loading
Only affects CO2 transport, not O2
explanation: Bohr effect (Christian Bohr, 1904): ↑CO2 or ↑H+ (acidosis) → protonation of histidine residues (His-146β especially) → favors salt bridges in T-state deoxy-Hb → ↓O2 affinity. Physiological significance: exercising muscle: ↑CO2, ↑H+ (lactic acid), ↑temperature → right shift → ↑O2 unloading to muscle. Lung: CO2 blown off → ↓CO2, ↑pH → left shift → ↑O2 loading. 2,3-DPG also causes right shift but by a different mechanism (binds between β-chains, stabilizes T-state). CO: causes left shift (carboxyhemoglobin stabilizes R-state → higher O2 affinity → O2 is trapped, not released → tissue hypoxia despite SpO2 apparently normal).

subject: Physiology
stem: The cardiac output increases with all EXCEPT:
explanation: CO determinants: Increased CO: exercise, pregnancy, AV fistula, hyperthyroidism, Paget's disease, beriberi, anemia (↓Hb → ↓O2 carrying capacity → compensatory ↑CO). Decreased CO: cardiomyopathy, severe bradycardia/tachycardia, hypovolemia, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, hypothyroidism (↓T3 → ↓heart rate + ↓contractility + ↑SVR → ↓CO despite ↑afterload).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cardiac structure generates the normal intrinsic pacemaker rate of 60–100 bpm?
options: Sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium (near the junction of the SVC and right atrium) — fastest intrinsic automaticity (60–100 bpm) due to the steepest phase 4 spontaneous depolarization driven by If + ICaT
explanation: Pacemaker hierarchy (overdrive suppression): SA node → AV node → Bundle branches → Purkinje/ventricular. Each lower pacemaker is suppressed by the faster SA node rate (overdrive suppression via Na+ accumulation → hyperpolarization). If SA node fails: AV node takes over at 40-60 bpm (junctional rhythm). If AV node fails: ventricular escape at 20-40 bpm. SA node blood supply: SA nodal artery from RCA (60%) or LCX (40%).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which reflex can slow HR during SVT and is used in clinical management?
options: Vagal maneuvers — carotid sinus massage (CSM: stimulates carotid sinus baroreceptors → ↑vagal output → ↑AV nodal block → ↓HR/terminates SVT); also Valsalva maneuver (phase 4 → ↑BP → baroreceptor → ↑vagal tone), Diver's reflex (cold water on face → ↑vagal → ↓HR)
explanation: Vagal maneuvers for SVT (AVNRT, AVRT): (1) Valsalva (forced expiration against closed glottis): Phase 1: ↑intrathoracic pressure → ↑venous return → brief ↑BP → vagal. Phase 2: ↑intrathoracic pressure → ↓venous return → ↓CO → ↓BP → reflex tachycardia. Phase 3 (release): ↑venous return. Phase 4: ↑CO → baroreceptor → vagal. 'Modified Valsalva' (legs up during phase 4) + adenosine (first-line pharmacological). (2) CSM: gently massage carotid sinus for 5-10 seconds (CI: bruit, cerebrovascular disease).

subject: Physiology
stem: Aortic stenosis (AS) physiological consequences: which cardiac chamber hypertrophies?
options: Left ventricle (LVH, concentric) — because the LV must generate higher pressure to overcome the fixed obstruction (↑afterload) → ↑wall stress → concentric hypertrophy (↑wall thickness, ↓cavity size, ↑diastolic stiffness); classic triad of symptoms: angina (↑O2 demand + impaired coronary filling), syncope (effort-induced), heart failure (decompensated LVH)
explanation: AS physiology: Obstruction to LV outflow → pressure overload → ↑LV systolic pressure (may reach 200-300 mmHg) → ↑wall stress (Laplace) → concentric LVH (↑wall thickness normalizes wall stress). Diastolic dysfunction (stiff LV → ↑LVEDP → ↑LA pressure). Auscultation: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at right 2nd ICS, radiates to carotids, slow-rising/low-volume pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus). Severity: mean gradient >40 mmHg or AVA <1.0 cm² = severe. Intervention: SAVR (surgical) or TAVR (transcatheter).

subject: Physiology
stem: In mitral regurgitation (MR), which volume overloads the left atrium?
options: Blood from LV regurgitating backward into LA during systole (MR) → ↑LA pressure and volume → LA dilatation → pulmonary venous hypertension → pulmonary edema in acute severe MR; chronic MR → LA enlarges to accommodate (↓pressure despite ↑volume) → AF (from LA stretch)
None — MR is a left ventricular problem only
explanation: MR physiology: During systole, incompetent mitral valve → regurgitant volume into LA → ↑LA preload. LV: eccentric hypertrophy (volume overload from regurgitant blood returning via pulmonary veins → ↑LV EDV). Chronic MR: LA enlarges (↑compliance) → AF (LA stretch → fibrosis → re-entry). Acute severe MR (chordae rupture, papillary muscle infarct): LA suddenly overloaded (non-dilated, non-compliant LA) → acute ↑LA pressure → pulmonary edema. Murmur: pansystolic (holosystolic), apex → axilla, with S3 if severe. Cause of apex beat displacement.

subject: Physiology
stem: The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm and arises from:
options: C3, C4, C5 (mnemonic: C3, C4, C5 keeps the diaphragm alive); the phrenic nerve is the sole motor nerve to the diaphragm (also sensory to central diaphragm, pericardium, and mediastinal pleura); injury → ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis (elevated on CXR, sniff test positive)
explanation: Phrenic nerve: arises from anterior rami C3, C4 (main), C5. Descends through the thorax (anterior to lung hilum, posterior to heart) → innervates ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Clinical: C3-C5 injury → diaphragm paralysis. Paradoxical movement: with inspiration, the paralyzed hemidiaphragm rises (passive, pushed by abdominal viscera and decreased intrathoracic pressure). Referred pain from diaphragmatic irritation → shoulder tip (C3-C5 dermatome = shoulder). Causes of elevated hemidiaphragm: phrenic nerve palsy, lung collapse/atelectasis, liver/subphrenic abscess (right), hepatomegaly, phrenic nerve compression (mediastinal tumor, aortic aneurysm).

subject: Physiology
stem: Spirometry: which measurement requires a body plethysmograph (or gas dilution) and cannot be measured by spirometry alone?
options: Residual volume (RV) and TLC — because RV is the volume remaining after maximal expiration (the patient cannot breathe it out into the spirometer); measured by helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography; all volumes containing RV require these techniques
explanation: Spirometric limitations: Spirometry can measure: TV, IRV, ERV, VC, FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, PEFR, MVV (maximal voluntary ventilation). Cannot measure: RV, FRC, TLC (require body plethysmography or gas dilution — these volumes contain the portion of gas that never leaves the lung during max expiration). Body plethysmography: patient seated in sealed box, panting against closed shutter → pressure changes in box and airways → Boyle's law → calculate thoracic gas volume (TGV = FRC). Helium dilution: dilution of a known amount of He within the breathing circuit → FRC calculation.

subject: Physiology
stem: High altitude physiology: which compensatory mechanism occurs FIRST?
options: Hyperventilation (↑RR immediately) — ↓PaO2 at altitude → stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid body) → ↑ventilation → ↓PaCO2 → respiratory alkalosis; the respiratory alkalosis then limits further hyperventilation; over 3-5 days: renal compensation → ↓HCO3- excretion → corrects pH → allows further hyperventilation to continue ('ventilatory acclimatization')
↑Heart rate (secondary to catecholamines, immediate but ↑ventilation is the primary first response)
explanation: Acclimatization to high altitude: Immediate (seconds-minutes): carotid body → ↑ventilation → ↑PaO2 (partly) + ↓PaCO2 → respiratory alkalosis. Hours: ↑2,3-DPG → right shift ODC → ↑O2 unloading. Days (3-5): renal compensation (↓HCO3-) → pH normalizes → breathing drive can increase further (removes inhibitory effect of alkalosis on central chemoreceptors). Weeks: ↑EPO → ↑RBC mass (polycythemia) → ↑Hb → ↑O2 carrying capacity. Chronic: ↑lung diffusion surface, ↑capillarity of muscles.

subject: Physiology
stem: Anatomical dead space: which instrument measures it?
options: Fowler's method (single-breath nitrogen washout): breathe in 100% O2 → exhale slowly → N2 concentration monitored; Phase I (dead space = 100% O2, no N2) → Phase II (transitional mixing) → Phase III (alveolar plateau from N2); where Phase III begins = anatomical dead space (~150 mL); distinct from physiological dead space (measured by Bohr equation using PaCO2)
explanation: Fowler's single-breath N2 washout: measure anatomical dead space. Subject inhales single breath of 100% O2 → exhales slowly while N2 monitored at the mouth. Phase 1: pure O2 from dead space (N2 = 0%). Phase 2: transition (dead space gas mixes with alveolar gas → N2 rises). Phase 3: pure alveolar gas plateau. Anatomical dead space = volume of gas exhaled before the 50% N2 point on the rising portion (Phase 2). Normal: ~150 mL (2.2 mL/kg). FRC is measured separately by a multiple-breath nitrogen washout (breathe O2 until N2 washed out, calculate volume from total N2 exhaled).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which pituitary hormone is produced by the same corticotroph cell as ACTH?
options: Alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), β-endorphin, and CLIP (corticotropin-like intermediate lobe peptide) — all derived from the POMC (pro-opiomelanocortin) precursor molecule, which is cleaved by prohormone convertases 1 and 2 in corticotroph cells; ACTH itself cleaves to α-MSH + CLIP
explanation: POMC (pro-opiomelanocortin): 31 kDa precursor, synthesized in corticotrophs of anterior pituitary (also in hypothalamus and skin). PC1 cleaves → ACTH + β-LPH. ACTH → cleaved by PC2 in the intermediate lobe (in animals) → α-MSH + CLIP. β-LPH → β-endorphin. Relevance: in Addison's disease or Nelson's syndrome (↑ACTH production) → proportional increase in α-MSH → hyperpigmentation (both ACTH and α-MSH activate MCR-1 on melanocytes → ↑melanin). Ectopic ACTH from lung tumors → very high ACTH → severe hyperpigmentation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Estrogen's mechanism of action at the cellular level:
options: Nuclear receptor: estradiol (lipid-soluble) → diffuses across plasma membrane → binds to intracellular ERα or ERβ (estrogen receptor) → receptor dimerizes → binds to estrogen response elements (EREs) in DNA → recruits co-activators → transcription of estrogen-responsive genes (e.g., pS2/TFF1, progesterone receptor, lactoferrin)
explanation: Sex hormone receptors (nuclear receptor superfamily): ERα (ESR1, high in uterus, liver, breast, bone) and ERβ (ESR2, ovary, brain, vascular endothelium, GI). Steroid hormones (lipid-soluble): diffuse across membrane → bind nuclear receptors → heat-shock proteins dissociate → receptor-ligand complex dimerizes → nuclear translocation → bind to hormone response elements (HREs) in promoters → recruit coactivators/corepressors → activate or repress transcription. Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs): tamoxifen (ER antagonist in breast, ERα agonist in uterus + bone → used for ER+ breast cancer), raloxifene (antagonist in breast + uterus, agonist in bone → osteoporosis).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which insulin secretagogue acts independently of glucose (may cause hypoglycemia even when glucose is low)?
options: Sulfonylureas (glibenclamide, glipizide, glimepiride) — bind to SUR1 (sulfonylurea receptor 1, regulatory subunit of KATP channel) → KATP channel closes → membrane depolarization → L-type Ca2+ channel opens → insulin secretion, regardless of blood glucose level → risk of hypoglycemia, especially with renal impairment (↑drug accumulation)
explanation: Antidiabetic drugs and hypoglycemia risk: HIGH risk: insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides (repaglinide — same mechanism as SU but shorter acting). LOW risk: metformin (↓hepatic glucose output, insulin-sensitizer), GLP-1 agonists (glucose-dependent → no effect when glucose low), DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors (glycosuric only when blood glucose is elevated), thiazolidinediones (TZDs, PPAR-γ agonists → insulin sensitizers). Sulfonylurea mechanism: SUR1 (ABCC8, ABC transporter) + Kir6.2 (KCNJ11) = KATP channel complex → SU binds SUR1 → closes K+ channel → depolarization → insulin release.

subject: Physiology
stem: Grave's disease: what is the direct cause of hyperthyroidism?
options: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI/TRAb): IgG autoantibodies that bind and activate TSH receptor (TSHR) on thyroid follicular cells → constitutive activation of Gs/cAMP pathway → ↑T3/T4 synthesis and secretion → hyperthyroidism; TSHR is also on orbital fibroblasts → Graves' ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos, proptosis from retroorbital glycosaminoglycan accumulation)
explanation: Graves' disease: most common cause of hyperthyroidism (especially in women 20-40 years). Thyroid triad: diffuse toxic goiter + ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos, lid lag, lid retraction) + pretibial myxedema. Pathology: TRAb (thyroid receptor antibodies) stimulate TSHR → ↑cAMP → ↑T3/T4. Graves' ophthalmopathy: TSHR on orbital fibroblasts → activation → cytokine release → GAG accumulation → edema + orbital fat expansion → proptosis. Labs: ↓TSH, ↑free T3/T4, ↑TRAb, ↑RAIU (radioactive iodine uptake — diffuse, vs. toxic adenoma/nodule with focal uptake). Treatment: antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil, carbimazole), radioiodine, surgery.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction and acts on nicotinic receptors?
options: Acetylcholine (ACh): stored in vesicles in the axon terminal → released by exocytosis (Ca2+-dependent, triggered by AP → Ca2+ enters via P/Q-type VGCCs → vesicle fusion → ACh exocytosis) → binds Nm (muscle-type nicotinic AChR, pentamer with 2α1-β-γ/ε-δ subunits) → Na+/K+ influx → end-plate potential (EPP) → triggers AP in muscle
explanation: NMJ transmission: Motor AP → presynaptic terminal → opens P/Q-type Ca2+ channels → Ca2+ triggers ACh vesicle exocytosis (SNARE proteins: SNAP-25, synaptobrevin, syntaxin) → ACh diffuses across the synaptic cleft → binds nicotinic AChRs (Nm subtype) on the motor end-plate → opens Na+/K+ channel (non-selective cation) → EPP depolarization → triggers surrounding NaV channels → muscle AP. Termination: AChE hydrolyzes ACh → choline (re-uptaken by ChAT) + acetate. Botulinum toxin: cleaves SNAREs → blocks ACh release. Tetanus toxin: blocks GABA/glycine in spinal cord.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cell type synthesizes myelin in the peripheral nervous system?
options: Schwann cells — each Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one PNS axon (unlike oligodendrocytes which each myelinate multiple CNS axon segments); Schwann cells also produce growth factors (NGF, BDNF) and facilitate PNS regeneration after injury
explanation: Myelinating cells: CNS: oligodendrocytes (each myelinates up to 50 axon segments; cannot regenerate after damage → multiple sclerosis). PNS: Schwann cells (one per internode; regenerate after injury → guides axon regrowth; Cajal bands facilitate regeneration). Node of Ranvier: gap between myelin sheaths (~1 μm) → high Na+ channel density → saltatory conduction. Demyelinating diseases: PNS — Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), CIDP, CMT type 1 (PMP22 mutation); CNS — MS, PML, central pontine myelinolysis.

subject: Physiology
stem: The blood-brain barrier (BBB): what composes it?
options: Tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells (claudin-5, occludin, ZO-1), supported by astrocyte endfeet (perivascular), pericytes, and the basement membrane — forms a selective barrier; lipid-soluble molecules (O2, CO2, ethanol, steroid hormones, most anesthetics) cross freely; ion transport proteins regulate ionic composition
explanation: BBB composition: Endothelial cells with tight junctions (no fenestrations unlike most systemic capillaries) → restrict paracellular transport. Astrocyte endfeet: surround capillaries → induce and maintain BBB properties via TGF-β, GDNF, Ang1. Pericytes: regulate capillary tone. Transport mechanisms: passive diffusion (lipid-soluble: CO2, O2, ethanol, steroid hormones, most anesthetics). Carrier-mediated: GLUT1 (glucose, normal plasma 5 mM → brain 3 mM), amino acid transporters. Active efflux pumps: P-glycoprotein (MDR1), BCRP → pump many drugs out of brain (explains CNS drug resistance). Breakdown in: inflammation, trauma, hyperosmolarity.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the glymphatic system?
options: Lymphatic vessels within the brain parenchyma

The brain's pseudo-lymphatic waste clearance system: CSF from the subarachnoid space enters the brain along para-arterial (periarterial) spaces → driven by AQP4 (aquaporin-4) on astrocyte endfeet → convective flow through brain interstitium → exits along para-venous spaces → drains into lymphatics (cervical lymph nodes); clears metabolic waste (β-amyloid, tau, lactate); most active during sleep
explanation: Glymphatic system (glial-lymphatic, Maiken Nedergaard, 2013): CSF enters perivascular space via AQP4 on astrocyte endfeet → sweeps through brain interstitium → exits via perivenous space → cervical lymphatics → venous drainage. Key waste cleared: β-amyloid (Aβ), tau, lactate, CO2. Sleep: glymphatic flow ↑10× during sleep (neuronal activity ↓ → brain cells shrink slightly → more interstitial space for flow). Relevance: chronic sleep deprivation → ↑Aβ accumulation → ↑Alzheimer's risk. Traumatic brain injury: impaired glymphatic flow → ↑CTE risk.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which amino acid is most important for transporting nitrogen from peripheral tissues to the liver?
options: Alanine (alanine-glucose cycle / Cahill cycle): muscle catabolism → amino acids → transamination with pyruvate (from glycolysis) → alanine + α-ketoacid; alanine travels in blood to liver → liver: alanine + α-ketoglutarate (ALT/GPT reaction) → pyruvate + glutamate; pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → glucose → back to muscle; glutamate → urea cycle (glutamate → α-ketoglutarate + NH3 → carbamoyl phosphate → urea cycle)
Glutamine (transport of NH3 from brain and other tissues, not primary nitrogen carrier for muscle)
explanation: Glucose-alanine cycle (Cahill cycle): Fasting/stress → muscle protein breakdown → amino acids → transamination (ALT in muscle: pyruvate + glutamate → alanine + α-KG) → alanine released into blood → liver (ALT in liver: alanine + α-KG → pyruvate + glutamate) → pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → glucose → back to muscle. Net: glucose is synthesized from muscle protein-derived carbon (alanine = pyruvate + N). Nitrogen removed as urea. Glutamine: primary nitrogen carrier from brain and intestine → liver and kidney (converted to glutamate + NH3 → enters urea cycle / excreted as NH4+).

subject: Physiology
stem: Bilirubin metabolism: conjugated vs. unconjugated — which is water-soluble and can be excreted by the kidney?
options: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin — after hepatic glucuronidation (UGT1A1: bilirubin + UDP-glucuronic acid → bilirubin monoglucuronide or diglucuronide); conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble → excreted in bile → intestine → urobilinogen (by bacteria) → stercobilin (feces, brown) + absorbed urobilinogen → urobilin (urine, yellow); can also be excreted directly in urine (bilirubin in urine = conjugated = dark urine in obstructive jaundice/hepatocellular jaundice)
explanation: Bilirubin metabolism: Heme → biliverdin (biliverdin reductase) → unconjugated bilirubin (UCB, indirect, fat-soluble, albumin-bound, NOT in urine, toxic to brain = kernicterus in neonates). UCB → liver (OATP1B1/B3 uptake → UGT1A1 conjugation → bilirubin glucuronide, water-soluble). Canalicular MRP2 excretion → bile → gut → urobilinogen (colonic bacteria) → stercobilin (feces). ~20% urobilinogen reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation) → liver re-excreted + small amount in urine (urobilin). Jaundice types: pre-hepatic (↑UCB, ↑urobilinogen in urine/feces), hepatic (↑both), post-hepatic/obstructive (↑conjugated bilirubin in blood and urine, ↓fecal urobilinogen = pale stools + dark urine).

subject: Physiology
stem: Fasting and starvation: what is the primary fuel source for the brain after several days of fasting?
options: Ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate) — by 3-4 days of fasting, liver ketogenesis from FA oxidation → blood ketone levels rise → brain (normally impermeable to FFA) → upregulates monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1) → uses ketones as primary fuel (may meet 60-70% of brain energy needs) → spares glucose → reduces muscle proteolysis (less gluconeogenesis needed)
explanation: Fuel hierarchy during starvation: First 4-6 hours: glycogen (liver 100g, muscle 400g). 6-16 hours: gluconeogenesis (liver: from alanine, glycerol, lactate). 16-72 hours: ↑lipolysis → ↑FFA → β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → ketogenesis (liver; accumulates because TCA cannot use all acetyl-CoA → condenses → acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + β-hydroxybutyrate). Day 3+ fasting: brain increasingly uses ketones → glucose-sparing effect → ↓gluconeogenesis → ↓muscle proteolysis. True starvation (>4 weeks): basal metabolic rate ↓ (T3 ↓), gluconeogenesis ↓, near-complete ketone utilization by brain.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which enzyme defect in the red blood cell causes oxidative hemolysis with Heinz body formation in G6PD deficiency?
options: G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase): in the pentose phosphate pathway → G6P + NADP+ → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH; NADPH is the primary reducing agent in RBCs → maintains glutathione in reduced form (GSH) via glutathione reductase; absence of G6PD → ↓GSH → oxidized Hb = Heinz bodies (precipitated, denatured Hb) → mechanical removal by spleen (bite cells) + intravascular hemolysis
explanation: G6PD and oxidative protection: G6PD → NADPH → glutathione reductase (GSSG → GSH) → glutathione peroxidase (H2O2 + 2GSH → GSSG + 2H2O; also reduces lipid hydroperoxides). Without G6PD → ↓NADPH → ↓GSH → oxidative stress (H2O2 from metabolism, or from drugs/infections) → Hb oxidized → methemoglobin → precipitates as Heinz bodies → spleen removes inclusions (bite cells) → intravascular hemolysis. G6PD favism: fava beans contain vicine/convicine → oxidants. Diagnosis: enzyme assay (do after hemolytic episode — reticulocytes have higher G6PD, may give false normal).

subject: Physiology
stem: Thalassemia: β-thalassemia major (Cooley's anemia) — what is the pathophysiology?
options: Decreased hemoglobin A2 and fetal hemoglobin

Absent or markedly reduced β-globin chains → ↑α-globin chains (unpaired) → α4 aggregates (insoluble) → precipitate in RBC precursors → ineffective erythropoiesis (intracellular RBC destruction in bone marrow = intramedullar hemolysis = 'ineffective erythropoiesis') + peripheral hemolysis → severe anemia → ↑EPO → bone marrow expansion (facial bossing, 'hair-on-end' skull X-ray) + iron overload (even without transfusion, due to ↑GI absorption from high EPO/↓hepcidin)
explanation: β-Thalassemia major: HbA virtually absent (β0/β0 or severe β+/β0). Excess α-chains → oxidized → Heinz bodies → membrane damage → hemolysis (extravascular in spleen). Ineffective erythropoiesis: erythroblasts destroyed in marrow before maturation → ↑iron absorption (↓hepcidin due to high erythropoietic drive via erythroferrone) → iron overload (liver, heart, endocrine glands — secondary hemochromatosis). Treatment: regular transfusions + iron chelation (deferoxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone). Curative: allogeneic HSCT. Bone marrow expansion: hepatosplenomegaly, frontal bossing, maxillary hyperplasia.

subject: Physiology
stem: von Willebrand disease (vWD): what is the most common type?
options: Type 1 (70-80% of cases) — partial quantitative deficiency of structurally normal vWF; autosomal dominant; mild bleeding tendency (epistaxis, menorrhagia, bruising, prolonged bleeding after dental procedures); prolonged bleeding time + prolonged aPTT (vWF carries factor VIII, so ↓vWF → ↓factor VIII → ↑aPTT); normal PT
explanation: vWD overview: vWF is produced by endothelial cells (Weibel-Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes (α-granules). Functions: (1) bridges platelet GPIb to subendothelial collagen at high shear rates; (2) carrier for factor VIII (protects from degradation). Lab: prolonged bleeding time (primary hemostasis affected), prolonged aPTT (↓FVIII), normal PT. Types: Type 1 (partial quantitative ↓, most common, autosomal dominant). Type 2A/2B/2M/2N (qualitative). Type 3 (complete absence, autosomal recessive, severe). Treatment: DDAVP (releases vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, works for type 1) or vWF concentrates.

subject: Physiology
stem: The P-450 system: which is the most important CYP for drug metabolism in the liver?
options: CYP3A4 — accounts for ~30-40% of all hepatic CYP enzymes and metabolizes ~50% of clinically used drugs; induced by: rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St. John's Wort (→ ↓drug levels); inhibited by: grapefruit juice (furanocoumarins), erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, diltiazem, verapamil (→ ↑drug levels → toxicity)
explanation: CYP3A4 (most abundant hepatic CYP): major metabolizer of: benzodiazepines, Ca2+ channel blockers (nifedipine, amlodipine, diltiazem — also inhibitor), statins (lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin), tacrolimus, cyclosporine, protease inhibitors, buspirone, ondansetron, midazolam, codeine (to morphine via CYP2D6 also), many others. Grapefruit juice (furanocoumarins, e.g., bergamottin) → irreversibly inhibit CYP3A4 → ↑[drug] → ↑toxicity risk. Practical: check CYP3A4 interactions for all patients starting new drugs.

subject: Physiology
stem: Pinocytosis vs. phagocytosis vs. receptor-mediated endocytosis: which is used for LDL uptake?
options: Receptor-mediated endocytosis (RME): LDL particles bind LDL receptors (LDLR, a coated pit receptor) → LDLR-LDL complex clusters in clathrin-coated pits → membrane invagination → endosome → lysosome (acid lipase cleaves cholesteryl esters → free cholesterol + FAs) → LDLR recycled to surface; familial hypercholesterolemia: LDLR loss-of-function → ↓LDL uptake → ↑serum LDL
explanation: Receptor-mediated endocytosis: LDL pathway (Brown and Goldstein, Nobel 1985): LDL → LDLR (coated pit) → clathrin-coated vesicle → early endosome (pH drop → LDLR releases LDL) → LDLR recycles to membrane → LDL → late endosome → lysosome → free cholesterol (↑ACAT → cholesteryl ester storage; ↓HMGCR → ↓endogenous synthesis; ↓LDLR → ↓more uptake — feedback). Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH): autosomal dominant LDLR mutation → ↓LDL clearance → ↑serum LDL → premature atherosclerosis. Statin: ↓intracellular cholesterol → SREBP-2 → ↑LDLR → ↑LDL clearance.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'zona glomerulosa' of the adrenal cortex lacks which enzyme?
options: CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase) — the zona glomerulosa LACKS 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1); therefore it CANNOT synthesize cortisol or sex steroids (both require 17-OH intermediate); it CAN synthesize aldosterone via: progesterone → 11-deoxycorticosterone (CYP21A2) → corticosterone (CYP11B1) → aldosterone (CYP11B2/aldosterone synthase); the fasciculata and reticularis HAVE CYP17A1
explanation: Adrenal steroidogenesis zonal differences: Zona Glomerulosa: Has CYP11A1 (SCC), CYP21A2, CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase, unique to ZG). LACKS CYP17A1 → cannot make cortisol or androgens → only mineralocorticoids (aldosterone). Zona Fasciculata: Has CYP11A1, CYP17A1, CYP21A2, CYP11B1 (11β-hydroxylase). Makes cortisol. Zona Reticularis: Has CYP11A1, CYP17A1 (with 17,20-lyase activity). Makes DHEA, DHEAS, androstenedione. Key: CYP11B2 = aldosterone synthase (only in ZG) vs. CYP11B1 = 11β-hydroxylase (ZF + ZR, makes cortisol from 11-deoxycortisol).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which reflex protects the lung against over-inflation?
options: Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: lung distension → slowly adapting stretch receptors (SARs, in airway smooth muscle) → vagal afferents (CN X) → pontine apneustic center/DRG → inhibits inspiration → promotes expiration; in anesthetized humans and infants, helps set tidal volume; Breuer deflation reflex: lung deflation → SARs quiet → disinhibition → promotes inspiration
explanation: Pulmonary stretch reflexes: Hering-Breuer (1868): lung inflation → SARs (myelinated fibers in airway smooth muscle) → vagal nucleus tractus solitarius → inhibits pontine apneustic center + dorsal respiratory group → terminates inspiration → active Ewald's reflex at rest? Only significantly active at TV >1L in awake adult humans. In infants and anesthetized subjects → active at normal TV. Breuer deflation reflex: lung collapse/deflation → ↑RARs and SAR silence → inspiratory facilitation. Clinical: vagotomy (removes both reflexes) → slow deep breathing.

subject: Physiology
stem: Carbonic anhydrase II is present in which cells of the nephron?
options: Proximal tubule cells (both cytoplasmic CA-II and luminal CA-IV) and intercalated cells of the collecting duct (CA-II); CA-II catalyzes: H2O + CO2 ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3- (both in the lumen and in the cell) → essential for H+ secretion and HCO3- reabsorption; acetazolamide inhibits CA → ↓H+ secretion in PCT → ↓HCO3- reabsorption → bicarbonaturia → metabolic acidosis
explanation: CA (carbonic anhydrase) in nephron: PCT: CA-IV (luminal, membrane-bound) → converts filtered HCO3- + secreted H+ → H2CO3 → H2O + CO2 → CO2 enters cell → CA-II (cytoplasmic) → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-; H+ secreted via NHE-3 (apical) + V-type H-ATPase; HCO3- exits basolateral via NBC (Na+-HCO3- cotransporter). Collecting duct: alpha-intercalated cells (A-ICs): CA-II → H+ secreted by V-type H-ATPase (lumen) + HCO3- exits via AE1 (Cl-/HCO3- exchanger, basolateral). Acetazolamide (CA inhibitor): ↓H+ secretion → ↓HCO3- reabsorption → bicarbonaturia (type 2 RTA-like, metabolic acidosis); used for altitude sickness, glaucoma.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'cough reflex': which receptor mediates it and which cranial nerve?
options: Slowly adapting stretch receptors (SARs), CN IX

Rapidly adapting receptors (RARs, also called irritant receptors): in airway epithelium; stimulated by inhaled particles, chemical irritants, mucus, rapid lung deflation → myelinated Aδ fibers of CN X (vagus, also CN IX from pharynx) → medullary cough center → expiratory response: deep inspiration → glottic closure → forced expiration against closed glottis → rapid glottis opening → high-velocity airflow → clears mucus/irritant
explanation: Cough reflex: Sensors: RARs (larynx, trachea, carina, bronchi) + C-fibers (alveolar level, respond to capsaicin/bradykinin/citric acid). Afferents: CN X (vagus, most of airway) + CN IX (pharynx/upper larynx). Medullary cough center: in the nucleus tractus solitarius and adjacent areas. Efferents: CN X (vagus → larynx, bronchi) + spinal motor neurons (phrenic, intercostals, abdominals). Cough sequence: (1) inspiration (↑airflow), (2) glottic closure (↑intrathoracic pressure up to 300 mmHg), (3) glottis opens → high-velocity expiratory airflow (up to 250 m/s) → clears airways. Antitussives: opioids (codeine, dextromethorphan → suppress cough center), local anesthetics.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'aldosterone escape' phenomenon refers to:
