options: The observation that in states of chronic aldosterone excess (e.g., primary hyperaldosteronism), Na+ retention and volume expansion occur initially but then reach a maximum, after which urinary Na+ excretion normalizes ('escapes') despite continued aldosterone secretion — mediated by ↑ANP and ↑BP-induced pressure natriuresis; K+ and H+ continue to be secreted (hyperkalemia prevented but hypokalemia + alkalosis persist)
Loss of aldosterone effect over time
explanation: Aldosterone escape: In primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome): ↑aldosterone → ↑ENaC → ↑Na+ reabsorption → ↑ECF volume → ↑BP → pressure natriuresis (↑GFR + ↓tubular reabsorption) + ↑ANP (↑atrial stretch → ANP → ↓ENaC) → Na+ balance restored without massive edema. But K+ secretion NOT compensated (ROMK always active) → persistent hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis. Contrast with chronic HF: no 'escape' for Na+ (low BP and impaired natriuresis override → progressive Na+ retention + edema). Fludrocortisone in Addison's: some aldosterone escape occurs — explains why edema doesn't occur at normal replacement doses.

subject: Physiology
stem: Name the Purkinje cell neurotransmitter and its role in cerebellar output:
options: GABA (inhibitory) — Purkinje cells are the sole output of the cerebellar cortex, and they tonically inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN: dentate, interposed, fastigial); DCN are excitatory (glutamate) → thalamus (VL) → motor cortex; when Purkinje cells are transiently silenced (by learned activity patterns), DCN fire more → motor cortex activated → movement
explanation: Cerebellar circuit: Mossy fibers (from spinal cord, pons, reticular formation, use glutamate) → granule cells (most numerous neurons, excitatory, glutamate → parallel fibers). Climbing fibers (from inferior olivary nucleus, use glutamate, powerful synapses on Purkinje cells → error signal, LTD induction for motor learning). Purkinje cells (GABA, inhibitory) → DCN. DCN (glutamate, excitatory) → thalamus (VL/VA) → motor cortex. Also: mossy fibers → DCN directly (bypass Purkinje, excitatory). Cerebellum = error correction and adaptation (compares intended vs. actual movement).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which substance inhibits platelet aggregation and is produced by vascular endothelium?
options: Prostacyclin (PGI2, prostaglandin I2) from endothelial cells via COX-2 + prostacyclin synthase → binds IP receptor on platelets → ↑cAMP → ↓[Ca2+]i → ↓GPIIb/IIIa activation → ↓aggregation; also vasodilator; in balance with TXA2 from platelets
explanation: Endothelial anti-thrombotic mechanisms: (1) PGI2 (prostacyclin): ↑cAMP in platelets → inhibits aggregation; vasodilator; short t½ (2 min). (2) NO (eNOS): ↑cGMP → inhibits platelet activation + causes vasodilation; synergistic with PGI2. (3) Thrombomodulin: on endothelial surface → binds thrombin → activates protein C → inactivates Va and VIIIa (anticoagulant). (4) Heparan sulfate: binds and activates AT III → inhibits coagulation factors. (5) TFPI (tissue factor pathway inhibitor): inhibits TF-VIIa complex. (6) CD39 (ecto-ADPase): degrades ADP (platelet activator) from damaged cells.

subject: Physiology
stem: Smooth muscle: which property allows it to maintain force at longer sarcomere lengths than skeletal muscle?
options: The 'latch bridge' mechanism: smooth muscle myosin cross-bridges can remain attached in a low-cycling state (dephosphorylated MLC) → tonic force at minimal ATP cost; also, smooth muscle has a flatter length-tension relationship (lacks organized sarcomere structure) → can generate force over a much greater range of lengths (e.g., bladder can expand from 30 mL to 500 mL while maintaining the ability to generate force when needed)
Higher calcium sensitivity of the filaments
explanation: Smooth muscle adaptations: (1) No organized sarcomere → no clear resting length optimal (flatter length-tension curve). (2) Latch bridges: dephosphorylated (but still attached) myosin cross-bridges → slow-cycling, tonic force with low ATP consumption. (3) Caldesmon and calponin: thin filament regulatory proteins that dampen cross-bridge cycling when not fully activated. (4) Plasticity: smooth muscle can reset resting length (e.g., after chronic distension of the bladder → ↑cell length → myosin filaments reorganize → can still contract). Key: smooth muscle is suited for tonic, sustained contraction (vessels, gut, bladder, uterus) with high economy.

subject: Physiology
stem: Proprioception: which receptor detects static joint position?
options: Muscle spindle (Ia afferents for velocity + rate of change; II afferents for static length) and Golgi tendon organs (Ib afferents for tension); Ruffini endings in joint capsules also contribute to static position sense; together these provide conscious proprioception (via DCML → VPL thalamus → S1 cortex) and unconscious proprioception (spinocerebellar tracts → cerebellum for movement coordination)
explanation: Proprioceptors: (1) Muscle spindle intrafusal fibers: nuclear bag fibers (Ia, dynamic: velocity of stretch) + nuclear chain fibers (II, static: maintained length). Gamma motor neurons control intrafusal fiber tension (set sensitivity). (2) GTO (Ib afferents): muscle tension. (3) Joint receptors: Ruffini endings (SA-II, joint capsule stretch → static position), Golgi ligament endings, pacinian corpuscles in joint capsule (RA, movement). Conscious proprioception: DCML → VPL → S1. Unconscious: Spinocerebellar (dorsal SCT from legs; Clarke's column; cuneocerebellar from arms) → cerebellum.

subject: Physiology
stem: The normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) range is:
options: 6-12 mmHg — measured by inflating the balloon of a Swan-Ganz (pulmonary artery) catheter in a small pulmonary arterial branch; the wedge pressure reflects left atrial pressure (and hence LVEDP in the absence of mitral stenosis); elevated PCWP (>18 mmHg) indicates left heart failure/pulmonary congestion
explanation: Swan-Ganz catheter measurements: Right atrium (RA): 0-8 mmHg. Right ventricle (RV): 15-30/0-8 mmHg. Pulmonary artery (PA): 15-30/8-15 mmHg. PCWP: 6-12 mmHg (balloon wedged in small PA branch → static column of blood → reflects LA pressure). Normal CO: 4-8 L/min. SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO × 80 (normal 800-1200 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵). PVR = (PAP mean - PCWP)/CO × 80 (normal 50-150). Elevated PCWP (>18 mmHg): LV failure, mitral stenosis. Low PCWP with ↑HR + ↓CO: cardiogenic shock vs. hypovolemic shock (in hypovolemic: ↓PCWP + ↓CVP; cardiogenic: ↑PCWP + ↓CO).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which ECG finding is characteristic of right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)?
options: Right axis deviation (>+110°) with dominant R wave in V1 (R > S in V1) and deep S wave in V5-V6 (S1Q3 is seen in acute PE); also: right bundle branch block (RBBB) pattern may occur; p-pulmonale (tall peaked P waves in II, III, aVF > 2.5 mm) suggests RA enlargement; causes of RVH: pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary stenosis, chronic cor pulmonale (COPD)
explanation: RVH ECG criteria: Right axis deviation (QRS axis >+110°), R/S ratio >1 in V1, S/R ratio >1 in V5-V6, R in V1 + S in V5 or V6 >10.5 mm, RBBB pattern. P pulmonale: ↑RA pressure → peaked P wave >2.5 mm in limb leads. Causes of RVH: primary pulmonary hypertension, Eisenmenger syndrome (L→R shunt reversal), cor pulmonale (COPD, interstitial lung disease), mitral stenosis (↑PAP), pulmonary stenosis. Acute PE: S1Q3T3 pattern + sinus tachycardia + right heart strain; RBBB may appear.

subject: Physiology
stem: The Windkessel effect refers to:
options: The increase in heart rate during inspiration

The ability of the elastic aorta to act as a pressure reservoir: during systole, the aorta expands and stores energy (like a Windkessel/air chamber in a fire engine pump) → during diastole, the recoil of the elastic aorta propels blood forward to the periphery, maintaining diastolic pressure; this converts pulsatile ventricular output into a more continuous flow; arteriosclerosis (↓aortic compliance) → ↑pulse pressure
The flow of blood through capillaries
explanation: Windkessel model of the aorta: Elastic arteries (aorta, large arteries): during systole → wall distends (stores ~50% of SV) → slows flow velocity. During diastole → elastic recoil → pushes stored blood distally → maintains diastolic pressure → coronary perfusion (which occurs mainly in diastole). Aging/arteriosclerosis: ↓aortic compliance → ↑pulse pressure (↑SBP + ↓DBP); pulse wave velocity increases (PWV, marker of arterial stiffness). Normal SBP ~120 mmHg, DBP ~80 mmHg, pulse pressure = 40 mmHg. Pulse pressure >60 mmHg: aortic regurgitation, thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia, beriberi, Paget's, complete heart block.

subject: Physiology
stem: In hemorrhagic shock, which compensatory mechanism acts first to restore blood pressure?
options: Baroreceptor reflex (acts within seconds): ↓BP → ↓baroreceptor firing (from carotid sinus + aortic arch) → ↓inhibitory input to vasomotor center → ↑sympathetic output → (1) ↑HR and ↑contractility (β1) → ↑CO; (2) vasoconstriction (α1) → ↑SVR; (3) venoconstriction → ↑preload; together: ↑CO + ↑SVR = ↑MAP; tachycardia + cool clammy skin are clinical manifestations
Fluid shifts into vascular space from interstitium (takes minutes-hours)
explanation: Hemorrhagic shock responses (time course): Seconds: baroreceptor reflex → ↑sympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility, vasoconstriction, venoconstriction. Minutes: carotid/aortic body chemoreceptors (if PaO2 ↓) → ↑HR. Minutes-hours: fluid shift from interstitium and cells into capillaries (Starling forces: ↓capillary hydrostatic pressure → net absorption). Hours-days: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone (↑Na+/H2O retention), ADH (V1 → vasoconstriction; V2 → ↑H2O reabsorption), EPO (↑RBC production). Class I shock (<15% blood volume loss): compensated; Class II (15-30%): tachycardia; Class III (30-40%): ↓BP; Class IV (>40%): life-threatening.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'J point' on the ECG refers to:
options: The peak of the P wave

The junction between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the ST segment; elevation of the J point (J-point elevation or early repolarization) can be a normal variant in young adults; J-point elevation followed by horizontal/downsloping ST segment in V1-V3 = Brugada pattern (risk of ventricular fibrillation); J-point elevation with peaked T waves in V1-V5 in right bundle branch block morphology is seen in Brugada syndrome
The midpoint of the T wave
The end of the T wave
explanation: J point (ST junction): transition from QRS to ST segment. Causes of J-point elevation: (1) Early repolarization: common in young adults, athletes; benign (usually); slurred/notched J wave in inferior/lateral leads. (2) Myocardial infarction: acute STEMI → ST elevation (tombstone pattern). (3) Pericarditis: diffuse concave (saddle-shaped) ST elevation. (4) Brugada syndrome: coved-type ST elevation in V1-V2 + J-wave → ↑risk of sudden cardiac death. (5) Hypothermia: Osborn/J waves (positive deflection at J point, pathognomonic of hypothermia). ST depression: subendocardial ischemia, digoxin (reverse tick), NSTEMI.

subject: Physiology
stem: In a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the arterial blood gas shows pH 7.32, PaCO2 65 mmHg, PaO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 33 mEq/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
options: Chronic respiratory acidosis (↑PaCO2 → ↓pH) with renal metabolic compensation (↑HCO3-): pH 7.32 (acidotic); PaCO2 65 mmHg (primary respiratory acidosis — respiratory failure, hypoventilation); HCO3- 33 mEq/L (elevated, indicates chronic compensation: kidneys retain HCO3- to partially correct pH); expected chronic compensation: for every 10 mmHg ↑PaCO2, HCO3- rises ~3.5 mEq/L (chronic) → expected HCO3- = 24 + (25/10 × 3.5) = 24 + 8.75 ≈ 33 mEq/L ✓ consistent with PURE chronic respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis with acute respiratory acidosis
explanation: Chronic respiratory acidosis (type II respiratory failure): PaCO2 ↑ → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-. Acute: HCO3- rises 1 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑PaCO2. Chronic (>3 days, renal compensation): HCO3- rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↑PaCO2. Clinical: COPD, obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), neuromuscular disease, chest wall deformity. Hypoxic drive in COPD: these patients with chronic hypercapnia suppress central CO2 sensitivity → rely on hypoxic (peripheral chemoreceptor) drive; giving high-flow O2 → removes hypoxic drive → ↑PaCO2 (Haldane effect + Hering-Breuer + CO2 response curve blunted); use controlled O2 to maintain SpO2 88-92%.

subject: Physiology
stem: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted LEFT by which of the following?
options: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) — HbF (α2γ2) has weaker binding to 2,3-DPG (because γ chains have low affinity for 2,3-DPG compared with β chains) → higher O2 affinity → left-shifted ODC; this allows HbF to extract O2 from maternal HbA in the placenta; other left-shift factors: ↓CO2, ↓H+ (alkalosis), ↓temperature, ↓2,3-DPG (stored blood, HbF, hypophosphatemia, methemoglobin reducers)
explanation: Oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve: Left shift (↑O2 affinity, ↓P50): HbF, alkalosis (↓H+), ↓CO2, ↓temperature, ↓2,3-DPG (stored blood, HbF, hypophosphatemia), CO (carboxyhemoglobin shifts the curve left AND binds O2 site), methemoglobin (shifts remaining heme left). Right shift (↓O2 affinity = ↑O2 delivery to tissues): ↑CO2, ↑H+ (acidosis, Bohr effect), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-DPG (high altitude, chronic anemia, chronic hypoxia, pyruvate kinase deficiency), sickle cell. P50: normal = 26-27 mmHg. T50: temperature of 50% saturation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Surfactant: what is its primary component and where is it produced?
options: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, lecithin) — produced by Type II pneumocytes (granular pneumocytes) and stored in lamellar bodies; surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension (by inserting between water molecules at the air-fluid interface) → prevents alveolar collapse at end-expiration; Laplace's law: P = 2T/r; without surfactant, small alveoli (small r) would have very high surface tension pressure → collapse into larger alveoli → atelectasis
explanation: Surfactant components: DPPC (principal component, ~70%) + phosphatidylglycerol (PG, ~10%) + surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D; SP-B most critical for surface tension reduction) + cholesterol (~10%). Laplace's law for a bubble: P = 4T/r; for alveolus (one surface): P = 2T/r. Surfactant ↓T → ↓collapse pressure. Lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio: L:S >2 indicates lung maturity (sphingomyelin remains constant; lecithin rises after 35 weeks). Infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS): premature birth (<34 weeks) → ↓surfactant → hyaline membrane disease → ↑work of breathing → hypoxia. Treatment: antenatal corticosteroids (↑SP gene expression) + postnatal surfactant replacement.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for the CO2/HCO3- buffer system?
options: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-] / (0.03 × PaCO2)) — pK of carbonic acid = 6.1; dissolved CO2 = 0.03 × PaCO2 (Henry's law solubility coefficient = 0.03 mEq/L per mmHg); at normal values: pH = 6.1 + log(24 / (0.03 × 40)) = 6.1 + log(24/1.2) = 6.1 + log(20) = 6.1 + 1.301 = 7.40; this equation links metabolism (HCO3-, regulated by kidneys) and respiration (PaCO2, regulated by lungs)
explanation: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). For bicarbonate buffer: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-]/[H2CO3]); since H2CO3 ≈ 0.03 × PaCO2: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-]/(0.03 × PaCO2)). Uses: (1) Calculate pH from PaCO2 and HCO3- (or vice versa). (2) Understand compensation rules. Why bicarbonate is such a good physiological buffer: (a) Its pKa (6.1) is not ideal for buffering at pH 7.4, but its components are controlled independently (kidneys control HCO3-, lungs control CO2) → open buffer system → infinitely large buffering capacity. (b) In a closed system, the bicarbonate buffer would be less effective (pKa 6.1 vs pH 7.4 means ratio = 20:1 → only handles large acid loads at this ratio).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'tubuloglomerular feedback' (TGF) mechanism: what is the sensor?
options: Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells in the afferent arteriole (they sense pressure, not flow)

Macula densa cells in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle: sense tubular fluid [NaCl] via NKCC2 transporter → if flow/NaCl ↑ → macula densa signals JG cells → release of adenosine (A1 receptor on afferent arteriole → vasoconstriction → ↓GFR) → maintains constant distal tubule delivery; if NaCl ↓ → ↓adenosine → afferent arteriole dilates → ↑GFR + macula densa signals renin release from JG cells
explanation: TGF mechanism (prevents excessive GFR): Macula densa (specialized cells in TAL at the point where the distal tubule returns to touch the afferent arteriole of its own glomerulus — juxtaglomerular apparatus, JGA). ↑Distal NaCl delivery → ↑NKCC2 transport → ↑intracellular Na+/Cl- → macula densa releases ATP → extracellular → adenosine (via ecto-5'-nucleotidase) → A1 receptors on afferent arteriole → vasoconstriction → ↓GFR → ↓tubular NaCl delivery → feedback loop. Macula densa also regulates renin: ↓distal NaCl → ↑renin release (via PGE2 from macula densa → EP2/EP4 on JG cells → cAMP → ↑renin). TGF keeps GFR constant despite changes in blood pressure (myogenic autoregulation also contributes).

subject: Physiology
stem: Metabolic alkalosis: which conditions cause it?
options: Vomiting (loses HCl → net gain of HCO3-), loop/thiazide diuretics (ECF contraction → ↑aldosterone → ↑H+ secretion), primary hyperaldosteronism (↑aldosterone → ↑H+ secretion by collecting duct A-ICs + ↓K+ → hypokalaemic alkalosis), refeeding, milk-alkali syndrome, Bartter/Gitelman syndromes (volume contraction alkalosis)
explanation: Metabolic alkalosis generation: (1) Loss of H+: vomiting (↑gastric HCl loss), loop/thiazide diuretics (ECF contraction → ↑aldosterone). (2) Addition of HCO3-: antacid ingestion, milk-alkali syndrome, blood transfusions (citrate → HCO3-), post-hypercapnic alkalosis (slow renal HCO3- excretion after CO2 normalized). (3) K+ depletion: ↓K+ → H+ shifts into cells and is secreted by collecting duct. Maintenance (perpetuation): why doesn't the kidney excrete excess HCO3-? ECF contraction (vomiting/diuretics) → ↑aldosterone → ↑H+ secretion → keeps regenerating HCO3-. Treatment: saline (↑ECF → ↓aldosterone → kidney excretes HCO3-; 'chloride-responsive' alkalosis). If aldosterone-driven (chloride-resistant): treat underlying cause.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the 'anion gap' and what does it measure?
options: Anion gap = [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]); normal = 8-12 mEq/L; represents 'unmeasured anions' (plasma proteins — especially albumin, phosphate, sulfate, organic acids) which maintain electrical neutrality with cations; ↑AG = accumulation of organic acids (lactate, ketones, salicylate, methanol/formate, ethylene glycol/oxalate, uremia/sulfate) that replace HCO3- as anions; normal-AG metabolic acidosis (hyperchloremic): ↓HCO3- replaced by ↑Cl- (diarrhea, RTA, type 4 RTA, NH4Cl ingestion)
The difference between measured cations and anions (including all measured electrolytes)
explanation: Anion gap (AG): AG = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-); normal 8-12 mEq/L (or 12±4 with albumin correction). AG primarily reflects albumin (each 1 g/dL ↓albumin → AG ↓2.5 mEq/L → correct AG for hypoalbuminemia). High-AG metabolic acidosis (MUDPILES): Methanol (formate), Uremia (sulfate, phosphate), Diabetic ketoacidosis (β-hydroxybutyrate + acetoacetate), Propylene glycol/Paraldehyde, Isoniazid/Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol (oxalate), Salicylates (late). Osmolar gap: if suspected toxic alcohol → osmolar gap = measured osmolality - calculated osmolality; calculated = 2[Na+] + [glucose]/18 + [BUN]/2.8; elevated osmolar gap + high AG → methanol or ethylene glycol.

subject: Physiology
stem: Primary hypoparathyroidism: what are the expected calcium and phosphate levels?
options: ↓Ca2+ (hypocalcemia), ↑PO4 (hyperphosphatemia) — absent PTH → ↓osteoclast activity (↓bone Ca2+ resorption) + ↓renal Ca2+ reabsorption (DCT) + ↓renal phosphate excretion (PTH normally inhibits phosphate reabsorption in PCT via NPT2a/b) + ↓1,25-(OH)2D3 production (↓PTH → ↓1α-hydroxylase) → ↓GI Ca2+ absorption; signs of hypocalcemia: Chvostek's sign, Trousseau's sign, tetany, QT prolongation, seizures
explanation: PTH effects (normally): ↑Ca2+: (1) bone resorption ↑ (via RANKL → osteoclasts); (2) DCT Ca2+ reabsorption ↑ (TRPV5); (3) PCT phosphate excretion ↑ (↓NPT2a/b → phosphaturia); (4) ↑1α-hydroxylase in kidney → ↑1,25-(OH)2D3 → ↑GI Ca2+/PO4 absorption. In hypoparathyroidism: all effects lost → ↓Ca2+ + ↑PO4. Causes: post-thyroidectomy (most common, parathyroids removed/devascularized), autoimmune (type 1 APS), DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, parathyroids absent). Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP): PTH is present but target cells resistant (Gs-α mutation, GNAS) → same lab picture (↓Ca2+, ↑PO4) but ↑PTH levels; Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which phase of insulin secretion is lost first in type 2 diabetes?
options: First-phase insulin secretion — the rapid, sharp spike occurring within 1-3 minutes of glucose stimulation (from readily releasable pool of pre-formed insulin granules docked at the plasma membrane); in T2DM, chronic hyperglycemia + lipotoxicity + glucotoxicity → impaired KATP channel closure + impaired granule docking → loss of first-phase → postprandial hyperglycemia; second phase (slower, 10-60 min, from reserve pool of granules) is more preserved initially but also declines with disease progression
explanation: Insulin secretion phases: First phase (0-10 min): rapid spike → due to pre-docked granules at the plasma membrane (readily releasable pool, RRP) → fused immediately on glucose sensing. Second phase (10-60 min): slower sustained release → from reserve granule pool requiring ATP-dependent transport to plasma membrane. Loss of first-phase: earliest marker of β-cell dysfunction in T2DM; detected by IVGTT (intravenous glucose tolerance test). Clinical consequence: ↑postprandial blood glucose (normally first-phase insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output and primes peripheral tissues). Incretin effect exploited by GLP-1 agonists/DPP4 inhibitors → both phases.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the half-life of cortisol in the circulation and what is its binding protein?
options: 70-90 minutes; most (~90%) bound to CBG (corticosteroid-binding globulin/transcortin, a serpin); ~7% albumin-bound; ~3% free (bioactive); total plasma cortisol = mostly CBG-bound; total cortisol rises with ↑CBG (pregnancy, OCP — estrogen ↑CBG → ↑total cortisol but free cortisol normal); late-night salivary cortisol reflects free cortisol (gold standard for Cushing's screening); 24h urinary free cortisol also measures only free cortisol
explanation: Cortisol pharmacokinetics: t½ ≈ 70-90 min in plasma. Binding: CBG (transcortin, 70 kDa globulin synthesized in liver): ↑by estrogen (pregnancy, OCP → ↑CBG → ↑total cortisol, appears as 'hypercortisolism' if you only measure total cortisol) → not true Cushing's. Albumin binds ~7%. Free (3%) = biologically active. Normal cortisol secretion: 15-25 mg/day (≈ 50-80 μmol). Diurnal rhythm: highest in early morning (6-8 AM, before waking), lowest at midnight; loss of diurnal rhythm = early sign of Cushing's (↑midnight cortisol). Stress response: ACTH spikes → cortisol ↑ within 15-30 min.

subject: Physiology
stem: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): which immunoglobulin increase promotes rouleaux formation and raises ESR?
options: Fibrinogen and immunoglobulins (especially IgM and IgG) — these large asymmetric proteins coat RBCs, reduce negative surface charge (which normally keeps RBCs apart by zeta potential), promote rouleaux (stack of coins) formation → faster sedimentation; fibrinogen is the single most important acute-phase protein affecting ESR; high ESR: inflammation, infection, malignancy, pregnancy, anemia (fewer cells to exclude), myeloma (high IgG/IgM paraprotein)
explanation: ESR Westergren method: Blood in a tube, measure how far RBCs fall in 1 hour. Normal: males <15 mm/h; females <20 mm/h; elderly can be higher. Factors ↑ESR: Fibrinogen (most important; acute phase reactant) + IgM (biggest, best rouleaux), IgG, IgA, anemia, pregnancy, macrocytes. Factors ↓ESR: polycythemia (↑viscosity), sickle cell (can't form rouleaux), hypofibrinogenemia, hyperviscosity, congestive heart failure. Limitation: non-specific, slow to respond (lags inflammation). CRP: faster acute phase protein (rises within 6h of inflammation, half-life 19h), good monitoring marker. Sickle cells: cannot form rouleaux → normal or low ESR despite active disease.

subject: Physiology
stem: The neutrophil respiratory burst: which enzyme is deficient in chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)?
options: NADPH oxidase (encoded by gp91phox subunit, X-linked = most common form, or autosomal recessive p47phox) — catalyzes: 2 O2 + NADPH → 2 O2•- + NADP+ + H+ (superoxide radical) → SOD → H2O2 → HOCl (via MPO) → kills bacteria; CGD: NADPH oxidase absent → can't produce superoxide → no oxidative killing; susceptible to catalase-positive organisms (e.g., S. aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Serratia — these produce catalase which breaks down their own H2O2, leaving no substrate for the MPO-dependent killing pathway)
explanation: NADPH oxidase complex: Membrane-bound: gp91phox (NOX2) + p22phox. Cytoplasmic: p47phox + p67phox + p40phox + Rac2. Assembled on membrane → electrons from NADPH → O2 → O2•- → dismutase → H2O2 → MPO → HOCl (hypochlorous acid = bleach, most potent bactericidal). CGD: defect in respiratory burst → can't kill catalase+ organisms (they destroy their own H2O2, leaving no H2O2 substrate for MPO). NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test: normal neutrophils reduce NBT (blue); CGD neutrophils cannot → remains colorless. DHR test (dihydrorhodamine): flow cytometry-based, more sensitive. Treatment: prophylaxis with TMP-SMX, itraconazole (Aspergillus); IFN-γ (upregulates oxidase activity in some).

subject: Physiology
stem: Factor V Leiden mutation: what is the mechanism?
options: Point mutation in Factor V (Arg506Gln substitution in the APC cleavage site) → Factor Va becomes resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (APC) → Factor Va persists → ↑thrombin generation → hypercoagulable state (most common inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians, ~5% prevalence); leads to venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE), especially when combined with other risk factors (OCP, pregnancy, immobility)
explanation: Factor V Leiden: autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance; most common inherited thrombophilia in Europeans. Normal: APC (activated protein C, via thrombomodulin + protein S as cofactor) cleaves Va at Arg506 + Arg306 + Arg679 → inactivates Va → ↓thrombin. FVL: Arg506Gln → APC cannot cleave at Arg506 → Va persists → ↑thrombin. 10× risk of first VTE in heterozygotes, 80× in homozygotes. Inherited thrombophilias (risk of VTE): Factor V Leiden (most common), Prothrombin G20210A mutation (#2), Protein C deficiency, Protein S deficiency, Antithrombin III deficiency. ATIII deficiency: highest absolute risk per episode; antithrombin is irreplaceable (no backup pathway).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which chemical triggers rigor mortis?
options: Depletion of ATP after death: without ATP → myosin heads cannot detach from actin (ATPase activity on myosin is needed for cross-bridge cycling to enter the 'cocked' position); myosin + actin remain bound in a rigor complex → muscle stiffness; begins 2-6 hours after death, peaks at 12 hours (when muscle glycogen is depleted), resolves 24-48 hours later (due to proteolysis/decomposition); ambient temperature affects the rate
explanation: Rigor mortis mechanism: Death → cessation of metabolism → ATP depletion → SERCA (SERCA-pump) on SR fails → [Ca2+]i rises (from SR leak + mitochondrial release) → thin filament activation (troponin-C binding). Simultaneously: ATP depletion → myosin cannot detach (the detachment/re-cocking step requires ATP hydrolysis) → permanent cross-bridge attachment → rigor. Begins: first in face and jaw (smaller muscle fibers, more rapid ATP depletion). Order: ascending rigor (face → neck → trunk → limbs). Disappears in same order due to proteolysis by lysosomal enzymes. Forensic: rigor helps estimate time of death. Rate: slowed by cold (hypothermia → slower ATP depletion and enzymatic breakdown) → helps forensic estimation.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'treppe' (staircase) effect in cardiac muscle refers to:
options: Progressive increase in contractile force during sustained rapid stimulation: when a series of stimuli at rapid rate is applied, each successive contraction is stronger (positive staircase = Bowditch staircase) → due to progressive accumulation of intracellular Ca2+: each rapid AP → slight residual Ca2+ inside → subsequent Ca2+ transient builds on residual → ↑[Ca2+] available for next contraction; opposite of skeletal muscle fatigue; basis for force-frequency relationship (FFR) in cardiac muscle
Decrease in force with each contraction
All-or-none response to a single stimulus
explanation: Force-frequency relationship (FFR) / Bowditch staircase: Cardiac muscle: ↑heart rate → ↑Ca2+ entry per unit time → NCX operates in reverse (less Ca2+ export) → ↑SR Ca2+ load → ↑Ca2+ transient per beat → ↑force. Positive FFR = 'positive staircase' = Bowditch phenomenon. This is why exercise increases CO: ↑HR → ↑force (plus catecholamines contribute). In heart failure: FFR blunted or reversed (negative FFR) due to ↓SR Ca2+ stores, ↓SERCA activity, ↓NCX function. Clinical: rate-adaptive pacing — uses FFR principle. Differs from Treppe in skeletal muscle (post-tetanic potentiation also uses residual Ca2+ but skeletal context), but FFR in cardiac is distinct.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which condition is associated with absent consensual pupillary light reflex but preserved direct reflex?
options: Optic neuritis (direct reflex absent due to afferent defect)

Contralateral optic tract lesion behind the optic chiasm affecting only the crossed fibers: illuminating the eye on the side of the lesion causes a direct reflex (intact ipsilateral CN II afferent + ipsilateral CN III efferent) but the consensual response (which requires crossed pretectal input to the contralateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus) may be reduced — actually this is complex; most commonly tested: right optic neuritis → right direct reflex absent + right eye illumination → no left consensual; left optic neuritis → similar; CN III lesion → ipsilateral direct + consensual ABSENT (efferent defect); Argyll Robertson pupil: accommodates but doesn't react to light (syphilis, affects pretectal dorsal midbrain)
Horner syndrome (no pupillary light defect, only miosis + ptosis + anhidrosis)
CN VII palsy (facial nerve, no pupillary effect)
explanation: Pupillary light reflex pathway: Afferent: retina → CN II → optic tract → pretectal nucleus (midbrain, just anterior to SC) → BILATERAL Edinger-Westphal (EW) nuclei. Efferent: EW → preganglionic parasympathetic fibers (travel with CN III) → ciliary ganglion → postganglionic → sphincter pupillae → pupil constriction. RAPD (relative afferent pupillary defect): optic neuritis or severe retinal disease → swinging flashlight test → paradoxical dilation when light moves to the affected eye (direct consensual both reduced because afferent is damaged). CN III palsy: efferent lesion → both direct and consensual responses absent in the ipsilateral eye; ptosis, 'down-and-out' eye, fixed dilated pupil. Argyll Robertson: small irregular pupils, accommodate but don't react (tabes dorsalis, neurosyphilis — dorsal midbrain pretectal lesion).

subject: Physiology
stem: The anterior visual pathway: lesion at the right optic nerve would cause:
options: Right monocular blindness (right eye) — complete loss of vision in the right eye only; the optic nerve carries all fibers from the ipsilateral (right) eye; after the optic chiasm, fibers from both eyes are combined in each optic tract; so lesion at the optic nerve → monocular visual field loss; bitemporal hemianopia → chiasm lesion (pituitary adenoma compresses decussating nasal fibers → loss of both temporal fields); homonymous hemianopia → optic tract or radiation or cortex lesion
explanation: Visual pathway lesions: (1) Right optic nerve (pre-chiasm) → right monocular blindness (complete right visual field loss). (2) Optic chiasm (central, pituitary adenoma) → bitemporal hemianopia (both temporal fields lost = tunnel vision). (3) Right optic tract (post-chiasm) → left homonymous hemianopia (loss of left half of both visual fields). (4) Right temporal lobe/Meyer's loop (lower fibers of optic radiation) → left superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'). (5) Right parietal lobe/upper optic radiation → left inferior quadrantanopia. (6) Right occipital cortex → left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (dual blood supply: calcarine artery + MCA). (7) Tip of occipital cortex (MCA territory) → monocular central scotoma / macular vision loss.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which hormone is responsible for maintaining the corpus luteum in early pregnancy?
options: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) — secreted by syncytiotrophoblast cells of the developing placenta from implantation (~7-10 days post-conception) onwards; hCG has LH-like activity (binds LH/hCG receptor on corpus luteum → ↑cAMP → ↑progesterone and estrogen production) → 'rescues' corpus luteum from luteal-follicular transition → maintains corpus luteum function until the placenta takes over progesterone production (luteo-placental shift, ~8-10 weeks)
explanation: hCG: glycoprotein, α-subunit (shared with LH, FSH, TSH) + unique β-subunit (pregnancy test detects β-hCG). Rises from implantation → peaks at 8-10 weeks (doubling time 48-72h in normal pregnancy) → falls to low plateau at 12-16 weeks. hCG functions: (1) Maintains corpus luteum → ↑progesterone (prevents menstruation, maintains decidua). (2) Stimulates thyroid (TSH-like activity due to shared α-subunit) → gestational hyperthyroidism in high hCG states (hyperemesis gravidarum, molar pregnancy). (3) Fetal Leydig cell → testosterone → male genital development. Molar pregnancy: very high hCG (no 8-week fall). Ectopic: slow doubling of hCG. Intrauterine: normal doubling q48h.

subject: Physiology
stem: Menopause: which gonadotropin rises first and higher?
options: FSH — as follicular reserve depletes (beginning 5-10 years before menopause) → ↓inhibin B from granulosa cells of early antral follicles → ↑FSH (inhibin B normally provides negative feedback specifically to FSH, not LH); FSH rises in the early follicular phase in perimenopausal women; after menopause: both FSH and LH rise (no estradiol/progesterone/inhibin B) → FSH typically >30-40 IU/L, LH also rises but FSH is consistently higher (because LH has shorter t½ ~20 min vs. FSH t½ ~4h + LH is cleared faster)
Neither rises — pituitary fails with age
explanation: Menopause sequence: (1) Perimenopause: ↓primordial follicle pool → ↓granulosa cells → ↓inhibin B → ↑FSH (before estrogen changes significantly). (2) Late perimenopause: irregular cycles, ↓estradiol. (3) Menopause (12 months no menses): FSH >40 IU/L, LH also ↑, estradiol <20 pg/mL. Inhibin A (from dominant follicle, late follicular to luteal phase) vs. Inhibin B (from early antral follicles, early follicular phase) — inhibin B is the first to decline. AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone, from small antral follicles): best marker of ovarian reserve; falls earliest, undetectable after menopause. Symptoms: vasomotor (hot flashes, due to ↑GnRH pulsatility ± central noradrenergic dysregulation), urogenital atrophy, osteoporosis (↓estrogen → ↑osteoclast activity).

subject: Physiology
stem: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS): what is the pathophysiology?
options: Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCC, P/Q-type) → ↓Ca2+ entry into motor nerve terminal during AP → ↓ACh vesicle exocytosis → ↓EPP → ↓muscle contraction; distinguishing features from MG: proximal limb weakness that IMPROVES with repetitive stimulation (incremental response on EMNG, vs. decrement in MG); autonomic features (dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction); deep tendon reflexes initially absent but may appear after exercise; often paraneoplastic (small cell lung cancer, 60% of cases)
explanation: LEMS vs MG: LEMS: anti-P/Q-VGCC Ab → ↓presynaptic Ca2+ → ↓ACh release → EPG decrement at rest → exercise/repetitive stimulation → ↑Ca2+ accumulation → ↑ACh release → incremental EMG response (>100-200% increment at high frequency). MG: anti-nAChR (or anti-MuSK) → post-synaptic receptor loss → decremental EMG (fatigability worse with repeated stimulation). LEMS diagnosis: antibodies (anti-VGCC), EMG (high-frequency increment), imaging for lung cancer. Treatment: 3,4-diaminopyridine (DAP, blocks K+ channels → prolongs AP → ↑Ca2+ entry), immunosuppression. MG treatment: pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor), immunosuppression (steroids, azathioprine), IVIG, plasmapheresis, thymectomy.

subject: Physiology
stem: Sleep physiology: which stage is characterized by K-complexes and sleep spindles?
options: Stage N2 (NREM stage 2) — deeper than N1 (light sleep with theta waves + vertex sharp waves); N2 is characterized by: (1) sleep spindles (bursts of 12-15 Hz sigma waves, generated by thalamic reticular nucleus inhibiting thalamo-cortical relay neurons — gate for sensory input during sleep); (2) K-complexes (large amplitude negative-then-positive EEG waves, triggered by external stimuli or spontaneous, thought to protect sleep by inhibiting cortical arousal); N2 makes up ~50% of total sleep time
Stage N3 (slow wave sleep, delta waves, no spindles/K-complexes at this depth)
Stage N1 (theta waves, vertex sharp waves only)
explanation: Sleep stages and EEG signatures: Awake: beta (>13 Hz, active) / alpha (8-13 Hz, relaxed, eyes closed). NREM N1 (~5% of sleep): theta (4-7 Hz), vertex sharp waves, hypnic jerks. NREM N2 (~50%): sleep spindles (12-15 Hz, thalamic reticular nucleus) + K-complexes (response to external stimuli). NREM N3 (~20%): delta waves (<4 Hz, high amplitude, slow wave sleep, SWS); most restorative, growth hormone secreted (first third of night), hardest to wake. REM (~25%): rapid eye movements, sawtooth waves, muscle atonia (brainstem), dreaming, memory consolidation; cardiac/respiratory variability ↑. Sleep cycle: N1→N2→N3→N2→REM (~90 min); more SWS early, more REM late in the night.

subject: Physiology
stem: Phantom limb pain: what is the neurophysiological basis?
options: Peripheral sensitization of the stump only

Maladaptive cortical reorganization (somatosensory cortex plasticity) following amputation: deafferentation → neighboring cortical regions expand into the deprived cortex (e.g., face representation expands into the former hand/arm area in the somatosensory homunculus) → abnormal sensory perception arising from this remapping → phantom sensations; additionally: ectopic firing from neuromas at the stump, dorsal horn sensitization (central sensitization), and mirror neuron system activation; more frequent when pain was present before amputation
Only central sensitization of the dorsal horn
Purely psychological phenomenon with no neurophysiological basis
explanation: Phantom limb pain: after amputation of a limb, ~70% of patients experience phantom sensations (non-painful) and ~50% phantom pain. Mechanisms: (1) Peripheral: stump neuroma → ectopic discharge → abnormal sensory input. (2) Spinal: central sensitization (NMDA-mediated wind-up) in dorsal horn. (3) Supraspinal/cortical: Penfield's homunculus: after arm amputation, face-related sensory input can trigger phantom hand sensations (since face map is adjacent to hand map in SI) — demonstrated by Ramachandran's mirror box therapy + neuroimaging. Treatment: mirror visual feedback (mirror therapy), graded motor imagery, virtual reality, central analgesics (ketamine, gabapentinoids), DRG/spinal cord stimulation.

subject: Physiology
stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis in the liver is:
options: Hexokinase (liver uses glucokinase/hexokinase IV, but it's not rate-limiting)

Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1, converts fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate) — the committed, irreversible, rate-limiting step of glycolysis; regulated allosterically: activated by AMP, ADP, fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP, most potent activator — product of PFK-2, itself activated by insulin/↑glucose → Fed state → ↑glycolysis); inhibited by ATP (high energy state), citrate (excess FA oxidation → ↑citrate → ↓glycolysis)
explanation: Glycolytic regulation — key enzymes: (1) Hexokinase (all tissues) / Glucokinase (HK-IV, liver + pancreatic β cells): glucose → G6P. Glucokinase: not saturated at normal plasma glucose, no product inhibition by G6P, high Km → acts as glucose sensor. (2) PFK-1 (rate-limiting): F6P → F-1,6-BP. F-2,6-BP (from PFK-2): most potent activator. Insulin → ↑PFK-2 activity (via protein phosphatase) → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis. Glucagon (fasting) → PKA → phosphorylates PFK-2 → ↓PFK-2 → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis → ↑gluconeogenesis. (3) Pyruvate kinase: PEP → pyruvate. Irreversible glycolytic steps: hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase (all bypassed in gluconeogenesis by alternative enzymes).

subject: Physiology
stem: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is required as a cofactor for which enzyme complexes?
options: Fatty acid synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA), α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (KGDH: α-KG → succinyl-CoA, in TCA cycle), branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH: valine, leucine, isoleucine metabolism), and transketolase (pentose phosphate pathway); deficiency: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia → chronic: Korsakoff psychosis with confabulation), beriberi (wet: high-output HF; dry: peripheral neuropathy)
explanation: Thiamine (B1) = thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP): (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH complex, also requires FAD, NAD, CoA, lipoate): converts pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (junction of glycolysis and TCA). (2) α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (TCA step 4): α-KG → succinyl-CoA. (3) Branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH): BCKA metabolism (MSUD = maple syrup urine disease if mutated). (4) Transketolase (pentose phosphate pathway): TPP-dependent sugar rearrangements → transketolase activity in RBCs used as a functional marker of thiamine status. B1 deficiency: Wernicke's encephalopathy (triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia — mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, cranial nerve nuclei lesions); 'never give glucose without thiamine' (↑demand → precipitates Wernicke's).

subject: Physiology
stem: During intense exercise, which shuttle moves reducing equivalents from cytoplasmic NADH into the mitochondria?
options: The citrate shuttle (exports acetyl-CoA from mitochondria)

The malate-aspartate shuttle (in heart, liver, skeletal muscle): NADH (cytoplasm) + OAA → malate + NAD+; malate enters mitochondria (via malate-aspartate carrier) → malate + NAD+ → OAA + NADH (in mitochondria); OAA → aspartate (via AST) → transported out; regenerates OAA in cytoplasm; net: 1 cytoplasmic NADH → 1 mitochondrial NADH → ~2.5 ATP (via complex I); contrasted with glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (muscle, brain) which yields FADH2 → ~1.5 ATP — less efficient
explanation: NADH shuttle systems (inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to NADH): (1) Malate-aspartate shuttle (M-A shuttle): heart, liver, kidney, resting skeletal muscle — cytoplasmic NADH → mitochondrial NADH → 2.5 ATP (efficient). (2) Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (G3P shuttle): brain, fast-twitch skeletal muscle, insect flight muscle — cytoplasmic NADH → mitochondrial FADH2 → 1.5 ATP (less efficient but faster, less regulated). During aerobic exercise: M-A shuttle dominates in heart and type I fibers. During anaerobic exercise: NADH regenerated by LDH (pyruvate → lactate) instead of shuttle. Clinical: malate-aspartate shuttle components impaired in ischemia → less ATP from glycolytic NADH → energy deficit.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which lipid-modifying drug primarily acts by inhibiting intestinal cholesterol absorption?
options: Ezetimibe — inhibits the Niemann-Pick C1-like 1 (NPC1L1) protein on the brush border of small intestinal enterocytes → ↓cholesterol absorption from the gut lumen; ↓intracellular cholesterol in enterocytes → ↑LDL receptor expression → ↑LDL clearance; combination with statins: additive ↓LDL (IMPROVE-IT trial showed ezetimibe + simvastatin → ↓CV events vs simvastatin alone); does not affect bile acid pool (unlike bile acid sequestrants)
explanation: Lipid-lowering drug mechanisms: Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors): ↓endogenous cholesterol synthesis → ↑hepatic LDLR → ↑LDL clearance → ↓LDL 30-50%; also anti-inflammatory. Ezetimibe (NPC1L1 inhibitor): ↓intestinal cholesterol absorption → ↑hepatic LDLR → ↓LDL ~20%; synergistic with statins. Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam): bind bile acids in gut → ↑hepatic bile acid synthesis from cholesterol → ↑LDLR → ↓LDL ~15-25%. PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab): block PCSK9 (degrades LDL receptors) → ↑LDLR recycling → ↓LDL 50-60% (most potent). Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate): PPAR-α → ↑LPL → ↓TG 30-50%, ↑HDL. Niacin: ↓hepatic VLDL secretion → ↓TG + ↓LDL + ↑HDL (but side effects limit use).

subject: Physiology
stem: Brown adipose tissue (BAT): what is its role and where does it predominate?
options: Non-shivering thermogenesis: BAT mitochondria contain uncoupling protein 1 (UCP-1/thermogenin) in the inner mitochondrial membrane → UCP-1 creates a proton leak pathway (bypasses ATP synthase) → proton gradient dissipated as heat instead of ATP; BAT is abundant in neonates (thermoregulation in newborns who cannot shiver efficiently) and hibernating animals; in adults: interscapular, perirenal, periaortic BAT (active in cold exposure → FDG-PET visible)
explanation: BAT vs WAT: WAT (white adipose tissue): unilocular lipid droplet, few mitochondria, energy storage, endocrine (leptin, adiponectin, resistin). BAT: multilocular lipid droplets, densely packed mitochondria, rich vascularity, brown color (from iron in cytochromes), express UCP-1. UCP-1: proton channel in IMM → dissipates proton motive force → heat. Activation: cold exposure → SNS → β3 adrenergic receptor on BAT → ↑cAMP → ↑PKA → ↑lipolysis (FFA → β-oxidation → FADH2/NADH → electron transport → UCP-1-mediated heat). BAT in humans: adults have active BAT (cervical, supraclavicular, paraaortic, perirenal) — detectable by 18F-FDG PET in cold conditions. Obesity/T2DM: ↓BAT activity.

subject: Physiology
stem: Shivering thermogenesis: where is the shivering center?
options: Posterior hypothalamus (dorsomedial hypothalamus and posterior hypothalamic area): receives cold signals from peripheral cold receptors (skin) and core temperature sensors → activates descending pathways → ↑somatic motor neuron activity → rhythmic, involuntary muscle contractions (shivering) → ↑heat production (3-5× resting metabolic rate); anterior hypothalamus (POAH) detects core warming → activates heat loss mechanisms (vasodilation, sweating)
explanation: Hypothalamic thermoregulation: POAH (preoptic area of anterior hypothalamus): 'thermostat' set point. Warm-sensitive neurons (WANs): activated by ↑temperature → trigger heat loss (cutaneous vasodilation via α2 + sweating via sympathetic cholinergic). Cold-activated neurons: activate heat gain. Posterior hypothalamus: integrates heat production. Set point normally 37°C. Fever: PGE2 (from hypothalamic cyclooxygenase activated by IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) → EP3 receptors → ↑cAMP → resets set-point ↑ → body feels 'cold' at normal temperature → shivering + vasoconstriction → ↑temperature until new set point reached. Antipyretics: aspirin/NSAIDs (↓COX → ↓PGE2) lower set point → vasodilation + sweating → fever breaks.

subject: Physiology
stem: A 28-year-old runner starts a marathon. After 20 km, which metabolic substrate shift occurs?
options: Initially glycogen + fatty acids (first 30 min) → as glycogen depletes (~2 h at moderate intensity): ↑fat oxidation (from adipose lipolysis → ↑circulating FFA → β-oxidation in muscle) + ↑gluconeogenesis (liver uses lactate/alanine/glycerol) + ↑ketogenesis; crossover concept (Brooks): at low intensity, fat predominates; as intensity ↑ → carbohydrate oxidation ↑; at high intensity: nearly 100% carbohydrate; at marathon pace (moderate-high intensity), both substrates are used, with progressive shift toward fat as glycogen depletes; the 'wall' (hitting the wall, bonking) = glycogen depletion around 30-35 km
Only amino acids are metabolized after 20 km
Stops using oxygen (switches to anaerobic only)
explanation: Exercise metabolism: Rest/light exercise: ~50-65% fat, ~35-50% carbohydrate. Moderate intensity (~65% VO2max): ~50% fat + 50% CHO. High intensity (>80% VO2max): ~90% CHO. 'Crossover point' (Brooks): point at which CHO > fat as substrate (usually ~60-65% VO2max). Marathon specifics: pace is ~70-75% VO2max → moderate-high; glycogen provides dominant fuel; glycogen stores last ~90-120 min at this intensity → after 30-35 km glycogen depletes → forced shift to fat → ↓power output ('hitting the wall'). Prevention: carbohydrate loading (supercompensation), mid-race glucose gels. Trained marathoners: ↑fat oxidation capacity, ↓glycogen utilization at same absolute speed (adaptation: ↑mitochondria, ↑LPL, ↑FABP, ↑β-oxidation enzymes).

subject: Physiology
stem: Dialysis: in hemodialysis, which type of membrane transport is primarily used?
options: Diffusion (down concentration gradient) + ultrafiltration (convection, driven by transmembrane pressure) + osmosis: (1) Diffusion: solutes (urea, creatinine, K+, phosphate) move from blood (high concentration) across semipermeable membrane to dialysate (low/zero concentration); (2) Ultrafiltration: hydrostatic pressure drives fluid (water + dissolved solutes) across membrane = convective transport; (3) Osmosis: in peritoneal dialysis, glucose in dialysate creates osmotic gradient → ↑water removal; in hemodialysis, ultrafiltration is pressure-driven
explanation: Hemodialysis (HD) vs peritoneal dialysis (PD): HD: blood → dialyzer (semipermeable hollow fiber membrane) → dialysate (counter-current flow); achieves clearance of small molecules (urea, creatinine, K+, phosphate) via diffusion; Kt/V is measure of dialysis adequacy (K = clearance, t = time, V = volume of distribution). PD: dialysate infused into peritoneal cavity; uses peritoneal membrane as dialyzer; osmotic agent (usually glucose, icodextrin) → ultrafiltration; less efficient per session but continuous. Membrane characteristics: molecular weight cutoff determines what passes; small molecules (<500 Da): easily diffuse; middle molecules (500-15,000 Da): require convection (hemofiltration/hemodiafiltration); large molecules (>15,000 Da): not removed.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which renal tubular acidosis (RTA) type presents with hypokalemia AND nephrolithiasis?
options: Type 1 RTA (distal RTA) — defect in α-intercalated cells' H+-ATPase (or anion exchanger AE1) → inability to secrete H+ in the collecting duct → cannot acidify urine maximally (urine pH >5.5 despite severe acidemia); characteristic features: hyperchloremic normal-AG metabolic acidosis + hypokalemia (alkaline tubular lumen → K+ secretion ↑ via ROMK, since H+ and K+ exchange) + nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis (alkaline urine → ↑Ca2+ precipitation as calcium phosphate) + osteomalacia (bone buffering chronic acidosis → Ca2+ release); causes: Sjögren's syndrome, amphotericin B toxicity, SLE, hereditary
Type 2 RTA (proximal, hypokalemia but NO nephrolithiasis — urine can still acidify distally)
explanation: RTA classification: Type 1 (Distal): ↓H+ secretion in CD → urine pH >5.5 always, normal-AG metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis (alkaline urine → ↑stone risk). Type 2 (Proximal): ↓HCO3- reabsorption in PCT (PCT threshold for HCO3- lowered) → once HCO3- is below threshold → distal nephron can still acidify urine (urine pH <5.5 when HCO3- is low/threshold is exceeded); hypokalemia; bicarbonaturia. No nephrolithiasis (urine acidified distally when HCO3- depleted). Associated with Fanconi syndrome (proximal tubule dysfunction: bicarbonaturia + phosphaturia + glucosuria + aminoaciduria + uricosuria). Type 4 (Hypoaldosteronism or pseudohypoaldosteronism): ↓aldosterone → ↓H+/K+ secretion → hyperkalemia + acidosis.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'gastrin' hormone: which cell secretes it and what stimulates its release?
options: G cells (gastrin cells) in the antrum of the stomach and the duodenum — stimulated by: (1) partially digested proteins and amino acids in the antral lumen (especially phenylalanine, tryptophan); (2) antral distension (vagal-GRP mechanism: vagus → GRP (gastrin-releasing peptide) from antral nerve endings → G cells → ↑gastrin); (3) hypercalcemia; inhibited by: (1) antral acidification (pH <3: somatostatin from D cells → inhibits G cells); (2) secretin (from S cells when pH <4 in duodenum)
Enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells — these produce histamine which acts on parietal cells
explanation: Gastrin (G17 in antrum, G34 in duodenum): actions via CCK-B receptors: (1) ↑HCl secretion by parietal cells (directly and via ECL cells → histamine → H2 → parietal cell). (2) ↑Pepsinogen from chief cells. (3) ↑Gastric motility. (4) Trophic effects on gastric mucosa (↑cell proliferation). Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma): ectopic gastrin-secreting tumor (pancreas most common, also duodenum) → very high gastrin → maximal acid secretion → multiple, atypical peptic ulcers (postbulbar), secretory diarrhea (↑acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes → fat malabsorption → diarrhea). Fasting serum gastrin: >1000 pg/mL + basal acid output = diagnostic. Secretin stimulation test: in ZE, secretin paradoxically ↑gastrin (unlike normal where ↓).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which segment of the GI tract is responsible for vitamin B12 (cobalamin) absorption?
options: Terminal ileum (distal 60-90 cm) — via specific receptors (cubilin) that recognize the intrinsic factor (IF)-B12 complex; intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells of the stomach; IF binds B12 in the duodenum → IF-B12 complex is stable → reaches terminal ileum → cubilin receptor (coiled-coil domain protein, also known as intrinsic factor-B12 receptor) + amnionless co-receptor → endocytosis → B12 enters portal blood (bound to transcobalamin II)
Duodenum (B12 binds IF here but is not absorbed here)
explanation: Vitamin B12 absorption: Dietary B12 (meat, fish, dairy) → bound to food protein → stomach: acid + pepsin releases B12 → binds R proteins (haptocorrins, from saliva and gastric juice) → R-B12 complex enters duodenum → pancreatic proteases digest R proteins → free B12 + intrinsic factor (IF, from gastric parietal cells) → IF-B12 complex. Terminal ileum: IF-B12 binds cubilin (+ amnionless) → endocytosis → B12 released intracellularly → enters blood bound to transcobalamin II → liver stores (3-5 years supply). Causes of B12 deficiency: pernicious anemia (autoimmune anti-IF antibodies), total gastrectomy, terminal ileal disease/resection (Crohn's, tropical sprue), vegan diet (no animal products), fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium, competes for B12).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which interleukin is the major endogenous pyrogen that acts on the hypothalamus to cause fever?
options: IL-1β (and IL-6, TNF-α) — these cytokines are released by activated macrophages in response to infection/inflammation (via TLR-NF-κB pathway); they are endogenous pyrogens that cross the blood-brain barrier (at circumventricular organs, e.g., OVLT — organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis, which lacks a BBB) → stimulate arachidonic acid metabolism in hypothalamic glial cells via COX-2 → ↑PGE2 → EP3 receptors on POAH neurons → ↑cAMP → resets thermoregulatory set-point higher → fever
explanation: Fever cascade: Infection/tissue injury → macrophage activation (TLR/PAMPs → NF-κB) → release of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α (endogenous pyrogens). These cytokines act at the OVLT (lacks BBB) or cross BBB (especially small amounts of IL-1β via transport) → stimulate COX-2 in hypothalamic arachidonic acid → PGE2 → EP3 (Gi) or EP4 receptors → ↑cAMP → raises thermoregulatory setpoint → shivering + vasoconstriction → fever. Antipyretics: aspirin, ibuprofen (nonselective COX inhibitors → ↓PGE2); paracetamol/acetaminophen (primarily in CNS COX-3 inhibition). IL-6: most potent for hepatic acute phase response (CRP, fibrinogen, complement production) + also a pyrogen. Exogenous pyrogens: LPS (bacterial), peptidoglycan → induce IL-1β/IL-6/TNF-α.

subject: Physiology
stem: Natural killer (NK) cells: what activates them to kill target cells?
options: MHC class I on target cell (which INHIBITS NK cells)

'Missing self' hypothesis: NK cells are inhibited by self-MHC class I (via killer inhibitory receptors, KIRs, e.g., KIR2DL1 binds HLA-C, CD94/NLG2A binds HLA-E) — normal cells express MHC I → NK cells held in check; virally infected cells or tumor cells → ↓MHC I expression (to evade T cells) → loss of inhibitory signal (loss of 'self') + ↑expression of stress ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP — bind NKG2D activating receptor) → NK activation → perforin + granzyme B → apoptosis
Antigen-specific T cell help (NK cells are not antigen-specific)
explanation: NK cell biology: Large granular lymphocytes (CD56+, CD16+, CD3-). Balance of activating + inhibitory signals. Inhibitory receptors (KIRs, CD94/NKG2A): recognize self-MHC I → inhibit killing. Activating receptors (NKG2D, NKp46, NKp30, NKp44, DNAM-1, CD16/FcγRIII): recognize stress ligands (NKG2D ligands: MICA/B, ULBPs — ↑in virally infected cells, tumor cells, DNA damage) → trigger activation. ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity): antibody on target cell → CD16 (FcγRIII) on NK cell → crosslinks → NK activation → cytotoxicity. NK cytotoxicity mechanisms: perforin (pores in target cell membrane) + granzymes (serine proteases → enter through perforin pores → activate caspases → apoptosis). Also: TNF, IFN-γ, FasL.

subject: Physiology
stem: Atropine mechanism: which receptor does it block and what are the cardiovascular effects?
options: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs), specifically M2 in the heart: competitive antagonist → blocks vagal (parasympathetic) effects on the heart → ↑HR (blocks SA node inhibition), ↑AV conduction velocity (blocks AV nodal inhibition), and increases sinus rate; used clinically for bradycardia, AV block, organophosphate poisoning (reverses muscarinic excess); also blocks M3 (glands → ↓salivary, ↓GI secretions + ↓sweating + dilated pupils), M1 (CNS: confusion at high doses — 'mad as a hatter')
explanation: Atropine mnemonic: 'Dry as a bone, Blind as a bat, Red as a beet, Hot as a hare, Mad as a hatter' → dry mouth (↓salivation, M3), cycloplegia + mydriasis (↓accommodation + dilated pupil, M3), flushing (↓sweating → ↑temperature → skin flushing, M3), fever (↓sweating), confusion/delirium (CNS, M1). Cardiovascular: ↑HR (M2 block), ↑AV conduction. Note: low doses may paradoxically ↓HR (central vagotonia? or peripheral pre-junctional M1 facilitation). Organophosphate poisoning: irreversible AChE inhibitors → ↑ACh everywhere → muscarinic excess (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI distress, emesis) + nicotinic excess (fasciculations, paralysis) → atropine (large doses) for muscarinic symptoms; pralidoxime (2-PAM) to regenerate AChE if given early.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which drug blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin (SNRI)?
options: Venlafaxine (and duloxetine): inhibit the serotonin transporter (SERT) and the norepinephrine transporter (NET) → ↑synaptic serotonin and NE → antidepressant effects; used for: major depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, neuropathic pain (duloxetine — particularly for diabetic peripheral neuropathy, fibromyalgia); side effects: ↑BP (from ↑NE), ↑HR, nausea, sweating
Tricyclic antidepressants (also block SERT + NET but additionally block muscarinic, H1, α1 — more side effects)
Mirtazapine (α2 antagonist + 5-HT2/3 antagonist, not reuptake inhibitor)
explanation: Antidepressant mechanisms: SSRIs: citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline — SERT inhibition → ↑synaptic 5-HT. SNRIs: venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine — SERT + NET inhibition. TCAs: amitriptyline, imipramine — SERT + NET + H1 + M1 + α1 blockade → sedation, anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation. MAOIs: phenelzine, tranylcypromine — ↓MAO → ↑5-HT + NE + dopamine; tyramine reaction with cheese/wine → hypertensive crisis. Mirtazapine: α2 antagonist (↑NE + 5-HT release) + 5-HT2A/2C antagonist (↑sleep) + H1 antagonist (sedation) + antiemetic. Bupropion: NDRI (NE + dopamine reuptake inhibitor); smoking cessation; ↑seizure risk.

subject: Physiology
stem: Pulsus paradoxus: what is the mechanism?
options: Paradoxical increase in systolic BP during inspiration

Exaggerated normal inspiratory ↓ in systolic BP (>10 mmHg): in cardiac tamponade (or severe asthma, tension pneumothorax), inspiration → ↑venous return to RV → RV expands → ventricular interdependence (shared pericardium/interventricular septum) → IVS bows leftward → ↓LV filling (↓LVEDV) → ↓LV stroke volume → ↓aortic pressure during inspiration; plus: ↑pulmonary vascular bed during inspiration traps blood → ↓LV preload; normal ↓SBP inspiration is <10 mmHg
Rise in jugular venous pressure during inspiration (Kussmaul's sign)
explanation: Pulsus paradoxus (PP): measured with sphygmomanometer (SBP during expiration - SBP during inspiration); normal <10 mmHg. Cardiac tamponade: pericardial effusion → ↑pericardial pressure → limits cardiac chamber filling → tachycardia (compensatory) + ↓CO + hypotension; Beck's triad: ↓BP, ↑JVP (Kussmaul's sign: JVP rises on inspiration, opposite of normal), muffled heart sounds. PP >10 mmHg in cardiac tamponade (virtually always), severe asthma (↑intrathoracic pressure swings), tension pneumothorax. Kussmaul's sign: ↑JVP with inspiration (constrictive pericarditis, RV failure, cardiac tamponade) — opposite of normal (normally JVP ↓ with inspiration as ↑intrathoracic pressure sucks blood into thorax).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cardiac auscultation: which murmur is heard at the upper right sternal border and radiates to the carotids?
options: Aortic stenosis: harsh crescendo-decrescendo (diamond-shaped) systolic ejection murmur (SEM), best heard at the right 2nd intercostal space (aortic area) → radiates to carotids (direction of turbulent flow); peak intensity late in systole (severe AS); associated signs: soft/absent A2, paradoxical split S2 (severe AS → delayed LV ejection → delayed aortic valve closure), S4 (from stiff hypertrophied LV), pulsus parvus et tardus (narrow, slowly rising carotid pulse), LVH on ECG/echo
Ventricular septal defect (VSD): pansystolic, left sternal border)
explanation: Systolic murmur locations: Right 2nd ICS (aortic area): aortic stenosis (SEM), pulmonary stenosis (SEM, radiates to left shoulder). Left 2nd ICS (pulmonary area): pulmonary stenosis, ASD (fixed split S2). Left 3rd-4th ICS (tricuspid area): VSD (pansystolic), HOCM (SEM + dynamic). Apex (mitral): MR (pansystolic, radiates axilla), MVP (mid-systolic click + late systolic murmur). Diastolic murmurs: aortic regurgitation (blowing decrescendo, left sternal border, sitting forward), mitral stenosis (rumbling mid-diastolic, apex, opening snap). Innocent murmurs: Still's murmur (musical, ejection-type, left sternal border, normal heart in children).

subject: Physiology
stem: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): which physiological mechanism causes hypoxemia during apneic episodes?
options: Shunting from left to right (increased cardiac shunt)

Upper airway collapse during sleep → cessation of airflow → continued O2 consumption by tissues without replenishment → ↓PAO2 → ↓PaO2; simultaneously ↑PaCO2 → hypercapnia; the alveolar gas equation explains: PAO2 = FiO2 × (Patm - PH2O) - PaCO2/R; as PaCO2 rises → PAO2 falls → hypoxia; the combination of hypoxemia (↓PaO2) + hypercapnia (↑PaCO2) → ↑sympathetic activity + arousals → repeated nocturnal surges in BP → hypertension (systemic and pulmonary), cardiac arrhythmias, metabolic syndrome
V/Q mismatch (which occurs chronically but the acute mechanism is airway obstruction)
explanation: OSA physiology: Repetitive complete (apnea) or partial (hypopnea) collapse of the upper airway during sleep → cessation of airflow → desaturation (↓SaO2) → hypercapnia → arousal (restores airway tone) → resumed breathing → cycle repeats throughout night. Oxygen desaturation kinetics: depend on lung O2 stores (FRC) + O2 consumption rate → obese patients with ↓FRC + ↑O2 consumption desaturate faster. Consequences: intermittent hypoxia → ↑sympathetic → ↑BP; endothelial dysfunction → atherosclerosis risk; ↑cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α); metabolic dysregulation. Diagnosis: polysomnography (PSG); AHI (apnea-hypopnea index) >5 events/h = OSA (mild 5-14, moderate 15-30, severe >30).

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the mechanism of action of furosemide (frusemide) on the kidney?
options: Inhibits Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the proximal convoluted tubule

Inhibits NKCC2 (Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter 2, SLC12A1) in the thick ascending limb (TAL) of the loop of Henle from the luminal side → ↓Na+, K+, Cl- reabsorption → ↓countercurrent multiplication (↓medullary hypertonicity) → ↓free water reabsorption in collecting duct → net diuresis (large volumes); also ↑Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion (paracellular Ca2+ absorption driven by lumen-positive potential created by NKCC2 — furosemide destroys this driving force); used for: pulmonary edema, hypertension, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia
Inhibits ENaC in the collecting duct
Inhibits Na+/Cl- cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule
explanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid): Inhibit NKCC2 in TAL lumen → ↓Na+/K+/Cl- reabsorption → (1) ↑urinary Na+, Cl-, K+ excretion; (2) ↓medullary interstitial osmolality (↓countercurrent multiplier) → ADH cannot concentrate urine effectively; (3) ↓lumen-positive potential (NKCC2 recycles K+ back to lumen via ROMK → creates + potential that drives paracellular Ca2+/Mg2+ absorption → furosemide ↑Ca2+/Mg2+ wasting → useful in hypercalcemia). Side effects: hypokalemia (↑Na+ delivery to CD → K+ secretion), metabolic alkalosis, hyponatremia, ototoxicity (NKCC in cochlea, especially high-dose/rapid IV), prerenal azotemia. Furosemide ototoxicity: damage to stria vascularis (contains NKCC1) → aminoglycosides + furosemide = synergistic ototoxicity.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the function of the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells?
options: Renin-secreting granular cells: modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole near the glomerulus; they secrete renin (aspartyl protease) in response to: (1) ↓renal perfusion pressure (myogenic stretch → ↓wall tension → ↑renin); (2) ↑sympathetic stimulation (β1 adrenergic → ↑cAMP → exocytosis of renin granules); (3) ↓NaCl at the macula densa (TGF → PGE2/prostacyclin → ↑renin); renin cleaves angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → ACE → Ang II
They produce erythropoietin (that's interstitial cells of the peritubular capillaries)
They are the site of vasopressin (ADH) action
explanation: RAAS (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system): Renin (from JG cells) → cleaves angiotensinogen (α2-globulin, from liver) → angiotensin I (decapeptide) → ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme, mainly pulmonary endothelium, also kidney) → angiotensin II (octapeptide). Ang II actions (via AT1 receptor): (1) ↑aldosterone (ZG) → ↑Na+/H2O reabsorption (CD). (2) ↑ADH release (posterior pituitary). (3) Vasoconstriction (↑SVR → ↑BP). (4) ↑Na+ reabsorption in PCT (via NHE3). (5) Thirst (circumventricular organs). (6) Cardiac/vascular remodeling (AT1 → PKC → proliferative signals). ACE inhibitors: ↓Ang II → ↓aldosterone, ↓SVR, ↑bradykinin (→ cough, angioedema). ARBs: block AT1 → similar effects minus bradykinin accumulation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Where are cell bodies of the lower motor neurons (LMNs) of the corticospinal tract located?
options: Anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord (alpha motor neurons): large multipolar neurons → axons exit via ventral roots → peripheral nerves → NMJ → innervate skeletal muscle; UMN: cell bodies in motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Betz cells), descend via corticospinal tract (CST) → synapse on LMN or interneurons; UMN lesion signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, clonus, weakness; LMN lesion signs: flaccid paralysis, ↓/absent reflexes, denervation atrophy, fasciculations, fibrillations (on EMG)
explanation: LMN vs UMN lesions: LMN (alpha motor neuron, anterior horn): flaccid paralysis, ↓DTRs, muscle atrophy (denervation, rapid), fasciculations (spontaneous motor unit discharge), fibrillations (EMG), no Babinski; segmental (muscle or nerve root pattern). UMN (corticospinal tract above anterior horn): spastic paralysis (↑tone, clasp-knife), hyperreflexia, Babinski sign (↑plantar reflex → upgoing big toe), clonus, no atrophy (only disuse), weakness (UMN pattern: UE extensors + LE flexors weaker). Corticospinal tract: motor cortex (precentral gyrus) → internal capsule (posterior limb) → brainstem (pyramids) → decussates at pyramidal decussation (medulla) → contralateral spinal cord (lateral CST) → anterior horn LMN.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which brainstem nucleus contains the cell bodies of the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons supplying the heart?
options: Nucleus ambiguus (CN X, motor to pharynx/larynx)

Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMNV): in the dorsal medulla oblongata → preganglionic parasympathetic fibers travel in CN X (vagus nerve) → synapse in ganglia within or near the heart wall (mainly SA node, AV node) → postganglionic short neurons → M2 muscarinic receptors → ↓HR + ↓AV conduction; also nucleus ambiguus contributes parasympathetic fibers to the SA node; heart parasympathetic: primarily via right vagus → SA node; left vagus → AV node
Superior salivatory nucleus (CN VII, lacrimal + submandibular glands)
explanation: Brainstem parasympathetic nuclei (craniosacral): CN III: Edinger-Westphal (EW) nucleus → ciliary ganglion → pupillary sphincter + ciliary muscle (accommodation). CN VII: Superior salivatory nucleus → pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal + nasal + palatal glands) + submandibular ganglion (submandibular + sublingual). CN IX: Inferior salivatory nucleus → otic ganglion → parotid gland. CN X: Dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (DMNV) + nucleus ambiguus → thoracic ganglia (heart, lungs) + abdominal ganglia (GI to 2/3 transverse colon). Sacral S2-S4: pelvic splanchnic nerves → bladder, lower GI, genitals (erection via cavernous nerves).

subject: Physiology
stem: Horner's syndrome: what is the triad?
options: Exophthalmos, lid retraction, lid lag (Graves' disease)

Miosis (small pupil), ptosis (drooping upper lid, partial, from Müller's superior tarsal muscle denervation), and anhidrosis (absent sweating on the ipsilateral face, from ↓sympathetic to face sweat glands): caused by interruption of the sympathetic pathway to the eye at any point: first-order neuron (hypothalamus → ciliospinal center of Budge C8-T1, via lateral tegmentum of brainstem and cervical cord), second-order (preganglionic: ciliospinal center → superior cervical ganglion, runs near apex of lung + subclavian artery), third-order (postganglionic: superior cervical ganglion → carotid → orbit)
Ptosis, diplopia, large pupil (CN III palsy)
explanation: Horner's syndrome: sympathetic denervation of the eye and face. Complete triad: ptosis (partial, 2 mm; vs. CN III: complete ptosis), miosis (dilation reflex lost; ↑dark-room anisocoria), anhidrosis (only if lesion is pre-ganglionic, proximal). Also: enophthalmos (apparent, not true), upside-down ptosis (slight elevation of lower lid, from ↓inferior tarsal muscle). Causes by neuron order: 1st order: Wallenberg syndrome (posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion → lateral medullary syndrome → Horner + dysphasia + ataxia + ipsilateral face numbness + contralateral body pain/temperature loss). 2nd order: Pancoast tumor (lung apex → compresses C8-T1 preganglionic), neck trauma, thyroid surgery. 3rd order: carotid artery dissection (periorbital pain + Horner = emergency), cavernous sinus thrombosis, cluster headache.

subject: Physiology
stem: Diarrhea types: osmotic vs. secretory — which feature distinguishes them?
options: Secretory diarrhea persists with fasting (and stool osmolar gap <50 mOsm/kg); osmotic diarrhea stops with fasting because the osmotically active agent (poorly absorbed solute: e.g., Mg2+-containing laxatives, lactulose, lactose in lactase deficiency) is no longer ingested; in secretory diarrhea (cholera, VIPoma, carcinoid, microscopic colitis): active secretion of Cl-/Na+ and water occurs independently of luminal solutes → persists fasting; stool osmolar gap = measured stool osmolality - 2×([Na+]stool + [K+]stool) → <50 mOsm/kg in secretory (mostly electrolytes, few other osmoles); >50 mOsm/kg in osmotic
Osmotic diarrhea has no stool osmolar gap
explanation: Diarrhea mechanisms: (1) Secretory: ↑active secretion by enterocytes (↑cAMP via cholera toxin → ↑Cl- secretion via CFTR; VIPoma → VIP → ↑cAMP; carcinoid → serotonin → ↑motility + secretion; BAM — bile acid malabsorption → irritates colon; microscopic colitis). Large volume (>1L/d), watery, persists fasting, low stool osmolar gap, isotonic. (2) Osmotic: poorly absorbed solute draws water into lumen (Mg2+ laxatives, lactulose, sorbitol, lactase deficiency, fructose malabsorption). Stops with fasting. ↑Stool osmolar gap. (3) Exudative/inflammatory: IBD, pseudomembranous colitis (C. diff) → blood/mucus. (4) Motility: hyperthyroidism (↑gut motility), IBS. (5) Malabsorptive/osmotic: celiac disease, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency → fat malabsorption → fatty stools.

subject: Physiology
stem: Vomiting reflex: which receptor triggers vomiting with chemotherapy agents?
options: D2 receptor in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) — the primary receptor for dopaminergic-mediated nausea, but not the dominant receptor for chemotherapy-induced

5-HT3 receptor (serotonin type 3 receptor): chemotherapy → enterochromaffin cells in the gut mucosa → ↑serotonin release → 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents → nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) + chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ, area postrema, lacks BBB) → vomiting center (lateral reticular formation) → vomiting; NK1 receptor (substance P) also mediates delayed CINV (chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting); 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron) are the cornerstone of acute CINV prevention; NK1 antagonists (aprepitant) + dexamethasone are added for complete prophylaxis
explanation: Vomiting control center (medullary): chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ/area postrema): outside BBB → samples blood for toxins/drugs/metabolites. Contains: D2 receptors, 5-HT3, NK1 (substance P/neurokinin 1), μ-opioid, H1, M1. Vomiting center (VC): nucleus tractus solitarius + lateral reticular formation (inside BBB). Receives input from CTZ, vagal afferents (gut), vestibular system, cortex, limbic. CINV pathways: Acute CINV (0-24h): serotonin (5-HT3) from gut enterochromaffin cells + dopamine + substance P. Delayed CINV (>24h): mainly substance P (NK1 pathway). Antiemetic targeting: 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, palonosetron — acute CINV), NK1 antagonists (aprepitant — delayed), dexamethasone (both, synergistic), D2 antagonists (metoclopramide, haloperidol — BTR), H1 antagonists (promethazine — motion sickness), anticholinergics (scopolamine — motion sickness).

subject: Physiology
stem: Pancreatic enzyme: which enzyme is responsible for fat digestion in the duodenum?
options: Pepsin (gastric protease, pH <3 — inactivated in duodenum)

Pancreatic lipase (triacylglycerol lipase, PTL): secreted as active enzyme (not a zymogen); requires colipase (also secreted by pancreas; activated from procolipase by trypsin) to function at oil-water interfaces (colipase displaces bile salts to allow lipase access to triglyceride); lipase hydrolyzes TG → 2-monoacylglycerol + 2 free fatty acids; absorbed with bile salts as mixed micelles → enterocytes → re-esterified → chylomicrons → lacteals → lymph → thoracic duct → blood
Salivary amylase (carbohydrate digestion, partly inactivated in stomach)
explanation: Fat digestion and absorption: (1) Emulsification: bile salts in the duodenum emulsify fat into small droplets (↑surface area). (2) Hydrolysis: pancreatic lipase (+ colipase) → TG → MAG + 2FFA; also phospholipase A2 (PLA2: → lysophospholipids + FA) + cholesterol esterase. (3) Micelle formation: bile salts + MAG + FFA + fat-soluble vitamins → mixed micelles → diffuse to brush border → lipids released at membrane → absorbed by enterocytes. (4) Re-esterification: enterocyte SER: MAG + FFA → TG (via MGAT pathway) → packaged with cholesterol + phospholipid + apolipoproteins (B-48, A-I, A-II, C-III, E) → chylomicrons. (5) Exocytosis → lacteals → cisterna chyli → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein → systemic circulation. Fat malabsorption: pancreatitis (↓lipase), ileal disease (↓bile acid reabsorption), cholestasis (↓bile in lumen).

subject: Physiology
stem: The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP): which important coenzyme does it generate?
options: NADPH (reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate) — generated in the oxidative phase of the PPP (G6P → 6-PGL → ribulose-5-P); NADPH is used for: (1) antioxidant defense (glutathione reductase: GSSG + NADPH → 2GSH); (2) fatty acid synthesis (acetyl-CoA → FA via FAS); (3) cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA → mevalonate); (4) neurotransmitter hydroxylations; (5) cytochrome P450 reactions; the PPP also generates ribose-5-phosphate (DNA/RNA synthesis); cells with high NADPH demand: RBCs (antioxidant defense), lactating mammary glands (FA synthesis), adrenal cortex (steroidogenesis), hepatocytes
explanation: Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP, hexose monophosphate shunt): Location: cytoplasm. Two phases: Oxidative (irreversible): G6P → NADPH + 6PGL (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, G6PD, rate-limiting) → 6PG → NADPH + CO2 + ribulose-5-P (6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase). Non-oxidative (reversible): interconverts sugar phosphates via transketolase (TPP-dependent) + transaldolase. Products: 2 NADPH + CO2 + ribose-5-P per G6P. Active PPP cells: RBCs (sole antioxidant source), adrenal cortex (steroidogenesis), activated neutrophils (NADPH oxidase), hepatocytes (FA/cholesterol synthesis), lactating breast, lens (antioxidant). G6PD deficiency: can't make NADPH → no GSH → oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies (bite cells).

subject: Physiology
stem: Glycogenolysis in the liver: which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting phosphorolysis step?
options: Glycogen synthase (does the opposite — adds glucose to glycogen)

Glycogen phosphorylase (liver form: PYGL) — cleaves glucose from glycogen branches via phosphorolysis (not hydrolysis): glycogen(n) + Pi → glycogen(n-1) + glucose-1-phosphate; G1P → G6P (phosphoglucomutase) → G6P → glucose (glucose-6-phosphatase in liver ER) → exported to blood; activated by: glucagon (via PKA → phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylates phosphorylase b → phosphorylase a, active) + epinephrine (hepatic α1 + β2 → ↑Ca2+/cAMP) + AMP (in muscle); inhibited by: glucose-6-phosphate (in muscle, not liver), insulin
Debranching enzyme (removes α-1,6 branches after phosphorylase hits 4 glucose branch points)
