explanation: Glycogenolysis regulation: Hormonal: glucagon (fed → fasted: ↑glucagon → β2 receptor on hepatocyte → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation cascade → ↑phosphorylase activity + ↓glycogen synthase activity). Epinephrine (stress → hepatic β2/α1 and muscle β2 → same cAMP cascade in liver; muscle: α1 → Ca2+ → calmodulin → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase). Allosteric: AMP (↑in energy-depleted muscle → activates phosphorylase b without phosphorylation = 'AMP bypass'); Ca2+ (exercise → ↑Ca2+ → calmodulin → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase activation). Liver glycogenolysis → ↑blood glucose. Muscle glycogenolysis → G6P (no glucose-6-phosphatase in muscle) → glycolysis locally. Von Gierke disease (GSD I): G6Pase deficiency → ↑G6P → ↑glycogen in liver → massive hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is the role of coenzyme A (CoA) in fatty acid metabolism?
options: CoA delivers fatty acids directly to the mitochondria

CoA activates fatty acids to acyl-CoA (fatty acyl-CoA): Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi (catalyzed by fatty acyl-CoA synthetase/ligase, in the outer mitochondrial membrane); this activation step is required before fatty acids can be transferred to carnitine for transport into the mitochondrial matrix (for β-oxidation) or used in the cytoplasm (for anabolic processes like phospholipid synthesis); CoA is derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)
CoA provides the carbon skeleton for fatty acid synthesis
CoA directly regenerates NAD+ for glycolysis
explanation: Fatty acid activation and transport: Step 1: FFA + CoA + ATP → fatty acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi (ΔG -ve due to PPi hydrolysis by pyrophosphatase → drives the reaction). Step 2 (transport into mitochondria for β-oxidation): fatty acyl-CoA + carnitine → acylcarnitine (carnitine acyltransferase I, CAT-I, on outer IMM) → inner membrane carnitine carrier → matrix. Acylcarnitine + CoA → fatty acyl-CoA + carnitine (CAT-II, on inner IMM). Step 3: β-oxidation: acyl-CoA → acetyl-CoA (by repeated: FAD → FADH2, NAD+ → NADH, hydration, NAD+ → NADH, thiolysis). CPT-I deficiency: cannot transport LCFA into mitochondria → hypoketotic hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy.

subject: Physiology
stem: A patient with bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's develops Nelson's syndrome: what is the mechanism?
options: Loss of cortisol-mediated negative feedback → ↑CRH + ↑ACTH from pituitary → pituitary corticotroph adenoma grows → ↑ACTH + ↑α-MSH (from POMC cleavage) → hyperpigmentation (MCR-1 activation on melanocytes) + mass effect (headache, visual field defects); bilateral adrenalectomy removes the source of cortisol → cortisol can no longer suppress ACTH → pituitary corticotroph proliferates; treated with pituitary irradiation or stereotactic radiosurgery
explanation: Nelson's syndrome: Bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease → cortisol absent → no feedback on CRH/ACTH → explosive growth of residual corticotroph adenoma → very high ACTH levels. ACTH → α-MSH (both from POMC) → intense hyperpigmentation (striking, generalized including mucous membranes). Symptoms: progressive hyperpigmentation, pituitary mass effects (headache, visual field defects, hypopituitarism from compression). Cortisol is replaced lifelong (hydrocortisone) but ACTH keeps rising. Incidence: ~20% of bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease. Prevention: adjuvant pituitary radiotherapy at time of bilateral adrenalectomy. Treatment established Nelson's: transsphenoidal surgery, Gamma Knife, cabergoline (↓ACTH in some).

subject: Physiology
stem: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH): what are the characteristic laboratory findings?
options: Hyponatremia (serum Na+ <135 mEq/L), ↓serum osmolality (<280 mOsm/kg), inappropriately HIGH urine osmolality (>100 mOsm/kg, typically >300-400) despite hyponatremia, HIGH urine Na+ (>40 mEq/L, euvolemic → no aldosterone activation → Na+ in urine), NORMAL or ↑blood volume (euvolemic to slightly hypervolemic, but no overt edema — Na+ wasting balances water retention), normal thyroid and adrenal function
explanation: SIADH diagnostic criteria (Schwartz-Bartter): (1) Serum Na+ <135 mEq/L + serum osmolality <280 mOsm/kg. (2) Urine osmolality inappropriately high (>100 mOsm/kg despite hypo-osmolality, usually >300). (3) Urine Na+ >40 mEq/L (no volume depletion → no aldosterone → urinary Na+ wasting). (4) Clinical euvolemia (no edema, no dehydration). (5) Normal renal, thyroid, adrenal function. (6) Not on diuretics. Causes: CNS disease (meningitis, SAH, stroke, TBI), pulmonary (SCLC — ectopic ADH, pneumonia, TB), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, oxytocin, chemotherapy, desmopressin overuse), pain, nausea. Treatment: fluid restriction (mainstay), vaptan (vasopressin receptor antagonists: tolvaptan, conivaptan → aquaresis); hypertonic saline for severe symptomatic hyponatremia. Caution: correction rate ≤8-10 mEq/L per 24 h → avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which of the following best describes the 'functional residual capacity' (FRC)?
options: The volume of gas remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal passive expiration: FRC = ERV (expiratory reserve volume) + RV (residual volume); at FRC, the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall is balanced by the inward elastic recoil of the lungs (the equilibrium point of the respiratory system); measured by helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography (cannot be measured by spirometry alone, as it contains RV); FRC is reduced in: supine position (abdominal contents push diaphragm up), obesity, ARDS, fibrosis; FRC is increased in: emphysema (air trapping + ↓lung recoil → new equilibrium at higher lung volume)
explanation: Lung volumes and capacities: TV (tidal volume, ~500 mL) = normal breath. IRV (~3000 mL) = extra volume inspirated above TV. ERV (~1200 mL) = extra volume expired below TV. RV (~1200 mL) = after maximal expiration. IC = IRV + TV. FRC = ERV + RV (~2400 mL) = resting lung volume. VC = IRV + TV + ERV = ~4700 mL. TLC = all four = ~6000 mL. FRC changes: ↓FRC: supine (abdominal contents), obesity (↓chest compliance), ARDS (consolidation/atelectasis), pulmonary fibrosis. ↑FRC: emphysema (↓elastic recoil of lung → chest wall recoil pulls lung to higher volume equilibrium), asthma (air trapping → dynamic hyperinflation). Normal FRC provides O2 reserve during apnea (why RSI pre-oxygenation is critical in obese patients who have ↓FRC).

subject: Physiology
stem: A patient has a urine pH of 6.5, hypokalemia, and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Type 1 (distal) RTA: inability to lower urine pH below 5.5 due to defective H+-ATPase (or AE1) in alpha-intercalated cells of the collecting duct → urine pH always >5.5 (here 6.5); hypokalemia (alkaline lumen of collecting duct → ↑K+ secretion via ROMK, plus secondary hyperaldosteronism from volume depletion); hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (HCO3- falls → Cl- rises to maintain electroneutrality, normal anion gap); causes: Sjögren's syndrome, amphotericin B, primary biliary cirrhosis, lithium; nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis (alkaline urine → Ca-phosphate stones)
Type 2 RTA can lower urine pH acutely to <5.5 (once serum HCO3- falls below threshold)
Type 3 RTA is very rare (carbonic anhydrase II deficiency)
explanation: RTA type 1 (distal): Key: cannot acidify urine (pH always >5.5). Hypokalemia: alkaline lumen → ↑K+ secretion → hypokalemia (and volume depletion → ↑aldosterone → further K+ loss). Normal AG metabolic acidosis. Complications: nephrocalcinosis, nephrolithiasis (calcium phosphate), osteomalacia (chronic acidosis buffers with bone). Treatment: oral NaHCO3 or Na/K citrate. Type 2 RTA (proximal): ↓PCT HCO3- reabsorption → bicarbonaturia until serum HCO3- falls below the lowered threshold → once below threshold, distal nephron CAN still acidify → urine pH CAN go <5.5 (distinguishing from type 1). Hypokalemia. Fanconi syndrome. Type 4: ↓aldosterone or pseudohypoaldosteronism → ↓H+/K+ secretion → hyperkalemia + mild acidosis; urine pH may be normal or slightly ↑.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which growth factor is primarily responsible for angiogenesis (new blood vessel formation)?
options: Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF — promotes smooth muscle/pericyte recruitment)

Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF-A) — binds VEGFR-2 (KDR) on endothelial cells → tyrosine kinase activation → PI3K/Akt + MAPK pathways → endothelial cell proliferation, migration, tube formation, and increased vascular permeability; also promotes lymphangiogenesis (VEGF-C/D → VEGFR-3); anti-VEGF agents: bevacizumab (anti-VEGF-A antibody — colorectal cancer, glioblastoma, wet AMD), ranibizumab (anti-VEGF-A Fab, anti-VEGF injection for wet AMD), aflibercept (VEGF trap); VEGF upregulated by HIF-1α (hypoxia-inducible factor) in hypoxic tissues
Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1, promotes bone/cartilage growth)
explanation: Angiogenesis: (1) VEGF-A: most important; released by hypoxic cells (HIF-1α → ↑VEGF transcription), tumor cells, activated macrophages. Causes: endothelial activation, degradation of basement membrane (MMPs), sprouting (tip cells guided by Dll4/Notch), proliferation (stalk cells), lumen formation, anastomosis. (2) Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1, via Tie-2 → vessel stability/quiescence) vs. Ang-2 (destabilizes vessels → promotes sprouting when combined with VEGF; promotes regression without VEGF). (3) FGF-2 (bFGF): also pro-angiogenic. Clinical: tumor angiogenesis: HIF-1α (von Hippel-Lindau disease: VHL mutations → can't degrade HIF → ↑VEGF → hemangioblastomas). Anti-angiogenic: bevacizumab, sunitinib/sorafenib (tyrosine kinase inhibitors → ↓VEGFR signaling).

subject: Physiology
stem: Prion diseases: what is the abnormal form of the prion protein?
options: PrPSc (scrapie isoform): misfolded form of the normal prion protein (PrPc) that is: enriched in β-sheet secondary structure (normal PrPc = α-helical); protease-resistant; insoluble; transmissible (PrPSc acts as a template → induces conformational conversion of normal PrPc → more PrPSc → exponential accumulation → spongiform encephalopathy); diseases: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD: sporadic most common, familial, iatrogenic, variant CJD from BSE), Kuru, Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker (GSS), fatal familial insomnia (FFI)
explanation: Prion diseases (transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, TSEs): Pathology: PrPSc accumulates in CNS → neurodegeneration + spongiform vacuolation + astrogliosis + amyloid plaques (in some). CJD: rapidly progressive dementia + myoclonus + periodic sharp wave complexes on EEG (PSWCs) + 14-3-3 protein in CSF; MRI: DWI/FLAIR cortical ribboning + pulvinar sign (variant CJD). Variant CJD: younger patients, ataxia first, florid plaques, from beef (BSE exposure) or blood products. Fatal familial insomnia (FFI): thalamic degeneration → insomnia, dysautonomia, dementia; PRNP D178N mutation + Met/Met polymorphism at codon 129. No treatment exists. Unique: protein-only infectivity (Nobel 1997, Stanley Prusiner).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which pathway mediates the sensation of pain and temperature from the body?
options: Dorsal column medial lemniscal pathway (discriminative touch + proprioception)

Spinothalamic tract (STT): pain (C and Aδ fibers → enter spinal cord → synapse in dorsal horn laminae I, II, V → second-order neuron crosses midline within 1-2 spinal segments via anterior commissure → ascends in contralateral lateral STT) → thalamus (VPL nucleus) → primary somatosensory cortex (S1, postcentral gyrus); temperature (C fibers → same pathway); crude touch via anterior STT; clinical: hemisection of spinal cord (Brown-Séquard): ipsilateral loss of proprioception/touch + contralateral loss of pain/temperature (below the level) because STT has already crossed
explanation: Anterolateral system (spinothalamic tract): Pain: Aδ (sharp, fast, bright pain) and C fibers (slow, burning, aching) → dorsal horn → lamina I (Aδ, sharp pain) + lamina II (substantia gelatinosa, C fibers) → second-order neurons → cross midline (anterior white commissure, within 1-2 segments) → lateral spinothalamic tract (STT) → thalamus (VPL). Temperature: C fibers and Aδ → same dorsal horn laminae → same lateral STT pathway. Crude touch: anterior STT. Clinically: (1) Contralateral loss of pain/temperature below lesion level (STT is crossed). (2) Syringomyelia: centrally expanding spinal cord cavity destroys anterior white commissure → bilateral loss of pain/temperature at the level of the syrinx (suspended level), preserving light touch and proprioception (DCML unaffected). (3) Cauda equina vs. conus medullaris: pain pattern important.

subject: Physiology
stem: The ABO blood group system: which antibodies are present in blood group O individuals?
options: No antibodies (O is the universal donor for cells only)

Anti-A AND anti-B IgM antibodies (naturally occurring, developed by age 6 months via exposure to environmental A-like and B-like antigens from gut flora/food): blood group O individuals have neither A nor B antigens on RBCs → their immune system does not suppress anti-A or anti-B → both are present; type O RBCs (no A/B antigens) can be transfused to any ABO type in emergencies (universal donor for packed RBCs); however type O individuals have anti-A + anti-B in plasma → cannot receive A, B, or AB blood (would cause hemolytic transfusion reaction)
explanation: ABO blood groups: Group A: A antigen on RBCs, anti-B antibody in plasma. Group B: B antigen, anti-A antibody. Group AB: A + B antigens, no antibodies (universal plasma recipient). Group O: no A/B antigens, anti-A + anti-B antibodies (universal RBC donor but not universal plasma donor). ABO antibodies: IgM (naturally occurring, immediate intravascular hemolytic transfusion reaction, complement activation). Rh system: Rh antibodies are IgG (immune-mediated, cross placenta → hemolytic disease of newborn). Crossmatching tests compatibility. Type and screen vs. type and crossmatch. Blood bank: major crossmatch = donor cells + recipient serum (tests for recipient antibodies against donor); minor crossmatch = donor serum + recipient cells (tests for donor antibodies against recipient cells, less critical in packed RBCs).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which is the most important factor in determining oxygen delivery to tissues?
options: Cardiac output × arterial oxygen content (DO2 = CO × CaO2): CaO2 = (Hb × 1.34 × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2); the main component is the Hb-bound oxygen (Hb × 1.34 × SaO2); dissolved O2 (0.003 × PaO2) is negligible normally; therefore Hb concentration and SaO2 (and CO) are the key determinants of O2 delivery; anemia is more critical than ↓PaO2 in limiting O2 delivery (a patient with Hb 7 g/dL and normal SaO2 delivers far less O2 than with Hb 15 g/dL even if their PaO2 is 100 mmHg)
explanation: Oxygen delivery (DO2): DO2 = CO × CaO2. CaO2 (mL O2/dL blood) = (Hb × 1.34 × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2). Normal: Hb 15 g/dL × 1.34 mL O2/g × 0.98 + 0.003 × 100 = 19.7 + 0.3 ≈ 20 mL O2/dL. Normal CO = 5 L/min = 50 dL/min. DO2 = 50 × 20 = 1000 mL O2/min. VO2 (O2 consumption) = 250 mL/min. Oxygen extraction ratio (O2ER) = VO2/DO2 = 25% at rest. Fick equation: CO = VO2/(CaO2 - CvO2). DO2 threshold: below ~300-350 mL/min → O2 delivery-dependent metabolism → anaerobic → lactic acidosis. Improving DO2: transfuse (↑Hb), ↑CO (inotropes, fluids), ↑SaO2 (supplemental O2, intubation). 100% O2 increases dissolved O2 minimally (0.003 × 673 mmHg = 2 mL O2/dL vs. 0.3 at room air).

subject: Physiology
stem: Nitric oxide (NO): where is it produced and what is its primary vascular effect?
options: Endothelial cells via eNOS (endothelial nitric oxide synthase, NOS3): L-arginine + O2 + NADPH → NO + L-citrulline (cofactors: tetrahydrobiopterin/BH4, calmodulin, FAD, FMN); NO diffuses to adjacent vascular smooth muscle cells → binds soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) → ↑cGMP → activates PKG → phosphorylates MLCK (↓activity) + K+ channels (opens) → ↓[Ca2+]i → dephosphorylation of MLC → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation; also: inhibits platelet aggregation (↑cGMP → ↓GPIIb/IIIa) + anti-atherosclerotic
iNOS in macrophages (inducible, produces large amounts for microbicidal effects)
explanation: NOS isoforms: eNOS (NOS3): constitutive, Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent, produces low levels of NO → endothelial function, vasodilation, anti-platelet. nNOS (NOS1): neurons, constitutive, neurotransmitter (non-adrenergic non-cholinergic, NANC) → penile erection (parasympathetic → nNOS in corpus cavernosum → NO → vasodilation → erection). iNOS (NOS2): macrophages, astrocytes, smooth muscle → induced by LPS + cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-γ) → large amounts of NO → peroxynitrite (NO + O2•- → ONOO-) → cytotoxic → kills bacteria/tumor cells → also causes vasodilation in septic shock. Drug: sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor → ↓cGMP breakdown → ↑vasodilation → erectile dysfunction + pulmonary hypertension).

subject: Physiology
stem: During exercise, which mechanism maintains plasma glucose?
options: Entirely from glycogen breakdown in the liver

Hepatic glucose output via two mechanisms: (1) glycogenolysis (liver glycogen, primary in early exercise, ~90 min supply) + (2) gluconeogenesis (from lactate/Cori cycle, alanine/Cahill cycle, glycerol from lipolysis); glucagon ↑ slightly with prolonged exercise; catecholamines (↑epinephrine) → ↑glycogenolysis in liver + ↑lipolysis in adipose + ↑muscle glycogenolysis; insulin ↓ with exercise (despite normal plasma glucose) → ↑hepatic glucose output + ↑fat oxidation; at the same time, exercising muscle ↑GLUT4 translocation (contraction-mediated, insulin-independent) → ↑glucose uptake by muscle
Only from exogenous carbohydrates consumed during exercise
explanation: Hepatic glucose homeostasis during exercise: Rest: liver glucose output = 1.5-2 mg/kg/min. Moderate exercise: ↑to 3-4 mg/kg/min. Intense exercise: ↑to 6-8 mg/kg/min. The parallel ↑in muscle glucose uptake and hepatic glucose output is remarkably matched (glycemic homeostasis during exercise). Hormonal: ↑epinephrine + ↑glucagon → hepatic glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis. ↓Insulin → less inhibition of hepatic glucose production. Muscle: ↑GLUT4 via AMPK + Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent pathways → insulin-independent glucose uptake. Post-exercise: ↑insulin sensitivity (24-48 h) → enhanced GLUT4 expression + glycogen resynthesis. Relevance for diabetics: aerobic exercise improves insulin sensitivity; risk of hypoglycemia in T1DM (↓insulin dose or eat CHO before exercise).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'starling forces' across a capillary: which force favors fluid filtration OUT of the capillary?
options: Plasma oncotic pressure (π_c) draws fluid INTO capillary

Capillary hydrostatic pressure (P_c) — the blood pressure within the capillary drives fluid OUT through the porous capillary wall; the net filtration pressure = (P_c - P_if) - σ(π_c - π_if); where P_c (~35 mmHg at arteriolar end, ~15 mmHg at venular end) is the hydrostatic pressure of blood, P_if (~-3 mmHg) is interstitial hydrostatic pressure, π_c (~28 mmHg) is plasma oncotic pressure (inward), π_if (~8 mmHg) is interstitial oncotic pressure (outward); net fluid filtered at arteriolar end and mostly reabsorbed at venular end (Starling hypothesis) with remainder drained by lymphatics
Interstitial oncotic pressure favors reabsorption only
explanation: Starling equation: Jv = Kf × [(Pc - Pif) - σ(πc - πif)]. Normal values: Pc arterial end = 35 mmHg, Pc venous end = 15 mmHg; Pif = -3 to 0 mmHg; πc = 28 mmHg; πif = 8 mmHg. Net filtration at arterial end: (35-0) - (28-8) = 35 - 20 = +15 mmHg (outward). Net reabsorption at venous end: (15-0) - (28-8) = 15 - 20 = -5 mmHg (inward). Approximate: 90% of filtered fluid reabsorbed at venous end; 10% via lymphatics. Edema formation: ↑Pc (heart failure, venous obstruction), ↓πc (hypoalbuminemia: liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition), ↑capillary permeability (inflammation, burns), ↓lymphatic drainage (lymphedema). Pulmonary edema: normal Pc = 7-12 mmHg (low to keep alveoli dry); ↑with LV failure → pulmonary edema.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'tension pneumothorax' causes hemodynamic compromise by:
options: Compressing the heart and great veins: air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space → pushes the mediastinum to the opposite side (tracheal deviation away from the affected side) → compresses the contralateral lung + kinks the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava → ↓venous return → ↓preload → ↓CO → obstructive shock; also compresses the heart itself (↓cardiac filling); treatment: immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS, midclavicular line) followed by chest drain
Causing hypoxia as the only mechanism
explanation: Tension pneumothorax: one-way valve mechanism → air enters pleural space on inspiration, cannot exit → progressive pressure build-up. Clinical: tracheal deviation (away from side of tension), absent breath sounds (ipsilateral), ↑JVP (impaired venous return), ↓BP, hypoxia, tachycardia. Obstructive shock: ↓preload → ↓CO despite normal myocardium. Causes: penetrating chest trauma, rib fractures with pleural laceration, iatrogenic (central line, positive pressure ventilation with PEEP). Management: emergency needle decompression → large-bore 14G needle → 2nd ICS MCL (or 4th-5th ICS, anterior axillary line per updated guidelines) → followed by chest drain (2nd-6th ICS, anterior axillary line). Do NOT wait for CXR in tension pneumothorax (clinical diagnosis).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cell type is the precursor of both osteoclasts and macrophages?
options: Mesenchymal stem cells (give rise to osteoblasts)

Monocyte/macrophage lineage (myeloid progenitor → monocyte in blood → tissue macrophage, or → macrophage fusion → osteoclast): osteoclasts are multinucleated giant cells (fusion of macrophage precursors) → activated by RANKL (from osteoblasts + T cells) binding RANK on osteoclast precursors → differentiation → bone resorption; osteoprotegerin (OPG, decoy receptor for RANKL from osteoblasts) inhibits osteoclastogenesis; osteoblasts produce both RANKL (stimulates osteoclasts) and OPG (inhibits osteoclasts) → coupling of bone formation and resorption
explanation: RANK-RANKL-OPG axis: Osteoblasts express RANKL (receptor activator of NF-κB ligand) + OPG (osteoprotegerin, soluble decoy receptor). RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → NF-κB activation → osteoclast differentiation + activation → ↑bone resorption. OPG competes with RANK for RANKL binding → ↓osteoclast activation → ↓resorption. Regulation: PTH, 1,25-OH2D3, IL-1β, TNF-α, glucocorticoids → ↑RANKL + ↓OPG → ↑bone resorption. Estrogen → ↑OPG + ↓RANKL → ↓bone resorption; menopause → ↓estrogen → ↑osteoclast activity → osteoporosis. Denosumab (anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody) → ↓osteoclast activity → used for osteoporosis, bone metastases.

subject: Physiology
stem: The mechanism of hypercalcemia in primary hyperparathyroidism:
options: ↑PTH from parathyroid adenoma (most common cause, 85%) → (1) ↑bone resorption (osteoclasts via RANKL) → ↑Ca2+ release from bone; (2) ↑renal Ca2+ reabsorption (DCT, TRPV5) → less Ca2+ lost in urine; (3) ↑1α-hydroxylase in kidney → ↑1,25-(OH)2D3 → ↑GI Ca2+ absorption; net: ↑serum Ca2+; PTH simultaneously ↓renal phosphate reabsorption (NPT2a) → ↑urine phosphate → ↓serum PO4 (hypophosphatemia); classic labs: hypercalcemia + hypophosphatemia + ↑PTH + ↑alkaline phosphatase + ↑urinary Ca2+
explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism (1° HPT): Cause: parathyroid adenoma (85%), hyperplasia (MEN1, MEN2A), carcinoma (rare). Symptoms: 'bones (osteitis fibrosa cystica, brown tumors), stones (nephrolithiasis, hypercalciuria), groans (constipation, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis), psychic moans (confusion, depression)'. Labs: ↑Ca2+, ↓PO4, ↑PTH (intact PTH, distinguishes from hypercalcemia of malignancy where PTH is suppressed + PTHrP may be elevated), ↑24h urinary Ca2+ (↑GFR + ↑tubular load), ↑ALP. Imaging: Tc-99m sestamibi scan (parathyroid scintigraphy) + neck USS. Treatment: surgery (parathyroidectomy) for symptomatic cases; cinacalcet (calcimimetic, activates CaSR → ↓PTH) for medical management.

subject: Physiology
stem: Maximum urine osmolality that can be achieved by a normal human kidney:
options: 1200-1400 mOsm/kg — achieved in the presence of maximal ADH stimulation (severe dehydration): ADH (arginine vasopressin, AVP) → V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates AQP2 → AQP2 vesicles fuse with apical membrane → ↑water permeability → water flows out (driven by the hyperosmotic medullary interstitium, ~1200 mOsm/kg in the deepest part of the inner medulla) → concentrated urine; minimum urine volume = ~0.5 L/day
explanation: Urine concentrating ability: Max urine osmolality: 1200-1400 mOsm/kg (vs. plasma 285-295 mOsm/kg → concentration ratio ~4-5×). Required for this: (1) Intact countercurrent multiplier (loop of Henle, NKCC2): builds medullary hyperosmolarity. (2) Urea recycling (inner medulla → very high osmolality from urea). (3) Maximal ADH (V2 → AQP2 in collecting duct). (4) Normal tubular function. Minimum urine osmolality: ~50 mOsm/kg (maximal water diuresis = no ADH). Disorders: Diabetes insipidus (central: ↓ADH → urine cannot concentrate → low osmolality <300 mOsm/kg; nephrogenic: ADH present but collecting duct unresponsive → similar result; responds to desmopressin in central, not nephrogenic). SIADH: urine inappropriately concentrated (>100 mOsm/kg) despite serum hypo-osmolality.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'Fick principle' for measuring cardiac output requires measuring:
options: O2 consumption (VO2) + arteriovenous O2 content difference: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2); O2 consumption measured by spirometry (indirect calorimetry); CaO2 from arterial blood gas + Hb; CvO2 from mixed venous blood (pulmonary artery catheter, must be truly mixed in the PA); normal CO = 250 mL/min ÷ 50 mL/L (5 mL/dL × 10 dL/L) = 5 L/min; also used: Fick principle for CO2, dye dilution (indocyanine green), thermodilution (cold saline bolus via Swan-Ganz)
Only blood pressure and heart rate
Only O2 saturation in pulmonary artery
explanation: Fick's principle (conservation of mass): Whatever O2 is consumed by the body must equal what the heart delivers minus what it returns: VO2 = CO × (CaO2 - CvO2). Rearranging: CO = VO2/(CaO2 - CvO2). Normal: VO2 = 250 mL/min; CaO2 = 20 mL/dL; CvO2 = 15 mL/dL; A-vO2 = 5 mL/dL = 50 mL/L; CO = 250/50 = 5 L/min. Thermodilution: inject cold saline into RA → PA catheter thermistor measures temperature change over time → Stewart-Hamilton equation → CO. Indicator dilution: CO = (amount of indicator) / (concentration × time); indocyanine green most used. Exercise: VO2 ↑ → must be matched by ↑CO × ↑O2 extraction; max VO2 (VO2max) = maximal CO × maximal AV-O2 difference; determines aerobic fitness.

subject: Physiology
stem: Erythropoiesis: which vitamin is required for normal nuclear maturation?
options: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid, for iron absorption)

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate (folic acid): both required for thymidylate synthesis (folate: THF → 5,10-methylene-THF → deoxythymidylate via thymidylate synthase); B12 required to regenerate THF from 5-methyl-THF (methionine synthase: 5-methyl-THF + homocysteine → THF + methionine); without THF → ↓DNA synthesis → erythroblasts arrest in S phase → enlarge (↑RNA/protein synthesis continues) → megaloblasts; result: macrocytic megaloblastic anemia (↑MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, macro-ovalocytes)
Vitamin A (retinol, for vision and epithelium)
explanation: Megaloblastic anemia: B12 or folate deficiency → ↓DNA synthesis → nuclear maturation arrest → megaloblasts in bone marrow → peripheral blood macro-ovalocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5-lobed, 'right shift'). B12 vs. folate deficiency distinction: B12 deficiency → ↑homocysteine + ↑MMA (methylmalonic acid, B12 is cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA); neurological signs (subacute combined degeneration: posterolateral column demyelination → loss of vibration + proprioception + upper + lower motor neuron signs). Folate deficiency → ↑homocysteine but NORMAL MMA; no neurological signs; cause: poor diet, pregnancy ↑requirement, methotrexate, alcohol, phenytoin. Treatment: replace specific vitamin; both together (if unclear) may mask B12-induced neurological damage (folate treats anemia but not neurology).

subject: Physiology
stem: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV): what does it do?
options: Generates ATP (that is Complex V, ATP synthase)

Final electron acceptor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain: accepts electrons from cytochrome c (reduced, from Complex III) → transfers to O2 (final acceptor) → reduces O2 to H2O (4 electrons per O2 + 4 H+); simultaneously: pumps H+ across the IMM (4H+ per O2 reduced) → contributes to proton motive force → ATP synthesis by Complex V; inhibitors: cyanide (CN- binds Fe3+ in Complex IV → blocks electron transfer to O2 → no ATP → ↑lactic acidosis), carbon monoxide (CO, lower affinity than cyanide for Complex IV but also inhibits other heme proteins), azide, H2S
Pumps H+ into the matrix (Complex V uses H+ gradient, not generates it)
explanation: Mitochondrial ETC complexes: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): NADH → NAD+ + 2e- → ubiquinone (Q); pumps 4H+ across IMM. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase): FADH2 → FAD + 2e- → Q; does NOT pump H+. Complex III (cytochrome bc1): Q → cytochrome c; pumps 4H+ (Q cycle). Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): cytochrome c → O2 → H2O; pumps 4H+. ATP synthase (Complex V / F1F0-ATPase): H+ flows down gradient through F0 → rotary mechanism → F1 synthesizes ATP; ~2.5 ATP per NADH (10H+ pumped / 4H+ per ATP ≈ 2.5). Inhibitors: Complex I: rotenone, amytal; Complex II: malonate; Complex III: antimycin A; Complex IV: cyanide, CO, azide, H2S; Complex V: oligomycin (blocks H+ channel), FCCP (uncoupler).

subject: Physiology
stem: Phosphocreatine (PCr) system: how long can it fuel maximal exercise?
options: 5-10 seconds only: at the onset of intense muscular activity, PCr (stored in muscle) + ADP → Cr + ATP (creatine kinase reaction, reversible); provides immediate ATP without O2 (anaerobic); PCr stores are limited (~20 mmol/kg muscle) and exhausted within 5-10 seconds at maximal effort (e.g., 100m sprint power phase); replenishment: requires ~2-3 minutes of rest/low-intensity exercise (oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP → creatine kinase runs in reverse → PCr resynthesis)
explanation: Energy systems for exercise: Immediately available ATP: ~5 mmol/kg muscle → powers ~1-2 seconds. Phosphocreatine (PCr): ~20 mmol/kg → extends to ~5-10 seconds (100m sprint). Anaerobic glycolysis (lactate system): glycogen → pyruvate → lactate; ~30-60 seconds of maximal effort; faster than oxidative but limited by H+ accumulation (lactic acidosis). Aerobic (oxidative): slowest but most sustained; uses glucose (glycolysis + TCA + ETC), FFA (β-oxidation + TCA + ETC), ketones; predominates from ~2 minutes of maximal effort and throughout endurance events. Creatine supplementation: ↑intramuscular PCr stores → may improve repeated high-intensity bouts. ATP production rates: PCr > anaerobic glycolysis > oxidative phosphorylation (power vs. capacity trade-off).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'law of Laplace' for a hollow sphere: pressure = 2T/r. What is the implication for smaller vs. larger alveoli?
options: Smaller alveoli have LOWER pressure and are more stable

Smaller alveoli have HIGHER transmural pressure (P = 2T/r; smaller r → higher P with same T) → tendency to collapse into larger alveoli unless surfactant reduces surface tension (T) proportionally more in smaller alveoli; in IRDS, absent surfactant → small alveoli have very high pressure relative to large alveoli → collapse → atelectasis; lung surfactant has the remarkable property of reducing surface tension MORE when the film is compressed (smaller alveolus) → equalizes pressure across alveolar sizes → prevents collapse; this is why surfactant reduces the tendency of different-sized alveoli to communicate catastrophically
Larger alveoli have higher pressure (incorrect for same T)
explanation: Laplace law and lung stability: P = 2T/r (single surface) or 4T/r (bubble with two surfaces). Without surfactant: smaller alveoli (r ↓) → P ↑ → air moves from high P (small) to low P (large) → small alveoli collapse into large ('unstable'). With surfactant (DPPC): as alveoli shrink during expiration → surfactant film compressed → ↑surface density of surfactant molecules → ↓T proportionally → P stabilized. Also: surfactant's unique surface tension vs. area hysteresis loop means T decreases as r decreases → stabilizes alveoli. Type II pneumocytes: produce surfactant (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D + phospholipids) → stored in lamellar bodies → secreted by exocytosis → form tubular myelin → surface film at air-liquid interface.

subject: Physiology
stem: In the ECG, what does the PR interval represent?
options: The time from onset of atrial depolarization (P wave) to onset of ventricular depolarization (start of QRS): includes: (1) atrial conduction time; (2) AV nodal delay (main contributor: slow Ca2+-dependent conduction in AV node, 50-150 ms) + His-bundle + bundle branches; normal PR: 120-200 ms (0.12-0.20 sec); ↑PR (>200 ms) = first-degree AV block (prolonged AV conduction); variable PR increasing → dropped QRS = Wenckebach (Mobitz type I); fixed PR, sudden drop = Mobitz type II; complete dissociation = third-degree AV block
Repolarization of the ventricles (that is the QT interval)
explanation: PR interval: normally 120-200 ms. Measured from onset of P to onset of QRS (Q or R, whichever comes first). AV block classification: 1st degree: PR >200 ms, every P followed by QRS (not a true 'block', just ↓conduction). 2nd degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach): PR progressively ↑ → dropped QRS → cycle repeats; AV nodal level; often benign; no pacemaker needed unless symptomatic. 2nd degree Mobitz II: fixed PR, sudden non-conducted P → dropped QRS (no PR change); infranodal (His or bundle branches); ↑risk progression to complete block → pacemaker indicated. 3rd degree (complete): P and QRS independent (AV dissociation); escape rhythm from junctional (40-60 bpm) or ventricular (20-40 bpm); emergency pacemaker. PR delta wave (short PR + slurred QRS): Wolf-Parkinson-White (accessory pathway bypasses AV node → ventricular pre-excitation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Pacemaker potential (If current): what ions carry it?
options: Na+ and K+ through a non-selective channel gated by hyperpolarization

Both Na+ and K+ flow through HCN (hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated) channels (funny channels, If = inward = net depolarizing): when membrane potential is very negative (after repolarization of SA node, ~-60 mV) → HCN channels open → Na+ and K+ enter/leave (predominantly Na+ inward under these conditions, net depolarizing) → 'funny current' → phase 4 spontaneous depolarization; HCN channels are activated at very negative voltages AND sensitized by cAMP (sympathetic stimulation → ↑cAMP → shift HCN activation curve to more positive voltages → ↑If → faster depolarization → ↑HR); ivabradine: HCN blocker → ↓HR without affecting contractility or BP
explanation: SA node pacemaker potential (phase 4): Three currents contribute: (1) If (funny current, HCN channels): activated by hyperpolarization, carries inward Na+ (mainly) + outward K+ → net depolarization. (2) ICaT (T-type Ca2+, CaV3.1): activates at -50 mV → small Ca2+ inward. (3) Slowly decreasing IK (delayed rectifier K+ channels deactivate) → less outward K+ → net depolarization. Phase 0 of SA node: L-type Ca2+ (ICaL, CaV1.2/1.3) → slow response (not fast Na+). Autonomic modulation: Sympathetic (β1 → ↑cAMP → ↑If + ↑ICaL + ↑IKs) → steeper phase 4 + shortened action potential → ↑HR. Vagal (M2 → ↑KACh via Gi → hyperpolarizes SA node + slows phase 4) → ↓HR. Ivabradine (If blocker): rate-specific, used in HF with ↑HR.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'hepatic acinus' (of Rappaport) zones: which zone is most susceptible to ischemic hepatocellular necrosis?
options: Zone 3 (centrilobular, around the central vein): furthest from the portal tracts → receives blood last → lowest O2 tension → most susceptible to ischemia/hypoxia (centrilobular necrosis in right heart failure, shock, Budd-Chiari, carbon tetrachloride/halothane toxicity) and hepatotoxic drugs (paracetamol: CYP2E1 highest in zone 3 → toxic metabolite NAPQI preferentially in zone 3 → glutathione depleted → hepatocyte necrosis); zone 1 = most O2 (first to receive portal blood), most susceptible to viral hepatitis and phosphorus toxicity (which are metabolically activated in zone 1)
Zone 2 (mid-zone, rare to be affected in isolation)
Zone 1 is most susceptible to ischemia
explanation: Hepatic acinus zones (Rappaport): Zone 1 (periportal): richest in O2 + nutrients (first to receive portal blood); highest enzyme activity for: fatty acid oxidation, gluconeogenesis, amino acid metabolism. Most susceptible: viral hepatitis (enters via portal tract), phosphorus, yellow fever. Zone 3 (centrilobular, perivenular): poorest in O2 (last to receive), lowest O2 tension; highest CYP450 (CYP2E1, CYP1A2), highest glutathione content. Most susceptible: ischemic necrosis (congestive heart failure → 'nutmeg liver'), paracetamol/APAP toxicity (CYP2E1 → NAPQI → glutathione depletion → zone 3 necrosis), halothane hepatitis (reductive metabolism by CYP in zone 3), CCl4, CHCl3. Zone 2: rare selective involvement. Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis): zone 3 congestion/necrosis.

subject: Physiology
stem: Myoglobin vs. hemoglobin: which molecule has a HIGHER O2 affinity and why?
options: Myoglobin: monomeric protein (single globin chain + heme) → binds O2 with high affinity and a HYPERBOLIC O2 dissociation curve (not sigmoidal); P50 ~1-2 mmHg (vs. Hb P50 ~27 mmHg); purpose: stores O2 in muscle and facilitates O2 diffusion within muscle cells to mitochondria; it becomes saturated at low PO2 (even at the low PO2 of exercising muscle interstitium ~20-30 mmHg); hemoglobin's lower affinity (higher P50) is appropriate for O2 delivery: loads O2 in high-PO2 pulmonary capillaries and unloads in low-PO2 tissues
Carboxyhemoglobin (which has similar affinity as oxyhemoglobin for remaining sites)
explanation: Myoglobin vs. hemoglobin: Myoglobin: monomer (1 heme), no cooperativity → hyperbolic curve, P50 ~1-2 mmHg, highest affinity. O2 storage + intracellular O2 transport to mitochondria. Releases O2 only at very low PO2 (e.g., intense exercise). Hemoglobin: tetramer (4 subunits, α2β2), cooperativity (T→R state shift) → sigmoidal curve, P50 ~27 mmHg. Functional: loads O2 in lungs (high PO2, near saturation), delivers in tissues (↓PO2, Bohr effect, 2,3-DPG). Sigmoidal curve advantage: large amounts of O2 delivered for small drops in PO2 (steep middle portion); efficient 'off-loading'. Myoglobinuria: crush injury (rhabdomyolysis) → myoglobin released from injured muscle → filtered in kidney → acute tubular necrosis (tea-colored urine, ↑CK, ↑LDH).

subject: Physiology
stem: Capillary recruitment during exercise: what mechanism increases muscle O2 supply?
options: Opening of previously closed capillaries (capillary recruitment) in skeletal muscle: at rest, only ~30-50% of muscle capillaries are open (the others are closed/non-perfused); during exercise, local metabolic vasodilation (CO2 ↑, pH ↓, O2 ↓, adenosine ↑, K+ ↑, prostaglandins, NO) → precapillary sphincters relax → ↑capillary recruitment → ↑functional surface area for exchange → ↑O2 delivery + ↑CO2/heat removal; also: ↑erythrocyte transit time (slower) → more time for O2 unloading; ↓O2-Hb affinity (Bohr effect: ↑CO2 + ↓pH)
Cardiac output decreases to redirect blood to the skin
explanation: Vascular adaptations to exercise: Local metabolic vasodilation: ↑CO2 (↑PCO2 → H+), ↓PO2, ↑adenosine, ↑K+, ↑prostaglandins (PGI2, PGE2), ↑NO from endothelium + shear stress → ↑arteriolar dilation + precapillary sphincter relaxation → ↑capillary blood flow. Capillary recruitment: ↑perfused capillaries → ↑surface area → ↑diffusion capacity → ↑O2 delivery. Functional hyperemia (exercise hyperemia): in contracting muscle, blood flow can increase 20× above rest. Neural: sympathetic ↑HR/contractility; sympathetic restrains vasoconstriction but metabolic signals override. Nitric oxide: eNOS in endothelium (shear stress) + nNOS in muscle (contraction) → NO → relaxation. Training effects: ↑mitochondria, ↑myoglobin, ↑capillary density, ↑O2 extraction, ↑VO2max.

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α): what regulates it?
options: Intracellular O2 tension: in normoxia, prolyl hydroxylase (PHD, requires O2 as substrate) hydroxylates HIF-1α → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau protein, E3 ubiquitin ligase) binds → ubiquitination → proteasomal degradation; in hypoxia, PHD inactive (no O2 substrate) → HIF-1α accumulates → binds HIF-1β → translocates to nucleus → transcribes hypoxia response genes: EPO (↑RBC), VEGF (angiogenesis), GLUT1/3 (↑glucose uptake), glycolytic enzymes (LDH, PGK), inducible NOS; VHL disease (loss-of-function mutations) → ↑HIF-1α even in normoxia → hemangioblastomas, clear cell RCC (VEGF-driven)
explanation: HIF-1 system: HIF-1 = HIF-1α (O2-regulated) + HIF-1β (constitutive). PHD enzymes (PHD1/2/3): prolyl hydroxylases, require O2 + Fe2+ + 2-oxoglutarate + ascorbate → hydroxylate HIF-1α at Pro402 and Pro564 → VHL recognition → ubiquitin-proteasome degradation (t½ <5 min in normoxia). Factor inhibiting HIF (FIH): hydroxylates Asn803 → prevents coactivator (CBP/p300) binding → ↓transcription. HIF target genes: EPO (renal peritubular fibroblasts → ↑RBC), VEGF-A (angiogenesis), LDHA/PGK1 (↑glycolysis), GLUT1/3 (↑glucose import), PHD2/3 (negative feedback), transferrin + transferrin receptor (↑iron uptake), carbonic anhydrase IX (pH regulation). VHL loss: constitutive HIF → pseudohypoxic state → ↑VEGF → angiomatous tumors (hemangioblastoma, clear cell RCC). HIF also mediates hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) gene changes.

subject: Physiology
stem: Venous return: which law describes the relationship between venous return and right atrial pressure?
options: Guyton's venous return curve: venous return = (mean systemic filling pressure - right atrial pressure) / resistance to venous return; at normal conditions: MSFP ~7-8 mmHg, RAP ~0 mmHg, VR = ~5 L/min (equals CO); ↑blood volume → ↑MSFP → ↑VR; ↓TPR (vasodilation, exercise, AV fistula) → ↑VR (shift of curve); ↑RAP (heart failure, cardiac tamponade) → ↓VR; at RAP = MSFP → VR = 0 (mean circulatory filling pressure = equilibrium); the intersection of Guyton's venous return curve and Frank-Starling curve = operating point (determines CO and RAP simultaneously)
Poiseuille's law (relates flow to pressure and resistance in tubes)
Bernoulli's principle (relates velocity and pressure in flowing fluid)
explanation: Guyton's venous return curve: plotted as VR (y-axis) vs RAP (x-axis). Slope: 1/Rv (resistance to venous return). X-intercept: MSFP (mean systemic filling pressure = pressure if heart stopped → equilibrium point). VR = (MSFP - RAP)/Rv. Manipulation: ↑blood volume (transfusion) → ↑MSFP → curve shifts right → ↑VR. Exercise (vasodilation + muscle pump) → ↓Rv → ↑slope + ↑VR. SNS activation → ↑venous tone → ↑MSFP (redistributes blood from veins → ↑MSFP → ↑VR). Heart failure → ↑RAP → ↓VR (moves along the curve to the right). Cardiac output determination: intersection of VR curve + Frank-Starling curve on a RAP vs. flow graph → only one steady-state point where heart output = venous return.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which protein maintains ventricular muscle in a quiescent state between action potentials?
options: Troponin I (TnI) — in diastole when cytoplasmic Ca2+ is low (~100 nM): TnI inhibitory region binds actin and TnC to lock tropomyosin over the myosin-binding sites on actin → prevents cross-bridge formation → muscle quiescence; during systole: ↑[Ca2+] (~1-10 µM) → Ca2+ binds TnC (3 Ca2+ bind: 2 low-affinity regulatory Ca2+ sites + 1 high-affinity structural site) → conformational change in TnC → releases TnI inhibitory region from actin → tropomyosin shifts → myosin-binding sites exposed → cross-bridge cycling; cTnI (cardiac isoform) and cTnT are specific cardiac markers for myocardial injury (released by ischemic myocytes)
Dystrophin (links actin cytoskeleton to extracellular matrix)
explanation: Troponin complex (thin filament regulation): TnC (calcium-binding): ~18 kDa, 4 Ca2+-binding sites (2 regulatory N-terminal low-affinity: control activation; 2 structural C-terminal high-affinity). TnI (inhibitory): ~24 kDa; inhibitory region binds actin (in absence of Ca2+) + N-terminus binds TnC → stabilizes off state; phosphorylation of TnI by PKA (β1 adrenergic → ↑cAMP) → ↓Ca2+ sensitivity of TnC → faster relaxation (lusitropy) → important for heart rate increase (TnI phosphorylation allows rapid relaxation at ↑HR). TnT (tropomyosin-binding): anchors troponin complex to tropomyosin. Cardiac specificity: cTnI and cTnT are encoded by cardiac-specific genes → not expressed in healthy skeletal muscle → highly specific biomarkers for myocardial injury (MI diagnosis, rise within 3-4h, peak 12-24h, persist 5-14 days).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which lung disease shows an obstructive pattern on spirometry with gas trapping (↑TLC, ↑RV)?
options: Emphysema (a type of COPD): destruction of alveolar walls → ↓elastic recoil → airways collapse prematurely on expiration → air trapping (↑RV) → barrel chest (↑AP diameter); spirometry: ↓FEV1, ↓FVC, ↓FEV1/FVC (<70%), ↑TLC, ↑FRC, ↑RV; DLCO ↓ (↓alveolar surface area); distinct from chronic bronchitis (productive cough >3 months in 2 consecutive years, airways disease, normal or mildly ↑ air trapping)
Myasthenia gravis (normal spirometry except ↓MVC/NIF due to respiratory muscle weakness)
explanation: Spirometry patterns: Obstructive (↓FEV1/FVC <70%): emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma, bronchiectasis. In emphysema: ↑TLC (air trapping), ↑RV, ↑FRC, ↑RV/TLC ratio (>40%), ↓DLCO (↓alveolar surface area), normal or ↑compliance. In chronic bronchitis: same FEV1/FVC reduction but DLCO may be normal. In asthma: reversible obstruction (bronchodilator response: FEV1 ↑≥12% and ≥200 mL). Restrictive (↓TLC with normal or ↑FEV1/FVC): ILD (fibrosis, sarcoidosis), pleural disease, neuromuscular weakness, chest wall deformity (kyphoscoliosis, obesity). In fibrosis: ↓TLC, ↓DLCO, ↑FEV1/FVC (stiff lungs → both volumes down but FEV1 proportion maintained). Mixed pattern: ↓FEV1/FVC + ↓TLC (e.g., combined emphysema + fibrosis, old TB with fibrosis and air trapping).

subject: Physiology
stem: Insulin C-peptide: what is its diagnostic utility?
options: C-peptide is a pro-hormone with biological activity

C-peptide has no hormonal activity but its serum level reflects endogenous insulin secretion: proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide in equimolar amounts (both stored in β-cell secretory granules and released together by exocytosis); measuring C-peptide distinguishes: (1) exogenous insulin injection (no C-peptide produced, as it is not in commercial insulin preparations) vs. endogenous insulin secretion (↑C-peptide); (2) insulinoma (↑C-peptide + ↑insulin + hypoglycemia) vs. factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous insulin (↑insulin + ↓C-peptide); used also to monitor residual β-cell function in T1DM
C-peptide is the active fragment of proinsulin
explanation: C-peptide (connecting peptide): 31-amino-acid peptide connecting A and B chains of insulin in proinsulin. Prohormone convertases (PC1/PC2) cleave proinsulin in secretory granules → insulin + C-peptide + 2 dipeptides. C-peptide: no known significant hormonal action in humans (some argue: may have mild anti-inflammatory or microvascular effects). Clearance: C-peptide t½ ~30 min (longer than insulin t½ ~5 min, as it bypasses hepatic first-pass extraction). Clinical: (1) C-peptide in hypoglycemia: if low (near 0) → exogenous insulin or IGF-2 source; if high → endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma, sulfonylurea). (2) T1DM residual β-cell function: unstimulated or glucagon-stimulated C-peptide. (3) T2DM β-cell reserve assessment. Note: sulfonylurea abuse → ↑C-peptide (stimulates endogenous secretion, mimics insulinoma — differentiated by urine sulfonylurea screen).

subject: Physiology
stem: The major determinant of glomerular filtration rate (GFR):
options: Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC): GFR = Kf × (PGC - PBS - π_GC + π_BS), where PGC is the hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries (~55 mmHg) driving filtration; PBS is Bowman's space hydrostatic pressure (~15 mmHg, opposing filtration); π_GC is the oncotic pressure of glomerular capillary blood (~30 mmHg, opposing filtration); π_BS ≈ 0 (no protein in Bowman's filtrate); net filtration pressure ≈ 55 - 15 - 30 = 10 mmHg; ↑systemic arterial BP → ↑PGC unless autoregulated; efferent arteriolar constriction (angiotensin II) → ↑PGC → ↑GFR but eventually ↑π_GC → filtration equilibrium
explanation: GFR determinants: GFR = Kf × NFP; NFP (net filtration pressure) = (PGC - PBS) - (πGC - πBS). Normal values: PGC = 55 mmHg, PBS = 15 mmHg, πGC = 30 mmHg (rises along glomerulus as protein concentrates), πBS ≈ 0. NFP ≈ 10 mmHg. Kf (ultrafiltration coefficient) = Kf × A (hydraulic conductivity × surface area). Autoregulation (80-180 mmHg): myogenic reflex (afferent arteriole constricts when stretched) + tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa → adenosine → afferent vasoconstriction) keep GFR stable despite BP changes. Manipulations: ↑afferent dilation (dopamine, ANP) → ↑GFR. ↑Efferent constriction (Ang II) → ↑GFR but ↑filtration fraction. ACE inhibitors → ↓Ang II → dilate efferent → ↓GFR (caution in bilateral renal artery stenosis or single functioning kidney). NSAIDs → block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation → ↓GFR.

subject: Physiology
stem: Einthoven's triangle: which ECG lead represents the difference between left arm (LA) and right arm (RA) potentials?
options: Lead I is RA minus LA (incorrect sign)

Lead I = LA - RA: defined as the potential difference between the left arm (LA, positive electrode) and right arm (RA, negative reference electrode); when the net electrical vector of the heart points toward LA → positive deflection in Lead I; Einthoven's triangle: RA (−), LA (−), LL (−) form the triangle; Lead I = LA − RA; Lead II = LL − RA; Lead III = LL − LA; Einthoven's law: Lead II = Lead I + Lead III (algebraic sum of deflections)
Lead aVL represents the LA minus RA relationship
explanation: ECG lead system: Bipolar limb leads (Einthoven): Lead I: LA(+) − RA(−) → horizontal, leftward. Lead II: LL(+) − RA(−) → inferior (most concordant with electrical axis, often tallest QRS). Lead III: LL(+) − LA(−). Einthoven's law: II = I + III. Augmented unipolar limb leads (Goldberger): aVR: RA(+) vs. mean of LA+LL. aVL: LA(+) vs. mean of RA+LL. aVF: LL(+) vs. mean of RA+LA. Precordial leads (Wilson): V1 (right sternal border) → V6 (left midaxillary). Normal QRS axis: 0° to +90° (I positive, aVF positive). Left axis deviation: −30° to −90° (I positive, aVF negative, II negative). Right axis deviation: +90° to +180° (I negative, aVF positive). Extreme/Northwest axis: +180° to +270° (both I and aVF negative).

subject: Physiology
stem: Oxygen toxicity in the lung: which mechanism causes it?
options: Generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS): high PO2 → ↑superoxide (O2•-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), hydroxyl radical (OH•) in mitochondria and via non-mitochondrial oxidases → overwhelms antioxidant defenses (SOD, catalase, glutathione peroxidase) → oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, lipids (peroxidation) → type I pneumocyte injury → ↑permeability → pulmonary edema → ARDS (diffuse alveolar damage, hyaline membranes); clinical: >50-60% O2 for >24-48h begins to cause toxicity; infants: retinopathy of prematurity (ROP, retinal neovascularization from high PO2) + bronchopulmonary dysplasia
Absorption atelectasis from N2 washout (separate mechanism)
explanation: Oxygen toxicity: (1) Tracheobronchitis: first manifestation of O2 toxicity; substernal chest discomfort, cough, ↓ mucociliary clearance. (2) Absorptive atelectasis (different mechanism): high FiO2 → N2 washed out from alveoli → alveoli filled with O2 → O2 absorbed by blood → alveolar collapse. (3) Pulmonary O2 toxicity: type I pneumocyte injury → exudative phase (edema) → proliferative phase → fibrosis. (4) CNS O2 toxicity (hyperbaric O2 at >1.5 atm, Paul Bert effect): seizures. (5) ROP (retinopathy of prematurity): premature infants exposed to high O2 → immature retinal vasculature regresses (Wnt/Norrin pathway disruption) → retinal ischemia → compensatory VEGF → neovascularization. Safe: 30-50% FiO2 for days/weeks. Toxicity threshold: >60% for >24h.

subject: Physiology
stem: Renin: how is its activity regulated by the sympathetic nervous system?
options: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on JG cells stimulate renin

Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on juxtaglomerular (JG) cells: sympathetic activation → NE + E → β1 receptor on JG cells → ↑cAMP → ↑renin secretion; this is the mechanism by which stress/hemorrhage activates RAAS → ↑Ang II → ↑aldosterone + vasoconstriction + ↑ADH → ↑BP + ↑Na+/H2O retention; β-blockers (propranolol, atenolol, metoprolol) → ↓β1 stimulation → ↓renin → ↓Ang II → ↓BP; mechanism of β-blocker hypotensive effect includes ↓renin
explanation: Renin regulation (three mechanisms): (1) Renal baroreceptor (afferent arteriole wall): ↓perfusion pressure → ↓wall stretch → ↑renin. (2) Macula densa: ↓NaCl delivery → ↑PGE2 → ↑cAMP in JG cells → ↑renin. (3) Sympathetic nervous system: β1 on JG cells → ↑cAMP → ↑renin. Inhibitors of renin release: ↑BP (↑stretch), ↑NaCl (macula densa), adenosine (A1 receptor on JG cells → ↓cAMP → ↓renin), NO. Direct renin inhibitor: aliskiren (binds active site of renin → ↓Ang I generation). β-blockers: inhibit β1-mediated renin release → one of 3 mechanisms for BP lowering (others: ↓CO, central ↓sympathetic tone). ACE inhibitors → ↓Ang II → ↑renin (feedback: ↓Ang II removes negative feedback → ↑renin) → but since ACE is blocked, ↑renin → ↑Ang I but little Ang II.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which substance is the most important long-term regulator of blood pressure?
options: Baroreceptor reflex (short-term, resets with chronic hypertension)

The kidneys via pressure natriuresis (Guyton's infinite gain concept): ↑MAP → ↑renal perfusion → ↑GFR + ↓proximal tubule reabsorption → ↑Na+ and H2O excretion → ↓blood volume → ↓CO → ↓MAP back to normal; conversely ↓MAP → ↓natriuresis → Na+ and H2O retained → ↑blood volume → ↑MAP; the kidney-body fluid feedback loop has 'infinite gain' (sets a precise operating point for MAP = the equilibrium pressure for zero net renal fluid balance); all chronic hypertension must ultimately shift the renal pressure-natriuresis curve rightward (kidneys reset to excrete normal Na+ at higher BP)
explanation: Long-term BP regulation: Guyton's kidney-body fluid model: The kidney is the ultimate long-term regulator of BP. Steady-state equation: CO (= VR) and SVR determine MAP; but MAP also determines renal Na+ excretion; at any given MAP there is a specific urinary Na+ excretion rate; BP equilibrates where intake = output of Na+. Pressure-natriuresis: the fundamental renal response that integrates all long-term BP control. All humoral, neural, and intrinsic renal mechanisms work by shifting the pressure-natriuresis curve: RAAS (↑Ang II, ↑aldosterone) → shift right → hypertension at higher Na+ balance point. ANP, renal denervation → shift left → ↓BP. Essential hypertension: rightward shift of the P-N curve (whether due to ↑RAAS, ↑renal sympathetics, ↓NO, ↑TGF-β in the kidney, etc.) → kidneys require higher MAP to excrete the same Na+.

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'isovolumetric relaxation' phase of the cardiac cycle begins with:
options: Closure of the aortic valve (and pulmonary valve) — once ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, the aortic valve closes → LV is now a closed chamber (both mitral and aortic valves closed) → LV continues to relax (active process, Ca2+ reuptake by SERCA2a) → ↓LV pressure at constant volume → when LV pressure falls below LA pressure → mitral valve opens → rapid filling phase begins; isovolumetric relaxation is an energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) active process, NOT passive
Closure of the mitral valve at the start of systole
explanation: Cardiac cycle phases: 1. Isovolumetric contraction (IVC): MV and AV both closed; LV pressure rises; begins with S1 (MV closure). 2. Rapid ejection: AV opens (LV pressure > aortic); maximal ejection velocity early. 3. Reduced ejection: LV begins to relax, ejection continues but slows. 4. Isovolumetric relaxation (IVR): AV closes (S2); both valves closed; LV pressure falls; active Ca2+ reuptake by SERCA2a (energy requiring; impaired in ischemia). 5. Rapid filling: MV opens; blood rushes in (80% of diastolic filling); S3 if pathological (↑atrial pressure or ↓LV compliance in HF). 6. Diastasis: slow filling. 7. Atrial systole ('a' wave, contributes ~20% of filling): P wave → atrial contraction → active filling; S4 if pathological (stiff ventricle, hypertrophic LV). IVR duration: shortened at ↑HR (lusitropy by β1/cAMP/TnI phosphorylation).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which cytokine is the primary stimulus for hepatic acute phase protein synthesis (CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A)?
options: TNF-α (important but IL-6 is the primary hepatic stimulus)

IL-6 (interleukin-6): secreted by macrophages, T cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts in response to inflammation; binds IL-6R (gp80) + gp130 (signal transducer) → JAK1/2 → STAT3 phosphorylation → nuclear translocation → transcribes acute phase genes: CRP (C-reactive protein, major opsonin and complement activator), SAA (serum amyloid A, apolipoprotein displaces ApoA-I from HDL), fibrinogen, haptoglobin, ferritin, α1-antitrypsin, complement proteins; negative acute phase proteins (↓by IL-6): albumin, transferrin, prealbumin
explanation: Acute phase response: Within hours of infection/injury: macrophages/monocytes release IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6 → hepatocytes (IL-6 the dominant hepatic signal via JAK/STAT3) → synthesis of positive acute phase proteins. CRP: pentamer → binds phosphocholine on bacterial surfaces + dead cells → activates complement (classical pathway, C1q) + opsonizes → phagocytosis; clinical marker of inflammation (rises within 6h, peaks 48h, t½ 19h); high-sensitivity CRP (hsCRP) = cardiovascular risk. SAA: apolipoprotein → amyloid A precursor → AA amyloidosis in chronic inflammation. Fibrinogen: coagulation + ESR ↑. Haptoglobin: binds free Hb → ↓in hemolysis. Ferritin: iron sequestration (bacteriostatic). α1-antitrypsin: protease inhibitor (deficiency → emphysema + liver disease). Negative: albumin ↓ (common in chronic disease → 'anemia of chronic disease' picture).

subject: Physiology
stem: Vitamin D synthesis: which enzyme is rate-limiting and where does it occur?
options: 25-hydroxylase in the liver (first step, not rate-limiting)

1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) in the kidney (proximal tubule): converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 [25-(OH)D3, calcidiol] → 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 [1,25-(OH)2D3, calcitriol, active form]; rate-limiting because this step is tightly regulated: stimulated by ↑PTH (primary regulator), hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia, ↑FGF23 inhibits (from bone osteocytes in hyperphosphatemia); inhibited by ↑Ca2+, ↑PO4, ↑1,25-(OH)2D3 (product inhibition); deficiency of 1α-hydroxylase → type I vitamin D-dependent rickets (hereditary, responds to calcitriol); excess 1α-hydroxylase activity: granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, TB: activated macrophages express CYP27B1 unregulated → hypercalcemia)
Skin 7-dehydrocholesterol → pre-vitamin D3 (UV-B initiated, not enzymatic, not rate-limiting)
CYP24A1 (24-hydroxylase, this inactivates 1,25-OH2D3, not the activating enzyme)
explanation: Vitamin D metabolism: UVB → skin 7-dehydrocholesterol → pre-vitamin D3 → vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol, thermal isomerization). Liver CYP2R1 (25-hydroxylase): vitamin D3 → 25-(OH)D3 (calcidiol, major circulating form, t½ 2-3 weeks; used for clinical measurement of Vitamin D status). Kidney CYP27B1 (1α-hydroxylase): 25-(OH)D3 → 1,25-(OH)2D3 (calcitriol, active hormone, t½ 4-6h). 1,25-(OH)2D3 effects: ↑intestinal Ca2+ + PO4 absorption (TRPV6 + CALBINDIN expression), ↑renal Ca2+ + PO4 reabsorption, bone: at normal levels → ↑mineralization; at high levels → ↑resorption. CYP24A1 (24-hydroxylase): inactivates both 25-OH-D3 and 1,25-(OH)2D3 → 24,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (inactive); upregulated by 1,25-(OH)2D3 itself (catabolism/product inhibition).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'Cushing triad' in raised intracranial pressure (ICP): what are the three components?
options: Hypertension (Cushing's reflex: ↑ICP → brainstem ischemia → ↑sympathetic output → ↑SVR → ↑MAP), bradycardia (baroreceptor reflex response to ↑MAP → vagal → ↓HR), and irregular respiration (Cheyne-Stokes, Biot's, or ataxic breathing from brainstem compression → central respiratory center dysfunction); this triad indicates impending herniation and is a medical emergency
Hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea (Cushing's triad is NOT shock)
Hypertension, tachycardia, fever (fever is not part of the triad)
explanation: Cushing's triad (Cushing's response): ↑ICP → compresses posterior fossa and midbrain → cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP) falls → brainstem ischemia → ↑sympathetic discharge → ↑SVR → MAP rises (attempting to restore CPP) → baroreceptor response to ↑MAP → vagal → paradoxical bradycardia. Also: Cushing's vasopressor reflex directly stimulates vagal centers in brainstem. The three elements: (1) ↑systolic BP (widened pulse pressure). (2) Bradycardia. (3) Irregular respiration. Late and ominous sign → impending uncal or tonsillar herniation → emergency ICP management: head elevation 30°, mannitol (osmotic), hyperventilation (↓PaCO2 → vasoconstriction → ↓cerebral blood volume → ↓ICP, temporizing measure), neurosurgical decompression. CPP target in TBI: 60-70 mmHg.

subject: Physiology
stem: Gastric acid secretion: which receptor on the parietal cell has the GREATEST stimulatory effect?
options: Histamine H2 receptor — histamine from enterochromaffin-like cells (ECLs) → H2 receptor on parietal cells → Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA → activates H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) → HCl secretion; H2 is the dominant final common pathway: gastrin and ACh both ALSO stimulate ECL cells to release histamine (indirect amplification), and gastrin/ACh directly stimulate parietal cells (via CCK-B and M3 receptors, respectively) but the histamine-H2 pathway is quantitatively the most important for acid production; H2 blockers (ranitidine, famotidine) effectively suppress acid; PPIs (omeprazole etc.) block the pump itself, inhibiting all stimulated acid regardless of receptor
explanation: Gastric acid (HCl) secretion — parietal cells: Three stimulatory receptors: (1) H2 (histamine): Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA → H+/K+-ATPase activation. (2) CCK-B/gastrin: Gq → PLC → IP3 → ↑Ca2+ + PKC → activates H+/K+-ATPase. (3) M3 (muscarinic): Gq → ↑Ca2+ → activates H+/K+-ATPase. H2 = most important final pathway (histamine convergence point: gastrin + ACh stimulate ECLs → ↑histamine → H2 → parietal cell). Inhibition: somatostatin (D cells, SST receptors on parietal cells and ECLs → ↓cAMP → ↓acid) + prostaglandins (E1/E2 → EP3 receptor → ↓cAMP) + secretin (when duodenal pH <4). PPIs: irreversible (covalent bond) inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase → suppress all stimulated acid. H2 antagonists: competitive, reversible → less complete acid suppression than PPIs. Achlorhydria: pernicious anemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells → ↓IF + ↓acid).

subject: Physiology
stem: Which lymphocyte surface marker is used to identify helper T cells (Th cells)?
options: CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4): expressed on T helper (Th) cells, regulatory T cells (Tregs), and monocytes/macrophages/dendritic cells (at lower levels); CD4 binds non-polymorphic regions of MHC class II on APCs during TCR-MHC-II-peptide interaction → stabilizes the synapse + initiates signaling (Lck tyrosine kinase); CD4 is also the receptor for HIV-1 gp120 (with co-receptor CCR5 or CXCR4) → HIV depletes CD4+ T cells → immunodeficiency; normal CD4 count >500/µL; AIDS defined as CD4 <200/µL or AIDS-defining illness
explanation: T cell subsets by CD markers: CD4+ T cells: helper T (Th) cells: provide help to B cells (CD40L-CD40 interaction, cytokines), activate macrophages (IFN-γ), coordinate adaptive immunity. Also: Tregs (CD4+CD25+FoxP3+). MHC class II restricted. CD8+ T cells: cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs): kill virally infected cells, tumor cells. MHC class I restricted. CD3: all T cells (signal transduction component of TCR complex). CD4/CD8 ratio: normal ~2:1 (about 1000 CD4 vs. 500 CD8 per µL). HIV: CD4 depletion → opportunistic infections when <200 (PCP, toxoplasma, MAC, CMV retinitis, cryptococcal meningitis). Antiretroviral monitoring: CD4 count + HIV viral load. CD4+ cell types during infection: Th1 (IFN-γ, IL-2 → intracellular pathogens), Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13 → parasites, allergy), Th17 (IL-17 → fungi, bacteria, mucosal immunity), Tfh (IL-21 → B cell help in germinal centers), Treg (TGF-β, IL-10 → peripheral tolerance).

subject: Physiology
stem: Hypothyroidism: which lipid abnormality is most characteristic?
options: ↑LDL-cholesterol (and total cholesterol): thyroid hormones (T3) upregulate LDL receptor expression in the liver + ↑LDL receptor-mediated clearance; in hypothyroidism → ↓T3 → ↓LDLR → ↓LDL clearance → ↑LDL-C; also: ↓HMG-CoA reductase activity (T3 promotes cholesterol synthesis via HMG-CoA reductase, but net effect is ↓LDL) → hypothyroidism: ↑LDL (predominant effect), often ↑total cholesterol; also ↑TGs (↓LPL activity); treatment of hypothyroidism → normalizes lipids (important to check TFTs in dyslipidemia workup)
explanation: Hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia: T3 effects on lipid metabolism: ↑hepatic LDL receptor expression → ↑LDL clearance → ↓LDL-C (in euthyroid). ↑LPL (lipoprotein lipase) activity → ↑TG clearance. ↑HMG-CoA reductase (↑cholesterol synthesis) but net effect: ↑LDL clearance outweighs → ↓LDL in hyperthyroidism. Hypothyroidism: ↓T3 → ↓LDLR → ↑LDL; ↓LPL → ↑TGs; ↑cholesterol synthesis (relative). Lipid profile: ↑TC, ↑LDL, ↑TG, normal or ↑HDL. Clinical relevance: hypothyroidism is a secondary cause of dyslipidemia (screen TFTs in new hypercholesterolemia). Statins: may increase myopathy risk in hypothyroid patients (↑CK baseline). After thyroid replacement: lipids often normalize, reducing need for additional lipid-lowering therapy.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which class of antiarrhythmic drugs prolongs the action potential duration (APD) and effective refractory period (ERP) by blocking K+ channels?
options: Class I (Na+ channel blockers, shorten APD)

Class III antiarrhythmic drugs (K+ channel blockers): amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide, ibutilide; block IKr (rapidly activating delayed rectifier K+ channel, hERG gene) → delayed repolarization → ↑APD → ↑ERP → ↑QT interval on ECG; used for: VT/VF, atrial flutter/fibrillation (rate/rhythm control); risk: QT prolongation → torsades de pointes (TdP, polymorphic VT) — especially QT >500 ms; amiodarone: multi-class drug (I + II + III + IV effects)
Class II (β-blockers, ↓automaticity + ↓conduction, no significant APD change)
Class IV (Ca2+ channel blockers, slows AV nodal conduction, no K+ channel blockade)
explanation: Vaughan Williams antiarrhythmic classification: Class I (Na+ channel blockers): Ia (moderate Na+ block + K+ block → ↑APD: quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide), Ib (minimal Na+ block → ↓APD in ventricle: lidocaine, mexiletine), Ic (strong Na+ block, minimal APD change: flecainide, propafenone). Class II (β-blockers): ↓automaticity + AV conduction, ↓reentry in AVNRT; metoprolol, atenolol, esmolol. Class III (K+ channel blockers): ↑APD + ↑ERP; amiodarone (also I/II/IV + anti-thyroid → thyroid dysfunction), sotalol (also β-blocker), dofetilide, dronedarone. Class IV (L-type Ca2+ channel blockers): verapamil, diltiazem → ↓AV conduction. Digoxin: ↑vagal tone → ↓AV conduction; used for rate control in AF/flutter and HF. Adenosine: ↑IKACh → hyperpolarizes AV node → terminates AVNRT (very short t½ ~10s).

subject: Physiology
stem: The 'corneal blink reflex': what are the afferent and efferent limbs?
options: CN VII afferent, CN III efferent

CN V (ophthalmic division, V1) afferent — trigeminal nerve sensory fibers from the cornea → Gasserian ganglion → spinal nucleus of trigeminal → bilateral reflex arcs → CN VII (facial nerve) efferent: motor to orbicularis oculi → bilateral blink; loss of afferent: ipsilateral cornea stimulation produces NO blink (V1 lesion); loss of efferent: ipsilateral eye fails to blink but contralateral blinks normally when ipsilateral cornea stimulated (CN VII palsy; contralateral blinks = consensual blink response intact via V1)
CN IX afferent, CN VII efferent
CN II afferent, CN VII efferent
explanation: Corneal blink reflex: Clinical testing: light touch to cornea (avoid conjunctiva) → normal = bilateral blink. Afferent: V1 (ophthalmic branch of trigeminal, CN V) → spinal trigeminal nucleus (caudal part, similar to pain/temperature pathway). Efferent: VII (facial nerve, motor to orbicularis oculi muscles) → bilateral response (direct and consensual). Interpretation: Corneal afferent (V1 ipsilateral) lesion: both direct AND consensual blink absent when ipsilateral cornea stimulated; normal when contralateral cornea stimulated. Efferent (VII ipsilateral) lesion: ipsilateral eye fails to blink (orbicularis oculi paresis), but contralateral eye blinks normally whether either cornea is stimulated. Absent corneal reflex: deep coma (any cause), V1 or VII lesion, contact lens wearers (chronic desensitization), topical anesthetics.

subject: Physiology
stem: What is 'physiological jaundice of the newborn' caused by?
options: Blood group incompatibility (ABO or Rh — that is hemolytic jaundice, different)

Relative immaturity of hepatic UGT1A1 (bilirubin-UDP-glucuronosyltransferase): neonatal liver has low UGT1A1 activity (adult levels not reached until 1-2 months) + ↑hemolysis (fetal Hb turnover as HbF switches to HbA) + ↓albumin → unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; appears day 2-3 (not day 1, which suggests pathological cause), peaks day 3-5, resolves by day 7-10 in term infants; bilirubin largely unconjugated (indirect) → may cross BBB → kernicterus if severe (especially if predisposing factors: G6PD deficiency, prematurity, acidosis)
explanation: Physiological jaundice (neonatal): Normal in up to 60% of term neonates. Unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia. Causes: ↑bilirubin production (↑RBC breakdown: neonatal RBC lifespan 70-90 days vs adult 120 days; HbF → HbA switch; polycythemia). ↓Bilirubin clearance: low UGT1A1 (immaturity), ↓albumin. ↑Enterohepatic circulation (β-glucuronidase in neonatal intestine deconjugates bilirubin → reabsorbed; breastfeeding enhances this). Timing: appears day 2-3, resolves by day 7-10 (term). Pathological if: onset day 1 (suggests hemolytic), persists >2 weeks in term (>3 weeks preterm), direct (conjugated) bilirubin > 20% total, or requires phototherapy. Management: phototherapy (converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers → excreted in bile without conjugation); exchange transfusion for severe/refractory.

subject: Physiology
stem: Nociception: what is peripheral sensitization and when does it occur?
options: Central wind-up in the dorsal horn only

Changes in nociceptor properties at the site of injury/inflammation: inflammatory mediators (bradykinin, PGE2, serotonin, substance P, NGF, H+, histamine) → bind receptors on nociceptor terminals → lower activation threshold (e.g., TRPV1 activated at <37°C instead of >43°C) and increase spontaneous firing → primary hyperalgesia (↑pain sensitivity at the injury site, and allodynia = normally non-painful stimuli are now painful); differs from central sensitization (NMDA receptor-mediated wind-up in dorsal horn → secondary hyperalgesia in the undamaged area surrounding injury)
Descending facilitation from the brainstem only
explanation: Pain sensitization types: Primary hyperalgesia (peripheral sensitization): at site of injury. Inflammatory soup at injury: bradykinin (B2 receptor → ↑PKC), PGE2 (EP1/EP4 → ↑cAMP/PKA), serotonin (5-HT3 → direct depolarization), NGF (TrkA → changes TRPV1 expression and trafficking), H+ (ASIC channels), substance P, ATP (P2X3). Result: ↓threshold of TRPV1, Nav1.8/1.9 → ↑sensitivity. PGE2 and bradykinin are clinically the most important → why NSAIDs (↓PGE2 via COX inhibition) reduce inflammatory pain. Secondary hyperalgesia (central sensitization): spread beyond injury → dorsal horn: ↑glutamate + SP → NMDA receptor activation (removes Mg2+ block at depolarized membrane) → Ca2+ → PKC/PKA → ↑AMPA expression → wind-up → pain memory. Ketamine (NMDA blocker) → ↓central sensitization.

subject: Physiology
stem: Neuromuscular blocking drugs: what distinguishes depolarizing from non-depolarizing agents?
options: Both types cause flaccid paralysis by the same mechanism

Depolarizing (succinylcholine): acts as agonist at nAChR → sustained depolarization → initial fasciculations then muscle cannot repolarize (prolonged depolarization → Na+ channels enter inactivated state → neuromuscular blockade); not reversed by neostigmine (AChE inhibitor would increase ACh → worsen depolarization block); short duration (~10 min, metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase); phase II block can occur with repeated dosing (receptor desensitization → resembles non-depolarizing). Non-depolarizing (rocuronium, vecuronium, atracurium, pancuronium): competitive antagonists → block nAChR without depolarizing → no fasciculations; reversed by AChE inhibitors (neostigmine → ↑ACh → competes back) or sugammadex (encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium → reversal)
explanation: Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs): Depolarizing (only succinylcholine in clinical use, also called suxamethonium): (1) Fasciculations (brief, generalized muscle contractions during onset), (2) then paralysis, (3) no reversal with neostigmine (avoided or contraindicated). Hyperkalemia risk: in burns, spinal cord injury, crush injuries, prolonged immobilization → upregulated extrajunctional AChRs → massive K+ efflux with succinylcholine → fatal hyperkalemia. Malignant hyperthermia risk: susceptible patients with RYR1 mutations → avoid succinylcholine (+ volatile anesthetics). Non-depolarizing: no fasciculations, dose-dependent paralysis; reversed by: neostigmine + glycopyrrolate (prevents muscarinic side effects of ↑ACh: bradycardia, ↑secretions) OR sugammadex (for aminosteroidal agents: rocuronium, vecuronium). Duration: succinylcholine ~10 min; rocuronium 30-60 min; cisatracurium (metabolized by Hofmann elimination, safe in hepatic/renal failure).

subject: Physiology
stem: Calcium homeostasis: which organ is the most important reservoir?
options: Bone — contains 99% of total body calcium (stored as hydroxyapatite crystals [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2] in the organic bone matrix); serum Ca2+ is tightly maintained at 8.5-10.5 mg/dL (2.1-2.6 mmol/L) at the expense of bone stores; the bone acts as a buffer for serum Ca2+ via two mechanisms: (1) rapid Ca2+ exchange from the bone fluid compartment (hours, driven by osteocyte Ca2+-ATPase) and (2) slower bone resorption by osteoclasts (days, via PTH/RANKL); 1% of body Ca2+ is in cells + ECF (serum); total body Ca2+ = ~1000 g; daily flux: ~1000 mg absorbed from diet, ~1000 mg lost in urine/feces/sweat
Liver (hepatocytes are not a calcium reservoir)
Muscle (stores significant glycogen, not calcium as reservoir)
explanation: Calcium distribution: 99% in bone (hydroxyapatite). 1% in ECF + intracellular. Serum total calcium: ionized (50%, biologically active, measured with ion-selective electrode), protein-bound (40%, mainly albumin — decreases with hypoalbuminemia; correction: add 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL ↓albumin below 4), complexed to anions (10%, citrate, phosphate, bicarbonate). pH effect: alkalosis → ↑albumin-Ca2+ binding → ↓ionized Ca2+ → symptoms of hypocalcemia (tetany, paraesthesia) despite normal total calcium. PTH and 1,25-(OH)2D3 maintain serum Ca2+: bone reservoir is the primary buffer. Daily requirements: adults 1000 mg/d, pregnant/lactating/elderly 1200-1500 mg/d. Absorption: primarily in duodenum via TRPV6 (active, vitamin D-dependent) + passive paracellular. Bone calcium dynamics: bone remodeling cycle: osteoblast (formation) couples with osteoclast (resorption) via RANK-RANKL-OPG axis.

subject: Physiology
stem: Spirometry quality criteria: which FVC maneuver criterion ensures a valid test?
options: The American Thoracic Society (ATS)/European Respiratory Society (ERS) acceptability criteria require: (1) maximal effort (PEFR achieved within 120 ms of start of blow); (2) no hesitation at start; (3) no cough in first second; (4) no early termination (FVC curve must reach a plateau for ≥1 second, or blow must continue for ≥6 seconds in adults, ≥3 seconds in children); reproducibility: best FVC and best FEV1 from at least 2 acceptable maneuvers must agree within 150 mL (or 200 mL if below ATS/ERS threshold); report the highest FVC and the highest FEV1 from separate acceptable maneuvers (they do not need to come from the same blow)
One FVC maneuver regardless of effort
FVC completed in exactly 3 seconds always
explanation: Spirometry interpretation: Obstructive: FEV1/FVC <0.70 (or below LLN in some guidelines). ↓FEV1, normal or ↓FVC, ↑TGV/TLC (if measured). Severity by FEV1 % predicted: >80% = mild, 50-80% = moderate, 30-50% = severe, <30% = very severe (GOLD criteria for COPD). Restrictive: TLC <LLN (5th percentile). ↓TLC, ↓VC, ↑FEV1/FVC (>70%). Cannot diagnose restriction on spirometry alone — need full lung volumes (body plethysmography or gas dilution). Bronchodilator response (reversibility): FEV1 and/or FVC increase ≥12% AND ≥200 mL after SABA/SAMA → suggests asthma. FVC maneuver: maximal inspiration → blast out as fast and as long as possible. Flow-volume loop: provides additional information (variable vs. fixed upper airway obstruction).

subject: Physiology
stem: Protein digestion begins in the stomach via which enzyme?
options: Pepsin — secreted as pepsinogen by chief cells (zymogen cells) of gastric fundus and body; activated by gastric acid (HCl): pepsinogen (pH 5-6) → pepsin (pH <3.5, autocatalytic after initial HCl activation); pepsin is an aspartyl protease (optimum pH 1-3) that cleaves internal peptide bonds of proteins → large peptide fragments → denatures dietary proteins; inactivated in duodenum when pH rises above 4; supplemented by: HCl (protein denaturation → unfolds → accessible to peptidases), intrinsic factor (from parietal cells, B12 binding — not a digestive enzyme but gastric product)
explanation: Protein digestion overview: Mouth: salivary amylase (carbohydrate only); no protein digestion. Stomach: HCl (pH 1.5-3.5) → denatures proteins + activates pepsinogen → pepsin → large peptides. Pancreatic proteases (major): trypsinogen → trypsin (activated by enteropeptidase/enterokinase from duodenal brush border); trypsin then activates: chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin; proelastase → elastase; procarboxypeptidase → carboxypeptidase. Brush border: aminopeptidases, di/tripeptidases → amino acids, dipeptides, tripeptides. Enterocytes: cytoplasmic peptidases → further digestion; amino acid transporters (SGLT-1-like sodium-coupled, system L for neutral AA, etc.) → portal blood → liver. Absorption: neutral amino acids (aliphatic, aromatic) via SLC1A/SLC6A families; basic (dibasic) AA via CAT transporters; proline + small peptides via PepT1 (H+-coupled, also drug transporter for β-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors).

subject: Physiology
