stem: Lymphocyte recirculation: which molecule directs naive lymphocytes to secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes)?
options: L-selectin (CD62L) on naive T and B cells: constitutively expressed → binds GlyCAM-1, CD34, MAdCAM-1 on high endothelial venules (HEVs) of lymph nodes (peripheral node addressin, PNAd) → tethering and rolling → CCR7 (chemokine receptor on naive lymphocytes) binds CCL19/CCL21 (produced by stromal cells and DCs in the T cell zone) → integrin activation (LFA-1 → ICAM-1) → firm adhesion → transmigration into the lymph node T cell zone; memory cells: lose L-selectin, gain E-selectin/P-selectin ligands + tissue-homing integrins (gut: α4β7 → MAdCAM-1; skin: CLA + CCR4)
CXCR5 (B cell homing to follicles within lymphoid organs, not entry into lymph nodes)
explanation: Lymphocyte trafficking: Naive lymphocyte recirculation: L-selectin (CD62L) on naive T/B cells → binds PNAd on HEVs (in lymph node cortex) → rolling (selectin) → chemokine-triggered activation (CCR7 + CCL19/CCL21) → integrin activation (LFA-1 + ICAM-1) → firm adhesion and diapedesis. Activated T cell trafficking: ↓L-selectin, ↑tissue-specific integrins; Th1 cells home to sites of inflammation (↑CXCR3 + CCR5 → binds CXCL10 + CCL5 from inflamed endothelium). Memory T cells: central memory (TCM): L-selectin hi, CCR7 hi → recirculate through lymph nodes; effector memory (TEM): L-selectin low, CCR7 low → traffic to peripheral tissues. Gut homing: α4β7 (on lymphocytes activated in gut-associated lymphoid tissue) → MAdCAM-1 on gut endothelium (targeted by vedolizumab in IBD). Skin homing: CLA (cutaneous lymphocyte antigen) + CCR4 → E-selectin + CCL17 on skin endothelium.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which hormone decreases heart rate primarily through effects on If (the pacemaker funny current)?
options: Acetylcholine (muscarinic M2 receptor activation): M2 (Gi → ↓cAMP) → (1) ↓If sensitization: cAMP normally sensitizes HCN channels to voltage (shifts activation curve to less negative potentials → faster phase 4); ↓cAMP → HCN channels shift back → slower phase 4 depolarization; (2) ↑IKACh (G protein-activated inward rectifier K+ channel, GIRK/Kir3.1/3.4): Gβγ released from Gi → directly activates GIRK → ↑K+ outward current → hyperpolarization of SA node → ↓HR; also: M2 → ↓ICaL in AV node → ↓AV conduction (↑PR, ↑AV block)
Glucagon (increases HR via its receptor on SA node in pharmacological doses)
explanation: Autonomic control of heart rate: Parasympathetic (vagal) → ↓HR (negative chronotropy): M2 → Gi → ↓cAMP → ↓PKA → ↓If (HCN channels less sensitive) + ↑IKACh (GIRK channels via Gβγ → K+ outward current → hyperpolarization → slows phase 4). Also: ↓ICaL → ↓phase 0 amplitude → ↓conduction velocity in AV node → ↑PR interval. Vagal tone is dominant at rest (resting HR 60-80 bpm; atropine → ↑HR to ~90-100 bpm; complete vagal and sympathetic block → intrinsic HR ~100 bpm). Sympathetic (β1 → Gs → ↑cAMP): ↑If (HCN shifts) + ↑ICaL + ↑IKs → faster phase 4 + shorter AP → ↑HR. Ivabradine: directly blocks HCN (If) → slows SA node rate, used for chronic HF (↓HR without ↓contractility), stable angina (↓HR → ↓O2 demand). Does not affect AVR, BP, contractility.

subject: Physiology
stem: The main clinical use of aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) in cardiology is:
options: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, EF <40%): aldosterone antagonists added on top of ACEi/ARB + β-blocker → ↓mortality (RALES trial with spironolactone, EMPHASIS-HF trial with eplerenone); mechanism: ↓aldosterone-mediated Na+/H2O retention → ↓volume overload; also ↓cardiac fibrosis and remodeling (aldosterone → mineralocorticoid receptor in fibroblasts → collagen synthesis → myocardial fibrosis; block → ↓progressive LV dysfunction); also: primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) treatment; resistant hypertension; nephrotic syndrome
explanation: Aldosterone antagonists: Spironolactone (non-selective): competitive antagonist at mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) → ↓ENaC + ROMK expression → ↓Na+/H2O reabsorption, ↓K+/H+ secretion in collecting duct principal cells → natriuresis + K+ retention (K+-sparing diuretic). Eplerenone (selective MR antagonist): fewer androgen/progesterone receptor effects → less gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction. Cardiovascular: ↓cardiac aldosterone effects → ↓fibrosis. RALES trial: spironolactone in severe HFrEF (EF <35%) → 30% ↓mortality. EMPHASIS-HF: eplerenone in mild HFrEF → ↓CV death/HF hospitalization. Side effects of spironolactone: hyperkalemia (especially with ACEi/ARB, renal impairment), gynecomastia/mastodynia (anti-androgenic), menstrual irregularity. Monitor K+ and creatinine. Primary hyperaldosteronism: spironolactone or eplerenone → medical management; surgery (unilateral adenoma, laparoscopic adrenalectomy) for adenoma.

subject: Physiology
stem: During fetal development, which structure connects the ductus arteriosus to the systemic circulation?
options: Foramen ovale (bypasses pulmonary circulation at atrial level, shunts blood from RA → LA)

The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery (main or left PA) to the descending aorta (just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery): in the fetus → high PVR (uninflated lungs, hypoxia-mediated HPV) → blood in the PA bypasses the lungs → shunts via ductus arteriosus to the aorta → mixes with oxygenated blood from the descending aorta → reaches the lower body; maintained open by PGE2 + low O2 tension → at birth: lungs expand → ↑PaO2 → ↓HPV → ↓PVR → blood flows to lungs; ↑O2 + ↓PGE2 (loss of placenta) → DA constricts → functional closure within 10-15h → permanent closure by 3 weeks (ligamentum arteriosum)
The umbilical vein (carries oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus)
The ductus venosus (liver bypass, umbilical vein → IVC)
explanation: Fetal circulation bypasses: (1) Ductus venosus: umbilical vein (oxygenated blood from placenta) → bypasses liver → IVC → RA. (2) Foramen ovale: RA → LA (bypasses lungs at atrial level); maintained open by ↑RA pressure (large venous return from IVC/placenta); most oxygenated blood from IVC directed through FO to LA → LV → aorta → coronary arteries + brain. (3) Ductus arteriosus: PA → aorta (right-to-left, fetal); maintained by PGE2 + low PaO2. At birth: (a) Lungs expand, ↑PaO2 → DA constricts within hours (indomethacin: inhibits PGE2 → helps close PDA; alprostadil/PGE1: keeps DA open when needed for ductal-dependent CHD). (b) SVR ↑ (cord clamped) → LA pressure ↑ → FO closes (functional closure). Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA): continuous 'machinery' murmur, left-to-right shunt → pulmonary overcirculation.

subject: Physiology
stem: Which condition is characterized by a 'moonface,' 'buffalo hump,' central obesity, and purple striae?
options: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease — opposite: weight loss, hyperpigmentation)

Cushing's syndrome (hypercortisolism): excess cortisol → (1) central adiposity (cortisol redistributes fat centrally via ↑lipolysis in periphery + ↑lipogenesis in visceral depots); (2) moonface + buffalo hump (supraclavicular fat pads); (3) purple striae (↑skin fragility: ↓collagen synthesis by cortisol → thinned skin → underlying vessels visible); (4) proximal muscle weakness (protein catabolism); (5) hypertension + ↑blood glucose (insulin resistance); (6) hypokalemia (mineralocorticoid effects); (7) osteoporosis (↓OPG, ↑RANKL → ↑bone resorption); (8) immunosuppression; (9) psychosis; thin skin, easy bruising; causes: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease, 70%), adrenal adenoma/carcinoma (20%), ectopic ACTH (10%, SCLC)
Hypothyroidism (puffiness, weight gain but different distribution, no striae)
explanation: Cushing's syndrome diagnosis: (1) Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (DST): give dex at midnight → 8 AM cortisol; normal ≤1.8 µg/dL (suppresses ACTH → ↓cortisol); Cushing's: cortisol remains elevated (lack of feedback). (2) Late-night salivary cortisol: loss of diurnal rhythm → ↑midnight cortisol. (3) 24h urinary free cortisol (UFC): ↑. After confirmation: ACTH levels: low (< 10 pg/mL) → ACTH-independent (adrenal source, adenoma/carcinoma) → adrenal imaging. Elevated ACTH (>20) → ACTH-dependent → pituitary vs. ectopic. High-dose DST (8 mg): Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma) suppresses cortisol >50%; ectopic ACTH does NOT suppress. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS): catheterize IPS bilaterally, measure ACTH gradient vs. peripheral → localizes pituitary source. Treatment: surgery (transsphenoidal resection for Cushing's disease, adrenalectomy for adrenal tumors), medical: metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat (↓cortisol synthesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Michaelis-Menten constant (Km) is defined as:
options: The substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax (V = Vmax/2); Km reflects the affinity of an enzyme for its substrate — a LOW Km indicates HIGH affinity (enzyme is half-saturated at low substrate); a HIGH Km indicates LOW affinity; Km is independent of enzyme concentration; it is a property of the enzyme-substrate pair and is affected by temperature, pH, and ionic strength
The concentration of enzyme at saturation
The rate of product formation at infinite substrate
explanation: Michaelis-Menten equation: V = (Vmax × [S]) / (Km + [S]). At [S] = Km: V = Vmax/2. Lineweaver-Burk plot (double-reciprocal): 1/V (y-axis) vs 1/[S] (x-axis) → straight line; x-intercept = −1/Km; y-intercept = 1/Vmax; slope = Km/Vmax. Competitive inhibition: ↑apparent Km (↓affinity), same Vmax (can be overcome by excess substrate). Uncompetitive inhibition: ↓Km + ↓Vmax (binds ES complex only). Non-competitive/mixed inhibition: same Km, ↓Vmax. Km values (approximate): hexokinase (low Km, ~0.1 mM, high affinity for glucose), glucokinase/HK-IV (high Km, ~10 mM, glucose sensor in liver/β-cells).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which type of enzyme inhibition cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration?
options: Competitive inhibition (can be overcome by excess substrate)

Non-competitive (pure) inhibition: the inhibitor binds to a site OTHER than the active site (allosteric site) on both free enzyme (E) and enzyme-substrate complex (ES) → forms EI and ESI complexes; binding does not affect Km (same apparent Km on Lineweaver-Burk: same x-intercept) but ↓Vmax (y-intercept moves up = ↑1/Vmax); since the inhibitor doesn't compete with substrate at the active site, adding more substrate CANNOT overcome the inhibition; example: cyanide (non-competitive inhibitor of cytochrome c oxidase)
Uncompetitive inhibition (decreases both Km and Vmax)
Substrate inhibition (at very high substrate, some enzymes are inhibited)
explanation: Enzyme inhibition summary: Competitive: inhibitor resembles substrate → binds active site → ↑Km (apparent), same Vmax → parallel lines on Lineweaver-Burk if you plot multiple inhibitor concentrations (different x-intercepts, same y-intercept). Non-competitive: inhibitor binds allosteric site on E or ES → ↓Vmax, same Km → lines intersect at x-axis on Lineweaver-Burk (same x-intercept = same Km). Uncompetitive: inhibitor binds only ES complex → ↓Km AND ↓Vmax → parallel lines on Lineweaver-Burk (different y-intercepts, same slope). Irreversible inhibition: covalent modification of active site → permanent (aspirin → COX, organophosphates → AChE, penicillin → DD-transpeptidase/PBP).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The allosteric enzyme phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1): which molecule is its most potent ACTIVATOR?
options: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP): produced by PFK-2 (bifunctional enzyme) when insulin is present (fed state) → ↑glycolysis; F-2,6-BP is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1; also activated by: AMP, ADP (low energy state); inhibited by: ATP (high energy → inhibits glycolysis), citrate (excess TCA/FA oxidation → inhibits glycolysis), H+ (acidosis)
explanation: PFK-1 regulation: Central control point of glycolysis. Allosteric activators: F-2,6-BP (most potent), AMP, ADP, Pi. Allosteric inhibitors: ATP (high energy), citrate (excess fuel entry into TCA from FA oxidation), H+ (metabolic acidosis). PFK-2 (bifunctional, PFK-2/FBPase-2): insulin → protein phosphatase → dephosphorylates PFK-2 → PFK-2 kinase activity active → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis. Glucagon/epinephrine → PKA → phosphorylates PFK-2 → FBPase-2 activity → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis + ↑gluconeogenesis. Clinical: PFKM deficiency (muscle PFK, type VII glycogen storage disease, Tarui disease): exercise intolerance, hemolytic anemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which bond links amino acids in a peptide?
options: Peptide bond (amide bond): covalent bond formed between the carboxyl group (−COOH) of one amino acid and the amino group (−NH2) of the next amino acid, with elimination of water (condensation); the peptide bond has partial double-bond character (resonance: C−N bond has ~40% double-bond character → restricted rotation → planar peptide bond → two conformations: trans (most common, R groups on opposite sides) or cis (rare, seen in proline))
explanation: Peptide bond: formed in ribosomes during translation (peptidyl transferase activity of 23S rRNA / 28S rRNA). Characteristics: planar (partial double-bond character, C=O and C−N resonance → restricts rotation around C−N bond); trans configuration (most common, large R groups on opposite sides to minimize steric clash); Cis configuration: occurs specifically at X-Pro bonds (~5-7% frequency; proline's pyrrolidine ring is less strained in cis). Peptide chain direction: N-terminus → C-terminus (amino to carboxyl; written left to right). The backbone torsion angles: φ (phi, around N−Cα) and ψ (psi, around Cα−C) define secondary structure; plotted on a Ramachandran plot.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The product of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) reaction is:
options: Acetyl-CoA: pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH; PDC is a multienzyme complex of 3 enzymes: E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase, requires TPP/thiamine), E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase, requires lipoic acid + CoA), E3 (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase, requires FAD + NAD+); PDC requires 5 cofactors: TPP (thiamine B1), lipoic acid, CoA (pantothenate B5), FAD (riboflavin B2), NAD+ (niacin B3) — mnemonic: 'The Lovely Couple Finds Nothing' (Thiamine, Lipoate, CoA, FAD, NAD+); PDC is inhibited by: its products (acetyl-CoA, NADH) + ATP; activated by: AMP, ADP, pyruvate, ↑NAD+, ↑CoA; regulated by PDK (pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, phosphorylates/inactivates E1) and PDP (pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase, activates)
explanation: PDC (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex): Located in mitochondrial matrix. Irreversible reaction: links glycolysis to the TCA cycle. Cofactors: E1 (TPP/B1) → decarboxylation of pyruvate; E2 (lipoic acid, CoA) → transfer of acetyl group; E3 (FAD, NAD+) → regeneration of lipoamide, generation of NADH. Regulation: PDK (kinase): activated by high ATP, NADH, acetyl-CoA (products) + palmitate/FA → phosphorylates Ser on E1 → inactivates PDC. PDP (phosphatase): activated by Ca2+, Mg2+, insulin → dephosphorylates E1 → activates PDC. Deficiency: PDC deficiency (E1α mutation, X-linked) → lactic acidosis, neurological dysfunction, elevated pyruvate/lactate; treatment with thiamine + ketogenic diet + dichloroacetate (DCA, activates PDP).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is the rate-limiting step of the TCA cycle?
options: Citrate synthase (first step, important but not rate-limiting in the sense of control)

Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH): converts isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate + CO2 + NADH (also NAD+-dependent IDH1 in cytoplasm vs. NAD+-dependent IDH2 in mitochondria); it is the major regulated step (allosteric: activated by ADP, Ca2+, isocitrate; inhibited by ATP, NADH); the TCA cycle also has regulated steps at citrate synthase (inhibited by ATP, NADH, citrate) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (similar cofactors to PDC: TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD+; inhibited by succinyl-CoA, NADH; activated by Ca2+)
Malate dehydrogenase (thermodynamically unfavorable, driven by oxaloacetate removal)
explanation: TCA cycle steps (mnemonic: Citrate Is Kreb's Starting Substrate For Making Oxaloacetate): (1) Citrate synthase: OAA + acetyl-CoA → citrate. (2) Aconitase: citrate → isocitrate (via cis-aconitate). (3) Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH, rate-limiting): isocitrate → α-KG + CO2 + NADH. (4) α-KG dehydrogenase: α-KG → succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH (multi-enzyme like PDC). (5) Succinyl-CoA synthetase: succinyl-CoA → succinate + GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation). (6) Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II): succinate → fumarate + FADH2 (membrane-bound). (7) Fumarase: fumarate → malate. (8) Malate dehydrogenase: malate → OAA + NADH. Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP + 2 CO2. Total ATP per acetyl-CoA: ~10 ATP (3 NADH × 2.5 + 1 FADH2 × 1.5 + 1 GTP).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Gluconeogenesis bypasses which irreversible glycolytic step using pyruvate carboxylase?
options: The pyruvate kinase step (PEP → pyruvate in glycolysis): pyruvate kinase catalyzes an irreversible glycolytic step; in gluconeogenesis, the bypass is: (1) pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → OAA (pyruvate carboxylase, in mitochondria, requires biotin, stimulated by acetyl-CoA); (2) OAA → PEP + CO2 + GDP → GTP consumed (PEPCK, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, in cytoplasm); net: pyruvate → PEP (2 reactions replace 1); PEPCK is the key regulated enzyme of gluconeogenesis (induced by glucagon/cortisol/fasting; repressed by insulin)
explanation: Gluconeogenesis bypass reactions (irreversible glycolytic steps and their bypasses): (1) Pyruvate → PEP: pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → OAA, mitochondria, biotin-dependent) + PEPCK (OAA → PEP, cytoplasm or mitochondria). Pyruvate carboxylase activated by acetyl-CoA (signal: fat being oxidized → gluconeogenesis needed). (2) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate → F6P: fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1, inhibited by AMP and F-2,6-BP; activated by citrate, ATP). (3) G6P → glucose: glucose-6-phosphatase (in ER membrane of liver/kidney; absent in muscle/brain → muscle cannot release glucose). Gluconeogenesis substrates: lactate (Cori cycle), alanine (Cahill cycle), glycerol (from lipolysis), propionate (odd-chain FA, some amino acids). Gluconeogenesis is active in liver and kidney cortex.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycogen synthase is activated by:
options: Epinephrine (activates glycogen phosphorylase, inhibits glycogen synthase)

Insulin — insulin → PI3K → Akt (PKB) → phosphorylates and inactivates GSK-3 (glycogen synthase kinase-3) → GSK-3 can no longer phosphorylate (inactivate) glycogen synthase → glycogen synthase remains dephosphorylated → ACTIVE → glycogen synthesis ↑; also: glucose-6-phosphate (allosteric activator of glycogen synthase, independent of phosphorylation state)
Glucagon (activates glycogenolysis via PKA → phosphorylates glycogen synthase → inactivates it)
cAMP (via PKA → phosphorylates glycogen synthase → inactivates it + activates phosphorylase kinase)
explanation: Glycogen synthase regulation: Active (dephosphorylated, 'a' form) → synthesizes glycogen. Inactive (phosphorylated, 'b' form) → by PKA (cAMP-dependent, from glucagon/epinephrine), phosphorylase kinase, CaM kinase II, GSK-3. GSK-3: constitutively active; phosphorylates glycogen synthase → inactivates it. Insulin → Akt → phosphorylates GSK-3 (Ser9) → inactivates GSK-3 → glycogen synthase remains active → ↑glycogen synthesis. Glucose-6-phosphate: allosteric activator of dephosphorylated (active) glycogen synthase. After a meal: insulin + ↑glucose → ↑G6P → allosteric activation + insulin-mediated dephosphorylation = maximal glycogen synthesis. Glycogen storage diseases: GSD 0 (glycogen synthase deficiency → no glycogen → hypoglycemia). GSD III (debranching enzyme deficiency → accumulate limit dextrin). GSD VI (liver phosphorylase → hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the pentose phosphate pathway, which enzyme is rate-limiting and what is its product?
options: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) — produces NADPH + 6-phosphogluconolactone from G6P + NADP+; this is the first and rate-limiting step of the oxidative phase of the PPP; NADPH is essential for: (1) reductive biosynthesis (FA synthesis, cholesterol synthesis); (2) antioxidant defense (GSSG + NADPH → 2GSH via glutathione reductase); (3) cytochrome P450 reactions; (4) NADPH oxidase (respiratory burst in neutrophils); G6PD deficiency → ↓NADPH → ↓GSH → oxidative hemolysis
explanation: G6PD regulation: G6PD is inhibited by its product NADPH (product inhibition) → when NADPH is consumed (e.g., during oxidative stress), G6PD is activated → ↑NADPH production. G6PD deficiency: X-linked recessive; most common enzyme deficiency worldwide; protective against Plasmodium falciparum malaria (RBCs are susceptible to oxidative damage, which kills the parasite too). Triggers of hemolytic crisis: primaquine, dapsone, chloroquine, sulfamethoxazole, nitrofurantoin (oxidant drugs), fava beans, infections. Diagnosis: G6PD enzyme assay (false normal immediately after hemolytic episode — young reticulocytes have higher G6PD → test 3 months after episode); methemoglobin reduction test (Brewer); NBT screening. Blood film: bite cells (keratocytes), Heinz bodies (brilliant cresyl blue stain).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis is:
options: Fatty acid synthase (FAS, multi-enzyme complex — downstream)

Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC, also called ACC1): catalyzes: acetyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP → malonyl-CoA + ADP + Pi (carboxylation, requires biotin); this is the committed, rate-limiting step of FA synthesis; malonyl-CoA is the 2-carbon donor for chain elongation; ACC is: activated allosterically by citrate (excess acetyl-CoA in cytoplasm signals to ↑FA synthesis) + dephosphorylation (by insulin → PP2A activates ACC); inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA (product inhibition), glucagon/epinephrine (PKA → phosphorylates ACC → inactivates), AMPK (energy depletion → phosphorylates ACC → inactivates); malonyl-CoA also inhibits CPT-I → ↓FA import into mitochondria (prevents futile cycle of simultaneous FA synthesis + oxidation)
explanation: Fatty acid synthesis: Location: cytoplasm. Building block: malonyl-CoA (3C) + acetyl-CoA (2C primer). NADPH source: pentose phosphate pathway (major) + malate dehydrogenase (NADP+-dependent, malic enzyme). Fatty acid synthase (FAS/FASN): multi-enzyme complex in eukaryotes (single polypeptide chain with multiple domains: ACP, KS, KR, DH, ER, MAT, TE); catalyzes 7 rounds of elongation to produce palmitate (16:0). Each round: malonyl group condenses with acyl chain + CO2 released + NADPH (2 per cycle) for reduction. Net reaction for palmitate: acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH → palmitate + 7 CO2 + 14 NADP+ + 8 CoA + 6 H2O.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: What is the function of lipoprotein lipase (LPL)?
options: Hydrolyzes triglycerides in VLDL and chylomicrons in the capillary lumen: LPL is located on the luminal surface of capillary endothelium (activated by apoC-II on the surface of chylomicrons and VLDL) → cleaves TG → FFA + glycerol; FFA absorbed by adjacent tissues (heart, muscle for β-oxidation; adipose for re-esterification to TG storage); activated by insulin (↑LPL expression in adipose), thyroid hormone; inhibited by fasting (↓LPL in adipose), ApoCIII (displaces ApoCII from LPL → inhibits LPL; raised ApoCIII = ↑TG); deficiency of LPL or ApoCII → familial chylomicronemia (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia) → pancreatitis
Esterifies cholesterol in HDL (that is LCAT)
Transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL (that is CETP)
explanation: Lipoprotein metabolism overview: Exogenous pathway: dietary fat → chylomicrons (ApoB-48, ApoC-II, ApoE) in lymph → blood → LPL (muscle/adipose) → chylomicron remnants → liver (ApoE receptor). Endogenous pathway: liver → VLDL (ApoB-100, ApoC-II, ApoE) → LPL → IDL → hepatic lipase (IDL → LDL); LDL (ApoB-100 only) → LDLR (liver, peripheral cells). Reverse cholesterol transport: HDL (ApoA-I from liver/intestine) → LCAT (lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase, ApoA-I activation) → esterifies cholesterol in HDL core → cholesteryl ester → CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein) → transfers CE to LDL/VLDL → liver. SR-B1 receptor: direct uptake of HDL cholesteryl esters in liver.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Beta-oxidation of a 16-carbon saturated fatty acid (palmitate) generates how many acetyl-CoA molecules?
options: 8 acetyl-CoA — palmitate (16:0) undergoes 7 rounds of β-oxidation; each round produces: 1 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 acetyl-CoA (from the 2 carbons cleaved off); 7 rounds yield 7 NADH + 7 FADH2 + 8 acetyl-CoA (the final round releases 2 acetyl-CoA from the 4-carbon intermediate); ATP yield: 8 acetyl-CoA × 10 ATP = 80; 7 NADH × 2.5 = 17.5; 7 FADH2 × 1.5 = 10.5; minus 2 ATP (activation of palmitate to palmitoyl-CoA) = 106 ATP net
explanation: β-Oxidation of palmitate (16:0): Activation: palmitate + CoA + ATP → palmitoyl-CoA + AMP + PPi (costs 2 ATP equivalents). Transport into mitochondria: carnitine shuttle (CPT-I on outer IMM → CAT on inner IMM → CPT-II). β-Oxidation (7 cycles): each cycle: (1) acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD → FADH2); (2) enoyl-CoA hydratase (water added); (3) L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (NAD+ → NADH); (4) thiolase (CoA cleaves, releases acetyl-CoA). Products per round: FADH2 + NADH + acetyl-CoA. 7 rounds for C16: 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH + 8 acetyl-CoA. Odd-chain FA: final round produces propionyl-CoA → propionyl-CoA carboxylase → methylmalonyl-CoA → (vitamin B12-dependent mutase) → succinyl-CoA → TCA. Unsaturated FA: requires additional isomerase (cis-Δ3-enoyl-CoA isomerase) and/or reductase (2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase, requires NADPH) → fewer FADH2 produced.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: HMG-CoA reductase: what is its function and where is it located?
options: Mitochondrial enzyme for ketone body synthesis

Endoplasmic reticulum (smooth ER) enzyme that catalyzes the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis: HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH → mevalonate + 2 NADP+ + CoA; this is the committed, irreversible, rate-limiting step of the mevalonate pathway (sterol synthesis); inhibited by: statins (competitive inhibitors, e.g., lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin → ↓cholesterol → ↑LDLR) + cholesterol itself (↓HMGCR transcription via SREBP-2 pathway); activated by: ↓cholesterol (SCAP releases SREBP → ↑HMGCR transcription), insulin (dephosphorylation activates HMGCR)
explanation: Cholesterol synthesis: Liver is the major site. HMG-CoA: acetoacetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (in both cytoplasm [for cholesterol] and mitochondria [for ketones]). HMG-CoA reductase (in ER): rate-limiting. Products downstream: mevalonate → isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) → farnesyl-PP (via squalene → lanosterol → cholesterol). Total ATP equivalents: ~18 acetyl-CoA + 16 NADPH + 14 ATP for 1 cholesterol. SREBP (sterol regulatory element binding protein) system: when cholesterol is low → SCAP escorts SREBP from ER to Golgi → PCSK9 cleaves → active SREBP1/2 → nucleus → ↑HMGCR + ↑LDLR transcription. Statins → ↓cholesterol → ↑SREBP → ↑LDLR → ↑LDL clearance. PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab): prevent LDLR degradation → ↑LDLR on hepatocyte surface → most potent LDL reduction.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The urea cycle: which enzyme is deficient in the most common urea cycle disorder?
options: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency: the most common urea cycle defect (X-linked recessive); OTC catalyzes: ornithine + carbamoyl phosphate → citrulline (in the mitochondrial matrix); deficiency → accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate → spills into cytoplasm → pyrimidine synthesis ↑ → orotic aciduria (elevated urine orotic acid); clinical: hyperammonemia, encephalopathy; presentation: neonate with lethargy, vomiting after protein feeds; treatment: low-protein diet + nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate) + arginine supplementation + liver transplant; elevated ammonia + low BUN + ↑orotic acid = OTC deficiency
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I, first step — no orotic aciduria as carbamoyl phosphate stays in mitochondria)
explanation: Urea cycle: Location: begins in mitochondria, completed in cytoplasm. Steps: (1) CPS I: NH3 + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate (mitochondria; activated by N-acetylglutamate from arginase + NAG synthase; deficiency → ↑ammonia, ↓orotic acid). (2) OTC: ornithine + carbamoyl phosphate → citrulline (mitochondria). (3) ASS (argininosuccinate synthetase): citrulline + aspartate → argininosuccinate (cytoplasm). (4) ASL (argininosuccinate lyase): argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate. (5) Arginase: arginine → urea + ornithine. Nitrogen sources: 1 NH3 (from amino acid deamination/glutamate dehydrogenase) + 1 aspartate (from transamination). Deficiencies: hyperammonemia + elevated specific upstream metabolites. Orotic acid elevated: OTC deficiency (carbamoyl phosphate → cytoplasm → CPS II → pyrimidines → orotic acid). NOT elevated in CPS I or NAG synthase deficiency.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of:
options: Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH): catalyzes phenylalanine + O2 + BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) → tyrosine + BH2 + H2O; deficiency → phenylalanine accumulates → alternative transamination pathway → phenylpyruvate, phenyllactate, phenylacetate (musty/mousy odor); tyrosine becomes an essential amino acid (cannot be synthesized from Phe) → ↓melanin (fair skin/hair/eyes), ↓neurotransmitters (dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin — all require Tyr/Trp as precursors); neurological damage from phenylalanine toxicity (inhibits brain amino acid transport); autosomal recessive; newborn screening (Guthrie test, now tandem mass spectrometry); treatment: low-phenylalanine diet + phenylalanine-free AA formula + sapropterin (BH4 cofactor supplement for PAH-responsive PKU)
explanation: PKU: AR mutation in PAH gene (12q22-24); >1000 alleles known. BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin): cofactor for PAH, TH (tyrosine hydroxylase → DOPA), TPH (tryptophan hydroxylase → 5-HTP). BH4-deficient PKU: PAH is normal but BH4 not made (GTP cyclohydrolase I or PTPS deficiency) or recycled (DHPR deficiency) → same phenotype but sapropterin alone insufficient (also need neurotransmitter precursors L-DOPA + 5-HTP). Maternal PKU: untreated hyperphenylalaninemia in mother → teratogen to fetus → microcephaly, cardiac defects, intellectual disability, growth retardation (even if fetus is heterozygous/unaffected). PKU labs: ↑Phe, ↓Tyr, ↑phenylpyruvate (ferric chloride test: green urine), Guthrie bacterial inhibition assay (old), now LC-MS/MS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Alkaptonuria: what enzyme is deficient and what is the hallmark finding?
options: Homogentisate oxidase (homogentisic acid oxidase, HGO) deficiency — autosomal recessive; homogentisic acid (an intermediate in tyrosine catabolism) accumulates → polymerizes into dark melanin-like pigment (alkapton/homogentisic acid oxidase polymer); hallmarks: (1) urine darkens on standing (homogentisic acid oxidizes to dark polymer in alkaline/exposed urine; ferric chloride turns urine dark); (2) ochronosis: deposition of dark pigment in connective tissues (cartilage, tendons, sclera → ear cartilage gray-blue, corneal pigmentation); (3) ochronotic arthritis (knee, hip, spine) in middle age; benign condition otherwise; no treatment required (vitamin C may slow progression)
explanation: Tyrosine catabolism pathway: Tyrosine → 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (by TAT, tyrosine aminotransferase) → homogentisate (by HPPD, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase) → maleylacetoacetate (by HGO, deficient in alkaptonuria) → fumarylacetoacetate → fumarate + acetoacetate. Clinical significance: Alkaptonuria: HGO deficiency, benign, ochronosis. Tyrosinemia type 1 (hepatorenal): fumarylacetoacetase (FAH) deficiency → accumulation of succinylacetone → inhibits porphobilinogen synthase → ↑ALA, ↑porphyrins → neurological crises; liver failure/cirrhosis; ↑risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; treatment: nitisinone (NTBC, HPPD inhibitor → reduces toxic metabolites) + low-Tyr/Phe diet + liver transplant. Tyrosinemia type 2: TAT deficiency → ↑tyrosine → pseudodendrites on cornea + palmar-plantar hyperkeratosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: De novo purine synthesis: which molecule provides the purine ring carbon and nitrogen atoms?
options: Multiple precursors contribute: Glycine (C4, C5, N7 of the purine ring), CO2 (C6), N10-formyl-THF (C2, C8 — 2 one-carbon units from folate), glutamine (N3, N9 — amide nitrogen), aspartate (N1); mnemonic for purine ring atoms: Glycine provides the 'backbone' (C4-C5-N7), formyl-THF adds C2 and C8, glutamine provides N3 and N9, CO2 adds C6, aspartate adds N1; the pathway starts with PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) and builds IMP (inosine monophosphate) as the common precursor of both AMP and GMP
Uric acid (this is a product, not a precursor)
explanation: De novo purine synthesis: Starts with PRPP (from ribose-5-P + ATP, by PRPP synthetase). Rate-limiting: PRPP amidotransferase (PRPP + glutamine → 5-phosphoribosylamine + glutamate + PPi; inhibited by AMP, GMP, IMP). 10 steps → IMP. IMP → AMP (via adenylosuccinate + ASL, requires GTP) or GMP (via IMP dehydrogenase → XMP + glutamine, requires ATP). 2 folate-dependent steps: formyltransferases use N10-formyl-THF for C2 and C8. Methotrexate (folate antagonist) → ↓de novo purine synthesis → ↓proliferation. Purine salvage: HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase): hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP; guanine + PRPP → GMP. APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase): adenine → AMP. HGPRT deficiency: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (X-linked): uric acid overproduction (PRPP diverted to de novo synthesis) + self-mutilation + choreoathetosis + gout.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome?
options: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT): X-linked recessive; the salvage enzyme that converts hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP and guanine + PRPP → GMP; without HGPRT, purines cannot be salvaged → hypoxanthine and guanine degraded to uric acid → ↑uric acid production; PRPP accumulates → ↑de novo purine synthesis → further ↑uric acid; clinical: hyperuricemia, gout/urate nephropathy, neurological features (choreoathetosis, dystonia, cognitive disability, self-mutilating behavior — lip/finger biting), normal at birth then develops in first months
Xanthine oxidase (gout from ↑uric acid, but not Lesch-Nyhan; allopurinol inhibits this)
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP deficiency → T cell immunodeficiency)
explanation: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: X-linked (HPRT1 gene, Xq26.2-27.2). Complete deficiency = Lesch-Nyhan (partial deficiency = Kelley-Seegmiller, gout + renal stones without severe neurological features). Pathophysiology: ↓HGPRT → ↑PRPP (not consumed by salvage) → ↑de novo purine synthesis → ↑IMP/AMP/GMP → ↑uric acid (via xanthine oxidase: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid). Treatment: allopurinol/febuxostat (↓uric acid → prevents gouty arthropathy and nephrolithiasis) but does NOT improve neurological symptoms; behavioral management for self-injury. Lesch-Nyhan diagnosis: 24h urine uric acid:creatinine ratio, HGPRT enzyme assay (RBCs), gene sequencing.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: DNA replication is said to be 'semi-conservative' because:
options: Each new DNA molecule contains two new strands

Each new double helix contains one original (template) parental strand and one newly synthesized strand — demonstrated by Meselson-Stahl experiment (1958): E. coli grown in 15N medium (heavy isotope) → switched to 14N medium → after 1 generation: all DNA was 'hybrid' density (one 15N + one 14N strand); after 2 generations: half hybrid + half light (14N/14N) — consistent only with semi-conservative model
Both strands of the original DNA are conserved in one daughter molecule (conservative model, disproved)
DNA is synthesized in fragments (this describes Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, a separate concept)
explanation: DNA replication features: Semi-conservative: each daughter has one old + one new strand. Bidirectional: replication proceeds in both directions from the origin of replication (ori). Requires: (1) Helicase (unwinds double helix, breaks H bonds between bases). (2) Primase (RNA polymerase → synthesizes short RNA primer, ~10 nt). (3) DNA polymerase III (prokaryotes) / Pol δ and ε (eukaryotes): elongates 5'→3' only. (4) Single-strand binding proteins (SSBPs): stabilize unwound DNA. (5) Topoisomerase (relieves supercoiling: topo I, single-strand nicks; topo II, double-strand breaks → target of fluoroquinolones in bacteria and irinotecan/topotecan in cancer). Leading strand: continuous synthesis 5'→3'. Lagging strand: discontinuous (Okazaki fragments, 100-200 nt each in eukaryotes) → RNA primers removed by RNase H/FEN1 → filled by Pol δ → joined by DNA ligase.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The TATA box in eukaryotic gene promoters is recognized by:
options: TATA-binding protein (TBP), a subunit of the TFIID (transcription factor IID) complex: TBP binds the TATA box (consensus TATAAA, ~25-30 bp upstream of the transcription start site in many but not all genes) → causes a 90° bend in the DNA → platform for assembly of the general transcription factors (GTFs: TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIID, TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH) → forms the pre-initiation complex (PIC) → RNA polymerase II recruited + phosphorylated at CTD (C-terminal domain) by TFIIH (CDK7) → transcription begins
Sigma factor (σ, in bacteria recognizes the -10 and -35 elements in prokaryotic promoters; eukaryotes do not have sigma factors)
explanation: Eukaryotic transcription initiation: Core promoter elements: TATA box (~-30): most genes, recognized by TBP/TFIID. Inr (initiator, at TSS): present in many genes (with or without TATA). DPE (downstream promoter element, +28-32): in some TATA-less promoters. BRE (TFIIB recognition element): upstream of TATA. Assembly order: TFIID (TBP + TAFs) binds TATA → TFIIB → RNA Pol II + TFIIF → TFIIE + TFIIH. TFIIH: CDK7 kinase phosphorylates Ser5 on CTD of Pol II (initiates transcription) → later CDK9 phosphorylates Ser2 (elongation). Enhancers: thousands of bp away → loop to promoter via Mediator complex (coactivator). Activators bind enhancers → interact with Mediator → recruit GTFs + Pol II. Repressors: bind silencers or repressor-binding sites → recruit HDACs (histone deacetylases → chromatin compaction → repression).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Post-translational modification: which modification targets a protein for proteasomal degradation?
options: Ubiquitination: ubiquitin (76-amino acid protein) is activated by E1 (ubiquitin-activating enzyme) → transferred to E2 (ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme) → E3 ubiquitin ligase (catalyzes transfer to a lysine on the target protein, provides substrate specificity); polyubiquitin chain (linked at Lys48) → marks protein for recognition by the 26S proteasome → unfolded and degraded; Lys63-linked ubiquitin chains: DNA repair, endocytosis (NOT proteasomal degradation); monoubiquitination: histone regulation, endocytosis
Phosphorylation (activates/inactivates, does not target for degradation directly)
explanation: Ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS): E1 + ATP + ubiquitin → E1-ubiquitin (thioester bond). E1 → E2 (ubiquitin-conjugating/carrier enzyme). E2 + E3 (ubiquitin ligase) → E3 transfers ubiquitin to Lys of substrate. Repeat (4+ ubiquitins on Lys48) → recognized by 26S proteasome (19S cap + 20S core): 19S unfolds protein, 20S cleaves. Clinical: MDM2 (E3 ligase) → ubiquitinates p53 → promotes p53 degradation; in cancer: mutant p53 or ↑MDM2 → escape from apoptosis. FBXW7 (E3 ligase) → targets cyclin E, c-Myc, Notch, Jun → tumor suppressor. Nutlin-3/MDM2 inhibitors: block MDM2-p53 interaction → ↑p53 → cancer treatment strategy. SCF complexes: Skp1-Cullin-F-box protein → major class of E3 ligases.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which vitamin deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia)?
options: Niacin (vitamin B3, nicotinic acid) deficiency — pellagra: niacin is required for synthesis of NAD+ and NADP+ (critical cofactors for hundreds of redox reactions); also: tryptophan (60 mg Trp = 1 mg niacin NE); can occur in: dietary deficiency (maize/corn-based diet without niacin, as corn niacin is bound as niacytin and poorly absorbed), Hartnup disease (↓tryptophan absorption), carcinoid syndrome (↑Trp → serotonin, not niacin), isoniazid (↑Trp → quinolinate, interferes with niacin synthesis); '3 Ds' of pellagra: Dermatitis (sun-exposed skin, Casal's necklace), Diarrhea, Dementia; '4th D' = Death (if untreated)
Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) — angular cheilitis, corneal vascularization, magenta tongue
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) — peripheral neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia, microcytic
explanation: Niacin/B3: NAD+ and NADP+ are derived from niacin. Diet: meat, poultry, fish, enriched grains. Niacin equivalents: 60 mg tryptophan = 1 mg niacin. Hartnup disease: defect in neutral amino acid transporter (SLC6A19) in small intestine and kidney → ↓tryptophan absorption → ↓niacin synthesis → pellagra-like rash + neuropsychiatric features; aminoaciduria (neutral amino acids in urine); nicotinic acid supplements → treat pellagra-like symptoms. Nicotinic acid (niacin) pharmacological use (1-2 g/d): ↓VLDL secretion → ↓TG (30-40%), ↑HDL (15-35%), ↓LDL-C; prostaglandin-mediated flushing (use aspirin 30 min before, or extended-release formulation). Nicotinamide (amide form): same deficiency prevention, but no flushing, no lipid effects.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which fat-soluble vitamin acts as an antioxidant and protects polyunsaturated fatty acids from peroxidation?
options: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol): the major lipid-soluble antioxidant; protects cell membranes from oxidative damage by scavenging lipid peroxyl radicals (ROO•) → prevents chain reaction of lipid peroxidation; regenerated by vitamin C (ascorbate reduces tocopheroxyl radical back to tocopherol); deficiency: rare (occurs in fat malabsorption — cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, abetalipoproteinemia); symptoms: peripheral neuropathy (spinocerebellar degeneration), ataxia (dorsal column + spinocerebellar tracts), hemolytic anemia (RBCs susceptible to oxidative damage), retinopathy; abetalipoproteinemia: no chylomicrons/VLDL → fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption → severe deficiency
explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K): stored in liver and fat tissue; toxicity possible (except K). Vitamin E (tocopherols + tocotrienols): α-tocopherol most active. Sources: vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, green vegetables. Mechanism: reacts with lipid peroxyl radical (LOO• + Vit E → LOOH + Vit E•) → Vit E• is relatively stable; regenerated by Vit C → Vit E radical + Vit C → Vit E + Vit C radical → Vit C radical + GSH → Vit C + GSSG. Abetalipoproteinemia (MTP mutation, microsomal triglyceride transfer protein): no apoB-48/apoB-100 → no chylomicrons or VLDL → severe fat-soluble vitamin deficiency → acanthocytosis (spiky RBCs, membrane lipid imbalance), retinitis pigmentosa, spinocerebellar ataxia, steatorrhea. Treatment: high-dose vitamins E, A, K, D.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hemoglobin S (HbS) in sickle cell disease: what is the amino acid substitution?
options: Lysine → glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-chain

Glutamic acid (Glu, charged, hydrophilic) → Valine (Val, hydrophobic) at position 6 (β6Glu→Val) of the β-globin chain: the single nucleotide change (GAG → GTG in codon 6 of HBB gene) causes HbS to polymerize under deoxygenated conditions; deoxygenated HbS exposes a hydrophobic 'sticky patch' (Val at β6) that inserts into a complementary hydrophobic pocket on adjacent HbS molecule → lateral contacts between HbS tetramers → polymerization → long fibers → 'sickling' of the RBC (crescent shape) → ↑viscosity → vascular occlusion + hemolysis
Lysine → glutamate at position 7 of the α-chain
explanation: Sickle cell disease (HbSS): AR mutation in HBB gene (chromosome 11). HbS polymerization: requires deoxyHbS (oxyHbS does not polymerize); nucleation → elongation → fibers align → distort RBC into sickle shape. Promoted by: ↓O2, ↓pH, ↑temperature, dehydration, hyperosmolarity. Heterozygotes (HbAS, sickle trait): protected from severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (sickling occurs in infected RBCs under conditions in spleen → parasite dies). HbF (γ chains) inhibits HbS polymerization → why infants with HbSS are relatively protected until ~6 months when HbF switches to HbA/HbS. Hydroxyurea: ↑HbF production (via ↑cyclin-dependent kinase pathway + NO-mediated sGC activation → HbF) → ↓sickling. Complications: vaso-occlusion (pain crisis, stroke, ACS, priapism), hemolysis, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 → ↓RBC production), splenic sequestration, functional asplenia (↑encapsulated bacteria infections — Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Salmonella osteomyelitis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Methemoglobin: what is its iron state and why does it not carry O2?
options: Fe2+ (ferrous, normal) — it carries O2 normally

Fe3+ (ferric): normal hemoglobin contains Fe2+ (ferrous) which can bind O2; methemoglobin has iron oxidized to Fe3+ (ferric) → cannot bind O2 → right shifts remaining normal Hb's ODC (Darling-Roughton effect) → ↓O2 delivery; appears brown-gray ('chocolate brown blood'); causes: oxidizing agents (dapsone, nitrites, benzocaine, prilocaine, nitric oxide, nitrates in well water in infants — 'blue baby syndrome' from well water), G6PD-deficient patients more susceptible; treatment: methylene blue (reduces MetHb → Hb via NADPH from PPP — requires G6PD!; IV 1-2 mg/kg) or ascorbic acid (in G6PD deficiency where methylene blue fails); diagnosis: co-oximetry (spectrophotometry, not regular pulse oximetry which overestimates SaO2)
Fe2+ in the deoxy state (normal deoxyHb, functional)
explanation: Methemoglobin: normally <1% of total Hb (cytochrome b5 reductase/methemoglobin reductase maintains Fe2+: NADH-dependent methemoglobin reductase reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ using NADH from glycolysis). Methemoglobinemia: congenital (cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency → AR) or acquired (oxidant drugs/chemicals). Darling-Roughton effect: if 50% of Hb is MetHb, remaining Hb shifts to R state → ↑O2 affinity → left-shifted ODC → poor O2 release to tissues. Pulse oximetry: reads MetHb as ~85% SaO2 regardless of actual MetHb% → gives falsely reassuring readings. Co-oximetry: direct measurement of all Hb species (OxyHb, DeoxyHb, MetHb, COHb). COHb vs MetHb: CO poisoning — CO binds Fe2+ tightly → not Fe3+; cherry-red skin; treated with 100% O2 / hyperbaric O2.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides?
options: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR): catalyzes the reduction of ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) → deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs); this is the essential committed step for DNA synthesis; RNR is the target of: hydroxyurea (inhibits RNR → ↓dNTP pool → ↓DNA synthesis → used for CML, sickle cell disease, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia), gemcitabine (incorporates into DNA + inhibits RNR), cladribine (lymphoid malignancies); RNR is highly regulated: allosteric (activity and specificity sites ensure balanced dNTP pools)
Thymidylate synthase (dUMP → dTMP, not ribonucleotide → deoxyribonucleotide)
Adenylate kinase (interconverts ATP/ADP/AMP, not RNR function)
explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase: Enzyme class: radical-dependent enzyme (uses a tyrosyl radical in mammalian enzyme). Reaction: NDP + thioredoxin(reduced) → dNDP + thioredoxin(oxidized). Overall reduction: NADPH → thioredoxin reductase → thioredoxin → RNR → dNDP. Regulation: overall activity site (ATP activates, dATP inhibits all activity). Specificity site: determines which NDP is reduced (dATP → reduces CDP/UDP; dTTP → reduces GDP; dGTP → reduces ADP). dNTP pools balanced for accurate DNA synthesis. Clinical: hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide): quenches tyrosyl radical on R2 subunit → ↓RNR → ↓dNTP → ↓S-phase → CML, polycythemia vera, sickle cell (↑HbF).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Collagen: which amino acid is unique and found in large amounts in collagen?
options: Hydroxyproline (and hydroxylysine): proline is converted to hydroxyproline AFTER translation (post-translational modification) by prolyl hydroxylase (prolyl 4-hydroxylase): requires: Fe2+, ascorbic acid (vitamin C), α-ketoglutarate, O2 as cofactors; hydroxyproline stabilizes the collagen triple helix (via hydrogen bonds between OH groups); hydroxyproline is unique to collagen (and a few other proteins) → urinary hydroxyproline measurement indicates collagen turnover; ascorbate deficiency (scurvy) → ↓prolyl hydroxylase activity → unstable collagen → fragile vessels, bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhage, impaired wound healing
Glycine (most abundant at every 3rd position in Gly-X-Y repeat, but not unique to collagen)
explanation: Collagen structure and synthesis: Primary structure: repeating Gly-X-Y tripeptide (Gly at every 3rd position essential; X often Pro, Y often Hyp). Post-translational modifications in ER: (1) Prolyl hydroxylase: Pro → Hyp (4-hydroxyproline, requires vit C, Fe2+, α-KG, O2). (2) Lysyl hydroxylase: Lys → Hyl (5-hydroxylysine, same cofactors). (3) Glycosylation: Hyl residues → galactose/glucose added. Triple helix formation in ER (3 alpha-chains → right-handed superhelix). Secretion → extracellular: procollagen peptidases cleave propeptides → tropocollagen. Lysyl oxidase (requires Cu2+): cross-links lysine/hydroxylysine residues → strong collagen fibers. Scurvy: ↓vit C → ↓Hyp → unstable triple helix → collagen degradation ↑, synthesis ↓ → periosteal hemorrhage, 'cork-screw' hair, Fröhlich scoring sign. Ehlers-Danlos: defects in collagen genes or processing enzymes → hyperextensible skin/joints.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which step in fatty acid synthesis requires NADPH?
options: Activation of acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase

The reduction steps in each elongation cycle: in fatty acid synthesis by FAS, each 2-carbon addition cycle has 4 steps: (1) condensation (β-ketoacyl-ACP synthase, releases CO2 from malonyl-ACP); (2) first reduction: β-ketoacyl-ACP reductase (NADPH → NADP+) → β-hydroxyacyl-ACP; (3) dehydration: β-hydroxyacyl-ACP dehydratase → enoyl-ACP + H2O; (4) second reduction: enoyl-ACP reductase (NADPH → NADP+) → acyl-ACP; 2 NADPH consumed per cycle of 2-carbon addition; synthesis of palmitate (16C) requires 7 cycles × 2 NADPH = 14 NADPH; NADPH source: pentose phosphate pathway (major) + malic enzyme (malate + NADP+ → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH)
The carboxylation of acetyl-CoA (requires ATP and biotin)
The thiolase cleavage step (ATP is not required here)
explanation: FAS reaction details: Primer: acetyl-ACP (2C). Extension unit: malonyl-ACP (3C). Each condensation: releases CO2 (so net addition = 2C despite 3C malonyl). 7 cycles to produce 16C palmitoyl-ACP. Product released by thioesterase domain: palmitate (16:0, free acid) + 8 CoA + 6 H2O + 14 NADP+ + 7 ADP + 7 Pi. Overall: acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 7 H+ → palmitate + 7 CO2 + 8 CoA + 14 NADP+ + 6 H2O. NADPH sources for FA synthesis: primary = pentose phosphate pathway (oxidative phase: 2 NADPH per G6P in oxidative phase). Secondary = malic enzyme (cytoplasmic NADP+-linked malate dehydrogenase): malate + NADP+ → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH. Citrate shuttle transports acetyl-CoA from mitochondria to cytoplasm: citrate → cytoplasm → ATP-citrate lyase → OAA + acetyl-CoA; OAA → malate (MDH) → pyruvate + NADPH (malic enzyme).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The coenzyme forms of riboflavin (vitamin B2) are:
options: FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide): both are derived from riboflavin; FMN = riboflavin + phosphate (flavokinase, ATP-dependent); FAD = FMN + AMP (FAD synthetase, ATP-dependent); both FMN and FAD function as electron carriers (one-electron steps possible, forming FMNH•/FADH•) in oxidoreductases; key enzymes requiring FAD/FMN: complex I (FMN), succinate dehydrogenase (FAD, complex II), fatty acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD, β-oxidation), α-KG dehydrogenase (FAD in E3 subunit), PDC (FAD), glutathione reductase (FAD), monoamine oxidase (FAD)
explanation: Riboflavin (B2): water-soluble, yellow in high concentrations. Forms: FMN (prosthetic group of Complex I, L-amino acid oxidase, others) and FAD (prosthetic group of Complex II/succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, α-KG dehydrogenase, etc.). FAD/FMNH2 typically donates electrons to ubiquinone (Q) in the ETC. Deficiency: glossitis, angular stomatitis (cheilitis), seborrheic dermatitis, corneal vascularization ('conjunctival injection'), anemia (impaired Fe absorption), photosensitivity. Rare in isolation; often combined B-vitamin deficiencies. Riboflavin is photosensitive (degrades in light) → store in dark bottles. Flavoproteins generally have tightly bound (prosthetic) FAD/FMN vs. NAD+/NADP+ which are cosubstrates (not tightly bound).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acids are ketogenic ONLY (not glucogenic)?
options: Leucine and Lysine: both are exclusively ketogenic (their catabolism yields only acetoacetate and/or acetyl-CoA, neither of which can enter gluconeogenesis); all other amino acids are either glucogenic only or both glucogenic AND ketogenic; mnemonic: 'LuciLy LK are only ketogenic' (Leucine and Lysine); the remaining 18 amino acids are glucogenic (produce OAA, pyruvate, α-KG, succinyl-CoA, or fumarate) or mixed (Phe, Tyr, Trp, Ile — produce both glucogenic and ketogenic products)
explanation: Amino acid catabolism fates: Purely glucogenic (produce pyruvate or TCA intermediates that can enter gluconeogenesis): Gly, Ala, Ser, Cys, Thr, Val, Met, His, Arg, Pro, Gln, Glu, Asp, Asn. Purely ketogenic: Leu and Lys (the only two). Both glucogenic AND ketogenic: Ile, Phe, Tyr, Trp. Leucine catabolism: Leu → α-KIC (by BCAA aminotransferase) → isovaleryl-CoA → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA (ketogenic). Lysine is unique: not a substrate for aminotransferases (no amino group transfer); degraded by saccharopine pathway → glutaric acid → acetoacetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA. BCAA catabolism (Val, Leu, Ile): begin with branched-chain aminotransferase (in muscle, not liver) → then BCKDH (branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase, thiamine-dependent) → further oxidation; BCKDH deficiency = maple syrup urine disease.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is deficient in classic galactosemia?
options: Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT): classic galactosemia (autosomal recessive); galactose-1-phosphate (Gal-1-P) accumulates → toxic to liver, brain, kidney, lens; presentation in neonate: jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting/diarrhea after breast milk/lactose formula, E. coli sepsis (Gal impairs neutrophil bactericidal function), cataracts (galactitol accumulates in lens via aldose reductase), Fanconi syndrome (renal tubular toxicity → glucosuria/aminoaciduria/phosphaturia); girls: premature ovarian insufficiency (even with treatment); diagnosis: elevated erythrocyte Gal-1-P + absent GALT activity; treatment: galactose-free diet (soy formula)
Galactokinase (galactokinase deficiency → galactosuria + cataracts, but milder; only Gal accumulates, not Gal-1-P)
explanation: Galactose metabolism: Normal: galactose → Gal-1-P (galactokinase, ATP) → glucose-1-phosphate + UDP-galactose (GALT) → UDP-glucose (UDP-Gal 4-epimerase). Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency): Gal-1-P accumulates → hepatotoxic, nephrotoxic, neurotoxic. Galactitol: galactose → galactitol (aldose reductase, in lens, ovary) → accumulates → cataract + ? ovarian damage. Duarte galactosemia: variant GALT allele with ~50% activity → milder, dietary restriction may or may not be needed. Galactokinase deficiency (Type II galactosemia): galactose → galactitol (accumulates) but no Gal-1-P → cataracts only, no systemic toxicity; benign if galactose restricted. UDP-galactose deficiency (Type III): rarest, variable.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which level of protein structure is maintained by disulfide bonds?
options: Primary (amino acid sequence — covalent peptide bonds, not disulfide)

Tertiary (and quaternary) structure: disulfide bonds (S–S) form between the thiol (–SH) groups of two cysteine residues on the same polypeptide chain (tertiary) or between different chains (quaternary); they are covalent bonds that stabilize the folded 3D conformation; disulfide bonds in secreted/extracellular proteins (formed in the oxidizing environment of the ER, catalyzed by protein disulfide isomerase, PDI); intracellular proteins rarely have disulfide bonds (reducing environment of cytoplasm: reduced glutathione, thioredoxin); examples: insulin (2 inter-chain SS + 1 intra-chain SS), immunoglobulins (multiple SS bonds), keratin (extensive SS bonds → hair texture)
Secondary (α-helices, β-sheets maintained by hydrogen bonds)
Quaternary only (disulfide bonds stabilize both tertiary and quaternary)
explanation: Protein structural levels: Primary (1°): amino acid sequence, maintained by peptide bonds. Secondary (2°): local folding (α-helix, β-sheet, β-turn, random coil) maintained by H-bonds between backbone NH and C=O groups. Tertiary (3°): overall 3D shape of one polypeptide, maintained by: H-bonds, ionic bonds (salt bridges), hydrophobic interactions (most important for folding), van der Waals forces, disulfide bonds (covalent, between Cys residues, most stable). Quaternary (4°): arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits. Protein denaturation: disrupts non-covalent interactions (and can break disulfide bonds with reducing agents like DTT/β-mercaptoethanol) → loses function; primary structure (peptide bonds) usually intact. PDI (protein disulfide isomerase): in ER lumen → helps form correct disulfide bonds → important for protein quality control.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Prion diseases involve a conformational change in the prion protein from:
options: α-helical (PrPc, normal, cellular form, ~40% α-helix, ~3% β-sheet) → β-sheet rich (PrPSc, scrapie form, ~30% α-helix, ~43% β-sheet): the conformational change results in protease resistance, insolubility, and the ability to template normal PrPc into the misfolded form; the β-sheet enriched PrPSc forms aggregates → neurotoxic deposits in the brain → spongiform vacuolation; this is the key example of a protein-only infectious agent (no nucleic acid)
explanation: Protein misfolding diseases (proteinopathies): Prion diseases: conformational change → seeded aggregation → 'infectious' (PrPSc acts as template). Other protein misfolding: Alzheimer's (Aβ plaques: APP → β-secretase + γ-secretase → Aβ42 → β-sheet → plaques; neurofibrillary tangles: hyperphosphorylated tau → paired helical filaments). Parkinson's (α-synuclein → Lewy bodies, β-sheet-rich aggregates). Amyloidosis: misfolded proteins (various) → cross-β sheet amyloid fibers (bind Congo red → apple-green birefringence with polarized light). Type 2 DM: islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP/amylin) deposits in β cells. Huntington's: polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion in huntingtin → aggregates. Common theme: normal soluble protein → insoluble aggregated β-sheet → toxic gain of function or loss of function.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Allosteric enzymes do NOT follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics because:
options: They have only one active site

They exhibit cooperative kinetics (sigmoidal velocity vs. [S] curve rather than hyperbolic): allosteric enzymes have multiple subunits with multiple active sites; binding of substrate to one subunit changes the affinity of other subunits for substrate (cooperativity, similar to hemoglobin O2 binding); positive cooperativity → sigmoidal curve (Hill equation, Hill coefficient n > 1); regulation by allosteric effectors (heterotropic: activators shift curve left → ↑apparent affinity; inhibitors shift curve right → ↓apparent affinity; without changing Vmax in classical K-type regulation); Hill coefficient: n = 1 (no cooperativity), n > 1 (positive cooperativity), n < 1 (negative cooperativity, rare); Hill coefficient of hemoglobin ≈ 2.8
They are not found in metabolic pathways
explanation: Allosteric regulation: Homotropic effects: substrate itself is the effector (cooperative binding, e.g., HbO2 binding). Heterotropic effects: different molecule (activator or inhibitor) is the effector, alters enzyme activity. K-type regulation: effector changes Km (apparent affinity) without changing Vmax (K-type = changes the sigmoid curve horizontally). V-type regulation: effector changes Vmax without changing Km (V-type = changes Vmax). Concerted (MWC) model: all subunits exist in either R (relaxed, high affinity) or T (tense, low affinity) state simultaneously; effectors shift R/T equilibrium. Sequential (KNF) model: substrate binding induces conformational change in that subunit → affects neighboring subunit sequentially. Feedback inhibition: first enzyme of a metabolic pathway inhibited by the pathway's end product → prevents overproduction.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme 'thymidylate synthase' is the target of which chemotherapy drug?
options: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): converted intracellularly to FdUMP (fluorodeoxyuridine monophosphate) → FdUMP forms a covalent complex with thymidylate synthase (TS) + 5,10-methylene-THF (methylene-tetrahydrofolate) → suicide inhibition → blocks TS → ↓dTMP production → ↓DNA synthesis; also: 5-FU → FUTP → incorporated into RNA → RNA dysfunction (secondary mechanism); used for: colorectal cancer, head/neck cancer, breast cancer; leucovorin (folinic acid, 5-formyl-THF) augments 5-FU effect (↑5,10-methylene-THF → ↑ternary complex with FdUMP + TS → ↑inhibition)
Gemcitabine (incorporated into DNA + inhibits ribonucleotide reductase)
explanation: Thymidylate synthesis: dUMP + 5,10-methylene-THF → dTMP + DHF (dihydrofolate); enzyme: thymidylate synthase (TS). DHF + NADPH → THF (dihydrofolate reductase, DHFR). THF + serine → 5,10-methylene-THF (serine hydroxymethyltransferase, SHMT; requires PLP). 5-FU mechanism: FdUMP binds TS active site + trapped covalently with methylene-THF → suicide inhibition (irreversible complex, 'trapped ternary complex'). Leucovorin (folinic acid, 5-formyl-THF): directly provides 5,10-methylene-THF → ↑ternary complex → ↑5-FU effect. Capecitabine: oral prodrug of 5-FU (thymidine phosphorylase converts capecitabine → 5-FU preferentially in tumor tissue). Pemetrexed: multi-target antifolate → inhibits TS + DHFR + GARFT → used in mesothelioma, NSCLC.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The 'second messenger' for hormones acting via Gq-coupled receptors is:
options: cAMP (second messenger for Gs-coupled receptors → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP)

Inositol-1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG): Gq → phospholipase C-β (PLC-β) → cleaves PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate in plasma membrane) → IP3 + DAG; IP3 → binds IP3 receptor (IP3R, ER Ca2+ channel) → Ca2+ release from ER → ↑[Ca2+]i → activates calmodulin-dependent kinases, PKC (with DAG), calpains, phospholipase A2; DAG (stays in plasma membrane) → activates PKC (protein kinase C) → phosphorylates multiple substrates; Gq-coupled receptors: α1 adrenergic (vasoconstriction), M1/M3 muscarinic, angiotensin II (AT1), vasopressin (V1), oxytocin, GnRH, histamine H1, TRH, serotonin 5-HT2
cGMP (for NO/ANP signaling via guanylyl cyclase)
Arachidonic acid (eicosanoid precursor, released by PLA2)
explanation: G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of target proteins (CREB, glycogen phosphorylase kinase, HSL, CFTR, etc.). Gi → adenylyl cyclase inhibition → ↓cAMP (also activates GIRK via Gβγ). Gq → PLC-β → IP3 + DAG → Ca2+ + PKC. G12/13 → Rho GEF → RhoA → actin cytoskeleton. PKA targets: glycogen phosphorylase kinase (activates glycogenolysis), glycogen synthase (inactivates), triglyceride lipase (activates lipolysis), TF CREB (gene expression), L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban (relieves inhibition of SERCA → ↑Ca2+ reuptake → faster relaxation). PKC targets: Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE), transcription factors (AP-1 via JNK/ERK cascade), EGF receptor Ser/Thr residues.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Gout: what is the mechanism of hyperuricemia in primary gout?
options: Overproduction and/or underexcretion of uric acid (end product of purine catabolism in humans — humans lack uricase, so uric acid cannot be further degraded); in primary gout: overproduction (~10%): ↑PRPP synthesis (PRPP synthetase gain-of-function mutation → ↑PRPP → ↑de novo purine synthesis → ↑uric acid), or HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan, partial Kelley-Seegmiller → ↑PRPP diverted to de novo); underexcretion (~90%): SLC22A12/OAT4 and other uric acid transporters defective → ↓renal uric acid excretion; secondary gout: rapid cell turnover (leukemia, lymphoma, polycythemia, tumor lysis), thiazide diuretics (↓uric acid excretion), low-dose aspirin, ethanol (↑lactate competes with uric acid for renal excretion), myeloproliferative disorders
↑Xanthine oxidase activity leading to excess uric acid production — xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid; allopurinol inhibits this
explanation: Purine catabolism: Adenine nucleotides → AMP → adenosine → inosine (ADA, adenosine deaminase) → hypoxanthine. Guanine nucleotides → GMP → guanosine → guanine → xanthine. Hypoxanthine + O2 → xanthine + H2O2 (xanthine oxidase, XO). Xanthine + O2 → uric acid + H2O2 (XO). Uric acid: excreted by kidney (2/3) and GI tract (1/3). Normal serum uric acid: men <7.0 mg/dL, women <6.0 mg/dL. Gout crystal: monosodium urate (MSU) monohydrate crystals → phagocytosed by neutrophils → NLRP3 inflammasome activation → IL-1β release → inflammation (swollen, red, hot, exquisitely tender joint — big toe, podagra). Allopurinol/febuxostat: inhibit XO → ↓uric acid. Probenecid/lesinurad: ↑renal uric acid excretion. Pegloticase: recombinant uricase (converts uric acid → allantoin, water-soluble) for refractory gout. Rasburicase: uricase for tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biotin (vitamin B7) acts as a cofactor for which class of enzymes?
options: Carboxylases: biotin is the prosthetic group covalently attached (via ε-amino group of lysine) to the enzyme; acts as a CO2 carrier in carboxylation reactions; biotin-dependent carboxylases: (1) Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → OAA (gluconeogenesis, requires ATP); (2) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (rate-limiting step of FA synthesis); (3) Propionyl-CoA carboxylase: propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA (odd-chain FA + Val/Ile/Thr/Met metabolism); (4) β-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (leucine catabolism); mnemonic: 'ABC+P = Acetyl-CoA + Biotinyl-CoA-activated + Propionyl-CoA + Pyruvate carboxylases'
explanation: Biotin: synthesized by gut bacteria; dietary sources: egg yolk, liver, nuts, legumes. Biotin cycle: carboxylase reaction: Biotin-enzyme + CO2 + ATP → carboxybiotin-enzyme + ADP + Pi (bicarbonate attached to N1 of biotin). Then: carboxybiotin-enzyme + acceptor → product + biotin-enzyme. Biotinylation of enzymes: holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS) attaches biotin to lysine. Recycling: biotinidase cleaves biotin from enzyme (after proteolysis) → free biotin → re-use. Deficiency: raw egg white (avidin, glycoprotein that binds biotin with very high affinity → prevents absorption; destroyed by cooking), biotinidase deficiency, holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency. Symptoms of biotin deficiency: alopecia, seborrheic dermatitis, conjunctivitis, neurological features (ataxia, hypotonia, seizures in children), lactic acidosis (↓pyruvate carboxylase → pyruvate cannot enter gluconeogenesis → ↑lactic acid).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which vitamin deficiency causes 'beri-beri' (peripheral neuropathy and/or heart failure)?
options: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency: wet beri-beri = high-output cardiac failure (↑CO due to peripheral vasodilation from impaired aerobic metabolism → heart must compensate → eventually fails) + peripheral edema; dry beri-beri = peripheral neuropathy (demyelination of peripheral nerves, sensory > motor → glove-stocking distribution); Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome = CNS manifestation (alcoholism/malnutrition); infantile beri-beri = cardiac failure in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers; thiamine is required for: PDC, α-KGDH, BCKDH, transketolase (PPP); all energy-intensive tissues (brain, heart, peripheral nerves) most vulnerable
explanation: Thiamine (B1): active form = thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)/thiamine diphosphate (TDP). Functions: (1) PDC: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA. (2) α-KG dehydrogenase: α-KG → succinyl-CoA (TCA). (3) BCKDH: branched-chain α-keto acid catabolism (Val, Leu, Ile). (4) Transketolase: pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). Thiamine assessment: erythrocyte transketolase activity (or TPP effect — % increase in transketolase activity after adding TPP in vitro). Sources: enriched grains, pork, legumes, nuts. High-risk: alcoholics (↓intake + ↑metabolic demand + impaired intestinal absorption + liver storage impairment), polished rice diet, IV glucose without thiamine. Critically: NEVER give glucose without thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient (especially alcoholic) → precipitates/worsens Wernicke's encephalopathy (↑metabolic demand from glucose → rapidly depletes residual TPP → acute decompensation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ketogenesis occurs primarily in which organ, and is accelerated by:
options: Liver (hepatic mitochondria): HMG-CoA pathway: acetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase) → + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase, mitochondrial) → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA (HMG-CoA lyase) → acetoacetate reduced → β-hydroxybutyrate (NADH-dependent); accelerated by: fasting/starvation (↑fat mobilization → ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → overwhelms TCA → ↑HMG-CoA → ↑ketones), T1DM (absent insulin → unopposed glucagon + lipolysis → ↑FFA → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑ketogenesis → diabetic ketoacidosis), low-carbohydrate diet; inhibited by: insulin (↑malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I → ↓FA import into mitochondria → ↓β-oxidation → ↓ketogenesis), high-carbohydrate diet (↑OAA in TCA → consumes acetyl-CoA → ↓HMG-CoA)
Adipose tissue (only stores fat, does not make ketones)
Muscle (utilizes ketones, does not synthesize them)
explanation: Ketone bodies: acetoacetate (keto, major), β-hydroxybutyrate (reduced form, major in DKA), acetone (spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate → exhaled, fruity breath). Interorgan metabolism: Liver makes ketones (lacks succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid-CoA transferase, so cannot use ketones) → exported to extrahepatic tissues (brain, heart, muscle, kidney) → β-OHB → acetoacetate (β-OHB dehydrogenase, uses NAD+) → acetoacetyl-CoA (thiophorase/succinyl-CoA transferase) → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA. Brain: initially uses glucose exclusively → after 3-4 days of starvation, upregulates MCT (monocarboxylate transporters) → uses β-OHB preferentially (60-70% of energy during prolonged fast). DKA: absolute insulin deficiency (T1DM) → ↑glucagon → ↑lipolysis + ↑FA oxidation + ↑ketogenesis; β-OHB pKa 3.8 → dissociates at physiological pH → H+ + β-OHB- → metabolic acidosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which lipid transfer protein exchanges cholesteryl esters between HDL and LDL/VLDL?
options: LCAT (lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase, esterifies cholesterol ON HDL surface)

CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein): shuttles cholesteryl esters (CE) from HDL → VLDL/LDL in exchange for triglycerides (TG) from VLDL/LDL → HDL receives TG which is hydrolyzed by hepatic lipase → HDL shrinks; CETP inhibition: ↑HDL CE content → larger, more CE-rich HDL → initially thought to be cardioprotective; CETP inhibitors (torcetrapib, anacetrapib, evacetrapib, dalcetrapib): ↑HDL by 50-100% but major clinical trials failed to show CV outcome benefit (torcetrapib increased mortality — off-target BP elevation via aldosterone); anacetrapib was neutral; understanding CETP pathway important for metabolic physiology
Apolipoprotein A-I (structural protein of HDL, also activates LCAT)
Hepatic lipase (hydrolyzes TG in IDL → LDL + HDL TG)
explanation: Reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) pathway: (1) ABC-A1 (ATP-binding cassette A1, on peripheral cells/macrophages): exports free cholesterol + phospholipids → lipid-poor pre-β-HDL/ApoA-I (nascent HDL). (2) LCAT (ApoA-I activated): esterifies free cholesterol → CE → CE in HDL core → mature spherical HDL. (3) CETP: transfers CE from HDL → VLDL/LDL; transfers TG from VLDL/LDL → HDL; CETP activity → smaller, TG-rich HDL → more susceptible to hepatic lipase/HTGL. (4) SR-B1 (scavenger receptor class B type 1, on hepatocytes): selective uptake of CE from HDL → liver → bile acids or excretion. ABCG5/G8: ABC transporters in liver → export cholesterol into bile. Tangier disease: ABC-A1 deficiency → no lipid efflux → massive cholesterol accumulation in macrophages (orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly) + very low HDL.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which DNA repair mechanism removes UV-induced thymine dimers?
options: Nucleotide excision repair (NER): recognizes bulky lesions that distort the DNA helix (thymine dimers from UV, cisplatin-induced adducts, 6-4 photoproducts); process: XPC/XPA (damage recognition) → TFIIH (helicase to unwind around lesion) → XPG + XPF-ERCC1 (endonucleases cut at ~30 nt around the lesion) → excision of ~30-nt oligonucleotide containing the lesion → Pol δ/ε + PCNA + RFC fill in the gap using undamaged strand → DNA ligase seals; defect in NER: xeroderma pigmentosum (XP, AR mutations in XPA-XPG genes) → extreme UV sensitivity → early multiple skin cancers + neurological degeneration
Base excision repair (BER, removes small/non-bulky base damage like 8-oxoG, deaminated bases)
Homologous recombination (DSB repair using a sister chromatid as template)
explanation: DNA repair mechanisms: (1) Direct reversal: photolyase (in bacteria, not mammals) → reverses CPD pyrimidine dimers directly using light energy (photoreactivation). O6-methylguanine DNA methyltransferase (MGMT): removes O6-alkyl groups (e.g., from temozolomide → resistance mechanism in GBM). (2) Base excision repair (BER): small/non-bulky: DNA glycosylase (removes modified base → AP site) → AP endonuclease (APE1, cuts backbone) → Pol β + DNA ligase III/XRCC1. (3) NER: bulky adducts (see above). (4) Mismatch repair (MMR): corrects replication errors; MutS (MSH2/MSH6) recognizes mismatch → MutL (MLH1/PMS2) recruits exonuclease → excision + resynthesis. MMR deficiency: microsatellite instability (MSI-H) → Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) → colon, endometrial, ovarian cancers. (5) DSB repair: NHEJ (non-homologous end joining, error-prone, G1) or HR (homologous recombination, precise, S/G2). BRCA1/BRCA2: HR mediators.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During translation, which component of the ribosome catalyzes peptide bond formation?
options: 23S rRNA (in prokaryotes) / 28S rRNA (in eukaryotes): the large ribosomal subunit contains the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) in its core — it is the rRNA, not the protein components, that catalyzes the peptide bond formation; this was proven by ribozyme experiments (RNA with intrinsic catalytic activity = ribozyme); the PTC catalyzes: peptidyl-tRNA (P-site, growing chain) + aminoacyl-tRNA (A-site, new amino acid) → elongated peptidyl-tRNA in A-site + deacylated tRNA in P-site; then translocation: EF-G (prokaryotes)/EEF2 (eukaryotes) + GTP hydrolysis → moves mRNA 3 nt + tRNAs shift P→E and A→P
GTPase EF-Tu/EF1A (delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosome A-site, not catalytic)
explanation: Translation machinery: Prokaryote ribosomes: 70S (30S + 50S); 50S (23S + 5S rRNA + ~31 proteins). Eukaryote: 80S (40S + 60S); 60S (28S + 5.8S + 5S rRNA + ~50 proteins). Initiation (prokaryotes): fMet-tRNAfMet + 30S subunit + mRNA (Shine-Dalgarno, 16S rRNA base-pairs with SD sequence upstream of start codon AUG) → 70S initiation complex. Elongation: (1) aa-tRNA binding: EF-Tu/EEF1A + GTP + aminoacyl-tRNA → ribosome A site → GTP hydrolysis. (2) Peptide bond: PTC (23S/28S rRNA) catalyzes. (3) Translocation: EF-G/EEF2 + GTP → ribosome moves 3 nt 5'→3', tRNAs shift A→P→E. Termination: release factors (RF1 recognizes UAA/UAG; RF2 recognizes UAA/UGA in bacteria; eRF1 recognizes all 3 stop codons in eukaryotes) → hydrolyzes peptidyl-tRNA → releases polypeptide. Antibiotic targets at ribosome: 30S: aminoglycosides (misreading), tetracyclines (block A-site). 50S: chloramphenicol (PTC, blocks aa-tRNA accommodation), macrolides (block translocation), clindamycin, linezolid.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Steroid hormones cross the plasma membrane because they are:
options: Lipid-soluble (hydrophobic): steroids are derived from cholesterol → retain the steroid ring structure → highly nonpolar → freely cross the plasma membrane by passive diffusion; once inside the cell → bind to intracellular nuclear receptors (Type I nuclear receptors: glucocorticoid receptor, GR; mineralocorticoid receptor, MR; androgen receptor, AR; estrogen receptor, ERα/β; progesterone receptor, PR) → hormone-receptor complex translocates to nucleus → binds hormone response elements (HREs) in DNA → regulates transcription; thyroid hormones (T3/T4) are also lipid-permeable (although more hydrophilic than steroids) → bind nuclear receptors (TR) → gene regulation
explanation: Hormone receptor classification: Cell-surface receptors (for hydrophilic hormones): GPCRs (catecholamines, glucagon, LH, FSH, TSH, ADH, PTH, calcitonin, serotonin, histamine), receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin, IGF-1, EGF, PDGF, FGF), receptor guanylyl cyclases (ANP, BNP), cytokine receptors (GH, prolactin, EPO, cytokines — JAK/STAT). Intracellular receptors (lipid-soluble hormones): Type I nuclear receptors (steroid receptors in cytoplasm → nucleus upon ligand binding): GR, MR, AR, ER, PR. Type II nuclear receptors (in nucleus even without ligand, associated with corepressors): TR (thyroid hormone), RAR (retinoic acid), VDR (vitamin D), PPAR (fatty acids, thiazolidinediones). Both types bind HREs as homodimers (Type I) or heterodimers with RXR (Type II).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Homocystinuria: the most common form is caused by deficiency of:
options: Methionine synthase (causes homocysteine accumulation but different etiology)

Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS, pyridoxal phosphate/B6-dependent): catalyzes: homocysteine + serine → cystathionine (irreversible, first step of transsulfuration); CBS deficiency (AR) → homocysteine accumulates → elevated plasma and urine homocysteine; also: cysteine becomes essential (cannot synthesize from methionine → homocysteine → cystathionine → cysteine); clinical features: ectopia lentis (lens subluxation, DOWNWARD, distinguishes from Marfan's which is upward), tall stature + Marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, psychiatric disorders, thromboembolism (homocysteine promotes endothelial damage + platelet aggregation), osteoporosis
Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR, C677T polymorphism → mild ↑Hcy, not classic homocystinuria)
explanation: Methionine metabolism: Methionine → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine, by MAT/methionine adenosyltransferase) → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine, after methylation reactions) → Homocysteine + adenosine. Homocysteine fate: (1) Remethylation to methionine: by methionine synthase (MS, requires 5-methyl-THF + B12 → transfers methyl to Hcy → methionine + THF); or by BHMT (betaine homocysteine methyltransferase, uses betaine, liver-specific). (2) Transsulfuration → cysteine: CBS (B6, step 1: Hcy + Ser → cystathionine); CSE (B6, step 2: cystathionine → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate). Homocystinuria vs. mild hyperhomocysteinemia: Classic (CBS def): severe, all features. Mild (MTHFR polymorphism C677T): ↑cardiovascular risk? (debated).
