Treatment of CBS deficiency: B6 (PLP cofactor; B6-responsive if some residual CBS activity) → large doses reduce Hcy in ~50% of patients; others: methionine restriction + cysteine supplementation + betaine (alternate remethylation) + folate/B12 (↑remethylation via MS).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD): which enzyme is deficient?
options: Branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH, also called BCKDC): deficiency → accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs: leucine, isoleucine, valine) and their corresponding α-keto acids (α-ketoisocaproate, α-keto-β-methylvalerate, α-ketoisovalerate); urine has characteristic maple syrup or burnt sugar odor (from sotolon, a metabolite); clinical: neonatal encephalopathy (1-2 weeks of age), opisthotonus, poor feeding, alternating hypotonia/hypertonia, seizures; leucine most neurotoxic; diagnosis: plasma amino acid profile (↑Leu, Ile, Val, alloisoleucine — hallmark; alloisoleucine is pathognomonic), urine organic acids; treatment: neonatal dialysis (acute), low-BCAA diet (lifelong), BCKDH cofactor (thiamine, some responsive forms), liver transplant (restores some BCKDH activity)
explanation: BCAA catabolism: BCAAs (Leu, Ile, Val) are the only amino acids catabolized primarily in extrahepatic tissues (especially muscle). Step 1: branched-chain aminotransferase (BCAT, reversible): BCAA + α-KG → BCKA (branched-chain α-keto acid) + glutamate. Step 2: BCKDH (irreversible, rate-limiting, thiamine-dependent — like PDC and α-KGDH): BCKA → branched-chain acyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. Further metabolism: Valine → succinyl-CoA (glucogenic); Isoleucine → succinyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA (both glucogenic + ketogenic); Leucine → HMG-CoA → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate (purely ketogenic). MSUD thiamine-responsive forms: E2 subunit mutation with residual BCKDH activity; high-dose thiamine (100-200 mg/d) → ↑BCKDH activity → ↓BCKA accumulation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Iron absorption: which form is best absorbed in the intestine?
options: Fe2+ (ferrous, heme iron and reduced non-heme): heme iron (from hemoglobin and myoglobin in meat) is absorbed via HCP1 (heme carrier protein 1/PCFT) → inside enterocyte, heme oxygenase releases Fe2+; non-heme iron (plant-based, Fe3+/Fe2+ mix): Fe3+ must be reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome b (DcytB, ferrireductase on brush border) + ascorbic acid → Fe2+ transported into enterocyte via DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1, H+-coupled); Fe2+ in enterocyte: used immediately or stored as ferritin; exported to blood via ferroportin (basolateral, FPN1, the sole known Fe exporter) + hephaestin (oxidizes Fe2+ → Fe3+) → binds transferrin (Fe3+, 2 per transferrin molecule)
explanation: Iron regulation: Hepcidin (liver-derived antimicrobial peptide): master regulator of systemic iron. Stimulated by: ↑iron stores, ↑BMP (bone morphogenetic protein, via BMP/SMAD signaling), IL-6 (acute inflammation → anemia of chronic disease), activated HJV (hemojuvelin). Inhibits ferroportin (FPN1): hepcidin binds FPN → FPN internalization + degradation → Fe trapped in enterocytes + macrophages + hepatocytes → ↓plasma iron. Deficiency states: iron deficiency anemia (IDA): ↓hepcidin → ↑DMT1 and FPN → ↑absorption. Anemia of chronic disease (ACD): ↑IL-6 → ↑hepcidin → ↓iron export → functional iron deficiency. Hemochromatosis (HFE gene mutations, AR): ↓hepcidin production → ↑iron absorption → ↑serum iron, ↑ferritin, ↑transferrin saturation → deposits in liver, pancreas, heart, pituitary, skin.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Selenium is a component of which antioxidant enzyme?
options: Superoxide dismutase (SOD uses Cu/Zn or Mn)

Glutathione peroxidase (GPx): contains selenocysteine at the active site (the 21st amino acid, encoded by UGA codon read as Sec with SECIS element in 3'UTR); catalyzes: H2O2 + 2GSH → GSSG + 2H2O; also reduces lipid hydroperoxides (LOOH + 2GSH → LOH + GSSG + H2O); selenium deficiency → ↓GPx → ↑oxidative stress; Keshan disease (dilated cardiomyopathy, endemic in selenium-deficient regions of China) and Kashin-Beck disease (chondrodysplasia); GPx1 is the major intracellular cytoplasmic form; GPx4 protects mitochondria; also: thioredoxin reductase (TrxR) contains selenocysteine → reduces oxidized thioredoxin → NADPH-dependent antioxidant
explanation: Antioxidant enzymes and cofactors: SOD (superoxide dismutase): Cu/Zn-SOD (cytoplasm, SOD1), Mn-SOD (mitochondria, SOD2), extracellular SOD (SOD3); catalyzes: 2 O2•- + 2H+ → H2O2 + O2 (disproportionation). Catalase (heme, Fe3+): H2O2 → H2O + O2; highest in liver, kidney, peroxisomes. GPx (Se): H2O2 → H2O (uses GSH). GSH synthesis: γ-glutamylcysteine synthetase (rate-limiting, requires Glu + Cys + ATP); then glutathione synthetase (+ Gly). GSSG → 2GSH: glutathione reductase (uses NADPH from G6PD/PPP). N-acetylcysteine (NAC): provides cysteine → ↑GSH synthesis → used as antioxidant (paracetamol overdose: replenishes hepatic GSH).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which modification of histones is associated with active transcription?
options: Histone deacetylation (removes acetyl groups → compacts chromatin → repression)

Histone acetylation (of lysine residues by histone acetyltransferases, HATs): HATs (e.g., p300/CBP, PCAF) transfer acetyl groups from acetyl-CoA to ε-NH2 of lysine residues in histone tails → neutralizes positive charge → ↓interaction between histone and negatively charged DNA → relaxes chromatin (euchromatin) → accessible to transcription factors + RNA Pol II → ↑transcription; also: histone H3K4 methylation (H3K4me3 at promoters = active transcription mark), H3K36me3 (within gene bodies = elongation), H3K27 acetylation (active enhancers)
H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3 = Polycomb repression, gene silencing)
explanation: Histone modification code: Acetylation: HATs (lysine acetylation → active), HDACs (deacetylation → repression). HDAC inhibitors: vorinostat (SAHA), romidepsin → cancer treatment (↑gene expression, cancer cell differentiation/apoptosis). Active marks: H3K4me3 (promoter), H3K27ac (active enhancer), H3K36me3 (elongation), H3K9ac (active promoter). Repressive marks: H3K27me3 (Polycomb, facultative heterochromatin), H3K9me3 (HP1/constitutive heterochromatin, centromeres), H3K20me3 (constitutive heterochromatin). Writers (add marks): HATs, KMTs (lysine methyltransferases, e.g., EZH2 for H3K27me3, SUV39H for H3K9me3). Erasers (remove marks): HDACs, KDMs (lysine demethylases). Readers (bind marks): BRD4 (reads acetylated lysine, BRD4 inhibitor: JQ1/BETs → cancer). DNA methylation: DNMT1/3A/3B → methylates CpG → gene silencing (at promoter CpG islands); hypermethylation of tumor suppressor genes in cancer.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme replicates the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes?
options: DNA polymerase δ (main lagging strand polymerase)

Telomerase (telomere terminal transferase): a reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template (TERC/TR, ~450 nt in humans) complementary to the telomeric DNA repeat (TTAGGG)n; adds TTAGGG repeats to the 3' ends of chromosomes to counteract the 'end-replication problem' (conventional DNA Pol cannot replicate the very ends due to requiring an RNA primer that leaves a 5' gap after removal); active in: germline cells, stem cells, cancer cells (→ immortality); inactive in most somatic cells (→ progressive telomere shortening with each cell division → Hayflick limit of ~50-70 divisions → cellular senescence/apoptosis); mutations in TERT (catalytic subunit) or TERC: dyskeratosis congenita, aplastic anemia, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (short telomere diseases)
DNA polymerase α (primase-DNA pol complex, initiates Okazaki fragments)
explanation: End-replication problem: Linear chromosomes → after lagging strand synthesis, the 5' end has a gap (where the last RNA primer was removed and cannot be filled → no 3' OH upstream) → progressive loss of telomeric DNA (~50-200 bp per division). Telomere: (TTAGGG)n repeats (up to ~10,000 in young humans, 1,500-3,000 in adults) + shelterin complex (TRF1, TRF2, POT1, TPP1, RAP1, TIN2) → forms T-loop structure → protects chromosomal ends from being recognized as DSBs. Telomerase: TERT (reverse transcriptase protein) + TERC (RNA template, 3'-AAUCCC-5' complementary to TTAGGG) + dyskerin (pseudouridylation of TERC). Telomere shortening → p53/p16 activation → senescence (p21 → cell cycle arrest). Cancer: reactivation of telomerase in ~85% of cancers → bypass senescence → immortalization. Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT): ~15% of cancers → recombination-based.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme converts pyruvate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) in gluconeogenesis?
options: Pyruvate kinase (catalyzes the reverse reaction in glycolysis — but this is irreversible)

Two enzymes working together: (1) Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → OAA (in mitochondria; requires biotin; allosterically activated by acetyl-CoA); (2) PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase): OAA + GTP → PEP + CO2 + GDP (in cytoplasm, cytosolic PEPCK1; also mitochondrial PEPCK2 exists); PEPCK is transcriptionally regulated: induced by glucagon (cAMP → CREB → PEPCK gene), cortisol, thyroid hormone, fasting; repressed by insulin (Akt/FOXO1 pathway → ↓PEPCK transcription); metformin: ↓hepatic PEPCK expression → ↓gluconeogenesis (partly via AMPK)
Phosphoglycerate kinase (only in glycolysis, not gluconeogenesis bypass)
PEP carboxykinase alone (only Step 2, Step 1 is pyruvate carboxylase)
explanation: Gluconeogenesis regulation: PEPCK is the rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis (in liver and kidney). Induction of gluconeogenesis: glucagon → cAMP → PKA → CREB phosphorylation (pCREB) → recruits CBP/p300 → transcription of PEPCK, G6Pase, FOXO1 target genes. Cortisol → GR → HRE → PEPCK, G6Pase, PEPCK. Fasting → ↑glucagon + ↑cortisol → maximal gluconeogenesis induction. Insulin → PI3K → Akt → phosphorylates FOXO1 (forkhead transcription factor) → FOXO1 exported from nucleus → ↓PEPCK/G6Pase transcription. Metformin: activates AMPK → ↑FOXO1 exclusion from nucleus + ↓hepatic SIRT1/PGC-1α complex → ↓PEPCK/G6Pase → ↓gluconeogenesis → ↓fasting blood glucose. G6Pase: endoplasmic reticulum membrane enzyme; deficiency = GSD type Ia (von Gierke disease) → severe fasting hypoglycemia + massive hepatomegaly.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glucuronic acid conjugation of bilirubin is catalyzed by:
options: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1, also called UDPGT): uses UDP-glucuronic acid as the donor → bilirubin + UDP-glucuronate → bilirubin glucuronide (water-soluble) + UDP; this reaction occurs in the smooth ER of hepatocytes; UGT1A1 also conjugates many drugs, estrogens, and other endogenous compounds; promoter polymorphism (TA)7TAA = UGT1A1*28 → ↓UGT1A1 expression → Gilbert's syndrome (benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia during fasting/illness/hemolysis); exon mutations → Crigler-Najjar syndrome (type I: complete UGT1A1 deficiency → severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia → kernicterus without treatment; type II: partial deficiency → treated with phenobarbital which induces UGT1A1)
explanation: UGT1A1: single gene with alternative exons 1A1 through 1A12 → generates multiple UGT1A1 isoforms in different tissues. UGT1A1 in liver: conjugates bilirubin at the C-8 and C-12 propionate side chains → bilirubin monoglucuronide (BMG) and diglucuronide (BDG). Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia: low UGT1A1 activity (immaturity) → physiological jaundice. Crigler-Najjar type I: autosomal recessive, complete absence of UGT1A1 → severe unconjugated bilirubin accumulates → crosses BBB → kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) → requires phototherapy 10-12 h/day or liver transplant. Crigler-Najjar type II (Arias syndrome): partial deficiency → bilirubin 6-25 mg/dL (vs >20 in type I) → phenobarbital (↑UGT1A1 induction → ↓bilirubin). Gilbert's syndrome: benign, autosomal recessive (TA)7TAA promoter → ~30% of Caucasians; bilirubin 1.2-4 mg/dL, rises with fasting/illness/exercise/stress; no treatment needed, but can affect drug metabolism (e.g., irinotecan → SN-38 accumulation → diarrhea/neutropenia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the synthesis of acetylcholine?
options: Monoamine oxidase (MAO, degrades catecholamines and serotonin)

Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT): synthesizes ACh from acetyl-CoA + choline → acetylcholine + CoA; located in cholinergic neurons (CNS: nucleus basalis of Meynert, medial septum, brainstem nuclei; PNS: parasympathetic + somatic motor); ↓ChAT activity in Alzheimer's disease (selective loss of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons → ↓ACh in hippocampus/cortex → memory impairment); ACh is stored in synaptic vesicles + released by exocytosis (Ca2+-dependent); terminated by AChE (acetylcholinesterase): ACh → choline + acetate; choline recaptured by high-affinity choline transporter (CHT1) for resynthesis
Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, makes DOPA → dopamine → NE → Epi)
explanation: Neurotransmitter biosynthesis: ACh: choline (taken up by CHT1) + acetyl-CoA (from mitochondria) → ChAT → ACh → stored in vesicles (VAChT, vesicular ACh transporter). Dopamine: tyrosine → TH (BH4, Fe2+) → DOPA → AAAD/DOPA decarboxylase (PLP) → dopamine → stored in vesicles (VMAT1/2). NE: dopamine → DBH (dopamine β-hydroxylase, Cu2+, vit C) → NE → VMAT2. Epinephrine: NE → PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, uses SAM as methyl donor, induced by cortisol) → Epi. Serotonin: tryptophan → TPH (tryptophan hydroxylase, BH4) → 5-HTP → AAAD (PLP) → serotonin → VMAT2. GABA: glutamate → GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase, PLP) → GABA. Glycine: serine → SHMT (PLP) → glycine (or direct from diet/synthesis from glyoxylate).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An enzyme that shows a positive cooperative effect on a V vs [S] plot would display:
options: A sigmoidal curve — positive cooperativity means that binding of the first substrate molecule increases the affinity of the enzyme for subsequent substrate molecules (T-state → R-state shift); this produces a sigmoidal (S-shaped) velocity vs. substrate curve rather than the hyperbolic Michaelis-Menten curve; described by the Hill equation: V = Vmax[S]n/(K0.5n + [S]n) where n > 1 is the Hill coefficient; examples: ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase, n ≈ 2.1), hemoglobin (n ≈ 2.8), phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1, allosteric)
explanation: Cooperative enzymes: The Km concept doesn't apply directly; instead use K0.5 (substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity). Hill equation: V = Vmax[S]n/(K0.5n + [S]n). Hill coefficient (nH): nH = 1: no cooperativity (Michaelis-Menten). nH > 1: positive cooperativity (sigmoidal, e.g., hemoglobin O2 binding nH ≈ 2.8). nH < 1: negative cooperativity (subunit binding interferes with next). Biological significance of positive cooperativity: switch-like behavior — enzyme stays relatively inactive at low [S] and then activates rapidly once a threshold [S] is reached → allows fine metabolic control at physiological substrate concentrations. ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase): first step of pyrimidine synthesis; CTP (end product) inhibits (feedback), ATP activates; sigmoidal kinetics.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is an example of covalent catalysis by an enzyme?
options: Metal ion catalysis by carbonic anhydrase (Zn2+)

Serine protease mechanism (chymotrypsin, trypsin, elastase): Ser195 of the active site acts as a nucleophile → attacks the carbonyl carbon of the peptide substrate → covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate formed (acyl-Ser) → water attacks the acyl-enzyme (deacylation) → releases carboxylic acid product and regenerates free enzyme; histidine (His57) acts as a general base (accepts proton from Ser195 OH to enhance nucleophilicity); aspartate (Asp102) stabilizes the imidazolium of His57 (catalytic triad: Ser-His-Asp)
Acid-base catalysis by RNase A (His residues)
explanation: Enzyme catalytic mechanisms: (1) Covalent catalysis: enzyme forms a transient covalent bond with substrate; examples: serine proteases (covalent acyl-enzyme), cysteine proteases (covalent thioester intermediate, e.g., papain, caspases), pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzymes (Schiff base with amino acid), transketolase (thiamine ester). (2) Acid-base catalysis: proton donation/acceptance by active site residues (His, Asp, Glu, Lys, Arg). (3) Metal ion catalysis: Zn2+ in carbonic anhydrase (activates H2O → OH-), carboxypeptidase, thermolysin; Fe2+/3+ in cytochrome P450; Cu2+ in cytochrome c oxidase; Mg2+ in kinases (chelates ATP). (4) Strain/distortion: enzyme distorts substrate into transition-state conformation → lowers Ea. (5) Proximity and orientation: substrates positioned optimally in active site.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Cori cycle transfers energy from liver to muscle in the form of:
options: Fatty acids (that is the more common energy transfer in fasting)

Glucose: during intense exercise, muscle produces lactate (anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate → lactate via LDH); lactate released into blood → liver (Cori cycle) → gluconeogenesis: lactate + NAD+ → pyruvate (LDH) → PEP (pyruvate carboxylase + PEPCK) → glucose-6-phosphate → glucose (glucose-6-phosphatase) → blood → muscle; NET: liver uses 6 ATP (via OAA, PEPCK requires GTP equivalent, plus other steps) to reconvert 2 lactate to 1 glucose; muscle extracts 2 ATP from 1 glucose; the liver 'subsidizes' muscle energy during intense exercise; this also prevents lactic acidosis (liver clears lactate)
Ketone bodies (those are for brain during prolonged fasting)
Alanine (Cahill cycle, from amino acid metabolism in muscle)
explanation: Cori cycle (lactate cycle): Lactate shuttling between muscle and liver during intense exercise. Muscle: Glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 lactate (net 2 ATP; anaerobic). Blood: lactate transported to liver. Liver: Lactate → pyruvate → glucose (requires 6 ATP total for gluconeogenesis vs 2 ATP gained in muscle → net energy cost to the organism, subsidized by liver's aerobic metabolism). The Cori cycle can handle about 40% of lactate produced during moderate-to-intense exercise (the rest is oxidized by heart, kidney, liver directly). After exercise: excess post-exercise O2 consumption (EPOC): lactate → pyruvate (aerobically, by heart/liver/kidney) → TCA → CO2 + H2O. Cori cycle is enhanced in cancer (Warburg effect: aerobic glycolysis → ↑lactate production even in O2 → glucose recycling by liver).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which disaccharide contains a β-1,4-glycosidic bond and is the major carbohydrate in milk?
options: Sucrose (α-1,2-glycosidic bond between glucose and fructose)

Lactose (galactose β-1,4 linked to glucose): milk sugar; hydrolyzed by lactase (β-galactosidase, brush border of small intestine, lingual-lactase or intestinal LPH, lactase-phlorizin hydrolase); lactase expression is highest in infancy and typically declines after weaning (lactase non-persistence, genetic lactase deficiency is the ancestral adult phenotype, common in East Asians, Africans, Middle Easterners; lactase persistence = adult expression of lactase, derived mutation, common in Europeans and some African populations with history of dairying); lactose intolerance: ↓lactase → undigested lactose → colon (osmotic effect + fermented by bacteria → gas H2, CO2, CH4 → bloating, flatulence, diarrhea, cramps)
Maltose (α-1,4-glycosidic bond between 2 glucose molecules, from starch digestion)
Cellobiose (β-1,4-glycosidic bond between 2 glucose molecules, from cellulose)
explanation: Common disaccharides: Maltose: α-1,4-glucosyl-glucose (starch hydrolysis product, by salivary/pancreatic amylase then maltase). Isomaltose: α-1,6-glucosyl-glucose (branch point product). Lactose: β-1,4-galactosyl-glucose (milk). Sucrose: α-1,2-glucosyl-fructose (table sugar, NON-reducing because anomeric carbons are linked to each other). Trehalose: α-1,1-glucosyl-glucose (mushrooms, insects). Cellobiose: β-1,4-glucosyl-glucose (cellulose). Reducing sugars: those with a free anomeric carbon → can reduce Fehling's or Benedict's reagent → glucose, galactose, fructose, maltose, lactose, all reducing; sucrose and trehalose are NON-reducing (both anomeric carbons are in the glycosidic bond). The Guthrie PKU test detects phenylalanine; glucose in urine can be detected by glucostrip (glucose oxidase-peroxidase) or Benedict's (reducing sugars, less specific).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H2 (PGH2)?
options: Cyclooxygenase (COX-1/COX-2, prostaglandin H2 synthase, PGHS): bifunctional enzyme with (1) cyclooxygenase activity: arachidonic acid + 2 O2 → PGG2 (prostaglandin G2); (2) peroxidase activity: PGG2 → PGH2; PGH2 is the common precursor of all prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and prostacyclin; COX-1 (constitutive, 'housekeeping': stomach, platelets, kidneys) vs. COX-2 (inducible by inflammation, growth factors, IL-1, TNF-α; also constitutive in kidney and brain); NSAIDs inhibit COX non-selectively (aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX, ibuprofen/naproxen reversible competitive); celecoxib/etoricoxib: selective COX-2 inhibitors
Phospholipase A2 (releases arachidonic acid from phospholipids — prior step)
explanation: Arachidonic acid cascade: AA (20:4 Δ5,8,11,14, from membrane phospholipids cleaved by PLA2) → COX pathway (prostaglandins, thromboxane, prostacyclin) or LOX pathway (leukotrienes). COX products: PGH2 → specific synthases: PGE2 (pain, fever, vasodilation, ↑uterine tone), PGI2 (prostacyclin, from endothelium, vasodilation + anti-platelet), PGD2 (mast cells, bronchoconstriction in asthma, sleep), PGF2α (vasoconstriction, bronchospasm, uterotonic), TXA2 (platelet aggregation + vasoconstriction, from platelets). LOX pathway: 5-LOX: AA + O2 → 5-HPETE → LTA4 → LTB4 (neutrophil chemotaxis) or LTC4/D4/E4 (cysteinyl leukotrienes, bronchoconstriction, mucus, SRS-A). 12-LOX: platelets → 12-HETE. 15-LOX: resolution lipoxins. Aspirin: irreversibly acetylates COX (Ser516 in COX-2, Ser530 in COX-1) → especially ↓TXA2 in platelets (no nucleus, can't resynthesize COX → permanent).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is the major nitrogen carrier in the blood during muscle protein catabolism?
options: Alanine (glucose-alanine cycle / Cahill cycle): muscle protein catabolism → amino acids → transamination with pyruvate (from glycolysis) via alanine aminotransferase (ALT/GPT): pyruvate + glutamate → alanine + α-ketoglutarate; alanine released from muscle → blood → liver → ALT (reverse reaction): alanine + α-KG → pyruvate + glutamate; pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → glucose → back to muscle; glutamate → α-ketoglutarate + NH3 (GDH) → enters urea cycle; NET: nitrogen transferred from muscle to liver in a non-toxic form (alanine, not NH3)
Urea (end product of nitrogen catabolism in liver, excreted by kidney)
Glutamine (from brain and intestine, not the primary muscle nitrogen carrier)
explanation: Nitrogen transport overview: Amino acid deamination: transamination transfers α-amino group to α-ketoglutarate → glutamate (most amino acids). Glutamate → GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase): glutamate + NAD(P)+ → α-KG + NH3 (in liver mitochondria, feeds NH3 into urea cycle). Muscle: limited urea cycle → uses alanine (to liver) and glutamine (synthesized by GS: glutamate + NH3 + ATP → glutamine; released to blood → liver + intestine + kidney). Brain: glutamine for NH3 detoxification (astrocytes synthesize glutamine from glutamate + NH3). Liver: major site of urea synthesis. Kidney: ammoniagenesis (glutamine → glutamate + NH4+ → urine) → acid-base regulation. Urine nitrogen: primarily urea (85%) + ammonium (3-5%), creatinine (2%), small amounts of uric acid, amino acids. Liver disease: ↑blood ammonia (↓urea cycle capacity) → hepatic encephalopathy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Propionic acidemia is caused by deficiency of:
options: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonic acidemia, not propionic acidemia)

Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC): biotin-dependent enzyme that converts propionyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP → methylmalonyl-CoA (D-form) → methylmalonyl-CoA racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12) → succinyl-CoA → TCA cycle; PCC deficiency (AR, PCCA or PCCB genes) → propionyl-CoA and propionic acid accumulate (↑propionyl-CoA → competes with acetyl-CoA in TCA → inhibits PDC + KGDH → impairs energy metabolism); clinical: neonatal metabolic crisis (acidosis, hyperammonemia, ketosis), pancytopenia (bone marrow suppression by propionate), cardiomyopathy, basal ganglia injury; diagnostic: ↑plasma propionic acid, ↑methylcitrate, ↑3-hydroxypropionate in urine organic acids; treatment: protein restriction, carnitine supplementation, liver transplant
explanation: Organic acidemias comparison: Propionic acidemia (PA): PCC deficiency → ↑propionyl-CoA → ↑propionate → ↑methylcitrate; biotin deficiency can mimic; ↑ammonia (propionyl-CoA inhibits CPS I). Methylmalonic acidemia (MMA): methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency (cobalamin B12 required) OR cobalamin metabolism defects (cblA, cblB, cblC, cblD) → ↑methylmalonic acid (↑plasma MMA) → mitochondrial toxicity; cobalamin-responsive forms: IM hydroxocobalamin; metabolic similarities: both have ketosis + hyperammonemia + neutropenia/anemia/thrombocytopenia (propionate/methylmalonate suppress bone marrow). Isovaleric acidemia: isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase → leucine metabolism → ↑isovaleric acid → 'sweaty feet' odor; treatment: glycine + carnitine. MSUD: BCKDH → ↑BCAA → maple syrup odor.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Heme synthesis: which enzyme catalyzes the first step (committed step) in heme synthesis in the cytoplasm?
options: Ferrochelatase (last step, in mitochondria, inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX)

ALA synthase (δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase, ALAS): catalyzes: succinyl-CoA (from TCA) + glycine → δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) + CO2 + CoA; requires PLP (pyridoxal phosphate, B6) as cofactor; occurs in the mitochondria (first step); rate-limiting step of heme synthesis; ALAS1 (ubiquitous, constitutive, regulated by heme via protein instability); ALAS2 (erythroid-specific, regulated by iron via IRE/IRP system); ALAS1 induced by: drugs (phenobarbital, sulfonamides, alcohol → induce CYP enzymes → ↑heme demand → ↑ALAS1) → can precipitate acute porphyria attacks; inhibited by heme (feedback)
Porphobilinogen synthase (ALA dehydratase, second step, cytoplasm): 2 ALA → porphobilinogen (PBG)
explanation: Heme synthesis pathway (cytoplasm → mitochondria → cytoplasm → mitochondria): Mitochondria: (1) ALAS: succinyl-CoA + Gly → ALA (B6). Cytoplasm: (2) ALA dehydratase (ALAD/PBGS, Zn2+, most sensitive to lead inhibition): 2 ALA → PBG. (3) HMB synthase (uroporphyrinogen I synthase/porphobilinogen deaminase, PBGD): 4 PBG → hydroxymethylbilane (HMB). (4) URO3 synthase: HMB → uroporphyrinogen III. (5) URO decarboxylase: uroporphyrinogen III → coproporphyrinogen III. Mitochondria: (6) CPG oxidase → protoporphyrinogen IX. (7) Protoporphyrinogen oxidase → protoporphyrin IX. (8) Ferrochelatase (Fe2+ insertion, inhibited by lead): → HEME. Porphyrias: enzyme defects in heme synthesis → accumulation of precursors → clinical features (photosensitivity from porphyrin accumulation + acute neurovisceral crises from ALA/PBG accumulation). AIP (acute intermittent porphyria): PBGD deficiency → ↑ALA + PBG in urine → acute attacks (abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric) precipitated by drugs/fasting.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP): what is accumulated in the urine during an acute attack?
options: Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG): AIP is caused by PBGD (hydroxymethylbilane synthase) deficiency → the pathway backs up → ↑ALA + ↑PBG accumulate; both detected in fresh urine during acute attack; PBG: Watson-Schwartz test (colorimetric) or Hoesch test; ALA: Ehrlich's aldehyde reaction (pink/red); IMPORTANT: urine darkens on standing (porphobilinogen polymerizes to porphobilin/uroporphyrin); symptoms: abdominal pain (colic), neuropathy (peripheral motor > sensory, can progress to respiratory paralysis), psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, confusion, psychosis); ↓Na+ (SIADH); precipitants: drugs (barbiturates, sulfonamides, estrogens, rifampin, anticonvulsants — avoid); fasting, infections, alcohol, hormonal changes (pre-menstrual); treatment acute: IV glucose (glucose suppresses ALAS1) + hemin (hematin, replenishes heme → ↓ALAS1 by feedback) + pain management
explanation: Porphyria classification: Hepatic porphyrias (defects in liver enzyme → neurological/abdominal): AIP (PBGD, most common acute, no photosensitivity); ALA-dehydratase deficiency porphyria (ALAD, rarest); variegate porphyria (VP, PPO deficiency → both skin + acute); hereditary coproporphyria (HCP, CPOX deficiency → both + acute). Erythropoietic (defects in developing RBCs → skin lesions): congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP/Günther, URO3S deficiency → ↑uroporphyrin I → severe photosensitivity, pink teeth, hypertrichosis); erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP, ferrochelatase deficiency → ↑protoporphyrin IX → photosensitivity without blistering). Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT): URO decarboxylase deficiency (most common porphyria) → ↑uroporphyrin III in urine + skin fragility → blistering on sun-exposed areas; iron worsens; treated with phlebotomy + hydroxychloroquine.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The CRISPR-Cas9 system cleaves DNA using a guide RNA (gRNA) complementary to the target sequence. What is the PAM sequence requirement?
options: The gRNA alone is sufficient for cleavage without a PAM

A protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) must be present immediately downstream of the target sequence in the DNA: for SpCas9 (from Streptococcus pyogenes, most widely used), the PAM is 5'-NGG-3' on the non-template strand; Cas9 recognizes the PAM → unwinds DNA → the gRNA base-pairs with the complementary strand (protospacer, 20 nt) → Cas9 HNH nuclease cleaves the complementary strand and RuvC nuclease cleaves the non-complementary strand → blunt-ended double-strand break (DSB) at position 3 bp upstream of the PAM → repaired by NHEJ (error-prone → insertions/deletions → gene disruption) or HDR (if donor template provided → precise edits)
The PAM sequence is only needed in bacteria, not in human cells
PAM sequences are found on the 5' end of the target sequence
explanation: CRISPR-Cas9 mechanism: Guide RNA (gRNA or sgRNA): ~100 nt single guide RNA = spacer sequence (20 nt, complementary to target DNA) + scaffold (binds Cas9). Steps: (1) Cas9-gRNA complex scans DNA for NGG PAM. (2) PAM recognized → local DNA unwinding → R-loop formation → gRNA base-pairs with complementary strand. (3) Cas9 cleaves both strands (HNH cuts gRNA-complementary strand; RuvC cuts non-complementary strand) → DSB. Repair: NHEJ: error-prone (indels → frameshift → gene knockout). HDR: precise (needs homology template → gene correction/insertion). Variants: Cas12a (AsCpf1): uses 5'-TTTN PAM, creates staggered cuts, processes own pre-crRNA. Cas13: RNA-targeting, no DSB. Base editors (CBE, ABE): convert C→T or A→G without DSB. Prime editing: PE, search-and-replace without DSB. Clinical: sickle cell/β-thalassemia (Casgevy/exa-cel, FDA 2023): editing BCL11A enhancer in HSCs to reactivate fetal hemoglobin (HbF) → reduces sickling.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In eukaryotic mRNA, which modification at the 5' end is required for cap-dependent translation?
options: 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap: added co-transcriptionally to the 5' end of pre-mRNA by: (1) RNA 5'-triphosphatase: removes γ-phosphate from 5'-pppRNA → 5'-ppRNA; (2) guanylyl transferase: transfers GMP → forms 5'-5' triphosphate linkage → GpppRNA; (3) guanine-N7-methyltransferase: SAM-dependent → m7GpppRNA (5' cap); functions: (a) protection from 5' exonuclease degradation; (b) export from nucleus (CBC, cap-binding complex); (c) cap-dependent translation initiation: eIF4E (cap-binding protein) + eIF4G + eIF4A (RNA helicase) = eIF4F complex → binds m7G cap → recruits 43S pre-initiation complex (40S + eIFs + Met-tRNAiMet) → scans 5' UTR → finds AUG (Kozak sequence)
Internal ribosome entry site (IRES) — alternative cap-independent mechanism
explanation: mRNA modifications: 5' Cap (m7G): co-transcriptional, required for cap-dependent translation (most mRNAs). Cellular target of IRES (internal ribosome entry site): cap-independent translation; used by some viruses (poliovirus, HCV) and some cellular mRNAs during stress (p53, c-myc, VEGF). 3' Poly-A tail: 100-200 adenine residues added by poly-A polymerase (PAP) to the 3' cleavage site (AAUAAA signal ~11-30 nt upstream); functions: mRNA stability (protected from 3' exonucleases), nuclear export, translation efficiency (PABP, poly-A binding protein, interacts with eIF4G → circular mRNA → efficient ribosome recycling). Splicing: pre-mRNA → mRNA by spliceosome (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNPs + proteins) → removes introns at conserved 5'-GU...AG-3' dinucleotides. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing: ADAR enzymes deaminate A → I (read as G) → changes codons or splice sites.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis relies on:
options: Polymerase chain reaction to amplify specific alleles

Restriction endonucleases that cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences: sequence variations (SNPs or small indels) can create or destroy restriction enzyme recognition sites → different individuals have different restriction patterns → Southern blotting (DNA → restriction digest → gel electrophoresis → transfer to membrane → hybridize labeled probe → detect fragment sizes) reveals RFLPs; used historically for: paternity testing, forensic analysis, genetic disease diagnosis (sickle cell, Huntington's), linkage analysis; largely replaced by PCR-based methods (STRs, SNP arrays, next-generation sequencing)
explanation: DNA analysis techniques: RFLP: restriction enzyme + Southern blot → size polymorphisms. PCR (polymerase chain reaction): primers + Taq DNA polymerase + dNTPs + thermal cycling → exponential amplification; uses: diagnosis (PCR for pathogens, allele-specific PCR for mutations), forensics (STR profiling), cloning, sequencing. Real-time PCR (qPCR): measures amplification in real time using fluorescent dyes (SYBR Green) or probes (TaqMan); quantitative. Southern blotting: detect specific DNA sequences. Northern blotting: detect specific RNA. Western blotting: detect specific proteins. ELISA: detect antibodies or antigens using enzyme-linked antibodies. Flow cytometry: cells labeled with fluorescent antibodies → laser excitation → detect multiple markers simultaneously (FACS for sorting). Microarray: hybridize labeled nucleic acids to thousands of probes → gene expression profiling or SNP genotyping. Next-generation sequencing (NGS): massively parallel sequencing → whole genome, exome, RNA-seq, ChIP-seq.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which metabolic change best explains the 'fruity breath'?
options: Accumulation of acetone: in DKA, absolute insulin deficiency → ↑glucagon → ↑lipolysis (↑FFA) + ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA (overwhelming TCA capacity, as ↑glucagon → ↓OAA availability) → ↑ketogenesis in liver → ↑acetoacetate + ↑β-hydroxybutyrate; acetoacetate spontaneously decarboxylates → acetone (volatile ketone, excreted by lungs) → sweet/fruity smell; in severe DKA: ↑β-OHB:acetoacetate ratio (because NADH is elevated from excessive β-oxidation → NADH drives reduction of acetoacetate → β-OHB); note: β-OHB is NOT detected by nitroprusside-based ketone tests (detects acetoacetate and acetone only → may underestimate severity); β-OHB measured directly (quantitative blood β-OHB assay)
Uremia causing ammonia smell (that is chronic kidney disease)
explanation: DKA biochemistry: Labs: ↑blood glucose (>250 mg/dL), ↑ketones (blood and urine), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, HCO3- <18 mEq/L), ↑anion gap (Na+ - Cl- - HCO3-, normally 12±2; in DKA = β-OHB- + acetoacetate-), ↑osmolality. Management: IV 0.9% NS → IVF, electrolyte replacement (K+ often depleted despite normo/hyperkalemia initially — insulin ↑K+ uptake into cells → hypokalemia can occur), insulin infusion (↑glucose uptake + ↓ketogenesis + ↓gluconeogenesis), bicarbonate only if pH <6.9 (risk of cerebral edema). Brain complications: cerebral edema (especially in children, from rapid osmolality change), venous sinus thrombosis, herniation. Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state (HHS): T2DM, elderly, no ketoacidosis (sufficient insulin to suppress ketogenesis but not enough to normalize glucose), glucose >600, osmolality >320, ↑mortality.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The normal blood glucose range for a fasting plasma glucose is:
options: 70-99 mg/dL (3.9-5.5 mmol/L): normal; 100-125 mg/dL = impaired fasting glucose (IFG, pre-diabetes); ≥126 mg/dL on two occasions = diabetes mellitus (ADA 2023 criteria); also: 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥6.5% or random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms = DM; HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the past 2-3 months (glycation of HbA, N-terminal valine of β-chain; HbA1c = 5.7-6.4% pre-diabetes, ≥6.5% diabetes)
explanation: Diabetes diagnostic criteria (ADA): Fasting plasma glucose (FPG, ≥8h fast): Normal <100 mg/dL; Pre-DM 100-125; DM ≥126 mg/dL (confirmed on 2 separate days). 2h-OGTT (75g glucose): Normal <140; Pre-DM 140-199 (IGT); DM ≥200. HbA1c: Normal <5.7%; Pre-DM 5.7-6.4%; DM ≥6.5%. Random PG: ≥200 mg/dL + symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) → DM. Type 1 DM: autoimmune destruction of β-cells, anti-GAD, anti-insulin, anti-IA-2 antibodies; absolute insulin deficiency; DKA. Type 2 DM: insulin resistance + relative insulin deficiency; progressive β-cell failure; metabolic syndrome (central obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension). MODY (maturity-onset diabetes of the young): monogenic, AR/AD; GCK (MODY2, glucokinase, glucose sensor) → mild fasting hyperglycemia. Gestational DM (GDM): 24-28 weeks gestation screening (1h 50g GCT or 3h 100g OGTT); risk: ↑T2DM risk to mother and child.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) converts pyruvate to lactate. Which cofactor does it use?
options: NAD+ (which is the PRODUCT, not the reactant)

NADH: LDH reaction: pyruvate + NADH + H+ ⇌ lactate + NAD+ (in hypoxic conditions, the reaction runs in the direction of lactate production, regenerating NAD+ for glycolysis to continue → critical for anaerobic energy production); in aerobic conditions the reverse reaction occurs (lactate → pyruvate, consuming NAD+); LDH has 5 isoforms (tetramers of H and M subunits); LDH-1 (H4, heart/RBCs): highest in heart, elevated in MI; LDH-5 (M4, liver/skeletal muscle): elevated in liver disease and myopathy; LDH-1 > LDH-2 pattern ('flipped') = characteristic of MI (historically); total LDH elevated in: MI, liver disease, hemolysis, lymphoma, megaloblastic anemia
explanation: LDH (lactate dehydrogenase): Reversible, equilibrium reaction, direction determined by relative concentrations of reactants/products and NADH/NAD+ ratio. Anoxia: ↑NADH (glycolysis produces NADH, ETC cannot regenerate NAD+) → ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio → LDH runs forward (pyruvate → lactate) → regenerates NAD+ → enables continued glycolysis → 2 ATP per glucose. Aerobic: ↓NADH (ETC regenerates NAD+) → LDH runs backward (lactate → pyruvate) → pyruvate enters TCA. Clinical uses of LDH: Hemolysis marker (LDH-2 > LDH-1 in intravascular hemolysis, but LDH-1 > LDH-2 in MI). Tumor lysis syndrome: massive LDH release. Lymphoma: elevated total LDH correlates with tumor burden and prognosis. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP): elevated LDH (>300 IU/L correlates with severity). Megaloblastic anemia: ↑LDH (ineffective erythropoiesis → intramedullary hemolysis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is NOT required for the TCA cycle to function?
options: Oxaloacetate (OAA) — TCA cycle starts and ends with OAA

Oxygen — the TCA cycle itself does NOT directly require O2; the TCA cycle enzymes use NAD+ and FAD as electron acceptors (generating NADH and FADH2), but O2 is required by the electron transport chain (ETC) to regenerate NAD+ and FAD from NADH and FADH2; in anaerobic conditions, NADH accumulates → ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio → inhibits TCA cycle (NADH inhibits isocitrate dehydrogenase, α-KG dehydrogenase, and malate dehydrogenase) → TCA cycle slows; O2 is indirectly required to keep the TCA cycle running via ETC
CoA-SH (required as substrate for citrate synthase and α-KG dehydrogenase)
NAD+ (required as electron acceptor at 3 steps)
explanation: TCA cycle and O2: Direct O2-requiring enzymes = NONE in TCA cycle. Indirect O2 requirement: the 3 NADH and 1 FADH2 generated per acetyl-CoA must be re-oxidized by ETC (Complex I-IV, ultimately O2 → H2O) to regenerate NAD+ and FAD for the cycle to continue. Without O2 → ETC fails → NADH/NAD+ ratio → TCA inhibited → cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis. TCA amphibolic: both catabolic (generates NADH, FADH2 → ATP) and anabolic (provides carbon skeletons: OAA → Asp (transamination), α-KG → Glu → Gln, succinyl-CoA → heme synthesis, malate/OAA → gluconeogenesis). Anaplerosis: replenishes TCA intermediates when removed for biosynthesis: pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate → OAA), GDH (glutamate → α-KG). Cataplerosis: removal of TCA intermediates for biosynthesis. PDC, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-KG dehydrogenase = major regulatory checkpoints.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose because:
options: They are too hydrophobic to enter gluconeogenesis

Acetyl-CoA (the product of fatty acid β-oxidation) cannot be converted to net glucose in animals because there is no net gain of OAA from the acetyl-CoA: the 2 carbons of acetyl-CoA enter the TCA cycle → 2 carbons are lost as CO2 at the isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-KG dehydrogenase steps → no net carbon remains to contribute to gluconeogenesis; unlike plants and some bacteria (which have the glyoxylate cycle: isocitrate → succinate + glyoxylate → glyoxylate + acetyl-CoA → malate → OAA → gluconeogenesis), animals lack isocitrate lyase and malate synthase → no glyoxylate cycle → even-chain FA → only ketone bodies, not glucose
Fatty acids cannot enter the liver
explanation: Glyoxylate cycle: Present in plants, bacteria, yeast, and invertebrates — NOT in mammals. Bypasses the two decarboxylation steps of TCA: isocitrate lyase → isocitrate → succinate + glyoxylate; malate synthase → glyoxylate + acetyl-CoA → malate. Net: 2 acetyl-CoA → 1 oxaloacetate → gluconeogenesis. Implications for humans: Even-chain fatty acids → CANNOT contribute to net glucose synthesis (only ketones). Odd-chain fatty acids: last 3-carbon product = propionyl-CoA → propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, B12) → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → TCA → OAA → gluconeogenesis → CAN contribute to glucose (minor). Glycerol from TG hydrolysis → glycerol kinase → glycerol-3-phosphate → DHAP → gluconeogenesis → CAN contribute to glucose. Propionate from ruminants (generated by fermentation) → propionyl-CoA → gluconeogenesis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the transfer of acyl groups from cytoplasm into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation?
options: Acyl-CoA synthetase (activates FA to acyl-CoA in the outer mitochondrial membrane)

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CPT-I): on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM); converts palmitoyl-CoA (long-chain acyl-CoA) + L-carnitine → palmitoylcarnitine + CoA; palmitoylcarnitine crosses the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) via carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase (CACT, antiporter exchanges acylcarnitine for free carnitine); CPT-II (on inner surface of IMM): palmitoylcarnitine + CoA → palmitoyl-CoA + carnitine (regenerates palmitoyl-CoA in the matrix for β-oxidation); CPT-I is the RATE-LIMITING step of FA oxidation; inhibited by malonyl-CoA (↑malonyl-CoA = fed state/active FA synthesis → inhibits FA oxidation → prevents futile cycle)
Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (first step within β-oxidation inside the mitochondrial matrix)
Carnitine acetyltransferase (transfers short-chain acyl groups, not long-chain)
explanation: Carnitine shuttle: Necessary for LCFA (C12+ long-chain fatty acids); SCFA (<C6) and MCFA (C6-C12) can diffuse across IMM without carnitine. Malonyl-CoA inhibition of CPT-I: insulin → ACC → ↑malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I → ↓FA import into mitochondria → ↓β-oxidation (prevents futile cycle when FA synthesis is active). Glucagon/fasting: ↓malonyl-CoA (↓ACC activity via PKA phosphorylation + ↑AMPK phosphorylation of ACC) → ↑CPT-I activity → ↑FA oxidation + ↑ketogenesis. CPT-I deficiency (liver/muscle types): failure to oxidize LCFA → hypoketotic hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly + skeletal myopathy/cardiomyopathy. Secondary carnitine deficiency: renal loss (Fanconi syndrome), organic acidemias (propionyl-carnitine/methylmalonyl-carnitine esters deplete free carnitine), valproic acid, pivampicillin. Primary systemic carnitine deficiency (OCTN2 transporter mutation): ↓carnitine uptake → ↓FA oxidation → cardiomyopathy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: N-glycosylation of proteins occurs where?
options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): as the nascent polypeptide is being synthesized by ribosomes on the RER and threaded into the ER lumen, oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) adds a preformed 14-sugar oligosaccharide (Glc3Man9GlcNAc2) from a dolichol-pyrophosphate carrier to asparagine residues in the consensus sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr (where X ≠ Pro) → N-linked glycosylation; then in ER: glucose residues removed by glucosidases I/II → GnT (N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase I) → further trimming by mannosidases → transferred to Golgi → further glycan modifications (complex-type or hybrid-type oligosaccharides) in Golgi cisternae → final structure added for secreted or membrane proteins
explanation: Glycosylation types: N-linked glycosylation: on Asn in Asn-X-Ser/Thr; initiated in RER (co-translational); dolichol-PP intermediate; high-mannose → complex type in Golgi. O-linked glycosylation: on Ser or Thr (or HyLys in collagen, HyPro in proteoglycans); added one sugar at a time in Golgi; no consensus sequence. GPI anchors: lipid anchors added in ER → anchors protein to outer leaflet of plasma membrane. Quality control in RER: calnexin (membrane lectin, binds monoglucosylated glycoproteins → retains misfolded proteins) + calreticulin (lumenal homolog) + ERp57 (disulfide isomerase) → UPR (unfolded protein response: BiP/GRP78 + IRE1 + PERK + ATF6) if overload. CDG syndromes (congenital disorders of glycosylation): mutations in glycosylation enzymes → multisystem disease.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Competitive inhibition with a fixed concentration of inhibitor: as substrate concentration increases infinitely (→ ∞), the apparent Vmax:
options: Remains permanently lower (that is non-competitive inhibition)

Approaches the true Vmax — in competitive inhibition, the inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site; at very high [S], the probability of inhibitor occupying the active site becomes negligible (inhibitor is out-competed) → enzyme behaves as if there is no inhibitor → the reaction rate can approach the same Vmax as the uninhibited enzyme; however, because more substrate is needed to achieve each fraction of Vmax, the apparent Km is INCREASED (↑K'M = Km × (1 + [I]/Ki)); on a Lineweaver-Burk plot: same y-intercept (same Vmax → same 1/Vmax) but different x-intercept (apparent Km, different -1/K'M) → lines converge at y-intercept for different inhibitor concentrations
Is zero (that is an irreversible inhibitor)
Doubles (substrate excess reverses even non-competitive inhibition — incorrect)
explanation: Competitive inhibition kinetics: Rate equation: V = Vmax[S] / (αKm + [S]) where α = 1 + [I]/Ki. Apparent Km: K'M = Km × α = Km(1 + [I]/Ki) → always higher than true Km. Vmax: unchanged (same y-intercept on LB plot). Km-based interpretation: ↑K'M means substrate must be at higher concentration to achieve half-Vmax → ↓apparent affinity. True Vmax is reached at infinite [S]: lim(V as [S] → ∞) = Vmax. Clinical/pharmacological example: sulfonamides (competitive inhibitors of dihydropteroate synthase in bacteria, structural analog of PABA) → overcome by high PABA in the host cells (selective toxicity). Methotrexate (competitive inhibitor of DHFR) → at high concentrations, can overwhelm high-dose rescue with leucovorin. Statins: competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase (structural analog of the HMG-CoA intermediate).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes:
options: Gout (uric acid overproduction — XO deficiency would cause xanthinuria, not ADA)

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID): ADA catalyzes adenosine → inosine (deamination); deficiency → accumulation of deoxyadenosine (dAdo) in lymphocytes (dAdo is phosphorylated to dATP by deoxykinases → extremely high dATP) → dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (↓dNTP pool, particularly ↓dCTP) → ↓DNA synthesis → selective lymphocyte toxicity (lymphocytes cannot proliferate) → ↓T cells + ↓B cells + ↓NK cells → complete immune deficiency (SCID); AR inheritance; 15-25% of SCID cases; treatment: HSCT, PEG-ADA (enzyme replacement), or Strimvelis (retroviral gene therapy, first approved in Europe 2016)
Hemolytic anemia (pyruvate kinase deficiency, not ADA)
explanation: Purine catabolism enzyme deficiencies and their consequences: ADA deficiency: ↑dATP in lymphocytes → inhibits RNR → ↓dCTP → ↓DNA synthesis → lymphopenia → SCID. PNP (purine nucleoside phosphorylase) deficiency: ↑dGTP accumulates in T cells (T cells highly express deoxyguanosine kinase) → inhibits RNR → selectively kills T cells → T-cell immunodeficiency with relatively preserved B cells. HGPRT deficiency: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (↑uric acid + neurological). ADSL (adenylosuccinate lyase) deficiency: ↑SAICAR + ↑succinyladenosine → psychomotor retardation + autism + seizures. ADA enzyme replacement therapy (PEG-ADA): modified bovine ADA conjugated to PEG → monthly IM injections → reduces toxic dATP accumulation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Amino acid transamination reactions require which vitamin as a cofactor?
options: Thiamine (B1) — required by PDC, KGDH, BCKDH

Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, the active form of vitamin B6): all aminotransferases (transaminases) require PLP as a prosthetic group; the mechanism involves formation of a Schiff base (aldimine) between the α-amino group of the amino acid and the aldehyde group of PLP → after deamination → pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP) intermediate → accepts amino group from α-ketoglutarate → regenerates PLP + glutamate (ping-pong mechanism); ALT (alanine aminotransferase/GPT): alanine + α-KG ⇌ pyruvate + glutamate; AST (aspartate aminotransferase/GOT): aspartate + α-KG ⇌ OAA + glutamate; both elevated in liver injury
explanation: PLP (pyridoxal-5'-phosphate): synthesized from pyridoxine (B6) by pyridoxal kinase. PLP is a cofactor for: (1) All aminotransferases (transaminases). (2) Amino acid decarboxylases: DOPA decarboxylase (DOPA → dopamine), histidine decarboxylase (His → histamine), glutamic acid decarboxylase (Glu → GABA), DOPA decarboxylase (5-HTP → serotonin). (3) Glycogen phosphorylase (structural, Lys residue of enzyme — unusual). (4) Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT). (5) Cystathionine β-synthase (transsulfuration pathway). (6) ALA synthase (first step of heme synthesis). B6 deficiency: peripheral neuropathy (most common — aminoaciduria, demyelination), sideroblastic anemia (↓ALA synthase → ↓heme → iron accumulates in mitochondria → ring sideroblasts), seborrheic dermatitis, glossitis, stomatitis. Drugs causing B6 deficiency: isoniazid (INH, forms hydrazide with PLP → ↓PLP activity → neuropathy → give B6 prophylactically with INH), penicillamine, cycloserine.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The 'rate-limiting' enzyme of cholesterol synthesis that is inhibited by statins:
options: Squalene synthase (not the rate-limiting step targeted by statins)

HMG-CoA reductase (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase): converts HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH → mevalonate + CoA + 2 NADP+; this is the rate-limiting step of the mevalonate pathway; statins (lovastatin, simvastatin [prodrugs, activated by hepatic metabolism], atorvastatin, rosuvastatin [active as given]) are structural analogs of HMG-CoA/mevalonate transition state → competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase → ↓mevalonate → ↓cholesterol synthesis → ↑SCAP/SREBP2 activation → ↑LDLR → ↑LDL-C clearance from blood; also ↓isoprenoids (geranylpyrophosphate, farnesylpyrophosphate → Ras/Rho prenylation → pleiotropic anti-inflammatory/anti-proliferative effects)
ATP-citrate lyase (cleaves citrate → acetyl-CoA + OAA in cytoplasm, supplies carbon for cholesterol synthesis)
explanation: Statin mechanism of action: Competitive inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase → ↓intracellular cholesterol → SCAP no longer inhibited → SCAP escorts SREBP1/2 from ER to Golgi → S1P/S2P proteases cleave SREBP → active SREBP enters nucleus → binds SREs (sterol regulatory elements) → ↑HMG-CoA reductase (feedback upregulation, limits statin effect), ↑LDLR, ↑PCSK9 (counteracts LDLR upregulation). Net result: ↑LDLR on hepatocyte surface → ↑LDL clearance → ↓serum LDL-C (20-60% reduction). Side effects: myopathy (↓mevalonate → ↓CoQ10 → mitochondrial dysfunction in muscle → myalgia → rhabdomyolysis risk); ↑LFTs; drug interactions (CYP3A4 metabolized statins: lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin → interactions with CYP3A4 inhibitors; rosuvastatin/pravastatin: not significantly metabolized by CYP3A4). Statin intensity: high (atorva 40-80mg, rosuva 20-40mg, →50% ↓LDL); moderate; low.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In which condition is unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia WITHOUT elevation of direct bilirubin seen?
options: Obstruction of common bile duct (↑direct bilirubin)

Hemolytic anemia: accelerated RBC destruction → ↑heme catabolism → ↑unconjugated bilirubin (UCB) production exceeding the liver's conjugation capacity; the liver can conjugate bilirubin ~3× the normal load before UCB rises; once capacity exceeded → ↑serum UCB; since RBCs contain no UGT1A1, and UCB is fat-soluble (not filtered by kidney) → no bilirubin in urine (acholuric jaundice); but ↑urobilinogen in urine (↑bilirubin enters GI tract → ↑urobilinogen production by gut bacteria → absorbed → ↑urinary urobilinogen); also: Gilbert's syndrome (↓UGT1A1 → ↓conjugation) + Crigler-Najjar syndrome (↓↓UGT1A1 → ↑UCB)
Hepatitis (usually both direct and indirect elevated)
Cholestasis (↑direct/conjugated bilirubin, also elevated in blood → bilirubin in urine = dark urine)
explanation: Jaundice differential: Pre-hepatic (hemolytic): ↑UCB, normal ↑ALP, normal ALT/AST, ↑urobilinogen in urine, urobilin in feces (↑, dark), no bilirubinuria, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin. Hepatic: ↑UCB + ↑CB, ↑ALT/AST (hepatocellular damage), ↑ALP (mild), ↑bilirubin in urine. Post-hepatic (obstructive/cholestatic): ↑CB, ↑ALP/GGT >> ALT/AST, bilirubinuria (dark urine), pale stools (↓stercobilin), ↓urobilinogen in urine, ↑direct: total bilirubin ratio. Classic scenario: Neonatal jaundice: ↑UCB (↓UGT1A1 immaturity + ↑bilirubin production). Sickle cell crisis: ↑UCB (hemolysis) + ↑LDH + ↓haptoglobin. G6PD deficiency attack: same pattern as hemolysis. Crigler-Najjar type I: ↑↑UCB (20-50 mg/dL), acholuric jaundice, kernicterus. Gilbert's: mild ↑UCB (<6 mg/dL), fasting triggers, benign.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is the precursor of both melanin and catecholamines?
options: Tyrosine: (1) catecholamine synthesis: Tyr → DOPA (TH, tyrosine hydroxylase, BH4, rate-limiting for catecholamines) → dopamine (AAAD, PLP) → NE (DBH, Cu2+, Vit C) → Epi (PNMT, SAM); (2) melanin synthesis: Tyr → DOPA (tyrosinase, Cu2+, first step in melanocytes) → dopaquinone → melanin (eumelanin: brown-black; pheomelanin: yellow-red, from DOPA + cysteine); tyrosine is also precursor of thyroid hormones (TH: iodination and coupling of Tyr on thyroglobulin → T3/T4); tyrosine is conditionally essential (synthesized from phenylalanine by PAH; in PKU or hyperphenylalaninemia → Tyr becomes essential)
explanation: Tyrosine metabolic pathways: (1) Protein synthesis. (2) Catecholamines: Phe → Tyr (PAH) → DOPA (TH) → dopamine → NE → Epi. Rate-limiting step for catecholamines: TH (tyrosine hydroxylase). (3) Melanin: Tyr → DOPA → dopaquinone (tyrosinase) → melanin; OCA1 (albinism type 1): tyrosinase deficiency → no melanin → white hair, pink eyes, pale skin, photophobia, nystagmus. OCA2: P-protein (melanosomal membrane protein) deficiency. (4) Thyroid hormones: Tyr on thyroglobulin → iodinated by TPO (thyroid peroxidase) → MIT/DIT → coupling → T3/T4 → proteolysis of thyroglobulin → T3/T4 secreted. (5) Degradation: Tyr → homogentisate → maleylacetoacetate → fumarylacetoacetate → fumarate + acetoacetate (glucogenic + ketogenic); HGO deficiency → alkaptonuria.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Type I glycogen storage disease (von Gierke disease) is caused by deficiency of:
options: Acid α-glucosidase (maltase) — that is Pompe disease (GSD II)

Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase): von Gierke disease (GSD Ia) — G6Pase catalyzes the final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (glucose-6-phosphate → glucose + Pi), expressed only in liver, kidney, and intestine; deficiency → G6P cannot be converted to free glucose → ↑G6P → ↑glycogen synthesis → ↑glycogen storage → massive hepatomegaly (liver stuffed with glycogen + fat) + renomegaly; presentation: severe fasting hypoglycemia (unable to produce free glucose from liver), lactic acidosis (↑G6P → ↑glycolysis → ↑pyruvate → ↑lactate), hyperuricemia (↑G6P → ↑PPP → ↑ribose-5-P → ↑purine synthesis → ↑uric acid), hypertriglyceridemia (↑G6P → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑FA synthesis), xanthomas; diagnosis: liver biopsy + enzyme assay; treatment: continuous glucose feeds (nasogastric), cornstarch (slowly absorbed), liver transplant
Debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase) — that is GSD III (Cori disease)
Glycogen phosphorylase (liver form) — that is GSD VI (Hers disease)
explanation: GSD classification: GSD I (von Gierke): G6Pase (Ia) or G6P translocase (Ib, also neutropenia + IBD) → liver/kidney, hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + ↑uric acid + ↑TG. GSD II (Pompe): acid α-glucosidase (acid maltase) → lysosomal glycogen accumulation → ALL organs, especially heart and muscle; infantile: cardiomegaly + hypotonia → death by 2 years; late-onset: myopathy; treatment: enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa). GSD III (Cori/Forbes): debranching enzyme → limit dextrin accumulates → hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia + muscle weakness; less severe than GSD I because gluconeogenesis intact. GSD IV (Andersen): branching enzyme → branching points reduced → amylopectin-like glycogen → cirrhosis. GSD V (McArdle): muscle phosphorylase → painful muscle cramps on exercise + myoglobinuria; ischemic forearm exercise test: no ↑lactate (can't break down glycogen in muscle); ↑ammonia (muscle purine catabolism ↑). GSD VI (Hers): liver phosphorylase → hepatomegaly + mild hypoglycemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In Pompe disease (GSD type II), glycogen accumulates in:
options: The cytoplasm, as a coating on organelles

Lysosomes: Pompe disease is the only GSD caused by deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme (acid α-1,4-glucosidase, acid maltase, GAA); all cells have lysosomes that normally degrade glycogen → in Pompe, glycogen accumulates within lysosomes → lysosomal distension → cell damage; unlike other GSDs (cytoplasmic glycogen excess), Pompe is a lysosomal storage disorder; this is why it affects ALL tissues with high glycogen content: heart (cardiomegaly), skeletal muscle (hypotonia), liver (hepatomegaly), diaphragm (respiratory failure); CNS involvement in severe infantile form; treatment: Myozyme (alglucosidase alfa, recombinant human GAA) — enzyme replacement therapy; newborn screening (dried blood spot): ↓GAA activity; genetics: AR, GAA gene; classic infantile: presents at 2-4 months with cardiomegaly + profound hypotonia ('floppy baby') + respiratory failure → death by 2 years without treatment
Only in striated muscle, not in the liver or heart
explanation: Pompe disease (GSD II): Deficient enzyme: GAA (acid alpha-glucosidase) — lysosomal. Gene: GAA (chromosome 17q25.3). Inheritance: AR. Phenotypes: Classic infantile (severe): onset <1 month; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + respiratory failure + hypotonia + hepatomegaly + feeding difficulties → untreated: death by 1-2 years from cardiorespiratory failure; ECG: short PR interval + large QRS voltages; Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly; Late-onset (juvenile/adult): skeletal muscle myopathy progressing to respiratory failure; no/mild cardiac involvement; Diagnosis: GAA enzyme activity (dried blood spot, lymphocytes, fibroblasts) + molecular (GAA gene sequencing); labs: ↑CK (in most), ↑LFTs; urine glucose tetrasaccharide (Glc4) as biomarker. Treatment: Myozyme (alglucosidase alfa); improved with miglustat combination; newborn screening (↓mortality when treated early).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: McArdle disease (GSD type V) is characterized by which of the following pathognomonic features?
options: Second wind phenomenon: McArdle disease = muscle phosphorylase deficiency → impaired glycogenolysis in exercising muscle → cramping + pain + weakness with exercise; after a rest period ('second wind'): the exercising muscles switch to use blood glucose (from liver glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis) and fatty acids as fuel, bypassing the blocked muscle glycogenolysis → symptoms transiently improve; this 'second wind' is pathognomonic for McArdle disease and is not seen in other metabolic myopathies; also: ischemic forearm exercise test shows no rise in lactate (but ammonia rises normally, showing AMP deamination is intact) → diagnosistic for GSD V; myoglobinuria after intense exercise (rhabdomyolysis risk); ↑CK at rest and markedly ↑CK after exercise; serum lactate does not rise after forearm ischemic exercise (normal: lactate rises due to anaerobic glycolysis in muscle)
Fixed, non-fatigable myopathy without exercise-related symptoms
explanation: McArdle disease (GSD V): Deficient enzyme: myophosphorylase (PYGM gene, muscle-specific glycogen phosphorylase). Tissues affected: skeletal muscle ONLY (liver phosphorylase PYGM gene different from liver PYGL). Inheritance: AR. Presentation: exercise-induced muscle cramps and fatigue, especially with isometric or high-intensity short-duration exercise; 'second wind' phenomenon; myoglobinuria (red/brown urine after heavy exercise → risk of AKI). Diagnosis: Forearm ischemic (non-ischemic) exercise test: venous ammonia rises (AMP → IMP → NH3) but venous lactate does NOT rise (muscle can't break down glycogen → no anaerobic glycolysis → no lactate); muscle biopsy (PAS: ↑glycogen deposits, myophosphorylase staining negative); molecular: PYGM sequencing (Arg50X common mutation). Serum CK: elevated at baseline, markedly ↑ after exercise. Treatment: avoid intense exercise; aerobic conditioning improves tolerance; sucrose before exercise (↑blood glucose → substrate for muscle); high-protein diet (controversial).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Gaucher disease, the most common lysosomal storage disease, is caused by deficiency of:
options: Hexosaminidase A (that is Tay-Sachs disease, deficiency of Hex-A)

Glucocerebrosidase (β-glucosidase, acid β-glucocerebrosidase, GBA gene): catalyzes: glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) → glucose + ceramide in lysosomes; deficiency → glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages/monocytes (especially Kupffer cells in liver, macrophages in spleen and bone marrow) → 'Gaucher cells' (lipid-engorged macrophages, wrinkled paper or crumpled tissue paper appearance on histology); types: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic, most common, especially in Ashkenazi Jews, GBA Asn370Ser most common): hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, bone disease (Erlenmeyer flask deformity of femur, bone pain, osteonecrosis), no CNS; Type 2 (acute neuronopathic, infantile): rapid neurological deterioration, death by 2-3 years; Type 3 (subacute neuronopathic): intermediate; treatment: enzyme replacement (imiglucerase/velaglucerase) or substrate reduction (miglustat/eliglustat)
Sphingomyelinase (that is Niemann-Pick disease types A and B)
explanation: Gaucher disease: GBA gene (1q22). Gaucher cells: PAS-positive, 'wrinkled tissue paper' cytoplasm → ↑tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP, CD68+, CD14+). Biomarker: ↑plasma chitotriosidase + ↑glucosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb1) → diagnosis and monitoring. Bone disease mechanism: Gaucher cells in marrow → ↑osteoclast activity + ↓osteoblast function → osteoporosis + bone crises (acute pain, warmth, swelling → 'bone crisis' mimics osteomyelitis). Hematologic: anemia, thrombocytopenia (sequestration in spleen), leukopenia. Ashkenazi Jewish founder mutations: N370S (most common, type 1, milder), L444P (more severe, neuronopathic risk), 84GG (frameshift, severe). ERT: imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa, taliglucerase alfa → very effective for type 1 (non-neuronopathic). SRT: miglustat, eliglustat → oral; eliglustat (specific CYP2D6 metabolism, poor metabolizers need dose adjustment). GBA mutations are also the most common genetic risk factor for Parkinson disease (heterozygous carriers have 5× ↑PD risk).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by accumulation of:
options: GM2 ganglioside: Tay-Sachs = deficiency of hexosaminidase A (Hex-A, α-subunit of HEXA gene), the enzyme that cleaves the terminal GalNAc from GM2 ganglioside → GM2 accumulates in neuronal lysosomes → progressive neurological disease; Sandhoff disease: deficiency of both Hex-A AND Hex-B (HEXB gene, β-subunit) → same GM2 accumulation but also globoside accumulation; clinical (Tay-Sachs): infantile form: normal at birth → regression of milestones at 3-6 months → cherry-red spot on macula (lipid-engorged ganglion cells rim the fovea, which lacks ganglion cells → normal fovea appears red against the surrounding pale macula) → progressive neurodegeneration → blindness, deafness, spasticity → death by 3-4 years; no organomegaly (unlike Gaucher/Niemann-Pick); Ashkenazi Jewish (1 in 30 carriers); diagnosis: Hex-A activity in serum or leukocytes; no treatment available (supportive only)
Sphingomyelin (accumulated in Niemann-Pick types A and B)
explanation: Sphingolipidoses (enzyme, substrate, features): Tay-Sachs: Hex-A (α subunit, HEXA), GM2 → progressive neurodegeneration, cherry-red spot, Ashkenazi Jewish, infantile form most common. Sandhoff: Hex-A + Hex-B (both, HEXB), GM2 + globoside → similar to Tay-Sachs + organomegaly (globoside in viscera). Fabry: α-galactosidase A (GLA), globotriaosylceramide (Gb3/CTH) → X-linked, angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias (burning pain in hands/feet, a:childhood/adolescence), corneal whorling (cornea verticillata), renal failure, cardiomyopathy; ERT: agalsidase alfa/beta. Gaucher: glucocerebrosidase (GBA), glucocerebroside → hepatosplenomegaly, bone disease. Niemann-Pick A/B: sphingomyelinase (SMPD1), sphingomyelin → hepatosplenomegaly; type A + neurodegeneration. Krabbe: galactocerebrosidase (GALC), galactocerebroside (psychosine also accumulates) → AR, leukodystrophy, globoid cells, peripheral neuropathy, spastic quadriplegia. MLD: arylsulfatase A (ARSA), sulfatide → demyelination, peripheral neuropathy. Farber: ceramidase (ASAH1), ceramide → hoarse cry, joint nodules, orange-red cherry spots.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Niemann-Pick disease types A and B are caused by deficiency of:
options: N-acetylglucosaminidase (that is Sanfilippo syndrome type B, MPS III-B)

Sphingomyelinase (acid sphingomyelinase, ASM, SMPD1 gene): catalyzes: sphingomyelin → ceramide + phosphocholine; deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulates in lysosomes of macrophages, CNS neurons; types: Type A (severe neuronopathic): infantile onset, massive hepatosplenomegaly, progressive neurological deterioration (hypotonia, psychomotor regression), cherry-red spot (in 50%), pulmonary infiltrates (foam cells) → death by 2-3 years; Ashkenazi Jewish; Type B (non-neuronopathic, 'visceral'): hepatosplenomegaly + progressive pulmonary disease + atherogenic dyslipidemia (↓HDL, ↑LDL), some survive into adulthood, no/minimal CNS; treatment: olipudase alfa (ERT for type B); Type C (NPC1/NPC2 genes, different mechanism — defect in cholesterol/sphingolipid intracellular trafficking, not sphingomyelinase deficiency): NPC1/2 → free cholesterol trapping in late endosomes/lysosomes → vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, seizures, dementia, cataplexy; treatment: miglustat (substrate reduction); filipin staining: ↑cholesterol in lysosomes (diagnosis of NPC)
explanation: Niemann-Pick type C (NPC) is a distinct disease: NPC1 (95%): late endosomal/lysosomal protein, cholesterol transporter-related. NPC2: soluble lysosomal protein binds free cholesterol. Together: mediate cholesterol egress from late endosomes/lysosomes. Deficiency: cholesterol accumulates in late endosomes → impaired cholesterol recycling → secondary sphingolipid accumulation. Presentation: vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (VSGP) — hallmark, downward gaze affected first; childhood-onset ataxia, dystonia, dysarthria; seizures; cognitive decline; gelastic cataplexy (atonic episodes triggered by laughter). Diagnosis: filipin staining (fluorescent cholesterol stain) of fibroblasts shows perinuclear cholesterol accumulation; NPC1/NPC2 sequencing; plasma oxysterols (7-ketocholesterol, etc.) as biomarker. Treatment: miglustat (iminosugar, substrate reduction — delays neurological progression); ERT trials ongoing. Niemann-Pick A/B (SMPD1 ASM deficiency): sphingomyelin + cholesterol accumulation (Niemann-Pick cells = foam cells with 'sea-blue' histiocytes in bone marrow = macrophages with blue-green granules on Giemsa stain).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hurler syndrome (MPS I-H) is caused by deficiency of which enzyme?
options: Iduronate-2-sulfatase (that is Hunter syndrome, MPS II, X-linked)

α-L-iduronidase (IDUA gene): catalyzes hydrolysis of the α-L-iduronate sulfate residues in dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate → both accumulate in lysosomes; autosomal recessive; severe form (Hurler, MPS I-H) vs. attenuated (Scheie, MPS I-S) vs. intermediate (Hurler-Scheie); Hurler presentation: coarse facial features (gargoylism), macroglossia, corneal clouding (dermatan sulfate deposits), hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac disease (coronary artery narrowing, valvular), skeletal dysplasia (gibbus deformity, claw hand, short stature, vertebral beaking on X-ray), intellectual disability (severe → profound), hearing loss, recurrent otitis media/URI; diagnosis: urine GAGs (↑dermatan sulfate + ↑heparan sulfate), enzyme assay, molecular; treatment: ERT (laronidase/Aldurazyme) for non-CNS symptoms; HSCT (if early, <2 years, before significant cognitive decline → slows neurological progression); death in first decade without treatment
N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (that is Morquio A syndrome, MPS IVA)
β-glucuronidase (that is Sly syndrome, MPS VII)
explanation: MPS classification: MPS I (Hurler/Scheie): α-L-iduronidase → ↑dermatan sulfate + heparan sulfate → coarse features + corneal clouding + intellectual disability. MPS II (Hunter): iduronate-2-sulfatase → ↑dermatan + heparan sulfate → X-LINKED (only X-linked MPS) → no corneal clouding (key distinction from Hurler!), pebbly skin lesions, intellectual disability (severe form) or preserved intelligence (mild form). MPS III (Sanfilippo A-D): 4 different enzymes for heparan sulfate degradation → ↑heparan sulfate → severe intellectual disability + behavioral problems (aggressive behavior, sleep disturbance), MILD somatic features. MPS IV (Morquio A/B): N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (A) or β-galactosidase (B) → ↑keratan sulfate → SKELETAL DYSPLASIA (short trunk, odontoid hypoplasia → atlantoaxial instability, genu valgum) WITHOUT intellectual disability. MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy): N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase → ↑dermatan sulfate → somatic features like Hurler, NO intellectual disability. MPS VII (Sly): β-glucuronidase → rare, variable. Key differentiator: corneal clouding = MPS I, IV, VI (NOT MPS II or III). X-linked = MPS II only.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hunter syndrome (MPS type II) differs from Hurler syndrome in which key feature?
options: Urine shows heparan sulfate only (both MPS I and II excrete dermatan + heparan sulfate)

Absence of corneal clouding and X-linked inheritance: Hunter (MPS II) = iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency (IDS gene, Xq28) → X-LINKED RECESSIVE (only MPS that is X-linked; females rarely affected; female carriers can have mild disease if unfavorable lyonization); accumulates dermatan sulfate AND heparan sulfate (same GAGs as Hurler) but corneal clouding does NOT occur (iduronate-2-sulfatase is important for corneal keratan/dermatan sulfate but the dermatan sulfate deposit pattern in cornea is different from α-L-iduronidase; the corneal stroma remains clear in Hunter because iduronate-2-sulfatase is present in corneal fibroblasts at sufficient residual levels in most patients); also: pebbly (cobblestone) skin lesions on back/arms (MPS II-specific); hearing loss, hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex; severe form (MPS IIA): intellectual disability, progressive; mild form (MPS IIB): relatively preserved intellect; treatment: ERT (idursulfase, Elaprase); intrathecal idursulfase-IT (for CNS involvement)
Absent cardiac disease (cardiac involvement is the key distinguishing feature)
Normal skeletal development (both MPS I and II have severe skeletal dysplasia)
explanation: Distinguishing MPS I vs MPS II (key boards differentiator): Both: dermatan + heparan sulfate in urine; coarse features; hepatosplenomegaly; cardiac disease; hearing loss; skeletal dysplasia. MPS I (Hurler): AR; corneal clouding present; α-L-iduronidase; treatment HSCT + ERT (laronidase). MPS II (Hunter): X-linked; NO corneal clouding; cobblestone skin lesions; iduronate-2-sulfatase; treatment ERT (idursulfase). Pearly/cobblestone skin: pathognomonic for Hunter — whitish, pebbly, ivory-colored papules between scapulae and on lateral trunk. GAGs in urine (screening): dermatan + heparan sulfate (MPS I, II, VI); heparan sulfate alone (MPS III); keratan sulfate (MPS IV); dermatan sulfate alone (MPS VI). Toluidine blue O spot test (urine): metachromasia (purple-red) = positive screening; dimethylmethylene blue quantitative assay.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Nucleotide excision repair (NER) is the primary DNA repair mechanism for:
options: Single-base mismatches (corrected by mismatch repair, MMR)

Bulky DNA adducts and UV-induced pyrimidine dimers (CPDs and 6-4 PPs): NER excises a ~25-30 nucleotide oligonucleotide containing the lesion → filled by DNA Pol δ/ε using the intact strand as template → ligated; two sub-pathways: (1) Global genome NER (GGR): removes lesions anywhere in the genome → requires XPC-RAD23B + DDB1-DDB2 (XPE, UV-DDB) for damage recognition; (2) Transcription-coupled NER (TCR): removes lesions specifically from the template strand of active genes → initiated by stalling of RNA Pol II at a lesion → CSA (ERCC8) + CSB (ERCC6) recognize the stalled polymerase; shared steps for both: TFIIH (contains XPB and XPD helicases) → unwind DNA around lesion; XPA verifies damage; XPG (3' endonuclease) + XPF-ERCC1 (5' endonuclease) → excise ≈25-30 nt oligonucleotide; replication machinery fills gap (Pol δ/ε + RPA + RFC + PCNA); DNA ligase I/III seals
explanation: DNA repair pathways: (1) BER (base excision repair): for small, non-helix-distorting lesions (oxidized bases: 8-oxoG by OGG1; deaminated cytosine = uracil by UNG; AP sites); steps: glycosylase removes base → APE1 cleaves backbone → Pol β fills → ligase III seals; MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP): defective MUTYH removes adenine mispaired with 8-oxoG → ↑G:C→T:A transversions → CRC. (2) NER: bulky adducts (UV dimers, benzo[a]pyrene-G, cisplatin cross-links); XP proteins (XPA through XPG); Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP): defective GGR → extreme UV sensitivity, 1000× ↑skin cancer risk, photophobia, neurological degeneration in some forms. (3) MMR (mismatch repair): for base mismatches and small indels from replication errors; MSH2/MSH6 (MutSα heterodimer) recognizes mismatch; MLH1/PMS2 (MutLα) → excision + re-synthesis; Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): germline mutations in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM → ↑CRC, endometrial, ovarian, urinary tract, gastric cancers; MSI (microsatellite instability). (4) HR: DSBs in S/G2 phase, uses sister chromatid → high fidelity; BRCA1/2 essential. (5) NHEJ: DSBs in G1 → error-prone.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The hallmark of Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) on tumor pathology is:
options: Loss of APC protein (APC loss = FAP, familial adenomatous polyposis)

Microsatellite instability (MSI): microsatellites are short tandem repeats (STRs) throughout the genome; normally maintained by MMR (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2); in Lynch syndrome, germline MMR gene mutation → tumor cell acquires somatic second hit → MMR deficiency → replication errors at microsatellites not corrected → MSI (accumulation of new repeat alleles not present in normal tissue); testing: PCR of 5 microsatellite markers (Bethesda panel: BAT-25, BAT-26, D5S346, D2S123, D17S250) → compare tumor vs. normal → MSI-H = ≥2/5 loci unstable; immunohistochemistry (IHC): absence of nuclear staining for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2 protein → loss of expression → suggests MMR deficiency (MMR-D); ≈15% of sporadic CRC also MSI-H (via MLH1 promoter hypermethylation + BRAF V600E mutation); pembrolizumab (PD-1 inhibitor): approved for MSI-H/MMR-D cancers regardless of histology (tissue-agnostic approval)
p53 mutation (occurs in many cancers but not the defining hallmark of Lynch syndrome specifically)
KRAS mutation (present in ~40% of CRC but not Lynch syndrome-specific)
explanation: Lynch syndrome (HNPCC): Most common hereditary CRC syndrome (~3% of all CRC). Genes: MLH1 (50%), MSH2 (40%), MSH6 (10%), PMS2, EPCAM (MSH2 silencing via deletion of 3' exons). Lifetime CRC risk: 60-80% (MLH1/MSH2); 25-50% (MSH6/PMS2). Cancer spectrum: CRC (right-sided predominance), endometrial (~50%), ovarian, gastric, small bowel, urothelial. Amsterdam criteria II: ≥3 relatives with Lynch cancers, spanning ≥2 generations, at least 1 <50 years old. Revised Bethesda guidelines (when to test for MSI): CRC <50 years; synchronous/metachronous Lynch cancers; CRC with MSI-H features (TILs, mucinous/signet-ring differentiation); CRC in 1st-degree relative with Lynch cancer/adenoma <50. MSI-H tumors: better prognosis in early-stage CRC; paradoxically resistant to 5-FU monotherapy; respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1/PD-L1 blockade). POLE/POLD1 mutations: proofreading deficiency → ultra-mutated (TMB very high) → hypermutation → respond to immunotherapy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The RAS oncogene encodes a protein with GTPase activity. In cancer, how is RAS commonly mutated?
options: RAS is deleted (loss-of-function, so it can't activate MAPK signaling)

Point mutations in codons 12, 13, or 61 that impair GTPase activity: normal RAS protein acts as a binary switch — GDP-bound (OFF) → activated by GEFs (guanine nucleotide exchange factors) → GTP-bound (ON) → activates effectors (RAF→MEK→ERK; PI3K→Akt→mTOR) → signal terminated when RAS hydrolyzes GTP to GDP (intrinsic GTPase + stimulated by GAPs, GTPase-activating proteins); in cancer, mutations at codon 12 (Gly12 → Val, Asp, Ala, Cys, Ser, Arg) or 13 (Gly13 → Asp) or 61 (Gln61) prevent GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis → RAS constitutively active (stuck in ON state) → continuous cell proliferation; KRAS most common (pancreatic: ~95%, CRC: ~40%, NSCLC: ~25%), NRAS (melanoma, AML), HRAS (head and neck, bladder); treatment: KRAS G12C-specific inhibitors (sotorasib, adagrasib) target the cysteine in G12C via covalent bond in the GDP-bound state
RAS is amplified, increasing the total amount of protein without changing GTPase activity
RAS acquires a novel catalytic domain to activate other oncoproteins
