explanation: RAS signaling pathway: RTK (e.g., EGFR) → GRB2-SOS complex → SOS (GEF) exchanges GDP for GTP on RAS → RAS-GTP → RAF (ARAF, BRAF, CRAF) → MEK1/2 → ERK1/2 → transcription factors (ELK1, c-Myc, c-Fos) → cell proliferation. Also: RAS → PI3K → PIP2 → PIP3 → Akt → mTOR → protein synthesis, survival. Oncogenic RAS: constitutively active → bypass receptor signals → sustained proliferation. Therapeutic targeting: EGFR antibodies (cetuximab, panitumumab) or EGFR TKIs: ONLY work if RAS is wild-type (mutant KRAS = downstream of EGFR → anti-EGFR agents ineffective → RAS must be tested before giving). KRAS G12C inhibitors: sotorasib (AMG 510) and adagrasib (MRTX849) → approved for KRAS G12C NSCLC and CRC; G12C is unique because cysteine can be covalently modified; other KRAS mutations (G12D, G12V) — inhibitors in development. Neurofibromatosis (NF1): neurofibromin is a GAP for RAS → NF1 loss → ↑RAS-GTP → benign nerve sheath tumors (neurofibromas) + ↑cancer risk.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The p53 protein acts as a tumor suppressor by:
options: Activating DNA synthesis at replication origins

Activating transcription of genes that halt the cell cycle or promote apoptosis when DNA is damaged: TP53 (tumor protein 53, chromosome 17p13.1) encodes a transcription factor (sequence-specific DNA binding); normally, p53 is rapidly degraded by MDM2 (E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates p53 → proteasomal degradation); DNA damage (DSBs, UV, oxidative stress) → ATM/ATR kinases phosphorylate p53 → stabilized + transactivates: (1) CDKN1A (p21, WAF1/CIP1): inhibits CDK4/CDK6-Cyclin D → arrests cell in G1; (2) GADD45: DNA repair; (3) BAX (↑Bax/Bcl-2 ratio → mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization → cytochrome c → apoptosome → caspase cascade → apoptosis); (4) PUMA, NOXA: pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins; if repair fails or damage too extensive → p53 promotes apoptosis rather than cycle restart; TP53 is mutated in ~50% of all human cancers (most commonly missense mutations in the DNA-binding domain: R175H, G245S, R248W, R248Q, R249S, R273H, R282W)
Directly repairing DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination
Inhibiting oncogene expression at the transcriptional level
explanation: p53 tumor suppressor: TP53: most commonly mutated gene in human cancer (~50%). Missense mutations (gain-of-function): dominant negative effect (mutant p53 tetramerizes with wild-type p53 → inactivates wild-type); also acquire novel oncogenic functions (↑invasion, ↑angiogenesis, ↑drug resistance). Li-Fraumeni syndrome: germline TP53 mutation → ↑lifetime risk of many cancers (sarcomas, breast, brain, adrenal cortex, leukemia). MDM2 amplification: ↑MDM2 → ↑p53 degradation → functional p53 loss despite wild-type TP53 → sarcomas (MDM2 amplification ~20% of liposarcomas, osteosarcomas). MDM2 inhibitors (nutlin, idasanutlin): block MDM2-p53 interaction → stabilize wild-type p53 → therapeutic potential in MDM2-amplified cancers. HPV E6 protein: binds p53 → targets for proteasomal degradation → p53 functional loss in HPV+ cancers (cervical, oropharyngeal). Rb (retinoblastoma protein): another major tumor suppressor; hypophosphorylated Rb sequesters E2F → G1 arrest; CDK4/6+CyclinD phosphorylates Rb → E2F release → S phase entry; Rb loss → uncontrolled E2F → proliferation; CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib): effective in Rb+ ER+HER2- breast cancer.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Vitamin K is required as a cofactor for which post-translational modification?
options: Hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen (that is Vitamin C, ascorbic acid)

γ-Carboxylation of glutamate residues: vitamin K (phylloquinone K1 from plants, menaquinones K2 from bacteria/animal products, menadione K3 synthetic) is the cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase enzyme that converts glutamate (Glu) residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues in specific proteins; Gla residues chelate Ca2+ → conformational change required for activity; coagulation factors requiring vitamin K: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X ('1972' mnemonic) + anticoagulant proteins C, S, Z; also: osteocalcin (bone), matrix Gla protein (vascular calcification inhibitor), Gas6 (tyrosine kinase ligand); warfarin mechanism: warfarin inhibits VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase) → blocks vitamin K recycling (vitamin K epoxide → active vitamin K hydroquinone cannot occur) → ↓γ-carboxylation → ↓functional coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X → anticoagulation; INR reflects factor VII (shortest half-life, first to fall after warfarin initiation)
Phosphorylation of serine residues on signaling proteins (protein kinase reactions)
Methylation of DNA cytosine residues (DNA methyltransferase reactions)
explanation: Vitamin K-dependent proteins and clinical aspects: Coagulation factors: II (prothrombin, t½ ~60h), VII (t½ ~6h, first to fall with warfarin/liver disease), IX, X (intrinsic + common pathway). Anticoagulant: Protein C (t½ ~6h, first anticoagulant to fall → transient hypercoagulability when warfarin started → warfarin-induced skin necrosis in protein C deficiency), Protein S, Protein Z. Bone: osteocalcin (binds hydroxyapatite, bone mineralization). Vascular: MGP (matrix Gla protein, inhibits vascular calcification → MGP gene mutations → Keutel syndrome, soft tissue calcification). Warfarin reversal: for urgent surgery/major bleeding: fresh frozen plasma (FFP) = immediate full factor replacement; prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) = faster, smaller volume; vitamin K (1-10mg IV) = restores synthesis over hours (2-6h oral, slower). VKORC1: polymorphisms affect warfarin dose requirement (VKORC1 1639G>A: lower warfarin dose needed). Hemorrhagic disease of newborn (HDN): neonates have low Vitamin K (poor placental transfer, sterile gut, poor Vit K in breast milk) → give IM Vitamin K at birth (prophylaxis for VKDB, vitamin K deficiency bleeding).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylation reactions. Which of the following is NOT a biotin-dependent enzyme?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate + CO2 → OAA, in gluconeogenesis)

Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (Propionyl-CoA + CO2 → D-methylmalonyl-CoA, requires both biotin AND cobalamin B12 for subsequent step): WAIT — propionyl-CoA carboxylase IS a biotin-dependent enzyme; the question asks what is NOT biotin-dependent; Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC): converts pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO2; requires TPP (B1), lipoic acid, CoA (B5), FAD (B2), NAD+ (B3) → NOT biotin-dependent; PDC is NOT a carboxylase — it is a decarboxylase (removes CO2); biotin-dependent carboxylases all use the same mechanism: biotin (covalently attached to Lys residue via biotinyl domain) is carboxylated by ATP + CO2 → carboxybiotin → transfers CO2 to substrate; ALL four biotin-dependent carboxylases: pyruvate carboxylase (PC), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC, rate-limiting for FA synthesis), propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC), β-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCC)
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (rate-limiting step in fatty acid synthesis, ACC1 in cytoplasm)
β-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCC) — in leucine catabolism pathway
explanation: Biotin (Vitamin B7): water-soluble B vitamin; covalently attached to enzymes via Lys residue (biotinylation by holocarboxylase synthetase, HLCS); recycled by biotinidase (cleaves biocytin → free biotin). Biotin-dependent carboxylases (all use ATP + HCO3- → add CO2 to substrate): (1) Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): pyruvate → OAA; mitochondria; gluconeogenesis initiation + TCA anaplerosis. (2) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1): cytoplasm; acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA; rate-limiting for FA synthesis; ACC2: outer mitochondrial membrane; malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I → blocks FA import into mitochondria. (3) Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC): propionyl-CoA → D-methylmalonyl-CoA; mitochondria; catabolism of Ile, Val, Met, Thr + odd-chain FA. (4) β-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCC): in leucine catabolism; mitochondria. Biotin deficiency: raw egg whites (avidin binds biotin tightly → bioavailability = 0); prolonged parenteral nutrition without biotin; biotinidase deficiency (neonatal screening); multiple carboxylase deficiency: organic acidemia (↑lactate, ↑pyruvate, ↑propionylcarnitine), alopecia, perioral/perianal dermatitis, conjunctivitis, ataxia, intellectual disability.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which protein is the major transport form of cortisol in the blood?
options: Albumin (nonspecific, transports ~10-15% of cortisol + many other molecules)

Corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, transcortin): alpha-2 globulin synthesized by liver; high affinity but low capacity for cortisol (binds ~75% of plasma cortisol); also binds progesterone; conditions affecting CBG: ↑CBG: estrogen/OCP, pregnancy, hyperthyroidism (↑total cortisol but normal free cortisol and no clinical hypercortisolism); ↓CBG: nephrotic syndrome (urinary loss), liver disease (↓synthesis), hypothyroidism; only FREE cortisol is biologically active (crosses blood-brain barrier, enters cells, binds GR); urinary free cortisol (UFC) reflects free (active) cortisol; salivary cortisol also measures free cortisol; morning serum cortisol: measures total cortisol (includes CBG-bound); Cushing syndrome screening: 24h UFC or late-night salivary cortisol (LNSC) or 1mg overnight DST
Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) — binds testosterone and estradiol, not cortisol
explanation: Plasma protein transport: Albumin: binds many hydrophobic substances nonspecifically (FFA, bilirubin, drugs [warfarin, diazepam, aspirin], cortisol 10-15%, steroids, Ca2+ 40-50%). CBG (transcortin): cortisol (~75%), progesterone, aldosterone (some). SHBG (sex hormone binding globulin): testosterone + estradiol (~60-70% of sex steroids bound; ↑SHBG in hyperthyroidism, liver disease, estrogen; ↓SHBG in obesity, hypothyroidism, androgen excess, insulin resistance). Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG): T4 (~70% of T4), T3 (low affinity); ↑TBG: estrogen, pregnancy, hepatitis; ↓TBG: androgens, nephrotic syndrome, liver disease, niacin. Transthyretin (TTR, prealbumin): T4 (15-20%), T3, retinol-RBP complex; negative acute phase reactant (↓in malnutrition, inflammation, liver disease); used as nutritional marker. RBP4 (retinol-binding protein): retinol transport; filtered and reabsorbed by kidney; ↑plasma RBP4 in AKI (↓filtration) and insulin resistance (↑secretion from fat). Haptoglobin: binds free Hb in hemolysis → ↓haptoglobin in hemolysis (consumed). Transferrin (siderophilin): iron transport (2 Fe3+ per molecule); normally 1/3 saturated; ↑TIBC in iron deficiency; ferritin: iron storage (acute phase reactant, ↑in inflammation/malignancy even with iron deficiency).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Activation of the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) → Akt → mTOR pathway: which downstream effect is most directly regulated by mTORC1?
options: Gene transcription via direct binding of Akt to DNA

Protein synthesis: mTORC1 (mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1, mTOR + Raptor + mLST8 + PRAS40 + DEPTOR) activates protein synthesis via two main substrates: (1) S6K1 (p70 S6 kinase): phosphorylates ribosomal protein S6 → ↑ribosome biogenesis + ↑translation of mRNAs with 5' TOP motifs (terminal oligopyrimidine tract, encoding ribosomal proteins and elongation factors); (2) 4E-BP1 (eIF4E-binding protein 1): phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 releases eIF4E → eIF4E joins eIF4F complex → cap-dependent translation initiation ↑; net: mTORC1 activation → ↑translation of many mRNAs → protein synthesis for cell growth; ALSO: mTORC1 inhibits autophagy (phosphorylates ULK1 → ↓autophagy initiation); mTORC2 (rapamycin-insensitive): activates Akt (Ser473 phosphorylation) + SGK1 + PKCα → cytoskeletal organization
Phosphorylation of nuclear histones to activate gene expression
Degradation of cell cycle inhibitors in the nucleus
explanation: PI3K-Akt-mTOR signaling: Activation: RTK/GPCR → PI3K → PIP2 + PI → PIP3 → PDK1 (phosphorylates Akt Thr308) + mTORC2 (phosphorylates Akt Ser473) → fully active Akt → phosphorylates: TSC2 (inhibits TSC1/2 complex → disinhibits Rheb-GTP → mTORC1 ON), PRAS40 (↓mTORC1 inhibition), BAD (↓apoptosis), GSK-3β (↑glycogen synthesis), FOXO (nuclear export → ↓cell death genes). mTORC1 substrates: S6K1, 4E-BP1 (see above), ULK1 (↓autophagy), LIPIN1, HIF-1α (↑ hypoxia response), c-MYC. Negative regulators: PTEN phosphatase (degrades PIP3 back to PIP2; PTEN is a major tumor suppressor; loss of PTEN → constitutive Akt-mTOR activation → PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome: Cowden, Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba); TSC1/TSC2 (tuberous sclerosis complex; GAP for Rheb; loss → mTORC1 constitutively active → TSC syndrome: hamartomas in brain, kidney, lung, skin). Rapamycin (sirolimus, everolimus): binds FKBP12 → complex inhibits mTORC1 (allosterically); used in transplant (immunosuppression), oncology, TSC (hamartoma reduction), vascular restenosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the insulin signaling cascade, glucose transporter translocation occurs via:
options: Receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylation of GLUT4 directly to activate it

Vesicle-mediated trafficking: insulin binds IR (insulin receptor, RTK, α2β2 heterotetramer) → β-subunit autophosphorylation (Tyr) → IRS-1/IRS-2 phosphorylation → PI3K → PIP3 → Akt (PDK1 + mTORC2) → Akt phosphorylates AS160/TBC1D4 (a Rab-GAP) → inactivated AS160 can no longer convert Rab10-GTP → Rab10-GDP → Rab10-GTP remains active → GLUT4-containing vesicles (GSVs, GLUT4 storage vesicles) translocate from intracellular compartment to plasma membrane → GLUT4 fusion with PM → ↑glucose uptake into muscle and adipose; in basal state: GLUT4 is sequestered intracellularly (~95% intracellular); insulin → rapid (within minutes) redistribution to PM (5× to 40× ↑PM GLUT4); also: muscle contraction → AMPK → AS160 phosphorylation → GLUT4 translocation (independent of insulin — important for exercise-induced glucose uptake)
Direct transcriptional upregulation of GLUT4 gene by the insulin receptor
Cyclic AMP-mediated phosphorylation of GLUT4 channels to open them
explanation: GLUT transporters: GLUT1 (ubiquitous, RBCs, brain, fetal, basal glucose uptake; ↑in cancer — Warburg effect). GLUT2 (liver, pancreatic β-cells, small intestine, kidney; high Km/low affinity → glucose sensor; transports fructose, galactose too). GLUT3 (brain neurons; high affinity/low Km → efficiently uptakes glucose even at low concentrations). GLUT4 (insulin-sensitive: skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, adipose; intracellular storage vesicles → insulin/exercise → PM translocation → ↑glucose uptake; predominantly responsible for post-prandial glucose disposal; ↓GLUT4 → insulin resistance). GLUT5 (small intestine, testes; fructose-specific transporter; does NOT transport glucose). GLUT7 (intracellular, ER membrane; exports glucose from ER → blood in liver → part of glucose-6-phosphatase system). Fructose absorption: GLUT5 → enterocyte → GLUT2 → portal blood. Glucose + galactose absorption: SGLT1 (Na+-glucose co-transporter, apical brush border, secondary active transport) → enterocyte → GLUT2 → portal blood.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane, proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972), describes:
options: A rigid bilayer with protein channels embedded at fixed locations

A phospholipid bilayer with freely moving integral and peripheral proteins: the lipid bilayer is a dynamic fluid — phospholipids diffuse laterally within their leaflet (lateral diffusion, ~1 µm/s) but rarely flip from one leaflet to the other (flip-flop is slow, requires flippases/floppases/scramblases enzymes with energy input); integral (transmembrane) proteins span the bilayer one or multiple times (single-pass: type I with extracellular N-term, type II with cytoplasmic N-term; multi-pass: 7-TM GPCRs, ion channels, transporters); peripheral proteins: attached to surface by electrostatic or hydrogen bonds (e.g., spectrin in RBC cytoskeleton); lipid rafts: microdomains enriched in sphingomyelin + cholesterol + GPI-anchored proteins → more ordered (liquid-ordered phase) than surrounding bilayer → signaling platforms
A trilaminar structure with proteins forming the inner and outer layers
A symmetrical bilayer where both leaflets have identical phospholipid composition
explanation: Membrane lipid composition: Phosphatidylcholine (PC): most abundant; outer leaflet. Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE): inner leaflet. Phosphatidylserine (PS): inner leaflet (exposure on outer leaflet = apoptosis signal → phagocytosis by macrophages/clearance); also involved in coagulation factor binding. Sphingomyelin: outer leaflet; enriched in lipid rafts. Cholesterol: both leaflets; intercalated between fatty acid chains → modulates membrane fluidity (↓fluidity at high temperature, ↑fluidity at low temperature → 'fluidity buffer'). Membrane fluidity factors: ↑unsaturated FA → ↑fluidity (cis double bonds create kinks → ↓packing). ↑cholesterol → ↓fluidity (fills gaps between FA chains). ↑temperature → ↑fluidity. ↑chain length → ↓fluidity. Asymmetry maintained by: flippases (ATP8A, TMEM30, flip PS from outer → inner), floppases (ABCA1, MRP1, flip lipids outward), scramblases (XKR8, TMEM16F — calcium-activated; scramble all phospholipids → PS exposure on outer leaflet during apoptosis and platelet activation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Na+/K+-ATPase: which of the following best describes its transport stoichiometry and energy requirement?
options: 2 Na+ out, 3 K+ in per ATP (incorrect)

3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP hydrolyzed: the Na+/K+-ATPase (sodium-potassium pump) is a P-type ATPase (phosphorylated intermediate during cycle, Asp residue phosphorylated); α/β heterodimer (α: catalytic, β: glycosylated, required for maturation/targeting); pump cycle (Post-Albers mechanism): (1) E1 state: faces cytoplasm, high affinity for Na+, binds 3 Na+ → ATP hydrolysis → Asp phosphorylation → E2-P conformation; (2) E2-P state: faces extracellular, releases 3 Na+ (low affinity), binds 2 K+ → dephosphorylation → E1 conformation; (3) E1: releases 2 K+ into cytoplasm; NET: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in → electrogenic (net +1 charge out = hyperpolarizing); maintains resting membrane potential (~-70 mV in neurons); maintains cell volume (Na+ pumped out → water follows → prevents cell swelling); inhibited by cardiac glycosides (ouabain, digoxin) → ↑intracellular Na+ → ↓Na+/Ca2+ exchanger → ↑intracellular Ca2+ → ↑cardiac contractility
1 Na+ out, 1 K+ in per ATP (electroneutral but incorrect)
3 Na+ in, 2 K+ out per ATP (direction reversed)
explanation: Transport mechanisms: Primary active transport: uses ATP directly (Na+/K+-ATPase, H+/K+-ATPase [proton pump, parietal cells, kidney collecting duct, osteoclasts], Ca2+-ATPase [SERCA: ER; PMCA: plasma membrane], ABC transporters). Secondary active transport: uses electrochemical gradient established by primary active transport; symport (same direction): SGLT1 (Na+-glucose, intestine/kidney), NKCC1/2 (Na+K+2Cl- cotransporter); antiport (opposite directions): Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE), Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX), Na+/HCO3- cotransporter. Facilitated diffusion: passive, requires channel or carrier, down concentration gradient (GLUT transporters, aquaporins, ion channels). Simple diffusion: O2, CO2, N2, lipid-soluble molecules, alcohol → directly through lipid bilayer. Osmosis: water moves from low to high solute concentration through aquaporins or lipid bilayer. Digoxin toxicity: ↓Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑intracellular Na+ → ↓NCX activity → ↑intracellular Ca2+ → ↑contractility (therapeutic) but can → arrhythmias (toxicity). Hypokalemia ↑digoxin toxicity (K+ normally competes with digoxin for pump binding site).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: De novo pyrimidine synthesis: which enzyme catalyzes the FIRST committed step?
options: UMPS (UMP synthase, catalyzes the last two steps in pyrimidine synthesis)

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II): rate-limiting step; CPS II (cytoplasmic, uses glutamine as nitrogen donor, uses HCO3- + 2 ATP) → carbamoyl phosphate; note the distinction from CPS I (mitochondrial, uses NH4+ as nitrogen donor, requires N-acetylglutamate as allosteric activator, in urea cycle); carbamoyl phosphate → ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase) → carbamoyl aspartate → ring closure (dihydroorotase) → dihydroorotate → dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH, mitochondrial, only mitochondrial enzyme in the pyrimidine pathway) → orotate → OPRT (orotate phosphoribosyltransferase) → OMP → OMP decarboxylase → UMP; from UMP: UMP → UDP → UTP → CTP (by CTP synthetase, adds NH2 from glutamine); first three steps (CPS II, ATCase, DHOase) are activities of a single trifunctional protein CAD
Thymidylate synthase (converts dUMP to dTMP in salvage, separate from de novo synthesis)
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (OPRT) — downstream step, not the first
explanation: De novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway: CPS II (cytoplasm, Gln, HCO3-, 2ATP → carbamoyl-P): rate-limiting. ATCase (aspartate transcarbamoylase): carbamoyl-P + Asp → carbamoyl-Asp. Dihydroorotase: carbamoyl-Asp → dihydroorotate (ring closure). [DHODH (mitochondria)]: dihydroorotate → orotate (FAD-dependent oxidation). [Back to cytoplasm]: OPRT: orotate + PRPP → OMP + PPi. OMP decarboxylase: OMP → UMP. UMP kinases: UMP → UDP → UTP. CTP synthetase: UTP + Gln → CTP. For DNA: UTP → dUDP → dUTP → dUMP (dUTPase); thymidylate synthase (TS): dUMP + CH2-THF → dTMP + DHF; DHFR: DHF → THF (target of methotrexate/trimethoprim). For RNA: UTP → CTP directly used. Regulation: CPS II activated by PRPP, ATP; inhibited by UMP (feedback). ATCase activated by ATP; inhibited by CTP (feedback). DHODH inhibitors: leflunomide/teriflunomide (active metabolite A771726) → ↓de novo pyrimidine synthesis → ↓activated lymphocyte proliferation → immunosuppression (RA, MS). Hereditary orotic aciduria: UMP synthase (UMPS, bifunctional enzyme with OPRT + OMP decarboxylase activities) deficiency → ↑orotic acid in urine; megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to B12/folate; treatment: uridine supplementation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis?
options: ATP (ATP is a SUBSTRATE and also an allosteric INHIBITOR at high concentrations)

AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP): AMP activates PFK-1 → signals low energy state (↓ATP/AMP ratio → need more ATP from glycolysis); F-2,6-BP is the most potent allosteric activator → synthesized by PFK-2 from F-6-P when insulin is high (fed state, PKA is inactive; glucagon/epinephrine → PKA → phosphorylates PFK-2 [bifunctional enzyme: PFK-2 kinase domain + FBPase-2 phosphatase domain] → ↑FBPase-2 domain activity → ↑degradation of F-2,6-BP → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis → promotes gluconeogenesis in liver); citrate is an INHIBITOR of PFK-1 (↑citrate in fed state → ↓glycolysis when TCA is overloaded); low pH inhibits PFK-1 (prevents runaway lactic acidosis)
Citrate (allosteric INHIBITOR of PFK-1, signals TCA cycle saturation)
High ATP (allosteric INHIBITOR at high concentrations, substrate at normal concentrations)
explanation: PFK-1 regulation (most important control point of glycolysis): Activators: ↑AMP, ↑ADP (low energy → need glycolysis). Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP): most potent activator; in liver, ↑insulin → dephosphorylated PFK-2 (kinase domain active) → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis. Inhibitors: ↑ATP (high energy, allosteric inhibition at regulatory site distinct from substrate site → sigmoidal kinetics with substrate F-6-P). Citrate (↑TCA intermediates → ↓glycolysis). Low pH (lactic acidosis → negative feedback). H+ ions. Glucagon action on liver: ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates PFK-2 → FBPase-2 domain active → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis; also phosphorylates pyruvate kinase → ↓glycolysis; promotes gluconeogenesis. Cancer: ↑PFK-1 activity → aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect); PFK-1 also regulated by phosphorylation (PKA, AMPK) and O-GlcNAcylation. The three irreversible glycolytic steps: hexokinase/glucokinase (step 1), PFK-1 (step 3), pyruvate kinase (step 10) → these are bypassed in gluconeogenesis by G6Pase, FBPase-1, PC+PEPCK.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) differs from hexokinase (I-III) in which key property relevant to the liver's role in glucose sensing?
options: Glucokinase has a lower Km for glucose (higher affinity) than hexokinase

Glucokinase has a high Km (~10 mM) and is NOT inhibited by its product G6P: hexokinase I-III (found in brain, muscle, RBCs): low Km (~0.1 mM, near-saturation at physiological glucose), inhibited by its product G6P (product inhibition), ubiquitously expressed, ensures glucose phosphorylation even at low blood glucose; glucokinase (Hex IV, GCK): high Km (~10 mM, not saturated at normal fasting blood glucose of 5 mM), NOT inhibited by G6P, sigmoidal kinetics (cooperative, Hill n ~1.7), high Vmax → acts as a glucose sensor (only phosphorylates glucose when portal glucose is HIGH → after a meal → responds proportionally to glucose concentration); expressed in: liver (glucose trapping after meal) and pancreatic β-cells (glucose sensing → trigger insulin release when blood glucose rises)
Glucokinase is found only in brain (critical for neuronal glucose uptake)
Glucokinase uses fructose-6-phosphate as substrate instead of glucose
explanation: Glucokinase (GCK) clinical relevance: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 2 (MODY2): heterozygous loss-of-function GCK mutations → ↑fasting blood glucose threshold (glucose setpoint for insulin release is higher) → mild, stable, non-progressive fasting hyperglycemia (usually 5.5-8.0 mmol/L); doesn't require treatment (no microvascular complications due to mild elevation); homozygous GCK mutation → permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus. GCK activators: new drug class (PF-04937319, dorzagliatin) → allosteric GCK activators → ↑glucose sensitivity of β-cells → ↑insulin secretion → ↓post-prandial glucose. Glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP) in liver: sequesters GCK in nucleus when glucose is low → fructose-6-P favors sequestration (blocks GCK); fructose-1-P (from fructose metabolism) dissociates GKRP from GCK → GCK enters cytoplasm → ↑glucose phosphorylation → that's why fructose ingestion lowers glucose. Diabetes: in T2DM, glucokinase expression in β-cells decreases → ↓glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycolysis produces a net gain of how many ATP molecules per molecule of glucose (anaerobic)?
options: 4 ATP (that is the GROSS ATP produced; the NET calculation requires subtracting investment)

2 ATP (net): investment phase (steps 1-5): HK uses 1 ATP (glucose → G6P); PFK-1 uses 1 ATP (F6P → F1,6BP) → total 2 ATP consumed; payoff phase (steps 6-10, x2 because 2 trioses): 2× substrate-level phosphorylation at PGK (3-PG → 1,3BPG → 3-PG: actually 1,3BPG + ADP → 3-PG + ATP; wait: 1,3-BPG → 3-PG by PGK: 1 ATP per triose × 2 = 2 ATP); 2× substrate-level phosphorylation at PK (PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP; 1 ATP × 2 = 2 ATP); also 2× NADH (at GAPDH step: G3P + NAD+ → 1,3-BPG + NADH; in aerobic conditions → 2 NADH → 5 ATP via ETC [malate-aspartate shuttle, 2.5 ATP each] or 3 ATP [glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, 1.5 ATP each]; in anaerobic conditions NADH oxidized by LDH [pyruvate → lactate] to regenerate NAD+); gross ATP in payoff phase = 4; net = 4 - 2 = 2 ATP
explanation: Energy yield from glucose oxidation (aerobic): Glycolysis: 2 ATP (net) + 2 NADH (cytoplasmic). PDC (2× per glucose): 2 NADH. TCA cycle (2× per glucose): 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP per acetyl-CoA × 2 = 6 NADH + 2 FADH2 + 2 GTP. ETC: NADH → 2.5 ATP (P/O ratio, old value: 3); FADH2 → 1.5 ATP (old value: 2). Total (modern estimates): Glycolysis: 2 (net ATP) + 2 NADH × 2.5 = 5; but cytoplasmic NADH must enter mitochondria (shuttle costs: malate-aspartate shuttle → no cost, 2.5 ATP; glycerol-3-P shuttle → 1.5 ATP). TCA inputs: 2 NADH from PDC × 2.5 = 5; 6 NADH from TCA × 2.5 = 15; 2 FADH2 × 1.5 = 3; 2 GTP = 2. Net total: ~30-32 ATP per glucose (modern estimates). Classic/old estimates: 36-38 ATP. RBC: no mitochondria → only 2 ATP from glycolysis → entirely anaerobic. Brain: mostly aerobic, highly dependent on glucose; hypoglycemia → coma. Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP): no ATP produced; produces NADPH + ribose-5-P; NADPH used for: reductive biosynthesis (FA synthesis, cholesterol), antioxidant (GPx reaction, thioredoxin reductase), NADPH oxidase (phagocytosis, ROS production).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which coagulation factor is deficient in classic hemophilia A?
options: Factor IX (Christmas factor) — that is hemophilia B

Factor VIII (antihemophilic factor, AHF): X-linked recessive (F8 gene, Xq28); hemophilia A is the most common severe inherited bleeding disorder (1 in 5,000 male births); deficiency → ↓intrinsic pathway (tenase complex: F IXa + F VIIIa + Ca2+ + phospholipid → activates FX → FXa) → ↓thrombin generation → ↓fibrin clot; clinical: hemarthroses (joint bleeds, knees > elbows > ankles, most characteristic), muscle hematomas, soft tissue bleeding, CNS bleeding, prolonged bleeding after trauma/surgery; rarely: mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, purpura) — those are platelet disorders; labs: ↑aPTT (measures intrinsic + common pathway), normal PT, normal bleeding time (platelet function is intact), ↓Factor VIII activity; treatment: Factor VIII concentrates (recombinant, e.g., octocog alfa), desmopressin (DDAVP — releases endogenous vWF + FVIII from Weibel-Palade bodies — for mild hemophilia A), emicizumab (bispecific antibody bridging FIXa + FX, mimics FVIIIa function, SC injection — now preferred prophylaxis)
Factor X (Stuart-Prower factor) — deficiency in some rare factor X disorders
Factor XI (PTA, hemophilia C, autosomal, milder)
explanation: Hemophilia types: Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency, X-linked recessive, 1:5,000 males, most common. Hemophilia B (Christmas disease): Factor IX deficiency, X-linked recessive, 1:25,000 males. Hemophilia C: Factor XI deficiency, autosomal (chromosome 4), Ashkenazi Jewish, variable bleeding, milder. Severity: Severe <1% factor activity (spontaneous bleeds), Moderate 1-5% (bleeds with minor trauma), Mild 5-40% (bleeds with significant trauma). aPTT prolonged in all (intrinsic pathway). Distinguish A from B: specific factor assays. vWD vs hemophilia: vWD also has ↑aPTT (due to ↓FVIII as vWF is FVIII carrier protein) + platelet-type bleeding (mucocutaneous) + ↑bleeding time → distinguish by vWF antigen, activity (ristocetin cofactor), FVIII. Inhibitors: ~30% of severe hemophilia A patients develop alloantibodies against FVIII after treatment → inhibitors (measured in Bethesda units) → bypass therapy: FEIBA (factor eight inhibitor bypass activity, contains FXa, FIIa, FVIIa, FIXa), recombinant FVIIa (NovoSeven), emicizumab.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Protein C and Protein S act as natural anticoagulants by:
options: Directly inhibiting thrombin (that is antithrombin III/heparin mechanism)

Inactivating activated Factor V (FVa) and Factor VIII (FVIIIa): thrombin-thrombomodulin (TM) complex on endothelial surfaces activates protein C (PC) → activated PC (APC) + protein S (PS, cofactor, also Vitamin K-dependent) → cleaves and inactivates FVa and FVIIIa → ↓amplification loops of coagulation (FVa is component of prothrombinase complex, FVIIIa is component of intrinsic tenase complex); this limits thrombin generation to the site of injury; Factor V Leiden mutation: FV Arg506Gln → APC cannot cleave FVa at Arg506 → APC resistance → ↑FVa activity → hypercoagulable state (most common inherited thrombophilia, autosomal dominant, 5% of European population are heterozygous, 20-40× ↑DVT risk in homozygotes)
Activating plasminogen to plasmin (that is tPA/urokinase mechanism — fibrinolysis)
Binding heparan sulfate on endothelium to activate antithrombin III
explanation: Natural anticoagulant pathways: (1) Antithrombin III (AT-III, now called AT): inhibits thrombin, FXa, FIXa, FXIa, FXIIa by forming covalent complex; heparin (unfractionated, UFH): binds AT-III → 1000× ↑rate of inactivation; LMWH: primarily ↑FXa inactivation. AT-III deficiency: hereditary thrombophilia; thrombus in unusual sites. (2) Protein C/S pathway (Vit K-dependent): APC + PS → inactivates FVa + FVIIIa (see above). Protein C deficiency: ↑DVT, PE; also warfarin-induced skin necrosis (protein C has short t½ → falls first when warfarin started before other Vit K factors → transient hypercoagulable state → thrombosis in skin vessels). Protein S deficiency: similar to protein C deficiency. (3) TFPI (tissue factor pathway inhibitor): inhibits FXa and TF-FVIIa complex → limits extrinsic pathway. (4) Prostacyclin (PGI2): inhibits platelet aggregation + vasodilation (from endothelium). (5) NO: vasodilation + ↓platelet aggregation. Hypercoagulable states (thrombophilias): Factor V Leiden (most common), Prothrombin G20210A (second most common), AT-III deficiency, Protein C deficiency, Protein S deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome (acquired).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which B vitamin acts as a single-carbon carrier in the form of tetrahydrofolate (THF)?
options: Cobalamin (B12) — carries methyl groups, is involved in folate recycling but THF is not B12

Folate (B9, folic acid): dietary folate → reduced to dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF) by DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase, NADPH-dependent); THF can carry single carbon units in various oxidation states: methyleneTHF (5,10-CH2-THF): thymidylate synthesis (TS: dUMP + 5,10-CH2-THF → dTMP + DHF), serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT: Ser + THF → Gly + 5,10-CH2-THF); methenyl-THF (5,10-CH=THF); formyl-THF (5-CHO-THF = leucovorin, 10-CHO-THF): de novo purine synthesis (formylation steps), histidine catabolism; methyl-THF (5-methyl-THF, N5-methylTHF): methionine synthesis (methionine synthase: homocysteine + 5-methyl-THF → methionine + THF; requires B12 as cofactor); methyltrap: B12 deficiency → 5-methyl-THF cannot donate methyl group → THF cannot be regenerated → ↑5-methyl-THF (trapped) → ↓active THF → ↓DNA synthesis → megaloblastic anemia (even with normal folate levels because trapped THF is not available)
Riboflavin (B2) — part of FAD/FMN, not a single-carbon carrier
explanation: Folate deficiency: ↓DNA synthesis (dTMP) → megaloblastic anemia (↑MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, pancytopenia); also ↑homocysteine (↑CVD risk + teratogenicity). Neural tube defects (NTDs): folate deficiency in peri-conceptional period → ↑risk of anencephaly, spina bifida → periconceptional folic acid supplementation (400-800 µg/day; 4 mg/day in women with prior NTD child) prevents 70% of NTDs. Methotrexate (MTX): DHFR inhibitor → ↓THF → ↓dTMP + ↓purines → ↓DNA synthesis → antiproliferative; rescue: leucovorin (5-formyl-THF) bypasses DHFR inhibition. Trimethoprim: DHFR inhibitor (bacterial DHFR >> human DHFR selectivity → antibacterial). Pyrimethamine: DHFR inhibitor (protozoal selectivity → malaria, toxoplasmosis). Megaloblastic anemia differential: B12 deficiency: neurological (subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord, demyelination of dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts + peripheral nerves; B12 deficiency → ↓methionine synthase → ↑homocysteine; ↓methylmalonyl-CoA mutase → ↑methylmalonate → neurological toxicity); folate deficiency: NO neurological symptoms. Lab: both: ↑MCV, ↑LDH, ↑bilirubin, ↓Hb, hypersegmented neutrophils; B12 deficiency also ↑MMA, ↑homocysteine; folate deficiency: ↑homocysteine only.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is essential for collagen synthesis because it is required for:
options: Glycosylation of procollagen in the Golgi apparatus (glycosylation happens in ER/Golgi by enzymatic reactions, not vitamin C)

Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen: collagen synthesis steps — (1) synthesis of procollagen α-chains on RER ribosomes → (2) signal peptide removed → into ER lumen → (3) hydroxylation of Pro (→ 4-hydroxyPro, by prolyl hydroxylase) and Lys (→ hydroxylysine, by lysyl hydroxylase) residues within Gly-X-Y repeat triplets (X is often Pro, Y is often HydroxyPro) → vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a COFACTOR for these hydroxylases (reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+ in the active site, keeping iron in the reduced form required for enzyme activity); (4) glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues (Gal-Glu); (5) triple helix formation (N-terminal propeptide); (6) secretion as procollagen; (7) extracellular: procollagen peptidases cleave N- and C-propeptides → tropocollagen; (8) lysyl oxidase (Cu2+ dependent) cross-links lysine/hydroxylysine residues between adjacent triple helices → pyridinoline/deoxypyridinoline cross-links → collagen fibrils; vitamin C deficiency (scurvy): ↓hydroxylation → unstable collagen (cannot form triple helix without hydroxyPro) → perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding, poor wound healing
Activation of lysyl oxidase (that enzyme requires Cu2+, not Vit C)
Assembly of collagen fibrils from tropocollagen (spontaneous, no Vit C needed)
explanation: Scurvy (Vitamin C deficiency): Vitamin C: L-ascorbic acid, water-soluble; obtained from fruits/vegetables (citrus, bell peppers, kiwi, strawberries, broccoli). Functions: (1) Collagen synthesis (prolyl + lysyl hydroxylases). (2) Antioxidant (reduces free radicals, regenerates Vit E). (3) Enhances non-heme iron absorption (reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ in gut lumen, acidic pH also helps). (4) Carnitine synthesis (β-hydroxylation of γ-butyrobetaine → carnitine, two hydroxylase steps requiring Vit C). (5) Dopamine-β-hydroxylase (Asp → DOPA → dopamine → NE; DBH requires Cu2+ + Vit C as cofactor → Vit C deficiency → ↓NE synthesis). (6) Amidation of peptide hormones (peptidylglycine α-amidating monooxygenase — requires Vit C, amidates C-terminus of peptide hormones: CCK, VIP, oxytocin, CRH). Scurvy features: perifollicular petechiae, corkscrew/swan-neck hairs, gingival bleeding + hyperplasia, poor wound healing, hemarthroses, periosteal hemorrhage in children (Fröhlich spots on X-ray — subperiosteal hematomas). Trümmerfeld zone and Frankel's line: metaphyseal changes in infantile scurvy. Diagnosis: plasma ascorbate or leukocyte vitamin C level. Treatment: ascorbic acid 300-1000 mg/day.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) is synthesized from 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin. Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting hydroxylation step in the production of the active form?
options: 25-hydroxylase in the liver (produces 25-OH D3, calcidiol — the storage form, not the active form)

1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) in the kidney proximal tubule: 25-OH D3 (from liver) → 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol, the most active form) by 1α-hydroxylase; 1α-hydroxylase is stimulated by: ↓Ca2+, ↓PO4-, ↑PTH (parathyroid hormone — the most potent stimulator: PTH → ↑cAMP in proximal tubule → ↑CYP27B1 expression), ↑FGF-23 (fibroblast growth factor 23 from osteocytes: ↑FGF-23 → ↓CYP27B1 + ↑CYP24A1 → ↓calcitriol [as in X-linked hypophosphatemia and tumor-induced osteomalacia]); 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1): inactivating enzyme, converts 25-OH D3 → 24,25-(OH)2 D3 (inactive) and 1,25-(OH)2-D3 → 1,24,25-(OH)3 D3 (inactive); CYP24A1 is induced by calcitriol itself (feedback limitation); CYP24A1 mutations: ↑calcitriol → ↑Ca2+ → idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia
24-hydroxylase in the kidney (that is the INACTIVATING enzyme)
Dihydrotachysterol conversion in the skin — no, that is a synthetic form
explanation: Vitamin D metabolism: Skin: UV-B (290-315 nm) → 7-dehydrocholesterol → (non-enzymatic, 290-320 nm photons) → pre-Vitamin D3 → heat → Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol); diet: D3 (animal) or D2 (ergocalciferol, plant/fungi). Liver: CYP27A1 or CYP2R1: D3 → 25-OH-D3 (calcidiol, storage form, t½ ~3 weeks) — not tightly regulated. Kidney (proximal tubule): CYP27B1 (1α-hydroxylase): 25-OH-D3 → 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol) — tightly regulated. Actions of calcitriol (via nuclear VDR, vitamin D receptor): ↑intestinal Ca2+ absorption (↑TRPV6 + calbindin-D9k), ↑intestinal PO4- absorption (↑NaPi-IIb), ↑renal Ca2+ reabsorption (↑TRPV5 in DCT), ↑bone resorption (↑osteoclast activity, paradoxically), ↑bone formation (↑osteocalcin, bone γ-carboxylation). Net: ↑serum Ca2+ and PO4-. Anti-inflammatory, antiproliferative effects (VDR on immune cells, epithelium). Vitamin D deficiency: rickets (children, ↑alkaline phosphatase, ↑PTH, ↓serum 25-OH D3, rachitic rosary, Harrison's groove, bow legs); osteomalacia (adults, ↑ALP, bone pain, pseudofractures). Vitamin D toxicity (hypervitaminosis D): ↑calcitriol → hypercalcemia → nephrocalcinosis, band keratopathy, ectopic calcification.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine is catalyzed by:
options: Tyrosinase (that is the melanin synthesis enzyme — tyrosine → DOPA)

Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH): phenylalanine + BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) + O2 → tyrosine + BH2 (dihydrobiopterin) + H2O; BH4 is regenerated by dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR) using NADH; PAH is expressed in liver (and small amounts in kidney and pancreas); phenylketonuria (PKU): AR deficiency of PAH → ↑phenylalanine in blood + tissues → ↑phenylpyruvate/phenylacetate/phenyllactate in urine (musty odor) → intellectual disability (phenylalanine competes with Trp, Tyr, other large neutral amino acids for transport across BBB → ↓neurotransmitters), fair skin and blue eyes (↓tyrosine → ↓melanin), eczema; maternal PKU (untreated mother): fetal exposure to ↑Phe → congenital heart disease, microcephaly, IUGR; treatment: Phe-restricted diet + large neutral amino acid supplementation; sapropterin (BH4) for PAH-responsive PKU (~25-50% of mild PKU)
Homogentisate oxidase (that is the enzyme deficient in alkaptonuria)
explanation: Phenylalanine catabolism pathway and disorders: Phe → Tyr (PAH, BH4): PKU. Tyr → DOPA → dopamine → NE → Epi (TH, AAAD, DBH, PNMT). Tyr → p-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (p-HPPA, TAT) → homogentisate (homogentisate oxidase, HGO) → maleylacetoacetate → fumarylacetoacetate (FAAH) → fumarate + acetoacetate. Disorders: PKU (PAH) → ↑Phe → urine phenylketones. Tyrosinemia type I (FAAH, fumarylacetoacetase) → ↑fumarylacetoacetate → hepatic failure, renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi), hepatocellular carcinoma risk; treatment: NTBC (nitisinone, 2-(2-nitro-4-trifluoromethylbenzoyl)-1,3-cyclohexanedione) → blocks p-HPPA dioxygenase → reduces toxic intermediates. Tyrosinemia type II (TAT) → skin and eye lesions. Alkaptonuria (HGO) → ↑homogentisic acid → urine darkens on standing, ochronosis (arthritis + dark deposits in sclerae, cartilage, connective tissue). Albinism (tyrosinase) → ↓melanin → hypopigmentation. BH4 deficiency (DHPR or GTP cyclohydrolase I) → hyperphenylalaninemia + ↓neurotransmitters (dopamine, serotonin) → profound neurological disease despite Phe-restricted diet → needs BH4 supplementation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) leucine, isoleucine, and valine are unique in that their first catabolic step occurs primarily in:
options: The liver (which is where most amino acid catabolism begins)

Skeletal muscle (and other peripheral tissues, NOT primarily the liver): BCAAs (Leu, Ile, Val) are unusual because the liver has very low BCAA aminotransferase activity and limited BCAA catabolism → BCAAs pass through the liver into the systemic circulation → taken up by skeletal muscle, brain, kidney, adipose tissue; in muscle: BCAT (branched-chain aminotransferase) → transamination of BCAAs → α-keto acids (KIV, KIC, KMV) + glutamate (donates nitrogen for alanine synthesis via ALT → alanine exported to liver [Cahill cycle]); BCKDH (branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, requires B1/lipoic acid/CoA/FAD/NAD, mitochondrial, rate-limiting for further BCAA oxidation) → inactivated by BCKDK (kinase, inhibits) + BCKDPHOSPHATASE (activates); MSUD: BCKDH deficiency → ↑BCAAs + ↑BCKAs in blood/urine → maple syrup odor + encephalopathy + ketoacidosis
Adipose tissue (adipose is not a major site of amino acid catabolism)
explanation: BCAA catabolism: L: purely ketogenic → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate. I: ketogenic + glucogenic → acetyl-CoA + propionyl-CoA (succinyl-CoA). V: purely glucogenic → succinyl-CoA. BCAA as muscle fuel: BCAAs can be oxidized for energy in muscle (especially during prolonged exercise and stress) → nitrogen exported as alanine/glutamine. In liver: ↑BCAA uptake after insulin-stimulated meals is minimal (liver lacks BCAT). BCAA supplements: marketed for muscle protein synthesis but evidence is mixed for healthy individuals. MSUD (maple syrup urine disease): BCKDH complex deficiency (BCKDHA/BCKDHB/DBT gene, E1α, E1β, E2) → ↑Leu, Ile, Val + BCKAs → neonatal encephalopathy, altered tone, apnea, poor feeding, seizures → death without treatment; maple syrup smell in urine (from sotolon formed from α-ketoisocaproate, KIC); treatment: BCAA-restricted diet + thiamine supplementation (some thiamine-responsive forms due to E1 component mutation → B1 supplementation reduces dietary restriction); HSCT in some; liver transplant (provides BCKDH). Neurological damage from leucine (most neurotoxic BCAA): ↑Leu → ↑neurotoxicity.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which RNA polymerase transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes) in eukaryotes?
options: RNA Polymerase I (Pol I) — transcribes large ribosomal RNA (rRNA): 28S, 18S, 5.8S

RNA Polymerase II (Pol II): transcribes all protein-coding mRNAs + most snRNAs + most microRNAs; largest of the three, ~12 subunits; requires general transcription factors (GTFs: TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIID [contains TBP + TAFs], TFIIE, TFIIF, TFIIH [with helicase activity for promoter melting + CDK7 for CTD phosphorylation]); preinitiation complex (PIC) assembles at promoter core (TATA box or Inr element); CTD (C-terminal domain) of Pol II largest subunit (RPB1): tandem heptad repeat (YSPTSPS × 52 in humans); phosphorylation of CTD Ser5 → transcription initiation + capping; phosphorylation of CTD Ser2 → transcription elongation + splicing; alpha-amanitin (amatoxin from Amanita phalloides death cap mushroom): inhibits Pol II (→ Pol III at higher concentrations) → lethal hepatotoxicity; Pol II also required for siRNA (processed from Pol II transcripts), lncRNAs, and enhancer RNAs (eRNAs)
RNA Polymerase III (Pol III) — transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNA U6, 7SL RNA
Primase — synthesizes RNA primers during DNA replication, not mRNA
explanation: Eukaryotic RNA polymerases: Pol I: nucleolus; rRNA (28S + 18S + 5.8S pre-rRNA, the major rRNA genes); insensitive to α-amanitin. Pol II: nucleus; mRNA + most ncRNA; highly sensitive to α-amanitin (IC50 ~0.02 µg/mL). Pol III: nucleus; tRNA + 5S rRNA + U6 snRNA + 7SL RNA + other small non-coding; sensitive to high α-amanitin (IC50 ~20-60 µg/mL). Mitochondrial RNA Pol (POLRMT): a phage-type single-subunit enzyme; transcribes mitochondrial genome → all 13 OXPHOS protein mRNAs + 22 mt-tRNAs + 2 mt-rRNAs. Promoter elements for Pol II: TATA box (~30 bp upstream), Inr (initiator at +1), BRE, DPE, MTE. Enhancers: distal regulatory elements (up to Mb away), loop with promoter via mediator/cohesin → ↑transcription. Pol II transcription cycle: assembly → initiation → promoter clearance → elongation (with pause sites, paused Pol II released by P-TEFb complex) → termination (cleavage/polyadenylation at poly-A site or Pol II read-through with torpedo mechanism).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During DNA replication, Okazaki fragments are formed on the lagging strand. Which enzyme removes the RNA primer?
options: DNA Pol III (prokaryotic enzyme that synthesizes, not removes primers)

RNase H + DNA Pol I (prokaryotes): RNase H degrades RNA in RNA:DNA hybrid; DNA Pol I 5'→3' exonuclease activity removes RNA primer while simultaneously synthesizing DNA to fill the gap (nick translation); in eukaryotes: the situation is more complex: flap endonuclease 1 (FEN-1) + RNase H1 → remove RNA primers; DNA Pol δ (with PCNA clamp) synthesizes replacement DNA; the flap structure (RNA primer displaced ahead of Pol δ) is cleaved by FEN-1 (endonuclease/5' exonuclease activity) → creates a nick → DNA ligase I seals the nick; also: Dna2 (helicase/nuclease) helps process longer flaps; in prokaryotes (E. coli): RNase HI + DNA Pol I (5'→3' exonuclease) → nick translation fills gap; DNA ligase (NAD+-dependent in E. coli, ATP-dependent in eukaryotes) seals final nick
Telomerase (extends telomeres, not involved in Okazaki fragments)
Topoisomerase II (relieves torsional stress ahead of replication fork)
explanation: DNA replication machinery (eukaryotic): Helicase: MCM2-7 complex (licensed by ORC→CDC6→CDT1→MCM; fired by DDK+CDK in S phase) → unwinds DNA → replication fork. SSB proteins: RPA (replication protein A) → stabilizes ssDNA. Primase: PriS/PriL (part of Pol α-primase complex) → synthesizes RNA primer (~8-12 nt). Pol α: adds ~20 nt DNA primer extension (initiates both strands). PCNA: sliding clamp (loaded by RFC, replication factor C) → tethers Pol δ/ε to DNA. Pol ε: leading strand synthesis (continuous). Pol δ: lagging strand synthesis (discontinuous Okazaki fragments, 200-400 nt in humans). Pol γ: mitochondrial DNA replication. RNase H1 + FEN-1 + DNA2 → primer removal. Ligase I → joins Okazaki fragments. Topoisomerase I (nicks one strand → relieves positive supercoiling ahead of fork; camptothecin/irinotecan inhibit topo I → DSBs → cancer cell death). Topoisomerase II (breaks both strands → relieves catenation; etoposide/doxorubicin inhibit topo II). Telomerase: TERT (reverse transcriptase) + TERC (RNA template); adds 5'-TTAGGG-3' repeats to lagging-strand ends → prevents chromosomal shortening; active in germ cells, stem cells, 85-90% of cancers; inhibited in somatic differentiated cells → Hayflick limit (~50 cell divisions).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Methylation of DNA at CpG islands in promoter regions leads to:
options: Transcriptional silencing (gene repression): DNA methylation at CpG dinucleotides (cytosine-5 methylation → 5-methylcytosine, 5mC) is a major epigenetic gene-silencing mechanism; performed by DNMT3A/DNMT3B (de novo methylation, establish new methyl marks) and DNMT1 (maintenance methylation, replicates methyl pattern on daughter strand after replication, recognizes hemi-methylated DNA); CpG islands: regions (~500-2000 bp) with high CpG density, usually unmethylated in active gene promoters (protected by TET enzymes [active demethylation: 5mC → 5hmC → 5fC → 5caC → C] and transcription factor binding); aberrant methylation of CpG island promoters → silencing of tumor suppressor genes (e.g., CDKN2A/p16 in many cancers, MLH1 in sporadic MSI-H CRC, BRCA1 in sporadic ovarian cancer, RB1 in retinoblastoma) → cancer; DNMT inhibitors (5-azacytidine/azacitidine, 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine/decitabine): cytidine analogs → incorporated into DNA → trap DNMT → hypomethylation → re-expression of silenced genes → used in MDS/AML
Translation inhibition without affecting mRNA stability
explanation: Epigenetics: Heritable changes in gene expression without DNA sequence change. DNA methylation: CpG methylation → gene silencing (heterochromatin). Histone modifications: Acetylation (HAT adds, HDAC removes) of H3/H4 Lys residues → euchromatin (active transcription) [HDAC inhibitors: vorinostat, romidepsin → cancer treatment]. Methylation of H3K4me3: active promoters. H3K27me3 (by PRC2/EZH2): repressive, Polycomb. H3K36me3: active gene bodies. H3K9me3 (by SUV39H): constitutive heterochromatin (pericentromeric). Phosphorylation of H3S10: mitosis. Ubiquitination of H2B-K120: active transcription. Chromatin remodeling: SWI/SNF (BAF complex): uses ATP to remodel nucleosomes → active transcription; loss-of-function mutations in ARID1A, SMARCA4 in many cancers. EZH2 gain-of-function: ↑H3K27me3 → silencing of tumor suppressors → follicular lymphoma, DLBCL → tazemetostat (EZH2 inhibitor). X-inactivation: one X chromosome is inactivated in females (lyonization) → XIST RNA coats inactive X → Polycomb-mediated H3K27 trimethylation + DNA methylation → condensed Barr body.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent venous thromboembolism (DVT and PE) and three pregnancy losses. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) is suspected. Which antibody is NOT part of the diagnostic criteria for APS?
options: Anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies (medium-to-high titer IgG or IgM) — part of criteria

Anti-histone antibodies: these are associated with drug-induced lupus (e.g., from procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, methyldopa, chlorpromazine) and NOT part of the Sapporo/Sydney criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) diagnosis; APS diagnostic criteria include: (1) lupus anticoagulant (LA, prolonged aPTT that does NOT correct with 1:1 mixing with normal plasma [inhibitor pattern] and DOES correct with excess phospholipid [phospholipid-dependent inhibitor] → detected by DRVVT, SCT, KCT tests); (2) anticardiolipin antibodies (aCL, IgG or IgM, medium-to-high titer ≥40 GPL/MPL or >99th percentile); (3) anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies (IgG or IgM, >99th percentile); all must be positive on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart to confirm
Anticardiolipin antibodies (medium-to-high titer IgG or IgM) — part of criteria
Lupus anticoagulant (prolonged aPTT not corrected by mixing, corrected by phospholipid) — part of criteria
explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS): Acquired autoimmune thrombophilia. Pathophysiology: antiphospholipid antibodies bind phospholipid-binding proteins (especially β2-GPI) → activate endothelium and platelets → ↑thrombosis; also directly inhibit phospholipid-dependent anticoagulants (Protein C, AT-III). Clinical features: Arterial thrombosis (stroke, TIA, MI), venous thrombosis (DVT, PE, Budd-Chiari), obstetric morbidity (recurrent pregnancy loss, pre-eclampsia, IUGR, premature delivery), thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis, Sneddon syndrome. Catastrophic APS (CAPS): ≥3 organs in <1 week → multiorgan failure (>50% mortality). LA paradox: lupus anticoagulant prolongs aPTT IN VITRO (because antibodies compete with coagulation factors for phospholipid surface in the test) but causes HYPERCOAGULABLE state IN VIVO. Treatment: anticoagulation (warfarin, target INR 2-3 for VTE; 3-4 for recurrent arterial events; LMWH during pregnancy); hydroxychloroquine for SLE-associated APS. Note: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are not recommended in triple-positive APS (LA+ aCL+ anti-β2GPI+) due to higher thrombosis risk vs. warfarin.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The main function of surfactant in lung alveoli is to:
options: Transport oxygen from the alveolus to the bloodstream

Reduce surface tension at the air-liquid interface: surfactant (pulmonary surfactant) is a lipoprotein complex synthesized by Type II pneumocytes → secreted into the alveolar surface liquid; composition: ~90% lipids (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, DPPC, the main surface-tension-lowering component, ~40%), other phospholipids (~40%), neutral lipids (cholesterol ~5-10%); ~10% proteins (SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D); function: DPPC adsorbs to the air-water interface → disrupts hydrogen bonds between water molecules → ↓surface tension (Laplace law: P = 2T/r, smaller alveoli have higher inward pressure → tend to collapse into larger alveoli without surfactant; surfactant ↓T proportionally MORE in smaller alveoli [because molecules are more concentrated when radius is smaller] → equalizes pressure across different alveolar sizes → prevents atelectasis); SP-B and SP-C: hydrophobic, help DPPC spread rapidly; SP-A and SP-D (collectins): immune functions (opsonization of pathogens); surfactant deficiency: premature neonates (synthesis begins ~24 weeks, adequate by ~34-35 weeks) → RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) → ↑work of breathing, ↑O2 requirement, diffuse atelectasis (ground-glass opacity on CXR); treatment: antenatal corticosteroids (↑surfactant synthesis by ↑SP mRNAs + ↑type II cell maturation) + exogenous surfactant (beractant, poractant alfa, calfactant)
Facilitate the immune clearance of pathogens via complement activation
Provide structural support to the alveolar wall (that is elastin and collagen)
explanation: Surfactant synthesis and maturation: Type II pneumocytes: synthesize surfactant → stored in lamellar bodies → secreted by exocytosis → unraveled as tubular myelin → monolayer at air-water interface. Stimulated by: corticosteroids (primary), thyroid hormones (synergistic with glucocorticoids in fetal lung maturation), prolactin, cyclic AMP, β-adrenergic agonists. Inhibited by: insulin (delays maturation, explains why infants of diabetic mothers have higher RDS risk despite being large for gestational age). Fetal lung maturity assessment: lecithin:sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio in amniotic fluid → ≥2 = mature (lecithin = primarily DPPC, increases with maturity; sphingomyelin remains constant → ratio rises as lecithin ↑). Phosphatidylglycerol (PG): appears at ~35 weeks, presence = further confirmation of maturity. Lamellar body count (LBC) in amniotic fluid: ≥50,000/µL = mature. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone IM): ↑L:S ratio, ↑PG, ↑SP mRNA, ↑lamellar body formation → ↓RDS severity; recommended at 24-34 weeks for threatened preterm delivery (and 34-36+6 weeks per ALPS trial).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Myoglobin is the oxygen-storing protein in muscle. How does its oxygen affinity compare to hemoglobin?
options: Myoglobin has lower O2 affinity than hemoglobin (wrong direction)

Myoglobin has HIGHER O2 affinity than hemoglobin and shows hyperbolic (not sigmoidal) O2 dissociation curve: myoglobin (Mb): single polypeptide (monomer), one heme group, NO cooperativity → hyperbolic O2-saturation curve; Km for O2 (P50) ~1-2 mmHg → near-saturated even at low O2 tensions → Mb HOLDS O2 until muscle O2 tension falls very low (during intense exercise) → releases O2 to the mitochondria; hemoglobin (Hb): tetramer (α2β2), 4 heme groups, positive cooperativity (T→R state shift as O2 binds successively) → sigmoidal curve; Hb P50 ~26-27 mmHg → loads in lungs (PO2 ~100 mmHg, ~97% saturated) and UNLOADS in tissue (PO2 ~40 mmHg, ~75% saturated, releases ~22%); Mb stores O2 in muscle → buffers against O2 fluctuations during exercise; after rhabdomyolysis, myoglobin released into plasma → filtered by kidney → myoglobinuria → proximal tubular necrosis (AKI, from direct toxicity + cast formation in acidic urine)
Myoglobin has the same P50 as adult hemoglobin (HbA)
Myoglobin shows allosteric modulation by 2,3-BPG similar to hemoglobin
explanation: O2 binding comparison: Mb: monomer, no cooperativity, hyperbolic curve, P50 ~1-2 mmHg. HbA (adult): tetramer, cooperative, sigmoidal, P50 ~26-27 mmHg. HbF (fetal): tetramer, sigmoidal, P50 ~20 mmHg (lower than HbA, higher O2 affinity → facilitates O2 transfer from maternal to fetal blood across placenta; γ-chains replace β-chains in HbF; γ-chains have ↓affinity for 2,3-BPG → ↑O2 affinity). HbS (sickle): HbA with Val6 (Glu→Val, β-chain) → deoxyHbS polymerizes into fibers → sickle-shaped cells → hemolysis + vaso-occlusion. Factors shifting ODC (O2-dissociation curve): Right shift (↓O2 affinity, unloads more O2 in tissues): ↑CO2 (Bohr effect), ↑[H+] (acidosis), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG (binds β-chains of deoxyHb → stabilizes T-state). Left shift (↑O2 affinity, loads more in lungs but unloads less in tissue): ↓CO2, ↓[H+] (alkalosis), ↓temperature, ↓2,3-BPG, HbF, CO poisoning (carboxyhemoglobin also shifts ODC left for remaining O2 binding sites), methemoglobin.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the electron transport chain, which complex is inhibited by cyanide and carbon monoxide?
options: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): inhibited by rotenone, amytal, MPTP

Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): cyanide (CN-) and carbon monoxide (CO) both inhibit Complex IV by binding to the Fe in the heme a3-CuB binuclear center (the oxygen-binding/reduction site); cyanide binds to Fe3+ (Fe3+-CN) → irreversible inhibition; CO binds to Fe2+ (similar to O2 binding at heme a3) → competitive inhibition (reversed by high O2); both → prevent O2 reduction to H2O → ETC completely blocked → NADH + FADH2 cannot be reoxidized → no proton pumping → no ATP synthesis → cellular hypoxia (histotoxic/cytotoxic hypoxia: cells cannot use O2 even if O2 is available); treatment of cyanide poisoning: nitrites (amyl nitrite inhaled + sodium nitrite IV → methemoglobin formation: Fe3+ heme in methHb competes with cytochrome c oxidase for CN- → shifts CN- from ETC to methHb → buys time) + sodium thiosulfate (provides sulfur → rhodanese [thiosulfate:cyanide sulfurtransferase] → SCN- thiocyanate, less toxic) + hydroxocobalamin (B12a: CN- + hydroxocobalamin → cyanocobalamin → excreted in urine)
Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase): inhibited by malonate
Complex III (bc1 complex, ubiquinol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase): inhibited by antimycin A
explanation: ETC inhibitors and clinical relevance: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase, NADH-Q oxidoreductase): Inhibitors: rotenone (insecticide), barbiturates (amobarbital), MPTP (contaminant in synthetic heroin → parkinsonism by destroying dopaminergic neurons, which have high ETC demand). Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, SDH): Inhibitors: malonate, TTFA; SDH is also tumor suppressor (SDHB/C/D mutations → paraganglioma, pheochromocytoma). Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex): Inhibitors: antimycin A (binding to Qi site), myxothiazol, stigmatellin. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): Inhibitors: cyanide (binds Fe3+ of heme a3), CO (binds Fe2+), H2S, azide. ATP synthase (Complex V, F0F1-ATPase): Inhibitors: oligomycin (blocks F0 c-ring, prevents proton flow → ↓NADH oxidation since ETC stalled when ΔµH+ too high). Uncouplers (ETC continues but ATP not made; energy dissipated as heat): 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP, proton ionophore, used dangerously as weight-loss drug); thermogenin (UCP1 in brown fat: physiological uncoupling → heat generation for thermogenesis in newborns and cold-adapted adults). Ionophores: valinomycin (K+ ionophore → collapses membrane potential but not a proton carrier).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Collagen type I is the most abundant protein in the body. Which of the following is a unique structural feature of collagen?
options: Extensive α-helices stabilized by intramolecular disulfide bonds

Triple helix of left-handed polyproline-II (PPII) helices stabilized by Gly-X-Y repeats and hydroxyproline: collagen is characterized by a repeating tripeptide unit Gly-X-Y (where X = often Pro, Y = often 4-hydroxyPro or hydroxylysine); every third residue MUST be glycine (smallest amino acid) to fit into the interior of the triple helix (the triple helix center is too small for any other amino acid); each α-chain is a left-handed PPII-type helix (not a conventional α-helix) with ~3.3 residues/turn → three chains twist around each other as a right-handed superhelix (triple helix); 4-hydroxyproline (HydroxyPro): in the Y position, forms interstrand hydrogen bonds + water-mediated bridges → critical for triple helix stability → requires Vitamin C (prolyl hydroxylase needs Vit C to maintain Fe2+); hydroxylysine in the Y position: glycosylated → provides sites for cross-linking; intermolecular cross-links (pyridinoline, deoxypyridinoline) formed by lysyl oxidase (Cu2+-dependent) → tensile strength
β-sheet structure that forms a barrel-like channel in the membrane
Extensive Glu-Asp-Arg repeats that bind calcium for structural stability
explanation: Collagen types and diseases: Type I: skin, bone, tendon, cornea, blood vessels; Gly-Pro-HydroxyPro triplets. Type II: cartilage, vitreous humor. Type III: fetal skin, blood vessels, uterus; important in wound healing. Type IV: basement membranes; non-fibrillar (reticular network); Alport syndrome: Col4A3-5 mutations (X-linked, 80%) → hematuria, ESRD, sensorineural hearing loss, ocular abnormalities. Type VII: anchoring fibrils in BMZ of skin; epidermolysis bullosa acquisita + dystrophic EB (COLG7A1). Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS): heterogeneous group of connective tissue disorders; most common: classical (COL5A1/A2, Type V collagen), hypermobile (pathogenic variants in TNXB or other genes), vascular EDS (COL3A1, Type III collagen, most dangerous → arterial rupture). Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI): most common: Type I COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations (Type I collagen) → brittle bones, blue sclerae (Type I: mild, autosomal dominant; Type II: lethal perinatal; Type III: severe; Type IV: moderate). Menkes disease: ATP7A (Cu transporter) mutation → ↓Cu → ↓lysyl oxidase → defective collagen/elastin cross-linking → kinky hair, neurodegeneration, connective tissue laxity; X-linked.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the initial hydroxylation of cholesterol in steroidogenesis?
options: 17α-hydroxylase (CYP17A1) — acts later in the steroidogenic pathway, not the first step

CYP11A1 (cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme, P450scc): located in the inner mitochondrial membrane; catalyzes the rate-limiting step of steroidogenesis: cholesterol → pregnenolone by sequential hydroxylation at C22 and C20 then cleavage of the C20-22 bond → releases isocaproic aldehyde + pregnenolone; the enzyme requires: adrenodoxin (ferredoxin, Fe-S protein), adrenodoxin reductase (FAD-dependent, uses NADPH), molecular O2; pregnenolone is the common precursor of ALL steroid hormones → diffuses from mitochondria to ER (or back); StAR (steroidogenic acute regulatory protein): transports cholesterol from outer to inner mitochondrial membrane → rate-limiting step of ACUTE steroidogenesis (StAR synthesis increases within minutes of ACTH/LH stimulation) → mutations cause congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia (most severe form, excess cholesterol lipid droplets accumulate in steroidogenic cells, adrenal failure, XY sex reversal)
HSD3B (3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase) — converts pregnenolone to progesterone
Aromatase (CYP19A1) — converts androgens to estrogens, much later in pathway
explanation: Steroidogenesis pathway: Cholesterol → [CYP11A1/P450scc, mitochondria] → Pregnenolone → two branches: Δ5-pathway (via pregnenolone, DHEA) and Δ4-pathway (via progesterone). Key enzymes: HSD3B (3β-HSD): pregnenolone → progesterone; DHEA → androstenedione (Δ5→Δ4). CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase): in ER; 17α-hydroxylation: progesterone → 17OH-progesterone; 17,20-lyase: 17OH-progesterone → androstenedione. CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase): progesterone → DOC; 17OH-progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol (most common form of CAH, see below). CYP11B1 (11β-hydroxylase): 11-deoxycortisol → cortisol; DOC → corticosterone. CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase): corticosterone → 18-OH-corticosterone → aldosterone. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH): most common: CYP21A2 deficiency (21-hydroxylase) → ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone → ↑ACTH → adrenal hyperplasia → ↑17OH-progesterone + ↑androgens → virilization + salt-wasting crisis (in 75%); 2nd most common: CYP11B1 deficiency (11β-hydroxylase) → ↓cortisol + ↑DOC (mineralocorticoid effect → hypertension + hypokalemia) + ↑androgens → virilization. Diagnosis of CAH: ↑17OH-progesterone (AM, 3rd day neonatal screening).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Copper (Cu) is a cofactor for which of the following enzymes?
options: Carbonic anhydrase (that is a Zn2+-dependent enzyme)

Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV, Cu-A and Cu-B centers), lysyl oxidase (Cu2+, cross-links collagen/elastin), ceruloplasmin (ferroxidase activity, oxidizes Fe2+→Fe3+ for loading onto transferrin), dopamine β-hydroxylase (dopamine→NE), superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn-SOD, SOD1), tyrosinase (melanin synthesis), peptidylglycine α-amidating monooxygenase (PAM, bioactive peptide amidation): ALL of these require copper; Wilson disease (AR, ATP7B gene, Chromosome 13): Cu cannot be exported from hepatocytes or incorporated into ceruloplasmin → Cu accumulates in liver + brain + kidneys + cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings, Cu deposits in Descemet's membrane, seen in >95% of neurological Wilson's); presentation: liver disease (hepatitis, cirrhosis), neuropsychiatric (dysarthria, tremor, dyskinesia, personality change, psychosis), Kayser-Fleischer rings (green-brown at peripheral cornea); labs: ↓ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), ↑24h urine Cu (>100 µg/day), ↑liver Cu on biopsy; treatment: penicillamine (chelation) or trientine (chelation) + zinc (induces metallothionein → binds Cu in enterocytes)
Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) — zinc is not required; activated by ADP, inhibited by ATP/GTP
Pyruvate carboxylase — that is a Zn2+ + Mg2+ + biotin enzyme, not copper
explanation: Trace mineral cofactors: Zinc (Zn2+): carbonic anhydrase, alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), carboxypeptidase, thermolysin, matrix metalloproteinases, DNA polymerase (structural), zinc finger transcription factors (Sp1, steroid hormone receptors), superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn-SOD). Zn deficiency: acrodermatitis enteropathica (ZIP4 mutations → ↓Zn absorption: perioral/acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea), ↓taste (hypogeusia) and smell (hyposmia), poor wound healing, growth retardation, infertility. Selenium (Se): GPx (glutathione peroxidase, 4 selenocysteine-containing GPxs), thioredoxin reductase, iodothyronine deiodinases (T4→T3 + rT3→T2), selenoprotein P. Se deficiency: Keshan disease (dilated cardiomyopathy, endemic in Se-deficient areas of China), Kashin-Beck disease (osteoarthropathy), myopathy. Iron (Fe): hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes (Fe-heme), Fe-S clusters (Complex I, II, III), ribonucleotide reductase (Fe2+ diiron center), prolyl hydroxylase (requires Fe2+ + Vit C). Manganese (Mn): mitochondrial SOD (Mn-SOD/SOD2), glutamine synthetase, pyruvate carboxylase, arginase (urea cycle). Molybdenum (Mo): xanthine oxidase (purine catabolism → uric acid), sulfite oxidase, aldehyde oxidase.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is the nitrogen donor for both nitrogens in the urea molecule?
options: Glutamine (carries one nitrogen from tissue to liver, but is NOT the direct donor in urea cycle)

Aspartate provides one nitrogen; NH3 (from glutamate dehydrogenase) provides the other: in the urea cycle, the two nitrogen atoms in urea come from: (1) NH3 (free ammonium) from the mitochondria → enters as carbamoyl phosphate (CPS I: NH3 + HCO3- + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate, requires N-acetylglutamate [NAG] as allosteric activator); (2) Aspartate (in the cytoplasm) → argininosuccinate synthetase: citrulline + aspartate → argininosuccinate; then argininosuccinase: argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate (recovers the aspartate carbon skeleton as fumarate → TCA cycle); then arginase: arginine → urea + ornithine; so the two nitrogens in urea = one from NH3 (carbamoyl-P step) + one from aspartate; aspartate is the immediate nitrogen donor in the cytoplasmic portion
Glutamate provides both nitrogens directly to urea
Alanine provides both nitrogens via the alanine aminotransferase reaction
explanation: Urea cycle enzymes and locations: Mitochondria: (1) CPS I: NH3 + HCO3- + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate (requires NAG as obligate activator: arginine → NAG by NAGS; so ↑arginine → ↑NAGS → ↑NAG → ↑CPS I activation). (2) OTC (ornithine transcarbamoylase): carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline (citrulline transported to cytoplasm via ornithine-citrulline antiporter). Cytoplasm: (3) ASS (argininosuccinate synthetase): citrulline + aspartate + ATP → argininosuccinate. (4) ASL (argininosuccinase/argininosuccinate lyase): argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate. (5) Arginase I (liver): arginine → urea + ornithine (ornithine transported back to mitochondria). Clinical: OTC deficiency: most common urea cycle disorder, X-linked; males severely affected; ↑ammonium, ↑orotic acid (excess carbamoyl phosphate → enters pyrimidine pathway → orotic acid overproduction); ↓citrulline + ↓arginine in plasma; no orotic aciduria in CPS I deficiency or NAGS deficiency (unlike OTC). Treatment of acute hyperammonemia: stop protein, ↑glucose (dextrose) + sodium benzoate/phenylacetate (alternative nitrogen excretion: hippurate + phenylacetylglutamine) + dialysis if severe.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) deficiency causes accumulation of which compound in the urine?
options: Orotic acid (accumulates in OTC deficiency and CPS I deficiency, NOT ASL deficiency)

Argininosuccinic acid: ASL catalyzes argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate; ASL deficiency → argininosuccinate accumulates in blood and is excreted in urine (argininosuccinicaciduria); plasma argininosuccinate markedly elevated + ↑urine argininosuccinate; also: ↑ammonium (like all urea cycle disorders); clinical: neonatal-onset hyperammonemia + encephalopathy, OR later-onset (vomiting, growth retardation, trichorrhexis nodosa — brittle hair), hepatomegaly, hypertension; treatment: arginine supplementation (ASL deficiency → ↓arginine synthesis → arginine becomes essential) + nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate + sodium phenylacetate)
Citrulline (accumulates in citrullinemia from argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency, NOT ASL)
explanation: Urea cycle disorders — key metabolite elevations: OTC deficiency (X-linked): ↑NH3, ↑orotic acid (because excess carbamoyl-P flows into pyrimidine synthesis), ↓citrulline, ↑glutamine. CPS I deficiency (AR): ↑NH3, ↓citrulline, NO ↑orotic acid (orotic acid is elevated in OTC but not CPS I — important distinction). ASS deficiency (citrullinemia type I): ↑NH3, ↑↑citrulline (hallmark). ASL deficiency: ↑NH3, ↑↑argininosuccinate (hallmark), trichorrhexis nodosa. Arginase deficiency: ↑arginine (unlike other urea cycle disorders which cause ↑NH3 primarily), spastic diplegia/tetraplegia, intellectual disability, ↑serum arginine. Neonatal screening: NH3 (if elevated → reflex to amino acid panel), amino acid panel (↑citrulline → citrullinemia or ASL deficiency; ↑argininosuccinate → ASL deficiency; ↑arginine → arginase deficiency). HHH syndrome (ORC1 gene): ↑ornithine (↑mitochondrial ornithine antiporter deficiency → ornithine cannot enter mitochondria → ↓urea cycle → ↑NH3) + homocitrullinuria (carbamoyl-P transfers to lysine → homocitrulline in urine).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Vitamin A (retinol) is stored primarily in which cell type in the liver?
options: Kupffer cells (liver macrophages, phagocytic, not storage cells for Vitamin A)

Stellate cells (Ito cells, hepatic stellate cells, perisinusoidal cells): hepatic stellate cells store ~70-80% of total body retinol as retinyl esters in lipid droplets within the cytoplasm; when activated (e.g., in liver injury → fibrosis), stellate cells lose retinoid droplets, become activated myofibroblasts (express α-SMA), and produce collagen I/III → hepatic fibrosis; serum retinol-binding protein (RBP) + transthyretin (TTR) complex transports retinol from liver to peripheral tissues; retinoic acid (RA, active form): all-trans-RA and 9-cis-RA → nuclear receptors RAR (retinoic acid receptor) + RXR (retinoid X receptor) → gene regulation (cell differentiation, epithelial integrity, vision [11-cis-retinal + opsin → rhodopsin], immune function, spermatogenesis); 11-cis-retinal (in rod photoreceptors): light → all-trans-retinal → triggers nerve impulse (visual cycle); Vitamin A deficiency: most common preventable cause of blindness worldwide; xerophthalmia (dry eyes), Bitot's spots (foamy white patches on conjunctiva), keratomalacia (corneal ulceration → blindness), night blindness (↓rhodopsin), follicular hyperkeratosis, immunodeficiency; excess: teratogenic (isotretinoin/Vit A in pregnancy → cardiac, CNS, ear malformations)
Hepatocytes (synthesize retinol-binding protein but store minimal retinol)
explanation: Vitamin A: Forms: retinol (storage, transport), retinal (11-cis-retinal in photoreceptors; all-trans-retinal after light), retinoic acid (gene regulation, irreversible oxidation), retinyl esters (storage form: retinyl palmitate in hepatic stellate cells + enterocytes). Sources: preformed Vit A (retinol, retinyl esters) in animal products (liver, cod liver oil, egg yolk, dairy). Provitamin A carotenoids: β-carotene (plant foods: carrots, sweet potato, squash) → cleaved by β-carotene 15,15'-oxygenase → 2 retinal molecules. Visual cycle (rhodopsin): 11-cis-retinal + opsin → rhodopsin (rod cells); light → rhodopsin → photoactivation → all-trans-retinal + opsin (meta-II rhodopsin) → G protein (transducin, Gαt) → ↑cGMP phosphodiesterase → ↓cGMP → close cyclic nucleotide-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels → hyperpolarization → reduced glutamate release → bipolar cell signal. Recovery: all-trans-retinal → all-trans-retinol → transported to RPE → 11-cis-retinal (by RPE65 isomerase, requires retinylamine/Ret-NH2 for recycling in visual cycle) → back to rod cell. RPE65 mutations: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) + severe early-onset retinal dystrophy; voretigene neparvovec (AAV-RPE65 gene therapy, FDA 2017). Isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid): teratogen → iPledge REMS program; not a source of retinol.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which form of Vitamin E has the highest biological activity?
options: γ-tocopherol (most abundant in US diet but LOWER biological activity than α-tocopherol)

α-tocopherol: Vitamin E consists of tocopherols and tocotrienols (8 natural forms); α-tocopherol (RRR-α-tocopherol, natural form) has the highest biological activity (1 IU = 1 mg all-rac-α-tocopherol = 0.67 mg RRR-α-tocopherol); α-tocotrienol has ~30% of α-tocopherol activity; γ-tocopherol (most common in North American diet) has only ~10-15% of the activity of α-tocopherol; function: lipid-soluble antioxidant → scavenges peroxyl radicals in lipid membranes → prevents lipid peroxidation (chain-reaction terminator: RO• → α-tocopherol-OOH [radical quenched] → Vit C (ascorbate) regenerates α-tocopherol from the tocopheryl radical [Vit C → semidehydroascorbate + tocopherol]; also: inhibits platelet aggregation (non-antioxidant mechanism); clinical deficiency: rare in healthy adults, seen in: premature neonates (↓Vit E stores + ↑lipid peroxidation → hemolytic anemia + neurological), fat malabsorption (abetalipoproteinemia, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis) → ataxia (spinocerebellar degeneration), neuropathy, ↑hemolysis, retinopathy
explanation: Vitamin E absorption and transport: Fat-soluble, requires bile + pancreatic lipase for absorption (like all fat-soluble vitamins); transported in chylomicrons → liver → VLDL (alpha-tocopherol transfer protein, αTTP in liver, preferentially retains RRR-α-tocopherol → incorporates into VLDL → tissues); αTTP mutations: ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (AVED) → spinocerebellar ataxia mimicking Friedreich's ataxia, treatable with high-dose Vit E. Abetalipoproteinemia (AR, MTP microsomal triglyceride transfer protein mutation): cannot assemble chylomicrons/VLDL → ↓absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) → acanthocytosis (spiculated RBCs), steatorrhea, ataxia (↓Vit E), retinitis pigmentosa, ↓plasma cholesterol + ↓TG. Clinical uses of Vit E: premature infant RDS supplement; prevention of retinopathy of prematurity (high O2 → lipid peroxidation); no proven benefit for CVD (HOPE trial) or cancer prevention in most RCTs; potential benefit in NAFLD/NASH (PIVENS trial: Vit E 800 IU/day → ↑liver histology in non-diabetic NASH). Tocotrienols: more potent antioxidants in some contexts + additional anti-inflammatory effects; rice bran, palm oil.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which type of inhibitor INCREASES both the apparent Km and lowers the apparent Vmax?
