options: Mixed inhibitor (non-competitive when α = α'): mixed inhibition occurs when the inhibitor can bind both the free enzyme (affects Km, allosteric site) AND the enzyme-substrate complex (affects Vmax, ES site); if binding affinity for E and ES is equal (α = α'), it is called 'non-competitive' (a special case of mixed inhibition); effect: ↑apparent Km (αKm) + ↓apparent Vmax (Vmax/α'); on Lineweaver-Burk plot: lines intersect in the second quadrant (to the left of y-axis) — both slope and y-intercept change; unlike competitive inhibition (lines intersect AT y-axis) and uncompetitive inhibition (lines are parallel — both slope and y-intercept change by same factor); examples: heavy metal ions (Pb2+, Hg2+, Ag+ bind non-specifically to enzyme and ES complex), LY294002 (PI3K inhibitor)
Uncompetitive inhibitor (↓apparent Km AND ↓apparent Vmax — lines parallel on LB plot)
Irreversible inhibitor (destroys enzyme activity, not a kinetic type in the Michaelis-Menten framework)
explanation: Inhibition types summary: Competitive: Inhibitor binds E only. α↑, Vmax unchanged, K'm = αKm. LB plot: same y-intercept, different x-intercept. High [S] overcomes. Non-competitive (special case of mixed, α=α'): Inhibitor binds E and ES equally. Vmax↓ (Vmax/α), Km unchanged. LB plot: same x-intercept, different y-intercept (increased). Not overcome by high [S]. Uncompetitive: Inhibitor binds ES only (not free E). Both Km and Vmax decrease by same factor α' (apparent Km = Km/α', apparent Vmax = Vmax/α'). LB plot: parallel lines (same slope, different intercepts). High [S] makes it WORSE (more ES → more inhibitor binding). Clinically important: competitive inhibition seen with most drugs that are substrate analogs. Uncompetitive inhibition: Li+ (inhibits inositol monophosphatase — used in bipolar disorder; mechanism: Li+ accumulates in brain, preferentially inhibits enzyme-substrate complex → uncompetitive inhibition → depletes inositol → ↓phosphatidylinositol signaling → mood stabilization). Substrate inhibition: at very high [S], substrate can occupy both the catalytic site AND an allosteric site simultaneously → inhibition (some enzymes show this at supraphysiological [S]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which sphingolipid accumulates in Fabry disease?
options: Globotriaosylceramide (Gb3, GL-3, ceramide trihexoside): Fabry disease = α-galactosidase A (GLA gene, Xq22) deficiency → X-linked; GLA cleaves terminal galactose from Gb3 → deficiency → Gb3 accumulates in endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, cardiomyocytes, renal tubular cells, dorsal root ganglia neurons; clinical: pediatric/adolescent onset in males: acroparesthesias (burning pain, tingling in hands and feet; triggered by heat, exercise, fever, fatigue), angiokeratomas (red-purple punctate lesions on bathing trunk distribution: umbilicus to knees), hypohidrosis (↓sweating → heat intolerance), corneal verticillata (whorled corneal deposits, bilateral, detected by slit lamp, does NOT affect vision), posterior lenticular opacity (Fabry cataract); adult onset: progressive CKD (podocyte Gb3 deposits → proteinuria → ESRD), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (LV hypertrophy, outflow tract obstruction), stroke/TIA (small vessel disease); females: highly variable (due to X-inactivation); treatment: ERT: agalsidase alfa (0.2 mg/kg EOW) or agalsidase beta (1 mg/kg EOW); chaperone: migalastat (pharmacological chaperone for amenable GLA mutations → stabilizes misfolded enzyme → ↑lysosomal GLA activity); substrate reduction: lucerastat (ongoing trials)
explanation: Fabry disease diagnostic tips: Only X-linked lysosomal storage disease besides Danon disease (LAMP2, GSD IIb). Enzyme activity: plasma or leukocyte α-galactosidase A (↓in affected males; females can be normal if favorable lyonization → must test GLA gene). Biomarker: plasma lyso-Gb3 (elevated even in females with normal enzyme activity → best biomarker for disease activity and treatment response). Urine: Gb3 (globotriaosylceramide) and lyso-Gb3. Renal biopsy: podocyte inclusions (zebra bodies/myelin figures on EM), glomerular and tubular Gb3 deposits. ECG: short PR interval (accessory conduction + Gb3 deposits), LVH, various arrhythmias. Brain MRI: posterior circulation white matter lesions. Skin biopsy: angiokeratoma histology (dilated vessels in dermis) + lipid deposits in eccrine glands. Angiokeratomas (differential): Fabry (bathing trunk), angiokeratoma of Fordyce (scrotum/vulva, benign, no enzyme deficiency), angiokeratoma circumscriptum (solitary), Fucosidosis + Schindler disease + galactosialidosis (also have angiokeratomas in other enzyme deficiencies).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of de novo fatty acid synthesis in the cytoplasm is:
options: Fatty acid synthase (FAS/FASN): multi-domain protein, not the rate-limiting enzyme

Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1): catalyzes: acetyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP → malonyl-CoA + ADP + Pi; ACC1 is the committed step and rate-limiting enzyme of de novo fatty acid synthesis; regulation: allosteric: citrate activates (↑ATP + ↑NADPH in fed state → ↑citrate efflux from mitochondria → ↑cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA via ATP-citrate lyase → ↑citrate binds ACC1 → polymerization → activation); palmitoyl-CoA inhibits (product inhibition); covalent: insulin → PP2A → dephosphorylates ACC (ACTIVE form); glucagon/epi → PKA → phosphorylates ACC at Ser79 (INACTIVE); AMPK → phosphorylates ACC Ser79 (INACTIVE, same site as PKA → explains why AMPK activation mimics fasting/exercise → ↓FA synthesis + ↑FA oxidation via ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I inhibition); malonyl-CoA: not only substrate for FAS, but also inhibits CPT-I (prevents FA oxidation when synthesis is active — prevents futile cycle)
Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (catalyzes the REVERSE of ACC1, i.e., malonyl-CoA → acetyl-CoA)
ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, ACLY): converts cytoplasmic citrate → acetyl-CoA + OAA; upstream of ACC1
explanation: Fatty acid synthesis pathway: Source of carbons: glucose → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (in mitochondria) → cannot directly cross IMM → condensed with OAA (citrate synthase) → citrate → exported via citrate carrier → ATP-citrate lyase (ACL, ACLY): citrate + CoA + ATP → acetyl-CoA + OAA. NADPH source for FA synthesis: pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD → 6-PGD → 2 NADPH) + malic enzyme (malate + NADP+ → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH; malate from OAA via malate dehydrogenase in cytoplasm). Fatty acid synthase (FAS/FASN): 7 enzymatic activities in one multifunctional polypeptide (mammals): KS (ketoacyl-ACP synthase), AT (malonyl/acetyl transacylase), DH (dehydratase), ER (enoyl reductase), KR (ketoreductase), ACP (acyl carrier protein), TE (thioesterase); produces 1 palmitate (C16:0) from 1 acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH per cycle; each cycle adds 2 carbons; thioesterase releases palmitate. FAS overexpression: in many cancers (breast, prostate, ovarian) → target for anticancer drugs (TVB-2640, oral FAS inhibitor, in trials). FASN gene: chromosome 17q25, regulated by SREBP1 (insulin-driven transcription factor → ↑FA synthesis genes).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the orientation of newly synthesized DNA strands?
options: Both new strands synthesized 3'→5' following the template

DNA is always synthesized 5'→3': DNA polymerases add deoxyribonucleotides to the 3'-OH group of the growing chain (the nucleotide arriving carries 5'-triphosphate: the 3'-OH of the growing chain attacks the α-phosphate of the incoming dNTP → forms phosphodiester bond → releases PPi → PPi → 2 Pi by pyrophosphatase → drives reaction forward); since the template is read 3'→5', the new strand grows 5'→3'; problem at replication fork: one template strand runs 3'→5' in the direction of fork movement → leading strand synthesized continuously 5'→3' in the direction of replication (needs only ONE primer); the other template runs 5'→3' in the direction of fork movement → lagging strand must be synthesized in DISCONTINUOUS short segments (Okazaki fragments, 100-200 bp in eukaryotes, 1000-2000 bp in prokaryotes) each primed and synthesized 5'→3' but in the opposite direction to overall fork movement; each Okazaki fragment: primase + RNA primer + DNA Pol → when next fragment reaches it, RNA primer removed + gap filled + ligated
DNA synthesis proceeds 3'→5' on the lagging strand only
Both strands synthesized from the same template at the same time in the same direction
explanation: Key rules of DNA replication: Template: 3'→5'. New strand: 5'→3'. Energy: provided by hydrolysis of PPi from incoming dNTP. No de novo synthesis: DNA polymerases cannot start a chain; need an RNA primer (primase provides 3'-OH). Proof-reading: DNA Pol δ/ε (eukaryotes), DNA Pol III (prokaryotes) have 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading → ↓error rate to ~10-7. Processivity: PCNA clamp (eukaryotes) or β-clamp (prokaryotes) → DNA pol stays on template → copies thousands of bp without dissociating. Fidelity mechanisms: Watson-Crick base pairing selectivity (~10-5), induced-fit conformation change (~10-3), and 3'→5' proofreading (~10-2) → combined error rate ~10-9 to 10-10 per base pair per replication. Semi-conservative replication: demonstrated by Meselson-Stahl experiment (1958) — E. coli grown in 15N → shifted to 14N medium → density gradient ultracentrifugation → hybrid (intermediate density) 14N/15N bands after one round → demonstrated each parental strand serves as template. Bidirectional replication: eukaryotic chromosomes have multiple origins (autonomously replicating sequences, ARS) → replication bubbles merge → allows rapid duplication of large chromosomes.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Translation termination occurs when a stop codon enters the ribosomal A site. The eukaryotic release factor (eRF) involved is:
options: EF-G (translocase) in prokaryotes — responsible for translocation, not termination

eRF1 (eukaryotic release factor 1): recognizes all three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) in eukaryotes (omnipotent release factor — unlike prokaryotes where RF1 recognizes UAA/UAG and RF2 recognizes UAA/UGA); eRF1 enters the A site → mimics a tRNA structurally; eRF1 + eRF3 (GTPase): eRF3-GTP hydrolysis → conformational change → eRF1 catalyzes peptidyl-tRNA hydrolysis (via Asn-Ile-Lys motif → water + peptide bond of peptidyl-tRNA → releases completed polypeptide from the P-site tRNA); then ABCE1 (ABC-family ATPase) → ribosome splitting (subunit recycling) → 60S + 40S separate → ready for next round; in prokaryotes: RF1 (UAA/UAG) and RF2 (UAA/UGA) → RF3 (GTPase) facilitates RF1/RF2 release; RRF (ribosome recycling factor) + EF-G → disassemble ribosome
eIF4E (cap-binding protein — involved in translation initiation, not termination)
eEF2 (elongation factor 2 — translocates peptidyl-tRNA from A to P site, not for termination)
explanation: Translation: major steps: Initiation (eukaryotes): cap-binding (eIF4E) → eIF4F complex → 43S PIC (40S + eIF3 + Met-tRNAi + eIF2-GTP) → mRNA loading → scanning 5'→3' for AUG in Kozak context (A/GCC-AUG-G) → 60S joining (eIF5B-GTP hydrolysis) → 80S. Elongation: A-site delivery (eEF1A-GTP → aminoacyl-tRNA) → peptidyl transfer (peptide bond formation at PTC of 23S/28S rRNA — rRNA is the true enzyme/ribozyme) → translocation (eEF2-GTP, moves peptidyl-tRNA from A to P, deacylated tRNA from P to E site, mRNA advances 3 nt). Termination: stop codon in A site → eRF1 + eRF3 → polypeptide released → ABCE1 → ribosome recycling. Diseases of translation: Diphtheria: DT (diphtheria toxin) → ADP-ribosylates eEF2 at 'diphthamide' (modified His715) → inhibits translocation → stops protein synthesis → cell death (mainly cardiomyocytes + neurons). Ricin: A chain (rRNA N-glycosidase) → removes adenine from 28S rRNA → ↓ribosome function → cell death. Aminoglycosides (prokaryotic): bind 16S rRNA → ↑misreading → mistranslation + premature termination. Chloramphenicol: inhibits prokaryotic (and mitochondrial) peptidyl transferase (50S). Linezolid (oxazolidinone): inhibits 70S ribosome assembly + initiator Met-tRNA binding.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which metabolite is elevated in the blood during diabetic ketoacidosis that causes the anion gap to increase?
options: Lactate (elevated in lactic acidosis, not the primary cause of anion gap in DKA)

β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB) and acetoacetate: in DKA, both are negatively charged ketoacid anions at physiological pH (pKa ~3.8 for acetoacetate, ~4.7 for β-OHB → essentially fully deprotonated at pH 7.4) → accumulate in plasma → replace bicarbonate as an anion → ↑anion gap (AG = Na+ - Cl- - HCO3-; normally 8-12 mEq/L; in DKA → 20-35+ mEq/L); β-OHB:acetoacetate ratio is normally ~3:1, can rise to 10:1 in severe DKA (↑NADH from β-oxidation → ↑beta-OHB dehydrogenase: acetoacetate + NADH → β-OHB + NAD+); CRITICAL: nitroprusside test (urine ketones, Acetest tablet, Multistix) detects acetoacetate + acetone but NOT β-OHB → may underestimate ketosis severity; direct β-OHB measurement (blood, point-of-care device) is preferred; acetoacetate → acetone (non-enzymatic decarboxylation, volatile → fruity breath)
Acetone (volatile, excreted via lungs, does not contribute to anion gap)
Glucose (does not contribute to anion gap)
explanation: Anion gap (AG) acidosis causes (MUDPILES mnemonic): M = Methanol (→ formic acid, severe optic nerve toxicity), U = Uremia (organic anions retained in renal failure), D = DKA (β-OHB + acetoacetate), P = Propylene glycol (lactic acidosis + osmol gap), I = Isoniazid/Infection (sepsis, lactic acidosis), L = Lactic acidosis (type A: tissue hypoperfusion; type B: metformin, linezolid, thiamine deficiency, liver failure, malignancy), E = Ethylene glycol (→ glycolic acid + oxalic acid → oxalate nephropathy + ↑osmol gap), S = Salicylates (early: respiratory alkalosis from direct respiratory center stimulation; late: AG metabolic acidosis). Mixed AG acidosis with osmolal gap: think methanol + ethylene glycol + isopropanol (but isopropanol → acetone not an acid → osmol gap without anion gap). DKA vs HHS (Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State): DKA: ↑AG + ketones + acidosis + glucose usually 250-600; HHS: no/minimal ketones + osmolality >320 + glucose often >600, elderly T2DM; HHS mortality > DKA. Key labs in DKA monitoring: glucose, potassium (K+ shifts with insulin therapy → hypokalemia risk), pH, HCO3-, AG closure.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In β-oxidation of an odd-chain fatty acid, propionyl-CoA is ultimately converted to succinyl-CoA via which pathway?
options: Directly via carnitine palmitoyltransferase without further modification

Propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA (D) → methylmalonyl-CoA (L) → succinyl-CoA: three steps: (1) propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC, biotin-dependent): propionyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → D-methylmalonyl-CoA; (2) methylmalonyl-CoA racemase (epimerase): D-methylmalonyl-CoA → L-methylmalonyl-CoA; (3) methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12/cobalamin-dependent, adenosylcobalamin form): L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → enters TCA cycle → gluconeogenesis; thus ODD-chain fatty acids CAN contribute to net glucose synthesis (via succinyl-CoA → OAA → gluconeogenesis) — unlike even-chain fatty acids; propionate also from: intestinal bacteria, catabolism of isoleucine + valine + methionine + threonine
Propionyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle directly without conversion
explanation: Odd-chain fatty acid catabolism: Final product after β-oxidation of odd-chain FA: propionyl-CoA (3C) + multiple acetyl-CoA. Propionate from other sources: (1) Gut bacteria (propionate is a major short-chain FA [SCFA] produced by gut microbiome fermentation → absorbed → liver → propionyl-CoA). (2) Amino acids: Ile, Val, Met, Thr → propionyl-CoA in catabolism. (3) Cholesterol side chain. Biotin + Cobalamin(B12) link: PCC (propionyl-CoA carboxylase) needs biotin; methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs adenosylcobalamin (B12 cofactor — distinct from methylcobalamin used by methionine synthase). Clinical significance: propionyl-CoA accumulation (MMA or PA [propionic acidemia]) → inhibits CPS I (→ ↑NH3), inhibits PDC (→ ↑lactate), depletes carnitine (propionylcarnitine ester → urinary loss). Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency (MMA): B12-unresponsive (MUT gene mutations, enzyme defect) vs B12-responsive (cobalamin metabolism defects: cblA/cblB → defective synthesis of adenosylcobalamin; cblC/D → defective synthesis of BOTH adenosylcobalamin AND methylcobalamin → MMA + homocystinuria). Methylmalonic acid (MMA): measured in plasma/urine → elevated in MMA + B12 deficiency (elevated in B12 deficiency even before clinical symptoms → sensitive biomarker).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) is the enzyme responsible for:
options: Metabolizing methanol to formaldehyde (that is alcohol dehydrogenase/ADH, which metabolizes ethanol AND methanol)

Oxidizing acetaldehyde to acetic acid (acetate) in the mitochondria: ethanol metabolism: (1) Cytoplasm: ADH (alcohol dehydrogenase, zinc-dependent) or CYP2E1 (microsomal ethanol oxidizing system, MEOS, induced by chronic alcohol) → ethanol + NAD+ → acetaldehyde + NADH; (2) Mitochondria: ALDH2 (mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase 2) → acetaldehyde + NAD+ → acetate + NADH; acetate → acetyl-CoA (by acetyl-CoA synthetase in peripheral tissues); net: ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio from both steps → inhibits TCA cycle → impairs gluconeogenesis → fasting hypoglycemia (↑NADH → ↑reduction of OAA to malate → ↓OAA for PEPCK → ↓gluconeogenesis) → ↑FA synthesis (↑NADH + ↑acetyl-CoA) → fatty liver; ALDH2*2 (Glu504Lys, East Asian 'Asian flush' mutation, dominant negative): ↓↓ALDH2 activity → acetaldehyde accumulates → flushing + tachycardia + nausea after drinking → 'Asian glow/flush syndrome' (~36-40% of East Asians are carriers); disulfiram (Antabuse): ALDH2 inhibitor → same effect → aversion therapy for alcohol dependence
Converting glucose to sorbitol in the polyol pathway (that is aldose reductase)
Generating free radicals from xanthine oxidase in reperfusion injury
explanation: Ethanol metabolism and consequences: ADH Km for ethanol: low (~1 mM → saturated at even low BAC) → zero-order kinetics for ethanol elimination (~15 mg/dL/h). CYP2E1 (MEOS): higher Km (~10 mM) → operates when [ethanol] is higher (chronic drinkers have ↑CYP2E1) → generates ROS + NAPQI-like metabolites. Zero-order kinetics: rate independent of [ethanol] → ≈1 drink/hour eliminated (0.015% BAC/hour). ↑NADH/NAD+ consequences: (1) Inhibition of pyruvate → OAA (malate dehydrogenase: malate → OAA requires NAD+; with ↑NADH, reaction reversal → OAA → malate → ↓OAA for gluconeogenesis → ↓glucose → hypoglycemia especially in fasting). (2) ↑lactate (LDH: pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD+ → lactic acidosis). (3) ↑β-OHB (acetoacetate + NADH → β-OHB + NAD+ → ↑β-OHB:acetoacetate ratio → alcoholic ketoacidosis). (4) ↑VLDL secretion + ↑TG → fatty liver. ALDH2*2 allele: heterozygotes (ALDH2*1/*2): ~30% reduction in ALDH2 activity → flushing; homozygotes (*2/*2): ~99% reduction → very sensitive to acetaldehyde. Disulfiram mechanism: irreversibly inhibits ALDH2 by carbamoylating active-site Cys302 → acetaldehyde accumulates → ↑flushing, nausea, hypotension, tachycardia → negative reinforcement (aversion).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Reverse transcriptase (RT) in retroviruses synthesizes DNA from RNA. Which of the following properties is unique to reverse transcriptase?
options: It uses a single DNA strand as a template exclusively

It has both RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity AND RNase H activity: RT (also called RNA-directed DNA polymerase) performs two key enzymatic activities: (1) RNA-dependent DNA polymerase: uses genomic ssRNA as template → synthesizes cDNA (complementary DNA, first strand) → forms RNA:DNA hybrid; (2) RNase H (H for Hybrid): degrades the RNA strand of the RNA:DNA hybrid → leaves single-stranded cDNA; then (3) DNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity of RT: uses ssDNA as template → synthesizes the second DNA strand → dsDNA; finally: integrase (another viral enzyme) integrates the dsDNA (provirus) into host chromosomal DNA; RT lacks proofreading (3'→5' exonuclease) → error rate ~10-4 to 10-5 per bp per replication cycle → rapid mutation rate → viral diversity + drug resistance; used in molecular biology: AMV-RT (avian myeloblastosis virus) or MMLV-RT (Moloney murine leukemia virus) → reverse transcription of mRNA → cDNA for cloning/PCR (RT-PCR); HIV RT inhibitors: NRTIs (nucleoside RT inhibitors: zidovudine/AZT, emtricitabine, lamivudine, tenofovir → chain terminators) + NNRTIs (non-nucleoside RT inhibitors: efavirenz, nevirapine, rilpivirine → bind allosteric site of RT)
It can replicate DNA with higher fidelity than cellular DNA polymerase
It requires a double-stranded RNA template to initiate synthesis
explanation: HIV replication cycle: Attachment: gp120 + CD4 receptor → conformational change → gp120 + CCR5 (R5-tropic, macrophages) or CXCR4 (X4-tropic, T cells) co-receptor → gp41 fusion peptide → membrane fusion. Entry: viral core → cytoplasm. Reverse transcription: RT → RNA→DNA, RNase H, DNA→dsDNA. Nuclear import: pre-integration complex (PIC) through nuclear pore → unique among lentiviruses (can infect non-dividing cells). Integration: integrase → provirus (flanked by LTRs). Transcription/splicing: host RNA Pol II + viral Tat (enhances elongation via TAR RNA hairpin + P-TEFb recruitment). Translation: structural proteins (Gag: MA, CA, NC; Pol: PR, RT, IN; Env: gp160 → gp120 + gp41) + regulatory (Tat, Rev) + accessory proteins (Vif, Vpr, Vpu, Nef). Assembly: Gag + Pol → assembled at PM (or endosome). Budding: ESCRT machinery. Maturation: HIV protease (PR) cleaves Gag-Pol polyprotein → mature virion. Antiretroviral targets: Entry (maraviroc: CCR5 antagonist; ibalizumab: CD4 antibody); RT (NRTIs, NNRTIs); Integrase (INSTIs: dolutegravir, elvitegravir, bictegravir); Protease (PIs: darunavir, atazanavir); Maturation inhibitors (lenacapavir: capsid inhibitor, also entry/integration/uncoating stages).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Km value of an enzyme represents:
options: The maximum rate of the reaction

The substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of the maximum velocity (Vmax/2): Km (Michaelis constant) is defined as [S] at V = Vmax/2; mathematically from the Michaelis-Menten equation: V = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); when V = Vmax/2: Vmax/2 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) → Km + [S] = 2[S] → Km = [S]; Km reflects the AFFINITY of the enzyme for its substrate: LOW Km → HIGH affinity (enzyme is half-saturated at low [S]) → needs less substrate to reach Vmax/2; HIGH Km → LOW affinity → needs more substrate to reach Vmax/2; if k3 (kcat) >> k2 (forward rate of ES complex formation), then Km ≈ Kd (dissociation constant of ES complex) → Km ≈ true affinity; for most enzymes this approximation is reasonable but not exact (Km = [k-1 + k2]/k1, the full expression)
The equilibrium constant for the enzyme-substrate reaction
The affinity of the enzyme for its product
explanation: Michaelis-Menten kinetics: Rate equation: V = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). Assumptions: steady-state: d[ES]/dt = 0 → [E][S]k1 = [ES](k-1 + k2). Km derivation: Km = (k-1 + k2)/k1. Vmax = kcat × [Et] (total enzyme). kcat (turnover number): catalytic constant, number of substrate molecules converted per active site per unit time. kcat/Km (catalytic efficiency): second-order rate constant for the reaction of free enzyme with free substrate; best measure of enzyme efficiency; diffusion-controlled upper limit = 108-109 M-1s-1. Clinically relevant Km values: hexokinase: low Km (~0.1 mM) → near-saturated at physiological glucose → ensures glucose phosphorylation even at low concentrations. Glucokinase: high Km (~10 mM) → not saturated at physiological glucose → glucose sensor. LDH: low Km for pyruvate → favors lactate production in anaerobic conditions. Hemoglobin: not strictly a Km (cooperative) but P50 = 26-27 mmHg (partial pressure for 50% saturation) — analogous concept. Substrate Km determines specificity: if enzyme must choose between two substrates → binds the one with lower Km more tightly (under low [S] conditions).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the pentose phosphate pathway, the oxidative phase generates:
options: NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate: the oxidative phase (irreversible): (1) G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase): G6P + NADP+ → 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone + NADPH (rate-limiting, first step); (2) lactonase: 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone + H2O → 6-phosphogluconate; (3) 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6-PGD): 6-phosphogluconate + NADP+ → ribulose-5-P + CO2 + NADPH; total: 1 G6P + 2 NADP+ + H2O → ribulose-5-P + CO2 + 2 NADPH; ribulose-5-P → (non-oxidative phase) → ribose-5-P (for nucleotide synthesis) and/or glycolytic intermediates (F6P, G3P); NADPH uses: (a) reductive biosynthesis (FA synthesis via FAS: needs 14 NADPH/palmitate; cholesterol synthesis); (b) antioxidant (GSH peroxidase: GSH + H2O2 → GSSG + H2O; glutathione reductase: GSSG + NADPH → 2 GSH + NADP+); (c) NADPH oxidase (phagocyte ROS for killing); (d) cytochrome P450s (detoxification); (e) folate reduction (DHFR); (f) nitric oxide synthesis (NOS: arginine + O2 + NADPH → citrulline + NO• + NADP+)
Only ATP (no ATP generated in the pentose phosphate pathway — incorrect)
Acetyl-CoA (wrong pathway — that is from pyruvate dehydrogenase complex or citrate in cytoplasm)
explanation: Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) non-oxidative phase: interconverts sugar phosphates without NADPH production: transketolase (TPP-dependent, B1): 2-carbon transfer; transaldolase: 3-carbon transfer; produces F6P and G3P (can enter glycolysis) from excess ribose-5-P; also: xylulose-5-P, sedoheptulose-7-P, erythrose-4-P (precursor for aromatic amino acid synthesis). G6PD deficiency: most common enzyme deficiency of RBCs (X-linked recessive, Xq28); ↓NADPH → ↓GSH → RBCs cannot protect against oxidative damage → hemolytic anemia triggered by: oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin), fava beans (divicine + isouramil → oxidants), infections (most common trigger, generates ROS in activated phagocytes + RBCs); G6PD A- (African variant): milder (affects older RBCs, reticulocytes spared); G6PD Mediterranean: more severe (affects all RBCs). Labs during G6PD crisis: ↑LDH, ↑bilirubin (indirect), ↓haptoglobin, ↑reticulocytes, Heinz bodies (precipitated oxidized Hb), bite cells (macrophages bite out Heinz bodies leaving 'bite cells' on peripheral smear). Normal G6PD activity in crisis (↑reticulocytes have ↑G6PD → assay must be timed after resolution).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: ATP is produced at which steps of glycolysis by substrate-level phosphorylation?
options: Steps 1 and 3 (these are ATP-CONSUMING steps by hexokinase and PFK-1)

Steps 7 (phosphoglycerate kinase) and 10 (pyruvate kinase): substrate-level phosphorylation (SLP) = direct transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy phosphorylated substrate to ADP → ATP (without ETC or proton gradient); step 7: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) + ADP → 3-phosphoglycerate + ATP (by PGK, phosphoglycerate kinase; 1,3-BPG has a high-energy acyl-phosphate [mixed anhydride] bond at C1); step 10: phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) + ADP → pyruvate + ATP (by pyruvate kinase; PEP has a very high phosphoryl transfer potential due to the enol-keto tautomerism of pyruvate after phosphate release → very negative ΔG); 2 trioses from 1 glucose → 2× each step → 4 ATP produced (steps 7 × 2 + step 10 × 2); minus the 2 ATP consumed (steps 1 and 3) = net 2 ATP
Steps 1, 3, 7, and 10 (mixing investment and payoff phases)
explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation (SLP) — all reactions: Glycolysis: PGK (step 7): 1,3-BPG → 3-PG + ATP (2× per glucose). PK (step 10): PEP → pyruvate + ATP (2× per glucose). TCA cycle: succinyl-CoA synthetase (step 5): succinyl-CoA + GDP/ADP → succinate + GTP/ATP (1× per acetyl-CoA). Oxidative phosphorylation (OP): H+ gradient drives ATP synthase (complex V) → ATP from ADP + Pi; produces ~25-27 of the ~30-32 ATP from glucose oxidation. SLP vs OP: SLP does not require O2, proton gradient, or ETC → important in: anaerobic conditions (sole ATP source), cytoplasm (glycolysis SLP), hypoxic tumors. 1,3-BPG: also regulated by 2,3-BPG mutase → 2,3-BPG (allosteric Hb regulator); 2,3-BPG in RBCs: ↑1,3-BPG → ↑2,3-BPG (by 2,3-BPG mutase); 2,3-BPG phosphatase → 3-PG. 2,3-BPG bypasses PGK → no ATP production in this shunt (Rapoport-Luebering shunt, RBC-specific → allows O2 delivery regulation without metabolic energy cost).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Thymidylate synthase (TS) converts dUMP to dTMP. The folate cofactor it uses is:
options: N10-formylTHF (this is the folate used in de novo purine synthesis at 2 steps)

5,10-methyleneTHF (methylene-THF): TS reaction: dUMP + 5,10-CH2-THF → dTMP + DHF (dihydrofolate); the 5,10-methyleneTHF donates both a methyl group (carbon) AND two hydrogen atoms (a hydride) to the methylene group of dUMP → dTMP; this oxidizes the reduced 5,10-methyleneTHF → DHF (oxidized); DHF must be reduced back to THF by DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase, NADPH-dependent) → THF → SHMT (serine hydroxymethyltransferase, B6) or other reactions → replenish 5,10-methyleneTHF; importance: TS provides the ONLY de novo source of dTMP (thymidine, the thymine deoxyribonucleotide) → critical for DNA synthesis; therefore, TS is essential for cell proliferation; 5-FU (5-fluorouracil) → metabolized to FdUMP → FdUMP + 5,10-methyleneTHF forms a ternary covalent complex with TS → irreversibly inhibits TS → ↓dTMP → ↓DNA synthesis → anticancer (colorectal, breast, head & neck); leucovorin (folinic acid, 5-formylTHF) → stabilizes the FdUMP-TS complex → potentiates 5-FU effect
N5-methylTHF (this is the folate involved in methionine synthesis)
Methylcobalamin (this is the B12 cofactor for methionine synthase)
explanation: Thymidylate synthesis and anticancer drug targets: TS reaction: dUMP + CH2-THF → dTMP + DHF. DHFR: DHF + NADPH → THF (target of methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine). SHMT (serine hydroxymethyltransferase, B6): Ser + THF → Gly + CH2-THF (regenerates substrate for TS). Anti-cancer: 5-FU metabolism: 5-FU → FUMP (by OPRT) → FUDP → FUTP (incorporated into RNA → ↓RNA function) or FdUMP (by thymidine phosphorylase [TP] + ribonucleotide reductase). FdUMP: the active inhibitor of TS. Capecitabine (prodrug): oral 5-FU prodrug (5'-deoxy-5-fluorouridine activated by TP in tumors → higher tumor concentration than liver). Folinic acid (leucovorin) + 5-FU: standard regimen (FOLFOX, FOLFIRI) — leucovorin ↑CH2-THF → ↑ternary complex stability → ↑TS inhibition. Methotrexate (antifolate): ↓DHFR → ↓THF → ↓CH2-THF → ↓TS substrate → ↓dTMP → ↓DNA; also: ↓de novo purine synthesis (↓formyl-THF for formylation steps). MTX rescue with leucovorin: high-dose MTX (bypasses DHFR at high dose) → leucovorin 24h later → provides THF without needing DHFR → rescues normal cells (which actively divide) but not as effectively as cancer cells (which have accumulated even more MTX intracellularly as polyglutamates [FPGS]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the citric acid cycle, which step is directly catalyzed by a flavoenzyme (FAD-dependent)?
options: Isocitrate dehydrogenase (this is NAD+-dependent, produces NADH)

Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH, Complex II): SDH catalyzes: succinate + FAD → fumarate + FADH2; this is unique because: (1) SDH is the only TCA enzyme embedded in the INNER mitochondrial membrane (all other TCA enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix); (2) SDH is also Complex II of the ETC (electrons from FADH2 → CoQ/ubiquinone → Complex III → Cytochrome c → Complex IV); FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) is covalently attached to SDH subunit A (SDHA, via His) → cannot dissociate; inhibitors: malonate (competitive inhibitor of succinate → used to study TCA cycle in vitro); SDH mutations → tumor suppressor role (subunits SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2 are all tumor suppressors) → hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndrome (HPPS): SDHB/C/D → extra-adrenal paragangliomas, SDHB → aggressive malignant pheochromocytoma; also Carney syndrome, Cowden-like syndromes
α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (α-KGDH uses FAD in its E3 subunit, but also uses NAD+ as the terminal electron acceptor — so the net oxidized product is NADH, not FADH2)
Malate dehydrogenase (this is NAD+-dependent, produces NADH)
explanation: TCA cycle reactions and cofactors: (1) Citrate synthase: OAA + acetyl-CoA → citrate; regulated by ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA, citrate. (2) Aconitase: citrate ⇌ isocitrate; [Fe-S] cluster; inhibited by fluoroacetate (which forms fluorocitrate, 'suicide inhibitor'). (3) Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1/2): isocitrate + NAD(P)+ → α-KG + CO2 + NAD(P)H; rate-limiting for TCA; IDH1 (cytoplasm) + IDH2 (mitochondria) → gain-of-function mutations in R132 (IDH1) and R172/R140 (IDH2) → produce 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) → onco-metabolite → inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (TET2, KDM histone demethylases) → DNA/histone hypermethylation → blocked differentiation → cancer (AML, glioma, chondrosarcoma). (4) α-KG dehydrogenase complex (KGDH): α-KG + CoA + NAD+ → succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH; requires TPP (B1) + lipoic acid + CoA + FAD + NAD+ (same cofactors as PDC). (5) Succinyl-CoA synthetase: succinyl-CoA + GDP + Pi → succinate + GTP + CoA (SLP). (6) SDH (FAD, see above). (7) Fumarase (fumarate hydratase, FH): fumarate + H2O → malate; FH tumor suppressor (FH mutations → ↑fumarate → inhibits TET2/KDM → renal cell carcinoma, leiomyomata, HLRCC syndrome). (8) Malate dehydrogenase: malate + NAD+ → OAA + NADH.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Carnitine is essential for the transport of long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria. Its biosynthesis requires which two vitamins?
options: Thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3) — incorrect; these are not required for carnitine synthesis
Vitamin C and niacin (B3) — WRONG; niacin is not required
Vitamin C (ascorbate) and niacin (B3) — still wrong for niacin

Lysine and methionine as amino acid precursors, with Vitamin C (B vitamins B3 and B6 as cofactors): carnitine is synthesized from lysine (provides the carbon skeleton — ε-amino group of lysine residues in protein is trimethylated to trimethyllysine by SAM → released by proteolysis → trimethyllysine hydroxylase [Fe2+ + Vit C + α-KG + O2] → 3-OH-trimethyllysine → 3-OH-trimethyllysine aldolase [PLP, B6] → trimethylaminobutyraldehyde → trimethylaminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase [NAD+] → γ-butyrobetaine → γ-butyrobetaine hydroxylase [Fe2+ + Vit C, rate-limiting] → L-carnitine; key vitamins: Vitamin C (ascorbate) is required at TWO steps (the two hydroxylation steps); B6 (PLP) for the aldolase step; niacin (B3) for the NADH-producing dehydrogenase step; methionine contributes methyl groups via SAM; therefore: carnitine deficiency can occur in scurvy (Vit C deficiency) → explains weakness/fatigue of scurvy partially
explanation: Carnitine biosynthesis summary: Lysine → [methylation of ε-NH2 by SAM × 3] → trimethyllysine (protein-bound) → [proteolysis] → free trimethyllysine → [TML hydroxylase, Fe2+, α-KG, O2, Vit C] → 3-OH-TML → [TML aldolase, PLP/B6] → trimethylaminobutyraldehyde + glycine → [TMABA dehydrogenase, NAD+/NIACIN] → γ-butyrobetaine → [γ-BB hydroxylase, Fe2+, α-KG, O2, Vit C — RATE-LIMITING] → L-carnitine. Vitamins required: Vit C (2 hydroxylation steps), B6 (PLP, aldolase step), Niacin/B3 (NAD+ for dehydrogenase). Sources: endogenous synthesis + diet (mainly from meat/dairy). Primary systemic carnitine deficiency (OCTN2, SLC22A5 transporter): ↓uptake of carnitine into cells → ↑urinary carnitine loss → ↓intracellular carnitine → ↓LCFA transport → myopathy + cardiomyopathy + hypoketotic hypoglycemia; treatment: high-dose oral L-carnitine. Secondary carnitine deficiency: organic acidemias (acylcarnitine esters deplete free carnitine), renal tubular dysfunction (↑urinary loss), valproate (forms valproylcarnitine), pivampicillin (pivaloylcarnitine). Carnitine forms: free carnitine + acylcarnitines (used in newborn screening: acylcarnitine profiles diagnose FA oxidation disorders and organic acidemias).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The 'second messenger' that mediates effects of hormones that act via receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) is:
options: Phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3): RTKs (e.g., insulin receptor, EGFR, PDGFR, VEGFR) undergo autophosphorylation → recruit PI3K → PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 → PIP3 → recruits PDK1 + Akt → downstream signaling; PIP3 is the key lipid second messenger of RTK signaling; note: Ras (small G protein) is also recruited and activates MAPK pathway; unlike GPCRs that use cAMP or IP3/DAG, RTKs primarily signal via PIP3, Ras/MAPK, and downstream phosphorylation cascades
Cyclic AMP (cAMP) — second messenger for Gs-coupled GPCRs (glucagon, epinephrine β)
Inositol trisphosphate (IP3) — second messenger for Gq-coupled GPCRs (not RTKs)
Cyclic GMP (cGMP) — for NO, ANP, guanylyl cyclase-linked receptors
explanation: RTK signaling details: RTK activation: ligand binding → dimerization → autophosphorylation of Tyr residues in cytoplasmic domain → docking sites for SH2-domain proteins (GRB2, PI3K regulatory subunit p85, PLCγ, SHC, etc.). Downstream: MAPK pathway: GRB2 → SOS (GEF) → Ras-GTP → Raf → MEK → ERK → transcription. PI3K pathway: PI3K catalytic p110 → PIP3 → PDK1 + mTORC2 → Akt → mTOR, GSK-3β, FOXO. PLCγ pathway: PLCγ hydrolyzes PIP2 → IP3 + DAG (→ Ca2+ mobilization + PKC). JAK-STAT pathway: cytokine receptors (not RTKs but similar mechanism): Jak1/2/3 → phosphorylate STAT dimers → gene expression. RTK downregulation: ligand-induced internalization → ESCRT pathway → lysosomal degradation (reduces signaling). Mutations: activating: erbB2/HER2 amplification (breast cancer, targeted by trastuzumab/pertuzumab/T-DM1); EGFR mutations (NSCLC, exon 19del/L858R → sensitive to TKIs: erlotinib, gefitinib, osimertinib). Loss-of-function: no known RTK tumor suppressors (Ras pathway tumor suppressors = NF1 [RAS-GAP], PTEN [PIP3 phosphatase]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) are lysosomal storage diseases caused by defects in the catabolism of:
options: Sphingolipids (these are degraded by specific acid hydrolases; defects → sphingolipidoses like Gaucher, Tay-Sachs)
Glycogen (defects in glycogen metabolism → glycogen storage diseases, not MPS)

Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs, mucopolysaccharides): GAGs are long, unbranched polysaccharides composed of repeating disaccharide units with alternating uronic acid (glucuronic or iduronic) and amino sugar (N-acetylglucosamine or N-acetylgalactosamine) residues, many of which are sulfated; GAGs are attached to core proteins → proteoglycans (PGs); types of GAGs: heparan sulfate (HS), dermatan sulfate (DS), chondroitin sulfate (CS), keratan sulfate (KS), heparin, hyaluronic acid (HA, not sulfated); GAG degradation occurs in lysosomes by sequential removal of terminal sugars + sulfate groups by specific exohydrolases; deficiency of any one enzyme → accumulation of undegraded GAG → swelling of lysosomes → cell dysfunction; MPS are diagnosed by: urine spot test (dimethylmethylene blue / toluidine blue → metachromasia) + specific GAG identification (electrophoresis) + enzyme assay in leukocytes or fibroblasts
Fatty acids (these are catabolized in mitochondria by beta-oxidation; not a lysosomal process)
explanation: GAG structure: Repeating disaccharide: [uronic acid - amino sugar]n. HS/Heparin: GlcA or IdoA + GlcNAc/GlcNS (heparan sulfate). DS: IdoA + GalNAc (dermatan sulfate). CS: GlcA + GalNAc (chondroitin sulfate). KS: Gal + GlcNAc (keratan sulfate). HA: GlcA + GlcNAc, not sulfated, not attached to protein. GAG functions: structural support in ECM (aggrecan in cartilage: CS + KS; versican in blood vessels), perlecan (basement membrane), syndecan/glypican (cell surface), binding growth factors (FGF binds HS → required for FGF receptor signaling), anticoagulant (heparin binds AT-III). Clinical correlation: 'shark fin' deformity (broad, clumsy hands), odontoid hypoplasia (atlantoaxial instability → cord compression in Morquio), corneal clouding (GAG deposits in corneal stroma → common in MPS I, IV, VI, not II or III). Urine GAG pattern distinguishes MPS types: HS + DS: MPS I, II, VI. HS alone: MPS III (Sanfilippo). KS: MPS IV (Morquio). DS alone: MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy, pure DS). Both KS + CS: MPS IVA if using more sensitive tests. ERT: laronidase (MPS I), idursulfase (MPS II), elosulfase alfa (MPS IVA), galsulfase (MPS VI).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is found at every third position of the collagen triple helix?
options: Proline (found at the X position but not every third)
Hydroxyproline (found at the Y position but not every third — and not in plants)
Alanine (found in some repeats but not every third)

Glycine: the collagen triple helix has a repeating Gly-X-Y sequence where Gly (glycine) occupies every third position; this is essential because the three collagen chains are wound tightly around each other → only glycine (the smallest amino acid, with only a hydrogen atom as a side chain) can fit in the interior of the triple helix without steric clash; X is often proline, Y is often 4-hydroxyproline; the Gly-Pro-HyPro sequence maximizes triple helix stability; mutations that replace Gly with a bulkier amino acid (e.g., in osteogenesis imperfecta: Gly → Cys, Ser, Arg, Asp, Val, or Glu in type I collagen chains) → disrupt triple helix folding → unstable collagen → brittle bones
explanation: Collagen biosynthesis (detailed): Intracellular: (1) Ribosome (RER): translation of preprocollagen → signal peptide cleavage. (2) ER lumen: prolyl 4-hydroxylase (P4H, requires Fe2+, O2, α-KG, Vit C) → 4-Hyp; prolyl 3-hydroxylase → 3-Hyp. Lysyl hydroxylase (PLOD, requires Fe2+, O2, α-KG, Vit C) → 5-hydroxylysine. Glycosylation of hydroxylysine (galactosyltransferase + glucosyltransferase). (3) ER/Golgi: trimerization (disulfide bonds between C-propeptides initiate chain alignment → triple helix forms from C to N terminus, 'zipper' mechanism). (4) Packaging in Golgi → secretory vesicles. Extracellular: (5) Procollagen peptidases (BMP-1/tolloid family for C-propeptide, ADAMTS for N-propeptide) → tropocollagen. (6) Fibril assembly (spontaneous, nucleation-dependent). (7) Cross-linking: lysyl oxidase (LOX, requires Cu2+) → oxidizes lysine/hydroxylysine → allysine/hydroxyallysine → aldol condensation → Schiff base → pyridinoline (Pyr) + deoxypyridinoline (DPyr) cross-links. LOX inhibited by β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN) → lathyrism (connective tissue fragility in animals consuming sweet peas). Kyphoscoliosis EDS (classical-like EDS 2, TNXB or PLOD1 deficiency): ↓LH1 (lysyl hydroxylase) → ↓hydroxylysine → ↓cross-linking → fragile connective tissue.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which reagent is used to detect reducing sugars in urine (Benedict's/Fehling's test) — and which COMMON reducing sugar would be positive?
options: Glucose: reducing sugars contain a free anomeric carbon (aldehyde group in open-chain form or free hemiacetal) → can reduce Cu2+ (in Benedict's/Fehling's) or Ag+ (Tollens') solutions; glucose (aldose, free C1-OH in solution) is a reducing sugar → gives a positive Benedict's test (brick red/orange precipitate of Cu2O); also positive: galactose, fructose (ketose but has an adjacent hydroxyl → can tautomerize to an aldose form), lactose, maltose, arabinose, ribose; NON-reducing: sucrose (anomeric carbons linked to each other → no free aldehyde), trehalose; clinical: glucosuria: positive Clinitest (Benedict's) AND positive glucostrip (glucose oxidase, specific for glucose); galactosuria: positive Clinitest but NEGATIVE glucostrip (galactose oxidase not present) → suggests galactosemia; fructosuria: positive Clinitest but negative glucostrip; Clinitest tablet (modified Benedict's, copper sulfate based) detects any reducing sugar in urine
Sucrose (non-reducing sugar — anomeric carbons are linked → no free aldehyde → NEGATIVE)
Starch (polysaccharide — not a reducing sugar in the usual sense, and not in urine)
explanation: Urine sugar tests: Clinitest (tablet, copper reduction, non-enzymatic): detects ALL reducing sugars (glucose + galactose + fructose + pentoses + lactose + maltose). Glucostrip/Clinistix (glucose oxidase + peroxidase): SPECIFIC for glucose. Therefore: Positive Clinitest + Positive glucostrip → glycosuria (diabetes, renal glycosuria threshold ↓). Positive Clinitest + NEGATIVE glucostrip → non-glucose reducing sugar (galactose in galactosemia; fructose in fructosuria/hereditary fructose intolerance; pentosuria [xylulose, benign]; reducing substance from drugs). Galactosemia screening: positive Clinitest in neonate + jaundice + hepatomegaly + E. coli sepsis (galactose-1-phosphate inhibits immune function) → urgent test for GALT enzyme. Phenylketonuria: NOT detected by reducing sugar tests (phenylalanine is not a sugar). Reducing power: ability of a compound to donate electrons → oxidized → reduces Cu2+ → Cu1+ (Cu2O, red precipitate). Note: Clinitest is rarely used now; direct quantitative blood glucose + HbA1c are standard. Neonatal screening in India: glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency + PKU + CAH + MSUD + hypothyroidism are part of expanded newborn screening panels.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the context of hemoglobin function, what is the Bohr effect?
options: The binding of 2,3-BPG to the β-chain of hemoglobin causing a right shift of the ODC
The Hill coefficient of hemoglobin (n ≈ 2.8) indicating cooperative binding

The decrease in hemoglobin oxygen affinity (right shift of ODC) caused by increased CO2 and H+ (acidosis): in exercising or metabolically active tissues, CO2 is produced → dissolved CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3- (carbonic anhydrase) → ↑[H+] → ↑[CO2]; these factors decrease Hb oxygen affinity (shift ODC right → lower affinity → releases O2 to tissues at the same pO2); mechanism: H+ + imidazole of His146 β-chain (βHis146) + Val1 α-chain → forms salt bridges stabilizing the deoxy (T) state of Hb → ↑T-state stability → ↓R-state → ↓O2 affinity; CO2 also forms carbaminohemoglobin (CO2 + N-terminal amino groups of Hb chains → carbaminoHb) → also stabilizes T-state → further ↓O2 affinity; reverse Bohr effect: in lungs, CO2 exhaled → ↓pCO2 → ↓H+ → alkalosis → ↑O2 affinity → O2 loading onto Hb; in placenta: fetal HbF has higher O2 affinity (↓BPG binding) → maternal HbA transfers O2 to fetal HbF
The release of CO2 from hemoglobin when oxygen binds (reverse of the Bohr effect)
explanation: Allosteric effectors of hemoglobin: T-state (tense, deoxy, lower O2 affinity) stabilized by: H+ ions (Bohr effect: CO2 → H+), CO2 (carbaminoHb), 2,3-BPG (binds to central cavity between β-chains in T-state), Cl- ions, temperature ↑. R-state (relaxed, oxy, higher O2 affinity): stabilized by O2 binding. 2,3-BPG: synthesized in RBCs by 2,3-BPG mutase (from 1,3-BPG); increases at high altitude (days) → ↑2,3-BPG → right shift ODC → ↑O2 delivery to tissues; HbF has γ-chains instead of β → γ-chains have ↓affinity for 2,3-BPG (Ser143 vs His143 in β → cannot form same contacts with 2,3-BPG) → HbF binds O2 more tightly → facilitates maternal-to-fetal O2 transfer. ODC right shift (↓affinity): ↑CO2, ↑H+, ↑temp, ↑2,3-BPG, sickle Hb (polymer form). ODC left shift (↑affinity): ↓CO2, ↓H+, ↓temp, ↓2,3-BPG, HbF, CO poisoning (raises affinity for remaining binding sites by + Bohr effect), methemoglobin (Fe3+ → cannot bind O2, shifts remaining Fe2+ hemes to higher affinity). CO poisoning: left shift + ↓O2-carrying capacity → very dangerous (cannot adequately deliver O2 even at high pO2).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is deficient in classic galactosemia (Duarte variant has lower activity but is milder)?
options: Galactokinase (deficiency causes only benign galactosemia → cataracts without intellectual disability)
Galactose epimerase (UDP-galactose 4-epimerase/GALE deficiency — rarer, variable severity)
Phosphoglucomutase (not a galactosemia enzyme, this interconverts G1P and G6P)

Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT, enzyme III in the Leloir pathway): classic galactosemia: AR, GALT gene → galactose-1-phosphate (gal-1-P) accumulates (toxic) + galactose accumulates → reduced by aldose reductase → galactitol (accumulates in lens → cataracts); clinical: neonatal (after milk feeding starts): vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice (↑bilirubin), hepatomegaly, E. coli sepsis (gal-1-P inhibits immune function), hypoglycemia; if untreated → cirrhosis, intellectual disability, cataracts; long-term (even treated): premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) in females (~80%), neurological complications, speech difficulties; diagnosis: newborn screening → ↑total galactose (galactose + galactose-1-P) in blood; enzyme assay (GALT activity in RBCs); molecular (GALT gene sequencing); treatment: lactose/galactose-restricted diet (eliminate breast milk, soy formula); galactose cannot be entirely eliminated from diet (endogenous production from UDP-galactose in human cells)
explanation: Galactose metabolism (Leloir pathway): (1) Galactokinase (GALK): galactose + ATP → galactose-1-P (gal-1-P). (2) GALT (galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase): gal-1-P + UDP-glucose → glucose-1-P + UDP-galactose. (3) GALE (UDP-galactose 4-epimerase): UDP-galactose ⇌ UDP-glucose (interconversion). Disorders: GALK deficiency (benign galactosemia, type II): galactose → galactitol (aldose reductase) → cataracts only; no intellectual disability (gal-1-P does not accumulate); treatment: lactose restriction. GALT deficiency (classic galactosemia, type I): ↑gal-1-P → toxic to liver, brain, kidney, ovary; ↑galactose → ↑galactitol (cataracts); ↑galactonate (from galactose oxidation); treatment: lactose/galactose-free diet; cataracts can reverse but neurological/ovarian damage can be permanent. GALE deficiency (type III): may affect only RBCs (benign) or all tissues (severe form resembles classic galactosemia). Duarte variant: GALT activity ~25% of normal (N314D allele in cis with reduced expression alleles); milder phenotype; management controversial (some centers restrict diet, others do not). Newborn screening: measured by: (1) Beutler test (GALT activity in RBCs on dried blood spot) — can be false negative after blood transfusion; (2) Hill method (total galactose measurement).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with homocystinuria due to cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) deficiency is at highest risk for:
options: Ochronosis and arthritis (that is alkaptonuria from homogentisate oxidase deficiency)

Thromboembolic events (arterial and venous): CBS deficiency → ↓conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine → ↑homocysteine in blood and urine (homocystinuria); ↑Hcy → multiple vascular effects: (1) endothelial injury (Hcy is directly toxic to endothelium, promotes oxidative stress, inhibits endothelium-dependent vasodilation); (2) ↑platelet aggregation; (3) promotes thrombosis; (4) ↑LDL oxidation; clinical features: ectopia lentis (downward lens subluxation — classic, differentiates from Marfan syndrome where lens subluxation is upward), intellectual disability, marfanoid habitus (tall, thin, long limbs), osteoporosis; cardiovascular: MI, stroke, PE, DVT — major cause of morbidity and mortality (thrombosis is the most common cause of death); treatment: B6 (pyridoxine, cofactor of CBS; ~50% of patients are B6-responsive → high-dose B6 supplement + folate + B12 → ↓Hcy), betaine (B6-nonresponsive: methyl donor → Hcy → methionine via BHMT [betaine homocysteine methyltransferase]), methionine-restricted diet; aspirin for thromboprophylaxis
Acute attacks of abdominal pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms (acute intermittent porphyria)
Megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to B12 or folate (that is hereditary orotic aciduria)
explanation: Homocystinuria differential: CBS deficiency (most common form of homocystinuria): ↑Hcy, ↑methionine, ↓cysteine; Hcy accumulates → features above; B6 (PLP) is CBS cofactor. Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency: ↑Hcy, ↓methionine (cannot remethylate Hcy); neurological symptoms. Cobalamin metabolism defects (cblC, E, G): ↑Hcy + MMA (in cblC, D) or just ↑Hcy (cblE, G); treat with B12. Mild hyperhomocysteinemia (common polymorphism MTHFR C677T → ↓enzyme activity → ↑Hcy moderately → ↑CVD risk; treat with folate). Homocysteine metabolism: Transsulfuration: Hcy + serine → [CBS, B6] → cystathionine → [cystathionine γ-lyase, B6] → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate + NH3. Remethylation: Hcy + 5-methyl-THF → [methionine synthase, B12] → methionine; or Hcy + betaine → [BHMT, liver/kidney] → methionine + dimethylglycine. Lens subluxation: CBS deficiency = DOWNWARD (ectopia lentis inferior or down-and-in); Marfan syndrome = UPWARD (ectopia lentis superior). Marfan (FBN1, fibrillin-1 mutations): lens dislocation upward, aortic root dilation (not caused by ↑Hcy but by structural FBN1/TGF-β pathway defects), tall stature, long fingers (arachnodactyly), high arched palate, AR/mitral valve prolapse.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme that synthesizes hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan, HA) differs from other GAG synthesis enzymes in that:
options: It is located in the Golgi apparatus (most GAG synthesis occurs in Golgi, but HA synthesis is different)
It requires PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate) as a sulfate donor (HA is not sulfated)
It transfers sugar residues from UDP-sugars to a core protein first (HA is synthesized without a core protein)

It synthesizes HA directly at the plasma membrane without a protein core and without sulfation: hyaluronan synthases (HAS1, HAS2, HAS3) are integral plasma membrane enzymes — they polymerize alternating UDP-GlcA and UDP-GlcNAc units directly at the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane and extrude the growing HA chain through the membrane into the extracellular space; HA is unique among GAGs: (1) synthesized at the cell surface, not in the Golgi; (2) NOT covalently attached to a protein core (not a proteoglycan chain); (3) NOT sulfated; (4) can be extremely large (MW up to 10 MDa, 25,000 disaccharide units); HA plays roles in: space-filling and hydration (cartilage matrix, vitreous humor, synovial fluid, umbilical cord Wharton's jelly), cell migration (wound healing, cancer metastasis), CD44 receptor signaling
explanation: Hyaluronic acid (HA): Sugar residues: alternating D-glucuronic acid (GlcA) + N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (GlcNAc). No sulfate groups. No core protein. Molecular weight: 400 kDa to 10 MDa. Structure: unbranched, random coil; occupies enormous volume relative to molecular weight (highly hydrated, holds ~1000× water relative to dry weight). Functions: Synovial fluid: HA (secreted by synoviocytes) provides viscoelasticity + lubrication (tribolubrication). Cartilage: HA backbone + aggrecan (via link protein) → bottle-brush proteoglycan aggregates → resist compression. Vitreous humor: HA + collagen II network. Skin dermis: HA + chondroitin sulfate/dermatan sulfate in ground substance. Cell signaling: CD44 (transmembrane HA receptor): ↑in cancer (cancer stem cells), promotes invasion/metastasis; RHAMM (receptor for HA-mediated motility). Catabolism: HA → hyaluronidase (in lysosomes + sperm: sperm hyaluronidase [PH-20/SPAM1] penetrates cumulus oophorus around egg) + β-glucuronidase + hexosaminidases. Clinical uses of HA: intra-articular injections (viscosupplementation, knee OA), ophthalmic (viscoelastic during cataract surgery), dermal fillers (cosmetic), wound care, drug delivery. PAPS: 3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate, the universal sulfate donor for sulfotransferases in GAG sulfation (NOT needed for HA). PAPS synthesis: ATP + SO4²⁻ → APS + PPi (ATP sulfurylase) → PAPS + ADP (APS kinase).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The active form of Vitamin D that regulates calcium absorption in the intestine is:
options: 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol, 1,25(OH)2D3): synthesized in the kidney by CYP27B1 (1α-hydroxylase) from 25-OH-D3; calcitriol is the most potent, biologically active form of Vitamin D; in intestinal enterocytes: calcitriol binds VDR (Vitamin D Receptor) → VDR + RXR forms heterodimer → binds VDREs (Vitamin D response elements) in DNA → ↑transcription of: TRPV6 (apical Ca2+ channel → Ca2+ entry into enterocyte), calbindin-D9k (intracellular Ca2+ shuttle), PMCA1b (basolateral Ca2+ pump → Ca2+ efflux to blood); net: ↑Ca2+ absorption from gut lumen into blood

25-hydroxycholecalciferol (calcidiol, 25-OH-D3): the storage form, produced in the liver; less active than calcitriol; measured in serum to assess Vitamin D status (most abundant circulating form; t½ ~3 weeks; normal: 30-100 ng/mL; deficiency: <20 ng/mL)
Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol): inactive precursor produced in skin, requires two hydroxylation steps
7-dehydrocholesterol: provitamin D (precursor in skin, not the active form)
explanation: Vitamin D physiology: Synthesis: 7-dehydrocholesterol → [UV-B, skin] → pre-D3 → [thermal isomerization] → D3 (cholecalciferol). Liver: D3 → [CYP27A1 or CYP2R1, 25-hydroxylase] → 25-OH-D3 (calcidiol, storage form, measured for Vit D status). Kidney proximal tubule: 25-OH-D3 → [CYP27B1/1α-hydroxylase, stimulated by PTH, ↓Ca2+, ↓PO4-] → 1,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol, active). FGF-23 (from osteocytes, ↑with ↑PO4-): ↓CYP27B1 + ↑CYP24A1 → ↓calcitriol + ↑inactivation; X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH, PHEX mutation → ↑FGF-23): ↓calcitriol → ↓phosphate absorption → rickets + short stature; treated with burosumab (anti-FGF-23 antibody). Serum 25-OH-D3 testing: best indicator of body vitamin D status (abundant, long t½, from multiple sources); 1,25(OH)2D3 not used for routine status (short t½, ↑with ↑PTH even in deficiency). Vitamin D deficiency: rickets (children: growth plate failure, craniotabes, rachitic rosary, bowing of legs) or osteomalacia (adults: bone pain, pseudofractures, ↓bone density, ↑ALP, ↓Ca, ↑PTH). Vitamin D toxicity (hypervitaminosis D): ↑25-OH-D3 (from oversupplementation) → granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB: activated macrophages express CYP27B1 → 1,25(OH)2D3 from 25-OH-D3 without PTH regulation) → hypercalcemia + hypercalciuria → nephrocalcinosis. Serum Ca normal in Vit D deficiency (PTH maintains normocalcemia) → late stage: ↓Ca.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) differs from nuclear DNA in which of the following ways?
options: mtDNA is linear with histone-wrapped chromatin structure (INCORRECT — nuclear DNA is linear and histone-wrapped)
mtDNA is replicated semi-conservatively just like nuclear DNA (semi-conservative replication is correct for both but the NEXT answer has a key unique feature)

mtDNA uses a different genetic code: unlike the universal nuclear genetic code, mtDNA uses a slightly modified genetic code: (1) UGA (stop codon in nuclear) = Trp in human mtDNA; (2) AGA and AGG (Arg in nuclear) = Stop codons in human mtDNA; (3) AUA (Ile in nuclear) = Met in human mtDNA; this is why mitochondrial protein synthesis can be selectively targeted by antibiotics (similar to bacterial ribosomes — mito ribosomes are 55S [28S + 39S], not 80S) → aminoglycosides, chloramphenicol, linezolid, tetracyclines affect mitochondrial protein synthesis; other unique features of mtDNA: circular, double-stranded (H strand and L strand); 16,569 bp; 37 genes (13 polypeptides of OXPHOS, 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs); lacks histones (associated with mitochondrial transcription factor A, TFAM instead); very few non-coding sequences; no introns; maternally inherited (paternal mitochondria destroyed in fertilized egg); heteroplasmy (mixture of mutant and wild-type mtDNA)
mtDNA is encoded entirely on the leading strand (incorrect)
explanation: mtDNA and mitochondrial genetics: Inheritance: maternal (sperm mitochondria are ubiquitinated and degraded by autophagosomes [mitophagy] after fertilization → leaky paternal mtDNA in rare cases; Leber hereditary optic neuropathy [LHON] is maternally inherited). Heteroplasmy: cells contain a mixture of mutant and wild-type mtDNA → phenotype depends on heteroplasmy level + threshold effect (most pathogenic mtDNA mutations must exceed 60-90% before clinical disease). Threshold effect: differs by tissue (tissues with high energy demand — brain, retina, muscle, heart — are most sensitive; cells with lowest threshold for disease). Bottleneck effect during oogenesis: rapid reduction of mtDNA copy number → random amplification → daughter cells have different heteroplasmy levels → explains variable clinical expression within families. mtDNA diseases: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy + lactic acidosis + stroke-like episodes): m.3243A>G (tRNA-Leu MT-TL1, most common); stroke-like episodes affect posterior cortex (occipital) disproportionately; ↑lactate (↓OXPHOS → anaerobic glycolysis). MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers): m.8344A>G (tRNA-Lys MT-TK). LHON (m.11778G>A in ND4/Complex I, m.3460G>A, m.14484T>C): bilateral painless optic neuropathy → central scotoma, young males; idebenone treatment. KSS (Kearns-Sayre: large deletions, >1kb of mtDNA); CPEO (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis + ophthalmoplegia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During starvation, the brain initially uses glucose but progressively shifts to using which alternative fuel?
options: Free fatty acids (FFAs cannot cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently — brain uses ketones instead)

Ketone bodies (acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate): during prolonged fasting (>3-4 days), hepatic ketogenesis increases dramatically (↑glucagon → ↑lipolysis → ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → overwhelmed TCA → HMG-CoA pathway → ↑acetoacetate + ↑β-OHB); the brain is initially glucose-obligate but adapts to use ketone bodies via ketolysis: β-OHB → [β-OHB dehydrogenase, NAD+] → acetoacetate → [succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (SCOT) — not in liver! only in extra-hepatic tissues] → acetoacetyl-CoA → [thiolase] → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA + ATP; after 4-7 days of fasting, ketone bodies provide ~60-70% of brain's energy; reduces glucose requirements → less muscle protein catabolism (↓gluconeogenic substrate from muscle)
Ethanol (not a fuel for the brain in physiological fasting)
Lactate (brain can use lactate but it must be converted to pyruvate and metabolic dependency is not like ketones)
explanation: Metabolic fuels in starvation: Hours: glucose (from glycogenolysis — liver glycogen depleted ~18-24h). Days: gluconeogenesis (liver + kidney) using amino acids (Ala, Gln from muscle), glycerol (from TG), lactate/pyruvate + ↑ketogenesis (β-OHB + AcAc) as alternative fuel. Weeks: ↑↑ketogenesis → ↑brain adaptation → ↓glucose utilization → ↓muscle protein catabolism → preservation of lean body mass → survival. Tissue fuel preferences: Brain: glucose primarily → ketone bodies in prolonged starvation. RBCs: OBLIGATE glycolytic (no mitochondria) → glucose ONLY. Cardiac muscle: preferentially uses FAs (70%) > lactate > glucose > ketones. Skeletal muscle at rest: FAs; during exercise: glucose/glycogen. Liver in fasting: gluconeogenesis + ketogenesis (NOT glucose consumer — produces glucose for others). Adipose: TG stores; releases FFAs + glycerol. Nitrogen balance in starvation: negative (muscle catabolism > synthesis); ketone sparing of protein: ↑ketones → ↓protein catabolism (mechanism: ketones → ↓leucine oxidation → ↓mTOR substrate that drives protein synthesis? more complex). Glucose-6-phosphatase in the body: ONLY in liver, kidney, intestine (not brain, muscle) → only these tissues can export free glucose from gluconeogenesis or glycogenolysis. Muscle glycogen: cannot export glucose (no G6Pase) → provides pyruvate/lactate to liver (Cori cycle) or alanine (Cahill cycle).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which is the most abundant protein in human plasma?
options: Fibrinogen (important but not the most abundant; ~2-4 g/dL)
Immunoglobulin G (IgG, ~7-16 g/L; not the most abundant)
Transferrin (iron transport protein; ~250-380 mg/dL — relatively low concentration)

Albumin: albumin is the most abundant plasma protein (~3.5-5.5 g/dL, ~60% of total plasma protein); synthesized by hepatocytes (rate ~10-15 g/day); major functions: (1) oncotic pressure (plasma colloid osmotic pressure ~25 mmHg → retains fluid in vessels; ↓albumin → edema); (2) transport: FFAs (6-7 binding sites), bilirubin (UCB), drugs (warfarin, diazepam, aspirin, furosemide, sulfonamides), hormones (cortisol ~10%, T4 ~15%), Ca2+ (40-50% of total plasma Ca2+ is protein-bound, mainly to albumin); (3) antioxidant (most abundant thiol in plasma, Cys34 scavenges ROS); (4) pH buffering (minor); (5) anticoagulant (minor — inhibits platelet aggregation); half-life: ~20 days; synthesized as preproalbumin → proalbumin → albumin (signal peptide + propeptide removed); negative acute phase reactant (↓in inflammation, ↑CRP, ↑fibrinogen, ↑ferritin)
explanation: Hypoalbuminemia causes: Decreased synthesis: liver failure (acute or chronic → ↓hepatic synthetic function → ↓albumin), malnutrition (↓amino acid substrate), acute phase response (cytokines → ↓albumin gene transcription → albumin is a negative APP). Increased losses: nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria >3.5 g/day → ↑renal albumin loss), protein-losing enteropathy (intestinal loss: IBD, celiac, lymphangiectasia), burns (↑skin protein loss), exudates (ascites, pleural effusion). Increased catabolism: sepsis, trauma, burns. Dilution: massive fluid resuscitation (↓concentration). Clinical consequences of ↓albumin: edema + ascites (↓oncotic pressure → fluid shift into interstitium); ↓drug binding (↑free fraction → ↑drug effect, toxicity risk); ↓calcium (↑ionized Ca2+ — true Ca2+ may be normal; must correct: corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × [4 - albumin g/dL]); ↑risk of drug-drug interactions. Analbuminemia (rare AR disorder): ↓plasma albumin but surprisingly mild edema (compensation by ↑IgG, ↑fibrinogen, ↑lipoproteins). Prealbumin (transthyretin, TTR): shorter t½ (~2 days) → more sensitive nutritional marker than albumin; also negative APP; used as nutritional assessment in critical care.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The glycolytic enzyme that is specifically inhibited by 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) as an allosteric effector:
options: None — 2,3-BPG does NOT inhibit any glycolytic enzyme; it binds Hb instead: 2,3-BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) is produced from 1,3-BPG by bisphosphoglycerate mutase in RBCs (Rapoport-Luebering shunt); 2,3-BPG binds to the central cavity of deoxyhemoglobin (β-chains) → stabilizes T-state → ↓O2 affinity → right-shift ODC; 2,3-BPG does NOT inhibit phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) or other glycolytic enzymes; rather, it BYPASSES PGK → the 2,3-BPG shunt diverts 1,3-BPG away from PGK (→ NO ATP generated in this bypass); 2,3-BPG phosphatase converts 2,3-BPG → 3-PG which re-enters glycolysis; clinical: stored blood (bank blood): ↓2,3-BPG over days → ↑O2 affinity → ↓O2 delivery (especially after mass transfusion); adenine + phosphate storage solutions partially maintain 2,3-BPG levels
Phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) is inhibited by 2,3-BPG (incorrect — 2,3-BPG acts on Hb)
Pyruvate kinase (PKu) is the main target of 2,3-BPG (incorrect)
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is inhibited by 2,3-BPG in RBCs (incorrect)
explanation: Rapoport-Luebering shunt: RBC-specific (mature RBCs have ↑bisphosphoglycerate mutase [BPGM] activity). 1,3-BPG → [BPGM] → 2,3-BPG → [BPG phosphatase] → 3-PG. This bypass of PGK sacrifices 1 ATP per glucose → trade-off for ↑2,3-BPG → ↑O2 delivery (important at high altitude, in anemia). Regulation: ↓pO2 (deoxyHb binds 2,3-BPG better → 2,3-BPG sequestered → ↑available 2,3-BPG relative to oxyHb); ↑pO2 → 2,3-BPG released. High altitude adaptation: days → ↑BPGM → ↑2,3-BPG → right shift ODC → ↑O2 unloading in tissues (compensates for ↓pO2 in lungs but ensures adequate O2 delivery to tissues). PK deficiency (pyruvate kinase deficiency): most common non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia; ↓PK → ↑1,3-BPG + ↑2,3-BPG (accumulated upstream of PK) → paradoxically: 2,3-BPG ↑↑ → right shift ODC → better O2 delivery (explains why symptoms may be less severe than expected for degree of anemia — 'compensated' by 2,3-BPG) + ↑reticulocytosis (EPO-driven). G6PD deficiency: normal 2,3-BPG. Hexokinase deficiency: ↓G6P → ↓glycolysis → ↓1,3-BPG → ↓2,3-BPG → left shift ODC → worse O2 delivery at given Hb level.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The hormone glucagon exerts its primary metabolic effects in the liver by activating which intracellular messenger?
options: Inositol trisphosphate (IP3) — that is a Gq-GPCR effect (PTH, ADH, oxytocin, angiotensin II, thromboxane, acetylcholine at M1/M3)
Phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) — that is an RTK/PI3K effect

Cyclic AMP (cAMP): glucagon → Gs-coupled GPCR (GCGR, Gs protein) → adenylyl cyclase → ATP → cAMP → PKA (protein kinase A) → phosphorylation of multiple targets in liver: (1) glycogen synthase → INACTIVE (phospho-GS) → ↓glycogen synthesis; (2) phosphorylase kinase → ACTIVE → phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase → ACTIVE (phospho-GP = GP-a) → ↑glycogenolysis → ↑G1P → ↑G6P → ↑glucose-6-phosphatase → ↑glucose release; (3) PFK-2 kinase domain → INACTIVE (FBPase-2 active) → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis; (4) pyruvate kinase → INACTIVE → ↓glycolysis; (5) hormone-sensitive lipase (in adipocytes) → ACTIVE → ↑lipolysis; (6) ACC → INACTIVE → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓FA synthesis + ↑CPT-I → ↑β-oxidation + ↑ketogenesis; phosphodiesterase (PDE) degrades cAMP → ↓cAMP; methylxanthines (theophylline, caffeine) inhibit PDE → ↑cAMP
Diacylglycerol (DAG) — that is a Gq-GPCR second messenger for PKC activation
explanation: Glucagon vs insulin signaling: Glucagon (fasting state): Gs → ↑cAMP → PKA → ↑glycogenolysis, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↓glycolysis, ↑lipolysis, ↑ketogenesis. Net: ↑blood glucose, ↑FFAs, ↑ketones. Insulin (fed state): RTK → IRS → PI3K → Akt → ↑GLUT4 translocation, ↑glycogen synthesis, ↑FA synthesis, ↓gluconeogenesis, ↓lipolysis, ↓ketogenesis. Gs pathway: glucagon (liver, adipocyte), PTH (kidney, bone), TSH (thyroid → ↑T4/T3), ACTH (adrenal → ↑cortisol), LH/FSH (gonad), ADH/V2 (collecting duct → ↑aquaporin 2 → ↑water reabsorption), dopamine D1/D5, β1/β2 adrenergic, secretin (↑HCO3- from pancreatic duct), GLP-1/GIP (↑insulin from β-cells). Gi pathway: ADH/V1a → not in kidney, ↑vasoconstriction (different receptor); α2 adrenergic (↓insulin from β-cells); M2/M4 muscarinic; dopamine D2/D3/D4; somatostatin; adenosine A1. Gq pathway (IP3+DAG → PKC + ↑Ca2+): M1/M3/M5 muscarinic, α1 adrenergic, H1 histamine, AT1 angiotensin, ET-A endothelin, GnRH, TRH, oxytocin, vasopressin V1, substance P.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme that converts homocysteine to methionine is:
options: Methionine synthase (cobalamin-dependent): uses N5-methylTHF + cobalamin (methylcobalamin) → transfers methyl group to homocysteine → methionine; reaction: homocysteine + CH3-THF → [methionine synthase, methylcobalamin] → methionine + THF; B12 deficiency → methionine synthase cannot function → 'methyltrap' (5-methyl-THF cannot donate its methyl group → THF not regenerated → ↑5-methyl-THF trapped, functionally equivalent to folate deficiency) → ↓dTMP synthesis → megaloblastic anemia; also B12 deficiency → ↑homocysteine (remethylation blocked) + ↑methylmalonate (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase also requires B12/AdoCobalamin)
CBS (cystathionine β-synthase, B6): converts Hcy + serine → cystathionine (transsulfuration, away from methionine)
MTHFR (methyleneTHF reductase): converts 5,10-methyleneTHF → 5-methyl-THF (not a direct Hcy→Met enzyme)
SAM synthetase (activates Met to SAM, not the Hcy→Met enzyme)
explanation: Methionine cycle: Met → [SAM synthetase, ATP] → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine, universal methyl donor). SAM + acceptor → [methyltransferase] → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine) + methylated product. SAH → [SAH hydrolase] → Hcy + adenosine. Hcy → two fates: (1) Remethylation: Hcy + 5-methyl-THF → [methionine synthase, B12] → Met + THF (most tissues); OR Hcy + betaine → [BHMT, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase] → Met + dimethylglycine (liver/kidney only). (2) Transsulfuration: Hcy + Ser → [CBS, B6] → cystathionine → [cystathionase, B6] → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate (irreversible direction → cysteine becomes conditionally essential in CBS deficiency). SAM function (SAM is the major biological methyl donor): DNA methylation (DNMT3A, DNMT1), histone methylation (HKMTs), RNA methylation (m6A by METTL3), neurotransmitter methylation (norepinephrine → Epi by PNMT), phosphatidylcholine synthesis (PE → PC via PEMT), creatine synthesis (guanidinoacetate → creatine by GAMT). SAM decarboxylation → decarboxylated SAM → aminopropyl donor for spermidine/spermine synthesis (polyamine synthesis). SAM is made from Met + ATP; SAM production depends on folate cycle (regeneration of Met) → folate or B12 deficiency → ↓SAM → global hypomethylation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The most common mutation in cystic fibrosis (CF) results in deletion of which amino acid from CFTR?
options: Phenylalanine at position 508 — ΔF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508 of CFTR, cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator): accounts for ~70% of CF alleles worldwide; ΔF508 causes: (1) protein misfolding in ER → retained by quality control machinery (calnexin, Hsp70) → targeted for ERAD (ER-associated protein degradation) via ubiquitin-proteasome pathway → ↓CFTR at cell surface; (2) even if protein reaches cell surface, it has temperature-sensitive gating defect; CFTR is a chloride channel (ATP-gated, also allows HCO3- transport); lumacaftor/tezacaftor: 'correctors' → stabilize ΔF508 CFTR folding → ↑trafficking to cell surface; ivacaftor: 'potentiator' → opens CFTR channel at cell surface; Trikafta (elexacaftor + tezacaftor + ivacaftor): highly effective for ΔF508/ΔF508 and many other genotypes (FDA 2019)
explanation: CFTR mutations classification: Class I: premature stop/splice → no protein (G542X, W1282X); treated with read-through agents (ataluren for nonsense, if UGA stop). Class II: misfolding → ERAD (ΔF508, most common) → correctors + potentiators. Class III: gating mutations → protein at surface but channel doesn't open properly (G551D, ~4% of CF) → ivacaftor monotherapy very effective (FDA 2012, first CFTR modulator). Class IV: conductance mutations → ↓Cl- transport per channel. Class V: reduced abundance (promoter, splice). Class VI: ↑degradation at surface. CF diagnosis: sweat chloride test (pilocarpine iontophoresis): >60 mEq/L = positive (definitive); 40-60 = borderline; <40 = negative; CFTR mutation genotyping; nasal potential difference (NPD) for unusual cases. Newborn screening: immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT, ↑in CF neonates due to blocked pancreatic ducts) on dried blood spot → if ↑IRT → reflex CFTR genotyping → if mutation → sweat test. Lung disease: thick, dehydrated mucus → impaired mucociliary clearance → chronic infection (Pseudomonas aeruginosa [biofilm, antibiotic-resistant], Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia [poor prognosis]) → bronchiectasis. Pancreatic: exocrine insufficiency (most patients), diabetes (CFRD, CF-related diabetes), recurrent pancreatitis. Liver: biliary cirrhosis (~5-10%). Male infertility (obstructive azoospermia, congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens, CBAVD).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which step in gluconeogenesis requires the enzyme that also requires biotin as a cofactor?
options: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase step (FBPase-1): fructose-1,6-BP → fructose-6-P (no biotin needed, just Mg2+)
Glucose-6-phosphatase step: G6P → glucose + Pi (no biotin, only in ER, requires G6P translocase)

Pyruvate carboxylase step: pyruvate → OAA (requires biotin + Mg2+ + ATP): this is the first bypass step of gluconeogenesis that circumvents pyruvate kinase (irreversible in glycolysis); pyruvate carboxylase (PC) is in the mitochondrial matrix; requires: biotin (CO2 carrier, covalently attached to Lys residue), Mg2+, ATP, and N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as allosteric activator (PC is activated when acetyl-CoA is high — signals that TCA cycle substrates are adequate → promote gluconeogenesis); OAA from PC → mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase (MDH) → malate → exported to cytoplasm via dicarboxylate carrier → cytoplasmic MDH → OAA + PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, requires GTP) → PEP → enters gluconeogenesis pathway upstream
PEPCK step (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase): OAA → PEP + CO2, requires GTP but NOT biotin
explanation: Gluconeogenesis overview: Irreversible steps of glycolysis bypassed: PK → PC (biotin) + PEPCK (GTP). PFK-1 → FBPase-1 (Mg2+, inhibited by AMP, fructose-2,6-BP; activated by citrate). HK/GK → G6Pase (in ER, via G6P translocase). Sources of substrates: Pyruvate: from alanine (ALT), lactate (LDH). OAA: from aspartate (AST), from citrate (cytoplasm), directly from TCA (via malate). Phosphoenolpyruvate: from OAA via PEPCK. Glycerol: glycerol → glycerol-3-P (glycerol kinase, liver) → DHAP → glycolysis/gluconeogenesis. Propionyl-CoA (odd-chain FA, Val, Ile, Met, Thr): → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → → OAA → gluconeogenesis. Regulation: Fasting/glucagon: ↑cAMP → ↑PKA → phosphorylates/activates: PEPCK transcription (FoxO1-mediated), PC activity, FBPase-2 (↓F-2,6-BP → relieves PFK-1, less relevant in gluconeogenesis regulation). ↑Acetyl-CoA: activates PC (ensures carbon availability for OAA production). Insulin: inhibits gluconeogenesis via Akt → phospho-FOXO → nuclear exclusion → ↓PEPCK/G6Pase transcription + ↑PK + ↑F-2,6-BP (↓FBPase-1). Metformin: inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis (partially via Complex I inhibition → ↑AMP → AMPK → ↑ACC phosphorylation; also direct inhibition of mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase → ↑NADH/NAD+ in mitochondria → ↓oxidation of lactate/glycerol → ↓GNG substrates).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Lactate dehydrogenase isoform flipping (LDH-1 > LDH-2) classically indicated myocardial infarction. LDH-1 is rich in which subunit?
options: M subunit (muscle) — LDH-5 (M4) is the liver/skeletal muscle isoform

H subunit (heart): LDH-1 (H4, four H subunits) is the cardiac/RBC isoform; the 5 isoforms of LDH are tetramers of H and M subunits: LDH-1: H4 (heart, erythrocytes); LDH-2: H3M1; LDH-3: H2M2; LDH-4: HM3; LDH-5: M4 (liver, skeletal muscle); normally LDH-2 > LDH-1 in serum; in MI: cardiac cell necrosis → LDH-1 released → serum LDH-1 > LDH-2 ('flipped LDH') was historically used days 2-7 post-MI (CK-MB rises earlier at 3-6h, peaks 10-24h; LDH-1 rises 24-48h, peaks 72h, remains elevated 5-10 days); now replaced by troponin I/T (rise within 3-6h, peak 12-24h, remain elevated 7-14 days for troponin I, 2-3 weeks for cTnT); LDH is still used as biomarker in: hemolysis (LDH-1 from RBCs), lymphoma (total LDH for tumor burden), PCP (LDH > 300 IU/L), testicular germ cell tumors (LDH as one of three tumor markers along with AFP + hCG)
Both H and M equally (LDH-3 is H2M2)
Neither — LDH-1 contains L subunit (incorrect subunit designation)
explanation: Cardiac biomarkers timeline: Myoglobin: rises 2-4h, peaks 6-12h, normalizes 24-36h (most sensitive early but not specific). CK-MB: rises 3-6h, peaks 10-24h, normalizes 48-72h; high specificity for cardiac muscle (vs. total CK which ↑in skeletal muscle too). Troponin I (cTnI): rises 3-6h, peaks 12-24h, remains elevated 7-14 days. Troponin T (cTnT): rises 3-6h, peaks 12-24h, remains elevated 10-14+ days. High-sensitivity troponin (hsTn): detects troponin in ~99% of healthy people; enables faster MI rule-out (0h/1h algorithms); diagnostic threshold: 99th percentile of normal reference population; also ↑in: ACS, PE, myocarditis, sepsis, CKD (↓renal clearance), heart failure, cardioversion. LDH: total LDH ↑in: MI, liver disease, hemolysis, PE, lymphoma, megaloblastic anemia. Classic LDH flip: historical, no longer primary diagnostic test. AST: rises 8-12h, peaks 18-36h; now used mainly as liver marker. CK total: skeletal muscle (MM), cardiac (MB), brain (BB); total ↑in: MI, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, hypothyroidism, dystrophies, trauma, strenuous exercise. BNP/NT-proBNP: heart failure biomarkers (myocyte stretch → ↑BNP synthesis in ventricles; proBNP → BNP + NT-proBNP; NT-proBNP longer t½ and higher levels).
