HsTnI delta (change) over 1-3 hours: ≥5-6 ng/L change = highly sensitive for ACS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the extrinsic pathway of coagulation, Tissue Factor (TF) activates which factor?
options: Factor X directly (less accurate — TF-FVIIa complex primarily activates X but also IX)

Factor VII: Tissue Factor (TF, FIII, thromboplastin) is a transmembrane protein expressed on subendothelial cells (fibroblasts, smooth muscle) exposed upon vessel injury; TF binds Factor VII → TF-FVII complex → FVII auto-activated to FVIIa by TF (and by FXa/FXIa/FIXa at low concentrations); TF-FVIIa complex (extrinsic tenase): activates Factor X → FXa AND Factor IX → FIXa; FXa → prothrombinase complex (FXa + FVa + Ca2+ + phospholipid) → prothrombin (II) → thrombin (IIa); thrombin: (1) fibrinogen → fibrin monomer → fibrin polymer; (2) activates FXIII → cross-linked fibrin (with isopeptide bonds); (3) activates FV, FVIII, FXI (amplification); (4) activates protein C (via thrombomodulin) → anticoagulant pathway; TFPI (tissue factor pathway inhibitor): inhibits TF-FVIIa-FXa ternary complex → limits extrinsic pathway → after TF-FVII initiates clotting, sustained thrombin generation requires FXI-FIXa (intrinsic pathway amplification)
explanation: Coagulation cascade (cell-based model): Initiation: TF exposure → TF + FVII → FVIIa → activates FX → FXa + FVa → thrombin burst (small amount) → activates platelets + FV + FVIII. Amplification: thrombin activates FV, FVIII, FXI on platelet surface. Propagation: FIXa + FVIIIa (tenase) → ↑↑FXa → FXa + FVa (prothrombinase) → ↑↑↑thrombin → ↑↑↑fibrin clot. Laboratory tests: PT (prothrombin time): tests extrinsic (FVII) + common (FX, FV, FII, fibrinogen) pathways; result: PT in seconds or INR (international normalized ratio: PT patient/PT normal ISI); prolonged PT: FVII deficiency, warfarin (FVII short t½ → first to fall), liver disease (↓synthesis of factors), Vit K deficiency. aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time): tests intrinsic (FXII, XI, IX, VIII, prekallikrein, HMWK) + common pathways; prolonged aPTT: hemophilia A (FVIII) or B (FIX), intrinsic factor deficiencies, lupus anticoagulant (inhibitor + clinical thrombosis despite prolonged aPTT). Mixing study: patient plasma + normal plasma 1:1; corrects → factor deficiency; does not correct → inhibitor present. Thrombin time (TT): thrombin added to plasma → fibrinogen → fibrin; prolonged: ↓fibrinogen, dysfibrinogenemia, heparin (↑AT-III → inhibits thrombin), direct thrombin inhibitors.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In which cellular compartment does fatty acid synthesis (de novo) primarily occur in mammals?
options: Mitochondrial matrix (fatty acid beta-oxidation occurs here; synthesis is cytoplasmic)

Cytoplasm (cytosol): de novo fatty acid synthesis in mammals occurs exclusively in the cytoplasm (cytosol); acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1, rate-limiting) and fatty acid synthase (FAS/FASN, 7-in-1 multifunctional enzyme) are both cytoplasmic; contrast with β-oxidation (occurs in mitochondrial matrix) and ketogenesis (HMG-CoA pathway in mitochondrial matrix); even-chain saturated fatty acids produced: mainly palmitate (C16:0, 16 carbons); further elongation and desaturation occur in the ER (elongases: ELOVL1-7; desaturases: SCD, Δ9-desaturase → stearoyl-CoA [18:0] → oleyl-CoA [18:1Δ9]; FADS1 [Δ5] + FADS2 [Δ6] → PUFA synthesis from essential FA precursors [LA and ALA])
Smooth ER (that is where triglyceride assembly and lipid desaturation/elongation occur)
Peroxisomes (very long chain fatty acid β-oxidation and synthesis of ether lipids/plasmalogens occur here, not de novo fatty acid synthesis)
explanation: Fatty acid synthesis location vs. other lipid metabolic pathways: De novo FA synthesis: cytoplasm (ACC1 + FAS). FA β-oxidation: mitochondrial matrix (main); peroxisomes (VLCFA, H2O2-generating). FA elongation + desaturation: ER. Triglyceride synthesis (GPAT, AGPAT, PAP/lipin, DGAT): ER and mitochondrial outer membrane; TG assembled in ER → VLDL/LDL assembly. Ketogenesis (HMG-CoA pathway: acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA [HMGS2] → acetoacetate [HMGCL]): mitochondria of liver. Cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase): ER. Prostaglandin/thromboxane/leukotriene synthesis: ER (COX, LOX enzymes) and nuclear membrane. Sphingolipid synthesis: ER (ceramide synthesis: serine palmitoyltransferase) and Golgi (complex sphingolipids). Ether lipid/plasmalogen synthesis: peroxisomes (initial steps, then ER). Bile acid synthesis: ER + mitochondria. Eicosanoid synthesis: from membrane phospholipids (PLA2 releases arachidonate → COX or LOX in smooth ER). Essential fatty acids: linoleic acid [LA, 18:2ω6, omega-6] and α-linolenic acid [ALA, 18:3ω3, omega-3] → must be obtained from diet → precursors for long-chain PUFAs (LA → GLA → DGLA → AA [20:4ω6] via FADS1/2; ALA → EPA [20:5ω3] → DHA [22:6ω3]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for generating the 2',3'-cyclic phosphate intermediate in RNA splicing?
options: RNA Pol II (synthesizes pre-mRNA, not involved in splicing chemistry)

Spliceosomal RNA (catalytic: U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNAs do the chemistry): splicing is catalyzed by the spliceosome, a ribonucleoprotein complex; the chemical steps are: Step 1 (branching): free 2'-OH of the branch point adenosine (in the intron, ~20-50 nt upstream of 3' splice site, YYYYURAY branch point sequence) attacks the 5' splice site (GU dinucleotide) → forms 2',5'-phosphodiester bond → releases the 5' exon as a free 3'-OH end + a lariat intermediate (intron folded back onto itself as a lasso/lariat); Step 2 (exon ligation): 3'-OH of freed 5' exon attacks the 3' splice site (AG) → joins exons + releases lariat intron; these are two transesterification reactions (no net ATP consumed in phosphodiester bond formation/breaking, but spliceosome assembly requires ATP); the 2',3'-cyclic phosphate is actually more relevant to certain ribozymes (group I/II) and RNase L; U2AF65/U2AF35 (heterodimer): recognize polypyrimidine tract and AG at 3' splice site
eIF4E cap-binding protein (involved in translation initiation)
Branch point binding protein (SF1/mBBP): recognizes branch point sequence, not the catalytic transesterification
explanation: Spliceosome assembly (ordered pathway): E complex: U1 snRNP binds 5' SS. A complex: U2 snRNP binds branch point (SF3A/B help). B complex: addition of U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP → B complex. B* (activated): U1 released, U4 released; U6 base-pairs with 5' SS; U2-U6 helices form active site. C complex: post-step-1 (lariat formed). mRNP: exons joined + lariat released. snRNAs: U1 (5' SS recognition, base-pairing), U2 (branch point; U2 snRNA ACUAAC pairs with UACUAAC in intron), U4/U6 (U4 sequesters U6 until activation), U5 (aligns exon ends for step 2). NMD (nonsense-mediated mRNA decay): premature termination codon (PTC) >50-55 nt upstream of last exon-exon junction → EJC (exon junction complex deposited by spliceosome) remains at junction → during translation, ribosome encounters EJC downstream of PTC → recruits UPF1-UPF2-UPF3 → mRNA degradation; prevents translation of truncated/dominant negative proteins. Alternative splicing: >90% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing → ↑proteome diversity from ~20,000 genes; regulated by ESE (exonic splicing enhancers, bound by SR proteins) and ESS (silencers, bound by hnRNPs); mutations creating/destroying splice signals → disease (e.g., β-thalassemia IVS1-110 G→A mutation creates new 3' splice site in intron 1 → aberrant splicing → ↓β-globin).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biliverdin is the first product of heme catabolism. It is produced by which enzyme?
options: Heme oxygenase (HMOX1, HMOX2): cleaves the porphyrin ring of heme at the α-methene bridge; reaction: heme (Fe-protoporphyrin IX) + 3 O2 + 3 NADPH → biliverdin (green, linear tetrapyrrole) + Fe2+ + CO; requires: (1) O2 as substrate; (2) NADPH; microsomal enzyme (smooth ER, mainly in spleen macrophages + Kupffer cells); HMOX1 (inducible, HO-1) is induced by: heme, heavy metals, heat shock, oxidative stress, hypoxia, cytokines → protective/anti-inflammatory; HMOX1 deficiency: rare but causes hemolytic anemia + hemosiderin deposits in multiple organs; HMOX2 (constitutive, HO-2) in brain, testes; CO produced: acts as signaling molecule (vasodilation, anti-inflammatory, neurotransmission) at physiological levels; biliverdin → biliverdin reductase (cytoplasm) → bilirubin (yellow-orange, UCB); UCB bound to albumin → transported to liver
Biliverdin reductase (this converts biliverdin to bilirubin, the second step)
Glucuronyl transferase (UGT1A1, in liver ER: bilirubin → bilirubin diglucuronide, a different step)
Stercobilinogen → urobilinogen (intestinal bacteria reduce bilirubin diglucuronide)
explanation: Heme catabolism pathway: RBCs (lifespan 120 days) → destroyed in spleen by macrophages → hemoglobin disassembled → globin (recycled amino acids) + heme. Heme → HMOX1 → biliverdin + Fe2+ + CO. Biliverdin → biliverdin reductase → unconjugated bilirubin (UCB, fat-soluble, NOT water-soluble, cannot be directly excreted). UCB + albumin → blood → liver hepatocytes → OATP1B1/1B3 (organic anion transport polypeptides) → UCB taken up into hepatocyte. UGT1A1 (UDP-glucuronyl transferase 1A1, in ER, induced by phenobarbital): UCB + 2 UDP-glucuronate → bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated bilirubin, CB, water-soluble) → secreted via MRP2 (ABCC2) into bile canaliculus. Bile → small intestine → large intestine → bacteria (β-glucuronidases + reductases): bilirubin diglucuronide → urobilinogen + stercobilinogen → stercobilin (brown color of feces) + urobilin (yellow color of urine — small fraction of urobilinogen reabsorbed enterohepatic circulation → blood → kidney → urine). Neonatal jaundice: UGT1A1 immature (prenatal: UGT1A1 is suppressed in fetus, because placenta handles bilirubin; after birth: must upregulate UGT1A1) + ↑bilirubin production (fetal Hb → adult Hb transition → HbF breakdown) → UCB builds up. Gilbert's syndrome: ↓UGT1A1 activity (promoter mutation, 7 TA repeats [A[TA]7TAA] instead of normal 6) → mild ↑UCB, episodic jaundice triggered by fasting/illness; benign.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ammonia is toxic to the brain primarily because it depletes which TCA cycle intermediate?
options: Alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG): in the brain (and liver), excess ammonia (NH3/NH4+) is detoxified by glutamine synthetase (GS) reaction: glutamate + NH3 + ATP → glutamine; the glutamate used in this reaction must be replenished → the major source of glutamate in the brain is transamination of α-KG (α-ketoglutarate) → Glu (using GABA or aspartate as amino donors); thus: ↑NH3 → ↑GS activity → ↑glutamate consumption → ↑α-KG consumption; ↓α-KG → ↓flux through TCA cycle → ↓NADH + ↓ATP → impaired oxidative phosphorylation in neurons; additionally: ↑glutamine in astrocytes → osmotic swelling (cytotoxic cerebral edema) → ↑ICP; also: ↑ammonia inhibits α-KG dehydrogenase (α-KGDH) directly (NH4+ competes with Mg2+); GABA/glutamate imbalance (↑glutamine → ↑GABA in some pathways → sedation); false neurotransmitters (octopamine, phenylethanolamine); ↑brain lactate (↓NADH oxidation)
explanation: Ammonia toxicity mechanisms in brain: (1) α-KG depletion → ↓TCA → ↓ATP in neurons (energy crisis). (2) Glutamine accumulation in astrocytes → osmotic swelling → astrocyte dysfunction → cerebral edema. (3) Glutamine excess → ↑glutamine transport into mitochondria → mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) → mitochondrial dysfunction. (4) Altered neurotransmitter balance (GABA/glutamate imbalance). (5) Direct NH4+ effect: NH4+ substitutes for K+ in Na+/K+-ATPase → impaired neuronal ion homeostasis. Hyperammonemia causes: liver failure (acute hepatic failure, cirrhosis with shunting), urea cycle disorders, organic acidemias (propionyl-CoA inhibits CPS I), Reye syndrome (salicylate + viral illness → mitochondrial damage → ↑NH3 + ↑liver enzymes + encephalopathy; avoid aspirin in children with viral illness), urease-positive bacteria (GI: Helicobacter pylori, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas → generate NH3 from urea in gut → absorbed → ↑portal NH3), carnitine transport deficiency, THAN (transient hyperammonemia of the newborn). Treatment of hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose (↓NH3 production: osmotic laxative + acidifies colon → NH4+ trapped → excreted; also alters gut flora); rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic → ↓urease-producing bacteria); protein restriction; zinc supplementation (activates urea cycle enzymes); ornithine phenylacetate (L-ORN-L-PBA → ornithine + PA → PhenylAcetylGlutamine in muscle + NH3 fixation); LOLA (L-ornithine L-aspartate); liver transplantation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the irreversible conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA?
options: Pyruvate carboxylase (pyruvate + CO2 → OAA, not acetyl-CoA)

Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC): pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH; irreversible (thermodynamically); multi-enzyme complex in the inner mitochondrial membrane/matrix: E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase, TPP/B1 cofactor, requires Mg2+), E2 (dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase, lipoic acid + CoA/B5 cofactor), E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, FAD/B2 cofactor → NADH/B3); overall, PDC requires 5 cofactors: TPP (B1), lipoic acid, CoA (pantothenic acid/B5), FAD (riboflavin/B2), NAD+ (niacin/B3); inhibited by: ↑acetyl-CoA (product inhibition), ↑NADH (product inhibition), ATP (end product), pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK); activated by: ↑CoA, ↑NAD+, ↑pyruvate (substrate), pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase (PDP); PDK activated by: ↑acetyl-CoA/CoA, ↑NADH/NAD+, ATP; PDK inhibited by: pyruvate (paradoxical substrate activation), dichloroacetate (DCA, experimental PDK inhibitor → ↑PDC activity → ↑pyruvate oxidation); PDC deficiency: most commonly E1α (PDHA1, X-linked): neonatal lactic acidosis, brain Leigh syndrome or Wernicke-like encephalopathy, ↑pyruvate + lactate, ↑alanine (alanine aminotransferase acts on excess pyruvate)
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT): alanine + α-KG ⇌ pyruvate + glutamate (reversible transamination)
explanation: PDC regulation and disease: Activation: insulin → activates PDP (phosphatase) → dephosphorylates + activates PDC; ↑pyruvate, ↑CoA, ↑NAD+ → activate. Inhibition: glucagon → activates PDK (kinase) → phosphorylates Ser264 of E1α → inactivates PDC; ↑acetyl-CoA, ↑NADH, ↑ATP → activate PDK. Clinical: Thiamine (B1) deficiency: PDC, α-KGDH, transketolase all require TPP; Wernicke encephalopathy (ataxia + ophthalmoplegia + confusion), Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia, confabulation), beriberi (wet: high-output HF; dry: peripheral neuropathy). Leigh syndrome: mtDNA or nuclear gene mutations affecting OXPHOS/PDC → bilateral symmetric basal ganglia + brainstem lesions on MRI (↑T2 signal); multiple genes (SURF1 [Complex IV], NDUFS genes [Complex I], PDC, PDHX, ATP synthase genes, etc.). Pyruvate: elevated in pyruvate kinase deficiency? No — PK deficiency causes ↑PEP/upstream intermediates, not specifically ↑pyruvate. Elevated pyruvate in: PDC deficiency, thiamine deficiency (PDC cannot function), Complex I deficiency (↑NADH → ↓PDC activity indirectly), severe hypoxia (pyruvate → lactate when ETC impaired). Arsenic poisoning: arsenic forms a complex with lipoic acid (dihydrolipoamide, E2 component) → inhibits PDC and α-KGDH → ↑pyruvate + lactate + peripheral neuropathy + skin/nail changes (Mees' lines).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The MTHFR C677T polymorphism leads to elevated homocysteine because:
options: It directly impairs methionine synthase activity
It reduces the methylation of adenosine in tRNA

It decreases the production of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-methyl-THF) which is needed to remethylate homocysteine: MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase) catalyzes: 5,10-methyleneTHF → 5-methyl-THF (N5-methyl-THF, the predominant circulating form of folate); this is the folate species required by methionine synthase (+ cobalamin/B12) to methylate homocysteine → methionine; MTHFR C677T variant (Ala222Val): thermolabile enzyme, ↓activity → ↓conversion of 5,10-methylene-THF → 5-methyl-THF → ↓folate available for Hcy remethylation → ↑Hcy; frequency: ~10% homozygous TT worldwide; associated with: ↑CVD risk, ↑NTD risk (neural tube defects), ↑thrombosis, ↑pregnancy complications; manageable with folate supplementation (↑substrate → partially compensates for reduced MTHFR activity); C677T + A1298C compound heterozygotes: ↓↓MTHFR activity > single variant; MTHFR is NOT directly involved in DNA synthesis (that role belongs to thymidylate synthase and de novo purine synthesis which use other THF forms)
It blocks UGT1A1 from conjugating bilirubin
explanation: MTHFR pathway and clinical significance: 5,10-methylene-THF is reduced to 5-methyl-THF by MTHFR (irreversible, NADPH-dependent); this step is committed to methylation (methionine cycle) and cannot be reversed → once committed to methylation. Methyl trap: B12 deficiency → methionine synthase non-functional → 5-methyl-THF cannot donate methyl group → THF cannot be regenerated → all folate eventually becomes 5-methyl-THF (trapped) → functional folate deficiency → ↓DNA synthesis. MTHFR C677T: homozygous TT: significant ↓MTHFR activity (~35-50% of normal in vivo); heterozygous CT: intermediate (~65% activity). Note: MTHFR TT homozygotes respond to folate supplementation → increase in substrate (5,10-methylene-THF) → increased product (5-methyl-THF) despite low MTHFR activity. Hyperhomocysteinemia associated risks: CVD (modest, causal relationship debated — Mendelian randomization studies suggest weak causal effect on stroke but less so on CAD); venous thrombosis (CBS deficiency >> MTHFR); NTDs (periconceptional folate ↓risk); adverse pregnancy outcomes. Testing: plasma total homocysteine (fasting); reference: <15 µmol/L normal; >100 µmol/L severe (CBS deficiency). B12 + folate + B6 supplementation: lower Hcy but not consistently shown to reduce CVD events in RCTs (HOPE-2, B-PROOF trials).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The activation energy (Ea) of a biochemical reaction is reduced by an enzyme by:
options: Providing additional thermodynamic energy to make the reaction exergonic
Changing the ΔG of the reaction (enzymes do NOT change the overall free energy of the reaction)

Stabilizing the transition state: the enzyme active site is complementary in shape/charge to the transition state (not the substrate or product); by binding the transition state preferentially → enzyme LOWERS the activation energy (Ea) required to reach the transition state; mechanisms: (1) proximity + orientation (substrates held optimally near each other → ↑effective concentration); (2) strain/distortion (enzyme distorts substrate toward transition state conformation); (3) electrostatic stabilization (charge complementarity between active site and transition state); (4) acid-base catalysis; (5) covalent catalysis; (6) metal ion catalysis; the enzyme does NOT change the equilibrium position (ΔG° is unchanged) → it only speeds up the reaction by lowering Ea; catalytic antibodies (abzymes): antibodies raised against transition state analogs → some catalytic activity → proof that TS stabilization is the key
Permanently binding to the substrate and releasing it slowly
explanation: Enzyme catalysis fundamentals: Transition state theory: every reaction must pass through a high-energy intermediate state (transition state, TS) with partial bond formation/breaking → highest energy point on the reaction coordinate; Ea = difference in energy between ground state (reactants) and TS; enzymes: Eauncat − Eacat > 0 → ↑rate by factor of e^(ΔEa/RT) (Arrhenius equation); for every 10°C ↑temperature: rate approximately doubles (Q10 ≈ 2); at >40-50°C: protein denaturation (thermostable enzymes: Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, stable to 95°C; pyroglutamate aminopeptidase from T. thermophilus). Lock-and-key model: substrate fits active site exactly (Koshland — induced fit model: substrate binding causes conformational change in enzyme → better active site complementarity to TS). Induced fit (Koshland 1958): enzyme 'wraps around' substrate → induced complementarity → explains specificity + cooperativity in allosteric enzymes (global conformation change from T→R upon substrate binding). Catalytic perfection: kcat/Km close to diffusion limit (10^8-10^9 M-1s-1) for enzymes like triose phosphate isomerase (TPI): kcat/Km = 2.4 × 10^8 M-1s-1 — nearly every substrate molecule is catalyzed upon encounter. Rate enhancement by enzymes: Orotidine decarboxylase (OMPDC) — 17-orders-of-magnitude rate acceleration (Ea reduction from 47 kcal/mol uncatalyzed to 15 kcal/mol catalyzed); remarkable because it uses no cofactor, just active site residues.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acid disorders is characterized by an 'odor of sweaty feet'?
options: Maple syrup urine disease (maple syrup/caramel odor from BCKAs)

Isovaleric acidemia (IVA): caused by isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency → leucine catabolism is blocked → isovaleryl-CoA accumulates → isovaleric acid (3-methylbutanoic acid) + 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid + isovalerylglycine in urine → distinctive 'sweaty feet' or 'cheesy' odor; presentation: neonatal acute form: overwhelming acidosis, vomiting, lethargy → coma and death if untreated; chronic intermittent form: episodes of decompensation triggered by fasting/illness; diagnosis: plasma acylcarnitines (↑isovalerylcarnitine, C5-acylcarnitine), urine organic acids (↑isovalerylglycine + 3-OH-isovaleric acid), IVDH enzyme assay; treatment: glycine + carnitine supplementation (form isovalerylglycine + isovalerylcarnitine → detoxify + excrete excess isovaleryl-CoA), leucine-restricted diet
Glutaric aciduria type I (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency — no characteristic odor)
explanation: Distinctive odors in metabolic diseases: Phenylketonuria (PKU): musty/mousy (phenylpyruvate/phenylacetate). Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD): maple syrup/caramel (sotolon, from BCKAs — mainly α-keto-isocaproate from leucine). Isovaleric acidemia (IVA): sweaty feet/cheesy (isovaleric acid). Trimethylaminuria (fish odor syndrome, TMAU): fishy odor (TMA from FMO3 [flavin-containing monooxygenase 3] deficiency → TMA not oxidized to TMAO → TMA excreted in sweat, urine, breath). Glutaric aciduria type II (MADD): also sweaty feet (isovaleric + glutaric acids). Tyrosinemia type I: cabbage/rotten smell (sulfur compounds). 3-methylcrotonylglycinuria: cat urine odor (3-hydroxyisovaleric acid + 3-methylcrotonylglycine). Dimethylglycinuria: fish smell (DGM, FAD deficiency → ↑dimethylglycine). Hawkinsinuria: swimming pool smell (unusual tyrosine metabolite, hawkinsins, transient). Alkaptonuria: urine darkens on standing (not a smell, but a classic visual sign — homogentisic acid polymerizes to dark pigment on air exposure). Methionine malabsorption syndrome (oast-house urine disease): α-hydroxybutyric acid from bacterial methionine degradation → fermented ale odor + blue-diaper syndrome. Propionic acidemia: rancid butter smell. These odors can help distinguish metabolic disorders when laboratory confirmation is pending.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency develops hemolytic anemia after taking primaquine. The mechanism is:
options: Inhibition of hemoglobin synthesis (that is lead poisoning affecting ALA dehydratase or heme pathway)

G6PD deficiency → ↓NADPH in RBCs → ↓reduced glutathione (GSH) → RBCs cannot neutralize oxidative stress from primaquine → Heinz body formation + hemolysis: in G6PD-deficient RBCs, NADPH production is severely impaired (G6PD is the ONLY enzyme producing NADPH in mature RBCs [which have no mitochondria]) → ↓NADPH → ↓glutathione reductase activity (glutathione reductase: GSSG + NADPH → 2 GSH + NADP+) → ↓GSH → ↓GPx activity (H2O2 + 2 GSH → 2 H2O + GSSG) → ↑H2O2 + ↑oxidative radicals from primaquine/its metabolites → oxidize hemoglobin (Fe2+ → Fe3+ = methemoglobin, then further → hemichromes) → precipitate as Heinz bodies (seen on crystal violet stain, NOT on routine Wright-Giemsa) → macrophages bite off Heinz bodies → 'bite cells' on peripheral smear → ↓RBC deformability → intravascular hemolysis
Direct lysis of RBCs by primaquine without any enzyme deficiency
Autoimmune destruction of RBCs (IgG antibodies, as in Coombs-positive hemolysis from drug — different mechanism)
explanation: G6PD deficiency (more detail): G6PD assay: normally done on non-crisis blood (reticulocytes have higher G6PD activity than mature RBCs → during crisis with ↑reticulocytosis → G6PD may appear falsely normal or near-normal → assay must be repeated 3-6 months after resolution for accurate diagnosis). Oxidant triggers: Drugs: antimalarials (primaquine, pamaquine, chloroquine [less so]), antibiotics (dapsone [most potent trigger], sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin), analgesics (aspirin at high doses), chloramphenicol. Foods: fava beans (Vicia faba) → divicine (4,6-diamino-5-formamidopyrimidine) + isouramil → oxidants → more likely to trigger hemolysis in Mediterranean variant than African A- variant. Infections: oxidative burst from activated phagocytes. Neonatal jaundice: ↑bilirubin from ↑hemolysis + ↓bilirubin conjugation capacity. G6PD variants: G6PD A- (common in sub-Saharan Africa): exon 5 mutation (Val68Met + Asn126Asp, etc.) → enzyme with normal activity in young RBCs but rapid inactivation → older RBCs more susceptible (reticulocytes protected). G6PD Mediterranean: exon 6 (Ser218Phe) → severely ↓enzyme activity even in reticulocytes → more severe hemolysis. G6PD Canton (Southeast Asia): also severe. G6PD Class I (rare): enzyme absent → chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia even without triggers.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The synthesis of heme is completed in the mitochondria. Which enzyme performs the final step?
options: Uroporphyrinogen III synthase (converts HMB → uroporphyrinogen III — step 4 of 8)
Protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (PPO, penultimate step — protoporphyrinogen IX → protoporphyrin IX)

Ferrochelatase (FECH): catalyzes the final step: protoporphyrin IX + Fe2+ → heme (iron protoporphyrin IX); located in the inner mitochondrial membrane (matrix-facing side); requires Fe2+ (not Fe3+; iron must be in the reduced form); inhibited by lead (Pb2+) and other heavy metals (compete with Fe2+); ferrochelatase deficiency: erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP, AR, FECH mutations) → protoporphyrin IX accumulates in erythrocytes and skin → severe photosensitivity (burning pain in sun, no blistering — unlike porphyria cutanea tarda) + liver disease (protoporphyrin deposits in hepatocytes → cirrhosis in severe cases); treatment: afamelanotide (MC1R agonist → ↑melanin in skin → photoprotection), givosiran (siRNA targeting ALAS1 → ↓heme synthesis intermediates)
ALA synthase 2 (ALAS2, erythroid, first step of heme synthesis in erythroid cells)
explanation: Heme catabolism connections: Ferrochelatase requires iron in Fe2+ form → STEAP3 (3-ketosteroid reductase-like protein) reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ in endosome for erythroid iron delivery from transferrin-TfR1 pathway → DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1) exports Fe2+ from endosome → mitoferrin-1/2 (SLC25A37/A28) imports Fe2+ into mitochondria → ferrochelatase. Lead poisoning effects on porphyrin pathway: Lead inhibits: ALA dehydratase (ALAD, most sensitive enzyme, 50% inhibition at very low lead levels → ↑urine ALA before clinical symptoms) + ferrochelatase → accumulation of ↑ALA, ↑zinc-protoporphyrin (ZPP, zinc substitutes for lead-inhibited ferrochelatase → ZPP in RBCs, measured by hematofluorometer) + ↑coproporphyrinogen → ↑urine coproporphyrin III. Labs in lead poisoning: ↑blood lead level (most direct), ↑ZPP, ↑urine ALA + coproporphyrin III, ↓ALAD activity in RBCs; anemia (microcytic, hypochromic + basophilic stippling [ribosomes, from lead ↓RNase → ribosome aggregates] + sideroblastic anemia). EPP (erythropoietic protoporphyria): FECH mutations → protoporphyrin IX → phototoxicity (protoporphyrin is a photosensitizer → generates singlet O2 on UV exposure → cell damage); no dark urine, no blistering → different from CEP/PCT.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Warburg effect in cancer cells refers to:
options: Metastasis of cancer cells to distant organs
Cancer cells switching from anaerobic to aerobic metabolism

Preferential use of aerobic glycolysis even in the presence of adequate oxygen: cancer cells preferentially convert glucose to lactate even when O2 is available (aerobic glycolysis → Warburg effect, described by Otto Warburg in 1924); this is thermodynamically inefficient (2 ATP vs ~30 ATP per glucose) but provides advantages for cancer cells: (1) rapid glucose uptake + high glycolytic flux → substrates for biosynthesis (nucleotides, FA, amino acids) from glycolytic intermediates; (2) generates lactate (excreted → acidifies tumor microenvironment → ↑invasion + ↑immune evasion); (3) maintains high NADPH (via PPP) → antioxidant defense; (4) keeps mitochondria from generating excessive ROS; PET scan (18F-FDG): exploits Warburg effect → cancer cells ↑glucose uptake (↑GLUT1 + ↑hexokinase II) → trap ↑18F-FDG-6-P (cannot be further metabolized) → ↑FDG uptake on PET; molecular basis: oncogene activation (c-Myc → ↑HK2, ↑LDH-A, ↑GLUT1; HIF-1α → ↑GLUT1, ↑HK2, ↑LDHA, ↑PDK1 [inhibits PDC → blocks pyruvate → mitochondria]); tumor suppressor loss (p53 → normally ↑TIGAR [fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase → ↓PFK-1] + ↑SCO2 [mitochondrial complex IV subunit]; p53 loss → ↑Warburg); isocitrate dehydrogenase mutations (IDH1/2 → 2-HG oncometabolite → HIF-1α activation)
Increased oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells to meet energy demands
explanation: Cancer metabolism (beyond Warburg): Glutamine addiction: many cancer cells depend heavily on glutamine as carbon/nitrogen source for biosynthesis (nucleotide + non-essential AA synthesis, TCA anaplerosis via glutaminolysis: Gln → Glu → α-KG → TCA). Fatty acid synthesis: ↑de novo FA synthesis in cancer (↑FASN, ↑ACC, ↑ATP-citrate lyase) → supports membrane biosynthesis + lipid raft signaling; lipid-droplet formation for energy storage. One-carbon metabolism: serine → glycine + formate (via SHMT2 in mitochondria) → THF derivatives → nucleotide synthesis (↑demand in proliferating cells). Hexosamine pathway: fructose-6-P → glucosamine-6-P → UDP-GlcNAc → O-GlcNAc protein modifications (WT epigenetic regulation of many cancer proteins). Pentose phosphate pathway: ↑PPP flux → ↑NADPH (antioxidant) + ↑ribose-5-P (nucleotide synthesis) → cancer proliferation + survival. Oncometabolites: 2-HG (IDH1/2 mut): inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases → epigenetic changes. Fumarate (FH mut): same. Succinate (SDH mut): same. These inhibit TET2 (DNA demethylase), KDM histone demethylases → CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). Tumor mutational burden (TMB) and microsatellite instability (MSI): high TMB/MSI-H → more neoantigens → better response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following vitamins can be synthesized by the human body in adequate amounts under normal sunlight exposure?
options: Vitamin C (must be obtained from diet — humans lost the ability to synthesize ascorbic acid due to GULO [L-gulonolactone oxidase] pseudogene mutation)
Vitamin E (must be obtained from diet — no known synthesis pathway in humans)

Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol): synthesized in the skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol (a cholesterol derivative) upon exposure to UV-B radiation (290-315 nm); 7-dehydrocholesterol → [UV-B photolysis] → pre-vitamin D3 → [heat, thermal isomerization, 37°C body temperature] → Vitamin D3; the photochemical reaction is rapid (minutes of sun exposure can produce adequate Vit D3); factors affecting synthesis: latitude (less UV-B at higher latitudes in winter), season, time of day (best: midday), skin pigmentation (↑melanin → ↑UV-B filtering → ↓Vit D synthesis), sunscreen (SPF15 → ↓95% of UVB → ↓Vit D synthesis), aging (↓7-dehydrocholesterol in skin), obesity (sequestration in fat), clothing; this is why dark-skinned populations at northern latitudes and veiled individuals are at high risk for deficiency; note: adequate sunlight exposure alone is often insufficient at northern latitudes, especially in winter → supplementation needed
Niacin (B3) — synthesized from tryptophan (60 mg Trp = 1 mg niacin equivalent, NE) but this requires adequate dietary Trp; not from sunlight
explanation: Vitamin D adequacy: 25-OH-D3 serum level (assessment): ≥30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L): sufficient (optimal >40-60 ng/mL by some guidelines). 20-29 ng/mL: insufficient. <20 ng/mL: deficient. <10 ng/mL: severe deficiency. Sunlight vs diet: casual sun exposure (15-20 min, arms + face, midday, without sunscreen) in summer at temperate latitudes → up to 10,000-20,000 IU/day potential → much more than RDA (600-800 IU/day). Excess UV-B → destroys pre-Vit D3 → photoproducts (lumisterol, tachysterol) → prevents Vit D3 toxicity from sun (unlike oral supplementation which can → toxicity). Dietary sources: naturally rich: cod liver oil, fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines), egg yolks; fortified foods: milk, orange juice, cereals. Supplementation: recommended in: infants (exclusively breastfed → Vit D-free), dark skin + northern latitude, institutionalized elderly, malabsorption syndromes, certain medications (anticonvulsants, glucocorticoids → ↑Vit D catabolism). Optimal Vit D dose: adults → 1000-2000 IU/day typical supplementation; treatment of deficiency → 50,000 IU/week × 8-12 weeks. Toxicity (from supplementation, NOT from sun): ↑25-OH-D3 > 150 ng/mL → hypercalcemia + hypercalciuria → nephrocalcinosis, weakness, polyuria, constipation, mental confusion.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme responsible for the conversion of testosterone to estradiol is:
options: Aromatase (CYP19A1): a cytochrome P450 enzyme in the ER of: ovarian granulosa cells (primary site in premenopausal women), adipose tissue stromal cells (primary site in postmenopausal women and obese men), brain (local estrogen for neural function), placenta (during pregnancy), testes Sertoli cells (small amount); reaction: testosterone + NADPH + 3 O2 → estradiol (E2) + H2O + CO2 (three steps: C19 methyl group oxidized × 2 + aromatization of ring A); androstenedione → estrone (E1) by aromatase (also occurs); aromatase inhibitors (AIs): anastrozole, letrozole (non-steroidal, reversible), exemestane (steroidal, irreversible) → ↓estrogen synthesis → used in: ER+HER2- breast cancer (adjuvant therapy in postmenopausal women, preferred over tamoxifen in postmenopausal), male gynecomastia (unlabeled), endometriosis, McCune-Albright syndrome (↑aromatase activity in bone, skin, adrenal)
17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (HSD17B): converts androstenedione ↔ testosterone AND estrone ↔ estradiol; important but not the aromatization step
explanation: Sex steroid synthesis: Androgens (testosterone, DHT, DHEA): synthesized in adrenal cortex (zona reticularis: DHEA, DHEAS, androstenedione) and gonads (Leydig cells in testes → testosterone). Testosterone: most potent androgen; converted to DHT by 5α-reductase (type 1 in skin/liver; type 2 in prostate, seminal vesicles, epididymis, skin); DHT is 5× more potent than testosterone. 5α-reductase deficiency (AR): 46,XY DSD — appears female at birth (↓DHT → ↓virilization of external genitalia in utero) but masculinizes at puberty (testosterone → intact) + ↓prostate. 5α-reductase inhibitors (finasteride — type 2; dutasteride — types 1 and 2): ↓DHT → shrink prostate (BPH), androgenetic alopecia, prevention of PCa. Estrogens: estradiol (E2, most potent) → estrone (E1, main estrogen after menopause) → estriol (E3, main estrogen in pregnancy, from placenta using DHEAS from fetal adrenal). Estrogen receptors: ERα (breast, uterus, bone, cardiovascular) + ERβ (brain, ovary, prostate, colon); nuclear receptors → genomic effects; also membrane-bound ERs → rapid non-genomic effects. Tamoxifen: SERM (selective estrogen receptor modulator): antagonist in breast tissue (blocks ER) → prevents breast cancer cells from proliferating; agonist in bone (↑bone density) and uterus (risk of endometrial cancer). Aromatase amplification: in some ER+ breast cancers → ↑local estrogen → AI resistance mechanism.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with suspected Wilson disease has which of the following characteristic lab findings?
options: ↓Ceruloplasmin, ↑liver copper, ↑24h urine copper (after penicillamine challenge): in Wilson disease (AR, ATP7B gene, chromosome 13q14) — copper cannot be incorporated into ceruloplasmin (ATP7B pumps Cu into secretory pathway for ceruloplasmin loading) and cannot be exported into bile → copper accumulates in liver → liver injury (hepatitis → cirrhosis) → copper redistributes to brain, cornea, kidney; labs: ↓ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL, in ~80-90% of patients — but can be normal in up to 20% including in acute liver failure from WD); ↑liver copper (>250 µg/g dry weight, gold standard); ↑24h urine copper (>100 µg/day, or >40 µg/day baseline is suspicious; after penicillamine challenge ↑↑); serum copper: LOW or normal (most serum copper is ceruloplasmin-bound; ↓ceruloplasmin → ↓ceruloplasmin-bound Cu; but ↑free [non-ceruloplasmin-bound] copper; total serum copper = ceruloplasmin-bound + free); KF rings (Kayser-Fleischer): in >95% of patients with neuropsychiatric WD; 50% with hepatic-only WD
↓Ceruloplasmin, ↓serum copper, ↓urine copper (like copper deficiency, not WD)
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration): ATP7B: copper-transporting ATPase (P-type, like ATP7A in Menkes) in hepatocytes; function: (1) incorporates Cu into ceruloplasmin in trans-Golgi; (2) exports Cu into bile (excretion). ATP7B loss → Cu not incorporated into ceruloplasmin → apo-ceruloplasmin (not secreted → ↓serum ceruloplasmin) + Cu not excreted in bile → Cu accumulates. Organs affected: Liver (most common presentation in children): hepatitis, steatosis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure (can mimic fulminant hepatitis, with very high UCB from Coombs-negative hemolysis [Cu directly oxidizes RBCs] + ↑AST/ALT but relatively low ALP [↑ALP typically expected in liver failure — ↓ALP in WD acute liver failure is a clue]). Brain: basal ganglia > cortex: dysarthria, tremor, dystonia (wing-beating tremor in limbs), ataxia, personality change, psychiatric symptoms (psychosis). Eye: KF rings (copper in Descemet's membrane, seen on slit lamp, not by naked eye usually) + sunflower cataract (Cu in lens). Kidney: Fanconi syndrome (Cu in proximal tubule → renal tubular acidosis + aminoaciduria + phosphaturia). Treatment: penicillamine (D-penicillamine, copper chelator, first-line historically), trientine (triethylene tetramine, less side effects than penicillamine), zinc (↑metallothionein in enterocytes → binds Cu → blocks absorption + reduces endogenous secretion; used for maintenance), liver transplant (severe/fulminant; corrects the underlying defect — restores normal liver ATP7B). Tetrathiomolybdate: rapidly lowers free copper — used for severe neurological cases (experimental in some countries).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The primary control point for regulating de novo purine synthesis is:
options: Xanthine oxidase (XO): catalyzes hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (last steps of catabolism); not de novo synthesis
IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH): converts IMP → XMP in guanine nucleotide branch; an important control but not the primary feedback control for the entire pathway
Adenylosuccinate synthetase (ADSS): converts IMP → SAMP in adenine nucleotide branch; important but branch-specific

PRPP amidotransferase (amidophosphoribosyltransferase): the rate-limiting first committed step of de novo purine synthesis; catalyzes: PRPP + glutamine → 5-phosphoribosylamine (5-PRA) + glutamate + PPi; this step is allosterically regulated: inhibited (feedback) by: AMP, ADP, GMP, GDP (the end products of purine synthesis, each working at their own inhibitory sites — AMP/ADP inhibit the adenyl site; GMP/GDP inhibit the guanyl site → cross-product regulation ensures balance); activated by: PRPP (substrate) + Mg2+; the balanced inhibition prevents over-production of purines; glutamine PRPP amidotransferase is the key committed step — deletion/inactivation would block all de novo purine synthesis
explanation: De novo purine synthesis (summary): All 10 steps occur in the cytoplasm (except the two formylation steps which use 10-formyl-THF, produced from 5-methyl-THF cycling). Starting material: PRPP (5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, from ribose-5-P + 2 ATP via PRPP synthetase). Key intermediates: 5-PRA → GAR → FGAR → FGAM → AIR → CAIR → SAICAR → AICAR → FAICAR → IMP (inosine monophosphate, the common purine precursor). From IMP: two branches: (1) IMP → SAMP [AdSS, GTP] → AMP [adenylosuccinase]; (2) IMP → XMP [IMPDH, NAD+] → GMP [GMPS, ATP + Gln]. Atoms in purine ring (mnemonic G-C-A-A-G at positions): N1 from Asp; C2 from 10-formyl-THF; N3 from Gln (amide); C4,C5,N7 from glycine; C6 from CO2; N10 from 10-formyl-THF; and N9 from Gln. Energy cost: 6 ATP equivalents per purine nucleotide synthesized de novo. Salvage pathway (much more efficient): HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase): hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP; guanine + PRPP → GMP; APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase): adenine + PRPP → AMP. Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency): ↑PRPP (not consumed by salvage) + ↑PRPP amidotransferase activity → ↑de novo synthesis → ↑uric acid.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The biosynthesis of nitric oxide (NO) from arginine requires which cofactor, among others?
options: NADPH and tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4): nitric oxide synthase (NOS) reaction: L-arginine + O2 + NADPH → L-citrulline + NO + NADP+; NOS requires: NADPH (electron donor), tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4, pterin cofactor, 2 electrons from BH4 → dihydrobiopterin [BH2] → regenerated by dihydrofolate reductase [DHFR] using NADPH), molecular O2 (two O2 molecules per arginine), calmodulin (Ca2+-dependent, for eNOS and nNOS, not iNOS), heme (Fe-S) prosthetic group in NOS; NOS isoforms: eNOS (NOS3, endothelial, constitutive, Ca2+/CaM-dependent, mainly in endothelium → vasodilation); nNOS (NOS1, neuronal, constitutive, Ca2+/CaM-dependent, in neurons → neurotransmission); iNOS (NOS2, inducible, CaM-independent, in macrophages, hepatocytes → innate immunity/inflammation, produces large amounts of NO for prolonged periods); physiological NO: ↑cGMP (soluble guanylyl cyclase: NO → GC → cGMP → PKG → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation); also S-nitrosylation of proteins (covalent modification of Cys residues by NO → alters protein function)
explanation: Nitric oxide (NO) biology: Production: NOS (eNOS, nNOS, iNOS) → L-Arg + O2 → L-Citrulline + NO. eNOS activation: shear stress (Akt → eNOS Ser1177 phosphorylation), VEGF, acetylcholine (M3 receptors → Gq → IP3 → Ca2+ → calmodulin → eNOS). Signaling: NO → activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) → GTP → cGMP → PKG → MLCK inhibition + MLCP activation + ↓Ca2+ release → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation. Also: NO → cGMP → PDE5 inhibition → ↑cGMP (pharmacological target: sildenafil/tadalafil: PDE5 inhibitors → ↑cGMP → vasodilation → erectile dysfunction treatment + PAH). Cardiovascular: endothelial NO: (1) vasodilation (↓BP); (2) anti-platelet (↓aggregation + adhesion); (3) anti-proliferative (↓smooth muscle growth); (4) anti-inflammatory. L-NMMA (competitive NOS inhibitor) → ↑BP. Arginine paradox: high dietary arginine → ↑NO production despite plasma arginine already exceeding NOS Km → NOS compartmentalization + BH4 availability are limiting. BH4 deficiency → eNOS uncoupling: BH4 deficient eNOS uses O2 but passes electrons to O2 instead of arginine → produces superoxide (O2•-) instead of NO → ↑vascular oxidative stress → endothelial dysfunction (atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes). iNOS-derived NO (innate immunity): large, sustained NO production → combines with O2•- → peroxynitrite (ONOO-) → DNA damage, protein nitration → pathogen killing but also tissue damage in sepsis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: GLUT2 transporter is found in pancreatic beta-cells where it acts as a glucose sensor. What is its distinguishing property?
options: Low Km (~0.1 mM), high affinity for glucose, always saturated — THAT IS GLUT1 and hexokinase properties

Very high Km (~15-20 mM) and not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate: GLUT2 has a HIGH Km for glucose (~15-20 mM) compared to physiological blood glucose (5-6 mM fasting, ~8-10 mM post-prandial) → GLUT2 is not saturated at normal physiological glucose levels → glucose transport rate increases proportionally with blood glucose concentration → acts as a glucose sensor; in β-cells: ↑blood glucose → ↑glucose enters via GLUT2 → ↑glucokinase (hexokinase IV, also high Km, not inhibited by G6P) → ↑G6P → ↑glycolysis → ↑pyruvate → ↑TCA → ↑ATP → ATP/ADP ratio ↑ → KATP channel closes → membrane depolarization → L-type Ca2+ channel opens → Ca2+ influx → insulin vesicle exocytosis; also: GLUT2 in liver (high Km → captures glucose after a meal when portal glucose is highest) + intestine/kidney (GLUT2 at basolateral surface after SGLT1 at apical brush border)
Exclusive expression in brain neurons (that is GLUT3 which has very low Km)
Active transport (GLUT transporters are all facilitated diffusion, passive)
explanation: GLUT isoform comparison (key features): GLUT1: Km ~1 mM, constitutive glucose uptake, ubiquitous; ↑in cancer cells (Warburg effect, regulated by HIF-1α). GLUT2: Km ~15-20 mM, liver + β-cells + intestine + kidney; glucose sensor. GLUT3: Km ~1.5 mM, neurons (ensures glucose uptake even at low plasma glucose; brain glucose transport is not insulin-dependent). GLUT4: Km ~5 mM, insulin-sensitive (muscle, fat, heart); translocated to PM by insulin signaling or exercise (AMPK). GLUT5: fructose transporter (Km ~6 mM for fructose, no glucose), small intestine (apical) + testes. GLUT7: in ER of liver → pairs with G6Pase → exports glucose from ER lumen. GLUT9: urate transporter (SLC2A9, not primarily glucose). GLUT10: aorta, smooth muscle; mutations → arterial tortuosity syndrome. SGLT transporters (Na+-glucose co-transporters, secondary active): SGLT1: intestine apical + kidney S1/S2 (high affinity, low capacity for glucose + galactose); SGLT2: kidney proximal tubule S1 (low affinity, high capacity → reabsorbs ~90% of filtered glucose); SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins: empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin): block renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria → ↓blood glucose + ↓body weight + ↓blood pressure + ↓HbA1c; also: ↓cardiovascular events + ↓CKD progression (likely via hemodynamic + metabolic non-glycemic effects).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Iron absorption in the gut is facilitated by which specific transporter at the apical brush border of duodenal enterocytes?
options: Ferroportin (FPN1/IREG1/SLC40A1): this is the BASOLATERAL iron exporter (exports Fe2+ from enterocyte to bloodstream) — not the apical importer

Hepcidin is NOT a transporter but a peptide hormone from the liver that inhibits ferroportin (causes FPN1 internalization and degradation → ↓iron export from enterocyte and macrophage → ↓serum iron → ↑storage; ↑hepcidin in: inflammation/infection [IL-6 → hepcidin], iron overload; ↓hepcidin in: iron deficiency, hypoxia [↑EPO → ↑TMPRSS6/matriptase-2 → ↓BMP6 signaling → ↓SMAD → ↓hepcidin], hemolytic anemia, dyserythropoiesis)

Divalent metal transporter-1 (DMT1, SLC11A2): DMT1 is the primary transporter for non-heme iron (Fe2+) at the apical brush border of duodenal enterocytes; in the brush border: dietary Fe3+ → DcytB (duodenal cytochrome b, also called DCYTB, SDR2) → reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ using intracellular vitamin C as a cofactor; Fe2+ → DMT1 (proton-coupled, imports Fe2+ into enterocyte); inside enterocyte: Fe2+ either stored as ferritin or exported at basolateral surface via ferroportin-1 → Fe2+ + hephaestin (or serum ceruloplasmin) oxidize Fe2+ → Fe3+ → binds transferrin in blood; heme iron: dietary heme (from meat hemoglobin/myoglobin) absorbed via HCP1 (heme carrier protein 1, SLC46A1) or other mechanism → FLVCR (feline leukemia virus C receptor) may export heme → heme oxygenase → Fe2+ inside enterocyte

Transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1): mediates receptor-mediated endocytosis of diferric transferrin in most cell types; NOT the primary iron transporter at the apical brush border of enterocytes (dietary iron absorption)
explanation: Iron metabolism: Daily requirement: adult male 8 mg/day, premenopausal female 18 mg/day, pregnant ~27 mg/day. Dietary sources: heme iron (meat, high bioavailability ~15-35%); non-heme iron (plant-based, lower bioavailability ~1-10%, enhanced by Vit C, reduced by phytate/tannins/calcium). Absorption: duodenum + upper jejunum (DMT1, maximal absorption). Serum transferrin: transports 2 Fe3+ per molecule; normally 1/3 saturated (TIBC = total iron binding capacity = transferrin capacity). Ferritin: iron storage (liver, spleen, bone marrow macrophages); ferritin is an acute phase reactant (↑in inflammation even with iron deficiency). Iron deficiency anemia: microcytic, hypochromic (↓MCV, ↓MCH, ↓MCHC); ↓serum iron, ↑TIBC, ↓transferrin saturation (<20%), ↓serum ferritin (<12 µg/L, most specific low-iron test). Anemia of chronic disease (ACD): ↓serum iron (hepcidin ↑ → ↓FPN → iron trapped in macrophages/enterocytes), ↓TIBC (↓transferrin synthesis), ↑ferritin (↑storage, ↑acute phase reactant) → differentiates from IDA. Hemochromatosis: HFE hereditary: HFE C282Y mutation → ↑iron absorption (↑DMT1 expression in enterocyte, despite iron overload — normally iron overload → ↑hepcidin → ↓DMT1/FPN; HFE C282Y → impaired HFE-TfR1 interaction → ↑HFE-dependent signaling → ↓hepcidin regulation → ↑iron absorption). Treatment: venesection (phlebotomy) + deferoxamine/deferasirox (chelators for severe/transfusion hemochromatosis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Uric acid is the end product of purine catabolism in humans. The enzyme responsible for the last step is:
options: Xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH): the same enzyme as xanthine oxidase (XO) but uses NAD+ as electron acceptor instead of O2; under physiological conditions, predominantly in XDH form in tissues; converts to XO form (uses O2 → H2O2 + superoxide) during ischemia (calcium-activated protease cleaves XDH → XO) — important in ischemia-reperfusion injury

Xanthine oxidase (XO, actually the same as XDH, just a different redox state; XO is the O2-using form): XO catalyzes: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (two sequential oxidations); produces H2O2 and O2•- (superoxide) as byproducts; the molybdenum cofactor (MoCo) at the active site accepts electrons from the purine substrate; xanthine oxidoreductase (XOR) is the gene encoding both XDH and XO forms (same polypeptide, different redox states); allopurinol: xanthine oxidase inhibitor (hypoxanthine analog, converted to alloxanthine/oxypurinol by XO → tight-binding inhibitor of XO) → ↓uric acid production → treats gout + tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis + kidney stones (uric acid); febuxostat: non-purine, selective XO inhibitor (does not affect other molybdenum enzymes) → treats gout (FDA approved)
Adenosine deaminase (ADA): converts adenosine → inosine (not the last step in uric acid production; ADA acts upstream); ADA deficiency → SCID
Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP): cleaves inosine → hypoxanthine + ribose-1-P (not the final step, and PNP deficiency → T-cell immunodeficiency)
explanation: Purine catabolism pathway: AMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → adenosine → [ADA] → inosine. GMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → guanosine → [PNP] → guanine → [guanine deaminase] → xanthine. Adenosine → [PNP] → inosine → [PNP] → hypoxanthine → [XOR, step 1] → xanthine → [XOR, step 2] → uric acid. Uric acid (pKa 5.4): at physiological pH (7.4) → urate (sodium urate, soluble). At lower pH → uric acid (less soluble). Uric acid solubility: ~6.8 mg/dL at physiological pH → gout flares when >6.8 mg/dL (monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints, especially first metatarsophalangeal joint [podagra], knees, ankles; precipitated by alcohol, dehydration, rich protein meal, aspirin [low-dose aspirin ↓urate secretion in kidney], cyclosporine). Gout treatment: acute: colchicine (↓microtubule-dependent neutrophil function → ↓MSU crystal phagocytosis + ↓IL-1β release from NLRP3 inflammasome), NSAIDs, glucocorticoids. Chronic/prophylaxis: allopurinol (start low, increase slowly, check HLA-B*5801 in Han Chinese/Thai for SJS risk), febuxostat (no SJS risk), probenecid (uricosuric, blocks URAT1 renal tubular urate reabsorption → ↑uric acid excretion). Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency): ↑de novo purines → ↑uric acid + self-mutilation + intellectual disability + dystonia → treat with allopurinol for gout but no effect on neurological symptoms.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During exercise, AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) is activated. Its activation leads to all of the following EXCEPT:
options: ↑Fatty acid oxidation (AMPK → phospho-ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I inhibition → ↑FA import into mitochondria → ↑β-oxidation)
↑Glucose uptake in muscle (AMPK → phospho-AS160 → ↑Rab10 → GLUT4 vesicle translocation → ↑GLUT4 at PM → ↑glucose uptake; exercise-induced glucose uptake is AMPK-dependent and INSULIN-INDEPENDENT)

↑Glycogen synthesis (WRONG — AMPK phosphorylates and INHIBITS glycogen synthase [GS], just like PKA does → ↓glycogen synthesis; ATP is low during exercise → cell doesn't want to waste ATP on glycogen synthesis when it needs to generate ATP; additionally AMPK phosphorylates and INHIBITS ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA, as above): this is the EXCEPTION — AMPK INHIBITS glycogen synthesis

↑Mitochondrial biogenesis (AMPK → PGC-1α [peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1α] → ↑mitochondrial biogenesis: AMPK directly phosphorylates PGC-1α + indirectly activates SIRT1 (NAD+-dependent deacetylase) → deacetylates + activates PGC-1α → ↑nuclear transcription of mitochondrial genes [NRF1/2, TFAM] → ↑mitochondrial number + capacity → long-term exercise adaptation)
explanation: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase): Sensor of cellular energy status (AMP/ATP ratio). Activated when: AMP↑ (from ATP hydrolysis during exercise, hypoxia, ischemia), ADP↑; binding of AMP or ADP to regulatory γ subunit → conformational change → expose Thr172 on α subunit → phosphorylation by LKB1 (tumor suppressor, major upstream kinase; STK11 gene; Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: LKB1 mutations → GI hamartomas + pigmentation + ↑cancer risk) or CaMKKβ (in response to Ca2+ → relevant in muscle contraction). Also activated by: AICAR (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide → ZMP → mimics AMP; used experimentally), metformin (indirectly via ↑AMP from Complex I inhibition → AMPK activation). Metformin and AMPK: AMPK-dependent and independent effects; major effect is ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis (AMPK phosphorylates CRTC2 → nuclear export → ↓PEPCK/G6Pase transcription) + ↑GLUT4 translocation in muscle (AMPK-dependent). AMPK substrates: ACC1/2 (→ ↓FA synthesis + ↑FA oxidation), HMGCR (↓cholesterol synthesis), glycogen synthase (↓glycogen synthesis), PFKFB3 (↑F-2,6-BP → ↑glycolysis in some contexts), ULK1 (↑autophagy), TSC2 (↑mTORC1 inhibition → ↓protein synthesis). AMPK as tumor suppressor: LKB1 → AMPK → ↓mTORC1 → ↓cell growth + proliferation (LKB1 is one of the most commonly mutated genes in NSCLC: ~20-30%; also in pancreatic, cervical cancer).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which vitamin is required for the synthesis of BOTH clotting factors AND anticoagulant proteins, and its deficiency can paradoxically cause thrombosis?
options: Vitamin C (required for collagen only, not for clotting factors)
Vitamin B12 (required for methionine synthesis + methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; not for clotting factor synthesis)

Vitamin K: required for γ-carboxylation of Glu residues → Gla residues in: coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X) AND anticoagulant proteins (Protein C [t½ ~6h, FIRST anticoagulant protein to fall when warfarin started], Protein S, Protein Z); when warfarin is initiated: Protein C (very short t½ ~6h) falls faster than the procoagulant factors (Factor VII t½ ~6h but factors II [~60h], IX [~24h], X [~36h] take longer to fall) → transient ↑coagulant/anticoagulant ratio → TRANSIENT HYPERCOAGULABLE STATE → risk of warfarin-induced skin necrosis (especially in patients with underlying Protein C or Protein S deficiency who have even lower baseline PC/PS); to prevent: overlap with heparin for ≥5 days when starting warfarin (heparin immediately anticoagulates while warfarin takes 3-5 days to fully suppress procoagulant factors); Vitamin K deficiency itself: can cause both bleeding (↓factors II, VII, IX, X) and paradoxically contribute to thrombosis if Protein C/S are preferentially reduced
Vitamin D (↑bone density, calcium homeostasis; not directly involved in coagulation)
explanation: Protein C system and warfarin safety: Protein C (PC) deficiency: inherited (AR → homozygous neonatal purpura fulminans; heterozygous → ↑VTE risk, ~5-fold) or acquired (liver failure, DIC, warfarin initiation). Mechanism of warfarin-induced skin necrosis: Protein C short t½ → rapid decline → transient loss of natural anticoagulation → microvascular thrombosis in skin (adipose-rich areas: breasts, buttocks, thighs) → skin necrosis; esp. in PC deficiency + warfarin loading dose without heparin bridge. Management: 1. Always bridge with heparin/LMWH for ≥5 days when starting warfarin. 2. Avoid large loading doses of warfarin. 3. If necrosis occurs: stop warfarin, give FFP (or PCC, includes Protein C) + heparin + Vitamin K. Warfarin pharmacogenomics: CYP2C9 (metabolizes warfarin S-enantiomer): *2 (Arg144Cys), *3 (Ile359Leu) → ↓warfarin metabolism → need ↓dose. VKORC1 (target of warfarin): 1639G>A promoter variant → ↓VKORC1 expression → more sensitive to warfarin → need ↓dose. FDA-approved pharmacogenomic dosing algorithms (e.g., IWPC algorithm incorporating CYP2C9, VKORC1, and clinical factors) → more accurate initial dosing. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs): dabigatran (thrombin inhibitor), rivaroxaban/apixaban/edoxaban (FXa inhibitors) → do not require Vit K → no bridging issues with initiation → rapidly effective.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In renal handling of amino acids, which transport defect leads to Hartnup disease?
options: Cystine transport defect (SLC3A1/SLC7A9 mutations → cystinuria: 'COAL' amino acids: Cys, Ornithine, Arginine, Lysine — dibasic + cysteine)
Dibasic amino acid transport defect (that is lysinuric protein intolerance, SLC7A7 mutations)

Neutral amino acid transport defect in intestine and kidney (SLC6A19, B0AT1, large neutral amino acids): Hartnup disorder (AR, SLC6A19 gene): defective renal tubular and intestinal reabsorption of neutral amino acids (especially tryptophan, alanine, serine, threonine, glutamine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, phenylalanine, histidine, tyrosine) → ↑urinary neutral aminoaciduria + ↓intestinal absorption; gut bacteria convert non-absorbed tryptophan → indolic compounds (indole, indolepyruvate, indoleacetate) → absorbed → ↑urine indolylacetyl compounds (distinguishes from primary Trp deficiency); ↓intestinal Trp absorption → ↓niacin synthesis (Trp → nicotinic acid, kynurenine pathway) → pellagra-like rash (photosensitive, niacin deficiency); features: 3 Ds of pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) + cerebellar ataxia; intermittent presentation; treatment: nicotinamide (niacin) supplementation + high-protein diet
Proline transport defect (iminoglycinuria: proline + hydroxyproline + glycine in urine; usually benign)
explanation: Renal amino acid transport disorders: Generalized aminoaciduria: Fanconi syndrome (proximal tubular dysfunction → ↑all amino acids + glucose + phosphate + uric acid + bicarb in urine; causes: cystinosis, Wilson, galactosemia, LCAT deficiency, heavy metals). Specific transport defects: Cystinuria (SLC3A1 [type A], SLC7A9 [type B]): COLA (Cys, Orn, Lys, Arg) amino acids in urine → cystine stones (hexagonal, radiopaque, poorly soluble in acidic urine; treat: hydration + alkalinize urine + D-penicillamine or tiopronin [reduces cystine to cysteine]). Hartnup (SLC6A19): neutral amino acids → see above. Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI, SLC7A7): basolateral transport of Arg, Lys, Orn from gut + kidney → these AA not exported → ↑blood Gln/Glu, ↓Arg/Orn/Lys → ↑NH3 (Orn needed for urea cycle) → ↑protein intolerance + failure to thrive + osteoporosis + interstitial lung disease; treat: low-protein diet + citrulline (converted to Orn in urea cycle, bypasses LPI transporter). Iminoglycinuria: SLC36A2 (PAT2) or SLC6A19 deficiency → Pro, HyPro, Gly in urine; benign. Dicarboxylic aminoaciduria: SLC1A1 (EAAC1) deficiency → Glu + Asp in urine; benign.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Sphingomyelin is synthesized from:
options: Ceramide + choline phosphate from CDP-choline (via phosphocholine transfer): sphingomyelin synthase catalyzes: ceramide + phosphatidylcholine (or CDP-choline) → sphingomyelin + diacylglycerol (DAG) [or CMP]; the phosphocholine head group is transferred from PC to ceramide at the Golgi apparatus; ceramide (N-acyl sphingosine) is made in the ER: serine + palmitoyl-CoA → [serine palmitoyltransferase, SPT, rate-limiting, uses PLP] → 3-ketosphingosine → [3-ketosphingosine reductase] → sphinganine → [dihydroceramide synthase + acyl-CoA] → dihydroceramide → [dihydroceramide desaturase] → ceramide; fumonisin B1 (mycotoxin from Fusarium in corn) inhibits dihydroceramide synthase → ↓ceramide → ↓sphingolipid synthesis → ↑sphinganine + ↓sphingosine → cytotoxic effects → equine leukoencephalomalacia, porcine pulmonary edema, possibly human esophageal cancer
Ceramide + galactose (that makes galactocerebroside, a glycosphingolipid)
Ceramide + glucose (that makes glucocerebroside = glucosylceramide, the storage substrate in Gaucher disease)
Sphingosine + fatty acid (that forms ceramide, an upstream intermediate, not sphingomyelin itself)
explanation: Sphingolipid synthesis: Serine + palmitoyl-CoA → [SPT, ER] → 3-ketosphingosine → sphinganine → dihydroceramide → ceramide (the hub/backbone). Ceramide + phosphocholine → sphingomyelin (Golgi). Ceramide + glucose → glucocerebrosidase (GlcCer) → [LacCer synthase] → lactosylceramide → [further glycosylation] → complex glycosphingolipids (gangliosides GM1/GM2/GM3, globosides, etc.). Ceramide + galactose → galactocerebroside (GalCer, in myelin). Ceramide + phosphate-inositol → ceramide-1-phosphate or phosphoinositol-ceramide. Ceramide is also a second messenger: generated from sphingomyelin by sphingomyelinase (SMS → ceramide + phosphocholine) → ceramide activates: protein phosphatase 1/2A, Raf-1 (pro-apoptotic), inhibits PKB/Akt → promotes apoptosis + cell cycle arrest + stress responses; ceramide-1-phosphate (from ceramide kinase): anti-apoptotic, pro-inflammatory (activates cPLA2 → ↑AA → eicosanoids). Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P): produced by sphingosine kinase (SphK1/2) from sphingosine (ceramide → ceramidase → sphingosine + FA; sphingosine + ATP → S1P) → binds S1P receptors (S1P1-5) → anti-apoptotic, pro-angiogenic, immune cell trafficking; fingolimod (FTY720): sphingosine analog → phosphorylated by SphK2 → FTY720-P binds S1P1 → lymphocyte sequestration in lymph nodes → ↓lymphocyte traffic to CNS → immunosuppression in MS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme that is uniquely absent in mature erythrocytes compared to other cells, explaining why stored blood loses its ability to deliver O2 effectively:
options: Pyruvate kinase (PK is present in RBCs; PK deficiency causes hemolytic anemia)
Hexokinase (HK is present in RBCs; HK deficiency causes rare hemolytic anemia)
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD is present; its deficiency causes hemolytic anemia in response to oxidants)

Mitochondria: mature RBCs have NO mitochondria (mitochondria are extruded during reticulocyte maturation as part of terminal erythropoiesis) → RBCs cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation → entirely dependent on glycolysis for ATP (2 ATP net per glucose) → also no TCA, no β-oxidation, no de novo lipid synthesis; consequences: RBCs cannot regenerate NADH via ETC → if excessive methemoglobin forms (Fe3+), the back-up reduction system (methemoglobin reductase/cytochrome b5 reductase, NADH-dependent) is limited; RBCs use G6PD/PPP for NADPH; RBCs have unique dependence on carbonic anhydrase II (CA-II, present in large amounts) for CO2 transport; RBCs maintain 2,3-BPG via Rapoport-Luebering shunt; mature RBCs also lack a nucleus → cannot synthesize new proteins
explanation: Mature RBC unique features: Biconcave disc shape: ↑surface area/volume ratio → ↑gas exchange efficiency; maintained by spectrin-actin cytoskeleton anchored to lipid bilayer via ankyrin (binds band 3 + spectrin) and protein 4.2 + adducin; RHCE/RHD → Rh antigens (band 3 is the anion exchanger [AE1, SLC4A1], transports HCO3-/Cl- exchange for CO2 transport). No nucleus: cannot transcribe new proteins; cannot repair DNA; finite lifespan ~120 days. No mitochondria: pure glycolysis → 2 ATP/glucose; no aerobic metabolism; must use NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase for methemoglobin reduction + G6PD/PPP for NADPH + antioxidant defense. No organelles: no ER → no protein synthesis; no Golgi → no membrane trafficking. Membrane stability: phospholipid bilayer maintained by aminophospholipid translocase (flippase, ATP8A1) → keeps PS on inner leaflet; lipid raft-associated proteins (glycophorin, ABO blood group antigens). Stored blood (bank blood) deterioration: storage lesion → ↓2,3-BPG (→ ↑O2 affinity → ↓O2 delivery), ↑potassium (K+ leaks out), ↑free Hb (hemolysis), ↓ATP, ↓NO (scavenged by free Hb → vasoconstriction), shape changes (echinocytes), cell membrane stiffening; generally deteriorates functionally over 42 days storage.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The product of the reaction catalyzed by aconitase in the TCA cycle is:
options: Citrate (aconitase converts citrate to isocitrate, not the other way for the forward reaction)

Isocitrate: aconitase (aconitate hydratase, Fe-S [4Fe-4S] enzyme) converts citrate ⇌ isocitrate (reversible but proceeds forward under TCA conditions) via a cis-aconitate intermediate (enzyme-bound, not released); the reaction: citrate → cis-aconitate (dehydration) → isocitrate (rehydration); net: citrate → isocitrate with migration of hydroxyl group from C3 to C2; isocitrate is then the substrate for isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH, NAD+) → α-KG + CO2 + NADH (rate-limiting step of TCA); inhibited by fluorocitrate (formed from fluoroacetate [rat poison: sodium fluoroacetate/compound 1080] which enters as fluoroacetyl-CoA via ACL and condenses with OAA → fluorocitrate → suicide inhibitor of aconitase → TCA blocked → cell death + particularly affects heart [depends heavily on TCA])
Oxaloacetate (OAA is the TCA cycle starter → condensed with acetyl-CoA by citrate synthase → citrate)
explanation: TCA cycle aconitase details: Enzyme: aconitate hydratase (ACON1/ACON2); contains a [4Fe-4S] cluster. Mechanism: two-step: (1) citrate → [dehydration] → cis-aconitate (Fe-S facilitates); (2) cis-aconitate → [rehydration, but different -OH added to C2] → isocitrate. Stereochemistry: citrate is a pro-chiral molecule (the two -CH2COO- arms are chemically identical but enzyme distinguishes them via the 'prochiral center') → aconitase adds -OH to the pro-S arm → (2R,3S)-isocitrate specifically → isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) is also stereospecific. IRP regulation: Aconitase has a dual function: when Fe is ADEQUATE, Fe-S cluster is intact → aconitase enzymatic activity. When Fe is LOW: Fe-S cluster disassembles → apoprotein becomes IRP1 (iron regulatory protein 1) → IRP1 binds IRE (iron response elements, hairpin loops in 5' or 3' UTR of mRNAs): 5' IRE: ferritin mRNA (storage), ↑IRP1 → blocks translation → ↓ferritin (don't store when Fe low); DMT1 mRNA 3' IRE, TfR1 mRNA 3' IRE: ↑IRP1 → stabilizes mRNA (prevents degradation) → ↑DMT1 + ↑TfR1 → ↑iron uptake + transport (absorb more Fe when Fe low). Fluoroacetate (1080 rat poison): metabolized to fluoroacetyl-CoA → fluorocitrate by citrate synthase → fluorocitrate is a potent COMPETITIVE inhibitor of aconitase (suicide substrate) → TCA arrested at citrate step → ↑citrate, ↓ATP → cardiac arrest and CNS toxicity; used in rodenticide; antidote: glycerol monoacetate (glycerol acetate, 'companion' that bypasses the acetyl-CoA deficiency).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 2-year-old child presents with recurrent infections, failure to thrive, and is found to have absence of T and B lymphocytes. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) enzyme replacement therapy is initiated. In which metabolic pathway does ADA function?
options: Purine nucleotide salvage: ADA catalyzes the deamination of adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine respectively (adenosine + H2O → inosine + NH3; deoxyadenosine + H2O → deoxyinosine + NH3); this is part of the purine nucleotide degradation/recycling pathway; ADA deficiency → ↑deoxyadenosine (dAdo) in lymphocytes → dAdo is phosphorylated to dATP by deoxykinases → ↑↑dATP accumulates → dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) → ↓dCTP supply → ↓DNA synthesis → lymphocyte apoptosis → SCID; ADA gene therapy (Strimvelis): γ-retroviral vector, autologous HSCs transduced ex vivo → infused back → approved in Europe 2016; also: ADA-PEG (pegademase bovine): PEGylated bovine ADA injected IM; reduces dATP in lymphocytes → partial immune reconstitution; definitive treatment: HSCT
Pyrimidine synthesis (ADA is specific to purines, not pyrimidines)
De novo purine synthesis (ADA degrades purines, not synthesizes; and ADA deficiency causes T and B cell loss)
Urea cycle (this involves arginine/citrulline metabolism, not purine metabolism)
explanation: SCID differential diagnosis by molecular mechanism: ADA deficiency (AR): ↑dATP → inhibits RNR → ↓dCTP → ↓DNA synthesis; T-B-NK- SCID (all lymphocytes absent). PNP deficiency (AR): ↑dGTP → inhibits RNR in T cells → T-B+NK- SCID (B cells relatively spared). IL2RG (X-linked, common γ chain): T-B+NK- SCID (X-linked, most common, affects T and NK not B; T+ B+ NK+ activity requires IL-2/4/7/9/15/21 signaling through γc). RAG1/RAG2 deficiency (AR): no V(D)J recombination → T-B-NK+ SCID. Artemis deficiency (AR): defect in NHEJ repair of V(D)J recombination breaks → T-B-NK+ SCID + radiation sensitivity. JAK3 deficiency (AR): JAK3 associates with IL2RG → same phenotype as X-linked SCID but AR. IL7Rα deficiency (AR): ↓T cell development → T-B+NK+ SCID. MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II): AR; ↓CD4 T cells; recurrent bacterial + fungal infections. Omenn syndrome: RAG1/2 or other V(D)J genes hypomorphic mutations → some autoreactive T cells generated → eosinophilia, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly + SCID features. SCID treatment: HSCT curative (best outcome if done early + HLA-matched sibling donor); gene therapy for ADA-SCID, X-linked SCID.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the role of 'UGA' codon in human mitochondrial translation?
options: It is a stop codon in human mitochondria, just as in the nuclear-encoded cytoplasmic translation
UGA codes for Cysteine in mitochondria (UGA = Sec [selenocysteine] by redefinition in cytoplasmic translation at specific Sec insertion sequences, SECIS elements; in mito UGA = Trp)

UGA codes for Tryptophan in human mitochondria: human mitochondria use a slightly different genetic code than the nuclear/cytoplasmic genetic code; in human mtDNA: (1) UGA (nuclear stop) → Trp (added as an amino acid); (2) AUA (nuclear Ile) → Met (in mito, both AUG and AUA serve as Met codons); (3) AGA and AGG (nuclear Arg) → Stop codons (UAG remains a stop codon too; TGA/UGA becomes Trp in mito); this allows the 22 mt-tRNAs to decode all 60+ sense codons by allowing wobble at the third position (super-wobble rules); mammalian mitochondria can decode all 64 codons with just 22 tRNAs (the minimum possible) by using extended wobble rules (U in anticodon position 34 can pair with all 4 bases at codon position 3; called four-way wobble or 'U wobble')
UGA codes for Selenocysteine in human mitochondria (that is the 21st amino acid, but this occurs in cytoplasmic ribosomes at UGA + SECIS element; not related to mitochondria)
explanation: Mitochondrial genetic code deviations from universal (in human mtDNA): Universal → Mitochondrial: UGA (Stop) → Trp. AGA (Arg) → Stop. AGG (Arg) → Stop. AUA (Ile) → Met. (All other codons same as universal). Consequences: (1) Mitochondrial proteins from 13 genes (ND1-6, ND4L, COX1-3, ATP6, ATP8, Cytochrome b) use UGA for Trp insertion → incompatible with cytoplasmic ribosomes. (2) AGA/AGG = stop in mito → the mito CYTOCHROME c OXIDASE subunit 1 (COX1) terminates with TAAGGGT (where AGG is the mito stop codon for the +1 reading frame); many mitochondrial open reading frames use incomplete stop codons (U or UA at end of coding sequence → polyadenylation adds A's to create UAA stop codon → 'UAA generation by polyadenylation'). (3) Only 22 tRNAs in mito → super-wobble (single U at wobble position pairs with all four bases → 1 tRNA decodes 4 codons rather than needing multiple tRNAs). Mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases: encoded by nuclear genes, imported into mitochondria; distinct from cytoplasmic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases; mutations in mt-aaRS genes (e.g., RARS2, DARS2, AARS2) → mitochondrial diseases with distinctive clinical phenotypes (LBSL for DARS2, various encephalomyopathies).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Transferrin receptor 2 (TFR2) and HFE protein interact to regulate hepcidin synthesis. In hereditary hemochromatosis type 1 (HFE hemochromatosis), what is the primary consequence of HFE C282Y mutation?
options: ↑Hepcidin production → ↑iron absorption (incorrect — HFE hemochromatosis has DECREASED hepcidin, causing iron overload)

↓Hepcidin production → ↑intestinal iron absorption → iron overload: HFE protein normally associates with TFR1 and participates in sensing iron-saturated transferrin → signal to liver to produce hepcidin (via BMP6-SMAD signaling); HFE C282Y mutation → HFE cannot associate properly with TFR1/TFR2 → ↓iron-sensing → ↓hepcidin production despite iron overload → ↓hepcidin → ↓binding to ferroportin → FPN not internalized → FPN continues to export iron from enterocytes + macrophages → ↑serum iron → ↑transferrin saturation (>45-50%, often >75%) → ↑NTBI (non-transferrin-bound iron) → free iron deposited in liver, pancreas, heart, joints, pituitary; clinical: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC, ↑risk ~20×), cirrhosis, 'bronzed diabetes' (diabetes + skin pigmentation), arthritis (calcium pyrophosphate/chondrocalcinosis in metacarpophalangeal joints), hypogonadism (pituitary iron), cardiomyopathy
↑Absorption of all metals including copper, leading to Wilson-like disease
Normal hepcidin + normal iron absorption but abnormal storage in macrophages
explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HH): Type 1 (HFE, most common, AR): HFE C282Y/C282Y homozygous (~85% of HH); C282Y/H63D compound heterozygous (~5%); ↓hepcidin → ↑iron absorption → iron overload. Type 2 (juvenile HH, severe): HJV (hemojuvelin, type 2A) or HAMP (hepcidin, type 2B) mutations → ↓hepcidin → severe iron overload by 20-30 years. Type 3: TFR2 mutations → ↓hepcidin signaling. Type 4 (ferroportin disease): SLC40A1 mutations → two subtypes: 4A (FPN loss-of-function → iron trapped in macrophages, ↑ferritin, ↑hepcidin, relatively resistant to FPN-IM); 4B (FPN gain-of-function → FPN resistant to hepcidin → iron overload similar to type 1). Labs: ↑serum ferritin, ↑transferrin saturation (best early screening), ↑serum iron, normal TIBC or ↓TIBC. Liver biopsy: ↑hepatic iron index (HII = µmol Fe/g dry liver ÷ age; >2 = HH in HFE era, now molecular testing preferred). MRI liver: ↓signal on T2* (Fe deposits ↑T2* relaxation → dark liver). Treatment: phlebotomy (remove 500 mL blood [~250 mg Fe] weekly until ferritin < 50 ng/mL → then maintenance); chelators (deferoxamine/deferasirox) if phlebotomy not possible; avoid alcohol + Vit C supplements. Prognosis: early treatment (before cirrhosis/diabetes) → normal life expectancy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In which disease is an elevated level of phytanic acid (a branched-chain fatty acid) in serum a diagnostic finding?
options: Refsum disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type IV): caused by deficiency of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase (PHYH, also called PhyH or PAHX) → cannot perform alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid (phytanic acid has a methyl branch at the alpha carbon → cannot directly enter beta-oxidation → must first undergo alpha-oxidation: phytanic acid → [phytanoyl-CoA dioxygenase/hydroxylase, requires O2, iron, 2-oxoglutarate, Vit C] → 2-hydroxyphytanic acid → [2-hydroxy phytanoyl-CoA lyase] → pristanal (aldehyde) → [aldehyde dehydrogenase] → pristanic acid → can now enter beta-oxidation); PHYH deficiency → phytanic acid accumulates → deposits in nervous system, retina; phytanic acid source: chlorophyll from plant food (phytol in chlorophyll → phytanic acid after digestion); clinical: progressive peripheral neuropathy (mixed motor + sensory), cerebellar ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness), sensorineural deafness, ichthyosis, cardiac arrhythmia; treatment: phytanic acid-restricted diet (avoid green vegetables, ruminant fat/liver); plasmapheresis for rapid reduction
Zellweger syndrome (defective peroxisome biogenesis, PEX gene mutations — has ↑VLCFA, not ↑phytanic acid specifically as the diagnostic test)
Adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD, ABCD1 mutations → ↑VLCFA [C22-C26], not phytanic acid)
Propionic acidemia (defective PCC → ↑propionylcarnitine, ↑propionic acid, not phytanic acid)
explanation: Peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation diseases: Alpha-oxidation (peroxisomal): phytanic acid (3-methyl FA) → requires PHYH (hydroxylase) → pristanal → pristanic acid → beta-oxidation; Refsum disease: PHYH deficiency → ↑phytanic acid. Beta-oxidation (peroxisomal, for VLCFA): VLCFA (C22-C26+) → must be shortened in peroxisome before transport to mitochondria; ABCD1 (adrenoleukodystrophy protein, ALDP): imports VLCFA-CoA into peroxisome; X-ALD (X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, ABCD1 mutations): ↑VLCFA (C24:0, C26:0) → demyelination (ALD brain form: childhood, fatal) + adrenal insufficiency (Addison) + slowly progressive spinal cord disease (AMN, adrenomyeloneuropathy, adult males); treatment: Lorenzo's oil (4:1 glyceryl trioleate:trierucate ratio, ↓VLCFA synthesis) + HSCT (for early cerebral ALD). Zellweger spectrum (PBD, peroxisome biogenesis disorders, PEX gene mutations): ↑VLCFA + ↑phytanic acid (cannot import or form peroxisomes → all peroxisomal functions lost); severe neurological disease + liver disease + adrenal insufficiency + retinopathy; Zellweger syndrome (most severe), neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy, infantile Refsum disease (ISD). IRD: ↑phytanic + ↑VLCFA but less severe phenotype than ZS. Peroxisomal beta-oxidation produces H2O2 (from acyl-CoA oxidase → oxidation uses O2, produces H2O2 → catalase breaks down H2O2; unlike mitochondrial beta-oxidation that produces FADH2 → ETC).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature that distinguishes non-competitive inhibition from uncompetitive inhibition on a Lineweaver-Burk (LB) plot?
options: Uncompetitive inhibition lines intersect at the x-axis (incorrect)
Both types of inhibition show parallel lines on the LB plot (this describes only uncompetitive inhibition, NOT non-competitive)
