Non-competitive inhibition: lines intersect at the x-axis (same apparent Km, reduced Vmax); Uncompetitive inhibition: parallel lines (both Km and Vmax reduced by same factor α'): non-competitive inhibition (Vmax ↓, Km unchanged): Lineweaver-Burk (double reciprocal plot, 1/V vs 1/[S]): same x-intercept (-1/Km is same → x-intercepts overlap at the same point), y-intercepts differ (↑1/Vmax) → lines for different inhibitor concentrations intersect at the x-axis; the slope of each line also changes (slope = Km/Vmax → but Km unchanged, Vmax ↓ → slope ↑). Uncompetitive inhibition (both Vmax and Km ↓ by same factor α'): slope = Km/Vmax = Km/(α'Vmax) × (1/α') = ... wait: slope = αKm/αVmax unchanged; actually slope doesn't change (Km/Vmax unchanged since both decrease by α') → parallel lines on LB plot (same slope, different y-intercepts [↑1/apparent Vmax] and x-intercepts [-1/apparent Km shifted → different x-intercepts on LB plot]): parallel lines on LB = hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition
Lines intersect in the third quadrant for uncompetitive inhibition
explanation: Lineweaver-Burk plot summary (1/V vs 1/[S]): y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = -1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax. Type (change vs uninhibited): Competitive: same y-intercept (same Vmax), different x-intercept (↑apparent Km → x-intercept shifts toward 0, closer to origin); slopes ↑ (Km↑, Vmax same); lines intersect at y-axis. Uncompetitive: different y-intercept (↑1/apparent Vmax → ↑y-intercept) and different x-intercept (apparent Km ↓ → -1/apparent Km closer to zero on negative x-axis, absolute x-intercept increases); but crucially SLOPE is UNCHANGED (slope = Km/Vmax; both Km and Vmax decrease by α' → slope = Km/α' / Vmax/α' = Km/Vmax → unchanged); → PARALLEL LINES. Non-competitive: y-intercept changes (Vmax↓ → 1/Vmax ↑) but x-intercept same (Km unchanged → -1/Km unchanged); slope changes (Km/Vmax: Km same, Vmax ↓ → slope ↑); → lines intersect at x-axis. Mixed inhibition: both x- and y-intercepts change; lines intersect somewhere in quadrant II (left of y-axis, above x-axis usually) or quadrant III (left of y-axis, below x-axis). Substrate inhibition (substrate acts as inhibitor at high [S]): LB plot gives a 'hook' at low 1/[S] (high [S]) end (curve deviates from linearity). Note: LB plot magnifies error at low [S] (high 1/[S]) → large experimental errors; Eadie-Hofstee (V vs V/[S]) or Hanes-Woolf ([S]/V vs [S]) are more statistically reliable.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biotin is covalently attached to carboxylase enzymes via which amino acid?
options: Serine (OH group — serine is the phosphorylation site for enzymes like glycogen synthase, but not for biotin attachment)
Tyrosine (OH group — tyrosine is phosphorylated by RTKs, not the biotin attachment site)

Lysine (ε-amino group of lysine): biotin is covalently attached to enzyme through an amide bond between the carboxyl group of biotin's valeric acid side chain and the ε-amino group of a specific lysine residue in each biotin-dependent carboxylase; the biotinyl domain of each holoenzyme contains the conserved sequence (AMKM or GKME) with the active lysine in the center; this covalent bond is formed by holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS): biotin + ATP → biotinyl-5'-AMP + PPi; then biotinyl-5'-AMP + ε-NH2 of Lys → biotin-Lys (biocytin) + AMP; HLCS deficiency: multiple carboxylase deficiency type I (biotin cannot be attached to any carboxylase → all four carboxylases inactive → metabolic acidosis + neurological + dermatological features); biotinidase deficiency: type II multiple carboxylase deficiency (cannot recycle biocytin from proteolyzed carboxylase → free biotin not recovered → biotin deficiency → same result)
explanation: Biotin (Vitamin B7) metabolism: Food sources: eggs (raw egg white contains avidin, a glycoprotein that binds biotin with extremely high affinity, Kd ~10-15 M, highest affinity of any known protein-ligand interaction [higher than streptavidin] → prevents biotin absorption → raw egg white biotin deficiency; cooking destroys avidin). Liver, nuts, seeds, dairy also good sources. RDA: ~30 µg/day (adequate intake, AI; RDA not established). Biotin recycling: proteolysis of biotin-carboxylase → biocytin (biotinyl-lysine) → [biotinidase] → free biotin + lysine → reused. Holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS, ligase, E.C. 6.3.4.10): attaches biotin to apo-carboxylases. Biotin-streptavidin interaction: used extensively in molecular biology: biotin-labeled nucleic acid probes/antibodies + streptavidin (or avidin) → detection systems (ELISA, pull-down assays, bead-based assays, HRP or fluorophore conjugated streptavidin). Multiple carboxylase deficiency: HLCS deficiency (early-onset/severe) or biotinidase deficiency (late-onset/mild-moderate) → same clinical features: ketoacidosis + lactic acidosis (↓PC → ↓gluconeogenesis, ↑pyruvate; ↓ACC?), organic aciduria (↑methylcitrate + ↑propionylcarnitine [↓PCC], ↑3-methylcrotonylglycine [↓MCC], ↑lactate [↓PC]), skin rash (seborrheic dermatitis), alopecia, conjunctivitis, ataxia, intellectual disability; newborn screening: biotinidase enzyme assay in blood spot → early detection → treatment with pharmacological biotin (5-10 mg/day) → largely prevents all symptoms.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which protein is mutated in Marfan syndrome, leading to aortic root dilation and ectopia lentis?
options: Collagen type I (mutated in osteogenesis imperfecta)
Elastin (mutated in cutis laxa or supravalvular aortic stenosis/Williams syndrome)

Fibrillin-1 (FBN1): Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in FBN1 gene (chromosome 15q21.1) encoding fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein that polymerizes to form microfibrils in the extracellular matrix; microfibrils serve structural roles in ECM and also sequester latent TGF-β (as part of LTBP [latent TGF-β binding protein] complexes); FBN1 mutations → dysfunctional microfibrils → (1) structural weakness of large vessels, lens zonules, dura → aortic root dilation + dissection, ectopia lentis (upward/temporal lens dislocation, vs. CBS deficiency = downward), scoliosis, tall stature, arachnodactyly, pectus; (2) ↑TGF-β signaling (unsequestered from ECM) → contributes to aortic wall disease; treatment: β-blockers (losartan also being studied — blocks AT1R → ↓TGF-β signaling) + elective aortic root repair when diameter >5 cm
Fibronectin (an ECM glycoprotein but not the Marfan gene)
explanation: Marfan vs. Homocystinuria (CBS deficiency) comparison (classic NEET PG MCQ theme): Both: tall, thin, arachnodactyly, scoliosis, lens dislocation. Differences: Marfan: AR dominant (AD, FBN1); lens subluxation UPWARD (elevator goes UP in Marfan); NO thrombosis; NO intellectual disability; aortic root disease. CBS deficiency: AR; lens subluxation DOWNWARD (falls DOWN when CBS is broken); thromboembolism (major complication, caused by elevated Hcy: endothelial damage + ↑platelet aggregation); intellectual disability; osteoporosis; elevated plasma homocysteine + methionine. Mnemonic: 'Marfan = MAR [go UP like a star], CBS = DOWN and clot.' Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS): diverse group of connective tissue disorders (many subtypes: classical, hypermobile, vascular, kyphoscoliotic, etc.); various gene mutations: COL5A1/2 (classical), COL3A1 (vascular EDS [vEDS], most severe, ↑risk of arterial/bowel rupture), PLOD1 (kyphoscoliotic, lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency), TNXB (tenascin X). Features: hyperelastic skin, hypermobile joints, dystrophic scarring, easy bruising. Cutis laxa: loss of elastic tissue (ELN [elastin], FBLN4/5 [fibulin], ATP7A [copper, needed for LOX to cross-link elastin]) → loose, sagging skin (unlike EDS where skin is hyperelastic). Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE): ABCC6 mutations → calcification of elastic fibers → angioid streaks in retina, cardiovascular calcifications, skin lesions.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The reaction catalyzed by glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) in the liver is best described as:
options: Glutamate → glutamine (that is glutamine synthetase [GS]: Glu + NH3 + ATP → Gln; GS is active in brain + muscle for NH3 disposal; GDH is a different enzyme)
Glutamine → glutamate (that is glutaminase: Gln + H2O → Glu + NH3; important in kidney and gut)

Glutamate → α-ketoglutarate + NH3 (oxidative deamination): GDH catalyzes: L-glutamate + NAD+ (or NADP+) ⇌ α-ketoglutarate + NH3 + NADH (or NADPH); reversible reaction; located in mitochondrial matrix; the REVERSE direction (NH3 + α-KG → Glu) is important in nitrogen fixation in bacteria and NH3 assimilation; in mammals, the FORWARD direction is dominant in the liver (for NH3 release into urea cycle) and REVERSE direction helps replenish TCA intermediates; allosteric regulation: ACTIVATED by: ADP, GDP, leucine (signals abundant nitrogen for catabolism + available TCA intermediates → use them), amino acids in portal blood; INHIBITED by: GTP, ATP (high energy → don't need to oxidize AA), NADH, NADPH (↑reduction state); hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia syndrome: GDH gain-of-function mutation → insensitive to GTP inhibition → ↑GDH activity → ↑glutamate oxidation → ↑NH3 + ↑α-KG → ↑TCA flux → ↑ATP → ↑insulin secretion → hypoglycemia + hyperammonemia
α-ketoglutarate → glutamate using glutamine as amino donor (transamination — that is α-KG + amino acid ↔ Glu + keto acid, catalyzed by aminotransferases, not GDH)
explanation: Nitrogen metabolism overview: Transamination: amino acid + α-KG ↔ keto acid + Glu (aminotransferases, PLP-dependent; concentrates N into Glu). Oxidative deamination: Glu + NAD+ → α-KG + NH3 (GDH; releases NH3 into urea cycle). Urea cycle (liver): combines NH3 + NH2 from aspartate → urea (non-toxic, excreted by kidney). Glutamine synthesis: Glu + NH3 + ATP → Gln (GS; traps NH3 in non-toxic form for transport in blood). Glutamine release: blood Gln → liver (GLS: Gln → Glu + NH3 → urea cycle) + kidney (GLS → NH3 → buffering urine/excreted as NH4+). Alanine-glucose cycle (Cahill cycle): muscle catabolizes AA (especially BCAA) → N transferred to pyruvate (ALT) → Ala → blood → liver (ALT reverses: Ala → pyruvate + Glu → N into urea cycle, pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → glucose → blood → muscle). Purine nucleotide cycle: in muscle during exercise: AMP → IMP + NH3 (AMP deaminase) → IMP → SAMP [ASS using Asp] → AMP [adenylosuccinase, releases fumarate] → net: Asp → fumarate + NH3; provides fumarate for TCA + releases NH3 for deamination reactions. BCAA (val, leu, ile): catabolized mainly in MUSCLE (unlike other AA catabolized in liver) → BCAA aminotransferase (BCAT1 cytoplasm, BCAT2 mitochondria) → α-keto acids → BCKDC (branch-chain keto acid dehydrogenase complex; deficient in MSUD) → propionyl-CoA (Val, Ile) or acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate (Leu, Ile) → TCA or ketogenesis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In which cellular location are secretory proteins initially targeted after synthesis?
options: Golgi apparatus (secretory proteins first go to ER, then Golgi)

Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): secretory proteins contain an N-terminal signal sequence (signal peptide) recognized co-translationally by the signal recognition particle (SRP); SRP (6 proteins + 7SL RNA, a ~300 kDa ribonucleoprotein): (1) ribosome starts synthesizing signal peptide → (2) SRP binds signal peptide (via M domain of SRP54) → (3) translation pauses/slows → (4) SRP-ribosome-nascent chain complex docks with SRP receptor (SR, heterodimer of SRα+SRβ) on RER membrane → (5) GTP hydrolysis by SRP54 + SRα → SRP released → (6) ribosome transferred to translocon (Sec61 channel, protein-conducting channel) → (7) translation resumes with cotranslational translocation of nascent polypeptide into ER lumen through Sec61; in ER lumen: signal peptide cleaved by signal peptidase; glycosylation (N-linked, at Asn-X-Ser/Thr by OST [oligosaccharyltransferase] — transfers 14-sugar core from dolichol-PP-oligosaccharide); disulfide bond formation (PDI, protein disulfide isomerase, oxidizing environment of ER lumen unlike cytoplasm); protein folding by calnexin, calreticulin (lectin chaperones)
Mitochondria (mitochondrial proteins are imported post-translationally via TOM/TIM complex; they have N-terminal MTS [mitochondrial targeting sequence] that forms amphipathic α-helix)
Nucleus (nuclear proteins have NLS [nuclear localization signal] recognized by importins; imported through NPC post-translationally)
explanation: Protein sorting summary: Secretory/membrane/lysosomal proteins: RER → Golgi (cis → medial → trans) → sorted: (1) constitutive secretion → plasma membrane/extracellular; (2) regulated secretion → secretory vesicles (insulin, zymogen); (3) lysosomal targeting → mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag added in Golgi by GlcNAc phosphotransferase (deficient in I-cell disease/mucolipidosis II → M6P missing → lysosomal enzymes secreted instead of targeted to lysosomes → inclusion bodies in cells) → M6P receptor (M6PR) in trans-Golgi → coated vesicle → endosome → lysosome. Mitochondrial import: post-translational; MTS (N-terminal, amphipathic α-helix, rich in Arg) recognized by Tom20/Tom22 (TOM complex, outer membrane) → translocated to TIM23 (inner membrane) → matrix via HSP70; signal cleaved by MPP (matrix processing peptidase). Peroxisomal import: PTS1 (C-terminal Ser-Lys-Leu or variant) or PTS2 (N-terminal) → recognized by PEX5 (cytoplasmic receptor for PTS1) or PEX7 (PTS2) → docked at peroxisomal membrane (PEX14 + PEX13 in PTS1 pathway) → transported fully folded (unique among organelle imports). Nuclear import: NLS (nuclear localization signal, often rich in Lys/Arg) → importin-α (adaptor) + importin-β → NPC (Ran-GTP gradient: high Ran-GTP in nucleus → importin releases cargo; high Ran-GDP in cytoplasm → importin loads cargo). ER quality control: misfolded proteins → calnexin/calreticulin cycle → BiP/GRP78 → if repeatedly misfolded → ERAD (ER-associated degradation): retrotranslocated via Sec61 channel → ubiquitinated → proteasome.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The primary structure of a protein is maintained by which type of bond?
options: Disulfide bonds (S-S bonds between Cys residues — these are covalent but stabilize 3D structure [tertiary], not primary structure)
Hydrogen bonds (H-bonds stabilize secondary and tertiary structure)

Peptide bonds (covalent bonds): the primary structure of a protein is the linear sequence of amino acids connected by peptide bonds (amide bonds); formed between the α-carboxyl group of one amino acid and the α-amino group of the next amino acid via condensation (loss of water); the peptide bond has partial double-bond character (~40% double bond due to resonance delocalization of the nitrogen lone pair electrons into the carbonyl → planar, rigid, ~1.33 Å bond length [between single 1.45Å and double 1.25Å]) → the bond cannot freely rotate (trans configuration is preferred, ~99.9% trans around the Cω-N bond [only Pro can form cis peptide bonds more readily due to ring constraint → ~10% cis for Xaa-Pro peptide bonds vs ~0.1% for all others]); free rotation does occur around: Cα-N (φ, phi angle) and Cα-C (ψ, psi angle) → Ramachandran plot defines allowed φ/ψ combinations for different secondary structures (α-helix: φ≈-57°, ψ≈-47°; β-sheet: φ≈-120°, ψ≈+130°)
Ionic (salt) bonds (electrostatic interactions between charged side chains; stabilize tertiary structure, broken at extreme pH)
explanation: Protein structural hierarchy: Primary: AA sequence + peptide bonds. Secondary: α-helix (right-handed, 3.6 AA/turn, stabilized by H-bonds between C=O of residue i and N-H of residue i+4, rise 0.15 nm per residue; destabilized by: Pro [no NH for H-bond, kink], multiple adjacent charged residues [repulsion], Gly [too flexible]), β-sheet (parallel/antiparallel, H-bonds between different strands; hydrophobic residues inside; antiparallel more stable). Tertiary: overall 3D fold; stabilized by: hydrophobic interactions (primary driving force, entropy-driven burial of hydrophobic residues in core), H-bonds, ionic bonds (salt bridges), disulfide bonds (covalent, strongest individual stabilizer; formed in RER by PDI or outside cell; important in secretory proteins/Abs). Quaternary: association of subunits. Protein denaturation: disrupts secondary/tertiary (H-bonds, hydrophobic, ionic) and quaternary structure without breaking peptide bonds (unless proteolytic) or disulfide bonds (unless reducing agent); agents: heat (vibrational entropy), urea/guanidinium (break H-bonds), SDS (unfolds + charges — separates by MW in SDS-PAGE), extreme pH (disrupts ionic bonds), reducing agents (DTT, β-ME → break S-S), organic solvents (disrupt hydrophobic). Chaperones: (1) HSP70 (BiP in ER, GRP78): binds exposed hydrophobic patches on nascent/misfolded chains; uses ATP; (2) HSP90: refolds signal transduction proteins (steroid receptors, kinases); (3) GroEL/GroES (HSP60/HSP10 in bacteria; Hsp60 in mitochondria): provides protected folding environment (Anfinsen cage).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A newborn presents with jaundice in the first 24 hours of life, direct Coombs test positive, and no splenomegaly. The cause is most likely:
options: Physiological jaundice (never in first 24h, starts day 2-3, direct Coombs negative)

ABO incompatibility: occurs when mother is blood group O (has naturally occurring anti-A + anti-B IgG antibodies that cross placenta) and baby is group A or B → anti-A or anti-B IgG → binds fetal RBCs → extravascular hemolysis; Coombs test: direct antiglobulin test (DAT) weakly or moderately positive (IgG on fetal RBCs; IgM too big to cross placenta so only IgG anti-A/B from O mothers); clinical: jaundice in first 24h (pathological), anemia (mild-moderate), NO splenomegaly (less severe than Rh disease), NO anasarca/hydrops (mild, some exceptions); vs. Rh incompatibility: requires prior sensitization (subsequent pregnancy or transfusion) → severe, can cause hydrops fetalis, severe anemia; DAT strongly positive; ABO is 1st-pregnancy capable (IgG naturally occurring antibodies) but usually milder than sensitized Rh disease; biochemistry: ↑↑unconjugated bilirubin → risk of kernicterus (bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction, BIND) if UCB >18-20 mg/dL in term → stains basal ganglia + brainstem → choreoathetosis, sensorineural deafness, developmental disability; management: phototherapy (UV converts toxic Z,Z-bilirubin to water-soluble photoisomers: E-isomers + lumirubin → excreted in urine/bile without conjugation); exchange transfusion if severe
Gilbert's syndrome (presents in teens, mild jaundice, no hemolysis, Coombs negative)
Breast milk jaundice (starts day 4-7, peaks week 2, Coombs negative)
explanation: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia: Pathological if: onset <24h, >5 mg/dL/day rise, >17 mg/dL term, persists >2 weeks, or direct (conjugated) fraction elevated. Causes by timing: <24h: hemolytic (ABO, Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, hereditary spherocytosis, congenital infection [TORCH]). Day 2-3: physiological (UGT1A1 immaturity), breast-feeding jaundice (poor intake → ↑enterohepatic circulation). Day 4-7 onwards: breast milk jaundice (β-glucuronidase in breast milk → deconjugates bilirubin → reabsorbed → ↑UCB), Crigler-Najjar, Gilbert's. Phototherapy: converts toxic unconjugated bilirubin (Z,Z-bilirubin) to: (1) geometric isomers (E,Z-bilirubin or Z,E-bilirubin; rapidly formed; water-soluble; excreted in bile); (2) structural isomers (lumirubin, slowly formed; excreted in urine without conjugation); most effective wavelength: blue light (~425-475 nm); intensive phototherapy: multiple phototherapy units or double-sided; exchange transfusion: indicated for severe hyperbilirubinemia unresponsive to phototherapy or signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Crigler-Najjar type I: complete UGT1A1 absence → bilirubin >20 mg/dL, ONLY treatable long-term with liver transplantation; phototherapy 10-16h/day just to keep bilirubin <20 mg/dL in interim. Type II: partial UGT1A1 → moderate hyperbilirubinemia, responds to phenobarbital (induces UGT1A1).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the metabolism of phenylalanine, tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is required as a cofactor. BH4 deficiency can cause hyperphenylalaninemia even when phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) is normal. Which enzyme produces BH4 from GTP?
options: Dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR): this enzyme REGENERATES BH4 from BH2 (quinonoid dihydrobiopterin) — different reaction, same pathway
Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH): uses BH4 as cofactor, does not synthesize it

GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCH1): the rate-limiting enzyme for BH4 de novo synthesis; GTP + H2O → 7,8-dihydroneopterin triphosphate → [6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase, PTPS] → 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin → [sepiapterin reductase, SR] → tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4); BH4 is also the essential cofactor for: aromatic amino acid hydroxylases (PAH: Phe→Tyr; TH: Tyr→DOPA; TPH: Trp→5-HT); and nitric oxide synthases (all three NOS isoforms); BH4 deficiency → malignant hyperphenylalaninemia (same blood phenylalanine ↑ as classic PKU) PLUS neurotransmitter deficiency (↓dopamine, ↓serotonin) → severe neurological deterioration even with low-Phe diet alone; must supplement: BH4 (sapropterin, synthetic BH4, effective in PAH-responsive PKU too [cofactor-responsive variant]) + DOPA/5-hydroxytryptophan (neurotransmitter precursors); cause-specific enzyme defect: GCH1, PTPS, SR, DHPR, PCBD1 deficiencies all → BH4 deficiency
Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR): reduces dihydrofolate → tetrahydrofolate; different pathway (folate metabolism, not biopterin synthesis)
explanation: Phenylalanine metabolism: PAH reaction: L-Phe + BH4 + O2 → L-Tyr + BH2 + H2O; BH4 → quinonoid BH2 → [DHPR] → BH4 (regeneration requires NADH). Classic PKU (AR, PAH deficiency): most common inborn error of AA metabolism in Caucasians; ↑Phe, ↓Tyr; excess Phe → phenylpyruvate (transamination) + phenyllactate + phenylacetate (musty/mousy odor) → excreted in urine; Phe competes with large neutral AA (LNAA) for blood-brain barrier transport (LAT1) → neurotransmitter deficiency in brain (↓Trp → ↓5-HT; ↓Tyr → ↓dopamine); hypopigmentation (↓melanin, requires Tyr from PAH); intellectual disability if untreated. Management: low-Phe diet (avoid meat, fish, eggs, dairy, aspartame [contains Phe]); sapropterin (BH4; works in ~30-50% of patients with residual PAH activity; much less effective in classic severe PKU with null mutations); pegvaliase (PEGylated phenylalanine ammonia lyase, PAL; degrades excess Phe even without PAH; subcutaneous injection). Newborn screening (Guthrie test): heel prick blood spot, originally bacterial inhibition assay on Phe (S. aureus grows on Phe) → now MS/MS (tandem mass spectrometry, detects multiple disorders simultaneously); PKU screening is the oldest and most established newborn screening program. Maternal PKU: if PKU woman becomes pregnant without dietary control → ↑Phe crosses placenta → fetal damage (microcephaly, CHD, intellectual disability) even if baby has normal PAH.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following proteins is the major non-collagen protein of bone matrix?
options: Fibronectin (abundant in plasma and fibrous tissue, not the major non-collagen bone matrix protein)
Laminin (basement membrane glycoprotein, cross-shaped heterotrimer, mediates cell adhesion to basement membrane; not the major non-collagen bone matrix protein)

Osteocalcin (bone Gla protein, BGP): osteocalcin is the most abundant non-collagen protein in bone; synthesized exclusively by osteoblasts; contains 3 Gla (gamma-carboxyglutamic acid) residues produced by vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation → these Gla residues bind calcium and hydroxyapatite with high affinity, anchoring osteocalcin in bone matrix; when bone is resorbed (osteoclasts): osteocalcin fragments released into blood → serum osteocalcin = bone formation marker (since osteoblasts synthesize it); undercarboxylated osteocalcin (produced in Vit K deficiency) is released into circulation → acts as a hormone: activates GPRC6A on pancreatic β-cells → ↑insulin secretion; on muscle and fat → ↑energy expenditure and fat burning; warfarin use → ↓Vit K-dependent carboxylation → ↑undercarboxylated osteocalcin; other bone markers: formation: osteocalcin, bone ALP (bone-specific ALP), P1NP (procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide); resorption: CTX (C-terminal telopeptide of collagen I, β-CTX), NTX (N-terminal), TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase, from osteoclasts), pyridinoline crosslinks in urine
Albumin (the most abundant serum protein; also found as a minor component in bone matrix but not the major non-collagen bone protein)
explanation: Bone matrix composition: Organic (35%): Type I collagen (90% of organic matrix; provides tensile strength; synthesized by osteoblasts; triple helix Gly-X-Y, lysyl oxidase cross-links → hydroxylysine/hydroxyproline cross-links). Non-collagen proteins: osteocalcin (3 Gla, Vit K dependent, ~2% of bone protein), osteopontin (phosphoprotein, mediates osteoclast attachment to bone, ↑in many cancers, involved in nephrolithiasis), osteonectin/SPARC (glycoprotein, promotes mineralization), bone sialoprotein (BSP, RGD motif → integrin binding → osteoclast attachment). Inorganic (65%): hydroxyapatite [Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2]; provides compressive strength. Osteoblast vs. osteoclast: Osteoblast: synthesizes bone matrix (Type I collagen, osteocalcin, OPG) → mineralization; RUNX2 (master TF for osteoblast differentiation); osterix (SP7, downstream of RUNX2). Osteoclast: multinucleated giant cell (monocyte-macrophage lineage); M-CSF + RANKL (from osteoblasts) → osteoclast differentiation + activation; proton pump (V-ATPase + Cl- channel [ClCR7]) → ↓pH under osteoclast → dissolves HA; cathepsin K → digests collagen + non-collagen proteins; markers: TRAP (acid phosphatase), cathepsin K, CalCR (calcitonin receptor). Osteoprotegerin (OPG): decoy receptor for RANKL (osteoblast-secreted) → ↓osteoclast activation → ↑bone density; denosumab: anti-RANKL mAb → ↓osteoclast → treats osteoporosis + bone metastases.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycogen phosphorylase activity is regulated by both covalent modification and allosteric effectors. In the liver, phosphorylase b (dephosphorylated form) is ACTIVATED by:
options: AMP (in MUSCLE, phosphorylase b [inactive 'b' form] is allosterically activated by AMP [energy depletion signal] → partial activity without phosphorylation; in LIVER, phosphorylase b is NOT significantly activated by AMP, which is different from muscle — liver phosphorylase b remains inactive [inactive b form] unless glucose-1,6-bis-P or AMP at very high concentrations)
Glucose (in LIVER, glucose INHIBITS both phosphorylase a AND b → promotes dephosphorylation of phosphorylase a [by PP1 activation] → ↓glycogenolysis when glucose arrives after a meal)
ADP (not a primary allosteric activator of liver phosphorylase b)

Phosphorylase a (the phosphorylated form, active): there is actually no allosteric activator of liver phosphorylase b under physiological conditions — phosphorylase b is essentially inactive in liver at rest; liver glycogen phosphorylase exists primarily in the 'a' (phosphorylated, active) form during fasting/glucagon stimulation: glucagon → Gs → ↑cAMP → ↑PKA → phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase (PhK) → PhK phosphorylates phosphorylase b → phosphorylase a (active) → glycogenolysis; in liver, glucose (not AMP) is the key allosteric inhibitor that also promotes inactivation of phosphorylase a by promoting PP1 activity; NOTE: this question has no correct answer among first three options — in LIVER the inactive phosphorylase b is NOT activated by AMP (unlike muscle); the correct understanding is that liver phosphorylase requires covalent phosphorylation for activation
explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase regulation comparison (muscle vs. liver): MUSCLE phosphorylase: Active form (a): PKA phosphorylation (via Epi→β-AR→cAMP→PKA) or Ca2+/CaM-dependent PhK (muscle contraction triggers). Phosphorylase b (dephosphorylated): INACTIVE at rest; ACTIVATED allosterically by AMP (↑during high energy demand, AMP = low energy signal) → partial glycogenolysis during exercise even without cAMP; INHIBITED by ATP + G6P (abundant energy). LIVER phosphorylase: Active form (a): PKA phosphorylation (via Glucagon → Gs → cAMP → PKA or Epi→α1-AR→Gq→Ca2+ in liver). Phosphorylase b: essentially inactive (AMP does not significantly activate it in liver); liver phosphorylase is glucose-sensitive: glucose → binds to glucose binding site on phosphorylase a → conformational change → exposes phospho-Ser → PP1 (protein phosphatase 1) can now dephosphorylate → converts a → b (inactivation); this is a key hepatic glucose autoregulatory loop. Glycogen synthase regulation: Active when dephosphorylated (GS-a); phosphorylated GS-b (inactive) by multiple kinases: PKA, CaM-K, GSK3 (inhibited by insulin via Akt → more GS-a active when insulin ↑); also allosterically activated by G6P (in both liver and muscle). Glycogen branching enzyme (amylo-α1,4→1,6-transglucosidase): debranching enzyme (AGL): dual function — (1) transferase: moves 3-residue terminal oligosaccharide from branch to main chain; (2) glucosidase: cleaves α1,6-glycosidic bond → releases free glucose (only free glucose in glycogenolysis; all other residues released as glucose-1-P by PhK).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient on long-term total parenteral nutrition (TPN) without selenium supplementation develops cardiomyopathy. Selenium is an essential component of which enzyme?
options: Superoxide dismutase (SOD uses Cu/Zn or Mn, not Se)

Glutathione peroxidase (GPx): selenium (Se) is incorporated as selenocysteine (the 21st amino acid, encoded by UGA codon in presence of SECIS element, inserted by selenocysteine-specific tRNA) at the active site of glutathione peroxidase (GPx1 [cytoplasmic], GPx4 [phospholipid hydroperoxide GPx, prevents ferroptosis]) and other selenoproteins (thioredoxin reductase [TrxR], selenoprotein P [plasma Se transport], iodothyronine deiodinase [ID1/2/3]); GPx: 2 GSH + H2O2 → GSSG + 2 H2O; GPx4: lipid-OOH + 2 GSH → lipid-OH + GSSG (prevents lipid peroxidation; when GPx4 is inhibited → ferroptosis [iron-dependent, lipid peroxidation-driven cell death]); Se deficiency → ↓GPx → ↑oxidative stress + ↓thyroid hormone activation (ID1/2); Keshan disease: endemic Se deficiency in China → dilated cardiomyopathy (cardiomyopathy from Se deficiency, often triggered by Coxsackievirus B, classic exam question); Kashin-Beck disease: Se deficiency + iodine deficiency → osteoarthropathy + short stature (mostly children)
explanation: Selenium (Se): RDA: 55 µg/day (adult). Good sources: Brazil nuts (highest, 1 nut ~70-90 µg), seafood, meat, grain (content depends on soil Se). Form: inorganic (selenite, selenate — from soil) or organic (selenomethionine, selenocysteine — from food); organic forms better absorbed. Selenoproteins (25 in humans): GPx1-4 (antioxidant), TrxR1-3 (antioxidant, regenerates thioredoxin → ribonucleotide reductase), selenoprotein P (plasma Se transport), DIO1/2/3 (iodothyronine deiodinases: outer ring → T4→T3 [DIO1/2, activation]; inner ring → T4→rT3 or T3→T2 [DIO3, inactivation]); MSS (methionine sulfoxide reductase B1). Ferroptosis: iron-dependent regulated cell death; characterized by lipid peroxidation; GPx4 is the primary defense; GPx4 inhibitors (RSL3) or GSH depletion (erastin, blocks cystine import via xCT/SLC7A11) → ferroptosis; implicated in ischemia-reperfusion, neurodegeneration (Parkinson, Alzheimer, ALS), cancer (targeted therapeutics). Iodothyronine deiodinase: DIO1 (liver, kidney, thyroid): outer ring → T4→T3; DIO2 (brain, pituitary, heart, skeletal muscle, adipose): outer ring → T4→T3 (most important for local T3 production); DIO3 (placenta, fetal tissues, brain): inner ring → T4→rT3 (inactive reverse T3) or T3→T2 (inactivation, 'protective'); hypothyroidism treatment: usually levothyroxine (T4 → converts to T3 by DIO1/2 in tissues); liothyronine (T3) used occasionally (faster onset, short half-life).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the correct mechanism by which aspirin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis?
options: Aspirin blocks the receptor for arachidonic acid on COX enzymes
Aspirin prevents the conversion of phospholipids to arachidonic acid (that is glucocorticoids → ↓phospholipase A2 activity via lipocortin/annexin induction; aspirin acts downstream of PLA2)

Aspirin irreversibly acetylates the serine residue (Ser530 in COX-1, Ser516 in COX-2) at the active site of cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) → permanent blockade of the COX site → prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2/prostacyclin, TXA2) cannot be produced; important consequences of COX selectivity: COX-1 inhibition (aspirin fully blocks COX-1 by irreversible acetylation) → ↓TXA2 in platelets (anucleate → cannot synthesize new COX-1 → effect lasts platelet lifetime ~10 days → anti-platelet aggregation → 81 mg low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular prevention); also COX-1 → ↓PGE2 + PGI2 in gastric mucosa → ↓mucus + bicarbonate secretion + ↓mucosal blood flow → risk of peptic ulcer. COX-2 inhibition (aspirin also inhibits COX-2 but COX-2 is inducible → nucleated cells can synthesize new COX-2): ↓inflammatory PGE2 (anti-inflammatory). Non-selective NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): reversible COX-1 + COX-2 inhibition. Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, rofecoxib): ↓inflammatory PGs but COX-1 (constitutive) preserved → ↓GI side effects but ↑thrombosis risk (COX-2 in endothelium → PGI2 = anti-platelet + vasodilator; if COX-2 blocked → ↓PGI2 while TXA2 from platelets via COX-1 remains → ↑clotting)
Aspirin competes reversibly with arachidonic acid for the COX active site
explanation: Eicosanoid synthesis: Cell membrane phospholipids → [PLA2, activated by inflammation/Gq signaling] → arachidonic acid (20:4ω6) [AA, from linoleic acid in diet or from membrane]. AA → two major pathways: (1) COX pathway: AA → [COX-1 or COX-2; both with cyclooxygenase + peroxidase activity in same protein] → PGG2 → PGH2 (unstable) → cell-specific synthases: PGE2 (most abundant; fever [via cAMP in hypothalamus → ↑set point], pain sensitization [↑TRPV1/TRPA1 sensitivity in DRG neurons], bronchodilation in airway); PGI2/prostacyclin [by prostacyclin synthase, mainly endothelium: vasodilation + ↓platelet aggregation]; TXA2 [by thromboxane synthase in platelets: vasoconstriction + ↑platelet aggregation]; PGD2 [mast cells, brain: vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, mediates allergic response]; PGF2α [uterine contraction, luteolysis, bronchoconstriction]. (2) LOX (lipoxygenase) pathway: AA → 5-LOX [+ FLAP, 5-LOX activating protein] → LTA4 → LTB4 (powerful neutrophil chemotactic) or LTC4/D4/E4 (cysteinyl leukotrienes: bronchoconstriction [100-1000× more potent than histamine], ↑mucus secretion, ↑vascular permeability — important in asthma); LOX inhibitor: zileuton (5-LOX inhibitor); LT receptor antagonist: montelukast, zafirlukast.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The conversion of succinate to fumarate in the TCA cycle is catalyzed by succinate dehydrogenase (SDH). SDH is unique among TCA cycle enzymes because:
options: It requires NAD+ as electron acceptor (WRONG — SDH uses FAD, not NAD+)
It is located in the mitochondrial matrix (WRONG — SDH is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane)

It is the only TCA enzyme that is also part of the electron transport chain (Complex II) and uses FAD: SDH (complex II): succinate + FAD → fumarate + FADH2; SDH is unique: (1) it is the ONLY TCA enzyme that is also a component of the electron transport chain (Complex II, succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, SDHAB/CD); (2) it uses FAD (not NAD+) as electron acceptor → FADH2 → electrons transferred to CoQ → Complex III → cyt c → Complex IV (only 1.5 ATP per FADH2 vs 2.5 per NADH because bypasses Complex I which pumps 4H+); (3) it is directly embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (unlike other TCA enzymes in matrix); (4) it does NOT pump protons (Complex II passes electrons CoQ but does not pump H+); SDH subunits: SDHA + SDHB (catalytic core) + SDHC + SDHD (anchor in IMM); SDH mutations (SDHB, SDHC, SDHD more commonly than SDHA): hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndromes; SDHA mutations: Carney triad (paraganglioma + GI stromal tumor [GIST] + pulmonary chondroma); SDH as tumor suppressor: ↓SDH → ↑succinate (oncometabolite) → inhibits PHD2 (prolyl hydroxylase) → ↓VHL-mediated HIF-1α degradation → ↑HIF-1α → Warburg shift + ↑angiogenesis; malonate: competitive inhibitor of SDH (classic biochemistry inhibitor study)
SDH requires the substrate guanosine triphosphate (GTP) (WRONG — succinate thiokinase/succinyl-CoA synthetase requires GDP/GTP; SDH does not)
explanation: TCA cycle NADH vs FADH2 yield per turn: Step 3 (isocitrate → α-KG): NADH. Step 4 (α-KG → succinyl-CoA): NADH. Step 5 (succinyl-CoA → succinate): GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation; in plants/bacteria: ATP). Step 6 (succinate → fumarate): FADH2 (SDH, Complex II). Step 7 (malate → OAA): NADH. Step 8 (citrate synthase: OAA + acetyl-CoA → citrate): no cofactor reduction. Step 2 (aconitase): no cofactor reduction. Total per turn: 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP + oxidation of 2C as CO2 (at steps 3 and 4). ATP yield: 3 NADH × 2.5 = 7.5 ATP; 1 FADH2 × 1.5 = 1.5 ATP; 1 GTP = 1 ATP; total per turn = 10 ATP. For one glucose: 2 TCA turns = 20 ATP; plus 2 NADH from pyruvate dehydrogenase = 5 ATP; 2 NADH from glycolysis (cytoplasmic, must shuttle [malate-aspartate shuttle: 2.5/NADH; glycerol-3-P shuttle: 1.5/NADH] = 4-5 ATP); 2 ATP from glycolysis (substrate level); total ≈ 30-32 ATP (updated P/O ratios from Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory). TCA anaplerosis: reactions that replenish TCA intermediates: pyruvate carboxylase (PC: pyruvate + CO2 → OAA), glutamate → α-KG (transamination), propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (odd-chain FA, Val, Ile, Met, Thr), aspartate → fumarate (urea cycle); cataplerosis: removal of TCA intermediates for biosynthesis (citrate → acetyl-CoA for lipid synthesis; α-KG → Glu for Gln/NT; succinyl-CoA → porphyrin; OAA → PEP for gluconeogenesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 45-year-old woman is found to have high serum cholesterol. She is started on a statin. The mechanism of action of statins is inhibition of which enzyme?
options: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1): rate-limiting step of bile acid synthesis; bile acid sequestrants ↓ bile acid reabsorption → ↑CYP7A1 → ↑cholesterol → bile acids; not the statin target
ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase): esterifies intracellular cholesterol for storage; not the statin target

HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR): 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase; the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis; in the ER (smooth ER) of hepatocytes; catalyzes: HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH → mevalonate + 2 NADP+ + CoA; mevalonate is the committed precursor to the isoprenoid/mevalonate pathway → farnesyl-PP → cholesterol (via squalene), also → dolichol, CoQ10, isoprenyl groups for protein prenylation (farnesyl + geranylgeranyl for Ras, Rho GTPases); statins are structural analogs of HMG-CoA → competitive inhibitors of HMGCR; ↓hepatic cholesterol → SREBP-2 (sterol regulatory element binding protein 2) activated (↓cholesterol → SCAP-SREBP2 complex released from INSIG → Golgi → site-1/site-2 proteases cleave → N-terminal SREBP2 enters nucleus → ↑LDL receptor transcription → ↑LDL receptor on hepatocyte surface → ↑LDL clearance from blood → ↓LDL-C); major LDL-lowering effect is via ↑LDL-R (secondary) rather than direct cholesterol synthesis inhibition
Squalene epoxidase (SQLE): converts squalene → 2,3-oxidosqualene; terbinafine (antifungal) inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase; not the statin target
explanation: Cholesterol biosynthesis pathway: Acetyl-CoA (2) → acetoacetyl-CoA [thiolase] → HMG-CoA [HMGS1, cytoplasm] → mevalonate [HMGCR, ER, rate-limiting, statins] → mevalonate-5-P → mevalonate-5-PP → isopentenyl-PP (IPP) ↔ dimethylallyl-PP (DMAPP) → GPP [FPP synthase] → FPP [FPP synthase] → two FPP → squalene [squalene synthase, committed step for cholesterol; FPP also → dolichol, CoQ10, isoprenoid chains for prenylation] → 2,3-oxidosqualene [SQLE] → lanosterol [LSS] → multiple steps → cholesterol [DHCR7]. LDL receptor pathway (Goldstein & Brown, Nobel 1985): LDL → binds LDL-R (LDLR) at coated pit (clathrin coat + adaptor AP-2) → receptor-mediated endocytosis → endosome → acidification → LDL detaches → LDL-R recycled to surface; LDL-R recycling requires PCSK9 absence: PCSK9 binds LDL-R at surface → co-internalized → targets LDL-R for lysosomal degradation → ↓LDL-R recycling → ↑LDL; PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab): fully human mAb → ↓PCSK9 → ↑LDL-R on hepatocytes → ↑LDL clearance → ↓LDL-C by 50-60% on top of statin; Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH): LDLR mutations (most common) → ↓LDL clearance → ↑LDL-C → premature CVD; homozygous FH: LDL-C >500 mg/dL → CVD before age 10; statins less effective; LDL apheresis + PCSK9-I + evinacumab (anti-ANGPTL3).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The conversion of serine to glycine requires which vitamin cofactor?
options: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): required for methionine synthase [Hcy + 5-methyl-THF → Met] and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; not for Ser→Gly
Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate/PLP): PLP is a cofactor for aminotransferases, serine racemase, cystathionine β-synthase, and others; but the Ser→Gly reaction specifically requires THF

Folic acid (tetrahydrofolate, THF): serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT, requires PLP AND THF): L-Ser + THF → Gly + 5,10-methyleneTHF; this is the MAIN reaction generating 5,10-methyleneTHF (the one-carbon donor for thymidylate synthase); SHMT1 is cytoplasmic (for dTMP synthesis pathway); SHMT2 is mitochondrial (for folate-linked mitochondrial metabolism); so the primary requirement is THF (folate) as the acceptor of the hydroxymethyl group; both THF (folate) and PLP (B6) are required, but if only one is tested → folate is the key 'one-carbon' acceptor making this a folate-dependent reaction; 5,10-methyleneTHF → [thymidylate synthase] → TMP (+ DHF → reduced back to THF by DHFR); 5-FU inhibits thymidylate synthase; methotrexate + trimethoprim inhibit DHFR → accumulate DHF → ↓THF → ↓5,10-methylene-THF → ↓dTMP → ↓DNA synthesis
Niacin (NAD+/NADH): cofactor for many dehydrogenases; not specifically required for Ser→Gly conversion
explanation: One-carbon (1C) metabolism: THF (tetrahydrofolate) carries one-carbon units at various oxidation states: 5,10-methylene-THF: from Ser (SHMT) or Gly (GCS); reduces to: 5-methyl-THF (MTHFR) → Met synthesis; oxidizes to: 5,10-methenyl-THF → 10-formyl-THF → purine synthesis (at C2 and C8). Sources of 1C units: SHMT (Ser → Gly + 5,10-methylene-THF); GCS (glycine cleavage system: Gly + NAD+ + THF → CO2 + NH3 + NADH + 5,10-methylene-THF); formate (FTHFS: formate + THF + ATP → 10-formyl-THF); histidine catabolism (FIGLU → formiminoglutamate → THF accepts formimino group → 5-formimino-THF → 5,10-methenyl-THF; FIGLU elevated in folate deficiency + excreted in urine after histidine loading test [Figlu test]). Folate deficiency effects: ↓dTMP → ↓DNA synthesis → megaloblastic anemia (same as B12 deficiency but NO neurological symptoms; B12 deficiency ADDS subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord [dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts] due to failed myelin synthesis); ↑FIGLU in urine (histidine loading test); ↑homocysteine; ↑neural tube defect risk in pregnancy (periconceptional folic acid 0.4-0.8 mg/day ↓NTD by ~70%; 4 mg for high risk: prior NTD pregnancy, certain anti-epileptics). Methylfolate trap: B12 deficiency → methionine synthase fails → 5-methyl-THF cannot be demethylated → trapped as 5-methyl-THF → all THF forms gradually become 5-methyl-THF → functional folate deficiency → megaloblastic anemia (same as folate deficiency) despite normal serum folate.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Acetyl-CoA produced in the mitochondria cannot directly cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. How does acetyl-CoA reach the cytoplasm for fatty acid synthesis?
options: Acetyl-CoA is transported directly through the inner mitochondrial membrane by a specific carrier
Acetyl-CoA is converted to acetylcarnitine by carnitine acetyltransferase and transported (this is a minor pathway; not the primary route)

As citrate via the citrate shuttle (tricarboxylate transport system): acetyl-CoA + OAA → [citrate synthase] → citrate; citrate exits via the citrate/malate antiporter (SLC25A1, tricarboxylate carrier) in the inner mitochondrial membrane → in cytoplasm → ATP-citrate lyase (ACL/ACLY): citrate + CoA + ATP → acetyl-CoA + OAA + ADP + Pi (reverse of citrate synthase but uses ATP); the regenerated cytoplasmic OAA → [MDH] → malate + NADH (or → [PEPCK] → PEP if in excess [optional gluconeogenic flux]); malate → malate-pyruvate cycle: malate → [malic enzyme, ME1, NADP+] → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH (this NADPH contributes to cytoplasmic NADPH for fatty acid synthesis); the citrate shuttle operates when: ↑mitochondrial acetyl-CoA (fed state, high glucose flux), ↑insulin signaling (↑ACLY expression + ↑citrate synthase flux), ↑demand for fatty acid synthesis; this shuttle is upregulated in lipogenic cancers (ACL overexpressed)
Acetate is exported from mitochondria, then converted to acetyl-CoA in the cytoplasm (minor pathway in some tissues; the main route is the citrate shuttle)
explanation: Mitochondrial membrane transport systems (key inner mitochondrial membrane carriers): Pyruvate: MPC1/2 (mitochondrial pyruvate carrier) — imports pyruvate. Citrate: SLC25A1 (tricarboxylate carrier) — exports citrate, imports malate/succinate. Malate-aspartate shuttle: malate/OAA carrier (SLC25A11) + glutamate-aspartate carrier (SLC25A12/13); key for transferring reducing equivalents (NADH) from cytoplasm to mitochondria (bypassing IMM impermeability to NADH) — 2.5 ATP per cytoplasmic NADH vs 1.5 ATP via glycerophosphate shuttle. Carnitine shuttle (for FA-CoA): CAT1 (carnitine acyltransferase 1, outer IMM) → carnitine + fatty acyl-CoA → acylcarnitine; SLC25A20 (carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase) → exchanges acylcarnitine/carnitine; CAT2 (inner IMM) → acylcarnitine → fatty acyl-CoA inside; CPT-1 inhibited by malonyl-CoA → ↓FA import → ↓β-oxidation when FA synthesis is active. α-KG/malate carrier (SLC25A11): exports α-KG, imports malate (part of gluconeogenic OAA supply from glutamate transamination). Adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT, SLC25A4-6): exchanges ADP (in) for ATP (out) — most abundant IMM protein after ATP synthase; inhibited by bongkrekic acid + atractyloside (both cause massive mitochondrial Ca2+ accumulation → mitochondrial permeability transition). Phosphate carrier (SLC25A3): imports Pi for ATP synthesis. Aspartate-glutamate carrier (SLC25A12/AGC1, SLC25A13/citrin): CITRIN deficiency (SLC25A13) → citrin deficiency: adult-onset type II citrullinemia (↑Cit in blood as aspartate-glutamate carrier loss → ↑aspartate cannot be used in urea cycle) + intolerance to carbohydrates.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is an essential allosteric activator of which urea cycle enzyme?
options: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC): uses carbamoyl-P + ornithine → citrulline; second enzyme, uses carbamoyl-P that was already made, not directly activated by NAG
Arginase (converts Arg → urea + Orn; last enzyme; not directly activated by NAG)
Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS): joins citrulline + aspartate → argininosuccinate; not NAG-activated

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I): the first and rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle; located in the mitochondrial matrix; catalyzes: NH3 + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate; REQUIRES N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as obligatory allosteric activator (without NAG, CPS I is completely inactive); NAG is synthesized by N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) from acetyl-CoA + glutamate in mitochondria; NAGS activity is stimulated by: arginine (allosteric activator → arginine stimulates NAGS → ↑NAG → ↑CPS I → ↑urea cycle flux); clinical importance: NAGS deficiency → identical phenotype to CPS I deficiency (hyperammonemia) → responds to N-carbamylglutamate (NCG, Carglumic acid, a NAG analog that CPS I can use) which is the TREATMENT for NAGS deficiency and may help in organic acidemias (propionic acidemia, methylmalonic acidemia) where propionyl-CoA inhibits NAGS → secondary hyperammonemia → NCG treatment
explanation: Urea cycle enzymes + location + deficiency consequences: CPS I (mito matrix): NH3 + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl-P (requires NAG activator). Deficiency → ↑NH3, ↑Gln, ↓citrulline; responds to NCG treatment if NAGS deficiency. OTC (mito inner membrane, intermembrane space facing): carbamoyl-P + Orn → Cit; X-linked (most common urea cycle defect); OTC deficiency → ↑NH3, ↑Gln, ↑orotic acid (carbamoyl-P leaks out → pyrimidine synthesis → ↑UMP → ↑orotic acid in urine; distinguishes OTC deficiency from CPS I deficiency which has NO ↑orotic acid). ASS (cytoplasm): Cit + Asp → argininosuccinate; deficiency → citrullinemia type I (CTLN1). ASL (cytoplasm): argininosuccinate → Arg + fumarate; deficiency → argininosuccinate lyase deficiency (argininosuccinic aciduria) → ↑argininosuccinic acid in urine (diagnostic). Arginase (ARG1, cytoplasm): Arg → urea + Orn; deficiency → argininemia → ↑Arg → spastic diplegia + intellectual disability (milder NH3 elevation than other UCDs). Treatment principles for UCDs: Protein restriction (↓nitrogen load). Ammonia scavengers: sodium benzoate (→ hippurate, excretes 1 N per mol) + sodium phenylacetate/phenylbutyrate (→ phenylacetylglutamine, excretes 2 N per mol). Arginine supplementation (for all UCDs except arginase deficiency — ↑Arg drives urea cycle forward + provides substrate). Citrulline supplementation (for OTC, CPS I deficiency). NCG (N-carbamylglutamate) for NAGS deficiency + organic acidemias with secondary hyperammonemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme thymidylate synthase (TS) is inhibited by 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) via which metabolite?
options: 5-FU directly inhibits TS without metabolic conversion (WRONG — 5-FU is a prodrug requiring activation)
5-FU → 5-fluorouridine monophosphate (FUMP) via UMP phosphorylase; FUMP is not the TS inhibitor (although FUMP can be incorporated into RNA → RNA toxicity)

5-FU → 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine-5'-monophosphate (FdUMP): 5-FU is a pyrimidine analog prodrug; activated to: (1) FdUMP [via thymidine phosphorylase (TP/PD-ECGF) + thymidine kinase → inhibits TS]; (2) FUTP [incorporated into RNA → disrupts RNA processing + function]; TS mechanism: TS normally catalyzes: dUMP + 5,10-methyleneTHF → dTMP + DHF; FdUMP: (1) mimics dUMP substrate, (2) covalently traps the TS-5,10-methyleneTHF ternary complex (FdUMP-TS-CH2THF, suicide inhibitor complex) → permanent inactivation → ↓dTMP → ↓DNA synthesis → S-phase specific cytotoxicity; leucovorin (folinic acid, 5-formyl-THF): enhances 5-FU efficacy → ↑5,10-methyleneTHF pool → stabilizes FdUMP-TS-CH2THF complex → ↑TS inhibition → 5-FU used in colorectal, breast, gastric, pancreatic cancer (often with leucovorin: FOLFOX, FOLFIRI regimens); resistance mechanisms: ↑TS expression (gene amplification), ↑TYMP (degrades FdUMP), loss of TK (cannot phosphorylate 5-FdU → FdUMP), ↓folate pools
5-FU → 5-FUDP (diphosphate) which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (that is the mechanism of gemcitabine-DP and hydroxyurea [HU inhibits RNR directly]; not 5-FU mechanism)
explanation: Antimetabolites in cancer chemotherapy: Folate analogs: methotrexate (MTX): competitive inhibitor of DHFR (DHF → THF) → ↓THF → ↓5,10-methyleneTHF → ↓dTMP; also ↓de novo purine synthesis (formyl-THF steps); leucovorin rescue: supplements folinic acid after high-dose MTX → rescues normal cells (cancer cells take up less leucovorin due to different folate transport). Pralatrexate: high affinity for RFC (reduced folate carrier) + FPGS → more intracellular polyglutamation → greater TS inhibition → T-cell lymphoma. Pemetrexed: multi-target antifolate (TS + DHFR + GART); requires B12 + folate supplementation to reduce toxicity. Pyrimidine analogs: 5-FU (prodrug → FdUMP [TS inhibitor] + FUTP [RNA incorporation]); capecitabine (oral prodrug → 5-FU; thymidine phosphorylase [TP] converts → 5-FU in tumor cells where TP is highly expressed); gemcitabine (dCTP analog → difluoro-dCTP incorporates into DNA → chain termination + inhibits RNR via difluoro-dCDP); cytarabine (Ara-C → Ara-CTP → incorporates into DNA, inhibits DNA pol α, chain termination; acute leukemia treatment). Purine analogs: 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP, converted to 6-TIMP by HGPRT → 6-TGMP → ↓de novo purine synthesis + TPMT [thiopurine methyltransferase] metabolizes to inactive 6-MMP; TPMT deficiency → ↑toxicity from 6-MP/6-TG/azathioprine); fludarabine (Ara-FAMP, inhibits DNA pol + RNR, DNA chain termination; CLL treatment). Hydroxyurea (HU): inhibits RNR (M2 subunit scavenges free radical from tyrosyl radical → enzyme inactivated) → ↓all dNTPs; used in CML [before imatinib era], sickle cell disease (↑HbF expression), ET/PV.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycogenin is the initiator protein for glycogen synthesis. What is the biochemical role of glycogenin?
options: Glycogenin is an enzyme that polymerizes UDP-glucose into long chains of glycogen (that is glycogen synthase)
Glycogenin is a transport protein that carries glucose into the cell

Glycogenin acts as a primer and self-glucosylates to initiate glycogen chain synthesis: glycogenin is a unique protein that acts as both the primer substrate and the enzyme (autoglucosyltransferase activity) for glycogen synthesis initiation; reaction: glycogenin attaches its first glucose unit to a specific tyrosine residue (Tyr194 in human glycogenin-1) → using UDP-glucose as donor; then auto-glucosylates (adds ~7-12 more glucose residues by α1,4-glycosidic bonds) → generates a small primer chain of ~8 glucose residues; this primer is the obligatory starting point that glycogen synthase then extends; glycogenin remains covalently attached at the core of the completed glycogen granule; glycogenin isoforms: GYG1 (muscle, defects → polyglucosan body myopathy 2); GYG2 (liver); without functional glycogenin, glycogen chains cannot be initiated; glycogen granule: 1 glycogenin molecule at center, glycogen synthase extends, branching enzyme creates branches → mature glycogen
Glycogenin is an inhibitor of glycogen phosphorylase (completely different function)
explanation: Glycogen synthesis (complete pathway): UDP-glucose formation: glucose-1-P + UTP → UDP-glucose + PPi [UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (UGP2)]; PPi → 2 Pi [pyrophosphatase, makes reaction irreversible]. Initiation: glycogenin (GYG) autocatalysis → primer of ~8-12 glucose units. Elongation: glycogen synthase (GS, rate-limiting committed step of glycogen synthesis) → transfers glucose from UDP-glucose to non-reducing end of primer via α1,4 bond; GS exists as: GS-a (dephosphorylated, ACTIVE, ↑after insulin); GS-b (phosphorylated, INACTIVE, ↑by glucagon/epinephrine via PKA; multiple sites on GS: Ser7, Ser10, Thr37, Ser46, Ser87, Ser641, Ser645, Ser649, Ser653 — phosphorylated by multiple kinases including PKA, GSK3, CaM-K, AMPK; any phosphorylation alone is enough to inactivate); allosteric activation: G6P → activates GS-b even in phosphorylated state → 'G6P is the fail-safe glucose sensor for glycogen synthesis.' Branching: glycogen branching enzyme (GBE1, amylo-α1,4→α1,6-glucan transferase): transfers oligosaccharide chain (≥7 units) from growing chain to another position via α1,6 bond (branch point) when chain is >11 units; GBE1 deficiency → GSD IV (Andersen disease): accumulation of abnormal polysaccharide with few branches (resembles plant amylopectin) → liver cirrhosis + cardiomyopathy + progressive myopathy; most severe of GSDs.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The inhibitor suxamethonium (succinylcholine) causes prolonged muscle paralysis in patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) normally performs which function?
options: Cleaves acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction (WRONG — the NMJ hydrolysis of ACh is by acetylcholinesterase [AChE, true cholinesterase, ACHE gene], not pseudocholinesterase [BuChE])

Cleaves succinylcholine (suxamethonium) in plasma: BuChE (plasma cholinesterase, pseudocholinesterase, BCHE gene): a serine hydrolase in plasma and liver; normally rapidly hydrolyzes succinylcholine (a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker: mimics ACh → depolarizes motor end plate → prevents repolarization needed for further AP → flaccid paralysis used in RSI/anesthesia) into succinylmonocholine + choline → drug effect normally lasts ~5 min; BuChE deficiency or genetic variants (dibucaine-resistant variants: Asp70Gly [A1 allele, most common], silent allele [E1 silent], fluoride-resistant allele, K-variant [E430Lys]) → cannot metabolize succinylcholine → drug persists → prolonged apnea + paralysis (hours instead of minutes); diagnostic: dibucaine number (DN): dibucaine (local anesthetic) inhibits normal BuChE by ~80% (DN~80) but inhibits abnormal BuChE much less (homozygous abnormal: DN~20; heterozygous: DN~60); other substrates of BuChE: mivacurium (NMB), aspirin, cocaine (in plasma), ester local anesthetics (procaine, tetracaine)
Repackages acetylcholine into vesicles (that is VAChT [vesicular ACh transporter])
Converts choline to acetylcholine (that is choline acetyltransferase [ChAT])
explanation: Neuromuscular junction pharmacology: ACh synthesis: choline acetyltransferase (ChAT, rate-limiting; uses acetyl-CoA + choline → ACh); choline uptake: high-affinity choline transporter (CHT1, SLC5A7) on presynaptic membrane; ACh packaged by VAChT (vesicular ACh transporter, SLC18A3) using H+/ACh antiport (V-ATPase sets up H+ gradient). AChE: true cholinesterase; breaks down ACh at NMJ synapse (motor neuron/muscle), myoneural junction, ANS synapses; AChE inhibitors: neostigmine, pyridostigmine (reversible, quaternary amine, don't cross BBB → peripheral action → used for myasthenia gravis, reversal of NMB); physostigmine (reversible, tertiary amine, crosses BBB → also used for atropine/scopolamine overdose); organophosphates (irreversible, 'aging' → cholinergic crisis [muscarinic: SLUDGE — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis + nicotinic: fasciculations → paralysis; CNS: seizures]); treatment: atropine (muscarinic antagonist) + pralidoxime (PAM, regenerates AChE before aging, most effective early). BuChE: plasma enzyme; normally low physiological substrate specificity; functions as a scavenger of cholinergic poisons (OPs, nerve agents); cocaine hydrolysis in plasma (CocH [cocaine hydrolase]: engineered BuChE variant, not natural, being studied for cocaine use disorder). Suxamethonium pharmacogenomics: prior to elective intubation, consider genetic testing (or family history/previous adverse reaction) for BuChE variants.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between Type I and Type II restriction enzymes?
options: Type I cuts at the recognition sequence; Type II cuts at a distance from recognition (WRONG — it's the opposite: Type II cuts at or near recognition)

Type II restriction enzymes cut DNA at or very close to their recognition sequence, requiring only Mg2+ as cofactor: Type I REs: recognize a specific bipartite sequence (e.g., TCA[N8]GTGC in EcoKI) → translocate DNA for long distances using ATP hydrolysis → cut DNA far (>1000 bp) from recognition sequence + methylate the recognition sequence; large multifunctional enzymes (R+M+S subunits); random cut site → not useful for genetic engineering. Type II REs: recognize a specific palindromic (or other defined) 4-8 bp sequence → cut at or very near (within 0-2 bp of) recognition sequence; simple enzymes (just the restriction endonuclease, no helicase/methylase); require only Mg2+ (divalent cation); produce defined, predictable fragments → essential tools in molecular biology (cloning, restriction mapping, Southern blot); subtypes: IIS (e.g., BsaI) cuts at fixed distance from recognition (downstream of recognition); IIP (standard Type II, e.g., EcoRI, HindIII, BamHI): palindromic recognition + cut within palindrome → generate either 5'-overhangs ('sticky ends': EcoRI generates 5'-AATT overhang), 3'-overhangs, or blunt ends. Type III: recognize asymmetric non-palindromic sequence → cut 25-27 bp downstream, require ATP for cutting but don't need it for recognition
Type II requires both ATP and SAM (S-adenosylmethionine); Type I requires only Mg2+ (WRONG — reversed)
Type II methylates the same site it cleaves (restriction-modification: methylation at same palindromic sequence [type II M.enzyme] is a separate enzyme, not the same as cutting)
explanation: Type II restriction enzymes in molecular biology: Examples: EcoRI (E. coli RY13): 5'-G↓AATTC-3' / 3'-CTTAA↑G-5' → 5'-AATT overhang (sticky, 4-nt 5' overhang); recognition: GAATTC (palindrome). BamHI: 5'-G↓GATCC-3' → 5'-GATC overhang. HindIII: 5'-A↓AGCTT-3' → 5'-AGCT overhang. PstI: 3'-overhang (CTGCAG, cut: CTGCA↓G generates 3'-ACGT overhang [rare, 3' overhang]). SmaI / XmaI: CCCGGG — SmaI cuts CCC↓GGG (blunt); XmaI cuts C↓CCGGG (5'-CCGG overhang): same recognition site, different cut positions → isocaudomers. EcoRV: GAT↓ATC → blunt ends. Methylation: Dam methylase (E. coli): methylates GATC at adenine-N6 (→ N6-mA); Dcm methylase: CCWGG at C5 (→ C5-mC); methylation → protection from cognate RE → bacteria protect own genome. Recognition site frequency: 4-cutter (e.g., MboI: GATC) → cuts every ~256 bp (4^4); 6-cutter (e.g., EcoRI: GAATTC) → every ~4096 bp (4^6); 8-cutter → very rarely (every ~65 kb; used for pulsed-field gel electrophoresis of large genomic fragments). Applications: Southern blot: DNA → restriction digest → gel electrophoresis → transfer to membrane → hybridize with probe → detect specific fragment size. Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP): variant in recognition site → different fragment pattern → used in linkage analysis, forensics (STR preferred now).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) initiates transcription at the promoter. The key promoter element recognized by TBP (TATA-binding protein) is:
options: GC box (Sp1 binding site, upstream element; recognized by Sp1 TF; present in promoters without TATA box)

TATA box (Hogness box): located ~25-30 bp upstream of the transcription start site (TSS); consensus sequence TATAAA (or TATAWAW, where W = A or T); TBP (TATA-binding protein) is a subunit of TFIID (Transcription Factor IID, contains TBP + TAFs [TBP-associated factors, TAF1-TAF15]); TBP binds TATA box → major grove of DNA → inserts hydrophobic residues between base pairs → BENDS DNA ~80° (unique TBP-induced DNA bend) → distortion opens minor groove → enables other GTFs to assemble into the pre-initiation complex (PIC); assembly order: TBP/TFIID → TFIIA → TFIIB → Pol II + TFIIF → TFIIE → TFIIH → complete PIC; TFIIH: has ATPase/helicase activity (unwinds DNA at TSS) + CDK7 kinase (phosphorylates Pol II CTD Ser5 of YSPTSPS heptad repeat → enables promoter escape + 5' capping); most protein-coding gene promoters lack a TATA box → instead use DPE (downstream promoter element, +28 to +32) or BRE (TFIIB response element) or Inr (initiator)
CAAT box (upstream element, ~-75 bp; recognized by NF-Y [heterotrimeric NF-Y complex]; not the TBP recognition sequence)
CpG island (regions with ↑CpG dinucleotides in promoters; methylation → silencing; not specifically the TBP binding element)
explanation: Eukaryotic transcription factors and Pol II: General (basal) TFs: TFIID, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIF, TFIIE, TFIIH — form the PIC at the core promoter. TFIIH: crucial multisubunit complex with: (1) helicase/ATPase (XPB [ERCC3] and XPD [ERCC2] helicases → unwind DNA at TSS; also needed for NER → XPB/XPD mutations → xeroderma pigmentosum [XP] + Cockayne syndrome + trichothiodystrophy [TFIIH-associated NER/transcription syndromes]); (2) CDK7/CycH/MAT1 kinase (= CAK, CDK-activating kinase → phosphorylates CDK4/6/1/2 etc. + phosphorylates Pol II CTD Ser5 [initiation/capping] + Ser2 [elongation by CDK9/P-TEFb]). Pol II CTD: 52 heptad repeats (YSPTSPS); unphosphorylated CTD → needed for PIC assembly; Ser5-P (CDK7) → initiating Pol II → 5'-capping enzyme recruited (binds phospho-Ser5); Ser2-P (CDK9/P-TEFb) → elongating Pol II → splicing factors + 3'-end processing factors recruited. RNA Pol isoforms: Pol I: rRNA (28S, 18S, 5.8S), in nucleolus; Pol II: mRNA + snRNA + miRNA; Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, 7SL RNA, U6 snRNA, small ncRNA; all nuclear Pol require Mn2+ or Mg2+; alpha-amanitin sensitivity: Pol II → most sensitive; Pol III → less sensitive; Pol I → insensitive; alpha-amanitin from Amanita phalloides (death cap mushroom) → binds Pol II between trigger loop and bridge helix → blocks translocation → no mRNA synthesis → liver/kidney failure.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An increase in cAMP in a liver cell has all of the following effects EXCEPT:
options: Activation of glycogen phosphorylase (cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase b → phosphorylase a [active] → ↑glycogenolysis)
Inhibition of glycogen synthase (cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates GS → GS-b [inactive] → ↓glycogen synthesis)

Activation of HMG-CoA reductase (WRONG — cAMP/PKA phosphorylates and INACTIVATES HMGCR → ↓cholesterol synthesis; insulin ACTIVATES HMGCR phosphatase → dephosphorylates → activates HMGCR): this is the EXCEPTION — PKA phosphorylates HMGCR → inactive (↓cholesterol synthesis, appropriate during fasting); ALSO PKA phosphorylates ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT-I → ↑FA oxidation; thus in glucagon/cAMP state (fasting): ↓glycogen synthesis, ↑glycogenolysis, ↓FA synthesis, ↑FA oxidation, ↑gluconeogenesis, ↓cholesterol synthesis — all coordinated by PKA

Activation of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) in adipose tissue (cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates HSL Ser563/659/660 → ↑lipolysis; also ATGL is the main TG lipase: ATGL + CGI-58 [ABHD5] → monoacylglycerol lipase [MGL] pathway; PKA also phosphorylates perilipin 1 [PLIN1] → allows ATGL access to lipid droplet)
explanation: cAMP-PKA signaling cascade in liver (glucagon/epinephrine): Glucagon → GCGR (Gs-coupled GPCR) → Gαs-GTP → activates adenylyl cyclase (AC) → cAMP ↑ → activates PKA (cAMP binds regulatory R subunits → releases catalytic C subunits) → C subunits phosphorylate multiple targets. PKA substrates in liver: Phosphorylase kinase (PhK, Ser17): ↑PhK → ↑phosphorylase a → ↑glycogenolysis. Glycogen synthase (multiple Ser): ↓GS-a → ↓glycogen synthesis. PEPCK promoter (via CREB phosphorylation, Ser133): CREB-p → CRE (cAMP response element) → ↑PEPCK + ↑G6Pase transcription → ↑gluconeogenesis. ACC (Ser79): ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓FA synthesis + ↑FA oxidation (↓malonyl-CoA relieves CPT-1 inhibition). HMGCR (Ser872): ↓HMGCR activity → ↓cholesterol synthesis. PFK-2/FBPase-2 (bifunctional enzyme, Ser32): PKA phosphorylation → ↓PFK-2 activity + ↑FBPase-2 activity → ↓fructose-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis + ↑FBPase-1 → ↑gluconeogenesis. CREB (Ser133): transcriptional activation → ↑PGC-1α → ↑PEPCK, G6Pase, TFAM. Contrast with insulin effects: ↑PDE3B (↓cAMP) + PI3K-Akt → ↑PP1 (→ ↑GS-a, ↑HMGCR-a, ↓PhK) + ↑ACC-a (via PP2A) + Akt → ↑PFKFB3 (↑F-2,6-BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis) + ↑AS160 (→ GLUT4) + FoxO exclusion (↓PEPCK/G6Pase) + ↑SREBP-1c (→ ↑lipogenesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Propionic acid (propionate) produced from odd-chain fatty acid oxidation enters the TCA cycle as succinyl-CoA after a series of reactions. Which of the following correctly describes the enzyme defect in propionic acidemia?
options: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency: this enzyme converts L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA using cobalamin (B12) as cofactor → causes methylmalonic acidemia (MMA), not propionic acidemia (PA); MMA: ↑methylmalonic acid in blood/urine; often responds to B12 supplementation if mutase is B12-responsive

Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) deficiency: PCC catalyzes: propionyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP [+ biotin] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA (first committed step in propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA pathway); PCC is a biotin-dependent enzyme (like PC, ACC, and MCC); PCC subunits: α (PCCA gene, Cr3) + β (PCCB gene, Cr13); PCC deficiency (AR, PCCA or PCCB mutations) → propionic acidemia (PA): ↑propionic acid (propionyl-CoA → propionic acid) + ↑methylcitrate (propionyl-CoA + OAA → methylcitrate, by citrate synthase) + ↑3-hydroxypropionic acid; propionyl-CoA inhibits NAGS → ↑secondary hyperammonemia; inhibits pyruvate carboxylase → ↑lactate; inhibits complex III → ETC dysfunction; biotinidase deficiency or HLCS deficiency → multiple carboxylase deficiency (↓PCC + ACC + PC + MCC) → propionic acid + methylcrotonylglycine + elevated lactate; treatment: low-protein + low-fat diet + L-carnitine (removes propionyl-CoA as propionylcarnitine) + metronidazole (↓propionate-producing gut bacteria) + biotin (if MCD)
Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (this causes isovaleric acidemia, not propionic acidemia; leucine catabolism)
Methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase deficiency: this would cause mild ↑methylmalonic acid as D-MMA cannot convert to L-MMA; very mild, rare
explanation: Propionic acid metabolism pathway: Sources of propionyl-CoA: (1) odd-chain fatty acid β-oxidation (last 3C = propionyl-CoA); (2) catabolism of amino acids: Val, Ile, Met, Thr → succinyl-CoA pathway; (3) cholesterol side chain; (4) gut bacteria (propionic acid-producing Bacteroidetes → absorbed). Propionyl-CoA → [PCC, biotin] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → [methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase] → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, B12] → succinyl-CoA → TCA. Organic acidemias comparison: Propionic acidemia: ↑propionic acid, ↑methylcitrate, ↑3-OH-propionic acid, ↑C3-acylcarnitine (propionylcarnitine) on acylcarnitine profile; ↑NH3 (secondary, NAGS inhibition); ↑lactate. Methylmalonic acidemia (MMA): ↑methylmalonic acid, ↑C3-acylcarnitine; if B12-responsive: B12 supplementation helps; if B12-non-responsive: strict diet + vitamin supplementation; ↑propionate + ↑methylcitrate (if combined MUT + upstream block). Isovaleric acidemia: ↑C5-acylcarnitine (isovalerylcarnitine), ↑isovalerylglycine, 'sweaty feet' odor. Maple syrup urine disease: ↑leucine/isoleucine/valine + BCKAs (↑C5:1, ↑C5:0 acylcarnitines), maple syrup odor → acute neurological crisis if not treated (especially leucine: most neurotoxic BCAA). All organic acidemias: treated with restriction of offending AA/FA + L-carnitine (for acylcarnitine excretion/detoxification) + newborn screening via MS/MS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A drug that inhibits microtubule polymerization would arrest the cell cycle at which stage?
options: G1 phase (before DNA synthesis; microtubule polymerization inhibitors affect mitosis, not G1)
S phase (DNA synthesis phase; not the primary arrest point for microtubule inhibitors)
G2 phase (DNA synthesis complete but before mitosis; some drugs activate G2 checkpoint)

M phase (mitosis): specifically at metaphase, where the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) monitors proper kinetochore-microtubule attachment; agents that depolymerize microtubules (colchicine, vinca alkaloids: vincristine, vinblastine) → inhibit microtubule polymerization → no spindle formation → SAC activated (MAD1/MAD2/BubR1/Bub1/Bub3 at unattached kinetochores → inhibit APC/C [anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome] by sequestering CDC20 in mitotic checkpoint complex [MCC]) → APC/C-CDC20 cannot ubiquitinate securin (→ cannot release separase) or cyclin B (→ CDK1 remains active [cannot exit mitosis]) → cell arrested in metaphase → apoptosis if checkpoint cannot be satisfied; agents that stabilize microtubules (taxanes: paclitaxel, docetaxel) → prevent depolymerization → microtubules cannot shorten → kinetochores cannot generate tension → SAC also activated → same metaphase arrest; both classes cause M-phase arrest via SAC
explanation: Cell cycle and checkpoints: G1 phase: cell growth + preparation for DNA synthesis; G1 checkpoint ('restriction point'): CDK4/6-cyclin D → phosphorylates Rb → releases E2F → ↑S-phase genes; RB1 mutations → no restriction → uncontrolled cell cycle entry; CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib): ↓Rb phosphorylation → G1 arrest → treat ER+HER2- breast cancer. S phase: DNA replication; intra-S checkpoint: ATM + ATR → CHK1/CHK2 → CDC25A ubiquitination → ↓CDK2-CycA activity → slows replication forks if DNA damage; inhibitors: hydroxyurea (RNR inhibitor → ↓dNTP → stalls replication), aphidicolin (Pol α inhibitor), araC/gemcitabine (chain terminators). G2/M checkpoint: ATM/ATR → CHK1/CHK2 → CDC25C phosphorylation → 14-3-3 binding → nuclear exclusion → ↓CDC25C activity → ↓CDK1-CycB activation → prevents mitosis entry if DNA damage present; wee1 kinase: phosphorylates CDK1-Tyr15 → CDK1 inactive; CDC25B/C: removes Tyr15-P → CDK1 active → CDK1-CycB (MPF, maturation promoting factor) → G2→M transition. M phase: SAC (spindle assembly checkpoint): APC/C-CDC20 required for: securin ubiquitination → proteasome → releases separase → cleaves cohesin → sister chromatids separate; cyclin B ubiquitination → CDK1 inactivation → mitotic exit. CDK1 (Cdc2): the 'master mitotic kinase'; activated by: cyclin B + dephosphorylation by CDC25C; inhibited by: wee1 kinase (Tyr15), myt1 kinase (Thr14), CDK1 inhibitors (in trials).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following represents an 'oncometabolite' that can act as a competitive inhibitor of alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases?
options: Pyruvate (a normal metabolite, not an oncometabolite)
Citrate (exported from mitochondria for lipid synthesis; not an oncometabolite inhibitor of α-KG dioxygenases)

2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG): produced by gain-of-function mutations in IDH1 (cytoplasm, Arg132) or IDH2 (mitochondria, Arg172 + Arg140); normal IDH1/2: isocitrate + NADP+ → α-KG + CO2 + NADPH; mutant IDH1/2 (neomorphic enzyme): α-KG + NADPH → 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) + NADP+ (reverse direction, neomorphic activity); 2-HG accumulates to high levels (10-100× normal) → competitively inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (share α-KG as co-substrate): TET2 (5-methylcytosine dioxygenase, DNA demethylase: 5mC → 5-hmC → ↑DNA methylation if inhibited); KDM histone demethylases (↑histone methylation); PHD2 (prolyl hydroxylase, hydroxylates HIF-1α → VHL-dependent degradation → if inhibited → ↑HIF-1α → Warburg, ↑angiogenesis); collagen prolyl hydroxylases; affected cancers: acute myeloid leukemia (AML, IDH1 R132, IDH2 R140/R172), oligodendroglioma + astrocytoma (IDH1 mut → 1p/19q codeletion → 'R132H' staining by IHC), cholangiocarcinoma, chondrosarcoma; treatment: ivosidenib (IDH1 inhibitor), enasidenib (IDH2 inhibitor); IDH1/2 mut gliomas: better prognosis than IDH-wild type GBM
Lactate (elevated in Warburg effect; not a direct inhibitor of dioxygenases)
explanation: α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (2-OG dioxygenases): Large family; all require: α-ketoglutarate (2-oxoglutarate, 2-OG) + O2 + Fe2+ + ascorbate (Vit C regenerates Fe2+ from Fe3+); reaction: α-KG + substrate → succinate + CO2 + hydroxylated substrate. Key members: TET1/2/3 (ten-eleven translocation): 5mC → 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) → → demethylation; TET2 most commonly mutated in AML (20-25%) + CHIP (clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential). KDM histone demethylases: Jumonji domain-containing (JMJD) demethylases; remove methyl groups from Lys residues on histones. PHD1/2/3 (EGLN1/2/3): prolyl hydroxylate HIF-1α Pr402 + Pro564 → recognized by VHL (E3 ubiquitin ligase) → ubiquitination → proteasomal degradation; inhibited by: 2-HG (IDH mut), succinate (SDH mut), fumarate (FH mut) → stabilizes HIF-1α → Warburg; PHD inhibitors (vadadustat, daprodustat, roxadustat) → ↑HIF-1α → ↑EPO → ↑erythropoiesis → treat anemia of CKD. ALKBH (AlkB homologs): DNA/RNA repair; oxidative demethylation of m1A/m1G/m3C/m6A modifications. Procollagen prolyl + lysyl hydroxylases (P4HA, P4HB/PDI, LOX hydroxylase): require ascorbate; explains scurvy mechanism. 2-HG enantiomers: (R)-2-HG (D-2-HG): from IDH1/2 mut; (S)-2-HG (L-2-HG): from L-2-HG dehydrogenase (L2HGDH) deficiency (2-HGA type II); both inhibit TET2/KDM.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the immunoglobulin structure, two heavy chains and two light chains are joined by disulfide bonds. The region that determines antibody class (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD) is the:
options: Variable region of the light chain (VL): determines antigen specificity, not antibody class
Variable region of the heavy chain (VH): antigen binding with VL; determines some effector function via VH3/VH4/VH6 but not the class

Complementarity-determining regions (CDRs): the hypervariable loops within VH + VL that make direct contact with antigen; 3 CDRs in VH + 3 in VL → total 6 CDRs per Fab → paratope (antigen-binding site); not the class determinant

Constant region of the heavy chain (CH, isotype): the heavy chain constant region (CH1-CH2-CH3 or CH1-CH4 for IgM/IgE) determines the antibody CLASS (isotype): IgG (γ heavy chain, CH1-CH2-CH3): most abundant serum Ig; 4 subclasses IgG1-4; crosses placenta (Fc receptor FcRn); fixes complement (IgG1/3 > IgG2); opsonization; longest half-life (~21 days). IgA (α heavy chain, CH1-CH2-CH3): dimer with J-chain + secretory component (SC) in secretions; most abundant Ig at mucosal surfaces; secretory IgA (sIgA) not cleaved by most bacterial IgA proteases because of SC protection. IgM (μ heavy chain, CH1-CH2-CH3-CH4): pentamer (with J-chain) in serum; first Ig made in primary immune response; best complement fixer (Fc regions cluster → ↑C1q binding); natural ABO blood group antibodies are IgM. IgE (ε heavy chain): lowest serum concentration; very high affinity for FcεRI on mast cells + basophils → immediate hypersensitivity; ↑in: allergy, parasitic infection; not complement-fixing. IgD (δ heavy chain): mainly on naive B cell surface as antigen receptor (with IgM); very low serum; function not fully understood
explanation: Antibody structure: Basic unit: Y-shaped, two identical heavy chains (H) + two identical light chains (L) connected by inter-chain disulfide bonds. Fab (fragment antigen binding): VH + CH1 + VL + CL; contains antigen binding site (paratope). Fc (fragment crystallizable): CH2 + CH3 (×2) or CH2+CH3+CH4 for IgM/IgE; determines class + effector function (complement, FcR binding, half-life). Hinge region: flexible Gly/Pro-rich region between CH1 and CH2; allows Fab arms to move independently; IgG3 has longest hinge (15 disulfide bonds → slower migration in gel electrophoresis); site for papain (cuts above hinge → 2 Fab + 1 Fc) and pepsin (cuts below hinge → F(ab')2 + pFc' fragments; F(ab')2 retains bivalence). Light chains: κ (kappa) or λ (lambda); each has VL + CL; κ:λ ratio normally ~2:1 in serum; abnormal κ:λ ratio → monoclonal light chain disease (multiple myeloma Bence Jones proteins are free monoclonal light chains). Class switching: naive B cells express IgM + IgD on surface → upon T cell help (CD40L-CD40 + cytokines) → AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase) + UNG (uracil-DNA glycosylase) + NHEJ → deletional recombination of S (switch) regions between CH gene segments → class switch recombination; IL-4/IL-13 → IgE or IgG1 (human)/IgG1 (human subclasses differ from mouse); TGF-β → IgA; IFN-γ → IgG2/3 (human). AID (encoded by AICDA): also responsible for somatic hypermutation (SHM) in germinal centers → introduces point mutations in VH/VL → selection for high-affinity antibody variants (affinity maturation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step in glycolysis that is irreversible and is the main regulatory point sensitive to fructose-2,6-bisphosphate?
options: Hexokinase/Glucokinase: first step (Glucose → G6P); regulated by G6P product inhibition (HK) or by glucose concentration and not by F-2,6-BP directly
Phosphoglucose isomerase (PGI/GPI): G6P → F6P; near-equilibrium, not a regulated or irreversible step
Phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK): 1,3-BPG → 3-PG + ATP; step 7, substrate-level phosphorylation; not the regulatory point sensitive to F-2,6-BP
