Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1): fructose-6-phosphate + ATP → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate + ADP; the COMMITTED, RATE-LIMITING, and IRREVERSIBLE step of glycolysis; allosteric regulation: ACTIVATED by: AMP (low energy), ADP, F-2,6-BP (most potent activator; made by PFK-2 which is a bifunctional enzyme: PFK-2 domain synthesizes F-2,6-BP from F6P + ATP; FBPase-2 domain degrades F-2,6-BP back to F6P; insulin → activates PFK-2 → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis; glucagon/PKA → phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2 bifunctional enzyme → FBPase-2 active → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis in liver); also activated by: Pi, NH4+; INHIBITED by: ATP (high energy), citrate (↑TCA intermediates → signals adequate oxidative capacity → pause glycolysis), H+ (acidosis → protects from excessive lactate production); in cancer: Warburg effect → ↑PFK-1 via ↑F-2,6-BP (↑PFKFB3 [PFK-2 isoform 3], hypoxia → ↑PFKFB3 via HIF-1α)
explanation: Glycolytic control points (irreversible steps): Hexokinase/Glucokinase (HK/GK): Glucose → G6P (step 1, irreversible in vivo). HK (I-III): high affinity (Km ~0.1 mM), inhibited by G6P. GK/HK IV: low affinity (Km ~10 mM), NOT inhibited by G6P, S-curve kinetics (cooperative), induced by insulin in liver/β-cells → glucose sensor. PFK-1: F6P → F-1,6-BP (step 3, irreversible, main regulatory point). Pyruvate kinase (PK, step 10): PEP → pyruvate + ATP (irreversible in vivo); regulated: activated by F-1,6-BP (feedforward from step 3); inhibited by ATP, alanine (as product of pyruvate → Ala by ALT; fasting → ↑Ala → ↑PK inhibition); L-PK (liver): phosphorylated by PKA (glucagon) → inactive (↓PK → ↓glycolysis, ↑gluconeogenesis in liver); PK deficiency (AR): most common enzyme defect in hereditary non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia (RBCs depend entirely on glycolysis → ↓ATP → ↓Na+/K+ ATPase → osmotic lysis; but ↑2,3-BPG → right-shifted ODC → better O2 delivery → less clinical severity than equivalent anemia from other causes; Heinz bodies NOT seen; ↑osmotic fragility is NOT a feature [unlike spherocytosis]; blood smear: echinocytes [poikilocytes]). Fructokinase (liver/intestine/kidney): fructose → F1P (not part of glycolysis control but important in fructose intolerance: aldolase B [F1P → DHAP + glyceraldehyde] deficiency → HFI; fructokinase deficiency → essential fructosuria [benign, F1P not made → no toxicity]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The complement system's membrane attack complex (MAC) is formed by polymerization of:
options: C3b oligomers only (C3b is important for opsonization and convertase formation, not MAC)

C5b + C6 + C7 + C8 + C9 (poly-C9): MAC formation: C5b binds C6 → C5b-6 → binds C7 (amphiphilic, partially inserts into membrane) → C5b-7 → binds C8 (C8α-C8β-C8γ; inserts into bilayer, creates small pore) → recruits multiple C9 molecules (12-18 C9 monomers) → C9 polymerizes around C5b-678 to form the MAC channel (C5b-9, terminal complement complex, TCC); MAC: a protein-lined pore (~10 nm diameter) through bacterial/cell membrane → unregulated ion flux + osmotic lysis; complement activation pathways: (1) Classical: Ag-Ab (IgG1/IgG3 or IgM) → C1q binds Fc → C1r autoactivation → C1r cleaves C1s → C1s cleaves C4 → C4a + C4b; C4b binds surface → + C2 → C1s cleaves C2 → C4b2a (C3 convertase, classical) → C3 → C3a + C3b; C4b2a3b (C5 convertase) → C5 → C5a + C5b → MAC; (2) Lectin (MBL/MASP): MBL/ficolins/CL-11 bind mannose/GlcNAc → MASP1/MASP2 activation → cleave C4 + C2 → same as classical from C4; (3) Alternative: C3 spontaneous hydrolysis → C3(H2O) + Factor B → Factor D cleaves Bb → C3(H2O)Bb (initiation convertase) → C3b on surface → C3bBb (stabilized by properdin, Factor P) + C3b → C3bBbC3b (C5 convertase, alternative)
C1q + C4 + C2 + C3 (these form the C3 convertase, not the MAC)
C3a + C4a + C5a (these are anaphylatoxins [small cleavage fragments], not the MAC components)
explanation: Complement components and clinical relevance: C1q deficiency: most common cause of hereditary angioedema type III; also ↑SLE risk (C1q needed to clear apoptotic cells/chromatin → if absent → chromatin accumulates → autoimmunity). C3 deficiency: most severe immunodeficiency of complement pathway → recurrent bacterial infections with ALL organisms; ↑susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria (which use complement-mediated opsonization). C5-C9 deficiency: defective MAC formation → susceptibility specifically to Neisseria infections (N. meningitidis, N. gonorrhoeae — Gram-negative, evade complement poorly without MAC). DAF (CD55) + CD59 (protectin): regulators of complement activation on host cells: DAF: accelerates decay of C3/C5 convertases → ↓complement activation on host cells; CD59: inhibits MAC by preventing C9 polymerization onto host cell membranes; PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria): somatic mutation in PIG-A (phosphatidylinositol glycan anchor biosynthesis class A) → absent GPI-anchor biosynthesis → deficient DAF + CD59 on RBC + platelet surface → uncontrolled complement-mediated hemolysis + thrombosis; treatment: eculizumab (anti-C5 mAb → prevents C5 cleavage → no C5a/MAC formation → ↓hemolysis, but ↑meningococcal risk → vaccinate); ravulizumab (anti-C5, longer t½). C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF): autoantibody (IgG) against C3bBb → stabilizes alternative pathway C3 convertase → ↑C3 consumption → ↓C3 → recurrent infections + MPGN type II (dense deposit disease).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the enzyme lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT)?
options: LCAT transfers phospholipids from HDL to VLDL (this is PLTP [phospholipid transfer protein] or CETP [cholesterol ester transfer protein, which transfers CE from HDL to VLDL/LDL in exchange for TG]; not LCAT)

LCAT converts free cholesterol to cholesterol esters on HDL particles using phosphatidylcholine as the acyl donor: LCAT (lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase): synthesized by liver → secreted into plasma; activated by ApoA-I (main activator) on HDL; reaction: phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) + free cholesterol → cholesterol ester + lysolecithin (lysophosphatidylcholine); the cholesterol ester (CE) moves to the hydrophobic core of HDL → nascent disk-shaped HDL (pre-β HDL) → accumulates CE → becomes spherical HDL3 → HDL2; this is a key step in reverse cholesterol transport (RCT): cholesterol removed from peripheral tissues → ABC A1 (on macrophages) → ApoA-I → LCAT → CE in HDL core → liver: hepatic scavenger receptor B-I (SR-BI) → selective uptake of CE from HDL → bile/recycling; LCAT deficiency (AR): familial LCAT deficiency (full deficiency) → anemia (↑unesterified cholesterol in RBC membrane → target cells + hemolysis) + corneal opacity (Lp-X deposits) + nephropathy (proteinuria → ESRD); fish-eye disease (partial LCAT deficiency): corneal opacity only without full clinical syndrome; ↓LCAT activity → ↓HDL-C
LCAT hydrolyzes triglycerides from chylomicrons to release free fatty acids (that is lipoprotein lipase [LPL], on capillary endothelium)
LCAT transfers apolipoprotein C-II (ApoC-II) to chylomicrons for LPL activation (this is HDL donating ApoC-II and ApoE to chylomicrons after they enter circulation)
explanation: Reverse cholesterol transport (RCT): ABCA1 (macrophage, hepatocyte) → transfers free cholesterol + phospholipid → to lipid-poor ApoA-I → forms nascent pre-β HDL (discoidal). LCAT (activated by ApoA-I) → esterifies cholesterol → CE → pre-β HDL → spherical HDL3 → HDL2. CETP: transfers CE from HDL → VLDL/LDL + TG from VLDL/LDL → HDL; ↑CETP → ↓HDL-C, ↑VLDL-CE → proatherogenic; CETP inhibitors (anacetrapib, dalcetrapib, evacetrapib) → ↑↑HDL-C but failed to show CV benefit (dalcetrapib, evacetrapib failed; anacetrapib showed marginal benefit in REVEAL trial but not pursued); torcetrapib failed due to ↑aldosterone + ↑BP (off-target CETP effects). SR-BI (scavenger receptor BI, SCARB1): selective lipid uptake at liver + steroidogenic tissues (adrenal, gonads); takes CE from HDL without internalizing whole particle → RCT endpoint. ABCG5/ABCG8: liver + intestine → excrete phytosterols (plant sterols) + cholesterol into bile; mutations → sitosterolemia (↑plant sterols → premature atherosclerosis). Apolipoproteins (key roles): ApoA-I: HDL structural, LCAT activator, ABCA1 ligand. ApoB48: chylomicron structural (intestine). ApoB100: VLDL/IDL/LDL structural; LDLR ligand. ApoC-II: LPL activator (on chylomicrons + VLDL); ApoC-II deficiency → familial hyperchylomicronemia type I (↑↑TG, pancreatitis). ApoC-III: LPL inhibitor (↓TG clearance). ApoE: VLDL remnant/IDL clearance by LDL-R + LRP; ApoE2 (↓LDLR affinity → ↑remnants, but lower risk of CAD in ApoE2/E2); ApoE4 (↑Alzheimer risk, ↓lifespan, ↑LDL, ↑CV risk); ApoE3 most common.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) oxidative branch produces NADPH. In which phase of the cell cycle is demand for PPP-derived NADPH particularly high?
options: G1 phase only (demand is high in all rapidly dividing cells, not just G1)

S phase: actively dividing cancer cells and rapidly proliferating normal cells show increased PPP flux during S phase when DNA synthesis occurs; however, demand for NADPH is not uniquely tied to any one cell cycle phase — NADPH is needed continuously for: (1) reductive biosynthesis (FA synthesis via FAS, cholesterol via HMGCR, nucleotide synthesis); (2) antioxidant defense (GPx via GSH + glutathione reductase, catalase in peroxisomes, thioredoxin reductase); (3) NADPH oxidase (NOX, phagocytic burst); the correct frame is that all highly proliferating cells have elevated PPP; this question has no single correct answer — but NADPH demand is highest during S phase when nucleotide synthesis (ribose-5-P from PPP for dNTPs) AND reductive biosynthesis for membrane components (needed for two daughter cells) peak
G0 (quiescent phase — minimal biosynthesis, minimal PPP demand)
M phase (mitosis — DNA replication complete, division occurring; biosynthesis has peaked)
explanation: Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP): Location: cytoplasm. Glucose-6-P → [G6PD, rate-limiting, NADP+] → 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone → [6-phosphogluconolactonase] → 6-phosphogluconate → [6-PGDH, NADP+] → ribulose-5-P + CO2 + NADPH. Total per turn: 2 NADPH + 1 CO2 (per glucose-6-P in the oxidative branch). Non-oxidative branch: ribulose-5-P → ribose-5-P [phosphopentose isomerase] → nucleotide synthesis; transketolase (TK, thiamine/B1 cofactor) + transaldolase interconvert C3-C7 sugars → can regenerate F6P + G3P that re-enter glycolysis. NADPH uses: (1) Fatty acid synthesis (FAS: ~14 NADPH per palmitate). (2) Cholesterol synthesis (HMGCR: 2 NADPH per mevalonate). (3) GSH regeneration (glutathione reductase: GSSG + NADPH → 2 GSH). (4) Detoxification of H2O2 (GPx: 2 GSH + H2O2 → GSSG + 2 H2O; NADPH regenerates GSH). (5) Microsomal P450 reactions (CYP450 + NADPH cytochrome P450 reductase). (6) NADPH oxidase (NOX, phagocytic burst: 2 O2 + NADPH → 2 O2•- + NADP+ + H+). (7) Nitric oxide synthesis (NOS: NADPH cofactor). Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD): X-linked (CYBB, gp91-phox [NOX2 catalytic subunit]) or AR (CYBA [p22], NCF1 [p47], NCF2 [p67], NCF4 [p40]); NADPH oxidase cannot generate superoxide → cannot kill phagocytosed bacteria → recurrent life-threatening infections with catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Nocardia, Burkholderia, Granulibacter); NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test → normal PMNs reduce NBT (→ formazan, blue) using O2-; CGD PMNs cannot reduce NBT → negative test. DHR (dihydrorhodamine) flow cytometry: more sensitive/specific.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Cholesterol esterification for intracellular storage is catalyzed by which enzyme?
options: LCAT (lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase): esterifies cholesterol on HDL in PLASMA, not for intracellular storage

ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase): ACAT1 (SOAT1, ER, ubiquitous — macrophages, adrenal) and ACAT2 (SOAT2, ER, liver + intestine): esterify intracellular free cholesterol for storage as cholesterol esters (CE) in lipid droplets; reaction: free cholesterol + acyl-CoA → cholesterol ester + CoA; regulation: ↑free cholesterol in ER → ACAT activated → CE formation → stored in lipid droplets (LD) → prevents cholesterol toxicity; ACAT1 in macrophages: major pathway for foam cell formation (excessive LDL uptake → ↑free cholesterol → ACAT1 → CE lipid droplets → foam cell → atherosclerotic plaque); ACAT inhibitors (avasimibe): reduce foam cell formation but clinical trials did not show reduction in atherosclerosis; ACAT2 in intestine: esterifies cholesterol for packaging into chylomicrons; ACAT2 in liver: esterifies cholesterol for VLDL assembly
CETP (cholesterol ester transfer protein): transfers CE between lipoproteins in PLASMA; not intracellular esterification

Pancreatic cholesterol esterase (CEase, bile salt-activated lipase): hydrolyzes dietary cholesterol esters in lumen → free cholesterol + FA for absorption; this is a hydrolase, not an esterification enzyme
explanation: Cellular cholesterol homeostasis: Cholesterol sensing in ER: INSIG-1/2 (ER membrane proteins) sense ↑cholesterol → retain SCAP-SREBP2 complex in ER → ↓LDLR + ↓HMGCR transcription + ↑ACAT (via ↑free cholesterol). When cholesterol ↓: SCAP-SREBP2 travels to Golgi → S1P + S2P proteases cleave → SREBP2 N-terminal domain enters nucleus → ↑LDLR + HMGCR transcription. PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9): secreted, binds LDLR → co-internalized → directs LDLR to lysosomal degradation; PCSK9 is transcribed from LDLR regulatory elements (SREBP2-responsive); statins → ↑SREBP2 → ↑LDLR + ↑PCSK9 → PCSK9 partially counteracts LDL-R increase; PCSK9-I (evolocumab, alirocumab) + statin → additive LDL lowering. NPC1/NPC2 (Niemann-Pick type C): endosomal/lysosomal proteins that export free cholesterol from late endosome → ER; NPC1 mutations → cholesterol trapped in late endosome + lysosome → ↓ER cholesterol → paradoxically activates SREBP2 → ↑LDL-R + ↑HMGCR (but cholesterol can't be utilized) → NPC disease (progressive ataxia, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dementia, liver disease). NPC1: most common (95%), large transmembrane protein; NPC2: soluble lysosomal; filipin staining: fluorescent marker for unesterified cholesterol → ↑filipin staining in NPC cells (cholesterol trapped in lysosomes).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glucose enters red blood cells by which mechanism?
options: Active transport requiring Na+ gradient (this is SGLT mechanism in intestine/kidney; RBCs use facilitated diffusion)

Facilitated diffusion via GLUT1: red blood cells (RBCs) rely solely on glucose as their energy source → critical demand for glucose uptake; GLUT1 (encoded by SLC2A1, chromosome 1p34.2) is the primary glucose transporter in RBCs; GLUT1 is a 12-transmembrane domain protein (class I GLUTs: 1, 2, 3, 4) that mediates facilitated diffusion of glucose down its concentration gradient (no ATP, no Na+ required); in fetal erythrocytes/placenta: GLUT1 expression very high; GLUT1 on blood-brain barrier (luminal side): ensures brain glucose supply; GLUT1 deficiency syndrome (GLUT1-DS; De Vivo disease): mutations in SLC2A1 → ↓glucose transport across BBB → low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) with normal serum glucose (ratio CSF/blood glucose <0.4, normally >0.6) → brain energy deprivation → drug-resistant epilepsy, developmental delay, movement disorder, microcephaly; treatment: ketogenic diet (ketones cross BBB independently → bypass GLUT1 deficiency) → ↓seizures + ↑development
Pinocytosis (endocytosis — used for large macromolecules, not glucose)
Co-transport with Na+ ions (secondary active transport — SGLT1 in gut, SGLT2 in kidney; not in RBCs)
explanation: Glucose transport systems: Class I facilitated GLUTs: GLUT1 (ubiquitous, BBB, RBC, placenta), GLUT2 (liver, β-cells, kidney, intestine — basolateral), GLUT3 (neurons, testes), GLUT4 (muscle, fat, heart — insulin-dependent). Class II: GLUT5 (fructose, intestine, testes), GLUT7 (ER of liver). SGLT (Na+-glucose cotransporter, secondary active, Na+ enters down gradient driving glucose uptake against gradient): SGLT1 (intestine apical, kidney tubule S1/S2): 2 Na+:1 glucose. SGLT2 (kidney tubule S1 predominant, ~90% of glucose reabsorption): 1 Na+:1 glucose — target of gliflozins (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). GLUT1-DS: hallmark → CSF glucose <2.2 mM (40 mg/dL) + CSF:plasma glucose ratio <0.4; also ↓CSF lactate; EEG: diffuse slowing; treatment: ketogenic diet (4:1 fat:carb+protein ratio) dramatically reduces seizures and improves cognition if started early. Transporter kinetics: GLUT1 Km ~1-2 mM for glucose → nearly saturated at physiological blood glucose (5 mM) → rate limited more by available GLUT1 than substrate. GLUT3 Km ~1.5 mM → even higher affinity → neurons can extract glucose even when blood glucose falls. GLUT4 translocation: AS160 (Akt substrate of 160 kDa, TBC1D4) → normally, AS160 GAP (GTPase-activating protein) keeps Rab10 in GDP-bound state → GLUT4 vesicle docked in intracellular pool; insulin → Akt phospho-AS160 → ↓GAP activity → Rab10-GTP → GLUT4 vesicle exocytosis → ↑PM GLUT4; exercise: AMPK → similar pathway independent of insulin.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An inherited condition in which the rate of synthesis of alpha-globin chains exceeds beta-globin chains results in:
options: Alpha thalassemia (this occurs when ALPHA synthesis is REDUCED relative to beta; ΔΔ or Δ condition)
Beta thalassemia major (this occurs when BETA synthesis is REDUCED, leaving excess alpha chains)

This scenario describes neither thalassemia but rather an imbalance that does not naturally occur in inherited hemoglobin disorders (alpha excess over beta is physiologically unusual in inherited diseases)

Hemolytic anemia from beta-globin chain precipitation (in beta thalassemia): this question tests the understanding that the PATHOLOGICAL situation is when ALPHA chains are IN EXCESS (after losing beta synthesis), NOT the reverse; in beta thalassemia: ↓beta globin → excess alpha chains precipitate → Heinz bodies in RBC precursors → ineffective erythropoiesis + hemolysis; in alpha thalassemia: ↓alpha → excess BETA chains form β4 (HbH) or excess GAMMA chains form γ4 (Hb Barts); IF (hypothetically) alpha synthesis was truly elevated over beta: this would not naturally occur because hemoglobin synthesis is tightly coordinated; the correct clinical condition is the REVERSE of what's stated: alpha EXCESS (reduced beta) = beta thalassemia
explanation: Thalassemia molecular basis: Alpha thalassemia: α-globin genes on chromosome 16 (4 genes: α1α2/α1α2); most common: gene deletions (Southeast Asian type: --SEA/αα or --SEA/--SEA). Loss of 1 gene: silent carrier (αα/α-). Loss of 2: alpha thal trait (mild microcytic anemia, Hb Bart 1-2%; --/αα [trans] or -α/-α [cis]). Loss of 3 (HbH disease): HbH (β4 tetramers, unstable, oxidize → Heinz bodies → hemolytic anemia); Hb Barts ~25-30% at birth. Loss of 4 (Hb Barts hydrops fetalis): γ4 tetramers (Hb Barts, very high O2 affinity → can't deliver O2 to tissues → severe tissue hypoxia + fetal hydrops → stillbirth or immediate neonatal death); requires in utero transfusion. Beta thalassemia: β-globin gene on chromosome 11 (1 gene per chromosome, 2 total): β+ (reduced), β0 (absent); excess α-chains: aggregate → oxidative damage → ineffective erythropoiesis (premature destruction of erythroid precursors in marrow) + peripheral hemolysis; thalassemia minor (β/β+ or β/β0): mild; thalassemia intermedia: transfusion-occasionally; thalassemia major (β0/β0 or β0/β+): transfusion-dependent; skull X-ray: 'hair-on-end' pattern (marrow expansion → diploe expansion of skull); treatment: regular transfusions + deferasirox/deferoxamine (chelation), HSCT (curative), luspatercept (TGF-β ligand trap → ↑late erythroid maturation → ↓transfusion need), gene therapy (betibeglogene autotemcel, bb2121 targets β-globin gene).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Transglutaminase 2 (TG2) crosslinks which proteins in celiac disease pathogenesis?
options: Gliadin peptides are crosslinked to each other by TG2 (TG2 deamidates gliadin, then in some cases crosslinks gliadin to itself, but the pathologically important T-cell-activating modification and the HLA-DQ2/DQ8-presented peptides involve deamidation, not crosslinking per se)
Collagen fibers in the intestinal wall (TG2 does crosslink ECM proteins like collagen and fibronectin but this is not central to celiac pathogenesis)

TG2 deamidates glutamine residues in gliadin peptides, converting them to glutamate, and also crosslinks gliadin to itself or to TG2 itself — the anti-TG2 IgA antibody is the diagnostic marker: TG2 (tissue transglutaminase, TGM2) is the autoantigen in celiac disease; TG2 has two activities in celiac pathogenesis: (1) DEAMIDATION: converts glutamine (Q) → glutamic acid (E) in gliadin peptides (e.g., QLQPFPQPQLPY → after deamidation has more negative charge) → deamidated gliadin peptides have much higher affinity for HLA-DQ2 (DQα1*05:01/DQβ1*02:01) and HLA-DQ8 (DQα1*03:01/DQβ1*03:02) → better presented to CD4+ T cells → Th1 response + ↑IFN-γ + ↑IL-21 → damage; (2) CROSSLINKING: TG2 crosslinks gliadin-deamidated peptides to TG2 itself → gliadin-TG2 complex → acts as hapten-carrier → B cells make anti-TG2 IgA antibodies (which cross-react with gliadin peptides → anti-deamidated gliadin antibodies); serology: anti-TG2 IgA (most sensitive + specific screening test); anti-endomysial IgA (EMA-IgA, anti-TG2 on endomysium, highly specific); anti-deamidated gliadin peptide IgA/IgG (less sensitive but useful in IgA-deficient patients)
Alpha-1-antitrypsin is inhibited by TG2 crosslinking (incorrect)
explanation: Celiac disease pathophysiology: Genetics: >95% carry HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 (necessary but not sufficient; 30-40% of general population have DQ2/DQ8 but only 1-3% develop celiac). Environmental trigger: gluten (storage proteins of wheat [gliadin], barley [hordein], rye [secalin]); safe grains: rice, corn, oats (usually tolerated if uncontaminated). Gliadin fractions: α-gliadin (most immunogenic, e.g., α-gliadin 33mer), γ-gliadin, ω-gliadin; resistant to digestive proteases (high Pro + Gln content → proline-specific endopeptidases needed for full digestion; ALV003/latiglutenase: protease mix being studied). Immune response: Innate: IL-15 (from enterocytes) → activates intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL, CD8+ T cells) → kill enterocytes (epithelial apoptosis) → villous atrophy; IEL express NKG2D (recognizes MICA/MICB stress proteins on enterocytes). Adaptive: gliadin-TG2 complex → HLA-DQ2/8-restricted presentation → CD4+ Th1 cells (IFN-γ, IL-21 → activate macrophages + IEL) + Tfh → B cells → IgA (anti-TG2, anti-EMA, anti-DGP). Histology: Marsh classification: Marsh 0 (normal); Marsh 1 (↑IEL >25/100 enterocytes); Marsh 2 (+ crypt hyperplasia); Marsh 3a/b/c (partial/subtotal/total villous atrophy + crypt hyperplasia); Marsh 3c = flat mucosa (classic celiac). Treatment: strict gluten-free diet (GFD) → reversal of symptoms, normalization of histology, normalization of antibodies (IgA-TG2 normalizes in 6-12 months on GFD); small amount of gluten → relapse; associated conditions: dermatitis herpetiformis (DH, IgA deposits in dermal papillae → pruritic vesicular rash on extensor surfaces; responds to dapsone + GFD).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The primary mechanism by which glucocorticoids suppress inflammation involves:
options: Direct inhibition of TNF-α by binding to TNF-α receptors (glucocorticoids are not TNF-R antagonists; biologics like etanercept/adalimumab are)
Direct binding to and inactivating NFκB (glucocorticoids do interact with NFκB but this is indirect, not the primary mechanism described here)

Induction of lipocortin-1 (annexin A1) which inhibits phospholipase A2 (PLA2): glucocorticoids (GCs) bind the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, a nuclear receptor) in the cytoplasm → GC-GR complex → (1) direct transactivation: GR homodimer binds GRE (glucocorticoid response element) in DNA → ↑transcription of anti-inflammatory genes including annexin A1 (lipocortin-1): annexin A1 → inhibits cytoplasmic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) → ↓arachidonic acid (AA) release from membrane phospholipids → ↓prostaglandins + leukotrienes + PAF; (2) transrepression: GR-p65 (NFκB subunit) interaction → ↓NFκB activity → ↓pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8); also: ↓COX-2 expression, ↓iNOS expression; net effect: ↓eicosanoids (upstream of both COX and LOX pathways, unlike aspirin/NSAIDs that only block COX); GC side effects: ↑gluconeogenesis (PEPCK ↑), ↑protein catabolism, ↑lipolysis, ↓calcium absorption (↓TRPV6, ↓calbindin), ↓bone formation + ↑bone resorption → osteoporosis, immunosuppression (↓lymphocyte migration, ↓antibody production), HPA axis suppression, ↑appetite, ↑BP
Selective inhibition of COX-2 (GCs inhibit COX-2 transcription via NFκB suppression but this is indirect and incomplete; the primary molecular mechanism centers on PLA2 inhibition via annexin A1)
explanation: Glucocorticoid molecular pharmacology: GR (NR3C1, nuclear receptor superfamily): cytoplasmic at rest (bound to HSP90 + HSP70 complex → maintains GR in ligand-binding conformation, prevents nuclear translocation); GC → binds ligand-binding domain (LBD) → HSP90 dissociates → GR nuclear translocation (NLS exposed) → GR dimerization → binds GRE (TGGTACAAATGTTCT) or nGRE (negative GRE) → transactivation or transrepression. Anti-inflammatory effects: Transactivation: ↑annexin A1 (↓PLA2 → ↓AA), ↑MKP-1 (MAPK phosphatase → ↓JNK/p38 activity), ↑IκBα (↓NFκB by trapping in cytoplasm), ↑GILZ (GC-induced leucine zipper → ↓AP-1 + NFκB), ↑SLPI (secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor). Transrepression: GR tethering to p65 (NFκB) → ↓NFκB-mediated transcription of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, COX-2, iNOS, VCAM-1, ICAM-1; GR-AP1 (Fos/Jun) interaction → ↓AP-1-mediated IL-2, IL-4 transcription. Cellular effects: ↓leukocyte migration to sites of inflammation (↓adhesion molecules), ↑neutrophil count in blood (demargination, ↓apoptosis), ↓eosinophils + basophils + mast cells in tissue, ↓T + B lymphocytes (lymphocyte redistribution + ↑apoptosis), ↓monocyte/macrophage function. Specific GC side effects by mechanism: Adrenal suppression (HPA axis): chronic GC → ↓CRH + ACTH → adrenal atrophy; abrupt cessation → Addisonian crisis (cardiovascular collapse); taper required. Osteoporosis: ↓osteoblast function + ↑osteoclast → bisphosphonate prophylaxis if >3 months use. Steroid diabetes: ↑hepatic gluconeogenesis + ↑insulin resistance. Cushing's phenotype: central obesity, moon facies, buffalo hump, thin skin, striae, proximal myopathy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Familial dysalbuminemic hyperthyroxinemia (FDH) is caused by a mutation in albumin that leads to:
options: Decreased binding of albumin to thyroid hormones (WRONG — FDH causes INCREASED binding, leading to spuriously high total T4)

A point mutation in albumin (Arg218His, most common in European families; also Leu66Pro in Asian families) that creates an albumin variant with greatly increased affinity for T4 but not T3: albumin is the main carrier protein for many hydrophobic ligands; the specific mutation in FDH increases albumin affinity for T4 → ↑bound T4 (cannot be measured as 'free') → ↑total T4 assay; important: free T4 (fT4) is NORMAL + TSH is NORMAL → patient is EUTHYROID; but many conventional immunoassay platforms for fT4 cross-react with the mutant albumin-bound T4 → falsely ↑fT4 result + normal TSH → this pattern (↑total T4 + ↑fT4 by immunoassay + normal TSH) can mimic thyroid hormone resistance or TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma; diagnosis: equilibrium dialysis (gold standard for fT4) or LC-MS/MS → shows truly normal fT4; family history (AD inheritance); albumin electrophoresis → double albumin band (bisalbuminemia) not always present; clinical management: no treatment needed (patient is euthyroid); recognition prevents unnecessary thyroid investigation and treatment
A mutation in the gene for thyronine-binding globulin (TBG) — that is TBG deficiency/excess which also affects thyroid hormone assays but via different mechanisms
Elevated thyroid hormone production from autonomous thyroid nodules
explanation: Thyroid hormone transport proteins: TBG (thyroxine-binding globulin, 55-60% of serum T4 and T3 binding): highest affinity for T4 and T3; synthesized in liver; ↑TBG: pregnancy (estrogen ↑ glycosylation → ↑t½ of TBG → ↑TBG → ↑total T4+T3 but free T4/T3 normal → TSH normal → euthyroid); oral estrogen; viral hepatitis; tamoxifen; perphenazine; ↓TBG: androgens; glucocorticoids; hepatic failure; large protein losses (nephrotic syndrome); acromegaly. Transthyretin (TTR, prealbumin, ~15%): transports T4 (preferentially) and retinol-binding protein-retinol complex; half-life 2-4 days (used as nutritional marker); TTR amyloidosis (ATTR): Val30Met (hereditary, FAP [familial amyloid polyneuropathy] + cardiomyopathy); wild-type ATTR: cardiac amyloidosis in elderly (age-related); tafamidis (TTR tetramer stabilizer) approved for ATTR cardiomyopathy. Albumin (~25%): low affinity but high capacity; bound T4/T3 dissociates readily (high off-rate) → 'easily dissociable' thyroid hormone pool; FDH: albumin mutation → ↑T4 affinity; mimics hyperthyroxinemia. Assay interference with thyroid tests: Biotin (high-dose supplements/therapy) → many immunoassays use biotin-streptavidin → biotin competes → falsely high fT4 + falsely low TSH (biotin patients appear to have hyperthyroidism, thyroid cancer suppression) → hold biotin ≥2 days before testing; heterophilic antibodies (HAMA, human anti-mouse antibodies): can falsely elevate or lower TSH/T4/T3 in immunoassays.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In cobalamin (vitamin B12) deficiency, which of the following organic acids accumulates in the urine?
options: Orotic acid (↑in OTC deficiency [urea cycle], not B12 deficiency)

Methylmalonic acid (MMA): cobalamin (B12) is required as a cofactor in TWO reactions: (1) methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM, mitochondrial) → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (requires adenosylcobalamin, AdoCbl); (2) methionine synthase (cytoplasmic) → 5-methyl-THF + homocysteine → THF + methionine (requires methylcobalamin, MeCbl); in B12 deficiency: MCM impaired → L-methylmalonyl-CoA cannot be converted → accumulates → hydrolyzed → methylmalonic acid (MMA) → excreted in urine; simultaneously, methionine synthase impaired → ↑homocysteine; thus B12 deficiency causes: ↑urine MMA + ↑serum/urine homocysteine; B12 deficiency markers (most sensitive → least): ↑MMA in urine/serum (very sensitive, functional B12 marker) > ↑homocysteine > ↓serum B12 (can be normal in functional deficiency); folate deficiency: ↑homocysteine but NOT ↑MMA → the MMA test differentiates B12 from folate deficiency (MMA only elevated in B12 deficiency)
Homogentisic acid (accumulates in alkaptonuria, HGD/homogentisate oxidase deficiency, Tyr metabolism)
explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): Structure: corrin ring with central cobalt (Co), deoxyadenosine or methyl group attached. Sources: animal products exclusively (meat, fish, eggs, dairy); vegans/vegetarians at risk; fortified foods. Absorption: requires intrinsic factor (IF, secreted by gastric parietal cells) → IF-B12 complex → absorbed in terminal ileum via cubilin-amnionless receptor; IF deficiency: pernicious anemia (autoimmune destruction of parietal cells or anti-IF antibodies); loss of terminal ileum: surgical (Crohn's, resection) or disease → B12 malabsorption. Transport: transcobalamin II (TC-II, main transport protein; TC-II-B12 = holotranscobalamin [holoTC], the active B12 in serum) → hepatocytes + other cells take up B12 via TC-II receptor. Stores: liver (several years supply) → deficiency takes years to develop even after B12 intake stops. B12 deficiency clinical features: (1) Megaloblastic anemia (same as folate deficiency): hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes, or ≥1 with 6 lobes), macrocytic RBCs (MCV >100 fL). (2) Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (SCD): UNIQUE to B12, NOT seen in folate deficiency: bilateral ↓proprioception + vibration sense (dorsal columns: dorsal funiculi → posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway) + spastic leg weakness with ↑DTRs (lateral corticospinal tracts); dementia + peripheral neuropathy in severe cases; mechanism: ↓methionine → ↓SAM → ↓myelin basic protein methylation → myelin instability. (3) Glossitis. (4) ↑MMA + ↑Hcy (as above). Treatment: IM hydroxocobalamin (1000 µg IM for 7 days then weekly then monthly) OR high-dose oral B12 (~1-2 mg daily; even without IF, passive absorption ~1% of dose → enough at high dose).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The amino acid that donates the ring nitrogen atoms to the purine ring in de novo synthesis is:
options: Aspartate alone (Asp donates only N1 to the purine ring, at the step ASL → AMP from IMP; and provides NH2 at C1 in SAMP step)
Glutamine alone (Gln provides N3 and N9 [amide nitrogen] in de novo synthesis but not both ring nitrogens)

Both glutamine (Gln) and aspartate (Asp) contribute nitrogen atoms to the purine ring: the purine ring has 4 nitrogen atoms (N1, N3, N7, N9); their origins: N1: aspartate (in the SAICAR → AICAR step: ASL/adenylosuccinase releases fumarate, leaves N1-derived nitrogen; or more precisely, in AMP synthesis from IMP: N1 comes from Asp); N3: glutamine (amide N, in the FGAM → FGAM + PFAS step); N7: glycine (within the glycine-donated C4-C5-N7 unit; actually N7 is part of the glycine molecule [Gly backbone: C2 = C4 of purine, N of Gly = N7 of purine]); N9: glutamine (amide N in first step: PRPP + Gln → 5-PRA, N9 comes from Gln amide); so N9 = Gln, N7 = Gly, N3 = Gln, N1 = Asp; two of the four nitrogens are from Gln, one from Asp, one from Gly

Glycine, glutamine, and aspartate all contribute nitrogen atoms to the purine ring: N9 from Gln [step 1: PRPP amidotransferase], N7 from Gly [step 2: GAR synthetase, Gly C-N-C unit: C4-C5-N7], N3 from Gln [step 4: PFAS/FGAR amidotransferase], N1 from Asp [step 8: SAICAR → AICAR by ASL, or in AMP from IMP: N1 specifically from Asp via SAMP]
explanation: Purine ring atom origins (mnemonic 'GAG-GA' or use a diagram): The purine ring (bicyclic: imidazole [C4-C5-N7-C8-N9] fused to pyrimidine [N1-C2-N3-C4]): N9: glutamine amide (step 1, PRPP amidotransferase). C4 + C5 + N7: glycine (step 2, GAR synthetase: whole glycine molecule incorporated as C4-C5-N7; Gly = NH2-CH2-COOH → NH2 → N7, CH2 → C5, COOH → C4 after condensation). C8: 10-formyl-THF (step 9, AIRS-forming step, PFAS). N3: glutamine amide (step 4, PFAS [FGAR amidotransferase] adds Gln amino to FGAR → FGAM). C6: CO2 (step 5, AIRS → CAIRS, AIR carboxylase, one of the steps where CO2 is used). N1: aspartate amino group (step 8, SAICAR → AICAR by adenylosuccinase; Asp N goes to N1; fumarate released). C2: 10-formyl-THF (step 10, FAICAR → IMP by IMPCH). So origins of all purine ring atoms: C2 = 10-formyl-THF; N1 = Asp; C6 = CO2; C5+C4 = Gly; N7 = Gly; C8 = 10-formyl-THF; N9 = Gln (amide); N3 = Gln (amide); back to top: N3 from Gln (4th step), N9 from Gln (1st step); N7 from Gly (2nd step); N1 from Asp (8th step). Total nitrogen donors: Gln (N3, N9), Gly (N7), Asp (N1). Total carbon donors: Gly (C4, C5), 10-formyl-THF (C2, C8), CO2 (C6), PRPP provides C1' (ribose).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) is caused by a deficiency of which enzyme?
options: Fructokinase: deficiency → essential fructosuria (benign, fructose not phosphorylated, excreted in urine unchanged — the BENIGN version of fructose intolerance)

Aldolase B (fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase, ALDOB): deficiency → hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI, AR, ALDOB gene, chromosome 9q22.3); ALDOB in liver cleaves F1P → DHAP + glyceraldehyde; in HFI: fructose → [fructokinase] → fructose-1-phosphate (F1P) ACCUMULATES (fructokinase is intact, so fructose is phosphorylated to F1P which CANNOT be cleaved because ALDOB is absent) → F1P: (1) inhibits fructokinase (product inhibition) → ↑serum fructose; (2) depletes inorganic phosphate (Pi) → inhibits glycogenolysis (phosphorylase needs Pi) + gluconeogenesis → HYPOGLYCEMIA; (3) depletes ATP (fructokinase uses ATP to phosphorylate fructose → Pi not recycled); (4) directly toxic to hepatocytes → hepatotoxicity; (5) inhibits glycogen phosphorylase + fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; clinical: vomiting, hypoglycemia (severe), liver disease (hepatomegaly → cirrhosis if untreated), renal tubular Fanconi syndrome, AVOIDANCE of sweets (children self-select → hallmark: absence of dental caries); diagnosis: DNA testing (ALDOB mutations) + fructose loading test (↑urine fructose + ↑serum Glu fall + ↑uric acid + ↑Mg drop — now rarely done [dangerous]); treatment: strict dietary fructose/sucrose/sorbitol elimination
Glucokinase (hexokinase IV): deficiency → MODY2 (mild hyperglycemia from ↓glucose phosphorylation in β-cells + liver); not related to fructose
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase: deficiency → ↑gluconeogenesis precursors → ketosis + hypoglycemia during fasting but NOT related to fructose intake
explanation: Fructose metabolism: Dietary fructose → absorbed by GLUT5 (apical) and GLUT2 (basolateral) in small intestine → portal blood → liver (main site of fructose metabolism). Liver fructose pathway: Fructose → [fructokinase, KHK, ketohexokinase] → F1P [uses ATP]; F1P → [ALDOB] → DHAP + glyceraldehyde; glyceraldehyde → [TK] → glycerol-3-P or → [aldehyde oxidase] → glycerate → [GK] → 2-PG → glycolysis; DHAP + G3P → glycolysis. Note: Unlike glucose, fructose entry into glycolysis bypasses PFK-1 (the rate-limiting step) → fructose metabolism in liver is unregulated → large substrate flux → ↑malonyl-CoA → ↑de novo FA synthesis → hypertriglyceridemia; ↑VLDL synthesis; chronically: hepatic steatosis (fructose-driven) even without excess caloric intake → concern about high-fructose corn syrup in metabolic syndrome. Galactose metabolism: Galactose → [galactokinase, GALK] → galactose-1-phosphate (Gal-1-P) [uses ATP]; Gal-1-P + UDP-Glu → [GALT, Gal-1-P uridylyltransferase] → Glu-1-P + UDP-Gal → [GALE, UDP-galactose 4'-epimerase] → UDP-Glu. Classic galactosemia (GALT deficiency): ↑Gal-1-P (toxic) → liver disease (jaundice, cirrhosis) + cataracts (galactitol in lens [aldose reductase: Gal → galactitol, not metabolized → osmotic lens damage]) + intellectual disability + E. coli neonatal sepsis (galactosemia impairs neutrophil function → susceptibility to gram-negative sepsis); treat: galactose-free diet (lactose-free formula). Galactokinase deficiency: only cataracts (galactitol accumulation) without liver or CNS disease (Gal-1-P is NOT made → less toxic). GALE deficiency: mild (UDP-Gal needed for glycolipid + glycoprotein synthesis → some residual activity always present).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following molecules acts as the methyl group donor in most biological transmethylation reactions?
options: Methylcobalamin (B12): this is a carrier of methyl groups for ONE specific reaction: homocysteine → methionine [methionine synthase]; not the general donor for most methylation reactions

Tetrahydrofolate (THF): THF is a carrier for various one-carbon units including 5-methyl (→ Met), 10-formyl (→ purines), 5,10-methylene (→ dTMP) but THF itself is not the direct methyl donor; the methyl on 5-methyl-THF is donated to B12/methionine synthase, not directly to most substrates

S-adenosylmethionine (SAM, AdoMet): the universal methyl donor in biological transmethylation reactions; SAM is formed from methionine + ATP → [methionine adenosyltransferase, MAT1A in liver] → SAM + PPi + Pi; SAM donates its methyl group to acceptors → S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) → [SAH hydrolase, reversible] → homocysteine + adenosine; methylation reactions using SAM: (1) DNA methylation: DNMT (DNMT1/3A/3B) → 5-methylcytosine at CpG; (2) RNA methylation: m6A (METTL3/14 complex), m1A, pseudouridine; (3) Histone methylation: KMT (SET-domain enzymes, e.g., G9a → H3K9me1/2, EZH2 → H3K27me3); (4) mRNA 7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap; (5) Protein methylation: arginine (PRMT1-9) or lysine methyltransferases; (6) Small molecule methylation: norepinephrine → epinephrine (PNMT: phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase); guanidinoacetate → creatine (GAMT: guanidinoacetate methyltransferase); histamine → N-methylhistamine (HNMT); phosphatidylethanolamine → phosphatidylcholine (PEMT); melatonin (ASMT); RNA cap (CMTR1); (7) Arsenic methylation (detoxification)
Pyruvate (a central metabolite, not a methyl donor)
explanation: SAM cycle and methylation: Methionine cycle: Met + ATP → [MAT] → SAM + PPi + Pi. SAM → [methyltransferase, MTase] → product + SAH. SAH → [SAH hydrolase, equilibrium strongly toward synthesis] → Hcy + adenosine. Hcy: (1) remethylation: Hcy + 5-methyl-THF → [methionine synthase + B12] → Met + THF (in most tissues); betaine → [BHMT, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase] → Hcy → Met (liver + kidney; an alternative remethylation using dietary choline-derived betaine). (2) transsulfuration: Hcy → [CBS, cystathionine β-synthase, B6/PLP] → cystathionine → [CGL, cystathionine γ-lyase, B6] → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate; requires B6 (both CBS + CGL are PLP-dependent). Cysteine → glutathione (GSH: Glu-Cys-Gly; rate-limiting: γ-glutamylcysteine synthetase [GCS, GCLC/GCLM]); taurine (decarboxylation + oxidation); coenzyme A (pantothenate + cysteine-derived). SAM as 'high-energy' compound: the C-S bond in SAM has a large negative ΔG for transfer of the adenosyl or methyl group → SAM is thermodynamically poised to donate its methyl group. Ratio SAM/SAH ('methylation index'): high ratio → ↑transmethylation; folate/B12 deficiency → ↓SAM/SAH → ↓global methylation. Creatine synthesis: Arg + Gly → [AGAT, arginine:glycine amidinotransferase, kidney] → guanidinoacetate + Orn; guanidinoacetate → [GAMT, liver, uses SAM] → creatine; most abundant acceptor of SAM methyl group in the body; creatine → muscle/brain → creatinine (excreted by kidney at constant rate → creatinine used to estimate GFR). Epinephrine: PNMT (in adrenal medulla, induced by cortisol from adrenal cortex) → converts NE → Epi using SAM.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the 'wobble hypothesis' in translation?
options: The mRNA moves in the 3' to 5' direction during translation
The ribosome itself 'wobbles' mechanically between two conformations during translocation

The first two positions of the codon-anticodon base pair must be Watson-Crick, but the third (3') position of the codon (the 'wobble position') can tolerate non-standard base pairing with the first (5') position of the anticodon: Crick's wobble hypothesis (1966): strict Watson-Crick base pairing required at codon positions 1 and 2 (from 5' end of codon = positions 1, 2, 3 from 5' end); the 3rd position (3' end of codon) allows 'wobble' non-standard pairing → one tRNA can decode multiple synonymous codons differing at the 3rd position; standard wobble pairs: G (anticodon pos 34) : C or U (codon pos 3); inosine (I, hypoxanthine base, at anticodon pos 34, from A→I deamination by ADAT enzyme) : C, U, or A (codon pos 3) → inosine is the most flexible wobble base (pairs with 3 different bases); uridine at anticodon pos 34 → normally only pairs C (strict) but with modifications (mnm5U, mcm5U, etc.) can wobble to A or G; this allows ~45 tRNA species (in humans) to decode 61 sense codons; mitochondria: 22 tRNAs decode all 60+ sense codons via 'super-wobble' (U in anticodon pos 34 pairs with all 4 possible bases at codon pos 3)
The Km value 'wobbles' around the true value in enzyme kinetics
explanation: Translation overview and ribosome structure: Prokaryotic ribosome: 70S (50S + 30S); 50S: 23S rRNA + 5S rRNA + ~31 proteins (large subunit); 30S: 16S rRNA + ~21 proteins (small subunit). Eukaryotic ribosome: 80S (60S + 40S); 60S: 28S + 5.8S + 5S rRNAs + ~49 proteins; 40S: 18S rRNA + ~33 proteins. Ribosome sites: A site (aminoacyl site): accepts charged tRNA-AA; P site (peptidyl site): holds tRNA with growing peptide chain; E site (exit site): deacylated tRNA exits. Peptide bond formation: peptidyl transferase center (PTC) in 23S/28S rRNA (ribozyme activity): α-NH2 of A-site AA attacks ester bond between P-site AA and tRNA → peptide bond formed + P-site tRNA deacylated. Translocation: GTP-dependent (EF-G/eEF2 catalyze + GTP) → A→P shift for tRNA, P→E for deacylated tRNA; ribosome moves 3 nt in 5'→3' direction along mRNA. EF-Tu (bacteria)/eEF1A (eukaryotes): delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to A site + GTP; GTP hydrolysis → confirmation of correct codon-anticodon pairing (proofreading) before full accommodation. eIF2B/eIF2 cycle: eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi → initiates; upon start codon recognition → eIF2-GTP hydrolysis → eIF2-GDP; eIF2B (GEF) → exchanges GDP→GTP (regenerates eIF2-GTP); eIF2α phosphorylation (by HRI, PKR, GCN2, PERK in ISR [integrated stress response]) → eIF2α-P is a competitive inhibitor of eIF2B → ↓global translation; mTORC1 → phospho-4E-BP1 → releases eIF4E → cap-dependent translation initiation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The biochemical basis of the 'hungry bone syndrome' after parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism involves:
options: ↑PTH causing calcium loss from bones after surgery (WRONG — hungry bone occurs after PTH-dependent hypercalcemia is REMOVED; PTH is removed by parathyroidectomy)

Rapid uptake of calcium into remineralizing bone depleting serum calcium: hungry bone syndrome (HBS) occurs after successful parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) or after effective treatment of severe secondary hyperparathyroidism; mechanism: chronic ↑PTH → ↑osteoclastic bone resorption → bones demineralized (high bone turnover); after parathyroidectomy → ↓PTH → ↓osteoclast activity → osteoblasts continue (uncoupled briefly → predominant) + bones 'hungry' to remineralize → rapid calcium uptake from serum into skeleton → hypocalcemia (can be severe, prolonged); features: severe hypocalcemia (may need IV calcium infusion) + hypomagnesemia (Mg also taken up into bone, needed as cofactor for PTH secretion from remaining parathyroid tissue) + hypophosphatemia (phosphate also deposits into bone); risk factors for HBS: higher preoperative PTH + higher preoperative calcium + higher bone alkaline phosphatase (marker of bone turnover) + longer duration of disease + degree of preoperative bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica); management: preoperative Vit D optimization, IV calcium gluconate for severe symptoms + oral calcium + calcitriol postoperatively; may need weeks to months of intensive calcium supplementation
Decreased absorption of calcium in the intestine after surgery
Increased renal calcium excretion following parathyroid gland removal
explanation: Calcium homeostasis: PTH (parathyroid hormone): target organs — kidney + bone + (indirectly through Vit D) intestine. Kidney: ↑Ca reabsorption (distal tubule), ↑phosphate excretion (proximal tubule, inhibits NaPi-IIa), ↑1α-hydroxylase (↑calcitriol). Bone: ↑osteoclastic activity (osteoclasts don't have PTH-R directly; PTH acts on osteoblasts → ↑RANKL + ↓OPG → ↑osteoclast activation); intermittent low-dose PTH (like teriparatide/abaloparatide) → anabolic (↑osteoblast [RUNX2, osterix] > ↑osteoclast → net bone gain); continuous high PTH → catabolic (net bone loss). Calcitonin: from parafollicular C cells of thyroid; ↓serum calcium (↓osteoclast activity, ↑renal Ca excretion); used in Paget's disease + hypercalcemia (short-term). Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT): most common causes: single adenoma (85%), multi-gland hyperplasia (10-15%), carcinoma (<1%); biochemistry: ↑Ca, ↓PO4, ↑PTH, ↑urine Ca, ↑urine cAMP, ↑ALP (if bone disease); symptoms: bones (osteitis fibrosa cystica, pathological fractures, subperiosteal bone resorption of radial side of middle phalanges on hand X-ray), stones (nephrolithiasis, Ca-oxalate or Ca-phosphate), groans (peptic ulcer, constipation, pancreatitis), moans + psychic overtones (depression, confusion, weakness, fatigue); management: surgical parathyroidectomy for symptomatic cases + asymptomatic cases meeting criteria (Ca >1 mg/dL above normal, eGFR <60, T-score <-2.5, age <50). MEN1 (PHPT + pituitary + pancreatic tumors — PHPT most common and earliest in MEN1, MEN1 gene).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) uses GTP to convert OAA to PEP in gluconeogenesis. This enzyme is found in two isoforms: cytosolic (PEPCK-C) and mitochondrial (PEPCK-M). What is the key difference?
options: PEPCK-C uses GTP while PEPCK-M uses ATP (WRONG — both isoforms use GTP; the difference is location and role in gluconeogenesis shuttle)
PEPCK-C is present only in the liver while PEPCK-M is present only in kidney (WRONG — both isoforms are expressed in liver; PEPCK-C predominates in humans)

PEPCK-C (cytosolic PEPCK2) is regulated primarily at the transcriptional level by glucagon/insulin, while PEPCK-M (mitochondrial PEPCK1) provides PEP directly to the mitochondrial export pathway: in human liver: PEPCK-C (PEPCK2, PCK2 gene): mitochondrial form; PEPCK-M (PEPCK1, PCK1 gene): cytoplasmic form — NOTE: this is counterintuitive naming; the commonly discussed regulated cytoplasmic form in humans is PCK1 (cytoplasmic; responds to glucagon → ↑cAMP → CREB → ↑PCK1 transcription); the mitochondrial form PCK2 provides PEP to the intermembrane space or cytoplasm depending on metabolic state; in humans PCK1 (cytoplasmic) is the primary regulated gluconeogenic isoform; PCK2 (mitochondrial) is less regulated transcriptionally but provides rapid PEP generation; glucagon → ↑cAMP → PKA → CREB → ↑PCK1 transcription + FoxO1 → ↑G6Pase; insulin → ↑Akt → FoxO1 nuclear exclusion → ↓PCK1 + ↓G6Pase
PEPCK-C requires vitamin K as a cofactor while PEPCK-M requires biotin (WRONG — PEPCK requires GTP, Mn2+, no vitamin cofactors; pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin)
explanation: Gluconeogenesis regulation — key control points: Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): biotin-dependent, NAG+acetyl-CoA-activated (signals: FA oxidation occurring, TCA intermediates abundant). PEPCK (cytoplasmic isoform, PCK1): transcriptionally induced by glucagon (cAMP/CREB/PGC-1α) + glucocorticoids (GRE in PEPCK promoter) + thyroid hormone; repressed by insulin (Akt → FoxO1 exclusion → ↓transcription). FBPase-1: Mg2+-dependent, activated by citrate, inhibited by AMP + fructose-2,6-BP. G6Pase (ER): not allosterically regulated; transcription induced by glucagon (via FoxO1 + CREB-PGC1α); inhibited by insulin. Metformin effects on gluconeogenesis: direct mitochondrial: inhibits Complex I → ↑AMP/ATP → AMPK (inhibits FBPase-1 directly) + indirect signaling (CRTC2 phosphorylation → nuclear exclusion → ↓PGC-1α → ↓PEPCK/G6Pase). Also: metformin inhibits mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (mGPDH) → ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio in mitochondria → ↓oxidation of lactate and glycerol → ↓gluconeogenic substrate availability. Exercise: AMPK in muscle → ↑glucose uptake (insulin-independent); also AMPK in liver → ↓gluconeogenesis during exercise (short-term); post-exercise: epinephrine → ↑hepatic glycogenolysis + ↑gluconeogenesis → blood glucose maintained during prolonged exercise.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which reaction produces NADPH in the mitochondrial matrix (NOT the cytoplasm)?
options: G6PD reaction (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase in cytoplasm — PPP is a cytoplasmic pathway)
Malate dehydrogenase reaction (MDH uses NAD+, not NADP+, in both mitochondria and cytoplasm under most conditions; produces NADH)

Isocitrate dehydrogenase-2 (IDH2): the mitochondrial isoform of isocitrate dehydrogenase; IDH2 uses NADP+ (not NAD+) as electron acceptor: isocitrate + NADP+ → α-KG + CO2 + NADPH; this mitochondrial NADPH is used for: (1) antioxidant defense within mitochondria (mitochondrial glutathione reductase + thioredoxin reductase 2 + GPx4 → reduce H2O2 using NADPH); (2) regenerating reduced thioredoxin 2 (Trx2) + peroxiredoxin 3 (PRX3); compare: IDH1 (cytoplasmic isoform, uses NADP+) → produces cytoplasmic NADPH (for FA synthesis + antioxidant); IDH3 (mitochondrial, uses NAD+) → produces NADH (TCA cycle, rate-limiting step); IDH1/2 gain-of-function mutations → oncometabolite 2-HG production; IDH2 R140/R172 mutations: AML + cholangiocarcinoma; enasidenib: IDH2 inhibitor (FDA 2017 for IDH2-mutant AML); also: malic enzyme 3 (ME3, mitochondrial, NADP+-dependent): malate + NADP+ → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH; GLUD1 (glutamate dehydrogenase): Glu + NAD+ or NADP+ → α-KG + NH3 + NADH/NADPH
Succinate dehydrogenase reaction (SDH uses FAD, not NADP+, and produces FADH2, not NADPH)
explanation: Mitochondrial NADPH sources and uses: IDH2 (isocitrate dehydrogenase 2, TCA cycle, NADP+-linked): isocitrate → α-KG + CO2 + NADPH. Malic enzyme 3 (ME3, mitochondrial NADP+-linked): malate → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH (anaplerotic in reverse: α-KG → OAA → malate → pyruvate + NADPH = cataplerosis for lipid synthesis fuel). GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase, can use NADP+): Glu → α-KG + NH3 + NADPH/H. Nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT): NADH + NADP+ ↔ NAD+ + NADPH (uses proton gradient across IMM → NNT uses ΔΨ to drive NADPH synthesis in mitochondria; KO in mice → ↑oxidative stress + diabetes susceptibility; NNT variants in some human diseases). Mitochondrial NADPH uses: Glutathione reductase 2 → reduces GSSG → 2 GSH. Thioredoxin reductase 2 (TXNRD2) → Trx2(ox) → Trx2(red). GPx4 (mitochondrial isoform) → lipid-OOH → lipid-OH. Proline biosynthesis (PYCR, pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase, NADPH). Note: NADPH cannot cross IMM directly → mitochondrial + cytoplasmic NADPH pools are separate → must use metabolite shuttles. Mitochondrial ROS: Complex I (FMN site, ubiquinone site) and Complex III (ubiquinone [Qo] site) are main superoxide generators; Complex II (SDHA FAD site) also generates some O2•-; superoxide → MnSOD (SOD2) → H2O2 → GPx4/PRX3/CAT in peroxisomes → H2O; oxidative phosphorylation efficiency vs. ROS: ↑proton leak (uncoupling proteins UCP1-5) → ↓ΔΨ → ↓ROS production.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Galactosylation of antibodies is a post-translational modification that affects their effector functions. Where does protein O-glycosylation primarily occur?
options: Rough ER (N-glycosylation begins here; O-glycosylation occurs primarily in the Golgi)

Golgi apparatus: O-linked glycosylation (O-glycosylation) occurs primarily in the Golgi apparatus (cis, medial, and trans cisternae) and to a lesser extent at the cell surface; characteristics: (1) occurs on Ser or Thr (hydroxyl group); (2) sequential addition of sugars (no oligosaccharide 'core' transferred from lipid carrier, unlike N-glycosylation which uses dolichol-PP-oligosaccharide); (3) main types: O-GalNAc (mucin-type, initiated by ppGalNAcTs in Golgi) → core 1/2/3/4/6 O-glycan extensions → sialylation by ST enzymes; O-GlcNAc (cytoplasmic + nuclear [OGT, O-GlcNAc transferase]; ↑in hyperglycemia → OGT substrate is UDP-GlcNAc made from hexosamine pathway → O-GlcNAc modification of proteins [HCF-1, FoxO, PGC-1α] → epigenetic/metabolic regulation); (4) IgG Fc N-glycosylation (Asn297 in CH2 domain): actually N-linked glycan at Asn297 (common misconception — the IgG Fc glycan that modulates ADCC + complement is N-linked at Asn 297 of the CH2 domain; removal of this N-glycan [ADCP] or modification [afucosylation → ↑ADCC via FcγRIIIa] dramatically alters effector function); IgA1 heavy chain + IgA1 hinge: O-GalNAc glycans (mucin-type) → IgA nephropathy: undergoes galactose-deficient O-glycans (Gd-IgA1) → autoantibodies against Gd-IgA1 → mesangial immune complex deposition → glomerulonephritis
Mitochondria (lipid synthesis occurs here but not Golgi-type glycosylation)
Nucleus (O-GlcNAc is present on nuclear proteins, but the primary site of mucin-type O-glycosylation is Golgi)
explanation: N-glycosylation vs. O-glycosylation: N-glycosylation: occurs co-translationally in ER (initial) and modified in Golgi; on Asn-X-Ser/Thr (X ≠ Pro) sequon; dolichol-PP-GlcNAc2Man9Glc3 (14-sugar core) transferred en bloc by OST (oligosaccharyltransferase); three types after processing: high-mannose, complex, hybrid; functions: protein folding (calnexin/calreticulin quality control), cell-cell recognition (N-CAMs), receptor-ligand interactions, protein stability, half-life (terminal sialylation ↑stability; terminal Gal → ASGPR in liver → removal/clearance). O-glycosylation: mucin-type (ppGalNAcT → O-GalNAc on Ser/Thr → core 1-6 extensions); proteoglycan-type (Xyl on Ser → GAG chains of chondroitin/dermatan/heparan/keratan); collagen Glc-Gal on hydroxylysine (in ER by galactosyl-OHLys transferase + glucosyl-transferase, requires Vit C for hydroxylation); EGF-domain O-fucosylation + O-glucosylation (Notch pathway); C-mannosylation (on Trp residues, only type with C-C linkage to residue). Glycosylation of IgGs and biopharmaceuticals: IgG Fc Asn297 N-glycan: core (GlcNAc2Man3GlcNAc2) ± fucose ± galactose ± sialic acid; fucosylation: ↓ADCC (afucosylated IgG → ↑FcγRIIIa binding → ↑NK cell activation → ↑ADCC); obinutuzumab (anti-CD20, afucosylated → ↑ADCC vs rituximab); galactosylation + sialylation: ↑anti-inflammatory effects (IVIG therapeutic effect partly through sialylated Fc). IgA1 hinge O-GalNAc glycans: deficient galactosylation → IgA nephropathy (Berger disease, most common glomerulonephritis worldwide in young adults).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme LKBST11 (LKB1/serine-threonine kinase 11) phosphorylates and activates AMPK. LKB1 is also a tumor suppressor. Germline mutations in STK11 cause:
options: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 germline mutations → multiple early-onset cancers including sarcomas, breast, brain, adrenal)
MEN2A/2B (RET proto-oncogene germline mutations → MTC + pheochromocytoma ± parathyroid ± Marfanoid habitus)

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS): STK11/LKB1 (serine threonine kinase 11) germline loss-of-function mutations → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (AD, but ~50% arise de novo); features: (1) hamartomatous polyps (GI tract, especially small intestine — jejunum > ileum > duodenum > colon > stomach; polyps have characteristic 'arborizing' smooth muscle core); (2) mucocutaneous pigmentation (melanin deposits, macules on lips, perioral skin, buccal mucosa, digits, genital skin — appear in infancy, fade with age from skin but persist on mucosa); (3) markedly ↑cancer risk: GI (colorectal, gastric, small bowel), pancreatic, breast, cervical (adenoma malignum), ovarian (sex cord tumor with annular tubules, SCTAT), and testicular (Sertoli cell tumors); LKB1 mechanism: LKB1 → AMPK activation → TSC2 activation → ↓mTORC1 → ↓cell growth; LKB1 loss → ↑mTORC1 → ↑HIF-1α → Warburg + ↑cell proliferation; LKB1 is commonly mutated somatically in NSCLC (~20-30%), cervical, pancreatic cancers
Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1 mutations → nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome)
explanation: LKB1 (STK11) as tumor suppressor — mechanism: LKB1 → forms complex with STRAD (STE20-related adapter protein) and MO25 → active kinase; phosphorylates AMPK α subunit at Thr172 → activates AMPK → AMPK → TSC1/2 (tuberous sclerosis complex) → Rheb-GAP → ↓Rheb-GTP → ↓mTORC1 → ↓S6K1 + ↓4E-BP1 → ↓protein synthesis + ↓cell growth; LKB1 also activates 13 other AMPK-related kinases (MARK1-4, SIK1-3, NUAK1-2, BRSK1-2, SNRK, QSK). Loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) in PJS polyps → loss of remaining STK11 allele → ↑mTOR signaling → hamartoma growth. mTOR pathway relevance: mTORC1 inhibitors (rapamycin/sirolimus, everolimus) → used in TSC (tuberous sclerosis complex: TSC1/TSC2 germline mutations → hamartomas in brain [cortical tubers, SEGAs], skin [angiofibromas, shagreen patches], kidney [AMLs], lung [LAM], heart [rhabdomyomas]); NSCLC with LKB1 mutations: associated with KRAS co-mutation (most common oncogene in NSCLC); poor response to immunotherapy (PD-L1/PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors); mTOR pathway alterations; ongoing investigation of mTOR inhibitors. AMPK in cancer: dual role — tumor suppressor (via LKB1 → ↓mTOR → ↓growth) in established tumors; but AMPK can also be pro-survival (↑autophagy + ↑glycolysis during metabolic stress → helps tumor cell survive). AMPK activators (metformin, phenformin, AICAR): under investigation as cancer prevention/treatment agents.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A molecule that has an α-1,4-glycosidic linkage between glucose residues AND α-1,6-glycosidic linkages at branching points is:
options: Cellulose (β-1,4-glycosidic linkages between glucose; unbranched; found in plant cell walls; not digestible by human amylase)
Chitin (β-1,4-glycosidic linkages between N-acetylglucosamine; unbranched; structural polysaccharide of fungal cell walls + insect exoskeleton)
Sucrose (disaccharide: glucose + fructose via α1,2-glycosidic bond between their anomeric carbons; not a polymer; no 1,6-branch)

Glycogen: α-1,4-glycosidic bonds between most glucose residues in linear chains + α-1,6-glycosidic bonds at EVERY branch point (branches every 8-12 glucose units); glycogen is the storage form of glucose in liver (100-120 g) and muscle (400 g); the branched structure provides: (1) multiple non-reducing ends for simultaneous phosphorylase action → rapid glucose release; (2) increased solubility (compared to linear polymer); starch (plant equivalent): amylose (α-1,4 only, linear, ~25% of dietary starch) + amylopectin (α-1,4 + α-1,6 branches every 24-30 glucose units, ~75% of starch); amylopectin branches are less frequent than glycogen (~24-30 units between branches vs. ~8-12 for glycogen); amylase (salivary + pancreatic): cleaves internal α-1,4 bonds of starch → maltose + maltotriose + α-dextrins (with branch points) + glucose; α-1,6 bonds and terminal α-1,4 bonds not cleaved by α-amylase → brush border enzymes needed (sucrase-isomaltase [cleaves α-1,6 in isomaltose], maltase, lactase, trehalase)
explanation: Glycosidic bond types: α-1,4: starch (amylose, amylopectin), glycogen — digestible; α-1,6 (branches): glycogen + amylopectin — digestible by isomaltase. β-1,4: cellulose (Glc-Glc), chitin (GlcNAc-GlcNAc), lactose (Gal-Glc), cellobiose — not digestible by humans (no β-glucosidase in gut). α-1,2: sucrose (Glc-Fru, anomeric C of both blocked → non-reducing disaccharide). β-1,4 (with N-acetyl groups): hyaluronic acid (GlcUA-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4 repeating disaccharide). β-1,3: β-glucan (fungal/yeast cell wall → target of caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin — echinocandin class antifungals). α-1,2-linked fucose: ABO blood group antigens (H antigen: Fucα1,2-Galβ1,4-GlcNAc-). Blood group biochemistry: O: H antigen (Fucα1,2-Gal-); A: adds GalNAc to H (A-transferase, glycosyltransferase encoded by ABO gene on chr 9); B: adds Gal to H (B-transferase); AB: both transferases; O: frameshift/nonsense mutation in ABO gene → no transferase → H antigen only. Lewis antigens (Le): Le (Lewis a): Fucα1,4-GlcNAc on type 1 chain; Le (Lewis b): Fucα1,2 (on Gal) + Fucα1,4 (on GlcNAc) on type 1 chain; Secretor status: FUT2 (Se gene) → α1,2-fucosyltransferase → adds Fuc to H antigen in secretions; Se/Se or Se/se → secrete ABH antigens in saliva/mucus (secretors, ~80% of population); se/se → non-secretors (↑susceptibility to norovirus, H. pylori; ↓ABH in secretions).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The lysosomal enzyme that is deficient in metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) is:
options: Galactocerebrosidase (GALC): deficient in Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy) — accumulates galactocerebroside + psychosine (galactosylsphingosine, the toxic metabolite)
Hexosaminidase A (HEXA): deficient in Tay-Sachs disease — accumulates GM2 ganglioside

Arylsulfatase A (ARSA, cerebroside sulfatase, cerebroside-3-sulfate-3-sulfohydrolase): MLD is caused by ARSA deficiency (AR, ARSA gene at chr 22q13) → sulfatide (galactocerebroside-3-sulfate) accumulates in lysosomes of CNS + PNS myelin-forming cells (oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells) + kidneys, gallbladder; sulfatide is metachromatic (stains brown-red with cresyl violet or toluidine blue at acidic pH, vs normal metachromatically stained blue → 'metachromatic' deposits); clinical: late infantile form (most common, onset 1-2 years): regression of motor milestones, hypotonia → spastic tetraplegia, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, dementia → death by 5 years; juvenile form; adult form (psychiatric symptoms earliest); lab: ↓ARSA in leukocytes + fibroblasts, ↑urine sulfatides; MRI: diffuse white matter signal abnormality (leukodystrophy pattern); nerve conduction: ↓velocity (demyelinating neuropathy); treatment: HSCT (early pre-symptomatic patients; arrests progression in some), arsa-cel (OTL-200, gene therapy, HSC lentiviral vector, approved in EU/US 2024), substrate reduction therapy (being investigated)
Glucocerebrosidase (GBA): deficient in Gaucher disease — accumulates glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide)
explanation: Sphingolipidoses summary (enzyme + substrate + features): MLD: ARSA deficiency → sulfatide → leukodystrophy + demyelinating neuropathy + metachromatic deposits. Krabbe: GALC deficiency → galactocerebroside + psychosine (toxic → Schwann cell apoptosis → globoid cells [multinucleated macrophages with galactocerebroside]) → early infantile onset, extremely rapid progression → death by 2 years; newborn screening programs (dried blood spot GALC enzyme assay) → early HSCT (only effective before neurological symptoms); GALC uses galactocerebroside + galactosylsphingosine as substrates. Gaucher: GBA (glucocerebrosidase) deficiency → glucosylceramide → Gaucher cells (macrophages with 'wrinkled tissue paper' cytoplasm); type 1 (non-neuronopathic): hepatosplenomegaly + pancytopenia + bone disease; type 2/3: neuronopathic; treatment: enzyme replacement therapy (ERT): imiglucerase, velaglucerase alfa; substrate reduction: miglustat, eliglustat (GlcCer synthase inhibitors → ↓substrate). Tay-Sachs: HEXA (α subunit of Hex A [αβ heterodimer]); Hex A required for GM2 → GM3 → lysosomal degradation; ↑GM2 in neurons → cherry-red spot (normal ganglion cells [absent in fovea] contrast with pale macula) + exaggerated Moro reflex + rapid neurodegeneration → death by 4 years; Sandhoff: HEXB (β subunit) deficiency → both Hex A (αβ) and Hex B (ββ) deficient → ↑GM2 + ↑globoside (4-AS GB4, which uses Hex B for degradation); clinically similar to Tay-Sachs + organomegaly (globoside in visceral organs). AB variant: GM2 activator protein deficiency (normal Hex A enzyme but cofactor absent). Fabry: GLA (α-galactosidase A) deficiency → Gb3 (globotriaosylceramide) → acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, corneal verticillata, renal failure, cardiac hypertrophy; X-linked; ERT: agalsidase alfa/beta; migalastat (pharmacological chaperone for amenable mutations).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) uses which principle to detect antigens?
options: Radioactive labeling of antibodies (that is RIA, radioimmunoassay; ELISA uses enzyme-linked antibodies)

Antigen-antibody interaction detected by enzyme-catalyzed colorimetric/fluorescent reaction: ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) relies on specific antigen-antibody (Ag-Ab) immunological interactions with detection via enzyme activity; general principle: (1) antigen or capture antibody immobilized on solid phase (microplate well); (2) sample added → specific antibody (or antigen in competitive ELISA) binds; (3) enzyme-conjugated detection antibody (secondary Ab) binds; (4) enzyme substrate added → enzyme converts substrate → colored/fluorescent product → measured by spectrophotometer/fluorometer; common enzymes used: HRP (horseradish peroxidase → TMB [3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine] substrate → blue → H2SO4 stop → yellow, read at 450 nm) or AP (alkaline phosphatase → pNPP [para-nitrophenyl phosphate] → yellow, read at 405 nm); ELISA types: (a) direct: enzyme-linked primary Ab binds Ag; (b) indirect: unlabeled primary Ab + enzyme-linked secondary Ab (amplification + versatility); (c) sandwich: two Abs (capture + detection) sandwich the Ag (most sensitive, requires two epitopes); (d) competitive: sample Ag competes with labeled Ag for limited Ab — more Ag in sample → less signal (inverse relationship)
Flow cytometry (uses fluorescent labels + laser detection; not ELISA)
Western blot (uses gel electrophoresis + antibody detection; different technique)
explanation: Immunological assays comparison: ELISA: quantitative, high throughput, can be highly sensitive (fg/mL range with enhanced detection), requires purified antigen/antibody. Western blot (immunoblot): protein separated by SDS-PAGE → transferred to nitrocellulose → probed with antibody → visualizes specific protein by size; confirms ELISA in HIV diagnosis (ELISA screen → WB confirm). Immunohistochemistry (IHC): antibody binding in tissue sections → visualize protein location in situ; uses enzyme (HRP → DAB, brown) or fluorescence (IF, immunofluorescence); Ki-67 (proliferation), CD20 (B cells), ER/PR (breast cancer), HER2 (IHC + FISH). CLIA (chemiluminescence immunoassay): replaces colorimetric with luminescent reaction → more sensitive; used in most modern immunoassay platforms (e.g., troponin, TSH, HCG, PSA, drug levels). RIA (radioimmunoassay): original sensitive immunoassay (Yalow + Berson, Nobel 1977 for Yalow); uses I-125 or I-131 labeled antigen competing with unlabeled antigen for limited antibody; now largely replaced by ELISA/CLIA (avoid radioactivity). FACS (fluorescence-activated cell sorting)/flow cytometry: single-cell analysis + sorting; fluorescent Ab (primary or secondary) binds cell surface/intracellular marker → laser excites → fluorescence detected; used for: CD4+ T cell count (HIV monitoring), leukemia immunophenotyping, cytokine production (intracellular staining), cell cycle analysis (PI [propidium iodide] DNA staining).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The 'rate of transcription' of a gene is primarily regulated by factors that bind to:
options: The ribosome (ribosomes regulate translation, not transcription)

Promoter and enhancer sequences in the DNA: transcription is primarily regulated by DNA-binding proteins (transcription factors, TFs) that recognize specific DNA sequences; promoter elements (upstream of TSS): core promoter (TATA box, Inr, DPE, BRE — recognized by GTFs); proximal promoter (~100-200 bp upstream of TSS); distal regulatory elements: enhancers (can be kilobases or even megabases from the gene; can act upstream or downstream or in introns; orientation-independent; function: bind activator TFs → recruit co-activators → chromatin remodeling [SWI/SNF, NuRD] → HAT [p300/CBP, add H3K27ac at enhancers] → increased RNAPII recruitment and activity); silencers: repressors bind → HDACs → remove acetyl groups → compact chromatin → ↓transcription; insulators (CTCF-binding): prevent enhancer from acting on genes beyond the insulator (boundary element between topologically associating domains, TADs); mediator complex: ~26-subunit complex bridging enhancer-bound activators to the core promoter via 3D DNA looping (enhancer-promoter looping); the frequency of transcription initiation is the key determinant of mRNA abundance (in most cases)
The 5' UTR of the mRNA (5' UTR contains IRES or structured elements that regulate TRANSLATION, not transcription)

The 3' UTR of the mRNA (3' UTR contains AU-rich elements [ARE] that regulate mRNA stability, and miRNA binding sites — these regulate post-transcriptional stability and translation, not transcription directly)
explanation: Transcriptional regulation mechanisms: cis-regulatory elements: promoter (core: TATA, Inr, DPE; proximal: CAAT, GC-box/SP1, CRE, etc.) + enhancers/silencers (distal, cell-type specific) + insulators (CTCF). trans-acting factors: TFs recognize specific DNA sequences via DBDs (zinc finger [C2H2, C4, C2C2], helix-turn-helix, leucine zipper [bZIP], helix-loop-helix [bHLH], Homeodomain, ETS domain, Forkhead, MADS). TF activation domains: TAD (transactivation domain) recruits: coactivators (Mediator, p300/CBP, PCAF), chromatin remodelers (SWI/SNF complex = BAF complex; or ISWI, NuRD). Chromatin: accessible (euchromatin): H3K4me3 (active TSS), H3K27ac (active enhancers), H3K4me1 (enhancers, poised), H3K36me3 (active gene bodies); repressed (heterochromatin): H3K27me3 (Polycomb, facultative hetero), H3K9me3 (HP1-mediated, constitutive hetero), DNA methylation (5mC at CpGs). Super-enhancers: large clusters of enhancers with very high concentrations of coactivators + Mediator + BRD4; associated with cell identity genes and oncogenes in cancer; BET bromodomain inhibitors (JQ1, BETi) → displace BRD4 from super-enhancers → disproportionate ↓transcription of super-enhancer-driven oncogenes (c-Myc, etc.) → cancer treatment strategy. CRISPR-dCas9 (dead Cas9, no nuclease): can be fused to: VP64/p65/Rta (activators → CRISPRa) or KRAB/DNMT3A (repressors → CRISPRi) → targeted transcriptional modulation without cutting DNA.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A carnitine transporter deficiency leads to systemic carnitine deficiency. What is the primary function of carnitine in fatty acid metabolism?
options: Carnitine is a cofactor for fatty acid synthesis enzymes (WRONG — carnitine is for FA oxidation, not synthesis; FA synthesis occurs in cytoplasm without carnitine)

Carnitine activates fatty acids by forming acyl-carnitine esters that enter the TCA cycle directly (WRONG — acyl-carnitines are the transport form; they re-form CoA thioesters inside mitochondria for beta-oxidation, not TCA)

Carnitine serves as a shuttle to transport long-chain fatty acyl-CoA groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane: long-chain fatty acids (C12-C20) must be activated to acyl-CoA by FACS (fatty acyl-CoA synthetase, requires ATP: FA + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi) at the outer mitochondrial membrane; acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane (CoA cannot be transported) → carnitine shuttle: (1) CPT-I (carnitine palmitoyltransferase-I, on outer face of IMM) → transfers acyl from CoA to carnitine → acylcarnitine + CoA; (2) SLC25A20 (carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase, CACT, IMM transporter) → exchanges acylcarnitine (in) for carnitine (out); (3) CPT-II (inner face of IMM) → re-transfers acyl to intramitochondrial CoA → acyl-CoA enters β-oxidation; CPT-I (liver isoform: CPTI-A; muscle/heart: CPTI-B) is the rate-limiting step, inhibited by malonyl-CoA → prevents FA oxidation when FA synthesis is active; in systemic carnitine deficiency: very long-chain + long-chain FA cannot enter mitochondria → cannot undergo β-oxidation → energy crisis in heart and muscle → skeletal myopathy + cardiomyopathy + hypoglycemia (no FA for ketogenesis when glucose low)
Carnitine directly stimulates beta-oxidation by activating the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase enzyme (WRONG — carnitine has no direct enzyme-activating role; it functions only as a transport carrier)
explanation: Carnitine deficiency syndromes: Primary carnitine deficiency (SCD): AR, SLC22A5 mutations (OCTN2, organic cation/carnitine transporter 2); ↓carnitine uptake in intestine, kidney (renal reabsorption), and cells; ↑urinary carnitine loss → ↓plasma carnitine → ↓intracellular carnitine; manifestations: cardiomyopathy (dilated), skeletal myopathy, episodic hypoglycemia (↓fatty acid oxidation → depends on glucose → fasting → hypoglycemia without ketosis); treatment: high-dose oral L-carnitine (50-100 mg/kg/day) → dramatic improvement of cardiomyopathy if treated early; excellent prognosis if diagnosed and treated. Secondary carnitine deficiency: most organic acidemias (propionyl-CoA/isovaleryl-CoA/methylmalonyl-CoA → conjugates with carnitine → acylcarnitines excreted → ↓free carnitine) → carnitine supplementation is standard in organic acidemias. CPT-I deficiency: hypoketotic hypoglycemia (hepatic form: CPTI-A deficiency — long-chain FA cannot enter mito in liver → ↓ketogenesis → hypoglycemia without ketones; but muscle/heart unaffected because CPTI-B is different gene). CPT-II deficiency: CPTII gene; most common inherited disorder of long-chain FA oxidation in adults; myopathic form: exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis (muscle cannot oxidize FA for sustained exercise) + myoglobinuria; neonatal/infantile: severe multiorganic. LCHAD/MTP deficiency: long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (part of MTP, mitochondrial trifunctional protein); ↑3-hydroxy-long-chain acylcarnitines → hepatic + cardiac + skeletal myopathy + peripheral neuropathy + retinopathy + maternal AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy) in heterozygous mothers carrying LCHAD-deficient fetus.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency impairs which of the following enzyme complexes?
options: Glutamate dehydrogenase + pyruvate carboxylase (GDH uses NAD+/NADP+, not TPP; PC uses biotin, not TPP)

Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex (α-KGDC), and transketolase: ALL THREE require thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP = ThPP, the active coenzyme form of thiamine/B1): (1) PDC (E1 component, pyruvate decarboxylase): pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (mitochondria); (2) α-KGDC (E1 component, alpha-ketoglutarate decarboxylase): α-KG → succinyl-CoA (TCA cycle, step 4 equivalent, mitochondria); (3) transketolase (cytoplasm, PPP): transfers 2C units between sugars (X5P + R5P ↔ G3P + S7P; X5P + E4P ↔ F6P + G3P); TPP is a cofactor for all three — loss of any of these activities → metabolic blockade; also: (4) BCKDC (branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase complex, E1α/E1β subunit) requires TPP → impaired in severe thiamine deficiency; clinical: Wernicke encephalopathy (triad: ophthalmoplegia [lateral gaze palsy, nystagmus], ataxia, confusion) → treat with high-dose IV thiamine BEFORE glucose in any high-risk patient (giving IV glucose first can precipitate/worsen Wernicke by depleting remaining TPP); Korsakoff syndrome (irreversible: anterograde + retrograde amnesia + confabulation + apathy); wet beriberi (high-output heart failure, vasodilation, ↓TPR, ↑CO); dry beriberi (sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy)
Fatty acid synthase (FAS) + acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) (these are zinc-dependent [FAS] and biotin-dependent [ACC]; not TPP)
explanation: Thiamine (B1) biochemistry: Active form: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate), made by thiamine pyrophosphokinase (thiokinase) using thiamine + ATP → TPP + AMP. TPP-dependent enzymes mechanism: TPP's thiazole ring has an acidic C2-H between N and S atoms → ionizes to form a nucleophilic carbanion/ylide → attacks the carbonyl carbon of keto acids → forms a 2-α-hydroxy-ethyl-TPP ('active acetaldehyde') intermediate → specific to each enzyme. Medical significance: High-risk groups for thiamine deficiency: alcoholism (↓dietary intake + ↓intestinal absorption [ethanol directly inhibits thiamine transporter] + ↑metabolism), chronic IV nutrition without supplementation, hyperemesis gravidarum, malabsorption (Crohn's, gastric bypass, short bowel), chronic diuretics (↑thiamine loss), CKD patients on dialysis. Diagnosis: (1) RBC transketolase activity: baseline + after addition of TPP; ↑activity with TPP addition (>25% increase = TPP effect [TPPE] = thiamine deficiency); most functional test. (2) Serum or whole blood thiamine (less sensitive). (3) Erythrocyte thiamine or TPP by HPLC. (4) MRI brain in Wernicke: ↑T2 signal in periaqueductal gray, medial thalami, mammillary bodies (most specific finding: mammillary body atrophy). Treatment: IV thiamine (100 mg IV × 3 days) → then daily orally; thiamine → TPP → PPP-transketolase activity recovers; neurological findings from Wernicke can largely reverse with timely treatment except in chronic Korsakoff. Gayet-Wernicke encephalopathy: same as Wernicke, term used in French literature.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the 'Bohr effect' in oxygen transport by hemoglobin?
options: ↑pH causes a rightward shift in the oxygen-dissociation curve (WRONG — ↑pH = ↓H+ = LEFT shift; RIGHT shift = ↓pH/↑H+/↑CO2)
↑CO2 causes increased oxygen affinity of hemoglobin (WRONG — ↑CO2 → ↓pH + direct carbamino binding → DECREASED O2 affinity = right shift)
