↑Temperature causes a leftward shift in the ODC (WRONG — ↑temperature → RIGHT shift [↓O2 affinity, ↑O2 release]; ↓temperature → LEFT shift, fetal circulation operates at slightly lower temp = one reason HbF has higher affinity)

↑CO2 and ↑H+ (↓pH) shift the oxygen-dissociation curve rightward, decreasing hemoglobin's affinity for O2 and promoting O2 release to metabolically active tissues: the Bohr effect: in metabolically active tissues (muscle, liver): CO2 is generated → dissolved in blood → CO2 + H2O ↔ [carbonic anhydrase] ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3-; ↑H+ → binds ionizable groups on Hb (mainly β-His146 at C-terminus forms salt bridges with Asp94 in T-state) → stabilizes T-state (deoxy) → ↓O2 affinity → ↑P50 (rightward shift of ODC) → more O2 released to tissues per drop in PO2; CO2 directly: forms carbamino groups (CO2 + N-terminus -NH2 → -NH-COO-) on Hb (preferentially on deoxy-Hb) → further stabilizes T-state → additive rightward shift; 2,3-BPG: also stabilizes T-state (binds central cavity of deoxy-Hb, makes electrostatic interactions with β-chain residues including β-His143, β-Lys82, β-N-terminus) → ↑P50; HbF: has γ-chains instead of β-chains; γ-chains have reduced 2,3-BPG binding → less T-state stabilization → ↑O2 affinity vs HbA → appropriate for fetal O2 extraction from maternal circulation
explanation: Hemoglobin oxygen transport — modifiers: All 4 listed (↑CO2, ↑H+, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑temperature) cause a RIGHTWARD shift (↓O2 affinity, ↑P50, ↑O2 delivery to tissues) — physiologically beneficial in metabolically active/hypoxic tissues. ALL cause LEFT shift in opposite direction (favoring O2 binding): ↓CO2, ↓H+ (↑pH), ↓2,3-BPG, ↓temperature. HbF (γ2α2): ↓2,3-BPG binding (γ-His143→Ser143 → no His for BPG electrostatic interaction) → ↑O2 affinity vs HbA → extracts O2 from maternal HbA in placental circulation (where PO2 is intermediate) → appropriate fetal oxygenation. Carboxyhemoglobin (HbCO): CO binds Hb with ~250× higher affinity than O2 → ↓available sites + paradoxically LEFTWARD shift (remaining heme sites have ↑O2 affinity because T→R transition is facilitated) → impaired O2 delivery even at high PO2. Methemoglobin (MetHb, Fe3+): cannot bind O2 → remaining heme groups in Fe2+ form have ↑O2 affinity → leftward shift → ↓O2 delivery. Sickle cell: βS mutation (Glu6Val): HbS polymerizes in deoxy state → sickling → chronic hemolysis + vaso-occlusion. HbSC, HbS-β-thal variants less severe. ODC (oxygen-dissociation curve): Hill equation: Y = PO2^n / (P50^n + PO2^n); n (Hill coefficient) = 2.8 for Hb (cooperative; n=1 = non-cooperative [myoglobin]). P50 = PO2 at 50% saturation; normal human Hb P50 ≈ 26-28 mmHg. Higher P50 = lower affinity = more O2 delivered; Lower P50 = higher affinity = retains O2.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The term 'phospholipid' refers to a lipid containing a phosphate group. Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in most mammalian cell membranes. It is synthesized in which pathway?
options: Beta-oxidation pathway (FA breakdown, not phospholipid synthesis)

Kennedy pathway (CDP-choline pathway): phosphatidylcholine (PC, lecithin) synthesis via the CDP-choline (Kennedy) pathway: step 1: choline → [choline kinase (CK), ATP] → phosphocholine (P-choline); step 2: P-choline + CTP → [phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase (CCT), rate-limiting step] → CDP-choline + PPi; step 3: CDP-choline + diacylglycerol (DAG) → [CPT1 (cholinephosphotransferase), in ER] → phosphatidylcholine + CMP; this is the main pathway in most tissues; CCT is the rate-limiting enzyme (activated by ↑DAG, ↑unsaturated FA, ↑phospholipid demand, membrane-binding activation); alternative: PEMT pathway (phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase): PE → (3 SAM-dependent methylation steps, PEMT enzyme, mainly in liver) → PC; provides ~25-30% of hepatic PC; dietary choline can spare this pathway; choline deficiency → ↓PEMT flux → ↓PC → ↓VLDL assembly (hepatic steatosis) + altered membrane composition; betaine (from choline oxidation via CHDH → betaine aldehyde → BHMT or BDMT) → SAM regeneration via BHMT (betaine-Hcy methyltransferase) → Met → SAM → PC via PEMT
De novo fatty acid synthesis (FA synthesis, not phospholipid headgroup attachment)
explanation: Phospholipid synthesis and remodeling: CDP-choline (Kennedy) pathway: major PC synthesis (all tissues). PEMT (liver only): SAM-dependent methylation (3 methylations: PE → N-methyl-PE → N,N-dimethyl-PE → PC); important when dietary choline inadequate. CDP-ethanolamine pathway: same as Kennedy but with ethanolamine → phosphoethanolamine → CDP-ethanolamine → PE + DAG. Phosphatidylserine (PS) synthesis: in ER, PS synthase 1: PC + serine → PS + choline; PS synthase 2: PE + serine → PS + ethanolamine; PS → PE (PS decarboxylase, mitochondrial → major PE source in mitochondria). Phosphatidylinositol (PI): CDP-DAG + inositol → PI (CDP-DAG pathway); PI → PIP → PIP2 → [PLCγ] → IP3 + DAG (signaling). Plasmalogens (ether lipids): peroxisomal synthesis; alkyl-glycerophospholipids with vinyl ether at sn-1 position (plasmenylcholine, plasmenylethanoamine); ~20% of all phospholipids in humans; very abundant in heart (plasmalogens in cardiac membranes); functions: antioxidant (vinyl ether preferentially oxidized → sacrificial antioxidant), membrane structure, ↑membrane fusogenicity; deficiency in Zellweger syndrome (PEX gene mutations → ↓peroxisomes → ↓plasmalogen synthesis). Phospholipid remodeling (Lands cycle): phospholipase A1/A2 → lysophospholipid + FA; lysophospholipid + acyl-CoA → [LPCAT/LPAAT] → new phospholipid with different FA composition; maintains membrane FA composition (↑PUFA incorporation into membranes via Lands cycle). PAF (platelet-activating factor): 1-O-alkyl-2-acetyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine; lipid mediator of inflammation + platelet activation; made in activated neutrophils, macrophages, eosinophils, mast cells; PAF receptor antagonists: being investigated in inflammatory conditions.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I?
options: ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme): converts Ang I → Ang II (not angiotensinogen → Ang I)
Chymase: a serine protease in heart mast cells that can convert Ang I → Ang II (tissue pathway, alternative to ACE); not the angiotensinogen-cleaving enzyme

Renin (aspartyl protease): renin is the rate-limiting enzyme of the RAAS; secreted by juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the kidney in response to: ↓renal perfusion pressure, ↓NaCl delivery to macula densa (detected by NKCC2 sensor), ↑sympathetic tone (β1-AR on JG cells → ↑cAMP → ↑renin release); renin cleaves the Leu10-Val11 bond of angiotensinogen (an α2-globulin synthesized by liver, also by adipocytes, brain, adrenal, cardiac tissue — increased by estrogen/glucocorticoids/thyroid hormone/Ang II [positive feedback]) → decapeptide angiotensin I (Ang I); Ang I → [ACE, lung endothelium, also kidney] → Ang II (cleaves His9-Leu10 dipeptide from C-terminus); Ang II: (1) AT1R → ↑aldosterone (zona glomerulosa, CYP11B2) → ↑Na+ reabsorption + ↑K+/H+ excretion in principal cells of collecting duct; (2) AT1R → vasoconstriction (↑IP3 → ↑Ca2+ → smooth muscle contraction); (3) AT1R → ADH release + thirst; (4) AT2R (counterbalances AT1R) → vasodilation + natriuresis

Neprilysin (neutral endopeptidase, NEP): cleaves ANP, BNP, and Ang II + endothelin; inhibited by sacubitril [in sacubitril/valsartan, Entresto] → ↑BNP → vasodilation + natriuresis; not the angiotensinogen-cleaving enzyme
explanation: RAAS pharmacology: ACE inhibitors (ACEi): enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril; block Ang I → Ang II; also ↑bradykinin (ACE = kininase II → degrades bradykinin; ACEi → ↑bradykinin → ↑prostaglandins → vasodilation; also → dry cough [bradykinin in lungs → ↑substance P → cough; ~10-20% incidence] + angioedema [rare, 0.1-0.7%, more common in Black patients due to higher basal kallikrein activity; bradykinin-mediated, not IgE-mediated]). ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers): losartan, valsartan, candesartan; block AT1R directly; no bradykinin → no cough; ↑Ang II (not blocked from AT2R) → AT2R effects (vasodilation, antiproliferative). ACEi + ARB combo: not recommended (↑adverse events, ↑hyperkalemia, ↑renal failure, no additional CV benefit in RCTs [ONTARGET]). Direct renin inhibitors: aliskiren; blocks renin activity; used in hypertension; not first-line. Aldosterone antagonists: spironolactone (competes with aldosterone at MR [mineralocorticoid receptor] → ↑Na+/water excretion + ↑K+ retention; side effects: gynecomastia [anti-androgen effect], hyperkalemia); eplerenone (selective MR antagonist, fewer hormonal effects). RAAS in HFrEF: ACEi/ARB + BB + MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone) + SGLT2-I + beta-blocker = 'fantastic four' for HFrEF management (↓mortality). Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI): inhibits neprilysin (↑ANP/BNP) + blocks AT1R → ↓preload/afterload → superior to enalapril in PARADIGM-HF trial.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hyperhomocysteinemia can result from deficiency of all of the following vitamins EXCEPT:
options: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate/PLP): required for cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) and cystathionine γ-lyase (CGL) in the transsulfuration pathway; B6 deficiency → impaired CBS → Hcy cannot enter transsulfuration → ↑Hcy
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): required for methionine synthase; B12 deficiency → ↓methionine synthase activity → Hcy cannot be remethylated → ↑Hcy
Folic acid (B9): provides 5-methyl-THF for methionine synthase; folate deficiency → ↓5-methyl-THF → ↓methionine synthase activity → ↑Hcy

Vitamin B1 (thiamine): required for PDC, α-KGDC, and transketolase; NOT directly involved in homocysteine metabolism; thiamine deficiency → ↑pyruvate + ↑lactate + neurological effects (Wernicke-Korsakoff) but does NOT cause hyperhomocysteinemia; this is the correct EXCEPTION
explanation: Homocysteine metabolism summary: Remethylation: Hcy + 5-methyl-THF → Met (methionine synthase, B12 cofactor) → requires folate (B9) + B12; alternatively, Hcy + betaine → Met (BHMT, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, liver/kidney only). Transsulfuration: Hcy → Cys-thionine (CBS, B6/PLP) → Cys + α-ketobutyrate (CGL, B6/PLP) → cysteine → GSH + taurine + CoA. Hyperhomocysteinemia causes: CBS deficiency (homocystinuria): most severe; Hcy >100 µmol/L; MTHFR C677T: moderate ↑; B12/folate/B6 deficiency: mild-moderate ↑; hypothyroidism (↓CBS activity); CKD (↓renal clearance + ↓folate absorption); methotrexate (↓folate), nitrous oxide (irreversibly oxidizes B12 → ↓methionine synthase); medications: phenytoin, carbamazepine (↑folate metabolism), isoniazid (B6 antagonist). Tests: fasting plasma total Hcy (tHcy): normal <15 µmol/L; methionine loading test: post-load Hcy >40 µmol/L = abnormal (detects partial CBS deficiency or mild B6 deficiency not captured by fasting levels). Clinical significance of hyperhomocysteinemia: CVD (endothelial damage, thrombophilia, ↑platelet aggregation); VTE (3-4× ↑risk in CBS deficiency); pregnancy complications (NTD, placental abruption); cognitive decline; B12 + folate + B6 supplementation: lowers Hcy but CV benefit in large trials (HOPE-2, B-PROOF) was modest/inconsistent.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Krabs disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy) causes accumulation of psychosine. What makes psychosine particularly toxic?
options: Psychosine activates ceramide synthesis which is pro-apoptotic in neurons

Psychosine (galactosylsphingosine) is a potent detergent-like molecule that directly disrupts myelin membranes and causes oligodendrocyte apoptosis: psychosine = galactosylsphingosine = lysogalactocerebroside; it is the predominant sphingolipid intermediate that accumulates in Krabbe disease (GALC deficiency); unlike galactocerebroside (GalCer), psychosine has a cationic head with the free amino group of sphingosine (no fatty acid) → amphipathic, detergent-like properties; at high concentrations, psychosine: (1) intercalates into membranes → disrupts lipid bilayer integrity; (2) triggers apoptosis in oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin-forming cells) and Schwann cells (PNS) → oligodendrocyte/Schwann cell death → demyelination; (3) activates PP2A (protein phosphatase 2A) → dephosphorylation of signaling proteins → neurodegeneration; (4) ↑ROS production; mechanism of globoid cell formation: galactocerebroside deposits (not degraded) attract macrophages → macrophages fuse → multinucleated globoid cells (with galactocerebroside inclusions); psychosine is the toxic culprit; diagnosis: ↓GALC enzyme in leukocytes, ↑psychosine in DBS/plasma (most sensitive and specific), MRI white matter changes, NCV slowing
Psychosine inhibits hexosaminidase A leading to GM2 ganglioside accumulation (this is Tay-Sachs mechanism)
Psychosine blocks the transport of galactose across the lysosomal membrane
explanation: Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy, GLD): Gene: GALC (chromosome 14q31.3). Enzyme: galactocerebrosidase (GALC), a lysosomal hydrolase; breaks down: galactocerebroside (GalCer) → ceramide + galactose; psychosine (galactosylsphingosine) → sphingosine + galactose. Both substrates accumulate in GALC deficiency; psychosine is the main toxic species. Forms: Early infantile (85%): onset <6 months → extreme irritability, feeding difficulties, hyperreflexia → motor regression, seizures, blindness, deafness, death by 2-3 years. Late infantile/juvenile: 6 months-3 years → slower; vision/hearing loss + ataxia + progressive neurological decline. Adult form: rare; ataxia + peripheral neuropathy slowly progressive. Pathology: globoid cells (PAS-positive, galactocerebroside deposits, multinucleated macrophages) + severe demyelination; lack of inflammation (unlike MS). Treatment: HSCT (stem cell transplant): only for pre-symptomatic newborns identified by newborn screening (NBS); must be done before 30 days of life for best outcome; NBS programs for Krabbe expanded after pivotal studies (NY adopted 2006; ~14 states now screen). Intrathecal enzyme replacement + gene therapy: under investigation (GALC is large → AAV capacity challenges). Psychosine biomarker: DBS (dried blood spot) psychosine level: elevated in GALC patients; correlates inversely with GALC enzyme activity; useful for confirming diagnosis + monitoring treatment response.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the catabolism of tryptophan to produce niacin (nicotinic acid) is:
options: Aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC): converts 5-HTP → 5-HT (serotonin) and DOPA → dopamine; not the first step in niacin synthesis from Trp
Tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH1/TPH2): converts Trp → 5-HTP (serotonin pathway, not niacin pathway); these two pathways COMPETE for Trp

Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO1/IDO2) or tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2): the first step of the kynurenine pathway (Trp → kynurenine → → nicotinic acid) is catalyzed by TDO2 (tryptophan dioxygenase, liver, heme enzyme, induced by cortisol + Trp itself) or IDO1 (extrahepatic, including intestine, macrophages, DCs, induced by IFN-γ — a major immune regulation enzyme); reaction: L-Trp + O2 → N-formylkynurenine → [kynurenine formamidase] → kynurenine; subsequent steps: kynurenine → 3-OH-kynurenine → 3-OH-anthranilic acid → 2-amino-3-carboxymuconic semialdehyde → quinolinic acid → [QPRT] → NMN → [NMNAT] → NAD+ (niacin equivalent); conversion efficiency: 60 mg tryptophan = 1 mg niacin equivalent (NE); pellagra (niacin deficiency): insufficient dietary niacin + insufficient Trp (e.g., in Hartnup disease → ↓Trp absorption; carcinoid syndrome → ↑Trp → 5-HT at expense of kynurenine pathway → ↓niacin synthesis → pellagra despite adequate Trp intake)
Quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT): converts quinolinate → NMN (this is a later step in niacin synthesis, not the first)
explanation: Tryptophan metabolism pathways: Trp is the precursor for THREE major products (competition between pathways): (1) Serotonin (5-HT) pathway: Trp → [TPH1, peripheral/gut; TPH2, brain, BH4 cofactor] → 5-HTP → [AADC, PLP] → 5-HT → [MAO-A] → 5-HIAA (in urine; elevated in carcinoid tumor → diagnostic). (2) Kynurenine pathway (>95% of Trp catabolism): Trp → [TDO2 in liver; IDO1 extrahepatic] → N-formylkynurenine → kynurenine → [kynurenine aminotransferase: kynurenic acid (KynA, neuroactive)] or [kynurenine 3-monooxygenase (KMO): 3-OH-kynurenine → 3-OH-anthranilic acid → quinolinic acid (QUIN, NMDAR agonist, excitotoxic) → NMN → NAD+]. (3) Melatonin: 5-HT (in pineal gland) → [AANAT, arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase] → N-acetylserotonin → [ASMT/HIOMT] → melatonin; regulated by circadian rhythm (light → suprachiasmatic nucleus → ↓AANAT at daytime; dark → ↑melatonin production at night). IDO1 in immunity: IFN-γ (from T cells, NK) → ↑IDO1 in macrophages/DCs → ↑kynurenine pathway → ↓Trp → (1) Trp depletion starves local bacteria/parasites; (2) Trp depletion inhibits T cell proliferation (T cells sensitive to Trp depletion via GCN2 sensor); (3) ↑kynurenines → immunosuppressive (inhibit Th1, promote Treg via AhR [aryl hydrocarbon receptor] activation); IDO1 overexpression in some tumors → local immunosuppression → immune evasion; IDO1/TDO inhibitors (epacadostat, navoximod) + checkpoint inhibitors: combination trials (disappointing results so far).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Cori cycle involves shuttling of which metabolite from muscle to liver?
options: Alanine (that is the glucose-alanine cycle [Cahill cycle]; alanine carries amino nitrogen from muscle to liver; separate from Cori cycle)
Glucose (glucose goes FROM liver TO muscle in both Cori cycle and Cahill cycle; the Cori cycle returns glucose from liver to muscle)

Lactate: the Cori cycle (glucose-lactate cycle, named after Carl and Gerty Cori) involves: (1) Muscle (especially under anaerobic/high-intensity exercise): glucose → [glycolysis] → pyruvate → [LDH] → lactate; lactate exported into blood (via MCT1/4, monocarboxylate transporters); (2) Blood: lactate transported from muscle to liver; (3) Liver: lactate → [LDH] → pyruvate → [gluconeogenesis: pyruvate → OAA [PC] → PEP [PEPCK] → → glucose]; glucose released back into blood → muscle; net: Cori cycle 'recycles' lactate from anaerobic muscle back to glucose in liver; energetics: muscle gets 2 ATP from glucose → lactate; liver uses 6 ATP to convert lactate back to glucose → net cost of 4 ATP to the organism (liver pays the ATP debt of the muscle); this allows sustained muscular activity by disposing of lactate (prevents acidosis) and regenerating glucose; RBCs also use the Cori cycle (exclusively glycolytic → produce lactate constantly)
Fatty acids (fatty acids go FROM liver/adipose TO muscle for oxidation; not the Cori cycle)
explanation: Cori cycle details: Key enzymes: Muscle LDH (pyruvate → lactate, predominantly LDH-5 [M4], favors lactate formation under high NADH/NAD+ ratio). Liver LDH (lactate → pyruvate, predominantly LDH-1 [H4], favors lactate oxidation). Hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate: lactate → pyruvate (LDH) → OAA (PC, mito, biotin) → PEP (PEPCK, GTP) → … → glucose-6-P → [G6Pase, ER] → glucose. Cori cycle quantification: at rest: ~25-30% of hepatic gluconeogenesis from lactate; during exercise: up to 50% of glucose comes from recycled lactate. Regulatory considerations: ↑epinephrine during exercise → ↑hepatic gluconeogenesis + ↑hepatic lactate uptake; glucagon → ↑PEPCK, G6Pase → ↑gluconeogenesis; insulin → ↓gluconeogenesis → ↓Cori cycle efficiency. Comparison with Cahill (glucose-alanine) cycle: Muscle: AA (especially BCAA) → transamination with pyruvate → Ala + keto acid; Ala released to blood → liver; Liver: Ala → pyruvate (ALT) + Glu → pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → glucose; Glu → GDH → α-KG + NH3 → urea cycle; net: transfers amino nitrogen from muscle to liver (for urea cycle) AND recycles carbon as glucose. Both cycles: serve as substrate shuttle; both require hepatic gluconeogenesis; both cost ATP in liver. Difference: Cori = lactate (energy substrate); Cahill = alanine (nitrogen carrier + carbon).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the context of DNA repair, which pathway specifically corrects single-base mismatches arising from DNA replication errors?
options: Nucleotide excision repair (NER): removes bulky helix-distorting lesions (pyrimidine dimers from UV, cisplatin adducts, large adducts); not for single-base mismatches
Base excision repair (BER): repairs small base modifications (oxidized, alkylated, deaminated, or missing bases) — initiated by DNA glycosylases; not for replication mismatches

Mismatch repair (MMR): the MMR pathway specifically corrects: (1) base-base mismatches (e.g., G-T instead of G-C, from replication polymerase error); (2) insertion/deletion loops (IDLs) in repetitive sequences (microsatellites); key MMR proteins: MutS (MutSα=MSH2+MSH6 detects base mismatches; MutSβ=MSH2+MSH3 detects IDLs) recognizes mismatch; MutL (MutLα=MLH1+PMS2; MutLβ=MLH1+PMS1; MutLγ=MLH1+MLH3) recruits downstream factors + PCNA; EXO1 or other exonucleases excise the newly synthesized strand (the error-containing strand identified by hemimethylation [bacterial] or strand discontinuities [eukaryotic]); DNA Pol δ + PCNA + ligase I re-synthesize + seal; Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, HNPCC): germline mutations in MMR genes (MLH1 [40%], MSH2 [35%], MSH6 [15%], PMS2 [<5%]) → ↑microsatellite instability (MSI-H) → ↑risk of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial, small bowel, brain cancers; diagnosis: IHC for MMR proteins (absent staining) + PCR for MSI; MLH1 promoter methylation: common in sporadic MSI-H CRC (different from Lynch); MSI-H tumors respond well to PD-1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) — FDA approved MSI-H as biomarker irrespective of tumor type (site-agnostic approval)
Double-strand break repair (DSBR): handles double-strand breaks via NHEJ (error-prone) or HR (error-free in S/G2); not for single-base mismatches
explanation: DNA repair pathways summary: BER (base excision repair): specific DNA glycosylase recognizes and removes abnormal base → AP site → APE1 endonuclease → Pol β inserts correct base → Ligase III/XRCC1 seals; types: UDG (removes U→G mismatches from cytosine deamination), OGG1 (removes 8-oxoG, oxidized guanine), MUTYH (removes A opposite 8-oxoG), MPG (removes alkylated bases); short-patch (1 nt) or long-patch (2-10 nt). NER (nucleotide excision repair): two pathways: GG-NER (genome-global: XPC+RAD23B recognize helix distortion → opens DNA → XPA+TFIIH+RPA → dual incision [XPF-ERCC1 5', XPG 3'] → removes 25-30 nt oligonucleotide → Pol δ/ε + RFC + PCNA resynthesize + Lig I); TC-NER (transcription-coupled: stalled RNA Pol II triggers CSB+CSA → recruits GG-NER machinery, more rapid repair of actively transcribed genes); NER defects: XP (xeroderma pigmentosum, XPA-XPG → ↑skin cancer + neurodegeneration), CS (Cockayne syndrome, ERCC8/CSA + ERCC6/CSB → no ↑cancer but premature aging + photosensitivity), TTD (trichothiodystrophy, TFIIH components). HR (homologous recombination): error-free; uses sister chromatid as template; requires: BRCA1/2, RAD51, MRN complex (MRE11-RAD50-NBS1), ATM/CHEK2; BRCA1/2 mutations → ↑breast/ovarian cancer; defective HR → sensitivity to PARP inhibitors (synthetic lethality: HR-deficient cells depend on PARP for single-strand break repair → PARP inhibition → lethal double-strand breaks) → olaparib, niraparib, rucaparib. NHEJ (non-homologous end joining): error-prone, main DSB pathway in G1; Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer → binds DSB ends → recruits DNA-PKcs → Artemis/XRCC4/Lig IV seal.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During starvation, ketone body synthesis occurs primarily in the liver. Ketogenesis is initiated by:
options: Activation of fatty acid synthase (FAS) — FAS makes fatty acids, not ketone bodies; the two pathways are opposite (FA synthesis vs. FA oxidation)
Inhibition of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) — inhibiting ACC reduces malonyl-CoA, which ENABLES ketogenesis by relieving CPT-I inhibition, but ACC inhibition alone does not initiate ketogenesis

The accumulation of acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation of fatty acids, which condenses to form HMG-CoA via the HMG-CoA pathway: in starvation → ↑glucagon/↓insulin → ↑hormone-sensitive lipase + ATGL in adipose → ↑fatty acid release → ↑NEFA to liver → ↑hepatic β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA; simultaneously, low insulin → ↓malonyl-CoA (↓ACC activity via phosphorylation by PKA + AMPK) → ↓CPT-I inhibition → ↑FA import into mitochondria → ↑β-oxidation; ↑acetyl-CoA + ↓oxaloacetate (OAA depleted for gluconeogenesis via PEPCK → PEP) → acetyl-CoA cannot fully enter TCA → condenses instead: 2 acetyl-CoA → [thiolase, ACAT1, reverse] → acetoacetyl-CoA → [HMG-CoA synthase 2 (HMGCS2), rate-limiting, mitochondrial] → HMG-CoA → [HMG-CoA lyase (HMGCL)] → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; acetoacetate → [β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, BDH1, NADH-linked] → β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB); acetoacetate → [spontaneous decarboxylation] → acetone (volatile, fruity breath in DKA); β-OHB is the main ketone body in blood (ratio β-OHB:acetoacetate ~3:1 at rest, can be 10:1 in DKA)
Overexpression of the liver's cytoplasmic HMG-CoA reductase — HMGCR is in ER and makes mevalonate for cholesterol (a different pathway); ketogenesis uses mitochondrial HMGCS2 + HMGCL
explanation: Ketone body metabolism: Synthesis (liver): β-OHB + acetoacetate + acetone; liver lacks the enzyme to use ketones (lacks succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid-CoA transferase [SCOT] for activating acetoacetate); liver MAKES ketones for export. Utilization (extrahepatic: brain, heart, kidney, skeletal muscle): acetoacetate + succinyl-CoA → [SCOT] → acetoacetyl-CoA + succinate; acetoacetyl-CoA → [thiolase] → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA; β-OHB → [BDH1] → acetoacetate → SCOT pathway. Brain during starvation: normally uses glucose exclusively; after 1-2 weeks of starvation: ↑ketones (β-OHB) cross BBB via MCT1/2 → brain utilizes ketones for ~2/3 of energy needs → spares muscle protein (less gluconeogenesis from AA needed). Regulation: ↑glucagon/↓insulin + ↑NEFA → ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑HMGCS2 activity (HMGCS2 is rate-limiting; inhibited when succinylated [high energy]; induced by PPAR-α during fasting via FGF21 axis); HMGCS2 is activated by FGF21 + PPARα + HNF4α. DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis): absolute insulin deficiency (type 1) or severe relative deficiency (type 2) → ↑glucagon/↑catecholamines → extreme lipolysis + ↑ketogenesis + ↑gluconeogenesis + ↓glucose uptake → ↑↑ketones + ↑↑glucose → anion gap metabolic acidosis + osmotic diuresis → dehydration + electrolyte losses (K+, Na+, PO4, Mg2+); K+ in DKA: total body K+ depleted (urinary losses + H+/K+ exchange in ECF) but serum K+ may appear NORMAL or HIGH (acidosis → H+ enters cells, K+ exits → hyperkalemia despite total body deficit; insulin + IV fluids → K+ returns to cells → hypokalemia → cardiac arrhythmia if not replaced). Treatment: IV fluids (normal saline initially → ↓osmolality), insulin (low-dose continuous infusion → ↓ketogenesis + ↓glucose), K+ replacement (start when K+ <5.5 mEq/L or after urine output established), monitor anion gap.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 3-year-old child presents with progressive muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, and on muscle biopsy shows 'ragged red fibers' on Gomori trichrome stain. The most likely diagnosis involves a defect in:
options: Nuclear-encoded ribosomal proteins causing cytoplasmic translation defects (ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia affect erythropoiesis, not classically causing ragged red fibers)
Glycogen metabolism (glycogenoses like GSD II/Pompe cause myopathy but not typically ragged red fibers on trichrome stain — glycogen-related myopathies show PAS-positive deposits)

Mitochondrial respiratory chain (oxidative phosphorylation): ragged red fibers (RRF) on Gomori modified trichrome stain represent subsarcolemmal and intermyofibrillar accumulations of abnormal mitochondria (appearing red/pink due to high protein content) in skeletal muscle; caused by defects in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) or nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins; mtDNA mutations: maternal inheritance (mtDNA transmitted exclusively through maternal oocyte); heteroplasmy (mixture of mutant and wild-type mtDNA within a cell/tissue → phenotype severity depends on proportion of mutant mtDNA [threshold effect]); common mtDNA mutation diseases: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes: m.3243A>G mutation in MT-TL1 [tRNA-Leu] gene → ~80% of MELAS); MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers: m.8344A>G in MT-TK [tRNA-Lys]); CPEO/KSS (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, Kearns-Sayre syndrome: large mtDNA deletions); Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON: point mutations in Complex I subunit genes); NARP (neurogenic atrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, ataxia: m.8993T>G in MT-ATP6); RRF = hallmark of mitochondrial myopathies but not pathognomonic (also in some inflammatory myopathies)
Peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation (peroxisomal disorders cause specific organ involvement patterns; ragged red fibers are not their hallmark)
explanation: Mitochondrial disease: electron transport chain (ETC) and OXPHOS: 5 complexes in inner mitochondrial membrane: CI (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, 44 subunits, 7 from mtDNA): rotenone inhibitor. CII (succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, all nuclear-encoded): malonate inhibitor. CIII (ubiquinol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase, cytochrome bc1 complex): antimycin A inhibitor. CIV (cytochrome c oxidase, 3 catalytic subunits from mtDNA): cyanide (Fe3+ site), CO (Fe2+ site), H2S inhibitors. CV (ATP synthase, ATP synthase F0F1): oligomycin (F0 channel), DCCD inhibitors. Proton gradient: CI, CIII, CIV pump H+ from matrix → IMS → driving force for ATP synthase (Mitchell's chemiosmotic hypothesis). Uncoupling: DNP, FCCP, thyroid hormone (↑UCP1 expression in BAT) → ↑proton leak → ↓ΔΨ → ↑O2 consumption → heat generation without ATP synthesis → UCP1 (thermogenin) in brown adipose tissue → nonshivering thermogenesis. mtDNA: 16,569 bp circular dsDNA; 37 genes: 13 ETC subunits (7 CI: ND1-6, ND4L; 1 CII: none; 1 CIII: Cytb; 3 CIV: COX1-3; 2 CV: ATP6, ATP8), 22 tRNAs, 2 rRNAs (12S, 16S); rest of OXPHOS subunits (>1000 total) encoded by nuclear genome → imported post-translationally. Mutations: heteroplasmy (mixed wt+mutant) vs. homoplasmy; threshold: generally >70-80% mutant mtDNA before clinical phenotype; different tissues have different thresholds (brain + heart + muscle most sensitive due to high energy demand).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The lysosomal acid hydrolases are targeted to lysosomes via which post-translational modification?
options: O-linked glycosylation at serine residues in the Golgi (this is mucin-type O-glycosylation; not the lysosomal targeting signal)
Palmitoylation (S-palmitoylation, adding palmitate to Cys via thioester bond — a lipid modification for membrane anchoring, not lysosomal targeting)

Mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) residues on N-linked oligosaccharides: lysosomal acid hydrolases are glycoproteins synthesized in the ER → moved to Golgi → in cis-Golgi: a unique two-step phosphorylation adds M6P to high-mannose N-glycans: step 1: UDP-GlcNAc → [GlcNAc phosphotransferase (GNPTAB)] → GlcNAc-1-PO4 attached to mannose-6-OH; step 2: [α-N-acetylglucosaminidase 1 (NAGPA/UCE)] → removes GlcNAc → exposes M6P; M6P recognized by M6P receptors (M6PR, also called CI-MPR/CD222 = cation-independent, 300 kDa; or CD-MPR = cation-dependent, 46 kDa) in trans-Golgi network (TGN) → coated vesicle (clathrin) → endosome → lysosome → acid pH → M6PR releases enzyme → enzyme retained in lysosome; I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II, ML-II): GNPTAB deficiency → cannot add M6P → lysosomal enzymes lack M6P → secreted into plasma instead of targeted to lysosomes → ↑plasma lysosomal enzymes (diagnostic) + large intracellular inclusions (inclusion bodies → 'I-cell') of undigested substrates → severe progressive lysosomal storage disease (coarse facies, severe psychomotor retardation, skeletal abnormalities, death in childhood); pseudo-Hurler polydystrophy (ML-III): partial GNPTAB deficiency → milder; mucolipidosis IV (ML-IV): MCOLN1 (mucolipin-1, TRPML1 channel) deficiency → different mechanism
GPI-anchor attachment in the ER (glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored proteins are targeted to plasma membrane lipid rafts, not to lysosomes)
explanation: Lysosomal biogenesis and disease: Lysosomes: pH ~4.5-5 (maintained by V-ATPase [vacuolar H+-ATPase]); contain ~50+ acid hydrolases (proteases [cathepsins B, D, L, S], lipases, nucleases, sulfatases, glucosidases); membrane proteins: LAMP1/2 (structural, highly glycosylated → protect from self-digestion), NPC1/2 (cholesterol export), NHE7 (Na+/H+), LAMP3 (CD63). M6PR: after lysosome delivery, M6PR recycled back to TGN (by GGA proteins + AP1 adaptors). M6P-independent lysosomal targeting: some lysosomal membrane proteins (LAMP1/2) → sorted by AP3 adaptor from TGN to lysosomes bypassing M6PR. Lysosomal storage diseases (LSDs): 50+ disorders; most AR; accumulation of specific substrate in lysosomes; classified by substrate: sphingolipidoses, mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS), glycoproteinoses, glycogenosis (Pompe), mucolipidoses, lipid storage diseases, lysosomal transport defects. Treatment approaches: ERT (enzyme replacement therapy): available for Gaucher (imiglucerase), Fabry (agalsidase), Pompe (alglucosidase alfa, cipaglucosidase alfa), MPS I, II, IVA, VI, VII; must be modified with M6P for lysosomal targeting. Substrate reduction therapy (SRT): miglustat + eliglustat (Gaucher), cysteamine (cystinosis — not enzyme deficiency but substrate accumulation; cysteamine + cysteine → cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide → exits lysosome via PQLC2 transporter). Pharmacological chaperones: migalastat (Fabry, stabilizes missense GALA variants → improved lysosomal trafficking). Gene therapy: AAV-based for some LSDs (SMA, CLN3 Batten disease, MPS).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Gaucher disease is treated with enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) using imiglucerase. What is the recombinant enzyme in imiglucerase?
options: Hexosaminidase A (recombinant HEXA would treat Tay-Sachs, not Gaucher)

Glucocerebrosidase (acid β-glucosidase, GBA1): Gaucher disease (AR, GBA1 gene mutations, chromosome 1q22) → deficiency of acid β-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase) → accumulation of glucosylceramide (glucocerebroside, GlcCer) in lysosomes of macrophages (liver Kupffer cells, spleen, bone marrow) → Gaucher cells (distended macrophages with 'crumpled tissue paper' or 'wrinkled silk' cytoplasm — packed GlcCer sheets); ERT: imiglucerase (modified GBA1 expressed in CHO cells, mannose-terminated oligosaccharides → M6P pathway + direct mannose receptor [CD206] on macrophages → targeted delivery to tissue macrophages where Gaucher cells accumulate); velaglucerase alfa (GBA1 expressed in fibrosarcoma cells); taliglucerase alfa (carrot cell-expressed); substrate reduction: miglustat (GlcCer synthase inhibitor, BBB-penetrant → also used for NPC neurological involvement [↓glucosylceramide/ganglioside substrates]) and eliglustat (peripheral only, not BBB)
Acid sphingomyelinase (recombinant ASMase, olipudase alfa, treats NPC and NPD type B, not Gaucher)
explanation: Gaucher disease types: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic, most common, especially Ashkenazi Jewish): N370S (most common mutation) homozygous/compound heterozygous; hepatosplenomegaly (massive splenomegaly, 'world's largest spleen' associations), pancytopenia (hypersplenism → bone marrow infiltration), bone disease (Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur on X-ray, osteonecrosis/avascular necrosis, pathological fractures), no neurological involvement; ↑risk of PD (Parkinson disease — GBA1 heterozygous mutations are most common genetic risk factor for PD, ~5% of PD patients) and multiple myeloma. Type 2 (acute neuronopathic): L444P mutation common; severe neurological (oculomotor abnormality → retroflexion of head → spasticity → seizures) + systemic; death before 2 years; ERT does not help neurological (cannot cross BBB). Type 3 (sub-acute neuronopathic): L444P/L444P or other mutations; milder neurological (oculomotor palsies) + systemic; ERT helps systemic; most common in Sweden (Norrbottnian type, type 3c). ERT monitoring: hemoglobin, platelet count, spleen/liver volume (MRI), bone marrow involvement (quantitative chemical shift imaging, DXA). GBA1-PD (Gaucher + Parkinson connection): GBA1 heterozygous mutation → ↓GCase activity → accumulation of GlcCer/GlcSph in dopaminergic neurons → promotes α-synuclein aggregation (amyloidogenic) → Lewy bodies + neurodegeneration; GCase activators + GBA1 gene therapy for GBA1-PD under investigation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is the immediate precursor of nitric oxide (NO) AND is also involved in the urea cycle?
options: Citrulline (intermediate in both urea cycle and NOS pathway — but not the IMMEDIATE precursor of NO; citrulline is formed FROM arginine in the NOS reaction, and is the urea cycle product of OTC)
Ornithine (urea cycle intermediate but not a precursor to NO)
Glutamine (provides nitrogen to carbamoyl-P in urea cycle but is not an immediate NO precursor)

Arginine: L-arginine is the substrate for all three NOS isoforms: NOS reaction: L-Arg + O2 + NADPH → L-Citrulline + NO + NADP+; L-Arg is also a direct participant in the urea cycle as the substrate of arginase (the final step: Arg → Orn + urea); in the urea cycle: OTC produces citrulline → ASS joins citrulline + Asp → argininosuccinate → ASL releases fumarate → Arg → arginase → urea + Orn; thus arginine is: (1) the immediate precursor of NO (in NOS reaction); (2) the immediate product of ASL (last step before arginase in urea cycle); (3) the substrate of arginase (last step of urea cycle); additionally: Arg → [GDH? No] → guanidinoacetate → creatine (AGAT: arginine + glycine → guanidinoacetate + ornithine); Arg provides the guanidinium group for creatine synthesis; Arg in polyamine synthesis: Arg → [arginase] → Orn → [ODC, ornithine decarboxylase, the rate-limiting step] → putrescine → spermidine → spermine (all polyamines)
explanation: Arginine biochemistry and urea cycle connection: In the urea cycle, arginine is at the penultimate step: ASL → Arg + fumarate (ASL, argininosuccinate lyase, cytoplasm). Arginase I (liver cytoplasm) → Arg → urea + Orn (final step). In NOS reaction: Arg → NO + Cit (mitochondria or cytoplasm depending on NOS isoform); NOS products: citrulline (same as urea cycle intermediate!) + NO; citrulline from NOS can recycle back to arginine via ASS + ASL ('citrulline-NO cycle') in endothelium and other cells → allows sustained NO production. Arginine semi-essential amino acid: typically classified as 'conditionally essential'; adults can synthesize sufficient Arg via urea cycle (intestine → kidney loop: gut synthesizes citrulline [CPS I + OTC, enterocytes] → kidney → ASS + ASL → Arg); but in stress, growth, pregnancy → dietary Arg needed. Arginine as secretagogue: stimulates insulin secretion (cationic amino acid → depolarizes β-cell via unknown mechanism → Ca2+ influx → insulin release); also stimulates growth hormone release (used in GH stimulation tests); used pharmacologically to diagnose argininosuccinic aciduria (oral Arg → bypasses OTC/CPS but not ASL step → accumulation proximal to block). Arginine in mTOR signaling: cytoplasmic arginine sensed by SLC38A9 (lysosomal Arg transporter) + CASTOR1 (cytoplasmic Arg sensor) → activate mTORC1 via GATOR complex; dietary Arg deprivation → ↓mTORC1 → autophagy (relevant in some tumors that can't synthesize Arg themselves → 'arginine auxotrophic tumors' → therapeutic arginine deprivation with pegylated arginase [BCT-100]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following lipoproteins is primarily responsible for transporting dietary cholesterol from the intestine to peripheral tissues?
options: LDL (low-density lipoprotein): delivers hepatic cholesterol to peripheral tissues; NOT dietary cholesterol from intestine
VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein): delivers hepatically synthesized TG + cholesterol to peripheral tissues; not dietary cholesterol
HDL (high-density lipoprotein): collects cholesterol from peripheral tissues → reverse cholesterol transport; not dietary cholesterol transport FROM intestine

Chylomicrons: intestinal cells (enterocytes) absorb dietary fatty acids + cholesterol → package as chylomicrons in the ER + Golgi: core: dietary TG + dietary cholesterol ester; surface: phospholipids + free cholesterol + ApoB-48 (intestine-specific, encoded by APOB gene, RNA editing by APOBEC1 converts CAA [Gln] codon 2153 → UAA [Stop] → truncated protein; ApoB-48 = N-terminal 48% of ApoB-100; unlike ApoB-100, ApoB-48 does NOT bind LDL receptor, so chylomicrons not directly cleared by LDL-R but by remnant receptors); chylomicrons secreted into lymphatic lacteals → thoracic duct → left subclavian vein → systemic circulation; in capillaries of adipose and muscle: lipoprotein lipase (LPL, anchored by GPIHBP1 on capillary endothelium; activated by ApoC-II [received from HDL] and ApoA-V) hydrolyzes TG → glycerol + FFA → taken up by cells; ApoC-II, ApoC-III, ApoE transferred from HDL to chylomicrons after entering bloodstream; chylomicron remnants (depleted of TG, enriched in cholesterol ester) → liver via ApoE-LRP1 (LDL receptor-related protein) + ApoE-LDL-R receptors
explanation: Lipoprotein metabolism cascade: Exogenous path: chylomicrons (intestine) → capillary LPL → remnants → liver (LRP1/LDL-R via ApoE). Endogenous path: VLDL (liver) → IDL (partially delipidated by LPL + HL [hepatic lipase]) → LDL (further delipidated, ApoC/E transferred off; IDL → LDL by HL; LDL = mainly ApoB-100 + cholesterol ester) → LDL-R (liver + peripheral cells; ApoB-100 binds; endocytosis; cholesterol released for membrane synthesis + steroid hormones). LDL receptor: regulated by: ↑intracellular cholesterol → INSIG-mediated retention of SCAP-SREBP2 → ↓LDLR transcription + ↑ACAT (store); ↓intracellular cholesterol → SCAP-SREBP2 released → Golgi → proteolysis → nSREBP2 → ↑LDLR + ↑HMGCR transcription; statins → ↓intracellular cholesterol → ↑LDLR (major mechanism of LDL-C lowering). Lp(a): ApoB-100 particle covalently linked to Apo(a) via disulfide bond; Apo(a) is structurally similar to plasminogen (contains kringle domains) → may inhibit plasminogen binding to fibrin → thrombotic risk; Lp(a) also carries oxidized PL (oxidized phospholipids, OxPL) → pro-inflammatory + pro-atherogenic; elevated Lp(a) (>50 mg/dL) → independent CVD risk factor; NOT lowered by statins (↑statins can actually ↑Lp(a) due to upregulation of LDL-R recycling pathway); lowered by: PCSK9-I (~20-25% ↓), niacin (~25-35% ↓), lipoprotein apheresis, olpasiran/zerlasiran/pelacarsen (siRNA/ASO targeting APOA1 gene → ↓Lp(a) synthesis, >90% ↓).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) requires molecular oxygen and which other co-substrate?
options: NADH (niacin) — PAH uses NADPH indirectly through BH4 regeneration, not NADH directly
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) — PLP is a cofactor for aminotransferases including phenylalanine aminotransferase; not for PAH

Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4): PAH catalyzes the irreversible hydroxylation: L-Phe + BH4 + O2 → L-Tyr + BH2 (quinonoid dihydrobiopterin) + H2O; co-substrates: O2 AND BH4 (both consumed in the reaction); BH4 is oxidized to BH2 (qBH2) → regenerated by DHPR (dihydropteridine reductase) using NADH: qBH2 + NADH → BH4 + NAD+; PAH is an iron-containing enzyme (Fe2+ at active site, non-heme iron); PAH reaction mechanism: BH4 donates 2 electrons + O2 → one O is inserted into Phe ring → Tyr + BH2 formed; stoichiometry: 1 Phe + 1 O2 + 1 BH4 → 1 Tyr + 1 H2O + 1 BH2; same co-substrates required for all aromatic amino acid hydroxylases: tyrosine hydroxylase (TH: Tyr → DOPA, dopamine synthesis) and tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH1/2: Trp → 5-HTP, serotonin synthesis)
Adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl, vitamin B12 coenzyme form) — required for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, not for phenylalanine hydroxylase
explanation: Aromatic amino acid hydroxylases: All three require BH4 + O2: PAH (phenylalanine → tyrosine): liver → Tyr production; rate-limiting step = deficiency → PKU. TH (tyrosine → DOPA): rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis (DOPA → dopamine → NE → Epi); TH is activated by: phosophorylation by PKA (Ser40), CaM-K (Ser19, Ser40), MAPK; inhibited by: catecholamines (product inhibition), BH4 depletion (end-product oxidation). TPH1 (tryptophan → 5-HTP): peripheral (gut, pineal, mast cells) → serotonin (gut, platelets); rate-limiting for 5-HT synthesis. TPH2: brain (raphe nuclei) → brain serotonin. BH4 deficiency clinical implication: BH4 deficiency → ↓PAH + ↓TH + ↓TPH1/2 + ↓NOS → malignant hyperphenylalaninemia (like PKU biochemically) + neurological symptoms (↓dopamine + ↓serotonin in brain) + ↓immune function (↓NOS → ↓NO). BH4 synthesis: GCH1 → PTPS → SR (see earlier question). DHFR vs. DHPR: DHFR (dihydrofolate reductase) reduces DHF → THF (folate pathway); DHPR (dihydropteridine reductase, QDPR gene) reduces qBH2 → BH4 (biopterin pathway); both use NADPH [for DHFR] or NADH [for DHPR]; methotrexate inhibits DHFR (not DHPR) → folate deficiency but does NOT cause BH4 deficiency (different enzyme); these two reductases handle different cofactors (folate vs. biopterin).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the context of membrane lipids, what is the main role of cholesterol in animal cell plasma membranes?
options: Cholesterol is the primary energy storage lipid in cell membranes (energy storage is TG in lipid droplets; cholesterol serves structural/regulatory roles)

Cholesterol serves as a precursor for vitamin D synthesis only in membranes (Vit D synthesis requires UV radiation on 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin; cholesterol's membrane role is primarily structural, not as a Vit D precursor)

Cholesterol modulates membrane fluidity by preventing both excessive rigidity at low temperatures and excessive fluidity at high temperatures: cholesterol is an amphipathic molecule (3-OH group = hydrophilic; flat steroid ring + hydrocarbon tail = hydrophobic); intercalates between phospholipid acyl chains at an angle with the 3-OH near the glycerol backbone; effects on membrane properties: (1) AT LOW TEMPERATURES: cholesterol disrupts ordered packing of saturated FA chains → prevents crystallization → maintains membrane fluidity (cholesterol as 'fluidizer'); (2) AT HIGH TEMPERATURES: cholesterol restricts motion of unsaturated FA chains (the flat rigid ring fills space between chains) → reduces fluidity (cholesterol as 'rigidizer'); net effect: cholesterol BUFFERS membrane fluidity changes with temperature → maintains membrane in 'liquid-ordered' (Lo) phase; also: increases membrane permeability barrier (reduces permeability to ions + polar molecules); part of lipid rafts (Lo phase microdomains enriched in cholesterol + sphingolipids + GPI-anchored proteins + signaling molecules)

Cholesterol acts as the direct receptor for steroid hormones on the membrane surface (steroid hormone receptors are intracellular [nuclear receptors], not on the membrane surface; membrane steroid receptors [mPR] exist but cholesterol is not their ligand)
explanation: Membrane lipid composition and properties: Phospholipid bilayer: amphipathic phospholipids spontaneously form bilayers (hydrophobic effect + electrostatic stabilization); dynamic structure → 'fluid mosaic model' (Singer & Nicolson, 1972). Asymmetry: PS + PE predominant in inner (cytoplasmic) leaflet; PC + SM (sphingomyelin) + glycolipids predominant in outer leaflet; maintained by: flippases (ATP8A1/2: PS to inner), floppases (ABCB4: PC to outer), scramblases (TMEM16F: bidirectional, Ca2+-activated → scrambles during apoptosis → PS flipped to outer leaflet → 'eat-me signal' for macrophages). Lipid rafts: detergent-resistant membrane (DRM) microdomains; enriched in cholesterol + SM + GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59, GFRα, CEA); raft-associated signaling proteins: Lyn (Src kinase), LAT (linker for T cell activation), Lck, eNOS; rafts may concentrate signaling components → amplify signals. Membrane fluidity regulation: FA unsaturation: ↑double bonds (kinks → less packing → ↑fluidity); FA chain length: shorter → ↑fluidity; cholesterol: maintains intermediate fluidity (as described). Bacterial membranes: no cholesterol; maintain fluidity by adjusting FA unsaturation (↑cold → ↑unsaturation); some bacteria (Mycoplasma) scavenge host cholesterol as they lack a cell wall. DHA (22:6ω3): highly unsaturated → very fluid bilayers; most concentrated in photoreceptor outer segments + brain synaptic membranes + sperm flagella → functions requiring high membrane fluidity; also modulates immune cells (↓NFκB signaling, ↓NLRP3 inflammasome activation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM) requires which vitamin as its cofactor?
options: Folate (B9) — required for methionine synthase and thymidylate synthesis; not for MCM
Biotin (B7) — required for carboxylases (PC, ACC, PCC, MCC); PCC makes methylmalonyl-CoA but MCM acts on it downstream; MCM itself does not require biotin

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin), specifically the adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) form: MCM (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) is a mitochondrial enzyme; catalyzes: L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA; this reaction requires adenosylcobalamin (5'-deoxyadenosylcobalamin, AdoCbl) as a cofactor; mechanism: AdoCbl provides a 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical → radical-based 1,2-shift rearrangement of the methylmalonyl-CoA substrate → succinyl-CoA; this is an intramolecular carbon-skeleton rearrangement (CoA + carboxyl groups switch positions); MCM deficiency (MMUT gene mutations) → methylmalonic acidemia (MMA) — some forms respond to B12 supplementation (B12-responsive MMA: MMAB [AdoCbl synthesis] or MMACHC [cblC; processing of B12 before both AdoCbl + MeCbl synthesis] defects → ↑serum B12 doesn't help if AdoCbl synthesis is blocked; MMUT mutations usually B12-non-responsive)
Riboflavin (B2) — cofactor for FAD-linked oxidases/dehydrogenases (ETC Complex I, II; FADH2 generation); not for MCM
explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) cofactor forms: Methylcobalamin (MeCbl): cofactor for methionine synthase (cytoplasm): Hcy + 5-methylTHF → Met + THF; MeCbl deficiency → ↑Hcy + megaloblastic anemia + methyl-trap (functional folate deficiency). Adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl): cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (mitochondria): L-MMA-CoA → succinyl-CoA; AdoCbl deficiency → ↑MMA (methylmalonic acid) in blood/urine. Clinical: B12 deficiency elevates BOTH Hcy + MMA (both enzyme pathways impaired); isolated folate deficiency: ↑Hcy but NOT ↑MMA (MCM is B12-dependent, not folate). B12 cobalamin processing: dietary B12 → parietal cell IF (intrinsic factor) → IF-B12 complex → ileal cubilin-amnionless → absorbed → haptocorrin (transcobalamin I, ~80% of serum B12, biologically inactive, storage); transcobalamin II (TC-II, holotranscobalamin = ~20% but biologically active form) → binds TC-II receptor → endocytosis → lysosomal processing: MMACHC (cblC gene) processes incoming cobalamin → 'cob(II)alamin' → two pathways: MMAB (cblB) + ATR (cblA) → AdoCbl (mitochondria); MTRR (cblE) + MTR (cblG) → MeCbl (cytoplasm). Common mutations: MMACHC/cblC: most common late-onset form; causes combined MeCbl + AdoCbl deficiency → homocystinuria + MMA + megaloblastic anemia + visual loss. MMUT: most common non-B12-responsive form (enzyme itself mutated).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The glucuronic acid (glucuronidation) pathway is important for drug metabolism. The main enzyme responsible for drug glucuronidation in the liver is:
options: CYP3A4 (cytochrome P450 3A4): Phase I enzyme (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis); most abundant hepatic CYP; metabolizes ~50% of all drugs; not a glucuronidase — glucuronidation is Phase II
N-acetyltransferase (NAT1/NAT2): Phase II enzyme for acetylation (isoniazid, hydralazine, procainamide, dapsone); not glucuronidation
Glutathione S-transferase (GST): Phase II enzyme for glutathione conjugation to electrophilic substrates (detoxification); not glucuronidation

UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT, specifically UGT1A1 + UGT1A3-9 + UGT2B family): UGT enzymes are membrane-bound enzymes in the ER of hepatocytes (and intestine, kidney, lung); reaction: drug (or metabolite/endogenous substrate) + UDP-glucuronate → glucuronide conjugate + UDP; glucuronate added to nucleophilic groups: -OH, -COOH, -NH2, -SH; product (glucuronide): more polar, water-soluble → excreted in urine or bile; clinical examples: morphine-6-glucuronide (active, more potent analgesic than morphine itself — clinical importance in CKD where it accumulates); morphine-3-glucuronide (inactive, may cause neuroexcitatory effects); bilirubin-glucuronide (UGT1A1 → bilirubin diglucuronide, critical for bile excretion); lamotrigine, lorazepam, propofol, irinotecan (SN-38 glucuronidation by UGT1A1 — important in irinotecan toxicity: UGT1A1*28 [7 TA repeats] reduces UGT1A1 activity → ↑SN-38 → ↑diarrhea + neutropenia with irinotecan — same variant as Gilbert's syndrome)
explanation: Phase I vs Phase II drug metabolism: Phase I (functionalization): introduce or unmask a reactive group (-OH, -COOH, -NH2, -SH); CYP450 family (mainly CYP3A4, 2D6, 2C9, 2C19, 1A2, 2E1, 2B6): oxidation (hydroxylation, epoxidation, N-/O-/S-dealkylation, N-oxidation, sulfoxidation); FMO (flavin-containing monooxygenase, S/N-oxidation); MAO (monoamine oxidase, oxidative deamination of catecholamines, serotonin, tyramine); esterases, hydrolases, reductases; Phase I may activate prodrugs (codeine → morphine via CYP2D6; irinotecan → SN-38 via carboxylesterase) or create reactive intermediates. Phase II (conjugation): adds polar group to Phase I product (or directly to parent drug); makes water-soluble conjugates for excretion; UGT (glucuronidation): most common Phase II; N-acetyltransferase (acetylation: NAT2 polymorphism → slow/fast acetylators; isoniazid: slow acetylators → ↑isoniazid levels → ↑toxicity [neuropathy, hepatotoxicity]; fast acetylators → ↓isoniazid exposure → more treatment failures); sulfotransferase (SULT: adds sulfate; important for estrogen + DHEA inactivation); glutathione S-transferase (GST: adds GSH to reactive electrophiles → mercapturic acid eventually); methyltransferases (COMT: catecholamine inactivation; TPMT: thiopurine methylation). Drug-drug interactions via CYP inhibition/induction: Inducers (↑CYP → ↓drug levels): rifampicin (CYP3A4, CYP2C9 → ↓warfarin, ↓OCP → contraceptive failure), phenytoin, carbamazepine, St. John's Wort, phenobarbital. Inhibitors (↓CYP → ↑drug levels): erythromycin, fluconazole (CYP3A4 + CYP2C9 → ↑warfarin → bleeding risk), ketoconazole (strongest CYP3A4 inhibitor), ciprofloxacin (CYP1A2 → ↑theophylline), grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 [intestinal] → ↑many drugs: statins, cyclosporine, felodipine).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Collagen contains hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine residues. The enzyme responsible for hydroxylation of proline residues in collagen is:
options: Lysyl oxidase (LOX): oxidizes specific Lys + HydroxyLys residues in collagen + elastin → aldehyde derivatives → covalent cross-links (allysine); requires copper; inhibited by BAPN (β-aminopropionitrile, lathyrogen from sweet peas → lathyrism, osteogenesis imperfecta-like syndrome); NOT responsible for hydroxylation of proline residues
Prolyl isomerase (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase, PPIase): changes Pro cis-trans conformation; assists in protein folding (cyclophilins + FK506-binding proteins [FKBPs]); NOT hydroxylation

Prolyl 4-hydroxylase (P4H, P4HA1/2/3 + P4HB subunits): P4H is the main enzyme that hydroxylates proline residues in collagen at the 4-position (Pro → 4-hydroxyproline, Hyp); located in the ER lumen (where collagen pro-peptide chains are modified during folding); requires: Fe2+ (ferrous iron, in active site), O2, ascorbate (vitamin C, reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+ → keeps enzyme active), α-ketoglutarate (co-substrate → oxidized to succinate + CO2 per Pro hydroxylated); hydroxyproline forms H-bonds between collagen chains → stabilizes triple helix → essential for collagen structural integrity; scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) → ↓P4H activity (Fe3+ not reduced → ↓Hyp) → unstable collagen → perivascular bleeding (↓collagen in vessel walls), poor wound healing, loose teeth (↓periodontal ligament collagen), hemarthroses, petechiae, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, poor dentition
Prolyl 3-hydroxylase (P3H, LEPRE1/P3H1): hydroxylates Pro at 3-position → 3-hydroxyproline (less abundant than 4-Hyp); P3H1 mutations → OI type VIII
explanation: Collagen synthesis and modifications: Step 1: Genes transcribed → pre-pro-α chains (with signal peptide) → ER; signal peptide cleaved → pro-α chains. Step 2: ER modifications: (1) Prolyl 4-hydroxylase (P4HA): Pro → 4-Hyp (requires Fe2+, O2, Vit C, α-KG); (2) Prolyl 3-hydroxylase: Pro → 3-Hyp; (3) Lysyl hydroxylase (LH1/2/3, PLOD1/2/3): Lys → hydroxylysine (Hyl) [requires Fe2+, O2, Vit C, α-KG; LH2 specifically hydroxylates Lys in triple-helical domain → galactosyl-Hyl cross-links in fibrillar collagen]; (4) O-glycosylation of Hyl: Gal-Glc-Hyl (glycosylated hydroxylysines help direct collagen fibril assembly); (5) Chaperone-assisted folding (HSP47, prolyl isomerases). Step 3: Triple helix formation: three pro-α chains assemble C-terminus → N-terminus (zipper-like); propeptides (PICP + PINP, C- and N-terminal propeptides, used as biomarkers) still attached → procollagen (soluble). Step 4: Secretion: procollagen → Golgi → secretory vesicles → extracellular space. Step 5: Extracellular processing: (1) Procollagen N-protease (BMP1/tolloid) → cleaves N-propeptide; (2) C-protease → cleaves C-propeptide; → tropocollagen (insoluble, self-assembles). Step 6: Cross-linking: lysyl oxidase (LOX, requires Cu2+ + O2): oxidizes ε-amino group of Lys/HyLys → allysine (aldehyde) → spontaneous condensation + Schiff base → covalent cross-links between collagen monomers → mature fibrils. Types I collagen: most abundant (bone, tendon, skin, cornea, blood vessels): α1(I)2α2(I) trimer; OI (osteogenesis imperfecta, COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ketoacidosis occurs in type 1 diabetes. The metabolic change that drives ketone body overproduction is best described as:
options: ↑Glucose utilization leading to excess pyruvate → ↑ketones (WRONG — in T1D, glucose is not utilized; ↓glucose uptake → ↑ketones)

↑Fatty acid synthesis in liver leading to ↑FA available for ketogenesis (WRONG — insulin absence → ↓FA synthesis [↓ACC], ↑FA oxidation; the fatty acids come from adipose lipolysis, not hepatic synthesis)

Absolute insulin deficiency → ↑glucagon/↑HSL/↑ATGL → ↑lipolysis → ↑NEFA → ↑hepatic β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑ketogenesis; combined with ↑glucagon → ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT-I: in type 1 diabetes (T1DM) → absolute insulin deficiency → ↑glucagon (unopposed) → activates hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) + ATGL in adipose tissue (via ↑cAMP → ↑PKA → phospho-HSL Ser563 + ATGL-CGI-58 interaction) → ↑lipolysis → ↑NEFA (non-esterified FA) release into plasma → ↑hepatic uptake → ↑β-oxidation [acyl-CoA → acetyl-CoA]; simultaneously: ↑glucagon → ↑PKA → phospho-ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I inhibition → ↑FA import into mitochondria → ↑β-oxidation; ↑acetyl-CoA + ↓OAA (glucagon → ↑gluconeogenesis → OAA depleted) → acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA pathway → ↑ketogenesis (HMGCS2 is rate-limiting, induced by PPARα + FGF21 during fasting/T1DM); also: ↑glucagon → ↓hepatic malonyl-CoA directly (↑FBPase-2/PFK-2 → ↓F-2,6-BP) [not the primary mechanism but contributes]

↑Protein catabolism providing amino acids as ketogenic substrates (while amino acids contribute to ketogenesis, the primary driver in DKA is FA oxidation from adipose lipolysis, not protein breakdown)
explanation: DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis) biochemistry: Three major metabolic effects of insulin deficiency + glucagon excess: (1) ↑Hepatic gluconeogenesis (PEPCK, G6Pase upregulated + substrates: AA from muscle, glycerol from lipolysis, lactate) → ↑blood glucose. (2) ↓Peripheral glucose uptake (↓GLUT4 translocation, ↓glycogen synthesis) → ↑blood glucose. (3) ↑Ketogenesis (as above) → ↑ketone bodies → anion gap metabolic acidosis. Biochemical hallmarks: ↑glucose (usually >250 mg/dL), ↑ketones (↑β-OHB + acetoacetate, ratio typically 3:1, but in severe DKA can be 10:1 or more → acetoacetate dipstick may underestimate ketosis; measure β-OHB for accuracy), ↑anion gap ([Na+] - [Cl-] - [HCO3-]; normal 8-12; in DKA usually >20 due to ketoacid accumulation), ↓pH, ↓HCO3-, ↑osmolality. K+ in DKA: total body K+ depleted (urinary K+ loss from glucosuria-induced osmotic diuresis + vomiting) but serum K+ normal or HIGH due to: H+/K+ exchange (↑H+ extracellular → enters cells in exchange for K+), insulin deficiency (no insulin → ↓Na+/K+-ATPase → ↓K+ uptake), hyperosmolality → cellular dehydration → K+ efflux. Treatment: IV fluid (NS first 1-2L → 0.45% NaCl → 5%D in 0.45% NS when glucose <200) + insulin (0.1 units/kg/h IV) + K+ replacement (start once K+<5.3 + urine output established; if K+<3.5 → give K+ BEFORE insulin to prevent life-threatening hypokalemia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme produces acetylcholine from acetyl-CoA and choline?
options: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE): BREAKS DOWN ACh → choline + acetate (not the synthesis enzyme)

Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT): ChAT (encoded by CHAT gene, chromosome 10q11.2) synthesizes ACh: acetyl-CoA + choline → ACh + CoA; the reaction occurs in the cytoplasm of cholinergic neurons; acetyl-CoA comes from mitochondria (primarily from pyruvate via PDC or from citrate via ATP-citrate lyase/ACLY in axon terminals); choline is taken up by the high-affinity choline transporter-1 (CHT1, SLC5A7) from the synaptic cleft or extracellular space → the choline for ACh synthesis is recycled from ACh hydrolysis by AChE (recycling loop); ChAT is synthesized in the cell body → transported down the axon to the nerve terminal; rate-limiting factor: choline availability (because ChAT Km for choline ~1 mM is higher than typical cytoplasmic choline concentration → choline uptake by CHT1 limits ACh synthesis); ACh storage: VAChT (vesicular ACh transporter, SLC18A3) loads ACh into synaptic vesicles using H+ gradient (V-ATPase → ↑H+ in vesicle → VAChT: H+/ACh antiport)
Choline kinase (CK-α/β): phosphorylates choline → phosphocholine (first step of CDP-choline pathway for phosphatidylcholine synthesis; not ACh synthesis)
Acetate kinase: bacterial enzyme (converts acetate + ATP → acetyl-phosphate + ADP); not present in neurons; not the ACh-synthesizing enzyme
explanation: Cholinergic neurotransmission: Distribution of ChAT-positive (cholinergic) neurons: CNS: basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei (NBM [nucleus basalis of Meynert] → cortex; medial septum → hippocampus; Ch1-Ch4 groups); brainstem (pedunculopontine + laterodorsal tegmental nuclei → thalamus + basal ganglia); striatal interneurons. PNS: all preganglionic ANS neurons (sympathetic + parasympathetic); all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons; neuromuscular junction (somatic motor neurons); enteric nervous system (most cholinergic). Alzheimer's disease: selective degeneration of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (particularly NBM + diagonal band of Broca) → ↓ACh in cerebral cortex → ↑central AChE → cognitive impairment; treatment: AChE inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine → ↑ACh at synapse → symptomatic improvement); amyloid hypothesis: Aβ deposition → neuroinflammation → tau hyperphosphorylation → NFTs → neurodegeneration. Drugs affecting cholinergic synthesis: hemicholinium-3 (HC-3): blocks CHT1 → ↓choline uptake → ↓ACh synthesis → experimental neurotoxin. Botulinum toxin (BoNT, multiple serotypes A-G): A-zinc metalloprotease cleaves SNAP-25 (synaptosomal associated protein 25 kDa) → blocks ACh vesicle fusion → ↓ACh release → flaccid paralysis + autonomic dysfunction (A, C) → SNARE cleavage. Tetanus toxin (TeNT): retrograde transport to spinal cord → cleaves synaptobrevin/VAMP → ↓GABA/Gly release from inhibitory interneurons → spastic paralysis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Proton pumps in the electron transport chain pump protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space. The resulting electrochemical gradient drives ATP synthesis. The protein directly synthesizing ATP from ADP and Pi is:
options: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV): transfers electrons to O2 → H2O; pumps protons but does not synthesize ATP
Cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III): transfers electrons from CoQH2 to cytochrome c; pumps protons; not ATP synthase
NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I): transfers electrons from NADH to CoQ; pumps protons; not ATP synthase

ATP synthase (Complex V, F1Fo-ATP synthase): the machine that uses the proton electrochemical gradient (ΔΨ + ΔpH) to synthesize ATP from ADP + Pi; structure: Fo (membrane-embedded, subunits a/b/c): proton channel; c-ring (10-15 c subunits in mammals): rotary motor driven by H+ flow down gradient; stator: a + b2 subunits; F1 (matrix-projecting, α3β3γδε): catalytic site; γ subunit rotates with c-ring (connects Fo to F1) → rotary mechanism: γ rotation causes conformational changes in alternating β subunits (Boyer's binding change mechanism: 3 states of β: O [open, low affinity for ADP+Pi], L [loose, ADP+Pi bind], T [tight, ATP formed] rotate with each 120° turn of γ; ATP synthesis is essentially free energy goes into conformational change, not into direct Pi-ADP chemistry → ATP released spontaneously from T site when O-L-T cycle drives next turn); P/O ratio: 2.5 ATP per NADH → Complex I (4H+), III (4H+), IV (2H+ per 2e-) pump total 10H+; ATP synthase requires ~2.7H+ per ATP (10 c-subunits, each H+ rotates c-ring 36°, 3 ATP per full rotation [360°] → 10H+/3 ATP ≈ 3.3H+/ATP but accounting for H+ used for Pi transport → ~2.5 ATP per NADH)
explanation: Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory (Nobel 1978): proton gradient (ΔμH+ = ΔΨ + ΔpH × 2.3RT/F) provides the driving force; ΔΨ (membrane potential, ~−180 mV, negative inside matrix) contributes ~2/3; ΔpH (~0.5 units, acidic IMS) contributes ~1/3 of the proton motive force. ATP synthase inhibitors: oligomycin: blocks F0 proton channel → no rotation → ↓ATP synthesis; ↑ΔΨ (proton gradient builds up since ATP synthase cannot discharge it). Uncouplers: DNP (dinitrophenol), FCCP, CCCP: lipophilic weak acids that carry H+ across IMM directly → collapse ΔΨ → no ATP made despite O2 consumption → energy released as heat; UCP1 (thermogenin) in BAT: physiological uncoupler → nonshivering thermogenesis; uncouplers increase O2 consumption but not ATP production → weight loss (some misuse DNP for this → dangerous hyperthermia + metabolic acidosis + death). P/O ratio: NADH → 2.5 ATP; FADH2 → 1.5 ATP; the '10H+ per NADH' model: CI pumps 4H+, CIII pumps 4H+ (per 2e- via Q-cycle: 4H+ consumed from matrix, 4H+ released to IMS = net 4H+ per 2e-), CIV pumps 2H+; F-ATP synthase: c10-ring (bovine mitochondria) requires 3.3H+/ATP (10/3 per rotation making 3 ATP); ~1H+ used for Pi transporter (PiC) and ADP/ATP exchanger (ANT) → total ~4H+ per ATP from ETC gradient → 10H+/(4H+/ATP) = 2.5 ATP/NADH. Rotary motor: verified by direct observation of F1 rotating with fluorescent bead (Noji et al., 1997); Boyer mechanism confirmed (ΔG° synthesis = 7.3 kJ/mol on F1, essentially ΔG° ≈ 0, actual synthesis driven by proton flow through F0 → mechanical energy → releases ATP).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (α-KGDH) complex deficiency, which intermediate of the TCA cycle would accumulate?
options: Succinate (downstream of the block; ↓not ↑succinate with α-KGDH deficiency)

Alpha-ketoglutarate (α-KG, 2-oxoglutarate): α-KGDH complex (also called 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, OGDH complex) catalyzes step 4 of TCA: α-KG + CoA + NAD+ → succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH; deficiency → α-KG CANNOT be converted to succinyl-CoA → α-KG accumulates (+ glutamate, which is in rapid equilibrium via GDH); α-KGDH complex is structurally and mechanistically analogous to PDC: E1 (OGDH, oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, TPP cofactor), E2 (DLST, dihydrolipoamide succinyltransferase, lipoic acid + CoA cofactor), E3 (DLD, shared E3 with PDC, α-KGDC, BCKDC — shared lipoamide dehydrogenase; FAD + NAD+ cofactors); same 5 cofactors as PDC: TPP, lipoic acid, CoA-SH, FAD, NAD+; isolated α-KGDH deficiency: OGDH or DLST mutations → Leigh syndrome/encephalopathy + lactic acidosis + ↑urinary α-KG; DLD (E3) deficiency: affects all three complexes (PDC + α-KGDC + BCKDC) simultaneously → combined defect: ↑pyruvate + ↑lactate + ↑α-KG + ↑branched-chain amino acids → severe metabolic encephalopathy; α-KG accumulation also seen in: IDH1/2 mutations (↑α-KG production paradoxically — mutant IDH makes 2-HG FROM α-KG)
Oxaloacetate (OAA): the starting point of TCA; would be regenerated from the cycle, not specifically accumulated at α-KGDH block
explanation: TCA cycle enzyme deficiencies and their metabolite accumulations: PDC deficiency: ↑pyruvate + ↑lactate + ↑alanine; → Leigh syndrome + lactic acidosis. α-KGDH deficiency: ↑α-KG in blood/urine (urinary α-KG also ↑in α-KG aciduria and transient hyperammonemia); → Leigh syndrome-like. DLD (E3) deficiency: ↑pyruvate + ↑α-KG + ↑BCKAs → combined features of PDC + α-KGDH + BCKDC deficiencies. Fumarase (FH) deficiency: ↑fumarate → encephalopathy + brain malformations; FH also acts as tumor suppressor (see oncometabolite section: fumarate → inhibits PHD2/TET → ↑HIF-1α). SDH (Complex II) subunit deficiencies: SDHA/B/C/D; ↑succinate → oncometabolite (inhibits dioxygenases); → paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma. IDH3 deficiency: ↑isocitrate (not a clinical syndrome per se). Citrate synthase: extremely rare; ↑OAA+AcCoA theoretically. Aconitase deficiency: ↑citrate; ferritin mRNA (5' IRE) sensitive to IRP1 (= aconitase without Fe-S); acute porphyrias: succinyl-CoA → δ-ALA (ALA synthase) → porphyrin pathway — relevant as succinyl-CoA is the starting point for heme synthesis; α-KGDH treatment: no specific treatment; supportive; thiamine supplementation (provides TPP cofactor) may partially improve some cases.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A drug that irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) for the entire platelet lifetime is:
options: Ibuprofen (reversible non-selective COX inhibitor; platelet COX recovers when drug level falls; no permanent anti-platelet effect)
Celecoxib (selective COX-2 inhibitor; COX-1 preserved; no significant anti-platelet effect)

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid): aspirin is the classic irreversible COX inhibitor; mechanism: aspirin is hydrolyzed to salicylate + acetate → the acetate group irreversibly acetylates a serine residue (Ser530 in COX-1, Ser516 in COX-2) at the cyclooxygenase active site → sterically blocks arachidonic acid access → irreversible loss of COX activity; platelets: anucleate → cannot synthesize new COX proteins → COX-1 inhibition is permanent for platelet lifetime (~10 days/8-10 days); after 7-10 days: new platelets (from megakaryocytes, which have COX) replace the old ones → COX activity recovers; anti-platelet effect: ↓TXA2 (thromboxane A2 from platelet COX-1 → vasoconstriction + ↑platelet aggregation) → net anti-platelet effect; COX-2 in endothelial cells recovers more rapidly (nucleated cells → new COX-2 synthesized → ↑PGI2 [prostacyclin] → anti-thrombotic), so net effect is anti-thrombotic; low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg) sufficient to irreversibly inhibit platelet COX-1 (once-daily dosing sufficient due to irreversibility); higher doses needed for anti-inflammatory effects (COX-2 also needs to be inhibited); pharmacogenomics: aspirin 'resistance' (partial pharmacodynamic resistance in some patients — possibly due to COX-2 upregulation producing TXA2 in platelets of some individuals, or insufficient dose)
Indomethacin (more potent reversible/tight-binding COX inhibitor than most NSAIDs, but still reversible; used for gout + PDA closure [inhibits ductal PGE2])
explanation: Aspirin pharmacology and clinical uses: Antiplatelet: 75-100 mg/day → irreversible COX-1 in platelets → ↓TXA2 → ↓platelet activation; cardiovascular prevention: secondary prevention (strong evidence: ACS, post-MI, post-stroke, post-PCI) + primary prevention (limited benefit vs. bleeding risk in most; ASA 81 mg considered in certain high-risk patients). Anti-inflammatory/analgesic/antipyretic: higher doses (325-650 mg TID/QID) → inhibits COX-1 + COX-2 → ↓PGE2 + PGI2 → ↓fever (PGE2 in hypothalamic thermoregulation), ↓pain (PGE2 sensitizes nociceptors), ↓inflammation. Adverse effects: GI toxicity (↓mucosal PGE2 + PGI2 → ↓mucus/bicarb + ↓mucosal blood flow → ↑peptic ulcer risk; minimize with PPI cotherapy or enteric coating); bleeding (platelet inhibition + GI mucosal damage); Reye syndrome (aspirin + viral illness in children → mitochondrial dysfunction + acute hepatic failure + encephalopathy → avoid aspirin <18 years with viral illness; mechanism involves mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation impairment); salicylate toxicity: low dose → metabolic alkalosis (↑renal HCO3- excretion) followed by respiratory alkalosis (direct CNS stimulation of respiratory center → ↑ventilation); high dose → uncouples OXPHOS → metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis + tinnitus + encephalopathy (aspirin triad: N/V + tinnitus + dyspnea); management: NaHCO3 IV (alkalinize urine → trap ionized salicylate → ↑renal excretion); hemodialysis if severe.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulation by fingolimod (FTY720) is used to treat multiple sclerosis. The biochemical mechanism involves:
options: Fingolimod directly blocks TNF-α signaling in the brain
Fingolimod inhibits the sphingolipid synthesis enzyme serine palmitoyltransferase

Fingolimod is phosphorylated by sphingosine kinase-2 (SphK2) to form fingolimod-phosphate (FTY720-P), which acts as a functional antagonist at S1P1 receptors on lymphocytes: fingolimod (FTY720, Gilenya) is a sphingosine analog (structurally similar to sphingosine): administered as a prodrug → phosphorylated by SphK2 (predominantly) in the body → FTY720-phosphate (active form); FTY720-P binds S1P1 (S1PR1) + S1P3 + S1P4 + S1P5 receptors (all except S1P2); on naive T and B lymphocytes: S1P1 normally acts as a 'GPS signal' directing lymphocytes to egress from lymph nodes + thymus into blood (S1P is high in blood/lymph, low in lymphoid organs → S1P1 signaling directs lymphocyte migration OUT); FTY720-P binds S1P1 → agonist binding → receptor internalization (downregulation) → functional S1P1 LOSS from cell surface → lymphocytes cannot respond to S1P gradient → TRAPPED in lymph nodes + thymus → ↓circulating lymphocytes (lymphopenia, ≥70% ↓) → ↓inflammatory lymphocyte trafficking into CNS → ↓MS relapses; paradoxically: FTY720-P is a FUNCTIONAL ANTAGONIST (agonist → internalization → net loss of signaling) rather than a classic competitive antagonist
Fingolimod inhibits myelin basic protein degradation by lysosomal cathepsin D
explanation: S1P biology and pharmacology: S1P (sphingosine-1-phosphate): bioactive lipid mediator; synthesized: sphingosine + ATP → [SphK1 (cytoplasm, exports S1P via SPNS2) + SphK2 (nucleus/mitochondria)] → S1P; degraded: S1P phosphatase (SGPP1/2, in ER → recycled to sphingosine) or S1P lyase (SGPL1 → irreversibly cleaved → ethanolamine-1-phosphate + hexadecanal). S1P in blood: mainly produced by RBCs (very high SphK1 activity) and endothelium; ~1 µM in plasma (high); very low in lymphoid tissues (→ gradient drives lymphocyte egress). S1P receptors (S1PR1-5): S1P1 (Gi-coupled): lymphocyte egress, endothelial function, cardiac chronotropy. S1P2 (G12/13-coupled): inverse: promotes lymphocyte retention (opposes S1P1). S1P3 (Gi + Gq): cardiac: bradycardia (fingolimod causes transient bradycardia after first dose due to S1P3 on heart); vascular: vasodilation. S1P4 (Gi): lung, lymphoid tissue. S1P5 (Gi): NK cell egress, brain. MS treatment with fingolimod: first-line for highly active relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS); oral (once daily); reduces annual relapse rate by ~54% vs placebo; side effects: transient bradycardia (first dose monitoring required for 6h; S1P3 on SA node), macular edema (S1P3 on retinal vasculature), herpes reactivation (PML from JC virus if immunocompromised), hypertension, liver enzyme elevation, teratogenic. Newer S1P modulators: siponimod (S1P1+5, fewer off-target effects, approved for secondary progressive MS), ozanimod, ponesimod.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step of cholesterol catabolism to bile acids is:
options: CYP7B1 (oxysterol 7α-hydroxylase): alternative bile acid pathway enzyme; acts on oxysterols (25-hydroxycholesterol, 27-hydroxycholesterol); NOT the rate-limiting step of classic pathway

CYP27A1 (sterol 27-hydroxylase): mitochondrial, involved in both pathways; produces 27-hydroxycholesterol → bile acid precursors via the alternative pathway; deficiency → cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX): accumulation of cholestanol + cholesterol in tendons + brain → tendon xanthomas + cerebellar ataxia + premature atherosclerosis

CYP7A1 (cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase): the rate-limiting enzyme of the CLASSIC (neutral) bile acid synthesis pathway; located in hepatocyte smooth ER; catalyzes: cholesterol + O2 + NADPH → 7α-hydroxycholesterol; this is the COMMITTED, RATE-LIMITING step; regulation: feedback inhibition by bile acids returning via enterohepatic circulation (FXR [farnesoid X receptor] activation → SHP [small heterodimer partner] → ↓CYP7A1 transcription); induced by: cholesterol, LXR (liver X receptor, activated by oxysterols → ↑CYP7A1); primary bile acids produced: cholic acid (from cholesterol via 7α-hydroxylation pathway) + chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA); then conjugated with glycine or taurine in hepatocytes → bile salts (more water-soluble); gut bacteria → secondary bile acids (deoxycholate from CA, lithocholate from CDCA)
ABCB4 (MDR3): phospholipid flippase in bile canalicular membrane; exports PC into bile to dilute bile salts → prevents bile salt toxicity; not a bile acid synthesis enzyme
explanation: Bile acid synthesis and enterohepatic circulation: Classic (neutral) pathway (≥75% in normal adults): CYP7A1 (rate-limiting) → 7α-hydroxycholesterol → [multiple CYP steps] → 7α-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one (C4, used as bile acid synthesis marker) → cholic acid (CA) or chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA); CYP8B1 (sterol 12α-hydroxylase, adds 12α-OH → cholic acid; controls CA:CDCA ratio). Alternative (acidic) pathway: CYP27A1 → 27-OH-Chol → CYP7B1 → 3β-hydroxy-5-choleste-en-27-oic acid → bile acids; produces mainly CDCA; important in fetus + early neonatal period. Conjugation: BA + CoA → [BACS] → BA-CoA; BA-CoA + glycine/taurine → [BAAT] → glyco- or tauro-conjugated BA; pKa of unconjugated BA ~6, glyco-conj ~4, tauro-conj ~2 → tauro-BA more soluble/ionized in gut. Enterohepatic circulation: bile → ileum (ASBT/SLC10A2 apically absorbs bile acids) → portal blood → liver (OATP1B1/B3 [SLC21A] import BA from portal blood); ~95% of bile acids recirculated per meal; ~5% lost in stool → feces = primary route of cholesterol excretion. Bile acid therapy: UDCA (ursodeoxycholic acid, 3α,7β-diol, tertiary BA from gut microbiota): hydrophilic, cytoprotective → used in primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) + primary sclerosing cholangitis + intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; obeticholic acid (OCA, semi-synthetic CDCA analog, potent FXR agonist) → used in PBC + NASH. Bile acid sequestrants: cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam: bind BA in gut → ↑BA excretion → ↑CYP7A1 (feedback relieved) → ↑cholesterol → bile acids → ↓serum cholesterol; also ↑TG (in some patients, as ↑VLDL secretion). Zollinger-Ellison: impaired BA function from low pH in duodenum → malabsorption.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Farber lipogranulomatosis (Farber disease) is caused by deficiency of which enzyme?
