options: Acid ceramidase (ASAH1): Farber disease (Farber lipogranulomatosis, Farber disease) is an ultra-rare AR lysosomal storage disease caused by mutations in the ASAH1 gene (chromosome 8p22) encoding acid ceramidase (N-acylsphingosine deamidase, AC); acid ceramidase is a lysosomal enzyme that degrades ceramide → sphingosine + fatty acid; ASAH1 deficiency → ceramide accumulates in lysosomes throughout the body (especially macrophages) → granulomatous inflammation → classic triad: (1) painful swollen joints (arthropathy, especially peri-articular); (2) subcutaneous nodules (lipogranulomas, especially over pressure points: interphalangeal joints, wrists, Achilles tendon area); (3) hoarse cry (laryngeal granulomas); additional: hepatosplenomegaly, CNS involvement (in classic severe forms → psychomotor regression); diagnosis: ↓acid ceramidase activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts; urine ceramide + ceramide analogs elevated; treatment: hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) for non-neurological manifestations; cerliponase alfa (enzyme replacement) under investigation; distinct from: Niemann-Pick (sphingomyelinase), Gaucher (glucocerebrosidase), Krabbe (galactocerebrosidase), MLD (arylsulfatase A)
Glucocerebrosidase (deficient in Gaucher disease, GBA1 gene)
Galactocerebrosidase (deficient in Krabbe disease, GALC gene)
Sphingomyelinase (deficient in Niemann-Pick A/B, SMPD1 gene)
explanation: Sphingolipid catabolism pathway: sphingomyelin → [sphingomyelinase] → ceramide → [acid ceramidase] → sphingosine + FA. Ceramide is the hub: generated from SM (sphingomyelinase), GSLs (after carbohydrate head group removal), and de novo synthesis; ceramide → sphingosine → S1P (sphingosine + SphK1/2); ceramide → [ceramide kinase] → ceramide-1-phosphate; ceramide is pro-apoptotic (activates PP2A, BAX translocation), S1P is anti-apoptotic and pro-survival — the ceramide/S1P 'rheostat' of cell fate; ASAH1 mutations also cause: spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME, a distinct allelic disorder; milder ASAH1 mutations that retain some acid ceramidase activity → SMA-like anterior horn + epilepsy without granulomas). Lysosomal sphingolipid storage diseases with their enzyme/gene: Fabry: α-galactosidase A (GLA gene) → Gb3/globotriaosylceramide accumulation. Krabbe: GALC → psychosine + GalCer. Gaucher: GBA1 → glucocerebroside. Niemann-Pick A/B: SMPD1 → sphingomyelin. MLD: ARSA → sulfatide. GM1 gangliosidosis: GLB1 (β-galactosidase). GM2 (Tay-Sachs): HEXA. GM2 (Sandhoff): HEXB. Farber: ASAH1 → ceramide.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In de novo purine synthesis, the carbon atoms of the purine ring are contributed by which set of molecules?
options: Glutamine, glycine, aspartate, CO2, and N10-formyl-THF: the purine ring is built de novo on PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) in 10 enzymatic steps; the atoms of the purine ring (C4, C5, N7, C8, N9 = imidazole ring; C2, N1, C6, N3 = pyrimidine ring) come from: N1 = aspartate (Asp); C2 = N10-formyl-THF (N10-fTHF, a one-carbon unit from the folate pool); N3 = glutamine (Gln, amide nitrogen); C4, C5, N7 = glycine (the entire glycine molecule incorporates: C4+C5 come from glycine, N7 = glycine's amino group); C6 = CO2 (bicarbonate, from ATP-driven carboxylation step); N9 = glutamine (amide nitrogen, in the very first step where PRPP → PRA [5-phosphoribosylamine]; amide nitrogen of Gln is transferred → N9 of purine; this step is catalyzed by PPAT [PRPP amidotransferase] and is inhibited by AMP + GMP [feedback]); C8 = N10-formyl-THF (a second one-carbon unit, different folate for C2 vs C8); summary: Gln contributes N3 + N9; Gly contributes C4+C5+N7; Asp contributes N1; CO2 contributes C6; 2× N10-formyl-THF contributes C2 + C8; these are all the non-hydrogen atoms of purine ring
Glutamine, glycine, aspartate, N10-formyl-THF, CO2, and ribose from PRPP (ribose contributes the sugar backbone, not atoms of the purine ring itself)
Glutamine, serine, aspartate, CO2, and N5-methyl-THF
Glycine, alanine, aspartate, folate, and CO2
explanation: De novo purine synthesis (10 steps, all in cytoplasm in mammals): Step 1: PRPP + Gln → PRA (5-phosphoribosylamine) [PPAT, glutamine PRPP amidotransferase; rate-limiting, inhibited by AMP+GMP]; Step 2: PRA + Gly + ATP → GAR (glycinamide ribonucleotide) [GART]; Step 3: GAR + N10-formyl-THF → FGAR (formylglycinamide ribonucleotide) [GART, trifunctional]; Step 4: FGAR + Gln + ATP → FGAM (formylglycinamidine RN) [PFAS]; Step 5: FGAM + ATP → AIR (5-aminoimidazole RN) [PFAS]; Step 6: AIR + CO2 + ATP → CAIR (carboxyaminoimidazole RN) [PAICS]; Step 7: CAIR + Asp + ATP → SAICAR [PAICS]; Step 8: SAICAR → AICAR + fumarate [ADSL, adenylosuccinate lyase, same enzyme also in purine salvage — ADSL deficiency → purinoautism [autism + psychomotor retardation + epilepsy]]; Step 9: AICAR + N10-formyl-THF → FAICAR [ATIC]; Step 10: FAICAR → IMP (inosine monophosphate) + H2O [ATIC, bi-functional AICAR transformylase/IMP cyclohydrolase]; IMP → AMP (via adenylosuccinate synthetase + ADSL; uses GTP) or IMP → XMP → GMP (via IMPDH1/2 using NAD+; then GMPS using Gln); Methotrexate/aminopterin: inhibit DHFR → ↓THF pool → ↓N10-formyl-THF → blocks steps 3 + 9 → ↓purine synthesis (and ↓pyrimidine synthesis via ↓methylene-THF for TYMS). AICA-riboside (AICAR, acadesine): pharmacological AMPK activator (mimics AMP) — used to study AMPK in lab; exogenous AICAR → cell → phosphorylated → ZMP → activates AMPK.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In Menkes disease, what is the primary biochemical defect?
options: Impaired copper export from intestinal cells due to ATP7A mutation: Menkes disease (Menkes kinky hair syndrome) is an X-linked recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene (chromosome Xq21.1), encoding a P-type Cu-ATPase (copper-transporting ATPase alpha, MNK); ATP7A functions: (1) in intestinal enterocytes (and other peripheral cells): exports Cu2+ from cell interior into trans-Golgi network (TGN) for secretion into portal blood; in Menkes, ATP7A is absent/non-functional → Cu2+ absorbed from gut but CANNOT be exported → trapped in enterocytes (intestinal copper retention) → ↓serum copper + ↓ceruloplasmin (despite normal/high intestinal Cu); (2) in non-hepatic cells: provides Cu to secretory cuproenzymes (dopamine β-hydroxylase → NE synthesis; lysyl oxidase → collagen/elastin cross-linking; tyrosinase → melanin; cytochrome c oxidase → mitochondrial respiration; Cu-Zn-SOD → antioxidant defense); result of ATP7A deficiency: ↓activity of all these cuproenzymes → features: kinky (pili torti), brittle, depigmented hair (↓tyrosinase); neurodegeneration (↓dopamine β-hydroxylase → ↓NE; ↓COX); hypotonia; bladder diverticula, arterial aneurysms (↓lysyl oxidase → poor collagen/elastin cross-linking); hypothermia; serum: ↓copper + ↓ceruloplasmin; liver copper: NOT elevated (liver dumps Cu via ATP7B [Wilson gene], different transporter)

Impaired copper export from hepatocytes due to ATP7B mutation (this is Wilson disease: AR, ATP7B deficiency → Cu accumulates in liver + brain + eyes [Kayser-Fleischer rings]; ↑urinary Cu + ↓serum ceruloplasmin [structurally but copper-depleted])
Excess copper absorption from the intestine due to DMT1 overactivity
Impaired synthesis of ceruloplasmin leading to copper toxicity in the liver
explanation: Copper metabolism: Absorption: Cu2+ → brush-border Cu reductase (? or direct Cu+) → CTR1 (SLC31A1, high-affinity Cu importer) in enterocyte apical surface → intracellular chaperones (ATOX1, CCS, COX17) → TGN (ATP7A transports Cu to secretory pathway and efflux to blood) → portal blood → liver. Liver: CTR1 uptake → ATOX1 delivers to ATP7B (hepatocyte TGN Cu pump): normally exports Cu into bile canalicular lumen (biliary excretion = main Cu excretion route); during Cu overload: ATP7B redistributes to canalicular membrane → ↑biliary Cu excretion; also loads ceruloplasmin (Cp) with Cu in TGN → holoCp secreted into blood (contains 6-7 Cu atoms per Cp molecule; Cu-loaded Cp has ferroxidase activity; apoCp [Cu-free] is rapidly degraded → serum Cp low in Wilson disease despite normal transcription). Wilson disease (ATP7B): AR; accumulation in liver (hepatitis → cirrhosis) + brain (lenticular degeneration → extrapyramidal + psychiatric) + eyes (Kayser-Fleischer rings in Descemet's membrane) + kidney (Fanconi) + hemolytic anemia (Coombs-negative, from Cu release); labs: ↓ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL, usually), ↑24h urine Cu (>100 µg/day), ↑liver Cu (biopsy, >250 µg/g dry weight), serum Cu may be paradoxically LOW (if Cp ↓↓, most serum Cu is bound to Cp); treatment: D-penicillamine (chelates Cu → ↑urinary excretion; initial neurological worsening in ~10-50%; also anti-Wilson via Cu excretion + anti-inflammatory via -SH); trientine (alternative chelator); zinc acetate (↑MT [metallothionein] in enterocytes → sequesters Cu → ↓absorption); liver transplant for fulminant hepatic failure.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the de novo synthesis of sphinganine (dihydrosphingosine), the first committed step of sphingolipid synthesis?
options: Serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT, SPTLC1/2/3 + SPTSSA/SPTSSB subunits): SPT catalyzes the condensation of palmitoyl-CoA (C16:0-CoA) + L-serine → 3-ketodihydrosphingosine (3-keto-sphinganine) + CO2 using PLP (pyridoxal phosphate) as cofactor; this is the RATE-LIMITING, COMMITTED step of sphingolipid de novo synthesis; occurs in the ER (cytoplasmic face); 3-ketodihydrosphingosine → [3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase, KDSR, NADPH-dependent] → sphinganine (dihydrosphingosine, d18:0); sphinganine + acyl-CoA → [ceramide synthases 1-6, CerS1-6, each with tissue-specific FA chain length selectivity] → dihydroceramide; dihydroceramide → [dihydroceramide desaturase, DEGS1, inserts 4,5-trans double bond] → ceramide; ceramide is the hub for all complex sphingolipids: SM, glucosylceramide, galactosylceramide, etc.; regulation of SPT: SPT is inhibited by: ORM1/ORM2 proteins (ER sensors); when ceramide/sphingolipids are adequate → ORM1/2 phosphorylated (by TORC2 in yeast) → ORM1/2 bind SPT → inhibit; when ceramide is low → ORM1/2 dephosphorylated → SPT activated; mammalian ORMDL3 (linked to asthma susceptibility) similarly regulates SPT; SSSPTA (SPTSSA/SPTSSB subunits) affect substrate specificity — can shift SPT toward shorter-chain acyl-CoAs, generating atypical 1-deoxy-sphingolipids (no 1-OH → cannot be phosphorylated → cannot be degraded by S1P lyase → accumulates) → hereditary sensory neuropathy type IA (HSAN1A, SPTLC1/SPTLC2 gain-of-function mutations → ↑1-deoxy-sphinganine, which is toxic to neurons)
Sphingomyelinase (degrades sphingomyelin → ceramide; not involved in de novo sphingolipid synthesis)
Ceramide synthase (CerS1-6, adds FA to sphinganine; this is downstream of SPT in the de novo pathway)
Sphingosine kinase (SphK1/2, phosphorylates sphingosine → S1P; acts on pre-formed sphingosine, not the de novo synthesis committed step)
explanation: Sphingolipid de novo synthesis: SPT (ER) → 3-ketodihydrosphingosine → [KDSR] → sphinganine → [CerS1-6 + FA-CoA] → dihydroceramide → [DEGS1] → ceramide; then ceramide moves to Golgi (CERT, ceramide transfer protein, bridges ER-Golgi) for SM synthesis (SMS1/2: ceramide + phosphocholine from PC → SM + DAG) or stays in ER/Golgi for GSL synthesis (UGCG: ceramide + UDP-Glu → GlcCer, then Golgi → LacCer + further additions). Ceramide synthase isoforms (tissue specificity and chain length): CerS1 (C18): brain, neurons. CerS2 (C22-C24): liver, kidney, oligodendrocytes. CerS4 (C18-C20): skin. CerS6 (C14-C16): widespread; inhibited by fumonisin B1 (Fusarium mycotoxin, CerS inhibitor → ↑sphinganine/sphingosine → hepatotoxicity, esophageal cancer [Africa/Asia] + neural tube defects in livestock). FB1 (fumonisin B1) inhibition of CerS → ↑sphinganine (Sa/So ratio) → NTD in corn-consuming populations (folate-independent NTD risk from mycotoxin exposure). Clinical significance: DEGS1 deficiency (hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 18, HLD18): dihydroceramide accumulates → leukodystrophy + progressive neurodegeneration; dihydroceramide (lacks 4,5 double bond) is pro-apoptotic and accumulates in chemo-treated cells (chemotherapy → ↑dihydroceramide intermediate).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The classic biochemical triad of lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly, and hypoglycemia in a neonate points to which enzyme deficiency?
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (GSD Type Ia, Von Gierke disease): neonatal presentation: hypoglycemia (often severe, within 4h of fasting), hepatomegaly (↑glycogen + fat deposits in liver), lactic acidosis (↑pyruvate → ↑lactate, as glucose-6-P cannot exit liver), hyperuricemia (↑purine degradation + ↓uric acid excretion → gout in adolescence), hypertriglyceridemia (↑VLDL from ↑glycerol-3-P + FA synthesis), hyperlipidemia; biochemistry: G6Pase (in ER membrane of hepatocytes, renal proximal tubules, small intestinal mucosa) catalyzes the final step in both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis: glucose-6-phosphate → glucose + Pi → glucose exits liver; G6Pase deficiency → glucose-6-P accumulates → cannot release free glucose → hypoglycemia (cannot maintain fasting glucose despite large glycogen stores + active gluconeogenesis); diverted glucose-6-P → glycolysis (↑pyruvate/lactate) → PPP (↑NADPH/purine) → fatty acid synthesis; distinguishing from other GSDs: doll-like facies (puffy cheeks, fat deposits), growth retardation, protuberant abdomen; diagnosis: liver biopsy (↓G6Pase activity; excess PAS+ glycogen), or mutation analysis (G6PC gene, chromosome 17q21); treatment: frequent oral corn starch feeds + uncooked cornstarch (slow digestion → sustained glucose release)

Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase deficiency (classic galactosemia) — causes similar neonatal crisis but triggered by lactose/galactose, not fasting; features: jaundice, cataracts (galactitol), E. coli sepsis, NOT the triad of hypoglycemia+lactic acidosis+hepatomegaly as a fasting defect

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency — FBPase deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis → lactic acidosis + hypoglycemia (with FASTING) but glycogen breakdown intact; fasting hypoglycemia without hepatomegaly as prominent; triggers: fasting + high fructose; similar lactic acidosis but different mechanism
Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency — ↑lactate/pyruvate, neurological, hyperammonemia; NOT hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia as the main triad
explanation: Glycogen Storage Diseases (GSD) — exam summary: GSD I (Von Gierke): G6Pase (Ia) or G6PT [glucose-6-P translocase] (Ib); liver + kidney; fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly + hyperuricemia + hyperlipidemia; Ib: additionally neutropenia + inflammatory bowel disease; GSD II (Pompe, Acid Maltase Deficiency): GAA (acid α-glucosidase, lysosomal); cardiac + muscle; infantile: cardiomegaly → cardiac failure by 1 year; late-onset: proximal myopathy (limb-girdle pattern) ± respiratory failure; enzyme: GAA (normally degrades lysosomal glycogen → Glc); treatment: alglucosidase alfa (ERT); GSD III (Cori/Forbes): debranching enzyme (AGL); liver + muscle; milder hypoglycemia; ↑AST/ALT (muscle); normal lactate; GSD IV (Andersen): branching enzyme (GBE1); liver → cirrhosis; amylopectin-like polysaccharide accumulates; liver failure; GSD V (McArdle): muscle phosphorylase (PYGM); exercise-induced cramps, myoglobinuria, ↑CK; NO hypoglycemia (liver phosphorylase normal); forearm ischemic exercise test: ↑NH4+ but NO ↑lactate (lactate needs glycogenolysis which is blocked in muscle); GSD VI (Hers): liver phosphorylase (PYGL); hepatomegaly + mild hypoglycemia; benign; GSD VII (Tarui): PFK-M (muscle PFK-1 subunit); like GSD V but also hemolytic anemia (RBCs have PFK-1 with M subunit + partial PFK-L); GSD IX: liver phosphorylase kinase (PHKA2, X-linked); mild hepatomegaly + mild hypoglycemia. Fanconi-Bickel: GLUT2 (SLC2A2) deficiency; hepatomegaly + glycogen accumulation + Fanconi renal tubular syndrome (↑glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Conversion of methionine to cysteine requires which vitamin cofactor?
options: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) — B12 is required for methionine SYNTHASE (Hcy → Met), not for the transsulfuration pathway from Met to Cys
Folate (B9) — folate (5-methyl-THF) is required for remethylation of Hcy to Met, not for Met → Cys conversion
Niacin (B3) — NAD+ is a cofactor for many reactions but not the direct cofactor for transsulfuration

Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6): the transsulfuration pathway converts Met → Hcy → Cys using two PLP-dependent enzymes: (1) cystathionine β-synthase (CBS, CSAD in some species): Hcy + Ser → cystathionine; PLP (at Lys residue of CBS as internal aldimine) facilitates the β-elimination + condensation; CBS is also allosterically activated by SAM (AdoMet) → when SAM is high (excess Met) → more flux through transsulfuration → more Cys + disposal of Met; (2) cystathionine γ-lyase (CGL, CSE): cystathionine → Cys + α-ketobutyrate + NH3; also PLP-dependent; the overall sequence: Met → SAM → SAH → Hcy → [CBS, PLP] → cystathionine → [CGL, PLP] → Cys; thus B6/PLP is the critical vitamin for Cys synthesis from Met; classical homocystinuria (CBS deficiency): accumulation of Hcy (homocysteine) + Met (as Hcy cannot enter transsulfuration) → ↑Hcy in blood/urine → thromboembolism, Marfanoid features (tall, thin, downward lens subluxation [downward = CBS; upward = FBN1 Marfan]), intellectual disability, premature vascular disease; B6-responsive form (~50%): residual CBS activity → high-dose B6 supplementation → ↑flux through transsulfuration → ↓Hcy; B6-non-responsive: treat with betaine (Hcy + betaine → Met via BHMT, only in liver)
explanation: Methionine metabolism and transsulfuration: Met → [MAT (methionine adenosyltransferase) + ATP] → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine, the universal methyl donor); SAM → [methyltransferases] → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine, a product inhibitor of methyltransferases); SAH → [SAHH, adenosylhomocysteinase (reversible, drives forward if Hcy removed)] → Hcy; Hcy can: (1) Remethylate: Hcy + 5-methyl-THF → Met (methionine synthase, B12 cofactor); or Hcy + betaine → Met (BHMT, only liver/kidney); (2) Transsulfuration: Hcy + Ser → cystathionine (CBS, PLP) → Cys (CGL, PLP); (3) Export: elevated Hcy excreted in urine (homocystinuria). CBS regulation: allosteric activation by SAM → when Met/SAM is high, transsulfuration is favored (shifts Met toward Cys, disposes of excess Met); inhibited by: nitric oxide (NO nitrosylates CBS heme), by CO (binds CBS heme); CBS contains: heme (redox sensor), PLP (catalytic), and SAM-binding regulatory domain. Cysteine downstream products: GSH (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly; rate-limiting: γ-GCS = γ-glutamylcysteine synthetase; requires Cys availability); taurine (Cys + SO3^2- → cysteine sulfinic acid → hypotaurine → taurine; important in: bile salt conjugation [taurocholic acid], retina, heart, osmoregulation); coenzyme A (requires pantothenic acid + cysteine); H2S (Cys → [CBS + CGL] → H2S, a gasotransmitter); sulfate (urinary excretion).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine biosynthesis de novo is:
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH, Complex III-associated, in the inner mitochondrial membrane) — this is a key step in pyrimidine synthesis and the target of leflunomide (→ teriflunomide), but it is NOT the rate-limiting step

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II): the rate-limiting, committed step of de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis; CPS II is the cytoplasmic isoform (distinct from CPS I in urea cycle [mito]); catalyzes: Gln + 2 ATP + HCO3- → carbamoyl phosphate + Glu + 2 ADP + Pi; CPS II is the first step in pyrimidine synthesis; regulated by: allosteric activation by PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate); allosteric inhibition by UTP (end product feedback); in mammals, CPS II is part of a trifunctional enzyme (CAD protein = CPS II + ATCase [aspartate transcarbamylase, step 2] + DHOase [dihydroorotase, step 3], all three steps on one polypeptide); downstream: carbamoyl-P + Asp → [ATCase, step 2] → carbamoylaspartate → [DHOase, step 3, ring closure] → dihydroorotate → [DHODH, step 4, mito IMM, oxidizes with FMN+FAD, electrons → CoQ → Complex III] → orotate → [UMPS: OPRT, step 5] → OMP → [UMPS: ODC, step 6] → UMP → [NDPK] → UDP → dUDP or CDP or [UTP synthase] → UTP → [CTP synthetase, CTPS1/2] → CTP; PRPP required as ribose donor in step 5 (OPRT)

Aspartate transcarbamylase (ATCase): step 2, but CPS II (step 1) is rate-limiting overall; ATCase is the classic allosteric enzyme in E. coli (T-state/R-state), regulated by ATP (activator) + CTP (inhibitor), but in mammals ATCase is part of the CAD trifunctional enzyme and is NOT rate-limiting
UMP synthase (UMPS, bifunctional: OPRT + ODC): performs steps 5+6; hereditary orotic aciduria from UMPS deficiency — not rate-limiting
explanation: Pyrimidine vs. purine synthesis comparison: Both start with PRPP; but order differs: Purine: PRPP is the scaffold → ring built on it (PRPP participates in step 1: PRPP + Gln → PRA). Pyrimidine: ring is built FIRST (as UMP/OMP), THEN attached to PRPP (step 5: orotate + PRPP → OMP [OPRT]). Pyrimidine feedback: UTP → inhibits CPS II (classical product feedback in mammals); note: ATP + PRPP activate CPS II (stimulate pyrimidine synthesis when energy and purines available). Orotic aciduria types: Type I (now called hereditary orotic aciduria): UMPS deficiency → cannot convert orotate to OMP → orotic acid accumulates in urine + crystals + megaloblastic anemia (↓pyrimidines → ↓DNA synthesis → megaloblastic); treatment: uridine supplementation (↑UMP → ↓CPS II via ↑UTP). Type II (Reye, DLD deficiency): combined UMPS deficiency-like picture not a genetic form. Drug-induced orotic aciduria: (1) Allopurinol → inhibits OPRTase (competes with PRPP) → ↑orotic acid (allopurinol ribotide inhibits OPRTase); (2) 6-azauridine; (3) hyperammonemia → ↑carbamoyl-P in excess → ↑pyrimidine synthesis → ↑orotate → orotic aciduria WITHOUT megaloblastic anemia (different from hereditary). DHODH inhibitors: leflunomide (prodrug → teriflunomide, A77 1726): blocks DHODH → ↓pyrimidine synthesis → ↓proliferating T+B cells → immunosuppression; used in RA + relapsing-remitting MS (teriflunomide/Aubagio); also blocks SARS-CoV-2 replication in vitro (pyrimidines needed for RNA synthesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with McArdle disease (GSD Type V) is asked to perform a forearm ischemic exercise test. What would be the expected result?
options: Both lactate and ammonia rise normally (this is the normal response; in McArdle, lactate does not rise)
Lactate rises normally but ammonia does not rise (this would suggest a defect in AMP deaminase or purine nucleotide cycle, not McArdle)

Lactate does not rise but ammonia rises normally: McArdle disease (GSD V) is caused by deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (PYGM gene; myophosphorylase); during the forearm ischemic exercise test (FIET): the patient squeezes a hand grip repetitively with the arm occluded → normally: muscle glycogenolysis → glucose → glycolysis → pyruvate → lactate (venous lactate rises 3-5× baseline, peaks in 1-3 min) AND AMP deaminase reaction (AMP → IMP + NH3, part of purine nucleotide cycle → venous ammonia rises 3-5×); in McArdle disease: glycogenolysis blocked (no myophosphorylase) → no glucose-1-P → no glycolysis → no lactate → VENOUS LACTATE DOES NOT RISE; but AMP deaminase is INTACT → AMP → IMP + NH3 → venous AMMONIA RISES NORMALLY; interpretation: flat lactate + normal ammonia response = diagnostic of glycogenolytic/glycolytic defect (GSD V, VII, or other myophosphorylase/PFK-1 defects); flat lactate + flat ammonia = myoadenylate deaminase deficiency (MADD); GSD VII (Tarui): PFK-M deficiency → also flat lactate + normal ammonia (like McArdle, but additional hemolytic anemia); modern modification: non-ischemic FEIT (without tourniquet) avoids risk of ischemic injury; same interpretation
Neither lactate nor ammonia rises (suggests myoadenylate deaminase deficiency or very poor effort — both would be flat; this is not McArdle's expected result)
explanation: GSD V (McArdle disease): Gene: PYGM (chromosome 11q13.1). Enzyme: myophosphorylase (PYGM, muscle isoform); liver phosphorylase (PYGL) is INTACT → hepatic glycogenolysis normal → blood glucose maintained → NO hypoglycemia (key distinguishing feature). Clinical: exercise-induced cramps + weakness + myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis after strenuous exercise); second wind phenomenon (after 5-10 min of exercise, pain resolves → oxidative metabolism from glucose + FA takes over; can be accelerated by glucose or sucrose intake before exercise); ↑CK at rest (chronically elevated due to repeated micro-rhabdomyolysis); labs during attack: ↑CK + myoglobinuria + AKI (risk); treatment: avoid strenuous anaerobic exercise + warm up slowly; carbohydrate-rich meal before exercise; sucrose 75g before exercise → ↑blood glucose → muscle can use glucose via GLUT4 (not glycogen) → ↑exercise tolerance; high-protein diet (some patients); vitamin B6 (pyridoxine): no convincing benefit; creatine supplementation: mixed evidence; no disease-modifying therapy currently. PYGM mutations: R49X most common in European populations (40-50% of alleles); ΔexE16 also common. Myoadenylate deaminase deficiency (MADA, AMPD1 gene): most common myopathy-related metabolic disorder (~2% of muscle biopsies); FIET: flat lactate (if they also have GSD) + flat ammonia; alone: ↑lactate (glycolysis intact) + flat ammonia; usually mild/asymptomatic or mild exercise intolerance; AMPD1 common variant (Q12X polymorphism): ~10-15% of Caucasians are homozygous but most asymptomatic.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme specifically removes the RNA primer during DNA replication in eukaryotes?
options: RNase H (RNase HI/RNHIA; H stands for 'Hybrid' — degrades RNA in RNA:DNA hybrids; involved in replication, transcription, and in the case of retroviruses, removal of RNA template after reverse transcription); RNase H PARTIALLY removes the RNA primer but cannot complete removal at the 5' end (the remaining 5'-terminal ribonucleotide must be removed by FEN1)

FEN1 (Flap endonuclease 1, also called DNase IV, RAD27 in yeast): in eukaryotes, after each Okazaki fragment is extended by Pol δ, DNA synthesis displaces the 5' end of the preceding RNA primer → forms a 5'-flap (single-stranded RNA/DNA) → FEN1 cleaves the 5'-flap (structure-specific endonuclease) → leaves a nick → DNA ligase I seals; the partnership for Okazaki fragment maturation: Pol δ extends until it reaches primer of downstream fragment → strand displacement synthesis → FEN1 cleaves the flap → ligase seals; RNase H1 may also assist (degrades RNA in the RNA:DNA hybrid primer region), but FEN1 is essential for completing primer removal in eukaryotes; FEN1 null mice: embryonic lethal; haploinsufficiency → genome instability → increased cancer risk; FEN1 requires PCNA (sliding clamp) for efficient activity in vivo

DNA Pol δ (Pol delta): the main lagging strand polymerase in eukaryotes; has 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease but NOT 5'→3' exonuclease (lacks 5'→3' exonuclease activity); so Pol δ alone cannot remove RNA primer
DNA Pol I (in bacteria this enzyme has 5'→3' exonuclease that removes the RNA primer; but in eukaryotes, the equivalent function is performed by FEN1/RNase H)
explanation: Eukaryotic DNA replication primer removal: Primers synthesized by: primase (DnaG subunit of Pol α-primase complex, synthesizes RNA-DNA hybrid primer ~8-10 RNA + ~20-30 DNA; the only polymerase that initiates new strands de novo). Primer removal on lagging strand (Okazaki fragments): Pol δ + PCNA + RFC displaces Pol α from primer → extends Okazaki fragment → strand displacement synthesis creates 5'-flap; FEN1 cleaves the flap (a 5'-flap specific endonuclease that cuts at the base of the flap); DNA ligase I (DNLI, requires PCNA) → seals the nick; maturation also involves: Pol ε (leading strand synthesis in metazoans + some Okazaki maturation); DNA2 (backup 5'-flap nuclease, helicase: processes longer flaps before FEN1); LIG1 (DNA ligase I): seals nicks; human LIG1 is the predominant nick-sealing ligase in replication. On the leading strand: only one primer at the origin → removed by FEN1/RNase H1 at origin end; some evidence that the 5'-end of leading strand is sealed differently or contains an unresolvable gap (relevant to telomere-like stability issues). Ribonucleotide excision repair (RER): misincorporated ribonucleotides by Pol δ/ε during replication (estimated ~10^5 per replication event, the most common lesion during replication) → removed by RNase H2 → PCNA → Pol δ → FEN1 → ligase (similar mechanism to Okazaki maturation). RNase H2 mutations → Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (inflammatory encephalopathy, mimics congenital viral infection; elevated type I interferons due to unprocessed RNA:DNA hybrids accumulating in the nucleus → innate immune activation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Propionyl-CoA is produced from the catabolism of which of the following groups of amino acids?
options: Lysine and leucine (these are PURELY ketogenic; they are NOT glucogenic and do not produce propionyl-CoA; leucine → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate; lysine → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetyl-CoA)
Alanine, glutamate, and aspartate (these are purely glucogenic amino acids: Ala → pyruvate; Glu → α-KG; Asp → OAA; none produce propionyl-CoA)

Methionine, isoleucine, valine, threonine (and odd-chain fatty acids): these amino acids produce propionyl-CoA as a metabolic intermediate; Met: Met → SAM → SAH → Hcy → [CBS] → cystathionine → Cys + α-ketobutyrate → [α-ketobutyrate dehydrogenase, similar to PDC] → propionyl-CoA + CO2; Ile: Ile → [BCKDC] → 2-methylbutyryl-CoA → → propionyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA; Val: Val → [BCKDC] → isobutyryl-CoA → → methylmalonyl-CoA (bypasses propionyl-CoA? No — actually Val → methylmalonyl-CoA via propionyl-CoA intermediate: Val → 2-oxoisovalerate → methylmalonyl semialdehyde → methylmalonyl-CoA [via propionyl-CoA step or directly?]); more precisely: Val catabolism → isobutyryl-CoA → methacyrloyl-CoA → 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA → 3-hydroxyisobutyrate → methylmalonyl semialdehyde → propionyl-CoA [controversial; some textbooks show direct methylmalonyl-CoA from Val]; Thr: Thr → [threonine aldolase, in some species] → Gly + acetaldehyde OR [threonine dehydratase, PLP-dependent] → α-ketobutyrate → propionyl-CoA; odd-chain fatty acids: β-oxidation of odd-chain FA → final product is propionyl-CoA (last 3 carbons); propionyl-CoA metabolism: propionyl-CoA → [PCC, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, biotin + CO2 + ATP] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MMCE, methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase] → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, AdoCbl] → succinyl-CoA → TCA
Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan (these are aromatic AAs; Phe/Tyr → fumarate + acetoacetate [both glucogenic + ketogenic]; Trp → alanine + acetyl-CoA; NONE produce propionyl-CoA)
explanation: Amino acid carbon skeleton catabolism categories: Glucogenic only (7 pure): Ala, Gly, Ser, Cys, Pro, Glu, Gln, Asp, Asn, Arg, His, Met, Val, Thr (most are glucogenic). Ketogenic only (2 pure): Leu + Lys (purely ketogenic → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate; NEVER enter gluconeogenesis directly). Both glucogenic + ketogenic (5): Ile, Phe, Tyr, Trp, Lys [Note: Lys is debated; predominantly ketogenic]. Propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA pathway: relevant in: methylmalonic acidemia (MCM deficiency → ↑MMA in blood/urine); propionic acidemia (PCC deficiency → ↑propionylcarnitine + ↑MMA + ↑BCAA precursors in blood); diagnosis: tandem mass spectrometry (TMS) in newborn screening (NBS): ↑C3-carnitine (propionylcarnitine) in PA and MMA; ↑C3:C0 and C3:C2 ratios; treatment of PA/MMA: low-protein diet (restrict BCAA precursors), carnitine supplementation, B12 supplementation (B12-responsive MMA), liver transplant (corrects enzymatic defect in MCM, reduces metabolic crises — but does not fully prevent neurological complications), OHCbl injections. MMA spectrum: isolated MMA (MCM, MMAB, MMAA mutations) vs. combined MMA+homocystinuria (MMACHC/cblC = most common combined; or cblD/E/G variants). Ureato cycle connection: propionic acid metabolism produces NH3 (from amino acid catabolism) + reduces available acetyl-CoA → ↑hyperammonemia (secondary, without primary urea cycle enzyme deficiency) → common in PA/MMA crises.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Lipid-lowering agent ezetimibe works by inhibiting which transporter in the intestine?
options: ABCG5/G8 (ABC transporter in enterocyte brush border that effluxes sitosterol/plant sterols + cholesterol back into intestinal lumen; loss-of-function mutations → sitosterolemia [phytosterolemia]; ezetimibe does NOT inhibit ABCG5/G8)
LPL (lipoprotein lipase, in capillary endothelium — hydrolyzes TG in chylomicrons; not a cholesterol uptake transporter in intestine)

NPC1L1 (Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 protein): NPC1L1 (encoded by NPC1L1 gene, chromosome 7p13) is the major sterol transporter responsible for intestinal cholesterol (and plant sterol) absorption at the brush border of enterocytes (duodenum and jejunum); mechanism: cholesterol + bile acid micelle → cholesterol transferred to brush border → NPC1L1 (at apical surface, interacts with caveolin-1, uses vesicle-mediated internalization) → cholesterol imported into enterocyte; ezetimibe: a selective inhibitor of NPC1L1 → ↓intestinal cholesterol absorption by ~54% → ↓LDL-C by ~18-25% as monotherapy; ezetimibe also expressed in liver (canalicular NPC1L1 → reabsorbs biliary cholesterol; ezetimibe → ↓biliary cholesterol reabsorption → ↑cholesterol excreted in bile/feces); ezetimibe + statin (combo): additive LDL-C lowering; IMPROVE-IT trial: ezetimibe + simvastatin vs. simvastatin alone → 6.4% ↓ in CV events → established that further LDL-C lowering beyond statin adds benefit; SHARP trial: ezetimibe + simvastatin → ↓major vascular events in CKD; no cancer signal (earlier concern disproved)

PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9: serine protease that targets LDL-R for lysosomal degradation → ↑LDL-R degradation → ↓LDL clearance; PCSK9 inhibitors [alirocumab, evolocumab] target PCSK9 protein; ezetimibe does not inhibit PCSK9)
explanation: NPC1L1 and cholesterol absorption: NPC1L1 vs. NPC1 (Niemann-Pick C1): NPC1 is a different protein (OMIM 607623) involved in intracellular cholesterol trafficking from late endosomes/lysosomes → ER; NPC1 mutations → Niemann-Pick type C disease (unesterified cholesterol + GSL accumulation in late endosomes → cerebellar ataxia + vertical supranuclear gaze palsy + dementia + visceral storage); NPC1L1 is the apical intestinal transporter only. Ezetimibe pharmacokinetics: absorbed in intestine → undergoes glucuronidation (UGT1A1 + UGT1A3) → ezetimibe-glucuronide (active conjugate) → enterohepatic recycling (biliary secretion → reabsorption from ileum → long duration of action; T1/2 ~22h). PCSK9 physiology: synthesized in liver → secreted into plasma → binds extracellular domain of LDL-R → LDL-R/PCSK9 complex → endocytosis → PCSK9 directs LDL-R to lysosome (degradation) instead of recycling → ↓LDL-R on hepatocyte surface → ↓LDL clearance; gain-of-function mutations: familial hypercholesterolemia type 3 (↑PCSK9 → ↓LDL-R → severe hypercholesterolemia); loss-of-function mutations: PCSK9 LOF → ↑LDL-R recycling → ↓LDL-C → protection from CVD (first identified in African Americans with Y142X and C679X mutations → 88% ↓CHD events; foundational evidence for PCSK9 as target). PCSK9 inhibitors: evolocumab (Repatha) + alirocumab (Praluent): monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9 → ↓LDL-C 55-65%; FOURIER trial (evolocumab): ↓CV events; approved for FH, ASCVD on max-tolerated statin with inadequate LDL-C control. Inclisiran: siRNA targeting PCSK9 mRNA synthesis in liver → ~50% ↓LDL-C with twice-yearly dosing.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The reverse transcriptase of HIV has which unique enzymatic activities?
options: DNA-dependent DNA polymerase + RNase A + strand-exchange activity

RNA-dependent DNA polymerase + RNase H + DNA-dependent DNA polymerase: HIV reverse transcriptase (HIV-RT) is a p66/p51 heterodimer (p66 = active polymerase + RNase H domain; p51 = structural, lacks RNase H activity); it has THREE enzymatic activities in one protein: (1) RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (RDDP): reads the HIV RNA genome (sense strand) → synthesizes complementary DNA (cDNA) → forms RNA:DNA hybrid; (2) RNase H (ribonuclease H): degrades the RNA template from the RNA:DNA hybrid → leaves single-stranded cDNA; (3) DNA-dependent DNA polymerase (DDDP): uses the ssDNA as template → synthesizes the second DNA strand → forms dsDNA provirus; the dsDNA provirus → integrase (HIV integrase enzyme) → integrated into host genome; note: HIV RT has NO 3'→5' proofreading exonuclease → very high error rate (~3×10^-5 per base per replication cycle) → rapid generation of HIV variants → drug resistance; NRTIs (nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors): zidovudine (AZT), tenofovir, emtricitabine, lamivudine → chain terminators (lack 3'-OH → block RT elongation); NNRTIs (non-nucleoside RTIs): efavirenz, rilpivirine, nevirapine → bind allosteric pocket on p66 near active site → conformational change → ↓RDDP activity
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase + helicase + ligase (these are functions of eukaryotic transcription machinery, not reverse transcriptase)
explanation: HIV replication cycle (relevant biochemistry steps): Attachment: gp120 (surface glycoprotein) binds CD4 (T cell + macrophage/DC + microglial cell); conformational change → gp120 binds co-receptor (CCR5 [macrophage-tropic M-tropic] or CXCR4 [T-tropic X4]); gp41 undergoes fusion peptide insertion → membrane fusion → viral nucleocapsid enters. Uncoating + reverse transcription: RT uses tRNA3-Lys (anticodon CUU) as primer, annealing to PBS (primer binding site) near 5' end of HIV RNA → (-) strand cDNA synthesis → RNase H removes RNA → (+) strand synthesis from PPT (polypurine tract) → dsDNA (complete provirus). Integration: dsDNA transported to nucleus (as pre-integration complex [PIC] with integrase + matrix protein + LEDGF/p75 [lens epithelium-derived growth factor/p75, integrase cofactor that tethers PIC to active chromatin]); integrase catalyzes: 3'-processing (removes 2 nt from each 3' end) + strand transfer (cuts host DNA + inserts provirus); INSTI (integrase strand transfer inhibitors): raltegravir, elvitegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir → block strand transfer step; bind integrase + viral DNA ends + Mg2+ → block integration. Transcription: host RNA Pol II transcribes provirus → HIV mRNA; Tat (Trans-Activator of Transcription): Tat binds TAR (trans-activation response element RNA stem-loop at 5' end of nascent HIV mRNA) → recruits P-TEFb (CDK9+cyclin T1) → phosphorylates RNAPII CTD (Ser2 of heptapeptide repeat) → releases paused RNAPII → productive elongation → efficient HIV transcription. Assembly + budding + maturation: Gag + Gag-Pol polyproteins → membrane; HIV protease (aspartyl protease, active as dimer) cleaves Gag → MA (matrix), CA (capsid), NC (nucleocapsid), p6; PI (protease inhibitors): atazanavir, darunavir, lopinavir → block HIV PR → immature, non-infectious virions.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas (EMP) pathway energetics under aerobic conditions?
options: Net gain: 2 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose; under aerobic conditions, NADH is reoxidized via ETC → additional ATP generated; the EMP pathway (glycolysis) itself produces: 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation (at PGK and PK steps) − 2 ATP consumed (at HK and PFK-1 steps) = net 2 ATP; plus 2 NADH (at GAPDH step); under aerobic conditions, the 2 NADH (cytoplasmic) → shuttled into mitochondria via: malate-aspartate shuttle (heart, liver: generates 2 NADH in mito → 2 × 2.5 = 5 ATP) or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle (muscle, brain: generates FADH2 in mito → 2 × 1.5 = 3 ATP); net ATP from complete glucose oxidation (malate-aspartate shuttle): 2 (glycolysis substrate) + 5 (malate-asp shuttle NADH) + 3 (PDC NADH) + 20 (TCA NADH) + 3 (TCA FADH2) + 2 (TCA substrate-level) = 30-32 ATP; the correct net from EMP pathway alone = 2 ATP (substrate level) + 2 NADH per glucose; the 'standard' NEET answer for total aerobic glycolysis: the EMP portion yields 2 net ATP + 2 NADH; total oxidation (old textbook): 36-38 ATP; current: 30-32 ATP depending on shuttle
Net gain: 4 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose (this incorrectly counts gross, not net; 4 ATP minus 2 consumed = 2 net ATP)
Net gain: 2 ATP + 2 FADH2 per glucose (FADH2 is not produced in glycolysis; GAPDH produces NADH)
Net gain: 6 ATP per glucose from substrate-level phosphorylation alone (this is incorrect; substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis produces only 4 gross / 2 net ATP)
explanation: Glycolysis (EMP pathway) step-by-step ATP accounting: ATP-consuming steps: Step 1 (HK/GK): Glucose → G6P: -1 ATP; Step 3 (PFK-1): F6P → F1,6-BP: -1 ATP; total: -2 ATP. ATP-producing steps: Step 7 (PGK, substrate level): 1,3-BPG → 3-PG: +2 ATP (2 molecules per glucose); Step 10 (PK, substrate level): PEP → pyruvate: +2 ATP; total: +4 ATP. Net ATP from glycolysis: 4 − 2 = +2 ATP per glucose. NADH from glycolysis: Step 6 (GAPDH): G3P → 1,3-BPG: +2 NADH (2 per glucose); Pyruvate fate: aerobic: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (PDC, in mito) + NADH; anaerobic: pyruvate → lactate (LDH) + NAD+ [NAD+ recycling to allow continued glycolysis]. Irreversible steps of glycolysis (regulatory enzymes, cannot be directly reversed in gluconeogenesis): HK (step 1): Glc → G6P; PFK-1 (step 3): F6P → F1,6-BP [most regulated; F-2,6-BP is the main activator, [AMP] activates, [ATP] + [citrate] inhibit]; PK (step 10): PEP → Pyr [inhibited by ATP + alanine; activated by F-1,6-BP (feedforward); PK deficiency → hemolytic anemia (2,3-BPG ↑ → ↑O2 delivery, which is an interesting compensatory mechanism); gluconeogenesis bypasses: G6Pase (bypasses HK), FBPase-1 (bypasses PFK-1), PC+PEPCK (bypasses PK). Substrate-level phosphorylation also occurs in TCA (succinyl-CoA synthetase: succinyl-CoA → succinate + GTP, equivalent to ATP).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A mutation that prevents RNA polymerase II from phosphorylating its C-terminal domain (CTD) would most likely impair which process?
options: tRNA processing in the nucleolus (tRNA is made by RNA Pol III, not Pol II; and is processed in the nucleus, not nucleolus [rRNA is in nucleolus]; CTD phosphorylation is specific to RNAPII)

mRNA 5'-capping, splicing, and polyadenylation: the CTD (C-terminal domain) of the largest subunit (RPB1/POLR2A) of RNA Pol II is a unique, highly conserved heptapeptide repeat (consensus: Tyr1-Ser2-Pro3-Thr4-Ser5-Pro6-Ser7; 52 repeats in mammals) that serves as a platform for co-transcriptional mRNA processing: at initiation: Ser5 + Ser7 of CTD are phosphorylated (by CDK7, part of TFIIH/CAK); phospho-Ser5 CTD recruits: (1) capping enzyme (guanylyltransferase adds 7-methylguanosine cap to 5'-end of nascent mRNA; cap added when RNA is 25-30 nt); at elongation: Ser2 phosphorylated (by P-TEFb/CDK9+cyclin T1, which also releases paused RNAPII); phospho-Ser2 CTD recruits: (2) splicing factors (SR proteins, U snRNPs → co-transcriptional splicing); (3) cleavage and polyadenylation factors (CPSF, CstF → recognizes AAUAAA + cleaves + poly-A polymerase adds poly-A tail of ~200 A residues); if CTD cannot be phosphorylated → RNAPII can initiate but cannot recruit capping/splicing/polyadenylation machinery → all three mRNA processing steps impaired; α-amanitin (Amanita phalloides mushroom toxin): inhibits RNAPII (binds between bridge helix and trigger loop of RNAPII → prevents translocation → traps RNAPII → no elongation) → CTD never phosphorylated for elongation → same net effect on mRNA processing
Ribosome biogenesis (rRNA synthesis is by RNA Pol I in nucleolus; 5S rRNA by Pol III; ribosome assembly involves rRNA + ribosomal proteins [nuclear-encoded, translated in cytoplasm])
Mitochondrial gene transcription (mitochondrial genome is transcribed by mitochondrial RNA Pol [POLRMT], a single-subunit enzyme related to bacteriophage T7 RNAP; not by RNAPII; no CTD)
explanation: CTD phosphorylation code: the CTD 'code' (analogous to histone code) coordinates transcription with mRNA processing: Tyr1-P: promotes elongation, prevents premature termination. Ser2-P: elongating RNAPII signature; recruits splicing (SF3b, U2snRNP) + 3'-processing (CPSF73, poly-A-polymerase). Ser5-P: initiating/capping RNAPII; recruits cap methyltransferase. Ser7-P: involved in snRNA/snoRNA 3'-end processing. Thr4-P: elongation-related (yeast). CDK7 (TFIIH component): phosphorylates Ser5 + Ser7 during initiation; CDK9/P-TEFb: phosphorylates Ser2 during elongation; inhibited by: DRB (5,6-dichlorobenzimidazole riboside, early CTD kinase inhibitor); flavopiridol (CDK9 inhibitor, anticancer; arrests RNA Pol II); cancer relevance: some cancers depend on P-TEFb → super-enhancers with high Ser2-P RNAPII at oncogene loci; BRD4 (bromodomain protein 4) recruits P-TEFb to super-enhancers → JQ1 (BET bromodomain inhibitor) → blocks BRD4 → ↓P-TEFb recruitment → ↓Pol II Ser2 phosphorylation → ↓oncogene elongation → anti-tumor in some cancers (MYC-driven, BRD4-NUT fusion in NUT midline carcinoma). Phosphatases: Fcp1 (FCP1): dephosphorylates Ser2-P → recycling of RNAPII; Ssu72: dephosphorylates Ser5-P at 3'-end → recycling.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In patients with cystinuria, renal tubular transport of which group of amino acids is defective?
options: All amino acids (non-specific aminoaciduria, Fanconi syndrome, involves all AAs; not specifically cystinuria)
Neutral amino acids including tryptophan (this is Hartnup disease: SLC6A19 deficiency → neutral amino acid malabsorption [Trp predominantly] → pellagra-like symptoms)
Acidic amino acids (glutamate + aspartate; deficient in dicarboxylic aminoaciduria from SLC1A1/EAAC1 deficiency; very benign)

Dibasic amino acids (cystine, lysine, arginine, ornithine): cystinuria is caused by mutations in SLC3A1 (rBAT, type A, chromosome 2p21) or SLC7A9 (b0,+AT, type B, chromosome 19q13) → defective renal tubular reabsorption (and intestinal absorption) of COLA amino acids: Cystine (cystine = oxidized disulfide form of two cysteines; the poorly soluble form), Ornithine, Lysine, Arginine (the shared transporter b0,+AT + rBAT is the heterodimeric cationic + neutral amino acid transporter in renal proximal tubule and intestinal brush border); cystine (insoluble at physiological pH) accumulates in urine → crystallizes → cystine kidney stones (hexagonal crystals, yellow-brown, radio-opaque on CT); clinical: recurrent nephrolithiasis starting in childhood/young adulthood → CKD; diagnosis: ↑urinary cystine (>250 mg/g creatinine) + hexagonal crystals; sodium cyanide-nitroprusside test: positive (turns purple-red, qualitative screen); treatment: high fluid intake (>3-4L/day), alkalinize urine (K-citrate, pH >7.5 → ↑cystine solubility), D-penicillamine (thiol drug → cleaves S-S bond → mixed penicillamine-cysteine disulfide [soluble]) or tiopronin (preferred, fewer side effects than D-penicillamine)
explanation: Aminoaciduria types: Overflow aminoaciduria: plasma AA levels exceed tubular reabsorption threshold → spillover into urine (e.g., PKU → Phe; maple syrup urine disease → BCAA; homocystinuria → Hcy); renal transport is normal, but concentration too high. Transport aminoaciduria: tubular transport defect → ↑urine AA despite normal/low plasma levels; examples: Cystinuria (SLC3A1/SLC7A9): dibasic AAs; Hartnup disease (SLC6A19): neutral AAs; dicarboxylic aminoaciduria (SLC1A1): Glu + Asp; iminoglycinuria (SLC6A20 + others): Pro + hydroxyPro + Gly; lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI, SLC7A7 [y+LAT1]): Lys + Arg + Orn fail to be reabsorbed but Cys not affected → hyperammonemia (Orn can't enter urea cycle → ↑NH3) + low plasma Lys/Arg → protein aversion, osteoporosis, immune dysfunction; different from cystinuria (both rBAT/b0,+ and y+LAT1 transport Lys/Arg, but different transporters). Cystine stone characteristics: radio-OPAQUE (contain S → slightly opaque on plain X-ray; more clearly seen on CT as hyperdense); hexagonal crystals; recurrent; treatment-resistant. Cystine stone vs. uric acid stone: uric acid: radiolucent, forms in acidic urine (pH<5.5), associated with gout/DM/metabolic syndrome; cystine: radio-opaque, hexagonal crystals, occurs in young patients with cystinuria. Penicillamine side effects: membranous nephropathy, drug-induced lupus, myasthenia, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, pemphigus (important adverse effect profile).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The first urine test positive for phenylketonuria (PKU) in a newborn would be:
options: Elevated phenylalanine on tandem mass spectrometry (TMS-NBS): PKU diagnosis: in the newborn screening era, PKU is detected by: (1) Guthrie test (bacterial inhibition assay): first NBS method (1960s, Robert Guthrie); Bacillus subtilis requires Phe for growth; β-2-thienylalanine inhibits growth; phenylalanine in blood spot reverses this inhibition → bacterial halo proportional to Phe concentration; now largely replaced. (2) Fluorometry: quantitative Phe level in dried blood spot (DBS). (3) Tandem mass spectrometry (TMS, LC-MS/MS): current gold standard NBS method; measures Phe + Tyr simultaneously; Phe:Tyr ratio is the main diagnostic criterion (normal Phe:Tyr <3; classical PKU >10; mild PKU 3-10); advantages: can detect Phe, Tyr, MSUD, organic acids (propionic, methylmalonic), fatty acid oxidation disorders, etc. in a single assay from one DBS; PKU NBS: blood spot collected at 24-48h of life (not before 24h — AA levels still equilibrating); recall rate ~0.1-0.3%; confirmatory: plasma amino acid profile (quantitative); screen timing: classical PKU Phe levels >20 mg/dL (>1200 µmol/L); mild hyperphenylalaninemia (mHPA): Phe 120-360 µmol/L; mild PKU: 360-1200 µmol/L; classical PKU >1200 µmol/L

Elevated phenylpyruvic acid in urine (the ferric chloride test turns green with phenylpyruvate; historically used, but unreliable in first 2-4 weeks because Phe must first accumulate to levels that drive alternate metabolism via transaminase → phenylpyruvate; NOT the first abnormality; NBS Phe elevation precedes urinary phenylpyruvate)
Elevated urinary homogentisic acid (this is alkaptonuria, a different aromatic AA disorder: HGD deficiency → HGA accumulates → dark urine on standing + ochronosis; not PKU)

Decreased pterins in urine (pterin analysis by HPLC of urine is done AFTER PKU is confirmed, to rule out BH4 deficiency [biopterin forms, neopterin] as the cause of hyperphenylalaninemia; this is a follow-up test, not the first positive result)
explanation: PKU (phenylketonuria): Gene: PAH (chromosome 12q23.2); Enzyme: phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH); Mechanism: ↓PAH → Phe not converted to Tyr → Phe accumulates → (1) ↑Phe transported across BBB via LAT1 (large neutral AA transporter 1, SLC7A5 [shares transport with all neutral AAs including BCAA/Tyr/Trp/Met]) → competes with Tyr+Trp+other LNAA → ↓dopamine/serotonin/thyroid hormones in brain → neurotoxicity; (2) Alternative Phe metabolism: Phe → [transaminase] → phenylpyruvate (in liver) → phenylacetate (by oxidative decarboxylation) + phenyllactate; musty/mousy odor from phenylacetate in urine/sweat; (3) ↓Tyr (now essential in PKU) → ↓melanin → fair complexion, blue eyes, blonde hair; classical PKU untreated: severe intellectual disability (IQ <50), microcephaly, seizures, eczema, musty odor; maternal PKU: untreated mother → embryotoxic effect of high Phe on fetus (even if fetus heterozygous, non-PKU): microcephaly, CHD, FGR, intellectual disability (even if child's own PAH normal → maternal Phe crosses placenta → fetal damage); dietary Phe restriction must be maintained throughout pregnancy in PKU mothers. Treatment: Phe-restricted diet (low-Phe formula, avoid high-Phe foods: meat, fish, eggs, dairy, regular bread) with Tyr supplementation; dietary treatment goal: Phe <360 µmol/L (ideally 120-360); BH4 therapy: sapropterin dihydrochloride (Kuvan, synthetic BH4) → for BH4-responsive PAH mutations (mostly mild PKU/mHPA; BH4 acts as pharmacological chaperone + provides additional cofactor → ↓Phe); PAH gene therapy (AAV-PAL or mRNA therapy): under investigation; Pegvaliase (PEGylated phenylalanine ammonia lyase from Anabaena): enzyme substitution therapy → Phe → trans-cinnamic acid + NH3 (bypasses PAH) → approved for adults with uncontrolled PKU.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) results in defective collagen synthesis. The specific biochemical defect is:
options: Deficiency in lysyl hydroxylase activity (lysyl hydroxylase [LH1/2/3, PLOD1/2/3] also requires Vit C/ascorbate as cofactor — so this IS also affected in scurvy; but prolyl 4-hydroxylase is the more classic and rate-limiting defect; in Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome kyphoscoliotic type [EDSKS], LH1 mutation → ↓hydroxylysine → ↓cross-links → hypermobility + kyphoscoliosis + fragile skin, a different genetic cause of similar biochemical defect)

↓Prolyl 4-hydroxylase (P4H) activity due to lack of ascorbate as a reducing cofactor: P4H requires: O2, Fe2+ (ferrous iron in active site), α-ketoglutarate (co-substrate, oxidized to succinate), and ascorbate (vitamin C, acts as a reducing agent to regenerate Fe2+ from Fe3+ between catalytic cycles; without ascorbate, Fe2+ is oxidized to Fe3+ after each catalytic cycle and cannot return to Fe2+ → P4H becomes inactive); without P4H activity: proline residues in collagen are not hydroxylated → insufficient hydroxyproline → the collagen triple helix cannot form stable intermolecular hydrogen bonds (4-Hyp forms H-bonds between chains; without Hyp, triple helix is thermodynamically unstable at body temperature → collagen denatures/unfolds at physiological 37°C) → secreted collagen is structurally weak → clinical scurvy: bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs (follicular changes), poor wound healing, loose teeth (loss of periodontal attachment), hemarthroses; biochemical marker: ↑urinary hydroxyproline (from degradation of existing collagen; during active scurvy, collagen synthesis is impaired but degradation continues → urinary Hyp paradoxically may be ELEVATED from breakdown of existing collagen, not from newly-synthesized Hyp); diagnosis: serum ascorbate <11 µmol/L (< 0.2 mg/dL); leukocyte ascorbate: better index of tissue stores
↑Crosslink formation between collagen chains due to excessive lysyl oxidase activity (scurvy causes DEFICIENT crosslinks, not excess; lysyl oxidase is copper-dependent, not Vit C-dependent directly)
↓Synthesis of glycine, which is the most abundant amino acid in collagen (glycine is non-essential; body can synthesize glycine; Vit C deficiency does not impair Gly synthesis)
explanation: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) biochemistry: Chemical: L-ascorbic acid; reduced form (active); oxidized → dehydroascorbate → can be reduced back by NADH or glutathione; DRI: 75-90 mg/day (adults); smokers need +35 mg/day; UL: 2000 mg/day. Functions of Vit C: (1) P4H + LH cofactor (collagen synthesis) — PRIMARY. (2) Dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH): Tyr → DOPA → dopamine → [DBH, Vit C + Cu] → NE; Vit C keeps Cu in Cu+ state in DBH. (3) Peptidyl-glycine α-amidating monooxygenase (PAM): amidates neuroendocrine peptides (CRH, CRF, GRP, etc.) at their C-terminus; requires Vit C. (4) Collagen-specific hydroxylase in biosynthesis of elastin (same P4H mechanism). (5) 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases in general (>60 enzymes in humans, e.g., HIFs, TETs, JmjC-KDMs, all use α-KG + O2 + Fe2+ + Vit C as cofactor). (6) Iron absorption: Vit C in GI tract reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ (DMT1 only transports Fe2+) → ↑non-heme Fe absorption; separate from enzyme cofactor role. (7) Antioxidant: quenches ROS, regenerates Vit E (tocopheroxyl radical back to Vit E). (8) Immune function: high concentration in neutrophils/lymphocytes → unclear exact role but ↓infection duration (mild benefit vs. common cold). Scurvy clinical: classic findings: perifollicular hemorrhages with corkscrew (coiled, swan-neck) hairs; bleeding gums (↓periodontal collagen + capillary fragility); Woody edema of lower limbs; sicca syndrome-like features; mood changes/depression (↓NE synthesis from DBH deficiency); subperiosteal hemorrhage (in children, resembles scurvy-rickets). RBC lysis in scurvy: NO, scurvy alone does not cause hemolysis (↓Vit E [tocopherol] deficiency → hemolytic anemia [↓GSH-Px + ↓catalase support from ↓ascorbate might be relevant but not the primary hemolytic cause]). Diagnosis: serum ascorbate + clinical features; leukocyte ascorbate (more accurate tissue store indicator); urinary 4-Hyp.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Niemann-Pick disease Type C (NPC) differs from Types A and B in that the enzymatic defect involves:
options: A different lysosomal acid lipase (LAL, LIPA gene → LAL deficiency → Wolman disease [infant] or CESD [adult]; accumulates cholesterol ester + TG; not NPC)
Reduced activity of sphingomyelinase (this is NPC TYPE A/B: SMPD1 mutations → acid sphingomyelinase deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation; NPC TYPE C is a completely different molecular defect)

Defective intracellular cholesterol trafficking due to NPC1 or NPC2 mutation: NPC1 (chromosome 18q11.2, ~95% of NPC): a 13-transmembrane domain protein in the late endosomal/lysosomal (LEL) membrane; NPC2 (~5% of NPC): a small soluble luminal protein in the endosome/lysosome; mechanism: LDL-derived cholesterol enters cells via LDL-R → endosome → lysosome; in lysosomes, NPC2 binds unesterified cholesterol from the lipid bilayer → transfers to NPC1 → NPC1 transports cholesterol out of LEL → to ER (for ACAT1-mediated esterification + storage) or to plasma membrane; in NPC1/2 deficiency: unesterified cholesterol (+ sphingomyelin + glycolipids including GM2/GM3 gangliosides and glucosylceramide) accumulates in late endosomes/lysosomes → cannot be mobilized → ER cholesterol sensing is impaired (despite excess intracellular cholesterol, ER doesn't 'see' it → SCAP-SREBP2 pathway activated as if cholesterol-depleted → ↑HMG-CoA reductase + ↑LDL-R = paradoxical upregulation despite cellular cholesterol excess); clinical NPC: vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (VSGP, pathognomonic; saccadic downgaze impaired → patients compensate by head bobbing; due to accumulation in midbrain pretectal region); progressive cerebellar ataxia; dementia; gelastic cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion/laughter, like narcolepsy); psychiatric symptoms; hepatosplenomegaly; foam cells in liver/spleen; diagnosis: filipin staining (filipin binds free cholesterol → fluorescent, bright LEL inclusions [positive filipin staining] in fibroblasts); plasma oxysterols (25-OH-cholesterol, 7-keto-cholesterol) elevated; NPC1 biomarker: ↑lyso-sphingomyelin-509 and 7-keto-cholesterol in plasma; treatment: miglustat (N-butyldeoxynojirimycin, GlcCer synthase inhibitor → ↓substrate [GSLs] → slower neurological decline; stabilizes NPC disease); arimoclomol (co-inducer of heat shock response → HSP70 → chaperone → some benefit in NPC1 [clinical trial showed benefit])
Defective transport of sphingosine across the lysosomal membrane (this is a feature of ASAH1-deficiency related pathology; not the primary NPC mechanism)
explanation: NPC disease overview: Prevalence: ~1:120,000-150,000; pan-ethnic but higher in Nova Scotian Acadians. NPC genetics: NPC1 (18q11.2, 97 mutations known; p.I1061T most common in Caucasians) and NPC2 (14q24.3, rarer); both AR. Intracellular cholesterol homeostasis (normal): LDL-cholesterol ester → lysosome → LAL (acid lipase) cleaves CE → free chol; free chol extracted from lysosomal membrane by NPC2 → NPC1 (cooperative handoff; NPC2 binds cholesterol in luminal pocket → contacts NPC1 transmembrane domain [loop of NPC2 = direct interaction with NPC1 N-terminal domain] → transfers cholesterol to NPC1) → NPC1 pumps cholesterol out via an exosite on its SSD (sterol-sensing domain) → non-vesicular transport via Rab9-mediated vesicles OR direct transfer to ER via VAMP7/SNARE. Filipin staining: unesterified (free) cholesterol brightly fluorescent with filipin (polyene antibiotic); NPC fibroblasts: intense perinuclear filipin staining of enlarged LELs; normal fibroblasts: faint PM + ER staining only. NPC2 protein: a soluble lysosomal NPC2 (binds cholesterol in lumen → donates to NPC1 TM domain) → NPC2 also secreted (found in urine, milk, bronchoalveolar fluid); NPC2 deficiency identical clinical phenotype to NPC1. Statins in NPC: statins are NOT beneficial (↓cholesterol synthesis but does NOT mobilize the ER-invisible lysosomal pool; may worsen by stimulating LDL-R → more cholesterol import).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The 'pentose phosphate pathway' (PPP) produces NADPH. In which subcellular compartment does the oxidative phase of the PPP occur?
options: Mitochondria (the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation are in the mitochondria; NADPH produced by mitochondria via IDH2/NNT/ME3 serves mitochondrial antioxidant defense; the PPP is not mitochondrial)
Nucleus (the nucleus contains enzymes for DNA repair and replication; PPP enzymes are not localized to the nucleus)

Cytoplasm (cytosol): the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP, hexose monophosphate shunt) occurs entirely in the cytoplasm; oxidative phase: G6P → [G6PDH, NADP+ → NADPH] → 6-phosphoglucono-δ-lactone → [lactonase] → 6-phosphogluconate → [6-PGD, NADP+ → NADPH + CO2] → ribulose-5-phosphate; products: 2 NADPH + 1 CO2 + ribulose-5-P per G6P; non-oxidative phase: interconversion of sugars (R5P, Xu5P, S7P, E4P, GAP, F6P); key enzymes: transketolase (uses TPP [thiamine]; Wernicke-Korsakoff → ↓transketolase activity → erythrocyte transketolase activity used to assess B1 status; stimulation by TPP in vitro [TPP effect]) + transaldolase; NADPH uses: ↓GSSG → 2 GSH (by glutathione reductase); ↑fatty acid synthesis (FAS requires NADPH); ↑cholesterol + steroid synthesis; cytochrome P450 reductase (↑drug metabolism); phagocyte respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase [NOX2, Nox2] in phagocytes: 2 NADPH + O2 → 2 NADP+ + H2O2 [→ HOCl via MPO]; G6PD deficiency → ↓NADPH → ↓GSH → ↑ROS → Heinz body hemolytic anemia AND ↓respiratory burst → ↑susceptibility to catalase-positive bacteria [S. aureus, Aspergillus, Klebsiella, Serratia] — similar to but distinct from Chronic Granulomatous Disease [CGD, NOX2 mutation directly])
Peroxisome (peroxisomes are the site of very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation, plasmalogen synthesis, bile acid intermediary metabolism; not PPP enzymes)
explanation: G6PD deficiency (X-linked, most common enzyme disorder, affects 400 million people): G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the oxidative PPP; X-linked (Xq28); males hemizygous (fully affected); females may be heterozygous (intermediate, depends on X-inactivation pattern in RBCs). G6PD deficiency: ↓NADPH in RBCs → ↓GSH → ↑oxidative stress → hemoglobin oxidized (methemoglobin) → precipitates → Heinz bodies (denatured Hb inclusions, seen on supravital staining) → splenic sequestration + intravascular hemolysis → non-immune hemolytic anemia. Triggers: (1) Infection (most common): oxidative stress from respiratory burst in macrophages + neutrophils → oxidative damage to G6PD-deficient RBCs; (2) Oxidant drugs: primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase; (3) Fava beans (vicine + convicine, oxidant compounds in Vicia faba) → 'favism'; (4) Naphthalene (mothballs); (5) Neonatal jaundice (G6PD deficiency is a major cause of severe neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, especially in African + Mediterranean + Asian neonates). G6PD variants: G6PD A- (African, c.202 G>A, p.Val68Met + c.376 G>A, p.Asp126Asn; ~10% normal activity; mild, episodic hemolysis); G6PD Mediterranean (p.Ser188Phe; <5% activity; more severe); G6PD Canton, G6PD Viangchan (Southeast Asian); G6PD Hektoen (↑activity → polycythemia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme synthesizes UTP from CTP in the pyrimidine nucleotide interconversion pathway?
options: CTP synthetase (CTPS1/2): this enzyme converts UTP to CTP (the reverse direction: UTP + Gln + ATP → CTP + Glu + ADP + Pi), not CTP to UTP

Nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDPK, NME1/2): NDPK catalyzes: NDP + ATP ↔ NTP + ADP; this IS the enzyme that equilibrates all nucleotide diphosphate/triphosphate pairs; it produces UTP (from UDP + ATP) and CTP (from CDP + ATP); BUT note: NDPK is a general enzyme, not specifically for UTP synthesis from CTP
Uridine kinase (UK, UCK1/2): phosphorylates uridine + cytidine → UMP + CMP (salvage); not relevant to UTP-CTP interconversion

CTP phosphohydrolase (CTPH, also called 5'-nucleotidase variant or NDP phosphatase): hydrolyzes CTP → CMP + PPi or CDP → CDP; not directly producing UTP from CTP; note: there is no direct CTP → UTP enzyme in mammalian cells; the pathway is: CTP → [CTPS inhibition reversal / or via CTP → CDP → UDP → UTP pathway]; in practice: CDP → [NDPK] → CTP; or CTP → [cytidine triphosphate hydrolase] → CDP → [CTP reductase? no] → UDP → [NDPK] → UTP; the simplest answer: UTP and CTP are interconverted primarily through the CDP/UDP pool via NDPK equilibrating nucleoside diphosphates; the specific enzyme producing UTP from CTP (top-down): CTP → CDP → UDP → UTP involves deamination (CTP → UTP via CTP deaminase in some organisms, but mammalian cells: UTP → CTP via CTPS; reverse of CTPS does not readily occur); in mammals, the main interconversion: UTP → [CTPS] → CTP is unidirectional in practice; CTP → UTP would require CDP → UDP → UTP; there is no specific standalone enzyme for this; NDPK is the main interconverter of NDP ↔ NTP
explanation: Pyrimidine nucleotide pool regulation: UMP (from de novo or salvage) → [UMPK/CMPK1] → UDP → [NDPK] → UTP → [CTPS1/2: UTP + Gln + ATP → CTP]; CTP synthase (CTPS) is the committed step to CTP from UTP; feedback: CTP and UTP inhibit CPS II (start of de novo pathway); CTPS is inhibited by CTP (product inhibition). Nucleotide kinases: UMP/CMP kinase (CMPK1, adenylate kinase family): phosphorylates UMP → UDP; also CMP → CDP; NDPK: non-specific NDP → NTP (uses ATP as phosphate donor); essential for maintaining NTP pools. Nucleoside salvage (pyrimidine): uridine + ATP → [UCK1/2, uridine kinase] → UMP; cytidine + ATP → [UCK1/2] → CMP; thymidine + ATP → [TK1, thymidine kinase 1, S-phase inducible] → dTMP → [DTYMK] → dTDP → [NDPK] → dTTP; TK1 level in plasma: tumor marker (elevated in rapidly proliferating cancers; used in NHL monitoring); TMPK (dTMP kinase, DTYMK): phosphorylates dTMP → dTDP; important in 5-FU metabolism: 5-FdUMP inhibits TYMS (thymidylate synthase, TS) → ↓dTMP → ↓dTTP → ↓DNA synthesis; 5-FU also incorporated into RNA (5-FUTP) → impairs RNA function.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the process of beta-oxidation, odd-chain fatty acids ultimately yield which unique product NOT generated from even-chain FA oxidation?
options: Acetyl-CoA (produced by ALL fatty acid beta-oxidation; even odd-chain FAs make acetyl-CoA for all cycles except the last)

Propionyl-CoA: when an odd-chain FA (e.g., C15, C17, C19) undergoes beta-oxidation, each cycle removes a 2-carbon acetyl-CoA unit; when only 3 carbons remain in the final thioester, the last cycle produces one molecule of propionyl-CoA (C3-CoA) instead of two acetyl-CoA molecules; propionyl-CoA is the unique product of odd-chain FA oxidation; propionyl-CoA metabolism: propionyl-CoA → [PCC, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, biotin-dependent] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MMCE, racemase] → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, AdoCbl-dependent] → succinyl-CoA → TCA cycle (anaplerotic substrate, can contribute to gluconeogenesis via OAA); even-chain FA oxidation: yields ONLY acetyl-CoA (+ NADH + FADH2); no propionyl-CoA, no succinyl-CoA, no gluconeogenic precursors (acetyl-CoA cannot be net converted to OAA in mammals [TCA is a cycle; oxaloacetate is regenerated but not formed net from acetyl-CoA due to the cycle stoichiometry — confirmed by the fact that pure ketogenic states produce no net glucose]; thus EVEN-chain fat CANNOT be gluconeogenic in net terms; ODD-chain fat CAN provide net gluconeogenic precursor via propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → OAA)
NADH (NADH is produced in beta-oxidation by L-3-hydroxy-acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, both even and odd chain)

Succinyl-CoA (a downstream product of propionyl-CoA metabolism; but propionyl-CoA is the direct product of odd-chain FA beta-oxidation; succinyl-CoA is downstream, not the direct unique product from beta-oxidation)
explanation: Beta-oxidation energetics: For palmitic acid (C16:0, even-chain): 7 cycles → 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 NADH + 7 FADH2; ATP yield: 8 acetyl-CoA → 8 × 10 = 80 ATP; 7 NADH → 7 × 2.5 = 17.5 ATP; 7 FADH2 → 7 × 1.5 = 10.5 ATP; subtract 2 ATP (activation: palmitate → palmitoyl-CoA by ACSL: uses ATP → AMP + PPi → equivalent to 2 ATP); net: 80 + 17.5 + 10.5 − 2 = 106 ATP. For heptadecanoic acid (C17:0, odd-chain): 7 cycles → 7 acetyl-CoA + 1 propionyl-CoA + 7 NADH + 7 FADH2; propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA via PCC + MMCE + MCM (requires 1 ATP for PCC) → succinyl-CoA → succinate + GTP (substrate-level) → ... overall net. Propionyl-CoA in nutrition: odd-chain FA sources: dairy fat (esp. ruminant milk, C15:0 pentadecanoic acid + C17:0 heptadecanoic acid) and bacterial fermentation in ruminant animals; C15:0 and C17:0 are emerging as beneficial fatty acids (epidemiologically associated with ↓CVD, ↓T2DM, ↓liver disease); proposed as essential fatty acid 'AC16:1' by some (not currently accepted EFA). Propionic acid: SCFA produced by gut bacteria → propionyl-CoA → gluconeogenic → contributes to hepatic glucose synthesis; elevated in propionic acidemia (PCC deficiency) and methylmalonic acidemia (MCM deficiency) → toxic at high levels. Branched-chain FA oxidation: methyl-branched FA (e.g., phytanic acid = 3,7,11,15-tetramethylhexadecanoic acid) cannot undergo direct beta-oxidation at C3 (methyl branch blocks) → requires alpha-oxidation first (in peroxisomes: phytanic acid → [PHYH, phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, removes 1 carbon + CO2] → pristanic acid → then beta-oxidation); PHYH deficiency → Refsum disease.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is precipitated by drugs that induce CYP450 enzymes. The biochemical basis involves:
options: Inhibition of ALA dehydratase (ALA-D) by heavy metals such as lead — this is lead poisoning / ALA-D deficiency porphyria; NOT AIP

Induction of ALA synthase 1 (ALAS1) leading to increased δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG) accumulation above the block: AIP (the most common acute hepatic porphyria; AD, HMBS gene, chromosome 11q23.3) is caused by ~50% ↓ in hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMB synthase, also called porphobilinogen deaminase [PBGD]); normally, the hepatic heme synthetic pathway is regulated by the rate-limiting enzyme ALAS1 (housekeeping ALA synthase), which is feedback-inhibited by free heme; precipitating factors (drugs that induce CYP450s: barbiturates, rifampicin, griseofulvin, sulfonamides, hormones [estrogen/progesterone], alcohol, starvation, infection): → ↑CYP enzyme synthesis → ↑hepatic heme demand → ↓free heme pool → DEREPRESSION of ALAS1 (heme normally inhibits ALAS1 transcription [via Bach1-HRE pathway] + import into mitochondria [feedback at mTF/TOM pathway] + mRNA stability) → ↑ALAS1 → ↑ALA synthesis → ↑PBG → accumulate proximal to the partial HMBS deficiency block → ↑ALA + ↑PBG excreted in urine (Port-wine or tea-colored urine); ALA + PBG are directly neurotoxic (mechanisms: ALA is structurally similar to GABA → may act as a GABA agonist → neurological effects; ↑ROS from ALA oxidation; ↓pyridoxal phosphate availability); clinical: abdominal pain (the most common presenting symptom) + neuropsychiatric (motor neuropathy, psychiatric) + autonomic (hypertension, tachycardia, hyponatremia [SIADH]); diagnosis: ↑urinary PBG during attack (Watson-Schwartz test: Ehrlich reagent [p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde] + urine → red complex with PBG; non-specific — uroporphobilin also positive); definitive: quantitative urinary PBG + ALA by HPLC; treatment: IV glucose (↓ALAS1 via ↑glucose → carbohydrate loading suppresses ALAS1) + IV hemin (Panhematin, Normosang: exogenous heme → ↑free heme → ↓ALAS1 derepression → ↓ALA/PBG); givosiran (Alnylam, siRNA targeting ALAS1 mRNA → ↓ALAS1 → ↓ALA/PBG; approved for recurrent acute attacks)
Depletion of free heme due to increased ferrochelatase activity, causing substrate accumulation

Inhibition of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase causing accumulation of uroporphyrin — this is Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT): UROD deficiency → ↑uroporphyrin I → photosensitivity + fragile bullous skin lesions; triggers: alcohol, estrogens, iron overload, HCV, HBV; treatment: phlebotomy + hydroxychloroquine
explanation: Porphyria overview: Acute (neurological/abdominal): ALL due to accumulation of ALA + PBG; dark/port-wine urine with attack; ALAS1 induction + hepatic CYP induction + female hormones trigger. AIP (HMBS, PBGD): most common acute; AD; PBG accumulates (highest ↑). ALA-D deficiency porphyria (ALAD): rarest; AR; ALA accumulates; similar to lead poisoning. Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP, CPOX/coproporphyrinogen oxidase): AD; ALA + PBG + coproporphyrin III. Variegate porphyria (VP, PPOX/protoporphyrinogen oxidase): AD; ALA + PBG + protoporphyrin IX; skin blistering ALSO present (because PPOX produces proto-porphyrin IX which is photosensitizing). Cutaneous (photosensitizing): no elevated ALA/PBG; porphyrins accumulate → absorb 400-410nm (Soret band) → excited → ROS → skin damage. PCT (UROD): ↑uroporphyrin; blistering photosensitivity; most common overall porphyria. EPP (erythropoietic PP, FECH): ↑protoporphyrin IX in RBCs/stool; painful (NOT blistering) photosensitivity (burning/stinging immediately on sun exposure); X-linked protoporphyria (XLPP, ALAS2 gain-of-function). Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP, UROS): ↑uroporphyrin I; severe blistering + mutilation + red fluorescent teeth (erythrodontia) + hypertrichosis; allelic to adult-type EPP in some families. Heme synthesis pathway (mnemonic: Succinyl-CoA + Gly → ALA → PBG → hydroxymethylbilane → uro'gen III → copro'gen III → proto'gen IX → PPIX → Heme): ALA synthase (ALAS1 hepatic, ALAS2 erythroid, mito, PLP + succinyl-CoA + Gly) → ALA dehydratase (ALAD, cytoplasmic, Zn2+, 2ALA → PBG) → HMB synthase/PBGD (4 PBG → hydroxymethylbilane) → uroporphyrinogen III synthase (UROS) → uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) → coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (CPOX, mito) → protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (PPOX, mito) → ferrochelatase (FECH, mito, inserts Fe2+).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hyperammonemia in ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency leads to increased urinary orotic acid because:
options: Ammonium ions directly stimulate orotic acid synthase activity in the urea cycle

Carbamoyl phosphate produced in excess accumulates in the cytoplasm and enters the pyrimidine synthesis pathway: OTC deficiency is the most common urea cycle enzyme defect (X-linked; OTC catalyzes: carbamoyl-P + Orn → citrulline, the second step of the urea cycle, in the mitochondrial matrix); in OTC deficiency: carbamoyl phosphate (made by CPS I in mitochondria) cannot enter the urea cycle (no OTC) → accumulates in mitochondria → SPILLS INTO THE CYTOPLASM; in the cytoplasm: excess carbamoyl-P → enters the de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway: carbamoyl-P + Asp → [ATCase, step 2, in CAD complex] → carbamoylaspartate → → eventually → OMP → UMP → further metabolism; the increased flux of carbamoyl-P into pyrimidine synthesis overwhelms the pathway → intermediate orotate accumulates + is excreted as orotic acid in urine; this explains why OTC deficiency presents with ↑urinary orotic acid (unlike CPS I deficiency, which is UPSTREAM of carbamoyl-P synthesis → LOW carbamoyl-P → no overflow into pyrimidine pathway → NORMAL or LOW urinary orotic acid — this distinguishes CPS I deficiency from OTC deficiency biochemically); diagnostic significance: OTC deficiency: ↑urinary orotic acid + ↑glutamine (as NH3 is detoxified by glutamine synthetase in brain → ↑Gln) + ↑urine uracil + ↑uridine; CPS I deficiency: normal/low urinary orotic acid; N-acetylglutamate synthetase (NAGS) deficiency: same as CPS I (cannot activate CPS I → ↓carbamoyl-P → normal orotic acid)
Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase is inhibited by excess ammonia, causing orotate backup
Ornithine depletion leads to reduced urea cycle activity causing alternative pyrimidine synthesis upregulation
explanation: Urea cycle defects (UCDs) — key differentials: All UCDs: ↑blood ammonia + ↑glutamine + ↓BUN (blood urea nitrogen, because urea synthesis is impaired → ↓urea in blood). Neonatal presentation (within 24-48h): profound hyperammonemia → encephalopathy → coma → respiratory alkalosis (NH3 stimulates respiratory center → ↓PaCO2) → later metabolic acidosis. Urinary orotic acid: ELEVATED: OTC deficiency (X-linked, most common UCD; carbamoyl-P spills into cytoplasm → ↑pyrimidine synthesis → ↑orotic acid); AS (argininosuccinate synthetase) deficiency (citrullinemia type I) — some ↑OA; AL (argininosuccinate lyase) deficiency (argininosuccinic aciduria) — variable OA elevation; arginase deficiency — moderate ↑OA. NORMAL or LOW orotic acid: CPS I deficiency; NAGS deficiency (NAG synthetase; OTC normally needs CPS I to supply carbamoyl-P; NAGS makes N-acetylglutamate, the essential allosteric activator of CPS I; NAGS deficiency → ↓NAG → ↓CPS I → ↓carbamoyl-P → low OA + hyperammonemia; treatment: N-carbamoylglutamate [Carbaglu] is a NAG analog that activates CPS I directly, bypassing NAGS deficiency — effective treatment); transient hyperammonemia of newborn (THAN): benign, mechanism unclear (↑shunting?), large right-to-left shunt → resolves; not enzymatic. OTC presentation: males severely affected (hemizygous); females: carrier → mild symptomatic (heterozygous; degree of symptoms depends on X-inactivation pattern in liver; most carriers asymptomatic; ~15% of female carriers have clinically significant disease); trigger: high protein meal, catabolic stress, illness, surgery; treatment: nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate: Gly + benzoate → hippurate [excreted, removing 1 N]; sodium phenylbutyrate [→ phenylacetate → conjugates with Gln → phenylacetylglutamine, excreted, removing 2 N per molecule] = Ravicti/glycerol phenylbutyrate) + Arg/citrulline supplementation (replenishes cycle intermediates) + low-protein diet + liver transplant (corrects enzymatic defect).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Insulin stimulates the uptake of glucose in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle primarily by:
options: Increasing the affinity of the glucose transporter for glucose (insulin does not change the intrinsic affinity [Km] of GLUT4 for glucose; it increases the number of transporters on the cell surface)

Activating the Na+/glucose cotransporter on the cell membrane (Na+/glucose cotransporters [SGLT1, SGLT2] are in the intestine and kidney; SGLT1 in intestine absorbs dietary glucose; SGLT2 in renal proximal tubule; they are NOT the primary insulin-responsive transporters in muscle/adipose)
