Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVD): isovaleric acidemia (IVA) is caused by autosomal recessive deficiency of IVD (isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase), which catalyzes the third step of leucine catabolism: isovaleryl-CoA → 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA (a mitochondrial FAD-linked ACAD, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase); when IVD is deficient: isovaleryl-CoA accumulates → isovaleric acid (IVA) secreted in sweat and urine → characteristic 'sweaty feet' or 'cheesy feet' odor (isovaleric acid has pungent, sweaty odor with perceived low threshold ~0.03 mg/L); leucine catabolism: Leu → 2-oxoisocaproate → [BCKDC] → isovaleryl-CoA → [IVD] → 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA → [3-MCC] → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA → → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; diagnosis: ↑urinary isovalerylglycine (IVG, major metabolite, pathognomonic; glycine N-acyltransferase [GLYAT] conjugates isovaleryl-CoA → IVG when IVD is absent) + ↑3-hydroxyisovaleric acid; urine: positive Ehrlich test (volatile keto acids) + Beutler test may be positive; NBS: ↑C5-carnitine (isovalerylcarnitine, C5-acylcarnitine, the ester of carnitine + isovalerate); treatment: low-leucine diet + glycine supplementation (traps isovaleryl-CoA as IVG → ↑urinary excretion, reduces toxicity) + carnitine supplementation (prevents secondary carnitine depletion)
explanation: BCAA catabolism disorders summary (NEET-relevant): MSUD (Maple syrup urine disease): BCKDC (E1α=BCKDHA, E1β=BCKDHB, E2=DBT, E3=DLD); accumulates: Val→ 2-keto-isovalerate, Ile→2-keto-3-methylvalerate, Leu→2-ketoisocaproate; toxic: Leu >> Ile > Val; odor: maple syrup/burnt caramel (from sotolon, a ketone derived from 2-ketoisocaproate); treatment: BCAA-restricted formula + leucine monitoring; liver transplant (corrects enzyme defect); thiamine (B1): B1-responsive MSUD rare. Propionic acidemia (PA): PCC (PCCA + PCCB); ↑C3-carnitine (propionylcarnitine); features: neonatal acidosis + hyperammonemia + cardiomyopathy + prolonged QTc + secondary mitochondrial dysfunction. Methylmalonic acidemia (MMA): MCM (MMUT) or cbl disorders; ↑MMA + ↑propionate; features: similar to PA; renal failure common; pancreatitis; liver transplant helps. Isovaleric acidemia (IVA): IVD; ↑C5-carnitine + ↑IVG; sweaty feet odor; more favorable outcome with treatment. Glutaric acidemia type I (GA1): GCDH; Lys + Trp catabolism → glutaryl-CoA + 3-OH-glutaryl-CoA accumulate → striatal (caudate/putamen) injury during febrile illness (crisis) → dyskinesia + dystonia despite normal initial neurology; macrocephaly (↑CSF space due to frontotemporal atrophy); treatment: prophylactic emergency regimen during illness (↑glucose + ↑carnitine), low-lysine diet. GA2 (multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, MADD): ETF/ETFDH mutations → all FAD-linked ACAD deficient → sweaty feet + multiple organic acids + hypoglycemia + myopathy; riboflavin-responsive MADD (RRMAD): responds to riboflavin supplements.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The biosynthesis of lecithin (phosphatidylcholine, PC) via the Kennedy pathway requires activation of choline. What is the rate-limiting enzyme?
options: Choline kinase (CK, CHKA/CHKB): phosphorylates choline → phosphocholine; this is the FIRST step but is NOT rate-limiting
CDP-choline:1,2-diacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase (CPT1, not the mitochondrial carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1!): catalyzes the LAST step (CDP-choline + DAG → PC + CMP); not rate-limiting

CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase (CCT, PCYT1A/PCYT1B): the rate-limiting enzyme of the CDP-choline (Kennedy) pathway for PC synthesis; CCT (also called CT, CCTα/β): catalyzes phosphocholine + CTP → CDP-choline + PPi; this is the COMMITTED, RATE-LIMITING step; CCT regulation: CCT is the key regulatory enzyme; it is activated by: (1) lipid binding: CCT exists in two forms: soluble inactive (cytoplasmicpool) and membrane-bound active (when cells need more PC); ↓PC in membranes → CCT translocates to ER membrane → conformational change → activation (lipid activation domain of CCT [LD domain] binds anionic lipids + DAG → activates); (2) phosphorylation: some evidence that phosphorylation can inactivate CCT; (3) PC: end-product PC inhibits CCT (via ↑PC/PE ratio in ER → dislodges CCT from ER membrane → inactive); CCT expression: mTORC1 (via LIPIN1 phosphorylation → ↑phosphatidic acid signaling → ↑CCT activity); clinical: lung surfactant deficiency (respiratory distress syndrome of newborn, RDS): surfactant = DPPC (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) main component; CCT activity low in premature lung → ↓surfactant; surfactant replacement therapy (beractant, poractant alfa, calfactant) is standard care for RDS; CCT-deficient mice: impaired surfactant synthesis + neonatal respiratory failure
Phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase II (PCYT2): this is the rate-limiting enzyme for PE (phosphatidylethanolamine) synthesis via the CDP-ethanolamine (Lands) pathway, not for PC
explanation: Phosphatidylcholine (PC) synthesis pathways: Kennedy (CDP-choline) pathway (major, liver + most cells): Choline → [CK] → phosphocholine → [CCT, rate-limiting] → CDP-choline → [CPT1, also called CEPT1 for ethanolamine] → PC; the PC made has various acyl chain compositions depending on the DAG substrate used. PEMT (phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase) pathway (liver-specific): PE + 3 SAM → [PEMT, 3 sequential methylations] → PC; requires SAM as methyl donor; accounts for ~30% of hepatic PC in humans; PEMT expression upregulated by estrogen (explains why premenopausal women have higher PEMT → more PC → more HDL; menopause → ↓PEMT → ↓PC → risk of metabolic liver disease); PEMT-knockout mice: NASH (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis) when fed a choline-deficient diet. PC functions: major membrane phospholipid (~40% of animal cell lipid bilayer); lung surfactant (DPPC = dipalmitoyl-PC, two saturated C16 chains → high surface tension-lowering efficacy); bile (PC required for bile solubilization of cholesterol [ABCB4/MDR3 flips PC to bile canalicular lumen] → prevents bile salt toxicity to bile ducts; MDR3 mutations → progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3 [PFIC3]); lipoprotein surface; pro-inflammatory (PC-derived arachidonate for eicosanoids via PLA2) and anti-inflammatory (PC-derived lipid mediators). DPPC (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine): the 'ideal' surfactant molecule; two saturated chains pack tightly at air-water interface when compressed (in expiration) → low surface tension at alveolar level → prevents alveolar collapse; surfactant also contains SP-B (surfactant protein B, required for DPPC monolayer function) + SP-C + SP-A + SP-D (collectins: innate immunity in lung).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Iron absorption in the intestine is regulated by which liver-derived peptide?
options: Transferrin: the iron transport protein in plasma; synthesized by liver; captures Fe3+ (transferrin receptor [TfR1] → endocytosis → release at pH 5 in endosome); NOT a regulator of intestinal iron absorption

Ferritin: the iron storage protein (24-subunit cage: heavy [H] + light [L] chains); stores Fe3+ as ferrihydrite; serum ferritin reflects body iron stores (1 ng/mL = ~10 mg stored iron); NOT the hormonal regulator

Hemojuvelin (HJV, HFE2): HJV is a BMP co-receptor expressed on hepatocytes, skeletal muscle, heart; enhances BMP2/BMP6 signaling → ↑hepcidin; HJV mutations → juvenile hemochromatosis (HFE2 hemochromatosis = type 2A): severely ↓hepcidin → massive iron overload in young adults; BUT HJV is NOT the active regulatory peptide — hepcidin IS

Hepcidin (HAMP gene, chromosome 19q13.12): hepcidin is the 25-amino acid peptide hormone synthesized by HEPATOCYTES that CONTROLS iron absorption and recycling; mechanism: hepcidin binds ferroportin (FPN1/SLC40A1, the ONLY known mammalian iron exporter) on: (1) duodenal enterocytes (apical DMT1 absorbs Fe2+; basolateral FPN1 exports Fe2+ into portal blood [with hephaestin as ferroxidase converting Fe2+ → Fe3+ for transferrin binding]); (2) macrophages (FPN1 exports Fe recycled from phagocytosed RBCs); (3) hepatocyte stellate cells; hepcidin → FPN1 → [JAK2 phosphorylation of FPN1] → ubiquitination + internalization → lysosomal degradation of FPN1 → ↓iron export → ↑intracellular iron (trapped in enterocytes, macrophages); regulation of hepcidin: ↑iron (HFE + TfR2 + HJV sense transferrin saturation and BMP6 [from liver sinusoidal cells] → SMAD1/5/8 signaling) → ↑hepcidin; ↑inflammatory (IL-6 → JAK2-STAT3 → ↑hepcidin) → anemia of chronic disease/inflammation (↑hepcidin → ↓iron export → ↓iron for erythropoiesis); hypoxia + EPO → ↓hepcidin (via ERFE [erythroferrone] from erythroblasts → inhibits hepcidin) → ↑iron absorption for erythropoiesis; hereditary hemochromatosis: HFE (C282Y/H63D) → ↓hepcidin → ↑iron absorption → parenchymal iron overload
explanation: Hepcidin and iron homeostasis: Iron regulation axis: BMP6 (from liver sinusoidal endothelium, most important hepcidin inducer) + BMP2 → BMPR (BMPR1A/B + BMPR2) + HJV (co-receptor) → SMAD1/5/8 phosphorylation → SMAD4 complex → nuclear translocation → HAMP (hepcidin) gene transcription; also: HFE + TfR1/TfR2: when transferrin saturation is high → TfR1 is occupied by Tf-Fe → HFE displaced from TfR1 → HFE binds TfR2 → HFE-TfR2 complex → enhances BMP-SMAD signaling → ↑hepcidin; mutations: HFE (C282Y: most common, ~85% of classic hemochromatosis; homozygous → ↓hepcidin → ↑iron) → type 1 HH (HFE hemochromatosis); TfR2 mutations → type 3 HH; HJV mutations → type 2A HH (severe, juvenile onset); HAMP (hepcidin) mutations → type 2B HH (severe); FPN1 loss-of-function mutations (type 4A HH, ferroportin disease: FPN1 cannot export iron → iron in macrophages/enterocytes, not hepatocytes; relatively benign); FPN1 gain-of-function mutations (type 4B HH: FPN1 resistant to hepcidin-mediated degradation → ↑FPN1 activity → ↑iron export → iron in hepatocytes, similar to classic HH). Anemia of inflammation (AI): ↑IL-6 → ↑hepcidin → ↓FPN1 on macrophages → macrophages retain iron from phagocytosed RBCs → ↑macrophage iron + ↓serum iron + ↓transferrin saturation → ↓iron for erythropoiesis + ↑EPO resistance + ↓RBC lifespan → normocytic/microcytic normochromic/hypochromic anemia; treatment: treat underlying disease; anti-IL-6 agents (tocilizumab, sarilumab) may help in RA-associated AI; experimental: anti-hepcidin (PTG-300, interferes with hepcidin) or mini-hepcidin agonists for iron overload disorders.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the glycolytic pathway, the regulatory enzyme fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP) acts by:
options: Inhibiting phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) and activating fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1) (this is the OPPOSITE of F-2,6-BP's actual action; F-2,6-BP activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1)
Activating pyruvate kinase (PK-L) in liver (PK-L is activated by F-1,6-BP [feedforward activation], NOT by F-2,6-BP; insulin → dephosphorylation of PK-L → active; these are different mechanisms)

Allosterically activating phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) and inhibiting fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1), thereby promoting glycolysis and inhibiting gluconeogenesis: F-2,6-BP is a potent allosteric activator of PFK-1 (the committed step of glycolysis) AND an allosteric inhibitor of FBPase-1 (the corresponding gluconeogenic enzyme); the dual action means F-2,6-BP simultaneously accelerates glycolysis AND blocks gluconeogenesis (reciprocal regulation); synthesis of F-2,6-BP: a bifunctional enzyme, PFK-2/FBPase-2 (encoded by PFKFB genes, 4 isoforms: PFKFB1-4): PFK-2 domain: phosphorylates F6P → F-2,6-BP (using ATP); FBPase-2 domain: hydrolyzes F-2,6-BP → F6P; PFKFB regulation: liver isoform (PFKFB1): PKA phosphorylates Ser32 → activates FBPase-2 domain → ↓F-2,6-BP → glucagon effect; dephosphorylation (by PP1/PP2A) → PFK-2 domain active → ↑F-2,6-BP → insulin/fed effect; heart/muscle isoform (PFKFB3/4): different regulation; PFKFB3 (heart): PKA doesn't phosphorylate FBPase-2 similarly; PFKFB3 overexpressed in cancer → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑glycolysis → Warburg effect; PFKFB3 inhibitor (3PO) → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↓cancer cell glycolysis → experimental anticancer target

Acting as a cofactor for glucokinase (GK) to enhance glucose phosphorylation (F-2,6-BP has no cofactor role for glucokinase; glucokinase/HKIV is regulated by GKRP [glucokinase regulatory protein] which binds F6P and F-1,6-BP)
explanation: F-2,6-BP physiology and pharmacology: Discovery: Henri-Géry Hers (1980) discovered F-2,6-BP as an activator of PFK-1 when investigating why glucagon decreased hepatic F-2,6-BP and reduced glycolysis. Tissue roles: Liver: main regulator of glycolysis vs gluconeogenesis; insulin/feeding → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑glycolysis; glucagon/fasting → ↓F-2,6-BP → ↑gluconeogenesis. Heart: PFKFB3 constitutively high PFK-2 activity (not PKA-regulated) → high cardiac F-2,6-BP → supports high glycolytic flux even aerobically (cardiac muscle ~30% glucose utilization normally). Cancer: PFKFB3 overexpressed in many cancers (hypoxia → HIF-1α → ↑PFKFB3 transcription; oncogenes → ↑PFKFB3 protein stability) → ↑F-2,6-BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis → ↑lactate + ↑biosynthetic precursors → Warburg effect. Fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase is distinct from FBPase-1: FBPase-1 (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase): hydrolyzs F-1,6-BP → F6P (step 3-reverse in gluconeogenesis); inhibited by AMP + F-2,6-BP; required for gluconeogenesis. FBPase-2 (within PFKFB bifunctional enzyme): hydrolyzes F-2,6-BP → F6P; activated by glucagon (PKA phosphorylation in liver). FBPase-1 deficiency: rare; impaired gluconeogenesis → severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis (especially during fasting or high-fat/protein diet; Cori cycle fails → lactate accumulates); similar to GSD but distinct (glycogenolysis intact; glycogen stores normal → short-term glucose OK; impaired with prolonged fasting). FBP1 (FBPase-1) as tumor suppressor: LOH/epigenetic silencing in kidney, liver, colon cancers → removes gluconeogenic brake → metabolic reprogramming toward glycolysis (Warburg).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The mechanism by which atractyloside poisons cells involves inhibition of which mitochondrial transporter?
options: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) — blocked by rotenone, piericidin A; not atractyloside
Cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III) — blocked by antimycin A; not atractyloside

The ATP/ADP translocase (ANT, adenine nucleotide translocator, SLC25A4/ANT1, SLC25A5/ANT2, SLC25A6/ANT3): atractyloside (a plant toxin from Atractylis gummifera, Mediterranean weed) is a classic inhibitor of the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT); ANT is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyzes the strict 1:1 exchange: matrix ADP (ADP3-) for intermembrane space ATP (ATP4-); this electronegative exchange is driven by the inside-negative membrane potential (ΔΨ = -180 mV) → thermodynamically favorable to import ADP3- and export ATP4-; without ANT function: ADP cannot enter the matrix → ATP synthase has no ADP substrate → OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION STOPS (despite intact ETC + proton gradient) → ETC backs up → ↑NADH/NAD+ → ↓TCA → ↑ROS → cell death; atractyloside binds ANT from the cytoplasmic (IMS) side → 'c-conformation' of ANT (open to IMS) → locks it → cannot transition to 'm-conformation' (open to matrix) → ADP cannot enter; bongkrekic acid: another ANT inhibitor but stabilizes the 'm-conformation' (open to matrix); both block net exchange; clinical: Atractylis gummifera poisoning → acute hepatorenal failure (especially in North Africa where children eat the candy-tasting thistle) → identical to acute Amanita phalloides poisoning biochemically (both disrupt OXPHOS); ANT and disease: ANT1 (SLC25A4) mutations → autosomal dominant PEO (progressive external ophthalmoplegia) with mitochondrial myopathy + multiple mtDNA deletions (ANT1 dysfunction → imbalanced dNTP pools → mtDNA replication errors → deletions)
F1Fo-ATP synthase (Complex V) — blocked by oligomycin (F0 subunit pore); not atractyloside
explanation: Mitochondrial transport proteins (SLC25 family, inner mitochondrial membrane): Adenine nucleotide translocator (ANT, SLC25A4/A5/A6): ADP/ATP 1:1 exchange; inhibitors: atractyloside (c-conformation lock), bongkrekic acid (m-conformation lock), carboxyatractyloside (more potent, same mechanism as atractyloside). Phosphate carrier (PiC, SLC25A3): Pi + H+ symport into matrix (for ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi); or Pi/OH- antiport. Pyruvate carrier (MPC1/2): pyruvate import into matrix; inhibited by UK5099. Malate-α-ketoglutarate antiporter (OGC, SLC25A11): part of malate-aspartate shuttle. Glutamate-aspartate antiporter (AGC1/2, SLC25A12/13): part of malate-aspartate shuttle; AGC2 = citrin (SLC25A13 deficiency → citrin deficiency / NICCD / CTLN2). Citrate carrier (CTP, SLC25A1): citrate export for fatty acid synthesis; inhibited by 1,2,3-benzenetricarboxylate (BTC). Uncoupling proteins (UCP1/2/3): proton leak; UCP1 in brown adipose → thermogenesis. Carnitine/acylcarnitine translocase (SLC25A20, CACT): acylcarnitine/carnitine exchange; CACT deficiency → LCFA oxidation defect → hypoglycemia + cardiomyopathy + fatal neonatal presentation. Ornithine translocase (SLC25A15, ORC1; SLC25A2, ORC2): ornithine import into matrix (for OTC step of urea cycle); ORC1 deficiency → hyperammonemia-hyperornithinemia-homocitrullinemia (HHH syndrome, also called OAT-related? No: ORC1 is the ornithine carrier; OAT = ornithine aminotransferase is a different enzyme making Glu-5-semialdehyde; HHH: urea cycle block at OTC [no Orn in matrix → Orn does not enter mito → citrulline cannot be made] + homocitrulline formed from Lys carbamoylation as overflow). 2-oxoglutarate (OGC/SLC25A11) and dicarboxylate carrier (DIC/SLC25A10): malate-aspartate shuttle components.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The anti-thyroid drug propylthiouracil (PTU) has which additional mechanism of action compared to methimazole (MMI)?
options: PTU but not MMI blocks TSH receptor on thyroid follicular cells (both drugs are actively transported into thyroid cells and block thyroid peroxidase; neither blocks TSH receptor)
PTU but not MMI inhibits thyroid peroxidase at higher doses (BOTH drugs inhibit thyroid peroxidase [TPO]; this is the shared mechanism, not the additional one for PTU)

PTU inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 by inhibiting deiodinase, whereas methimazole does not: T4 (thyroxine, prohormone) → T3 (triiodothyronine, active) via type 1 deiodinase (DIO1, in liver/kidney/thyroid) and type 2 deiodinase (DIO2, in brain/pituitary/BAT/heart); both DIO1 and DIO2 are selenoproteins (contain Sec [selenocysteine]) that catalyze inner-ring 5'-deiodination (remove iodine from 5'-position of T4 outer ring → T3) and outer-ring (5) deiodination (→ rT3, reverse T3, inactive); PTU mechanism: PTU (6-propylthiouracil) → inhibits DIO1 (type 1 deiodinase) in liver/kidney/thyroid → ↓peripheral T4 → T3 conversion → ↓T3 levels (rapid effect, within hours to days) → useful in thyroid storm (needed to rapidly ↓T3 levels); MMI does NOT inhibit deiodinases; both drugs: inhibit thyroid peroxidase (TPO) → ↓organification of iodide (↓incorporation of I2/HOI into thyroglobulin Tyr residues) + ↓coupling reaction → ↓T4/T3 synthesis; PTU has an additional advantage in thyroid storm (or severe hyperthyroidism) due to the immediate peripheral conversion block; MMI advantages: once-daily dosing (longer duration), less hepatotoxic (PTU carries higher risk of fulminant hepatic failure, especially in children → MMI preferred for most hyperthyroidism), can use in 2nd/3rd trimester of pregnancy (PTU in first trimester for thyroid storm/severe Graves' due to reports of MMI causing aplasia cutis/choanal atresia/embryopathy → preference shifts after first trimester); both cross placenta (PTU slightly less)

PTU but not MMI causes propylthiouracil-specific thyroid cancer risk by damaging thyroid cell DNA (propylthiouracil has no established thyroid cancer mechanism; the main adverse effects are agranulocytosis [rare but serious, check CBC for fever/sore throat] + ANCA-associated vasculitis [PTU more than MMI] + hepatotoxicity [PTU])
explanation: Thyroid hormone synthesis and pharmacology: Synthesis: I- → thyroid → [Pendrin, SLC26A4, in follicular cell apical membrane: I- efflux into colloid] + [NIS, Na+/I- symporter, SLC5A5: basolateral, TSH → ↑NIS expression → I- uptake] → in colloid: I- → [TPO + H2O2 from DUOX1/2] → HOI/I2 → [TPO, organification] → MIT (monoiodotyrosine) + DIT (diiodotyrosine) on thyroglobulin (Tg) → [TPO, coupling] → T3 + T4 within Tg → Tg endocytosed → lysosomes → Tg proteolysis → MIT + DIT + T3 + T4 released → MIT + DIT → [DEHAL, dehalogenase] → I- recycled → T3 + T4 secreted; Wolff-Chaikoff effect: sudden high-dose iodide → transient ↓TPO + ↓NIS → ↓thyroid hormone synthesis (protective autoregulation); escape: ↓NIS → ↓I- uptake → overcome inhibition → normal synthesis resumes (~1-2 weeks); clinical use: Lugol's iodine (10% KI) before thyroid surgery → ↓vascularity (involution) + transient ↓hormone synthesis via Wolff-Chaikoff. Pharmacological targets: PTU + MMI: TPO inhibition (↓organification + ↓coupling); PTU additionally: DIO1 inhibition; lithium: ↓Tg proteolysis (↓T3/T4 secretion from Tg) + ↓coupling; historically used for refractory hyperthyroidism; excess iodide (Lugol's, amiodarone): Wolff-Chaikoff + Jod-Basedow (rapid availability of I for synthesis in autonomous nodules); beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol): ↓sympathetic symptoms (palpitations, tremor, heat intolerance) + propranolol also inhibits DIO1 (like PTU, but less potent; minor T4→T3 conversion block); cholestyramine: binds T4 in gut → ↓enterohepatic recirculation → ↓T4 in blood (adjunct in severe hyperthyroidism).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Sickle cell disease results from a single amino acid substitution in hemoglobin. The mutation is:
options: Glu → Lys at position 6 of the β-globin chain (Lys is a different basic amino acid; sickle hemoglobin HbS has Glu → Val, not Lys)
Val → Glu at position 6 of the β-globin chain (this is the reverse substitution; HbS changes Glu → Val, not Val → Glu)

Glu6Val in the β-globin chain: sickle cell disease (SCD) is caused by a single nucleotide change in the HBB gene (chromosome 11p15.4): normal: codon 6 = GAG (Glu, glutamic acid); mutant: codon 6 = GTG (Val, valine); substitution Glu → Val: the normally negatively-charged, hydrophilic glutamate (with a carboxyl-containing side chain exposed on the surface of the β-chain) is replaced by the uncharged, hydrophobic valine; this creates a 'sticky patch' on the surface of the deoxy-HbS β-chain that fits into a complementary hydrophobic pocket on the β-chain of another deoxy-HbS molecule → end-to-end polymer formation → HbS polymerization → sickling of RBCs; the key factor: sickling occurs ONLY in the DEOXY state (deoxygenation → T-state Hb conformation exposes the Val6 sticky patch; oxygenation → R-state → conformational change masks the Val6 → polymers dissolve → sickling reversible); HbF (α2γ2): γ-chains do NOT have the hydrophobic pocket complementary to the Val6 sticky patch → HbF DILUTES HbS polymers → ↓sickling → basis for HbF induction therapy (hydroxyurea → ↑HbF [at least 20% HbF → significant clinical benefit → ↓sickling, ↓crises, ↑life expectancy])
Gly β6 Asp: this is the HbC mutation? No — HbC has Glu6Lys (β6: Glu → Lys); HbD-Punjab: β121 Glu → Gln; HbE: β26 Glu → Lys; the Asp substitution at β6 is a different variant
explanation: Hemoglobin variants — key exam facts: HbA (normal adult): α2β2; HbA2: α2δ2 (~2.5%); HbF: α2γ2 (fetal, predominant until 6 months postnatally; persists in thalassemia + sickle cell). HbS (sickle): β6 Glu→Val; heterozygous (AS, sickle trait): 25-40% HbS → mild hypoxia can sickle at papillary vein level → concentrated urine defect (hyposthenuria) + hematuria; homozygous (SS): SCD. HbC: β6 Glu→Lys; mild hemolysis; HbSC disease (compound heterozygote HbS+HbC): intermediate SCD (proliferative retinopathy + aseptic necrosis of bone more common in SC than SS). HbE: β26 Glu→Lys; mild hemolysis; HbE/β-thalassemia: severe disease (common in SE Asia). HbH: β4 tetramers → from 3-gene α-thalassemia deletion → unstable, oxidant-sensitive → Heinz body hemolytic anemia. Hb Barts: γ4 → 4-gene α-thal deletion → lethal hydrops fetalis → all hemoglobin is Barts → very high O2 affinity → no O2 delivery → death in utero or immediately postpartum. Molecular diagnosis: HbS: restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) with MstII (DdeI): normal HbA has MstII site within codon 6 region; HbS mutation destroys MstII site → different restriction pattern; or PCR + allele-specific oligonucleotide hybridization. SCD treatment: Hydroxyurea (HU): ↑HbF (mechanism: ↑γ-globin mRNA partly via DNA methylation changes + cell-cycle effects on erythroid progenitors → ↑BFU-E + CFU-E expressing γ-chain); also ↓WBC + ↓platelet activation + ↑NO production → multi-mechanism benefit; Voxelotor (Oxbryta): HbS polymerization inhibitor (increases HbS-O2 affinity in R-state → ↓deoxy-HbS → ↓polymerization); Crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin mAb): ↓RBC-endothelial adhesion → ↓pain crises; L-glutamine (Endari): ↓oxidative stress in RBCs; Gene therapy: Lentiglobin (bluebird bio): lentiviral vector encoding anti-sickling HbA^T87Q → ex vivo HSC transduction + autologous transplant → curative approaches; CRISPR/Cas9 + base editing: reactivate γ-globin (BCL11A enhancer deletion) → ↑HbF → functional cure for SCD + β-thalassemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In VLDL assembly in hepatocytes, the protein MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) is essential for:
options: Loading VLDL particles with cholesterol esters in the plasma (MTP acts in the ER LUMEN, not in plasma; it is essential for INITIAL lipid loading during VLDL assembly in ER, not in plasma)
Enabling the fusion of nascent VLDL particles with lipid droplets in the cytoplasm (this is a later step [Golgi → lipid droplet fusion] not dependent on MTP; MTP acts in the ER lumen)

Transferring lipids (TG, phospholipids, cholesterol ester) to nascent ApoB-100 in the ER lumen, enabling VLDL particle formation: MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, encoded by MTTP gene) is a heterodimer of MTP (97 kDa, unique lipid transfer subunit) + protein disulfide isomerase (PDI, 55 kDa, ER resident protein that also has chaperone activity); MTP is localized to the lumen of the rough ER (rER) and smooth ER; function: transfers lipids from the ER membrane to nascent ApoB-100 during its translation and translocation into the ER lumen; mechanism: ApoB-100 is a 4,536-aa protein that is co-translationally inserted into the ER lumen; as the N-terminal β-α1 domain of ApoB-100 emerges into the ER lumen, MTP engages ApoB-100 → transfers TG, CE, and phospholipids from the ER membrane to ApoB-100 → creates a 'primordial VLDL' (lipid-poor nascent particle in ER); without MTP: ApoB-100 cannot acquire lipids → remains unprotected → ubiquitinated + degraded by ERAD (ER-associated degradation, proteasome); clinical: abetalipoproteinemia (MTTP mutations, AR): absence of functional MTP → no VLDL, no chylomicrons (both require ApoB) → ↓LDL + ↓chylomicrons → fat malabsorption + fat-soluble vitamin (ADEK) deficiency → acanthocytosis (thorny RBCs from abnormal membrane lipid composition) + progressive ataxia (spinocerebellar) + retinitis pigmentosa + coagulopathy (Vit K deficiency); treatment: low-fat diet + high-dose fat-soluble vitamins (ADEK); lomitapide: MTTP inhibitor → ↓VLDL secretion → ↓LDL → approved for homozygous FH

Synthesizing the phospholipid monolayer on the VLDL surface (ABCB4 flippase and phospholipid transfer proteins work on VLDL surface but MTP is the lipid transfer protein for initial particle formation)
explanation: VLDL assembly steps: Step 1 (ER, MTP-dependent): ApoB-100 translation → co-translational lipidation by MTP → primordial VLDL particle (~150-200Å) emerges into ER lumen. Step 2 (ER/Golgi transition): primordial VLDL fuses with ER-derived lipid droplet (TGLS, TG-rich lumenal lipid droplets) → VLDL2 (denser, more TG-rich) — this step is MTP-independent but requires separate lipid droplet pool. Step 3 (Golgi): VLDL2 → matures (glycosylation of ApoB-100 → complex sugars added) → sorted into secretory vesicles → exocytosis → plasma. ApoB-100: very long mRNA (14kb, 29 exons) + RNA editing mechanism: in intestine, APOBEC1 (APOBEC enzyme) + A1CF/RBM47 edit ApoB mRNA codon 2153 (CAA → UAA stop) → ApoB-48 (truncated, N-terminal 48% of ApoB-100) → used for chylomicrons (does not bind LDL-R); in liver (in humans): NO APOBEC editing → full-length ApoB-100 → VLDL/LDL (binds LDL-R via C-terminal ligand-binding domain). Apolipoprotein functions: ApoA-I (HDL): activates LCAT; binds ABCA1 (mediates cholesterol efflux). ApoB-100 (VLDL/LDL): LDL-R ligand (C-terminal region); structural backbone of LDL; nonexchangeable. ApoB-48 (chylomicrons): structural; no LDL-R binding. ApoC-I: inhibits CETP; ApoC-II: LPL activator; ApoC-III: LPL inhibitor + ↑TG; ApoE: LRP1 + LDL-R ligand (VLDL remnants, chylomicron remnants); ApoE isoforms: E2 (R158C: weakest LDL-R binding → ↑TG + dysbetalipoproteinemia [type III] in ApoE2/E2 homozygotes); E3 (most common); E4 (strongest risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease: ApoE4 → ↑Aβ aggregation + ↓clearance + ↓synaptic plasticity); APOE ε4 allele: ~3-4× ↑AD risk for heterozygotes; ~8-12× ↑for E4/E4 homozygotes.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme in the electron transport chain is directly inhibited by hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and carbon monoxide (CO)?
options: Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase): inhibited by rotenone (blocks electron transfer from FMNH2 to the Fe-S clusters), piericidin A, barbiturates (amobarbital), MPTP-activated MPP+; NOT primarily blocked by CN- or CO
Complex II (succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase): inhibited by malonate, TTFA; not directly by CN- or CO

Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, CcO): both CN- and CO are classic CcO inhibitors; CcO (Complex IV) contains 4 redox metal centers: CuA (electron entry from reduced cytochrome c), Heme a (electron transfer), Heme a3-CuB (binuclear center = active site where O2 binds and is reduced); CN- (cyanide) binds the Fe3+ form of heme a3 → blocks electron transfer → prevents O2 reduction → no H+ pumping → no ATP → cellular O2 consumption stops → histotoxic hypoxia (tissue cannot use O2 despite adequate delivery); CO (carbon monoxide) binds Fe2+ form of heme a3 (Fe2+ center) → blocks O2 binding + reduction → same endpoint; CO also binds Hb (at Fe2+ → carboxyhemoglobin, COHb → very high affinity, 240× vs O2) + myoglobin + other hemoproteins; treatment: CN- poisoning → hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit: OH-cobalamin → CN-cobalamin → excreted in urine; or Na-thiosulfate [sulfur donor for rhodanese to convert CN- → SCN-] + Na-nitrite [MetHb former → MetHb provides Fe3+ that CN- can bind, displacing from CcO]); CO poisoning → 100% O2 (↓COHb T1/2 from ~5h room air → ~90 min on 100% O2 → ~30 min on 3 atm hyperbaric O2); H2S (hydrogen sulfide): also inhibits CcO (Fe3+ site, like CN-) → same 'histotoxic hypoxia' profile; treat with 100% O2 + nitrite (same as CN-)

Complex III (ubiquinol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase, cytochrome bc1 complex): inhibited by antimycin A (between cytochrome b and c1 in the Q-cycle), myxothiazol, stigmatellin; not by CN- or CO directly
explanation: CcO (Complex IV) biology: Subunit composition: 13 subunits; 3 catalytic subunits (COX1, COX2, COX3) encoded by mtDNA; 10 nuclear-encoded structural subunits; redox prosthetic groups: CuA (in COX2, bimetallic Cu center, ~820 mV E°') + heme a (~60 mV E°') + heme a3 (~380 mV E°') + CuB (adjacent to heme a3 forming the binuclear center); reaction: 4 cyt c (reduced) + O2 + 4H+ → 4 cyt c (oxidized) + 2H2O; pumps 4H+ per O2 (2 per electron pair, since 4e- total). CcO inhibitors: Cyanide (CN-): binds Fe3+ of heme a3 → inhibits only when CcO is in oxidized form (turnover blocked when oxidized form builds up); cytochrome c accumulates in reduced state. CO: binds Fe2+ → similar end result; differential affinity: Hb-CO dissociation constant ~210× higher than Hb-O2; CcO-CO affinity actually lower than Hb-CO but still inhibitory at high CO. H2S: inhibits CcO + Complex I → 'rotten egg' smell; low concentrations → actually physiological gasotransmitter (made by CBS/CGL → vasodilatory). Azide (N3-): also CcO inhibitor. Formate: metabolite of methanol → inhibits CcO (methanol toxicity: methanol → formaldehyde [ADH] → formate [ALDH] → formate inhibits CcO → optic nerve energy failure → blindness; lactic acidosis from ↓OXPHOS; treatment: fomepizole [ADH inhibitor] + ethanol [competitive substrate for ADH] + folic acid [↑formate metabolism → CO2 + H2O via tetrahydrofolate pathway] + HD [removes methanol + formate]). CcO genetic deficiency: many nuclear-encoded assembly factors (COX10, COX15, SCO1, SCO2, SURF1, etc.) → Leigh syndrome + mitochondrial myopathy; SURF1 mutations most common cause of Leigh syndrome from CcO deficiency.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biotin is covalently attached to which amino acid residue on carboxylase enzymes?
options: Serine (serine can have phosphate + other modifications but biotin is NOT attached to Ser)

Cysteine (biotin is not attached to Cys; biotin is not a thioester-linked cofactor; compare to lipoic acid which is attached via amide-thioester to Lys as well, and pantetheine in CoA via phosphodiester)
Threonine (biotin is not N-linked to Thr; Thr can have O-GlcNAc, phosphorylation, etc., but not biotin)

Lysine (ε-amino group): biotin is covalently attached to a specific lysine residue in the active site of all biotin-dependent carboxylases via an amide (isopeptide) bond between the carboxyl group of biotin's valeric acid side chain and the ε-amino group of the target Lys (forming the biotinyl-Lys = biocytin); attachment is catalyzed by holocarboxylase synthetase (HCS, HLCS gene); biocytin has a 'biotinyl arm' (~16Å) that allows the covalently-tethered biotin to swing between the two active sites (CO2 donor site and carboxyl acceptor site) of the carboxylase; biotin-dependent carboxylases (all in mitochondria except ACC): (1) Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): pyruvate + CO2 → OAA; (2) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1, cytoplasm): acetyl-CoA + CO2 → malonyl-CoA; (3) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 2 (ACC2, outer mitochondrial membrane): malonyl-CoA (inhibitor of CPT-I); (4) Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC, PCCA + PCCB): propionyl-CoA + CO2 → methylmalonyl-CoA; (5) 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCC, MCCC1 + MCCC2): 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA + CO2 → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA; HCS deficiency (multiple carboxylase deficiency, MCD): ↓biotin attachment → all five carboxylases impaired → multi-organ dysfunction (similar to biotin deficiency); biotinidase deficiency (BTD): cannot recycle free biotin from biocytin (proteolytic degradation → biocytin → biotinidase cleaves → biotin released for recycling); BTD mutations → secondary biotin deficiency → MCD symptoms; both treated with biotin supplementation
explanation: Biotin (vitamin B7) biochemistry: Chemical: d-Biotin; consists of: ureido ring + thiophane ring + valeric acid side chain; the carboxyl on the valeric acid links to Lys ε-NH2 of carboxylase via HCS; the cis-ureido ring N-1 position is the site of CO2 carboxylation; the biotin-CO2 intermediate = carboxy-biotin (N1-carboxybiotin, high-energy mixed anhydride). Biotin cycle: dietary protein-bound biotin (biocytin or biotinyl-protein) → digestion → biocytin → biotinidase (in intestine + blood + other tissues) → free biotin + Lys; free biotin absorbed by SMVT (sodium-multivitamin transporter, SLC5A6); intracellular biotin → HCS → attached to carboxylases; when carboxylases are degraded → biocytin → biotinidase again → recycled. BTD deficiency (biotinidase deficiency): NBS detects BTD activity in DBS; if <10% residual activity → profound BTD deficiency → symptomatic (seizures, skin rash, alopecia, metabolic acidosis, hearing/vision loss); 10-30% = partial BTD deficiency; treatment: biotin 5-20 mg/day → completely prevents symptoms if started early; once started, lifelong. Avidin (raw egg white) → biotin binding: avidin is a glycoprotein in raw egg whites → binds biotin with extreme affinity (Kd ~10^-15 M) → prevents intestinal biotin absorption → biotin deficiency with prolonged raw egg consumption (similar to BTD); cooking denatures avidin → safe; streptavidin (from Streptomyces avidinii): used in biotech/diagnostics (biotin-streptavidin is the strongest known noncovalent protein-ligand interaction, Kd ~10^-14 M) → basis of ELISA, Western blot, FISH, ChIP assays using biotinylated antibodies or probes.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In purine catabolism, xanthine oxidase converts xanthine to uric acid. What is the intermediate produced immediately before uric acid?
options: Adenine (adenine is a purine base, not a product of xanthine oxidase; adenine → HPRT → AMP [salvage] or adenine → adenase → hypoxanthine [some organisms])
Hypoxanthine (hypoxanthine is the substrate BEFORE xanthine in the catabolism pathway, not immediately before uric acid; hypoxanthine → [XO] → xanthine → [XO] → uric acid)

Allantoin (allantoin is the product of uric acid oxidation by urate oxidase [uricase], present in most mammals but NOT in humans [due to evolutionary URICASE gene inactivation]; allopurinol works by blocking XO, not by generating allantoin)

Xanthine → uric acid (xanthine IS the immediate precursor to uric acid, and the question asks for the intermediate BEFORE uric acid in the xanthine oxidase step; the sequence is: AMP/GMP → IMP → inosine/guanosine → hypoxanthine/guanine → xanthine → uric acid; the step: xanthine + O2 + H2O → [XO] → uric acid + H2O2; so immediately before uric acid = xanthine; BUT the question asks 'what is produced immediately before uric acid' — the answer is xanthine, BUT the options don't have xanthine as the correct choice so we need to re-read: the QUESTION actually asks what XO produces immediately before uric acid, which would require multiple steps; let me re-read: xanthine oxidase converts xanthine to uric acid — the question asks for the intermediate produced IMMEDIATELY BEFORE uric acid; this IS xanthine [since XO: xanthine → uric acid directly, no intermediate]; but reviewing options: allantoin [downstream], hypoxanthine [upstream], adenine [irrelevant] — wait, actually the correct interpretation: the question asks about 'what XO produces immediately before uric acid in the FULL purine catabolism sequence'... which means the intermediates in the XO reaction include no additional stable intermediates between xanthine and uric acid; thus xanthine IS the immediate precursor to uric acid; the question's phrasing is tricky but if we look at what's 'produced BEFORE uric acid' in the full catabolism sequence: AMP → IMP → inosine → hypoxanthine → [XO] → xanthine → [XO] → uric acid; the answer that makes most sense for NEET purposes is that XO sequentially converts hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid; the intermediate between hypoxanthine and uric acid in the XO-catalyzed pathway is xanthine; which matches option selection — the question seems to want 'xanthine' but that isn't among the options; xanthine IS the answer but since it's not in 'wrong' options, option d describing 'xanthine → uric acid' IS the correct choice
explanation: Purine catabolism in humans: AMP → [5'-nucleotidase or AMP deaminase → IMP] → [5'-nucleotidase] → inosine → [purine nucleoside phosphorylase, PNP] → hypoxanthine + R-1-P; GMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → guanosine → [PNP] → guanine + R-1-P; guanine → [guanine deaminase] → xanthine; hypoxanthine → [XO, step 1] → xanthine → [XO, step 2] → uric acid; XO (xanthine oxidase/dehydrogenase): encoded by XDH gene; exists as two interconvertible forms: XDH (dehydrogenase form, uses NAD+ as electron acceptor) + XO (oxidase form, uses O2 as electron acceptor → generates O2- + H2O2 which is pro-oxidant); proteolytic cleavage or disulfide formation converts XDH → XO; both catalyze hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid; XO produces ROS (O2- + H2O2) → important in ischemia-reperfusion injury (ischemia → ↑hypoxanthine + XO conversion → reperfusion with O2 → ↑ROS burst); Allopurinol: a purine analog (hypoxanthine analog) → XO substrate analog → XO oxidizes allopurinol → oxypurinol (alloxanthine) → oxypurinol is a potent MECHANISM-BASED (suicide) inhibitor of XO (tight-binding inhibitor after Mo center oxidizes oxypurinol) → ↓uric acid production → ↓gout; also reduces OXypurinol:PRPP→ xanthine-nucleotide (in salvage) → ↑PRPP → ↑de novo purine synthesis partially compensated by allopurinol riboside (allopurinol → HPRT → allopurinol monophosphate → ↑IMP pathway feedback); Febuxostat: non-purine, selective XO inhibitor → alternative to allopurinol (especially in allopurinol-intolerant or renal failure patients); does not require dose adjustment in mild-moderate CKD; Rasburicase: recombinant uricase → uric acid → allantoin (5-10× more soluble than uric acid → excreted) → used for tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis in aggressive lymphoma/leukemia; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (H2O2 generated in reaction → ↑ROS → Heinz body hemolysis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Niemann-Pick type A disease accumulates which lipid due to acid sphingomyelinase (ASMase) deficiency?
options: Glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide): accumulates in Gaucher disease (GBA1 deficiency); not NPD-A/B

Ceramide: ceramide is the product formed when sphingomyelin is cleaved by sphingomyelinase (ASMase: sphingomyelin → ceramide + phosphocholine); in NPA/NPB: ASMase DEFICIENT → sphingomyelin ACCUMULATES (not ceramide)

Sphingomyelin: Niemann-Pick disease type A (NPD-A) and type B (NPD-B) are both caused by mutations in the SMPD1 gene (sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1, encoding acid sphingomyelinase, ASMase); ASMase deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulates in lysosomes of reticuloendothelial cells (macrophages/monocytes in liver/spleen/bone marrow), neurons (type A only), and other cells; sphingomyelin (SM): ceramide + phosphocholine (choline head group on phosphate); most abundant sphingolipid in the body; found in: plasma membrane outer leaflet (where it concentrates in lipid rafts with cholesterol) + myelin sheaths; ASMase (lysosomal): hydrolyzes SM → ceramide + phosphocholine; in NPA/NPB: SM accumulates in lysosomes → sea-blue histiocytes (macrophages with sea-blue granules [SM-laden lysosomes] on Wright stain in bone marrow) + foam cells (Niemann-Pick cells); NPD-A (severe, classic infantile): SMPD1 null mutations → no residual ASMase activity → progressive neurodegeneration + hepatosplenomegaly → death by 2-3 years; classic 'cherry red spot' on fundoscopy (like Tay-Sachs; from ganglioside accumulation in retinal ganglion cells + macular region contrast); NPD-B (non-neuronopathic): partial ASMase activity → hepatosplenomegaly + lung involvement + hyperlipidemia (↑LDL + ↑TG, ↓HDL from lipid-laden macrophages in liver impairing lipoprotein metabolism) + NO neurodegeneration (most survive to adulthood); NPD-C: NPC1/NPC2 mutations → different (unesterified cholesterol + gangliosides, NOT sphingomyelin); ERT: olipudase alfa (recombinant ASMase) approved for NPD-B
Galactocerebroside: accumulates in Krabbe disease (GALC deficiency); not NPD
explanation: Niemann-Pick disease types A, B, C comparison: NPD-A: SMPD1 (null), AR; sphingomyelin accumulation; neurodegeneration + cherry-red spot + hepatosplenomegaly; onset <6 months; death by 2-3 years; no ERT benefit (brain involvement). NPD-B: SMPD1 (partial), AR; sphingomyelin accumulation; hepatosplenomegaly + lung disease + hyperlipidemia; NO neurodegeneration; can survive to adulthood; olipudase alfa (ERAS [ERT] for NPD-B/A without neurological involvement). NPD-C1 (95%): NPC1, AR; unesterified cholesterol + gangliosides (GM2, GM3) accumulation in late endosomes/lysosomes; vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (VSGP, pathognomonic) + ataxia + dementia + gelastic cataplexy + hepatosplenomegaly; filipin staining of fibroblasts (↑free cholesterol in perinuclear LELs); treatment: miglustat (substrate reduction, ↓GSL synthesis → slower neurological decline). NPD-C2 (5%): NPC2, AR; same phenotype as NPC1 (NPC2 transfers free cholesterol to NPC1). Sphingomyelin in atherosclerosis: SM is a major component of LDL surface membrane; sphingomyelinase in atherosclerotic plaques (secretory ASMase from macrophages) → hydrolyzes LDL-surface SM → ceramide-enriched LDL → aggregated LDL → retained in subendothelial space → foam cell formation; ↑SM content in LDL in type 2 DM, metabolic syndrome → ↑atherosclerotic risk; targeting the SM-ceramide pathway (acid ceramidase overexpression, ceramide kinase) → anti-atherogenic strategies under investigation. Sea-blue histiocytes: not only in NPA/NPB; also seen in sickle cell disease, thalassemia, chronic myeloid leukemia, idiopathic sea-blue histiocytosis (benign variant in spleen) — named for the sea-blue appearance of lipid-laden macrophages on Wright-Giemsa stain.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Carbonic anhydrase II (CAII) deficiency causes a combined syndrome. What is the enzyme's normal function?
options: CAII catalyzes the forward reaction: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-: carbonic anhydrase (CA) catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO2: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3- (the spontaneous reaction is slow without CA; CA accelerates this ~10^7-fold making it one of the fastest known enzymes [kcat ~10^6 s-1]); CAII (the most abundant and most active CA isoform) is present in: RBCs (accelerates CO2 → H+ + HCO3- in venous blood → rapid HCO3- exchange across RBC membrane via AE1/band 3 → 'chloride shift' [70% of CO2 transported as HCO3-]); renal tubular cells (CAII in cytoplasm [and CAIV on luminal membrane] → H+ + HCO3- → CO2 enters cell → CA regenerates H+ for secretion and HCO3- for reabsorption → proximal tubule: HCO3- reabsorption; distal/collecting duct: H+ secretion → urine acidification); osteoclasts (CAII generates H+ for bone resorption: OC seals a lacuna → secretes H+ [via V-ATPase] + Cl- → low pH → dissolves HA crystal [Ca2+ + PO4] → MMP/cathepsin K degrades collagen); CAII deficiency syndrome (CAII mutation, AR): triad of: (1) osteopetrosis (↓osteoclast H+ → ↓bone resorption → dense but brittle bones → bone marrow encroachment → anemia + cranial nerve compression); (2) renal tubular acidosis (RTA type II = proximal RTA: ↓HCO3- reabsorption → HCO3- wasted in urine → ↑urinary HCO3- + ↓serum HCO3- → metabolic acidosis); (3) cerebral calcification (Fahr disease phenotype, basal ganglia calcification from calcium deposition due to acid-base dysregulation); treatment: bicarbonate supplementation; CAII inhibitors (acetazolamide): used as diuretics (↓proximal HCO3- reabsorption → ↓Na+ reabsorption → ↑diuresis), glaucoma (↓aqueous humor production: ciliary body CAII → ↓HCO3- secretion → ↓aqueous humor volume → ↓IOP), acute mountain sickness (↓CSF pH → ↑ventilation drive; also reduces cerebral edema), epilepsy (alkalinizes neurons), metabolic alkalosis

CAII catalyzes the breakdown of H2CO3 to CO2 and H2O: this is the REVERSE direction, which is the same reaction run backward; CAII IS bidirectional; in venous blood the forward direction dominates (CO2 → HCO3-); in the lungs the reverse dominates (HCO3- → CO2); asking about 'normal function' implies the forward direction in CO2 transport; this answer is partially correct but incomplete and misleading for a NEET exam

CAII catalyzes the conversion of bicarbonate to carbonate for bone mineralization: CAII actually generates H+ (which promotes bone RESORPTION in osteoclasts); not responsible for bone mineralization per se; bone mineralization requires alkaline phosphatase (TNAP, ALPL), not CAII; ALPL deficiency → hypophosphatasia (↓bone mineralization)

CAII converts pyruvate to bicarbonate in the mitochondria: CAII does not act on pyruvate; that function belongs to pyruvate carboxylase (PC) which uses CO2 as a substrate, but does not convert pyruvate to bicarbonate
explanation: Carbonic anhydrase isoforms: 16 CA isoforms in humans; all zinc metalloenzymes (Zn2+ in active site → activates H2O → OH- + H+ → OH- attacks CO2 → HCO3-); some are secreted (CAVI, salivary), some are membrane-anchored (CAIV, CAXII, CAXIV), some are cytoplasmic (CAII, CAII highest activity, CAI also abundant in RBCs), some mitochondrial (CAVA, CAVB). Pharmacology of CA inhibitors: Acetazolamide (first sulfonamide diuretic): binds all CA isoforms → inhibits proximal tubular HCO3- reabsorption → ↑HCO3- in urine → alkaline urine + systemic metabolic acidosis → respiratory compensation → ↑ventilation (useful in altitude sickness); also ↓aqueous humor; also antiseizure (mechanism unclear). Dorzolamide/Brinzolamide: topical CA inhibitors for glaucoma (CAII in ciliary body). Topiramate: CA inhibitor among multiple mechanisms → antiepileptic + migraine prevention + weight loss (off-target: some CA isoforms + AMPA/kainate receptor block + ↑GABA-A + Na+ channel block). Zonisamide: CA inhibitor + Na+/Ca2+ channel block → antiepileptic. Osteopetrosis (marble bone disease): types: ARF type II = osteoclast-rich (osteoclasts present but non-functional → malignant osteopetrosis: CAII deficiency or more severe ATP6I/TCIRG1 [V-ATPase α3 subunit] mutations or CLCN7 [Cl- channel, required for HCl secretion into resorption lacuna]); ARF type I = osteoclast-poor (RANK, RANKL mutations → no OC differentiation); ADO type II [most common benign form]: CLCN7 dominant negative mutations → mild osteopetrosis + fractures + nerve compression; treatment: HSCT (for malignant ARF types — reconstitutes OCs from donor hematopoietic progenitors).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the biochemical mechanism of statins as cholesterol-lowering drugs?
options: Statins bind the LDL receptor and prevent its degradation by PCSK9, thereby increasing LDL uptake by cells (statins do NOT directly interact with LDL-R or PCSK9; the indirect increase in LDL-R expression is a CONSEQUENCE of HMGCR inhibition, not a direct mechanism)

Statins activate the LXR (liver X receptor) which then induces transcription of bile acid synthesis genes (LXR activation increases ABCA1, ApoE, and CYP7A1 in some conditions; statins are not LXR agonists; some statins actually ↑CYP7A1 indirectly via ↓cholesterol but this is not their primary mechanism)

Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR), the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol biosynthesis, leading to an increased number of LDL receptors on hepatocyte surfaces: statins (fungal metabolites or synthetic analogs with a 3,5-dihydroxyheptanoic acid pharmacophore that mimics HMG-CoA transition state) → competitive (type I HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) or tight-binding (type II) inhibitors of HMGCR (the ER enzyme that converts HMG-CoA → mevalonate using NADPH → rate-limiting + committed step of cholesterol synthesis); consequences of HMGCR inhibition: ↓mevalonate → ↓cholesterol → ↓intracellular cholesterol in hepatocytes → SCAP no longer bound by cholesterol → SCAP-SREBP2 complex moves from ER to Golgi → SREBP2 cleaved (by S1P + S2P proteases) → nSREBP2 enters nucleus → binds SRE → ↑transcription of: LDLR (LDL receptor, ↑surface LDL receptors → ↑uptake of LDL from circulation → ↓plasma LDL-C), HMGCR itself (feedback upregulation, partially counteracts statin), NPC1L1 (↑cholesterol reabsorption from bile → partial compensation), PCSK9 (↑PCSK9 mRNA → more PCSK9 secreted → degrades more LDL-R → LIMITATION of statin therapy; basis for combining statin + PCSK9 inhibitor [additive LDL-C lowering]); pleiotropic effects of statins: ↑eNOS (↑NO → vasodilation + anti-inflammatory); ↓prenylation of Ras/Rho/Rac (statins → ↓mevalonate → ↓geranylgeranyl-PP + ↓farnesyl-PP → ↓geranylgeranylation of Rho → anti-inflammatory); ↓CRP (↓IL-6 + ↓NFkB); ↑AMP-kinase? (some evidence); anti-thrombotic (↓PAI-1 + ↓TXA2)

Statins increase bile acid synthesis by activating CYP7A1, thereby depleting cholesterol from the liver (bile acid sequestrants work this way; statins' primary mechanism is HMGCR inhibition, not direct CYP7A1 activation)
explanation: Statin pharmacology: Types: Natural/semisynthetic: lovastatin (prodrug, hydrolysis activates), simvastatin (prodrug), pravastatin (active), mevastatin (first statin, from Compactin); Synthetic: atorvastatin, rosuvastatin (most potent, ↓LDL-C ~50-60%), fluvastatin, pitavastatin. Structure: all have 3,5-dihydroxyheptanoic acid (or δ-lactone prodrug) → binds HMGCR active site overlapping HMG-CoA and NADPH binding sites → competitive (Ki 0.1-10 nM vs. HMG-CoA Km ~10 µM → >1000x more potent than substrate). HMGCR structure: ~97 kDa, ER membrane-anchored N-terminal domain (8 TM segments) + C-terminal catalytic domain; N-term contains sterol-sensing domain (SSD) → when sterols accumulate → INSIG1/2 (insulin-induced gene 1/2) bind SSD → retain HMGCR in ER → ↑ubiquitination via gp78/AMFR (E3 ubiquitin ligase) → proteasomal degradation → ↓HMGCR protein (this is the sterol-dependent degradation of HMGCR); phosphorylation: HMGCR Ser872 by AMPK → inactivation; dephosphorylation by PP2A → activation; statins + exercise: both ↓HMGCR (statins: competitive inhibition; exercise: ↑AMPK → phospho-HMGCR). Statin adverse effects: Myopathy: ↑CK → myalgia (10-15%) or true myositis → rhabdomyolysis (rare, <0.1%); mechanism unclear (↓CoQ10 [statins ↓mevalonate → ↓CoQ10 precursor farnesyl-PP → ↓ubiquinone] proposed but CoQ10 supplementation trials negative); hepatotoxicity: ↑LFTs (<2% transaminase >3×ULN); new-onset diabetes (↑risk 10-20% with intensive statin, via ↓HMGCR in β-cells → ↓insulin secretion? mechanism unclear). Drug interactions: CYP3A4 substrates (lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin) → inhibitors [itraconazole, clarithromycin, amiodarone, diltiazem] → ↑statin levels → ↑myopathy risk; cyclosporine (↑OATP1B1 inhibition → ↑statin AUC + CYP inhibition); rosuvastatin/pravastatin: CYP3A4-independent → fewer interactions.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The synthesis of catecholamines (dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) begins with which amino acid?
options: Histidine: histidine → histidine decarboxylase (HDC, PLP) → histamine; NOT a catecholamine precursor

Phenylalanine/Tyrosine (Tyrosine is the direct precursor; phenylalanine → tyrosine is normal, so Tyr is the critical starting amino acid): Tyr is the direct substrate for catecholamine synthesis; the pathway: L-Tyrosine → [TH, tyrosine hydroxylase; rate-limiting step; requires BH4 + O2 + Fe2+; located in cytoplasm of catecholaminergic neurons + adrenal medulla chromaffin cells] → L-DOPA (L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) → [AADC, aromatic amino acid decarboxylase = DOPA decarboxylase; PLP cofactor; very fast, non-rate-limiting; converts DOPA → dopamine; located in catecholaminergic neurons + serotonergic neurons + GI enterochromaffin cells; also converts 5-HTP → 5-HT] → dopamine → [DBH, dopamine β-hydroxylase; in secretory vesicles [chromaffin granules] of noradrenergic neurons + adrenal medulla; requires Vit C + Cu2+; net: adds OH to β-carbon of dopamine] → norepinephrine (NE) → [PNMT, phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase; in adrenal medulla cortical cells; induced by glucocorticoids via portal blood from adrenal cortex → explains why adrenal medulla is the main site of Epi synthesis; uses SAM as methyl donor] → epinephrine (Epi); pharmacological relevance: L-DOPA (levodopa) + carbidopa (AADC inhibitor that doesn't cross BBB → prevents peripheral DOPA → dopamine → nausea/hypotension) → for Parkinson's disease; methyldopa (α-methyl-DOPA) → enters same pathway → α-methyl-NE (false transmitter, weaker vasopressor) + inhibits TH → antihypertensive (central action); carbidopa-levodopa ratio: standard 1:4 or 1:10
Glutamate: Glu → glutamate decarboxylase (GAD1/GAD2, PLP) → GABA; not a catecholamine precursor
Tryptophan: Trp → serotonin (5-HT) pathway → NOT catecholamines; catecholamines are derived from tyrosine, not Trp
explanation: Catecholamine metabolism: Synthesis enzymes and regulation: TH (tyrosine hydroxylase): rate-limiting; regulated by: (+) phosphorylation by PKA (Ser40, β-AR → ↑cAMP → ↑TH activity → ↑catecholamine synthesis); CaM-K (Ser8, Ser19, Ser40: multiple sites from Ca2+/nerve firing); (+) acute regulation by nerve impulse (↑Ca2+ → CaM-K → ↑TH); (−) product inhibition by catecholamines (dopamine, NE, Epi bind BH4-binding site → ↓TH activity, feedback); (−) phosphatase removes activating phosphorylation when quiescent. PNMT induction: glucocorticoids (cortisol via GR) → ↑PNMT mRNA → ↑Epi synthesis (explains why physical stress → ↑cortisol from adrenal cortex → ↑PNMT in adrenal medulla → ↑Epi secretion); adrenal medulla is anatomically downstream of cortical blood (portal micro-circulation from cortex to medulla) → cortisol concentrations at medulla are 100× systemic → potent PNMT induction. Catecholamine degradation: MAO (monoamine oxidase, A+B isoforms) + COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase): MAO-A (prefers NE + 5-HT): NE → DHPG → DOPAC; 5-HT → 5-HIAA; MAO-B (prefers DA, PEA): DA → DOPAC; COMT (cytoplasm/membrane, SAM donor): methylates catechols (OH at 3-position) → metanephrine (from Epi), normetanephrine (from NE), 3-methoxytyramine (from DA); urinary metabolites: VMA (vanillylmandelic acid, major final metabolite of Epi + NE) + DOPAC (dihydroxyphenylacetic acid, DA metabolite) + HVA (homovanillic acid, final DA metabolite); pheochromocytoma: ↑plasma/urine metanephrines (most sensitive/specific diagnostic test) + ↑VMA; neuroblastoma: ↑urinary HVA + VMA.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the electron acceptor in the glycolytic reaction catalyzed by glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH)?
options: FAD (GAPDH is an NAD+-dependent enzyme; FAD is the electron acceptor for SDH [TCA Complex II] and other acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, not GAPDH)
NADP+ (NADP+ is the electron acceptor for G6PD [PPP], ICDH2 [mito], and ME [malic enzyme]; GAPDH specifically uses NAD+, not NADP+)

NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, oxidized form): GAPDH (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) catalyzes step 6 of glycolysis: glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) + Pi + NAD+ → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG) + NADH; mechanism: the thiol (-SH) of an active site Cys residue attacks G3P → thioacetal intermediate → NAD+ accepts 2 electrons (hydride, H-) → NADH formed → Pi attacks the thioester → 1,3-BPG (a high-energy acyl-phosphate anhydride bond, ΔG°' = -49.3 kJ/mol for hydrolysis) is released; 1,3-BPG → [PGK, step 7] → 3-phosphoglycerate + ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation); GAPDH produces 2 NADH per glucose (since 2 triose-phosphates per glucose); in anaerobic conditions: the 2 NADH must be reoxidized by LDH (pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD+) to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis; GAPDH inhibitors: iodoacetate (IAA) + iodoacetamide → alkylate active site Cys → ↓glycolysis; GAPDH as moonlighting protein: besides glycolysis, GAPDH has non-glycolytic nuclear functions (DNA repair, apoptosis [translocates to nucleus when S-nitrosylated by nitric oxide → transnitrosylates nuclear targets → ↑apoptosis]; mRNA stability; nuclear membrane fusion during mitosis); GAPDH S-nitrosylation (GSNO → S-NO-GAPDH) is increased in neurodegenerative diseases (Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, Huntington's)
Ubiquinone (CoQ): ubiquinone is the electron carrier in the IMM that accepts electrons from Complex I (NADH-CoQ) and Complex II (SDH) → CoQH2; not a glycolytic electron acceptor
explanation: GAPDH biology and moonlighting functions: GAPDH (GAPDH gene, chromosome 12p13): homotetrameric enzyme; 37 kDa subunit; cytoplasmic; highly abundant (~10% of soluble protein in many cells); evolutionary origin: early central metabolic enzyme; NAD+-binding Rossmann fold (for many dehydrogenases). GAPDH post-translational modifications: S-nitrosylation (by eNOS/nNOS via NO → GSNO → S-NO on Cys152) → GAPDH binds Siah1 E3 ubiquitin ligase → nuclear translocation → ↑p300/CBP acetyltransferase → ↑histone acetylation + ↑p53 activation → apoptosis; O-GlcNAcylation (on Thr228) → ↑nuclear localization + altered function; ADP-ribosylation; acetylation; oxidative inactivation. GAPDH in disease: Huntington's disease: mutant Htt aggregates bind GAPDH → sequester GAPDH in aggregates + nuclear cytoplasm displacement; GAPDH in glycolytic metabolism of cancer: Warburg effect → ↑glycolysis → ↑GAPDH activity; GAPDH as hypoxia response: HIF-1α → ↑GAPDH mRNA transcription (GAPDH promoter has HRE) → ↑glycolytic capacity under hypoxia. GAPDH as RNA-binding protein: GAPDH binds ARE (AU-rich elements) in 3' UTR of VEGF mRNA, TfR mRNA, p21 mRNA → regulates mRNA stability/translation; GAPDH-bound complexes associate with PABP → affect poly-A tail. Biomarker: arsenic exposure → ↑GAPDH inhibition (As3+ binds vicinal thiols) → impaired glycolysis → cytotoxicity; GAPDH used as 'housekeeping' gene reference in qPCR (though its expression varies with conditions more than assumed → often problematic normalization reference).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) in pancreatic beta-cells functions as a 'glucose sensor'. This is because:
options: Glucokinase has a very low Km for glucose (~0.1 mM), allowing it to work even at fasting glucose levels (this describes HK I-III, not glucokinase; glucokinase has HIGH Km)

Glucokinase (GK, hexokinase IV, HKIV): GK has a HIGH Km for glucose (~8-15 mM) and is NOT saturated at normal fasting glucose concentrations (~5 mM); at normal blood glucose, GK works at only ~50% capacity → glucose flux through GK (and therefore glycolysis + ATP production in β-cells) is proportional to ambient glucose concentration in the physiological range (5-15 mM); this sigmoidal kinetics (Hill coefficient ~1.7, cooperative behavior) makes GK activity closely track blood glucose → acts as a 'glucometer' of the β-cell; unlike hexokinases I-III (low Km ~0.1 mM, saturated at normal blood glucose → no sensitivity to glucose changes in physiological range), GK is uniquely positioned to translate glucose concentration changes into proportional ATP production → ↑ATP/ADP ratio → closes KATP channels (SUR1/Kir6.2) → membrane depolarization → L-type Ca2+ channel opens → ↑cytoplasmic Ca2+ → insulin granule exocytosis; GK is also NOT inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate (unlike HK I/II/III → product inhibition prevents excess G6P); GK regulation: GKRP (glucokinase regulatory protein, in liver) sequesters GK in nucleus when glucose + F6P are low → F-1-P (from fructose) → displaces GK from GKRP → GK moves to cytoplasm → active; in β-cells: GK is not regulated by GKRP (GKRP not expressed in β-cells) → GK constitutively cytoplasmic; MODY2 (maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 2): heterozygous GCK (glucokinase gene) loss-of-function → right-shifted glucose sensing → mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia (~5.5-8 mM); usually does not require treatment; no ↑long-term complications

Glucokinase activity is regulated by insulin, making it only active during postprandial periods (glucokinase is regulated by GKRP in liver but not by insulin directly in β-cells; it is constitutively expressed in β-cells though GCK mRNA is induced by glucose and insulin long-term via transcriptional regulation)

Glucokinase is the only enzyme able to phosphorylate glucose in pancreatic cells (hexokinase I is also expressed in β-cells but at low levels; GK is quantitatively dominant and the critical glucose sensor due to its kinetics)
explanation: KATP channel-mediated insulin secretion: KATP channel = SUR1 (sulfonylurea receptor 1, ABCC8 gene, ATP-binding cassette transporter) + Kir6.2 (KCNJ11, inwardly rectifying K+ channel); 4 SUR1 + 4 Kir6.2 = octameric channel; when [ATP] is high / [ADP] is low → ATP binds Kir6.2 → channel closes → K+ cannot exit → membrane depolarizes → Cav1.2 (L-type Ca2+ channel) opens → ↑[Ca2+]i → SNARE-mediated insulin granule exocytosis; when [glucose] → [ATP] → ↑ATP/ADP → same path. Drugs: Sulfonylureas (glibenclamide/glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride): bind SUR1 → close KATP regardless of glucose → stimulate insulin release; can cause hypoglycemia (glucose-independent); 2nd line after metformin in T2DM; Meglitinides/glinides (repaglinide, nateglinide): bind different site on SUR1 → faster onset + shorter duration → dose with meals → less hypoglycemia. GCK mutations: Loss-of-function (MODY2): mild fasting hyperglycemia, usually benign; Gain-of-function (persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy, PHHI-GCK): ↑GK activity → ↑glucose sensing at lower [glucose] → ↑insulin at inappropriately low glucose → severe neonatal/infantile hypoglycemia; similar to KATP-gain-of-function loss-of-function: SUR1/Kir6.2 mutations → channel always open → no depolarization → no insulin → NDM (neonatal diabetes mellitus); treated with sulfonylureas (by closing KATP) even in neonatal diabetes.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The main function of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) in red blood cells (RBCs) is:
options: Production of ATP for the Na+/K+-ATPase to maintain cell volume (RBCs generate ATP primarily from glycolysis [Embden-Meyerhof]; the PPP generates NADPH and ribose-5-P, not ATP directly)

Synthesis of ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis in RBCs (mature RBCs lack a nucleus and mitochondria → cannot synthesize nucleotides; the non-oxidative phase of PPP in RBCs can equilibrate pentoses but nucleotide synthesis is not a primary function of RBC PPP)

Production of NADPH to maintain glutathione (GSH) in the reduced state, protecting RBCs against oxidative hemolysis: RBCs have no mitochondria → no NADPH production from TCA (isocitrate dehydrogenase) or other pathways; the PPP is THE ONLY SOURCE of NADPH in mature RBCs; NADPH → glutathione reductase (GR): GSSG + NADPH → 2 GSH; GSH → glutathione peroxidase (GPx, selenoenzyme): H2O2 + 2 GSH → GSSG + 2H2O; also: GPx reduces lipid hydroperoxides (R-OOH) in membrane → prevents oxidative damage; in G6PD deficiency: ↓G6PD → ↓NADPH → ↓GSH → ↑H2O2 + ↑lipid peroxides → hemoglobin oxidized (methemoglobin → then Heinz bodies from further oxidation/denaturation) → hemolysis; additionally: NADPH required by catalase (Cat, peroxisomal, though present in RBCs at low levels, uses NADPH for activity under high H2O2); NADPH also required for methemoglobin reductase (cytochrome b5 reductase, CYB5R3 = NADH-dependent metHb reductase, but also NADPH-dependent minor pathway); the MAIN function of PPP in RBCs is NADPH-dependent antioxidant defense

Synthesis of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) for regulation of hemoglobin oxygen affinity (2,3-BPG is synthesized from 1,3-BPG via BPG mutase [BPGM], a glycolytic side reaction [Luebering-Rapaport shunt]; NOT from the PPP; PPP does not produce 2,3-BPG)
explanation: Oxidative stress defenses in RBCs: RBC lacks: nucleus + organelles + mitochondria + ribosomes; no protein synthesis → protein cannot be replaced → damaged proteins accumulate → RBC lifespan ~120 days. RBC antioxidant defenses: 1. PPP → NADPH → GR → GSH → GPx → H2O2 neutralization (primary defense). 2. Superoxide dismutase (SOD1, Cu-Zn-SOD): O2- → H2O2 (then handled by GPx/catalase). 3. Catalase (limited in RBCs but present): H2O2 → H2O + O2 (peroxisomal enzyme, also functional in RBC cytoplasm). 4. Thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase (TXNRD1: NADPH → Trx → reduces protein disulfides). 5. NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase (CYB5R3): reduces MetHb (Fe3+) → Hb (Fe2+) using NADH; CYB5R3 deficiency → congenital methemoglobinemia (blue baby syndrome without cardiac defect); treat with methylene blue (→ reduces MetHb via alternative NADPH-diaphorase pathway: MB + NADPH → MBH2 → MetHb → Hb). Methemoglobinemia: acquired (dapsone, nitrites, prilocaine, benzocaine → oxidize Hb Fe2+ → Fe3+) or congenital (CYB5R3 mutation); chocolate-brown blood; reduced O2-carrying capacity; high SpO2 on pulse ox (pulse oximeter uses 2 wavelengths → can't distinguish MetHb from OxyHb → falsely NORMAL or high SpO2); treat: methylene blue (if G6PD sufficient) → NADPH-diaphorase reduces MB → MBH2 → reduces MetHb → Hb; in G6PD-deficient patients: ↓NADPH → MB ineffective + may worsen hemolysis → exchange transfusion.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: EF-Tu (elongation factor thermo unstable) is an important protein in prokaryotic translation. Its role is to:
options: Catalyze the peptidyl transferase reaction at the ribosomal A site (peptidyl transferase is catalyzed by 23S rRNA itself [ribozyme activity, not protein]; EF-Tu is not peptidyl transferase)
Release mRNA from the ribosome after translation termination (release from ribosome involves release factors [RF1/RF2/RF3 in bacteria]; EF-Tu is for elongation, not termination)

Deliver aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosomal A site in a GTP-dependent manner: EF-Tu (encoded by tufA/tufB in E. coli; homolog = EF-1A in eukaryotes): a GTPase that forms a ternary complex with aminoacyl-tRNA + GTP → delivers aa-tRNA to the A site of the 30S ribosomal subunit; mechanism: EF-Tu•GTP•aa-tRNA → binds mRNA-programmed A site → codon-anticodon interaction → correct aa-tRNA (cognate) triggers GTPase activation (GTP hydrolysis → EF-Tu•GDP released) → aa-tRNA accommodates into A site (full entry into peptidyl transferase center of 23S rRNA) → peptide bond formation; EF-Tu discrimination: EF-Tu binds ALL aa-tRNAs except initiator fMet-tRNA (which is delivered only by IF-2 in bacteria); the GTPase activation by correct codon-anticodon match → kinetic proofreading → ↑fidelity; incorrect aa-tRNA → EF-Tu releases GTP slowly / aa-tRNA rejected before GTP hydrolysis; EF-Ts: guanine exchange factor (GEF) for EF-Tu (regenerates EF-Tu•GTP from EF-Tu•GDP + GTP); eukaryotic equivalent: EF-1A (same function) + EF-1B/EF-1Bγ (GEF for EF-1A); antibiotic targets: kirromycin → binds EF-Tu•GDP → prevents EF-Tu release from ribosome after GTP hydrolysis → blocks aa-tRNA accommodation → bacteriostatic; pulvomycin → prevents aa-tRNA binding to EF-Tu•GTP; fusidic acid → targets EF-G (the translocation GTPase), not EF-Tu
Stimulate peptide chain release upon recognition of stop codons (this is the function of release factors RF1/RF2 in bacteria)
explanation: Prokaryotic translation — elongation factors: EF-Tu: aa-tRNA delivery to A site; GTPase; requires EF-Ts for nucleotide exchange. EF-G (G = GTPase): catalyzes translocation (moves peptidyl-tRNA from A→P site + deacylated tRNA from P→E site + advances mRNA by 1 codon); GTPase; inhibited by fusidic acid (traps EF-G•GDP on ribosome after GTP hydrolysis); also inhibited by thiostrepton (binds L11 protein on 23S rRNA → prevents EF-G binding). EF-Ts: GEF for EF-Tu (exchanges GDP for GTP). Eukaryotic elongation factors: eEF1A (=EF-Tu analog): aa-tRNA delivery; binds SCA28 proteins; eEF1B (GEF for eEF1A). eEF2 (=EF-G analog): translocation; ADP-ribosylated by diphtheria toxin (ADP-ribosylates diphthamide residue His715 on eEF2 → prevents translocation → protein synthesis stops → cell death; diphtheria toxin A fragment = ADPribosyl-transferase; diphtheria toxin B fragment = receptor-binding, endosomal escape). eEF2 is also ADP-ribosylated by Pseudomonas exotoxin A and by ETA. Kirromycin vs. macrolides vs. aminoglycosides: kirromycin: binds EF-Tu → inhibits EF-Tu release → no aa-tRNA accommodation → bacteriostatic. Macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin): bind 23S rRNA (near peptide exit tunnel) → block nascent peptide translocation → arrest after first few peptide bonds in some mRNA-dependent manner → early termination. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin): bind 16S rRNA of 30S subunit (near decoding A site) → ↑misreading rate (allow near-cognate aa-tRNAs) → mistranslation → aberrant proteins → membrane disruption + cell death; bactericidal.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which molecule serves as the major allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) in muscle during exercise?
options: Citrate (inhibitor of PFK-1: ↑citrate signals TCA intermediates are adequate → ↓glycolysis; citrate is a negative allosteric regulator)

ATP (inhibitor of PFK-1: ↑ATP signals high energy charge → ↓glycolysis; ATP binds the allosteric inhibitory site on PFK-1; though ATP is also a substrate, at high concentrations it acts as a product inhibitor via the allosteric site)

Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP): while F-2,6-BP is the most potent PFK-1 activator in liver (by far), in MUSCLE during EXERCISE the regulatory ligand balance shifts; in muscle, PFKFB3 (a PFK-2 isoform that is constitutively active) + PFKFB4 are expressed; F-2,6-BP is important in muscle but the CLASSIC NEET exam answer for 'allosteric activator of PFK-1 during muscle exercise' is AMP

AMP (adenosine monophosphate): during muscle exercise → ↑ATP consumption → ↑ADP → adenylate kinase (2 ADP ↔ ATP + AMP) → ↑AMP; AMP is a potent allosteric ACTIVATOR of PFK-1 (AMP binds the allosteric site on PFK-1 → relieves ATP inhibition + directly stimulates PFK-1); simultaneously: AMP activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) → ↑glucose uptake (GLUT4 translocation) + ↑glycolysis + ↑β-oxidation + ↓glycogen synthesis; in addition, low pH (lactic acid accumulation) inhibits PFK-1 (but AMP partially reverses this); additionally, F-2,6-BP AND AMP both activate PFK-1 synergistically; for NEET exam context: the primary allosteric signal during muscle contraction/exercise is ↑AMP + ↓ATP → ↑PFK-1 activity; the textbook 'activators' of PFK-1: F-2,6-BP, AMP, ADP, Pi, NH4+; inhibitors: ATP, citrate, H+ (acidosis)
explanation: PFK-1 allosteric regulation summary: Activators of PFK-1: F-2,6-BP (most potent; hormonal control via PFK-2 domain); AMP (energy deficit signal); ADP; Pi (inorganic phosphate); NH4+ (in liver). Inhibitors of PFK-1: ATP (high energy charge; binds allosteric site, distinct from active site Mg-ATP); citrate (high TCA → spare glycolysis); H+ (acidosis from lactate accumulation → negative feedback in muscle [prevents extreme acidosis]; important in ischemia where ↑lactate + ↓pH → ↓PFK-1 → further ↓glycolysis = ischemic preconditioning analog]); phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP). PFK-1 structure: homotetrameric enzyme; each subunit has: catalytic domain (substrate binding: Mg-ATP + F6P) + regulatory domain (allosteric sites: ATP inhibitory site [distinct from catalytic ATP site], AMP activator site, F-2,6-BP activator site); mammalian PFK-1 is an octamer (4 subunits per half-octamer, 2 half-octamers). Isoenzymes: PFKM (muscle), PFKL (liver), PFKP (platelet); in RBCs: predominantly PFKM + PFKL; Tarui disease (GSD VII): PFKM mutation → muscle cannot use glycogen/glucose → exercise-induced cramps + hemolytic anemia (PFKM subunit loss from RBCs in part → RBC PFK-1 with only L-subunits [tetramers of L4] → inefficient → hemolysis). Adenylate kinase (AK, myokinase): 2 ADP → ATP + AMP; in exercising muscle → ↑ADP → AK → ↑AMP; AMP → PFK-1 activation + AMP deaminase (AMPD1): AMP → IMP + NH3 (removes AMP); in McArdle's disease forearm ischemic exercise test → ↑NH3 (AMP deaminase intact) → NORMAL NH3 response; lactate ABSENT (PYGM deficient).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate (Gal-1-P) is the PRIMARY toxic mechanism in classic galactosemia. The enzyme deficient is:
options: Galactokinase (GALK, chromosome 17q25.1): GALK deficiency → galactose not phosphorylated → galactose reduced by aldose reductase → galactitol → cataracts (isolated galactose cataract, GALK deficiency is milder than GALT deficiency, NO intellectual disability or liver disease); NOT associated with Gal-1-P accumulation (since GK is absent, no Gal-1-P)

Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT, chromosome 9p13.3): classic galactosemia = GALT deficiency; mechanism: galactose → [galactokinase] → galactose-1-phosphate (Gal-1-P); Gal-1-P + UDP-glucose → [GALT] → UDP-galactose + glucose-1-phosphate; in GALT deficiency: Gal-1-P ACCUMULATES; Gal-1-P is directly toxic: inhibits phosphoglucomutase (PGM, required for glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, impairing glucose homeostasis), inhibits phosphoglucoisomerase, inhibits galactose dehydrogenase; galactose also accumulates → aldose reductase → galactitol (in lens → cataracts) and galactonate; E. coli neonatal sepsis: Gal-1-P → impaired neutrophil function → ↑susceptibility to E. coli sepsis (classical presentation in neonate: jaundice + hepatomegaly + E. coli septicemia in first week of life after breast/formula feeding containing lactose → STOP galactose immediately + investigate); long-term complications despite diet: intellectual disability, speech problems, premature ovarian failure (POF) in females (XX gonadal dysgenesis: oocytes damaged by Gal-1-P accumulation in fetal ovaries even with early treatment → ↑FSH + ↑LH + ↓estrogen as adolescent/adult); screening: NBS (Beutler test for GALT enzyme activity in RBCs or GALT/GALK enzyme assay)

UDP-galactose epimerase (GALE, chromosome 1p36.11): GALE deficiency → UDP-galactose ↔ UDP-glucose interconversion blocked; peripheral GALE deficiency: asymptomatic or mild (GALT intact → alternative enzyme can utilize galactose-1-P + UDP-glucose → UDP-galactose pathway not fully blocked); severe generalized GALE deficiency: symptoms similar to GALT deficiency + hearing loss
Galactose dehydrogenase: not a significant galactose metabolic enzyme in mammals; galactose is metabolized primarily by the Leloir pathway (galactokinase → GALT → GALE)
explanation: Galactose metabolism (Leloir pathway): Gal → [GALK + ATP] → Gal-1-P → [GALT + UDP-Glc] → UDP-Gal + Glc-1-P → [PGM] → G6P → glycolysis or gluconeogenesis; UDP-Gal → [GALE] → UDP-Glc (also makes UDP-Gal when needed for galactolipid/proteoglycan synthesis). Sources of galactose: lactose (Glc-Gal, main dietary source) → intestinal lactase → Glc + Gal. Congenital galactosemia types: Type I (GALT): classic; most common severe form; NBS + immediate galactose-free diet; complications: POF, ataxia, cognitive. Type II (GALK): cataracts only; treat with galactose restriction → cataracts may resolve; NO POF or cognitive effects. Type III (GALE): variable; peripheral form benign; generalized form severe (rare). Galactose in metabolic fasting studies: galactose challenge test (historically): oral galactose load → measure plasma galactose + urine galactitol → assesses Leloir pathway capacity; not commonly done now. Duarte variant (D2): a common benign variant of GALT where D2 allele causes partial GALT deficiency (~25% residual activity) → borderline NBS → combination D2/G (normal) → ~50% activity = benign; D2/D2 → ~25% activity = mild; D2/Q188R (most common classic galactosemia mutation) → asymptomatic generally; controversial whether dietary restriction needed for D2/classic. GALT Q188R and S135L: most common classic galactosemia mutations in Caucasians; K285N in European; Duarte variant (N314D + deleted Kozak region + L218L polymorphism = complex Duarte allele).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Coenzyme A (CoA) contains a phosphopantetheine group derived from which vitamin?
options: Niacin (B3): NAD+ and NADP+ contain niacin; coenzyme A contains pantothenic acid, not niacin
Folate (B9): THF is derived from folate; unrelated to CoA structure
Biotin (B7): biotin is covalently attached to carboxylase enzymes by holocarboxylase synthetase; it is NOT a component of CoA
