Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5): CoA (coenzyme A) structure: adenosine-3'-phosphate + 4-phosphopantothenate + cysteine-derived portion; biosynthesis: pantothenic acid (pantoic acid + β-alanine, made from Val + Asp in microorganisms; dietary in humans) → [pantothenate kinase 1/2/3/4, PANK1-4, ATP-dependent] → 4'-phosphopantothenate → [PPCS] → 4'-phosphopantothenoylcysteine → [PPCDC, decarboxylated] → 4'-phosphopantetheine → [PPAT] → dephospho-CoA → [DPCK] → CoA; the 4'-phosphopantetheine portion (pantetheine-4'-phosphate) contains pantothenic acid + cysteamine (from Cys); the thiol (-SH) of cysteamine is the reactive site of CoA for thioester formation; CoA functions: thioester-forming coenzyme: acetyl-CoA (from pyruvate, β-oxidation, amino acid catabolism) → TCA (entering as acetyl for citrate synthase reaction), FA synthesis (malonyl-CoA), ketone bodies (HMG-CoA), cholesterol (HMG-CoA), acetylcholine synthesis, acetylation reactions; acyl carrier protein (ACP): contains 4'-phosphopantetheine as an arm linked to Ser of ACP → FAS subunit (type II FAS in bacteria, plants; type I FAS multidomain enzyme in mammals); malonyl-ACP intermediate in FA synthesis; PANK2 mutations → PKAN (pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, NBIA type I): iron accumulation in globus pallidus + dystonia + 'eye-of-the-tiger' MRI sign; ↓CoA in specific brain regions + ↑cysteine (since PANK2 catalyzes first step in CoA synthesis; CoA deficiency → ↓pantetheine [iron chelator] → ↑iron accumulation in GP)
explanation: CoA biochemistry and PKAN: CoA structure memory: AdenoSINE-3'-phosphate-pantetheine-4'-phosphate (adenosine 3',5'-bisphosphate + 4-phosphopantetheine); thiol group (-SH) at end of cysteamine portion → reactive site for acyl transfer/thioester formation. CoA in metabolism: acetyl-CoA (C2): product of pyruvate (PDC), FA β-oxidation, AA catabolism → TCA, ketogenesis, lipogenesis, cholesterol synthesis; malonyl-CoA (C3): from acetyl-CoA + CO2 (ACC); ↓CPT-I (inhibitor); substrate for FAS; propionyl-CoA (C3): from odd-chain FA + AA (Met, Ile, Val, Thr) → PCC → methylmalonyl-CoA → MCM → succinyl-CoA; succinyl-CoA (C4): TCA intermediate → succinyl-CoA synthetase → GTP; also: succinyl-CoA + Gly → δ-ALA (heme synthesis via ALAS1). Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC): converts acetyl-CoA (C2) → malonyl-CoA (C3); key regulatory step of fatty acid synthesis; inhibited by phosphorylation (PKA [glucagon], AMPK [↑AMP]) → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I inhibition → ↑β-oxidation; in liver cells: ACC1 (cytoplasmic, FA synthesis) + ACC2 (OMM, CPT-I regulation); in cancer: ACC overexpressed (↑lipogenesis in Warburg effect); TOFA (5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid) = first ACC inhibitor; modern ACC inhibitors (firsocostat, MK-4074) for NASH under clinical investigation. PPAT (phosphopantetheine adenylyltransferase) converts 4'-phosphopantetheine → dephospho-CoA using ATP.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Insulin resistance is associated with altered lipid metabolism. Which enzyme is primarily responsible for the accumulation of ceramide in insulin-resistant states?
options: Sphingolipid transfer protein (CERT): CERT transfers ceramide from ER to Golgi for SM synthesis; ↑CERT might shunt ceramide away from toxic accumulation, not increase it

Ceramide synthase (CerS, CERS1-6): CerS adds fatty acids to sphinganine → dihydroceramide → DEGS1 → ceramide; ↑CerS activity (especially CerS6 with C14/C16:0 chains) has been implicated in ceramide accumulation in obesity/IR; HOWEVER, the de novo synthesis pathway begins with SPT

Serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT, SPTLC1/2): SPT catalyzes the COMMITTED, RATE-LIMITING STEP of ceramide de novo synthesis (palmitoyl-CoA + Ser → 3-ketodihydrosphingosine → sphinganine → ceramide); in obesity/insulin resistance: ↑circulating saturated fatty acids (SFA, particularly palmitate C16:0) → ↑palmitoyl-CoA availability → ↑SPT substrate → ↑de novo ceramide synthesis → ceramide accumulates in muscle, liver, adipose; ceramide effects on insulin signaling: ceramide → activates PP2A (protein phosphatase 2A) → dephosphorylates Akt (PKB) → ↓Akt activity → ↓GLUT4 translocation + ↓glycogen synthesis; ceramide → activates PKC-ζ → inhibits Akt (by direct phosphorylation Thr34 → ↓Akt membrane association); ceramide → ↑PTP1B (protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B) → ↓insulin receptor phosphorylation → ↓IRS-1 → ↓PI3K-Akt; thus: SFA → ↑ceramide → ↓Akt → insulin resistance; ORMDL3 (ER membrane protein): inhibits SPT (see earlier question); in Th17 inflammation → ORMDL3 downregulated → ↑SPT → ↑ceramide → ↑IR; ceramide and T2DM: ceramide levels elevated in: T2DM patients vs. controls (serum ceramide species C14:0, C16:0, C18:0, C20:0, C24:0 all elevated); steatohepatitis (↑hepatic ceramide from ↑SFA flux); pharmacological: SPT inhibitors (myriocin/ISP-1 from Isaria sinclairii): in mice → ↓ceramide → reverses diet-induced insulin resistance + ↓obesity-associated inflammation (research stage)
Acid ceramidase (ASAH1): degrades ceramide → sphingosine + FA; ↑acid ceramidase would DECREASE ceramide, not accumulate it; Farber disease = ceramide accumulation from ↓ASAH1 (loss-of-function)
explanation: Ceramide as a lipotoxic mediator: Obesity + high SFA diet → ↑circulating palmitate + stearate → enter cells → palmitoyl-CoA → ↑SPT → ↑de novo ceramide; also: ↑sphingomyelinase activation by inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β) → ↑sphingomyelin hydrolysis → ↑ceramide from membrane; ceramide species: C16:0-Cer (CerS6): associated with mitochondrial fragmentation (Drp1 activation → ↑fission → ↑ROS → ↑apoptosis); C18:0-Cer (CerS1): associated with neuronal apoptosis; C24-Cer (CerS2): may be protective (longer chains less toxic?); dihydroceramide vs. ceramide: dihydro-Cer (lacks 4,5-trans double bond) → much less biologically active; chemotherapy → ↑dihydroceramide (as DEGS1 inhibition) → accumulation → some anti-tumor effect but also pro-survival effects. S1P rheostat: ceramide (pro-apoptotic, pro-inflammatory) ↔ ceramidase → sphingosine ↔ [SphK1/2] → S1P (anti-apoptotic, pro-survival, angiogenic, pro-inflammatory); the ceramide:S1P ratio ('rheostat') determines cell fate; cancer exploits: ↑SphK1 → ↑S1P → ↑survival + ↑angiogenesis; SphK1 inhibitors (PF-543, SKI-I) → ↑ceramide → apoptosis in cancer cells. Glycosphingolipids in IR: ↑GM3 ganglioside in adipocytes of obese/T2DM patients; GM3 inhibits insulin receptor (by competing with IR for lipid raft association) → ↑GM3 → ↓IR signaling → IR; ST3Gal5 (GM3 synthase) knockout mice → ↑insulin sensitivity; miglustat/ibiglustat (GlcCer synthase inhibitors) → ↓GSL including GM3 → used in NPC + Gaucher (SRT) + under investigation for metabolic syndrome.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The genetic code is described as 'degenerate'. This means:
options: Each codon codes for more than one amino acid (this is the opposite — each codon encodes exactly ONE amino acid or a stop signal; the degeneracy is MANY codons → one amino acid)

Multiple codons can specify the same amino acid, but each codon encodes only one amino acid: 'degeneracy' of the genetic code means that more than one codon (triplet) can encode the same amino acid (synonymous codons); there are 64 codons total: 61 sense codons (encoding 20 amino acids + Sec [selenocysteine] in some contexts) + 3 stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); most amino acids are encoded by 2, 3, 4, or 6 codons; amino acids with the most codons: Leu (6: CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG, UUA, UUG), Arg (6: CGU, CGC, CGA, CGG, AGA, AGG), Ser (6: UCU, UCC, UCA, UCG, AGU, AGC); Met (1: AUG, also start codon) and Trp (1: UGG) are encoded by only ONE codon each (no degeneracy for these two); stop codons: UAA ('ochre'), UAG ('amber'), UGA ('opal' or 'umber'); UGA is also the codon for Sec (selenocysteine, 21st amino acid) in the presence of SECIS element (selenocysteine insertion sequence in 3'-UTR of mRNA + SECISBP2 + EFSec elongation factor); degeneracy is mainly at the 3rd position of codons (wobble position, as Crick's wobble hypothesis predicted); wobble: anticodon position 1 of tRNA (5'-anticodon) = position 34 in tRNA numbering → can pair with codon position 3 with less strict requirement: Inosine (I, modified from G in tRNA position 34 by ADAT deaminase) can pair with U, C, or A at the 3rd codon position → allows one tRNA to read multiple codons

The genetic code is read in an overlapping manner between codons (overlapping reading is NOT a feature of standard genetic code; codons are read as non-overlapping triplets sequentially; overlapping reading would mean nucleotides shared between codons — this does NOT occur in the standard code [though SOME viral/phage genomes have overlapping ORFs read in different frames])

The genetic code contains ambiguous codons that can be decoded by multiple tRNAs for different amino acids in different tissues (the genetic code is NOT ambiguous — each codon encodes one specific amino acid [or stop]; PRFB = programmed frameshifting creates apparent 'ambiguity' but the codon itself is not ambiguous)
explanation: Genetic code properties: Universal: same in all organisms (with rare exceptions: mitochondrial code [differs in stop codons + some aa assignments, e.g., UGA = Trp in human mito; AUA = Met in human mito; AGA/AGG = Stop codons in human mito; CUX codons all = Leu in human mito — standard: some are Ile, Leu, Val for CUX]; mycoplasma UGA = Trp [like mito]; some ciliates UAA/UAG = Gln instead of Stop). Non-ambiguous (unambiguous): each codon decodes to exactly one amino acid (or stop). Non-overlapping: read in sequential non-overlapping triplets from 5'→3'. Degenerate (redundant): one amino acid → multiple codons. Commaless: no spacers between codons. Polar: codons specifying similar amino acids tend to be similar (single nucleotide change often gives similar aa or silent change → error tolerance). Codon usage: 'codon bias' (organisms prefer some synonymous codons over others; correlates with tRNA abundance → efficient translation); codon optimization of recombinant genes for expression in heterologous hosts (replace rare codons with preferred ones → ↑protein yield). tRNA charging: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (aaRS): 20 aaRS enzymes (one per amino acid); recognition of correct tRNA by aaRS involves: anticodon loop (in some cases); acceptor stem sequence (especially for Gln, Glu); unusual bases; discriminator base (position 73); 'second genetic code' = structural features of tRNA recognized by aaRS. Isoacceptor tRNAs: multiple tRNAs recognizing different codons for the same amino acid; distinguished by anticodon; aminoacylated by the same aaRS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Km of an enzyme for its substrate represents:
options: The maximum velocity (Vmax) of the enzyme (Vmax is the maximum rate at saturating substrate; Km is a different parameter)

The concentration of substrate at which the reaction velocity is half the maximal velocity (Vmax/2): the Michaelis constant (Km) is defined as the substrate concentration [S] at which v = Vmax/2; derived from the Michaelis-Menten equation: v = Vmax × [S] / (Km + [S]); when [S] = Km → v = Vmax × Km / (2Km) = Vmax/2; interpretation: enzymes with LOW Km have HIGH affinity for their substrate (reach half-maximal velocity at low [S]); enzymes with HIGH Km have LOW affinity (need high [S] to reach half-saturation); for simple enzyme-substrate kinetics: Km ≈ Ks (dissociation constant of ES complex) = k_-1/k_1 (rate of ES dissociation / rate of ES formation); in reality, Km = (k_-1 + k_cat)/k_1 where k_cat is the catalytic rate → Km ≥ Ks; examples: hexokinase I (brain): Km for glucose ~0.1 mM → very high affinity (saturated at normal blood glucose); glucokinase (liver/β-cell): Km for glucose ~8-15 mM → low affinity (not saturated at normal fasting glucose); GLUT1 (RBC): Km for glucose ~1 mM; GLUT2 (liver/β-cell): Km ~15-20 mM → sensor

The inhibition constant of a competitive inhibitor (the inhibition constant is Ki, not Km; Ki is the affinity of an inhibitor for the enzyme; in competitive inhibition: apparent Km increases but Vmax unchanged; in noncompetitive: apparent Km unchanged but Vmax decreases)
The total enzyme concentration required for the reaction to proceed (enzyme concentration affects Vmax proportionally; Km is a property of the enzyme-substrate pair, not of enzyme concentration)
explanation: Michaelis-Menten kinetics — key concepts: Michaelis-Menten equation: v = Vmax × [S] / (Km + [S]); assumes: single substrate, single active site, steady-state approximation (d[ES]/dt = 0 → rate of ES formation = rate of ES breakdown), no product inhibition at early time points. Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot: 1/v vs 1/[S]; y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = -1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax; useful for graphically identifying inhibition type. Enzyme efficiency: kcat = Vmax/[E]_total = turnover number (reactions per enzyme per second); kcat/Km = specificity constant (measure of enzymatic efficiency; at low [S], v = (kcat/Km) × [E] × [S]); catalytic perfection: kcat/Km ≈ 10^8-10^9 M-1s-1 (diffusion limit) → enzymes like carbonic anhydrase, superoxide dismutase, acetylcholinesterase, triosephosphate isomerase approach this. Allosteric enzymes: do NOT follow simple Michaelis-Menten kinetics; sigmoidal v vs [S] curves (cooperative kinetics); Hill equation: v = Vmax × [S]^n / (K0.5^n + [S]^n); n = Hill coefficient (nH): nH = 1 = no cooperativity; nH > 1 = positive cooperativity (one substrate binding ↑affinity for next); nH < 1 = negative cooperativity (rare). S0.5 (not Km) = [S] at v = Vmax/2 for allosteric enzymes. Examples: hemoglobin: nH ~2.7 for O2 binding (positive cooperativity → sigmoidal ODC); ATCase: nH ~2 for aspartate binding; PFK-1: sigmoidal kinetics; K type vs V type effects: K-type allosteric effect: changes [S] at half-maximal velocity (S0.5) without changing Vmax; V-type: changes Vmax without changing S0.5; most real allosteric effectors have mixed effects.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme produces the 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) important for oxygen delivery?
options: Phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK): catalyzes 1,3-BPG → 3-PG + ATP (step 7 of glycolysis); NOT the 2,3-BPG synthase
Phosphoglycerate mutase (PGM, PGAM): converts 3-PG → 2-PG (step 8); NOT the BPG mutase

Bisphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM): 2,3-BPG is synthesized from 1,3-BPG via the Luebering-Rapaport shunt (in RBCs); the enzyme BPGM (bisphosphoglycerate mutase, chromosome 7q31-34) has two activities: (1) BPG synthase (BPGM mutase): 1,3-BPG → 2,3-BPG (intramolecular phosphate transfer from C1-acyl phosphate → C2 hydroxyl; monophosphate released = Pi); (2) 2,3-BPG phosphatase (same enzyme, BPGM phosphatase activity): 2,3-BPG → 3-PG + Pi; the Luebering-Rapaport shunt: 1,3-BPG → [BPGM synthase activity] → 2,3-BPG → [BPGM phosphatase activity] → 3-PG; bypasses PGK step → 1 ATP lost per triose (vs. glycolysis); normal 2,3-BPG concentration in RBC: ~4-5 mM (very high; equimolar to Hb tetramer); regulation: ↑pH → ↑BPGM synthase activity → ↑2,3-BPG; ↓pH → ↓BPGM → ↓2,3-BPG; 2,3-BPG function: binds the central cavity of deoxy-Hb (between β-chains of T-state Hb) → stabilizes T-state → ↓O2 affinity → rightward shift of ODC → ↑O2 delivery to tissues; physiological: high altitude → hypoxia → ↑2,3-BPG (within hours) → ↓O2 affinity → more O2 delivered; anemia → ↑2,3-BPG (compensatory); 2,3-BPG interaction: binds deoxy Hb A (Hb-F less sensitive because γ-chains don't bind 2,3-BPG as well → HbF has LEFT-shifted ODC → better O2 extraction from maternal blood in placenta)
Pyruvate kinase (PK): converts PEP → pyruvate + ATP (step 10); not involved in 2,3-BPG synthesis
explanation: 2,3-BPG physiology and clinical relevance: ODC (oxygen-dissociation curve) right shift factors (↓O2 affinity, ↑O2 delivery): ↑CO2 (Bohr effect, ↑PCO2); ↑H+ (Bohr effect, ↓pH = acidosis); ↑Temperature; ↑2,3-BPG; ↑Cl- (Hamburger shift). Left shift factors (↑O2 affinity, ↓O2 delivery): ↓CO2; ↓H+ (alkalosis); ↓Temperature; ↓2,3-BPG; HbF (better O2 affinity for fetal use); methemoglobin (remaining Hb has left shift); CO-HB (HbCO). Blood storage: stored blood (in CPDA-1 solution): 2,3-BPG levels fall dramatically after 1 week (RBCs cannot regenerate 2,3-BPG without adequate glycolysis; stored blood depleted of 2,3-BPG → transfused RBCs can't deliver O2 effectively for 24h [until 2,3-BPG regenerates in vivo] → tissue hypoxia from banked blood possible); adding inosine to stored blood (inosine → pentose phosphate → glycolysis) → ↑2,3-BPG maintenance in stored blood (experimental). BPGM deficiency: AR; ↑2,3-BPG is absent → very low 2,3-BPG in RBCs → severe left shift of ODC → ↑O2 affinity → tissues get less O2 → compensatory erythrocytosis (↑Hb, like high-altitude adaptation) but O2 delivery is IMPAIRED; rare; presents with compensatory polycythemia. Pyruvate kinase deficiency: PK-R deficiency → ↑1,3-BPG (substrate accumulation) → ↑2,3-BPG (via BPGM) → rightward ODC shift → surprisingly good O2 delivery relative to Hb level → PK-deficient patients tolerate relatively lower Hb without symptoms → 'adaptation'; treat: mitapivat (PK activator, activates both WT and some mutant PK-R) → approved for hemolytic anemia in PK deficiency.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Long-chain fatty acid oxidation defects (e.g., VLCAD deficiency) characteristically present with which combination?
options: Hyperglycemia, ketoacidosis, and marked ketosis (fatty acid oxidation defects cause HYPOKETOTIC hypoglycemia — the key distinguishing feature; marked ketosis would suggest normal fatty acid oxidation response to hypoglycemia; in FAOD [fatty acid oxidation disorders], ketogenesis is impaired because ketones require acetyl-CoA from beta-oxidation which is blocked)

Hypoketotic hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy, and rhabdomyolysis: VLCAD deficiency (very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, ACADVL gene mutations) is the most common long-chain FAOD; ACADVL catalyzes the first step of long-chain FA β-oxidation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase reaction for C12-C22 FA); in VLCAD deficiency: long-chain FAs cannot be oxidized → cannot generate acetyl-CoA → impaired ketogenesis → hypoketotic hypoglycemia (during fasting or illness → ↑glucagon → adipose lipolysis → ↑NEFA → liver uptake → BUT β-oxidation blocked → no ketone bodies → ↓energy for liver gluconeogenesis → hypoglycemia WITHOUT appropriate ketosis [ketones normally rise as a survival response to hypoglycemia; their absence = hypoketotic hypoglycemia]); also: long-chain acylcarnitines accumulate (C14:1-carnitine, the pathognomonic NBS biomarker [↑tetradecenoylcarnitine]) → toxic to heart → cardiomyopathy (DCM or HCM) + arrhythmias; skeletal muscle: can't use LCFA for energy → rhabdomyolysis + myoglobinuria (especially with fasting + exercise or febrile illness); NBS: ↑C14:1 carnitine (tetradecenoylcarnitine = hallmark); ↑C14:0, C12:0, C16:0 also elevated; management: frequent feeds (avoid prolonged fasting), low long-chain fat diet + medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs, C8/C10 → absorbed directly to portal → mitochondria as octanoyl-CoA or decanoyl-CoA, bypassing VLCAD) + carnitine supplementation; avoid fasting + exercise during illness

Methylmalonic acidemia, hyperammonemia, and lactic acidosis (this is the presentation of methylmalonic acidemia, a disorder of propionyl-CoA/methylmalonyl-CoA metabolism, not a fatty acid oxidation defect)
Galactosemia, E. coli sepsis, and cataracts (this is classic galactosemia [GALT deficiency]; not a FAOD)
explanation: Fatty acid oxidation disorders (FAOD) — key clinical concepts: Hypoketotic hypoglycemia: the hallmark of ALL FAOD; normal response to hypoglycemia = lipolysis → NEFA → ketogenesis (ketones fuel brain + spare glucose); in FAOD: NEFA cannot be oxidized → no ketone bodies → brain has no ketone backup + liver gluconeogenesis impaired (↓acetyl-CoA) → severe hypoglycemia without protective ketosis. FAOD types and NBS biomarkers (C = acylcarnitine): VLCAD (ACADVL): ↑C14:1 (tetradecenoyl), C14:0, C12:0; cardiomyopathy + rhabdomyolysis predominate. LCHAD (HADHA: trifunctional protein α-subunit; also long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase): ↑C16-OH, C18-OH, C18:1-OH; progressive peripheral neuropathy + pigmentary retinopathy + AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy, when carrier mother has LCHAD-deficient fetus → LCHAD fetus cannot oxidize LCFA → long-chain 3-OH-acylcarnitines from fetal circulation → cross placenta → maternal liver → mitochondrial dysfunction → AFLP/HELLP in mother); MCAD (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, ACADM; most common FAOD): ↑C8:0 (octanoylcarnitine) + C10:0, C10:1, C6:0; presents after 1st illness + fasting at 3-24 months; SUDDEN DEATH possible (most common single-gene cause of sudden death in infants before NBS); NBS has largely eliminated MCAD deaths; SCAD (ACADS): ↑C4:0 (butyrylcarnitine); generally benign. Treatment: avoid fasting, frequent feeds; high carbohydrate diet during illness; uncooked cornstarch for overnight fasting; MCT oil for VLCAD/LCHAD; triheptanoin (C7 odd-chain TG → propionyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA in β-oxidation) for VLCAD; carnitine (secondary carnitine depletion in FAOD → carnitine supplementation important; but primary carnitine deficiency [SLC22A5/OCTN2 mutations] → severe FAOD-like + cardiomyopathy → treat with carnitine).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Metformin's primary mechanism of action for glucose lowering is:
options: Insulin secretagogue action on pancreatic beta-cells (metformin does NOT stimulate insulin secretion; it is an insulin sensitizer; patients taking metformin alone do NOT get hypoglycemia, unlike sulfonylureas)
↑Insulin receptor tyrosine kinase activity in peripheral tissues (metformin does not directly activate insulin receptor kinase; it works upstream/parallel to insulin receptor)

Inhibition of hepatic gluconeogenesis, primarily through inhibition of mitochondrial complex I: metformin (biguanide, dimethylbiguanide): primary target = hepatic glucose production; mechanism: metformin → taken up by hepatocytes via OCT1 (organic cation transporter 1, SLC22A1) → accumulates in mitochondria (due to negative mitochondrial potential, biguanide cations accumulate) → inhibits mitochondrial Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) mildly → ↓NADH oxidation → ↓ATP/↑AMP ratio → ↑AMPK activation (AMP → activates AMPK by direct allosteric mechanism + CaMKK2/LKB1-mediated phosphorylation) → AMPK → phosphorylates ACC (↓malonyl-CoA → ↑β-oxidation), phosphorylates TORC2 (cAMP-response element binding protein [CREB]-regulated transcription coactivator 2) → ↓CREB/TORC2 → ↓PEPCK + ↓G6Pase transcription → ↓gluconeogenesis; AMPK-independent mechanisms also proposed: metformin → ↑AMP → directly inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1) [AMP inhibits FBPase-1 at the allosteric AMP-inhibitory site] → ↓gluconeogenesis even without AMPK activation; also: metformin → ↓hepatic NAD+/NADH ratio → ↓activity of PEPCK (which requires NAD+ as cofactor for oxaloacetate generation from malate) → ↓gluconeogenesis; weight-neutral or modest weight loss; no hypoglycemia (if used alone) → preferred first-line agent in T2DM

Activation of GLP-1 receptor in intestinal L-cells (GLP-1 agonists like liraglutide act on GLP-1R; metformin may increase GLP-1 levels secondarily [by altering gut microbiota + bile acid metabolism + L-cell GLP-1 release] but this is NOT the primary mechanism of glucose lowering)
explanation: Metformin pharmacology: PK: oral, low bioavailability (~50-60%), NOT metabolized (excreted unchanged by kidney via OCT1/OCT2); half-life ~6h; renally cleared → contraindicated if eGFR < 30 (↑lactic acidosis risk from ↑drug accumulation + ↑Complex I inhibition → ↑lactate from anaerobic glycolysis if hepatic OXPHOS impaired). Pleiotropic effects: ↓HbA1c by 1-1.5%; ↓CVD events in obese T2DM (UKPDS); ↑gut GLP-1 (secondary effect); ↑vitamin B12 absorption competition (via calcium-dependent IF-B12 receptor in ileum; B12 deficiency in ~10-30% of long-term metformin users → check B12 annually); gut microbiome: ↑Akkermansia muciniphila, ↑SCFA-producing bacteria → improved metabolic profile; cancer: epidemiological data → ↓colorectal, breast, prostate cancer risk → AMPK activation → ↓mTORC1 → ↓cancer cell proliferation; AMPK in cancer: LKB1 (STK11) is a tumor suppressor that phosphorylates AMPK → ↓mTORC1; LKB1 mutations (Peutz-Jeghers, some lung cancers) → AMPK cannot be activated → ↑mTOR → cancer. AMPK biology: heterotrimeric (α1/α2 catalytic + β1/β2 scaffold + γ1/γ2/γ3 regulatory); γ-subunit has CBS-domain pairs (Bateman domains) → bind AMP (activating) or ATP (inhibiting); LKB1 (STK11, liver kinase B1): phosphorylates AMPKα Thr172 (constitutively active LKB1, but AMPK is only active when it's both LKB1-phosphorylated AND AMP-bound); CaMKK2 (calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase kinase 2): activated by ↑Ca2+ → phosphorylates AMPKα Thr172 (independent of AMP → activates AMPK in muscle during exercise via Ca2+ waves from contracting sarcomere).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the urea cycle, the enzyme that condenses carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine is located in the:
options: Cytoplasm (the cytoplasmic steps of the urea cycle are ASS and ASL and arginase; OTC is mitochondrial)
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (the SER is important for drug metabolism [CYP450], steroid synthesis, and glucose release [G6Pase]; urea cycle enzymes are not in SER)

Mitochondrial matrix: ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC, OTCA gene, Xp21.1) catalyzes: carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline + Pi; OTC is located in the MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX; OTC is the second step of the urea cycle (CPS I is the first); both CPS I and OTC are in the mitochondrial matrix; citrulline (product of OTC) → transported from matrix into cytoplasm via the ornithine-citrulline antiporter (ORNT1, SLC25A15) → citrulline + aspartate → [ASS, argininosuccinate synthetase, CYTOPLASM] → argininosuccinate → [ASL, argininosuccinate lyase, CYTOPLASM] → Arg + fumarate → [arginase I, CYTOPLASM] → urea + ornithine; ornithine re-enters the mitochondrial matrix via ORNT1 (citrulline out, ornithine in = antiport); compartmentalization: MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX: CPS I + OTC (first two steps) + NAGS (makes NAG to activate CPS I); CYTOPLASM: ASS + ASL + Arginase I (steps 3-5); OTC deficiency: X-linked, most common UCD; see earlier questions for details
Lysosome (lysosomes contain acid hydrolases for macromolecule degradation; OTC is a mitochondrial enzyme)
explanation: Urea cycle compartmentalization and clinical relevance: Ornithine transport: ornithine (from cytoplasmic arginase-1 reaction) → imported into mitochondrial matrix by ORNT1 (SLC25A15) in exchange for citrulline; ORNT1 deficiency → HHH syndrome (hyperammonemia-hyperornithinemia-homocitrullinemia): ↑ornithine in blood + urine (because OTC reaction [in matrix] also deficient as no substrate ornithine despite enzyme being present) + ↑homocitrulline in urine (mitochondrial OTC uses Lys as backup for ornithine → Lys + carbamoyl-P → homocitrulline) + ↑ammonia + ↑urinary orotate (because carbamoyl-P still produced but can't enter urea cycle → spills into pyrimidine synthesis as in OTC deficiency). ASS (argininosuccinate synthetase): citrulline + Asp + ATP → argininosuccinate; MUTATIONS → citrullinemia type I (CTLN1): ↑citrulline + ↑ammonia + normal orotic acid (OTC intact → carbamoyl-P used normally by OTC → citrulline made → ASS missing → citrulline accumulates in blood); ↑citrulline is the diagnostic marker. ASL (argininosuccinate lyase): argininosuccinate → Arg + fumarate; MUTATIONS → argininosuccinic aciduria (ASA): ↑argininosuccinate in blood/urine + ↑citrulline (moderate) + ↑ammonia; characteristic trichorrhexis nodosa (friable hair like bamboo nodes due to Arg deficiency and abnormal hair protein synthesis); ↑fumarate bypass → argininosuccinate accumulates; treatment: Arg supplementation (provides end product directly, bypassing enzyme). Arginase I (ARG1): Arg → urea + ornithine; MUTATIONS → arginase deficiency: spastic diplegia + cognitive disability + ↑arginine; different presentation from other UCDs (less acute neonatal crisis; more neurological/developmental).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Propionic acidemia (PA) and methylmalonic acidemia (MMA) both present with ketoacidosis and hyperammonemia. The key enzyme deficiency distinguishing the two is:
options: Both have the same enzymatic defect (they do NOT; PA = PCC deficiency; MMA = MCM deficiency or cobalt disorder; these are two different enzymes in the same sequential pathway)
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM) is deficient in propionic acidemia while PCC is deficient in MMA (this is REVERSED; PCC is deficient in PA [upstream]; MCM is deficient in MMA [downstream])

Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) is deficient in propionic acidemia, while methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM) is deficient in methylmalonic acidemia: the sequential pathway: propionyl-CoA → [PCC, biotin + CO2 + ATP] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MMCE, epimerase] → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, AdoCbl] → succinyl-CoA → TCA; PCC (propionyl-CoA carboxylase): encoded by PCCA + PCCB genes; biotin-dependent; deficiency = propionic acidemia (PA): ↑propionyl-CoA → ↑propionic acid + propionylcarnitine (↑C3-carnitine on NBS) + secondary hyperammonemia (propionic acid inhibits NAGS → ↓NAG → ↓CPS I → ↑NH3) + secondary carnitine depletion + ketoacidosis; MCM (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase): encoded by MMUT gene; requires adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl); deficiency = methylmalonic acidemia (MMA): ↑methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonic acid (MMA) in blood + urine; MMA is also elevated from propionate pathway overflow as byproduct; ↑C3-carnitine (similar to PA on NBS) but ↑MMA + ↑methylcitric acid + ↑3-OH-propionic acid also present (vs. PA: ↑methylcitric acid + ↑3-OH-propionic acid WITHOUT ↑MMA); differentiating PA vs MMA: PA: ↑propionylcarnitine (C3), methylcitric acid + 3-OH-propionic acid, NO↑MMA (MMA normal); MMA: ↑C3-carnitine + ↑MMA + ↑methylcitric acid; both: hyperammonemia + ketoacidosis + ↑lactate (secondary mitochondrial dysfunction)
Propionic acid carboxylase is deficient in MMA while carbamoyl phosphate synthetase is deficient in PA (incorrect on both counts)
explanation: PA vs MMA biochemistry: Propionic acidemia (PA): PCC (PCCA α-subunit + PCCB β-subunit); α12β12 dodecamer; mitochondrial; biotin + CO2 + ATP; biotin delivered by HCS; propionyl-CoA sources: odd-chain FA, Met, Ile, Val, Thr, intestinal microbial propionate; ↑propionate → inhibits: PDC (complex competition), succinate dehydrogenase, NAGS (→ hyperammonemia), complex III; ↑propionic acid: can be incorporated into TCA as 'propionyl-CoA trap' competing with acetyl-CoA for oxaloacetate → ↑methylcitric acid; prolonged QTc (cardiac involvement; specific to PA vs MMA); pancreatitis (↑risk); bone marrow suppression (↑propionate → ↑methylmalonyl-CoA → inhibits succinyl-CoA synthetase → ↓succinyl-CoA → ↓heme synthesis → anemia). Methylmalonic acidemia: MCM (MMUT gene); AdoCbl-dependent; mito; if MCM absent → L-MMA-CoA accumulates → MMA; ALSO: methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (MMCE) deficiency → mild MMA (D-MMA-CoA cannot convert to L-form → mild elevation); Cobalamin disorders (cblA-G, MMACHC etc.): combined MMA + homocystinuria (cblC: most common; MMACHC → processes dietary B12 → both AdoCbl + MeCbl impaired → MMA + Hcy elevated; also retinal degeneration [CRD, cone-rod dystrophy]). NBS: ↑C3-carnitine is the marker for BOTH PA and MMA + propionic acidemia-like disorders; distinguish by urine organic acids: PA = ↑propionate + methylcitrate + 3-OH-propionate; MMA = ↑methylmalonic acid + methylcitrate + 3-OH-propionate; C3:C0 ratio + C3:C16 ratio helps. Treatment: PA and MMA: ↓BCAA/Met/Thr/odd-chain FA in diet; carnitine; biotin (for PA/PCC); B12 (for B12-responsive MMA); liver transplant (corrects enzyme in liver → reduces metabolic crises; does NOT prevent renal or neuro complications fully in MMA, since MMA also made in kidney + CNS); OHT (orthotopic hepatorenal transplant) for severe MMA; gene therapy under investigation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the conversion of pregnenolone to progesterone in the adrenal cortex?
options: CYP11A1 (P450scc): converts cholesterol → pregnenolone (the first step, the SIDE CHAIN CLEAVAGE enzyme); not the pregnenolone → progesterone step
CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase): hydroxylates pregnenolone → 17α-hydroxypregnenolone (and also has 17,20-lyase activity for DHEA synthesis); NOT the pregnenolone → progesterone step

3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3β-HSD, HSD3B1 in peripheral/placenta + HSD3B2 in adrenal + gonad; both use NAD+): 3β-HSD catalyzes: (1) the oxidation of the 3β-OH group of steroids + (2) isomerization of the double bond from Δ5 (between C5-C6) to Δ4 (between C4-C5); net: pregnenolone (3β-OH, Δ5) → progesterone (3-keto, Δ4); 3β-HSD acts on all Δ5-3β-hydroxy steroids: pregnenolone → progesterone; 17-OH-pregnenolone → 17-OH-progesterone; DHEA → androstenedione; androstenediol → testosterone; 3β-HSD deficiency: AR; congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) type IV (or HSD3B2 deficiency): accumulation of DHEA (weakly androgenic) + pregnenolone; both salt-wasting (↓aldosterone, ↓cortisol) + virilization in FEMALES (from ↑DHEA) + UNDERVIRILIZATION in MALES (insufficient testosterone from Δ5 pathway, as testosterone synthesis requires 3β-HSD → convert DHEA → androstenedione → testosterone); biochemical: ↑17-OH-pregnenolone + ↑DHEA + ↓17-OH-progesterone + ↓androstenedione + ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone; serum marker: ↑17-OH-pregnenolone:cortisol ratio + ↑DHEA-S
CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase): converts progesterone → deoxycorticosterone (DOC) and 17-OH-progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol; 21-hydroxylase is DOWNSTREAM of 3β-HSD, not the pregnenolone → progesterone step
explanation: 3β-HSD and steroidogenesis: 3β-HSD isoforms: HSD3B1 (type 1): placenta + peripheral tissues (skin, breast, brain); converts locally produced steroids; HSD3B2 (type 2): adrenal cortex + gonads; the MAJOR adrenal/gonadal enzyme; mutations → classical 3β-HSD deficiency (CAH IV). Δ5 vs. Δ4 steroids: Δ5 = double bond between C5-C6: pregnenolone, 17-OH-pregnenolone, DHEA; Δ4 = double bond between C4-C5: progesterone, 17-OH-progesterone, androstenedione, testosterone, aldosterone, cortisol; all active steroids are Δ4 (or have Δ4-3-keto structure); 3β-HSD: the KEY enzyme that converts all Δ5-steroids → Δ4; without 3β-HSD: you cannot make Δ4 steroids → no aldosterone, no cortisol, no testosterone. Spironolactone: MR (mineralocorticoid receptor) antagonist; also inhibits 3β-HSD at high doses (additional anti-androgen mechanism) + inhibits CYP enzymes (↓aldosterone synthesis + ↓testosterone synthesis) → gynecomastia side effect. Finasteride/dutasteride: 5α-reductase inhibitors (5α-reductase: testosterone → dihydrotestosterone [DHT], the active androgen in prostate/skin/hair follicles; 5α-R1: skin, liver; 5α-R2: prostate, seminal vesicles, genital skin; dutasteride inhibits both; finasteride primarily 5α-R2); used for BPH + androgenetic alopecia. DHT vs. testosterone: DHT has 3× higher affinity for AR (androgen receptor) than testosterone → prostate development + scrotal fusion + male pattern baldness + prostate cancer (↑AR activation). Flutamide/enzalutamide/bicalutamide: AR antagonists → used in prostate cancer (↓androgens or ↓AR signaling → ↓tumor growth); enzalutamide (2nd gen) → binds AR + prevents nuclear translocation + DNA binding.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Cystinosis differs from cystinuria in the site of cystine accumulation. In cystinosis, cystine accumulates in:
options: Renal tubular cells of the proximal tubule (the proximal tubule is DAMAGED by cystinosis → Fanconi syndrome; but cystine accumulates in LYSOSOMES of ALL body cells, not specifically in the tubule)
Urine (excess cystine in urine is the hallmark of CYSTINURIA [a transport defect, not a storage disease]; in cystinosis, cystine accumulates intracellularly in lysosomes)

Lysosomes of all body cells: cystinosis (CTNS gene, chromosome 17p13.2): AR lysosomal storage disease caused by mutations in CTNS (cystinosin), a lysosomal cystine transporter (7-transmembrane proton-cystine symporter in the lysosomal membrane); normally: protein degradation in lysosomes releases free cystine → cystinosin transports cystine out of lysosomes into cytoplasm → reduced to cysteine by GSH + other reductants; in cystinosis: cystinosin absent → free cystine cannot exit lysosomes → cystine accumulates in lysosomes of virtually ALL cells → crystals (rectangular birefringent) in: cornea (corneal crystals → photophobia, blepharospasm, most characteristic early finding), kidney (Fanconi syndrome from proximal tubular damage → generalized aminoaciduria + glucosuria + phosphaturia + bicarbonaturia + uricosuria + polyuria; later → ESRD by age 10 if untreated), thyroid, muscle, eye, CNS, leukocytes (diagnostic: ↑white blood cell cystine); systemic/extra-renal: hypothyroidism, myopathy (late), swallowing difficulties (pharyngeal weakness), male hypogonadism (Leydig cell failure), pancreatic exocrine + endocrine failure (insulin-dependent diabetes), CNS damage (cognitive involvement in adult); DIAGNOSIS: ↑WBC cystine (>1 nmol half-cystine/mg protein → diagnostic), slit-lamp corneal crystals, renal Fanconi syndrome, CTNS genotyping; TREATMENT: cysteamine (CYSTAGON): penetrates lysosomes → reacts with cystine (opens S-S bond) → cysteamine-cysteine mixed disulfide → exits lysosome via PQLC2 (SLC66A1) transporter (which transports cationic amino acids, including the mixed disulfide [which mimics Lys structurally]) → ↓lysosomal cystine → slows renal progression; cysteamine eye drops: topical → dissolves corneal crystals; nephropathic cystinosis: most common form; ESRD by ~10 years without treatment; renal transplant: corrects renal failure but does NOT prevent extra-renal manifestations (transplanted kidney is cystine-free [donor cells]; but non-renal tissues continue to accumulate cystine)
Plasma (plasma cystine levels may be slightly elevated in cystinosis but it is NOT the site of cystine accumulation; the intracellular lysosomal accumulation is the pathological hallmark)
explanation: Cystinuria vs. Cystinosis — key distinction: Cystinuria: Defect = SLC3A1/SLC7A9 (renal + intestinal COLA amino acid transport); Cystine accumulates in = URINE (insoluble at physiological pH → stones); Pathology = recurrent nephrolithiasis; No lysosomal storage; No systemic accumulation; Treat = hydration + urinary alkalization + thiol drugs (D-penicillamine, tiopronin). Cystinosis: Defect = CTNS (lysosomal cystinosin transporter); Cystine accumulates in = LYSOSOMES (all cells, but cornea + kidney most obvious); Pathology = Fanconi syndrome + ESRD + corneal crystals + multi-organ damage; Yes, lysosomal storage; Systemic accumulation; Treat = cysteamine (oral + topical eye drops). Lysosomal transport defects (similar to cystinosis): Sialic acid storage disorders (SIASD, SLC17A5/sialin deficiency): sialic acid accumulates in lysosomes → Salla disease (moderate) + ISSD (infantile sialic acid storage disease, more severe); cobalamin transport (LRBA/ABCA4 related? No — lysosomal B12 transport via MCOLN1-related pathway [mucolipin] and TMEM98 or related proteins; not well-characterized clinically). Free cystine in lysosome: once proteins are degraded in lysosome, the disulfide bond of cystine (Cys-Cys disulfide) can't be reduced in the acidic, oxidizing lysosomal lumen → free cystine must be exported by cystinosin; reduced cysteine (monomeric) CAN freely diffuse out; the problem is specifically the OXIDIZED disulfide form (cystine, not cysteine). Cysteamine mechanism: 2 reactions: (1) cysteamine (HOCH2-CH2-SH) → enters lysosome via plasma membrane → reacts with cystine (HOCH2-CH(NH2)-CO-S-S-CO-CH(NH2)-CH2OH) → forms cysteamine-cysteine mixed disulfide (structure similar to Lys) → exits via PQLC2; (2) some cystine may be directly reduced by lysosomal thiol compounds in the presence of cysteamine.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In translation, the peptidyl transferase activity that catalyzes peptide bond formation is attributed to:
options: The ribosomal protein L16 in the 50S subunit (L16 [bacterial] stabilizes the PTC structure but is not the catalytic RNA)

The ribosomal RNA (23S rRNA in prokaryotes, 28S rRNA in eukaryotes — the ribozyme hypothesis): peptide bond formation is catalyzed by the 23S rRNA of the large (50S) ribosomal subunit in bacteria (28S rRNA in eukaryotes, in the 60S large subunit); this makes the ribosome a RIBOZYME for this activity; key evidence: (1) Noller's experiments (1992): protein-free rRNA retains peptidyl transferase activity; (2) Crystal structures of Haloarcula marismortui + Thermus thermophilus 50S subunit (Ban et al., Nissen et al., 2000): the peptidyl transferase center (PTC) is entirely RNA-based → no protein side chains within 18Å of the peptide bond being formed; (3) Specific rRNA residues in 23S (A2451 in E. coli; A2602; U2585) form the PTC → mutations reduce activity; mechanism of peptide bond formation: aminoacyl-tRNA in A-site + peptidyl-tRNA in P-site → α-amino group of A-site aa attacks the carbonyl carbon of the ester bond linking peptide to P-site tRNA → tetrahedral intermediate → peptide bond formed + deacylated tRNA remains in P-site; ribosome as ribozyme: evolutionary significance → 'RNA world' hypothesis (RNA was both catalytic and informational in early evolution); antibiotic targets of PTC: chloramphenicol (binds A-site region of 23S rRNA near PTC → blocks aa-tRNA binding to A-site → inhibits peptidyl transferase; bacteriostatic; broad-spectrum but bone marrow toxicity + 'gray baby syndrome' [neonates lack UGT enzyme for Chloramphenicol glucuronidation → accumulate → cardiac toxicity]); clindamycin (binds 23S rRNA near PTC → blocks translocation; good for anaerobes)
The initiation factor IF-3 (IF-3 prevents premature association of the 50S with the 30S; it dissociates the 70S → allows mRNA + fMet-tRNA binding; has no peptidyl transferase activity)
The 30S ribosomal subunit (the 30S/40S small subunit is the decoding subunit [reads mRNA codons]; peptidyl transferase activity is in the 50S/60S large subunit)
explanation: Ribosome structure and function: Prokaryotic (70S): small subunit (30S): 16S rRNA + ~21 proteins; functions: mRNA binding (Shine-Dalgarno sequence pairs with 3'-end of 16S rRNA for initiation), A-site decoding (codon-anticodon recognition), E-site (exit site for deacylated tRNA). Large subunit (50S): 23S rRNA (2904 nt) + 5S rRNA + ~34 proteins; functions: peptidyl transferase center (PTC, in 23S rRNA), peptide exit tunnel (>100Å long → nascent peptide threads through; 60Å of this is surrounded only by rRNA; some antibiotic binding sites here). Eukaryotic (80S): small subunit (40S): 18S rRNA + ~33 proteins; large subunit (60S): 28S + 5.8S + 5S rRNA + ~49 proteins. Antibiotic targets: 30S (16S rRNA/proteins): Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, streptomycin → Decoding center, A1492/A1493 in 16S rRNA → misreading; bactericidal). Tetracyclines (block aa-tRNA/EF-Tu entry to A-site; bacteriostatic). 50S (23S rRNA/proteins): Chloramphenicol (PTC → A-site → ↓peptidyl transferase). Clindamycin (23S rRNA PTC/A-site → ↓translocation). Macrolides (23S rRNA near peptide exit tunnel → ↓translocation/premature peptide release). Linezolid (oxazolidinone, 23S rRNA → blocks IF-2/fMet-tRNA/mRNA assembly of 70S complex; inhibits initiator tRNA binding to P-site) → used for VRE, MRSA; bone marrow suppression + serotonin syndrome risk (MAO-A inhibitor + serotonergic drug → avoid SSRIs). Fusidic acid (EF-G → prevents GDP/GTP exchange, traps EF-G on ribosome after translocation; topical for MRSA skin infections).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In DNA replication, which enzyme is responsible for removing the RNA primers from Okazaki fragments in bacteria?
options: DnaB (helicase): the replicative helicase in E. coli that unwinds the DNA double helix ahead of the replication fork; not involved in primer removal
DnaG (primase): synthesizes the RNA primer for both leading and lagging strand initiation; does not remove primers

DNA Pol I (DNA polymerase I, polA gene): in bacteria, DNA Pol I has three enzymatic activities: (1) 5'→3' DNA polymerase (extends DNA); (2) 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading); (3) 5'→3' exonuclease (UNIQUE to Pol I among bacterial polymerases): removes RNA primers from the 5' end of Okazaki fragments while simultaneously synthesizing new DNA to fill the gap (nick translation); mechanism: Pol I binds at the 3'-OH of the upstream Okazaki fragment → moves 5'→3' → 5'→3' exonuclease removes the RNA primer nucleotides from the 5'-end of the downstream Okazaki fragment → simultaneously Pol I polymerase fills the gap with DNA → leaves a nick between the new DNA and the downstream fragment; DNA ligase (NAD+-dependent in bacteria, ATP-dependent in eukaryotes) → seals the nick → continuous lagging strand; in eukaryotes: Pol I 5'→3' exonuclease activity is replaced by RNase H1 + FEN1 (flap endonuclease 1) for primer removal (Pol δ + FEN1 + Lig I in eukaryotes); DnaA: initiator protein in bacteria (binds oriC)
SSB (single-strand binding protein): stabilizes ssDNA at the replication fork → prevents reannealing and secondary structure formation; does not remove RNA primers
explanation: DNA Pol I multi-functionality (E. coli vs. eukaryotes): E. coli DNA Pol I (polA gene): kcat ~20 nt/s; processivity ~3-200 nt; uses 5'→3' exonuclease for nick translation (primer removal + gap filling simultaneously) → highly efficient for Okazaki fragment maturation; the Klenow fragment (large fragment of Pol I): retains 5'→3' polymerase + 3'→5' exonuclease BUT LACKS 5'→3' exonuclease → used for DNA labeling/sequencing (without primer removal activity); the small N-terminal fragment = 5'→3' exonuclease alone. E. coli DNA Pol III (polC): the main replicative polymerase; very fast (~1000 nt/s) + highly processive (entire chromosome with few events); contains: α (polymerase), ε (3'→5' proofreading exonuclease), θ (stimulates ε); holoenzyme assembles at initiation; NO 5'→3' exonuclease → cannot do nick translation. E. coli DNA Pol II: DNA repair (UV damage bypass, SOS response); 3'→5' exonuclease; no 5'→3' exonuclease. Eukaryotic Okazaki maturation: Pol α-primase (synthesis of ~8-10 RNA + 20-30 DNA primer) → Pol δ (extension + strand displacement → 5'-flap formation → FEN1 cuts flap → Lig1 seals); Pol ε (primarily leading strand synthesis in yeast/metazoans). Dideoxy chain termination (Sanger sequencing): uses ddNTPs (2',3'-dideoxyNTPs lack 3'-OH → chain terminates when incorporated) → DNA Pol cannot add the next nucleotide → statistical mixture of fragments terminated at each dNTP → gel electrophoresis → sequence readout; now largely replaced by NGS (next-generation sequencing: Illumina: reversible dye terminators; nanopore: strand threading + ionic current).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) is degraded under normoxic conditions by which mechanism?
options: Caspase-mediated cleavage in the cytoplasm (caspases are cysteine proteases activated in apoptosis; HIF-1α degradation is NOT caspase-mediated)

Ubiquitin-proteasome pathway following prolyl hydroxylase-mediated modification: HIF-1α (hypoxia-inducible factor 1α): a transcription factor regulated at the protein stability level; under normoxia (normal O2): PHD (prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins, PHD1/EGLN2, PHD2/EGLN1, PHD3/EGLN3): use O2 + α-KG + Fe2+ + Vit C as cofactors → hydroxylate HIF-1α at Pro402 and/or Pro564 (within the oxygen-dependent degradation domain, ODD) → hydroxyl-Pro-HIF-1α; the prolyl-hydroxy-HIF-1α is recognized by the VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) protein → VHL recruits the CRL2-VHL E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (CUL2 + ELONGIN B/C + RBXL + VHL) → ubiquitinates HIF-1α → proteasomal degradation → normoxia → low HIF-1α → low HIF target gene expression; under hypoxia: PHD activity requires O2 (and α-KG) as co-substrates → when O2 is limited → PHDs not active → HIF-1α NOT hydroxylated → VHL cannot bind → HIF-1α NOT ubiquitinated → HIF-1α STABILIZED → accumulates → translocates to nucleus → dimerizes with ARNT (HIF-1β, constitutively expressed) → HIF-1α/β dimer binds HRE (hypoxia response elements, 5'-RCGTG-3') → ↑transcription of: VEGF (↑angiogenesis), EPO (↑erythropoiesis), GLUT1/3 (↑glucose uptake), LDH-A (↑lactate dehydrogenase → ↑lactate), PHD enzymes (feedback to sense O2 recovery), etc.; PHDs = O2 sensors of the cell; PHD2 (EGLN1) is the main PHD; inhibited by: ↓O2, ↓Fe2+, ↑succinate (oncometabolite from SDH mutations → competitive inhibitor of PHDs), ↑fumarate (oncometabolite from FH mutations), ↑2-HG (from IDH mutations); all these → ↑HIF-1α → pseudo-hypoxia → ↑VEGF → ↑angiogenesis → tumor growth
Dephosphorylation by calcineurin (calcineurin dephosphorylates NFAT [nuclear factor of activated T cells], not HIF-1α)
Nuclear export by exportin-1 (CRM1) under normoxia (CRM1 does export some nuclear proteins but HIF-1α degradation in normoxia is via PHD-VHL-proteasome, not nuclear export)
explanation: HIF pathway and disease: VHL syndrome (VHL tumor suppressor gene, 3p25.3): autosomal dominant; germline VHL mutations → hemangioblastomas (CNS + retinal), clear cell renal carcinoma (ccRCC, biallelic VHL loss → no VHL → constitutive HIF-1α → ↑VEGF → ↑angiogenesis → highly vascular tumors), pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts/neoplasms; VHL mutation → cannot ubiquitinate HIF-1α → constitutive HIF target gene expression; ccRCC: most common adult renal malignancy (~70% clear cell type, ~90% of clear cell have VHL mutations by LOH or methylation); treated with: anti-VEGF (bevacizumab) + VEGFR-TKI (sunitinib, pazopanib, cabozantinib) + mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, temsirolimus [↓mTOR → ↓HIF-1α translation]) + immunotherapy (nivolumab + ipilimumab). PHD inhibitors (HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors): roxadustat, daprodustat, molidustat: block PHD2 → ↑HIF-1α → ↑EPO transcription → ↑erythropoiesis → used for anemia of CKD (oral alternative to injectable ESAs); also iron mobilization via ↑hepcidin suppression pathway. Carbon monoxide (CO) and HIF: CO → binds PHD heme-Fe2+ → partially inhibits PHD → ↑HIF-1α at low CO concentrations (this may be a mechanism by which chronic CO exposure [tobacco smoke] stimulates erythropoiesis). Succinate and HIF pseudo-hypoxia: SDH (succinate dehydrogenase) mutations in paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma (SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHA genes) → ↑succinate accumulates → inhibits PHD (competitive with α-KG) → ↑HIF-1α → VEGF-driven tumor angiogenesis + growth; fumarate hydratase (FH) mutations in hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma (HLRCC) → ↑fumarate → PHD inhibition → ↑HIF-1α → similar mechanism.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) is a peroxisomal biogenesis disorder. The primary biochemical abnormality is:
options: Impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation causing lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy (this describes FAOD; Zellweger is a PEROXISOMAL disorder, not mitochondrial)
Deficiency of lysosomal α-glucosidase (acid maltase) causing glycogen accumulation (this is Pompe disease, GSD type II; not Zellweger)

Accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs) and phytanic acid due to absent or dysfunctional peroxisomes: Zellweger syndrome (ZS, cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) is the most severe form of the Zellweger spectrum disorder (ZSD); ZS + neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy (NALD) + infantile Refsum disease (IRD) form a continuum based on peroxisomal biogenesis disorder (PBD) severity; caused by mutations in PEX (peroxin) genes (PEX1 [most common, ~60%], PEX2, PEX3, PEX5, PEX6, PEX7 [Rhizomelic Chondrodysplasia Punctata, RCDP, different phenotype], PEX10, PEX12, PEX13, PEX16, PEX19, PEX26); PEX proteins are required for peroxisome biogenesis (import of peroxisomal matrix enzymes + peroxisomal membrane proteins) → absent functional peroxisomes → all peroxisomal functions impaired; peroxisomal functions impaired: (1) VLCFA β-oxidation (ABCD1 + ACSL4/FATP4 + ACOX1 + MFP1/2 + thiolase → peroxisomal β-oxidation of C22-C26+ FA → VLCFAs CANNOT be oxidized → VLCFA accumulates in plasma + tissues [especially brain white matter + adrenal cortex]); (2) Phytanic acid α-oxidation (PHYH → removes one carbon from C-3 position of phytanic acid → pristanic acid → then peroxisomal β-oxidation; impaired in ZS → ↑phytanic acid [like Refsum disease]); (3) Plasmalogen synthesis (DHAPAT + AGPS, dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase → ether lipid synthesis starting material; plasmalogen-deficient myelin); (4) Bile acid synthesis (peroxisomal enzymes for bile acid C27 chain → ↑C27-dihydroxy and trihydroxy-cholestanoic acids); (5) Amino acid oxidation (pipecolic acid oxidase → ↑pipecolic acid in ZS); features: hypotonia, seizures, hepatomegaly, cataracts, skeletal abnormalities, neuronal migration defects (cortical dysplasia, pachygyria) → death in first year; diagnosis: ↑plasma VLCFAs (C26:0, C26:0/C22:0 ratio) + ↑DHCA + THCA (bile acid intermediates) + ↑phytanic acid + ↑pristanic acid + ↑pipecolic acid + ↓plasmalogens in RBC membranes; PEX genotyping
Impaired glucocerebrosidase activity causing glucosylceramide accumulation (this is Gaucher disease, GBA1 deficiency; not Zellweger)
explanation: Peroxisomal disorders — two main categories: I. Peroxisomal biogenesis disorders (PBD): PEX gene mutations → no functional peroxisomes; all peroxisomal functions impaired: Zellweger spectrum (ZS, NALD, IRD) — most severe to least; RCDP (rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata type 1): PEX7 mutations → only import of PTS2-targeted proteins defective (PEX7 is the receptor for PTS2 signal); ↓plasmalogens + ↑phytanic acid (PHYH is a PTS2-targeted enzyme); skeletal anomalies + cataracts + intellectual disability. II. Single enzyme/transporter defects (peroxisomes PRESENT but specific function lacking): X-ALD (X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy): ABCD1 mutation → peroxisomal VLCFA transporter defective → ↑VLCFAs (C24:0, C26:0) in plasma/brain/adrenal → inflammatory cerebral demyelination (CCALD, childhood cerebral ALD, most severe, predominantly males) OR adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN, adults, axonal neuropathy + adrenal insufficiency); X-linked (ABCD1 on Xq28); female carriers may be symptomatic (AMN-like, rare CCALD); treatment: Lorenzo's oil (4:1 mixture of erucic acid [C22:1] + oleic acid [C18:1] → ↓VLCFA synthesis by competitive substrate; reduces plasma VLCFA but doesn't prevent neurological disease in symptomatic patients; may delay onset in asymptomatic boys if started early based on MRI monitoring); HSCT for early/pre-symptomatic CCALD. Refsum disease: PHYH mutation → phytanic acid α-oxidation blocked → ↑phytanic acid only (phytanic is a plant-derived FA from chlorophyll metabolism [via phytol]) → retinitis pigmentosa + cerebellar ataxia + peripheral neuropathy + anosmia; treated with diet restriction (avoid chlorophyll-rich foods: green vegetables, dairy fat, ruminant fat). Acatalasemia: CATALASE gene → ↓catalase → mild H2O2 accumulation → oral ulcers + ↑susceptibility to dental caries.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The translocon (Sec61 complex) is a protein-conducting channel in the ER membrane. Signal recognition particle (SRP) targets ribosome-nascent chain complexes to the ER. Which statement BEST describes what happens after SRP engages the signal peptide?
options: SRP delivers the ribosome directly to the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope (SRP delivers to the ER membrane, not nuclear envelope; these are different organelles)

SRP binding to the signal peptide PAUSES translation (elongation arrest) and then docks at the ER membrane via SRP receptor (SR), allowing translation to resume co-translationally through the Sec61 translocon: SRP (7S RNA + 6 protein subunits: SRP9/14, SRP19, SRP54, SRP68, SRP72; SRP54 contains the M-domain that recognizes the hydrophobic signal peptide) → binds the signal peptide emerging from the ribosome exit tunnel → ELONGATION ARREST (pauses translation to allow time for ER targeting; prevents premature folding of the nascent polypeptide) → SRP-ribosome-nascent chain complex → docks with SR (SRP receptor, a heterodimer: SRα [FtsY homolog, GTPase] + SRβ [integral ER membrane, GTPase]) → GTP hydrolysis by both SRP54 and SRα → SRP released from signal peptide + from SR → signal peptide inserts into Sec61 translocon (Sec61α/β/γ heterotrimer in mammals; SecY/E/G in bacteria = bacterial homolog) → translation RESUMES through the translocon → protein is extruded into ER lumen (for soluble secretory proteins) or retained in the lipid bilayer (for membrane proteins via stop-transfer anchor/signal anchor sequences); co-translational vs. post-translational: mammalian cells: mostly co-translational translocation; yeast: both co-translational (via SRP) and post-translational (via TRAP complex = Sec62/63/71/72 + BiP/Hsp70 pulling): small, moderately hydrophobic signal peptides → post-translational; bacteria: SecA (ATPase) pushes unfolded proteins post-translationally through SecYEG; Sec61 channel opening: lateral gate allows hydrophobic TM segments to exit into bilayer; plug (short helix) maintains channel in closed state when no signal peptide → prevents ion leak
SRP directly inserts the signal peptide into the lipid bilayer without the help of Sec61 (SRP is a targeting factor, not a translocon; Sec61 is the actual channel through which translocation occurs)

SRP binding leads to permanent arrest of translation, and the mRNA is stored until sufficient ER membrane is available (elongation arrest is transient, not permanent; translation resumes after ER docking)
explanation: ER targeting signals — types: N-terminal signal peptide (classical): 15-30 aa; hydrophobic core (h-region) + n-region (positive) + c-region (AXA cleavage site for signal peptidase); cleaved after insertion. Signal anchor (type I transmembrane): internal hydrophobic segment; not cleaved; serves as both signal + TM anchor; stops translocation (stop-transfer mechanism) → single-pass type I TM protein (N-terminus in lumen, C-terminus in cytoplasm). Reverse signal anchor (type II): N-terminal cytoplasmic; C-terminal luminal; signal anchor near N-terminus is not cleaved. Multiple TM segments: type III and beyond — alternating loop. GPI anchor addition: GPI (glycosylphosphatidylinositol)-anchored proteins: N-terminal signal peptide (co-translationally enters ER lumen) + C-terminal GPI signal (gets cleaved by transamidase + replaced with pre-formed GPI anchor in the ER lumen) → GPI-anchored protein in ER → transported to Golgi → PM; GPI-anchored proteins are enriched in lipid rafts (sphingomyelin + cholesterol microdomains); examples: CD14, CD59, DAF, FOLR, alkaline phosphatase, prions. PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria): acquired somatic mutation in PIGA gene (X-linked, PIG-A = phosphatidylinositol glycan biosynthesis class A; encodes an enzyme in the first step of GPI anchor synthesis) in a stem cell → clone of GPI-deficient hematopoietic cells → ↓CD59 (protectin, blocks C9 polymerization = MAC inhibitor) + ↓DAF/CD55 (decay-accelerating factor, inhibits C3/C5 convertases) on RBCs → complement attack at night (when CO2 from sleep-time breathing retention → mildly ↓pH → complement activation) → intravascular hemolysis + hemoglobinuria; diagnosis: flow cytometry (CD55-/CD59- RBCs + granulocytes); FLAER (fluorescently labeled aerolysin, binds GPI anchor → detects GPI-deficient cells); treatment: eculizumab/ravulizumab (anti-C5 mAb → blocks MAC + C5a).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In eukaryotic gene expression, alternative splicing is regulated by splicing regulatory proteins. Which RNA element promotes exon inclusion by recruiting splicing activators?
options: Intronic silencer sequences (ISS): these recruit hnRNP repressors → REPRESS splicing of adjacent exons → promote exon SKIPPING, not inclusion

Exonic splicing enhancer (ESE): ESEs are short degenerate sequences (typically 6-8 nt) located within exons → recognized by SR proteins (serine-arginine rich splicing factors: SRSF1/SF2/ASF, SRSF2/SC35, SRSF3, SRSF5/SRp40, SRSF7, etc.) → SR proteins bound to ESE: (1) recruit U1 snRNP to the nearby 5' splice site; (2) recruit U2AF to the polypyrimidine tract near the 3' splice site; (3) enhance E complex formation → promote exon inclusion into mRNA; SR protein domain structure: RNA-recognition motif (RRM) = N-terminal, binds RNA; RS domain = C-terminal, serine-arginine dipeptide repeats (heavily phosphorylated by SRPK1/SRPK2 kinases → phospho-RS domain mediates protein-protein interactions with spliceosomal components, especially U1-70K + U2AF35); ESE vs. ESS: ESE (exonic splicing ENHANCER) → recruits SR proteins → promotes exon inclusion; ESS (exonic splicing SILENCER) → recruits hnRNP A/B (heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins) → promotes exon skipping; ISE (intronic splicing ENHANCER) → promotes inclusion of upstream exon; ISS (intronic splicing SILENCER) → represses inclusion of adjacent exon; clinical significance: mutations in ESE sequences → exon skipping in disease (e.g., SMN2 ESE mutation in SMA [spinal muscular atrophy]: C6T transition in exon 7 → disrupts ESE for SRSF1 → exon 7 skipping → truncated SMN2 protein [SMNΔ7] that is unstable → SMA]; SMN1 deletion = classic SMA); exon inclusion therapy: nusinersen (intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide [ASO]) → binds ISS-N1 in SMN2 intron 7 → blocks hnRNP A1 binding → relieves repression → ↑SMN2 exon 7 inclusion → functional SMN protein; risdiplam (oral small molecule) → similarly promotes SMN2 exon 7 inclusion
Polypyrimidine tract binding protein (PTB): PTB is a REPRESSOR of splicing (PTB binds ESS + ISS → competes with U2AF65 at polypyrimidine tract → blocks exon inclusion → PTB is not an enhancer)

Branch point sequence (BPS): the branch point (A residue, ~20-50 nt upstream of 3' splice site) is recognized by SF1/BBP + U2 snRNA → forms the lariat intermediate; it is NOT an ESE and does not recruit SR proteins to promote exon inclusion
explanation: Spliceosome and splicing mechanism: Spliceosome = snRNPs (small nuclear ribonucleoproteins): U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNPs + non-snRNP proteins; step 1: E complex (early): U1 snRNP → binds 5' SS (via base-pairing with 5' end of U1 snRNA); SF1 → binds BPS; U2AF65/35 → binds polypyrimidine tract + 3' AG; step 2: A complex (prespliceosome): U2 snRNP → binds BPS (U2 snRNA base-pairs with BPS except at the branch A → looped-out bulge → later 2'-OH of A attacks 5' SS); step 3: B complex: U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP → joins; step 4: B* complex (activated): U1 + U4 dissociate; Prp28 helicase displaces U1 from 5' SS; Brr2 helicase unwinds U4/U6 duplex; now U6 snRNA base-pairs with 5' SS AND U2 snRNA; step 5: C complex (catalytic): two transesterification reactions: (1) branch A 2'-OH attacks 5' SS → free 5' exon (3'-OH) + lariat-3'-exon intermediate; (2) 3'-OH of free 5' exon attacks 3' SS → join exons + release lariat; RNA world: snRNAs perform the catalytic transesterification (spliceosomal ribozyme, similar to group II self-splicing introns → evolutionary origin of spliceosome from group II introns). Alternative splicing types: exon skipping (most common): one or more exons skipped; mutually exclusive exons: only one of two possible exons included; alternative 5' SS: different 5' splice site; alternative 3' SS: different 3' splice site; intron retention: intron retained in mRNA; alternative promoter/poly-A: changes first/last exon.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During cell starvation, a process called autophagy degrades cytoplasmic components in lysosomes. The initiation of autophagy is primarily regulated by:
options: Caspase-3 mediated cleavage of ATG proteins (caspase-3 is an executioner caspase in apoptosis; it can cleave some ATG proteins to suppress autophagy in late apoptosis, but is NOT the initiator of autophagy)

Ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation of Beclin-1 (Bcl-2 anti-apoptotic protein sequesters Beclin-1 [BCL2-interacting protein] to inhibit autophagy; but this is inhibitory control of autophagy, not initiation; proteasomal degradation of Beclin-1 would suppress autophagy)

ULK1/2 kinase complex activation following AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition: autophagy initiation hierarchy: (1) nutrient/energy sensing: AMINO ACIDS → mTORC1 active (via Rag GTPases + Ragulator on lysosomal membrane + GATOR complexes [GATOR1 = GAP for RagA/B, GATOR2 = scaffold/regulator] + v-ATPase lysosomal amino acid sensing → mTORC1 phosphorylates ULK1 [Ser757] → INHIBITS ULK1 → ↓autophagy) + ENERGY: ↑ATP/↑glucose → ↓AMPK → ↓ULK1 activation → ↓autophagy; during starvation: ↓amino acids + ↓ATP → ↓mTORC1 activity (Rag GTPases become inactive → mTORC1 released from lysosomal surface) + ↑AMPK (AMP/ADP-bound) → AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 [Ser317, Ser777, Ser555] → ACTIVATES ULK1; ULK1 is also released from mTORC1 inhibition; (2) ULK1 complex: ULK1/2 (kinase) + ATG13 + FIP200 (RB1CC1) + ATG101; activated ULK1 complex → translocates to ER or mitochondrial-associated membrane (MAM) → phosphorylates Beclin-1 + VPS34 (class III PI3K); (3) PI3K complex I (Beclin-1 complex): VPS34 (PI3K class III) + Beclin-1 (ATG6) + VPS15 + ATG14L → produces PI3P (phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate) at the phagophore assembly site (PAS, also called the omegasome or ER subdomain); PI3P → recruits WIPI2 (PH-domain protein that reads PI3P) + DFCP1 (also reads PI3P, marks omegasome); (4) ATG5-ATG12-ATG16L1 complex + ATG3/7: two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems: (a) ATG12~ATG7(E1)~ATG10(E2)→ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 complex; (b) ATG8 family (LC3-I/LC3-II: LC3A/B/C + GABARAP/GABARAPL1/2) → ATG7(E1) + ATG3(E2) + ATG5 conjugation → LC3-II (lipidated with PE on the phagophore membrane; LC3-II = LC3-PE = marker of autophagosome); (5) Phagophore → elongation → autophagosome (double membrane) → fusion with lysosome → autolysosome → degradation of contents → amino acids recycled
CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation of LC3 (CaMKII is a Ca2+-calmodulin-dependent kinase involved in synaptic plasticity; LC3 lipidation is mediated by ATG7/3/5, not CaMKII)
explanation: Autophagy types: Macroautophagy (canonical): double-membrane phagophore engulfs cargo → autophagosome → lysosome → autolysosome → bulk degradation; non-selective (bulk) vs. selective (specific cargo): selective autophagy: cargo receptors (p62/SQSTM1, NBR1, NDP52, OPTN) → bind cargo (protein aggregates, organelles) via UBA domain (ubiquitin binding) + LIR motif (LC3-interacting region, Trp-x-x-Leu; binds LC3-II) → tethers cargo to phagophore membrane. Types of selective autophagy: mitophagy: damaged mitochondria (↓ΔΨm → PINK1 stabilized on OMM → PINK1 phosphorylates Ub on OMM proteins [pUb] → recruits Parkin E3 ligase → more ubiquitination → p62/NDP52/OPTN recruit LC3-II → mitophagy); PINK1/Parkin pathway defects: Parkinson's disease (AR early-onset PD). Reticulophagy (ER-phagy): FAM134B, RTN3, TEX264 as receptors. Xenophagy: pathogen destruction (NDP52, optineurin [OPTN]). Aggrephagy: protein aggregates. Lipophagy: lipid droplets. Ribophagy: ribosomes (NUFIP1). Microautophagy: direct invagination of lysosomal membrane → engulfs cytoplasmic material; organelle microautophagy (e.g., microlipophagy in yeast). Chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA): KFERQ-like motif on substrate → bound by Hsc70 + co-chaperones → LAMP-2A on lysosomal membrane → substrate unfolded + translocated into lysosome via LAMP-2A channel; selective, no vesicle; upregulated by oxidative stress, lipid starvation; relevant to α-synuclein degradation (impaired CMA → ↑α-synuclein → Parkinson). Beclin-1 regulation: Bcl-2/Bcl-XL binds Beclin-1 BH3 domain → sequesters Beclin-1 → inhibits VPS34/PI3P → INHIBITS autophagy; DAPK (death-associated protein kinase) phosphorylates Beclin-1 → releases from Bcl-2 → allows autophagy; UVRAG: positive regulator of Beclin-1 complex; Rubicon: negative regulator of autophagosome-lysosome fusion.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the RATE-LIMITING enzyme in the catabolism of branched-chain amino acids (BCAA: leucine, isoleucine, valine)?
options: BCAA aminotransferase (BCAT): first step; transfers amino group from BCAA → α-KG → branched-chain α-keto acid (BCKA) + glutamate; this is REVERSIBLE and not rate-limiting in catabolism

Branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH): the second and RATE-LIMITING step; BCKDH (branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase complex, analogous to PDC and OGDH; all three are α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes): catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation of all three BCKAs (α-keto-isocaproate [from Leu] + α-keto-β-methylvalerate [from Ile] + α-keto-isovalerate [from Val]) → branched-chain acyl-CoA derivatives (isovaleryl-CoA + α-methylbutyryl-CoA + isobutyryl-CoA) + CO2 + NADH; structure: E1 (decarboxylase, TPP), E2 (acyltransferase, lipoic acid), E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase = DLDH, FAD); regulation: BCKDH kinase (BDK, encoded by BCKDK) → phosphorylates E1α-Ser293 → INACTIVATES BCKDH; BCKDH phosphatase (PP2Cm, encoded by PPM1K) → dephosphorylates → ACTIVATES BCKDH; DEFICIENCY → MSUD (maple syrup urine disease, BCKDH deficiency): all three BCKAs accumulate → ↑BCAA + BCKA in blood + urine → sweet maple syrup odor (from sotolon/maple furanone formed from Leu BCKA); neonatal encephalopathy + spasticity + cerebral edema → death if untreated; NBS: ↑Leu/Ile/Val + ↑alloisoleucine (pathognomonic marker, not normally present → made from the unusual α-keto-β-methylvalerate intermediate); thiamine-responsive form (E1 component → some mutations respond to very high-dose thiamine [cofactor of E1]); treatment: BCAA-restricted diet; BCKDH kinase inhibitor (BT2, sodium phenylbutyrate → activates BCKDH by inhibiting its kinase → may be useful in MSUD or obesity-related BCAA metabolic dysregulation)

Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVD): third step in Leu catabolism only; IVD deficiency → isovaleric acidemia (isovaleryl-CoA accumulates → isovaleric acid + 'sweaty feet' odor); it acts only on the Leu pathway, not on Ile or Val — so NOT the rate-limiting enzyme for ALL BCAA catabolism
BCAA acyl-CoA carboxylase: this is not a single enzyme in the BCAA catabolism pathway; ACC (acetyl-CoA carboxylase) is for fatty acid synthesis
explanation: BCAA metabolism — complete pathway: Location: first step (BCAT) in muscle; second step (BCKDH) in mitochondria; subsequent steps in liver for Ile/Val (anaplerotic) and liver/extrahepatic for Leu (ketogenic only). Leu catabolism: Leu → BCKA (α-ketoisocaproate) → isovaleryl-CoA → methylcrotonyl-CoA → methylglutaconyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; Leu is PURELY KETOGENIC (no gluconeogenic carbons) and activates mTORC1 via leucyl-tRNA synthetase sensing mechanism. Val catabolism: Val → BCKA → isobutyryl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (TCA, anaplerotic); Val is purely glucogenic. Ile catabolism: Ile → BCKA → α-methylbutyryl-CoA → propionyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (via MCC) + ketone bodies; Ile is both glucogenic + ketogenic. MSUD variants: Classic MSUD (E1α/E1β/E2 mutations, most common): neonatal encephalopathy; requires strict dietary restriction + frequent BCAAs monitoring. Intermediate MSUD: less severe; elevated Leu/BCKA present but tolerated longer. Intermittent MSUD: normal between attacks; high protein intake / illness → crisis. Thiamine-responsive MSUD: mutations in E2 or E1 that respond to megadose thiamine. E3-deficient MSUD (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase [DLD] deficiency): most severe; affects PDC + OGDH + BCKDH (all share the E3 subunit) → ↑pyruvate + ↑α-KG + ↑BCKA; lactic acidosis + neurological dysfunction; poor outcome. Alloisoleucine: generated from stereoisomer enrichment of allo-isoleucine (2S,3R-Ile) from incomplete transamination/metabolism; pathognomonic for MSUD; NOT present in normal plasma.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The complement system can be activated by spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 thioester. This pathway is called:
options: Classical pathway (CP): activated by C1q binding antibody-antigen complexes [IgM (most potent on a molar basis, one pentamer activates C1q) or IgG (especially IgG1 and IgG3)]; requires antibody → NOT spontaneous hydrolysis)
Lectin pathway (LP): activated by mannose-binding lectin (MBL) + ficolin binding to carbohydrate patterns on microbial surfaces; NOT spontaneous C3 hydrolysis; also: collectin-10/11 can activate LP

Alternative pathway (AP): the alternative pathway is initiated by SPONTANEOUS (tick-over) hydrolysis of the internal thioester bond in C3 → C3(H2O) [iC3 or C3-H2O, a conformational change exposes the thioester making it reactive]; C3(H2O) + Factor B → C3(H2O)B → [Factor D cleaves B] → C3(H2O)Bb (initial fluid-phase C3 convertase) → cleaves C3 → C3a (anaphylatoxin) + C3b; C3b deposits on microbial surfaces (or host, where it is rapidly inactivated by Factor H, Factor I, CR1, DAF, MCP) → C3b + Factor B + Factor D → C3bBb (surface-bound AP C3 convertase, further stabilized by properdin/Factor P) → ↑C3 cleavage (AMPLIFICATION LOOP) → C3bBb3b (C5 convertase) → C5 → C5a + C5b → MAC assembly; tick-over rate: C3 thioester spontaneously hydrolyzes at low rate in plasma (~1% per hour) → always generating small amounts of C3(H2O) → constant surveillance; on microbial surfaces (lacking inhibitors): AP proceeds to MAC; on host cells: complement regulatory proteins (CRPs): Factor H (plasma, binds host polyanions), DAF/CD55 (cleaves Bb from C3bBb), MCP/CD46 (cofactor for Factor I to cleave C3b → iC3b), CR1/CD35 (cofactor + DAF), CD59/protectin (blocks MAC); factor H-related proteins (FHR1-5) and CFHR gene cluster: polymorphisms in CFHR/CFH locus → ↑risk for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) [CFH Y402H → weaker factor H binding to OCN/CRP on drusen → ↑AP activation → drusen + RPE damage] and atypical HUS (aHUS)

Terminal complement pathway: MAC (membrane attack complex) = C5b-9; assembly: C5b + C6 + C7 + C8 + polyC9 (up to 18 C9 molecules); inserts into lipid bilayer → lytic pore → cell lysis; MAC is not a 'pathway' of initiation but the final effector complex
explanation: Complement pathways and regulation: All three pathways → C3 convertase → C3b → C5 convertase → C5a + C5b → MAC (C5b-9). CP: C1q-C1r-C1s → C4a + C4b; C4b + C2 → C4b2a (CP C3 convertase); C4b2a3b (CP C5 convertase). LP: MBL-MASP1/2 → cleave C4 + C2 → same C4b2a as CP. AP: C3(H2O)Bb (initiation) → C3bBb (surface-bound, amplification) → C3bBb3b (AP C5 convertase). Complement components mnemonic: CP activators: IgM (single molecule) > IgG1 ≈ IgG3 > IgG2 >> IgG4 (IgG4 cannot activate complement; IgM, IgG1, IgG3 most important). Complement deficiencies: C1q/r/s, C4, C2 (most common) deficiency → ↑SLE risk (↓opsonization + ↓immune complex clearance → IC accumulation → autoimmunity): C2 deficiency = most common hereditary complement deficiency in Caucasians → ↑SLE/Sjögren-like disease + ↑encapsulated bacteria. C3 deficiency: most severe → ↑ALL three pathway deficits → ↑ encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. flu) + ↑immune complex disease. C5-C9 (terminal) deficiency: ↑Neisseria infection (gonorrhoeae + meningitidis) specifically → MAC is critical for Gram-negative bacteria lysis; no ↑SLE risk. MBL deficiency: ↑infection in early childhood (before adaptive immunity matures). Complement therapeutics: Eculizumab (anti-C5 mAb → blocks C5a + MAC): PNH, aHUS, NMOSD. Ravulizumab (longer-acting anti-C5). Avacopan (C5a receptor [C5aR1] antagonist): ANCA vasculitis. Pegcetacoplan (PEGylated C3 inhibitor): PNH. Iptacopan (Factor B inhibitor): PNH. Danicopan (Factor D inhibitor): PNH. Sutimlimab (anti-C1s): cold agglutinin disease.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Reverse transcriptase (RT) of HIV can synthesize DNA from RNA. It also degrades the RNA template. This degradation activity is called:
options: 5'→3' exonuclease activity (5'→3' exonuclease activity is found in bacterial DNA Pol I for primer removal [nick translation]; HIV RT does not have 5'→3' exonuclease activity)

Ribonuclease H (RNase H): HIV RT is a heterodimeric enzyme (p66/p51 subunits; p66 has: fingers, palm, thumb, connection, RNase H domain; p51 lacks RNase H domain); RT functions: (1) RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (RDDP): synthesizes (−)-strand DNA from viral genomic RNA template → creates RNA:DNA hybrid; (2) RNase H: degrades the RNA strand of the RNA:DNA hybrid → removes genomic RNA template after first-strand DNA synthesis; (3) DNA-dependent DNA polymerase (DDDP): synthesizes (+)-strand DNA from (−)-strand DNA template → produces double-stranded viral DNA (vDNA); process: (+)ssRNA genome + tRNA3Lys primer → RDDP → (−)ssDNA + RNase H removes RNA → PPT (polypurine tract) remains as primer for (+) strand → DDDP → dsDNA → nuclear import → integrase → integrate into host chromosome; NO proofreading: RT lacks 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading activity → error rate ~3×10-5 per base per cycle (10× higher than cellular DNA polymerases) → high mutation rate → rapid generation of HIV quasispecies → drug resistance + immune evasion; NRTI mechanism: NRTIs (nucleoside/nucleotide RT inhibitors: tenofovir [TFV; actually a NtRTI], abacavir, emtricitabine [FTC], lamivudine [3TC], zidovudine [ZDV/AZT]) → must be phosphorylated intracellularly → incorporated into growing DNA chain → chain termination (lack 3'-OH) → BOTH RDDP and DDDP inhibited; NNRTIs (non-nucleoside RT inhibitors: efavirenz, nevirapine, rilpivirine, doravirine) → bind allosteric site on p66 (NNRTI-binding pocket [NNIBP] at junction of fingers/palm/thumb domains) → conformational change → ↓RDDP + DDDP; RNase H is NOT directly targeted by any current approved HIV drug (RNase H inhibitors are under research)
Ligase activity (RT does not have ligase activity; ligase joins nicks in DNA; HIV uses host cell DNA ligase during integration)
DNase activity (DNase cleaves DNA non-specifically; RT's RNase H selectively cleaves RNA in an RNA:DNA hybrid; it does not cleave pure DNA or pure RNA effectively)
explanation: HIV replication cycle — biochemistry of each step: 1. Viral entry: gp120 (SU) + CD4 (T cells, macrophages) → conformational change → gp120 binds co-receptor (CCR5 [macrophages, R5-tropic HIV, main transmissible strain] or CXCR4 [T cells, X4-tropic, late in disease; 'SI' syncytia-inducing]) → gp41 (TM) hairpin formation → fusion → viral core enters cytoplasm; maraviroc: CCR5 antagonist (prevents R5-HIV entry); ibalizumab: anti-CD4 mAb (blocks HIV binding without impairing CD4 T cell immune function, targets domain 2 of CD4). 2. Reverse transcription (as above). 3. Nuclear import: pre-integration complex (PIC = vDNA + integrase + reverse transcriptase + Vpr + capsid remnants) → nuclear pore → importin-α/β; HIV (lentivirus) can infect non-dividing cells → intact nuclear envelope is not a barrier (unlike simple retroviruses that need cell division + nuclear envelope breakdown). 4. Integration: integrase (IN): (a) 3' processing: removes 2 nt from each 3' end of vDNA → recessed 3'-OH; (b) strand transfer: inserts 3'-OH into host chromosome → 5-bp staggered cut in host DNA → 5-bp direct repeats flanking provirus after repair; INSTI (integrase strand transfer inhibitors: raltegravir, elvitegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir) → bind active site + Mg2+ chelation → block strand transfer step (most active class, very high barrier to resistance especially dolutegravir/bictegravir). 5. Transcription: Tat (transactivator of transcription): HIV tat → TAR (transactivation response element RNA stem-loop at 5' end of all HIV mRNAs) → recruits P-TEFb (CDK9/cyclin T1) → phosphorylates Pol II CTD Ser2 → ↑elongation; without Tat → Pol II pauses (promoter-proximal pause) → no productive transcription. Rev: nuclear export: Rev → RRE (Rev Response Element) in env/gag/pol mRNAs → binds CRM1 (exportin-1) → cytoplasmic export of unspliced/partially spliced mRNAs (needed for structural proteins Gag/Pol/Env); early mRNAs (tat/rev/nef) fully spliced → don't need Rev. 6.
