Assembly + budding: Gag polyprotein (MA-CA-SP1-NC-SP2-p6) → assembles at PM → Env (gp120/gp41 from gp160 processing by furin) → incorporated; budding → HIV protease (PR) → cleaves Gag + GagPol → mature virus; PIs (protease inhibitors): ritonavir, lopinavir, darunavir, atazanavir → mimic substrate transition state → bind PR active site → block maturation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Transsulfuration pathway converts homocysteine to cysteine. Which vitamin-dependent enzyme is specifically responsible for condensing homocysteine with serine?
options: Methionine synthase (MS, MTR gene): remethylates homocysteine → methionine using 5-methylTHF + methylcobalamin; does NOT condense Hcy with Ser

Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS): CBS (pyridoxal-5'-phosphate [PLP/B6] dependent enzyme, chromosome 21q22.3): catalyzes: homocysteine + serine → cystathionine + H2O (β-replacement reaction; the β-carbon of serine is displaced); PLP cofactor: forms Schiff base with the amino group of serine (or Hcy) at the active site Lys → facilitates the elimination + addition reactions; CBS structure: homotetrameric; N-terminal heme domain (inhibits CBS; CO/NO can bind heme → modulate CBS; CBS is activated by S-adenosylmethionine [SAM → activates CBS by relieving autoinhibition → shunts Hcy toward transsulfuration when SAM is high] → CBS is unique in having both a PLP active site AND a SAM regulatory binding site + heme domain); CBS deficiency (homocystinuria type I): AR; most common cause of inherited homocystinuria; features: marfanoid body habitus (downward lens subluxation [ectopia lentis, inferior/nasal dislocation] vs. upward in Marfan [fibrillin mutation → superior/temporal]; tall + arachnodactyly + kyphoscoliosis) + intellectual disability + thromboembolism (venous AND arterial; Hcy → endothelial damage + ↑platelet aggregation + ↑coagulation) + osteoporosis; biochemical: ↑urine homocystine (oxidized Hcy dimer) + ↑serum homocysteine + ↑methionine (Met accumulates as remethylation overwhelmed) + ↓cystathionine + ↓cysteine; treatment: PLP-responsive forms (50% of patients; CBS has enough residual activity if excess PLP cofactor) → high-dose pyridoxine (vitamin B6) + folate + B12 + betaine (alternative Hcy remethylation via BHMT, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, using betaine → methionine); PLP-non-responsive: betaine + Met-restricted diet; CBS regulates H2S: CBS (in combination with CGL [cystathionine γ-lyase/CSE]) generates H2S (hydrogen sulfide) from cysteine/cystathionine → H2S = gasotransmitter (like NO, CO) → ↑cGMP + Kir6.1 KATP → vasodilation; CBS is the predominant H2S-generating enzyme in the brain

Cystathionine γ-lyase (CGL, CSE gene): second enzyme of transsulfuration; cleaves cystathionine → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate + NH3; PLP-dependent; cystathioninuria (CGL deficiency): generally benign (most patients normal); ↑urine cystathionine; B6 responsive

Betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase (BHMT): remethylates Hcy → Met using betaine (trimethylglycine) as methyl donor → dimethylglycine; liver-specific; alternative remethylation (not transsulfuration)
explanation: Homocysteine metabolism — complete picture: Normal Hcy fate: 1. Remethylation to Met: (a) MS/MTR (methionine synthase): 5-Me-THF + Hcy → THF + Met; requires B12 (methylcobalamin, MeCbl) + folate; ubiquitous; (b) BHMT: betaine + Hcy → DMG + Met; liver + kidney specific; important when folate/B12 limited. 2. Transsulfuration to Cys: CBS (B6) → cystathionine; CGL (B6) → Cys + α-ketobutyrate. 3. Excretion: when production > metabolism → ↑plasma Hcy → ↑urine homocystine. Hyperhomocysteinemia: mild (>15 µM): most common; diet + lifestyle (folate/B12/B6 deficiency, smoking, age, CKD); moderate (>30 µM): nutritional + mild enzyme defects; severe (>100 µM): usually enzymatic (CBS deficiency, MTHFR TT genotype severe [rare], CblC deficiency). Cardiovascular risk: Hcy → oxidative stress + endothelial dysfunction + LDL oxidation + ↑tissue factor expression → thrombosis; each 5 µmol/L ↑Hcy → ~20% ↑CVD risk; but supplementation trials with B-vitamins → ↓Hcy but did NOT reduce CVD events in primary/secondary prevention trials (HOPE-2, VITATOPS) → Mendelian randomization studies suggest Hcy-CVD relationship may be partially confounded; however, ↓stroke risk with B-vitamins (CSPPT China trial: folate+enalapril vs. enalapril alone → ↓stroke in Chinese population [where low dietary folate is endemic + food is not fortified]). MTHFR polymorphisms: C677T (p.A222V): thermolabile MTHFR → ↓activity (especially TT genotype homozygous) → ↓5-Me-THF → ↑Hcy (esp with low folate intake); A1298C: less severe. NTDs: low maternal folate → ↑NTD risk; folic acid fortification (USA 1998) + supplementation → ↓NTD by 50-70%.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Heme oxygenase (HO) is the enzyme that degrades heme. Products of HO reaction include all EXCEPT:
options: Carbon monoxide (CO): HO cleaves the α-meso position of heme (Fe-protoporphyrin IX) → biliverdin + CO + Fe2+; CO is generated (1 mol CO per mol heme) → CO is a gasotransmitter (activates sGC → ↑cGMP → vasodilation, anti-inflammatory); HMOX1 (HO-1, inducible): induced by heme, heavy metals, oxidative stress, hypoxia, CO → protective (Nrf2 target); HMOX2 (HO-2, constitutive): brain + testis
Iron (Fe2+): released from heme during HO reaction → Fe2+ → either stored as ferritin or exported via ferroportin → ferrokinetics; HO reaction is the major source of endogenous carbon monoxide

Biliverdin: first product of heme breakdown; blue-green pigment; further reduced by biliverdin reductase (BVR, cytoplasmic NADPH-dependent enzyme) → bilirubin (IXα, yellow) → transported bound to albumin to liver → conjugation by UGT1A1 (glucuronidation) → bilirubin diglucuronide → bile → intestine → urobilinogen (by gut bacteria) → excreted in feces (stercobilin, brown) or reabsorbed + urinary urobilinogen → urobilin (yellow)

Protoporphyrin IX: protoporphyrin IX is the SUBSTRATE porphyrin ring of heme; the HO reaction opens the porphyrin ring at the α-meso bridge → releases protoporphyrin ring as biliverdin (the linear tetrapyrrole); porphyrin ring is NOT a product of HO — it is converted to biliverdin; in erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP): ferrochelatase (FECH) deficiency → protoporphyrin IX accumulates (cannot be converted to heme) → skin photosensitivity (porphyrin fluorescence + singlet oxygen generation on sun exposure → severe burning pain without blistering [characteristic of EPP vs. bullae in PCT]); HO activity: NOT elevated in EPP (heme is still degraded normally; it is the SYNTHESIS of heme that is blocked at last step)
explanation: Bilirubin metabolism and jaundice: Heme sources: 80% from senescent RBC hemoglobin (macrophages of spleen/liver/bone marrow) + 20% from myoglobin, cytochromes, other hemoproteins. HO-1 (HMOX1, ER-associated, inducible): rate-limiting step of heme catabolism → biliverdin + Fe2+ + CO; HO-2 (HMOX2, constitutive, brain): mainly makes CO for neural signaling + O2 sensing. Biliverdin reductase: biliverdin + NADPH → bilirubin IXα (unconjugated, UCB) + NADP+; UCB: water-INsoluble, lipid-soluble, can cross BBB → kernicterus in neonates. Transport: UCB bound to albumin (2 binding sites: high-affinity + low-affinity) → liver → hepatocyte uptake by OATP1B1/1B3 (organic anion transporting polypeptides) → bound to ligandin (GST, glutathione S-transferase) in cytoplasm → UGT1A1 in ER → bilirubin mono/diglucuronide (CB, conjugated bilirubin, water-SOLUBLE); secretion into bile via MRP2 (ABCC2, canalicular membrane). Neonatal jaundice: physiological (↑UCB): immature UGT1A1 (50% adult activity at birth, matures by 6-14 weeks) + high RBC turnover (fetal Hb replacement); pathological: Rh/ABO incompatibility (hemolysis); Crigler-Najjar type I (UGT1A1 absent → severe → kernicterus); Crigler-Najjar type II (UGT1A1 reduced → intermediate); Gilbert syndrome (UGT1A1*28 [TA repeat in TATA box → ↓transcription] → mild, benign, stress-induced, fasting-induced UCB ↑ → no treatment needed; UGT1A1 also reduces irinotecan's SN-38 → UGT1A1*28 homozygotes → ↑SN-38 → ↑diarrhea + neutropenia from irinotecan). Dubin-Johnson (MRP2/ABCC2 deficiency → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia; benign; liver grossly black [lipofuscin pigment accumulation]; urinary coproporphyrin I ↑ [normally mainly III]); Rotor syndrome (OATP1B1/1B3 mutations → impaired hepatic CB uptake for excretion/reuptake).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During gluconeogenesis, pyruvate is converted to oxaloacetate (OAA) by pyruvate carboxylase (PC). OAA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. How does OAA exit the mitochondria?
options: OAA is exported directly through a specific OAA transporter in the IMM (no such dedicated OAA transporter exists in the IMM; OAA must first be converted to another metabolite)

OAA is transaminated to aspartate (by mitochondrial GOT2) → aspartate exits via AGC (aspartate-glutamate carrier) → cytoplasmic GOT1 converts aspartate back to OAA: in the liver, for gluconeogenesis, OAA generated by PC (mitochondrial matrix) exits via TWO routes: ROUTE 1 (transamination/aspartate): mito OAA + Glu → [mito GOT2/mito AST] → Asp + α-KG; Asp exits mito via AGC (SLC25A12/13, aspartate-glutamate carrier, electrogenic, exchanges Asp [out] + Glu [in]); in cytoplasm: Asp + α-KG → [cytoplasmic GOT1/cAST] → OAA + Glu → PEPCK (GTP-dependent in cytoplasm, PCK1) → PEP; ROUTE 2 (malate): mito OAA → [mito MDH2 + NADH] → malate; malate exits via OGC (SLC25A11, 2-oxoglutarate carrier, exchanges malate [out] + α-KG [in]); in cytoplasm: malate → [cytoplasmic MDH1 + NAD+] → OAA + NADH → PEPCK; route 2 also provides cytoplasmic NADH (from malate→OAA [MDH1]) which is needed for gluconeogenesis when using lactate (lactate→pyruvate by LDH uses NAD+ → but net the reducing equivalents from lactate go to cytoplasm via this malate shuttle); both routes provide cytoplasmic OAA → PEPCK-C (PCK1) → PEP → gluconeogenesis; PEPCK-M (PCK2, mitochondrial isoform): makes PEP directly in matrix from mito OAA → PEP exits via a pyruvate/phosphate transporter; PCK2 important in kidney and some tumors

OAA is reduced to malate by mito MDH2 ONLY; then malate diffuses freely through the IMM (OXA and malate cannot freely diffuse through the IMM; malate requires the OGC/SLC25A11 carrier; it is NOT free diffusion)

OAA is spontaneously decarboxylated to pyruvate and CO2 in the mitochondrial matrix, then pyruvate is re-carboxylated in the cytoplasm (OAA does slowly decarboxylate to pyruvate but this is wasteful; the cell actively converts OAA to malate or aspartate for transport, not spontaneous decarboxylation followed by re-carboxylation)
explanation: Gluconeogenesis substrate entry and OAA transport: PC (pyruvate carboxylase): mitochondrial matrix; biotin-dependent; Mg2+ + ATP; OAA formation: pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → OAA + ADP + Pi; activated by acetyl-CoA (↑acetyl-CoA → signal of excess substrate → ↑GNG); PC is absent in muscle (muscle cannot do GNG). PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase): OAA + GTP → PEP + CO2 + GDP; Rate-limiting REGULATORY enzyme of gluconeogenesis (transcriptionally regulated): insulin → ↓PCK1 transcription; glucagon + cortisol → ↑PCK1 transcription; metformin → ↓PCK1 via ↓TORC2/CREB. GNG substrate entry points: Lactate → LDH → pyruvate → PC → OAA → PEPCK → PEP; Glycerol → glycerol kinase → G3P → GAPDH (reverse) → 1,3-BPG → GNG; Amino acids (Ala, Gln, Asp → various entries into TCA → OAA route); Propionate → propionyl-CoA → MCC → succinyl-CoA → TCA → OAA → GNG. Rate-limiting enzymes of GNG: PEPCK (key regulated step); FBPase-1 (fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase) → F1,6BP → F6P; G6Pase (glucose-6-phosphatase) → G6P → glucose (only in liver + kidney + intestine = gluconeogenic tissues); PC (substrate availability control). FBPase-1 regulation: inhibited by AMP + F-2,6-BP; activated by Ca2+/CaM indirectly; ↓F-2,6-BP (glucagon → PKA → FBPase-2 active) → ↑FBPase-1 activity (F-2,6-BP removed from inhibition) → ↑GNG. G6Pase: liver + kidney + intestine (Cori cycle gluconeogenesis + dietary glucose handling); located in SER lumen; G6P transporter (G6PT/SLC37A4) transports G6P into SER lumen where G6Pase cleaves to glucose → transported out; GSD Ia (G6Pase) + GSD Ib (G6PT, also neutrophil dysfunction) = Von Gierke disease.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (ACC1) catalyzes the first committed step of fatty acid synthesis. Which molecule DIRECTLY inhibits ACC1 in muscle under conditions of low energy (↑AMP)?
options: Malonyl-CoA (product inhibition: while malonyl-CoA is the product of ACC1 and inhibits CPT-I, this is a downstream effect; the direct inhibitor of ACC1 under low energy/↑AMP is AMPK-mediated phosphorylation, and malonyl-CoA is the product, not the direct inhibitor of ACC1 activity itself)

Citrate (citrate is an ACTIVATOR of ACC1 [allosteric]; citrate induces polymerization of ACC1 from inactive dimers → active filaments; citrate provides acetyl-CoA signal from TCA → more FA synthesis; citrate is not an inhibitor of ACC1 under low energy)

Palmitoyl-CoA (long-chain acyl-CoA [e.g., palmitoyl-CoA, C16:0-CoA] allosterically inhibits ACC1 by binding the allosteric inhibitory site → prevents polymerization → ↓activity; this is a product feedback loop [end product of FAS inhibiting ACC1]; palmitoyl-CoA is indeed an allosteric inhibitor of ACC1, BUT the main inhibitor under ↑AMP / low energy is AMPK-mediated phosphorylation)

Phosphorylation of ACC1 by AMPK: under low cellular energy (↑AMP, ↑ADP/ATP) → AMPK activated (AMP binds γ-subunit + LKB1/CaMKKβ phosphorylate Thr172 of AMPK α-subunit) → AMPK phosphorylates ACC1 at Ser79 (and ACC2 at Ser221) → phosphorylated ACC1 LOSES activity → ↓malonyl-CoA synthesis; in muscle: ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I inhibition → ↑fatty acid import into mitochondria → ↑β-oxidation (to regenerate ATP); this mechanism: exercise → ↑AMPK → ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑β-oxidation = the primary metabolic switch during muscle exercise for energy provision from fat; AMPK also phosphorylates and inactivates HMGCR (HMG-CoA reductase) → ↓cholesterol synthesis (+ statins competitively inhibit HMGCR enzymatic activity); ACC1 dephosphorylation/reactivation: insulin → PI3K → Akt → inhibits AMPK (via phosphorylation of AMPKα) → ↓AMPK → ↑ACC1 activity (dephosphorylated by PP2A) → ↑malonyl-CoA → ↑FA synthesis
explanation: ACC isoforms and their roles: ACC1 (ACACA gene): cytoplasmic; provides malonyl-CoA for de novo fatty acid synthesis (substrate for FAS/FASN); expressed in lipogenic tissues (liver, adipose, lactating mammary gland). ACC2 (ACACB gene): outer mitochondrial membrane (N-terminal ER-targeting/mitochondrial association motif); makes malonyl-CoA locally at OMM → inhibits CPT-I (carnitine palmitoyltransferase-I) → prevents FA entry into mito → when malonyl-CoA ↑ (anabolic state) → CPT-I inhibited → no β-oxidation; when AMPK active → ↓ACC2 → ↓malonyl-CoA at OMM → ↑CPT-I activity → ↑β-oxidation. In liver: ACC1 (cytoplasmic) also has a pool near mitochondria that may inhibit CPT-I locally. ACC activation: citrate (allosteric, crosses OMM + IMM via citrate carrier → cytoplasm → ACC1) + insulin (PI3K → Akt → PP2A deactivation of AMPK → ↓AMPK → ACC1 dephosphorylated [active]). TOFA (5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid): fatty acid-like ACC inhibitor (competitive with acetyl-CoA + allosteric); research use. Firsocostat (ND-630), MK-4074: liver-targeting ACC inhibitors in NASH clinical trials → ↓de novo lipogenesis → ↓liver fat (steatosis); but may ↑plasma TG (reduced malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT-I inhibition in liver → VLDL-TG secretion may increase → hypertriglyceridemia as side effect → combining with fibrates or ω-3 FA). FAS (FASN) complex: seven activities in a single ~270 kDa polypeptide in mammals (homodimer functional): KS (β-ketoacyl ACP synthase) + AT (malonyl/acetyltransferase, MAT) + DH (dehydratase) + ER (enoyl reductase) + KR (β-ketoreductase) + ACP (acyl carrier protein with 4'-PP) + TE (thioesterase, releases C16:0 palmitate).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is an oncofetal antigen that is used as a tumor marker. It is elevated in all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC): AFP is produced by fetal hepatocytes + yolk sac; re-expressed in HCC → ↑serum AFP (>400 ng/mL highly suggestive of HCC in cirrhosis; used for screening + surveillance in cirrhosis [every 6 months ± ultrasound]; however sensitivity for early HCC is moderate [50-70%]; higher values → ↑specificity)

Yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor): produces large amounts of AFP (classic tumor marker; peak AFP often >10,000 ng/mL; part of germ cell tumor marker panel [AFP + β-hCG + LDH]; AFP ↑ in yolk sac tumors of testis, ovary, extragonadal); pure seminoma does NOT produce AFP (if AFP elevated in presumed seminoma → suggests non-seminomatous GCT element)

Neural tube defects (NTDs) — open NTDs: amniotic fluid AFP (AFAFP) + maternal serum AFP (MSAFP) both elevated in OPEN NTDs (anencephaly, myelomeningocele, encephalocele if open) due to transudation of fetal AFP from exposed neural tissue into amniotic fluid → crosses into maternal circulation; closed NTDs (e.g., spina bifida occulta covered by skin) → no AFP elevation; Down syndrome (trisomy 21): MSAFP is DECREASED (part of the 'triple screen' AFP + hCG + uE3: AFP ↓, hCG ↑, uE3 ↓ in T21); and 'quad screen' adds inhibin A ↑

Colorectal carcinoma: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is the classical marker for colorectal carcinoma (and other GI malignancies, breast, lung); AFP is NOT typically elevated in colorectal cancer (AFP is liver/yolk sac-specific oncofetal antigen; colorectal cells don't reactivate AFP gene)
explanation: Tumor markers — biochemistry and clinical use: AFP (alpha-fetoprotein): normal level <10 ng/mL (adults); produced by fetal liver + yolk sac; major protein in fetal serum (like albumin in adult); reactivated in HCC + yolk sac tumors + hepatoblastoma + gastric hepatoid adenocarcinoma. β-hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin, β subunit): produced by syncytiotrophoblast; elevated in: hydatidiform mole + choriocarcinoma (very high, >100,000 mIU/mL) + germ cell tumors (embryonal carcinoma + choriocarcinoma components; NOT pure seminoma → if ↑AFP with β-hCG in 'seminoma' → rethink diagnosis); also elevated in normal pregnancy + some pituitary hCG. CA-125 (cancer antigen 125, MUC16): elevated in epithelial ovarian cancer + peritoneal carcinoma + endometriosis + pelvic inflammatory disease; used for monitoring treatment response in ovarian cancer; not specific for screening. CA 19-9 (sialylated Lewis antigen): elevated in pancreatic carcinoma + cholangiocarcinoma + gastric cancer; Note: patients who are Lewis antigen-negative cannot produce CA 19-9 → may have pancreatic cancer with normal CA 19-9 (false negative). PSA (prostate-specific antigen, KLK3 kallikrein): prostate-specific (not cancer-specific); elevated in BPH, prostatitis, prostate cancer, post-DRE; free vs. total PSA: low free/total ratio → ↑cancer risk. CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen): colorectal > other GI > breast > lung; NOT diagnostic (elevated in smoking, IBD); used to monitor recurrence after colorectal cancer resection. Chromogranin A: neuroendocrine tumors (NETs, pheochromocytoma, carcinoid). PLAP (placental alkaline phosphatase): seminoma. Inhibin A/B: granulosa cell tumor + mucinous ovarian tumor.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 (VKORC1) is inhibited by warfarin. The effect of this inhibition on coagulation factors is:
options: ↑ activity of vitamin K-dependent factors (warfarin INHIBITS, not activates, vitamin K-dependent factor synthesis; warfarin prevents reduced vitamin K formation → ↓carboxylation → ↓active factors)

Reduced carboxylation of the glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C, and protein S: warfarin mechanism: warfarin (racemic mixture; S-warfarin more potent via CYP2C9) → inhibits VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase) → prevents recycling of vitamin K epoxide → reduced vitamin K (KH2, hydroquinone form); KH2 is required as cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase (GGCX): KH2 + O2 → KO (vitamin K epoxide) + CO2 used for carboxylation of Glu → Gla (γ-carboxyglutamate) residues; Gla residues (in the Gla domain of vit K-dependent proteins) → chelate Ca2+ → bind phosphatidylserine (PS) on activated platelet/cell surfaces → membrane binding → conformational change → coagulation factor activation; without KH2 → GGCX non-functional → Glu NOT converted to Gla → PIVKAs (proteins induced by vitamin K absence/antagonists) are synthesized but cannot bind Ca2+/PS → non-functional; Vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors: II (prothrombin), VII (shortest half-life → first affected by warfarin → INR rises first), IX, X + natural anticoagulants protein C (shortest half-life among vit K-dep proteins → initially can drop faster → WARFARIN SKIN NECROSIS [especially in protein C/S deficiency: early warfarin therapy → protein C falls before factors fall → transient procoagulant state → microthrombi in small vessels → skin necrosis]; also protein S + protein Z; warfarin monitoring: PT/INR (predominantly reflects factors II, VII, X → extrinsic + common pathway); goal INR: 2-3 for most indications (AF, DVT/PE, mechanical valves [depends on valve type/position]); drug interactions: ↑INR (potentiate): amiodarone (↓CYP2C9 = ↓S-warfarin metabolism → ↑warfarin effect), metronidazole, fluconazole, clarithromycin, SSRIs, ↑vitamin K-containing antibiotics, liver disease; ↓INR (antagonize): rifampicin (induces CYP2C9 + CYP3A4 → ↑S- and R-warfarin metabolism → ↓warfarin effect)

↑ synthesis of thromboxane A2 (TXA2) by platelets (aspirin inhibits COX-1 → ↓TXA2; warfarin does not affect TXA2 synthesis; warfarin works at a completely different level — carboxylation of coagulation proteins)

Direct inhibition of thrombin (thrombin is factor IIa; direct thrombin inhibitors [DTIs] = dabigatran [oral], hirudin/lepirudin/bivalirudin; warfarin does not directly inhibit thrombin but reduces the amount of functional prothrombin [factor II] available)
explanation: Vitamin K metabolism and antagonism: Dietary sources: vitamin K1 (phylloquinone): leafy greens (spinach, kale, broccoli) + plant oils; vitamin K2 (menaquinones, MK-4 to MK-13): fermented foods, meat, cheese, gut bacteria (E. coli, Bacteroides); vitamin K3 (menadione): synthetic, can be toxic (hemolytic anemia). Mechanism of carboxylation: vitamin K1/K2 reduced to KH2 by VKOR (VKORC1 + VKORC1L1) + DTD (dithiol-dependent reductase = NQO1 can partially rescue); KH2 → GGCX → Glu → Gla + KO (epoxide); KO recycled by VKOR back to KH2; warfarin blocks VKOR (primarily VKORC1). VKORC1 genetics: VKORC1 -1639G>A (rs9923231): A allele → ↓VKORC1 expression → more sensitive to warfarin (lower dose needed); CYP2C9 *2, *3: reduced S-warfarin metabolism → lower dose; FDA approvals for pharmacogenomically-guided warfarin dosing; CYP4F2 V433M: reduces VK1 degradation → higher K1 availability → more warfarin resistance. Newer VKOR biology: VKORC1L1: paralog → not inhibited by warfarin (provides partial rescue); VKORC1L1 mediates vitamin K recycling in non-hepatic tissues (bone, vascular); important for osteocalcin Gla-carboxylation + MGP (matrix Gla protein, inhibits vascular calcification) → long-term warfarin use → ↑vascular calcification (reduces MGP Gla carboxylation → ↑vascular calcification, especially coronary arteries in CKD). Reversal of warfarin: FFP (fresh frozen plasma, immediate) + Vitamin K (phytonadione, IV/PO, 6-12h onset for factor synthesis); 4F-PCC (4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate = factors II + VII + IX + X + proteins C + S; faster + more predictable than FFP); andexanet alfa (anti-Xa reversal, NOT for warfarin; for apixaban/rivaroxaban); idarucizumab (anti-dabigatran).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In muscle glycogenolysis, activated phosphorylase kinase (PhK) phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase b → a. PhK itself is activated by two second messengers simultaneously. These are:
options: cAMP and diacylglycerol (DAG): PhK is NOT directly activated by DAG; DAG activates PKC which has different substrates; PhK is activated by Ca2+ + cAMP/PKA

Inositol triphosphate (IP3) and cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR): PhK is activated by Ca2+ (which IP3 releases, but IP3 itself is not the second messenger that acts on PhK) + cAMP via PKA; cADPR is a Ca2+-mobilizing messenger but not the primary PhK activator

Calcium (Ca2+) and cAMP (via PKA): PhK (phosphorylase kinase) = αβγδ tetrahedral subunit architecture; (αβγδ)4 holoenzyme (16 subunits); α-subunit: regulatory (phosphorylated by PKA at Ser); β-subunit: regulatory (phosphorylated by PKA at Ser); γ-subunit: CATALYTIC (kinase activity); δ-subunit = calmodulin (CaM, calcium-binding, permanently bound); activation: (1) Ca2+ binds the δ/CaM subunit → conformational change in γ subunit → partial activation of PhK (basal Ca2+-dependent activity); this allows muscle contraction (↑[Ca2+]i from SR → PhK partially active → ↑glycogenolysis → ↑energy for contraction) WITHOUT requiring PKA; (2) epinephrine → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates PhK α and β subunits → full activation of PhK (phospho-PhK can be further activated by Ca2+ → synergistic); thus: PhK is activated by BOTH Ca2+ (from SR, via ECC) + cAMP/PKA; in heart and skeletal muscle during exercise: Ca2+ is the primary signal (ECC couples contraction to glycogenolysis via Ca2+-calmodulin-PhK pathway, WITHOUT needing epinephrine/cAMP); in liver: no direct Ca2+ signal for glycogenolysis; glucagon + epinephrine → cAMP → PKA → PhK → phosphorylase; PhK deficiency: GSD type VIII (or IX in different nomenclature) = PhK deficiency: X-linked (PHKA2 [α-subunit liver-specific isoform, most common]) or AR (PHKB [β-subunit] or PHKG2 [liver γ-subunit isoform]) → liver PhK deficiency → benign hepatomegaly + mild hypoglycemia + ↑glycogen in liver; muscle PhK deficiency (PHKA1, X-linked): exercise intolerance + cramps (McArdle-like but NO myoglobinuria usually)

Glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) and AMP: G6P inhibits hexokinase (not PhK); AMP activates glycogen phosphorylase DIRECTLY (AMP binds allosteric site on phosphorylase b [inactive form] → converts it to phosphorylase b active conformation EVEN WITHOUT phosphorylation, in the AMP-bound active 'R-state') but AMP does NOT activate PhK; PhK is activated by Ca2+ + cAMP/PKA
explanation: Glycogen metabolism signaling cascade (full): Beta-adrenergic stimulation (epinephrine in muscle/liver): Epi → β-AR → Gαs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA (cAMP-dependent protein kinase = PKA holoenzyme [R2C2 tetramer] → 4 cAMP molecules bind R-subunits → release C-subunits → active C-subunits phosphorylate targets): PKA → phosphorylates: PhK (α+β subunits → ↑PhK → ↑phosphorylase b→a → ↑glycogenolysis); GS kinase (phosphorylates GS → ↓glycogen synthesis); phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibited by methylxanthines [theophylline, caffeine → ↑cAMP by blocking degradation]; Phosphorylase a: serine-phosphorylated form; active regardless of AMP levels (constitutively active in T/R state balance → predominantly in R state); Phosphorylase b: unphosphorylated; normally inactive (T-state) UNLESS AMP is bound (AMP → allosterically converts T→R → active but less so than phosphorylase a); ATP + G6P → allosterically inhibit phosphorylase b (compete with AMP binding); glucose alone → inhibits phosphorylase a in liver (by binding active site → T-state preference → becomes better substrate for phosphatase PP-1G); PP-1G (protein phosphatase 1, glycogen-associated, regulatory subunit GL/RGL in liver): PP-1G dephosphorylates: PhK (↓activity) + phosphorylase a → b (↓glycogenolysis) + GS-phospho → GS (↑glycogen synthesis); PP-1G is activated by: insulin → PI3K → Akt → phosphorylates PHLPP2 + inhibits GSK-3β; insulin also phosphorylates PDE → ↓cAMP → ↓PKA → ↑PP-1G → ↑GS activity → ↑glycogen storage. Ca2+ signaling in muscle (exercise without epinephrine): ECC (excitation-contraction coupling): motor neuron AP → nicotinic ACh → muscle AP → T-tubule voltage sensor (DHPR, dihydropyridine receptor, Cav1.1) → physical interaction → RyR1 (ryanodine receptor 1) → ↑SR Ca2+ release → [Ca2+]i ↑ from 0.1µM → 10µM → troponin C (TnC) binds Ca2+ → conformational change → exposes actin-myosin binding sites → contraction; SIMULTANEOUSLY: Ca2+ → CaM (PhK δ-subunit) → ↑PhK → ↑phosphorylase a → ↑glycogenolysis → ↑ATP for contraction.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: An infant presents with recurrent bacterial infections, albinism (partial), and giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils. The underlying defect involves:
options: Defect in RAG1/RAG2 recombinase (RAG1/2 are required for VDJ recombination in T and B cell development → RAG deficiency → SCID with absent T and B cells; Chediak-Higashi has normal lymphocyte numbers but dysfunctional NK cells and CTL)

Defect in CD40 ligand (CD40L, CD154) on T cells (CD40L deficiency → Hyper-IgM syndrome type I → ↑IgM + ↓IgG/A/E due to impaired isotype class switching [T cell CD40L-B cell CD40 interaction required for GC formation + class switch]; Chediak-Higashi does NOT present with impaired isotype class switching)

Defect in the LYST (lysosomal trafficking regulator) gene causing failure of lysosomal granule trafficking (Chediak-Higashi syndrome [CHS]: AR; LYST gene (also called BEACH domain-containing protein CHS1, chromosome 1q42.1-3): LYST is a large cytoplasmic protein required for proper formation and sizing of lysosomes + lysosome-related organelles (LROs); LYST deficiency → giant fused lysosomes/granules in virtually all granule-containing cells: (1) neutrophils → giant azurophilic granules (primary lysosomes fail to properly 'pinch off' → giant granules by fusion) → neutrophils cannot efficiently kill bacteria (granules cannot properly fuse with phagosomes → delayed intracellular killing) → recurrent pyogenic infections (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus); (2) melanocytes → large melanosomes that cannot properly distribute melanin → partial oculocutaneous albinism (diluted pigmentation in skin, hair, iris); (3) NK cells → defective NK cell lytic granule secretion → impaired NK killing; (4) CTL → defective cytotoxic granule exocytosis → impaired target cell killing; (5) platelets → dense granule defects → mild bleeding tendency; clinical phases: stable phase (recurrent infections + partial albinism + peripheral neuropathy [from giant granules in Schwann cells/neurons]) → accelerated phase (hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis [HLH]/lymphohistiocytic infiltration of organs: fever + hepatosplenomegaly + lymphadenopathy + cytopenias; triggered by EBV or other infections; mediated by uncontrolled NK/CTL activation because they can't kill targets efficiently → macrophage activation); treatment: HSCT (cures hematologic + immunologic aspects; does NOT cure neurological features); diagnosis: PBS showing giant neutrophil granules; gene sequencing of LYST

Defect in ADA (adenosine deaminase) enzyme causing lymphocyte toxicity (ADA deficiency → SCID via accumulation of deoxyadenosine → toxic to lymphocytes especially T cells; presents with profound lymphopenia; no giant granules; no partial albinism)
explanation: Lysosome-related organelle (LRO) diseases: LROs are organelles sharing biogenesis machinery with lysosomes: melanosomes (melanocytes), Weibel-Palade bodies (endothelial cells), dense granules (platelets), azurophilic granules (neutrophils), lytic granules (NK/CTL), lamellar bodies (type II pneumocytes). Diseases of LRO biogenesis: CHS (LYST): giant granules in all LRO-containing cells → partial albinism + immune dysfunction + bleeding. HPS (Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, HPS1-11): multiple genes encoding BLOC (biogenesis of lysosome-related organelle complex) proteins; ↓dense granules (platelets) → bleeding diathesis + ↓melanosomes → OCA; no giant granules; some subtypes → pulmonary fibrosis (HPS-1, HPS-4: BLOC-3 deficiency → disease in lamellar bodies of type II pneumocytes); neutropenia (HPS-2: AP3B1 deficiency = AP-3 adaptor protein → neutrophil granule + melanocyte + platelet LROs affected). Griscelli syndrome (GS): GS type 1 (MYO5A [myosin Va] mutation → melanosomes not transported in melanocyte dendrites → clumped melanosomes → silvery hair + hypopigmentation + neurological symptoms); GS type 2 (RAB27A mutation → lytic granule secretion defect → HLH without neurological symptoms); GS type 3 (MLPH/melanophilin mutation → silvery hair, benign, no immune/neurological). Familial HLH (fHLH/FHLH): primary HLH from defects in CTL/NK granule-mediated killing: perforin mutations (PRF1, FHLH2): ↓perforin pore formation; UNC13D (FHLH3): ↓lytic granule priming/docking; STX11 (FHLH4): ↓lytic granule fusion; STXBP2 (FHLH5): ↓fusion; all → CTL/NK cannot kill targets → unchecked macrophage activation → HLH.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 4-year-old child has recurrent episodes of vomiting and metabolic acidosis after high-protein meals. Urine organic acid analysis shows elevated isovalerylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovalerate. NBS showed elevated C5-acylcarnitine. Enzyme deficiency is:
options: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC): PCC deficiency → propionic acidemia; NBS marker = ↑C3 (propionylcarnitine), NOT C5; urine shows ↑3-OH-propionic acid + methylcitric acid, NOT isovalerylglycine; protein intake exacerbates but different pattern

3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (3-MCC, MCCA + MCCB genes): 3-MCC deficiency → ↑3-methylcrotonylglycine + 3-OH-isovalerate + 3-methylcrotonate in urine; NBS: ↑C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine), NOT C5 per se; 3-MCC deficiency is the MOST COMMON organic acidemia detected on NBS in many countries (but often benign/asymptomatic; considered largely benign in most cases); common false positive in maternal 3-MCC deficiency (mother's metabolites cross placenta → elevated in infant's NBS)

Isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVD): isovaleric acidemia (IVD deficiency); NBS: ↑C5-acylcarnitine (isovalerylcarnitine, C5:0-acylcarnitine); urine OA: ↑isovalerylglycine (formed by conjugation of isovalerate + glycine, catalyzed by glycine N-acyltransferase [GLYAT] → helps excrete isovalerate; this is the KEY diagnostic marker) + ↑3-OH-isovalerate + isovaleric acid; odor: 'sweaty feet' or 'cheesy' smell (from isovaleric acid); IVD is the first step after BCKDH in Leu catabolism (Leu → BCKA → isovaleryl-CoA → [IVD, FAD-dependent] → 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA → [3-MCC] → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA → [3-MGS] → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA); high protein (especially Leu-containing) → ↑isovaleryl-CoA → IVD enzyme saturated (or absent) → ↑isovalerate → isovalerylglycine; treatment: low-Leu diet + glycine supplementation (↑isovalerylglycine formation → more efficient excretion) + carnitine; prognosis: variable; if treated early (via NBS) → often normal development

Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM): methylmalonic acidemia; NBS: ↑C3-carnitine (propionylcarnitine; elevated because methylmalonyl-CoA accumulation → overflows to propionyl-CoA); urine: ↑methylmalonic acid + ↑propionic acid byproducts; NOT isovalerylglycine
explanation: Leucine catabolism and organic acidemias: Leu is PURELY KETOGENIC → feeds HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA (no gluconeogenic carbons). Leu catabolism cascade: Leu → [BCAT] → α-ketoisocaproate (KIC) + Glu → [BCKDH complex, rate-limiting, TPP+NADH+CoASH] → isovaleryl-CoA + CO2 + NADH → [IVD, FAD-dep] → 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA → [3-MCC, biotin+CO2+ATP] → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA → [3-methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase, AUH] → HMG-CoA → [HMGCL] → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. Enzyme deficiencies in Leu catabolism: MSUD (BCKDH): all 3 BCKAs; ↑C5, C3, C4 acylcarnitines (C5 from isovaleryl-CoA); urine: ↑BCKA; sweet maple syrup odor; alloisoleucine pathognomonic. Isovaleric acidemia (IVD): ↑C5 acylcarnitine; ↑isovalerylglycine + 3-OH-isovalerate; sweaty-feet odor; Leu restriction + glycine + carnitine. 3-MCC deficiency (3-MCC): ↑C5-OH acylcarnitine; ↑3-OH-isovalerate + 3-methylcrotonylglycine; mostly benign (discovered on NBS); maternal 3-MCC deficiency common cause of elevated C5-OH in infant. 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria (multiple causes): types I-V: type I (3-MGS deficiency, AUH mutations, ↑3-methylglutaconate + 3-OH-isovalerate); types II-V: secondary (↑3-methylglutaconate from other metabolic disturbances, not AUH deficiency); types II (Barth syndrome, tafazzin mutations, cardiomyopathy + neutropenia); type III (DNAJC19 mutations, DCMA syndrome); type IV/V (OPA3, CLPB mutations). HMG-CoA lyase deficiency (HMGCL): cannot generate acetoacetate from HMG-CoA → ↓ketones + ↑HMG-CoA → hypoketotic hypoglycemia + metabolic acidosis (↑HMG acid + 3-OH-3-methylglutarate in urine); similar to FAOD in presentation but different pathway.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Fanconi anemia (FA) is caused by mutations in FA proteins (FANC genes). The key molecular defect in FA is:
options: Impaired V(D)J recombination in lymphocyte development (VDJ recombination involves RAG1/2, Artemis, XRCC4, LigIV, Ku70/80 complex [NHEJ pathway]; FA proteins are not part of VDJ recombination; FA deficiency causes aplastic anemia, not lymphocyte-specific SCID-like immunodeficiency)

Inability to repair interstrand crosslinks (ICLs) in DNA: FA pathway: FA proteins (>23 FANC proteins, A/B/C/D1[BRCA2]/D2/E/F/G/I/J[BRIP1/BACH1]/K/L/M/N[PALB2]/O/P/Q/R/S/T/U/V/W) function in a common pathway for ICL repair (interstrand crosslinks covalently link both strands of dsDNA → prevent strand separation → block replication forks); ICL sources: bifunctional alkylating agents (nitrogen mustards, cyclophosphamide, melphalan), platinum compounds (cisplatin, oxaliplatin, carboplatin), mitomycin C, psoralens + UV; key FA pathway steps: (1) stalled replication fork at ICL → CMG helicase (CDC45-MCM2-7-GINS) stalls → FANCM (translocase) recruits FA core complex; (2) FA core complex (nuclear E3 ubiquitin ligase): FANC-A,-B,-C,-E,-F,-G,-L + UBE2T → monoubiquitinates FANCD2 and FANCI (FANCI-FANCD2 [ID] complex, called ID2 complex); monoubiquitin added to FANCD2-Lys561 by UBE2T (E2) + FANCL (cullin-like E3); (3) monoUb-ID2 complex → relocalizes to ICL site (chromatin foci, 'FA nuclear foci'); (4) recruited nucleases (FAN1, SLX4/FANCP as scaffold + SLX1, MUS81, XPF-ERCC1) → dual incisions flanking the ICL → unhooking the crosslink → one strand freed; (5) unhooked ICL → TLS (translesion synthesis) DNA polymerases (Rev1, Pol ζ [Rev3+Rev7+accessory subunits]) bypass the unhooked adduct → fill the gap; (6) FANCD1/BRCA2 + FANCN/PALB2 + FANCJ/BRIP1 → HR (homologous recombination) using sister chromatid → restores the other strand; clinical: FA → aplastic anemia (bone marrow failure, most often presenting as macrocytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + leukopenia) + cancer predisposition (AML/MDS [leukemia early], squamous cell carcinoma [especially head+neck+GU in adults]) + congenital anomalies (VACTERL: vertebral + anorectal + cardiac + tracheoesophageal fistula + renal + limb, especially radial ray defects [thumb + radius hypoplasia/aplasia] + other); key clinical detail: FA cells are hypersensitive to crosslinking agents (DEB [diepoxybutane] test or mitomycin C test → chromosomal breakage test → diagnostic; ↑chromosomal breaks + radial figures); treatment: HSCT (curative for hematologic manifestations); gene therapy (under investigation)

Failure of mismatch repair (MMR) causing microsatellite instability: MMR genes = MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; Lynch syndrome (HNPCC); deficient MMR → microsatellite instability (MSI); FA does NOT present with MSI or colorectal cancer predisposition (primarily squamous cell carcinoma)

Defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER) causing sensitivity to UV light: NER defects → Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP), Cockayne syndrome; FA is specifically an ICL repair defect; XP is a NER defect; both cause DNA repair failure but different pathways and different stimuli (UV vs. crosslinkers)
explanation: DNA repair overview — defects and associated diseases: BER (base excision repair): single-base damage (8-oxoG, alkylated bases, SSB) → OGG1, NEIL1/2, MUTYH, APE1, XRCC1/Lig3/Pol β; MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP): MUTYH (glycosylase for 8-oxoG:A mismatch) AR → colorectal polyposis. NER (nucleotide excision repair): bulky adducts + UV-induced CPDs (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers) + 6-4PP (pyrimidine-pyrimidone photoproducts) → XPC-RAD23B (GG-NER) or stalled Pol II (TC-NER) → TFIIH helicase (XPD, XPB) → single-strand excision (XPG at 3', XPF-ERCC1 at 5') → gap filled by Pol δ/ε; XP (A-G): xeroderma pigmentosum; XP Variant (Pol η/POLH deficiency, TLS). MMR (mismatch repair): base mismatches + insertion/deletion loops → MutSα (MSH2+MSH6) or MutSβ (MSH2+MSH3) → MutLα (MLH1+PMS2) → excision + resynthesis; Lynch syndrome (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 germline mutations, AD) → colorectal + endometrial + other cancers + MSI. DSB repair: NHEJ (non-homologous end joining): fast, error-prone, throughout cell cycle; Ku70+Ku80 → DNA-PK → XRCC4-LigIV-XLF → join; defects: Artemis mutations → SCID; Lig4 syndrome; XLF/Cernunnos deficiency; DNA-PKcs mutations. HR (homologous recombination): accurate, S/G2 phase; DSB → Mre11-Rad50-NBS1 (MRN) → CtIP → RPA-ssDNA → RAD51 (loaded by BRCA2/PALB2) → strand invasion into sister chromatid → Holliday junction → resolution; BRCA1 + BRCA2 → HR; PARP inhibitors (olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib, talazoparib) → synthetic lethality in BRCA1/2-deficient tumors (BRCA1/2 → ↓HR → rely on PARP-mediated SSB repair → PARP inhibition → SSBs → DSBs → cannot repair by HR → cell death). FA pathway bridges ICL repair + HR.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which lipoprotein carries the most cholesterol (as a percentage of its total lipid) and is primarily responsible for 'reverse cholesterol transport'?
options: VLDL (very-low-density lipoprotein): carries mostly triglycerides (~55% TG); produced by the liver; delivers TG to peripheral tissues → becomes IDL → LDL; NOT primarily a cholesterol carrier or involved in RCT

LDL (low-density lipoprotein): LDL carries the MOST cholesterol (approximately 45-50% cholesterol + CE; mainly cholesterol ester [CE] carried in core) and is the primary vehicle for delivering cholesterol to peripheral tissues; LDL is NOT involved in reverse cholesterol transport (which goes FROM periphery TO liver, not liver → periphery); LDL is formed by VLDL → IDL → LDL (CETP + lipolysis); LDL is cleared by LDLR (LDL receptor) in liver primarily (→ clathrin-coated pit → endocytosis → lysosome → CE → free cholesterol → ↓HMGCR + LDLR transcription via SCAP-SREBP2 pathway)

HDL (high-density lipoprotein): HDL primarily performs 'reverse cholesterol transport' (RCT) — transporting excess cholesterol FROM peripheral tissues TO the liver for excretion; HDL lipid composition: ~30% phospholipid (PC, SM) + ~20% unesterified + esterified cholesterol + ~15% TG + ~5% other; compared to LDL (45-50% cholesterol + CE), HDL has LESS cholesterol as % of total weight; but HDL is SPECIFICALLY responsible for RCT: nascent HDL (discoidal, apoA-I-containing) → ABCA1 (ABC transporter A1, Tangier disease gene) on macrophages + peripheral cells → accepts free cholesterol → LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase, activated by apoA-I → esterifies free cholesterol → CE in HDL core → converts discoidal to spherical mature HDL); CE-enriched HDL3 → HDL2; CETP (cholesterol ester transfer protein) → transfers CE from HDL → VLDL/LDL in exchange for TG → HDL TG → hepatic lipase → regenerates HDL3 ('HDL cycling'); final: CE-enriched HDL → SR-BI (scavenger receptor B-I, SCARB1) in liver → selective CE uptake (without apoA-I endocytosis) → CE → bile acids + free cholesterol → bile → feces; HDL as a fraction has only ~20% cholesterol but is the RCT vehicle; QUESTION likely tests: HDL = RCT vehicle; LDL = most cholesterol by % (45-50%); for NEET-relevant exam logic: 'reverse cholesterol transport' = HDL; 'highest cholesterol %' = LDL
Chylomicron: carries mostly dietary TG (~85% TG); produced by intestine; delivers dietary TG to peripheral tissues; relatively little cholesterol (%); NOT involved in RCT
explanation: Lipoprotein composition — key numbers: Lipoprotein | TG % | Chol+CE % | PL % | Protein %. Chylomicron: 85, 4, 9, 2. VLDL: 55, 20, 18, 7. IDL: 35, 36, 22, 10. LDL: 10, 48, 22, 20. HDL: 5, 20, 30, 50. Reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) — step by step: 1. Peripheral cells (macrophage foam cells, arterial wall) → ABCA1 → exports cholesterol + PL → apoA-I (free in plasma or just secreted by liver/intestine) → forms nascent pre-β-HDL (discoidal); 2. Peripheral cells also → ABCG1 → exports cholesterol to mature spherical HDL3; 3. Nascent HDL → LCAT (apoA-I activates LCAT) → PC + free Chol → CE + lysoPC; CE moves to core → discoidal → spherical HDL3; 4. HDL3 + more CE from LCAT → HDL2; 5. CETP: exchanges HDL-CE → VLDL/LDL-TG (and vice versa); ↑CETP → ↓HDL-C (and ↑LDL-C [CE-enriched LDL]); CETP inhibitors (anacetrapib, torcetrapib [off due to off-target BP effects], evacetrapib [failed CVD outcomes trial]) → ↑HDL dramatically; anacetrapib showed modest CVD benefit (HPS3/REVEAL trial) but not approved; genetically ↓CETP → ↑HDL (some Asians) but paradoxically NOT always ↓CVD (HDL-C is not fully predictive of function); 6. SR-BI (SCARB1) in liver: selective uptake of CE from HDL → CE → bile; 7. LDLR in liver: uptakes VLDL remnants/LDL (CE-enriched after CETP transfer from HDL); Tangier disease: ABCA1 mutations → cannot export cholesterol from macrophages → apoA-I/HDL cannot be lipidated → apoA-I rapidly catabolized → near-absent HDL + ↑TG + cholesterol deposits in lymphoid organs (orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy); paradoxically: not greatly ↑CVD in Tangier disease (despite very low HDL; highlights that HDL-C level ≠ CVD protection linearly); ABCA1 mutations in heterozygotes: familial hypoalphalipoproteinemia (↓HDL-C but not as severe as Tangier).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme that synthesizes UMP de novo from orotic acid is:
options: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH): converts dihydroorotate → orotate (step 4 of de novo pyrimidine synthesis); produces the pyrimidine ring precursor orotate; located in IMM (unlike other de novo pyrimidine enzymes which are cytoplasmic/bifunctional); target of leflunomide's active metabolite teriflunomide → ↓pyrimidine synthesis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation (used in rheumatoid arthritis + MS); NOT the enzyme that adds ribose-5-P to orotate

Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (OPRT): OPRT transfers a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate) to orotate → orotidine-5'-monophosphate (OMP); this is the step that converts orotic acid to a nucleotide (OMP); in mammals, OPRT activity is part of the bifunctional enzyme UMP synthase (UPS = UMPS gene), which has two activities: (1) OPRT (N-terminal domain): orotate + PRPP → OMP + PPi; (2) OMP decarboxylase (OMPD, C-terminal domain): OMP → UMP + CO2; orotic acid accumulates if: (a) OTC deficiency: carbamoyl-P overflows from urea cycle into pyrimidine synthesis → ↑carbamoyl-P → ↑orotic acid via DHODH → BLOCKED at OPRT step (substrate builds up) → ↑urinary orotic acid + hyperammonemia; (b) UMPS (UMP synthase) deficiency = orotic aciduria type I (hereditary orotic aciduria): very rare AR; ↑orotic acid in urine + megaloblastic anemia (↓UMP → ↓RNA + ↓DNA → ↓cell division of RBC progenitors → megaloblastic changes) + growth failure + normal ammonia [distinguishes from OTC deficiency where ammonia ↑]; treat with oral uridine (bypasses blocked enzyme, provides UMP precursor); (c) 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) + active metabolite 5-FDUMP → inhibits thymidylate synthase (TS) → ↓dTMP → orotic acid doesn't directly accumulate from 5-FU; but allopurinol → ↑PRPP availability → ↑orotic acid synthesis (allopurinol has some inhibitory effect on OPRT in some conditions, and also PRPP is redirected away from purine de novo)

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II): catalyzes the first and RATE-LIMITING step of pyrimidine de novo synthesis: Gln + 2 ATP + HCO3- → carbamoyl phosphate (in the cytoplasm; distinct from CPS I in mito for urea cycle); inhibited by UTP (end product inhibition, allosteric); activated by ATP + PRPP; forms a trifunctional enzyme with aspartate transcarbamylase (ATC) and DHOase on a single large polypeptide: CAD protein (CPS II + ATCase + DHOase)

Thymidylate synthase (TS): converts dUMP + 5,10-methylene-THF → dTMP + DHF; not involved in de novo UMP synthesis from orotic acid; TS is specifically for deoxyuridine → deoxythymidine conversion; inhibited by 5-FDUMP (FdUMP, from 5-fluorouracil)
explanation: De novo pyrimidine synthesis (6 steps): 1. CPS II (CAD): Gln + 2ATP + HCO3- → carbamoyl-P; CYTOPLASM; rate-limiting; inhibited by UTP. 2. ATCase (CAD): carbamoyl-P + Asp → N-carbamoyl-Asp. 3. DHOase (CAD): N-carbamoyl-Asp → dihydroorotate (ring closure). 4. DHODH: dihydroorotate → orotate; UNIQUE: located in IMM (uses ubiquinone as electron acceptor → FAD/FMN containing enzyme); inhibited by leflunomide metabolite (teriflunomide) → ↓T cell proliferation. 5. OPRT (UMPS): orotate + PRPP → OMP. 6. OMPD (UMPS): OMP → UMP + CO2. CAD = trifunctional protein for steps 1-3. UMPS = bifunctional protein for steps 5-6. UMP → [UMP kinase] → UDP → [NDP kinase] → UTP → [CTP synthase, Gln] → CTP; CTP → [RNR, ribonucleotide reductase] → dCDP → dCTP; UTP → [RNR] → dUDP → dUMP → [TS] → dTMP. Pyrimidine salvage: uridine phosphorylase (UP) + uridine kinase (UK): uridine → UMP (salvage); thymidine kinase (TK1): thymidine → TMP (important in S-phase, used to assess cell proliferation [↑TK1 in tumors]); thymidine phosphorylase (TP): converts thymidine ↔ thymine + deoxyribose-1-P; MNGIE (mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy): TP deficiency (TYMP gene) → ↑thymidine + ↑deoxyuridine in plasma → mitochondrial thymidine pool imbalance → mtDNA depletion/deletion → MNGIE (ophthalmoplegia + GI dysmotility + neuropathy + leukoencephalopathy); TYMP enzyme therapy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with recurrent pancreatitis has serum triglycerides > 1000 mg/dL and eruptive xanthomas. Genetic testing reveals LPL deficiency. The biochemical basis is inability to:
options: Synthesize triglycerides from fatty acids (TG synthesis is performed by DGAT enzymes in the ER; LPL is a lipolytic enzyme, not a synthetic one)
Transfer cholesterol from LDL to cell membranes (LDLR mediates LDL uptake; LPL does not function in LDL metabolism directly)

Hydrolyze triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL at the capillary endothelium: LPL (lipoprotein lipase): synthesized in parenchymal cells of adipose + muscle + heart → secreted → binds GPIHBP1 (GPI-anchored HDL-binding protein 1) on luminal surface of capillary endothelium; GPIHBP1: transports LPL from subendothelial surface to luminal surface; stabilizes LPL; GPIHBP1 mutations → TG > 1000, similar to LPL deficiency (familial chylomicronemia syndrome type II); LPL function: hydrolyzes TG in core of chylomicrons and VLDL at the capillary endothelial surface → FFA + glycerol → FFA taken up by adjacent cells (muscle → oxidation, adipose → re-esterification as TG for storage); LPL cofactors: ACTIVATED by: apoC-II (on chylomicrons and VLDL) → apoC-II deficiency = same TG > 1000 phenotype as LPL deficiency; ApoA-V (secreted by liver → associates with VLDL → ↑LPL activity → ↓TG); INHIBITED by: apoC-III (on VLDL → inhibits LPL + inhibits hepatic uptake of TG-rich remnants + inhibits ANGPTL3/4 cleavage of LPL) → ↑apoC-III → ↑TG; ANGPTL3/4 (angiopoietin-like proteins 3 and 4): inhibit LPL (especially in fasting states → ↑ANGPTL4 → ↑LPL inhibition in adipose → promotes FFA release vs. uptake [lipolysis of stored TG in adipose, not LPL-mediated chylomicron TG hydrolysis]; ANGPTL3 inhibits EL [endothelial lipase] + LPL); loss-of-function ANGPTL3 mutations → very low TG + LDL + HDL (all three ↓); evinacumab (anti-ANGPTL3 mAb): for homozygous FH; LPL deficiency = FCS (familial chylomicronemia syndrome, type I hyperlipoproteinemia): TG > 1000-2000 mg/dL consistently; chylomicronemia + eruptive xanthomas + pancreatitis; plasma appears milky (lactescent); fasting does NOT normalize TG; NO ↑atherosclerosis (chylomicrons too large to enter vessel wall); treatment: very-low-fat diet (<15g fat/day) + omega-3 FA (↓VLDL-TG), volanesorsen (anti-sense mRNA target ApoCIII → ↓ApoCIII → ↑LPL activity; approved in EU), alipogene tiparvovec (LPL gene therapy, AAV-LPL; first gene therapy approved in EU, 2012, later withdrawn for commercial reasons)
Synthesize HDL from apoA-I and phospholipids (nascent HDL formation involves ABCA1 lipidation of apoA-I; LPL is not required for HDL synthesis)
explanation: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (HTG) — clinical and biochemical: Chylomicronemia syndrome: TG > 1000 mg/dL (often > 5000 in homozygous LPL deficiency); milky plasma; Tyndall effect (plasma white due to chylomicron light scattering); eruptive xanthomas (TG-laden macrophages in skin); lipemia retinalis (white color in retinal vessels on fundoscopy); abdominal pain (due to pancreatic lipase overload + FFA from partial LPL activity or other lipase → pancreatitis risk); splenomegaly; hepatomegaly. Gene panel for severe HTG (familial chylomicronemia): LPL (most common), APOC2, APOA5, LMF1 (lipase maturation factor 1 — required for LPL/HL folding in ER), GPIHBP1. Moderate HTG (200-999 mg/dL): polygenic + secondary causes (T2DM, hypothyroidism, alcohol, CKD, medications [HAART, tamoxifen, corticosteroids, atypical antipsychotics]). Type V hyperlipoproteinemia: elevated chylomicrons + VLDL → TG 500-1000 mg/dL; often polygenic + secondary triggers; treated with fibrates (↑LPL transcription via PPARα + ↓ApoCIII transcription via PPARα) + omega-3 FA (↓VLDL production). ANGPTL proteins: ANGPTL3: mainly from liver; inhibits LPL + EL; elevated in insulin resistance; inhibited by evinacumab (approved for HoFH); ANGPTL4: from adipose + liver; inhibited during feeding → ↑LPL active → chylomicron TG cleared; elevated in fasting → ↓LPL → TG accumulation in plasma; ANGPTL8 (betatrophin): liver + adipose → complexes with ANGPTL3 to preferentially inhibit LPL in heart/muscle (spares adipose LPL during feeding → allows selective TG delivery to adipose).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) deficiency presents with lactic acidosis. All of the following are cofactors for PDC EXCEPT:
options: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, vitamin B1): E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase component of PDC) uses TPP as cofactor; TPP deficiency (Wernicke encephalopathy) → impairs PDC → ↑pyruvate + ↑lactate
Lipoic acid: E2 (dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase) uses lipoic acid covalently attached to Lys residue via amide bond; lipoic acid as a 'swinging arm' transfers acetyl group from E1 → CoA

Biotin: biotin is NOT a cofactor for PDC; biotin is covalently attached (amide bond via holocarboxylase synthetase) to carboxylase enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase (PC), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC1/2), propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC), 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (3-MCC); PDC does NOT use biotin; the cofactors of PDC are: TPP (E1), lipoic acid (E2), CoASH (E2 product), FAD (E3), NAD+ (E3); the enzymes using biotin in mitochondria include PC (in matrix); biotinidase (BTD) recycles biotin from biocytin; BTD deficiency → cannot recycle → secondary biotin deficiency → impairs PC + other carboxylases → ↑lactic acidosis (different from PDC deficiency)

FAD: E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, DLDH) uses FAD as prosthetic group; FAD oxidizes dihydrolipoamide → lipoamide while reducing FAD → FADH2; FADH2 then reduces NAD+ → NADH (via the FAD → NAD+ transfer in E3); E3 (DLDH) is shared by PDC + OGDH + BCKDH
explanation: PDC cofactors remembered by '5 cofactors = NAD+ FADH CoA TPP Lipoic acid' (Never Forget CoA Thru Life): PDC = 3 catalytic components + 2 regulatory: E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase): TPP → decarboxylates pyruvate → acetyl group attached to TPP; E2 (dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase): lipoic acid on Lys → accepts acetyl from E1→TPP → transfers to CoASH → acetyl-CoA; E3 (DLDH): FAD + NAD+ → oxidizes dihydrolipoamide → lipoamide; E3-binding protein (E3BP): tethers E3 to the E2 core; PDK (pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase 1-4): phosphorylates E1α → INHIBITS PDC; activated by: acetyl-CoA, NADH, ATP (all products of PDC/TCA/β-oxidation); inhibited by: ADP, CoASH, NAD+ (substrates); PDPase (pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase, Mg2+/Ca2+-dependent): dephosphorylates E1α → ACTIVATES PDC; activated by: Ca2+ (exercise), insulin; PDC deficiency (E1α most common, X-linked [PDHA1 gene on Xp22.33]; also E2 [DLAT], E3 [DLD], E3BP [PDHX]): PDHA1 deficiency → ↑pyruvate → ↓acetyl-CoA → ↓TCA + ↓ATP → neurological manifestations (brain is aerobic, glucose-dependent → pyruvate cannot be used aerobically → brain fails) + lactic acidosis; features: neonatal lactic acidosis (most severe), Leigh syndrome pattern (basal ganglia lesions), developmental delay; pyruvate:acetyl-CoA ratio ↑; thiamine-responsive PDC deficiency (some PDHA1 mutations → high-dose thiamine → ↑TPP → partially restore E1 activity); ketogenic diet (bypasses blocked PDC by providing ketone bodies as acetyl-CoA equivalent for TCA directly in brain).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Heparin is used as an anticoagulant. The PRIMARY mechanism of heparin's anticoagulant effect is:
options: Direct inhibition of thrombin (Factor IIa) by covalent modification of its active site serine (heparin does NOT covalently modify thrombin; direct thrombin inhibitors [hirudin, dabigatran, bivalirudin] bind thrombin's active site directly; heparin works via antithrombin)

Activation of antithrombin (AT, AT-III) → rapid inhibition of multiple coagulation factors: heparin mechanism: heparin (a sulfated GAG, mixture of polysaccharides [MW 3,000-30,000 Da for UFH, or MW ~5000 Da for LMWH]) → binds a specific pentasaccharide sequence on antithrombin (AT, SERPINC1); AT is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that slowly inactivates: thrombin (IIa), Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa, kallikrein; heparin binding → conformational change in AT → markedly accelerates AT inhibition rates (10,000-fold for thrombin; 1000-fold for Xa); mechanism differs for Xa vs thrombin: AT binds Xa directly via the pentasaccharide site (heparin bridges AT to Xa is not needed for Xa inhibition → even small pentasaccharide [fondaparinux] can inhibit Xa); AT inhibits thrombin by a TERNARY COMPLEX mechanism: heparin bridges AT to thrombin simultaneously (heparin chain ≥18 saccharides needed) → UFH inhibits both Xa + thrombin; LMWH (7000 Da, avg chain ~15 saccharides): mainly inhibits Xa (most chains too short to bridge AT to thrombin) → Xa:IIa inhibition ratio = 4:1 for enoxaparin vs 1:1 for UFH; fondaparinux (synthetic pentasaccharide): ONLY anti-Xa (no anti-IIa activity); UFH monitoring: aPTT (APTT, activated partial thromboplastin time: intrinsic + common pathway; most sensitive to heparin effect on IIa); LMWH monitoring: anti-Xa activity (calibrated for LMWH); platelet factor 4 (PF4): PF4 released from activated platelets → binds heparin (neutralizes heparin; one reason for heparin resistance); HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia): PF4-heparin complex → antibodies (IgG) → IgG-PF4-heparin immune complex → binds platelet FcγRIIA → platelet activation → THROMBOSIS + thrombocytopenia; treat HIT: STOP heparin (including LMWH, fondaparinux relatively safe); use non-heparin anticoagulants (argatroban, bivalirudin [DTIs], or rivaroxaban/apixaban)
Inhibition of the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in the liver (this is warfarin's mechanism; heparin does not affect factor synthesis; heparin acts immediately in plasma)
Chelation of calcium ions required for coagulation factor activation (EDTA chelates Ca2+ in laboratory settings; heparin is not a chelating agent; its anticoagulant effect is AT-III mediated)
explanation: Heparin pharmacology: UFH (unfractionated heparin): molecular weight 3,000-30,000 Da (mean ~15,000 Da); heterogeneous; mechanism = AT activation; both Xa + IIa inhibition (1:1 ratio); IV or SC; monitoring = aPTT (1.5-2.5× normal therapeutic range) or anti-Xa; reversible with protamine (positively charged → neutralizes heparin's negative sulfate groups); HIT risk 1-3% with UFH. LMWH (low-molecular-weight heparin: enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin, nadroparin): MW 4,000-6,500 Da; more predictable PK (better subcutaneous bioavailability ~90% vs ~30% UFH); predominantly anti-Xa; monitoring: anti-Xa for high-risk patients (CKD, pregnancy, extremes of weight); partial reversal with protamine (~60% reversal of Xa activity); HIT risk <0.5% with LMWH. Fondaparinux (Arixtra): synthetic pentasaccharide; MW ~1728 Da; ONLY anti-Xa; cannot be reversed with protamine; renally cleared; lower HIT risk; approved for DVT prophylaxis, ACS, DVT/PE treatment. Bivalirudin: direct thrombin inhibitor; semisynthetic; bound to thrombin catalytic site + fibrin-binding exosite; used in PCI; renally + enzymatically cleared; does NOT cause HIT antibodies (no PF4 involvement); good choice in suspected HIT. Argatroban: small-molecule direct thrombin inhibitor; hepatically cleared → preferred in CKD; used in HIT treatment; monitored by aPTT. New anticoagulant targets: TFPI (tissue factor pathway inhibitor) → marstacimab; FXI → factor XIa inhibitors (osocimab, abelacimab, asundexian, milvexian) in trials (FXI deficiency [Hemophilia C] → low thrombosis risk but minimal bleeding → FXI inhibition may provide anticoagulation without major bleeding risk).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: ABO blood group antigens are carbohydrate antigens on the surface of red blood cells. The H antigen is the precursor for both A and B antigens. The enzyme that synthesizes H antigen is:
options: Alpha-1,3-galactosyltransferase (ABO gene encodes the A- and B-transferases: for A antigen, GTA [alpha-1,3-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase] adds GalNAc to H-antigen; for B antigen, GTB [alpha-1,3-galactosyltransferase] adds Gal to H-antigen; H-antigen synthesis is a DIFFERENT enzyme)

Alpha-1,2-fucosyltransferase encoded by FUT1 (H gene): the H antigen is a carbohydrate structure (fucosylated type 2 chain): H antigen = Fucα1→2-Galβ1→4-GlcNAc-R (or type 1 chain in secretions); synthesis: Type 2 H on RBC: FUT1 (H gene, α-1,2-fucosyltransferase 1) → adds Fucose (α1→2) to terminal Gal on the precursor type 2 chain → H antigen; Type 1 H in secretions (saliva, plasma): FUT2 (Se gene, secretor gene, α-1,2-fucosyltransferase 2) → adds Fuc to type 1 precursor chains; modification of H antigen: A allele (GTA enzyme: α-1,3-N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase): H + UDP-GalNAc → A antigen (GalNAc added); B allele (GTB enzyme: α-1,3-galactosyltransferase): H + UDP-Gal → B antigen (Gal added); O allele: FUT1/ABO gene has frameshift/stop mutation → no functional enzyme → H remains unmodified → O blood group; AB: both A + B enzymes present → GalNAc + Gal both added; Bombay blood group (Oh): FUT1 (H gene) homozygous null mutations → NO H antigen → cannot make A or B → blood type 'Oh'; antibodies: anti-H, anti-A, anti-B, anti-AB in plasma → SEVERE hemolytic transfusion reaction if given A, B, AB, or O blood; rare (1 in 10,000 in India; rare in Europe); Bombay individuals can only receive Bombay donor blood (or autologous); Lewis antigens (Le): FUT3 (Lewis gene): adds Fuc to precursor type 1 chain → Lea antigen; if FUT2 (Se) also active → Leb antigen; Lewis antigens absorbed onto RBCs from plasma (not synthesized in RBCs themselves)

UDP-galactosyltransferase encoded by the B allele of the ABO gene (the B-transferase adds Gal to H antigen to make B antigen; it does NOT synthesize H antigen itself; H antigen is the substrate for B-transferase, not its product)
Neuraminidase (sialidase): neuraminidase removes sialic acid from glycoproteins/glycolipids; unrelated to H antigen synthesis; H antigen is a fucosyl structure, not a sialyl structure
explanation: ABO blood groups — complete biochemistry: Gene = ABO (chromosome 9q34.2): encodes glycosyltransferases; A allele (most common A1): GTA — adds GalNAc in α-1,3 linkage to terminal Gal of H → A antigen (terminates in GalNAc-α1→3-[Fucα1→2]-Gal-β1→4-GlcNAc-R); B allele: GTB — adds Gal in α-1,3 linkage to terminal Gal of H → B antigen; A and B alleles differ at 4 key amino acids (positions 176, 235, 266, 268) → determine sugar donor specificity; O allele (most common worldwide): single nucleotide deletion at codon 87 → frameshift → premature stop → no enzyme → H antigen unmodified; H gene (FUT1, chromosome 19p13.3): adds α-1,2-fucose to precursor chains; Se gene (FUT2, same chromosome): secretor status; ~80% of population are 'secretors' (FUT2 active) → express blood group antigens in secretions (saliva, gastric mucosa, etc.). Natural antibodies (allohemagglutinins): develop ~6 months postnatally (against dietary carbohydrate antigens similar to blood group antigens presented by gut bacteria): Group A → anti-B (IgM); Group B → anti-A (IgM); Group O → anti-A + anti-B; Group AB → no antibodies (universal recipient for RBCs); Group O → universal donor (only H antigen on RBCs; but plasma has anti-A+anti-B → only safe for RBC transfusions, not whole blood/plasma in non-emergency settings). Weak A subgroups: A1 (most common, ~80% of A individuals, highest GalNAc density, reacts with anti-A1 lectin from Dolichos biflorus); A2 (~20% of A, less GalNAc; some A2 individuals make anti-A1 → clinically relevant in crossmatching); A3, Ax, Aend, Am, Ael (rare). Clinically important transfusion reactions: immediate hemolytic transfusion reaction (IHTR): ABO mismatch → acute intravascular hemolysis → DIC + renal failure + shock → potentially fatal; caused by IgM ABO antibodies + complement activation. Delayed hemolytic reaction: 7-14 days post-transfusion; RBC antibodies (Kidd, Duffy, Kell, others) amnestic response; extravascular hemolysis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which phase of the cell cycle is characterized by the highest activity of cyclin D-CDK4/6?
options: G2/M phase (the G2/M transition is regulated by cyclin B-CDK1; cyclin D-CDK4/6 is active in G1 phase)
S phase (S phase entry and progression requires cyclin E-CDK2 [for origin licensing] and cyclin A-CDK2 [for replication fork progression]; cyclin D-CDK4/6 is G1-phase active)

G1 phase: cyclin D (D1, D2, D3) levels rise in response to mitogenic signals (growth factors → Ras → MAPK cascade → ↑cyclin D transcription); cyclin D-CDK4/6 complex: (1) phosphorylates RB (retinoblastoma protein, Rb, RB1) → hyperphosphorylated Rb → releases E2F transcription factors (E2F1/2/3a are transcriptional activators; E2F3b/4/5/6/7/8 are repressors) → E2F target genes activated (cyclin E, cyclin A, DNA polymerase, DHFR, thymidine kinase, CDC6, MCM2-7, etc.); (2) early G1: Rb is hypophosphorylated (active, represses E2F) → RESTRICTION POINT not yet passed; cyclin D-CDK4/6 initiates Rb phosphorylation → partial derepression; (3) late G1: cyclin E-CDK2 amplifies Rb hyperphosphorylation → ↑E2F → cyclin E (positive feedback) → RESTRICTION POINT crossed (irreversible commitment to S-phase even if growth factors withdrawn); (4) CDK4/6 inhibitors: palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib → block CDK4/6 → ↓Rb phosphorylation → ↓E2F → ↓cyclin E → G1 arrest → used in HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer (with letrozole or fulvestrant)
M phase (mitosis) (M-phase is regulated by cyclin B-CDK1 [MPF, maturation-promoting factor]; cyclin D-CDK4/6 activity falls as cells enter M phase)
explanation: Cell cycle — cyclin-CDK pairs: G1: Cyclin D1/2/3 + CDK4/6 → Rb phosphorylation → G1 restriction point; late G1: Cyclin E1/2 + CDK2 → complete Rb phosphorylation + origin activation. S: Cyclin A1/2 + CDK2 → replication elongation + origin firing regulation. G2: Cyclin A2 + CDK1 → G2 progression. M: Cyclin B1/2 + CDK1 (MPF) → nuclear envelope breakdown, chromatin condensation, spindle assembly, Golgi fragmentation. CDK inhibitors (CKIs): INK4 family (inhibit CDK4/6 specifically): p16INK4a (CDKN2A product, inhibits cyclin D-CDK4/6), p15INK4b, p18INK4c, p19INK4d; Cip/Kip family (inhibit multiple CDKs): p21CIP1 (CDKN1A, induced by p53 + TP53 → arrest in G1 after DNA damage), p27KIP1 (CDKN1B, withdrawal of growth factors → ↑p27 → CDK2 inhibition → G1 arrest), p57KIP2 (CDKN1C, imprinted gene, BWS). Rb pathway in cancer: Rb is a tumor suppressor; in many cancers: Rb inactivated by: hyperphosphorylation (excess cyclin D or cyclin E), LOH/mutation (retinoblastoma, osteosarcoma), or HPV E7 oncoprotein (binds Rb → destabilizes → E2F released constitutively). p16INK4a/CDKN2A: most frequently lost tumor suppressor gene in human cancers (homozygous deletion in ~25-30% of all cancers) → loss of CDK4/6 inhibition → unchecked Rb phosphorylation. CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib/Ibrance, ribociclib/Kisqali, abemaciclib/Verzenio): cause G1 arrest in Rb-proficient tumor cells; combined with endocrine therapy in HR+/HER2- MBC → ↑PFS significantly; abemaciclib also has CDK2 inhibitory activity; resistance: Rb mutation/loss, CDK4 mutation, cyclin D amplification, loss of p27.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Transglutaminase 2 (TG2) cross-links glutamine residues to lysine residues. This activity is pathologically relevant in celiac disease because:
options: TG2 digests gliadin peptides → making them small enough to pass through intestinal tight junctions (TG2 is a cross-linking enzyme, not a protease/digestive enzyme; gliadin transit through tight junctions is a separate mechanism)

TG2 deamidates glutamine residues of gliadin → creates negatively charged glutamate residues → ↑binding to HLA-DQ2/DQ8 → ↑T cell recognition and pathological immune response: TG2 function in celiac disease: tissue transglutaminase (tTG, TG2): normally cross-links fibronectin + collagen in ECM, regulates apoptosis; at gut mucosal sites: TG2 DEAMIDATES specific Gln residues in gliadin peptides → Gln → Glu (deamidation = removal of amide from side chain → adds negative charge); WHY this is pathological: deamidated gliadin peptides (DGP) have ↑affinity for HLA-DQ2 (DQ2.5: DQA1*05/DQB1*02, ~90-95% of celiac patients) or HLA-DQ8 (DQ8: DQA1*03/DQB1*03:02, ~5-10% of celiac patients); HLA-DQ2/DQ8 groove preferentially binds negatively charged peptides at P4, P6, P7 positions → DGP perfectly fits → CD4+ T cells recognize DGP-DQ2/DQ8 complex → TH1 cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-21) → mucosal inflammation + villous atrophy; ALSO: TG2 cross-links gliadin → gliadin-TG2 complexes → B cells recognize gliadin-TG2 complexes → anti-TG2 antibodies (IgA-anti-tTG) are the primary autoimmune antibody in celiac disease AND the serological test (anti-tTG IgA, sensitivity 94%, specificity 97% for celiac disease); anti-DGP (deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies, IgA and IgG): more specific but used in IgA-deficient patients or combined testing; the mechanism: TG2 deamidates gliadin → creates both the T cell antigen AND the autoantigen (TG2 complexed to gliadin); HLA-DQ2/DQ8 present deamidated gliadin → auto-reactive B cells make anti-TG2 (molecular mimicry between gliadin + TG2 in the immune complex)

TG2 acetylates gluten proteins → makes them stable against intestinal proteases (TG2 is a transglutaminase, not an acetyltransferase; gluten stability against intestinal proteases is due to its high proline content [proline inhibits most endopeptidases]
TG2 activates gliadin peptides by proteolysis into fragments that bypass the immune system (TG2 deaminates, not cleaves, gliadin; the result is MORE immunogenic, not less)
explanation: Celiac disease biochemistry: Gliadin structure: gliadin is the alcohol-soluble fraction of gluten (wheat + related: barley [hordein] + rye [secalin]; oat avenin may cross-react in some patients); gluten = gliadin + glutenin; gliadin is rich in Gln + Pro → Pro-rich sequences resist pancreatic endopeptidases → large Pro-Gln rich peptides survive to lamina propria. Critical peptides: 33-mer (33 amino acids from α-gliadin residues 57-89): the most immunodominant T-cell stimulatory peptide; contains 6 overlapping epitopes; all contain the motif QxP (Gln-x-Pro); highly resistant to digestion; deamidation by TG2 → ↑DQ2/DQ8 binding → ↑T cell activation. TG2 enzyme chemistry: reactions: (1) transamidation/cross-linking: Gln + Lys-NH2 → Gln-ε-Lys isopeptide bond + NH3; requires Ca2+ and is the classical cross-linking function; (2) deamidation: Gln + H2O → Glu + NH3; occurs at low Lys concentrations; (3) amine incorporation: Gln + RNH2 → Gln-NHR + NH3; GTP-binding regulatory function of TG2 (GDP/GTP-bound → closes enzyme active site, inhibits transamidation; Ca2+-bound + GDP → open conformation → transamidation/deamidation active). Diagnostic tests: IgA-anti-tTG (primary screen): measure IgA anti-tTG IgA; MUST check total serum IgA (IgA deficiency in ~3-5% celiac → false-negative; if IgA-deficient → measure IgG-anti-DGP or IgG-anti-tTG); anti-endomysial antibody (EMA): IgA against tTG in connective tissue (endomysium of primate esophagus or umbilical cord); highly specific (~99%) but operator-dependent IIF; HLA typing (DQ2/DQ8): negative predictive value >99% (if no DQ2/DQ8 → celiac very unlikely); gold standard: duodenal biopsy (modified Marsh classification: Marsh 1 = ↑IELs [>25/100 enterocytes]; Marsh 2 = ↑IELs + crypt hyperplasia; Marsh 3 = villous atrophy [3a partial, 3b subtotal, 3c total]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Cori cycle describes the relationship between actively glycolyzing muscle and the liver. Which statement BEST describes the Cori cycle?
options: Muscle takes up glucose, converts it to lactate, which is transported to the liver, where it is converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis; the net result is energy transfer from the liver to the muscle: CORRECT DESCRIPTION; Cori cycle: during intense exercise or ischemia → muscle anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate → LDH → lactate + NAD+ (regenerates NAD+ for glycolysis continuation); lactate exported from muscle → blood → liver; in liver: lactate + NAD+ → [LDH-liver, liver LDH-isoform 5 in cytoplasm] → pyruvate → [PEPCK, PC, etc. = gluconeogenesis] → glucose → released into blood → taken up by muscle again; KEY POINT: cycle does NOT generate net energy for the organism (gluconeogenesis in liver uses 6 ATP, glycolysis in muscle generates 2 ATP net → cycle costs the body 4 ATP per glucose turned over) → the liver subsidizes muscle contraction energetically using hepatic ATP (from oxidative phosphorylation) to regenerate glucose from muscle lactate → allows muscle to work beyond aerobic capacity; clinical relevance: phenformin (biguanide, withdrawn) + metformin → inhibit hepatic Complex I → impair lactate uptake + gluconeogenesis → ↑lactic acidosis (type B, from metformin toxicity in CKD or overdose); in sepsis: ↑lactate from peripheral tissue hypoxia + glycolysis → ↑Cori cycle demand but liver may be impaired → lactate accumulates → lactic acidosis

Muscle oxidizes lactate from red blood cells and converts it to glucose (muscle does not perform gluconeogenesis; liver does; this is the GLUCOSE-LACTATE cycle [Cori], but direction described here is wrong)

The liver exports lactate to the muscle which is used directly as fuel by oxidation (muscle can oxidize lactate directly to pyruvate via LDH → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → TCA; this is the 'lactate shuttle' [intracellular + cell-to-cell lactate shuttles] described by Brooks; but the CORI CYCLE specifically refers to muscle→liver lactate + liver→muscle glucose, not direct lactate oxidation)

Red blood cells produce glucose-6-phosphate from stored glycogen and export it to the liver (RBCs have no mitochondria, no gluconeogenesis, no glycogen; they produce lactate exclusively from glucose; this statement is incorrect in multiple ways)
explanation: Cori cycle vs. Alanine-glucose cycle: Cori cycle (lactate-glucose cycle): Muscle: Glucose → 2 lactate + 2 ATP (net, anaerobic); Liver: 2 lactate → glucose (costs 6 ATP per glucose = 2 ATP from PGK reversed equivalent + 4 more for PEPCK + PC + FBPase + G6Pase = overall 6 ATP); Net: 2 ATP gained in muscle, 6 ATP spent in liver → net cost = 4 ATP per cycle; Purpose: allows continued muscle work (anaerobic) at expense of hepatic oxidative phosphorylation. Glucose-alanine cycle: analogous for amino acid transfer during protein catabolism in muscle → transamination of pyruvate + Glu → Ala + α-KG (alanine aminotransferase, ALT in muscle) → Ala exported → liver → ALT liver: Ala + α-KG → pyruvate + Glu → pyruvate → GNG → glucose; simultaneously: Glu → transamination → aspartate → urea cycle (via OAA) → amino group eliminated as urea; Purpose: transfer of NH2 groups from muscle to liver for urea synthesis + glucose for muscle. Lactate as a fuel: lactate is the preferred fuel of the heart (oxidizes it via LDH1 [heart isoform, M2H2] → pyruvate → TCA; LDH1 has lower Km for lactate [higher affinity] than LDH5 [muscle isoform, M4]); lactate is fuel for gluconeogenic cells: kidney cortex can use lactate → gluconeogenesis; astrocytes produce lactate → neurons use lactate (Brooks' astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle); after exercise: lactate clearance is primarily by: liver (~35%), heart (~17%), slow muscle fibers (~50% combined for all oxidative tissues). VO2 max and lactate threshold: 'lactate threshold' (LT) = exercise intensity at which blood lactate begins to accumulate (>2 mM); LT1 ≈ ventilatory threshold; LT2 (OBLA, onset of blood lactate accumulation ≈ 4 mM) = anaerobic threshold; trained athletes have higher LT2 (more mitochondria → more aerobic capacity → less lactate at given workload).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Aldosterone acts on the principal cells of the collecting duct. The MAIN biochemical effect leading to sodium reabsorption is:
options: Rapid increase in ATPase pump activity due to direct phosphorylation of Na+/K+-ATPase by aldosterone (aldosterone is a STEROID → acts via NUCLEAR RECEPTOR → transcription/translation required; it does NOT directly phosphorylate Na+/K+-ATPase; this would be a non-genomic kinase-mediated effect which is minor)

↑Transcription of SGK1 (serum- and glucocorticoid-inducible kinase 1) → SGK1 phosphorylates NEDD4-2 → prevents NEDD4-2 from ubiquitinating ENaC → ↑ENaC cell-surface expression → ↑Na+ reabsorption: Aldosterone mechanism (GENOMIC): aldosterone (lipophilic steroid, ~MW 360) → passive diffusion into principal cells → binds MR (mineralocorticoid receptor, NR3C2, cytoplasmic) → MR-aldosterone complex dissociates from heat shock proteins → nuclear translocation → binds MREs (mineralocorticoid response elements) in promoters → ↑transcription of early response genes (within 30-60 min): SGK1 (SGK1: serum/glucocorticoid-inducible kinase 1): phosphorylates NEDD4-2 (E3 ubiquitin ligase) at Ser-444/Ser-338 → NEDD4-2 cannot bind and ubiquitinate β/γ-ENaC (epithelial sodium channel, composed of α/β/γ subunits; SCNN1A/B/G genes) → ENaC is NOT internalized → ↑ENaC at apical membrane → ↑Na+ entry from tubular lumen into principal cells → ↑intracellular Na+ → ↑Na+/K+-ATPase (basolateral) activity → exports Na+ to interstitium → Na+ reabsorption; late response genes (4-8h): ↑Na+/K+-ATPase α+β subunit expression → more pump molecules → ↑Na+ export to blood; ↑GILZ (glucocorticoid-induced leucine zipper) → additional ENaC regulation; ENaC ligand-independent channel: always open when present at membrane (gating by PIP2, Cl-, flow); Liddle syndrome: GAIN-of-function mutations in β or γ ENaC PY motifs → NEDD4-2 cannot bind → ENaC not internalized → constitutive Na+ reabsorption → hypertension + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis (same phenotype as hyperaldosteronism but aldosterone IS LOW) → treat with amiloride (blocks ENaC directly) or triamterene; Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 (PHA1): LOSS-of-function in ENaC (AR) or MR (AD) → same electrolyte pattern as aldosterone deficiency despite high aldosterone (RESISTANCE to aldosterone); ↑Na+ loss + ↑K+
