The change in quaternary structure of hemoglobin from the deoxy T-state (tense, low O2 affinity) to the oxy R-state (relaxed, high O2 affinity) through conformational changes propagated between subunits: Hemoglobin (Hb) tetrameric structure: α2β2 in adults (HbA); when deoxy: T-state (tense, constrained, low O2 affinity; Fe2+ is out of porphyrin plane [dome]; His F8 proximal [Fe-bound] + Val E11 steric constraint; 2,3-BPG pocket is open; salt bridges between subunits stabilize T-state: 8 intersubunit salt bridges including α1-β1 and α1-β2 + α2-β1 interfaces); when O2 binds to first heme (Fe2+): Fe2+ moves INTO the porphyrin plane (becomes planar) → pulls proximal His F8 → moves F helix → propagates conformational change through the α-β interface (switch + slider contacts) → loosens T-state constraints → ↑affinity of remaining 3 hemes → COOPERATIVE BINDING; after 4th O2 binds: full R-state (relaxed; maximum affinity); the sigmoidal O2 dissociation curve (ODC) results from: low affinity of T-state (flat portion of the curve at low pO2) → T→R transition → rapid O2 binding in R-state (steep rise) → saturation at high pO2; Hill coefficient (nH): for Hb ≈ 2.7 (positive cooperativity; maximum theoretical nH = 4 for 4 subunits); the cooperative mechanism is ALLOSTERIC (conformational change in one subunit transmitted to neighbors) → Monod-Wyman-Changeux (MWC/concerted model: all subunits switch T→R simultaneously) vs. Koshland-Nemethy-Filmer (KNF/sequential model: each O2 binding induces sequential conformational changes); reality: hybrid model, closer to MWC but with sequential elements

The presence of 2,3-BPG in the central cavity that independently triggers cooperative binding without structural changes in globin (2,3-BPG STABILIZES the T-state → right-shifts ODC → ↓O2 affinity; but cooperativity EXISTS even without 2,3-BPG; 2,3-BPG modulates the position of the ODC but is not the STRUCTURAL BASIS for cooperativity itself)

The dissociation of αβ dimers from the tetramer upon O2 binding (Hb does dissociate into α1β1 dimers in solution but this is NOT the basis of cooperativity; cooperativity is mediated by the α1β2 interface within the intact tetramer, not by subunit dissociation)
explanation: Hemoglobin structure-function: α1β1 interface (same-type dimer interface): tight, hydrogen bonds + hydrophobic contacts; non-flexible; does NOT change with oxygenation; these dimers are stable. α1β2 interface (αβ heterodimer interface): FLEXIBLE; changes significantly between T and R states; contains the SWITCH (Tyr42[α] contacts Asp99[β]) and SLIDER (Thr38/Arg40 region [α] contacts Asp94/Pro95 [β]); in T-state: Tyr42[α1]-Asp99[β2] contact; in R-state: this contact is broken, Asn97[β2]-Thr38[α1] contact forms instead → different geometry → subunit rotation by ~15° + one subunit pair shifts relative to other. The 'tension' model: O2 binding to first subunit → Fe2+ → plane of porphyrin → F8 His pulled → F helix moves → breaks some T-state salt bridges → partial R-state shift → next O2 binds with higher affinity. Hemoglobin variants affecting cooperativity: Hb S (β6 Glu→Val): polymerizes in deoxy (T) state → sickle cells; cooperativity intact per se but cells sickle before O2 unloads fully. Hb Chesapeake (α92 Arg→Leu): R-state stabilized → LEFT-shifted ODC → ↑O2 affinity → ↓O2 delivery to tissues → ↑EPO → polycythemia. Hb Kansas (β102 Asn→Thr): T-state stabilized → RIGHT-shifted ODC → ↓O2 affinity → peripheral cyanosis. Hemoglobin disorders: Hb M (Hb Milwaukee, Hb Boston, etc.): various mutations → stabilize Fe3+ (methemoglobin) → cannot bind O2 at that subunit → cyanosis + reduced cooperativity; heterozygous → cyanosis from birth. MCHC (mean corpuscular Hb concentration): normal 32-36 g/dL; if MCHC > 36: INDICATES spherocytosis (loss of membrane + concentrated Hb) → osmotic fragility ↑.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Schindler disease (angiokeratoma corporis diffusum type II) is caused by deficiency of:
options: Galactosidase A (GLA): α-galactosidase A deficiency = Fabry disease (X-linked; Gb3/GL-3 accumulation; angiokeratoma + neuropathy + renal failure; treated with agalsidase)
Acid ceramidase (ASAH1): deficiency = Farber lipogranulomatosis (ceramide accumulation; triad: painful joints + subcutaneous nodules + hoarse cry; laryngeal involvement is characteristic)

Alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase (NAGA, NAGA gene, chromosome 22q13.1): Schindler disease (type I/infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy form) and Kanzaki disease (type II/adult form, also called angiokeratoma corporis diffusum type II): both from NAGA mutations (AR); NAGA (lysosomal exoglycosidase) cleaves terminal α-N-acetylgalactosamine from glycopeptides and glycolipids; substrates include: glycopeptides with Tn antigen (GalNAc-α-O-Ser/Thr), blood group A antigens (GalNAc on type 2 chain), some gangliosides; Schindler disease TYPE I (infantile severe form): severe neuroaxonal dystrophy; psychomotor regression at 9-12 months → spasticity, seizures, blindness → vegetative state by age 4; type II (Kanzaki disease, adult form): milder; main features = angiokeratoma corporis diffusum (small purple-red papules over lower trunk/genitalia) + lymphedema + mild intellectual impairment + neuropathy; type III: intermediate; DIAGNOSIS: urine oligosaccharides (↑Tn antigen-containing glycopeptides) + NAGA enzyme assay (leukocytes/fibroblasts) + NAGA gene sequencing; TREATMENT: no approved ERT or SRT

Mannose-6-phosphate receptor (MPR): MPR is required for lysosomal targeting of enzymes; MPR defects → I-cell disease (GNPTAB) not Schindler disease; MPR itself is not an enzyme; Schindler disease is a specific α-NAGA enzyme deficiency
explanation: Rare lysosomal storage diseases — enzyme/substrate: Schindler (NAGA): α-N-acetylgalactosaminidase → glycopeptides with terminal α-GalNAc. Farber (ASAH1): acid ceramidase → ceramide. Pompe/GSD II (GAA): acid α-glucosidase → lysosomal glycogen. Wolman/CESD (LIPA): lysosomal acid lipase → cholesterol esters + TG. Sialidosis (NEU1): sialidase/neuraminidase → sialylated glycopeptides + gangliosides. Galactosialidosis (PPCA/CTSA): cathepsin A protects NEU1 + β-gal; PPCA (protective protein/cathepsin A) deficiency → NEU1 + GLBA unstable → combined sialidase + β-galactosidase deficiency → cherry-red spot + coarse features + myoclonus. Aspartylglucosaminuria (AGA): aspartylglucosaminidase (ASPA-glucosaminidase) → N-aspartylglucosamine. Mannosidosis: α-mannosidosis (MAN2B1): alpha-mannosidase → mannose oligomers; coarse features + intellectual disability + hearing loss; β-mannosidosis (MANBA): beta-mannosidase → mannose-containing oligosaccharides; very rare. Fucosidosis (FUCA1): alpha-fucosidase → fucosylated glycolipids/glycoproteins; coarse features + angiokeratoma + progressive neurological; AR. Blood group antigens and lysosomal enzymes: Schindler (NAGA) is relevant to blood group A (GalNAc component of A antigen); NAGA can cleave A antigen → Schindler patients may show changes in A blood group expression. Clinical comparison — angiokeratoma corporis diffusum: seen in Fabry disease (Galactosidase A deficiency, most common), Schindler/Kanzaki type II, Fucosidosis, Sialidosis, Aspartylglucosaminuria, GM1 gangliosidosis, and β-mannosidosis → angiokeratoma is not disease-specific but a key skin finding in multiple LSDs.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Watson-Crick base pairs A:T and G:C are held together by hydrogen bonds. Which statement about hydrogen bond numbers is CORRECT?
options: A:T pair has 3 hydrogen bonds and G:C pair has 2 hydrogen bonds (this is REVERSED; it is the G:C pair that has 3 hydrogen bonds and A:T that has 2; getting this wrong is a common error in exams)

A:T pair has 2 hydrogen bonds and G:C pair has 3 hydrogen bonds: the antiparallel complementary DNA strands (5'→3' + 3'→5') are held together by specific hydrogen bonds between complementary bases in the Watson-Crick base pairs: A:T (adenine-thymine): 2 hydrogen bonds (A N6-H···O4[T] and A N1···H-N3[T]); G:C (guanine-cytosine): 3 hydrogen bonds (G N1-H···N3[C]; G N2-H2···O2[C]; G O6···H-N4[C]); implications: (1) G+C content correlates with DNA melting temperature (Tm): ↑GC content → ↑Tm (because G:C has 3 H-bonds vs. A:T's 2 H-bonds → more energy needed to melt [separate strands]) → G+C rich DNA is more thermostable; formula: Tm ≈ 81.5 + 16.6 log[Na+] + 0.41 × (%G+C) − 675/n [for longer duplexes]; alternatively: Tm ≈ 2°C per A:T pair + 4°C per G:C pair (simple approximation); (2) Chargaff's rules: %A = %T and %G = %C in double-stranded DNA (not necessarily in single-stranded or RNA); (3) PCR annealing temperature: primer Tm related to GC content → for primers: Tm ≈ 2(A+T) + 4(G+C) [for short oligonucleotides]; (4) FRET-based DNA probes: G:C-rich probes have higher Tm → remain hybridized at higher temperatures → tighter probes; (5) AT-rich promoter TATA box: A:T-rich regions melt more easily → preferred for DNA strand separation at promoters (TATA box = TATAAA, all AT → melts easily to allow RNA Pol II access to template strand)
Both A:T and G:C have 2 hydrogen bonds each (G:C has 3 H-bonds, not 2; this statement is incorrect)
Both A:T and G:C have 3 hydrogen bonds each (A:T has only 2 H-bonds; this statement is incorrect)
explanation: DNA structure and stability: B-form DNA (physiological, Watson-Crick double helix, right-handed): 10 bp per turn (3.4 Å per bp, 34 Å per turn); major groove (wider, ~12 Å) + minor groove (narrower, ~6 Å); Major groove: base-specific contacts → where most DNA-binding proteins read sequence (helix-turn-helix, zinc finger, leucine zipper); Minor groove: also used by some proteins (TATA-binding protein TBP bends DNA into minor groove); antiparallel strands. A-form DNA: right-handed, 11 bp per turn; shorter, wider; double-stranded RNA + RNA-DNA hybrids; in dehydrated conditions. Z-form DNA: LEFT-handed; 12 bp per turn; GC-rich with alternating G+C; zig-zag backbone (Z); physiological role: at actively transcribed genes (negative supercoiling behind Pol II → Z-DNA); may regulate transcription. DNA topology: topoisomerases: Type I (nick one strand + religate after rotation → ↓supercoils; no ATP; types: IA [bacteria, ↓only negative supercoils] + IB [eukaryotes, ↓ either direction]); camptothecin/irinotecan/topotecan: inhibit topoisomerase IB (eukaryotic type I) by trapping cleavage complex → DNA DSBs; Type II (nick both strands + pass dsDNA through gap + religate; ATP-dependent; decatenates): bacterial: DNA gyrase (GyrA + GyrB = ↑negative supercoiling [introduction of negative supercoils ahead of replication fork] + ↓positive supercoiling; INHIBITED by fluoroquinolones [ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin → trap cleavage complex] and novobiocin [competes with ATP on GyrB]); topoisomerase IV (ParC + ParE; decatenation of replicated chromosomes → inhibited by fluoroquinolones [↑affinity to ParC] and quinolones; eukaryotic: Topo II (↑negative relaxation; ↓positive; decatenation); inhibited by doxorubicin/etoposide (etoposide/VP-16 → trap Topo IIα cleavage complex → DSBs → clinical: hematologic malignancies, solid tumors; secondary therapy-related AML risk [MLL rearrangements]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE-related) has high serum iron, high transferrin saturation, and high ferritin. The PRIMARY gene mutated is:
options: TF (transferrin): transferrin is the iron transport protein in blood; mutations are RARE and cause atransferrinemia (very rare AR → severe iron deficiency anemia paradoxically [transferrin is required for erythropoiesis] + iron overload in organs [no transferrin → no receptor-mediated delivery to erythroblasts → marrow failure; excess non-transferrin-bound iron accumulates elsewhere]); HH is NOT caused by TF mutations

SLC40A1 (ferroportin): ferroportin mutations → type 4 hemochromatosis (Ferroportin disease): type A (loss-of-function SLC40A1 mutations → ↓iron export from macrophages → iron sequestration in macrophages [MPS cells] → different phenotype: high ferritin but NORMAL transferrin saturation [macrophage iron, not plasma iron]; treated by phlebotomy but tolerates poorly); type B (gain-of-function SLC40A1 mutations → hepcidin resistance → ferroportin cannot be degraded → iron export from macrophages + enterocytes continues unchecked → same as HFE HH); NOT the primary HH gene (HFE is)

HFE (HFE gene, chromosome 6p21.3): HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis (HH type 1) = most common form; HFE protein: MHC class I-like protein (MHC-I related but non-classical; associates with β2-microglobulin) expressed on hepatocytes + duodenal crypts; HFE interacts with transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) + TfR2 → involved in sensing transferrin-iron levels → normally: ↑diferric transferrin → HFE-TfR1/TfR2 signaling → ↑BMP6 signaling → SMAD1/5/8 → ↑hepcidin; in HFE mutations → ↓hepcidin production → ↑ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes + macrophages → ↑plasma iron → ↑transferrin saturation → iron deposition in liver + heart + pancreas + joints + pituitary + skin; most common HFE mutations: C282Y (Cys282Tyr, rs1800562): most important (>80-90% of HH in North European ancestry; homozygous C282Y = classic HH; prevents HFE-β2M complex formation → unstable → cannot reach cell surface → ↓TfR1 interaction → ↓hepcidin → ↑iron); H63D (His63Asp, rs1799945): much milder; compound heterozygous C282Y/H63D has intermediate iron overload; S65C: minor variant; phenotypic penetrance of C282Y/C282Y: ~28% of homozygous males develop clinical iron overload; lower in females (menstrual losses protect); treatment: therapeutic phlebotomy (450-500 mL blood = ~250 mg iron per session → weekly until ferritin < 50 ng/mL; then maintenance every 3-4 months; very safe + effective); iron chelation (deferoxamine IV/SC, deferasirox oral, deferiprone oral) if phlebotomy not tolerated

HAMP (hepcidin): HAMP mutations → type 2B HH (juvenile hemochromatosis); HAMP null mutations → very high iron, early onset (2nd-3rd decade), cardiomyopathy + endocrine failure → most severe HH; NOT the most common form (HFE type 1 is most common)
explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HH) types: Type 1 (HFE-related): HFE C282Y mutation; commonest (1/200-300 of Northern European descent); autosomal recessive; penetrance incomplete. Type 2A (HJV mutation, hemojuvelin): HJV = BMP co-receptor for hepcidin induction → HJV null → severe ↓BMP6-SMAD signaling → ↓hepcidin → juvenile HH (2nd-3rd decade); severe cardiomyopathy + hypogonadism. Type 2B (HAMP mutation, hepcidin): direct hepcidin deletion → same as 2A (juvenile HH). Type 3 (TFR2 mutation, TfR2): TfR2 is a second transferrin receptor (abundant in hepatocytes; signals to HJV/BMP/hepcidin pathway); type 3 HH: similar to type 1 but milder + different geographic distribution. Type 4 (SLC40A1/ferroportin): as described above. Secondary iron overload: transfusion-dependent patients (sickle cell, thalassemia major, MDS): IV iron from RBC transfusions → 250 mg Fe per unit → RBC lifespan 90 days → 10-15 units/year → > 5 g excess Fe per year; chelation: deferoxamine (SC overnight infusion) → standard for 20 years; deferasirox (Exjade, oral, once daily, monitored renal function) → now preferred; deferiprone (oral, tid; best cardiac iron chelation; agranulocytosis risk). Iron overload complications: Liver (most first affected): fibrosis → cirrhosis → HCC (↑1% per year in cirrhosis); Heart: dilated cardiomyopathy + arrhythmias; Endocrine: diabetes (pancreatic β-cell iron → DM = 'bronze diabetes'), hypogonadism (pituitary iron → ↓LH/FSH → secondary hypogonadism, impotence, amenorrhea), hypothyroidism, adrenal; Joints: chondrocalcinosis (pyrophosphate arthropathy, especially 2nd/3rd MCP joints + knee); Skin: bronze/grey pigmentation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A researcher measures enzyme kinetics for an enzyme under two conditions: with and without an inhibitor. Results: without inhibitor, Km = 2 mM, Vmax = 100 nmol/min; with inhibitor, Km = 2 mM, Vmax = 50 nmol/min. This inhibitor is:
options: Competitive inhibitor (competitive inhibition: Km ↑ [apparent Km = Km(1 + [I]/Ki) → increases with inhibitor concentration], Vmax UNCHANGED; in this problem Km did NOT change → not competitive)

Pure noncompetitive inhibitor (pure noncompetitive inhibition = equal affinity for E and ES complex; Km UNCHANGED, Vmax DECREASED [apparent Vmax = Vmax/(1 + [I]/Ki)]): pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds to BOTH free enzyme (E) and enzyme-substrate complex (ES) with the SAME affinity (Ki_E = Ki_ES); effects: Km unchanged (because substrate can still bind; inhibitor doesn't affect substrate binding; Km is the ratio of on/off rates for substrate + kcat/k1 → if kcat ↓ proportionally and substrate binding unaffected, Km stays same); Vmax decreased (because the EI complex + ESI ternary complex are BOTH unable to form product; the fraction of enzyme molecules available for catalysis is reduced); Lineweaver-Burk (double reciprocal plot): intersect on x-axis (same −1/Km → Km unchanged) but y-intercept ↑ (1/Vmax ↑ → Vmax ↓); the lines have the SAME x-intercept but different slopes and y-intercepts; pure noncompetitive inhibitors in biochemistry: specific examples include: allosteric inhibitors that bind remote sites; heavy metal cations (Hg2+, Pb2+) inhibiting some enzymes; certain phytocompounds
Mixed noncompetitive inhibitor (mixed inhibition: inhibitor binds E and ES with DIFFERENT affinities [Ki_E ≠ Ki_ES]; both Km AND Vmax change; in this problem ONLY Vmax changes → not mixed)

Uncompetitive inhibitor (uncompetitive: binds ONLY ES complex, not free E; effects: BOTH Km AND Vmax decrease proportionally [apparent Km = Km/(1+[I]/Ki') and apparent Vmax = Vmax/(1+[I]/Ki')] → the ratio Km/Vmax [= slope in LB plot] is UNCHANGED → parallel lines in LB plot; in this problem ONLY Vmax changes → Km unchanged → not uncompetitive [which would also decrease Km])
explanation: Enzyme inhibition types — complete: Competitive inhibition: Inhibitor (I) binds E (not ES); competes with S for active site; reversible by ↑[S]; apparent Km ↑; Vmax UNCHANGED; LB plot: same y-intercept, different slopes; clinical example: statins (compete with HMG-CoA at HMGCR active site), methotrexate (competes with DHF at DHFR), sulfonamides (compete with PABA at dihydropteroate synthase). Pure noncompetitive: I binds E + ES equally; Km UNCHANGED; Vmax ↓; LB plot: same x-intercept, different y-intercepts (lines converge on x-axis); examples: cyanide on cytochrome oxidase (binds Fe3+ regardless of substrate), heavy metals, allosteric inhibitors (if allosteric site fully separate from substrate binding). Mixed noncompetitive: I binds E + ES with different affinities; both Km and Vmax change; LB plot: lines converge in second quadrant (not at x-axis); includes most 'noncompetitive' inhibitors in practice. Uncompetitive: I binds only ES; both Km AND Vmax DECREASE (proportionally); apparent Km/Vmax = true Km/Vmax (slope unchanged); LB plot: PARALLEL lines (same slope, different y- and x-intercepts); examples: lithium inhibits inositol monophosphatase (uncompetitive with inositol-1-P); some enzyme inhibitors at high substrate concentrations (substrate inhibition → uncompetitive inhibition by excess substrate). Irreversible inhibition: covalent modification of active site; Vmax decreases (fewer active E molecules); Km unchanged (remaining active E has same affinity); examples: organophosphates (Ser of AChE), aspirin (COX-1 Ser530), DFP (diisopropylfluorophosphate, all Ser proteases). Key: In this question, Km = 2 mM (SAME both conditions) + Vmax = 50 nmol/min (decreased) → pure noncompetitive; not competitive (Km would ↑); not uncompetitive (both Km + Vmax would ↓); not mixed (Km would also change).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Warburg effect refers to the preferential use of aerobic glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells. Which statement BEST explains the underlying reason for the Warburg effect?
options: Cancer cells have defective mitochondria that cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation (most cancer cells have FUNCTIONAL mitochondria; the Warburg effect is not primarily due to dysfunctional OXPHOS but rather to reprogrammed metabolic priorities; mitochondria in cancer are also used for biosynthesis and apoptosis evasion)

Cancer cells use aerobic glycolysis to support rapid biomass production (macromolecule synthesis, not primarily for ATP): the Warburg effect paradox: aerobic glycolysis generates only 2 ATP/glucose (vs. ~30-32 ATP/glucose via OXPHOS) → seems inefficient for energy production; BUT the reason cancer cells prefer aerobic glycolysis: (1) Biosynthetic demands: dividing cells need not just ATP but also carbon backbones for biosynthesis; glycolysis intermediates feed: PPP (ribose-5-P for nucleotides; NADPH for lipid synthesis), serine synthesis pathway (3-PG → serine → one-carbon metabolism, lipids, purines, glycine, GSH), lipogenesis (acetyl-CoA via citrate shuttle), etc.; OXPHOS simply oxidizes everything to CO2 + H2O with no carbon for biosynthesis; (2) Lactate production acidifies the tumor microenvironment (TME) → ↑matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity → ↑invasion + metastasis + ↓immune function in TME (low pH inhibits NK cells + CTL); (3) PKM2 (pyruvate kinase muscle isoform 2): expressed in cancer cells (alternative splicing of PKM pre-mRNA → exon 10 instead of exon 9 → PKM2 vs. PKM1); PKM2 has LOWER activity than PKM1 (can be inhibited by Tyr-phosphorylation [in cancer with constitutive TKs] + fructose-1,6-BP is its allosteric activator but if upstream builds up → feedback; PKM2 dimers are less active → upstream glycolytic intermediates shunt to PPP + serine synthesis); (4) HIF-1α: tumor hypoxia + oncogene signaling → ↑HIF-1α → ↑GLUT1/3 + ↑HK2 + ↑LDHA + ↑PDK1 (pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase → inactivates PDC → ↓acetyl-CoA entry to TCA → ↑pyruvate → ↑lactate) → promotes glycolytic phenotype even in O2 (aerobic)

Cancer cells lack glucose transporters and must compensate by maximizing ATP per glucose via glycolysis (this is incorrect; cancer cells OVEREXPRESS glucose transporters [GLUT1, GLUT3, GLUT12] → massive glucose uptake → PET scanning uses 18F-FDG precisely because tumors hyperaccumulate glucose; the problem is NOT lack of glucose transporters)

Cancer cells must use glycolysis because glucose is only available for 6 hours after meals (the Warburg effect occurs continuously regardless of feeding state; it is a constitutive feature of cancer cell metabolism driven by oncogenes, not by glucose availability timing)
explanation: Warburg effect — molecular drivers: Oncogene-driven metabolic reprogramming: RAS (constitutively active → RAF-MEK-ERK → ↑HIF-1α + ↑c-Myc → ↑glycolytic genes including HK2, LDHA, MCT4, GLUT1); PI3K-Akt-mTOR (↑GLUT translocation, ↑glycolytic enzyme expression, ↑HIF-1α translation); c-Myc: directly activates LDHA, PKM2 (exon 10 splicing via HNRNP repressors), GLS (glutaminase); HIF-1α: even in normoxia (pseudo-hypoxia from RAS, Myc, VHL loss) → ↑PDK1 (inhibits PDC → ↑lactate). Lactate metabolism: MCT4 (monocarboxylate transporter 4, SLC16A3): exports lactate from glycolytic/hypoxic cells; MCT1 (SLC16A1): imports lactate into oxidative cells (some tumor regions actually IMPORT lactate from neighboring glycolytic cells for OXPHOS = 'metabolic symbiosis'); CAFs (cancer-associated fibroblasts): aerobic glycolysis + autophagy → export lactate/pyruvate → tumor cells use for OXPHOS = 'reverse Warburg effect'. Glutamine metabolism in cancer (Warburg complement): cancer cells also hyperactivate glutamine uptake (via ASCT2/SLC1A5) → GLS (glutaminase) → glutamate → α-KG → TCA (anaplerosis) → replenishes TCA intermediates drained for biosynthesis (asparagine synthesis, fatty acid synthesis, etc.) → c-Myc drives GLS expression; some cancers (pancreatic) rely more on glutamine than glucose for energy. Metabolic vulnerabilities in cancer (therapeutic targets): LDHA inhibitors (FX11): ↓lactate → ↑pyruvate → ↑ROS → ↓tumor growth (preclinical). MCT1 inhibitors (AZD3965): solid tumors relying on lactate import. PKM2 activators: force PKM2 → PKM1-like activity → restore efficient glycolysis + ↑OXPHOS → ↓biosynthetic shunting → impair proliferation. Glutaminase inhibitors (CB-839/Telaglenastat): pancreatic cancer, T-ALL, RCC (PRCC, NF2-mut). IDH1/2 inhibitors: IDH-mutant cancers (AML, glioma) → 2-HG → metabolic addiction; ivosidenib (IDH1) + enasidenib (IDH2) approved for AML.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Cortisol is the primary glucocorticoid produced by the adrenal cortex. The biosynthetic step that specifically produces cortisol from 11-deoxycortisol is catalyzed by:
options: CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase): converts pregnenolone → 17-OH-pregnenolone (+ lyase activity: 17-OH-pregnenolone → DHEA); converts progesterone → 17-OH-progesterone; CYP17A1 is NOT the enzyme that makes cortisol from 11-deoxycortisol

CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase): converts 17-OH-progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol (in the zona fasciculata pathway to cortisol); also converts progesterone → deoxycorticosterone (DOC) [in zona glomerulosa pathway to aldosterone]; CYP21A2 is UPSTREAM of cortisol synthesis, not the final step

CYP11B1 (11β-hydroxylase): CYP11B1 (Cytochrome P450 11β-hydroxylase, also called steroid 11β-monooxygenase; encoded by CYP11B1 on chromosome 8q24.3): mitochondrial enzyme of the zona fasciculata; catalyzes: 11-deoxycortisol + O2 + NADPH → cortisol (hydroxylation at C11 position); similarly: deoxycorticosterone (DOC) + O2 → corticosterone (11β-hydroxylation); CYP11B1 vs CYP11B2: CYP11B1 (in zona fasciculata): makes cortisol from 11-deoxycortisol + corticosterone from DOC; CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase, in zona glomerulosa): makes aldosterone from DOC (3 steps: 11-hydroxylation → 18-hydroxylation → 18-oxidation, all on the same CYP11B2 enzyme); CYP11B1 CANNOT efficiently perform the 18-oxidation step → zona fasciculata cannot make aldosterone; CYP11B1 DEFICIENCY (congenital adrenal hyperplasia type V, or CAH due to 11β-hydroxylase deficiency): AR; second most common form of CAH (after CYP21A2 deficiency); ↑11-deoxycortisol + ↑DOC accumulate → ↑DOC (a mineralocorticoid) → ↑sodium retention → HYPERTENSION + hypokalemia (distinctive from 21-hydroxylase CAH which causes SALT-WASTING) + suppressed renin + suppressed aldosterone (due to DOC excess → negative feedback on renin-angiotensin → ↓aldosterone); virilization (excess androgens from shunting): in females → ambiguous genitalia, clitoromegaly; in males → precocious puberty; biochemistry: ↑serum 11-deoxycortisol + ↑DOC → confirmatory; ACTH stimulation test: ↑11-deoxycortisol; ↓cortisol; treatment: glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone or dexamethasone → suppress ACTH → ↓shunting to androgens + ↓DOC → resolves hypertension); does NOT need mineralocorticoid replacement (DOC provides enough mineralocorticoid effect)

CYP11A1 (P450scc, cholesterol side-chain cleavage): converts cholesterol → pregnenolone (first step of steroidogenesis, rate-limiting for ACUTE steroid synthesis; regulated by StAR [steroidogenic acute regulatory protein]); NOT the enzyme converting 11-deoxycortisol → cortisol
explanation: Steroidogenesis in adrenal cortex — complete: Zona glomerulosa (aldosterone): Cholesterol → [CYP11A1] → Pregnenolone → [3β-HSD] → Progesterone → [CYP21A2] → DOC → [CYP11B2 step 1] → Corticosterone → [CYP11B2 step 2] → 18-OH-corticosterone → [CYP11B2 step 3] → Aldosterone. Zona fasciculata (cortisol): Cholesterol → [CYP11A1] → Pregnenolone → [3β-HSD] → Progesterone → [CYP17A1] → 17-OH-Progesterone → [CYP21A2] → 11-Deoxycortisol → [CYP11B1] → Cortisol. Zona reticularis (DHEA + androgens): Pregnenolone → [CYP17A1 hydroxylase] → 17-OH-Pregnenolone → [CYP17A1 lyase] → DHEA → [DHEA-S by SULT2A1] → DHEA-S. CAH types — enzyme deficiency, biochemistry, clinical: CAH 21-OH (CYP21A2 def, most common ~90-95%): ↑17-OH-progesterone; ↑androgens; classic salt-wasting (↑urine Na+, ↓serum Na+, ↑K+, ↑renin, ↓aldosterone, shock); virilization females + male precocious puberty; Rx: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone. CAH 11β-OH (CYP11B1 def, ~5-8%): ↑11-deoxycortisol + ↑DOC; HYPERTENSION (not salt-wasting); virilization; Rx: glucocorticoids alone. CAH 17α-OH (CYP17A1 def, rare): ↑DOC + ↑corticosterone (without cortisol, without androgens); HYPERTENSION + hypokalemia; ABSENT sexual development (no androgens → females: primary amenorrhea; males: pseudohermaphroditism [46 XY but female phenotype due to no androgens]); Rx: glucocorticoids + sex steroid replacement. CAH 3β-HSD (HSD3B2 def, rare): ↑DHEA + ↑17-OH-pregnenolone; salt-wasting; virilization in FEMALES but UNDERVIRILIZATION in males (DHEA is weak androgen). CAH lipoid (StAR def or CYP11A1 def): cannot make any steroids; severe salt-wasting + absent sex development; male 46 XY = phenotypic female.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A point mutation in the anticodon loop of tRNALeu causes it to recognize UGA (normally a stop codon) as a leucine codon. This phenomenon is called:
options: Wobble base pairing (wobble base pairing = flexible [non-Watson-Crick] base pairing at the third position of the codon / first position of the anticodon; described by Crick's wobble hypothesis; allows one tRNA to read multiple codons; this is a normal process of tRNA decoding, not a mutation-caused suppression of stop codons)

Nonsense suppression (tRNA suppressor): a SUPPRESSOR tRNA is a mutant tRNA that reads a STOP CODON as an amino acid codon; in this case, a mutation in the anticodon loop of tRNALeu changes the anticodon from the normal Leu anticodon → to an anticodon complementary to UGA; the mutant tRNALeu → can be aminoacylated with leucine by LeuRS (leucyl-tRNA synthetase; the identity elements of the tRNA body are maintained → still charged with Leu) → can decode UGA as Leu → SUPPRESSES nonsense mutations (UGA stop → Leu insertion → read-through); types of suppressor tRNAs: UAG (amber) suppressor: most commonly studied; Gln (most common amino acid inserted); UGA (opal) suppressor: inserts Leu, Trp, Ser; UAA (ochre) suppressor: rarest; naturally occurring UGA suppressor: UGA is also read as Sec (selenocysteine) in selenoproteins via SECIS element + SelB/EFSec → Sec-tRNASec; experimentally: amber suppressors used in genetic code expansion (unnatural amino acid incorporation) using engineered aaRS + suppressor tRNA pairs; naturally occurring UGA read-through: some viruses (Moloney murine leukemia virus [MoMuLV], tobacco mosaic virus): UGA leakiness allows read-through → extended polyproteins; UGA read-through efficiency ~0-30% depending on context (surrounding nucleotide sequence [context effects])

Frameshifting (frameshifting = ribosome shifts reading frame by ±1 nucleotide; can be programmed [+1 or -1 frameshifting] or spontaneous; results in changed reading frame → different amino acid sequence from that point, not a stop codon suppression by altered tRNA recognition)
Wobble mismatch (wobble mismatch is already covered under wobble base pairing; mutation causing the tRNA to suppress a stop codon = nonsense suppression, not wobble)
explanation: Genetic code expansion and suppressor tRNAs: Natural amber suppressor in E. coli: the amber (UAG) suppressor supE (GLTX gene, glutamine amber suppressor): tRNAGln anticodon mutated to CUA → reads UAG → inserts Gln; 5-10% amber suppression efficiency (the ribosome competes between the suppressor tRNA and RF1 [which recognizes UAG → releases peptide]); higher suppression if: UAG in favorable context (C before UAG + A after) → allows drug selection in bacteria (UAG in essential gene → only with supE tRNA present do bacteria survive amber mutant). Unnatural amino acid (UAA) incorporation using orthogonal tRNA-aaRS pairs: evolved aaRS (usually from Methanosarcina mazei PylRS [pyrrolysyl-tRNA synthetase] or Methanocaldococcus jannaschii TyrRS) + cognate amber suppressor tRNA that are ORTHOGONAL (not recognized by endogenous aaRS or charged by endogenous charging enzymes) → charge with UAA → amber codon in gene of interest → protein with UAA incorporated at specific site; applications: site-specific fluorescent labeling, photo-crosslinkers, ketone handles for bioorthogonal chemistry, bispecific antibodies with unnatural linkers. Read-through therapy for nonsense mutations: ataluren (PTC124, 3-[5-(2-fluorophenyl)-1,2,4-oxadiazol-3-yl]benzoic acid): promotes ribosomal read-through of premature stop codons (UAG, UAA, UGA) → inserts near-cognate amino acid → near-full-length functional protein (approved in EU for nonsense mutation Duchenne muscular dystrophy [DMD] patients who can walk; promotes utrophin/dystrophin read-through); aminoglycosides (gentamicin): also promote read-through (bind 16S rRNA decoding center in bacteria → misreading; also cause some read-through in eukaryotes [via mammalian ribosome decoding site modification] → clinical studies in CF, Hurler, Duchenne); limited by: (1) tissue penetration; (2) amino acid identity inserted may affect protein function; (3) toxicity of aminoglycosides.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Insulin receptor (IR) is a receptor tyrosine kinase. After insulin binds to IR, which of the following is the FIRST intracellular signaling event?
options: Activation of adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP (insulin receptor is NOT coupled to Gαs/adenylyl cyclase; this is how glucagon and epinephrine signal; in fact, insulin OPPOSES cAMP effects by activating PDE [phosphodiesterase] → ↓cAMP)

Autophosphorylation of IR β-subunit tyrosine residues (Tyr1158, Tyr1162, Tyr1163 in the activation loop): Insulin receptor (IR, INSR gene): receptor tyrosine kinase; α2β2 heterotetrameric structure (2 extracellular α-subunits + 2 transmembrane β-subunits, linked by S-S bonds); insulin binds: sites 1 + 2 on α-subunit; binding → conformational change → β-subunit activation → AUTOPHOSPHORYLATION: (1) first event: IR β-subunit cytoplasmic domain trans-autophosphorylates (one β-subunit phosphorylates the other) at Tyr1158, Tyr1162, Tyr1163 in the kinase activation loop (A-loop) → opens A-loop → ↑kinase activity; also: Tyr960 (juxtamembrane, IRS-1 docking) + Tyr1328/1334 (C-terminal) phosphorylated; (2) then: activated IR → phosphorylates IRS proteins (IRS-1/2, insulin receptor substrate): IR phosphorylates multiple Tyr residues on IRS-1 (e.g., Tyr612 in mice, equivalent in humans) → pTyr motifs on IRS-1 → docking sites for SH2 domains of: PI3K p85 subunit → PI3K activity → PIP2 → PIP3 → PDK1 + mTORC2 → Akt (PKB) phosphorylation (Thr308 by PDK1 + Ser473 by mTORC2) → fully active Akt → GLUT4 vesicle translocation (AS160/TBC1D4 phosphorylation → Rab GTPase activates → GLUT4 docking + fusion) + glycogen synthesis (GSK-3β inactivation) + lipogenesis (SREBP-1c) + protein synthesis (S6K1 via mTOR); also: Grb2-SOS → Ras → MAPK cascade → gene expression; (3) IRS-1 Ser phosphorylation by IKK + JNK (in inflammation/obesity) → INHIBITS IRS-1 → impairs insulin signaling → insulin resistance (the molecular link between inflammation and type 2 diabetes)

Phospholipase C (PLC) activation → IP3 + DAG (PLC is activated by Gαq-coupled receptors, not by RTKs directly; though PLC-γ [PLCγ] can be activated by some RTKs [e.g., EGFR → SH2 domain of PLCγ → PLCγ phosphorylation → active] but IR does NOT primarily signal via PLCγ; IP3 + DAG are not the main insulin signaling intermediates)

Activation of JAK2 kinase → STAT5 phosphorylation (JAK-STAT signaling is used by cytokine receptors [GH receptor, Epo receptor, interferons, IL-2, etc.]; insulin receptor is a receptor TYROSINE KINASE that autophosphorylates directly, not via JAK kinases; though JAK2 can interact with IR at high concentrations, it is not the primary first signaling event)
explanation: Insulin signaling pathway — PI3K-Akt: IR → IRS-1/2 (Y-phosphorylation) → PI3K (p85 + p110) → PIP2 → PIP3 → PDK1 (PDPK1) → Akt (PKB) phospho-Thr308; mTORC2 (RICTOR complex) → phospho-Ser473 on Akt → full Akt activation; Akt substrates: AS160/TBC1D4 (Rab-GAP) → ↑Rab10 activity → GLUT4 vesicle translocation to PM → ↓blood glucose; GSK-3β (phospho → inactive) → ↑glycogen synthase (active) → ↑glycogen; TSC2 (phospho → TSC1/2 dissociation → Rheb-GTP) → mTORC1 active → S6K1 + 4E-BP1 → ↑protein synthesis; FOXO1 (phospho → nuclear exclusion) → ↓PEPCK + ↓G6Pase transcription → ↓gluconeogenesis; PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) → dephosphorylates PIP3 → PIP2 → opposes PI3K → ↓Akt; PTEN is a tumor suppressor → frequently mutated in cancer (↑PI3K-Akt → ↑proliferation + ↑survival). Akt isoforms: Akt1 (PKBα): growth + survival (Akt1 knockout → small animal, placental defect); Akt2 (PKBβ): metabolic regulation (Akt2 knockout → diabetes); Akt3 (PKBγ): brain size. IR-MAPK pathway (less dominant for metabolic effects, more for growth): IRS → Grb2 (SH2 domain) → SOS (GEF) → Ras-GDP → Ras-GTP → B-Raf/Raf1 → MEK1/2 → ERK1/2 → nuclear entry → Elk-1, c-Fos → ↑gene expression (→ some insulin effects on cell growth + proliferation); the MAPK pathway is what links insulin to cell growth/differentiation (less about GLUT4 translocation); insulin resistance and T2DM: selective impairment (PI3K-Akt branch impaired → ↓GLUT4 → ↑blood glucose) while MAPK branch often remains functional → this explains why insulin resistance → ↑insulin levels → over-activation of MAPK → vascular smooth muscle proliferation → accelerated atherosclerosis in T2DM.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glutamate is converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase (GS). This reaction is important for:
options: Synthesis of ketone bodies in the liver (ketone bodies [AcAc, 3-HB, acetone] are made from acetyl-CoA via HMG-CoA pathway in liver; glutamine is not a substrate for ketogenesis)

Excretion of excess ammonia in the brain and muscle, and as the primary nitrogen transport molecule in blood: GS (glutamine synthetase): glutamate + NH3 + ATP → glutamine + ADP + Pi + H2O; enzyme is ubiquitous but particularly important in: (1) Brain astrocytes: glutamine synthetase is HIGH in astrocytes; neurons release glutamate → astrocytes take up glutamate → GS → glutamine → released to blood or re-exported to neurons (glutamate-glutamine cycle); astrocyte GS also fixes NH4+ from blood → glutamine; GS in astrocytes prevents ammonia toxicity in brain (↑NH3 in hepatic encephalopathy → astrocytes cannot compensate → Alzheimer type II astrocytes [nuclear swelling], ↑glutamine in astrocytes → osmotic swelling → cerebral edema); methionine sulfoximine (MSO) inhibits GS → used experimentally to model hyperammonemia in brain; (2) Skeletal muscle: during prolonged exercise + protein catabolism → ↑NH3 from AMP deaminase + BCAA catabolism → muscle GS + BCAT: α-KG + NH4+ → Glu (transamination) → GS → Gln; glutamine is the primary nitrogen carrier in blood (plasma Gln ~500-700 µM = highest concentration of any amino acid in plasma); Gln exported from muscle → intestinal mucosal cells (glutamine is the primary fuel of rapidly dividing cells like enterocytes → GLS → glutamate + NH4+ → used for energy + nucleotide precursor) + kidney (renal GLS → Glu + NH4+ → NH4+ excreted in urine [important in acidosis: ↑urinary NH4+ → acid excretion]) + liver (urea cycle [urea synthesis from glutamine N]); (3) Nitrogen metabolism: GS activity: in liver → converts NH3 → Gln as 'safety net' for leftover NH3 not captured by urea cycle; high GS in perivenous hepatocytes (zone 3 of hepatic acinus); GLS (glutaminase, opposite reaction): liver periportal hepatocytes (zone 1) → glutamine → NH4+ + glutamate → urea cycle input; the peri-portal high GLS + peri-venous high GS = hepatic glutamine/glutamate zonation

Providing the amino group for pyrimidine synthesis by CPS II (CPS II uses glutamine [NOT glutamate] as the nitrogen donor: Gln + 2ATP + HCO3- → carbamoyl-P + Glu; but the question asks about the GS REACTION itself [Glu → Gln]; the reaction of GS is what MAKES Gln available for CPS II; technically correct but not the PRIMARY reason for GS importance described classically)
Converting Gln to α-ketoglutarate for the TCA cycle (that would be the reverse: glutaminase → Glu → glutamate dehydrogenase → α-KG; GS catalyzes Glu → Gln, not the reverse)
explanation: Ammonia metabolism — inter-organ: Sources of NH3: amino acid catabolism: transaminases → Glu → GDH → NH4+ + α-KG; AMP deaminase (AMPD1, especially muscle): AMP → IMP + NH4+ (released during exercise → McArdle forearm test: ↑NH4+ but no ↑lactate); intestinal bacteria: ureolysis → urea → urease (bacteria) → 2 NH3 + CO2; absorbed from colon into portal blood → liver → urea cycle; in liver failure → ↑NH3 bypasses urea cycle → systemic hyperammonemia. Transport: Alanine-glucose cycle (Ala as nitrogen carrier from muscle → liver); Glutamine (Gln from muscle/brain → liver/kidney); Purines (IMP from muscle → hypoxanthine → liver). Urea cycle (review): Liver periportal zone: CPS I (mito, NH4+ + CO2 + ATP → carbamoyl-P) + OTC (mito: carbamoyl-P + Orn → Cit) → cytoplasm: ASS (Cit + Asp → AS) → ASL (AS → Arg + fumarate) → Arginase I (Arg → Orn + urea) → urea excreted in urine. Hepatic encephalopathy (HE): ↑NH3 in hepatic failure → brain astrocytes → ↑GS → ↑glutamine → astrocyte swelling + glutamine-induced oxidative stress in mitochondria → MASH → 'Trojan horse' hypothesis; treatment: lactulose (acidifies colon → ↓NH4+ → ↑NH4+ trapping in colon → ↓NH4+ absorption; also acts as cathartic); rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic → ↓gut bacteria → ↓NH3 production); LOLA (L-ornithine L-aspartate): provides substrates for periportal urea cycle + perivenous GS → ↑NH3 disposal; sodium benzoate + phenylbutyrate: conjugate with Gly (benzoate → hippurate) and Gln (phenylbutyrate → phenylacetylglutamine [PAG]) → provide alternative nitrogen excretion pathways (not via urea); used in UCDs and HE.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Linoleic acid (18:2 Δ9,12) is an essential fatty acid. In the body, it can be converted to arachidonic acid (20:4 Δ5,8,11,14) by the action of:
options: Elongases only (elongases add 2 carbons to the carboxyl end of a fatty acid; while elongation is needed to go from 18→20 carbons, desaturases are ALSO required to add the extra double bonds needed to make arachidonic acid [20:4] from linoleic acid [18:2])
Desaturases only (desaturases add double bonds to FA chains; but to go from C18 → C20, elongation is also required; desaturase alone cannot change chain length)

Elongases (ELOVL5) and desaturases (FADS1 Δ5-desaturase + FADS2 Δ6-desaturase): the pathway from linoleic acid (LA, 18:2n-6 Δ9,12) to arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4n-6 Δ5,8,11,14): Step 1: LA (18:2 Δ9,12) → [FADS2, Δ6-desaturase, also called FADS2] → γ-linolenic acid (GLA, 18:3 Δ6,9,12); FADS2 (fatty acid desaturase 2, Δ6-desaturase): inserts a double bond at position Δ6 in C18 FA; uses O2 + NADH/NADPH + cytochrome b5 + FAD; in the ER membrane; FADS2 is ALSO the Δ6-desaturase for α-linolenic acid (ALA, 18:3n-3) → stearidonic acid (SDA, 18:4n-3); Step 2: GLA (18:3 Δ6,9,12) → [ELOVL5, elongase 5, adds 2 carbons at carboxyl end] → DGLA (dihomo-γ-linolenic acid, 20:3 Δ8,11,14); Step 3: DGLA (20:3 Δ8,11,14) → [FADS1, Δ5-desaturase] → Arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4 Δ5,8,11,14); FADS1 (fatty acid desaturase 1, Δ5-desaturase): inserts double bond at Δ5; the rate-limiting step of the pathway; DGLA (20:3n-6) is also a substrate for COX-1/2 → 1-series prostaglandins (PGE1) which are generally anti-inflammatory (unlike 2-series from AA); dietary significance: Western diets: high LA (from corn/soybean oil) but low conversion to AA (FADS1 + FADS2 are relatively inefficient) → most AA comes from diet (meat, eggs, liver); FADS2 polymorphisms: rs1535 (FADS2 variant): associated with ↓FADS2 activity → ↓ARA + ↓DHA from plant sources → populations with historically animal-based diets may have ↑FADS2 polymorphism frequency (less enzymatic need due to dietary AA); dietary n-3 FA (EPA, DHA from fish) → ↓FADS1/2 activity (competed for same enzymes) → ↓AA synthesis → ↓2-series PGs → anti-inflammatory

Lipoxygenases and cyclooxygenases (lipoxygenases [LOX: 5-LOX, 12-LOX, 15-LOX] + cyclooxygenases [COX-1/2] metabolize EXISTING polyunsaturated FA [especially AA] to eicosanoids [leukotrienes, prostaglandins, thromboxanes]; they do NOT synthesize AA from LA)
explanation: Essential fatty acids and eicosanoid biosynthesis: Essential fatty acids (EFA): cannot be synthesized de novo by mammals (lack Δ12 and Δ15 desaturases found in plants); must be obtained from diet: ω-6 series (n-6): LA (18:2n-6), found in plant oils (corn, soybean, sunflower) → GLA → DGLA → AA (20:4n-6) → ω-3 series (n-3): ALA (18:3n-3), found in flaxseed, chia, walnuts → SDA → EPA (20:5n-3) → DPA → DHA (22:6n-3); EPA + DHA primarily from marine oils. EFA deficiency: ↑Mead acid (20:3 Δ5,8,11, n-9) [triene] → ↑triene:tetraene ratio (Holman index) > 0.2 = EFA deficiency; dermatitis (scaly), ↑transepidermal water loss (TEWL) → 'impaired skin barrier' (ceramide + linoleic acid in epidermal ceramides are required for skin barrier integrity); ↓wound healing; in neonates on parenteral nutrition without lipid → EFA deficiency risk → IV lipid emulsions (Intralipid, soybean oil based) provide LA. Eicosanoids from AA (20:4n-6): COX pathway (PGs + TXs): COX-1/2 (cyclooxygenase, PGHS-1/2): AA + O2 → PGG2 → PGH2 (endoperoxide); PGH2 → isomerases: PGE2 (prostanoid E2), PGI2 (prostacyclin; vasodilation + antiaggregation), TXA2 (thromboxane A2; vasoconstriction + platelet aggregation), PGD2, PGF2α; 5-LOX pathway (leukotrienes): AA → [5-LOX + FLAP] → 5-HpETE → LTA4 → LTB4 (chemoattractant, PMN) or LTC4/D4/E4 (cysteinyl LTs, bronchospasm + vasoconstriction = slow-reacting substances of anaphylaxis, SRS-A); 12-LOX, 15-LOX pathways → lipoxins (anti-inflammatory), HETEs. SPM (specialized pro-resolving mediators from EPA/DHA): resolvins, protectins/neuroprotectins, maresins → actively resolve inflammation.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the process of intein splicing?
options: A process where pre-mRNA introns are removed by the spliceosome (intein splicing is a PROTEIN-level process; the spliceosome removes introns from pre-mRNA at the RNA level; these are completely different processes)

Protein self-splicing: inteins are intervening protein sequences that excise themselves from the precursor protein and ligate the flanking sequences (exteins) in a process requiring no external enzymes or ATP: inteins: defined as protein introns — internal sequences within precursor proteins that autocatalytically excise themselves; mechanism of intein splicing (self-splicing): step 1: N-terminal splice junction: N-Cys/Ser/Thr → forms thioester/ester with C-terminal residue of N-extein (N-S or N-O acyl shift); step 2: branching: C-terminal of N-extein ester → transfers to N-Cys of intein C-terminus → branched thioester intermediate; step 3: Asn cyclization: C-terminal Asn of intein → cyclizes (succinimide) → releases intein from N-extein + C-extein; step 4: S→N acyl shift: thioester between exteins → amide bond (permanent peptide bond between exteins); net result: N-extein + C-extein are joined by a new peptide bond; intein is released as a circular lariat (the Asn cyclization closes the intein as a thioester intermediate that resolves); inteins found in: bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes (fungi, algae, some unicellular organisms), bacteriophage; no introns in metazoans (nematodes are exception with rare cases); examples: Mycobacterium tuberculosis RecA intein; S. cerevisiae VMA1 (vacuolar ATPase catalytic subunit) has a 454-aa intein; split inteins: trans-splicing; two halves of intein in separate proteins → form complex → splice → ligate attached proteins (used for protein semisynthesis, conditional knock-outs); therapeutic potential: AAV gene therapy: large genes (>4.7 kb AAV capacity) can be split + delivered in 2 separate AAV vectors with split intein → proteins assemble after expression in cell → functional full-length protein

Removal of introns from ribosomal RNA by RNase P (RNase P is the ribozyme that cleaves the 5' leader of pre-tRNA → generates mature 5' end of tRNAs; it is NOT involved in ribosomal RNA intron removal or protein splicing)

Processing of signal peptides from secretory proteins by signal peptidase (signal peptidase [SPC, signal peptidase complex] cleaves the signal peptide from the nascent secretory protein as it enters the ER lumen; this is co-translational cleavage, not self-splicing and not 'intein splicing')
explanation: Types of protein splicing and analogous concepts: Protein splicing by inteins: self-catalytic, no external enzymes; catalytic residues: N-terminal Cys/Ser/Thr + C-terminal Asn + the penultimate His; conservation: intein sequences are diverse but the 'LAGLIDADG' motif (homing endonuclease-like) in some inteins is signature; engineered inteins: split inteins (DnaE split intein from Ssp and Npu cyanobacteria) → protein trans-splicing (PTS) used in: (1) protein semisynthesis; (2) split protein reporters (GFP complementation); (3) gene therapy with oversized genes; (4) traceless protein ligation (removing affinity tags); (5) biosensors. Post-translational processing events (NOT intein splicing): Signal peptide cleavage: signal peptidase (SPC complex) in ER lumen; N-terminal Met removal: methionine aminopeptidase (MAP) → cotranslational (many cytoplasmic proteins start with Ala/Gly/Val/Ser/Thr/Cys/Pro after Met removal). Propeptide removal: proenzymes activated by site-specific protease cleavage (trypsinogen → trypsin by enterokinase [duodenum]; chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin by trypsin); procollagen → collagen by procollagen protease (ADAMTS2/3/14). GPI anchor addition: co-translational, ER. Ubiquitin-mediated cleavage: ubiquitin is translated as part of a fusion protein (UBB + Ub-protein [ribosomal proteins] precursors → UCHL3/UCHL5 proteases → free ubiquitin monomers + active Ub moieties). Sortase (bacterial): SrtA (Staphylococcus aureus): sorts surface proteins; recognizes LPXTG motif → cleaves Thr-Gly + ligates to pentaglycine of peptidoglycan wall; used in bioconjugation (sortagging/Staudinger).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Succinyl-CoA is an intermediate in the Krebs cycle. It can also be formed from propionyl-CoA in the catabolism of odd-chain fatty acids. Which enzyme converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA?
options: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC): catalyzes propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA (upstream step); NOT the enzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA

Methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase (MMCE): interconverts D-methylmalonyl-CoA ↔ L-methylmalonyl-CoA; needed because PCC makes D-methylmalonyl-CoA but MCM uses L-methylmalonyl-CoA; MMCE is an important intermediate step but NOT the enzyme converting methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA

Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM, MMUT gene): MCM catalyzes: L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (intramolecular rearrangement: the thioester group migrates from one carbon to an adjacent one, 'carbanion-mediated 1,2 shift'); cofactor: adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl, 5'-deoxyadenosylcobalamin, the active coenzyme form of vitamin B12); mechanism: AdoCbl → homolytic cleavage of C-Co bond → 5'-deoxyadenosyl radical → abstracts H from substrate → substrate radical → isomerization → product radical → H returns from adenosyl → succinyl-CoA; MCM is in the mitochondrial matrix; MCM deficiency → methylmalonic acidemia (MMA); clinical presentation: neonatal metabolic crisis (hyperammonemia + ketoacidosis + hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis) or chronic (failure to thrive + developmental delay + chronic renal disease [methylmalonic acid nephrotoxicity]); biochemistry: ↑MMA in blood + urine + ↑plasma propionylcarnitine (C3) → odd-chain FA substrates diverted; AdoCbl deficiency also causes MMA (e.g., in cobalamin disorders [cblA, cblB, cblC, cblD] → cannot synthesize AdoCbl → functional MCM deficiency); vitamin B12 deficiency: ↑MMA in blood/urine (not as high as genetic MCM deficiency, but useful biomarker of B12 status → serum MMA better than serum B12 for functional B12 deficiency, especially in elderly or vegans; also ↑plasma homocysteine); succinyl-CoA role: TCA cycle → succinyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA synthetase → succinate + GTP; also: succinyl-CoA + Gly → [ALAS2] → δ-ALA (first step of heme synthesis in erythroid cells)
Methylmalonyl-CoA decarboxylase (found in some bacteria; converts methylmalonyl-CoA → propionyl-CoA + CO2; not the human enzyme for converting methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA; humans use MCM)
explanation: Odd-chain fatty acid catabolism: Odd-chain FA (C15:0, C17:0, etc., found in small amounts in dairy/ruminant fat): β-oxidation down to propionyl-CoA (C3) rather than ending at acetyl-CoA (C2); propionyl-CoA fate: propionyl-CoA + CO2 + biotin + ATP → [PCC] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MMCE] → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM + AdoCbl] → succinyl-CoA → TCA cycle (anaplerotic) + gluconeogenesis. Sources of propionyl-CoA: Odd-chain FA β-oxidation; Catabolism of BCAA (Ile, Val → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA; Met → homocysteine → Cys + α-ketobutyrate → propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA); Threonine catabolism (Thr → α-ketobutyrate → propionyl-CoA or Thr → Gly + acetyl-CoA); intestinal bacterial fermentation (propionate as SCF [short-chain fatty acid]). Cobalamin metabolism: Dietary B12 (in meat/dairy) → gastric intrinsic factor (IF, GIF gene: parietal cells) → IF-B12 complex → ileal cubilin/AMN receptor → endocytosis → lysosome → B12 released → transcobalamin II (TCII) → blood → cells; in cells: lysosomal Cbl → cytoplasmic → MMACHC (CblC, combines B12 with reductants) → AdoCbl (mitochondria, via CblA [MMAA] + CblB [MMAB]) or MeCbl (cytoplasm, via CblE [MTRR] + CblG [MTR/MS]) → AdoCbl → MCM; MeCbl → methionine synthase. Neurological effects of B12 deficiency: subacute combined degeneration (SCD) of spinal cord: ↑homocysteine → ↓methionine → ↓SAM → ↓myelin basic protein methylation → demyelination; also ↑MMA → mitochondrial dysfunction; posterior + lateral column degeneration: vibration sense + proprioception lost (posterior columns, dorsal) + upper motor neuron signs + spastic paraparesis (lateral columns, corticospinal).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A drug that specifically inhibits glycolysis by blocking the enzyme at step 9 (enolase) would prevent conversion of:
options: Glucose-6-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate (this is step 2: phosphoglucose isomerase / PGI; not step 9)

2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP): Enolase (step 9, phosphopyruvate hydratase, ENO1/2/3): 2-phosphoglycerate (2-PG) → phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) + H2O; dehydration reaction; generates PEP (high-energy phosphate compound, ΔG = -61.9 kJ/mol of hydrolysis) from 2-PG; Mg2+ required for catalysis; inhibited by fluoride (F-): F- + Mg2+ → MgF- → chelates second Mg2+ in active site → stops enolase → used in blood collection tubes to prevent glycolysis (gray-top tubes: sodium fluoride + potassium oxalate for blood glucose preservation); tumor marker: ENO1 (alpha-enolase, NSE [neuron-specific enolase] refers to ENO2 = gamma-enolase): NSE (ENO2) is a tumor marker for small cell lung cancer (SCLC), neuroblastoma, neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), and carcinoid; ↑serum NSE correlates with tumor burden + staging in SCLC; enolase isoenzymes: ENO1 (α-enolase, ubiquitous), ENO2 (γ-enolase, neurons + neuroendocrine cells = NSE), ENO3 (β-enolase, muscle-specific); ENO1 deletion: tumor suppressor function in some contexts (1p36 deletion [frequent in neuroblastoma] → ↓ENO1 → ↓cancer glucose metabolism)
3-phosphoglycerate to 2-phosphoglycerate (step 8 is phosphoglycerate mutase [PGAM] which converts 3-PG → 2-PG; step 9 [enolase] converts 2-PG → PEP)
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to DHAP + glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (this is step 4: aldolase [ALDOA]; cleaves F1,6BP into the two triose phosphates)
explanation: Glycolysis steps — enzymes and products: Step 1: Hexokinase/Glucokinase (HK/GK): Glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP (Mg2+; irreversible). Step 2: Phosphoglucose isomerase (PGI): G6P → F6P (reversible). Step 3: PFK-1: F6P + ATP → F1,6BP + ADP (Mg2+; irreversible; rate-limiting). Step 4: Aldolase (ALDOA): F1,6BP → DHAP + G3P (reversible). Step 5: TPI (triosephosphate isomerase): DHAP ↔ G3P (very fast; near-equilibrium). Step 6: GAPDH: G3P + NAD+ + Pi → 1,3-BPG + NADH (Mg2+; sulfhydryl at active site Cys149 → inhibited by iodoacetate, arsenate, GAPDH antibodies in autoimmunity). Step 7: PGK (phosphoglycerate kinase): 1,3-BPG + ADP → 3-PG + ATP (1st substrate-level phosphorylation; Mg2+; reversible). Step 8: PGAM (phosphoglycerate mutase): 3-PG → 2-PG (requires 2,3-BPG as cofactor in mammalian form [bisphosphoglycerate mutase activity activates PGAM by phosphorylating His at active site]; PGAM deficiency [rare] → exercise intolerance + myoglobinuria). Step 9: Enolase: 2-PG → PEP + H2O (Mg2+; inhibited by F-; see above). Step 10: Pyruvate kinase (PK): PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP (2nd substrate-level phosphorylation; Mg2+; K+ required; irreversible; activated by F1,6BP; inhibited by ATP, Ala). Pyruvate fates: Aerobic: PDC → acetyl-CoA → TCA. Anaerobic/anerobic conditions: LDH → lactate. In liver/kidney: PC → OAA (gluconeogenesis entry). In yeast: pyruvate decarboxylase → acetaldehyde → ADH → ethanol.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is a serine protease produced by the prostate gland. It belongs to which biochemical family?
options: Matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) family: MMPs are zinc-dependent endopeptidases (collagenase, gelatinase, stromelysin, etc.) that degrade ECM components; PSA is NOT an MMP; PSA is a serine protease

Aspartyl protease family: aspartyl proteases use two Asp residues in the active site (pepsin, cathepsin D, renin, HIV protease, secretases); PSA does NOT use Asp at its active site; PSA uses Ser (serine protease)

Kallikrein family (kallikrein-related peptidases, KLKs): PSA (Prostate-Specific Antigen) = KLK3 (Kallikrein-related peptidase 3), also known as hK3 (human kallikrein 3); the KLK family (KLK1-15) are serine proteases of the S1 peptidase family (chymotrypsin clan); KLK3 (PSA): expressed predominantly in prostate epithelium + secreted into seminal fluid (normal PSA in semen: very high, ~0.5-5 mg/mL; in blood: normal < 4 ng/mL); normal function: cleaves seminogelin I + II (semenogelin, major gel-forming proteins of the seminal vesicle secretion) → liquefies seminal clot after ejaculation → ↑sperm motility; PSA in blood: most is complexed to α1-antichymotrypsin (PSA-ACT, major form, ~65-90%) + some to α2-macroglobulin; FREE PSA (uncomplexed): ratio of free PSA / total PSA: ↓free:total ratio (< 0.10-0.25) → ↑probability of prostate cancer (cancer cells secrete more complexed PSA or less total PSA); HIGH free:total ratio → benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH); PSA clinical use: screening (controversial): systematic screening with PSA → ↓prostate cancer mortality by ~20-30% but ↑overdiagnosis + overtreatment; U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF): decision to screen for men 55-69 should be individualized; high-risk men (Black men, BRCA2 mutation) → earlier/more vigilant screening; PSA kinetics: PSA velocity (PSAV): > 0.75 ng/mL/year → concerning; PSA doubling time (PSADT): short PSADT after radical prostatectomy (< 12 months) → higher risk of metastasis; PSA density (PSAD) = PSA/prostate volume; 4K Score, phi (PSA-related index) = newer, more specific tests
Cysteine protease family: cysteine proteases use Cys in active site (caspases [apoptosis], cathepsins B/L/K, calpains, papain, cruzain); PSA is a serine protease, not a cysteine protease
explanation: Serine protease superfamily: Serine proteases: Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad (or Ser-His-Glu) → Ser nucleophile attacks carbonyl of peptide bond → acyl-enzyme intermediate → H2O → deacylation + product release; clans: PA clan (chymotrypsin-like): trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, thrombin, plasmin, urokinase, tPA, KLK family (including PSA/KLK3); SB clan (subtilisin-like): subtilisin, kexin, furin (PCSK9 activator); SC clan (α/β hydrolases): prolyl endopeptidase, DPP4; SF clan: signal peptidase. Chymotrypsin-like serine proteases (PA clan, S1 family): all have classic oxyanion hole (Gly193 backbone NH + Ser195 OH in chymotrypsin numbering → stabilize the tetrahedral intermediate); specificity determined by S1 binding pocket: chymotrypsin (large hydrophobic [Phe, Trp, Tyr] → large non-polar S1 pocket); trypsin (Arg/Lys → Asp189 in S1 pocket = negative charge attracts positive side chains); elastase (small neutral [Val, Ala] → small S1 pocket due to Val190 + Thr218 replacing Gly in chymotrypsin); PSA (KLK3): chymotrypsin-like specificity (cleaves after aromatic AA); other KLKs: KLK1 (tissue kallikrein): cleaves kininogens → kallidin (Lys-bradykinin); KLK2 (hK2): prostate specific, activates PSA precursor (pro-PSA); KLK4 (hK4): activates enamelins in tooth formation; KLK5 (hK5): skin desquamation (activates profilaggrin and corneodesmosin); KLK7 (hK7): skin desquamation; KLK6 (neuropsin): CNS, myelination; KLK14: skin; Netherton syndrome: SPINK5 (LEKTI) → serine protease inhibitor mutations → ↑KLK5/7 → excessive desquamation + ↑permeability.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A researcher studying mRNA turnover finds that an mRNA with a specific sequence in its 3'-UTR undergoes rapid degradation. This 3'-UTR element is called:
options: Internal ribosome entry site (IRES): IRES elements are in the 5'-UTR (not 3'-UTR) and allow cap-independent translation initiation by recruiting the ribosome directly to the mRNA; found in viral RNAs (HCV, IRES is highly structured) and some cellular mRNAs during stress
CpG island: CpG islands are found in DNA promoter regions (not mRNA); associated with gene regulation at the transcriptional level, not mRNA stability

AU-rich element (ARE): AREs (AU-rich elements, adenosine-uridine rich elements) are sequences in the 3'-UTR of certain mRNAs that target them for rapid degradation; typical ARE: AUUUA pentamer (single or in tandem) or UUAUUUAUUU (nonanucleotide) often in clusters; found in: proto-oncogene mRNAs (c-fos, c-myc, c-jun), cytokine mRNAs (TNF-α, IL-2, IL-3, GM-CSF), other short-lived mRNAs (COX-2, HIF-1α); ARE-binding proteins: (1) TTP (tristetraprolin, ZFP36): AU-rich element binding protein → promotes mRNA deadenylation → degradation; INDUCED by LPS + inflammation; p38 MAPK → MK2 phosphorylates TTP → stabilizes TTP (cannot bind ARE effectively) → ARE-containing mRNAs stabilized → ↑TNF-α (important inflammatory amplification); when inflammation resolves → ↑TTP activity → ↑TNF-α mRNA degradation; TTP knockout mice → chronic inflammatory arthritis; (2) HuR (ELAVL1): ARE-binding → stabilizes mRNA (positive effect on ARE-mRNAs); nuclear normally → stress → nuclear export → cytoplasmic stabilization of ARE-containing mRNAs; (3) AUF1/hnRNP D: destabilizes ARE-mRNAs; (4) KSRP: deadenylation + P-body targeting; mRNA decay pathways: deadenylation (CCR4-NOT complex + PAN2-PAN3 remove 3' poly-A tail) → then: 5'-decapping (DCP1a-DCP2) + 5'→3' exoribonuclease (XRN1) OR 3'→5' exoribonuclease complex (RNA exosome) → mRNA degraded in P-bodies (processing bodies) or stress granules

Kozak sequence: the Kozak sequence (5'-GCCACCAUGG-3', where AUG is the start codon) is in the 5'-UTR/start codon context; influences translation initiation efficiency; NOT in the 3'-UTR and NOT a destabilizing element; a strong Kozak sequence ↑translation efficiency of mRNA
explanation: mRNA stability regulation: mRNA half-life ranges from minutes (c-fos, proto-oncogenes) to hours (globin mRNAs) to days (xeroderma pigmentosum repair genes); 'average' mRNA half-life in mammals: ~10 hours; unstable mRNAs: cytokines, proto-oncogenes, transcription factors — this allows rapid changes in cellular response; stable mRNAs: structural proteins (β-globin: ~10h in reticulocytes), ribosomal proteins, housekeeping genes. ARE classes: class I ARE: AUUUA in U-rich context; class II: overlapping AUUUA repeats; class III: U-rich without canonical AUUUA (e.g., c-fos 3'-UTR). Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD): recognizes premature termination codons (PTC: > 50-55 nt upstream of an exon-exon junction = EJC [exon junction complex: eIF4A3 + MAGOH + RBM8A/Y14 + MLN51]); when ribosome reaches PTC before removing all EJCs → UPF1 (RENT1, NMD factor) + UPF2 + UPF3 + SMG1/6/7 complex → deadenylation + decapping + degradation; NMD eliminates aberrant mRNAs from premature stop codons (from nonsense mutations, frameshifts, leaky splicing); ~30% of PTC-containing mRNAs escape NMD → partial expression; NMD is exploited therapeutically (ataluren: read-through of PTC → produces some protein; NMD inhibitors: would let PTC mRNAs survive NMD → ↑read-through protein from leaky translation). Staufen-mediated mRNA decay (SMD): Staufen1 binds dsRNA structures in 3'-UTR (formed with Alu elements or with linc RNAs) → recruits UPF1 → degradation. miRNA pathway: RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex: AGO2 + miRNA) → binds 3'-UTR complementary sequences → mRNA degradation (AGO2 slicer activity if perfect complement, like siRNA) or translation repression (if partial complement, most miRNA in animals) → leading to mRNA deadenylation + decapping + degradation in P-bodies.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient presents with megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms (subacute combined degeneration). Both vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia, but ONLY B12 deficiency causes neurological symptoms. The UNIQUE biochemical function of vitamin B12 not shared with folate is:
options: Participation in the methionine synthase (MS) reaction as methylcobalamin (MeCbl) — this IS shared with folate (5-methylTHF is the donor of the methyl group in the MS reaction; B12 [MeCbl] accepts the methyl from 5-Me-THF and transfers it to homocysteine → methionine); both B12 + folate are needed for this reaction; if we're looking at what's UNIQUE to B12, it is the adenosylcobalamin-requiring MCM reaction

Methylcobalamin cofactor for methionine synthase converting methylTHF + Hcy → THF + Met (this IS the 'methylfolate trap' mechanism for megaloblastic anemia shared between B12 + folate deficiency; without B12 → methylTHF cannot donate its methyl group → cannot regenerate THF → ↓THF → ↓all THF-dependent reactions including dTMP synthesis → megaloblastic anemia; but this mechanism is shared; the UNIQUE B12 function is MCM)

Adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) as cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM), which is the ONLY cobalamin-dependent enzyme in humans NOT requiring folate: B12-dependent enzymes in humans: (1) Methionine synthase (MTR/MS): uses methylcobalamin (MeCbl) → methionine from homocysteine + 5-methyl-THF (INVOLVES FOLATE); (2) Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM): uses adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) → succinyl-CoA from methylmalonyl-CoA; DOES NOT INVOLVE FOLATE; this is the biochemically UNIQUE B12 function not shared with folate; neurological damage in B12 deficiency: two proposed mechanisms: (a) ↓MCM → ↑methylmalonyl-CoA + ↑MMA → incorporation of methylmalonyl-CoA into fatty acid synthesis → abnormal odd-chain FA in myelin (propionyl-CoA shunted to FA synthesis → ↑C15:0 + C17:0 in myelin → structural instability → demyelination); (b) ↓MS → ↓methionine → ↓SAM → ↓methylation of myelin basic protein (MBP) + other myelin lipids → ↓maintenance of myelin sheath; BOTH mechanisms may contribute; the MCM mechanism (unique to B12) is the principal reason SCD does NOT occur in folate deficiency (folate supplements methyl-group transfer, not AdoCbl/MCM pathway); subacute combined degeneration (SCD): posterior and lateral column degeneration: posterior columns (dorsal): ↓proprioception + vibration sense → Romberg sign; lateral corticospinal tracts: ↑DTRs → upper motor neuron signs → spastic weakness; also peripheral neuropathy (axonal degeneration); serum B12 vs MMA: serum B12 normal in ~25% of functional B12 deficiency; MMA + Hcy both elevated in B12 deficiency; MMA alone elevated → specific for MCM dysfunction (not folate-related); Hcy alone elevated can be folate OR B12 deficiency

Participation in one-carbon metabolism via the folate cycle for nucleotide synthesis (one-carbon metabolism and folate cycle for nucleotide synthesis [purine + dTMP] is the FUNCTION OF FOLATE primarily; B12's connection to folate is indirect [MS reaction releases THF from 5-methylTHF trap]; one-carbon metabolism is not B12-UNIQUE, it is primarily a folate function)
explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) forms and functions: Cobalamin structure: corrin ring (4 pyrrole rings with Co2+/3+ center) + 5'-deoxyadenosyl (AdoCbl) or methyl (MeCbl) or CN (cyanocobalamin, storage form, inactive) or OH (hydroxocobalamin, therapeutic form) upper ligand. Two active forms: MeCbl (cytoplasmic): methionine synthase cofactor; connects B12 to folate cycle + homocysteine remethylation. AdoCbl (mitochondrial): MCM cofactor; connects B12 to propionyl-CoA/odd-chain FA catabolism. Absorption pathway: food Cbl → HCl + pepsin → R-binder (haptocorrin, salivary/gastric) → duodenum → pancreatic proteases digest R-binder → intrinsic factor (IF, gastric parietal cells) binds Cbl → IF-Cbl complex → ileal receptor (cubilin + amnionless = cubam complex) → endocytosis → lysosomal release → TCII (transcobalamin II, secreted by endothelial cells + macrophages) + TCIb (haptocorrin, carries majority in blood but doesn't enter cells → reservoir) → cells via TCII receptor (CD320) → endocytosis → lysosomal processing → MMACHC (CblC) → intracellular Cbl metabolism. Causes of B12 deficiency: Pernicious anemia (PA): autoimmune gastritis → anti-parietal cell Ab (anti-H+/K+-ATPase) → type A gastritis (body + fundus) → ↓parietal cells → ↓IF + ↓HCl → ↓B12 absorption; anti-IF antibody (type I = blocking, prevents IF-Cbl binding; type II = precipitating, prevents IF-Cbl from binding ileal receptor); ↑gastrin (achlorhydria → no acid inhibition of gastrin → ↑G cells → ↑gastrin → can cause hyperplasia of ECL cells → ↑risk gastric carcinoid); diagnose with Schilling test (historically) or serum anti-IF antibody (best specificity); treat: IM hydroxocobalamin (monthly in UK) or oral cyanocobalamin/methylcobalamin (high doses, 1000 µg/day, can compensate if some gastric absorption or IF-independent absorption via passive diffusion). Dietary B12 deficiency (pure vegans + breastfed infant of vegan mother): no animal products → ↓B12 intake; infant breastfed by B12-deficient vegan → very low breast milk B12 → neonatal SCD + megaloblastic anemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the context of gene regulation, CRISPR-Cas9 can be repurposed as a gene activator (CRISPRa) by:
options: Replacing the Cas9 protein with a Cre recombinase to activate floxed promoters (Cre recombinase acts on loxP sites to recombine DNA; this is a different system entirely from CRISPRa and does not activate gene expression)

Fusing a transcriptional activation domain (e.g., VP64 or VPR) to a catalytically inactive Cas9 (dCas9): CRISPR activation (CRISPRa): Cas9 is an RNA-guided endonuclease; to ACTIVATE transcription without cutting DNA: use dCas9 (dead Cas9): two point mutations in Cas9 catalytic residues: D10A (RuvC nuclease domain) + H840A (HNH nuclease domain) → dCas9 cannot cleave DNA BUT can still be guided by sgRNA to specific genomic loci; fuse dCas9 to: (1) VP64 (tetrameric VP16 from herpes simplex virus = potent transcriptional activator; binds TBP + TFIIB → ↑Pol II recruitment): dCas9-VP64 + sgRNA targeting promoter → recruit transcriptional machinery → ↑gene expression; (2) VPR (VP64-p65-Rta, even more potent activation by combining VP64 with p65 [NF-κB activation domain] + Rta [Epstein-Barr virus transcriptional activator]); (3) SAM (synergistic activation mediator): dCas9-VP64 + sgRNA with aptamer hairpins that recruit MS2-p65-HSF1 → ↑transcription; (4) SunTag: dCas9-SunTag (GCN4 peptide array) + scFv-VP64 antibody fragments (10 copies of VP64 per dCas9 → very strong activation); applications: target gene overexpression without DNA insertion, disease modeling, screening for therapeutic targets (pooled CRISPRa libraries), epigenome editing (dCas9-TET1 → demethylation; dCas9-DNMT3A → methylation; dCas9-LSD1 → H3K4me1 removal; dCas9-p300 → H3K27ac deposition); CRISPRi (interference): dCas9-KRAB (KRAB domain of Krüppel-associated box → recruits KAP1/TRIM28 → recruits NuRD + SETDB1 → H3K9me3 → chromatin compaction) → gene repression without DNA cutting

Designing sgRNA to target the Cas9 protein to the RNA polymerase complex directly (sgRNA guides Cas9 to DNA sequences, not to protein complexes directly; Cas9 binds DNA, not protein targets [though modified systems like RCas9 target RNA or protein-tethered proximity labeling]

Expressing Cas9 as a fusion with GFP to visualize gene activation in live cells (GFP fusion is for visualization/tracking of dCas9 in the nucleus, not for transcriptional activation; visualization ≠ gene activation; CRISPRa requires a transcriptional activation domain fused to dCas9)
explanation: CRISPR-Cas9 system — mechanisms and applications: Natural CRISPR-Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats - CRISPR-associated proteins): adaptive immune system in bacteria/archaea against bacteriophage; mechanism: bacteria capture spacer sequences from phage DNA → insert between repeats in CRISPR array → upon re-infection: CRISPR array transcribed → pre-crRNA → processed into crRNA + tracrRNA (or sgRNA when fused) → crRNA:tracrRNA + Cas9 → scans DNA for PAM (protospacer adjacent motif: 5'-NGG-3' for SpCas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes) + 20-nt match → Cas9 unwinds DNA → R-loop → HNH domain (cleaves target/non-template strand at -3 position from PAM) + RuvC domain (cleaves non-target strand) → blunt DSB → phage DNA inactivated. SpCas9: most widely used; requires NGG PAM; ~1200 aa; gene editing: transfect sgRNA + Cas9 (plasmid, mRNA, or RNP [ribonucleoprotein complex]) → DSB at target → cellular repair: NHEJ (error-prone → indels → frameshift/knockout) or HDR (with donor template → precise edit). Base editing: CBE (cytosine base editor): dCas9-nCas9 [D10A nickase cuts non-target strand only] + APOBEC (cytidine deaminase) + UGI (uracil DNA glycosylase inhibitor) → C→U in window → U treated as T → C:G→T:A transition; ABE (adenine base editor): dCas9 + engineered adenosine deaminase (TadA evolved) → A→I (treated as G) → A:T→G:C transition; prime editing: PEgRNA + Cas9 nickase fused to reverse transcriptase → nick + RT-mediated insertion of precise edit; all types of transitions + transversions + small indels + insertions; no DSB required for prime editing. Therapeutic CRISPR: CTX001/exa-cel (exagamglogene autotemcel): BCL11A enhancer editing in HSCs → ↑γ-globin → ↑HbF → approved for SCD + β-thalassemia (2023, first approved CRISPR therapeutic). CRISPR for transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR): patisiran/inclisiran/siRNA approaches but NTLA-2001 (in vivo CRISPR-LNP → liver delivery → TTR gene editing → ↓TTR protein → ↓amyloid deposits) in phase II trials.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with macrocephaly, developmental regression, cherry-red spot, and an infant with hepatosplenomegaly. Enzyme assay shows marked deficiency of β-hexosaminidase A and B. The diagnosis is:
options: Tay-Sachs disease: Tay-Sachs has β-hexosaminidase A deficiency ONLY (deficient HexA = α+β subunit heterodimer; HexB = β+β homodimer is INTACT in Tay-Sachs); in Tay-Sachs there is NO hepatosplenomegaly (no GM2 accumulation in macrophages because Hex B is intact in macrophages and partially degrades GM2)

Fabry disease: Fabry is α-galactosidase A deficiency (GLA gene, X-linked; Gb3/GL-3 accumulation; angiokeratoma + neuropathy [burning pain] + renal failure; NO cherry-red spot; NO hexosaminidase deficiency)

Sandhoff disease (GM2-gangliosidosis type 2): Sandhoff disease = HEXB gene mutations → deficiency of BOTH β-hexosaminidase A (α+β subunit) AND β-hexosaminidase B (β+β homodimer, Hex B); because HexB subunit is absent → BOTH Hex A AND Hex B lose function; biochemistry: Hex A (α1β1 [αβ] heterodimer) requires HEXA-encoded α-subunit + HEXB-encoded β-subunit; Hex B (β2 homodimer) requires only HEXB-encoded β-subunit; in HEXB mutations: HEXB protein absent → no β-subunit available for either Hex A or Hex B → BOTH Hex A + Hex B profoundly deficient; GM2 and GA2 AND globoside (Gb4, a β-hexosaminidase substrate) accumulate in BOTH neurons (GM2 → cherry-red spot + neurodegeneration) AND macrophages/Kupffer cells (GA2 + globoside via HexB) → HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY (macrophage storage) + NEURODEGENERATION + cherry-red spot; CONTRAST with Tay-Sachs: HEXA mutation → Hex A deficient, Hex B intact → macrophages use Hex B to clear some substrates → NO hepatosplenomegaly; clinically: Sandhoff disease (infantile form) = clinically IDENTICAL to Tay-Sachs BUT with HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY + BONE INVOLVEMENT (globoside also accumulates in bone) + BIOCHEMICALLY both enzymes deficient; GM2-activator protein deficiency (GM2-AP, GM2A gene): activator protein for Hex A in GM2 degradation; mutations → same clinical phenotype as Tay-Sachs (Hex A present but cannot access substrate without GM2-AP); called 'AB variant' of GM2 gangliosidosis

Niemann-Pick disease type A (NPD-A): sphingomyelinase (SMPD1) deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation; cherry-red spot YES; hepatosplenomegaly YES; but Hex A and Hex B are NORMAL (NPD is not a hexosaminidase deficiency)
explanation: GM2 gangliosidoses — complete comparison: GM2 ganglioside structure: GalNAc-β1,4-(NeuAc-α2,3)-Gal-β1,4-Glc-β1,1'-Cer; degradation: Hex A (αβ heterodimer) + GM2-activator protein → cleaves terminal GalNAc from GM2 → GM3. Tay-Sachs disease (infantile most common; late-onset/juvenile forms also): HEXA gene → α-subunit absent → Hex A absent, Hex B INTACT; GM2 accumulates in neurons + glial cells (not macrophages/liver because Hex B handles some substrates); presentation: cherry-red spot (macular cherry-red in fovea = foveal ganglion cells swollen around the area, central fovea appears red due to lack of overlying ganglion cells) + psychomotor retardation from 3-6 months + startle response (hyperacusis) + seizures + blindness → vegetative state → death by 2-4 years; NO hepatosplenomegaly; Ashkenazi Jewish high carrier frequency (1/30); biochemical: ↑GM2 in brain + CSF; HexA activity absent in leukocytes + plasma; HexA activity ABSENT, HexB activity NORMAL; Sandhoff disease: HEXB gene → β-subunit absent → BOTH HexA + HexB absent; GM2 + GA2 + globoside all accumulate; clinically SAME as Tay-Sachs plus hepatosplenomegaly + bone involvement; HexA + HexB BOTH absent in leukocytes; less ethnic specificity (not Ashkenazi-enriched). GM2-AP deficiency (AB variant): HexA + HexB both NORMAL enzymatically (in vitro with artificial substrate) but GM2-AP absent → in vivo HexA cannot degrade GM2 (needs activator protein) → GM2 accumulates; diagnosis: ACTIVATOR PROTEIN assay; not detectable by routine enzyme assay (both enzymes appear normal!). NBS for Tay-Sachs: dried blood spot HexA enzyme activity assay (classic); molecular genotyping (three common Ashkenazi mutations: HEXA c.1278insTATC [+4 insertion], c.1421+1G>C IVS12, Gly269Ser); NBS expanding (DNA-based or enzyme-based); carrier screening: ACOG recommends carrier screening for Ashkenazi Jewish couples.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A muscle biopsy from a patient with exercise intolerance shows abnormal mitochondria on electron microscopy and ragged-red fibers with modified Gomori trichrome stain. Genetic testing reveals a deletion in mitochondrial DNA. This disease is classified as:
options: Autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT): CMT is a hereditary peripheral neuropathy from nuclear-encoded gene mutations (PMP22, MPZ, MFN2, GJB1/Cx32); not a mitochondrial DNA disorder; CMT presents with slowly progressive distal muscle weakness + pes cavus + stocking-glove sensory loss
