A storage disease due to enzyme deficiency (storage diseases like Pompe, Gaucher, Krabbe involve lysosomal enzyme deficiencies; they present with organomegaly + skeletal changes; ragged-red fibers + mtDNA deletion indicate primary mitochondrial disease)

A primary mitochondrial disease (mitochondrial myopathy): ragged-red fibers (RRF) on modified Gomori trichrome stain (MGT): caused by proliferation/accumulation of abnormal mitochondria in the subsarcolemmal region → appear as 'ragged red' edges under MGT (mitochondria stain red with MGT; massive subsarcolemmal aggregation → red ragged appearance); COX (cytochrome c oxidase/Complex IV) staining: COX-negative fibers (blue SDH staining against COX-negative background) → characteristic mosaic pattern (some fibers COX-positive [contain normal mtDNA] and some COX-negative [contain only deleted mtDNA]); mitochondrial DNA deletions: most common = 4977 bp 'common deletion' (between two 13-bp direct repeats in mtDNA → intramolecular homologous recombination → deletion of between ND4 to ATP8 region); KSS (Kearns-Sayre syndrome): single large mtDNA deletion + RRF + PIEOplus: progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO: ptosis + ophthalmoplegia) + pigmentary retinopathy + cardiac conduction block (AV block → sudden death) + ataxia + onset < 20 years; Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome (same deletion in early life/severe form): refractory sideroblastic anemia + exocrine pancreatic dysfunction + ring sideroblasts; survivor → may develop KSS; CPEO (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, single or multiple mtDNA deletions): ptosis + ophthalmoplegia; milder than KSS; often sporadic (single large deletion) or autosomal dominant (POLG, TWNK, SLC25A4 mutations → nuclear gene-driven multiple mtDNA deletions); inheritance: single large deletions: usually sporadic (not maternally inherited); MtDNA point mutations: maternally inherited (MELAS → MT-TL1 m.3243A>G; MERRF → MT-TK m.8344A>G); nuclear genes causing secondary mtDNA instability: maternally, AD, or AR

An autoimmune inflammatory myositis (inflammatory myopathies [dermatomyositis, polymyositis, IBM] show inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy; anti-ARS antibodies, anti-MDA5, anti-Mi-2 etc.; NOT ragged-red fibers or mtDNA deletions)
explanation: Mitochondrial diseases — inheritance and clinical: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke-like episodes): MT-TL1 gene → m.3243A>G mutation (>80%); tRNALeu(UUR) → impaired mitochondrial translation → ↓all mtDNA-encoded proteins → ↓ETC → ↑lactic acid + ↑stroke-like episodes (vascular endothelium mitochondria fail → vasogenic edema); MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers): MT-TK → m.8344A>G; ↓tRNALys → myoclonus + epilepsy + ataxia + RRF + ↑lactic acid; NARP (neurogenic weakness, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa): ATP6 gene m.8993T>G or T>C; LHON (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy): MT-ND4 (m.11778G>A, most common, ~70%), MT-ND1, MT-ND6 → complex I subunit mutations → ROS + complex I assembly failure → retinal ganglion cell degeneration → painless bilateral central vision loss in young males (12-30 years; 80-85% males affected vs. 10-15% females; maternal inheritance + male preponderance due to incomplete penetrance + gender modification); MtDNA heteroplasmy: each cell has 100-10,000 mtDNA copies; if mixture of mutant + wild-type mtDNA → heteroplasmy; threshold effect: usually >60-80% mutant mtDNA needed for biochemical defect; >85-90% for clinical disease; heteroplasmy varies between tissues (mtDNA segregates randomly during cell division); maternal inheritance: all mitochondria come from oocyte (paternal sperm mitochondria are ubiquitinated + degraded in early embryo); exceptions: VERY rare cases of paternal mtDNA inheritance (3 families reported) — evidence of mtDNA integrity gatekeeping failure. Nuclear genes encoding mitochondrial proteins: POLG (mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ) mutations → CPEO + ataxia + peripheral neuropathy + Alpers syndrome; TWNK (twinkle helicase) → KSS/CPEO; SURF1 → Leigh syndrome; SCO1/2 → COX deficiency; BCS1L → GRACILE.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: ADP-ribosylation by bacterial toxins is a virulence mechanism. Cholera toxin (CT) ADP-ribosylates Gsα, while pertussis toxin (PT) ADP-ribosylates Giα. What is the NET effect of CT on intestinal cAMP levels?
options: Decreased cAMP (↓cAMP is the effect of Giα stimulation; cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα to LOCK it in the active state → INCREASES cAMP, not decreases)
Unchanged cAMP (CT ADP-ribosylation permanently activates Gsα → cAMP ↑; not unchanged)

Increased cAMP leading to massive chloride secretion and watery diarrhea: CT (from Vibrio cholerae O1 and O139): AB5 toxin (one A subunit + 5 B subunits; B ring binds GM1 ganglioside on intestinal epithelial cells → endocytosis → retrograde transport to ER → ERAD machinery → A subunit enters cytosol as A1 fragment [active] + A2 fragment [connects to B]); CT-A1 subunit: ADP-ribosyl transferase: uses NAD+ → ADP-ribose → transferred to Arg201 of Gsα; ADP-ribosylation of Arg201 → INHIBITS intrinsic GTPase activity of Gsα → Gsα CANNOT hydrolyze GTP → Gsα REMAINS IN ACTIVE GTP-BOUND STATE → CONSTITUTIVE ACTIVATION of adenylyl cyclase → PERSISTENT ↑cAMP; in intestinal crypts (specifically): ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, ABCC7) → CFTR Cl- channel opens → Cl- secretion into lumen → Na+ follows (paracellular) → water follows osmotically → massive watery diarrhea ('rice water stools'); also: inhibits NHE3 (Na+/H+ exchanger 3) + NHE8 via PKA → ↓Na+ absorption + ↑H+ secretion → acidic loose stool; net: ↑secretion + ↓absorption → up to 20 liters of watery diarrhea/day → fatal dehydration + hypokalemia + metabolic acidosis; treatment: oral rehydration therapy (ORT: Na+ + K+ + Cl- + bicarbonate + glucose [glucose stimulates Na+ co-absorption via SGLT1, which is CFTR-independent and not directly affected by CT] → replaces losses); PT (pertussis toxin, Bordetella pertussis): ADP-ribosylates Cys351 of Giα → Giα CANNOT couple to receptor → Giα LOCKED IN INACTIVE GDP-BOUND STATE → cannot inhibit adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP in lymphocytes/macrophages → ↑histamine sensitization + ↑lymphocyte chemotaxis → whooping cough pathogenesis
No clinical effect, as intestinal cells lack Gsα (intestinal cells DO express Gsα; the G-protein signaling cascade in intestinal epithelium drives electrolyte/fluid secretion)
explanation: Bacterial toxin ADP-ribosylation targets: Toxin → Target → Effect → Disease: Cholera toxin (CT): Gsα Arg201 → GTPase blocked → constitutive AC activation → ↑cAMP → CFTR Cl- secretion → watery diarrhea. Pertussis toxin (PT): Giα Cys351 → cannot couple to receptor → ↑cAMP in immune cells + ↑lymphocytosis (T+B lymphocytes fail to recirculate to lymph nodes due to impaired Gi-coupled chemokine receptor function) → whooping cough. Anthrax toxin lethal factor (LF): MAPKK (MEK) Zn-metalloprotease cleavage → ↓MAPK signaling → ↓TNF-α + IL-12 → immune evasion + macrophage death; Anthrax toxin EF (edema factor): calmodulin-dependent adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → edema. E. coli heat-labile toxin (LT): same mechanism as CT (Gsα Arg201 ADP-ribosylation → ↑cAMP); heat-stable toxin (ST): activates guanylyl cyclase C (GC-C, GUCY2C) on intestinal cells → ↑cGMP → ↑cGMP-dependent protein kinase → ↑CFTR activity → Cl- secretion → watery diarrhea; linaclotide + plecanatide (drugs): GC-C agonist peptides → ↑cGMP → CFTR → ↑intestinal secretion → treat constipation (IBS-C, CIC). Pseudomonas exotoxin A + Diphtheria toxin: ADP-ribosylate EF-2 (eukaryotic elongation factor 2) → block protein synthesis → cell death; anthrax EF: calmodulin-activated adenylyl cyclase → supraphysiological cAMP → edema + immune suppression; E. coli CDT (cytolethal distending toxin): DNase activity → DNA damage + G2 arrest. CFTR as drug target: ivacaftor (VX-770): CFTR potentiator → opens CFTR channels that are at PM but gating-defective (class III mutation: G551D → ivacaftor approved); lumacaftor/tezacaftor/elexacaftor: CFTR correctors → increase folding/trafficking of misfolded CFTR (class II: ΔF508 → misfolded → trapped in ER → ↓surface CFTR) → cell surface expression + potentiation by ivacaftor; triple therapy (Trikafta: elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor) → most effective for ΔF508 (most common CF mutation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 40-year-old woman with a BRCA2 mutation-associated breast cancer receives olaparib, a PARP inhibitor. The mechanism of olaparib's anti-tumor selectivity for BRCA2-deficient cells involves:
options: Olaparib directly activates caspase-3, causing apoptosis specifically in cells with BRCA2 mutations (olaparib does NOT directly activate caspases; it works through DNA damage repair pathway dysfunction; no specific caspase-3 activation mechanism is involved directly)

Synthetic lethality: BRCA2-deficient tumor cells cannot repair DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination; olaparib blocks PARP-mediated repair of single-strand breaks → SSBs accumulate → become DSBs at replication forks → BRCA2-deficient cells cannot repair by HR → accumulation of lethal DSBs → selective tumor cell death: MECHANISM: PARP (poly-ADP ribose polymerase, specifically PARP1 + PARP2): detects single-strand DNA breaks (SSBs) → binds SSBs → auto-PARylation (PARP1 adds PAR [poly-ADP ribose] chains onto itself + histones nearby) → recruits BER (base excision repair) factors + XRCC1 + Pol β → SSB repaired + PARP1 released; olaparib (and rucaparib, niraparib, talazoparib): inhibit both PARP1 enzymatic activity AND TRAP PARP1 on DNA (PARP trapping = PARP1 stays bound to SSB → physically blocks DNA replication fork → 'PARP trapping cytotoxicity' is MORE IMPORTANT than simple inhibition of PARylation for anti-tumor effect; different PARPi have different trapping potency: talazoparib > rucaparib ≈ niraparib > olaparib > veliparib [weakest]); when fork reaches trapped PARP1 → fork collapse → DSB; in BRCA1/2-proficient cells: DSBs repaired by HR (BRCA2 loads RAD51 onto ssDNA → strand invasion into sister chromatid → accurate repair) → cell survives; in BRCA1/2-deficient tumor cells: HR non-functional → DSBs can only be repaired by error-prone NHEJ (if at all) → unrepaired DSBs → cell death (mitotic catastrophe, apoptosis) → selective killing of BRCA-deficient tumor cells; SYNTHETIC LETHALITY: two gene defects that are individually tolerated but lethal in combination; here: defect 1 = BRCA1/2 mutation (already in the tumor); defect 2 = PARP inhibition (added by drug); combination = lethal specifically in tumor cells; CLINICAL APPLICATIONS of PARPi: BRCA1/2-mutated breast + ovarian cancer; HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer with gBRCA1/2 mutations (olaparib, talazoparib); BRCA1/2-mutated ovarian cancer (maintenance therapy after platinum response); also: BRCAness (tumors with defects in other HR genes: RAD51C/D, BRIP1, PALB2, CDK12 → may respond to PARPi); homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) assays (Myriad myChoice CDx, FoundationOne Liquid CDx) → measure genomic scars (loss of heterozygosity, telomeric allelic imbalance, large-scale state transitions) → predict PARPi benefit even without BRCA mutation

Olaparib blocks topoisomerase II, causing DNA double-strand breaks that can only be repaired if BRCA2 is functional (olaparib inhibits PARP, not topoisomerase II; topoisomerase II is inhibited by doxorubicin/etoposide; the mechanism described is not how PARPi work)

Olaparib inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, depleting dNTP pools and causing replication fork stalling in BRCA2-deficient cells (ribonucleotide reductase is inhibited by hydroxyurea; olaparib does not affect dNTP pools; this is not the mechanism)
explanation: PARP biology and DNA repair: PARP superfamily: 17 members (PARP1-4, tankyrase 1/2, TNKS/TNKS2, etc.); PARP1 (main): 1014 aa; 3 functional domains: N-terminal zinc fingers (BRCT-like, DNA-binding), WGR domain (recognizes broken DNA ends), PARP catalytic domain (NAD+ binding → PAR synthesis using NAD+ as ADP-ribose donor; releasing nicotinamide); PARP2: similar to PARP1 but shorter; less important. PAR (poly-ADP ribose) signaling: PAR chains (homopolymers of ADP-ribose units via 1''→2' ribose-ribose O-glycosidic bonds) → attached to glutamate/aspartate/Lys/Ser on target proteins including PARP1 itself (auto-PARylation) → recruits repair factors (XRCC1, LIG3, Pol β, PAR-binding proteins: FHA-BRCT domains, WWE domains, OB-fold, macrodomains) → repair SSB → PARG (poly-ADP ribose glycohydrolase) degrades PAR → releases ADP-ribose; PARP1 TRAPPING: PARPi competitive with NAD+ at catalytic domain → but also traps PARP1 at DNA lesions (normally PARylation → PARP1 dissociates from DNA; PARPi prevents PARylation → PARP1 electrostatically attracted to DNA via zinc fingers + cannot dissociate → physical barrier); ARTD1/2 (alternative nomenclature for PARP1/2). BRCAness: HR deficiency signature: tumors with HR defects (BRCA1/2 + PALB2 + RAD51C/D + CDK12 mutations [CDK12 inactivation → acquired tandem duplications → HR deficiency in prostate cancer]) → HRD score [genomic instability score from LST + LOH + TAI] → HRD-high tumors → predict benefit from PARPi + platinum chemotherapy. FDA-approved PARPi indications: Olaparib (Lynparza): gBRCA1/2 HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer (2018); BRCA1/2-mutated advanced ovarian cancer maintenance (HRD-positive, 2017); gBRCA1/2 prostate cancer (2020); BRCA1/2 early-stage breast cancer adjuvant (2022). Niraparib (Zejula): first-line maintenance HRD-positive ovarian cancer (regardless of BRCA). Rucaparib (Rubraca): BRCA1/2 ovarian cancer. Talazoparib (Talzenna): gBRCA1/2 HER2-neg metastatic breast cancer.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Xanthine oxidase (XO) is the enzyme responsible for the final two steps of purine catabolism. Which of the following pairs correctly describes the substrates and products of XO-catalyzed reactions?
options: Adenosine → inosine + IMP (adenosine deaminase [ADA] converts adenosine → inosine; PNP converts inosine → hypoxanthine; these are XO substrates [hypoxanthine, xanthine] not adenosine)

Hypoxanthine → xanthine, and xanthine → uric acid: XO (xanthine oxidase, XDH gene, also called xanthine dehydrogenase [XDH] in NAD+-dependent form; XO is the O2-dependent form released by proteolysis or oxidation of XDH): catalyzes: (1) hypoxanthine + O2 + H2O → xanthine + H2O2 (+ O2•-); (2) xanthine + O2 + H2O → uric acid + H2O2 (+ O2•-); XO uses molybdenum (Mo cofactor, MoCo) + iron-sulfur clusters (2× [2Fe-2S]) + FAD; the reaction generates BOTH H2O2 and O2•- (superoxide anion radical) → important source of reactive oxygen species (ROS) after ischemia-reperfusion injury (I/R injury): during ischemia: hypoxanthine + xanthine accumulate (from ATP breakdown); XDH (dehydrogenase form) converts to XO form (oxidase form) by oxidation of sulfhydryl groups + limited proteolysis; upon reperfusion: O2 available → XO reacts with hypoxanthine/xanthine + O2 → burst of ROS (H2O2, O2•-) → tissue damage; XO inhibitors: allopurinol (hypoxanthine analog → converted to alloxanthine/oxypurinol by XO → alloxanthine tightly binds Mo at XO active site → suicide inhibitor [mechanism-based inhibitor]); febuxostat (Uloric): non-purine XO inhibitor → binds Mo channel; rasburicase: recombinant urate oxidase → converts uric acid → allantoin + H2O2 (allantoin is more soluble → used to prevent tumor lysis syndrome-associated hyperuricemia in children + adults; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency [H2O2 produced → hemolysis in absence of G6PD])
AMP → ADP → ATP (this is the adenylate kinase or ATP synthase reaction, not XO)

Guanine → xanthine only (guanine → guanosine → hypoxanthine or guanine → guanine [by HGPRT salvage] → xanthine [by guanine deaminase → xanthine] → uric acid [by XO]; XO catalyzes the last two steps [hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid])
explanation: Purine catabolism pathway: AMP → [AMP deaminase] → IMP + NH3; AMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → adenosine → [ADA, adenosine deaminase] → inosine; inosine → [PNP, purine nucleoside phosphorylase] → hypoxanthine + ribose-1-P; GMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → guanosine → [PNP] → guanine + ribose-1-P; guanine → [guanine deaminase/guanase] → xanthine; hypoxanthine → [XO] → xanthine; xanthine → [XO] → uric acid (end product in humans, primates, birds; excreted in urine); note: most mammals have uricase → allantoin (more soluble) → allantoate → glyoxylate + urea (fish). ADA deficiency: AR; SEVERE combined immunodeficiency (SCID): deoxyadenosine accumulates → dATP → inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) → ↓dNTP → ↓DNA synthesis in lymphocytes → ↓T cells (most affected) + ↓B cells + ↓NK cells; deoxyadenosine → SAH hydrolase inhibition → ↓SAM → ↓methylation; also deoxyadenosine → toxic to lymphocytes (lymphocytes high in 5'-nucleotidase activity normally, so ↑dATP accumulation); first gene therapy disease (1990, Ashanthi DeSilva); pegylated bovine ADA (pegademase, Adagen/PEG-ADA): ERT; gene therapy: ARSAAda (lentiviral delivery) approved; ADA-SCID: only SCID without marked lymphopenia at birth → becomes apparent at 6-12 weeks. PNP deficiency: AR; T-cell immunodeficiency with normal B cells (contrast ADA = T + B SCID); accumulation of dGuo (deoxyguanosine) → dGTP → ↓RNR specifically in T cells (high dGuo kinase in T cells); patients: recurrent viral + fungal infections; may develop autoimmune disease; not as severe as ADA-SCID. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency): X-linked; HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase; salvage enzyme: Hx + PRPP → IMP; Gua + PRPP → GMP) → absent/severely deficient; de novo purine synthesis ↑↑ (no feedback by salvage products) → ↑uric acid → gout + uric acid nephropathy; NEUROLOGICAL: self-mutilating behavior (lip/finger biting), choreoathetosis, intellectual disability, spasticity (unique feature).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) is an incretin hormone secreted by intestinal L-cells. Its main receptor (GLP-1R) signals via:
options: Gαi → ↓cAMP → ↓insulin secretion (GLP-1R signals via Gαs → INCREASES cAMP → INCREASES insulin secretion; Gαi would decrease cAMP and decrease insulin — opposite of GLP-1 effect)

Gαq → PLC → IP3/DAG → ↑Ca2+ → ↑glucagon secretion (Gαq/IP3 pathway raises Ca2+ and is used by some GPCRs; GLP-1R primarily signals via Gαs; also, GLP-1 INHIBITS glucagon secretion [inhibitory effect on α-cells], it does NOT increase it)

Gαs → ↑cAMP → PKA/Epac2 → ↑insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells and reduced glucagon from α-cells: GLP-1R is a class B GPCR (secretin family); mechanism: GLP-1 binds GLP-1R → Gαs activation → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA (phosphorylates + closes KATP channels, phosphorylates + activates exocytosis machinery) AND Epac2 (exchange protein activated by cAMP 2 / RAPGEF4) → ↑insulin secretion; cAMP also directly modulates KATP channel gating and Ca2+ channels (VDCC); GLUCOSE-DEPENDENT: GLP-1 only potentiates insulin secretion when glucose is elevated (requires concurrent glucose-stimulated insulin secretion [GSIS] → GLP-1 alone at normoglycemia causes little insulin release → low risk of hypoglycemia); GLP-1 effects: ↑insulin secretion (glucose-dependent) + ↑insulin gene expression (PDX-1 upregulation) + ↑β-cell mass (↑proliferation + ↓apoptosis of β-cells) + ↓glucagon secretion (direct α-cell effect via GLP-1R + indirect via SST) + ↓gastric emptying (extends time of nutrient absorption → postprandial glucose spike) + ↑satiety (central + peripheral effect → ↓appetite → weight loss); drugs: GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA): exenatide (Byetta: twice daily; Bydureon: once weekly; derived from exendin-4 from Gila monster saliva; 53% homology with human GLP-1 but resistant to DPP-4 degradation); liraglutide (Victoza [T2D], Saxenda [obesity]): C16 fatty acid linked → albumin binding → ↑half-life; once daily; semaglutide (Ozempic [T2D], Wegovy [obesity]: once weekly SC; Rybelsus: oral); tirzepatide: dual GIP/GLP-1 RA (GIP = glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide; both incretins); retatrutide: triple GIP/GLP-1/glucagon RA; DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins): sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin → inhibit DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase 4 → degrades GLP-1 N-terminal His-Ala → inactive within 2 min in blood) → ↑active GLP-1 + GIP → ↑insulin
Tyrosine kinase receptor autophosphorylation → IRS-1 → PI3K (this is the insulin receptor [IR/InsR] signaling mechanism, not GLP-1R; GLP-1R is a GPCR coupled to Gαs)
explanation: Incretin physiology: Incretins defined: gut-derived hormones that AMPLIFY glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) beyond what the glucose level alone would cause; this explains the INCRETIN EFFECT: oral glucose → ↑insulin secretion 2-3× more than equivalent IV glucose (bypasses gut-derived incretin release with IV glucose); GLP-1: proglucagon gene (GCG) product processed by PC1/3 in L-cells (ileum/colon, distal) → GLP-1(7-36)NH2 (active) + GLP-2 (intestinotrophic); secreted upon nutrient (fat + carbohydrate + protein) entering the intestine; t1/2 in blood ~2 min (rapidly degraded by DPP-4 enzyme [CD26, expressed on endothelial cells, T cells, etc.] which cleaves the N-terminal His-Ala dipeptide → inactive GLP-1(9-36)); GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide): proglucagon-independent; K-cells (duodenum/proximal jejunum) → GIP secretion → GIPR (Gαs/cAMP in β-cells + fat cells); GIP ↑adipogenesis + fat storage; GLP-1 vs GIP differences: GLP-1: strong insulin + glucagon suppression + central satiety + ↓gastric emptying; GIP: weaker glucagon suppression; GIPR also on fat cells → ↑fat storage (but in high GLP-1 context → ↓net adiposity due to ↓intake); high GIP seen in obesity → but GIP receptor in brain also linked to satiety when combined with GLP-1 (dual GIP/GLP-1 agonism [tirzepatide] → more weight loss than GLP-1 alone); Gut-brain axis: GLP-1R in vagal afferents → NTS (nucleus tractus solitarius) → satiety/nausea signal; hypothalamic GLP-1R → ARC → appetite suppression; area postrema GLP-1R → nausea/vomiting (side effect of GLP-1 RA especially at high doses); GLP-2 (also from PC1/3 in L-cells): intestinotrophic: ↑intestinal mucosal growth → ↑nutrient absorption; GLP-2R (also Gαs/cAMP); teduglutide (GLP-2 analog) → ↓parenteral nutrition dependence in short bowel syndrome (SBS).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In adipose tissue, adiponectin exerts its metabolic effects primarily through which receptor and signaling pathway?
options: Leptin receptor (Ob-R) → JAK2-STAT3 pathway (leptin, NOT adiponectin, signals via Ob-R/LepR; JAK2-STAT3 is activated by leptin to suppress appetite via hypothalamic POMC neurons; adiponectin uses AdipoR1/R2, not Ob-R)

Insulin receptor (IR) → PI3K-Akt (insulin signals via IR tyrosine kinase → PI3K → Akt; while adiponectin has insulin-sensitizing effects, it does NOT directly activate the insulin receptor; it signals via AdipoR1/R2 → AMPK/PPARα)

AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 → AMPK activation (↑fatty acid oxidation, ↑glucose uptake) and PPARα activation (↑FAO gene transcription): adiponectin (also called AdipoQ, Acrp30, ApM1): secreted exclusively by white adipocytes; exists as low-MW (trimer), medium-MW (hexamer), high-MW (HMW, 18-mer) multimers; HMW form: most biologically active; ↓adiponectin in obesity (PARADOX: adipose tissue produces adiponectin but ↓in obesity; due to ↑TNF-α + ↑FFA → ↓adiponectin secretion; ↓adiponectin = independent risk factor for T2D + CVD); adiponectin receptors: AdipoR1 (high affinity for globular adiponectin; expressed in muscle, liver, brain) + AdipoR2 (high affinity for full-length adiponectin; expressed in liver > muscle); both AdipoR1 + AdipoR2 are 7-TM proteins but NOT classic GPCRs (they are zinc-binding proteins [ceramidase activity: cleave ceramide → sphingosine + FA]); T-cadherin (CDH13) is also an adiponectin receptor (HMW form; expressed in heart/muscle; adiponectin protective effect on heart partly via T-cadherin); signaling: AdipoR1/R2 → AMPK activation (through LKB1-dependent phosphorylation of AMPK-α Thr172) → ↑ACC phosphorylation (↓malonyl-CoA) → ↑FAO + ↑CPT1; AdipoR2 → PPARα activation (↑FAO gene expression [ACOX, LCAD, etc.]) → adiponectin also: ↑GLUT4 translocation → ↑glucose uptake; ↑insulin sensitivity; ↓hepatic gluconeogenesis (↓PEPCK, ↓G6Pase); ↓ceramide levels (AdipoR ceramidase activity → ↓ceramide → less lipotoxicity); anti-inflammatory: ↓NF-κB → ↓TNF-α, ↓IL-6; cardiovascular: ↑NO production (via AMPK → eNOS) → vasodilation; anti-atherogenic; adiponectin knockout mice → ↑insulin resistance + ↑diet-induced atherosclerosis
GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) → cAMP → PKA (GLP-1R is activated by GLP-1 from intestinal L-cells; adiponectin acts on AdipoR1/R2, not GLP-1R)
explanation: Adipokines — comparative: White adipose tissue (WAT) secretes adipokines (adipose-derived cytokines/hormones): Pro-inflammatory/insulin-resistant (obesity-associated, ↑in obesity): Leptin: encoded by OB gene; promotes satiety (hypothalamic LepR → JAK2-STAT3 → ↑POMC/CART [anorexigenic] + ↓NPY/AgRP [orexigenic]); congenital leptin deficiency (ob/ob mouse) → morbid obesity + ↓reproduction + ↓immunity; leptin deficiency in humans (mutations in LEP or LEPR) → severe early-onset obesity (treat with recombinant metreleptin); leptin resistance in diet-induced obesity → high leptin but ↓CNS response; Resistin (RETN): mainly macrophage-derived in humans; ↑insulin resistance; ↓adiponectin expression; ↑in T2D, obesity, CVD; Visfatin (PBEF1/NAMPT): also called extracellular NAMPT (eNAMPT); intracellular NAMPT (iNAMPT) = rate-limiting enzyme in NAD+ salvage (NMN synthesis); eNAMPT → acts as NMK2 cytokine; ↑in obesity + T2D + inflammation; plasma NAMPT/visfatin correlates with obesity + CVD risk; RBP4 (retinol-binding protein 4): secreted by adipocytes + liver; ↑in obesity + insulin resistance; impairs glucose uptake in muscle; Chemerin (RARRES2): attracts DCs + macrophages to adipose tissue; ↑in obesity + MetS; PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor 1): ↑in obesity + insulin resistance → ↑thrombosis risk (PAI-1 inhibits tPA + uPA → ↓fibrinolysis). Anti-inflammatory/insulin-sensitizing (↓in obesity): Adiponectin: see above. Omentin-1 (ITLN1): ↑insulin sensitivity; ↓in obesity; secreted by visceral adipose tissue (VAT) stromal vascular fraction; ↑in lean individuals. FGF21 (fibroblast growth factor 21): PPARα-induced, hepatic + adipose; ↑FAO + ↑ketogenesis; ↑in obesity and alcoholic fatty liver (compensatory); pharmacological FGF21 → ↑insulin sensitivity + ↓TG; Adipsin (CFD, complement factor D): alternative complement pathway; ↓in obesity.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the ER with an acute hemolytic crisis after eating fava beans. The diagnosis of G6PD deficiency is suspected. Which pathway does G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) serve, and what is its critical product?
options: G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, producing ATP and NADH (G6PD is NOT in glycolysis; it is the first enzyme of the PENTOSE PHOSPHATE PATHWAY [PPP]; its product is NADPH [not NADH] and 6-phosphogluconolactone)

G6PD catalyzes the first committed step of glycogenesis, producing UDP-glucose (UDP-glucose is produced by UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase [UGP2] from glucose-1-phosphate; G6PD is in the PPP, not glycogenesis)

G6PD catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), producing NADPH and 6-phosphogluconolactone from glucose-6-phosphate: G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase): G6P + NADP+ → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH + H+; NADP+-dependent (NADPH produced, not NADH); first and RATE-LIMITING step of PPP; committed to PPP (6-phosphogluconolactone is not a substrate of glycolysis or any other major pathway); product NADPH is critical for: (1) GLUTATHIONE REDUCTASE: 2 GSH (reduced glutathione) regenerated from GSSG (oxidized glutathione) using NADPH → reduced GSH detoxifies H2O2 (via GPX, glutathione peroxidase: 2 GSH + H2O2 → GSSG + 2H2O) and eliminates peroxidized lipids → RBC protection; (2) CYTOCHROME P450 (CYP) reactions (hepatic oxidative metabolism); (3) NADPH oxidase (NOX2 in neutrophils/macrophages → O2•- → respiratory burst → kill bacteria); (4) fatty acid synthesis (FAS system uses NADPH); (5) cholesterol synthesis (HMG-CoA reductase uses NADPH); G6PD deficiency: X-linked recessive; most common enzyme deficiency worldwide (~400 million affected); >200 variants; common variants: G6PD Mediterranean (Ser188Phe in exon 6) → severe; G6PD A- (African; Asn126Asp [in exon 4] + Val68Met in exon 2) → mild-moderate; G6PD Canton (Arg459Leu, common in Southeast Asia) → moderate-severe; class I (severe, <1% residual activity, chronic HNSHA [hemolytic non-spherocytic anemia]), class II (<10%, acute/episodic hemolysis), class III (10-60%, generally asymptomatic unless triggered); triggers of hemolytic crisis: oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, phenazopyridine), infections, fava beans (favism): vicine + convicine → divicine + isouramil (powerful oxidants → oxidize glutathione → Heinz bodies [denatured Hb] → intravascular hemolysis); diagnosis: Fluorescent spot test (G6PD activity assay): NADPH fluoresces under UV light; ↓fluorescence = G6PD deficiency; do NOT test during acute hemolytic episode (young RBCs [reticulocytes] have higher G6PD activity → false-normal result during crisis); test 2-3 months after episode; laboratory features: Heinz bodies on crystal violet stain + bite cells on peripheral smear (splenic macrophages bite off Heinz body-containing RBC membrane) + ↑LDH + ↑bilirubin + ↓haptoglobin + hemoglobinuria (hemoglobinuria → 'cola-colored urine')
G6PD generates GTP used in the TCA cycle for energy production (G6PD is not in TCA; GTP is produced by succinyl-CoA synthetase in TCA; G6PD produces NADPH not GTP; completely different pathways)
explanation: Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) — complete: Oxidative phase (irreversible): G6P + NADP+ → [G6PD] → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH; 6-PGL + H2O → [6-phosphogluconolactonase/PGLS] → 6-phosphogluconate; 6-PG + NADP+ → [6PGD] → ribulose-5-P + CO2 + NADPH; net (oxidative): G6P + 2 NADP+ → Rib5P + CO2 + 2 NADPH; Non-oxidative phase (reversible, TKT + TAL): rearrangement of pentose phosphates → glycolytic intermediates (F6P, G3P) via transketolase (TKT, uses TPP/thiamine) + transaldolase (TAL); TKT is a thiamine-status marker (↓thiamine → ↓TKT activity → ↑erythrocyte TKT activity ratio [ETKR] > 1.25 = B1 deficiency). PPP products: NADPH (anabolic reductions + antioxidant), ribose-5-P (nucleotide + histidine synthesis), PRPP (phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate, purine/pyrimidine synthesis), glycolytic intermediates (F6P, G3P). Differential production: cell needs NADPH > ribose: flux goes oxidative → non-oxidative → F6P + G3P re-enter glycolysis; cell needs BOTH: oxidative phase only (Rib5P + NADPH); cell needs ribose only: reverse non-oxidative phase; Metabolic diseases of PPP: G6PD deficiency: above; 6-PGD deficiency: rare; hemolytic anemia; Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase deficiency: extremely rare; progressive leukoencephalopathy; transaldolase deficiency: liver fibrosis + cirrhosis in childhood + multi-organ involvement.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs: leucine, isoleucine, valine) are unique among essential amino acids because they are primarily catabolized in which tissue?
options: Liver (most amino acids are predominantly catabolized in the liver [hepatic first-pass removal]; however, BCAAs are an EXCEPTION: liver has VERY LOW BCAT activity [branched-chain aminotransferase] → BCAAs pass through liver relatively unmodified → catabolized in extra-hepatic tissues)
Kidney (the kidney does catabolize some amino acids [especially Gln → NH4+ for urinary acid excretion] but it is NOT the primary site of BCAA catabolism; skeletal muscle is the dominant site)

Skeletal muscle (and to a lesser extent brain and adipose): BCAA catabolism: the first step [transamination] is catalyzed by BCAT (branched-chain aminotransferase): BCAT1 (cytoplasmic, in brain, testis, ovary) + BCAT2 (mitochondrial, in muscle, adipose, kidney, brain) → Leu/Ile/Val + α-KG → α-KIC/α-KMV/α-KIV (branched-chain α-keto acids, BCKA) + Glu; then: BCKA dehydrogenase (BCKDH complex [rate-limiting], mitochondrial): analogous to PDC and OGDH complex: E1α/E1β (decarboxylase, TPP) + E2 (transacylase, lipoic acid) + E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase [DLD], same as in PDC and OGDH); product: Leu → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetyl-CoA (KETOGENIC ONLY); Ile → acetyl-CoA + succinyl-CoA (both ketogenic + glucogenic); Val → succinyl-CoA (GLUCOGENIC ONLY); WHY muscle is the primary site: BCAT2 highly expressed in muscle (HIGH BCAT2 activity in skeletal muscle); liver has very low BCAT activity; during exercise: BCAA from muscle protein → transamination → Glu → (with pyruvate via ALT) → Ala → Ala-glucose cycle to liver; also: Glu + NH4+ → Gln → exported to liver + kidney; skeletal muscle as BCAA sensor: Leu → activates mTORC1 (via Sestrin-GATOR2-Ragulator → mTOR → S6K1 + 4E-BP1 → ↑protein synthesis) → muscle hypertrophy signal (leucine is the most potent mTORC1 activator among amino acids); maple syrup urine disease (MSUD): BCKDH deficiency → accumulation of BCKA (alloisoleucine pathognomonic) + BCAA; neurotoxicity; sweet maple syrup odor of urine; treatment: BCAA-restricted diet + thiamine (some thiamine-responsive MSUD); transplantation (liver restores BCKDH); classification: classic (BCKDH activity < 2%) + intermediate + intermittent + thiamine-responsive forms
Intestinal epithelium (while glutamine is the preferred fuel of enterocytes, BCAAs are not primarily catabolized there; skeletal muscle is the primary site)
explanation: BCAA metabolism and integration: Leu catabolism: Leu → α-KIC → [BCKDH] → isovaleryl-CoA → [IVD = isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase] → 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA → [MCCC1/2 + biotin] → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → acetyl-CoA + acetoacetate (KETOGENIC only; Leu is the only strictly ketogenic ESSENTIAL amino acid); IVD deficiency → isovaleric acidemia (IVA): ↑isovalerylcarnitine [C5] → 'sweaty feet' odor (isovaleric acid) → neonatal or episodic metabolic crisis; IVD deficiency → severe neonatal form or mild episodic. Val catabolism: Val → α-KIV → [BCKDH] → isobutyryl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → TCA (GLUCOGENIC only; Val is purely glucogenic). Ile catabolism: Ile → α-KMV → [BCKDH] → 2-methylbutyryl-CoA → propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA AND acetyl-CoA → both glucogenic + ketogenic. BCKDH complex regulation: BCKDH kinase (BCKDK): phosphorylates E1α (Ser293) → INACTIVATES BCKDH → prevents BCAA catabolism (BCKDK expression: ↑in fed state, ↑by BCAA; inhibited by BCKA); BCKDH phosphatase (PP2Cm, PPM1K): dephosphorylates E1α → ACTIVATES BCKDH; PP2Cm knockout → BCAA accumulate → impair cardiac function; BT2 (BDK inhibitor): BT2 inhibits BCKDK → ↑BCKDH activity → ↓plasma BCAA → tested in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) models. BCAA in disease: T2DM + obesity: ↑plasma BCAA associated with insulin resistance (BCAA → mTORC1 activation → inhibitory S6K1 phosphorylation of IRS-1 → insulin resistance; branched-chain acylcarnitines [C3: propionylcarnitine; C5: isovalerylcarnitine] accumulate → mitochondrial stress); Heart failure: ↑BCKA in heart (↓PP2Cm → impaired BCKDH → ↑BCKA → ↑oxidative stress; PP2Cm KO recapitulates heart failure features); supplementation: Leu/BCAA supplements → ↑muscle protein synthesis (mTORC1 activation); beneficial in sarcopenia, cirrhosis (↑BCAA:LNAA ratio to improve hepatic encephalopathy via competing with aromatic AA for BBB transport → ↓false neurotransmitters).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During nucleotide synthesis, the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) catalyzes the conversion of ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDP) to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDP). RNR is regulated by:
options: Feedback inhibition by ADP only (RNR is regulated by activity site + specificity sites; it is NOT regulated by ADP alone; the regulation is complex involving multiple effectors at distinct allosteric sites)

Allosteric regulation at two sites: an activity site (regulated by ATP/dATP) and a specificity site (regulated by ATP, dATP, dGTP, dTTP) that coordinate production of a balanced dNTP pool for DNA replication: RNR (ribonucleotide reductase, RRM1 [large subunit R1] + RRM2 [small subunit R2, class Ia] or RRM2B [p53R2, injury-inducible small subunit]): class I RNR (mammalian): (α2β2) R1 homodimer + R2 homodimer → active complex; R2 contains diferric iron cluster (Fe3+-O-Fe3+) + tyrosyl radical (Tyr122•) → stable radical required for catalysis; mechanism: generates thiyl radical on Cys439 of R1 → substrate radical → 2'-OH removal + H• from C3' → ribonucleotide → deoxyribonucleotide; two thioredoxin (Trx)/thioredoxin reductase (TrxR) mediated Cys pairs on R1 → oxidized after each turnover → regenerated by thioredoxin (TRX1 + TrxR1 → NADPH-dependent) or glutaredoxin (Grx → GSH-dependent); ACTIVITY SITE (A-site on R1): ATP → ACTIVATES; dATP → INACTIVATES (inhibits) → when dATP accumulates → RNR off → protects against over-production of dNTPs; SPECIFICITY SITE (S-site on R1): ATP or dATP → favors reduction of CDP + UDP (pyrimidine rNDPs); dTTP → favors reduction of GDP; dGTP → favors reduction of ADP; HEXAMERIZATION SITE (H-site): dATP binds → R1 hexamerizes → sequestrates R2 → complete RNR inhibition (eukaryotes have additional H-site-mediated inhibition); clinical: hydroxyurea (HU): inhibits RNR by scavenging tyrosyl radical on R2 (iron-chelating hydroxamic acid → Fe3+ reduction → loss of Tyr•) → ↓dNTP → ↓DNA synthesis → used in: SCD (↑HbF via ↓S-phase cell cycling → γ-globin gene reactivation [or ↑NO → ↑cGMP → HbF] → ↑HbF → ↓sickling); CML (before TKI era); polycythemia vera; essential thrombocythemia; gemcitabine → incorporated as dFdCTP into DNA → also inhibits RNR (dFdCDP competes at the catalytic site) → antimetabolite used in pancreatic/lung/bladder cancer; cladribine (2-CdA): deoxyadenosine analog → dCTP-analog → inhibits RNR; used in hairy cell leukemia

Competitive inhibition by CTP only at the active site (RNR is not inhibited by CTP; the regulation is by multiple dNTP effectors at distinct allosteric sites as described; CTP is a product of pyrimidine synthesis regulated by CPS II, not RNR)

Activation by dCTP and inhibition by dGTP (the specificity-site regulation is: dTTP inhibits/redirects toward GDP; dGTP redirects toward ADP; dATP at activity site inhibits; not 'dCTP activates'; these are incorrect assignments)
explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) — classes: Class I (aerobic; mammals, herpes viruses): iron-dependent tyrosyl radical; R1 (catalytic + allosteric sites) + R2 (Fe-Tyr•); mammalian isoforms: R2 (highly expressed in S-phase, cytoplasm, rapidly degraded in G1) vs. p53R2/RRM2B (constitutive, nuclear, supplies dNTPs for DNA repair in non-dividing cells; p53-induced → important for mitochondrial DNA maintenance [p53R2 KO → mtDNA depletion syndrome]; mutations → mtDNA depletion = Alpers syndrome/SANDO/PEO with myopathy]). Class II (anaerobic + aerobic; bacteria): adenosylcobalamin-dependent (AdoCbl → radical generation). Class III (anaerobic; bacteria): glycyl radical enzyme. RRM1 gene is located on chr 11p15; RRM2 is on chr 2p25; RRM2B on chr 8q22.3. Thymidylate synthesis (TS): dUMP + N5,N10-methylene-THF → [TS, TYMS] → dTMP + DHF; DHF → [DHFR + NADPH] → THF; critical link: 5-FU → fluorouracil → 5-FdUMP (active metabolite: FdUMP) → inhibits TS (binds TS + locks TS-FdUMP-5,10-methylene-THF ternary complex → no dTMP → ↓DNA synthesis); also: 5-FU → FUTP incorporated into RNA → disrupts mRNA processing; pemetrexed (ALIMTA): multitargeted antifolate → inhibits TS + DHFR + GARFT + AICARFT (multiple folate-dependent enzymes in purine synthesis) → used in mesothelioma + NSCLC non-squamous; leucovorin (5-formyl-THF): 'folinic acid rescue' after high-dose methotrexate (MTX; MTX inhibits DHFR → ↑DHF → trapped → ↓THF → ↓nucleotide synthesis → ↓rapidly dividing cells; leucovorin bypasses DHFR step → 'rescues' normal cells).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycine is considered a non-essential amino acid synthesized in the body. Its biosynthesis primarily involves which substrate and enzyme?
options: Alanine → pyruvate → [alanine transaminase] → glycine (ALT catalyzes Ala → pyruvate + Glu; pyruvate is not directly converted to glycine; this is not the primary glycine synthesis pathway)

Serine → glycine via serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT): Gly biosynthesis: Ser + THF → [SHMT, serine hydroxymethyltransferase, mitochondrial SHMT2 + cytoplasmic SHMT1] → Gly + N5,N10-methylene-THF; cofactor: pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6); this is the PRIMARY route of glycine synthesis in humans; SHMT2 (mitochondrial isoform) is more important metabolically: transfers the β-carbon of serine as one-carbon unit to THF → methylene-THF (N5,N10-CH2-THF), which enters folate-dependent one-carbon metabolism → used for: (a) dTMP synthesis (TS: dUMP + CH2-THF → dTMP); (b) purine synthesis (C2 and C8 come from formate/10-formyl-THF) + SHMT generates glycine from serine; glycine cleavage system (GCS, also in mitochondria): catabolizes glycine: Gly + NAD+ + THF → [GCS: P protein [pyridoxalphosphate, Gly decarboxylase] + H protein [lipoic acid] + T protein [THF-dependent] + L protein [FAD, dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase]] → CO2 + NH3 + N5,N10-methylene-THF + NADH; GCS is the primary Gly degradation pathway; GCS deficiency → non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH): glycine accumulates → activates NMDA receptors in CNS (Gly is obligatory co-agonist of NMDA receptor [binds GluN1 subunit co-agonist site]) → severe neonatal seizures + hypotonia + coma; P-protein gene GLDC mutations most common (>80% of NKH); T-protein gene AMT mutations; treatment: sodium benzoate (conjugates Gly → hippurate → excreted) + NMDA antagonists (dextromethorphan); glycine functions: non-essential AA, but 'conditionally essential' in rapidly growing children + cancer/critical illness; conjugates with bile acids (glycocholate, glycochenodeoxycholate) → bile salts; component of glutathione (γ-Glu-Cys-Gly); collagen (Gly-X-Y repeat, every 3rd residue is Gly → fits into triple helix); one-carbon donor via GCS; heme synthesis co-substrate (Gly + succinyl-CoA → [ALAS] → δ-ALA); synthesis of purines (C4 N3 C4a framework from Gly in de novo purine synthesis); creatine synthesis: Arg + Gly → [AGAT, in kidney] → guanidinoacetate + Orn → [GAMT + SAM, in liver] → creatine → exported to muscle + brain → creatine kinase → phosphocreatine

Glutamine → glutamate → [glutamate decarboxylase] → GABA, which is then converted to glycine (GAD [glutamate decarboxylase] converts Glu → GABA [γ-aminobutyric acid], not glycine; these are entirely different amino acids; GABA → succinate semialdehyde → succinate, not Gly)

Threonine → [threonine aldolase] → glycine + acetaldehyde: In some organisms (bacteria, yeast): threonine aldolase (ThrA): Thr → Gly + acetaldehyde; In humans, this pathway is MINOR (humans have low L-threonine aldolase activity); primary glycine biosynthesis in humans = SHMT pathway from serine; some dietary Thr → Gly but major pathway remains Ser via SHMT
explanation: Serine-glycine-one-carbon axis (SGOC): SGOC pathway fuels rapidly proliferating cells (cancer cells → high SHMT2 + PHGDH expression → serine synthesis + one-carbon transfer): Serine biosynthesis: 3-PG → [PHGDH, 3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase] → 3-phosphopyruvate → [PSAT1] → 3-phosphoserine → [PSPH] → serine; PHGDH gene amplified in breast cancer + melanoma; serine → SHMT → Gly + CH2-THF; SHMT2 in mitochondria; SHMT1 in cytoplasm; Gly → GCS (mitochondria) → CO2 + NH3 + CH2-THF + NADH; net: serine → 2 CH2-THF (one from SHMT, one from GCS) + CO2 + NH3 + NADH; this mitochondrial one-carbon export → cytoplasm (as formate via MTHFD2 → formate exports to cytoplasm → MTHFD1 → THF cycle → TS → dTMP + purine synthesis); cancer dependency: many cancer cells are serine-addicted (↑PHGDH → de novo serine synthesis; serine restriction → ↓one-carbon units → ↓dTMP + ↓purines → ↓proliferation); SSP (serine synthesis pathway) inhibitors are in preclinical development. Metabolic roles of glycine: Creatine synthesis: Arg + Gly → [AGAT/GATM, L-arginine:glycine amidinotransferase, primarily in kidney] → guanidinoacetate (GAA) + Orn; GAA → blood → liver → [GAMT, guanidinoacetate methyltransferase + SAM] → creatine; creatine → muscle/brain → phosphocreatine (PCr) [by creatine kinase, CK] → PCr + ADP → [CK] → Cr + ATP (fast energy buffer); GAMT deficiency: ↑GAA → GAA is neurotoxic → intellectual disability + epilepsy; ↓phosphocreatine; creatine supplement helps; AGAT deficiency: ↓GAA → ↓creatine → intellectual disability responds to creatine; SLC6A8 deficiency (creatine transporter): X-linked intellectual disability; brain cannot take up creatine (creatine does not cross BBB freely; depends on SLC6A8 CRTR); creatinine: Cr → spontaneous non-enzymatic cyclization → creatinine → excreted in urine (stable production rate → marker of GFR).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with uncontrolled type 1 diabetes presents with ketoacidosis. On an arterial blood gas, the pH is 7.1, HCO3- is 8 mEq/L, PCO2 is 20 mmHg, and the anion gap is 28 mEq/L. Regarding the biochemistry of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), the ketone bodies that accumulate include:
options: Acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA (acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA are acyl-CoA intermediates, not the ketone bodies released from liver into blood; ketone bodies are water-soluble and exported; acetyl-CoA is the precursor but not itself a ketone body)

Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate (3-hydroxybutyrate), and acetone: In DKA: insulin deficiency → ↑glucagon/insulin ratio → (1) ↑lipolysis in adipose (↑HSL) → FFA to liver → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA overwhelms TCA (low OAA [OAA used for gluconeogenesis]) → HMG-CoA pathway in mitochondria: acetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → [ACAT/thiolase] → acetoacetyl-CoA; acetoacetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → [HMGCS2 [mitochondrial]] → HMG-CoA; HMG-CoA → [HMGCL] → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; KETONE BODIES: (a) acetoacetate (AcAc): pKa ~3.8; loses H+ at physiological pH → anionic (negative charge → ↑anion gap); (b) β-hydroxybutyrate (3-OHB, 3HB): AcAc + NADH → [β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, BDH1, inner mitochondrial membrane] → 3-OHB + NAD+; in DKA: ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio → equilibrium shifted → more 3-OHB than AcAc; 3-OHB : AcAc ratio normally ~3:1, in DKA can be >10:1; (c) acetone: AcAc → [spontaneous decarboxylation] → acetone + CO2 (volatile → excreted via lungs → fruity breath of DKA; acetone NOT metabolized; excreted via lung + urine); diagnostic: urine ketones (nitroprusside test, Acetest): detects AcAc + acetone but NOT 3-OHB; severe DKA → ↑↑3-OHB → urine ketone test may underestimate severity; serum 3-OHB assay (blood ketone meters, RANBUT assay) > urine ketones for monitoring DKA severity; anion gap: AG = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-); normal 8-12 mEq/L; in this patient: if Na=138, Cl=102: AG = 138 - (102+8) = 28 → elevated (AcAc- + 3-OHB- are unmeasured anions → ↑AG); Winter's formula for expected PCO2: pCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3- + 8 ± 2 = 1.5 × 8 + 8 = 20 (matches actual PCO2 → appropriate respiratory compensation); treatment: IV fluids + insulin + K+ (⚠️ ↓K+ shifts into cells with insulin → ↓serum K+ → arrhythmia → check K+ before insulin) + glucose (if BG < 250 mg/dL → add dextrose to IV while continuing insulin to clear ketosis)
Citrate and succinate (citrate + succinate are TCA cycle intermediates, not ketone bodies; they are NOT released from liver as ketone bodies; the three ketone bodies are AcAc, 3-OHB, and acetone)
explanation: Ketone body utilization in peripheral tissues: Liver: PRODUCES ketones (has HMGCS2 + HMGCL) but CANNOT USE THEM (lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase [SCOT, OXCT1]); extrahepatic tissues (brain, heart, muscle, kidney): CONSUME ketones via: 3-OHB → [BDH1, extramitochondrial or BDH2] → AcAc; AcAc + succinyl-CoA → [SCOT/OXCT1] → AcAcCoA + succinate; AcAcCoA + CoA → [ACAT] → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA; SCOT is absent in liver → liver cannot consume its own ketones (no futile cycle). During prolonged fasting/starvation: brain adapts to use ketones: normally brain uses glucose exclusively; fasting > 3 days → ↑3-OHB + AcAc cross BBB → supply up to 60-70% of brain energy; residual glucose use by brain drops to ~30-40 g/day (from ~120 g/day) → spares protein catabolism; regulatory point: insulin → promotes glucose oxidation + inhibits ketogenesis; glucagon + insulin deficiency → promotes FAO + ketogenesis; malonyl-CoA as gatekeeper: in fed state → ↑insulin → ↑citrate → ↑ACLY → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑ACC → ↑malonyl-CoA → inhibits CPT1 → ↓FAO → ↓ketogenesis; fasting → AMPK → phospho-ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT1 activity → ↑FAO → ↑ketogenesis; HMGCS2 gene: regulated by PPAR-α (fasting) + FGF21 + glucagon → ↑HMGCS2 mRNA; also: SIRT3 deacetylates HMGCS2 → activates it (fasting → ↑NAD+ → SIRT3 active → HMGCS2 deacetylated + active). Alcoholic ketoacidosis: alcohol → ↑NADH/NAD+ → ↓gluconeogenesis → ↓acetyl-CoA oxidation → ↑ketogenesis (↑3-OHB predominantly due to ↑NADH → equilibrium → 3-OHB); not usually hyperglycemic (unlike DKA); + volume depletion → starvation → ↑FAO. Neonatal ketosis: normal neonates have ↑fatty acid mobilization + ↑ketogenesis after birth (colostrum is high fat) → physiological ketonemia (different from pathological ketoacidosis); ketone bodies are fuels for neonatal brain development.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A competitive inhibitor increases the Km of an enzyme but does NOT change Vmax. In a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot, competitive inhibition is recognized by:
options: Parallel lines shifted upward (an upward shift of parallel lines on a Lineweaver-Burk plot indicates NONCOMPETITIVE inhibition where both the slope and y-intercept change but the x-intercept remains the same → Vmax decreases, Km unchanged)

Lines with the same x-intercept (= −1/Km is CHANGED) and different y-intercepts: Hmm — I need to be more careful. Actually in competitive inhibition: apparent Km = Km × (1 + [I]/Ki) → INCREASED apparent Km; Vmax UNCHANGED; Lineweaver-Burk: y = Km/Vmax × x + 1/Vmax; competitive inhibition: slope = Km/Vmax × (1 + [I]/Ki) → INCREASED slope; y-intercept (1/Vmax) = UNCHANGED (same as without inhibitor); x-intercept = −1/Km(apparent) → CHANGED (closer to 0, less negative since Km ↑); So: competitive inhibition on Lineweaver-Burk = lines with SAME Y-INTERCEPT (1/Vmax unchanged) but DIFFERENT SLOPES and DIFFERENT X-INTERCEPTS (−1/apparent Km is different). The lines intersect at the y-axis (x=0 point = 1/Vmax; all lines share this point on y-axis; the x-intercepts differ). Wait, let me re-examine: on Lineweaver-Burk: y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = −1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax. Competitive inhibition: Vmax same → y-intercept same; Km increases → x-intercept moves toward 0 (less negative; −1/apparent Km is a smaller negative number when Km_app is larger); slope = Km_app/Vmax increases. So on the L-B plot: competitive inhibition lines intersect AT THE Y-AXIS (same y-intercept), with different slopes and different x-intercepts. This means 'same y-intercept, different slopes' → lines cross ON THE Y-AXIS.

Lines with the same y-intercept (1/Vmax) but different slopes and different x-intercepts, intersecting on the y-axis: Lineweaver-Burk (L-B) plot: double reciprocal plot: x-axis = 1/[S]; y-axis = 1/v; Michaelis-Menten: v = Vmax×[S]/(Km+[S]); reciprocal: 1/v = Km/Vmax × (1/[S]) + 1/Vmax; y = m×x + b, where m = Km/Vmax (slope) and b = 1/Vmax (y-intercept); competitive inhibition: Km_app = Km(1 + [I]/Ki) [Km increased]; Vmax_app = Vmax [unchanged]; 1/v = Km_app/Vmax × (1/[S]) + 1/Vmax; y-intercept (1/Vmax): SAME (no inhibitor line and inhibitor line share same y-intercept); slope (Km_app/Vmax): INCREASED (steeper line); x-intercept (−1/Km_app): CLOSER TO ZERO (less negative, since Km_app > Km); lines intersect ON THE Y-AXIS (x=0) → classic competitive inhibition pattern; examples: Malonate → SDH (succinate dehydrogenase); Methotrexate → DHFR; Statins → HMGCR; Sildenafil → PDE5; Allopurinol → XO; pure NONCOMPETITIVE: Vmax_app ↓; Km unchanged; lines intersect ON THE X-AXIS (same x-intercept, y-intercepts differ); UNCOMPETITIVE: Km_app ↓ and Vmax_app ↓ (both in same proportion); lines PARALLEL (same slope, different intercepts); MIXED: lines intersect neither on x-axis nor y-axis (at a point in 2nd quadrant typically)

A line with a lower y-intercept (= higher Vmax) and same slope (lower y-intercept → higher Vmax would mean the inhibitor INCREASES Vmax, which no classical inhibitor does; this is not a real inhibition pattern)
explanation: Enzyme kinetics — inhibition patterns on Lineweaver-Burk: Inhibition type → Km_app / Vmax_app → L-B graph features: Competitive: Km↑ / Vmax same → same y-intercept, different slopes, lines intersect on y-axis. Uncompetitive: Km↓ / Vmax↓ (same factor) → parallel lines (same slope), different y + x intercepts. Pure noncompetitive: Km same / Vmax↓ → same x-intercept, different y-intercepts, lines intersect on x-axis. Mixed noncompetitive: Km↑ or ↓ / Vmax↓ → lines intersect in 2nd quadrant (left of y-axis, above x-axis for α>α') or 3rd quadrant. Allosteric inhibition: not typically shown on L-B (cooperative kinetics → sigmoidal v vs [S] → L-B plot is non-linear). Substrate inhibition: at very high [S] → 1/v goes up on L-B (curve bends upward = hook). Clinical enzyme inhibitors as examples: PFK-1 competitive inhibition: ATP inhibits PFK-1 at the catalytic active site (competitive with AMP) → high ATP → ↓glycolysis; DHFR + methotrexate: tightly competitive inhibition (Ki ~1 nM) → leucovorin rescue competes at same active site; carbonic anhydrase + acetazolamide: competitive inhibitor → ↑HCO3- loss in urine → metabolic acidosis (used for altitude sickness, glaucoma, seizures); ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) + captopril: competitive-like inhibitor (captopril = competitive inhibitor; lisinopril, enalaprilat also competitive); arginase + DFMO (difluoromethylornithine/eflornithine): irreversible (mechanism-based) inhibitor of ODC (ornithine decarboxylase) used for Pneumocystis pneumonia + West African trypanosomiasis. IC50 vs Ki: IC50 is substrate concentration-dependent (IC50 = Ki[1 + [S]/Km] for competitive inhibition); Ki is the true affinity of the inhibitor for the enzyme (independent of [S]); IC50 > Ki when [S] > 0 for competitive inhibition.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following molecules activates HIF-1α (hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha) by PREVENTING its degradation under hypoxic conditions?
options: VHL protein, which prevents PHD from ubiquitinating HIF-1α (this is BACKWARDS: VHL is the E3 ubiquitin ligase that causes HIF-1α degradation; VHL promotes HIF-1α degradation, not its stabilization)

PHD2 (prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2, EGLN1), which hydroxylates HIF-1α on Pro402 and Pro564, triggering VHL recognition and degradation (PHD2 promotes HIF-1α degradation [via hydroxylation → VHL recognition → ubiquitination → proteasome]; in hypoxia, PHD2 is INACTIVE [requires O2], so HIF-1α is NOT hydroxylated → accumulates; PHD2 inhibition = mechanism for HIF-1α stabilization but here the question asks what ACTIVATES HIF-1α by preventing degradation under hypoxia → answer is the absence/inhibition of PHD activity due to lack of O2)

Lack of oxygen: in normoxia, PHD1/2/3 (require O2, α-KG, Fe2+, ascorbate as cofactors) hydroxylate HIF-1α at Pro402 + Pro564 → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau, pVHL, part of Cul2-RING ubiquitin ligase [CRL2: VHL + elongin C + elongin B + Cullin-2 + RBX1]) recognizes pOH-Pro → polyubiquitinates → 26S proteasome degradation; in HYPOXIA: PHD O2 requirement not met → HIF-1α NOT hydroxylated → VHL cannot recognize → HIF-1α ESCAPES proteasomal degradation → accumulates in cytoplasm → translocates to nucleus → dimerizes with HIF-1β (ARNT) → recruits p300/CBP coactivators → binds HREs (hypoxia-response elements, 5'-RCGTG-3') → activates transcription of hypoxic response genes: target genes: EPO (erythropoietin, ↑RBC production); VEGF (angiogenesis); Glut1/3, LDHA, PGK1 (glycolytic switch: Warburg); CAIX (carbonic anhydrase IX; surface marker of hypoxic tumors); BNIP3 (mitophagy); PHD2/3 themselves (negative feedback); FIH (factor inhibiting HIF): ALSO hydroxylates HIF-1α at Asn803 → blocks interaction with p300/CBP → ↓transcriptional activity; FIH requires O2 (lower O2 affinity than PHDs → FIH inactivated at higher pO2 than PHDs; so HIF-1α can be stabilized but still not fully active until FIH is also inactivated at very low pO2); PHD inhibitors (roxadustat, daprodustat, vadadustat, molidustat): HIF-PHI (HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors) → prevent PHD activity → ↑HIF-1α → ↑EPO → treat anemia of chronic kidney disease (CKD); approved in multiple countries (Japan, EU, China; FDA approval for some); VHL syndrome: germline VHL mutations → ↑HIF-1α in normoxia → hemangioblastomas (cerebellum, retina, spinal cord), clear cell RCC (renal cell carcinoma), pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors; VHL loss → HIF-driven tumor angiogenesis; HIF-2α (EPAS1): ↑EPO production (kidney/liver); targeted by belzutifan (MK-6482, VHL disease + clear cell RCC HIF-2α inhibitor, FDA-approved 2021); HIF-1α more ubiquitous; HIF-2α more tissue-specific

Acetylation of HIF-1α by ARD1 acetyltransferase, which promotes HIF-1α stability (ARD1/NATH [N-terminal acetyltransferase A] was proposed to acetylate HIF-1α Lys532 → VHL recognition → degradation in some studies; however, this acetylation mechanism is controversial and largely NOT confirmed; the main mechanism is O2-dependent PHD hydroxylation of Pro402/564 → VHL; acetylation is not the established primary mechanism)
explanation: HIF pathway — cancer and therapeutics: PHD1/2/3 (EGLN2/1/3): require O2 (Km_O2 ~100-250 µM, near atmospheric O2 = ~230 µM → PHDs are sensitive O2 sensors), Fe2+ (inhibited by Fe3+ or competing divalent metals like Co2+, Ni2+, Mn2+), α-KG (2-oxoglutarate, co-substrate), and ascorbate (keeps Fe in 2+ state → activates PHDs; vitamin C deficiency may impair PHD activity → ↑HIF-1α → some vitamin C effects on angiogenesis via this pathway); FIH (factor inhibiting HIF, asparagine hydroxylase): asparaginyl hydroxylase; hydroxylates Asn803 in HIF-1α C-TAD (C-terminal transactivation domain) → prevents p300/CBP binding → ↓transcription; FIH is more O2-sensitive (lower Km) → inhibited at lower O2 than PHDs; PHD inhibitors (PHDI, HIF-PHI) mechanism: α-KG analogs + iron chelators → competitive with α-KG and Fe2+ → ↓PHD activity → ↑HIF-1α → ↑EPO + ↑hepcidin suppression (↑iron absorption) → ↑Hb; approved PHDIs: roxadustat (China 2018, EU 2021, FDA 2023 [in some markets]); daprodustat; vadadustat; molidustat; all are α-KG analogs. VHL E3 ligase complex: VHL binds HIF-α (recognizes Hyp402 + Hyp564 via its β-domain) → recruits elongin B/C (adapter) + Cullin-2 + RBX1 + E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme → K48-polyubiquitin chain → 26S proteasome. Cancer HIF activation: VHL mutation/deletion → ccRCC (clear cell RCC, 90% have VHL loss); SDHB/C/D mutations → pseudohypoxia (succinate accumulates → competitive inhibitor of PHD [succinate and α-KG compete at Fe-center] → PHD inhibited → HIF-1α stable → ↑HIF target genes → paraganglioma + pheo); IDH1/2 gain-of-function → 2-HG (R-2-HG) → inhibits PHD? (some evidence) + TET2 + JMJD histone demethylases → epigenetic dysregulation; FH mutations (fumarate hydratase) → ↑fumarate → PHD inhibition → HLRCC (hereditary leiomyomatosis + RCC); targeted therapy: bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) + TKI (sunitinib, pazopanib, axitinib, cabozantinib: anti-VEGFR1/2/3 → anti-angiogenesis → ccRCC treatment); belzutifan (HIF-2α inhibitor) → VHL disease + ccRCC (second-line).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The sickle cell mutation (HbS: Glu6Val) in the β-globin gene results from a single nucleotide change. The original codon for Glu6 (GAG) mutates to:
options: GUG (valine codon) — a transversion mutation changing A→U (in RNA terms): In DNA: Glu codon = GAG (on mRNA); Val codon = GTG → mRNA: GUG; Single nucleotide change: GAG → GTG (in DNA: coding strand) → mRNA: GAG → GUG; this is a TRANSITION mutation: A (purine) → T/U (pyrimidine) at the second position → TRANSVERSION (purine → pyrimidine = TRANSVERSION); WAIT: Let me reconsider. GAG → GTG: G (position 1) same; A → T (position 2); G (position 3) same; so the change is A → T (in DNA) / A → U (in mRNA); A is a purine; T/U is a pyrimidine; purine → pyrimidine = TRANSVERSION; specifically: purine (Adenine) → pyrimidine (Thymine/Uracil) = TRANSVERSION; HbS is caused by a TRANSVERSION: A→T in DNA (second position of codon 6); mRNA codon: GAG (Glu) → GUG (Val); This is a missense mutation (GAG [Glu] → GUG [Val]: one amino acid substituted for another); The first sickle mutation identified biochemically (1956, Vernon Ingram) using peptide mapping + fingerprinting; diagnosis: hemoglobin electrophoresis (alkaline pH: HbA migrates further than HbS → different charge due to loss of negative charge from Glu substitution by neutral Val → HbS moves less toward anode); isoelectric focusing (IEF) + HPLC (used for NBS); Sickle cell disease (SCD): HbSS, HbSC, HbS/β-thal, etc.; HbS polymerization: deoxy-HbS → Val6 inserts into hydrophobic pocket on adjacent β-chain (between Ala70 and Phe85) → polymer contact point → polymer nucleation → polymerization → fiber formation → RBC sickling → VOC (vaso-occlusive crisis), hemolysis, organ damage; HbF (γ-globin chains) does NOT sickle (no Val6 equivalent, + inhibits HbS polymer formation by dilution); treatment: hydroxyurea → ↑HbF; voxelotor (GBT440): Hx-modified HbS → ↑O2 affinity → ↓deoxy-HbS → ↓polymerization; crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin → ↓WBC/RBC/platelet adhesion → ↓VOC); L-glutamine (FDA-approved: ↓oxidative damage to RBC); gene therapy: CTX001/exa-cel (CRISPR: BCL11A erythroid enhancer editing → ↑γ-globin → ↑HbF) approved 2023 (first approved CRISPR therapeutic); lovo-cel (Bluebird Bio bb1111: lentiviral βA-T87Q-globin → creates anti-sickling β-globin) → ↑functional Hb → approved 2023

GTG (valine codon) — a transition mutation (technically: GAG → GTG change is A→T which is TRANSVERSION not transition; a TRANSITION would be purine → purine [A→G] or pyrimidine → pyrimidine [C→T]; HbS is caused by a transversion [A→T])

GCG (alanine codon) — changing Glu6 to Ala6 (GCG codes for Ala; changing GAG → GCG would require A→C at position 2, which is a transversion giving Ala, not Val; HbS is Glu→Val, requiring GTG at the codon; GCG would give HbC equivalent or different variant)
GGG (glycine codon) — a transition mutation at position 2 (GAG → GGG changes A→G [transition] but GGG = glycine, not valine; HbS has valine at position 6, not glycine)
explanation: Hemoglobin variants — molecular basis: HbS (sickle): β6 Glu→Val (GAG→GTG, transversion A→T); most common severe hemoglobinopathy; ~300,000 births per year globally with SCC. HbC: β6 Glu→Lys (GAG→AAG, transversion A→A? No: G→A at position 1 of codon: GAG→AAG is G→A [purine→purine = transition]; Lys replaces Glu → mild hemolytic anemia; HbSC: compound heterozygote → moderate disease. HbE: β26 Glu→Lys (GAG→AAG); very common in SE Asia; causes thalassemia-like picture (aberrant splicing + ↓HbE production); HbE/β-thal → severe disease. HbM: various histidine mutations in heme-binding region → met-Hb stabilized → cyanosis (Mhb does not respond to methylene blue since enzymatic [NADH-MetHb reductase] + non-enzymatic pathways cannot reduce it [wrong heme environment]). HbF (fetal hemoglobin): α2γ2; γ-globin has Ala136 instead of β-Gly136 → ↑O2 affinity (2,3-BPG binds γ chains less effectively → ↑affinity → placental O2 transfer); HbF normally ~<1% in adults; ↑HbF in: HPFH (hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin: δβ-thalassemia or BCL11A/ZBTB7A/KLF1 regulatory mutations), sickle cell disease (protective), β-thalassemia, certain drugs (hydroxyurea, decitabine). Electrophoresis at alkaline pH: Fast (toward anode) → Slow: HbH (α0 thalassemia, α4 tetramers) → C (= Bart's/Hb Bart's = γ4, also fast) → Bart's > A2 [HbA2 = α2δ2, ↑in β-thal] > A [normal] > S [sickle] > C [HbC]. IEF (isoelectric focusing) separates by pI (isoelectric point): HbC (pI~7.5) > HbS (pI~7.0) > HbA (pI~6.9) → used in NBS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Coagulation factor XIII (FXIII) is a transglutaminase activated by thrombin. Its function in hemostasis is to:
options: Activate protein C to inhibit thrombin formation (Protein C is activated by thrombin-thrombomodulin complex → activated protein C [APC] inactivates FVa + FVIIIa; Factor XIII does NOT activate protein C; their functions are entirely different)
Convert fibrinogen to fibrin by removing fibrinopeptides A and B (that is the function of THROMBIN; Factor XIII cross-links EXISTING fibrin, not converts fibrinogen to fibrin)

Cross-link fibrin polymers by forming covalent isopeptide bonds between glutamine and lysine residues, stabilizing the fibrin clot: FXIII (factor XIII): a transglutaminase (glutamine-amine γ-glutamyl transferase); in plasma as inactive zymogen (FXIII = 2 A-subunits [catalytic, FXIII-A2] + 2 B-subunits [non-catalytic, carrier/inhibitory, FXIII-B2] → α2β2 heterotetramer); activation: thrombin cleaves FXIII-A at Arg37 → releases B-subunit (in presence of Ca2+) → exposes active site Cys314 in A-subunit → active FXIIIa (= transglutaminase); platelet FXIIIa: platelets contain FXIII-A2 (no B subunits); FXIIIa (platelet-derived) activated more rapidly than plasma FXIII (due to Ca2+ release + thrombin generated locally); FUNCTION: FXIIIa cross-links γ (Lys406/Lys411 + Gln398/399) + α chains of fibrin → isopeptide bonds (γ-glutamyl-ε-lysyl bonds): (1) cross-links adjacent γ chains (γ-γ dimers; first and most rapid cross-links); (2) cross-links α chains to form polymers (α-α + α-γ cross-links); (3) cross-links α2-antiplasmin (α2AP, principal inhibitor of plasmin) to α-chain of fibrin → ↓fibrinolysis susceptibility; cross-linking converts non-covalent fibrin polymer → covalent → mechanically STRONGER, RESISTANT to plasmin degradation (protects clot from premature lysis); CLINICAL: FXIII deficiency: rare AR disorder; presents with: delayed bleeding (minutes to hours after injury, since initial primary hemostasis is normal [platelet plug forms] + fibrin initially forms but non-cross-linked → weak → dissolves); umbilical stump bleeding (hallmark in neonates!); intracranial hemorrhage (common cause of death in FXIII deficiency, even with trauma); poor wound healing (fibrin scaffold non-stable → impaired granulation tissue); habitual abortions (non-crosslinked fibrin insufficient for placental implantation); lab: normal PT, aPTT, TT (all normal! FXIII activity assay is SEPARATE → clot solubility test: 5M urea or 1% monochloroacetic acid dissolves non-cross-linked fibrin [FXIII-deficient clot] but not cross-linked fibrin [normal clot]); specific FXIII-A assay (quantitative); treatment: cryoprecipitate or FXIII concentrate (Corifact, Tretten)

Activate plasminogen to plasmin, initiating fibrinolysis (plasminogen is activated by tPA [tissue plasminogen activator] or urokinase-type PA [uPA]; Factor XIII does not activate plasminogen; it actually stabilizes the clot AGAINST fibrinolysis by cross-linking α2-antiplasmin to fibrin)
explanation: Coagulation cascade — biochemistry: Extrinsic pathway (TF pathway): TF (tissue factor, CD142) exposed after vessel injury → binds circulating FVIIa → TF-FVIIa complex (extrinsic tenase) → activates FX → FXa + FVa → prothrombinase complex → thrombin; small initial thrombin → amplifies: activates FVIII, FV, FXI + platelets → intrinsic tenase: FIXa-FVIIIa → ↑FXa → ↑thrombin → ↑fibrin + ↑FXIII; Intrinsic pathway: FXII activation (contact system: collagen, Hageman factor [FXII] + HMWK + prekallikrein) → FXI → FIX → extrinsic tenase-independent FXa. Common pathway: FX + FV + Ca2+ + platelet PF → prothrombinase → prothrombin (II) → thrombin (IIa) → fibrinogen → fibrin + FXIII → FXIII-a (by thrombin + Ca2+) → stable fibrin clot. Anticoagulant systems: TFPI (tissue factor pathway inhibitor): inhibits TF-FVIIa-FXa complex → limits initiation; thrombin-thrombomodulin (TM) complex on endothelium → activates protein C → APC + protein S → inactivates FVa + FVIIIa → ↓thrombin generation (negative feedback); antithrombin (SERPINC1): inhibits thrombin + FXa + IXa + XIa (serine protease inhibitor [SERPIN]); heparin → binds AT → conformational change → AT activity ↑1000-fold → LMWH (enoxaparin, dalteparin): anti-Xa primarily; UFH: anti-Xa + anti-IIa (thrombin); fondaparinux: selective anti-Xa; DOAC (direct oral anticoagulants): rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban (anti-Xa); dabigatran (anti-IIa/thrombin); reversal: idarucizumab (anti-dabigatran Fab antibody) or andexanet alfa (recombinant FXa decoy → binds anti-Xa DOACs + heparin → reverses anti-Xa effect). FXIII and wound healing: FXIIIa cross-links fibronectin, collagen, and other ECM components to fibrin → scaffolding for fibroblast migration → granulation tissue → FXIII deficiency → impaired wound healing (slow wound closure, recurrent dehiscence).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the committed step of purine de novo synthesis (the first unique step after PRPP formation)?
options: Adenylosuccinate lyase (ASL): catalyzes two steps in de novo purine synthesis (step 8: SAICAR → AICAR; step 10-ish: adenylosuccinate → AMP); NOT the committed step; ASL deficiency → purine synthesis defect + psychomotor retardation
IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH1/2): converts IMP → XMP in the GMP branch after IMP formation; NOT the committed or first step of purine synthesis

PRPP amidotransferase (phosphoribosylamine-glycine amide synthetase; PPAT, also called glutamine PRPP amidotransferase or amidophosphoribosyltransferase): step 1 of de novo purine synthesis: PRPP + Gln + H2O → [PPAT] → phosphoribosylamine (PRA) + PPi + Glu; this IS the committed step (first step unique to purine synthesis; PRPP itself is used in multiple pathways including pyrimidine synthesis + NAD synthesis; PRA is purine-specific); PPAT: allosteric enzyme regulated by feedback inhibition: end products AMP, GMP, IMP inhibit PPAT; AMP binds to one allosteric site + GMP binds to another → additive inhibition (two separate allosteric sites on PPAT); activated by PRPP (high PRPP → more PRA formation); full de novo purine synthesis sequence (10 steps to IMP, then 2 branches to AMP + GMP): step 1: PRPP + Gln → PRA [PPAT, committed step, rate-limiting] → step 2: PRA + Gly → GAR [GARS, glycinamide ribonucleotide synthetase; also uses ATP] → step 3: GAR + N10-formyl-THF → FGAR [GARFT, formyltransferase] → step 4: FGAR + Gln + ATP → FGAM [PFAS, formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide amidotransferase] → step 5: ring closure → AIR [PFAS, aminoimidazole ribonucleotide synthetase] → step 6: AIR + CO2 (mammals: direct carboxylation via PAICS/AIRcase) → CAIR → step 7: CAIR + Asp + ATP → SAICAR [PAICS] → step 8: SAICAR → AICAR [adenylosuccinate lyase/ASL] → step 9: AICAR + N10-formyl-THF → FAICAR [ATIC, AICAR formyltransferase] → step 10: FAICAR → IMP [ATIC, IMP cyclohydrolase] → IMP is the branch point; IMP → AMP branch: IMP → adenylosuccinate [ADSS/adenylosuccinate synthetase + GTP] → AMP [ASL]; IMP → GMP branch: IMP → XMP [IMPDH1/2 + NAD+] → GMP [GMPS + Gln + ATP]

Dihydroorotase (DHODH): part of the CAD trifunctional enzyme complex for PYRIMIDINE synthesis (step 3: carbamoyl-aspartate → dihydroorotate); nothing to do with PURINE synthesis; DHODH is in the inner mitochondrial membrane; DHODH inhibitor: leflunomide/teriflunomide (used for rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation by ↓pyrimidine synthesis)
explanation: De novo purine vs. pyrimidine synthesis — comparison: PURINE: assembles on ribose-5-P scaffold (PRPP → IMP → AMP/GMP); 10 steps; committed step: PRPP + Gln → PRA (PPAT); rate-limiting: PPAT; regulation: AMP + GMP feedback-inhibit PPAT; AMP branch: needs GTP (adenylosuccinate synthetase); GMP branch: needs ATP (GMP synthetase) → cross-regulation: overproduction of one inhibits its own branch but the other branch needs ATP or GTP of the first → balanced; uses: glycine (C4, N3, C4a backbone), aspartate (N1 of adenine), Gln (N9 + N3 of purine), N10-formyl-THF (C2 + C8), CO2 (C6 in birds, C4a in mammals), PRPP (ribose scaffold). PYRIMIDINE: assembles as free base then attached to ribose; 6 steps; committed step: CPS II (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II: Gln + 2ATP + HCO3- → carbamoyl-P) in cytoplasm (separate from CPS I in mitochondria [urea cycle]); rate-limiting: CPS II; regulation: UTP feedback-inhibits CPS II; PRPP activates CPS II (via UMP to UTP/CTP pathway); trifunctional CAD enzyme (CPS II + ATCase/aspartate transcarbamoylase + dihydroorotase) → carbamoyl-P → carbamoyl-Asp → dihydroorotate → DHODH (inner mitochondrial membrane → passes electrons to CoQ → ETC) → orotate → UMPS (bifunctional: OPRT + ODC: orotate + PRPP → OMP → UMP) → UMP → UDP → UTP → [CTP synthase] → CTP → nucleic acid/phospholipid synthesis. Key drugs targeting de novo synthesis: Purine synthesis: methotrexate (MTX, inhibits DHFR → ↓THF → ↓N10-formyl-THF → ↓steps 3 + 9 [GARFT + ATIC]) + pemetrexed (also inhibits GARFT/step 3 + ATIC directly); lometrexol (GARFT inhibitor); mycophenolate mofetil (MMF → mycophenolic acid → inhibits IMPDH → ↓GMP branch → selectively ↓lymphocyte proliferation [lymphocytes depend on de novo synthesis, lack adequate salvage]; immunosuppressant after transplant); pyrimidine synthesis: leflunomide/teriflunomide (DHODH inhibitor → ↓UMP → ↓lymphocyte proliferation → RA/MS); 5-FU (antimetabolite: FdUMP inhibits TS; FUTP incorporated into RNA); hydroxyurea (HU → inhibits RNR → ↓all dNDP → ↓DNA synthesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Pyruvate carboxylase (PC) deficiency presents in neonates with severe lactic acidosis, hyperammonemia, and hypoglycemia. The inability to make OAA from pyruvate in PC deficiency impairs:
options: Both gluconeogenesis (loss of OAA as GNG substrate) and the TCA cycle (loss of OAA for anaplerosis), explaining lactic acidosis (pyruvate cannot enter TCA via OAA → backs up → lactic acid) + hypoglycemia (GNG cannot proceed without OAA): PC (pyruvate carboxylase): pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → OAA + ADP + Pi; biotin-dependent (BCCP [biotin carboxyl carrier protein] domain of PC); exclusively mitochondrial; activated by acetyl-CoA (↑FA oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑PC → ↑OAA → ↑TCA flux AND/OR GNG); OAA has dual role: (1) GNG: OAA → [PEPCK, pyruvate carboxylase route] → PEP → gluconeogenesis; (2) TCA cycle: OAA + acetyl-CoA → [citrate synthase] → citrate → TCA continues; PC deficiency: PC gene mutations → ↓PC → pyruvate cannot be carboxylated → ↑pyruvate accumulates → LDH → ↑lactate → lactic acidosis; also acetyl-CoA accumulates but cannot enter TCA (no OAA for citrate synthase) → ketogenesis? Paradoxically some PC-deficient patients have ↑ketones because acetyl-CoA has nowhere to go except HMG-CoA pathway; main issues: (1) ↓OAA for TCA → ↓TCA cycle flux → ↓NADH → ↓ETC → ↓ATP → cell dysfunction; ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑HMGCS → ketosis; ↑lactate + pyruvate (↑L:P ratio normal in PC deficiency: L:P ratio often NORMAL even though ↑lactate + ↑pyruvate; this is because both are elevated proportionally; contrast with complex I/PDC deficiency where ↑L:P > 20 due to ↑NADH:NAD+); (2) ↓OAA for GNG → hypoglycemia; (3) hyperammonemia: OAA is needed for malate-aspartate shuttle → Asp synthesis in liver → Asp is a substrate for urea cycle (ASS) → without OAA → ↓Asp → ↓urea cycle function → ↑NH4+; types: type A (benign, partial PC deficiency: delayed psychomotor development + episodic lactic acidosis); type B (severe, French form: essentially no PC activity; neonatal onset, severe lactic acidosis + hypoglycemia + hyperammonemia + hypercitrullinemia/hyperprolinemia → mimics type 2 citrullinemia; → death in infancy); type C (variable); treatment: biotin supplementation (if biotin-dependent); high-fat, low-carb diet (↑acetyl-CoA → ↑TCA via anaplerosis from FAO without needing PC) + aspartate supplementation (restores urea cycle)
Only the TCA cycle, with no effect on gluconeogenesis (PC deficiency severely impairs BOTH TCA cycle anaplerosis AND gluconeogenesis; hypoglycemia is a hallmark → GNG impaired)
Only gluconeogenesis, explaining just the hypoglycemia (TCA cycle anaplerosis is also impaired → lactic acidosis + TCA failure; saying 'only GNG' is incomplete)

Only fatty acid oxidation (FA oxidation is IMPAIRED in carnitine deficiency or VLCAD/MCAD deficiency; PC deficiency primarily impairs OAA synthesis → TCA + GNG impaired; FAO itself is NOT directly impaired in PC deficiency)
explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase and related organicacidurias: PC gene: 11q13.2; AR; rare (~1 in 250,000); cofactor: biotin (covalently attached to BCCP domain Lys1119); biotin attachment enzyme: holocarboxylase synthetase (HLCS); biotinidase recycles biotin (from biocytin [biotin-ε-Lys] → free biotin); biotinidase deficiency → secondary deficiency of all biotin-dependent carboxylases (PC + PCC + MCC + ACC1/2); presentation of biotinidase deficiency: eczematous rash + alopecia + ataxia + seizures + lactic acidosis + ketoacidosis + organic acidemia pattern on GC-MS; treat with free biotin (10 mg/day) → prevents neurological damage; biotin-dependent carboxylases in humans: PC (pyruvate + CO2 → OAA, gluconeogenesis/TCA anaplerosis); PCC (propionyl-CoA + CO2 → D-methylmalonyl-CoA, odd-chain FA/BCAA catabolism); MCC (3-methylcrotonyl-CoA + CO2 → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA, Leu catabolism); ACC1/2 (acetyl-CoA + CO2 → malonyl-CoA, FA synthesis/CPT1 regulation); HCS (holocarboxylase synthetase) deficiency → same multi-carboxylase picture as biotinidase but no biotinidase; HCS mutations → BIOTIN in pharmacological doses helps only partially (HCS has ↑Km for biotin → needs more biotin to load all four carboxylases). OAA in metabolic integration: OAA is the 'hub' of intermediary metabolism: TCA: OAA + acetyl-CoA → citrate (condenses); TCA: malate → OAA (MDH, TCA step 9); GNG: OAA → PEP (PEPCK, rate-limiting step of GNG); Amino acid: OAA ↔ Asp (GOT2/AST transamination); Lipid: citrate → OAA + acetyl-CoA (ACLY, cytoplasm, lipogenesis); so OAA deficiency (as in PC deficiency) cascades into multiple defects.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 25-year-old woman is found to have hypercholesterolemia with total cholesterol 580 mg/dL, LDL 510 mg/dL, triglycerides 130 mg/dL, and a family history of premature MI in her father (died at age 45). She is diagnosed with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). The most common molecular defect in FH is:
options: Deficiency of hepatic lipase (HL, LIPC): HL deficiency → ↑IDL + HDL (Type III/V hyperlipidemia pattern); not the classic cause of FH; HL has 2 roles: remnant particle uptake aid (HL-TAG hydrolysis → smaller IDL → LDL receptor can grab it) + HDL remodeling (HDL2 → HDL3); LIPC mutations → ↑HDL + ↑IDL; not FH

Gain-of-function mutation in PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9): PCSK9 GOF mutations CAN cause FH (HeFH or HoFH); PCSK9 gain-of-function → ↑LDL receptor degradation → ↑LDL; mutations like D374Y (severe), S127R are RARE causes of FH; PCSK9 mutations account for only ~1% of FH cases; the MOST COMMON cause remains LDL receptor mutations
