Loss-of-function mutations in the LDL receptor (LDLR) gene: the most common molecular cause of FH (~85-90% of genetically confirmed FH cases); LDLR encodes the LDL receptor (LDL-R); LDL-R function: binds ApoB-100 (on LDL, VLDL remnants, IDL) and ApoE (on VLDL remnants, IDL, HDL) → endocytosis → LDL degraded in lysosome → cholesterol released → cholesterol: (1) inhibits HMGCR (↓cholesterol synthesis); (2) activates ACAT → esterified + stored; (3) inhibits LDL-R transcription (via INSIG → SCAP-SREBP2 retention in ER → ↓SREBP2 processing → ↓LDL-R gene expression); FH LDLR mutation classes: class I (null alleles, no LDLR produced → most severe); class II (transport defective: LDLR made but retained in ER → not transported to Golgi); class III (binding defective: LDL-R at cell surface but cannot bind LDL [ApoB-100]); class IV (internalization defective: LDLR can bind LDL but LDLR cannot cluster in clathrin-coated pits → not endocytosed); class V (recycling defective: LDL-R cannot release LDL in lysosome → degraded with LDL); >3000 LDLR variants; HeFH (heterozygous FH): 1/250-500 prevalence (most common monogenic hypercholesterolemia); LDL 190-400 mg/dL; premature ASCVD in 40-50s if untreated; HoFH: 1/300,000; LDL >400-500 mg/dL; severe premature ASCVD, aortic stenosis, cutaneous + tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus; treatment: statins (↑LDLR expression by ↑SREBP-2 activation → ↑LDL clearance; HOW: statins → ↓HMG-CoA → ↓cholesterol → ↓INSIG binding to SCAP → SCAP-SREBP-2 → Golgi → S1P/S2P → SREBP-2 active → ↑LDL-R transcription) + ezetimibe (NPC1L1 inhibitor → ↓intestinal cholesterol absorption) + PCSK9 inhibitors (alirocumab, evolocumab: anti-PCSK9 monoclonal → ↓PCSK9 → ↑LDL-R recycling → ↑LDL clearance); inclisiran (siRNA targeting PCSK9 mRNA); lomitapide (MTP inhibitor, HoFH); LDL apheresis

Gain-of-function mutation in HMGCR (HMG-CoA reductase): HMGCR GOF mutations are NOT known to cause FH; HMGCR (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase) is the target of statins and the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis; activating mutations would theoretically ↑cholesterol synthesis but this is not a recognized cause of FH; there are known HMGCR polymorphisms that affect statin response but not clinical FH
explanation: FH management — biochemistry of LDL-lowering: PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9): serine protease (S1P/kexin family); synthesized in liver (mainly), intestine, kidney; binds LDL-R on hepatocyte surface → endocytosis → lysosome → PCSK9 prevents acid-induced conformational change in LDLR that allows LDL release → LDLR degraded with LDL (instead of recycling to surface); net: ↑PCSK9 → ↓surface LDL-R → ↑LDL-C; PCSK9 gain-of-function (GOF) mutations: ↑LDL (FH3, ~1% of FH); PCSK9 loss-of-function (LOF) mutations: ↓LDL (up to 40%) → protective against ASCVD (African-Americans with PCSK9 LOF: C679X → LDL -28% → ASCVD risk -88%; demonstrates LDL causality in ASCVD); alirocumab (Praluent) + evolocumab (Repatha): fully human mAbs against PCSK9 → ↑LDL-R recycling → ↓LDL 50-60%; inclisiran (Leqvio): siRNA targeting PCSK9 mRNA in hepatocytes → ↓PCSK9 protein → ↑LDL-R → ↓LDL ~50%; dosing: every 6 months (s.c.); statins paradox: statins → ↓cholesterol → SREBP-2 → ↑LDL-R AND ↑PCSK9 (PCSK9 gene also has SREBP response element) → statins upregulate both LDL-R + PCSK9 → PCSK9 partially counters statin LDL-lowering → combination statin + PCSK9i is synergistic. LDL-C calculation: Friedewald: LDL-C = Total-C − HDL-C − TG/5 (mg/dL); inaccurate when TG > 400 mg/dL or TG/VLDL ratio unusual; Martin-Hopkins formula: TG/VLDL factor is adjustable by LDL quintiles + TG level → more accurate when TG is high; direct LDL measurement (ultracentrifugation or homogeneous assay): gold standard for high TG.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A newborn develops jaundice on day 1 of life. Total serum bilirubin is 18 mg/dL with unconjugated bilirubin 17 mg/dL. Coombs test is positive. This is consistent with hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN). Bilirubin is a breakdown product of heme. The sequence of heme catabolism is:
options: Heme → bilirubin → biliverdin → UDP-glucuronide (this reverses the correct order; biliverdin comes BEFORE bilirubin in heme catabolism; bilirubin is made FROM biliverdin, not the other way)

Heme → biliverdin → bilirubin → bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated bilirubin): Heme catabolism sequence: Step 1: heme + O2 + NADPH → [heme oxygenase 1/2, HO-1/HO-2, HMOX1/HMOX2] → biliverdin IXα + CO (carbon monoxide) + Fe2+; heme ring opens at α-methene bridge (HO-1 is INDUCIBLE [induced by heme, oxidative stress, LPS → HO-1 = cytoprotective enzyme: produces CO [vasodilator] + Fe [ferritin-stored] + biliverdin → bilirubin [antioxidant?]); HO-2 is constitutive (brain, testes); Step 2: biliverdin + NADPH → [biliverdin reductase BVR-A/B] → bilirubin IXα; bilirubin = yellow; water-INsoluble (internal H-bonds between propionic acid carboxylates and amide NH groups of the dipyrrolemethene rings → hydrophobic pocket → ↓ionization at physiological pH → not water-soluble → bound to albumin in blood → transported to liver); Step 3: bilirubin in hepatocyte → [UGT1A1, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1] → bilirubin-monoglucuronide (BMG) → bilirubin-diglucuronide (BDG, conjugated bilirubin); UGT1A1 uses UDP-glucuronic acid as glucuronyl donor; conjugation: ester linkage between glucuronic acid and propionic acid carboxylates of bilirubin → makes bilirubin water-soluble; Step 4: BDG → [MRP2/ABCC2, canalicular transporter] → bile → gut → bacteria → urobilinogen (UBG, by β-glucuronidase + anaerobic bacteria) → urobilin (oxidized UBG → urine yellow color) or stercobilin (fecal brown color) or urobilinogen absorbed → enterohepatic circulation → liver (reconjugated) or kidney (urobilinogen → urine); HDN: maternal IgG antibodies (Rh [anti-D] or ABO) cross placenta → opsonize fetal RBCs → hemolysis → ↑heme catabolism → ↑unconjugated bilirubin → crosses blood-brain barrier (unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble → kernicterus: bilirubin deposits in basal ganglia, hippocampus, cerebellum) → prevention: Rh immunoglobulin (anti-D Ig) given to Rh- mother after delivery of Rh+ baby or after any sensitizing event

Heme → protoporphyrin IX → iron + bilirubin (this is not the correct sequence; protoporphyrin IX is a PRECURSOR to heme [in heme biosynthesis: ferrochelatase adds Fe2+ to protoporphyrin IX → heme]; in catabolism, heme → biliverdin, NOT → protoporphyrin IX; heme oxygenase cleaves heme ring to biliverdin, not back to protoporphyrin)

Heme → urobilinogen → bilirubin (urobilinogen is produced from bilirubin by intestinal bacteria AFTER bilirubin reaches the gut; urobilinogen is a downstream product, not an intermediate between heme and bilirubin)
explanation: Bilirubin metabolism disorders: Physiological jaundice of newborn: days 2-3 peak (not day 1); due to: (1) ↑hemolysis (fetal RBC lifespan 70-90 days vs adult 120 days, + switch from HbF → HbA); (2) ↓UGT1A1 activity in neonatal liver (UGT1A1 matures in 2-3 months); treatment: phototherapy (blue light 430-490 nm → converts bilirubin IXα [Z,Z isomer] → lumirubin [photoisomers: E,Z or Z,E isomers, or structural isomers] → water-soluble → excreted in bile without conjugation); exchange transfusion if dangerously high. Neonatal jaundice on day 1 = always pathological (hemolytic disease); not physiological. UGT1A1 variants: Gilbert syndrome: UGT1A1 promoter polymorphism [TA]7 (7 TA repeats instead of normal 6 [TA6]) → ↓UGT1A1 expression (~30% of normal) → mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (< 5 mg/dL) → benign, no liver disease; exacerbated by fasting, stress, illness; affects ~10% of Caucasians; irinotecan toxicity: active metabolite SN-38 detoxified by UGT1A1 → [TA]7/7 homozygotes have ↓UGT1A1 → ↑SN-38 → ↑diarrhea + neutropenia → dose reduction indicated; Crigler-Najjar syndrome: CN-I: complete UGT1A1 deficiency → severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (>20 mg/dL) → kernicterus → death if untreated → liver transplant (only cure); CN-II (Arias syndrome): partial UGT1A1 deficiency → less severe (phenobarb → ↑UGT1A1); Dubin-Johnson syndrome (DJS): MRP2/ABCC2 mutations → ↓canalicular conjugated bilirubin export → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + normal liver function + liver pigmentation (melanin-like dark pigment) + coproporphyrin I ↑↑ in urine (normally coproporphyrin I:III ratio ≤ 0.9; DJS → reversed: coproporphyrin I = 80% in urine); benign; Rotor syndrome: OATP1B1 + OATP1B3 mutations (SLCO1B1 + SLCO1B3) → ↓hepatic uptake of conjugated bilirubin from portal blood → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + normal liver (no liver pigment); no MRP2 mutation (contrast DJS); coproporphyrin I in urine also ↑.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Nitric oxide (NO) is synthesized from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS). The type of NOS expressed constitutively in vascular endothelium and responsible for physiological vasodilation is:
options: iNOS (inducible NOS, NOS2): iNOS is INDUCIBLE (expressed after stimulation by LPS, cytokines [IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1] in macrophages, hepatocytes, smooth muscle cells); iNOS produces LARGE amounts of NO (high output, sustained) → cytotoxic effects on pathogens + tumor cells; NOT the constitutive endothelial isoform; iNOS activity is Ca2+-INDEPENDENT

nNOS (neuronal NOS, NOS1): nNOS is expressed constitutively in neurons (skeletal muscle: nNOS-μ, a splice variant) and in macula densa of kidney; responsible for NO in neuronal signaling (LTP, intestinal non-adrenergic non-cholinergic [NANC] relaxation, penile erection [parasympathetic]); Ca2+-CaM-dependent; NOT primarily responsible for endothelial vasodilation

eNOS (endothelial NOS, NOS3): Ca2+-CaM-dependent (activated by ↑intracellular Ca2+; shear stress on endothelium → ↑Ca2+ → calmodulin binds eNOS → displaces autoinhibitory loop → active; also activated by: Akt [PI3K-Akt-eNOS: Ser1177 phosphorylation by Akt → ↑eNOS activity even without ↑Ca2+; insulin, VEGF, exercise → this pathway]); eNOS: myristoylated (Gly2) + palmitoylated (Cys15, Cys26) → localized to caveolae (lipid rafts, caveolin-1); caveolin-1 INHIBITS eNOS (protein-protein interaction → autoinhibitory); ↑Ca2+ + CaM displaces caveolin-1; substrates: L-Arg + O2 + NADPH + FAD + FMN + BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) + heme → L-Cit + NO + NADP+; eNOS-derived NO diffuses to VSM → [soluble guanylyl cyclase, sGC: heme-containing; NO binds heme → conformational change → ↑cGMP from GTP] → ↑cGMP → PKG (cGMP-dependent protein kinase G) → phosphorylates MLCK (↓activity) + MLC phosphatase (↑activity) + MLCP → dephosphorylated MLC → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation; also: NO → S-nitrosylation of RyR (ryanodine receptor) → ↑Ca2+ leak? (complex); NO inhibits platelet aggregation (↑cGMP → ↓GPIIb/IIIa activation) + ↓leukocyte adhesion; eNOS uncoupling: in absence of BH4 (BH4 deficiency, oxidized BH4 = BH2 in oxidative stress) → eNOS 'uncouples' → produces O2•- (superoxide) instead of NO → ↑ROS + ↓NO → endothelial dysfunction → hypertension + atherosclerosis; endothelial dysfunction marker: ↓FMD (flow-mediated dilation)
mtNOS (mitochondrial NOS): a proposed isoform of nNOS in mitochondria; existence is debated; NOT the primary endothelial isoform responsible for vasodilation
explanation: NO signaling — full pathway: NO is a gaseous free radical; half-life in blood: 0.1 ms (rapidly scavenged by HbO2 → metHb + NO3-); yet exerts paracrine effects within tissue distances of ~200 µm; sgc (soluble guanylyl cyclase): heterodimer (α1β1 or α2β1); β1 subunit has heme (histidine-ligated Fe2+); NO binds heme → breaks Fe-His bond → activates catalytic site → ↑cGMP; riociguat (Adempas): sGC stimulator → ↑NO sensitivity → treats pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) + CTEPH; sildenafil/tadalafil/vardenafil: PDE5 inhibitors → ↓cGMP degradation → ↑cGMP → vasodilation (pulmonary + penile vasculature; PDE5 highest in smooth muscle); inhaled NO (iNO): direct pulmonary vasodilation → treats PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborn) + ARDS (selective pulmonary vasodilation without systemic hypotension); rebound effect if abruptly stopped → taper. Acetylcholine-mediated endothelium-dependent vasodilation: ACh → M3 receptors on endothelial cells → Gαq → PLC → IP3 + DAG → IP3 → ↑Ca2+ → CaM → eNOS → NO → VSM relaxation; classical experiment (Furchgott 1980): ACh dilated aortic rings ONLY when endothelium was intact → 'endothelium-derived relaxing factor' (EDRF) later identified as NO; Furchgott/Ignarro/Murad → Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1998. NOS cofactors: BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin): from GTP via GCH1 (GTP cyclohydrolase I, rate-limiting) → BH4; BH4 donates an electron to NOS → keeps heme in Fe2+ state → coupled NO production; BH4 deficiency (genetic PTPS/SR/DHPR variants causing atypical PKU [BH4 is also cofactor of PAH → BH4 deficiency → phenylketonuria phenotype!]) or oxidative stress oxidizes BH4 → BH2 (inactive) → eNOS uncoupling; sapropterin (Kuvan) = synthetic BH4 → PAH augmenter (PAH + sapropterin → ↑PAH activity in BH4-responsive PKU [~30% of PAH mutations]). Asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA): endogenous competitive inhibitor of all NOS isoforms (ADMA methylated on guanidino group of Arg by PRMT [protein arginine methyltransferases]); ↑ADMA in renal failure, diabetes, hypertension → endothelial dysfunction marker; degraded by DDAH (dimethylarginine dimethylaminohydrolase); homoARG (L-homoarginine) is a competitive substrate of NOS with lower affinity; ↑ ADMA:Arg ratio → ↓NO → CVD risk.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Warfarin inhibits the vitamin K epoxide reductase complex (VKORC1). This prevents recycling of vitamin K, thereby inhibiting which step in coagulation factor synthesis?
options: The carboxylation of glutamate residues to γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues on factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C, S, Z: Vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X [procoagulant] + Protein C, Protein S, Protein Z [anticoagulant + structural]; all these factors have Gla domains (N-terminal, contains multiple γ-carboxyglutamate [Gla] residues); Gla residues function: chelate Ca2+ → Ca2+-Gla complex → binds phospholipid membranes (especially negatively charged PS [phosphatidylserine] on activated platelet/endothelial surface) → allows assembly of tenase and prothrombinase complexes on membrane; Gla carboxylation: GGCX (γ-glutamyl carboxylase): requires: vitamin K hydroquinone (KH2, the active reduced form) + O2 + CO2 → Gla + vitamin K epoxide (KO) + H2O; CO2 is the carboxyl donor (NOT biotin; GGCX is not biotin-dependent; this is a UNIQUE CO2 fixation mechanism distinct from biotin-dependent carboxylases); warfarin (→ S-warfarin [active enantiomer] + R-warfarin; S-warfarin is 5× more potent; metabolized by CYP2C9 [S] + CYP3A4/1A2 [R]) → inhibits VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 [VKORC1; part of a complex on ER membrane]; VKORC1 reduces vitamin K epoxide → vitamin K quinone → further reduced by VKORC1 or NQO1 → KH2 [hydroquinone, active form]) → ↓KH2 → ↓carboxylation → PIVKA (proteins induced by vitamin K absence/antagonism) = under-carboxylated factors → cannot bind Ca2+/membranes → non-functional coagulation factors → ↑PT/INR; monitoring: INR (PT normalized by ISI [international sensitivity index of thromboplastin used]); therapeutic INR: 2.0-3.0 for most (AF, DVT, PE); 2.5-3.5 for mechanical heart valves; reversal: vitamin K (phylloquinone, takes 12-24h); 4F-PCC (4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate [factors II+VII+IX+X] for urgent reversal); FFP (contains all factors); andexanet alfa (not for warfarin specifically, for DOACs); vitamin K1 (phylloquinone, dietary, green vegetables) vs K2 (menaquinone, bacterial synthesis, long-chain MK-7, fermented foods) vs K3 (menadione, synthetic, not used therapeutically due to hemolysis); newborn vitamin K prophylaxis: IM vitamin K1 → prevents hemorrhagic disease of newborn (HDN, VKDB [vitamin K deficiency bleeding]): low placental transfer of vitamin K + low breast milk vitamin K + immature GI bacterial flora → ↓vitamin K → ↓clotting factors

Hydroxylation of Pro and Lys in collagen (collagen modifications: prolyl hydroxylase + lysyl hydroxylase require Fe2+, O2, ascorbate [vitamin C], α-KG; NOT vitamin K-dependent; prolyl + lysyl hydroxylation → collagen triple helix stability + cross-linking)

Phosphorylation of coagulation factors by protein kinases (vitamin K is not involved in phosphorylation reactions; phosphorylation of coagulation factors is not a major activation mechanism; the relevant post-translational modification is γ-carboxylation of Glu → Gla)

Cleavage of signal peptide from coagulation factor precursors (signal peptide cleavage is by signal peptidase in the ER lumen; unrelated to vitamin K; occurs during protein synthesis, not during post-translational modification of Gla domain)
explanation: Vitamin K metabolism pharmacology: VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1): gene on chr 16p11.2; common VKORC1 variants affect warfarin dose: VKORC1 1639G>A (rs9923231): AA genotype → lower VKORC1 expression → more sensitive to warfarin (need lower dose; Asian > European > African frequency of A allele); CYP2C9 variants (*2 = Arg144Cys; *3 = Ile359Leu) → ↓S-warfarin metabolism → ↑anticoagulation → need lower warfarin dose; CYP4F2 V433M → ↓vitamin K oxidation → ↑vitamin K available → needs higher warfarin dose; pharmacogenomics-guided warfarin dosing algorithms (IWPC algorithm) use VKORC1 + CYP2C9 + CYP4F2 genotypes + BSA + age + drugs → predicted warfarin dose; FDA updated warfarin label (2010) to include pharmacogenomics information. Vitamin K antagonists (VKA): warfarin (most used); acenocoumarol (faster off, shorter half-life); phenprocoumon (longer half-life, popular in Europe); all inhibit VKORC1. DOAC vs VKA comparison: DOACs (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban): fixed dose (with some adjustments), no routine INR monitoring, fewer drug-food interactions (no vitamin K from food matters), less ICP hemorrhage (especially apixaban vs warfarin), faster onset/offset; VKA: broad drug interactions (CYP2C9 inducers/inhibitors: rifampicin/fluconazole; also K-rich foods: green leafy vegetables ↑vitamin K → ↑VKORC1 substrate → ↑KH2 → overcome warfarin inhibition → ↓anticoagulation), narrow therapeutic index, teratogenic (warfarin crosses placenta → fetal warfarin syndrome: nasal hypoplasia + chondrodysplasia punctata + CNS abnormalities; heparin [LMWH] does NOT cross placenta → used during pregnancy). Protein C pathway: Protein C (PC) + Protein S (PS) are vitamin K-dependent ANTICOAGULANTS; Thrombin + TM (thrombomodulin) → APC (activated PC) + PS (cofactor) → inactivate FVa + FVIIIa → ↓thrombin generation; Factor V Leiden (FVL, R506Q, most common hereditary thrombophilia): FVa resistant to APC cleavage → ↑FVa activity → ↑thrombin → ↑thrombosis risk; Prothrombin G20210A mutation: second most common hereditary thrombophilia; ↑prothrombin mRNA stability → ↑FII levels → ↑risk DVT/PE.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Phosphatidylcholine (PC) is a major phospholipid in cell membranes. It is synthesized via the CDP-choline pathway (Kennedy pathway). The committed step is:
options: Choline kinase: choline + ATP → phosphocholine + ADP (choline kinase [CK, CHKA/CHKB] catalyzes the first step: choline → phosphocholine; this is not the committed step; CK phosphorylates choline but the product phosphocholine is a branch point [can also enter other pathways in some cells; however, in the CDP-choline pathway, the COMMITTED step is the next step: CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase])

CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase (CCT, PCYT1A): phosphocholine + CTP → CDP-choline + PPi: CDP-choline pathway (Kennedy pathway): choline → [CK] → phosphocholine → [CCT/PCYT1A] → CDP-choline → [CEPT1 or CPT1] → PC; CCT (CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase): rate-limiting + committed step of PC synthesis via CDP-choline pathway; PCYT1A (α isoform) + PCYT1B (β isoform); CCT is regulated by lipid activation: in cytosol (inactive, CCT-α soluble form) → translocates to membrane (ER, nuclear envelope) when lipid composition changes (↑DAG, ↑fatty acids, ↑PE, ↑diacylglycerol → CCT binds amphipathic helix-membrane interaction → ↑activity) → converts phosphocholine → CDP-choline (committed to PC synthesis); CCT is allosterically activated by: anionic lipids (PA, CL) + DAG + fatty acids → membrane binding → conformational change → ↑activity; also: phosphorylated by CK2 (casein kinase 2) → ↓activity; role: CCT is the 'sensor' of cellular need for PC; ↓PC → ↑DAG + ↑PA → CCT membrane association → ↑activity → restore PC; PCYT1A mutations → spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy (SMDCRD) — rare skeletal dysplasia; also: IPF (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis) → ↑PCYT1A in type II alveolar cells? (surfactant PC synthesis); lipid droplet biology: CCT is also recruited to lipid droplet (LD) surface to supply PC for LD monolayer expansion

Choline phosphotransferase: CDP-choline + DAG → PC + CMP (CPT1/CEPT1 [choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferase 1] catalyzes the last step: CDP-choline + DAG → PC + CMP; this is the final enzymatic step, not the committed step; the committed step is CCT)

Phospholipase D: PC → phosphatidic acid + choline (phospholipase D [PLD1/2] hydrolyzes PC → PA + free choline; this is a CATABOLIC step that generates PA [a signaling lipid]; it does not synthesize PC; PLD is not part of the Kennedy pathway synthesis)
explanation: Phospholipid metabolism — synthesis pathways: Major phospholipids: PC (phosphatidylcholine): ester of glycerol + 2 FA + phosphocholine; most abundant phospholipid in eukaryotic membranes (~50%); PE (phosphatidylethanolamine): ~25%; PI (phosphatidylinositol): ~5-10%; PS (phosphatidylserine): ~10%; PG (phosphatidylglycerol): mitochondrial + pulmonary surfactant; CL (cardiolipin, bis-PG): inner mitochondrial membrane (tightly associated with ETC complexes, especially complex I + III); MLCL (monolysocardiolipin)/tafazzin → Barth syndrome; SM (sphingomyelin): PC + ceramide [SMS1/2: transfers phosphocholine from PC to ceramide → SM + DAG]; PA (phosphatidic acid): central branch point of phospholipid synthesis; synthesis routes for PC: CDP-choline pathway (80% of PC synthesis, salvage of choline): Cho → phospho-Cho [CK] → CDP-Cho [CCT*] → PC [CPT1/CEPT1]; PEMT pathway (liver only, 20%): PE → PE-N-methyltransferase (PEMT) uses SAM × 3 → PC; important for liver PC in methionine/choline deficiency states; PEMT provides choline de novo (bypasses dietary choline requirement in liver); Landsmeer's rule: 'PEMT makes up the deficit' — when dietary choline is low, PEMT activity increases; PEMT KO mice → fatty liver (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, NASH) on choline-deficient diet + ↓plasma VLDL (PC needed for VLDL assembly/secretion by MTP [microsomal triglyceride transfer protein]). Lung surfactant PC: dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, 16:0/16:0-PC) = most abundant surface-active lipid in surfactant (reduces alveolar surface tension); synthesized in type II pneumocytes; surfactant protein A/B/C/D associate with DPPC; deficiency in NRDS (neonatal respiratory distress syndrome): premature lung → ↓type II cells → ↓surfactant → alveolar collapse; treatment: exogenous surfactant (beractant [Survanta: bovine derived], poractant alfa [Curosurf: porcine], calfactant [Infasurf]) + CPAP + oxygen.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hemoglobin's oxygen-binding curve is sigmoidal (S-shaped), unlike myoglobin's hyperbolic curve. This difference arises because:
options: Hemoglobin has a higher intrinsic O2 affinity than myoglobin at all O2 tensions (this is INCORRECT; myoglobin has HIGHER O2 affinity [lower P50, ~1 mmHg] than hemoglobin [P50 ~26 mmHg]; myoglobin binds O2 very tightly and does not release it until very low O2 tensions in exercising muscle)

Hemoglobin is a tetramer with cooperative O2 binding (allostery/cooperativity), while myoglobin is a monomer with non-cooperative binding: Myoglobin (Mb): single polypeptide + one heme → O2 binding = HYPERBOLIC: v = Vmax×[O2]/(P50 + [O2]) [Hill equation with n=1 = no cooperativity]; single O2 binding site → no allosteric communication; Hemoglobin (Hb): α2β2 tetramer → 4 heme groups → COOPERATIVE O2 binding (sigmoidal): when one heme binds O2 → conformation change (T→R transition, specifically: porphyrin ring flattens → Fe2+ moves into porphyrin plane → pulls proximal His (F8 His) → shifts F helix → moves α1-β2 interface → transmits to other subunits → ↑O2 affinity of remaining subunits); CONCERTED (MWC/Monod-Wyman-Changeux) model: Hb exists in T (taut/deoxy, low affinity) and R (relaxed/oxy, high affinity) states; O2 binding → stabilizes R state; SEQUENTIAL (KNF/Koshland-Nemethy-Filmer) model: O2 binding to one subunit → directly alters adjacent subunit affinity; real Hb: some elements of both; Hill coefficient (n): measure of cooperativity; Mb: n=1 (non-cooperative); normal Hb: n=2.7-3.0 (high cooperativity near P50); n=1 → hyperbolic; n>1 → sigmoidal; physiological significance of sigmoidal curve: at alveolar pO2 (~100 mmHg): Hb 97-98% saturated (near top of curve → loads O2 efficiently); at venous pO2 (~40 mmHg): Hb ~75% saturated → only ~25% of O2 unloaded (rest available for further exercise); at exercising muscle (~20 mmHg): Hb ~35% saturated → ~65% O2 unloaded → large delivery due to steep slope in physiological range; myoglobin: P50 ~1 mmHg → at muscle pO2 ~20 mmHg → Mb is >95% saturated → excellent O2 receiver from Hb; at extreme exercise → Mb P50 so low → only releases O2 at very low pO2 → O2 buffer for mitochondria

Hemoglobin contains iron in the Fe3+ state while myoglobin contains Fe2+ (normally BOTH Hb and Mb contain Fe2+ [ferrous iron] → can bind O2; Fe3+ [ferric, metHb/metMb] cannot bind O2 → formed by oxidation [nitrites, drugs] → methemoglobinemia; the Fe2+/Fe3+ state does not explain the curve shape difference)

Hemoglobin has a Bohr effect while myoglobin does not (the Bohr effect — right-shift of Hb O2 curve by ↑CO2 + ↑H+ — DOES apply to Hb but NOT Mb [Mb is a monomer without the T/R allosteric shift that mediates the Bohr effect]; HOWEVER, the PRIMARY reason for the sigmoidal curve is cooperativity/allostery from tetrameric structure; the Bohr effect modifies the Hb curve but it does not by itself explain why the curve is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic)
explanation: Hemoglobin allostery — complete: Allosteric effectors of Hb O2 affinity (all RIGHT-shift = ↓affinity = ↑O2 unloading at tissues): ↑H+ (↑CO2 from metabolism → H+ via carbonic anhydrase [CA: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3-]; H+ → binds β146 His + α122 His → stabilizes salt bridges → stabilizes T state → ↓O2 affinity → ↑O2 unloading at tissues = Bohr effect; Hb also buffers H+ [when Hb releases O2, becomes better base → accepts H+ → HbH+ → buffered]); ↑CO2 (direct: CO2 + Hb NH2 terminals → carbamino-Hb [HbNHCOO-]; T state stabilized); ↑2,3-BPG (binds central cavity of deoxy-Hb [T state]: Arg141, His143, Lys82 of β chains; ↑DPG → stabilize T state → ↓O2 affinity; ↑2,3-BPG in: high altitude, chronic anemia, COPD [to augment O2 delivery]; ↓2,3-BPG in: stored blood [blood bank storage → depleted; RBCs have no mitochondria but BPGM + PGAM → BPG from 1,3-BPG; storage → ↓BPG within 1-2 weeks → ↑O2 affinity of stored blood → less O2 delivered to tissues → '2,3-BPG depletion' of stored blood; additive solutions extend RBC viability and partially maintain 2,3-BPG]); ↑temperature (↑Temp → ↑O2 release → Hb delivers more O2 to hot tissues [exercising muscle]); LEFT-shift (↑O2 affinity → better loading but less unloading): HbF (γ-chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly → ↑O2 affinity → fetal blood takes O2 from maternal blood at placenta); HbH (β4 tetramer, α0-thal → no cooperativity, no 2,3-BPG binding → hyperbolic curve, very high O2 affinity → severe anemia because O2 not released to tissues despite near-normal saturation); ↓H+/↓CO2; CO (carbon monoxide): COHb: CO has 250× higher affinity for Hb than O2 → CO outcompetes O2; + COHb remaining O2-binding subunits SHIFT LEFT (↑O2 affinity of remaining sites → less O2 unloaded) = Haldane effect → double problem in CO poisoning; metHb (methemoglobinemia): oxidized Fe3+ → remaining Fe2+ subunits: ↑O2 affinity (left shift) → ↓O2 delivery despite near-normal SaO2 as measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2 falsely normal in metHb since pulse ox cannot distinguish COHb, metHb, OxyHb accurately).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the synthesis of UDP-glucuronic acid (UDP-GlcUA), which enzyme oxidizes UDP-glucose?
options: UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase (UGP2): UGP2 synthesizes UDP-glucose from glucose-1-P + UTP → UDP-Glc + PPi; NOT the enzyme that oxidizes UDP-glucose to UDP-GlcUA

UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT): UGTs conjugate glucuronic acid from UDP-GlcUA to aglycone substrates (bilirubin, drugs, hormones); NOT the enzyme that makes UDP-GlcUA; UGTs are the consumers, not the makers

UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase (UGDH): UDP-Glc + 2 NAD+ → [UGDH] → UDP-GlcUA + 2 NADH; UGDH (UDP-glucose 6-dehydrogenase, hexuronyl dehydrogenase): oxidizes C6 of glucose in UDP-glucose → UDP-glucuronic acid; requires 2 NAD+ → produces 2 NADH (two sequential NAD+-dependent oxidations: first → UDP-glucuronic aldehyde [intermediate], then → UDP-glucuronic acid); UDP-GlcUA is the activated form of glucuronic acid; functions of UDP-GlcUA: (1) Phase II drug metabolism: glucuronidation: UGT enzymes conjugate glucuronic acid from UDP-GlcUA to drugs, bilirubin, steroid hormones, bile acids → water-soluble glucuronide conjugates → excreted in bile or urine; most important phase II reaction (50% of drugs conjugated via glucuronidation); isoforms: UGT1A1 (bilirubin, CPT-11/SN-38, estradiol, NSAIDs), UGT1A4 (TCA [tricyclics], benzodiazepines), UGT2B7 (morphine→morphine-6-glucuronide [active analgesic metabolite] + morphine-3-glucuronide [inactive]), UGT2B15 (androgens); (2) Glycosaminoglycan (GAG) synthesis: glucuronic acid is a component of hyaluronic acid (HA), chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate → extracellular matrix; (3) Ascorbate synthesis: in most mammals (not humans/primates/guinea pigs): UDP-GlcUA → L-gulonolactone → L-ascorbic acid [via L-gulonolactone oxidase (GULO); GULO is MUTATED/absent in humans → cannot synthesize vitamin C]; UGDH inhibitor: UDP-xylose feedback-inhibits UGDH [UDP-xylose is made from UDP-GlcUA by UXS1 → then used for proteoglycan synthesis; ↑UDP-xylose → ↓UGDH → limits UDP-GlcUA production] → regulation of UDP-GlcUA availability

Glucuronidase (β-glucuronidase, GUS): GUS hydrolyzes glucuronide bonds → releases aglycone + GlcUA; it is a CATABOLIC enzyme in lysosomes (GUSB gene deficiency → Sly syndrome [MPS VII]); NOT the enzyme that makes UDP-GlcUA
explanation: UDP-glucuronic acid and glucuronidation: Phase I vs Phase II drug metabolism: Phase I (functionalization): CYP450 (mainly CYP3A4 > CYP2D6 > CYP2C9 > CYP2C19 > CYP2E1 > CYP1A2): oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis → introduce or expose reactive groups (OH, COOH, NH2, SH) → products may be more toxic than parent (CYP → reactive intermediate: acetaminophen → NAPQI [N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine] → toxic if excess; normally detoxified by GSH); Phase II (conjugation): glucuronidation (UGT1A/2B): most drugs → glucuronides → excretion; sulfation (SULT1A/2A): phenolic compounds + steroids; acetylation (NAT1/2): sulfonamides, isoniazid; GSH conjugation (GST, glutathione S-transferases): reactive epoxides, Michael acceptors; methylation (COMT, TPMT, HNMT); glycine conjugation: bile acids + benzoate → hippurate; enterohepatic circulation: glucuronides in bile → gut → β-glucuronidase (bacterial/mucosal) → aglycone released → reabsorbed (→ ↑effective drug half-life, e.g., estrogens, morphine, irinotecan); MPS (mucopolysaccharidoses): lysosomal enzyme deficiencies in GAG degradation: MPS I (Hurler/Scheie): α-L-iduronidase (IDUA) → dermatan + heparan sulfate ↑; MPS II (Hunter): iduronate-2-sulfatase (IDS); MPS III (Sanfilippo): various heparan sulfate hydrolases; MPS IV (Morquio): GALNS (N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase) or GLBV1 (β-galactosidase) → keratan + chondroitin sulfate; MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy): ARSB (N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase) → dermatan sulfate; MPS VII (Sly): GUSB (β-glucuronidase) → dermatan + heparan + chondroitin sulfate → presents with non-immune hydrops fetalis + dysostosis multiplex + hepatosplenomegaly; treatment: ERT (laronidase for MPS I, idursulfase for MPS II, elosulfase for MPS IVA, galsulfase for MPS VI) + HSCT (MPS I Hurler).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During translation of a protein destined for secretion, the ribosome is directed to the ER membrane. Which feature of the mRNA/protein determines ER targeting?
options: A stretch of acidic amino acids at the C-terminus (KDEL sequence: Lys-Asp-Glu-Leu is an ER RETENTION signal for soluble ER-resident proteins [HDEL in yeast]; it is at the C-terminus of SOME ER proteins; but it retains proteins in the ER, it does NOT direct the ribosome to the ER initially during synthesis)

A hydrophobic N-terminal signal sequence on the nascent peptide, recognized by SRP: Signal sequence (SS): N-terminal extension of secretory/membrane protein precursors; 15-30 amino acids; structure: (1) n-region (2-5 positively charged AA: +, +, +); (2) h-region (hydrophobic core: 7-15 hydrophobic AA: Leu, Val, Ile, Ala; ≥ 10 AA helix required for SRP recognition); (3) c-region (3-7 AA with small side chains at -1 and -3 positions of signal peptidase cleavage site [von Heijne rule: small neutral AA at -1/-3 → signal peptidase cleavage]; signal peptidase = SPC complex on ER lumen → cleaves after c-region → releases mature protein into ER lumen); SRP (signal recognition particle): 7SL RNA (Alu domain + S domain) + 6 proteins (SRP9, SRP14, SRP19, SRP54, SRP68, SRP72); SRP54 (NG domain + M domain) recognizes hydrophobic h-region of SS → SRP54 M domain binds h-region (hydrophobic groove) → translation elongation paused; SRP then GTP-dependent docking: SRP → SRP receptor (SR, α+β subunits) on ER membrane → SR-SRP GTPase activity → releases signal sequence → Sec61 translocon (Sec61α/β/γ) inserts in ER membrane → co-translational translocation of growing peptide into ER lumen; Sec61 forms protein-conducting channel (PCC) → gate opens for signal anchor/transmembrane domains or passes hydrophilic loops into lumen; signal peptidase (SPC: SEC11/SPC12/SPC18/SPC22/SPC25) → cleaves SS → mature protein; ribosome anchored to translocon during translation → co-translational → DURING synthesis (not post-translational); mammals: also post-translational translocation via SEC62/SEC63 complex (for short or post-translation signal sequences); differences: yeast has both; most mammalian SS → SRP-dependent

A poly-A tail at the 3' end of the mRNA (the poly-A tail is present on virtually all eukaryotic mRNAs and is involved in mRNA stability + translation initiation, not ER targeting; poly-A tail does not code for any signal sequence)
An m7G cap structure at the 5' end of the mRNA (the 5' cap is also universal on eukaryotic mRNAs; involved in cap-dependent translation initiation via eIF4E binding; not a signal for ER targeting)
explanation: Protein sorting signals — summary: ER import (co-translational): N-terminal signal sequence (SS) → SRP → Sec61 translocon → lumen or membrane; ER retention: KDEL (soluble luminal proteins: BiP/GRP78, PDI, GRP94, ERp57) → binds KDEL receptor (KDELR1/2/3) in Golgi → retrograde COPI transport → ER; KKXX motif (cytoplasmic tail of Type I membrane proteins) → COPI retrieval to ER. Nuclear import: classical nuclear localization signal (NLS): mono-partite (PKKKRKV of SV40 T antigen, basic residues) or bi-partite (2 stretches of basic AA separated by linker); recognized by importin-α (KPNA family, cargo-binding) + importin-β (KPNB1, RanGAP-activation) → RanGTP in nucleus → cargo release → importin export. Nuclear export: nuclear export signal (NES): hydrophobic leucine-rich export signal (LxxLxL motif); recognized by CRM1/exportin 1 (XPO1) + RanGTP → nuclear export; leptomycin B inhibits CRM1 → prevents NES-mediated export. Peroxisome import: PTS1 (peroxisomal targeting signal 1): C-terminal tripeptide (-SKL or variants like -SQL, -ANL, -PQL, -SRL, etc.) → recognized by PEX5 (cytoplasmic receptor) → PEX5 → docking complex (PEX13/14) → import; PTS2: N-terminal 9-mer motif → PEX7 receptor; PEROXIN genes (PEX1-26): >12 PEX mutations → Zellweger spectrum disorders (ZSD): PEX1 most common (70%) → Zellweger syndrome (most severe: liver failure + neurodegeneration + VLCFAs ↑ + phytanic acid ↑ + VLCFA ↑ + ↓plasmalogens), neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy (NALD), infantile Refsum disease (IRD). Mitochondrial import: MTS (mitochondrial targeting sequence): N-terminal amphipathic helix (alternating +/hydrophobic; forms helix with positive face on one side); TOM/TIM complexes (translocase of outer/inner membrane) → matrix or IMS or IMM; MPP (mitochondrial processing peptidase) → cleaves MTS → mature protein.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with sickle cell disease develops an aplastic crisis. The most likely cause is infection with parvovirus B19. Parvovirus B19 infects erythroid precursors via its receptor. The receptor for parvovirus B19 is:
options: CD4 (CD4 is the primary receptor for HIV-1 [gp120] + co-receptors CCR5/CXCR4 → CD4+ T cells and macrophages [CCR5 as co-receptor]; CD4 is NOT the parvovirus B19 receptor)

Globoside (Gb4Cer, blood group P antigen, P1PK blood group P antigen): Parvovirus B19 (B19V, genus Erythroparvovirus): primary receptor = globoside (Gb4Cer = blood group P [P1PK antigen P]): globoside is a neutral glycosphingolipid: GalNAcβ1-3Galα1-4Galβ1-4Glc-Cer; blood group P system (P1PK): individuals lacking P antigen (p phenotype, very rare) are naturally resistant to B19V infection; B19V targets erythroid precursors (BFU-E, CFU-E, pronormoblasts) because: (1) globoside is abundantly expressed on erythroid progenitors; (2) co-receptors: Ku80 autoantigen + αVβ5 integrin (facilitate viral entry after globoside binding); B19V clinical syndromes: erythema infectiosum (fifth disease): children → lacy rash (reticulate exanthem) + 'slapped cheek' appearance; fifth disease in pregnancy: B19V infection in pregnant woman (especially 9-20 weeks) → hydrops fetalis (B19V infects fetal erythroid progenitors → severe fetal anemia → high-output cardiac failure → ascites + edema → hydrops) → fetal loss; no vaccine available; treatment: IVIG for immunocompromised patients with chronic B19 infection (→ pure red cell aplasia [PRCA] with chronic anemia); hemolytic anemia patients (SCD, thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis): B19V infects erythroid precursors → transient aplastic crisis (TAC): abrupt halt in RBC production → severe anemia + reticulocytopenia (profound) → life-threatening in patients already hemolytic; normal adults: self-limited → reticulocyte nadir at day 10, recovery by day 17; immunocompromised: chronic B19 infection → persistent PRCA

ICAM-1 (intercellular adhesion molecule 1): ICAM-1 (CD54) is the receptor for rhinovirus (major group rhinoviruses use ICAM-1; minor group use LDLR [LDL receptor]); ICAM-1 is also used by Plasmodium falciparum (cytoadherence); NOT the parvovirus B19 receptor

GD1a ganglioside: GD1a is a receptor for influenza virus HA (hemagglutinin); influenza preferentially binds α2,3-SA (avian, GD1a/sialylated glycoprotein) or α2,6-SA (human, predominantly on tracheal epithelium); NOT the B19 parvovirus receptor
explanation: Glycosphingolipid (GSL) receptors for pathogens: GSLs as microbial receptors: Globoside (Gb4, P antigen): parvovirus B19; GM1: cholera toxin (CT B-subunit); LT (E. coli heat-labile toxin B-subunit) also uses GM1 (similar to CT); Gb3 (globotriaosylceramide, CD77, Pk antigen): verotoxin (Shiga toxin, VTEC/STEC: Shiga-toxin producing E. coli; e.g., O157:H7 → HUS [hemolytic uremic syndrome]); Gb3 expressed on renal tubular cells + glomerular capillary endothelium (kidney) + brain cells → Gb3 distribution explains why STEC HUS damages kidney + CNS; Shiga toxin: also receptor for Gb3 is abundantly expressed in children (P1PK antigens expressed earlier in development) → explains why HUS predominantly in children; also: Fabry disease (GLA deficiency → Gb3 accumulates, but this is enzyme deficiency in catabolism, not pathogen receptor); Sialyl-Lea (sialyl-Lewis A) and Sialyl-Lex: P-selectin/E-selectin ligands (leukocyte rolling); CD44 (HA-binding): receptor for many pathogens (H. pylori→ CD44); Neu5Ac (N-acetylneuraminic acid, sialic acid): receptor for influenza (α2,3- or α2,6-linked; hemagglutinin [HA] types: H1, H3 in seasonal flu prefer α2,6-SA on human upper respiratory epithelium; H5N1 [avian] prefers α2,3-SA on bird intestinal/respiratory epithelium; low binding to human α2,6-SA → poor human-to-human transmission; H5N1 mutations required for α2,6-SA binding → pandemic potential). Parvovirus B19 biology: ss linear DNA virus; 5.5 kb; very small (20 nm); obligate host: humans (erythroid progenitors); limited host range (primates only); no reverse transcriptase (linear ssDNA genome → dsDNA in nucleus by host DNA pol); NS1 protein: initiates rolling hairpin replication + transactivates gene expression; VP1 + VP2 (capsid proteins): VP1 has N-terminal unique region (VP1u) with phospholipase A2 (PLA2)-like activity → required for pore formation during endosome escape + viral uncoating.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient has hyperuricemia with gout and is treated with allopurinol. Allopurinol is a substrate analog of hypoxanthine and is metabolized by xanthine oxidase (XO) to alloxanthine (oxypurinol). Alloxanthine inhibits XO by:
options: Competitive inhibition with ATP at the adenylate site (alloxanthine does NOT inhibit XO competitively with ATP; it inhibits XO at the molybdenum center in a mechanism-based manner)

Irreversible covalent modification of the XO active-site cysteine (alloxanthine does NOT form a covalent bond with a cysteine; it is a tightly-bound non-covalent inhibitor; XO uses a molybdenum center, not an active-site cysteine [which is for thiol-dependent enzymes like caspases, cysteine proteases])

Mechanism-based (suicide) inhibition: allopurinol is first oxidized by XO to alloxanthine (oxypurinol) which remains tightly bound at the molybdenum (Mo) center of XO, inhibiting further XO activity: allopurinol (4-hydroxypyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine): hypoxanthine structural analog (isomer: N7 and C8 of hypoxanthine → C7 and N8 in allopurinol pyrazolo ring); MECHANISM: XO catalyzes allopurinol → alloxanthine [Mo6+ in XO reduced to Mo4+ during the reaction + alloxanthine generated → alloxanthine remains tightly but non-covalently bound to the Mo4+ form of XO at the active site → XO cannot complete catalytic cycle (Mo4+ → Mo6+ re-oxidation is blocked) → XO inactivated]; THIS IS A MECHANISM-BASED (SUICIDE) INHIBITOR: the drug (allopurinol) must be METABOLIZED BY THE TARGET ENZYME (XO) to form the ACTIVE INHIBITOR (alloxanthine) → alloxanthine is so tightly bound (Ki ~0.01 nM for reduced XO) it functions as essentially irreversible inhibitor; the XO activity can only recover when: (a) alloxanthine slowly dissociates (t1/2 ~300 min) or (b) new XO is synthesized; alloxanthine: plasma half-life ~18-30 hours → once-daily dosing of allopurinol; clinical use: gout (↓uric acid production); also used in chemotherapy (prevents tumor lysis syndrome hyperuricemia in children [rasburicase used in higher risk patients]); side effects: allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS): HLA-B*58:01 (Han Chinese, Thai, Korean) → severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR): DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms) + SJS/TEN; all patients of Han Chinese/Thai/Korean ancestry should be HLA-B*58:01 screened before allopurinol; febuxostat: non-purine XO inhibitor (2-[3-cyano-4-(2-methylpropoxy)phenyl]-4-methylthiazole-5-carboxylic acid) → binds in a different channel of Mo active site → does not require metabolic activation; different toxicity profile (no HLA-B*58:01 issue)

Allosteric inhibition at a regulatory site distant from the active site (alloxanthine inhibits XO by direct interaction with the molybdenum cofactor center at the active site after being generated from allopurinol; it is not an allosteric inhibitor at a remote site)
explanation: Mechanism-based (suicide) inhibitors — biochemistry: Mechanism-based inhibition (MBI) = suicide inhibition: the drug is an unreactive 'pro-inhibitor' → processed by target enzyme → generates reactive species that irreversibly (or tightly) inhibits the enzyme; distinguishing features: requires catalytic turnover of drug by enzyme; inhibition is time-dependent (t50% ↓ with time pre-incubation); excess substrate protects (substrate competes with drug for the enzyme during turnover); irreversibility (or very slow recovery); 'kinact/KI' ratio: key potency parameter for MBI (ratio of inactivation rate constant to apparent inhibitory constant). Clinical examples of MBI (suicide inhibitors): Allopurinol → alloxanthine: XO MBI (see above, gout). Aspirin (acetylsalicylate): acetylates Ser530 of COX-1 (+ Ser516 of COX-2 at higher doses) → irreversible covalent inhibition → platelets (no nucleus → cannot synthesize new COX-1) → ↓TXA2 → ↓platelet aggregation → 1 aspirin lasts platelet lifetime (7-10 days); aspirin is IRREVERSIBLE (not true mechanism-based since Ser530 acetylation is direct without enzymatic processing, but similar concept). Eflornithine (DFMO, α-difluoromethylornithine): ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) MBI → ↓polyamine synthesis (putrescine/spermidine/spermine) → used for African sleeping sickness (HAT, Trypanosoma brucei gambiense) + topical for unwanted facial hair. 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) → FdUMP: thymidylate synthase (TS) MBI: FdUMP + 5,10-methylene-THF → ternary complex with TS → TS inhibited. Vigabatrin (γ-vinyl GABA): GABA-aminotransferase (GABA-T) MBI: γ-vinyl GABA binds PLP in active site → forms Michael adduct → GABA-T inactivated → ↓GABA breakdown → ↑GABA → ↓seizures (used in infantile spasms + refractory partial epilepsy). Phenelzine/tranylcypromine: MAO-A + MAO-B MBI (oxidized by MAO → reactive alkylating intermediate → covalent inactivation); irreversible MAOIs vs reversible (moclobemide: MAO-A reversible inhibitor, RIMA). Clopidogrel/prasugrel/ticagrelor: clopidogrel + prasugrel = prodrugs metabolized by CYP2C19 → thiol metabolite → covalently alkylates P2Y12 receptor ADP-binding site (not enzyme suicide, but analogous irreversible receptor inhibition; ticagrelor = direct, reversible P2Y12 inhibitor; no CYP activation required).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Hartnup disorder is a rare autosomal recessive condition caused by a defect in neutral amino acid transport in the small intestine and kidney. The biochemical consequence that leads to clinical features (cerebellar ataxia + pellagra-like skin rash) is:
options: Accumulation of excess tryptophan in the intestinal lumen causing toxicity (in Hartnup, tryptophan is NOT absorbed → it is metabolized by intestinal bacteria → indole derivatives → excreted in urine; it does not accumulate intracellularly as a toxin)

Deficient tryptophan absorption → reduced tryptophan availability → reduced NAD+ synthesis (since tryptophan is a precursor for NAD+ via the kynurenine pathway): SLC6A19 (also called B0AT1, neutral amino acid transporter 1) encodes the brush border apical membrane transporter for neutral amino acids (including tryptophan [Trp], alanine, leucine, isoleucine, valine, phenylalanine, histidine) in small intestine + proximal tubule (kidney); Hartnup disorder (OMIM 234500): mutations in SLC6A19 → ↓intestinal absorption of neutral AA (especially Trp [since Trp is entirely neutral at physiological pH; other large neutral AA also affected]) → ↓blood Trp → ↓Trp available for: (1) NAD+/niacin synthesis (kynurenine pathway: Trp → IDO1/IDO2/TDO2 → N-formylkynurenine → kynurenine → 3-OH-kynurenine → ACMSD → quinolinate → QPRTase → NaMN → NAD+; normally provides ~50% of NAD+ from Trp [dietary niacin provides rest]; in Hartnup: ↓Trp → ↓NAD+ synthesis via this route → functional NAD+ deficiency → PELLAGRA-LIKE PICTURE: 4 D's of pellagra [dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death; in Hartnup: mainly photosensitive rash + ataxia]); (2) Serotonin synthesis (Trp → [TPH1/TPH2, tryptophan hydroxylase, BH4] → 5-hydroxytryptophan → [AADC, aromatic AA decarboxylase, PLP] → serotonin [5-HT]); (3) melatonin synthesis; cerebellar ataxia: possibly ↓serotonin/NAD+ in cerebellar neurons → Purkinje cell dysfunction → ataxia; diagnosis: urine: ↑neutral aminoaciduria (Trp + other neutral AA); stool: ↑indole compounds (from intestinal bacterial metabolism of unabsorbed Trp → indole → absorbed → converted to indican + excreted in urine → 'blue diaper syndrome' or similar indoluria); plasma AA: NORMAL or slightly low for neutral AA; clinical: intermittent cerebellar ataxia + photosensitive skin rash (like pellagra) + psychiatric symptoms; triggered by: sun exposure, fever, poor diet (low protein → ↓AA intake → worse); treatment: high-protein diet + nicotinic acid (niacin) supplementation → bypasses need for Trp-derived NAD+; skin: sunscreen; prognosis: generally good with treatment

Deficient absorption of all amino acids causing protein malnutrition (Hartnup specifically affects NEUTRAL amino acid transport; basic amino acids [Lys, Arg] are transported via SLC7A9/SLC3A1 [cystinuria transporter, different disease]; Hartnup does NOT affect all AA, only neutral AA; and the clinical picture is specifically due to Trp deficiency → NAD+ deficiency, not just generalized protein malnutrition)

Elevated blood cysteine and ornithine causing toxicity (elevated cystine + other dibasic AA = cystinuria [SLC7A9/SLC3A1 mutations]; Hartnup involves neutral AA [not cystine]; the transport defects are in different transporters)
explanation: Amino acid transport disorders — comparison: Cystinuria (OMIM 220100): SLC3A1 (rBAT) + SLC7A9 (BAT1) = b0,+AT-rBAT transporter complex; defect in intestinal + renal tubular reabsorption of DIBASIC amino acids (Cys, Orn, Lys, Arg — COLA mnemonic); most important: CYSTINE (Cys-Cys disulfide, poorly soluble) → cystine kidney stones (radiopaque, hexagonal crystals in urine) → recurrent nephrolithiasis from childhood; urine cyanide-nitroprusside test: positive (qualitative cystine test); treatment: high fluid intake, alkaline urine (Na bicarbonate → ↑cystine solubility [more ionized at pH >7.5]), D-penicillamine (chelates cystine → more soluble), tiopronin (thiol → forms tiopronin-cysteine mixed disulfide, more soluble); note: despite dibasic AA malabsorption, plasma AA relatively normal (other compensatory mechanisms); Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI; SLC7A7/y+LAT1 mutations): intestinal + renal defect for basic AA (Lys, Orn, Arg) → ↓plasma Lys/Orn/Arg → urea cycle impaired (↓Orn + Arg → ↓urea cycle flux → ↑NH4+ → hyperammonemia after protein meals) + ↓Lys → impaired collagen cross-linking + ↑Gln absorption → pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (Gln → Glu in pulmonary macrophages → ↑Glu → ↑reactive oxygen); clinical: protein aversion, post-prandial hyperammonemia, hepatosplenomegaly, osteoporosis, interstitial lung disease; treatment: low-protein diet + citrulline supplementation (Cit is not a dibasic AA → absorbed via different transporter → supports Orn + Arg supply for urea cycle). Iminoglycinuria: SLC36A2 (IMINO) + SLC6A20 defects → ↓reabsorption of Pro, Hyp, Gly; generally benign (no clinical symptoms in most). Blue diaper syndrome (congenital selective malabsorption of tryptophan — Drummond syndrome): SLC6A19? [in some patients] → ↑unabsorbed Trp → bacterial conversion to indole → intestinal oxidation → indigo (blue dye) → blue diaper discoloration.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In porphyrin synthesis, which enzyme catalyzes the FIRST step in the CYTOPLASM (after the initial delta-aminolevulinic acid [ALA] synthesis in the mitochondria)?
options: Porphobilinogen synthase (PBGS, ALA dehydratase): 2 ALA → [PBGS, also called ALA dehydratase or ALA-D] → porphobilinogen (PBG) + 2 H2O; this is the SECOND step overall (first cytoplasmic step); ALA made in mitochondria (by ALAS) → ALA exported to cytoplasm → PBGS in cytoplasm: condensation of 2 ALA molecules → porphobilinogen (pyrrole ring with acetic + propionic side chains); PBGS: zinc-dependent enzyme (Zn2+); inhibited by: LEAD (Pb2+): Pb replaces Zn → ↓PBGS → ↑ALA accumulates (↑urine ALA is a marker of lead poisoning) + ↓PBG and ↓heme; also: PBGS porphyria (rare, ALA dehydratase-deficient porphyria = ADP): PBGS gene mutations → ↑ALA accumulation → neurological symptoms (ALA is neurotoxic); also: hereditary tyrosinemia type I (fumarylacetoacetate accumulates → succinylacetone [chemical analog of ALA] → potent PBGS inhibitor → secondary porphyria-like picture); this is the FIRST CYTOPLASMIC STEP; ALAS is in MITOCHONDRIA (first step overall)

ALA synthase (ALAS): ALAS1 (ubiquitous, housekeeping) + ALAS2 (erythroid, X-linked): mitochondrial matrix enzyme (not cytoplasmic); Gly + succinyl-CoA → [ALAS + PLP] → ALA (delta-aminolevulinic acid) + CO2 + CoA; ALAS2 deficiency → X-linked sideroblastic anemia (XLSA): ring sideroblasts in bone marrow (iron deposits in mitochondria as RING around nucleus because mitochondrial iron accumulates when heme synthesis fails); responds to pyridoxine (PLP) supplementation in some patients; ALAS1 inhibited by heme (feedback inhibition); ALA synthesis is the COMMITTED STEP of heme synthesis; but ALAS is MITOCHONDRIAL, not cytoplasmic

Ferrochelatase (FECH): FECH is in the INNER MITOCHONDRIAL MEMBRANE (final step of heme synthesis, last step back in mitochondria); inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX → heme; FECH is NOT cytoplasmic; FECH deficiency → erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP): protoporphyrin IX accumulates → photosensitivity (pain, burning, swelling with light exposure; no blistering unlike PCT); X-linked dominant EPP (XLPP): ALAS2 gain-of-function mutations → ↑protoporphyrin (not EPP caused by FECH loss)

Uroporphyrinogen III synthase (UROS): UROS is in the CYTOPLASM (step 4 of heme synthesis); condenses 4 PBG molecules (from HMB [hydroxymethylbilane]) into uroporphyrinogen III (the physiological isomer); UROS deficiency → congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP, Günther disease): accumulation of uroporphyrin I (wrong isomer: I-isomer, uroporphyrinogen I, made spontaneously without UROS) → pink urine + severe photosensitivity + hemolytic anemia + red teeth (erythrodontia) → treatment: HSCT (most severe form), strict photoprotection
explanation: Heme synthesis steps — complete compartmentalization: MITOCHONDRIA (inner matrix): Step 1: Gly + succinyl-CoA → [ALAS1/2 + PLP] → ALA → CYTOPLASM: Step 2: 2 ALA → [PBGS/ALA-D, Zn2+] → porphobilinogen (PBG) → Step 3: 4 PBG → [HMBS/PBGD, hydroxymethylbilane synthase, porphobilinogen deaminase] → hydroxymethylbilane (HMB, preuroporphyrinogen) + 4 NH3 → Step 4: HMB → [UROS] → uroporphyrinogen III → Step 5: Uroporphyrinogen III → [UROD, uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase] → coproporphyrinogen III (removes 4 acetate → 4 methyl groups) → MITOCHONDRIA: Step 6: Coproporphyrinogen III → [CPOX, coproporphyrinogen III oxidase] → protoporphyrinogen IX + CO2 → Step 7: Protoporphyrinogen IX → [PPOX, protoporphyrinogen oxidase] → protoporphyrin IX + 6H → Step 8: Protoporphyrin IX + Fe2+ → [FECH, ferrochelatase] → heme. Porphyrias — summary: ADP (ALA-D/PBGS porphyria): PBGS mut; ↑ALA; acute neuropathic; very rare. AIP (acute intermittent porphyria): HMBS/PBGD mut (haploinsufficiency); ↑ALA + ↑PBG; NO skin; acute neuropsychiatric; AD; most common acute porphyria in most regions; triggers: drugs (P450 inducers: rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates), starvation, hormones (estrogen/progesterone, explains why attacks postovulatory); treatment: IV heme (hematin, heme arginate) → ↑ALAS1 negative feedback → ↓ALA accumulation; IV glucose + high caloric intake; avoid triggers. VP (variegate porphyria): PPOX mut; ↑ALA + ↑PBG + ↑porphyrins; BOTH acute + cutaneous; AD; South African founding mutation (R59W). HCP (hereditary coproporphyria): CPOX mut; ↑ALA + ↑PBG + ↑coproporphyrin III; BOTH acute + mild cutaneous; AD. PCT (porphyria cutanea tarda): UROD mut (familial) or acquired (alcohol + iron + HCV + estrogen → UROD inhibition by uroporphomethene); ↑uroporphyrin in urine (tea/wine-colored); photosensitivity + bullae + hypertrichosis + fragile skin; NO acute attacks; treatment: phlebotomy (↓iron → ↓UROD inhibition) + hydroxychloroquine. CEP (congenital erythropoietic porphyria): UROS mut; ↑uroporphyrin I; severe cutaneous + hemolytic anemia; AR. EPP (erythropoietic protoporphyria): FECH mut; ↑protoporphyrin IX; photosensitivity (painful, NO blistering); liver disease (protoporphyrin IX precipitates in bile ducts). X-linked EPP (XLPP): ALAS2 GOF mut; very high erythrocyte protoporphyrin.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Homocysteine accumulates in homocystinuria. The most common form of homocystinuria is caused by a deficiency of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS). CBS catalyzes:
options: Homocysteine + NADPH → methionine (methionine synthesis from homocysteine via methionine synthase [MTR] requires B12 + methylTHF, NOT NADPH; this is the remethylation pathway, not the transsulfuration pathway)

Serine + homocysteine → cystathionine: CBS (cystathionine β-synthase): condensation reaction: Hcy + Ser → cystathionine + H2O; cofactor: PLP (pyridoxal-5'-phosphate, vitamin B6); activated by: SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) allosterically activates CBS → ↑flux through transsulfuration when SAM is abundant (positive effector); heme (CBS has N-terminal heme domain; heme bound to His65 + Cys52 → structural/regulatory role; CO + NO can bind heme → may regulate CBS activity); CBS is a unique enzyme in that it has BOTH PLP (catalytic, C-terminal) AND heme (N-terminal regulatory); also note: CBS alternative reaction (minor): Hcy + Hcy → cystathionine (self-condensation); Hcy + cysteine → cystathionine + H2O (less common); Transsulfuration pathway: CBS → cystathionine → [CGL, cystathionase, also PLP-dependent] → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate + NH3 → cysteine + taurine [via CDO1 + sulfoalinine decarboxylase, ADO2, etc.] or cysteine → [GSH synthesis: GCL + GS] → glutathione; CBS deficiency (classic homocystinuria, OMIM 236200): AR; ↑plasma Hcy (>100 µmol/L) + ↑urinary Hcy + ↑Met (not cleared via transsulfuration → Met accumulates too); Hcy-thioglycolate crystals in urine → Nitroprusside test POSITIVE (cyanide-nitroprusside: urine + NaCN + NaOH → purple/magenta with thiol-containing compounds, including Hcy + cystine in cystinuria); clinical: Marfan-like appearance (lens dislocation [ectopia lentis] DOWNWARD [in Marfan: upward = toward 12 o'clock; in homocystinuria: downward = toward 6 o'clock + nasal] + tall, long limbs) + intellectual disability + seizures + thromboembolism (Hcy damages endothelium → promotes thrombus formation; ↑risk DVT + arterial thrombosis → stroke, MI) + osteoporosis; pyridoxine-responsive (~50% of patients): high-dose B6 → ↑residual CBS activity (B6 is cofactor; some mutant CBS has ↓affinity for PLP → pharmacological PLP restores activity); treatment: pyridoxine (if responsive) + low-methionine diet + betaine (trimethylglycine: Hcy + betaine → Met + dimethylglycine via BHMT [betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase] → ↓Hcy) + folate + B12 (remethylation pathway support)

Methionine + ATP → S-adenosylmethionine (SAM synthesis from methionine + ATP is catalyzed by MAT [methionine adenosyltransferase, MAT1A in liver / MAT2A elsewhere]; NOT by CBS; SAM is actually an ACTIVATOR of CBS, not a product)
explanation: Methionine cycle and one-carbon metabolism: Methionine → SAM → SAH → Hcy: SAM synthase (MAT): Met + ATP → SAM (major methyl donor: ~80 reactions, most important: DNA methylation [DNMT], histone methylation [HMTs], phosphatidylcholine [PEMT], creatine [GAMT], epinephrine [PNMT]); SAM → SAH after methyl transfer; SAH → [SAHH, SAH hydrolase] → Hcy + adenosine; Hcy fate: (1) REMETHYLATION → Met: MTR/MS + MeCbl + 5-methylTHF → Met (all tissues); BHMT (betaine-Hcy methyltransferase) + betaine → Met (liver only); (2) TRANSSULFURATION → Cys: CBS (B6) → cystathionine → CGL (B6) → Cys + α-ketobutyrate; Hcy is the 'toxin': damages endothelium (oxidative stress + ↑homocysteine thiolactone → carbamylation of protein Lys residues → ↑protein damage → foam cells in coronary arteries); ↑Hcy > 15 µmol/L = hyperhomocysteinemia → ↑CVD risk + thrombosis + neurological (Alzheimer risk); causes of elevated Hcy: B12 deficiency (↓MTR activity); folate deficiency (↓5-methylTHF → ↓MTR) [most common nutritional]; CBS deficiency (transsulfuration blocked); MTHFR mutations (especially 677C>T → thermolabile MTHFR → ↓5-methylTHF → ↑Hcy); renal failure (↓Hcy clearance); drugs (MTX blocks DHFR → ↓THF→↓methylene-THF→↓5-methyl-THF; also: metformin → ↓B12 absorption → ↑Hcy; nitrous oxide → irreversibly oxidizes MeCbl → ↓MTR activity → ↑Hcy); treatment of hyperhomocysteinemia: folate + B12 + B6 (supplements); betaine (BHMT-mediated remethylation); despite ↓Hcy with B vitamins, clinical CVD outcomes have not consistently improved in trials (HOPE-2, NORVIT, VISP) → suggests Hcy is a marker not cause, or other mechanisms.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a serine protease secreted by hepatocytes. Its gain-of-function mutations cause hypercholesterolemia because PCSK9:
options: Directly degrades apoB-100 on LDL particles in the blood (PCSK9 does NOT degrade apoB-100 in the bloodstream; PCSK9 binds to the LDL receptor on the hepatocyte surface → promotes receptor degradation; it does not cleave apoB)

Binds to LDL receptors on the hepatocyte surface and promotes their degradation in lysosomes: PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin 9): serine protease (S1P kexin family); primarily secreted by liver; structure: prodomain + catalytic domain + C-terminal CHRD (cysteine/histidine-rich domain); prodomain is NOT cleaved off (unlike most proprotein convertases: prodomain cleaved intracellularly by autocatalytic process but remains non-covalently associated → inactive until released); mechanism: PCSK9 → binds EGF-A domain of LDL-R on hepatocyte PM → PCSK9-LDL-R complex → clathrin-mediated endocytosis → endosome → pH drops → normally LDL-R releases LDL → LDL-R recycles back to PM (repeated ~150 cycle/receptor lifetime); with PCSK9 bound: at low endosomal pH, PCSK9 binds LDL-R even MORE tightly (affinity increases 50-fold at pH 5.4 vs pH 7.4) → LDL-R cannot recycle → directed to lysosome → lysosomal proteolysis (mainly cathepsin D) → LDL-R degraded; net effect: ↓surface LDL-R → ↓LDL clearance → ↑plasma LDL-C; GOF mutations (e.g., D374Y, S127R, F216L): ↑PCSK9 secretion or ↑PCSK9-LDL-R affinity → more receptor degradation → ↑LDL; LOF mutations (e.g., Y142X, C679X in African-Americans): ↑surface LDL-R → ↓LDL (~40%) → ↓ASCVD risk (genome-wide validation of LDL-ASCVD causality); PCSK9 inhibitors: evolocumab (Repatha) + alirocumab (Praluent): human IgG2 anti-PCSK9 mAbs → block PCSK9-LDL-R interaction → ↑LDL-R recycling → ↓LDL up to 60%; SC injection every 2-4 weeks; inclisiran (Leqvio): siRNA → hepatic PCSK9 mRNA knockdown → ↓PCSK9 protein → ↑LDL-R → ↓LDL ~50%; every 6 months dosing; lerodalcibep: small protein binder of PCSK9 (monthly); bempedoic acid: ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY) inhibitor → ↓hepatic acetyl-CoA → ↓cholesterol synthesis → SREBP-2 → ↑LDL-R (liver-specific: activated by ACSL1 in liver but not muscle → avoids myopathy seen with statins)

Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing cholesterol synthesis (HMGCR is inhibited by statins, not PCSK9; PCSK9 affects LDL receptor degradation, not cholesterol biosynthesis directly; statins → ↑PCSK9 expression [SREBP-2 upregulates both LDLR and PCSK9] → this is why PCSK9 inhibitors + statins are synergistic)

Activates SREBP-1c in the nucleus to promote lipogenesis (PCSK9 does not directly activate SREBP-1c; PCSK9 works at the hepatocyte cell surface on the LDL receptor; SREBP-1c is regulated by insulin and liver X receptor [LXR])
explanation: Cholesterol metabolism regulation — SCAP-SREBP-LDL-R axis: When cellular cholesterol is LOW: ER cholesterol ↓ → SCAP (SREBP cleavage activating protein) is NOT bound to INSIG1/2 (INSIG = insulin-induced gene; INSIG senses cholesterol and oxysterols; normally when ↑cholesterol → INSIG binds SCAP → SCAP-SREBP2 retained in ER) → SCAP-SREBP2 can traffic to Golgi → S1P (site-1 protease; MBTPS1) cleaves luminal loop of SREBP-2 → S2P (site-2 protease; MBTPS2) cleaves transmembrane domain → SREBP-2 N-terminal bHLH transcription factor released → nuclear entry → binds SRE (sterol regulatory element: ATCACCCCAC) → ↑LDLR + ↑HMGCR + ↑SQLE + ↑PCSK9 + ↑ABCG5/8 (bile acid/cholesterol excretion); statin mechanism (again): statins → ↓mevalonate → ↓cholesterol → ↓INSIG binding → ↑SCAP-SREBP2 → ↑LDL-R (net: ↑LDL clearance, primary effect) + ↑PCSK9 (partial counter); PCSK9 inhibitors added to statins → prevent statin-induced PCSK9 upregulation → greater LDL-R activity → ↓LDL further. Apolipoprotein B (apoB): VLDL assembly: apoB-100 (full-length, 4536 AA, liver) + MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) → lipidation of apoB → VLDL; intestinal: apoB-48 (N-terminal 48% of apoB-100, from RNA editing by APOBEC1 [stops codon for CAA→UAA at codon 2153]) → chylomicrons; familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (FHBL): apoB mutations → ↓apoB → ↓VLDL + ↓LDL; abetalipoproteinemia: MTP mutations → cannot lipidated apoB → no VLDL or chylomicrons → fat malabsorption + retinitis pigmentosa + ataxia (spinocerebellar degeneration from vitamin E malabsorption) + acanthocytosis; lomitapide (Juxtapid): MTP inhibitor → ↓VLDL → used for HoFH.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient has severe recurrent episodes of rhabdomyolysis with elevated CPK, myoglobinuria, and muscle pain triggered by prolonged exercise or fasting. Between episodes he is asymptomatic. The most likely diagnosis is deficiency of:
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase): G6Pase deficiency = GSD type Ia (von Gierke disease): presents with hypoglycemia + hepatomegaly + hyperlipidemia + hyperuricemia in infancy; NO rhabdomyolysis (G6Pase is in the liver/kidney/intestine, NOT in muscle); exercise-triggered rhabdomyolysis involves muscle energy metabolism enzymes

Lipoprotein lipase (LPL): LPL deficiency → chylomicronemia (hypertriglyceridemia type I) → pancreatitis; NOT rhabdomyolysis; LPL is extracellular (on capillary endothelium) and does not affect muscle energy production during exercise

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I or II (CPT I or CPT II): exercise/fasting → ↑need for FA oxidation in muscle → CPT II deficiency → long-chain FA cannot enter mitochondria for β-oxidation → muscle energy failure → myoglobinuria + rhabdomyolysis: FAO is the PRIMARY fuel for sustained aerobic exercise (especially > 30 min); fasting → ↑FAO in muscle (glycogen depleted, glucose limited); CPT SYSTEM: Long-chain fatty acids (LCFAs, ≥ C12) cannot cross inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) as free acids → carnitine shuttle: outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM): LCFA-CoA + carnitine → [CPT I / CPT1A(liver), CPT1B(muscle), CPT1C(brain)] → acylcarnitine + CoA; carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase (CACT/SLC25A20) in IMM: exchanges acylcarnitine (in) for carnitine (out); inner mitochondrial membrane: acylcarnitine → [CPT II] → LCFA-CoA + carnitine → β-oxidation; CPT II deficiency (CPTII gene): most common hereditary disorder of long-chain FA oxidation in adults; classic form: autosomal recessive; typically presents in adults (20-30 years) with episodic exercise/fasting-triggered rhabdomyolysis + myoglobinuria + elevated CPK (may reach 100,000-1,000,000 U/L) + pigmenturia ('coca-cola' urine) + potential acute renal failure; NO hypoglycemia or cardiomyopathy in adult form (preserved hepatic CPT I); BETWEEN EPISODES: COMPLETELY NORMAL (no weakness, no biochemical abnormality except ↑acylcarnitine [C16:0, C18:0, C18:1, C18:2] on acylcarnitine profile); contrast with severe neonatal/infantile CPT II form: cardiomyopathy + hypoglycemia + hepatic failure → often fatal; diagnosis: acylcarnitine profile (blood spot NBS or plasma): ↑long-chain acylcarnitines (C16, C18:1) + ↑C16/C2 ratio; CPT II enzyme activity (lymphocytes/fibroblasts); molecular: CPTII gene (1p32); most common mutation: S113L (60% of alleles); treatment: low-fat diet (↓LCFA → ↓need for CPT II) + avoid fasting + avoid prolonged exercise; MCT oil supplementation (medium-chain FAs bypass CPT system → enter mitochondria directly via diffusion); carnitine supplementation (controversial); riboflavin + glycerol (during acute episodes to provide glucose); similar presentations (exercise-induced myoglobinuria): VLCAD deficiency (very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, ACADVL gene) + LCHAD/TFP deficiency (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase/trifunctional protein) + CACT deficiency + CPT I deficiency (usually neonatal/infant hepatic disease more than muscle)

Myophosphorylase (PYGM, GSD type V, McArdle disease): McArdle disease is also exercise-induced myoglobinuria! But: GSD V → MUSCLE GLYCOGEN accumulates → cannot use muscle glycogen → first 10-15 min of exercise painful (glycolytic fuel depleted) → 'second wind' phenomenon (FA + blood glucose take over as fuel); triggered by INTENSE SHORT exercise (anaerobic, glycolytic) more than prolonged aerobic exercise; forearm ischemic test: ↑NH4+ but NO ↑lactate (in normal: both increase; in McArdle: ↑NH4 [AMP deaminase works] but no lactate [block in glycogenolysis]);  DISTINGUISHED from CPT II: McArdle = glycogen on muscle biopsy (Periodic acid-Schiff [PAS] positive); fasting does NOT specifically trigger McArdle (glycogen stores normal at rest; problem is glycogenolysis during exercise); CPT II = no abnormal glycogen but ↑acylcarnitines + triggered by FASTING + PROLONGED aerobic exercise (both exercise-intensity dependent)
explanation: Fatty acid oxidation disorders (FAODs) — clinical spectrum by chain length: Very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD, ACADVL, C12-C20): ↑C14:1 (C14:1 myristoylenic) on acylcarnitine profile; NEONATAL: cardiomyopathy + hypoglycemia + hepatic failure (most severe); milder forms: hypoketotic hypoglycemia (infancy) or exercise intolerance/rhabdomyolysis (adolescent/adult); Newborn screening: part of NBS in most developed countries (C14:1 elevation). LCHAD (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase): HADHA gene (α-subunit of TFP, trifunctional protein); G1528C + E474Q (most common mutations); clinical: neonatal cardiomyopathy + hypoglycemia + PN (peripheral neuropathy) + pigmentary retinopathy (unique!); MATERNAL COMPLICATION: LCHAD-heterozygous mothers carrying homozygous LCHAD-affected fetus → ↑risk AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy) + HELLP syndrome (hemolysis + elevated liver enzymes + low platelets) [long-chain hydroxy FA accumulate in fetal liver → cross placenta → maternal liver toxicity; heterozygous mothers have ↓capacity to handle ↑LCHAD substrates]). MCAD (medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, ACADM, C4-C12): most common FAOD in Northern European descendants; ↑C8 (C8:0 octanoylcarnitine) on NBS; presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemic encephalopathy with illness/fasting in infants 3-24 months; near-death events (Reye-like); diagnosis: NBS (C8 elevation) + urine OA (octanoic acid, suberic + adipic acid = dicarboxylic acids from ω-oxidation when β-oxidation blocked). SCAD (short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, ACADS, C4-C6): controversial clinical significance (C4 elevation on NBS; most asymptomatic → may not require intervention). SCHAD (short-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, HADH): hyperinsulinism (SCHAD inhibits glutamate dehydrogenase [GDH] in β-cells → HADH loss → ↑GDH → ↑insulin secretion → congenital hyperinsulinism; very rare).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme generates NADPH in the mitochondrial matrix, providing reducing equivalents for mitochondrial antioxidant defense?
options: Malate dehydrogenase (MDH2): MDH2 in the mitochondrial matrix catalyzes malate → OAA using NAD+; this generates NADH (not NADPH); NADH enters the ETC; MDH2 is part of the TCA cycle and the malate-aspartate shuttle, not mitochondrial NADPH generation

NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I): Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) OXIDIZES NADH (not NADPH) → transfers electrons to CoQ → NAD+ regenerated; does not produce NADPH; it oxidizes NADH from TCA + pyruvate oxidation

Isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2): IDH2 (NADP+-linked mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase): isocitrate + NADP+ → [IDH2] → α-KG + CO2 + NADPH; IDH2 provides NADPH in the MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX for: (1) mitochondrial glutathione peroxidase (GPX1 [Sec-containing] + GPX4 [in mitochondria]) → reduces H2O2 using GSH; (2) thioredoxin 2 (TRX2) + thioredoxin reductase 2 (TrxR2) system → ↑NADPH → TrxR2 → ↑TRX2-SH (reduced) → peroxiredoxin 3 (PRX3) → ↓mitochondrial H2O2; (3) NADPH-dependent reduction of GSSG → GSH by glutathione reductase (GR2? [or cytoplasmic GR]); note: other NADPH sources in mitochondria: ME3 (malic enzyme 3, mitochondrial: malate + NADP+ → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH), ALDH2-adjacent reactions; IDH2 is particularly important for mitochondrial antioxidant defense; IDH2 overexpression in cancer → ↑mitochondrial NADPH → ↑antioxidant defense → ↓ROS → ↑cancer cell survival; IDH2 GOF mutations (R172K in AML, R140Q in AML/MDS) → 2-HG production (onco-metabolite) instead of NADPH (normal IDH2 → ↑α-KG; mutant IDH2 → 2-HG using NADPH as cofactor → consumes NADPH instead of producing it → ↑ROS paradox); IDH2 inhibitor: enasidenib (Idhifa) → mutant IDH2 inhibition → differentiation of AML blasts → used in IDH2-mutated relapsed/refractory AML (FDA 2017)

G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase): G6PD is in the CYTOPLASM (cytosol); G6PD produces NADPH in the cytoplasm from the pentose phosphate pathway; it is NOT in the mitochondrial matrix; G6PD deficiency → ↓cytoplasmic NADPH → ↓GSH regeneration in RBCs (which have no mitochondria) → oxidative hemolysis
explanation: Mitochondrial NADPH generation: NADPH in mitochondria differs from cytoplasmic NADPH (separate pools, cannot cross IMM); mitochondrial NADPH sources: IDH2: isocitrate → α-KG + CO2 + NADPH (TCA step 3b variant); ME3 (mitochondrial malic enzyme 3): malate + NADP+ → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH (anaplerosis → cataplerosis cycle); THF-dependent: mitochondrial MTHFD2 (methylene-THF dehydrogenase 2) + MTHFD2L: metabolizes 10-formyl-THF → THF + CO2 + NADPH (feeds formate to cytoplasm for purine synthesis); NNT (nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase): inner mitochondrial membrane enzyme: NADH + NADP+ → NAD+ + NADPH (driven by Δp/proton gradient across IMM → ↑mitochondrial NADPH at expense of NADH; C57BL/6J mice have NNT deletion → ↑ROS + metabolic syndrome [famous model for diet-induced T2DM]; NNT loss → ↑glucocorticoid excess [adrenal requires mitochondrial NADPH for steroidogenesis → without NNT → ↓NADPH → ↑ROS → ↑cortisol excess]); IDH3 (NAD+ linked, TCA cycle): same enzyme in TCA cycle → NADH (not NADPH). Mitochondrial antioxidant systems: PRX3 (peroxiredoxin 3): mitochondrial; reduces H2O2 using TRX2; PRX5 (also mitochondrial); SOD2 (MnSOD, manganese-containing): converts O2•- → H2O2 (first line) → then H2O2 → GPX1/2 or catalase → H2O; Parkinson's disease: ↑mitochondrial ROS (complex I inhibitors → ↑O2•- → SOD2 → ↑H2O2); ↑4-HNE (4-hydroxynonenal, lipid peroxidation product) attacks mitochondrial proteins; sirtuins: SIRT3 (NAD+-dependent mitochondrial deacetylase): deacetylates SOD2 (Lys68) → ↑SOD2 activity → ↓ROS; deacetylates IDH2 → ↑IDH2 → ↑mitochondrial NADPH; SIRT3 is the primary 'guardian' of mitochondrial protein acetylation; fasting → ↑NAD+ → SIRT3 active → ↑FAO + ↑antioxidant defense.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the catabolism of phenylalanine and tyrosine, fumarylacetoacetate is hydrolyzed to fumarate and acetoacetate. The enzyme catalyzing this step is deficient in which condition?
options: Alcaptonuria (homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency, HGD gene): alcaptonuria is deficiency of HOMOGENTISATE 1,2-DIOXYGENASE (HGD) at step BEFORE fumarylacetoacetate is formed; homogentisic acid accumulates → dark urine [darkens on standing, oxidized to alkapton pigment/benzoquinonacetic acid] + ochronosis [black pigmentation of cartilage, ear wax, tendons] + arthropathy; alcaptonuria does NOT involve fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase

Phenylketonuria (PKU): PAH deficiency → Phe accumulates; tyrosine becomes essential; phenylpyruvate + phenyllactate + phenylacetate in urine; FAH is NOT deficient in PKU; PKU is at the first step (Phe → Tyr); fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase is several steps downstream of the PKU block

Hereditary tyrosinemia type I (HT1, fumarylacetoaceturia): FAH (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase) deficiency: FAH gene (15q23-q25): AR; FAH is the LAST enzyme in Phe/Tyr catabolism → fumarylacetoacetate (FAA) + maleylacetoacetate accumulate → FAA is spontaneously reduced to succinylacetoacetate → succinylacetoacetate → succinylacetone (SA); SUCCINYLACETONE (SA): the pathognomonic metabolite of HT1; SA: (1) potently inhibits PBGS (ALA dehydratase, delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase) → ↑ALA → porphyria-like symptoms (SA is a structural analog of ALA); ALA toxicity → neurological crises (acute porphyria-like: neuropathic pain, ascending paralysis, respiratory failure, SIADH [syndrome of inappropriate ADH]) → HT1 is the ONLY organic acidemia with true porphyria crisis (mimics AIP); (2) FAA + MAA = directly cytotoxic (alkylating agents) → liver cell death + fibrosis + cirrhosis → HCC (hepatocellular carcinoma) risk even in childhood (extremely high; HT1 without treatment has >50% HCC risk by 5 years of age); (3) renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome, type II RTA); diagnosis: urine succinylacetone (pathognomonic); ↑alpha-fetoprotein (↑AFP even without HCC: liver disease marker); ↑serum tyrosine + Met (secondary to liver failure); NBS (most countries): ↑succinylacetone or ↑Tyr ratio on NBS tandem MS + acylcarnitine; TREATMENT: NITISINONE (NTBC, 2-(2-nitro-4-trifluoromethylbenzoyl)-1,3-cyclohexanedione = HPD inhibitor): inhibits 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), 2 steps UPSTREAM of FAH → ↓FAA + MAA production → dramatically reduces liver disease + HCC risk + prevents porphyria crises; started IMMEDIATELY on diagnosis; + low-tyrosine + low-phenylalanine diet (since HPD is blocked → ↑HPA [4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate] + ↑Tyr if not restricted); liver transplant: curative (replaces deficient FAH) if detected late or nitisinone not available; gene therapy: ongoing trials
Homocystinuria (CBS deficiency): CBS catalyzes Hcy + Ser → cystathionine; CBS deficiency is in homocysteine/methionine metabolism, NOT in Phe/Tyr catabolism; FAH is unrelated to CBS deficiency
explanation: Phenylalanine/Tyrosine catabolism — full pathway: Phe → [PAH + BH4] → Tyr → [TAT, tyrosine aminotransferase] → 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (HPP) → [HPD, 4-HPD + ascorbate] → homogentisate → [HGD] → maleylacetoacetate → [GSTZ1, maleylacetoacetate isomerase, glutathione S-transferase zeta 1] → fumarylacetoacetate → [FAH] → fumarate + acetoacetate; fumarate → TCA; acetoacetate → ketone body metabolism (both glucogenic + ketogenic products from Phe/Tyr → both glucogenic AND ketogenic amino acids). HT1 vs HT2 vs HT3: HT2 (hereditary tyrosinemia type 2, Richner-Hanhart syndrome): TAT deficiency (tyrosine aminotransferase) → ↑blood tyrosine → (1) painful palmoplantar keratoderma (tyrosine crystallizes in skin) + (2) bilateral corneal ulcers/crystals (tyrosine deposits in cornea → photophobia + lacrimation) + (3) intellectual disability (some patients); treatment: low-Phe + low-Tyr diet. HT3 (hereditary tyrosinemia type 3): HPD deficiency → ↑blood Tyr + ↑4-HPA in urine; usually milder than HT1; treatment: low-Phe + low-Tyr diet; no liver disease.
