Transient tyrosinemia of newborn: most common neonatal hypertyrosinemia; preterm + some full-term neonates → ↓HPD activity (requires ascorbate/vitamin C) + high dietary protein → transient ↑Tyr; resolves spontaneously or with ascorbate. Nitisinone (NTBC): inhibits HPD (the 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase) → ↓downstream accumulation (↓FA accumulation) → ↑HPP + ↑Tyr in blood (dietary restriction needed); nitisinone + diet → transformed HT1 prognosis (from 50% HCC by age 5 to essentially no HCC with early treatment + monitoring).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with chronic alcoholism develops peripheral neuropathy, confusion, and ophthalmoplegia. The deficiency responsible for this Wernicke's encephalopathy is:
options: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration (posterior + lateral columns) + megaloblastic anemia + peripheral neuropathy; ophthalmoplegia is NOT a feature; the triad described (confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia) is classic for thiamine deficiency, not B12

Niacin (B3): niacin deficiency = pellagra (4 D's: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death); no ophthalmoplegia; chronic alcoholics may have pellagra but the specific triad described is thiamine deficiency

Thiamine (vitamin B1): Wernicke's encephalopathy (WE): classic triad: (1) ophthalmoplegia (6th nerve palsy [lateral rectus weakness] → diplopia, nystagmus; 3rd nerve palsy can occur); (2) ataxia (cerebellar); (3) confusion/altered mental status (encephalopathy); caused by thiamine (B1) deficiency; at-risk: chronic alcoholism (↓intake + ↑metabolic demand + impaired absorption), persistent vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum, post-bariatric surgery), cancer, refeeding syndrome (↑metabolic demand → ↑thiamine requirement); biochemistry: thiamine → thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, thiamine diphosphate) by thiamine pyrophosphokinase (TPK, in cytoplasm) using ATP; TPP-dependent enzymes: (1) PDC (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA; ↓PDC → ↑pyruvate → ↑lactate [lactic acidosis] + ↓acetyl-CoA → ↓ATP via TCA); (2) OGDH (α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase → α-KG → succinyl-CoA; ↓TCA flux); (3) BCKDH (branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase → BCKA → acyl-CoA products; relevant in MSUD); (4) transketolase (TKT, non-oxidative PPP → ↓ribose-5-P → ↓nucleotide synthesis; TKT activity in RBCs is classic biomarker of thiamine status: ↓TKT activity or ↑ETKR [erythrocyte transketolase reactivation ratio by exogenous TPP] > 1.25 → B1 deficiency); affected regions in WE: periaqueductal gray, mammillary bodies, medial thalamus → vulnerability due to ↑glucose oxidation demand + ↑PDC/OGDH need; MRI: characteristic T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in mammillary bodies + medial thalami + periaqueductal gray; Korsakoff syndrome: confabulatory amnesia (anterograde > retrograde) that persists after acute WE resolves → mammillary body atrophy; treatment: IV thiamine (100-200 mg) BEFORE glucose infusion (giving glucose without thiamine in deficient patient → uses up remaining thiamine → acute WE precipitation); high-risk patients should ALWAYS get thiamine before glucose
Riboflavin (vitamin B2): B2 deficiency: angular stomatitis, cheilosis, corneal vascularization, photophobia, scrotal dermatitis, normochromic-normocytic anemia; NOT the cause of the Wernicke's triad
explanation: Thiamine biochemistry and deficiency: TPP-dependent enzymes — all in mitochondria except TKT (cytoplasm): 1. PDC: pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH (irreversible); 2. OGDH/KGDH: α-KG + CoA + NAD+ → succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH (TCA step 5); 3. BCKDH: BCKA (α-KIC, α-KIV, α-KMV) → isovaleryl-CoA, isobutyryl-CoA, 2-methylbutyryl-CoA; 4. TKT: PPP non-oxidative phase; 5. AHAS (acetolactate synthase) in plants/microbes (not in humans). Beriberi syndromes: Dry beriberi: peripheral neuropathy (sensorimotor axonal, starts distally → stocking-glove pattern; burning feet → loss of sensation/reflexes); Wet beriberi: cardiomyopathy + high-output heart failure + peripheral edema (↓ATP → myocardial dysfunction + vasodilation → ↑cardiac output → edema); infantile beriberi: breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers → cardiac failure + aphonia (thin cry) + hoarse cry (laryngeal nerve involvement); Shoshin beriberi: acute fulminant wet beriberi → cardiovascular collapse + lactic acidosis (life-threatening; IV thiamine emergency); Thiamine transport: SLC19A2 (THTR1, high-affinity transporter) + SLC19A3 (THTR2); THTR1 mutations → thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anemia syndrome (TRMA/Rogers syndrome): megaloblastic anemia (responds to thiamine) + diabetes mellitus + sensorineural deafness → SLAD syndrome (SLC19A2-related anemia-DM); TRMA treated with high-dose thiamine (pharmacological). Biotin-responsive multiple carboxylase deficiency: biotinidase or HCS deficiency → ↓biotin → ↓all 4 carboxylases (PC, PCC, MCC, ACC) → ↑MMA + ↑lactic acid + ↑3-methylcrotonylglycinuria + ↑3-methylcitric acid → seizures + hypotonia + rash + alopecia → responds to biotin 5-10 mg/day; NBS by biotinidase enzyme assay.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Niacin (vitamin B3) can be synthesized endogenously from tryptophan. The relative efficiency of this conversion is approximately:
options: 1 mg niacin per gram of tryptophan (this is not the correct ratio; the actual conversion is approximately 1 mg of niacin equivalents from 60 mg of dietary tryptophan, meaning niacin from tryptophan is much less efficient than stated here)

60 mg of dietary tryptophan yields approximately 1 mg of niacin equivalents: niacin (vitamin B3) exists as nicotinic acid + nicotinamide; both are precursors to NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) and NADP+; ENDOGENOUS SYNTHESIS from tryptophan (kynurenine pathway): Trp → [TDO2 in liver, or IDO1/IDO2 in other cells + immune] → N-formylkynurenine → kynurenine → 3-hydroxykynurenine → 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid → ACMSD → quinolinate → [QPRT, quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase + PRPP] → NaMN (nicotinic acid mononucleotide) → NMNAT → NaAD → NADS → NAD+; 60 mg Trp = 1 mg niacin equivalent = 1 NE (niacin equivalent); EFFICIENCY FACTORS that reduce Trp → niacin conversion: (1) Estrogen: ↑kynureninase (via ↑PLP-dependent activity; estrogen → ↑PLP metabolism → kynureninase efficiency ↑ → ↑conversion Trp → niacin → explains why females may have slightly higher endogenous niacin synthesis); (2) Leucine (high leucine diet → inhibits QPRT → ↓conversion Trp → NaMN) → in corn-dependent diets (high Leu, low Trp + niacin → pellagra risk); (3) Vitamin B6 (PLP): kynureninase is PLP-dependent → B6 deficiency → ↓Trp → niacin conversion → secondary niacin deficiency in B6 deficiency; (4) IDO1 induction (infection, cancer, immune activation) → Trp consumed for immune modulation vs niacin synthesis (Trp 'depleted' by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase → immunotolerance at the expense of niacin synthesis); Hartnup disease (SLC6A19 defect) → ↓Trp absorption → ↓Trp → ↓niacin → pellagra-like rash; carcinoid tumor: ↑Trp → serotonin (TPH1 highly active in carcinoid) → ↓Trp available for niacin synthesis → pellagra can occur; treatment of pellagra: niacin (nicotinic acid) or nicotinamide supplementation; nicotinic acid (not nicotinamide) also used pharmacologically: ↑HDL + ↓TG + ↓LDL (though CVD benefit not proven in recent large RCTs like AIM-HIGH and HPS2-THRIVE); side effect: prostaglandin-mediated flushing (PGD2 from Langerhans cells → skin flushing; aspirin pretreatment ↓flushing; laropiprant [DP1 antagonist] was combined with niacin but withdrawn due to adverse events)

1 mg niacin is equivalent to 10 mg tryptophan (the correct ratio is 60 mg tryptophan = 1 mg niacin equivalent, not 10 mg; the 60:1 ratio is the standard used to calculate total niacin equivalents in diet)
explanation: NAD+ metabolism and its clinical relevance: NAD+ biosynthesis routes: De novo (from Trp): Trp → quinolinate → NaMN → NaAD → NAD+; requires QPRT. Preiss-Handler pathway (salvage from NA): nicotinic acid (niacin) + PRPP → NaMN → NaAD → NAD+. NAD+ salvage (main pathway in most cells): nicotinamide (Nam) → [NAMPT, rate-limiting] → NMN → [NMNAT1/2/3] → NAD+; Nampt = nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase; NAMPT is also secreted (eNAMPT/visfatin) with non-enzymatic cytokine-like functions; NAMPT inhibitors (FK866/APO866, daporinad) → deplete NAD+ → ↓cancer cell survival (rapidly dividing cells highly dependent on NAD+; targeting NAMPT → cancer therapy). NAD+ as signaling molecule: PARP1/2: consume NAD+ → poly-ADP-ribose (PAR) during DNA repair → ↑PARP activity (from DNA damage) → ↓NAD+ → ↓sirtuins (sirtuins also use NAD+) → feedback; SIRT1-7 (sirtuins): NAD+-dependent deacylases → consume NAD+ → NAM + acetyl-ADP-ribose; SIRT1 (nuclear): deacetylates PGC-1α → ↑mitochondrial biogenesis + ↑FAO; SIRT3 (mitochondrial): see previous; CD38: major NAD+ consumer (cyclic ADP-ribose [cADPR] signaling: Ca2+ mobilization; also produces ADPR + NAM); ↑CD38 in aging + inflammation → ↓NAD+ → ↓sirtuin activity → aging phenotype; NAD+ precursors as supplements: NMN (nicotinamide mononucleotide): converted → NMN → NAD+; orally absorbed; NR (nicotinamide riboside): NR → [NRK1/2] → NMN → NAD+; commercial supplements claim anti-aging via ↑NAD+ → ↑SIRT1 → mitochondrial function; animal studies promising; human RCTs ongoing; NAD+ in SCD (sickle cell disease): HU → ↑NO → ↑cGMP → ↑HbF + ↑NAD+? (some evidence); NMN in heart failure preclinical models → ↑NAD+ → ↑mitochondrial function → ↓hypertrophy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the electron transport chain, which complex is responsible for proton translocation but does NOT contain a prosthetic group directly involved in electron transfer?
options: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): Complex I translocates protons AND contains FMN + FeS clusters that directly transfer electrons from NADH to CoQ; its FeS clusters are directly involved in electron transfer

Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase): Complex II oxidizes succinate → FADH2 (covalent FAD) → FeS → CoQ; does NOT pump protons; has prosthetic groups directly involved in electron transfer (FAD + [2Fe-2S], [4Fe-4S], [3Fe-4S]); the question asks for a complex that DOES translocate protons but DOES NOT directly participate in electron transfer with a cofactor

ATP synthase (Complex V, FoF1-ATPase): ATP synthase DOES translocate protons (Fo subunit: proton channel a + c-ring; protons flow through c-ring → rotate c-ring → stalk → γ-subunit rotation → β-subunit conformational changes → ATP synthesis [Boyer's binding change mechanism: O [open] → L [loose] → T [tight] states for β subunits]) BUT Complex V does NOT have a prosthetic group involved in electron transfer (it uses the proton gradient to drive ATP synthesis, NOT electron transfer; no heme, no FeS, no flavin involved in electron transport in Complex V); Complex V proton translocation: 10-15 protons per ATP synthase revolution; c-ring (10 subunits in mammals) rotates → each proton: 10 c-subunits pass one proton → 1 full revolution (10 protons) = 3 ATP (3 β-subunits in F1 head) → ~3.33 ATP per 10 protons, or 2.5-2.7 ATP per 10 protons by revised estimates; also: FoF1-ATP synthase inhibitors: oligomycin (complex V Fo subunit, c-subunit ring blocker) → ↓ATP synthesis → ↓respiration (state 4 = no ADP present is similar); venturicidin, DCCD (covalently modifies Asp61 of c-subunit); efrapeptin; Bz-423 (BM40-1420 analog); clinical: mutations in MT-ATP6 (Fo a-subunit, subunit 6) or ATP5A1 → Leigh syndrome, NARP syndrome (Neurogenic weakness, Ataxia, Retinitis Pigmentosa)

Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): Complex IV reduces O2 → H2O AND translocates protons; contains prosthetic groups directly involved in electron transfer: CuA (dinuclear copper center in Cox2 subunit; accepts electrons from cytochrome c); heme a (in Cox1); CuB (binuclear center with heme a3 in Cox1; accepts electrons from CuA/heme a → reduces O2); so Complex IV has MULTIPLE prosthetic groups in electron transfer; does NOT satisfy 'NO prosthetic group in electron transfer'
explanation: ATP synthase — structure and mechanism: Complex V structure: Fo (membrane-embedded): subunits a (1), b (2), c (10 in mammals), e, f, g, DAPIT, 6.8 PL; c-ring (10 c-subunits) rotates; subunit a: provides proton half-channels (two half-channels: one facing IMS, one facing matrix → proton enters IMS-facing → binds conserved Asp (cAsp, Asp61 in c-subunit) → c-ring rotates → proton released into matrix-facing channel); F1 (matrix-facing): α3β3γδε; catalytic: β-subunits (3, on each is ATPase/synthase activity); γ-subunit (rotating asymmetric stalk) → as it rotates → β-subunits change conformation cyclically: O (open, low affinity for nucleotide) → L (loose, binds ADP + Pi) → T (tight, ATP formed spontaneously) → O (ATP released); binding change mechanism (Paul Boyer, Nobel 1997): rotation is the KEY: the actual synthesis of ATP from ADP + Pi in the T state is spontaneous (ΔG ~0 in T state); energy is used to release ATP from T (open it to O state) → conformational energy → mechanical energy → chemical product release; OSCP (oligomycin sensitivity conferring protein): stator subunit b/δ/OSCP; holds F1 α3β3 stationary while γ rotates; oligomycin sensitivity: oligomycin blocks Fo → ↓rotation → ↓ATP synthesis; mutations in OSCP → ↓oligomycin sensitivity + ↑permeability transition pore (PTP) open probability. ATP/ADP exchange: ANT (adenine nucleotide translocator, SLC25A4/A5/A6) in IMM: exchanges cytoplasmic ADP → matrix + matrix ATP → cytoplasm; 1 ADP[3-] in, 1 ATP[4-] out → electrogenic (net negative charge moves from matrix → IMS → ↓Δψ slightly); ANT is inhibited by: atractyloside + carboxyatractyloside (c-state inhibitors, fix ANT in 'cytoplasmic' conformation = facing IMS) and bongkrekic acid (m-state inhibitor, fixes ANT in matrix conformation); ANT1 (SLC25A4) mutations → adPEO (autosomal dominant PEO with mtDNA multiple deletions) + hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (ANT1 highly expressed in heart + skeletal muscle). P/O ratio debate: older textbook value: NADH → 2.5 ATP/O (per oxygen atom reduced = per NADH: 10 H+ pumped → 10H+/3.33 H+/ATP = 3 ATP, but energy cost of phosphate transport adjusts → ~2.5); FADH2 → 1.5 ATP/O (6 H+ pumped via complex III + IV only; revised from old 2 vs 3 estimates).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ganglioside GM3 is synthesized in the Golgi apparatus. Which enzyme catalyzes the first step in converting ceramide to gangliosides?
options: Glucosylceramide synthase (UGCG): UGCG (UDP-glucose ceramide glucosyltransferase): ceramide + UDP-glucose → [UGCG] → glucosylceramide (GlcCer, also called cerebroside) + UDP; this IS the first step in the synthesis of most glycosphingolipids (except sulfatides → GalCer which use galactosylceramide); UGCG is in the cytoplasmic leaflet of the Golgi → GlcCer synthesized on cytoplasmic face → flipped to luminal face (by ABCB1/MDR1 or FAPP2) → further glycosylation in Golgi lumen; GlcCer → [B4GALT5/6] → LacCer (lactosylceramide) = Gal-Glc-Cer → [ST3GAL5] → GM3 (NeuAc-Gal-Glc-Cer = Sialyl-LacCer = the simplest ganglioside) → [B4GALNT1] → GM2 → [B3GALNT1] → GM1 → further → GD1a, GD1b, GT1b; OR: LacCer → [B3GNT5] → Lc3Cer (lacto-series) → [various] → H antigen blood group and others; OR: LacCer → [A4GALT] → Gb3 (globo-series); UGCG inhibitors: PDMP (D-threo-1-phenyl-2-decanoylamino-3-morpholino-1-propanol), eliglustat: eliglustat (Cerdelga): UGCG inhibitor → approved for Gaucher disease (substrate reduction therapy [SRT]) → ↓glucosylceramide synthesis → ↓substrate for beta-glucocerebrosidase → ↓glucosylceramide accumulation (works best in Gaucher type 1 non-neuropathic); N-butyldeoxynojirimycin (miglustat, Zavesca): also UGCG inhibitor (less potent; also inhibits other glucosidases → GI side effects) → Gaucher type 1 SRT + Niemann-Pick type C SRT

Ceramide synthase (CERS1-6): CERS (ceramide synthase, laglas): sphinganine + fatty acyl-CoA → [CERS] → dihydroceramide; then DEGS (dihydroceramide desaturase) → ceramide; CERS is the synthase for ceramide ITSELF, not for glycosylation of ceramide → not the first step in ganglioside synthesis

Sialyltransferase ST3GAL5 (GM3 synthase): ST3GAL5 (SAT-I) transfers NeuAc from CMP-NeuAc to LacCer → GM3; this is NOT the first step (UGCG → GlcCer is first; then B4GALT5/6 → LacCer; then ST3GAL5 → GM3); ST3GAL5 is 2 steps downstream of UGCG

Sphingomyelin synthase (SMS1/2): SMS (SGMS1 in Golgi, SGMS2 in PM): PC + ceramide → SM (sphingomyelin) + DAG; this generates sphingomyelin (phospholipid), NOT ganglioside (glycosphingolipid); SMS uses ceramide but makes SM, not glyco-sphingolipids
explanation: Sphingolipid metabolism — synthesis and catabolism: Ceramide is the central molecule: synthesized de novo: palmitoyl-CoA + Ser → [SPT, serine palmitoyltransferase, B6] → 3-ketosphinganine → [3-KSR] → sphinganine (dihydrosphingosine) → [CERS + acyl-CoA] → dihydroceramide → [DEGS1] → ceramide; ceramide serves as: precursor for sphingomyelin (SGMS1/2), glucosylceramide (UGCG), galactosylceramide (UGT8), ceramide-1-phosphate (CERK); signaling: ceramide → apoptosis (activates PP2A → dephosphorylate Akt → ↓survival; also BAX activation → MOMP); sphingosine (from ceramide by ceramidase) → [SK1/2] → sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P): pro-survival, anti-apoptotic; the 'sphingolipid rheostat': Cer:S1P balance → life/death decisions. Lysosomal GSL catabolism: step-by-step hydrolysis in lysosomes: GM1 → [GLB1/β-galactosidase + GM2-AP] → GM2 → [HexA + GM2-AP] → GM3 → [β-galactosidase/NEU1] → LacCer → [GBA/β-glucocerebrosidase + saposin C] → GlcCer → [ceramidase/ASAH1] → ceramide → [ASMase/SMPD1] → sphingosine + FA; GalCer → [GalC, GALC] → ceramide (galactosylceramide galactosidase; Krabbe disease: GALC deficiency → psychosine [galactosylsphingosine] accumulation → oligodendrocyte death → demyelination); Gb3 → [GLA, α-galactosidase A] → LacCer (Fabry disease: GLA mutations, X-linked → Gb3 accumulation → renal/cardiac/neurological); SM → [SMPD1, ASMase] → ceramide (NPD type A/B: SMPD1 deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation → foam cells). GBA (glucocerebrosidase, acid beta-glucosidase 1): mutated in Gaucher disease; saposin C (PSAP gene) is the activator protein for GBA; saposin C deficiency → Gaucher-like disease despite normal GBA; ERT for Gaucher: imiglucerase (Cerezyme, CHO-derived) → biweekly IV infusion → ↓glucosylceramide in macrophages.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Selenocysteine (Sec) is the 21st amino acid. It is incorporated into proteins in response to UGA codons. The unique feature of selenocysteine incorporation is:
options: UGA is decoded normally as a stop codon in all organisms, and selenocysteine is added post-translationally (UGA IS normally a stop codon, but in specific mRNAs with a SECIS element, UGA is decoded as Sec [a co-translational incorporation]; it is NOT added post-translationally)

Sec is encoded by UGA and requires a SECIS element in the 3'-UTR, a specialized elongation factor (SBP2 + SelB/EFSec), and Sec-tRNASec charged with selenocysteine: Selenocysteine (Sec, U, the 21st amino acid): contains selenium (Se) rather than sulfur → lower pKa of SeH (~5.2) vs SH (~8.3) → Sec exists as selenolate anion (Se-) at physiological pH → more reactive nucleophile than Cys → used in catalytic mechanisms of selenoproteins; BIOSYNTHESIS of Sec: unusual: NOT made in cytoplasm and loaded onto tRNA; made on the tRNA itself: Ser charged onto tRNA[Sec] (by SerRS, seryl-tRNA synthetase); Ser-tRNA[Sec] → [PSTK, phosphoseryl-tRNA kinase] → phosphoseryl-tRNA[Sec]; phosphoseryl-tRNA[Sec] + H2Se (from SPS1 [selenophosphate synthetase 1] or SPS2 → selenophosphate) → [SecS/SEPSECS, selenocysteinyl-tRNA synthase [O-phosphoseryl-tRNA: selenium transferase]] → Sec-tRNA[Sec]; INCORPORATION: requires: (1) Sec-tRNA[Sec] (anticodon UCA, reads UGA); (2) SECIS element (selenocysteine insertion sequence): stem-loop structure in 3'-UTR of selenoprotein mRNAs (required in BOTH prokaryotes [SECIS in coding region] and eukaryotes [3'-UTR]); in eukaryotes: SECIS-BP2 (SBP2, SECISBP2 gene): binds SECIS element; SECIS + SBP2 → recruits SelB/EFSec (the specialized elongation factor for Sec, analogous to EF-Tu/EF1A but specifically for Sec-tRNA[Sec]) → ternary complex: EFSec-GTP-Sec-tRNA[Sec] → ribosome reads UGA as Sec → GTP hydrolysis → Sec inserted; SELENOPROTEINS in humans: ~25 genes encoding selenoproteins; major ones: GPX1/2/3/4 (glutathione peroxidases, Sec at active site); TrxR1/2 (thioredoxin reductases); DIO1/2/3 (iodothyronine deiodinases [T4→T3 by DIO1 and DIO2; T4+T3→rT3 by DIO3]); SelP (selenium transport protein in plasma); Sep15; MSRB1; Sec is essential for: ↑GPX activity (Sec has 100-1000x higher catalytic efficiency vs Cys; Cys-mutated GPX has ↓activity) → antioxidant; DIO activity (T4 → T3 conversion in liver [DIO1] and tissues [DIO2])

Sec is incorporated in response to UAG amber codons using a suppressor tRNA charged with Sec (Sec is incorporated in response to UGA [opal] stop codons, not UAG [amber] stop codons; amber suppression is for other purposes [genetic code expansion]; Sec uses UGA in a context-dependent manner dictated by SECIS element)

Sec is synthesized from cysteine by direct replacement of sulfur with selenium in the cytoplasm and then non-specifically added to any cysteine position in selenoproteins (incorrect; Sec synthesis involves Ser-tRNA[Sec] intermediate, phosphorylation, and then selenium addition; Sec is NOT derived from cysteine nor added post-translationally to Cys positions)
explanation: Selenium and selenoproteins — clinical relevance: Selenium (Se): essential trace mineral; dietary sources: Brazil nuts (highest), seafood, organ meats, whole grains; RDA ~55 µg/day; toxic at > 400 µg/day (selenosis: garlic breath [dimethylselenide], hair loss, nail changes, neurological); deficiency: Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy in children from Se-deficient soil in China → ↓GPX4 in cardiomyocytes → ↑ROS → cardiac damage); Kashin-Beck disease (osteoarthropathy of cartilage, Se + iodine + mycotoxin deficiency); white muscle disease in livestock. Selenocysteine vs. cysteine: catalytic advantage: Sec has pKa ~5.2 vs Cys pKa ~8.3 → at physiological pH 7.4 → Sec is ~99% deprotonated (nucleophilic Se-) vs Cys ~50% deprotonated (less active) → 100-1000× faster catalysis; evolutionarily: Sec is found in selenoproteins of most organisms but absent in some (fungi, Arabidopsis); some organisms (e.g., some bacteria) have secondary replacement of Sec → Cys in orthologous selenoprotein with ↓catalytic activity; GPX4 and ferroptosis: GPX4 (glutathione peroxidase 4): reduces phospholipid hydroperoxides (PL-OOH) using GSH → ↓lipid peroxidation; GPX4 is a key defender against ferroptosis (iron-dependent form of regulated cell death: ↑lipid peroxidation of PUFA-containing phospholipids → membrane disruption → cell death); GPX4 inhibitors (RSL3, ML162) → induce ferroptosis; GPX4 expression requires: Se (for Sec at active site) + GSH (as reductant) + CoQ10 (FSP1, ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 → reduces CoQ10 → ↓PL-OOH independently); ferroptosis is relevant in: ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cancer cell death (used therapeutically to kill drug-resistant cancer cells). DIO (deiodinases): DIO1 (5'-deiodinase, liver + kidney + thyroid): T4 → T3 [5'-deiodination, outer ring] + T4 → rT3 [5-deiodination, inner ring, minor]; DIO2 (5'-deiodinase, brain + pituitary + skeletal muscle + heart + BAT): T4 → T3 (primary source of local T3 in brain/pituitary); DIO3 (5-deiodinase, placenta + fetal tissues): T4 → rT3 + T3 → T2 → inactivates thyroid hormones; inhibited by PTU (propylthiouracil) → DIO1 inhibited (reduces peripheral T4→T3 conversion; methimazole only blocks thyroid synthesis); excess DIO3 in hemangiomas → consumptive hypothyroidism.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme adenylate kinase (also called myokinase) catalyzes which reaction in the cell?
options: ADP + Pi → ATP (this is the reaction of ATP synthase [Complex V], not adenylate kinase; adenylate kinase interconverts adenylate species without inorganic phosphate)

2 ADP ↔ ATP + AMP: adenylate kinase (ADK1/myokinase in muscle; AK1 = major cytoplasmic isoform; AK2 in IMS of mitochondria; AK3 in mitochondrial matrix; AK4 in IMS; AK6 in nucleus): 2 ADP → ATP + AMP (near-equilibrium reaction, Keq ~1); physiological roles: (1) maintains [AMP]/[ADP]/[ATP] ratios: when ATP is hydrolyzed rapidly (high energy demand) → 2 ADP accumulate → AK → ATP + AMP → ATP regenerated (provides additional ATP from 2 ADP); (2) ENERGY SIGNAL AMPLIFICATION: AMP is a more sensitive signal of energy depletion than ADP (AMP/ATP ratio changes more dramatically): ATP dropping from 5→4 mM = 20% change in ATP, but AMP rising from 0.1→0.5 mM = 500% change in AMP → AMP allosterically activates: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase, phospho-Thr172 also needed, activated by LKB1/CaMKKβ, but direct AMP binding to γ-subunit → allosteric activation + protects Thr172 from dephosphorylation) → catabolic pathways; PFK-1 (PFK is activated by AMP → ↑glycolysis); muscle adenylate kinase: AK1 (cytoplasmic, also called myokinase): high in skeletal muscle + smooth muscle; when ATP nearly depleted (intense exercise) → ↑ADP → AK → ATP + AMP → ATP available briefly; also: AMP → [AMP deaminase, AMPD1/2/3] → IMP + NH3 (AMPD reaction: irreversible → pushes AK equilibrium → provides additional driving force for ATP regeneration); IMP + Asp + GTP → [adenylosuccinate synthetase] → adenylosuccinate → [ASL] → AMP (purine nucleotide cycle, PNC) → regenerates AMP (a bit complex); forearm ischemic test: blocked blood flow → exercise → in McArdle disease → ↑NH3 (AMPD active) but NO ↑lactate; in AMPD deficiency → ↑lactate but NO ↑NH3; adenylosuccinate lyase (ASL) deficiency → ↓purine nucleotide cycle
ATP + GMP ↔ ADP + GDP (this is the reaction of nucleoside diphosphate kinase [NDPK, NME1/2]: uses ATP → phosphorylates other NDPs [GDP, CDP, UDP] → produces GTP, CTP, UTP; NOT adenylate kinase)
explanation: Energy sensing — AMPK axis: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase): heterotrimer: α-subunit (catalytic, Thr172 activation) + β-subunit (scaffold, glycogen-binding) + γ-subunit (regulatory, CBS [cystathionine β-synthase] domains that bind AMP/ADP/ATP); activation: ↑AMP or ↑ADP → binds γ-subunit → allosteric activation + protects α-Thr172 from PP2A dephosphorylation; also: LKB1 (STK11, the primary upstream kinase in liver + most tissues) → constitutively active → phosphorylates Thr172 when AMP protects it; CaMKKβ (CAMKK2, in brain + muscle): ↑Ca2+ → CaMKKβ → phosphorylates AMPK independently of AMP (exercise Ca2+ transients → AMPK via CaMKKβ); TAK1 (TGF-β-activated kinase): in some contexts; AMPK effects (catabolic activation, anabolic inhibition): ↑FAO (phospho-ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT1); ↑glycolysis (phospho-PFKFB3 → ↑F2,6BP → ↑PFK-1); ↑GLUT4 translocation in muscle (via AS160/TBC1D4); ↑autophagy (via ULK1 phosphorylation); ↑mitochondrial biogenesis (via PGC-1α phosphorylation + SIRT1 activation); ↓cholesterol synthesis (phospho-HMGCR → ↓activity); ↓fatty acid synthesis (phospho-ACC1/ACC2); ↓protein synthesis (phospho-TSC2 → ↑TSC1/2 → ↓mTORC1 → ↓S6K1 + ↓4E-BP1 → ↓protein synthesis); ↓gluconeogenesis (phospho-TORC2/CRTC2 → cannot activate CREB-dependent PEPCK + G6Pase transcription; also phosphorylates HMGCR + ACC); Metformin → complex I inhibition → ↑AMP → AMPK (partially; metformin's mechanism is multifactorial). Creatine kinase (CK): PCr (phosphocreatine) + ADP ↔ Cr + ATP; CK-MB (heart + skeletal muscle) + CK-MM (skeletal) + CK-BB (brain); cardiac troponins (cTnI, cTnT) are more specific for MI; CK-MB ratio (CK-MB/total CK > 6%): suggests cardiac origin; CK-MM elevation: rhabdomyolysis, McArdle, inflammatory myopathies, intense exercise; CK-BB: cerebral infarction, brain trauma, neonates.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following accurately describes a Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence?
options: A sequence in eukaryotic mRNA that recruits the 40S ribosomal subunit for cap-independent translation (IRES elements allow cap-independent translation in eukaryotes; the Shine-Dalgarno sequence is a PROKARYOTIC ribosome binding site concept; eukaryotes use Kozak sequence for ribosome positioning near the AUG start codon; eukaryotes do NOT have SD sequences)

A purine-rich sequence (AGGAGG or similar) 5-10 nucleotides upstream of the start codon in prokaryotic mRNA, complementary to the 3' end of 16S rRNA: Shine-Dalgarno sequence (1974, John Shine + Lynn Dalgarno): a purinerich sequence (consensus: 5'-AGGAGG-3') in the 5'-UTR of prokaryotic mRNA, centered ~5-10 nucleotides (7±2 nt) upstream of the AUG start codon; MECHANISM: 3'-UCCUCC-5' is the anti-SD sequence at the 3' end of 16S rRNA (positions 1536-1541 in E. coli 23S... wait: 16S rRNA [small 30S subunit] 3' end); SD sequence on mRNA base-pairs with the anti-SD sequence of 16S rRNA → positions the AUG exactly in the P-site for initiation → proper reading frame established; why important: prokaryotic mRNAs are polycistronic (multiple ORFs per mRNA) → each ORF has its own SD sequence for separate ribosome entry → allows individual ORF translation; contrast eukaryotic: mRNAs are monocistronic (one ORF usually); ribosomes scan from 5' cap → Kozak sequence near AUG (5'-GCCACCAUGG-3') → 48S complex → start codon recognized by eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi ternary complex; strength of SD sequence: determines translation initiation efficiency; 'strong' SD (AAGGAGG, close to AUG) → ↑translation of downstream ORF; 'weak' SD → ↓translation; applications: synthetic biology/protein expression: synthetic SD sequences in expression vectors (e.g., pET vectors in E. coli) → maximal protein expression; riboswitch + SD interaction: some regulatory elements occlude SD sequence → ↓translation (e.g., SAM riboswitches in biosynthetic gene regulation); SD-anti-SD interaction also used in trans-acting RNA regulation (rpsO autoregulation in E. coli)

A GC-rich stem-loop structure at the 5' end of mRNA that promotes ribosomal loading in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes (GC-rich stem-loops at the 5' end of mRNA do NOT promote ribosomal loading; they typically BLOCK translation [inhibitory secondary structure]; the cap and IRES recruit ribosomes in eukaryotes; SD is a specific linear sequence in prokaryotes)

A regulatory element at the 3' end of rRNA that activates transcription of ribosomal genes in response to growth signals (rRNA transcription is regulated by RNA Pol I, sigma factors, and growth signals; the 3' end of 16S rRNA contains the anti-SD sequence which base-pairs with mRNA SD; it is a translational initiation element in mRNA recognition, not a transcriptional regulatory element)
explanation: Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic translation initiation comparison: Prokaryotic initiation (70S ribosomes): fMet-tRNAfMet (formylmethionyl-tRNA; formylated at amino group by PDF and MTIF after Met-tRNAfMet is charged) + 30S (16S rRNA + ~21 proteins) + 50S (23S + 5S rRNA + ~33 proteins) → 70S; initiator tRNA: tRNAfMet (different from tRNAMet elongator; can directly enter P-site without being at A-site first); initiation factors: IF1 (30S A-site occupier → prevents elongator tRNAs from entering); IF2 (GTPase, carries fMet-tRNAfMet to P-site → GTP hydrolysis → IF2 release); IF3 (anti-association factor → prevents 30S + 50S joining before initiator tRNA is in place + proofreads codon-anticodon in P-site); Eukaryotic initiation (80S): met-tRNAi (initiator Met-tRNA; not formylated) + 40S + 60S; initiator tRNA: tRNAiMet (base pairs in P-site directly with AUG in start codon scanning); initiation factors (eIFs): eIF2 (GTPase, carries Met-tRNAi as ternary complex eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAiMet); eIF2B (GEF, reloads GDP→GTP on eIF2); eIF2α kinases (GCN2, PKR, HRI, PERK): phospho-eIF2α-Ser51 → sequester eIF2B → ↓GDP→GTP exchange → ↓ternary complex → ↓global translation → ISR (integrated stress response); eIF4E (cap-binding protein; 4E-BPs inhibit eIF4E, phospho-4E-BPs by mTORC1 release eIF4E → ↑cap-dependent translation); eIF4G (scaffold); eIF4A (RNA helicase); 43S preinitiation complex (43S PIC): 40S + eIF3 (13 subunit complex) + eIF1 + eIF1A + eIF5 + eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNAi ternary complex → binds 5'-cap mRNA (with eIF4F cap complex) → scans 5'→3' for AUG in Kozak context → AUG recognition → GTP hydrolysis (by eIF2) + eIF5B-GTP → 60S joins → 80S elongation-competent ribosome (eIF2-GDP released; eIF2B regenerates eIF2-GTP). IRES (internal ribosome entry site): cap-independent eukaryotic translation; Type I-IV IRESes differ in secondary structure + eIF requirements; HCV IRES: directly recruits 40S + 5S rRNA (minimal eIF2 and cap factors); used in bicistronic reporter vectors; IRES-dependent translation increases during stress (when cap-dependent is inhibited by phospho-eIF2α).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Thrombin activates platelets and cleaves fibrinogen. One major cleavage event by thrombin on protease-activated receptor 1 (PAR-1) is a tethered-ligand activation mechanism. This means:
options: Thrombin cleaves an extracellular loop of PAR-1 to release a soluble fragment that freely diffuses to activate neighboring platelets (the released N-terminal fragment does NOT act as a diffusible ligand; the tethered-ligand mechanism specifically means the new N-terminal peptide remains attached [tethered] to the receptor and acts as the ligand intramolecularly)

Thrombin uses a non-covalent serine protease mechanism to bind and activate PAR-1 without peptide bond cleavage (thrombin DOES cleave PAR-1; it hydrolyzes the Arg41-Ser42 peptide bond; the tethered-ligand mechanism involves actual proteolytic cleavage exposing a new N-terminus that then activates the receptor intramolecularly)

Thrombin cleaves the extracellular N-terminal domain of PAR-1 at Arg41-Ser42, exposing a new N-terminal sequence (SFLLRN) that acts as a tethered ligand by folding back to bind and activate the receptor's ligand-binding domain: PAR (protease-activated receptor) family: PAR-1, -2, -3, -4; GPCRs activated by serine proteases; PAR-1 (F2R): activated by thrombin (primary high-sensitivity receptor) + plasmin; PAR-4 (F2RL3): activated by thrombin at lower sensitivity; PAR-2 (F2RL1): activated by trypsin, tryptase, FXa, FVIIa; PAR-3: thrombin; MECHANISM: thrombin (serine protease) → cleaves Arg41-Ser42 bond in PAR-1 extracellular N-terminal domain → releases a short N-terminal fragment → exposes new N-terminal sequence (SFLLRN in PAR-1; this is the tethered ligand) → new N-terminal peptide 'folds back' → binds the 7-TM GPCR extracellular loops → intramolecular agonism → receptor activation → signal; downstream: PAR-1 → Gαq → PLC → IP3 + DAG → ↑Ca2+ + PKC → platelet activation; also Gαi → ↓cAMP; Gα12/13 → RhoA → ↑cytoskeletal changes → platelet shape change; SFLLRN peptide: synthetic peptide of tethered ligand sequence → can activate PAR-1 independently (used experimentally); antiplatelet drug: vorapaxar (Zontivity): selective PAR-1 antagonist → ↓platelet aggregation → ↓MACE in secondary prevention after MI (note: risk of ICH + GI bleeding); PAR-1 vs GP IIb/IIIa: vorapaxar targets PAR-1 (thrombin receptor); abciximab/tirofiban/eptifibatide target GP IIb/IIIa (fibrinogen receptor); P2Y12 (ADP receptor) targeted by clopidogrel/prasugrel/ticagrelor; TXA2 receptor (TP, TBXA2R) targeted by aspirin (inhibits COX-1 → ↓TXA2 → ↓TP activation)

Thrombin binds to PAR-1 and induces conformational change without proteolysis, and the occupied receptor then amplifies thrombin activity (PAR-1 activation requires PROTEOLYSIS by thrombin; it is not a simple occupancy mechanism; conformational change alone is insufficient; PAR-1 cannot 'amplify' thrombin directly)
explanation: Platelet activation biochemistry: Primary agonists of platelet activation: Thrombin (→ PAR-1/4): most potent; generated by the coagulation cascade at site of vascular injury; ADP (→ P2Y1 [Gαq, ↑Ca2+] + P2Y12 [Gαi, ↓cAMP; most important for sustained aggregation]): released from dense granules (δ-granules) of activated platelets → autocrine + paracrine amplification; TXA2 (→ TP receptor, Gαq + Gα12/13): generated by COX-1 pathway in platelets → vasoconstriction + ↑more TXA2 (amplification); Collagen (→ GPVI [FcγR-like, SFK → Syk → LAT → PLCγ2 → IP3 + Ca2+] + GP Ia/IIa [α2β1 integrin, collagen adhesion receptor] on platelets): direct platelet-collagen interaction at subendothelial collagen; GP Ib-IX-V (vWF receptor): vWF + collagen → vWF binds GP Ib-V-IX → platelet captures to endothelium at high shear → rolling → GPVI contact → activation; vWF disease (vWD): bleeding; thrombolytic drugs target: tPA + streptokinase → plasminogen → plasmin → degrades fibrin. Platelet degranulation: α-granules: fibrinogen, vWF, P-selectin, Factor V, Factor XIII, GP IIb/IIIa, platelet factor 4 (PF4), PDGF, TGF-β, VEGFs, coagulation factors; δ-granules (dense): ADP, ATP, serotonin (5-HT), Ca2+, polyphosphates; lysosomal granules (λ): acid hydrolases. GP IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3, integrin): fibrinogen bridge → platelet-platelet aggregation; activated by inside-out signaling (↑Ca2+ → talin-kindlin → integrin conformational change → ↑affinity for fibrinogen); abciximab (chimeric Fab) + tirofiban (RGD peptidomimetic) + eptifibatide (KGD cyclic peptide) → competitive antagonists of fibrinogen at GP IIb/IIIa → ↓aggregation → used for ACS PCI.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The lac operon of E. coli is a classic example of inducible gene regulation. Induction occurs when lactose is present but glucose is absent. The mechanism requires BOTH removal of the lac repressor AND activation by CAP-cAMP. Which statement about the role of cAMP in this system is correct?
options: cAMP directly binds to the lac repressor, causing its dissociation from the operator (the lac repressor is a DIFFERENT protein from CAP; allolactose [not cAMP] binds the lac repressor → conformational change → repressor dissociates from operator; cAMP interacts with CAP [catabolite activator protein], not the lac repressor)

cAMP is synthesized by adenylate cyclase, which is ACTIVATED when glucose is absent: in E. coli, glucose transport via PTS (phosphotransferase system) → EIIAGlc (IIAGlc): when glucose is absent → EIIAGlc remains phosphorylated (EIIAGlc-P) → EIIAGlc-P activates adenylate cyclase (CYA, adenylate cyclase) → ↑cAMP; when glucose is present → EIIAGlc donates its phosphate to incoming glucose (PTS transport) → EIIAGlc becomes unphosphorylated → EIIAGlc (unphosphorylated) inhibits adenylate cyclase → ↓cAMP; EFFECT of ↑cAMP: cAMP binds to CAP (catabolite activator protein, also called CRP [cAMP receptor protein]): CAP-cAMP complex → conformational change → CAP-cAMP binds to specific DNA sequence at CAP site (upstream of lac promoter: at -61.5 position from TSS) → bends DNA ~90° → directly contacts α-CTD (C-terminal domain of the α-subunit of RNA Pol II in E. coli) → RECRUITS RNA Pol → ↑lacZYA transcription; CATABOLITE REPRESSION (glucose effect): when glucose is present → ↓cAMP → ↓CAP-cAMP → ↓RNA Pol binding → ↓transcription of lac operon even if lactose removes the repressor; catabolite repression applies to: lac operon + ara operon + gal operon + mal regulon (all for alternative carbon source utilization that should only be expressed when glucose [preferred] is absent); INDIRECT regulation: EIIAGlc also directly inhibits permease (LacY) + other transporters when unphosphorylated → 'inducer exclusion' (lactose cannot enter the cell when glucose is present → no allolactose [lac operon inducer] formed even if lactose is extracellular) → double mechanism for glucose preference

cAMP binds directly to the -10 and -35 promoter regions, increasing RNA polymerase binding efficiency (cAMP does not directly bind DNA; cAMP binds to CAP protein → CAP-cAMP complex binds DNA; RNA Pol binds to -10 and -35 promoter elements independently of cAMP/CAP; the CAP site is upstream [at ~-61] of the promoter; CAP-cAMP contact with RNA Pol α-CTD activates transcription)

cAMP concentration is highest when glucose is present and decreases when glucose is absent (this is BACKWARDS; adenylate cyclase is activated when glucose is ABSENT → ↑cAMP → CAP-cAMP → ↑transcription; when glucose is present → ↓cAMP → ↓CAP-cAMP → ↓transcription [catabolite repression])
explanation: Lac operon regulation — integrated: Three states: No lactose + glucose: repressor bound (operator occupied → blocks lacZYA) + ↓cAMP (↓CAP-cAMP) → NO transcription. Lactose + glucose: allolactose (inducer, made by β-galactosidase from lactose traces) → binds repressor → repressor off operator → but ↓cAMP (↓CAP-cAMP) → MINIMAL transcription (low-level). Lactose + no glucose: repressor off (allolactose) + ↑cAMP (↑CAP-cAMP) → MAXIMAL transcription → lacZ (β-galactosidase) + lacY (lactose permease) + lacA (thiogalactoside transacetylase). Lac repressor (LacI protein): tetrameric; HTH (helix-turn-helix) DNA binding domain; inducer-binding domain binds allolactose → HTH cannot bind DNA → derepression; aTc (anhydrotetracycline) analogy: tet repressor + aTc works similarly (used in synthetic biology Tet-off/Tet-on systems). CAP-cAMP: transcriptional activator; class I (lac, gal: CAP contact with αCTD of RNA Pol) vs class II (araBAD: CAP at -41.5 → contacts σ70 directly); arabinose operon: AraC: in absence of arabinose → AraC dimerizes + binds araI1-araO2 (repressor loop) → represses araBAD; in presence of arabinose → arabinose binds AraC monomer → AraC binds araI1-araI2 (adjacent) → CAP-cAMP + AraC → ↑transcription; AraC = both activator (with arabinose + no glucose) AND repressor (without arabinose) → elegant bistable switch. Attenuation: additional regulation in amino acid biosynthetic operons (trp operon): leader peptide with tandem Trp codons → if Trp-tRNATrp plentiful → ribosome translates leader rapidly → RNA forms terminator hairpin → premature transcription termination; if Trp-tRNATrp scarce → ribosome stalls at Trp codons → RNA folds into anti-terminator → transcription continues; antitermination mechanism: NusA + rho-independent terminators vs rut (rho utilization) sites + Rho helicase for rho-dependent terminators.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Methemoglobin (MetHb) cannot carry oxygen because iron in MetHb is in the ferric (Fe3+) state. The major enzymatic mechanism for reducing MetHb back to Hb (Fe2+) in red blood cells is:
options: Glutathione peroxidase + reduced glutathione: GPX uses GSH to reduce H2O2 → GSSG; GSSG → reduced back to GSH by glutathione reductase + NADPH (from G6PD/PPP); GPX does NOT directly reduce MetHb; GSH does not reduce MetHb significantly under physiological conditions

NADPH-metHb reductase (using NADPH from PPP): NADPH-MetHb reductase (NADPH diaphorase, CYPB5R2) exists but is NOT the major pathway of MetHb reduction under basal conditions; it requires METHYLENE BLUE as an intermediate electron carrier → treatment of MetHb toxicity: methylene blue (MB) + NADPH diaphorase → leucomethylene blue → reduces MetHb → normal Hb; MB is the PHARMACOLOGICAL pathway for MetHb reduction, not the physiological primary pathway

NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase (NADH-diaphorase, CYB5R3) coupled with cytochrome b5: CYB5R3 (cytochrome b5 reductase 3, NADH-methemoglobin reductase, formerly called DIA1): the MAJOR physiological MetHb reductase in RBCs (~95% of MetHb reduction); mechanism: NADH (from glycolysis: GAPDH step → 1,3-BPG + NADH) → [CYB5R3] → cytochrome b5 (reduced, cytochrome b5 type B, CYB5B) → MetHb (Fe3+) → Hb (Fe2+) + cytochrome b5 oxidized; CYB5R3 accepts electrons from NADH → reduces cytochrome b5 (heme-containing electron carrier) → cyt b5 donates electrons to MetHb-Fe3+ → reduces to Fe2+; CYB5R3 is constitutive in RBCs (mature RBCs have no mitochondria + limited oxidative phosphorylation → rely on glycolysis for NADH); CYB5R3 deficiency (hereditary MetHb disease type I: RBC-only deficiency, autosomal recessive): persistent MetHb + cyanosis + polycythemia (compensatory erythrocytosis); treatment: methylene blue or ascorbic acid; type II CYB5R3 deficiency: generalized (all cells) → severe neurological impairment + fatal; CYB5R3 deficiency type I vs type II: same gene but different mutations → type I often milder missense that preserves some catalytic activity; treatment: riboflavin (cofactor for CYB5R3 [FAD-containing]) may partially help in some cases; ascorbic acid (reduces MetHb non-enzymatically via direct electron donation)

Hexokinase converting glucose → G6P which directly reduces MetHb: hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to G6P (glycolysis entry); G6P then enters glycolysis (→ NADH via GAPDH for CYB5R3) or PPP (→ NADPH for emergency MB-mediated pathway); hexokinase itself does NOT directly reduce MetHb; the indirect provision of NADH is via glycolysis + GAPDH → CYB5R3 pathway
explanation: Methemoglobinemia — causes and treatment: Acquired MetHb causes (oxidize Fe2+ → Fe3+): Dapsone (antibiotic/antiprotozoan; used for malaria prophylaxis, PCP, leprosy): oxidizes Hb → MetHb; hydroxylamine metabolite of dapsone is the direct oxidant; Nitrites: amyl nitrite (historically used for cyanide antidote: MetHb [Fe3+] avidly binds CN- → cyanomethemoglobin → frees respiratory chain from CN-; then sodium thiosulfate → thiocyanate; but methylene blue CANNOT be used for CN poisoning MetHb since MB would re-reduce MetHb → restore toxicity); sodium nitrite in well water → infant MetHb ('blue baby syndrome'); Benzocaine + prilocaine (local anesthetics): aminophenol metabolites → MetHb; Nitroglycerine + nitroprusside: SNP (sodium nitroprusside) → cyanide release → some MetHb; Phenazopyridine (urinary analgesic): MetHb; Industrial: aniline, nitrobenzene. Treatment of MetHb toxicity: methylene blue (MB, 1-2 mg/kg IV): MB → [NADPH diaphorase/G6PD-PPP-NADPH] → leucomethylene blue (reduced MB) → leucomethylene blue reduces MetHb → Hb + oxidized MB → recycled; rate-limiting: NADPH availability; CONTRAINDICATIONS for methylene blue: (1) G6PD deficiency: cannot generate NADPH → MB ineffective + hemolysis risk (G6PD deficiency → ↓NADPH → cannot reduce MB back → hemolysis without MetHb reversal; alternative: ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion, or hyperbaric O2); (2) NADPH-diaphorase deficiency (rare); high-dose MB itself causes MetHb (paradoxical; MB > 7 mg/kg → direct Hb oxidation). Ascorbic acid (vitamin C): reduces MetHb non-enzymatically (but slowly; used chronically in CYB5R3 deficiency type I [1000 mg/day] + in some toxin cases where MB is contraindicated). Cyanide antidote kits: hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit): binds CN directly → cyanocobalamin → safe; no MetHb induction needed; preferred in suspected mixed CO+CN poisoning (CO → carboxyhemoglobin; adding MetHb worsens O2 delivery; hydroxocobalamin better); or: sodium thiosulfate → sulfur donor for rhodanese (ThTST, mitochondrial thiosulfate sulfurtransferase) → CN + S2O3 → SCN- (thiocyanate) → excreted.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the synthesis of heme, the enzyme ferrochelatase (FECH) inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX. FECH activity is inhibited by:
options: Succinylacetone (from hereditary tyrosinemia type I): succinylacetone is a potent inhibitor of PBGS (ALA dehydratase, step 2 of heme synthesis), NOT ferrochelatase; succinylacetone inhibits ALA dehydratase by mimicking ALA (substrate analog) → ↑ALA accumulation; ferrochelatase is a separate enzyme

Hematin (heme in ferric form): hematin (hemin) can inhibit ALAS1 (negative feedback on committed step of heme synthesis) via negative feedback mechanisms, NOT ferrochelatase; ferrochelatase inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX → if the reaction is inhibited, protoporphyrin IX accumulates

Lead (Pb2+) and other heavy metals, which compete with Fe2+ at the active site: FECH (ferrochelatase, FECH gene, 18q21.3): mitochondrial inner membrane; contains [2Fe-2S] cluster (structural, not catalytic) → important for FECH structure + electron channeling; catalytic: inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX → heme; inhibited by: LEAD (Pb2+): Pb2+ competes with Fe2+ at the active site of FECH → ↓heme synthesis → ↑protoporphyrin IX accumulates as zinc protoporphyrin (ZPP: in RBC, zinc substitutes for iron in the blocked reaction → ZPP = zinc protoporphyrin; ZPP measured as ZPP/heme ratio by hematofluorometry → screening test for lead poisoning) + ↑free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP); also PBGS is inhibited by Pb → ↑ALA in urine; combined: ↑ALA + ZPP = lead poisoning; other metals: Hg2+, As3+ also inhibit FECH; FECH deficiency → EPP (erythropoietic protoporphyria): ↑protoporphyrin IX in erythrocytes + plasma + liver → photosensitivity (non-blistering, painful burning with light exposure; porphyrin absorbs light at 400 nm [Soret band] → singlet oxygen → oxidative damage to skin) + liver disease (protoporphyrin IX precipitates in bile → cholestasis + cirrhosis); diagnosis: erythrocyte protoporphyrin (free metal-free protoporphyrin IX) + stool protoporphyrin; treatment: beta-carotene (photoprotection), afamelanotide (MC1R agonist → ↑melanin → ↑photoprotection); liver transplant if end-stage liver disease

N-succinyl-5-aminolevulinic acid, which is the product of ALA dehydratase: this is not a real compound; ALA dehydratase condenses 2 ALA → porphobilinogen; succinyl-5-aminolevulinic acid does not exist; ferrochelatase is inhibited by Pb2+, not by ALA derivatives
explanation: Lead poisoning — biochemistry: Pb2+ inhibits MULTIPLE heme synthesis enzymes: (1) PBGS/ALA-D (most sensitive): ↑urine ALA (major biomarker); (2) FECH: ↑ZPP (zinc protoporphyrin in RBCs; Zn2+ substitutes for Pb-blocked Fe2+); (3) coproporphyrinogen oxidase (CPOX): ↑urine coproporphyrin III; neurological toxicity: Pb2+ → mimics Ca2+ → activates PKC → ↑Glu release (excitotoxicity) → also enters NMDA receptors; ↓dopamine → neurological damage; also interferes with Na+/K+-ATPase; inhibits ALAD (ALA dehydratase) → ↑ALA → ALA is neurotoxic (GABAergic system inhibition); Pb and non-heme effects: Pb inhibits δ-ALAS (indirectly, by ↑ALA which is normally at low concentration → feedback reduction of ALAS?); Pb → ↓Na+/K+-ATPase in brain → ↑extracellular K+ → depolarization + seizures; ↓IQ (by mechanism involving dopamine + NMDA receptor); calcium mimicry: Pb2+ → Ca2+-binding proteins (calmodulin, PKC); blood lead level (BLL) > 5 µg/dL = elevated in children (CDC reference value, 2012); treatment: chelation (CaNa2EDTA + BAL/dimercaprol: for severe cases with BLL > 70 µg/dL or encephalopathy; succimer [DMSA, meso-2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid] for outpatient, BLL > 45 µg/dL); remove from exposure first. Arsenic poisoning: ↑As3+ → inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase (lipoic acid arsenical adduct, 'arsenical paralysis'; As3+ chelates vicinal dithiols → PDC + OGDH disabled → lactic acidosis + neurological); also FECH + other enzymes; As5+ (arsenate) → substitutes for inorganic phosphate → uncouples oxidative phosphorylation (arsenolysis: 1,3-BPG replaced by 1-As-3-BPG → spontaneous hydrolysis → no ATP) → ↓GAPDH product stability → ↓ATP.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Autophagy is a cellular degradation pathway that delivers cytoplasmic contents to lysosomes. The initiation of autophagy is regulated by MTORC1 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1). When nutrients are abundant, mTORC1:
options: Is inactive, allowing ULK1 to phosphorylate Beclin-1 and initiate autophagy (when nutrients are abundant, mTORC1 is ACTIVE; active mTORC1 INHIBITS autophagy by phosphorylating ULK1 and Beclin-1 to PREVENT initiation; the scenario described is opposite of what happens)

Is active and phosphorylates and inhibits ULK1 (unc-51-like autophagy activating kinase 1), thereby suppressing autophagy initiation: mTORC1: kinase complex containing mTOR (FRAP1, MTOR gene) + Raptor (RPTOR) + mLST8 + PRAS40 + Deptor; activated by: nutrients (amino acids via Rag GTPase: RagA/B-GTP + RagC/D-GDP → active Rag heterodimer → recruits mTORC1 to lysosomal surface → RHEB-GTP activates mTOR kinase); PI3K-Akt pathway (↑Akt → phospho-TSC2 → TSC1/TSC2 inactive → RHEB remains GTP-bound → mTORC1 active); energy status (↑ATP/AMP ratio → low AMPK → ↓mTORC1 phosphorylation? [AMPK inhibits TSC2 phospho-Ser1387 to activate TSC, and directly inhibits Raptor phospho-Ser792 → ↓mTORC1]); WHEN mTORC1 IS ACTIVE (nutrient-abundant state): mTORC1 → phosphorylates ULK1 (Ser757 in ULK1 [serine 757 in human ULK1]) → INACTIVATES ULK1 → ↓autophagy initiation; mTORC1 → phosphorylates ATG13 (autophagy-related 13) + FIP200 (RB1CC1) → disrupts ULK1-ATG13-FIP200 complex → ↓autophagy; also: mTORC1 → phosphorylates TFEB (transcription factor EB) → TFEB remains cytoplasmic (14-3-3 sequestered) → ↓lysosomal biogenesis + ↓autophagy gene transcription; when mTORC1 is INHIBITED (starvation/rapamycin): ↓mTORC1 → ↓phospho-ULK1-Ser757 → AMPK can phosphorylate ULK1 Ser317 + Ser777 → ULK1 ACTIVE → initiates autophagy; ULK1 phosphorylates Beclin-1 (ATG6) + ATG14L → PI3KC3 complex (Beclin-1 + Vps15 + Vps34 + ATG14L) → ↑PI3P production → phagophore nucleation; SPECIFIC AUTOPHAGY TYPES: macroautophagy (discussed above); microautophagy (lysosomal membrane invagination → direct engulfment); CMA (chaperone-mediated autophagy: KFERQ-like sequences in cytosolic proteins → Hsc70 + cochaperones → LAMP-2A [LAMP-2 isoform on lysosome] → direct translocation); mitophagy (selective autophagy of damaged mitochondria: PINK1 [kinase, accumulates on depolarized Δψm-low mitochondria → Parkin [E3 ubiquitin ligase] recruitment + phospho-Ser65 of Ub on OMM proteins + phospho-Ser65 of Parkin → ubiquitination of OMM proteins → p62/SQSTM1 + NBR1 + NDP52/CALCOCO2 receptor-mediated autophagosome recognition)

Is active and directly upregulates lysosomal cathepsins to enhance protein degradation (lysosomal cathepsins are regulated by TFEB; active mTORC1 SUPPRESSES TFEB → ↓lysosomal biogenesis; so mTORC1 active → LESS cathepsin expression and LESS autophagy; the correct effect of mTORC1 is to INHIBIT autophagy, not to upregulate lysosomal cathepsins)
explanation: Autophagy — steps and selective forms: Initiation: ULK1/2 complex (ULK1/2 + ATG13 + RB1CC1/FIP200 + ATG101) → phagophore (isolation membrane, IM) nucleation; Nucleation: Beclin-1 complex (Beclin-1 + VPS34 + VPS15 + ATG14L/BARKOR) → PI3P generation at ER/mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCS) → phagophore; Elongation: ATG5-ATG12 complex (ATG7 [E1] → ATG10 [E2] → ATG12-ATG5 conjugate) + ATG16L1 → LC3 lipidation: LC3B [MAP1LC3B, PE conjugation; ATG4 → proLC3 → LC3-I [cytosol] → ATG7 [E1] + ATG3 [E2] + ATG12-ATG5/ATG16L1 [E3-like] → LC3-II [PE-conjugated to outer + inner IM]]; Completion: closure of phagophore → autophagosome (double-membrane vesicle); Maturation: autophagosome + lysosome → autolysosome (SNAREs: STX17/SNAP29 on autophagosome + VAMP8 on lysosome); Degradation: lysosomal cathepsins (B, D, L + others) + acid pH → degrade contents → AA + FA + etc. → exported via SLC transporters → cytoplasm; Rapamycin: allosteric mTORC1 inhibitor (binds FKBP12 → FK-rapamycin complex inhibits mTOR FRB domain → ↓S6K1 + ↓4E-BP1 phosphorylation → ↓protein synthesis + ↑autophagy); used as immunosuppressant (↓T-cell proliferation); rapalogs (everolimus, temsirolimus, ridaforolimus) for cancer (↓mTOR → ↓cell growth). Beclin-1 (ATG6/BECN1): pro-autophagy (activates PI3KC3) but also regulated by BCL-2 + BCL-XL: BCL-2 BH3-binding groove binds Beclin-1 BH3 domain → sequesters Beclin-1 → ↓autophagy (apoptosis regulator also inhibits autophagy); BH3-mimetics (venetoclax/ABT-199 → BCL-2) → displace Beclin-1 → ↑autophagy + ↑apoptosis in cancer; p62 (SQSTM1): autophagy receptor + signaling hub: binds ubiquitinated cargo (via UBA domain) + LC3/GABARAP (via LIR [LC3-interacting region, WDXL/I motif]) → bridges cargo to autophagosome; also activates NRF2 (anti-oxidant) + mTOR (via Raptor binding on lysosome); accumulates when autophagy is impaired → p62 bodies (IHC) → marker of defective autophagy; ↑p62 in ALS, FTLD, Parkinson, Huntington, liver disease, cancer.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Signal transduction via receptor tyrosine kinases often involves the small GTPase Ras. Ras normally cycles between GDP-bound (inactive) and GTP-bound (active) states. The protein that ACTIVATES Ras by catalyzing GDP→GTP exchange is:
options: GAP (GTPase-activating protein): RasGAP (RASA1/NF1): STIMULATES the intrinsic GTPase of Ras → converts GTP→GDP → INACTIVATES Ras; NF1 (neurofibromin 1): RasGAP → loss of NF1 → constitutive Ras-GTP → neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) → ↑MAPK signaling; the question asks for the ACTIVATOR (GDP→GTP exchange), which is GEF not GAP

SOS (son of sevenless), a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): SOS (SOS1/SOS2): RasGEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor for Ras): mechanism: SOS catalyzes release of GDP from Ras → GDP dissociates → Ras:empty → GTP (abundant in cytoplasm) replaces GDP → Ras-GTP (active); SOS activation pathway: activated RTK (e.g., EGFR) → pTyr → SH2-domain protein Grb2 (growth factor receptor-bound protein 2) → constitutively associated SOS (Grb2-SOS complex via SH3-proline-rich motif interaction) → Grb2 SH2 binds RTK pTyr → SOS recruited to plasma membrane → SOS catalyzes Ras nucleotide exchange → Ras-GTP; Ras-GTP → RAF (BRAF/CRAF) → MEK1/2 → ERK1/2 → nuclear (Elk-1, Fos, Myc) → gene expression (proliferation, survival); SOS feedback: Ras-GTP → SOS allosteric site on SOS → ACTIVATES SOS further (positive feedback via Ras switch II binding to SOS allosteric pocket = 'Ras-GTP positive feedback') + PLC-ε → ↑DAG → PKC → phospho-SOS → ↓SOS (negative feedback); Noonan syndrome: PTPN11 (SHP2) GOF mutations (most common, 50%) + SOS1 GOF → Ras-MAPK hyperactivation → Noonan syndrome phenotype (short stature, facial dysmorphism, cardiac defects [pulmonary stenosis, HCM], webbed neck, coagulopathy); also: KRAS/NRAS mutations in Noonan-like conditions; RASopathies: NF1, Noonan, LEOPARD, Costello, CFC (cardio-facio-cutaneous) syndromes; cancer: KRAS GOF mutations (most common oncogene mutation in human cancer: KRAS G12C, G12V, G12D → constitutive Ras-GTP → ↑MAPK + ↑PI3K → ↑proliferation); KRAS inhibitors: sotorasib (AMG 510, Lumykras): first approved KRAS inhibitor → covalently binds KRAS G12C in GDP-bound (inactive) form → prevents GTP exchange → ↓Ras-GTP → ↓signaling; adagrasib (MRTX849, Krazati): also KRAS G12C inhibitor

GDP exchange inhibitor (GDI): GDIs (GDP dissociation inhibitors) apply mainly to Rho GTPases (RhoGDI, GDI1/GDI2/GDI3) → bind prenylated Rho GTPases → sequester in cytoplasm → INHIBIT by preventing membrane association + GDP exchange; GDIs are NOT GEFs; for Ras, there are no classical GDIs; Ras is membrane-anchored (farnesylation + palmitoylation → RAS does not use GDIs
p120RasGAP (RASA1): same as option A's GAP; p120RasGAP is a GTPase-activating protein → inactivates Ras → same incorrect answer as A
explanation: Ras-MAPK cascade — clinical relevance: Ras: small GTPase (21 kDa); KRAS (Kirsten), NRAS (neuroblastoma), HRAS (Harvey) isoforms; farnesylated (via FNTA/FNTB [farnesyltransferase] using FPP from mevalonate pathway) + palmitoylated (HRAS, NRAS) or polylysine stretch (KRAS4B) → plasma membrane anchoring; GDP-Ras (inactive): Ras GTP off = inactive → GEF needed; GTP-Ras (active): effectors: RAF → MEK → ERK (proliferation/survival); PI3K → Akt (survival); RalGDS → Ral (vesicle trafficking); Tiam1 (Rac GEF) → Rac (cytoskeleton). GEFs for Ras: SOS1/SOS2 (main); RasGRF1/2 (calmodulin-sensitive, Ca2+-dependent, mainly in neurons; EPAC-related?); RasGRP1/2/3/4 (DAG-regulated → mast cells, lymphocytes); RIN proteins. GAPs for Ras: RASA1 (p120RasGAP); NF1 (neurofibromin, largest RasGAP, 250 kDa, Sec14 + PH + Ras-GRD [GAP-related domain] + GRD); DAB2IP (in endosome). MAPK cascade downstream of Ras: RAF1 (CRAF) + BRAF + ARAF → MEK1 + MEK2 → ERK1 + ERK2; ERK substrates: RSK (ribosomal S6 kinase) → S6 [↑translation]; MNK1/2 → eIF4E [↑cap-dependent translation]; c-Fos (rapid transcription → AP-1 complex → gene expression); ELK-1 (SRF coactivator → SRE → immediate-early genes); MSK1/2 → histone H3 Ser10/28 + CREB Ser133; ↑Cyclin D1 (BRAF → ERK → ↑Cyclin D expression → CDK4/6 activation → pRb → S-phase entry → proliferation); Therapeutic BRAF inhibitors: vemurafenib (PLX4032), dabrafenib: BRAF V600E (T1799A mutation → Val600Glu → constitutive BRAF kinase, no Ras needed) → melanoma (50-60% have BRAF V600E) + colorectal (20%) + thyroid papillary (40-60%) + hairy cell leukemia (100%); MEK inhibitors: trametinib + cobimetinib + binimetinib → combine with BRAF inhibitors to ↓resistance (BRAF inhibitor → paradoxical MAPK activation in KRAS-mutant/RAS-driven tumors via RAS → RAF dimerization → CRAF → MEK bypass; MEKi prevents this); ERK inhibitors: ulixertinib (in trials).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme that directly converts propionyl-CoA (C3) to methylmalonyl-CoA (C4) is propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC). PCC requires:
options: Adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl, vitamin B12 coenzyme): AdoCbl is the cofactor for METHYLMALONYL-COA MUTASE (MCM), NOT for propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC); AdoCbl catalyzes the isomerization of methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (a carbon skeleton rearrangement)

Biotin and ATP: PCC (propionyl-CoA carboxylase): propionyl-CoA + HCO3- + ATP → D-methylmalonyl-CoA + ADP + Pi; BIOTIN (covalently attached to BCCP subunit of PCC via ε-NH2 of Lys residue by holocarboxylase synthetase [HCS, HLCS gene]) is the CO2 carrier; ATP (provides energy for the carboxylation); MECHANISM: Step 1: biotin carboxylase (BC) subunit uses ATP → carboxylates biotin (N1 of biotin) from HCO3- → N1-carboxybiotin (CO2-biotin); Step 2: carboxyltransferase (CT) domain transfers CO2 from N1-carboxybiotin → propionyl-CoA → D-methylmalonyl-CoA; Biotin-dependent carboxylases in humans: PCC (PCCA + PCCB subunits, α6β6 dodecamer, mitochondrial); MCC (3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, MCCA + MCCB, Leu catabolism, mitochondrial); ACC1 (ACACA, cytoplasmic, lipogenesis); ACC2 (ACACB, outer IMM, CPT1 regulation via malonyl-CoA); PC (pyruvate carboxylase, PCCA gene, mitochondrial, gluconeogenesis/anaplerosis); HCS (holocarboxylase synthetase) attaches biotin to all four: PCC, MCC, ACC1, ACC2, PC; PCC deficiency (propionic acidemia, PA): PCCA or PCCB mutations → ↑propionylcarnitine (C3) on acylcarnitine NBS + ↑3-OH-propionic acid + ↑methylcitric acid (propionyl-CoA + OAA → [propionyl-CoA enters TCA via anaplerosis?] → methylcitrate, a toxic metabolite) + ↑propionate in urine; clinical: neonatal/early onset: metabolic crisis (ketoacidosis + hyperammonemia + hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis) + cardiomyopathy (propionate is cardiotoxic → QTc prolongation → arrhythmia → sudden death); treatment: low-protein diet + carnitine + cobalamin (B12 trial for MMA not PA); liver/liver-kidney transplant; OAA regeneration: propionyl-CoA is anaplerotic (→ D-methylmalonyl-CoA → L-methylmalonyl-CoA [MMCE] → succinyl-CoA [MCM + AdoCbl] → TCA); in PA: blocked → ↑propionyl-CoA → ↑methylcitrate + ↑odd-chain FA in membrane phospholipids

FAD and NAD+: FAD + NAD+ are cofactors for the α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes (PDC, OGDH, BCKDH) which contain E3 (dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, FAD-dependent) and regenerate NAD+; propionyl-CoA carboxylase does NOT use FAD or NAD+; biotin + ATP are the required cofactors

Tetrahydrofolate (THF) and cobalamin: THF is the one-carbon carrier in folate cycle (used in purine synthesis, thymidylate synthesis, amino acid metabolism); B12 (cobalamin) as MeCbl is used by methionine synthase + as AdoCbl by MCM; neither THF nor cobalamin is the cofactor for PCC
explanation: Biotin (vitamin B7/H) — biochemistry and deficiency: Biotin structure: bicyclic compound (imidazolidine ring + tetrahydrothiophene ring + valeric acid side chain); covalently attached to Lys ε-NH2 of BCCP domain of each carboxylase by HCS (holocarboxylase synthetase; HLCS gene; pyrophosphate release drives reaction); in food: biotin-Lys (biocytin) → biotinidase (BTDP gene, in serum + lysosome) → free biotin + Lys → recycling; biotinidase deficiency (BTD mutations; AR; most common cause of biotin deficiency in children): ↓biotinidase → cannot recycle biotin → functional biotin deficiency → ↓all four biotin-dependent carboxylases → ↑3-methylcrotonylglycinuria + ↑methylcitrate + ↑lactic acid + ↑3-OH-isovalerate; clinical: seizures + hypotonia + alopecia + eczematous rash + hearing loss + optic atrophy (if untreated); NBS (dried blood spot): BTD enzyme activity assay (included in newborn screening panels worldwide); treatment: free biotin 5-10 mg/day → prevents all symptoms if started early; HCS deficiency: newborn period; more severe; ↑HCS Km for biotin → needs pharmacological doses; BIOTIN in LABS: biotin interference in immunoassays: exogenous high-dose biotin (biotin supplements) → interferes with streptavidin-biotin immunoassay systems → FALSE high or false low test results depending on assay format (competitive vs sandwich): troponin I (falsely LOW in biotin interference, sandwich assay streptavidin-avidin based) → missed MI diagnosis; TSH (can be falsely LOW or HIGH depending on assay); requires stopping biotin ≥ 72 h before blood draw. Drug-nutrient interaction: raw egg white contains avidin (a glycoprotein that binds biotin with extremely high affinity Kd ~10-15 M → biotin trapped → not absorbed → biotin deficiency [egg-white injury]); cooking → avidin denatured → biotin available.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The coagulation cascade uses multiple serine proteases. The final step of the common pathway is the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin. Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen at:
options: The gamma-gamma crosslink sites between two fibrin molecules (gamma-gamma crosslinks are formed by FXIII after fibrin polymerization; thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to generate fibrin monomers BEFORE FXIII acts; thrombin does not create crosslinks)

The Arg-Gly bonds in the fibrinogen Aα and Bβ chains to release fibrinopeptides A and B: fibrinogen (FI): hexameric plasma glycoprotein: (Aα)2(Bβ)2(γ)2 = 340 kDa; 3 pairs of chains: 2 Aα + 2 Bβ + 2 γ; arranged with 2 terminal D domains + central E domain (trinodular structure in EM); fibrinopeptides A (FPA) and B (FPB): short N-terminal peptides that mask polymerization sites; thrombin (IIa) cleaves: Arg16-Gly17 on Aα chain → releases FPA (16 AA peptide, first cleaved); Arg14-Gly15 on Bβ chain → releases FPB (14 AA peptide, cleaved second, slower); removal of FPA + FPB → fibrin monomers (desAA-desAB fibrin or desAABB fibrin); fibrin monomers spontaneously polymerize: FPA removal → exposes knob A (central E domain, sequence GPRV) → fits into hole a (terminal D domain, γ-chain hole) → end-to-end (overlapping half-staggered) polymer; FPB removal → exposes knob B → fits into hole b (β-chain hole); network formation: FPA-mediated lateral + longitudinal association → loose fibrin clot (soluble); then FXIII cross-links → insoluble covalent clot; diagnostic uses: FPA (fibrinopeptide A) and FPB: ↑FPA + FPB in plasma → evidence of thrombin generation (thrombosis, DIC); D-dimer: crosslinked fibrin degradation product (FDP) after plasmin cleaves crosslinked fibrin → D-D dimer junction remains → elevated in DVT/PE (very sensitive but low specificity); negative D-dimer (<500 ng/mL) → high NPV for excluding PE/DVT

The C-terminal region of the fibrinogen γ-chain to create sticky ends for polymerization (thrombin cleaves the N-terminal fibrinopeptides, NOT the C-terminal regions; the C-terminal γ-chain has hole 'a' (complement binding site?) + γ-dimer crosslinking sites for FXIII; GPRV knob:hole a interaction is formed AFTER thrombin cleavage of FPA)

The D-D junction to produce fibrin degradation products directly (fibrin degradation products are produced by plasmin cleavage of crosslinked fibrin → D-dimers; thrombin cleaves fibrinogen → fibrin MONOMERS, not D-dimers)
explanation: Fibrinogen and fibrin clot formation: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation): simultaneous systemic activation of coagulation → microthrombi in small vessels + consumption of clotting factors + platelets → paradoxical BLEEDING; causes: sepsis (LPS → TF on monocytes/endothelium → extrinsic pathway), obstetric catastrophe (amniotic fluid embolism → TF-rich AF → DIC), trauma (massive), malignancy (acute promyelocytic leukemia [APL, APML]: t(15;17) → PML-RARα → APL cells release TF + annexin II → severe DIC; treated with ATRA [all-trans retinoic acid] → differentiation → ↓TF release → DIC resolves); labs: ↑PT + ↑aPTT + ↑fibrinogen degradation products (FDP) + ↑D-dimer + ↓fibrinogen + ↓platelets + microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA, schistocytes on smear). Fibrinolysis: tPA (tissue plasminogen activator; PLAT gene): released from endothelium by shear stress, thrombin, histamine; half-life ~5 min in blood (rapidly cleared by PAI-1); cleaves plasminogen (Glu-Plm → Lys-Plm active plasmin [serine protease] → degrades fibrin + fibrinogen + FV, FVIII); fibrin-bound tPA is 100-1000× more active than free tPA (fibrin as cofactor → ↑tPA + plasminogen colocalization); uPA (urokinase-type PA; PLAU gene): cell-surface receptor uPAR (PLAUR) → uPA → plasminogen → plasmin → extracellular matrix degradation (tumor invasion) + wound healing; PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1; SERPINE1): SERPIN; rapidly inhibits tPA + uPA; PAI-1 is the major fibrinolysis regulator; ↑PAI-1 in obesity + insulin resistance + MetS + pregnancy + sepsis → ↑thrombosis risk; α2-antiplasmin (SERPINF2): directly inhibits free plasmin (crosslinked by FXIII to fibrin → limits fibrin clot dissolution); therapeutic thrombolysis: alteplase (rtPA) + tenecteplase + reteplase: activate plasminogen → fibrinolysis → used for acute MI/PE/stroke (within time window: stroke ≤ 4.5h; STEMI if PCI unavailable; massive PE). Streptokinase: bacterial (Streptococcal) protein; binds + activates plasminogen → non-fibrin-specific thrombolysis; older agent; allergenic; no longer first-line.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Prostaglandin synthesis begins with arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4 n-6) released from membrane phospholipids. Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting steps of prostaglandin biosynthesis?
options: Phospholipase A2 (PLA2): PLA2 (cytosolic PLA2 [cPLA2, PLA2G4A] + secreted PLA2 [sPLA2]) → releases AA from sn-2 position of phospholipids; PLA2 does provide the substrate (AA) but is NOT the rate-limiting step of prostaglandin synthesis; AA release can limit flux but COX is the primary regulated step; also: PLA2 releases lysophospholipids [lyso-PC → PAF precursor]; PLA2 inhibited by glucocorticoids (↑lipocortin/annexin A1 → blocks cPLA2) → ↓all eicosanoid synthesis (NSAIDs only block COX)

Cyclooxygenase-1/2 (COX-1/2, PTGS1/2, prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 1/2): COX enzymes are the rate-limiting and committed step of the prostaglandin/thromboxane/prostacyclin branch; COX has two activities in the same protein: (1) cyclooxygenase activity: AA + 2 O2 → PGG2 (prostaglandin G2, endoperoxide with hydroperoxide at C-15); uses two O2; (2) peroxidase activity: PGG2 → PGH2 (prostaglandin H2, endoperoxide [5,6-endoperoxide] with OH at C-15); COX mechanism: radical mechanism: Tyr385 is oxidized to tyrosyl radical by heme [Fe3+] + GSH/ROOH → Tyr385• → abstracts H from C13 of AA → AA radical → O2 inserts → cyclization → cyclooxygenase reaction; NSAID mechanism: NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, indomethacin, naproxen, diclofenac) inhibit COX: aspirin: irreversible acetylation of Ser530 of COX-1 (+ Ser516 of COX-2 at higher dose) → sterically blocks AA binding channel → loss of AA binding → ↓PGG2 → ↓all prostaglandins + TXA2; COX-2 selective inhibitors (coxibs: celecoxib, etoricoxib, rofecoxib [withdrawn: ↑MI risk due to ↓PGI2 without ↓TXA2]): exploit structural difference: COX-2 has Val523 instead of Ile523 in COX-1 → creates larger side pocket → coxibs fit into this pocket → selective COX-2 inhibition; COX-1: constitutive (gastric mucosa, platelets, kidney); COX-2: inducible (inflammation, pain, fever); COX-3 (splice variant of COX-1): minor relevance; downstream prostaglandin synthases: PGH2 → tissue-specific isomerases: PGE2 [PTGES, cytosolic or microsomal]; PGD2 [PTGDS, lipocalin-type or hematopoietic]; PGF2α [AKR1C3, aldoketoreductase]; PGI2 (prostacyclin) [PTGIS]; TXA2 [TXAS/CYP5A1] → platelet vasoconstriction

Thromboxane synthase (TXAS, CYP5A1): TXAS converts PGH2 → TXA2 (thromboxane A2) specifically in platelets; TXA2 is NOT a prostaglandin; TXAS is not the rate-limiting step of all prostaglandin synthesis; it acts downstream of COX on a specific branch

5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX, ALOX5): 5-LOX with FLAP (5-lipoxygenase activating protein) catalyzes AA → 5-HpETE → LTA4 (leukotriene A4, an epoxide) → LTB4 or LTC4/D4/E4; this is the LEUKOTRIENE pathway (NOT prostaglandin synthesis); 5-LOX is NOT involved in prostaglandin synthesis
explanation: Eicosanoid biosynthesis — complete: AA (20:4 n-6) metabolism via: COX pathway: → PGG2 → PGH2 → PGE2/PGD2/PGF2α/PGI2/TXA2; 5-LOX pathway: → 5-HpETE → LTA4 → LTB4 (PMN chemoattractant) or LTC4/D4/E4 (cysteinyl LTs = SRS-A, bronchoconstriction); 12-LOX (ALOX12): AA → 12-HpETE → 12-HETE; 15-LOX (ALOX15): AA → 15-HpETE → 15-HETE → lipoxins (anti-inflammatory); CYP450 pathway: AA → EETs (epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) [CYP2J2, vasodilatory] or HETEs [CYP4A, vasoconstrictory]. Key PGs and their receptors: PGE2: EP1-4 receptors (EP1: Gαq; EP2: Gαs; EP3: Gαi; EP4: Gαs/cAMP) → fever (hypothalamic EP3), pain sensitization (spinal EP3/EP4), vasodilation (EP2/4), bronchoconstriction (EP1), gastric cytoprotection (EP3/4); PGD2: DP1 (Gαs, mast cells, ILC2, eosinophil suppression) + DP2/CRTH2 (Gαi, eosinophil + basophil chemoattractant → allergy) → dual: some anti-inflammatory (DP1) + some pro-allergic (DP2); PGI2 (prostacyclin, t½ ~2 min): IP receptor (Gαs) → vasodilation + anti-aggregation (opposes TXA2 in the Vane-moncada prostacyclin:TXA2 balance); TXA2 (t½ ~30 sec): TP receptor (Gαq/G12) → vasoconstriction + platelet aggregation; LTB4: BLT1/BLT2 (Gαi); LTC4/D4/E4 (cysteinyl LTs): CysLT1/2 (bronchoconstriction → anti-asthma drugs: montelukast, zafirlukast = CysLT1 receptor antagonists; zileuton = 5-LOX inhibitor → ↓all LTs). Anti-inflammatory resolution: lipoxins (LXA4, LXB4) from 15-HETE + 5-LOX; resolvins (from EPA/DHA: E-series from EPA + D-series from DHA via 15-LOX/aspirin-acetylated COX-2 + 5-LOX); protectins/neuroprotectins (from DHA): neuroprotectin D1 (NPD1) → ↓brain ischemia; maresins (from DHA via 12-LOX) → pro-resolution; aspirin-triggered resolvins (AT-resolvins): aspirin-acetylated COX-2 loses TXA2/PGE2 activity BUT gains 15R-HETE from AA → 15-epi-LXA4 (aspirin-triggered lipoxin, ATL) → anti-inflammatory; this is one mechanism of aspirin's anti-inflammatory effects beyond just COX inhibition.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with Wilson's disease has abnormal copper deposition in the liver and brain. Wilson's disease is caused by mutations in the gene encoding:
options: Ceruloplasmin (CP): Ceruloplasmin is the major copper transport protein in plasma (synthesized in liver, carries ~95% of plasma copper as 6 atoms of Cu2+); ceruloplasmin is a MARKER for Wilson's disease (↓ceruloplasmin in ~90% of WD) but is NOT the causative gene; aceruloplasminemia (CP gene mutations) → iron accumulation (not copper) in brain/liver/pancreas (ceruloplasmin is also a ferroxidase: Fe2+ → Fe3+ for transferrin loading); aceruloplasminemia presents with neurological + diabetes + retinal degeneration

ATP7B (Wilson disease protein), the copper-transporting P-type ATPase expressed in liver: ATP7B (ATPase copper transporting beta): P-type ATPase (P1B subfamily); expressed primarily in LIVER (also brain [less]); FUNCTION: intracellular copper trafficking: (1) in trans-Golgi network (TGN) of hepatocyte: loads copper onto ceruloplasmin (apoCP → + Cu → holoCeruloplasmin) → secretion; (2) under high copper: ATP7B relocates from TGN → canalicular membrane (bile canaliculus) → exports excess copper into bile → eliminated in feces; WILSON DISEASE (WD, hepatolenticular degeneration): AR mutations in ATP7B → ↓biliary copper excretion → copper accumulates in liver → liver disease (hepatitis → cirrhosis → liver failure) + copper 'overflows' to blood (↓ceruloplasmin [cannot load Cu onto apoCP] + ↑free copper) → deposits in: brain (basal ganglia: putamen + caudate → lenticular degeneration → motor symptoms: tremor, dysarthria, dysphagia, choreoathetosis + psychiatry); kidney (Fanconi syndrome); cornea (Kayser-Fleischer [KF] rings: golden-brown ring at Descemet's membrane [posterior cornea], seen with slit-lamp, caused by Cu deposition); sun-flower cataracts (Cu in lens); diagnosis: ↓serum ceruloplasmin (< 20 mg/dL) + ↑24h urine copper (> 100 µg/day) + KF rings + liver biopsy (↑copper content > 250 µg/g dry wt) + ATP7B mutation; treatment: D-penicillamine (Cu chelation, first-line historically) + trientine (alternative chelator, fewer side effects) + zinc (↑intestinal metallothionein → binds dietary copper → ↑fecal excretion, reduces absorption) + liver transplant (corrects hepatic ATP7B deficiency → cures liver + systemic disease; KF rings may resolve)

ATP7A (Menkes disease protein): ATP7A (ATPase copper transporting alpha): P-type ATPase; expressed ubiquitously EXCEPT LIVER; function: provides copper to cuproenzymes (dopamine β-hydroxylase [DBH] → catecholamine synthesis; peptidyl glycine α-amidating mono-oxygenase [PAM] → neuropeptide amidation; lysyl oxidase → connective tissue cross-linking; SOD3) in TGN; also pumps copper from enterocyte to portal blood → copper absorption; MENKES DISEASE (MD): X-linked recessive, ATP7A mutations → ↓copper in all cells except intestinal enterocytes (↑copper in intestine but cannot export to blood) → systemic copper deficiency; clinical: kinky/steely hair (pili torti, lusterless, brittle → ↓lysyl oxidase → ↓hair shaft crosslinks), neurodegeneration (↓DBH → ↓catecholamines → seizures + hypotonia + developmental regression), connective tissue abnormalities (↓LOX → lax joints + vascular fragility + skin redundancy), hypothermia, hypoglycemia; no KF rings (copper is DEFICIENT in brain, not accumulated); treatment: copper histidinate (SC injection) if started very early (neonatal period); most forms fatal in early childhood

Hephaestin (HEPH): hephaestin is a ceruloplasmin homolog (also a ferroxidase) expressed in intestinal epithelium; works WITH ferroportin (SLC40A1) to export iron from enterocytes → circulation (hephaestin oxidizes Fe2+ → Fe3+ on the luminal side of basolateral enterocyte membrane → Fe3+ loaded onto transferrin); hephaestin is involved in IRON absorption, not copper disease; HEPH gene not related to Wilson disease
explanation: Copper metabolism: Dietary copper (0.9 mg/day) → absorbed in duodenum/small intestine: CTR1 (SLC31A1) → copper into enterocyte; copper → MT (metallothionein) or → ATP7A → basolateral export → portal blood → ceruloplasmin (CP, liver) → distributed to tissues. MT (metallothioneins MT1-4): small cysteine-rich proteins → bind heavy metals (Cu, Zn, Cd, Hg) → sequester; MT synthesis induced by: Zn, Cu, Cd, corticosteroids, IL-6; MT protects against heavy metal toxicity (↑MT → ↑tolerance); competition: Cu and Zn compete for enterocyte MT binding → high Zn → ↑MT → binds dietary Cu → ↓Cu absorption → used therapeutically in WD. Cuproenzymes (copper-dependent enzymes): Ceruloplasmin (CP, ferroxidase); Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV, CuA + CuB + heme a3); SOD1 (Cu/Zn-SOD, cytoplasmic O2•- → H2O2); SOD3 (extracellular Cu/Zn-SOD); DBH (dopamine β-hydroxylase, Cu-dependent → dopamine → norepinephrine; ↓DBH in Menkes); PAM (peptidyl glycine α-amidating monooxygenase, Cu-dependent → C-terminal amidation of neuropeptides [VIP, NPY, CRF, etc.]; ↓in Menkes); Lysyl oxidase (LOX, Cu-dependent → oxidizes Lys/HylLys → aldehyde → crosslinks in collagen + elastin → ↓LOX in Menkes → connective tissue laxity, vascular fragility); Tyrosinase (melanin synthesis, Cu-dependent); Factor V + VIII (not enzymes but contain Cu in their structure).
