WD epidemiology: 1/30,000; highly variable presentation; liver disease dominant in children/young adults; neuropsychiatric symptoms more prominent in older; ATP7B mutations > 700 reported; common: H1069Q (40-70% in European patients, 2 alleles needed for WD; compound heterozygotes common); R778L common in Asian patients; 8-33% WD patients have normal ceruloplasmin → don't rely only on CP level.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which protein complex caps the free ends of actin filaments, thereby preventing both polymerization and depolymerization?
options: Profilin: profilin (PFN1/2) binds G-actin (monomeric actin) in a 1:1 complex → sequesters actin monomers (in PFN-bound form, actin preferentially adds to barbed [+] end of filaments); profilin maintains high-concentration pool of polymerizable actin → ↑rapid actin assembly at barbed ends; profilin does NOT cap actin filaments

Arp2/3 complex: Arp2/3 complex (7 subunits: Arp2, Arp3, ArpC1-5): creates new actin branches off existing filaments (nucleation of branch points at 70°); activated by NPFs (nucleation-promoting factors: N-WASP, WAVE/SCAR, WASH); Arp2/3 is an INITIATOR of actin branching, NOT a filament cap

CapZ (capping protein, also called CP, α1β1 heterodimer, CAPZA1 + CAPZB): CapZ (capping protein Z, barbed-end capper): heterodimer (α + β subunits); binds barbed (+) end of actin filaments with very high affinity (Kd ~1 nM) → caps barbed end → BLOCKS both addition AND loss of monomers at barbed end; POINTED (-) end: capped by Tropomodulin (TMOD) in sarcomeric myofibrils; FUNCTION: CapZ localizes to sarcomeric Z-disc (hence 'Cap' + 'Z'-disc); in non-muscle cells: CapZ limits filament growth → shorter, more numerous filaments; REGULATION: CapZ regulated by: PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate): ↑PI(4,5)P2 → ↓CapZ activity (dissociation from barbed ends) → ↑free barbed ends → ↑actin polymerization (mechanism by which Gαq [PLC] → DAG + IP3; and Gα12/13 → RhoA → ROCK → ↑PIP5K → ↑PI(4,5)P2 → ↑CapZ release → ↑actin); V-1 (myotrophin/MT): binds CapZ → inhibits capping; CARMIL (capping protein, Arp2/3, myosin I linker): ↓CapZ affinity for barbed ends; WASp-homology domain 2 (WH2): G-actin binding; CapZ role in cardiac disease: CapZβ mutations/deletions → dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM); CapZ overexpression → concentric hypertrophy in animal models; CapZα/β balance in myofibrils → sarcomere length regulation

Cofilin (ADF/cofilin, ADF/destrin): cofilin (CFL1/2, actin depolymerizing factor) severs actin filaments AND depolymerizes pointed end (promotes treadmilling by recycling ADP-actin from pointed end → ADP-actin released → profilin → ADP-actin → ATP-actin [nucleotide exchange] → G-actin available for barbed end → faster treadmilling); cofilin is a SEVER and DEPOLYMERIZER, not a filament cap; cofilin inhibited by: LIM kinase (LIMK, phosphorylates Ser3 of cofilin → inactive cofilin → ↓actin dynamics → stable actin filaments) → LIMK is downstream of ROCK + PAK; slingshot phosphatase (SSH1) → activates cofilin (dephospho-Ser3)
explanation: Actin dynamics — complete: G-actin (globular): monomeric (ATP-actin or ADP-actin); F-actin (filamentous): polymer; treadmilling: barbed (+) end addition (fast) + pointed (-) end dissociation (slow) → net directionality at steady state; Profilin supplies ATP-actin to barbed end; cofilin severs filaments + removes ADP-actin from pointed end; CapZ caps barbed end; TMOD caps pointed end; nucleation: Arp2/3 (branches), formins (mDia1/2; FHOD; unbranched cables; leaky barbed-end elongation via FH1-FH2 domain; profilin-actin fed through FH1); tandem-monomer nucleation (JMY, COBL); Ena/VASP (anti-capping? → promote processive barbed-end elongation); Actin-regulating RhoGTPases: RhoA → ROCK → LIMK → ↓cofilin → ↑actin stability + ↑stress fibers (mDia1 + ROCK → myosin II); Rac1 → PAK1 → LIMK → ↓cofilin + → WAVE/SCAR → Arp2/3 → lamellipodia (sheet-like protrusions); Cdc42 → N-WASP → Arp2/3 + MRCK → filopodia (spike-like protrusions); Invadopodia/podosomes: actin-rich matrix-degrading structures; require Arp2/3 + cortactin + WASP + MT1-MMP. Drugs targeting actin: Cytochalasin D/B: cap barbed ends → ↓polymerization (same effect as CapZ but pharmacological); Jasplakinolide: stabilizes actin filaments (like phalloidin for F-actin staining); Latrunculin A/B: sequesters G-actin → ↓polymerization (like profilin trap); Phalloidin (Amanita phalloides mushroom toxin): stabilizes F-actin → ↓depolymerization → hepatotoxicity; used in lab to stain F-actin (fluorescent phalloidin conjugates). Clinically: p21-activated kinase 1 (PAK1): activated by Rac/Cdc42 → phosphorylates LIMK → ↓cofilin → ↑actin stability; PAK1 amplified in breast + ovarian cancer → cytoskeletal rearrangements → invasion; WASp (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein): mutations → ↓WASp → ↓Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization in lymphocytes + platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (XL; thrombocytopenia [small platelets] + eczema + immunodeficiency).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The major rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis in the liver is:
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase): G6Pase (SLC37A4 is the glucose-6-phosphate translocase; the catalytic subunit is G6PC/G6Pase-α in liver/kidney): the terminal step of GNG → G6P → glucose + Pi; G6Pase deficiency = GSD Ia (von Gierke); while G6Pase is a regulated enzyme, the RATE-LIMITING step of GNG is PEPCK (which commits oxaloacetate exclusively to the GNG pathway)

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1): FBPase-1 (FBP1): F1,6BP → F6P + Pi; the reverse of PFK-1; regulated allosterically: inhibited by AMP + F2,6BP (same regulators in reverse direction from PFK-1); is an important regulatory enzyme BUT not CLASSICALLY called the PRIMARY RATE-LIMITING step of GNG

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK, PCK1): PEPCK (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1, cytoplasmic): OAA + GTP → PEP + CO2 + GDP; KEY POINT: PEPCK is the committed step AND rate-limiting enzyme of gluconeogenesis because: (1) PEPCK is the enzyme that converts OAA → PEP (entering the GNG pathway from oxaloacetate, which comes from amino acids [alanine, glutamine], lactate [via pyruvate + PC → OAA], and TCA intermediates → OAA is at the COMMITMENT BRANCH POINT: OAA can go to TCA [citrate synthase] or to GNG [PEPCK]; PEPCK commits OAA to GNG); (2) PEPCK is regulated at the TRANSCRIPTIONAL level (long-term regulation is the major mechanism): CREB + PGC-1α → ↑PEPCK1 transcription; glucagon → cAMP → PKA → CREB → ↑PEPCK1 (fasting/stress); glucocorticoids → GR → GRE → ↑PEPCK1; AMPK → ↓CRTC2 → ↓CREB-mediated PEPCK1 transcription (metformin mechanism partly); insulin → PI3K → Akt → FOXO1 phosphorylation → FOXO1 nuclear exclusion → ↓PEPCK1 + ↓G6Pase transcription (insulin suppresses GNG via FOXO1); thyroid hormone → ↑PEPCK1 (explains ↑GNG + ↓blood glucose in hypothyroidism = ↑weight vs. ↑GNG and ↑blood glucose in some hyperthyroidism states); glucocorticoids → GRE in PEPCK1 promoter → ↑PEPCK1; cortisol excess → ↑GNG → ↑blood glucose → Cushing syndrome hyperglycemia; isoforms: PCK1 (PEPCK-C, cytoplasmic): liver + kidney + small intestine + adipose (adipose PEPCK-C → glyceroneogenesis: glycerol-3-phosphate from PEP → TAG synthesis from FA + glycerol in adipocytes); PCK2 (PEPCK-M, mitochondrial): uses GTP from succinyl-CoA synthetase → feeds OAA into PEP → PEP exits to cytoplasm; PCK2 less regulated at transcription level vs PCK1

Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): PC catalyzes pyruvate → OAA (the FIRST step of GNG from pyruvate); PC is regulated (activated by acetyl-CoA → signal of ↑FAO → ↑need for GNG substrates) and provides OAA; however, PC is not the primary rate-limiting step that responds to fasting/glucagon signals; PEPCK is the classically designated rate-limiting step of GNG because it controls the flux from OAA → GNG pathway specifically
explanation: Gluconeogenesis bypass reactions (vs glycolysis irreversible steps): Glycolysis irreversible → GNG bypass: 1. Pyruvate kinase (PEP → Pyr): GNG bypasses via PEPCK + PC → 2. Phosphofructokinase-1 (F6P → F1,6BP): GNG bypasses via FBPase-1 (F1,6BP → F6P); 3. Hexokinase/glucokinase (Glc → G6P): GNG bypasses via G6Pase (G6P → Glc). GNG substrates: glucogenic amino acids (ALL EXCEPT Leu [purely ketogenic] and Lys [purely ketogenic]): Alanine (→ pyruvate via ALT → GNG via PC + PEPCK), Glutamine (→ glutamate → α-KG → TCA → OAA → PEPCK); Lactate (→ pyruvate via LDH → GNG); Glycerol (→ glycerol-3-P → DHAP → GNG); Propionate/odd-chain FA (→ propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → TCA → OAA → PEPCK). GNG energy requirement: net: 2 pyruvate → 1 glucose = 4 ATP + 2 GTP + 2 NADH consumed (very energy-costly = 6 high-energy equivalents: 4 ATP + 2 GTP); PEPCK uses GTP (not ATP), which comes from TCA cycle (succinyl-CoA synthetase → GTP in liver [uses SUCLG2, GTP-producing isoform]) → tight coupling of TCA to GNG energy supply. F2,6BP (fructose-2,6-bisphosphate) — master regulator: F2,6BP: synthesized by PFK-2 (bifunctional enzyme: kinase + phosphatase = PFKFB3 in muscle, PFKFB1 in liver, PFKFB4 in other tissues); PFK-2 kinase domain: F6P → F2,6BP; FBPase-2 domain: F2,6BP → F6P; in liver: glucagon → cAMP → PKA → phospho-PFK-2 (Ser32) → ↓PFK-2 kinase + ↑FBPase-2 → ↓F2,6BP → ↓PFK-1 (↓glycolysis) + ↑FBPase-1 (↑GNG); insulin → ↑PFK-2 → ↑F2,6BP → ↑PFK-1 (↑glycolysis) + ↓FBPase-1 (↓GNG); in muscle: AMPK → phospho-PFK-2-Ser466 → ↑PFK-2 kinase activity → ↑F2,6BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis (opposite to liver!).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Collagen synthesis involves multiple intracellular and extracellular modifications. The amino acid that is most characteristically hydroxylated by prolyl hydroxylase for triple helix stability is:
options: Tyrosine (Tyr hydroxylation is NOT a major modification in collagen; tyrosine residues are not hydroxylated for collagen triple helix stability; Tyr is present in collagen but not the characteristic hydroxylated residue)

Hydroxyproline (Hyp), formed from proline by prolyl hydroxylase (prolyl 4-hydroxylase, P4H): collagen triple helix is a Gly-X-Y repeat: Gly (every 3rd, smallest AA fits into core of triple helix), X (often Pro), Y (often Pro or Hyp = 4-hydroxyproline); P4H (prolyl 4-hydroxylase): hydroxylates Pro in the Y position → 4-hydroxyproline (Hyp; the 4-OH group of Hyp forms hydrogen bonds that STABILIZE the collagen triple helix through water-bridging H-bonds [water molecules bridge adjacent Hyp OH groups across chains → ↑Tm of triple helix by ~50°C]); COFACTORS of P4H: Fe2+ (iron in ferrous state; oxidizes to Fe3+ during catalysis → must be re-reduced back to Fe2+ → requirement for ASCORBATE [vitamin C] to re-reduce Fe3+ → Fe2+ → enzyme active again); O2 (co-substrate, inserted into Hyp); α-KG (co-substrate, decarboxylated → succinate + CO2, oxidative decarboxylation coupled to Pro hydroxylation); VITAMIN C DEFICIENCY → SCURVY: ↓ascorbate → P4H cannot re-reduce Fe3+ → enzyme inactive → procollagen cannot be hydroxylated → Hyp absent → triple helix UNSTABLE → procollagen mismatch (without stable triple helix, procollagen cannot be properly packaged/secreted → degraded in ER, accumulates in RER as unfolded protein) → ↓collagen secretion + structurally weak collagen; manifestations: bleeding gums (↓gingival collagen), perifollicular hemorrhages (↓skin capillary basement membrane), poor wound healing, corkscrew hair, hemarthrosis, hyperkeratosis; lysyl hydroxylase (PLOD1/2/3, procollagen-lysine 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase): SAME cofactors as P4H (Fe2+, α-KG, O2, ascorbate) → hydroxylates Lys in Y position → 5-hydroxylysine (HylLys); HylLys: (1) site for O-linked galactosyl-HylLys glycosylation (galactosyl by GT [GLT25D1/2] + glucosyl-galactosyl by GGT [no specific gene assigned in all species] → glycosylation varies between collagen types); (2) site for LOX crosslinking (LOX oxidizes HylLys/Lys → allysine/hydroxyallysine → Schiff base/aldol condensation → covalent crosslinks between chains); EDS (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, kyphoscoliotic type, EDS VI): PLOD1 mutations → ↓LH1 → ↓HylLys → ↓crosslinks → ↓collagen + elastin stability → hypermobile joints + kyphoscoliosis + eye involvement

Serine (Ser is O-glycosylated in some proteins but NOT characteristically hydroxylated in collagen; serine IS phosphorylated in many signaling proteins; in collagen, the characteristic hydroxylated amino acids are Hyp [from Pro] and HylLys [from Lys])
explanation: Collagen biosynthesis — steps: 1. Transcription/translation: procollagen α-chains (with propeptides at N + C terminus) in ribosome. 2. Co-translational modifications in ER lumen: prolyl 4-hydroxylation (P4H, requires Fe2+/O2/ascorbate/α-KG) → Hyp; lysyl hydroxylation (PLOD1-3) → HylLys; O-glycosylation of HylLys (Gal-HylLys ± Glc-Gal-HylLys). 3. Triple helix formation in ER: starts at C-terminal propeptides → registration peptides → zipper up N-terminally → collagen triple helix (disulfide bonds between C-terminal propeptides initiate coiling; HSP47/SERPINH1 [collagen-specific chaperone] stabilizes triple helix during transport; BiP/GRP78 + PDI also help). 4. Secretion via Golgi: TANGO1 (MIA3) packages procollagen into large COP II vesicles (procollagen is too long for standard COP II vesicles → TANGO1 + cTAGE5 → enlarged COP II coat for collagen export). 5. Extracellular processing: N-proteinase (ADAMTS2/3/14) cleaves N-terminal propeptides → N-propeptides accumulate in dermatosparaxis EDS (ADAMTS2 mutations); C-proteinase (BMP1 [bone morphogenetic protein 1], procollagen C-proteinase) cleaves C-terminal propeptides; both propeptides removed → tropocollagen; feedback: N-propeptide (pN-collagen) → feedback inhibits procollagen synthesis. 6. Fibril formation: spontaneous self-assembly → quarter-stagger arrangement → collagen fibril. 7. Crosslinking by LOX (lysyl oxidase, Cu2+-dependent, extracellular): Lys or HylLys → allysine (oxidative deamination → aldehyde) → aldol condensation or Schiff base with Lys → dehydro-LNL, DHLNL → mature crosslinks (HP = hydroxylysyl pyridinoline; LP = lysyl pyridinoline) → bone + cartilage crosslinks measurable in urine as markers of bone resorption. Collagen types: type I (skin, bone, tendon, cornea, dentin) = Osteogenesis Imperfecta; type II (cartilage) = achondrogenesis/Stickler; type III (vascular, bowel) = vascular EDS (COL3A1); type IV (basement membrane) = Alport syndrome (COL4A3/4/5) + Goodpasture (anti-GBM Ab targets α3/α4/α5 chains); type VII (anchoring fibrils) = dystrophic EB.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: During mitosis, cyclin B1 accumulates and then is rapidly degraded at the end of mitosis. The mechanism of cyclin B1 degradation involves:
options: Phosphorylation by CDK1 (cyclin B1-CDK1 itself phosphorylates cyclin B1 → targets it for degradation; this is not correct; cyclin B1 is destroyed by ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation; CDK1-cyclin B1 activity is what cyclin B1 activates, not the mechanism of cyclin B1 destruction)

Caspase-3 cleavage during apoptosis (caspase-3 cleaves cyclin B1 during apoptosis but this is an apoptotic mechanism, NOT the normal mechanism of cyclin B1 destruction at the end of mitosis; during normal mitosis → APC/C is the mechanism)

Ubiquitination by APC/C (anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome) + proteasomal degradation: APC/C: E3 ubiquitin ligase complex (~19 subunits); CDC20 is its activating subunit during mitosis; APC/C-CDC20: activated at the metaphase-anaphase transition; substrates recognized via D-box (destruction box: RXXL motif) or KEN-box: Securin (PTTG1): ubiquitinated → proteasome → separase (ESPL1) released → cleaves cohesin (SCC1/RAD21 + SMC1/3) → ↑sister chromatid separation → anaphase; Cyclin B1 (CCNB1): ubiquitinated via D-box (RXXL at N-terminus) → proteasomal degradation → ↓CDK1 activity (MPF, maturation promoting factor) → CDK1 inactivated → phosphatases (PP2A-B55, PPP1R12A) → remove CDK1-specific phosphates → mitotic exit → chromosome decondensation, nuclear envelope reformation, cytokinesis; APC/C activation timeline: APC/C-CDC20 activated at metaphase → destroys securin + cyclin B1 → anaphase + mitotic exit; APC/C-CDH1 (Cdh1): activated in late mitosis + G1 → destroys CDC20 + cyclin A2/B1 residuals + keeps cells in G1; SAC (spindle assembly checkpoint): unattached kinetochores → MCC (mitotic checkpoint complex: MAD2 + BUBR1/BUB3 + CDC20) → MCC inhibits APC/C-CDC20 → securin + cyclin B1 stable → keeps mitosis going until all chromosomes properly attached (bioriented) → ↑tension at bioriented kinetochore → remove MAD2 → APC/C-CDC20 released → rapid securin + cyclin B1 destruction → anaphase; cancer: SAC mutations (MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUB3, BUBR1): common in cancer → chromosomal instability (CIN) → aneuploidy → cancer progression
Serine protease degradation in the cytoplasm (cyclin B1 is NOT degraded by serine proteases in the cytoplasm; the mechanism is ubiquitin-26S proteasome system, specifically APC/C-CDC20 E3 ligase)
explanation: Cell cycle regulation — complete: G1/S CDKs: CDK4 + CDK6 + Cyclin D (D1/D2/D3): phosphorylate Rb → partial Rb inactivation → E2F partial release → ↑Cyclin E/A gene expression; CDK2 + Cyclin E: G1/S: hyperphosphorylates Rb → complete E2F release → S-phase gene expression; S-phase: CDK2 + Cyclin A: DNA replication licensing (prevents re-replication by phosphorylating CDC6 + Cdt1); G2/M: CDK1 + Cyclin A then CDK1 + Cyclin B1 (MPF): nuclear lamins (LMNA/B) phosphorylation → NE breakdown; condensins phosphorylation → chromosome condensation; WEE1 (kinase) phospho-CDK1-Tyr15 → ↓CDK1 activity (before G2/M entry); CDC25C (phosphatase) removes phospho-Tyr15 → ↑CDK1 → G2/M activation; CDK inhibitors (CKIs): INK4 family (p16-CDKN2A, p15-CDKN2B, p18-CDKN2C, p19-CDKN2D): specifically inhibit CDK4 + CDK6 → ↑pRb → ↑G1 arrest; Cip/Kip family (p21-CDKN1A, p27-CDKN1B, p57-CDKN1C): inhibit CDK1/2/4/6 broadly; p21 (CDKN1A): p53 target → ↑p21 → CDK2-CycE inhibition → ↑G1 arrest (DNA damage checkpoint mechanism); p27 (CDKN1B): ↓by: ↑mitogenic signaling → SKP2 (F-box protein in SCF complex) → p27 ubiquitination → proteasome (cancer: ↑SKP2 → ↓p27 → ↑CDK2 → ↑S-phase → ↑proliferation); CDK4/6 inhibitors (clinical): palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib → ↓CDK4/6 → ↑pRb → ↑G1 arrest → ↓ER+ HER2- breast cancer proliferation (FDA-approved, added to endocrine therapy). Rb (retinoblastoma protein): tumor suppressor; sequestrates E2F transcription factors (E2F1-7); hypophosphorylated Rb (active repressor): binds E2F1/2/3 → ↓S-phase genes; hyperphosphorylated Rb (inactive): releases E2F → ↑Cyclin A/E + other S-phase genes + E2F target genes; RB1 mutations → hereditary retinoblastoma (first tumor suppressor cloned; 'two-hit' hypothesis, Knudson 1971); also: bladder, lung small cell, osteosarcoma, Rb loss.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Proteolytic processing of proinsulin to insulin occurs in the pancreatic beta cell. The enzymes that cleave proinsulin are:
options: Trypsin and chymotrypsin in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen (trypsin and chymotrypsin are exocrine pancreatic enzymes in pancreatic juice for food digestion; they do NOT process proinsulin inside beta cells; proinsulin processing occurs in the Golgi and secretory granules by specific proprotein convertases)

Proprotein convertase 1/3 (PC1/3, PCSK3) and PC2 (PCSK2) in secretory granules: Proinsulin → Insulin processing: Proinsulin: A-chain + B-chain connected by C-peptide (connecting peptide, 31 AA); three disulfide bonds already formed in ER (A6-A11, A7-B7, A20-B19); Proinsulin cleavage in GOLGI + SECRETORY GRANULES: Step 1: PC1/3 (proprotein convertase 1/3, encoded by PCSK3): cleaves Arg31-Arg32 at the B-chain/C-peptide junction → des-31,32 proinsulin (= split proinsulin I); Step 2: PC2 (proprotein convertase 2, encoded by PCSK2): cleaves Lys64-Arg65 at the C-peptide/A-chain junction → des-64,65 proinsulin intermediate; Step 3: carboxypeptidase E (CPE, also called carboxypeptidase H): removes basic residues (Arg32, Arg64, Arg65) from C-termini → mature insulin (B-chain [30 AA] + disulfide + A-chain [21 AA]) + C-peptide (31 AA); PC1/3 + PC2 requirements: mildly acidic pH (pH 5-6, as in secretory granules; optimal for these proprotein convertases) + Ca2+ (required cofactor); WHY secretory granules: the immature secretory granules → pH drops (V-ATPase) → activates PC1/3 first (higher pH optimum, ~6.5) → PC2 (lower pH optimum, ~5.5) → sequential processing; C-peptide: equal molar production with insulin (1:1 ratio with insulin) → used clinically to measure residual beta cell function in insulin-treated diabetic patients (endogenous C-peptide not cross-reactive with exogenous insulin in C-peptide immunoassay); C-peptide: t½ ~30 min (> insulin t½ ~5 min) + not extracted by liver (contrast to insulin: 50% extracted by liver on first pass) → serum C-peptide levels more accurately reflect beta cell function; C-peptide: may have biological activities (signal transduction via GPCR?; controversial); MODY (maturity onset diabetes of the young): MODY 1 (HNF4A), MODY 2 (GCK), MODY 3 (HNF1A), MODY 4 (PDX1), MODY 5 (HNF1B), MODY 6 (NEUROD1), MODY 7 (KLF11); NEUROD1 (MODY 6) regulates insulin gene transcription + beta cell development; PDX1 (MODY 4) is required for pancreatic development + insulin gene transcription; PC1/3 deficiency: rare AR; ↑proinsulin secretion → impaired glucose sensing → obesity + hypocortisolism (↓ACTH processing, PC1/3 also cleaves POMC → ACTH/MSH/beta-endorphin) + hypogonadism

Kallikrein and renin in secretory granules (kallikreins are serine proteases for kinin generation; renin cleaves angiotensinogen → Ang I; neither has a role in proinsulin processing inside beta cell secretory granules)
explanation: Insulin gene → protein: Insulin gene (INS, chr 11p15.5): 3 exons; encodes preproinsulin; signal peptide (24 AA) → ER → cleaved by signal peptidase → proinsulin (86 AA); PDX1 (IPF1) + NeuroD1 + MafA → insulin gene transcription; glucose → ↑insulin gene transcription + ↑translation; GLUT2 (SLC2A2, low affinity, high capacity, Km 15-20 mM) → glucose enters beta cell proportional to blood glucose → glucokinase (GK, GKRP regulatory protein sequesters GK in nucleus at low glucose → ↑blood glucose → glucose → GK active → G6P → glycolysis → ATP/ADP ratio ↑ → KATP channel closes (Kir6.2/ABCC8 [SUR1]) → β-cell depolarization → VDCC (L-type [CaV1.2/1.3] → ↑Ca2+ → insulin granule exocytosis; FIRST PHASE: rapid secretion of pre-formed granules (within 1-5 min of glucose stimulus); SECOND PHASE: prolonged sustained secretion (5-60+ min; requires new insulin synthesis); Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glibenclamide, glyburide, glimepiride) → bind SUR1 (ABCC8) on KATP → close KATP → depolarize beta cells → ↑Ca2+ → ↑insulin secretion; independent of blood glucose (can cause hypoglycemia!). Potassium channel mutations: KCNJ11 (Kir6.2) + ABCC8 (SUR1) LOF mutations → congenital hyperinsulinism (KATP stays closed → persistent depolarization → ↑insulin secretion → ↓blood glucose → seizures); GOF mutations → neonatal diabetes (KATP stays open → ↓Ca2+ → ↓insulin → neonatal diabetes; some respond to high-dose sulfonylurea therapy → closes KATP → ↑insulin → treats diabetes without insulin injections); KATP GOF permanent neonatal diabetes (PNDM): diazoxide (KATP opener) can worsen; sulfonylurea (glibenclamide) → closes mutant KATP.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Long-term potentiation (LTP) in hippocampal neurons requires NMDA receptor activation. The signaling cascade downstream of NMDA receptor activation that leads to LTP maintenance involves:
options: Activation of adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA → CREB (cAMP-CREB pathway is important for late-phase LTP [L-LTP] involving protein synthesis + gene expression; early-phase LTP [E-LTP] requires CaMKII, NOT primarily the cAMP-PKA pathway; the question is about initial LTP maintenance which primarily involves CaMKII)

Calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) → phosphorylation of AMPA receptors, leading to their insertion into the postsynaptic membrane: LTP (long-term potentiation): persistent strengthening of synaptic connection; NMDA receptor (NMDAR): glutamate + glycine co-agonist + membrane depolarization (removes Mg2+ block) → Ca2+ influx → CaM (calmodulin) + ↑CaMKII activation → CaMKII autophosphorylation (Thr286 of CaMKII-α → constitutively active 'autonomous' CaMKII even after Ca2+/CaM dissociates → memory trace = 'molecular memory'); CaMKII effects: (1) phosphorylates AMPA receptors (GluA1 subunit, Ser831 [by CaMKII] + Ser845 [by PKA]) → ↑AMPA receptor conductance (opens longer) + ↑membrane insertion of AMPA receptors (AMPA receptor trafficking: AMPARs are normally cycling between intracellular stores [endosomes] and PM; LTP → CaMKII + PKA phosphorylation → ↑AMPA receptor exocytosis [SAP97 + GRIP1/2 and PICK1 auxiliary proteins involved] → ↑synaptic AMPA receptors → ↑EPSP [excitatory postsynaptic potential] → ↑synaptic strength); (2) phosphorylates SynGAP (synaptic RasGAP) → ↑Ras/ERK → ↑AMPA receptor insertion; (3) CaMKII directly binds GluA1 → stabilizes AMPA receptors at synapse; EARLY LTP (E-LTP, < 3 hours): requires CaMKII; NO new protein synthesis needed (dependent on existing proteins + post-translational modifications); LATE LTP (L-LTP, > 3 hours): requires new protein synthesis + transcription (BDNF → TrkB → ERK → CREB → IEG [immediate early genes: Arc/Arg3.1, Fos, Jun, Zif268/Egr1] → structural changes [spine enlargement]); LTD (long-term depression): low-frequency stimulation → modest ↑Ca2+ (insufficient for CaMKII) → calcineurin (PP2B) → PP1 → dephosphorylation of AMPA receptors → ↑AMPA receptor endocytosis → ↓synaptic AMPARs → ↓EPSP; LTP vs LTD: the 'Ca2+ amplitude' hypothesis: high Ca2+ spike → CaMKII → LTP; modest Ca2+ → PP2B + PP1 → LTD

Protein kinase C (PKC) activation leading to phosphorylation of transcription factors only (PKC is activated by DAG + Ca2+ from mGluR1/5 [metabotropic glutamate receptors] → PKC → various targets; PKC can contribute to AMPA receptor insertion but is NOT the PRIMARY downstream mediator of NMDAR-activated LTP; CaMKII is the key kinase; also: PKC affects transcription but E-LTP is NOT primarily transcription-dependent)

Inhibition of calcineurin (PP2B) leading to decreased phosphatase activity and constitutive CaMKII activation (calcineurin INHIBITION → ↑phosphorylation → LTP-like enhancement? This is not the standard primary mechanism; the key mechanism is Ca2+-CaM-CaMKII positive cascade; calcineurin is the LTD-associated phosphatase [activated by modest Ca2+ → LTD]; calcineurin inhibition would be anti-LTD but the primary LTP mechanism is CaMKII autophosphorylation following NMDAR Ca2+ influx)
explanation: Synaptic plasticity biochemistry: Glutamate receptors: ionotropic (ion channels): AMPA (fast, Na+/K+; GluA1-4 subunits [GRIA1-4]; GluA2 subunit determines Ca2+ impermeability [Q586R RNA editing by ADAR2 → Q → R → Ca2+-impermeable; if unedited → Ca2+-permeable AMPA receptors in some neurons/cancer]; AMPA receptors mediate fast excitatory transmission); NMDA (slow, Ca2+/Na+/K+, Mg2+ block at resting potential; GluN1 [required; binds glycine/D-serine] + GluN2A/B/C/D [binds glutamate; GluN2B has longer tail → more LTP signaling in young synapses] + GluN3; 'coincidence detector': needs both glutamate AND depolarization to remove Mg2+); kainate (GluK1-5); metabotropic glutamate receptors (mGluR1-8): GPCRs; group I (mGluR1/5): Gαq → PLC → IP3 + DAG → Ca2+ + PKC; group II (mGluR2/3): Gαi → ↓cAMP (presynaptic autoreceptors → ↓Glu release); group III (mGluR4/6/7/8): Gαi. AMPA receptor trafficking in LTP: constitutive cycling: AMPARs enter/exit synapses through lateral diffusion + exocytosis/endocytosis; GluA1 homomers: highly mobile, low basal synaptic concentration → preferentially inserted during LTP (by CaMKII + Rab11 recycling endosome → vesicular exocytosis near synapse → lateral diffusion into PSD); GluA2/3 heteromers: constitutively cycling (maintain basal AMPAR levels); Stargazin (TARP, transmembrane AMPAR regulatory protein, CACNG2): auxiliary AMPAR subunit → retains AMPA receptors at PM + enhances conductance; PSD-95 (DLG4): postsynaptic density scaffold (via MAGUK family); binds NMDAR C-terminus (GluN2B via PDZ1/2) → organizes NMDAR in PSD; also binds mGluR1 + signaling proteins; Shanks (SHANK1/2/3): scaffold for long-range PSD organization; SHANK3 mutations → Phelan-McDermid syndrome + autism spectrum disorder (ASD); spine morphology: stubby → thin → mushroom spines (LTP → ↑spine head volume → 'synaptic engram'); BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) → TrkB → PLCγ + PI3K + MAPK-CREB → ↑synaptic proteins + ↑L-LTP; critical period plasticity: OD plasticity (ocular dominance) requires CaMKII + Arc + mTOR.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glutamate is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. It is synthesized in neurons primarily from:
options: Aspartate via transamination in the cytoplasm (aspartate can donate its amino group to OAA → Glu + oxaloacetate [via GOT1], but aspartate is not the primary substrate for Glu synthesis in neurons; aspartate comes from OAA + Glu in the first place)

Acetylcholine, which is hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase to form glutamate (this is completely wrong; ACh is hydrolyzed to choline + acetate by AChE; there is no metabolic pathway from ACh to glutamate)

Glutamine (Gln) via glutaminase: glutamate-glutamine cycle: NEURONS release Glu at synapses → ASTROCYTES take up Glu (via EAAT1/2 [excitatory amino acid transporter 1/2, SLC1A2/1, GLAST/GLT-1]) → ASTROCYTES: Glu + NH4+ → [GS, glutamine synthetase] → Gln → Gln exported to neurons (via SN1 [SNAT3/SLC38A3] + SN2 [SNAT5/SLC38A5] from astrocytes, and ATA1/2 [SNAT1/2] import into neurons) → NEURONS: Gln → [phosphate-activated glutaminase, GLS/PAG, mitochondrial] → Glu + NH4+ → Glu packaged into vesicles (by VGLUTs [vesicular glutamate transporters, VGLUT1-3/SLC17A5-7]) → released by Ca2+-dependent exocytosis; PHOSPHATE-ACTIVATED GLUTAMINASE (GLS, glutaminase 1 [kidney-type], in neurons; GLS2 [liver-type] in liver/astrocytes): requires phosphate (Pi) as activating ligand → cleaves amide bond of Gln → Glu + NH4+; GLS is the primary route for neuronal Glu synthesis; ALSO: α-KG → [GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase)] → Glu (reverse of the catabolic direction; uses NH4+ + NADH/NADPH to aminatize α-KG; in brain under certain conditions); ALSO from BCAA: BCAT1 (cytoplasmic, brain) → BCAA + α-KG → BCKA + Glu (transamination; Leu/Ile/Val are major nitrogen donors in brain); clinical: GLS inhibitor CB-839 (telaglenastat): cancer metabolism drug → inhibits GLS → ↓Glu → ↓TCA anaplerosis → ↓cancer cell growth (cancer cells are 'glutamine-addicted'); hepatic encephalopathy: ↑NH4+ → ↑brain NH4+ → astrocyte GS → ↑Gln → astrocyte swelling (osmotic) → cerebral edema

α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) directly from the TCA cycle via the cytoplasm: α-KG from TCA cycle CAN give Glu (via BCAT or GDH) but this is a SECONDARY pathway; the PRIMARY and most quantitatively important source of Glu in neurons is the glutamine shuttle from astrocytes (glutamine → glutaminase → Glu); direct α-KG → Glu in neurons is much less significant than the Gln cycle
explanation: Neurotransmitter biochemistry — synthesis and reuptake: Glutamate (Glu): synthesis: Gln → [GLS] → Glu (main route in neurons); packaging: VGLUTs (VGLUT1-3) → vesicles; release: Ca2+-dependent; reuptake: EAAT1 (SLC1A3/GLAST, astrocytes) + EAAT2 (SLC1A2/GLT-1, astrocytes, 90% Glu transport) + EAAT3 (SLC1A1/EAAC1, neurons) + EAAT4 (SLC1A6, cerebellum) + EAAT5 (SLC1A7, retina). GABA (inhibitory): synthesis: Glu → [GAD1/GAD67 + GAD2/GAD65, glutamate decarboxylase, PLP-dependent] → GABA + CO2; packaging: VGAT (vesicular GABA transporter, SLC32A1); reuptake: GAT1/2/3 (SLC6A1/13/11); catabolism: GABA → [GABA-T, GABA transaminase, PLP, in mitochondria] → succinic semialdehyde → [SSADH, succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase] → succinate → TCA; GAD65 antibodies: type 1 diabetes (T1DM) + stiff-person syndrome (SPS, anti-GAD65 Ab → ↓GABA in spinal interneurons → ↑muscle stiffness + spasms); vigabatrin: GABA-T MBI → ↑GABA → ↓seizures. Dopamine: Tyr → [TH, tyrosine hydroxylase, BH4 + Fe2+] → L-DOPA → [AADC, aromatic AA decarboxylase, PLP] → DA; DA → [DBH, Cu2+] → NE → [PNMT, SAM] → Epi; DA pathways: mesolimbic (reward/addiction), mesocortical (cognition), nigrostriatal (motor), tuberoinfundibular (↑DA → ↓prolactin [DA inhibits prolactin from pituitary lactotrophs]). Serotonin (5-HT): Trp → [TPH1 [gut, BH4] or TPH2 [brain, BH4]] → 5-HTP → [AADC, PLP] → 5-HT; MAO-A (mainly in mitochondria) → 5-HT → 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) in CSF + urine (↑5-HIAA → carcinoid syndrome marker). ACh: choline + acetyl-CoA → [ChAT, choline acetyltransferase] → ACh; ChAT localized to presynaptic cholinergic terminals; ACh → [AChE, acetylcholinesterase] → choline + acetate; ChAT is the MARKER for cholinergic neurons (NuclBasMagn/Meynert cholinergic neurons → Alzheimer's pathology → ↓ChAT → ↓ACh).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the pentose phosphate pathway, transketolase transfers a 2-carbon unit from one sugar phosphate to another. Which vitamin serves as a cofactor for transketolase?
options: Pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6): PLP is the cofactor for transaminases, amino acid decarboxylases, ALA synthase, GABA decarboxylase, CBS, cystathionase, serine hydroxymethyltransferase, glycogen phosphorylase; PLP is NOT a cofactor for transketolase
Niacin (NAD+/NADP+, vitamin B3): NAD+/NADP+ are cofactors for dehydrogenases (G6PD, 6PGD, LDH, PDC-E3 etc.) in the PPP and other pathways; transketolase does NOT use NAD+ or NADP+; it uses TPP

Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, vitamin B1): transketolase (TKT/transketolase; cytoplasmic) uses TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate) as cofactor: TKT catalyzes transfer of 2-carbon unit (specifically an active glycolaldehyde unit bound to TPP) from a ketose phosphate donor → aldose phosphate acceptor; reactions in non-oxidative PPP: (1) TKT-1: xylulose-5-P + ribose-5-P → sedoheptulose-7-P + glyceraldehyde-3-P; (2) TKT-2: xylulose-5-P + erythrose-4-P → fructose-6-P + glyceraldehyde-3-P; mechanism: ylide form of TPP (resonance stabilized carbanion of C2 of thiazolium ring) → attacks C2 of ketose → C-C bond cleavage → releases aldose-3-P + transfers 2-C active glycolaldehyde-TPP (α,β-dihydroxyethyl-TPP) → attacks C1 of aldose acceptor → new ketose + TPP regenerated; CLINICAL USE: ETKR (erythrocyte transketolase reactivation ratio): gold standard for thiamine status assessment: TKT activity measured before and after addition of exogenous TPP to hemolysate; ETKR > 1.25 (25% ↑ in activity with added TPP) = thiamine deficiency (normal ETKR < 1.15); because thiamine-deficient cells have functional apoTKT protein but limited holo-TKT (insufficient TPP); adding TPP → reactivates apoTKT → large increase in TKT activity; TALDO (transaldolase): PPP enzyme that transfers 3-carbon unit; does NOT require any cofactor (no TPP; uses Schiff base with Lys-NH2 at active site)

Riboflavin (FAD/FMN, vitamin B2): FAD is required for FADH2 generation in ETC, β-oxidation (ACAD enzymes), succinate dehydrogenase, PDC E3; FMN is in Complex I; neither FAD nor FMN is used by transketolase; transketolase requires TPP
explanation: TPP-requiring enzymes — expanded: Transketolase (TKT): non-oxidative PPP; pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC): E1 component (TPP); α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (OGDH): E1α (TPP); branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH): E1α (TPP); acetolactate synthase (bacteria/plants, not mammals); other organisms: glyoxylate carboligase (E. coli), phosphoketolase (heterofermenters); HOW TPP works: thiazolium ring has C2-H (pKa ~17) → in active site → deprotonated → carbanion (ylide/aminoenamine) → REACTS WITH CARBONYL (attacks α-keto acid or ketose) → forms adduct → decarboxylation (for dehydrogenase complexes) or C-C bond formation/cleavage (for TKT); TPP history: thiamine identified as the anti-beriberi factor (1906-1926, Funk, Jansen); structure determined 1932; coenzyme (diphosphate) form described 1937 (Lohmann & Schuster); Wernicke's encephalopathy: mammillary bodies + periaqueductal gray (richest in PDC/OGDH → most sensitive to TPP depletion) → TPP-dependent enzyme failure → lactic acidosis (↑pyruvate → ↑LDH → lactate) + ↓TCA flux → ↓energy → neuronal death; ATPD (alcohol thiamine pyrophosphate deficiency): binge drinker given IV glucose without thiamine → ↑glucose → ↑PDC demand → uses up remaining TPP → acute WE precipitation; ALWAYS give thiamine (100 mg IM/IV) before or with glucose in alcohol/malnourished patients.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient has hypochromic, microcytic anemia. Serum ferritin is 200 µg/L (elevated), serum iron is low, and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is low. Peripheral smear shows dimorphic red cells. This pattern is consistent with:
options: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA): classic IDA: ↓serum ferritin (the EARLIEST and MOST SENSITIVE marker of iron deficiency) + ↓serum iron + ↑TIBC (transferrin is elevated as compensatory response to ↑iron need → ↑TIBC); ↑ferritin EXCLUDES simple IDA; the elevated ferritin + low TIBC in this case points to a different diagnosis

Anemia of chronic disease/inflammation (AoCI): AoCI: ↑serum ferritin (acute phase reactant, elevated in inflammation) + ↓serum iron + ↓TIBC (transferrin synthesized LESS in inflammation → ↓TIBC; hepcidin ↑ in AoCI → sequesters iron in macrophages/enterocytes → ↓iron release → ↓serum iron + ↑ferritin [iron stored]); USUALLY normocytic-normochromic (early) → microcytic-hypochromic (chronic, severe); but dimorphic cells (mixture of microcytic/hypochromic + normocytic populations) suggest a DIFFERENT process (pure AoCI would NOT show dimorphic cells; dimorphic cells suggest dual iron deficiency + another process, or treatment effect)

Sideroblastic anemia: Sideroblastic anemia (SA): HALLMARK = ring sideroblasts in bone marrow (abnormal iron-loaded mitochondria forming a ring around the erythroid cell nucleus; Prussian blue/Perl's stain); iron is AVAILABLE but CANNOT be incorporated into heme → iron accumulates in mitochondria → ring sideroblasts; LABS: ↑serum ferritin (iron overload) + ↓serum iron (some forms; in most SA iron is overloaded → ↑iron) + ↓TIBC (iron stores full → ↓transferrin → ↓TIBC); dimorphic red cell population: a HALLMARK of SA on peripheral smear (two populations: hypochromic microcytes [defective heme synthesis in pathological cells] + normochromic normocytes [normal cells]; dimorphic picture is particularly characteristic); causes of SA: X-linked SA (XLSA, ALAS2 deficiency, most common hereditary): ↓ALAS2 → ↓ALA → ↓heme synthesis → ↑Fe accumulation → ring sideroblasts; responds to pyridoxine (B6) in some patients; autosomal recessive SA (SIDBA: SLC25A38 or HSPA9 mutations; not B6-responsive); Pearson syndrome (mtDNA deletions → ALAS2 mRNA precursor import failure?; ring sideroblasts + pancreatic insufficiency + exocrine pancreatic failure); acquired SA: lead poisoning (Pb → ↓ALAD + ↓FECH → ↑protoporphyrin + ring sideroblasts + coarse basophilic stippling of RBCs [aggregated ribosomes, ribosomal RNA precipitation due to ↓RNase/altered RNA processing in Pb]); isoniazid, pyrazinamide, chloramphenicol, alcohol, copper deficiency (↓COX-1 → ↓Cu → ↓CCO → ↓electron transport → ↓mitochondrial function → ↓heme synthesis), hypothermia; MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS): somatic SF3B1 mutations (RNA splicing factor → aberrant ABCB7 mRNA splicing → ↓ABCB7 [iron transporter out of mitochondria] → Fe accumulates); treatment: pyridoxine for XLSA; iron chelation for overload

Thalassemia (β-thalassemia): β-thalassemia major: ↑ferritin (iron overload due to ineffective erythropoiesis + transfusions) + ↓serum iron can be normal-to-high; TIBC usually ↓ (iron overloaded); morphology: target cells, poikilocytosis, nucleated RBCs; but RING SIDEROBLASTS in MARROW and DIMORPHIC RBCs are NOT the classic finding of thalassemia (target cells + hypochromic + microcytic are more specific); elevated ferritin + low TIBC + dimorphic cells are most consistent with SA, not β-thalassemia specifically
explanation: Iron studies interpretation: Iron studies pattern comparison: IDA: Ferritin↓ + serum Fe↓ + TIBC↑ + Sat%↓ (transferrin saturation%). AoCI: Ferritin↑/N + serum Fe↓ + TIBC↓/N + Sat%↓. Sideroblastic anemia: Ferritin↑ + serum Fe↑ or ↓ + TIBC↓ + Sat%↑ or ↓ + ring sideroblasts. Hemochromatosis: Ferritin↑↑ + serum Fe↑↑ + TIBC↓ + Sat%↑↑ (>45-50%). B12/folate deficiency: Ferritin N + normocytic/macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented PMNs; no microcytosis. TIBC interpretation: TIBC = total iron-binding capacity of transferrin; each transferrin molecule binds 2 Fe atoms; ↑TIBC → ↑transferrin → ↑iron hunger (compensatory ↑protein synthesis in IDA); ↓TIBC → ↓transferrin (in inflammatory states: transferrin is a NEGATIVE acute-phase reactant = decreases in inflammation; also ↓in liver disease → ↓synthesis; also ↓in iron overload → no need for more transporting capacity). Hepcidin (HAMP gene, liver-derived): master regulator of iron homeostasis: ↑hepcidin → binds ferroportin (SLC40A1) → internalization + degradation of ferroportin → ↓Fe export from: enterocytes (↓Fe absorption) + macrophages (↓Fe release from recycled RBCs) + hepatocytes (↓Fe export) → ↓serum Fe → anemia when excessive; stimuli for ↑hepcidin: IL-6 (→ STAT3 → hepcidin [the main pathway in AoCI]) + BMP6/2 (liver iron sensing via BMP receptors + HJV [hemojuvelin, BMP co-receptor] → SMAD1/5/8 → hepcidin [the main pathway for iron overload response]); genetic hemochromatosis: HFE (HFE gene, C282Y most common, AR, Northern European descent) → ↓hepcidin expression → ↑ferroportin activity → ↑Fe absorption + ↑Fe release → ↑transferrin saturation → Fe deposits in liver (cirrhosis, HCC), heart (cardiomyopathy/arrhythmia), pancreas (bronze diabetes), skin (bronze), joints (chondrocalcinosis), anterior pituitary (↓GnRH → hypogonadism + erectile dysfunction).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) phosphorylates and inactivates the E1 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC). PDK is allosterically ACTIVATED by:
options: AMP and pyruvate (AMP activates AMPK which reactivates PDC by opposing PDK? No: AMP activates AMPK which activates FAO; pyruvate INHIBITS PDK [not activates]; so this answer is incorrect)

NADH, acetyl-CoA, and ATP (product feedback activation): PDK (pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase, PDK1-4): the 4 isoforms differ in tissue expression and regulatory properties; PDK1/2/3/4; PDK phosphorylates E1α at Ser293, Ser300, Ser232 (Ser293 is the primary phosphorylation site → inactivation of PDC); PRODUCT FEEDBACK: PDK is ACTIVATED by: acetyl-CoA (product of PDC → signals 'product buildup' → inactivate PDC via PDK); NADH (product of PDC via E3 → signals 'reducing equivalents abundant → no more PDC needed → PDK active → inactivate PDC); ATP (high energy → PDK active → ↓PDC → ↓further energy generation); SUBSTRATE ACTIVATION (keeps PDK inactive = keeps PDC active): PDK is INHIBITED by: pyruvate (PDK inhibitor: high pyruvate → keep PDC active to burn pyruvate → pyruvate directly inhibits PDK by binding the pyruvate-binding site on PDK [competing with ADP at the 'N-terminal' regulatory domain?; more precisely: pyruvate binds to the 'dichloroacetate [DCA] binding site' on PDK → ↓PDK phosphorylation of E1]); CoA (↓acetyl-CoA/CoA ratio → ↓PDK); NAD+ (↓NADH/NAD+ ratio → ↓PDK); ADP (↓ATP/ADP ratio → ↓PDK); ADDITIONAL: Ca2+ → activates PDC phosphatase (PDP1/2) → dephosphorylates E1α → ↑PDC activity (during exercise: ↑Ca2+ in muscle → ↑PDC) — but Ca2+ affects PDP not PDK; CLINICAL: DCA (dichloroacetate): PDK inhibitor → ↑PDC activity → ↑glucose oxidation → ↓lactate; used investigationally in lactic acidosis (MELAS, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency) + cancer (Warburg reversal: ↑OXPHOS → ↑ROS → ↑cancer cell apoptosis; DCA in glioblastoma clinical trials); PDHPC (pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase): PDP1 (calmodulin-binding, Ca2+/Mg2+-dependent) + PDP2 (constitutive, Mg2+-dependent) → dephosphorylates E1α → activates PDC; insulin → ↑PDP1 → ↑PDC (in fed state → ↑glucose oxidation); PDK4 highly induced by: fasting → ↑glucocorticoids → ↑PPAR-α/γ → ↑PDK4 → ↓PDC → ↓pyruvate oxidation → spare glucose (↑GNG) + ↑FA oxidation
Pyruvate and CoA (pyruvate INHIBITS PDK [keeps PDC active]; CoA INHIBITS PDK [keeps PDC active]; these are SUBSTRATES of the PDC reaction → activate PDC, NOT PDK)
explanation: PDC regulation — summary: PDC is regulated by: Covalent modification: PDK (kinase → phospho-Ser → inactivate) + PDP (phosphatase → dephospho → activate); Allosteric: PDK inhibited by pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ + ADP; PDK activated by acetyl-CoA + NADH + ATP; PDP activated by Ca2+ + Mg2+; PDP inhibited by acetyl-CoA + NADH (same products also inhibit PDP → biphasic product inhibition); Feed-forward: Pyruvate → INHIBITS PDK → KEEPS PDC ACTIVE → process more pyruvate; Feedback: products (acetyl-CoA, NADH, ATP) → ACTIVATE PDK → INACTIVATE PDC. PDK isoforms: PDK1: heart, lung, skeletal muscle; most responsive to DCA; PDK2: ubiquitous, most abundant; PDK3: testes, brain; PDK4: heart, skeletal muscle, kidney; highly induced by fasting + HFD via PPAR-α/γ → ↓PDC → ↓glucose oxidation → ↑fat oxidation (fasting adaptation). PDC deficiency (PDCD, inherited): most commonly E1α subunit mutation (PDHA1, X-linked; pyruvate cannot be decarboxylated → pyruvate + alanine + lactate accumulate → lactic acidosis + neurodegeneration; especially brain [high PDC demand] → Leigh syndrome/Leigh-like; basal ganglia + brain stem degeneration; ataxia); also: E1β (PDHB), E2 (DLAT), E3 (DLD), E3BP/PDX1 (PDK/PDP binding protein) deficiencies; treatment: ketogenic diet (provides acetyl-CoA directly from FA → bypasses PDC → TCA can proceed; limits glucose → ↓pyruvate overload; high-fat diet → ↑FADH2:NADH ratio from FA oxidation → different substrate for ETC; ↑ketone bodies → fuel brain); thiamine (B1) supplementation (if thiamine-responsive form); DCA: ↓lactic acidosis. EGL (E3-lipoamide dehydrogenase deficiency): DLD gene; E3 is SHARED among PDC, OGDH, BCKDH → E3 deficiency → dysfunction of ALL THREE complexes → ↑lactate + ↑α-KG + ↑BCKA → severe metabolic acidosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following CORRECTLY pairs a lysosomal storage disease with its deficient enzyme AND accumulated substrate?
options: Tay-Sachs: deficient β-glucocerebrosidase → accumulated glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) (INCORRECT: β-glucocerebrosidase [GBA] deficiency → Gaucher disease → glucosylceramide accumulation; Tay-Sachs has HEXA deficiency [β-hexosaminidase A] → GM2 ganglioside accumulation)

Niemann-Pick type A: deficient sphingomyelinase → accumulated sphingomyelin: NPD-A (Niemann-Pick disease type A): SMPD1 (sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1, acid sphingomyelinase [ASM]) deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation in lysosomes of macrophages, neurons, etc.; NPD-A: infantile; severe neurodegeneration + hepatosplenomegaly + foam cells (Niemann-Pick cells) + cherry-red spot (50%) + sea-blue histiocytes; SMPD1 gene; AR; NPD-B (partial SMPD1 deficiency): visceral disease (hepatosplenomegaly + lung infiltrates) but ↑or normal neuro function; NPD-C: NPC1/NPC2 mutations [cholesterol transporter/receptor in lysosome → intracellular cholesterol transport defect → free cholesterol + sphingomyelin accumulate in lysosomes]; NOT SMPD1; NPD-C is a CHOLESTEROL trafficking disorder; ERT (olipudase alfa, recombinant ASM) approved for NPD-B (2022); miglustat (substrate reduction) for NPD-C; this option is CORRECT

Gaucher: deficient hexosaminidase A → accumulated GM2 ganglioside (INCORRECT: Gaucher = GBA [beta-glucocerebrosidase] deficiency → glucocerebroside [glucosylceramide] accumulation; hexosaminidase A [HEXA] deficiency → Tay-Sachs → GM2 ganglioside)

Krabbe disease: deficient glucocerebrosidase → accumulated psychosine (INCORRECT: Krabbe = galactocerebrosidase [GALC] deficiency [NOT glucocerebrosidase] → galactosylceramide + psychosine [galactosylsphingosine, which is the psychosine] accumulation; glucocerebrosidase = GBA → Gaucher disease)
explanation: Lysosomal storage diseases — comprehensive table: ENZYME DEFICIENCY / DISEASE / ACCUMULATED SUBSTRATE / FEATURES: α-L-iduronidase (IDUA) → MPS I (Hurler/Scheie) → Dermatan sulfate + Heparan sulfate → coarse facies + short stature + corneal clouding + skeletal dysostosis multiplex; ERT = laronidase; HSCT for Hurler. Iduronate-2-sulfatase (IDS, X-linked) → MPS II (Hunter) → Dermatan + Heparan sulfate → similar to Hurler but milder + NO corneal clouding + X-linked; ERT = idursulfase. β-Glucocerebrosidase (GBA) + saposin C → Gaucher disease → Glucosylceramide (glucocerebroside) → Gaucher cells in BM/spleen/liver; hepatosplenomegaly + anemia + thrombocytopenia + bone pain/crisis; cherry-red spot ONLY in type 2; ERT imiglucerase/velaglucerase; SRT eliglustat/miglustat. α-Galactosidase A (GLA, X-linked) → Fabry → Gb3 → Angiokeratoma + neuropathy (burning pain, acroparesthesias) + renal failure + cardiomyopathy; ERT = agalsidase α/β. Acid sphingomyelinase (SMPD1) → NPD A/B → Sphingomyelin → foam cells; NPD-A: ↑neuro + hepatosplenomegaly + cherry-red spot; NPD-B: visceral only. NPC1/NPC2 → NPD-C → Cholesterol + sphingomyelin → progressive neurological + vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (pathognomonic) + seizures. β-Hexosaminidase A (HEXA α+β) → Tay-Sachs → GM2 ganglioside → progressive neurodegeneration + cherry-red spot + hyperacusis + macrocephaly; NO hepatosplenomegaly. β-Hexosaminidase A + B (HEXB β+β) → Sandhoff → GM2 + globoside → like Tay-Sachs + hepatosplenomegaly. α-Glucosidase (GAA, acid maltase) → Pompe (GSD II) → Glycogen in lysosomes → infantile: cardiomegaly + hypotonia + death; adult: myopathy; ERT alglucosidase. Galactocerebrosidase (GALC) → Krabbe → Galactosylceramide + PSYCHOSINE (galactosylsphingosine, toxic) → severe neurodegeneration; HSCT early. Arylsulfatase A (ARSA) → Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) → Sulfatide (galactocerebroside-3-sulfate) → progressive demyelination; HSCT (early); atidarsagene autotemcel (gene therapy, 2020 EU approval for early-onset). Neuraminidase 1 (NEU1/sialidase) → Sialidosis/mucolipidosis I → Sialooligosaccharides → cherry-red spot + neurologic.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent spontaneous abortions. Laboratory testing reveals prolonged aPTT, positive lupus anticoagulant test, and elevated anti-cardiolipin antibodies. Which phospholipid is the primary antigen targeted by these antibodies?
options: Phosphatidylserine (PS): antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL Abs) were originally thought to target cardiolipin directly, but later research showed they primarily target PROTEIN COFACTORS (β2-glycoprotein I, or β2GPI/apolipoprotein H) bound to negatively charged phospholipids; cardiolipin is one of these negatively charged phospholipids, but phosphatidylserine is ALSO a target; however, the antiGEN in the cardiolipin ELISA is cardiolipin, not PS; so this is partially correct but less specific

Cardiolipin (diphosphatidylglycerol, CL, bis-PG): anti-cardiolipin antibodies (aCL) detected by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay using cardiolipin-coated plates; cardiolipin is a negatively charged phospholipid (bis-phosphatidylglycerol, CL) found in: inner mitochondrial membrane (enriched, 20% of IMM lipids) + bacterial membranes; in antiphospholipid syndrome (APS, Hughes syndrome): APS is an autoimmune thrombophilia; criteria: THROMBOSIS (venous or arterial) or OBSTETRIC MORBIDITY (recurrent miscarriage, fetal death, IUGR) + LABORATORY: positive on 2+ occasions ≥12 weeks apart: aPTT-based LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT (LA): paradox: LA prolongs aPTT in VITRO (binds phospholipids needed for coagulation in test tube → apparent anticoagulant effect) but CAUSES THROMBOSIS in VIVO (antibodies → endothelium damage → ↑thrombin; anti-β2GPI Abs on platelet surface → ↑platelet activation; anti-LA Abs → inhibit protein C activation → ↓anticoagulation); anti-cardiolipin antibodies (IgG or IgM, medium-to-high titer) + anti-β2GPI antibodies (IgG or IgM); target: β2-glycoprotein I (β2GPI, apolipoprotein H [APOH]): main antigen of APS antibodies → β2GPI binds cardiolipin (domain V, positively charged) + PS → forms immunogenic complex → β2GPI conformational change → new epitopes exposed → APS antibodies recognize β2GPI-PL complex; syphilis cross-reactivity: false positive VDRL/RPR (non-treponemal tests for syphilis use cardiolipin-based reagent → aPL Abs → false positive VDRL; true syphilis antibodies are different from aPL); distinguish with treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, TPHA); treatment: hydroxychloroquine (↓APS events + ↓thrombosis risk); low-dose aspirin; anticoagulation for thrombotic APS (heparin/LMWH + warfarin [INR 2-3 for venous; 2.5-3.5 for arterial]; DOACs less evidence, some RCTs [TRAPS] suggest ↑risk with rivaroxaban vs warfarin → warfarin preferred especially for triple aPL positivity); obstetric APS: LMWH + low-dose aspirin during pregnancy

Sphingomyelin (SM): SM is NOT a cardiolipin homolog and is not the target antigen in APS; SM is involved in membrane structure + signaling via ASMase/SMS pathways; aPL antibodies target negatively charged phospholipids (cardiolipin, PS, PI, phosphatidic acid, PE to lesser extent) + β2GPI; SM is neutral (zwitterionic) → not a typical aPL target

Phosphatidylcholine (PC): PC is the most abundant phospholipid (zwitterionic, neutral charge); NOT a typical target of APS antibodies; aPL Abs favor negatively charged phospholipids + β2GPI; anti-PC Abs exist in some populations (natural Abs, B-1 cells) but are not part of APS criteria
explanation: Antiphospholipid antibodies — β2GPI biology: β2GPI (apolipoprotein H/ApoH): 50 kDa glycoprotein; produced by liver; circulates in plasma (150-500 µg/mL); structure: 5 CCP (complement control protein/short consensus repeat [SCR]) domains; domain V (5th): binds anionic phospholipids (PL-binding site = hydrophobic 'taco' loop); in normal state: β2GPI in solution has a 'closed' conformation (domain I faces domain V, Asn-Gly-Ser [NGS] cleavage site protected); after binding anionic PL → 'open' conformation → domain I fully exposed → cryptic epitopes on domain I NOW ACCESSIBLE → APS antibodies recognize domain I of open β2GPI (not free β2GPI or CL alone); APS antibody binding → β2GPI: (1) competes with protein C for PS on endothelium → ↓protein C activation → ↑coagulation; (2) binds annexin A5 (anti-coagulant shield on trophoblast + vascular endothelium; anti-β2GPI disrupts annexin A5 shield) → ↑thrombosis + ↑placental microthrombi; (3) activates endothelial cells (RAGE [receptor for advanced glycation end products] or TLR4 → NF-κB → ↑TF + ↑VCAM-1 + ↑ICAM-1 + ↑E-selectin → ↑thrombosis); (4) activates platelets (ApoER2/LRP8 as β2GPI receptor → PI3K → ↑platelet activation + ↑TXA2); complement: C3, C5a: ↑complement activation by APS Abs → ↑neutrophil NET (neutrophil extracellular trap) formation → ↑thrombosis; eculizumab (anti-C5) in catastrophic APS (CAPS). Catastrophic APS (CAPS, Asherson syndrome): <1% of APS; widespread microvascular thrombosis within days → multi-organ failure (kidney + lung + brain + adrenal + heart simultaneously); precipitants: infection, surgery, cessation of anticoagulation; treatment: anticoagulation + glucocorticoids + plasmapheresis + IVIG ± rituximab ± eculizumab. Lupus anticoagulant in vitro paradox: in aPTT assay tube: LA Abs bind phospholipids (on which prothrombinase complex assembles) → impede assembly → PROLONGED aPTT; in vivo: Abs on endothelium → PROMOTE clotting; 'anticoagulant in vitro, pro-coagulant in vivo'; DRVVT (dilute Russell's viper venom time): more specific for LA; LA confirmed if prolongation corrects with excess phospholipid (not with normal plasma → not just a factor deficiency).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Tangier disease is characterized by extremely low plasma HDL cholesterol and cholesterol ester deposition in tonsils and other tissues. The molecular defect is a mutation in:
options: LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase): LCAT deficiency → low HDL + high free cholesterol in plasma + corneal opacities + anemia + renal failure; LCAT transfers fatty acid from lecithin (PC) to cholesterol → cholesterol ester; in LCAT deficiency, nascent HDL (discoidal pre-β-HDL) cannot mature to spherical HDL-C (because CE formation is impaired) → flat discoidal HDL particles + ↑free cholesterol on membranes; LCAT deficiency is NOT Tangier disease; LCAT is a plasma enzyme

ABCA1 (ATP-binding cassette transporter A1): ABCA1 (ABCA subfamily, full ABC transporter with 2 NBDs + 2 TMDs): transport of cholesterol + phospholipids from intracellular membranes to lipid-poor apoA-I (apolipoprotein A-I); this is the FIRST STEP in reverse cholesterol transport (RCT): ApoA-I → ABCA1 on macrophage/peripheral cell → ABCA1 effluxes cholesterol + PL to apoA-I → nascent discoidal HDL (pre-β-HDL, discoidal) → LCAT → CE → mature spherical HDL → SR-BI (SCARB1) on liver → selective HDL-CE uptake (the liver pathway for RCT); ABCA1 mutations → Tangier disease (TD, AR): characteristics: (1) very low or absent plasma HDL-C (< 5 mg/dL; apoA-I rapidly catabolized when it cannot acquire lipids from ABCA1) + (2) cholesterol ester accumulation in macrophages/reticuloendothelial cells (because macrophages cannot efflux cholesterol → foam cells in unexpected locations): orange-yellow tonsils (cholesterol ester deposits, pathognomonic), enlarged liver + spleen (Kupffer cells + splenic macrophages), peripheral neuropathy; (3) mildly elevated TG (↓HDL → impaired TG clearance); (4) ↑atherosclerosis risk despite young age (severe HDL deficiency → impaired RCT); ABCA1 promoter SNPs: contribute to population-level HDL variability (common variant polymorphisms → ↓ABCA1 → ↓HDL-C); Apolipoprotein A-I Milano (R173C Cys substitution) PARADOX: ↓HDL-C but ↓CV events (apoA-I Milano forms dimers via Cys-Cys disulfide → different function → perhaps super-efficient RCT despite low HDL); basis of recombinant apoA-I Milano infusion trials (MILANO-PILOT, ASSAY trials)

CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein): CETP transfers CE from HDL → VLDL/LDL in exchange for TG; CETP inhibition → ↑HDL-C; CETP deficiency (AR) → hyperalphalipoproteinemia (very high HDL) + low LDL; NOT Tangier disease; CETP inhibitors (anacetrapib, dalcetrapib, evacetrapib, torcetrapib): ↑HDL-C but torcetrapib failed (↑aldosterone + BP); anacetrapib: ↑HDL + modest ↓LDL → mild CV benefit in REVEAL trial but not approved

SR-BI (scavenger receptor class B, type I, SCARB1): SR-BI is the liver HDL receptor for selective uptake of cholesterol ester from HDL (HDL → SR-BI on hepatocyte → CE selectively taken up → ↓cholesterol from HDL → 'lipid-poor' apoA-I particle recycled back to circulation); SR-BI/SCARB1 rare mutations in humans → ↑HDL-C + ↑CV risk (paradox: HDL cannot be 'drained' at the liver → CE accumulates in HDL → less efficient RCT despite ↑HDL); SR-BI is NOT the Tangier disease protein
explanation: Reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) — complete pathway: 1. ABCA1 (on macrophage/peripheral cells) → effluxes cholesterol + phospholipid → lipid-poor apoA-I → nascent discoidal HDL (pre-β-HDL); 2. ABCG1 (also on macrophage) → effluxes cholesterol → mature HDL-3; 3. LCAT (plasma) → CE (cholesteryl ester) from HDL phospholipid + free cholesterol → HDL-2 (spherical, CE-rich); 4. CETP → exchanges HDL-CE for VLDL-TG → more CE enters VLDL/LDL pathway → LDL-CE → liver LDLR → liver; 5. SR-BI (hepatocyte) → selective uptake of CE from mature HDL → liver; bile acid synthesis from cholesterol → biliary excretion → fecal elimination; RCT step 1 defect: ABCA1 mutations → Tangier disease; CETP deficiency → hyperalphalipoproteinemia (very ↑HDL); SR-BI deficiency → ↑HDL but ↑CV risk. Apolipoprotein A-I: major HDL protein (70% of HDL protein); amphipathic α-helices; receptor ligand for ABCA1 + SR-BI; LCAT activator; APOA1 gene; apoA-I serum level proportional to HDL-C + inversely proportional to CV risk; apoA-I amyloidosis: hereditary amyloidosis (R26G + L64P + W50R etc. APOA1 mutations → amyloid fibrils deposit in liver, kidney, heart, nerve). ApoA-II: second most abundant HDL protein; apoA-II/apoA-I ratio affects HDL function; APOA2 promoter polymorphism → ↓HDL-C + ↑BMI in some studies. ApoC-III: on HDL + VLDL/TG-rich lipoproteins; inhibits LPL + VLDL-hepatic uptake → ↑TG; APOC3 loss-of-function variants → ↓TG + ↓CV risk (eplontersen/volanesorsen target APOC3 mRNA for ↓TG in familial chylomicronemia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hereditary coproporphyria (HCP) results from deficiency of which enzyme in the heme biosynthetic pathway?
options: Uroporphyrinogen III cosynthase (UROS): UROS is the 4th enzyme in the heme pathway → converts hydroxymethylbilane → uroporphyrinogen III (the correct isomer); UROS deficiency → congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP, Günther disease): uroporphyrinogen I accumulates (wrong isomer) → severe photosensitivity + mutilating skin lesions + hemolytic anemia + pink urine + red/brown discoloration of teeth; NOT HCP

Coproporphyrinogen III oxidase (CPOX, coproporphyrinogen oxidase): HCP (hereditary coproporphyria): CPOX (CPOX gene, chromosome 3q12): enzyme that converts coproporphyrinogen III → protoporphyrinogen IX (removes 2 carboxyl groups via oxidative decarboxylation; the reaction requires O2 as electron acceptor; mitochondrial enzyme [intermembrane space + inner membrane?]); CPOX deficiency (AD, 50% of normal enzyme activity may be sufficient under basal conditions; attacks precipitated by same triggers as other acute porphyrias → buildup of ALA + PBG); CLINICAL: acute neurovisceral attacks (abdominal pain + nausea/vomiting + tachycardia + hypertension + psychiatric symptoms + hyponatremia) PLUS mild photosensitivity (coproporphyrin III accumulates in skin → mild blistering, not severe [unlike VP or PCT]); distinguishing feature: elevated URINARY COPROPORPHYRIN III (100-fold elevated, predominantly isomer III) during attacks; also ↑ALA + ↑PBG in urine; contrasted with VP (variegate porphyria, PPOX deficiency): VP also has PLASMA FLUORESCENCE at 626 nm (plasma fluorescence scanning for PPOX pathway products); HCP plasma: fluorescence at ~617 nm but ≤VP

Protoporphyrinogen IX oxidase (PPOX): PPOX deficiency → Variegate porphyria (VP): acute attacks + chronic skin photosensitivity; South Africa (Dutch founder mutation, R59W in PPOX, affects ~1/300 Afrikaners); characteristic: plasma porphyrin fluorescence peak at 626 nm (pathognomonic); stool: increased coproporphyrin III + protoporphyrin IX; NOT HCP

Ferrochelatase (FECH): FECH (ferrochelatase, FECH gene): inserts Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX → heme; FECH deficiency → erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP): autosomal dominant/recessive depending on allele; severe photosensitivity (burning, stinging, itching, redness IMMEDIATELY upon sun exposure without blistering or scarring → characteristic EPP [unlike PCT where blistering + fragile skin]); ↑free protoporphyrin in RBCs + liver → cholestasis + liver failure (EPP liver disease); treatment: afamelanotide (alpha-MSH analog → ↑melanin → ↑sun tolerance in EPP, approved 2019); X-linked EPP (XLEP): ALAS2 gain-of-function → ↑ALA/PBG → ↑PPIXprotoporphyrin IX; FECH deficiency is NOT HCP
explanation: Heme biosynthesis pathway — complete 8 steps: 1. ALA synthase (ALAS1 [liver], ALAS2 [erythroid], rate-limiting, mitochondrial): Gly + succinyl-CoA → δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) + CO2; cofactor: PLP; feedback: hemin → ↓ALAS1 (not ALAS2); heme → ↑HRI (heme-regulated inhibitor) [in RBC maturation → ↑hemin → ↑HRI → ↓eIF2α → ↓globin translation? No: hemin → ↓HRI → ↑translation; irony: LACK of heme → HRI active → ↓translation]; ALAS2 GOF → XLEP; ALAS2 LOF → X-linked sideroblastic anemia. 2. ALA dehydratase (ALAD, porphobilinogen synthase, ALAD, cytoplasm, Zn2+-dependent): 2 ALA → porphobilinogen (PBG) + 2 H2O; inhibited by Pb2+ (Pb displaces Zn) → ALA-D porphyria (ALADP, very rare, AR); also lead poisoning → ↑urine ALA (with normal PBG). 3. PBG deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase, HMBS, cytoplasm): 4 PBG → hydroxymethylbilane (HMB) + 4 NH4+; HMBS deficiency → Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP): most common acute porphyria; AD; NO skin disease (AIP has NO photosensitivity); ↑↑↑ urine ALA + PBG during attacks; Watson-Schwartz test + Ehrlich's aldehyde test: PBG + Ehrlich's (p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in HCl) → RED color (porphobilinogen also red; UBG also red — distinguished by chloroform extraction: PBG stays aqueous, UBG extracted). 4. UROS (see above, CEP). 5. Uroporphyrinogen III decarboxylase (UROD, cytoplasm): uroporphyrinogen III (8 carboxyl groups) → coproporphyrinogen III (4 carboxyl groups; removes 4 COOH from acetic acid side chains → methyl groups); UROD deficiency → Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT): most common porphyria overall; skin blistering + fragile skin on sun-exposed areas + hyperpigmentation + hypertrichosis; ↑uroporphyrin I + III in urine (tea-colored urine); triggers: alcohol + hepatitis C + HFE mutations + estrogens; treatment: phlebotomy (reduces hepatic iron → ↓UROD inhibition) or low-dose chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine (chelates porphyrins in liver → ↑urinary excretion); UROD inhibitor: iron (Fe3+ inhibits UROD via uroporphomethene metabolite produced by CYP1A2?). 6. CPOX (HCP, see above). 7. PPOX (VP, see above). 8. FECH (EPP, see above). Acute porphyria triggers: inducers of CYP450 (barbiturates, carbamazepine, rifampicin, sulfonamides, alcohol) → induce ALAS1 → ↑ALA + PBG → attacks; hormones (progesterone: explains menstrual attacks in AIP; estrogens); fasting/caloric restriction; stress/infections. Treatment of acute attack: IV glucose + heme arginate (hematin, ↓ALAS1 via heme feedback) + pain control + avoid triggers; givosiran (siRNA against ALAS1 mRNA → ↓ALAS1 → ↓ALA → ↓attacks in AIP/AHP, FDA approved 2019).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A patient with progressive muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, and lactic acidemia on exertion is found to have a homoplasmic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutation in the gene encoding subunit ND4 of Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase). In addition to reduced ATP production, this mutation is MOST directly expected to impair which of the following reactions?
options: Beta-oxidation of palmitate in the mitochondrial matrix (beta-oxidation [FAO]: ACAD enzymes → FADH2 [from the enoyl-CoA dehydrogenase step]; subsequent steps produce NADH [from 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase] + acetyl-CoA; the NADH produced feeds to Complex I [NADH → FMN → Fe-S clusters → CoQ]; therefore, Complex I deficiency → NADH cannot be oxidized → ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio → blocks HADHA [3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase] step of beta-oxidation → ↑acylcarnitines; but the QUESTION asks what is 'most directly impaired' by Complex I loss → reduction of NADH → NAD+ is the DIRECT reaction; beta-oxidation is secondary to this; also: FADH2 from FAO [ACAD enzymes] feeds to ETF/ETFDH → CoQ directly, BYPASSING Complex I → FAO can continue partly in Complex I deficiency via ETF pathway; so FAO is NOT the MOST directly impaired

Reduction of NAD+ to NADH in the tricarboxylic acid cycle (reverse: Complex I is a NADH oxidizer [NADH → NAD+]; the TCA cycle PRODUCES NADH [NAD+ → NADH by dehydrogenases]; if Complex I is deficient, NADH cannot be oxidized → ↑NADH → ↓NAD+ → ↓TCA dehydrogenases [isocitrate DH, α-KGDH, malate DH] → ↓TCA flux; but this is a SECONDARY effect due to NADH/NAD+ imbalance; the question asks what is 'most directly' impaired by the ND4 mutation in Complex I)

Oxidation of NADH to NAD+ by Complex I, thereby reducing ubiquinone (CoQ) to ubiquinol (CoQH2): Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, CI): the DIRECT catalytic reaction of Complex I: NADH + H+ + CoQ → NAD+ + CoQH2 (ubiquinol); simultaneously: 4 protons pumped from matrix → IMS per NADH oxidized (CI pumps 4H+ out of matrix per 2 electrons passed to CoQ); ND4 is one of the 7 core mitochondrially-encoded subunits of CI (ND1, ND2, ND3, ND4, ND4L, ND5, ND6 = the proton-pumping membrane arm of Complex I; all encoded by mtDNA [16,569 bp, 37 genes: 2 rRNAs, 22 tRNAs, 13 protein-coding: 7 CI subunits + 1 CII [none — wait: CII is entirely nuclear-encoded; the 13 mtDNA-encoded proteins are: 7 Complex I ND subunits + 1 Complex III Cyt b [cytochrome b] + 3 Complex IV subunits [COX1/COX2/COX3] + 2 Complex V subunits [ATP6/ATP8] = total 13]); NADH/NAD+ imbalance with CI deficiency: ↑NADH in matrix → ↑NADH/NAD+ ratio → ↓flux through NAD+-dependent dehydrogenases (↓PDC, ↓OGDH, ↓MDH, ↓isocitrate DH, ↓HADHA) → accumulation of pyruvate (cannot enter TCA → LDH → lactate) → LACTIC ACIDEMIA; Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON): mtDNA point mutations in CI subunits (ND4 G11778A → most common LHON mutation [~70% of LHON worldwide, Gly→Arg substitution]; ND1 G3460A; ND6 T14484C) → blindness (RGC [retinal ganglion cell] death → optic neuropathy → progressive vision loss usually in young males, incomplete penetrance, maternal inheritance, males >> females [4:1], females require higher mutant mtDNA threshold for expression); idebenone (reduced-form of CoQ analog) → bypasses CI → FDA/EMA approved for LHON; lenadogene nolparvovec (AAV2-ND4 gene therapy) approved in EU 2021 for LHON with ND4 mutation

Synthesis of GTP from GDP + Pi in the mitochondrial matrix by succinyl-CoA synthetase (GTP is produced by succinyl-CoA synthetase [SUCLG1/SUCLG2 for GTP-producing in liver; SUCLA2 for ADP-forming in muscle] as part of the TCA cycle; this is a substrate-level phosphorylation; GTP synthesis does NOT require Complex I; it is independent of the ETC; Complex I loss would NOT directly impair GTP synthesis)
explanation: Mitochondrial respiratory chain — complete: Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase): 45 subunits (7 mtDNA [ND1-6 + ND4L] + 38 nuclear); 4H+/2e-; NADH → FMN → 8 Fe-S clusters → CoQ; inhibited by: rotenone, amytal (barbiturate), piericidin; deficiency → Leigh syndrome (most common cause), MELAS-like, LHON. Complex II (succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase): 4 subunits, ALL nuclear-encoded (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD); 0H+/2e-; FADH2 → FAD → Fe-S → CoQ; inhibited by: malonate; SDHA mutations → paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma (chromaffin cell tumor) + Leigh syndrome; SDHB/C/D → hereditary pheochromocytoma + paraganglioma syndrome types 3/4; CII is the ONLY ETC complex also part of TCA (succinate dehydrogenase). Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex, ubiquinol:cytochrome c oxidoreductase): 11 subunits (1 mtDNA [cytochrome b/MTCYB] + 10 nuclear); 4H+/4e-; CoQH2 → cytochrome b → Rieske Fe-S (ISP) → cytochrome c1 → cyt c (shuttles to CIV); Q-cycle pumps 4H+ per 2e-; inhibited by: antimycin A (at Qi site of cyt b); stigmatellin (Qo site). Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, CcO): 14 subunits (3 mtDNA [COX1, COX2, COX3] + 11 nuclear); 4H+/4e-; 4 cyt c → CuA → heme a → heme a3-CuB → O2 + 4H+ → 2H2O; inhibited by: cyanide (CN-: Fe3+ of a3 → ferricyanide, cannot be reduced → block), azide (N3-, same), CO (binds a3, competes with O2, CO poisoning = apple-red skin + cherry-red blood = HbCO), H2S (sulfide → blocks CIV + CI). Complex V (ATP synthase, FoF1-ATPase): F1 (α3β3γδε, matrix-side, catalytic, 80 kDa), Fo (a, b, c-ring [c8-15 depending on species], d, e, f, g, A6L, F6, OSCP): a + c-ring: proton translocation through Fo; rotation of c-ring → rotation of γ (rotor) → catalytic conformational change in F1 β-subunits (Boyer's binding change mechanism: 3 β-subunits cycle through: L [loose, ADP+Pi bind] → T [tight, ATP synthesized] → O [open, ATP released]); 2 mtDNA subunits (ATP6 [= a-subunit of Fo] + ATP8 [MTATP8, involved in Fo assembly]); inhibited by: oligomycin (binds c-ring/a-subunit of Fo → blocks proton translocation → ↓ATP synthesis → used in research); DCCD (dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, same site); FCCP, DNP (uncouplers → dissipate ΔΨm by bringing protons back across IMM outside of CV → ↑O2 consumption + heat without ATP production); NARP (neuropathy, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa): mtDNA ATP6 mutations → CV dysfunction; MILS (maternally inherited Leigh syndrome): more severe ATP6 mutations. P/O ratio (ATP produced per O2): NADH → Complex I → ~2.5 ATP; FADH2 → Complex II → CoQ (bypasses CI) → ~1.5 ATP; actual vs theoretical: Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory gives theoretical 10 ATP + 2 GTP per acetyl-CoA cycle if using ΔμH+ efficiently; substrate-level: 4 ATP + 2 GTP per glucose; total: ~30-32 ATP per glucose (vs old calculation of 38 ATP [used fixed P/O of 3/2]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The JAK-STAT signaling pathway mediates the actions of many cytokines. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the mechanism of JAK-STAT signal transduction?
options: Cytokine → cytokine receptor dimerization → receptor intrinsic tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation → STAT phosphorylation (this describes growth factor receptors with intrinsic RTK activity, e.g. EPO receptor has SOME features but the JAK kinases are the ACTUAL kinases; most cytokine receptors do NOT have intrinsic kinase activity; they associate non-covalently with JAKs)

Cytokine → receptor homodimerization → cAMP elevation → PKA → STAT phosphorylation (cAMP-PKA pathway is for Gαs-coupled GPCRs, not JAK-STAT; PKA does not directly phosphorylate STATs in the canonical pathway)

Cytokine binding → receptor dimerization → JAK activation → STAT tyrosine phosphorylation → STAT homodimerization → nuclear translocation → target gene transcription: JAK-STAT pathway (complete mechanism): 1. CYTOKINE BINDING: cytokine (e.g., IFN-γ, IL-6, EPO, G-CSF, prolactin, GH, IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-12, IL-15, IL-21, leptin) binds to its receptor; 2. RECEPTOR DIMERIZATION (or oligomerization): cytokine-receptor engagement → receptor conformational change → receptor chains brought together (pre-formed dimers or induced dimers/trimers); 3. JAK ACTIVATION: JAKs (Janus kinase 1, 2, 3 [JAK1, JAK2, JAK3] and TYK2) constitutively associated with receptor intracellular domains (via FERM + SH2 domains binding receptor Box 1/Box 2 motifs); receptor dimerization → juxtaposition of JAKs → JAKs phosphorylate EACH OTHER (transphosphorylation, specifically activation loop Tyr → full activation); also phosphorylate receptor cytoplasmic Tyr → docking sites for SH2 domain-containing proteins; 4. STAT RECRUITMENT + PHOSPHORYLATION: STATs (signal transducer and activator of transcription 1-6) recruited via their SH2 domain to phospho-Tyr on receptor → STATs phosphorylated by JAKs (Tyr701 of STAT1; Tyr705 of STAT3; Tyr694 of STAT5, etc.) → 5. STAT DIMERIZATION + NUCLEAR TRANSLOCATION: pSTAT → dissociates from receptor → homodimerization (STAT1:STAT1 [GAS element], STAT3:STAT3 [GAS element]) or heterodimerization (STAT1:STAT2 + IRF9 → ISGF3 complex [ISRE element] → type I IFN signaling); pSTAT dimers: conformational change → Tyr on one monomer now interacts with SH2 of other monomer → stable antiparallel dimer; 6. NUCLEAR ENTRY: importin-α3/α6 → recognize NLS on STAT → nuclear import; 7. TRANSCRIPTION: pSTAT dimers bind GAS (IFN-γ activated sequence, TTCN2-4GAA palindrome) or ISRE (IFN-stimulated response element, AGTTTCNTTTTCNY/T) → recruit CBP/p300 → ↑target gene transcription; JAK-STAT negative regulation: SOCS proteins (suppressor of cytokine signaling, SOCS1-7 + CIS): induced by STATs (negative feedback) → SOCS SH2 domain → binds JAK + receptor pTyr → competes with STAT + promotes JAK ubiquitination (SOCS box → elongin/cullin E3) → ↓JAK signaling; PIAS proteins (protein inhibitor of activated STAT1-4, PIAS): SUMO E3 ligase → SUMOylates STAT → ↓DNA binding; PTP-TC45/PTPN2 (nuclear PTP) → dephosphorylates STAT1 in nucleus → ↓transcription; JAK2V617F: oncogenic somatic point mutation (Val617Phe) in JAK2 pseudokinase (JH2) domain → removes auto-inhibitory function → constitutive JAK2 activity → constitutive STAT3/5 signaling → polycythemia vera [PV], essential thrombocythemia [ET], primary myelofibrosis [PMF]; ALL three Philadelphia-negative MPN share JAK2V617F (PV: >95%; ET: ~60%; MF: ~50-60%); OTHER MPN mutations: CALR (calreticulin, exon 9 frameshift, ET/MF, ~25%; activates TPO receptor/MPL) + MPL (thrombopoietin receptor mutations, ~5%)

Cytokine binds → activates RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK cascade, which phosphorylates STAT proteins (RAS-MAPK pathway can cross-talk with STAT but the PRIMARY JAK-STAT pathway does NOT go through RAS-MAPK; the canonical pathway is JAK → STAT direct Tyr phosphorylation; some RTKs activate both RAS-MAPK and STATs but that is not the canonical JAK-STAT description)
explanation: JAK-STAT clinical pharmacology: JAK inhibitors (Jakinibs) — broad class approved for multiple indications: Ruxolitinib (JAK1 + JAK2): MF (myelofibrosis) → ↓splenomegaly + ↓constitutional symptoms; PV (polycythemia vera hydroxyurea-resistant); graft-versus-host disease (GvHD); tofacitinib (JAK1 + JAK3 >> JAK2): RA, psoriatic arthritis, ulcerative colitis; baricitinib (JAK1 + JAK2): RA, severe COVID-19 (↓IFN-driven immune hyperactivation); upadacitinib (JAK1 selective): RA, Crohn's, UC, atopic dermatitis, PsA, AS; filgotinib (JAK1 selective): RA; deucravacitinib (TYK2 selective, allosteric): psoriasis (TYK2 mediates IL-23 + IL-12 signaling in Th17/Th1; selective → spares JAK1/2/3). STAT proteins and pathways: STAT1: IFN-α/β (with STAT2 → ISGF3) + IFN-γ (STAT1:STAT1 homodimer → GAS → antiviral genes [IFIT1, ISG15, MxA, OAS, APOBEC3B]; pro-apoptotic, anti-proliferative); STAT2: IFN-α/β only (with STAT1+IRF9 → ISGF3 → ISRE); STAT3: IL-6 (acute-phase response + B-cell differentiation + anti-apoptotic [↑Bcl-2, Bcl-xL] + proliferative [↑cyclin D1] + immunosuppressive [↑IL-10, ↑Treg via FOXP3]), oncogenic in cancers (STAT3 GOF mutations → adult-onset immunodeficiency / lymphoma); STAT4: IL-12 + IL-23 → Th1/Th17 differentiation; STAT5A/B: GH (IGF-1 induction), EPO (↑anti-apoptosis in erythroid cells [↑Bcl-xL]), prolactin (↑milk protein genes), IL-2 (T-cell survival + regulatory T cells [FOXP3 + IL-2R α-chain expression]), IL-15; STAT6: IL-4 + IL-13 → Th2 differentiation, IgE class switch, allergic airway responses; STAT6 is an asthma target (dupilumab targets IL-4Rα → blocks both IL-4 + IL-13 → ↓STAT6 → ↓allergic inflammation). IFN signaling detail: Type I IFNs (IFN-α/β): IFNAR1 + IFNAR2 → JAK1 + TYK2 → STAT1:STAT2 hetero + IRF9 → ISGF3 → ISRE → antiviral ISGs; Type II IFN (IFN-γ): IFNGR1 + IFNGR2 → JAK1 + JAK2 → STAT1:STAT1 → GAS → antimicrobial + antigen presentation genes; Type III IFNs (IFN-λ1/2/3): IFNLR1 + IL-10Rβ → TYK2 + JAK1 → ISGF3 → ISRE (similar to type I IFN but restricted to epithelial cells [mucosal antiviral defense]; reduced systemic inflammation vs type I IFN → therapeutic advantage in GI/pulmonary virus infections).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step in the de novo biosynthesis of cholesterol, producing mevalonate?
options: Squalene synthase: squalene synthase (FDFT1/SQS): 2 farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) → squalene (30C) + 2 PPi; this is the first exclusively cholesterol-committed step (FPP also feeds geranylgeranylation [GGPP, 20C], farnesylation [15C → protein prenylation], CoQ/heme synthesis), but squalene synthase is NOT the rate-limiting or committed step of the entire cholesterol synthesis pathway; HMG-CoA reductase is the classic rate-limiting step and the pharmacological target

Lanosterol synthase (LSS, oxidosqualene cyclase): LSS → 2,3-oxidosqualene → lanosterol (first steroid ring formation); IS exclusively committed to steroid/cholesterol synthesis but is NOT the classically designated rate-limiting step

HMG-CoA reductase (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase, HMGCR): HMGCR: committed rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol de novo synthesis; reaction: HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH + 2H+ → mevalonate + 2 NADP+ + CoA; HMGCR: ER membrane enzyme (transmembrane domain + catalytic domain facing cytoplasm); REGULATION (multi-level): 1.
