TRANSCRIPTIONAL (SREBP-2 pathway): when ER cholesterol ↓: SCAP (SREBP cleavage-activating protein)-SREBP2 complex exits ER (not retained by INSIG) → Golgi → S1P (site-1 protease, MBTPS1) cleaves SREBP2 N-terminal domain → S2P cleaves transmembrane anchor → releases bHLH-Zip N-terminus of SREBP2 → enters nucleus → binds SRE (sterol regulatory element, CANNTG) → ↑HMGCR + ↑LDLR + ↑FDPS + ↑SQLE + ↑mevalonate pathway genes; when ER cholesterol ↑: INSIG1/2 (insulin-induced genes) retain SCAP-SREBP in ER → ↓SREBP2 nuclear → ↓HMGCR transcription; 2. TRANSLATIONAL: low sterol → ↑HMGCR mRNA translation efficiency; 3. POST-TRANSLATIONAL: AMPK phosphorylates HMGCR Ser872 → ↓HMGCR activity (inactivation by phosphorylation at Ser872, in the catalytic domain); also: mevalonate + sterols → ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of HMGCR (via MARCH6/TRC8 E3 ligases, and geranylgeraniol → accelerates HMGCR ubiquitination); 4. ALLOSTERIC: mevalonate + sterols → ↓HMGCR activity (product inhibition); STATINS: competitive inhibitors of HMGCR (the HMG-CoA analog moiety binds active site); mechanism: ↓intracellular cholesterol → ↑SREBP2 → ↑LDLR → ↑LDL uptake from blood → ↓LDL-C; statins: lovastatin/pravastatin/simvastatin (first generation, often prodrugs), atorvastatin/rosuvastatin (second gen, more potent); side effects: myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (SLCO1B1/CYP2C9 polymorphisms → ↑statin levels → ↑myopathy risk) + rare hepatotoxicity

Acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase (ACAT, acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase): first step of HMG-CoA synthesis pathway: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA; NOT the committed or rate-limiting step; ACAT has many isoforms (ACAT1 = mitochondrial thiolase, ACAT2 = cholesterol esterification in ER/intestine); very early and not specifically regulated for cholesterol synthesis
explanation: Mevalonate/isoprenoid pathway — complete with branches: Acetyl-CoA → (ACAT) → Acetoacetyl-CoA → (HMGS) → HMG-CoA → (HMGCR [rate-limiting]) → Mevalonate → (MVK [mevalonate kinase]) → Mevalonate-5-P → (PMVK) → Mevalonate-5-PP → (MVD [mevalonate pyrophosphate decarboxylase]) → IPP (isopentenyl-PP, 5C) ↔ (IDI1, isomerase) ↔ DMAPP (dimethylallyl-PP); IPP + DMAPP → (FDPS, farnesyl-PP synthase) → GPP (geranyl-PP, 10C) → FPP (farnesyl-PP, 15C): BRANCHES from FPP: → 2x FPP → (SQS) → squalene → (SQLE [squalene epoxidase]) → 2,3-oxidosqualene → (LSS) → lanosterol → → → cholesterol; → FPP → (GGPPS) → GGPP (geranylgeranyl-PP, 20C) → protein GGTases (GGTase-I/II: geranylgeranylates Rho GTPases [RhoA, Rac1, CDC42], Rab proteins) → membrane targeting; → FPP → protein farnesyltransferase (FTase) → Ras, HDJ2/DNAJ, nuclear lamins (LMNA/B → farnesylated) → farnesylation defects: progeria (LMNA H222R → partially farnesylated → Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome [HGPS]; lonafarnib [FTase inhibitor] approved for HGPS 2020); → IPP → (10+ IPP) → dolichol-PP (glycan carrier for N-linked glycosylation in ER; key: Dol-PP-oligosaccharide transferred en bloc to Asn by OST [oligosaccharyltransferase]); → IPP → → → CoQ10 (ubiquinone, coenzyme Q): ring from tyrosine; tail from GGPP+IPP extensions; CoQ10 deficiency (primary: PDSS1/2 + CoQ2 + CABC1/ADCK3 mutations → encephalopathy + myopathy; secondary: statin-associated CoQ10 depletion → ↑myopathy risk?; controversial) → IPP in erythrocytes → → → heme synthesis (minor); all branches from FPP explain why statins can inhibit non-cholesterol isoprenoids: ↓FPP → ↓protein prenylation (Ras farnesylation, Rho GGTylation) → pleiotropic statin effects: anti-inflammatory, endothelial NO ↑, ↓platelet aggregation, ↑plaque stability (↑fibrous cap, ↓MMPs) — beyond just LDL-C lowering.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Wnt/β-catenin (canonical Wnt) signaling plays a critical role in development and cancer. In the ABSENCE of Wnt ligand, β-catenin is degraded. What is the mechanism?
options: Wnt absent → LRP5/6 phosphorylation → β-catenin activation → nuclear entry (LRP5/6 phosphorylation occurs IN THE PRESENCE of Wnt, not the absence; Wnt → Frizzled + LRP5/6 co-receptor → Dvl → LRP5/6 phosphorylation by CK1γ → axin recruited to membrane → destruction complex disrupted → β-catenin accumulates; this describes the ACTIVE Wnt pathway)

Wnt absent → formation of the β-catenin destruction complex (APC + Axin + GSK3β + CK1α) → sequential phosphorylation of β-catenin → β-TrCP (ubiquitin ligase) recognition → proteasomal degradation: CANONICAL Wnt/β-catenin pathway: WNT ABSENT (OFF state): β-catenin destruction complex: APC (adenomatous polyposis coli, scaffold) + Axin1/2 (scaffold) + GSK3β (glycogen synthase kinase 3β) + CK1α (casein kinase 1α) → complex binds β-catenin at its N-terminal regulatory domain → SEQUENTIAL PHOSPHORYLATION: (1) CK1α: phospho-Ser45 of β-catenin (priming phosphorylation); (2) GSK3β: phospho-Thr41 → phospho-Ser37 → phospho-Ser33 (β-TrCP recognition motif: DSGxxS); phospho-Ser33/37 of β-catenin recognized by β-TrCP (beta-transducin repeat containing protein, an F-box protein of SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase: SCF-β-TrCP) → K48-ubiquitination → 26S proteasome → β-catenin degradation; WNT PRESENT (ON state): Wnt binds Frizzled (FZD1-10, 7-TM receptor) + LRP5/6 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5/6, co-receptor) → receptor complex → recruits Dishevelled (Dvl1/2/3) via its DIX + PDZ domains → Dvl → phosphorylation of LRP5/6 cytoplasmic tail by CK1γ (at PPPSP motifs) + GSK3β → phospho-LRP5/6 → Axin recruited to LRP5/6 → destruction complex falls apart (Axin no longer in complex) → free β-catenin → accumulates in cytoplasm → enters nucleus (via β-importin?) → β-catenin associates with TCF/LEF transcription factors (TCF1 [TCF7], TCF3, TCF4, LEF1) → displaces Groucho (transcriptional repressor) → recruits CBP/p300 → ↑Wnt target genes: CYCLIN D1 (CCND1), c-MYC (MYC), AXIN2 (negative feedback), DKK1 (negative feedback), CD44, LGR5 (adult stem cell marker), VEGFA, MMP7 etc.; CANCER: APC mutations: most common cause of colorectal cancer (CRC): ↓APC → destruction complex non-functional → ↑β-catenin → constitutive Wnt signaling → ↑cell proliferation; 80% CRC: somatic APC mutations (truncating); familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): germline APC mutation (→ thousands of polyps → 100% CRC risk without prophylactic colectomy); Gardner syndrome: FAP + desmoid tumors + osteomas + CHRPE (congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium); Turcot syndrome: FAP variant with brain tumors (medulloblastoma for APC/Wnt; glioblastoma for MMR/Lynch syndrome); CTNNB1 (β-catenin gene) missense mutations at Ser45/Thr41/Ser37/Ser33 (phosphorylation sites): deletion or mutation → cannot be phosphorylated → resistant to destruction → constitutive Wnt signaling → cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma, Wilms tumor, medulloblastoma); AXIN1/2 mutations (less common): same effect as APC loss; R-spondin (RSPO1-4) + LGR4/5/6 (Leucine-rich repeat-containing GPCR 4/5/6): Wnt amplifiers: RSPO → LGR4/5 → inhibits ZNRF3/RNF43 (E3 ligases that ubiquitinate and remove Frizzled from cell surface) → ↑Frizzled surface expression → ↑Wnt sensitivity; RSPO fusions/LGR5 amplifications: in colorectal + pancreatic + other cancers → Wnt hyperactivation

Wnt absent → Frizzled receptor constitutive kinase activity → STAT3 phosphorylation → c-Myc induction (this pathway is not the canonical Wnt/β-catenin mechanism; Frizzled is not a kinase; STAT3 and c-Myc are not directly regulated by Wnt via STAT3 in the canonical pathway; c-Myc IS a Wnt target but transcribed via TCF/LEF not STAT3)

Wnt absent → DKK1 secretion → LRP5/6 sequestration → β-catenin enters nucleus constitutively (DKK1 inhibits Wnt signaling by binding LRP5/6 → ↓LRP5/6 availability → ↓Wnt signaling; DKK1 is a WNT INHIBITOR, not something that constitutively activates Wnt; also DKK1 is a negative feedback target of Wnt signaling; when Wnt is absent, there is no DKK1 being induced by Wnt, and β-catenin is being degraded, not entering nucleus)
explanation: Non-canonical Wnt pathways: 1. Wnt/PCP (planar cell polarity) pathway: Wnt → FZD → Dvl → RhoA/ROCK → actin cytoskeleton + Rac1/JNK → morphogenetic movements (convergent extension in gastrulation); no β-catenin involvement; 2. Wnt/Ca2+ pathway: Wnt → FZD → Gαq → PLC → IP3 + DAG → Ca2+ → CaMKII + PKC → NFAT → cell adhesion + motility; Wnt inhibitors (therapeutic/clinical): Porcupine (PORCN) inhibitors: LGK-974, WNT-974, ETC-159 (preclinical/phase I-II trials): PORCN is an O-acyltransferase that palmitoylates Wnt ligands (palmitoleoyl group at Ser at conserved Cys-Ser-... motif in all Wnt ligands → required for Wnt secretion + receptor binding; without palmitoylation → Wnt retained in ER + cannot be secreted → ↓ALL Wnt signaling); PORCN inhibitors → ↓all Wnt ligand secretion → potential use in RSPO fusion cancers, Wnt-dependent CRC, TNBC; Tankyrase inhibitors (G007-LK, XAV939): tankyrase (TNKS1/2) PARylates Axin → Axin ubiquitination → ↑β-catenin degradation; by inhibiting tankyrase → ↑Axin stability → ↑destruction complex → ↓β-catenin; Frizzled 4 antibody (vantictumab) (preclinical/discontinued). APC domain structure: N-terminal → oligomerization domain; APC contains β-catenin binding repeats (15-AA + 20-AA repeats) and downregulation domain → physical interaction with β-catenin in destruction complex; also: APC has microtubule-binding domain (regulates mitotic spindle) and nuclear export signal (in chromosomal instability, loss of APC → mitotic errors).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: TGF-β (transforming growth factor-β) signals through Smad proteins to regulate gene transcription. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the TGF-β/Smad pathway?
options: TGF-β → Frizzled receptor → Dishevelled → β-catenin dephosphorylation → nuclear entry (this describes the Wnt pathway, not TGF-β; TGF-β signals through serine/threonine kinase receptors, not Frizzled GPCRs)

TGF-β → type II receptor (TβRII) → recruits and phosphorylates type I receptor (TβRI/ALK5) → TβRI phosphorylates R-Smads (Smad2/3) → R-Smad + co-Smad (Smad4) → nuclear translocation → gene regulation: TGF-β/Smad pathway: 1. TGF-β LIGAND BINDING: TGF-β dimer binds constitutively active TGF-β receptor type II (TβRII, TGFBR2), a serine/threonine kinase; 2. RECEPTOR COMPLEX: TβRII phosphorylates type I receptor (TβRI/ALK5 [activin receptor-like kinase 5], TGFBR1) at GS domain (Gly-Ser-rich domain N-terminal to kinase domain) → activates TβRI kinase; 3. R-SMAD PHOSPHORYLATION: TβRI (ALK5) phosphorylates R-Smads (receptor-regulated Smads): Smad2 + Smad3 at their C-terminal SSXS motif (Ser465/467 of Smad2); SMAD families: R-Smads (Smad1/2/3/5/8): receptor-regulated; Smad2/3 = TGF-β/activin pathway; Smad1/5/8/9 = BMP pathway (via ALK1/2/3/6); co-Smad (Smad4): common mediator for ALL pathways (obligate partner for R-Smads); I-Smads (Smad6/7): inhibitory; 4. CO-SMAD RECRUITMENT: R-Smad (Smad2/3) + Smad4 → heterotrimer (2 R-Smads + 1 Smad4 typically); 5. NUCLEAR TRANSLOCATION: Smad complex → nucleus (importin-β3 for Smad2/3); 6. GENE REGULATION: Smad complex + DNA-binding co-factors (FOXH1, ZEB1/2, AP-1 [Fos/Jun], Runx, p300/CBP) → bind Smad-binding element (SBE: GTCT or AGAC) → transcription of TGF-β target genes: pro-fibrotic (COL1A1, FN1, ACTA2 [α-SMA], PAI-1 [SERPINE1]); anti-proliferative (p21 [CDKN1A], p15 [CDKN2B] → CDK inhibition → ↓cyclin D + E → ↑Rb → ↓cell cycle); context-dependent pro-tumorigenic (TGF-β PARADOX: early cancer: tumor suppressor [↓proliferation → ↑apoptosis]; late cancer: tumor promoter [→ EMT via Snail/Slug/ZEB1/2 → invasion/metastasis + ↑immunosuppression + ↑angiogenesis]); I-Smad regulation: Smad7 is induced by TGF-β (negative feedback) → Smad7 binds activated TβRI → recruits Smurf1/2 (HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin ligases) → polyubiquitinates TβRI → proteasomal degradation → ↓TGF-β signaling; Smad6: inhibits BMP signaling specifically; FKBP12: binds unactivated TβRI → holds GS domain in inactive configuration → TβRII phosphorylation of GS releases FKBP12

TGF-β → JAK1 phosphorylation → STAT3 → SBE binding (TGF-β does not use JAK-STAT as its canonical signaling pathway; JAK-STAT is for cytokines like IFN/IL-6 etc.; TGF-β uses Smad2/3 as the canonical pathway; there is cross-talk [STAT3 can modulate TGF-β responses] but this is not the primary mechanism)

TGF-β → TβRI autophosphorylation without TβRII → Smad1/5 phosphorylation → BMP response genes (Smad1/5 phosphorylation is for the BMP pathway [through ALK1/2/3/6, not ALK5]; TGF-β/ALK5 specifically phosphorylates Smad2/3; also, TβRII is required for TβRI activation — TGF-β cannot activate TβRI alone; auto-phosphorylation without TβRII does not occur in the canonical pathway)
explanation: TGF-β superfamily — complete: TGF-β superfamily (>35 members): TGF-β1/2/3 (pleiotropic, most studied), Activins (A/B: FSH regulation, erythropoiesis, reproductive axis), Inhibins (reproductive axis), BMPs (1-20+: bone/cartilage/Wnt signaling), GDF (growth differentiation factors: GDF9, GDF11, myostatin [GDF8]), AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone, Sertoli cell → regression of Müllerian ducts in males), Nodal (L-R asymmetry in embryo). ALK (activin receptor-like kinase) type I receptors: ALK1 → pSmad1/5 (endothelial TGF-β + BMP9/10 signaling); ALK2 → pSmad1/5 (BMP + Activin); ALK3 → pSmad1/5 (BMP4/7); ALK4 → pSmad2/3 (Activin A/B, GDF11, Nodal); ALK5 → pSmad2/3 (TGF-β1/2/3); ALK6 → pSmad1/5 (BMP4/7); ALK7 → pSmad2/3 (Activin + Nodal). TGF-β pathological roles: Fibrosis: ↑TGF-β → Smad3 → ↑myofibroblast differentiation (α-SMA+) → ↑collagen → fibrosis in: lung (IPF), liver (cirrhosis), kidney (CKD), scleroderma; anti-TGF-β therapies in fibrosis: fresolimumab (anti-TGF-β1 monoclonal Ab), bintrafusp alfa (TGF-βRII-IgG1 trap), pirfenidone (mechanism partly anti-TGF-β); Cancer EMT: TGF-β → Smad2/3 + Snail1/2 + ZEB1/2 → ↓E-cadherin (CDH1) + ↑vimentin + ↑fibronectin + ↑N-cadherin → epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) → ↑invasion + metastasis + resistance to therapy; anti-TGF-β cancer therapy: targets both fibrosis and EMT; galunisertib (TβRI/ALK5 inhibitor, LY2157299) + vactosertib + SAR439459 (anti-TGFβ-PD-L1 bispecific); musculoskeletal: myostatin (GDF8) → pSmad2/3 → ↓muscle growth (negative regulator); anti-myostatin: bimagrumab (anti-ActRII/ActRIIB) + apitegromab (anti-GDF8 proform) → muscle mass in spinal muscular atrophy + myopathies; AMH/MIS: AMH → AMHRII (type II) + ALK2/3/6 (type I) → Smad1/5 → Müllerian duct regression; AMH serum assay: marker of ovarian reserve (AMH produced by small antral follicles); ↓AMH → ↓ovarian reserve → ↓IVF prognosis; ↑AMH → PCOS (↑antral follicle count → ↑AMH); FOP (fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva): ALK2 GOF mutation (R206H → constitutively active ALK2 → pSmad1/5 → ectopic bone formation in soft tissues → progressive ossification of muscles, tendons, ligaments; catastrophic disease; surgical removal worsens [heterotopic ossification flare]; palovarotene [RARγ agonist, retinoic acid] → ↓HO [heterotopic ossification], approved 2023].

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycogen debranching enzyme (amylo-alpha-1,6-glucosidase/alpha-1,4-glucanotransferase, AGL) is deficient in glycogen storage disease type III (Cori-Forbes disease). Which substrate accumulates in this disease?
options: Glucose-6-phosphate in lysosomes (G6P accumulation in lysosomes → GSD type Ia/Ib [von Gierke] — not GSD III; in GSD III, the primary accumulation is in the cytoplasm of glycogen with short outer branches)

Glycogen with abnormally SHORT outer branches (limit dextrin) in liver and muscle: Glycogen debranching enzyme (AGL, amylo-1,6-glucosidase/oligo-1,4→1,4-glucanotransferase; bifunctional enzyme): has TWO activities in ONE polypeptide: (1) 4-α-glucanotransferase (oligo-1,4→1,4-glucan transferase): transfers the 3 outer glucosyl residues from the branch to the main chain (a 1,4-bond at the branch) — leaves one glucose at branch point attached by α-1,6 bond; (2) amylo-1,6-glucosidase (α-1,6-glucosidase): cleaves the α-1,6 branch-point glucose (the single remaining glucose at the branch) → free glucose (the only GSD that releases free glucose during glycogenolysis) → debris-free glycogen main chain can be continued by phosphorylase; AGL deficiency → GSD III (Cori disease [Carlos Gori] / Forbes disease): glycogen with short outer branches (LIMIT DEXTRIN = phosphorylase limit dextrin; glycogen phosphorylase stalls 4 glucose residues from a branch point → cannot proceed further → limit dextrin formation; without debranching enzyme → limit dextrin cannot be resolved) → phosphorylase cannot fully degrade glycogen → limit dextrin accumulates; CLINICAL GSD III: AR (AGL gene); liver AND muscle involvement in type IIIa (most common, ~80%); LIVER ONLY in type IIIb (AGL mutations affecting only the 4-α-glucanotransferase activity); hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia (fasting) + growth retardation + elevated transaminases in CHILDHOOD → often IMPROVES with age (puberty); MUSCLE: progressive myopathy + CK elevation in ADULTS (GSD IIIa); cardiomyopathy (in some); URINE ORGANIC ACIDS: NOT acidic (no lactic acidosis unlike GSD I); ketosis during hypoglycemia (can oxidize FA); DIET: frequent meals + high-protein diet (protein → GNG → bypasses glycogenolysis); raw cornstarch (slow-release glucose); DIAGNOSIS: liver biopsy + AGL enzyme assay (in RBCs or liver/muscle); gene sequencing; DISTINGUISHING GSD I vs III: GSD I: NO ketosis (↑lactate, ↑uric acid, ↑TG, ↑lipids, no ketones); GSD III: KETOSIS (can oxidize fat partially, FA oxidation intact); GSD I: elevated lactate + lactic acidosis; GSD III: normal or mild lactate; GSD I: cannot produce glucose at all (G6Pase deficient); GSD III: CAN produce some glucose (from the outer chains via phosphorylase before limit dextrin → can produce some glucose until limit dextrin forms; after that → hypoglycemia)
Galactose-1-phosphate in red blood cells and liver (galactose-1-phosphate accumulation → galactosemia [classic, GALT deficiency]; NOT a glycogen storage disease)

Glycogen with abnormally LONG outer chains in liver (abnormally long outer chains → GSD IV [Andersen disease, branching enzyme deficiency] → polyglucosan [amylopectin-like structure with very few branch points → very long chains] → liver cirrhosis in childhood; NOT GSD III; GSD III has SHORT outer chains = limit dextrin)
explanation: Glycogen storage diseases — comprehensive: GSD I (von Gierke): G6Pase (Ia, G6PC gene) or G6P translocase (Ib, SLC37A4) deficiency → ↑G6P + glycogen in liver/kidney → NO hepatic glucose production → severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis (↑pyruvate → lactate) + hypertriglyceridemia + hyperuricemia (↑G6P → PPP → ribose-5-P → purines → uric acid; also ↓urate excretion) + gout (NOT in infancy — manifests later) + hepatomegaly; GSD Ib additionally: neutropenia + IBD-like colitis (SLC37A4 needed in neutrophils); treatment: raw cornstarch + G-CSF (Ib); GSD II (Pompe): α-glucosidase/acid maltase (GAA, lysosomal enzyme) deficiency → lysosomal glycogen accumulation in ALL tissues (heart >> muscle); infantile: cardiomyopathy + hypotonia + respiratory failure + macroglossia; adult: proximal myopathy + respiratory failure; ERT: alglucosidase alfa (Myozyme) + cipaglucosidase alfa (newer, better) + gene therapy (clinical trials); GSD III (Cori-Forbes): AGL, limit dextrin; GSD IV (Andersen): GBE (1,4-α-glucan branching enzyme, GBE1) deficiency → polyglucosan (amylopectin-like) accumulation → liver cirrhosis in first years of life; Lafora disease [EPM2A/EPM2B]: different cause of polyglucosan (laforin/malin mutations → intraneuronal Lafora bodies → progressive myoclonic epilepsy); adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD): GBE1 mutations in adults; GSD V (McArdle): myophosphorylase (PYGM) deficiency → glycogen in MUSCLE only → EXERCISE-induced muscle cramps + myoglobinuria + SECOND WIND PHENOMENON (after initial fatigue, patient feels better due to ↑FFA + gluconeogenesis) + ischemic forearm exercise test: ↑lactate normally (from glycolysis) → in McArdle, ↑↑↑ammonia (purine nucleotide cycle: AMP → [AMP deaminase] → IMP + NH3 → when AMP not re-aminatized due to ↑AMP) without ↑lactate (pathognomonic pattern); GSD VI (Hers): liver phosphorylase (PYGL) deficiency → milder; GSD VII (Tarui): PFK-M (muscle PFK-1, PFKM) deficiency → ↑G6P + F6P in muscle + RBCs → exercise intolerance + hemolytic anemia; GSD IX (PHK deficiency): phosphorylase kinase (PhK) deficiency → liver enlargement + hypoglycemia; most common GSD; PHKA2 (X-linked liver): boys; GSD 0 (glycogen synthase deficiency): ↓glycogen → fasting hypoglycemia + ketosis (no glycogen to release); GSD IXa: PHKA2; GSD IXb: PHKB; GSD IXc: PHKG2; GSD IXd: PHKA1 (muscle PHK).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Sirtuins (SIRTs 1-7) are NAD+-dependent protein deacylases that link cellular metabolism to epigenetic regulation. SIRT1 deacetylates and regulates which transcriptional coactivator to promote gluconeogenesis and fatty acid oxidation during fasting?
options: PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha): SIRT1 → deacetylates PGC-1α (at multiple Lys residues → removes acetyl groups → activates PGC-1α); PGC-1α activated (deacetylated form): PGC-1α coactivates: (1) FOXO1 + HNF4α → ↑PEPCK1 + G6Pase → ↑gluconeogenesis (fasting response); (2) PPARα → ↑FAO genes (CPT1A, ACOX1, HMGCS2 → ↑mitochondrial FA oxidation + ↑ketogenesis); (3) NRF1 + NRF2 + TFAM → ↑mitochondrial biogenesis (↑mt DNA copy number + ↑mtRNA transcription); (4) PPAR-γ → ↑adipogenesis (context-dependent); (5) MEF2C/D → ↑muscle gene expression; (6) ERRα → ↑OXPHOS genes; SIRT1 activation: ↑NAD+ (during fasting/caloric restriction → ↑NAD+/NADH ratio → ↑SIRT1 activity → ↑PGC-1α deacetylation → ↑metabolic adaptation); SIRT1 and AMPK cooperation: AMPK → ↑NAMPT (nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase, rate-limiting in NAD+ salvage: nicotinamide + PRPP → NMN → NAD+) → ↑NAD+ → ↑SIRT1 → ↑PGC-1α + FOXO1/3 → ↑FAO + ↑GNG + ↑autophagy; also: AMPK directly phosphorylates PGC-1α → synergistic with SIRT1 deacetylation; SIRT1 and TORC2 (CRTC2): SIRT1 deacetylates TORC2 (CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 2) at early fasting → promotes TORC2 ubiquitination → ↓CRTC2-CREB-PEPCK1 signaling (SIRT1 switches from TORC2/CREB-mediated early GNG to FOXO1/PGC-1α-mediated late GNG); resveratrol (polyphenol from red grape skins): SIRT1 activator? → activates SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of PGC-1α + other substrates → used as model for caloric restriction mimetic; controversy: resveratrol may be an indirect SIRT1 activator (via AMPK → ↑NAD+ → ↑SIRT1) rather than direct SIRT1 allosteric activator; SRT1720, SRT2104 (SIRT1 activating compounds, STACs): more specific in trials; NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR [nicotinamide riboside]) → ↑cellular NAD+ → ↑SIRT1/3/5 → metabolic benefits in aging models

STAT3 (signal transducer and activator of transcription 3): SIRT1 CAN deacetylate STAT3 (Lys685) → ↓STAT3 transcriptional activity → ↓IL-6/gp130-driven gene expression; but PGC-1α is the CANONICAL SIRT1 substrate linking fasting/NAD+ to metabolic gene expression; STAT3 deacetylation is not the primary answer for gluconeogenesis + FAO regulation by SIRT1

SREBP-2 (sterol regulatory element binding protein 2): SIRT1 deacetylates SREBP-2? → actually SIRT1 → deacetylates LXRα (liver X receptor α) → LXRα → ↑ABCA1 → ↑cholesterol efflux; SIRT1 can also suppress SREBP-1c processing → ↓lipogenesis; SREBP-2 is not the canonical PGC-1α replacement for fasting FAO/GNG regulation by SIRT1

HIF-1α (hypoxia-inducible factor 1α): SIRT1 deacetylates HIF-1α at Lys674 → ↓HIF-1α transcriptional activity (paradoxically inhibits HIF-1α target genes) → ↓glycolysis under hypoxia; SIRT1 and HIF-1α interaction is a HYPOXIA adaptation; NOT the answer for gluconeogenesis + FAO during fasting; fasting → ↑SIRT1 → ↑PGC-1α (not ↑HIF-1α targets)
explanation: Sirtuin family — complete: SIRT1 (nucleus + cytoplasm): deacetylates p53 (↓p53-dependent apoptosis), FOXO1/3 (↑autophagy + ↑stress resistance), PGC-1α (↑mitochondrial biogenesis + ↑FAO + ↑GNG), NF-κB (Lys310, ↓inflammatory genes), HIF-1α (↓glycolytic genes under hypoxia), TORC2 (modulates early GNG), H3K9ac + H4K16ac (chromatin compaction → gene silencing); SIRT1 responds to: ↑NAD+/NADH (fasting/CR) + caloric restriction + exercise → ↑SIRT1 → metabolic adaptations; SIRT2 (cytoplasm): deacetylates α-tubulin (Lys40) + FOXO3 + H4K16ac; cell cycle regulator; SIRT3 (mitochondrial matrix): deacetylates many mitochondrial proteins: LCAD (long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, ↑FAO), AceCS2 (acetyl-CoA synthetase 2 → ↑acetyl-CoA from acetate), MnSOD/SOD2 (Lys122, ↑antioxidant capacity) + GDH (Glu dehydrogenase, ↑Glu → α-KG in TCA), PDHA1 (PDC), IDH2 (↑NADPH → ↑glutathione reduction); SIRT3 KO → hyperacetylation of mitochondrial proteins → ↓FAO + ↓TCA efficiency + ↓ETC → cancer-like metabolism + ↑cancer risk (SIRT3 is a tumor suppressor in some contexts); SIRT4 (mitochondrial inner membrane): NAD+ glycohydrolase + lipoamidase (cleaves lipoamide from E2 of PDC/BCKDH → ↓PDC and BCKDH activity → ↓BCAA catabolism); ↑SIRT4 → ↓BCAA oxidation → conserves BCAAs during fasting? SIRT5 (mitochondrial matrix): NAD+-dependent desuccinylase + demalonylase + deglutarylase (removes succinyl/malonyl/glutaryl groups from Lys); targets: CPS1 (desuccinylation → ↑urea cycle) + HMGCS2 (demalonylation → ↑ketogenesis); SIRT5 important for ammonia detoxification during fasting. SIRT6 (nucleus): deacetylase for H3K9ac + H3K56ac → chromatin silencing at telomeres + ribosomal DNA + SIRT6 KO → premature aging phenotype in mice (progeroid syndrome); deacetylates HIF-1α → ↓glycolytic Warburg genes; SIRT6 tumor suppressor (promotes DNA repair, suppresses Warburg); SIRT7 (nucleus/nucleolus): H3K18ac deacetylase; RNA Pol I regulation; ↑rDNA transcription; SIRT7 KO → inflammatory cardiomyopathy. NAD+ metabolism: de novo synthesis (from Trp via quinolinate [kynurenine pathway]: Trp → IDO/TDO → kynurenine → → → quinolinate [QPRT] → NMN → NAD+); Preiss-Handler pathway (from nicotinic acid [niacin]: niacin → NAPRT → NaMN → NMNAT → NaAD → NADS → NAD+); salvage pathway (from nicotinamide: NAMPT → NMN → NMNAT → NAD+; from nicotinamide riboside [NR]: NRK1/2 → NMN → NAD+); NAMPT is the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway → NAMPT inhibitors (FK866, GMX1778) → ↓NAD+ → ↓energy + ↓PARP + ↓Sirtuin activity → cancer therapy trials.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with recurrent severe bacterial infections, omphalitis at birth, delayed umbilical cord separation (at 8 weeks), and elevated WBC count. Immunophenotyping shows normal lymphocyte subsets. Flow cytometry reveals absent CD18 on neutrophils. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Chediak-Higashi syndrome (CHS): CHS (LYST gene, lysosomal trafficking regulator): AR; giant granules in leukocytes (hallmark: giant lysosomes due to abnormal lysosomal trafficking/fusion); partial oculocutaneous albinism + recurrent infections + progressive neurodegeneration + accelerated phase (hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, HLH); CD18 expression is NORMAL in CHS; CHS has normal NEUTROPHIL count but impaired killing (CTL are also defective); elevated WBC + absent CD18 → NOT CHS

Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I (LAD-I): CD18 (ITGB2, integrin beta-2 chain) is the common β-chain of the β-2 integrins: (1) LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18, αLβ2, ICAM-1 ligand, lymphocytes + NK): T cell-APC adhesion, NK cytotoxicity; (2) Mac-1/CR3 (CD11b/CD18, αMβ2, ICAM-1 + C3bi + fibrinogen ligand, neutrophils + monocytes): phagocytosis + oxidative burst; (3) p150,95/CR4 (CD11c/CD18, αXβ2, C3bi ligand, monocytes); (4) CD11d/CD18 (αDβ2); LAD-I (ITGB2 gene mutations, AR): ↓CD18 → ↓all β-2 integrins → neutrophil adhesion defect: neutrophils CANNOT adhere to endothelium → CANNOT emigrate from blood to infected tissue; SELECTIN: binds; but firm adhesion (LFA-1/ICAM-1, Mac-1/ICAM-1) is absent → neutrophils roll but don't stop; CLINICAL: (1) omphalitis at birth (umbilical stump infection by skin flora; neutrophils cannot emigrate); (2) DELAYED UMBILICAL CORD SEPARATION (>21 days; normal: 7-14 days; mechanism: normally granulation tissue forming during cord detachment requires neutrophils; without neutrophils → delayed separation); (3) recurrent severe bacterial infections (S. aureus, Enterobacteriaceae, Aspergillus) WITHOUT pus (despite ↑WBC; pus requires neutrophil emigration into tissue → pus-less infections is classic); (4) LEUKOCYTOSIS (elevated WBC, often 40,000-100,000/µL) even without acute infection (because neutrophils cannot leave the blood → accumulate in blood → high WBC [leukocytosis is a cardinal feature of LAD]); (5) poor wound healing; DIAGNOSIS: flow cytometry: absent/reduced CD18 (+ CD11a/b/c) on neutrophils/monocytes; TREATMENT: aggressive antibiotics + G-CSF (partial help) + bone marrow transplant (HSCT is curative for severe LAD-I); gene therapy: early phase trials; SEVERITY: severe (< 1% CD18) → childhood death without HSCT; moderate (1-30% CD18) → less severe; mild (30-60% CD18) → periodontitis + milder infections

Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD): CGD: NADPH oxidase (NOX2/gp91phox = CYBB [X-linked, most common, ~65% of CGD] or NCF1/p47phox, NCF2/p67phox, CYBA/p22phox, NCF4/p40phox [AR forms]): deficiency → cannot generate superoxide (O2•-) → ↓oxidative burst → cannot kill catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Klebsiella, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Aspergillus); LABS: ↑WBC (may be elevated); NBT test (nitroblue tetrazolium): normal neutrophils + NBT → NBT reduced to blue formazan (by O2•- from NADPH oxidase); CGD neutrophils: NBT STAYS YELLOW (no O2•-); flow cytometry: DHR (dihydrorhodamine 123) assay: DHR oxidized by HOCl → rhodamine 123 (fluorescent); CGD: no fluorescence; CGD neutrophils EXPRESS NORMAL CD18 (the adhesion problem is not in CGD) → CD18 expression NORMAL in CGD; diagnosis would show negative NBT/DHR, not absent CD18

Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID): SCID: deficiency of BOTH T cells AND B cells (sometimes with NK cell involvement, depending on type); typical: ↓lymphocytes + ↓T cells + ↓B cells + absent CD3/CD4/CD8 on immunophenotyping + susceptibility to viral/fungal/bacterial infections; CD18 NORMAL in SCID; also: elevated WBC with normal lymphocytes does NOT fit SCID
explanation: Integrins — complete: Structure: heterodimers of α (18 types) + β (8 types) chains → 24 distinct combinations; transmembrane glycoproteins (with short cytoplasmic tails linking to cytoskeleton [talin, vinculin, α-actinin]); extracellular domain: binds ECM or cell-surface ligands; inside-out signaling: chemokines/activated GPCRs → talin (via kindlin) → pulls cytoplasmic tail of β-chain → conformational change from bent (inactive, low affinity) to extended (active, high affinity) → outside-in signaling: ligand binding → integrin clustering → FAK (focal adhesion kinase) + ILK (integrin-linked kinase) + Src → paxillin + p130CAS → ERK + PI3K → survival + proliferation + migration; LAD types: LAD-I: ITGB2 (CD18) → absent β-2 integrins; LAD-II (FUCT1/SLC35C1, GDP-fucose transporter): ↓sialyl-Lewis X (CD15s) on neutrophils → ↓selectin-mediated rolling (rolling phase of adhesion deficient); clinical: LAD-I-like infections + mild learning disability + short stature + blood group H+Ley absent (Bombay blood group: H antigen absent on RBC due to same fucosylation defect); treatment: fucose supplementation (partially corrects); LAD-III (FERMT3/KINDLIN-3 mutations): kindlin-3 required for inside-out integrin activation in ALL hematopoietic cells; ↓β-1, -2, -3 integrins activation → LAD-I phenotype + bleeding (↓platelet β-3 integrin [αIIbβ3/GPIIb-IIIa] activation → similar to Glanzmann thrombasthenia). Adhesion cascade (neutrophil extravasation): 1. Tethering/rolling: E/P-selectin (on endothelium, induced by TNF/IL-1/histamine) → sialyl-Lewis X (on neutrophil) → rolling (selectin step); 2. Activation: chemokines (IL-8/CXCL8, C5a, LTB4, fMLP) → GPCR on neutrophil → G-protein → ↑Ca2+ + PKC → inside-out integrin activation + degranulation; 3. Arrest/firm adhesion: LFA-1 (αLβ2) → ICAM-1/2 on endothelium + Mac-1 (αMβ2) → ICAM-1 → firm adhesion; 4. Diapedesis: PE-CAM-1 (CD31) → PE-CAM-1 homophilic + JAM-A/B/C → neutrophil squeezes through tight junction; 5. Chemotaxis: fMLP + C5a + IL-8 → GPCR → PI3K → PIP3 → WAVE/Arp2/3 → lamellipodia + pseudopodia toward gradient; LAD-I: steps 3-5 impaired (intact rolling but no firm adhesion or migration).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Hedgehog (Hh) signaling pathway is crucial for embryonic development. In the ABSENCE of Hh ligand, PTCH1 (Patched) inhibits SMO (Smoothened). When Hh binds PTCH1, SMO is released. What are the transcription factors that are activated in the canonical Hh pathway?
options: NFκB (nuclear factor kappa B): NF-κB is activated by multiple signaling pathways (TNF/IL-1 → TRAF → IKK → IκB phosphorylation + degradation → NF-κB nuclear entry); NF-κB has cross-talk with Hh signaling in some contexts but is NOT the canonical Hh transcription factor; the canonical Hh pathway transcription factors are GLI proteins
Smad1/5/8: Smad1/5/8 are the canonical transcription factors for the BMP pathway (BMP → ALK1/2/3/6 → pSmad1/5/8 → Smad4 → SBE); NOT the Hh pathway

GLI1, GLI2, and GLI3 (glioma-associated oncogene family): Hedgehog pathway (canonical): 1. HH ABSENT: PTCH1 (Patched 1, 12-TM tumor suppressor, 2 per tetramer) in primary cilia membrane → inhibits SMO (Smoothened, a 7-TM GPCR-like protein) — mechanism: PTCH1 inhibits SMO via regulation of a small molecule (oxysterol? or PI4P?) flux → SMO cannot accumulate in cilia; cytoplasmic: SUFU (suppressor of fused) + KIF7 (kinesin) + CK1/GSK3 → phosphorylate GLI2/3 full-length → partial proteasomal processing → GLI2/3 repressor forms (GLI2-R, GLI3-R) → nuclear entry → REPRESSES Hh target genes; 2. HH PRESENT: Sonic Hh (SHH) / Desert Hh (DHH) / Indian Hh (IHH) → bind PTCH1 (with SCUBE2/BOC/CDON co-receptors for SHH) → PTCH1 internalized + DEGRADED → SMO no longer inhibited → SMO accumulates in cilia (primary cilium is the signaling hub for Hh) → SMO → activates KIF3A (kinesin, cilia-dependent trafficking) → SUFU-GLI complex in cilia → Gli2/3 full-length dissociates from SUFU → GLI activator forms (GLI2-A predominantly; GLI1 is a target gene that amplifies the signal → GLI1-A) → GLI activators translocate to nucleus → ↑Hh target genes: PTCH1 (negative feedback loop!), GLI1 (positive feedback), CYCLIN D1/D2, SNAI1 (Snail, EMT), FOXF1, FOXA2, NKX2.1, VEGF; GLI family: GLI1 (GLIS family, chromosome 12q13): no repressor form; ACTIVATOR only; amplified in glioma (but not the primary TF in normal Hh); GLI2 (chromosome 2q14): mainly ACTIVATOR in Hh signal; GLI3 (chromosome 7p13): mainly REPRESSOR (GLI3-R) when Hh absent; Pallister-Hall syndrome = heterozygous GLI3 GOF mutation (truncating → constitutive GLI3-R → abnormal repressor → polydactyly + hypothalamic hamartoma + epiglottis + other defects); Greig cephalopolysyndactyly = GLI3 haploinsufficiency (LOF); CANCER: PTCH1 loss → Basal cell carcinoma (BCC, most common cancer; PTCH1 mutations in >90% of sporadic BCC; also Gorlin syndrome [NBCCS]: hereditary BCC + medulloblastoma + odontogenic keratocysts + bifid ribs + calcified falx cerebri); SMO GOF mutations → BCC + some MB; HH pathway-targeted drugs: Vismodegib (GDC-0449): first-in-class SMO inhibitor, FDA approved 2012 for locally advanced/metastatic BCC; Sonidegib (LDE225): SMO inhibitor for locally advanced BCC; Glasdegib (PF-04449913): SMO inhibitor for AML + MDS (in combo with LDAC); SMO mutations R180C/W535L = resistance mutations to vismodegib

p53 and Rb (p53 is a tumor suppressor activated by DNA damage via ATM/ATR → Mdm2 inhibition; Rb is a cell cycle regulator inactivated by CDK4/6-CycD; both can be regulated downstream of Hh in cancer contexts but neither is the canonical transcription factor activated by Hh/GLI signaling in the primary cilia pathway; the canonical Hh TFs are GLI1/2/3)
explanation: Hh pathway in development and cancer: Sonic Hedgehog (SHH): produced by notochord + floor plate → dorsal-ventral patterning of spinal cord; limb bud zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) → SHH gradient → digit identity (5 → 1 finger): Hh signaling errors → polydactyly (GLI3 haploinsufficiency → extra digits) or limb loss; SHH/IHH in growth plate (chondrocyte differentiation + PTHRP signaling); IHH → PTHrP signaling → cartilage-bone transition; Desert Hh (DHH): Sertoli cells → Leydig cell specification; peripheral nerve myelination (Schwann cells). SMO inhibitor mechanism: SMO protein: GPCR-like (7-TM) but signals without G-protein (couples to GLI via intracellular cilia-based scaffold); drug binding: SMO has extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) for oxysterol binding + transmembrane 7-TM groove for vismodegib/sonidegib binding; SMO activation: oxysterols (20S-hydroxycholesterol) → activate; cyclopamine (alkaloid from Veratrum californicum → natural teratogen → SMO inhibitor → holoprosencephaly in cattle [cyclopic calves] → led to discovery of Hh pathway); SUFU (suppressor of fused) role: SUFU binds GLI proteins via 5-residue YGHF/Y motif → keeps GLI in cytoplasm or targets for partial cleavage; SUFU mutations → medulloblastoma (desmoplastic variant) + basal cell carcinoma (SUFU tumor suppressor function); Primary cilia: non-motile single cilia on almost all mammalian cell types (9+0 doublet microtubule axoneme); Hh signaling is cilia-dependent in vertebrates: SMO, PTCH1, SUFU, GLI → all traffic to/from cilia; IFT (intraflagellar transport): IFT-B (anterograde, kinesin-2/KIF3A-KIF3B) + IFT-A (retrograde, cytoplasmic dynein 2); ciliopathies: primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD): DNAI1/DNAI2/DNAH5/DNAH11 → no ciliary motility → bronchiectasis + situs inversus + infertility (Kartagener syndrome if situs inversus present); Joubert syndrome: AHI1/NPHP1/CEP290 → cerebellar vermis aplasia + 'molar tooth' sign + breathing irregularity + retinal dystrophy + kidney; Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS): BBS genes (BBS1-21) → BBSome complex → cilia → obesity + rod-cone dystrophy + polydactyly + renal + cognitive impairment.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the urea cycle, which enzyme catalyzes the condensation of citrulline and aspartate to form argininosuccinate?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I): CPS I (mitochondrial, uses glutamine as N-donor? No: CPS I uses NH4+ as N-donor [unlike CPS II, which uses glutamine]): NH4+ + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate + 2 ADP + Pi; first step of urea cycle; NOT the condensation of citrulline + aspartate

Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC): OTC: citrulline [NOT aspartate] + ornithine? No: OTC: carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline + Pi; the second step of urea cycle; NOT the reaction with aspartate; OTC deficiency = most common urea cycle disorder; X-linked (OTCX chromosome)

Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS, ASS1): ASS1 (argininosuccinate synthetase 1): citrulline + aspartate + ATP → argininosuccinate + AMP + PPi; the THIRD step of the urea cycle; reaction: forms an amide bond between α-amino group of aspartate and ureido group of citrulline → argininosuccinate; this adds the SECOND nitrogen of urea (first N comes from NH4+ via CPS I; second N comes from aspartate → provided by the liver transamination network); ASS1 deficiency → Citrullinemia type I (CTLN1): ↑citrulline in blood + urine (citrulline is the substrate that cannot be processed forward → backs up) + hyperammonemia; AR; neonatal hyperammonemic crisis; treatment: protein restriction + arginine (to complete the cycle past the block) + Na-benzoate/phenylacetate (alternate N excretion: benzoate → hippurate [using Gly] + phenylacetate → phenylacetylglutamine [using Gln → removes 2 N per molecule]) + liver transplant; citrullinemia type II (CTLN2, adult onset): SLC25A13 (citrin/aspartate-glutamate carrier 2, mitochondrial inner membrane) deficiency → ↓aspartate export from mitochondria → ↓cytoplasmic aspartate → ↓ASS1 substrate → ↑citrulline; peculiar: adults with nocturnal hyperammonemia + liver dysfunction + preference for high-protein diet + aversion to carbohydrate (carbohydrate → ↑glycolysis → ↑NADH in cytoplasm → competes with aspartate-malate shuttle → ↑citrulline/ammonia worsening); treatment: MCT + protein diet; liver transplant; CTLN2 common in East Asia

Argininosuccinate lyase (ASL): ASL: argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate (the FOURTH step of urea cycle; NOT the step that condenses citrulline + aspartate; ASL lyase cleaves, ASS synthetase condenses); ASL deficiency → argininosuccinic aciduria (ASA): ↑argininosuccinate in blood/urine/CSF + hyperammonemia + liver disease + neurocognitive impairment; HAIR ABNORMALITY: TRICHORRHEXIS NODOSA (brittle hair with segmental structural defects, 'bamboo hair' on exam under microscopy, due to argininosuccinate as ammonia detoxification in hair follicle? Actually: ASL in hair follicles → arginine supply for NO synthesis → ↑eNOS → hair follicle vascularization?; ASL enzyme present in extrahepatic tissues and hair follicle; deficiency → secondary arginine deficiency + ↓NO → hair fragility)
explanation: Urea cycle — complete 5 enzymes + transporters: Location: mitochondria + cytoplasm: steps 1-2 in MITOCHONDRIA; steps 3-5 in CYTOPLASM: Step 1 (mitochondria): CPS I: NH4+ + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl-P + 2 ADP + Pi; cofactor: biotin (no), PLP (no); allosteric activation: N-ACETYLGLUTAMATE (NAG, synthesized by NAGS from glutamate + acetyl-CoA, activated by arginine → arginine stimulates NAGS → ↑NAG → ↑CPS I → ↑urea cycle; NAGS deficiency → ↓NAG → ↓CPS I → hyperammonemia; treatment: N-carbamylglutamate [Carbaglu] — synthetic NAG analog that allosterically activates CPS I → treats NAGS deficiency + propionic/methylmalonic acidemia-associated hyperammonemia); Step 2 (mitochondria): OTC: carbamoyl-P + ornithine → citrulline + Pi; X-linked; most common urea cycle disorder; carrier females: 50% enzyme → variable (lyonization; some may have neonatal-like crisis with protein load); neonates: lethargy + vomiting + encephalopathy + hyperammonemia + ↑orotic acid (orotic acid [diagnostic!]: carbamoyl-P backs up → cytoplasm → CPS II pathway → carbamoyl-P + aspartate → → orotate → ↑urinary orotic acid distinguishes OTC/ASS1/ASL from CPS I/NAGS/arginase [no ↑orotic acid in upstream defects or arginase]); Step 3 (cytoplasm): ASS1: citrulline + aspartate → argininosuccinate + AMP + PPi (see above); Step 4 (cytoplasm): ASL: argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate; Step 5 (cytoplasm): Arginase I (ARG1): arginine + H2O → ornithine + urea; ornithine → OTC1 (ORNT1/SLC25A15, ornithine:citrulline antiporter) → returns to mitochondria for next cycle; arginase I deficiency: hyperargininemia → progressive spastic diplegia/tetraplegia + intellectual disability + growth failure; ↑arginine in blood; milder course than other UCDs; treatment: low-protein + arginine-free amino acid supplementation + Na-benzoate/phenylacetate + liver transplant. Transport: citrulline exits mitochondria via SLC25A2/SLC25A15 (citrulline-ornithine antiporter); aspartate-malate shuttle (SLC25A11 [OGC] + SLC25A12/13 [AGC1/2/citrin]): aspartate → cytoplasm for ASS1 substrate; malate → mitochondria; EMERGENCY TREATMENT of hyperammonemia: IV Na-benzoate (10% solution) + Na-phenylacetate (Ammonul in USA) + L-arginine HCl (to restart blocked cycle, except arginase def) + dialysis (hemodialysis > peritoneal in neonates for rapid clearance).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: NAD+ metabolism is critical for many enzymatic reactions. In the kynurenine pathway for tryptophan catabolism, the committed step enzyme requires which cofactor?
options: Tetrahydrofolate (THF): THF is required for one-carbon transfer reactions (SHMT: Ser → Gly + CH2-THF; MTHFR: CH2-THF → CH3-THF; MTHFS: formyl-THF; TS: dTMP synthesis; GART: de novo purine synthesis); THF is NOT a cofactor for TDO or IDO in the kynurenine pathway

Pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6): PLP is involved LATER in the kynurenine pathway [kynurenine aminotransferases (KATs) → kynurenine → kynurenic acid (via KAT1/2/3/4, PLP-dependent aminotransferases) and kynureninase (→ anthranilic acid or 3-hydroxykynurenine → 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, PLP-dependent)]; but the COMMITTED STEP enzyme (IDO or TDO) does NOT use PLP as its cofactor; IDO and TDO use iron-containing heme

Heme (iron-protoporphyrin IX): Tryptophan catabolism via kynurenine pathway: COMMITTED STEP: IDO (indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, IDO1/IDO2 [extra-hepatic, immune cells] or TDO [tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase, TDOX/TDO2, liver]): reaction: Trp + O2 → N-formylkynurenine (ring-opening dioxygenation, inserts both atoms of O2 into the indole ring → N-formylkynurenine); COFACTOR: HEME (iron-protoporphyrin IX): both IDO and TDO are HEME-CONTAINING DIOXYGENASES (Fe2+ in heme needed for O2 binding + insertion); TDO: liver-specific; constitutive + induced by cortisol + tryptophan itself; IDO1: widespread (especially dendritic cells, macrophages, intestinal epithelium); induced by IFN-γ; IDO2: some expression in liver/placenta; immune regulation: IDO1 activation → ↓Trp in local environment → ↓T-cell proliferation (T cells highly sensitive to Trp depletion → ↓mTOR + GCN2 kinase activation → ↓T-cell cycle arrest → ↑T-reg differentiation) → peripheral immune tolerance; IDO1 in tumors → tumor immune escape; IDO1 inhibitors in cancer immunotherapy: epacadostat (IDO1 inhibitor) + PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors → clinical trials (ECHO-301/KEYNOTE-252: epacadostat + pembrolizumab in melanoma did NOT improve outcomes vs pembrolizumab alone — negative trial 2018); linrodostat, navoximod, BMS-986205: other IDO1/TDO inhibitors; KYNURENINE PATHWAY PRODUCTS: N-formylkynurenine → [AFMID, arylformamidase] → kynurenine → BRANCHES: (1) [KYNU, kynureninase, PLP] → anthranilic acid (→ minor); (2) [KAT1-4, kynurenine aminotransferase, PLP] → kynurenic acid (neuroprotective NMDA antagonist + AhR ligand); (3) [KMO, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, FAD] → 3-hydroxykynurenine → [KYNU, PLP] → 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid → [HAAO, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid oxygenase, Fe3+-nonheme] → 2-amino-3-carboxymuconic semialdehyde → [spontaneous/ACMSD] → picolinic acid (neuroprotective → AhR ligand + zinc chelation) or [ACMSD+picolinate carboxylase bypass] → quinolinic acid (QUIN, neuroTOXIC NMDA agonist → excitotoxicity; ↑QUIN in neuroinflammation) → [QPRT, quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase] → NMN → [NMNAT] → NAD+; thus: de novo NAD+ synthesis requires heme-containing enzyme (IDO or TDO) at the committed step
Biotin: biotin is for carboxylases (PC, ACC, PCC, MCC); NOT for TDO or IDO; biotin has no role in the kynurenine pathway
explanation: Tryptophan metabolism — complete: Daily Trp utilization: ~5% → serotonin/melatonin; ~95% → kynurenine pathway → NAD+ (and other end products); vitamin B3 (niacin) equivalence: 60 mg Trp → 1 mg niacin equivalent; in pellagra (niacin deficiency): ↓Trp → ↓NAD+ and ↑requirement for dietary niacin (or Trp-adequate diet) → symptoms: Dermatitis + Diarrhea + Dementia (3Ds) + Death (4th D); also: carcinoid tumor: ↑Trp → serotonin pathway → ↓Trp for kynurenine/NAD+ → can cause pellagra-like symptoms; HARTNUP disorder (SLC6A19, neutral amino acid transporter, intestine + kidney): ↓Trp (and other neutral AAs) absorption → ↓systemic Trp → ↓NAD+ → pellagra-like rash + cerebellar ataxia (variable) → treat with niacin + high-protein diet; Serotonin synthesis: Trp → [TPH1 (gut, enterochromaffin cells, BH4) or TPH2 (brain + enteric nervous system, BH4)] → 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) → [AADC, PLP] → serotonin (5-HT) → [MAO-A → 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, urinary carcinoid marker); or → N-acetylserotonin → [AANAT, arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase; SAM] → N-acetylserotonin → [HIOMT/ASMT] → MELATONIN (N-acetyl-5-methoxyserotonin); melatonin synthesis regulated by: suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) → NE (from superior cervical ganglion) → β1-AR on pineal gland → cAMP → ↑AANAT transcription → ↑melatonin at night; light → ↓melatonin (via retinohypothalamic tract → SCN); pharmacology: ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) + melatonin → sleep onset disorders (circadian rhythm shift). Kynurenic acid (KYNA): KAT enzymes (PLP) → KYNA: endogenous broad-spectrum antagonist at NMDA receptor (glycine site: Kd ~7 μM for NR1/NR2A), AMPA, and nicotinic α7 receptors; ↑KYNA in schizophrenia? (excess glutamate hypofunction model → symptoms similar to NMDA antagonism [ketamine, PCP] → ↑KYNA may worsen schizophrenia; vs ↑QUIN [neuroTOXIC excitotoxic] in HIV-associated dementia, ALS, Huntington's); IDO inhibition → ↓Kyn → ↓KYNA + ↓QUIN but immune effects dominate in cancer therapy rationale.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is the most common cause of autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Which toxic metabolite accumulates and is responsible for lymphocyte death?
options: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP) in all cell types equally

Deoxyadenosine triphosphate (dATP) preferentially in lymphocytes: ADA (adenosine deaminase): adenosine → inosine AND deoxyadenosine → deoxyinosine (deamination); ADA deficiency → ↑deoxyadenosine → phosphorylated by deoxycytidine kinase (dCK, highly active in lymphocytes) → ↑dATP accumulation PREFERENTIALLY in T and B lymphocytes (lymphocytes have high dCK activity + low 5'-nucleotidase activity → trap dATP); dATP toxicity: (1) dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) at the activity site (dATP competes with ATP at the activity site → ↓all dNTP synthesis → ↓DNA replication → ↓lymphocyte proliferation); (2) dATP → ↑SAH hydrolase inhibition (deoxyadenosine inhibits SAH hydrolase → ↑SAH → ↓methylation reactions → cytotoxic); (3) dATP activates apoptosome (Apaf-1 + cytochrome c + dATP → caspase-9 → apoptosis); CLINICAL: ADA-SCID: absent T + B + NK cells (T-B-NK- SCID); onset: infancy; opportunistic infections; failure to thrive; absent thymic shadow; TREATMENT: PEG-ADA (pegademase bovine → enzyme replacement → ↓dATP; first ERT for any genetic disease); HSCT (curative); GENE THERAPY: Strimvelis (first approved gene therapy, 2016 EU, γ-retroviral vector + autologous CD34+ cells → ADA gene insertion; also: lentiviral ADA gene therapy [OTL-101] clinical trials)
Uric acid crystals in renal tubules
explanation: Purine salvage and immunodeficiency: ADA pathway: adenosine → [ADA] → inosine → [PNP] → hypoxanthine → [HGPRT] → IMP (salvage) or → [XO] → xanthine → uric acid (degradation). PNP (purine nucleoside phosphorylase) deficiency: dGTP accumulation (same mechanism: deoxyguanosine → dGTP in lymphocytes via dCK → inhibits RNR → ↓DNA synthesis); PNP-SCID: T-cell deficiency predominantly (T-B+NK- pattern; dGTP more toxic to T cells; B cells relatively spared initially); ↑uric acid is LOW in PNP deficiency (PNP converts inosine/guanosine → hypoxanthine/guanine → xanthine → uric acid; ↓PNP → ↓uric acid, ↓hypoxanthine → HYPOURICEMIA is a diagnostic clue). HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) deficiency: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (X-linked): ↓purine salvage → ↑de novo purine synthesis (↑PRPP available → ↑PPAT → ↑IMP → ↑degradation → ↑uric acid → HYPERURICEMIA + gout + uric acid nephropathy); NEUROLOGICAL: self-injurious behavior (lip/finger biting, pathognomonic), choreoathetosis, spasticity, intellectual disability; mechanism of neuro symptoms: ↓HGPRT in basal ganglia → ↓dopamine (dopaminergic neurons in striatum particularly dependent on purine salvage for nucleotide supply → ↓function → movement disorders). Orotic aciduria (type I): UMP synthase deficiency (bifunctional: OPRT [orotate phosphoribosyltransferase] + OMP decarboxylase [orotidine-5'-monophosphate decarboxylase]): ↓UMP → ↓pyrimidine → ↑orotic acid (the substrate before UMP synthase → backs up → crystalluria); megaloblastic anemia (↓dTTP → ↓DNA synthesis → megaloblastic; does NOT respond to B12 or folate); treatment: uridine (bypasses block → UMP → feedback inhibits CPS II → ↓orotic acid production); DISTINGUISH from OTC deficiency orotic aciduria: OTC def → ↑carbamoyl-P → exits mito → enters pyrimidine pathway → ↑orotic acid + ↑hyperammonemia; orotic aciduria type I → ↑orotic acid but NO hyperammonemia (urea cycle intact).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Homocystinuria can result from deficiency of several different enzymes. Classical homocystinuria is caused by deficiency of:
options: Methionine synthase (MS, MTR): MS (5-methyltetrahydrofolate-homocysteine methyltransferase): homocysteine + N5-methyl-THF → methionine + THF; cofactor: methylcobalamin (MeCbl); MS deficiency (or MeCbl deficiency [cblE/cblG]) → homocystinuria + megaloblastic anemia (↓THF recycling → functional folate deficiency → ↓dTMP synthesis → megaloblastic); but this is NOT classical homocystinuria; MS deficiency is a RARE cause

Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS): CBS (cystathionine beta-synthase, CBS gene, chromosome 21q22.3): homocysteine + serine → cystathionine + H2O; cofactor: PLP (pyridoxal-5'-phosphate, vitamin B6); CBS is the FIRST enzyme of the transsulfuration pathway (Hcy → cystathionine → [cystathionase, also PLP] → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate + NH4+); CBS deficiency → CLASSICAL HOMOCYSTINURIA (most common cause): ↑↑homocysteine in blood + urine + ↑methionine (because Hcy cannot be converted to cystathionine → remethylation of Hcy → Met by MS → ↑Met); CLINICAL (Marfanoid habitus but DIFFERENT from Marfan): (1) LENS: ectopia lentis (lens subluxation) → downward and nasal (vs Marfan: upward and temporal); (2) SKELETAL: tall + thin + long limbs (Marfanoid) + osteoporosis (Hcy interferes with collagen cross-linking via LOX) + arachnodactyly + pectus; (3) VASCULAR: thromboembolism (arterial + venous; Hcy is prothrombotic: endothelial damage + ↑TF + ↓thrombomodulin + ↓protein C activation + ↑platelet aggregation + ↓fibrinolysis); DVT/PE/stroke/MI in young patients; (4) NEUROLOGICAL: intellectual disability (variable, can be mild if treated early) + seizures; (5) FAIR COMPLEXION (↓melanin: ↓Cys → ↓pheomelanin? + ↓tyrosinase inhibition by Hcy?); TREATMENT: pyridoxine (B6) supplementation (50% of CBS-deficient patients are B6-RESPONSIVE: residual CBS activity enhanced by ↑PLP; I278T mutation is commonly B6-responsive); B6-non-responsive: methionine-restricted diet + betaine (trimethylglycine: alternative Hcy remethylation via BHMT [betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase] → Hcy + betaine → Met + dimethylglycine; BHMT is liver/kidney only) + folate + B12 supplementation

MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase): MTHFR: N5,N10-methylene-THF → N5-methyl-THF (irreversible in vivo); MTHFR deficiency (severe, rare) → ↓N5-methyl-THF → ↓MS substrate → ↑Hcy (homocystinuria) + ↓Met (unlike CBS where Met is HIGH, MTHFR deficiency has LOW methionine); also: megaloblastic anemia is NOT a feature (folate is not trapped as N5-methyl-THF in MTHFR deficiency → THF available for dTMP synthesis); MTHFR C677T polymorphism (common, 10-15% homozygous in some populations): thermolabile variant → mild ↑Hcy → mild CV risk; treatment with folate; MTHFR deficiency is NOT classical homocystinuria

Cystathionase (cystathionine γ-lyase, CTH): CTH: cystathionine → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate + NH4+; PLP-dependent; CTH deficiency → cystathioninuria (↑cystathionine in urine); BENIGN condition (no clinical consequences in most patients); NOT associated with homocystinuria or thrombosis; NOT classical homocystinuria
explanation: Methionine-homocysteine metabolism: Methionine cycle: Met → [MAT, methionine adenosyltransferase] → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine, universal methyl donor: >200 methyltransferases use SAM; DNA methyltransferases [DNMT1/3A/3B → CpG methylation]; histone methyltransferases [EZH2 → H3K27me3; SET7/9]; COMT [catechol-O-methyltransferase → dopamine/NE metabolism]; PEMT [phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase → PE → PC]; GNMT [glycine N-methyltransferase → sarcosine; buffer enzyme for SAM levels]); SAM → [methyltransferase] → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine); SAH → [SAHH, S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase] → homocysteine + adenosine; Hcy fates: (1) REMETHYLATION → Met: (a) MS (MTR, MeCbl): Hcy + N5-CH3-THF → Met + THF; (b) BHMT (liver/kidney only): Hcy + betaine → Met + DMG; (2) TRANSSULFURATION → Cys: CBS (PLP): Hcy + Ser → cystathionine → CTH (PLP) → Cys + α-KB + NH4+; Cys → glutathione (GSH: Cys + Glu + Gly → γ-GluCys → GSH) or → taurine or → SO4²⁻ (sulfate); HOMOCYSTEINE MEASUREMENT: total plasma Hcy (tHcy): normal <15 µmol/L; mild ↑15-30; moderate 30-100; severe >100 (in CBS deficiency). Folate trap (methylfolate trap) hypothesis: in B12 deficiency: ↓MeCbl → ↓MS → ↓THF regeneration from N5-CH3-THF → N5-CH3-THF ACCUMULATES (trapped as methyl-THF) → ↓THF + ↓CH2-THF + ↓CHO-THF → ↓dTMP synthesis (thymidylate synthase needs CH2-THF) → megaloblastic anemia; ALSO: ↓MS → ↑Hcy → hyperhomocysteinemia; giving FOLATE to B12-deficient patient → temporarily ↑THF → corrects anemia BUT does NOT correct neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord; B12 deficiency → ↓MeCbl + ↓AdoCbl → ↓MS [Hcy→Met] + ↓MCM [methylmalonyl-CoA→succinyl-CoA] → ↑odd-chain FA incorporation into myelin → demyelination of posterior columns + lateral corticospinal tracts); ALWAYS check B12 before treating with folate alone.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease) is caused by deficiency of:
options: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase (PYGM, myophosphorylase): PYGM deficiency → GSD V (McArdle disease): exercise intolerance + muscle cramps + myoglobinuria + second wind phenomenon; MUSCLE only; NOT liver phosphorylase

Liver glycogen phosphorylase (PYGL): GSD VI (Hers disease): PYGL gene mutations (AR): LIVER glycogen phosphorylase deficiency → ↓glycogenolysis in liver → hepatomegaly + mild fasting hypoglycemia + ketosis + growth retardation; relatively MILD compared to GSD I; often improves with age; TREATMENT: frequent meals + raw cornstarch; GSD VI is sometimes called 'benign hepatic glycogenosis' because of its mild course compared to GSD I/III; PYGL is the liver-specific isoform of glycogen phosphorylase (3 isoforms: PYGM [muscle], PYGL [liver], PYGB [brain]); glycogen phosphorylase: cleaves α-1,4 glycosidic bonds from non-reducing ends → releases glucose-1-phosphate (G1P); REGULATION: phosphorylase exists as: phosphorylase b (less active, T state) → phosphorylase kinase (PhK) → phospho-Ser14 → phosphorylase a (more active, R state); ALLOSTERIC: phosphorylase b activated by AMP (muscle, energy-sensing) and inhibited by ATP + G6P; phosphorylase a: inhibited by glucose (liver: glucose binds phosphorylase a → R→T transition → susceptible to PP1 dephosphorylation → ↓glycogenolysis when blood glucose is adequate); PYRIDOXAL-5'-PHOSPHATE (PLP): PLP is a STRUCTURAL cofactor of glycogen phosphorylase (present at the active site; the 5'-phosphate of PLP participates in acid-base catalysis of the phosphorolysis reaction; PLP donates a proton to the leaving group during glycosidic bond cleavage → G1P release); this is one of the very few examples where PLP acts as a structural cofactor rather than a catalytic cofactor for amino acid metabolism
Glucose-6-phosphatase (G6Pase): G6Pase deficiency → GSD Ia (von Gierke): severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricemia + hyperlipidemia + hepatomegaly; NOT GSD VI
Acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA): GAA deficiency → GSD II (Pompe disease): lysosomal glycogen storage → cardiomyopathy (infantile) or myopathy (adult); NOT GSD VI
explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase cascade — complete hormonal regulation: GLUCAGON (liver) / EPINEPHRINE (liver + muscle): glucagon → Gαs → AC → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase (PhK) phosphorylation (at α-subunit Ser → ↑PhK activity) → PhK phosphorylates phosphorylase b → phosphorylase a → ↑glycogenolysis; SIMULTANEOUSLY: PKA phosphorylates glycogen synthase (GS) → ↓GS activity → ↓glycogen synthesis; NET: ↑glycogenolysis + ↓glycogenesis in fasting/stress; EPINEPHRINE IN MUSCLE: β2-AR → Gαs → cAMP → PKA pathway (same as glucagon in liver); ALSO: α1-AR → Gαq → PLC → IP3 → Ca²⁺ → CaM → CaM activates PhK directly (PhK δ-subunit = calmodulin; Ca²⁺ → CaM binds PhK δ → activates PhK even WITHOUT PKA phosphorylation → this is the Ca²⁺-activated glycogenolysis during muscle contraction); PhK structure: α4β4γ4δ4 hexadecamer; α + β: regulatory (phosphorylated by PKA → activation); γ: catalytic (kinase domain); δ: calmodulin (Ca²⁺ sensor); GSD IX: PhK deficiency (PHKA2 [X-linked, liver, most common GSD IX], PHKB [AR, liver+muscle], PHKG2 [AR, liver], PHKA1 [AR, muscle]); mild hepatomegaly + fasting ketotic hypoglycemia; often mild course; INSULIN: insulin → PI3K → Akt → PP1 activation (via PP1 regulatory subunits: GM in muscle [PPP1R3A], GL in liver [PPP1R3B]) → PP1 dephosphorylates: phosphorylase a → b (↓glycogenolysis) + GS phosphorylated → GS dephosphorylated (↑glycogenesis); NET: ↓glycogenolysis + ↑glycogenesis (fed state).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acid disorders is characterized by accumulation of succinylacetone, a pathognomonic metabolite detected on newborn screening?
options: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD): MSUD (BCKDH deficiency): ↑branched-chain amino acids (Leu/Ile/Val) + ↑BCKAs (α-ketoisocaproate, α-keto-β-methylvalerate, α-ketoisovalerate); urine smells of maple syrup (or burnt sugar); no succinylacetone involvement
Phenylketonuria (PKU): PKU (PAH deficiency): ↑phenylalanine (Phe) → ↑phenylpyruvate + phenylacetate + phenyllactate (Phe metabolites via transamination); musty/mousy odor; no succinylacetone

Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 (HT1, hepatorenal tyrosinemia): HT1: FAH (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, FAH gene) deficiency → ↑fumarylacetoacetate (FAA) + ↑maleylacetoacetate (MAA) → these compounds are REDUCED to SUCCINYLACETOACETATE → SUCCINYLACETONE (4,6-dioxoheptanoic acid); SUCCINYLACETONE is PATHOGNOMONIC for HT1 (no other condition produces it in detectable amounts); succinylacetone toxicity: (1) INHIBITS δ-ALA dehydratase (ALAD, porphobilinogen synthase, the second enzyme of heme synthesis) → ↑ALA in urine (like lead poisoning, where Pb also inhibits ALAD) → porphyria-like symptoms; (2) FAA + MAA are directly mutagenic (alkylating agents) → ↑hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk in untreated HT1 (highest cancer risk of any metabolic disorder in childhood); CLINICAL: LIVER: acute liver failure in infancy (HT1 is a cause of neonatal liver failure) → cirrhosis → HCC (untreated: >35% develop HCC by age 5); KIDNEY: renal Fanconi syndrome (proximal tubular dysfunction → ↑amino acids, glucose, phosphate in urine) + nephrocalcinosis; NEUROLOGICAL: acute porphyria-like crises (↑ALA → peripheral neuropathy + abdominal pain); DIAGNOSIS: ↑succinylacetone on newborn screening (tandem MS/MS) + ↑tyrosine + ↑methionine (liver dysfunction); confirmatory: FAH enzyme assay in fibroblasts or FAH gene sequencing; TREATMENT: NITISINONE (NTBC, 2-(2-nitro-4-trifluoromethylbenzoyl)-1,3-cyclohexanedione): inhibits 4-HPPD (4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase), the SECOND enzyme of tyrosine catabolism → blocks formation of homogentisic acid → ↓MAA/FAA/succinylacetone formation; nitisinone converts HT1 biochemistry into alkaptonuria phenotype (↑4-HPPD substrate → but no ochronosis clinically because 4-HPP is non-toxic); nitisinone + low-Tyr/Phe diet = standard of care → dramatically improved survival + ↓HCC risk; liver transplant: reserved for nitisinone non-responders or existing HCC

Alkaptonuria (AKU): AKU (HGD, homogentisic acid oxidase/homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency): ↑homogentisic acid (HGA) → darkens urine on standing (HGA oxidizes → benzoquinone acetic acid → polymer → dark pigment); ochronosis (blue-black pigment in cartilage + connective tissue); arthropathy; no succinylacetone; nitisinone also being trialed for AKU (↓HGA production by blocking 4-HPPD upstream)
explanation: Tyrosine catabolism — complete pathway: Tyr → [TAT, tyrosine aminotransferase, PLP, cytoplasmic] → 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate (4-HPP) → [4-HPPD, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, Fe²⁺ + ascorbate] → homogentisic acid (HGA, 2,5-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid) → [HGD, homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase, Fe²⁺] → maleylacetoacetate (MAA) → [GSTZ1, maleylacetoacetate isomerase, uses GSH] → fumarylacetoacetate (FAA) → [FAH, fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase] → fumarate + acetoacetate; tyrosine is both GLUCOGENIC (fumarate → TCA → OAA → GNG) and KETOGENIC (acetoacetate → ketone body or → acetyl-CoA); DISORDERS at each step: TAT deficiency → Tyrosinemia type II (Richner-Hanhart syndrome): ↑Tyr → corneal crystals (dendritic keratitis) + palmoplantar keratosis (painful hyperkeratotic skin lesions on palms/soles) + intellectual disability (if untreated); treatment: low-Tyr/Phe diet. 4-HPPD deficiency → Tyrosinemia type III (extremely rare): ↑Tyr + ↑4-HPP; mild neurological symptoms; low-Tyr diet. HGD deficiency → Alkaptonuria (AKU): see above. GSTZ1 deficiency → Maleylacetoacetate isomerase deficiency: extremely rare; ↑MAA + succinylacetone (MAA can be reduced to SA); similar to mild HT1. FAH deficiency → HT1 (see above). Newborn screening: Tyr is elevated in BOTH HT1 and transient tyrosinemia of the newborn (common, benign, due to immature 4-HPPD; resolves spontaneously); SUCCINYLACETONE is specific for HT1 (added to NBS panels to distinguish HT1 from benign transient tyrosinemia → ↓false positives); some NBS programs measure SA directly; others reflex to SA if Tyr is elevated.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is activated when misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum. Which of the following is one of the three canonical UPR sensor proteins?
options: AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase): AMPK is an energy sensor (↑AMP/ATP ratio → AMPK activation → ↑catabolic pathways + ↓anabolic pathways); AMPK is NOT a UPR sensor; AMPK is in the cytoplasm and responds to energy stress, not ER protein folding stress

mTORC1 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1): mTORC1 senses nutrients (amino acids via Ragulator/Rag GTPases on lysosome; growth factors via PI3K/Akt/TSC1-TSC2/Rheb); mTORC1 is NOT a UPR sensor; mTORC1 is inhibited during ER stress (via AMPK cross-talk) but is not one of the three canonical UPR sensors

IRE1α (inositol-requiring enzyme 1 alpha, ERN1): IRE1α is one of the THREE canonical UPR sensors: (1) IRE1α (ERN1, inositol-requiring enzyme 1α): ER transmembrane kinase/endoribonuclease; luminal domain senses unfolded proteins (BiP/GRP78 dissociation model: BiP normally binds IRE1α luminal domain → keeps IRE1α INACTIVE; unfolded proteins → sequester BiP away from IRE1α → IRE1α oligomerizes → autophosphorylation of kinase domain → activates RNase domain); IRE1α RNase: unconventional splicing of XBP1 mRNA (removes 26-nt intron → XBP1s [spliced form] → encodes active transcription factor XBP1s → ↑ER chaperones [BiP/GRP78, GRP94, calnexin, calreticulin] + ↑ERAD genes [HRD1, SEL1L, EDEM1] + ↑lipid synthesis [↑ER membrane expansion]); also: RIDD (regulated IRE1-dependent decay): IRE1α RNase degrades ER-localized mRNAs → ↓ER protein load (reduces incoming protein burden); (2) PERK (EIF2AK3, PKR-like ER kinase): ER transmembrane kinase; same BiP-release activation; PERK → phospho-eIF2α (Ser51) → GLOBAL translation attenuation (↓cap-dependent translation → ↓ER protein load) BUT selectively ↑translation of ATF4 (activating transcription factor 4; uORF-mediated translational upregulation: ATF4 mRNA has upstream ORFs that are bypassed when eIF2α is phosphorylated → ribosomes scan to main ORF → ↑ATF4 protein); ATF4 → ↑CHOP/DDIT3 (pro-apoptotic TF) + ↑GADD34 (PP1 regulatory subunit → dephosphorylates eIF2α → negative feedback → restores translation) + amino acid transporters + antioxidant genes; (3) ATF6 (activating transcription factor 6α): ER transmembrane TF; BiP dissociation → ATF6 → transported to Golgi → S1P + S2P (SAME proteases as SREBP processing!) cleave ATF6 → releases N-terminal bHLH-Zip domain → nucleus → ↑ER chaperone genes (BiP, GRP94, XBP1 [unspliced mRNA → provides substrate for IRE1α splicing]); UPR outcome: ADAPTIVE (if stress resolved): ↑chaperones + ↓protein load → proteostasis restored; APOPTOTIC (if stress unresolved): CHOP → ↑BIM + ↑DR5 + ↓Bcl-2 → mitochondrial apoptosis; IRE1α → TRAF2 → ASK1 → JNK → apoptosis

p53 (TP53): p53 is activated by DNA damage (ATM/ATR → Chk1/Chk2 → p53 stabilization; also Mdm2 inhibition); p53 can be activated DOWNSTREAM of UPR (CHOP can modulate p53; DNA damage from oxidative stress during ER stress) but p53 is NOT one of the three canonical UPR sensor proteins (IRE1α, PERK, ATF6)
explanation: ER stress and disease: Diabetes: ↑insulin demand → ↑proinsulin → ER overload in β-cells → chronic UPR → β-cell apoptosis (CHOP-mediated) → ↓β-cell mass → T2DM progression; Wolfram syndrome (WFS1 mutations): ER protein WFS1 → ↓ER Ca²⁺ homeostasis → chronic UPR → β-cell death + optic atrophy + diabetes insipidus + deafness (DIDMOAD); PERK mutations: Wolcott-Rallison syndrome (AR, EIF2AK3 mutations): neonatal diabetes + skeletal dysplasia + hepatic failure (earliest onset monogenic diabetes); Neurodegenerative: ↑misfolded proteins (Aβ, tau, α-synuclein, polyQ, SOD1, TDP-43) → ER stress → UPR → chronic CHOP → neuronal apoptosis; Alzheimer's: ↑Aβ + ↑phospho-tau → ↑PERK → ↑eIF2α phosphorylation → ↓synaptic protein translation → cognitive decline; cancer: many cancers activate UPR constitutively (hypoxia + nutrient deprivation in tumor microenvironment → ER stress) → IRE1α-XBP1s → ↑cancer survival + ↑angiogenesis; XBP1s → MYC cooperation in multiple myeloma (plasma cells have high secretory burden → dependent on XBP1s for ER expansion → proteasome inhibitors [bortezomib, carfilzomib] → ↑misfolded protein accumulation → overwhelm UPR → apoptosis; this is WHY proteasome inhibitors work in myeloma); ERAD (ER-associated degradation): misfolded ER proteins → retrotranslocated to cytoplasm via Sec61 channel (or Hrd1 retrotranslocation channel) → ubiquitinated by ER-associated E3 ligases (HRD1, gp78, MARCH6, TEB4) → proteasomal degradation; ERAD impairment → ↑ER stress → UPR.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol in the liver. The rate-limiting enzyme of the classic (neutral) bile acid synthesis pathway is:
options: HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR): HMGCR is the rate-limiting enzyme of CHOLESTEROL synthesis (not bile acid synthesis); statins inhibit HMGCR → ↓cholesterol → compensatory ↑LDLR; HMGCR acts far upstream of bile acid synthesis

Sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1): CYP27A1 catalyzes 27-hydroxylation of cholesterol → the ALTERNATIVE (acidic) bile acid pathway (NOT the classic/neutral pathway); CYP27A1 is expressed in many tissues; the alternative pathway produces chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) primarily; CYP27A1 deficiency → cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX): ↑cholestanol (5α-dihydrocholesterol) deposits in tendons + brain → xanthomas + progressive neurodegeneration + cataracts + diarrhea; treatment: CDCA supplementation

Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1): CYP7A1 (cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase, cytochrome P450 7A1): RATE-LIMITING enzyme of the CLASSIC (neutral) bile acid synthesis pathway; reaction: cholesterol + O2 + NADPH → 7α-hydroxycholesterol + NADP+ + H2O; CYP7A1 is the committed step → produces 7α-hydroxycholesterol → subsequent steps → 2 PRIMARY bile acids: cholic acid (CA, trihydroxy: 3α, 7α, 12α-OH) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA, dihydroxy: 3α, 7α-OH); CYP7A1 REGULATION: (1) FXR (farnesoid X receptor, bile acid nuclear receptor): bile acids (especially CDCA) → activate FXR in intestine → ↑FGF19 (fibroblast growth factor 19) → portal blood → liver → FGFR4 + β-klotho → ↓CYP7A1 transcription (negative feedback: bile acids → FXR → FGF19 → ↓CYP7A1 → ↓bile acid synthesis); ALSO: FXR in liver → ↑SHP (small heterodimer partner) → SHP inhibits LRH-1 (liver receptor homolog 1) → ↓CYP7A1 transcription; (2) Cholesterol: ↑cholesterol → ↑CYP7A1 (to eliminate excess cholesterol as bile acids → fecal excretion); bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam): bind bile acids in gut → prevent reabsorption → ↓enterohepatic circulation → ↓FXR activation → ↓FGF19 → ↑CYP7A1 → ↑bile acid synthesis from cholesterol → ↓hepatic cholesterol → ↑LDLR → ↓LDL-C; FXR agonists (obeticholic acid [OCA], approved for PBC [primary biliary cholangitis]): activate FXR → ↓bile acid synthesis + ↓inflammation + ↓fibrosis

Oxysterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7B1): CYP7B1 catalyzes 7α-hydroxylation of oxysterols (25-hydroxycholesterol, 27-hydroxycholesterol) → this is part of the ALTERNATIVE (acidic) pathway; CYP7B1 deficiency → neonatal cholestasis + liver failure; CYP7B1 is NOT the rate-limiting enzyme of the classic pathway
explanation: Bile acid metabolism — complete: Classic (neutral) pathway (~75% of BA synthesis): cholesterol → [CYP7A1, rate-limiting] → 7α-OH-cholesterol → [CYP8B1, sterol 12α-hydroxylase] → → → cholic acid (CA, if 12α-hydroxylated) or → → → chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA, if NOT 12α-hydroxylated); Alternative (acidic) pathway (~25%): cholesterol → [CYP27A1] → 27-OH-cholesterol → [CYP7B1] → 7α,27-diOH-cholesterol → → → CDCA primarily. Bile acid conjugation: primary BAs (CA, CDCA) → conjugated with glycine or taurine (via BACS [bile acid-CoA synthetase] → BA-CoA → BAAT [bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase] → glyco-CA/CDCA or tauro-CA/CDCA); conjugation → ↓pKa → ionized at intestinal pH → amphipathic → better detergent for fat emulsification → micelle formation for lipid/fat-soluble vitamin absorption. Enterohepatic circulation: conjugated BAs → bile canaliculus → [BSEP/ABCB11, bile salt export pump] → bile → gallbladder → duodenum → fat emulsification → terminal ileum: ASBT (apical sodium-dependent bile acid transporter, SLC10A2) → enterocyte → IBABP (ileal bile acid binding protein) → basolateral: OSTα/β (organic solute transporter) → portal blood → liver: NTCP (Na+-taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide, SLC10A1) → hepatocyte → recycled; 95% of BAs are recycled (enterohepatic circulation); 5% lost in feces → this is the ONLY significant route of cholesterol elimination from the body. Secondary bile acids: colon bacteria: CA → [7α-dehydroxylation by gut bacteria] → deoxycholic acid (DCA); CDCA → [7α-dehydroxylation] → lithocholic acid (LCA, toxic, hepatotoxic → sulfated in liver for detoxification + fecal excretion); ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, 3α, 7β-OH): naturally present in small amounts; hydrophilic BA → cytoprotective; therapeutic: UDCA for PBC (primary biliary cholangitis), PSC (primary sclerosing cholangitis), gallstone dissolution (cholesterol stones), ICP (intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy); PFIC (progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis): PFIC1 (ATP8B1/FIC1, ↓PS flippase), PFIC2 (ABCB11/BSEP, ↓BA export), PFIC3 (ABCB4/MDR3, ↓PC floppase → ↓biliary phospholipid → ↑BA toxicity to bile duct epithelium).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ether lipids, specifically plasmalogens, are synthesized beginning in peroxisomes. Which clinical condition results from a generalized defect in peroxisome biogenesis, leading to absent plasmalogens?
options: Gaucher disease: Gaucher is a lysosomal storage disease (GBA deficiency → glucosylceramide accumulation); peroxisomes are normal in Gaucher; NOT related to plasmalogen deficiency

Zellweger spectrum disorder (ZSD): ZSD (Zellweger syndrome spectrum, previously: Zellweger syndrome [severe] / neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy [intermediate] / infantile Refsum disease [mild]): caused by mutations in PEX genes (peroxin genes: PEX1 [most common, 65%], PEX6, PEX12, PEX26, PEX5, PEX7, etc.); PEX proteins are required for PEROXISOME BIOGENESIS (assembly of functional peroxisomes: PEX5 [PTS1 receptor: recognizes C-terminal -SKL/-SRL tripeptide peroxisomal targeting signal 1], PEX7 [PTS2 receptor: recognizes N-terminal cleavable nonapeptide (R/K)(L/V/I)X5(H/Q)(L/A)], PEX1/6 [AAA-ATPases for receptor recycling], PEX3/16/19 [peroxisomal membrane protein import]); PEROXISOME FUNCTIONS lost in ZSD: (1) PLASMALOGEN SYNTHESIS: first 2 steps occur in peroxisomes: DHAP-AT (dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase, GNPAT) → 1-acyl-DHAP → AGPS (alkyl-DHAP synthase/alkylglycerone phosphate synthase) → 1-alkyl-DHAP → → → plasmalogen (1-alk-1'-enyl-2-acyl-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine [plasmenylethanlamine] is the most abundant plasmalogen); plasmalogens: 50% of phospholipids in myelin + cardiac tissue; ↓plasmalogens → demyelination + cardiomyopathy; absent plasmalogen = diagnostic marker for ZSD (RBC plasmalogen assay); (2) VERY LONG CHAIN FATTY ACID (VLCFA) β-OXIDATION: C24:0, C26:0 → shortened by peroxisomal β-oxidation (different enzymes from mitochondrial FAO: ACOX1 [first step, generates H2O2 → catalase detoxifies], DBP/HSD17B4 [bifunctional protein], ACAA1 [thiolase]) → ↓VLCFA oxidation → ↑C26:0 in blood (diagnostic); (3) α-OXIDATION: phytanic acid (from phytol in dairy/ruminant fat) → pristanic acid (requires α-oxidation by PHYH [phytanoyl-CoA 2-hydroxylase]); ↓peroxisomes → ↑phytanic acid → Refsum-like symptoms; (4) bile acid synthesis (DHCA/THCA conjugation: peroxisomal β-oxidation of C27-bile acid intermediates → C24-bile acids); (5) glyoxylate detoxification (AGXT: glyoxylate → glycine; not in ZSD context but in primary hyperoxaluria type 1); CLINICAL ZSD: neonatal: severe hypotonia ('floppy baby') + seizures + distinctive facies (high forehead, large fontanelles, hypertelorism) + hepatomegaly + liver dysfunction + renal cysts + stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata) + sensorineural hearing loss + retinopathy; death usually in first year (severe Zellweger); DIAGNOSIS: ↑VLCFA (C26:0/C22:0 ratio), ↓plasmalogens (RBC), ↑phytanic acid, ↑pipecolic acid, ↑bile acid intermediates (DHCA/THCA); PEX gene sequencing

X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD): X-ALD: ABCD1 (peroxisomal VLCFA transporter) mutations → ↓VLCFA import into peroxisomes → ↑VLCFA in blood + tissues → adrenal insufficiency + cerebral demyelination; peroxisomes are PRESENT but cannot import VLCFA; plasmalogens are NORMAL (peroxisome biogenesis is intact; only VLCFA transport is defective); NOT a peroxisome biogenesis disorder
Niemann-Pick type C: NPC is a cholesterol trafficking disorder (NPC1/NPC2 mutations → cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes); peroxisomes and plasmalogens are normal
explanation: Peroxisomal disorders — classification: 1. PEROXISOME BIOGENESIS DISORDERS (PBDs): Zellweger spectrum (PEX gene mutations) → absent/ghost peroxisomes → all peroxisomal functions lost; rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (RCDP) type 1 (PEX7 mutations → PTS2 receptor deficiency → specifically ↓plasmalogen synthesis + ↓phytanic acid oxidation → epiphyseal stippling + proximal limb shortening + cataracts + ichthyosis); 2. SINGLE PEROXISOMAL ENZYME DEFICIENCIES: X-ALD (ABCD1 transporter → ↑VLCFA); Refsum disease (PHYH [phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase] → ↑phytanic acid → retinitis pigmentosa + peripheral neuropathy + cerebellar ataxia + ↑CSF protein; treatment: phytanic acid-restricted diet [avoid dairy fat, ruminant meat]); ACOX1 deficiency (pseudoneonatal ALD); D-bifunctional protein (DBP/HSD17B4) deficiency; RCDP type 2 (GNPAT, DHAP-AT deficiency → ↓plasmalogens); RCDP type 3 (AGPS deficiency → ↓plasmalogens); primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT deficiency in peroxisomes → glyoxylate cannot be converted to glycine → glyoxylate → oxalate → calcium oxalate kidney stones + nephrocalcinosis + renal failure; treatment: lumasiran [siRNA against glycolate oxidase HAO1, ↓glycolate → ↓glyoxylate → ↓oxalate; FDA approved 2020] + liver transplant). Plasmalogen biology: structure: sn-1 position has VINYL ETHER bond (alk-1-enyl, -O-CH=CH-R) instead of ester bond; sn-2: polyunsaturated FA (often AA or DHA); most abundant: plasmenylethanolamine (brain, heart, skeletal muscle myelin); function: (1) antioxidant (vinyl ether scavenges ROS → protects membrane PUFAs from peroxidation; plasmalogens sacrifice themselves to protect other lipids); (2) membrane structure (↑membrane fluidity, ↑fusion competence [important for synaptic vesicle fusion]); (3) signaling (source of AA/DHA for eicosanoid/docosanoid synthesis when PLA2 acts on sn-2 position).

subject: Biochemistry
