explanation: Metabolic cycles — Cori cycle vs glucose-alanine cycle vs Randle cycle: CORI CYCLE: muscle → lactate → liver → glucose → muscle (glucose-lactate shuttle; important during exercise + hypoxia); GLUCOSE-ALANINE CYCLE (Cahill cycle): muscle → alanine → liver → glucose → muscle; mechanism: muscle: pyruvate + [ALT/GPT, Glu → α-KG] → alanine + α-KG; alanine exported → liver: alanine + [ALT] → pyruvate + Glu; pyruvate → GNG → glucose; Glu → [GDH] → α-KG + NH4+ → urea; purpose: (1) transports amino nitrogen from muscle to liver (for urea synthesis) without releasing free NH4+ into blood (NH4+ is toxic; alanine is a safe nitrogen carrier); (2) provides GNG substrate (pyruvate from alanine); important during fasting/starvation when muscle proteolysis provides amino acids for GNG; RANDLE CYCLE (glucose-fatty acid cycle): competition between glucose and FA oxidation; ↑FA oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑citrate → inhibits PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis; ↑acetyl-CoA → ↑PDK → ↓PDC → ↓pyruvate oxidation; ↑NADH from FAO → ↑NADH/NAD+ → ↓isocitrate DH → ↓TCA from glucose-derived acetyl-CoA; NET: ↑FA oxidation SUPPRESSES glucose oxidation (fuel selection); clinical relevance: in diabetes: ↑FFA → Randle cycle → ↓glucose utilization → ↑blood glucose → worsens hyperglycemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). The essential cofactor for PAH that must be regenerated by dihydrobiopterin reductase (DHPR) is:
options: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4): PAH (phenylalanine hydroxylase): Phe + O2 + BH4 → Tyr + H2O + q-BH2 (quinonoid dihydrobiopterin); BH4 is the essential cofactor; BH4 donates electrons to reduce one atom of O2 → inserts into Phe ring → Tyr; BH4 is oxidized to q-BH2; DHPR (dihydropteridine reductase, QDPR gene): q-BH2 + NADH → BH4 + NAD+ (regenerates BH4); BH4 is also required by: TH (tyrosine hydroxylase: Tyr → L-DOPA), TPH1/2 (tryptophan hydroxylase: Trp → 5-HTP), NOS (all 3 isoforms); BH4 synthesis: GTP → [GCH1, GTP cyclohydrolase I] → dihydroneopterin triphosphate → [PTPS, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase] → 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin → [SR, sepiapterin reductase] → BH4; BH4 deficiency (GCH1/PTPS/DHPR mutations): hyperphenylalaninemia + SEVERE neurological disease (↓dopamine [↓TH] + ↓serotonin [↓TPH] → progressive neurodegeneration even with Phe restriction → Phe-restricted diet ALONE is insufficient); treatment: BH4 supplementation (sapropterin [Kuvan], synthetic BH4; also benefits ~30% of classic PKU patients with BH4-responsive PAH mutations [mild mutations where excess BH4 can partially rescue residual PAH activity]) + L-DOPA + 5-HTP (to replace neurotransmitter deficiency); Dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa disease): GCH1 heterozygous mutations (AD) → ↓BH4 → ↓TH → ↓dopamine → dystonia; dramatic response to low-dose L-DOPA; PKU: classic PKU: PAH activity <1% → ↑Phe >20 mg/dL → intellectual disability + seizures + eczema + musty odor + fair hair/skin (↓melanin because Phe competes with Tyr for entry into melanocytes + ↓Tyr → ↓melanin); maternal PKU: uncontrolled maternal Phe → teratogenic to fetus (microcephaly + CHD + IUGR + ID) even if fetus is heterozygous; treatment: lifelong Phe-restricted diet + sapropterin (BH4-responsive); pegvaliase (PEGylated phenylalanine ammonia lyase [PAL], enzyme substitution → Phe → trans-cinnamic acid + NH3; FDA 2018 for adults with uncontrolled PKU)
explanation: Aromatic amino acid hydroxylases — BH4-dependent: PAH (Phe → Tyr), TH (Tyr → L-DOPA), TPH (Trp → 5-HTP): all mixed-function monooxygenases using BH4 + O2; BH4 regeneration: DHPR; Newborn screening: PKU was the first disease screened at birth (Guthrie test: bacterial inhibition assay, 1963 → now tandem mass spectrometry [MS/MS] for Phe levels); NBS panel now includes >30 conditions (MSUD, galactosemia, hypothyroidism, CAH, sickle cell, biotinidase deficiency, CF, etc.).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glycine is conjugated with benzoate to form hippurate for urinary excretion. This reaction is used therapeutically in which clinical context?
options: Urea cycle disorders — sodium benzoate provides an alternate nitrogen excretion pathway: Na-benzoate + glycine → [GLYAT, glycine-N-acyltransferase, mitochondrial, liver/kidney] → hippurate (hippuric acid) + CoA; hippurate is excreted in urine; each mole of hippurate removes 1 mole of nitrogen (from glycine's amino group); glycine is then resynthesized from serine (SHMT: Ser + THF → Gly + CH2-THF) or from other sources → net removal of nitrogen from the body WITHOUT requiring the urea cycle; this is alternate pathway nitrogen excretion therapy for hyperammonemia/urea cycle disorders; Na-phenylacetate/phenylbutyrate removes 2 N per molecule (conjugates glutamine → phenylacetylglutamine [Gln has 2 N: amide + amino]) → even more efficient; USED IN: acute hyperammonemic crisis (IV Ammonul = Na-benzoate + Na-phenylacetate); chronic UCD maintenance (oral Na-phenylbutyrate [Buphenyl] or glycerol phenylbutyrate [Ravicti])

Treatment of isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy (isoniazid-induced neuropathy is treated with pyridoxine [B6] supplementation, not sodium benzoate; INH interferes with B6 metabolism → ↓PLP → peripheral neuropathy)
Management of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA is treated with insulin + IV fluids + electrolytes; sodium benzoate has no role in DKA management)
Treatment of methanol poisoning (methanol poisoning is treated with fomepizole/ethanol + dialysis + folinic acid; sodium benzoate is not used for methanol detoxification)
explanation: Alternate pathway therapy for nitrogen disposal: Principle: bypass the blocked urea cycle by conjugating nitrogen-containing amino acids with pharmacological agents → renally excreted conjugates remove nitrogen; Na-benzoate: benzoate → [acyl-CoA synthetase] → benzoyl-CoA → [GLYAT] → hippurate (removes 1 N as glycine); Na-phenylacetate: phenylacetate → phenylacetyl-CoA → [phenylacetyl-CoA:glutamine N-acyltransferase, kidney/liver] → phenylacetylglutamine (removes 2 N as glutamine); Na-phenylbutyrate (prodrug): phenylbutyrate → [β-oxidation] → phenylacetate → same as above; glycerol phenylbutyrate (Ravicti): prodrug of phenylbutyrate (triglyceride of phenylbutyrate → pancreatic lipase → phenylbutyrate → phenylacetate); advantages of Ravicti: no taste/smell issues, once-daily dosing; N-carbamylglutamate (Carbaglu): NOT alternate pathway; directly activates CPS I (replaces NAG) → treats NAGS deficiency specifically.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acids is both glucogenic AND ketogenic?
options: Leucine: Leu is PURELY KETOGENIC (catabolized entirely to HMG-CoA → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; no carbons enter gluconeogenic pathways); Leu and Lys are the only two purely ketogenic amino acids
Alanine: Ala is PURELY GLUCOGENIC (Ala → [ALT] → pyruvate → GNG → glucose); alanine is the major glucogenic amino acid transported from muscle to liver (glucose-alanine cycle)

Isoleucine: Ile is BOTH glucogenic AND ketogenic: Ile catabolism → propionyl-CoA (→ methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → TCA → GNG = glucogenic portion) + acetyl-CoA (→ TCA for energy or → ketone bodies = ketogenic portion); other amino acids that are both glucogenic AND ketogenic: Phe (→ fumarate [glucogenic] + acetoacetate [ketogenic]); Tyr (→ fumarate + acetoacetate); Trp (→ alanine/pyruvate [glucogenic] + acetoacetyl-CoA [ketogenic]); Thr (→ pyruvate [glucogenic] + acetyl-CoA [ketogenic] via threonine dehydratase pathway); mnemonic: PITTT = Phe, Ile, Trp, Thr, Tyr are both gluco+ketogenic
Valine: Val is PURELY GLUCOGENIC (Val → isobutyryl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA → TCA; all carbons can enter GNG)
explanation: Amino acid classification by metabolic fate: PURELY GLUCOGENIC (all except Leu, Lys, and the 5 'both'): Ala → pyruvate; Gly → pyruvate (via serine or threonine dehydrogenase); Ser → pyruvate; Cys → pyruvate; Asp → OAA; Asn → OAA (via Asp); Glu → α-KG; Gln → α-KG (via Glu); Pro → Glu → α-KG; Arg → Glu → α-KG (also → ornithine → glutamate semialdehyde → Glu); His → Glu → α-KG (via FIGLU [formiminoglutamate → THF] → Glu); Val → succinyl-CoA; Met → succinyl-CoA (via propionyl-CoA). BOTH GLUCOGENIC + KETOGENIC: Ile → succinyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA; Phe → fumarate + acetoacetate; Tyr → fumarate + acetoacetate; Trp → pyruvate (Ala) + acetoacetyl-CoA; Thr → pyruvate + acetyl-CoA (or → Gly via TDG). PURELY KETOGENIC: Leu → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA (via HMG-CoA); Lys → acetoacetyl-CoA (via saccharopine pathway: Lys + α-KG → saccharopine → [saccharopine dehydrogenase] → α-aminoadipic semialdehyde → → → acetoacetyl-CoA).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme phospholipase A2 (PLA2) cleaves membrane phospholipids to release arachidonic acid. At which position (sn-) of the glycerophospholipid does PLA2 act?
options: sn-1 position: PLA1 cleaves the sn-1 ester bond (releasing a fatty acid from position 1, typically saturated [palmitate/stearate]); PLA1 is NOT PLA2

sn-2 position: PLA2 specifically cleaves the sn-2 ester bond of glycerophospholipids → releases the fatty acid at sn-2 (typically polyunsaturated: arachidonic acid [AA, 20:4 n-6] is preferentially esterified at sn-2 of membrane phospholipids [especially phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine]) + lysophospholipid (lyso-PL, which has only the sn-1 acyl chain remaining); cPLA2 (cytosolic PLA2, PLA2G4A): Ca2+-dependent, preferentially cleaves AA-containing phospholipids → releases AA for eicosanoid synthesis (COX → PGs/TXA2; LOX → LTs; CYP → EETs); cPLA2 is activated by: ↑intracellular Ca2+ + MAPK (ERK1/2) phosphorylation; sPLA2 (secreted PLA2): multiple isoforms (PLA2G2A, PLA2G5, etc.); Ca2+-dependent; released during inflammation → extracellular PL hydrolysis; iPLA2 (Ca2+-independent PLA2, PLA2G6): housekeeping membrane remodeling; regulation: glucocorticoids → ↑lipocortin-1 (annexin A1) → inhibits cPLA2 → ↓AA release → ↓ALL eicosanoids (PGs, TXA2, LTs); NSAIDs only block COX (↓PGs/TXA2 but NOT LTs); glucocorticoids block PLA2 → ↓all eicosanoids → broader anti-inflammatory effect

sn-3 position: sn-3 is the position of the headgroup (choline/ethanolamine/serine/inositol attached via phosphodiester bond); phospholipase C (PLC) cleaves on the glycerol side of the phosphodiester → releases DAG + headgroup-phosphate; phospholipase D (PLD) cleaves on the headgroup side → releases phosphatidic acid (PA) + headgroup; neither PLC nor PLD is PLA2

The phosphodiester bond between glycerol and the headgroup: this describes phospholipase C or D activity, not PLA2; PLA2 cleaves an ESTER bond between glycerol and a FATTY ACID, not the phosphodiester bond
explanation: Phospholipases — complete: PLA1: sn-1 acyl ester → FA1 + 2-acyl-lysoPL; PLA2: sn-2 acyl ester → FA2 (often AA) + 1-acyl-lysoPL; PLC: phosphodiester bond (glycerol side) → DAG + phospho-headgroup (IP3 in PIP2 cleavage by PLCβ/γ); PLD: phosphodiester bond (headgroup side) → PA + headgroup (choline in PC cleavage); PLB (lysophospholipase): cleaves remaining acyl chain from lysoPL. Arachidonic acid cascade: AA (20:4 n-6) released by PLA2 → three major enzyme pathways: (1) COX-1/2 → PGG2 → PGH2 → PGE2/PGD2/PGF2α/PGI2/TXA2; (2) 5-LOX+FLAP → 5-HpETE → LTA4 → LTB4 or LTC4/D4/E4; (3) CYP450 epoxygenases → EETs (vasodilatory); also: 12-LOX → 12-HETE; 15-LOX → 15-HETE → lipoxins.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the most abundant protein in the human body?
options: Collagen type I: collagen (all types combined) constitutes ~25-35% of total body protein; TYPE I collagen is the MOST ABUNDANT PROTEIN in the human body; found in: skin (~70% of skin dry weight), bone (90% of organic matrix), tendon, ligament, cornea, dentin, vasculature; structure: [α1(I)]2[α2(I)] heterotrimer (two α1 chains + one α2 chain); genes: COL1A1 (chromosome 17q21.33) + COL1A2 (chromosome 7q21.3); mutations → osteogenesis imperfecta (OI): OI type I (mild, AD, null allele → ↓collagen quantity but normal quality → blue sclerae + fractures + hearing loss); OI type II (lethal perinatal, AD, dominant negative structural mutation → severely abnormal collagen → in utero fractures → death); OI type III (severe deforming, AD); OI type IV (moderate, AD); also: Caffey disease (COL1A1 Arg836Cys) → infantile cortical hyperostosis

Albumin: albumin is the most abundant PLASMA protein (~55% of plasma protein, 3.5-5.0 g/dL; synthesized by liver; functions: oncotic pressure, transport [bilirubin, FA, drugs, Ca2+, hormones], buffer); but albumin is NOT the most abundant protein in the whole body — collagen is

Hemoglobin: hemoglobin is the most abundant protein in RED BLOOD CELLS (each RBC contains ~270 million Hb molecules); Hb A (α2β2) is the major adult hemoglobin; but total body hemoglobin mass (~750 g) is less than total body collagen mass (~several kg)

Actin: actin (G-actin + F-actin) is one of the most abundant intracellular proteins (~5-10% of total cellular protein in non-muscle cells; higher in muscle with myosin); but total body actin is less than total body collagen
explanation: Major body proteins by abundance: 1. Collagen (type I > type II > type III): ~25-35% of total body protein; 2. Actin + Myosin: together comprise ~65-70% of muscle protein (muscle is ~40% of body mass → actin+myosin are 2nd most abundant); 3. Hemoglobin: ~750 g in adult (most abundant single protein in blood); 4. Albumin: ~300 g in adult (most abundant plasma protein); 5. Immunoglobulins: IgG is most abundant Ig in serum; Collagen types by tissue: Type I: bone, skin, tendon, dentin (90% of bone organic matrix); Type II: hyaline cartilage, vitreous humor; Type III: blood vessels, uterus, GI tract (reticular fibers); Type IV: basement membranes (non-fibrillar, network-forming); Type V: cell surfaces, placenta; Type VII: anchoring fibrils (dermal-epidermal junction).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the fed state, insulin activates protein phosphatase 1 (PP1). Which of the following metabolic effects does PP1 activation produce?
options: Activation of glycogen phosphorylase and inhibition of glycogen synthase (this is the OPPOSITE of PP1 action; PP1 DEPHOSPHORYLATES both enzymes: glycogen phosphorylase a → b [↓glycogenolysis] + glycogen synthase phosphorylated → dephosphorylated [↑glycogenesis]; the stated effect describes the FASTING state when PKA phosphorylates these enzymes)

Activation of glycogen synthase and inactivation of glycogen phosphorylase: PP1 (protein phosphatase 1): dephosphorylates key metabolic enzymes in the fed state (insulin → PI3K → Akt → PP1 activation via regulatory subunits [GM in muscle, GL in liver]); PP1 targets: (1) glycogen synthase (GS): phosphorylated GS (inactive) → dephosphorylated GS (ACTIVE) → ↑glycogen synthesis; (2) glycogen phosphorylase a (active) → dephosphorylated → phosphorylase b (LESS active) → ↓glycogenolysis; (3) phosphorylase kinase (PhK): dephosphorylated → less active → further ↓phosphorylase activation; NET EFFECT: ↑glycogen synthesis + ↓glycogen breakdown = ↑net glycogen storage (FED STATE); PP1 regulatory subunits: GM (PPP1R3A, muscle): targets PP1 to glycogen particle; GL (PPP1R3B, liver): targets PP1 to glycogen + sensitive to glucose (liver glucose → binds phosphorylase a → conformational change → phosphorylase a becomes better substrate for PP1 → rapid dephosphorylation → rapid shut-off of glycogenolysis when glucose is abundant); GM is phosphorylated by PKA (at site 2) → PP1 dissociates from glycogen → ↓PP1 activity at glycogen → allows PKA-mediated phosphorylation cascade to proceed (glycogenolysis in fasting/stress)

Phosphorylation of CREB and activation of gluconeogenic gene transcription (CREB is phosphorylated by PKA [not PP1]; PKA → phospho-CREB → CRE → ↑PEPCK + ↑G6Pase transcription; PP1 would DEPHOSPHORYLATE and INACTIVATE CREB → ↓gluconeogenic gene expression; so this answer describes the fasting/glucagon state, not insulin/PP1)

Activation of hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue (HSL is ACTIVATED by PKA phosphorylation [fasting: glucagon/epinephrine → cAMP → PKA → phospho-HSL → active → lipolysis]; PP1 would DEPHOSPHORYLATE HSL → INACTIVE → ↓lipolysis; insulin activates PP1 → ↓HSL → ↓lipolysis → anti-lipolytic effect of insulin)
explanation: Insulin signaling → metabolic effects: Insulin → insulin receptor (IR, RTK) → IRS1/2 phosphorylation → PI3K → PIP2 → PIP3 → PDK1 → Akt (PKB) activation → multiple downstream targets: GLUCOSE UPTAKE: Akt → AS160 (TBC1D4) phosphorylation → Rab10 GTPase activation → GLUT4 vesicle translocation to PM → ↑glucose uptake (muscle + adipose); GLYCOGEN: Akt → ↓GSK3 (glycogen synthase kinase 3; Akt phosphorylates GSK3β → inactive → ↓GS phosphorylation → ↑GS activity) + Akt → ↑PP1 → dephosphorylates GS (active) + phosphorylase (inactive) → ↑glycogenesis; LIPOGENESIS: Akt → ↑SREBP-1c processing → ↑FAS + ↑ACC → ↑FA synthesis; GLUCONEOGENESIS SUPPRESSION: Akt → phospho-FOXO1 → nuclear exclusion → ↓PEPCK + ↓G6Pase transcription → ↓GNG; PROTEIN SYNTHESIS: Akt → ↑mTORC1 (via TSC2 phosphorylation → ↓TSC1/2 → ↑Rheb-GTP → ↑mTORC1) → ↑S6K1 → ↑ribosomal protein phosphorylation + ↑4E-BP1 phosphorylation → release eIF4E → ↑cap-dependent translation → ↑protein synthesis; ANTI-APOPTOSIS: Akt → phospho-BAD (sequestered by 14-3-3) → ↓apoptosis; insulin resistance: ↓insulin signaling → ↓Akt → ↓GLUT4 translocation + ↓GS + ↑FOXO1 + ↑GNG → T2DM.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Alkaptonuria is caused by deficiency of which enzyme in the tyrosine catabolism pathway?
options: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH): FAH deficiency → hereditary tyrosinemia type I (not alkaptonuria); HT1 → ↑fumarylacetoacetate → ↑succinylacetone → liver damage + HCC

Homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase (HGD): HGD deficiency → ALKAPTONURIA (AKU): homogentisic acid (HGA) accumulates → ↑HGA in blood and urine; HGA undergoes oxidation and polymerization → benzoquinone acetic acid → dark pigment (ochronotic pigment); CLINICAL: (1) dark urine (on standing; HGA oxidizes when exposed to air + alkaline pH → dark brown/black; parents may notice dark diapers); (2) ochronosis (blue-black pigmentation of cartilage, sclera, ear cartilage, tympanic membrane, aortic/mitral valves); (3) ochronotic arthropathy (progressive degenerative arthritis; HGA polymer deposits in cartilage → ↓cartilage integrity → large joint [spine, knees, shoulders] degeneration; spine: intervertebral disc calcification visible on X-ray); (4) cardiac valve disease (aortic stenosis from ochronotic deposits); AKU is BENIGN in childhood (usually diagnosed incidentally by dark urine or stained diapers); arthropathy develops in 3rd-4th decade; treatment: nitisinone (blocks 4-HPPD upstream → ↓HGA production; ↑tyrosine → requires low-Tyr diet; phase III SONIA-2 trial showed ↓HGA + clinical benefit; approved in EU 2020 for AKU); ascorbic acid (antioxidant → may ↓HGA oxidation → ↓ochronosis; limited evidence)
Tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT): TAT deficiency → tyrosinemia type II (Richner-Hanhart); corneal crystals + palmoplantar keratosis; NOT alkaptonuria

4-Hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (4-HPPD): 4-HPPD deficiency → tyrosinemia type III (extremely rare); ↑Tyr + ↑4-HPP; NOT alkaptonuria; nitisinone (NTBC) INHIBITS 4-HPPD therapeutically (used in HT1 and AKU)
explanation: Aromatic amino acid catabolism — Phe and Tyr: Phe → [PAH, BH4] → Tyr → [TAT, PLP] → 4-HPP → [4-HPPD, Fe2+, ascorbate] → HGA → [HGD, Fe2+] → MAA → [GSTZ1] → FAA → [FAH] → fumarate + acetoacetate; Enzyme deficiency → Disease: PAH → PKU; TAT → Tyrosinemia II; 4-HPPD → Tyrosinemia III; HGD → Alkaptonuria; GSTZ1 → rare (similar to mild HT1); FAH → Tyrosinemia I.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Pellagra is caused by deficiency of which vitamin?
options: Thiamine (B1): thiamine deficiency → beriberi (wet: cardiac; dry: neurological) + Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; NOT pellagra

Niacin (B3, nicotinic acid/nicotinamide): Niacin deficiency → PELLAGRA; niacin is the precursor of NAD+ and NADP+; pellagra: 4 Ds = Dermatitis (photosensitive, bilateral, symmetrical; Casal's necklace [necklace-like rash around neck]; sun-exposed areas) + Diarrhea (GI mucositis) + Dementia (neuropsychiatric: confusion, memory loss, psychosis) + Death (if untreated); causes: dietary deficiency (corn-based diet: corn contains niacin in bound form [niacytin] that is not bioavailable unless treated with alkali [nixtamalization]; also: corn protein [zein] is low in Trp → ↓endogenous niacin synthesis); also: Hartnup disease (↓Trp absorption → ↓niacin); carcinoid syndrome (↑Trp → serotonin → ↓Trp available for niacin synthesis); isoniazid therapy (INH inhibits pyridoxine [B6] → ↓PLP → ↓kynurenine pathway → ↓niacin; also INH directly inhibits niacin metabolism); alcoholism + malnutrition; TREATMENT: nicotinamide (preferred; does not cause flushing) or nicotinic acid; niacin equivalents: 60 mg Trp = 1 mg niacin equivalent (NE); RDA: 14-16 mg NE/day; nicotinic acid (pharmacological doses, 1-3 g/day): ↓VLDL + ↓LDL + ↑HDL (most effective HDL-raising agent); mechanism: GPR109A (niacin receptor, HCA2) on adipocytes → ↓cAMP → ↓HSL → ↓lipolysis → ↓FFA → ↓hepatic VLDL synthesis; side effect: prostaglandin-mediated flushing (PGD2 → DP1 receptor → vasodilation → warm flushing; mitigated by aspirin or laropiprant [PGD2 receptor antagonist; withdrawn])
Riboflavin (B2): riboflavin deficiency → ariboflavinosis: angular cheilitis + glossitis + corneal vascularization; NOT pellagra
Pyridoxine (B6): pyridoxine deficiency → peripheral neuropathy + sideroblastic anemia + seizures (neonatal); NOT pellagra
explanation: Water-soluble vitamins — summary: B1 (thiamine): TPP cofactor (PDC E1, OGDH E1, BCKDH E1, transketolase); deficiency: beriberi, Wernicke-Korsakoff; B2 (riboflavin): FMN + FAD (Complex I, Complex II, ACAD, glutathione reductase, XO, MAO, MTHFR); deficiency: ariboflavinosis; B3 (niacin): NAD+ + NADP+ (>400 enzymes); deficiency: pellagra; B5 (pantothenic acid): CoA + ACP (acyl carrier protein of FAS); deficiency: rare (burning feet syndrome); B6 (pyridoxine/pyridoxal/pyridoxamine): PLP (transaminases, decarboxylases, ALA synthase, glycogen phosphorylase, CBS, cystathionase); deficiency: neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia, seizures; B7 (biotin): carboxylases (PC, ACC, PCC, MCC); deficiency: dermatitis, alopecia, lactic acidosis; B9 (folate): THF derivatives (one-carbon transfer: dTMP synthesis, purine synthesis, Hcy remethylation); deficiency: megaloblastic anemia, NTDs; B12 (cobalamin): MeCbl (MS) + AdoCbl (MCM); deficiency: megaloblastic anemia + subacute combined degeneration; C (ascorbic acid): antioxidant + collagen hydroxylation (prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase cofactor); deficiency: scurvy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which second messenger is generated by the activation of phospholipase C-beta (PLCβ) downstream of Gαq-coupled receptors?
options: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate): cAMP is generated by adenylyl cyclase (AC) downstream of Gαs-coupled receptors; PLCβ does NOT produce cAMP

Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG): Gαq-coupled receptor activation → Gαq-GTP → activates PLCβ → PLCβ cleaves PIP2 (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate) → IP3 (inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, water-soluble) + DAG (diacylglycerol, membrane-bound); IP3: binds IP3 receptor (IP3R) on ER → opens Ca2+ channel → ↑cytoplasmic Ca2+ → Ca2+/CaM → CaMKII + calcineurin + CaM-dependent enzymes; DAG: remains in membrane → activates PKC (protein kinase C; classical PKCs [α, βI, βII, γ]: require Ca2+ + DAG + phosphatidylserine; novel PKCs [δ, ε, η, θ]: require DAG but NOT Ca2+; atypical PKCs [ζ, ι/λ]: require neither Ca2+ nor DAG); PKC targets: ↑NF-κB, ↑MAPK, ↑NADPH oxidase (NOX2 assembly), cellular proliferation; Gαq-coupled receptors: α1-adrenergic (vasoconstriction), M1/M3 muscarinic (glandular secretion, smooth muscle contraction), H1 histamine (allergy), AT1 angiotensin II (vasoconstriction), V1 vasopressin (vasoconstriction), endothelin ETA (vasoconstriction), bradykinin B2, thromboxane TP, PAR-1 (thrombin); IP3 metabolism: IP3 → [IP3 kinase] → IP4 (inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate; may potentiate IP3 or have its own signaling); IP3 → [IP3 phosphatases] → IP2 → IP1 → inositol; Li+ (lithium) inhibits IP1 phosphatase (IMPase, inositol monophosphatase) + IPP (inositol polyphosphate 1-phosphatase) → ↓inositol recycling → ↓PIP2 resynthesis → ↓IP3/DAG signaling → basis for lithium therapy in bipolar disorder (inositol depletion hypothesis)
cGMP (cyclic guanosine monophosphate): cGMP is generated by guanylyl cyclase (soluble GC activated by NO; particulate GC activated by ANP/BNP); PLCβ does NOT produce cGMP

Phosphatidic acid (PA): PA is produced by phospholipase D (PLD) from phosphatidylcholine (PC → PA + choline); PLCβ produces IP3 + DAG (DAG can be phosphorylated by DAG kinase → PA, but PA is not the direct second messenger of PLCβ)
explanation: G-protein signaling — complete: Heterotrimeric G-proteins: Gα (GTPase, 4 families) + Gβ + Gγ; GPCR → Gα-GDP (inactive) → GEF activity → Gα-GTP (active) + free Gβγ → effectors; Gα families: Gαs: stimulates AC → ↑cAMP → PKA; examples: β1/β2/β3-AR, D1/D5 dopamine, H2 histamine, V2 vasopressin, PTHR, glucagon, TSH, ACTH, LH/FSH (Gs); Gαi: inhibits AC → ↓cAMP; examples: α2-AR, M2/M4 muscarinic, D2/D3/D4 dopamine, GABA-B, μ/δ/κ opioid, somatostatin; Gαi also: Gβγ from Gαi → activates GIRK channels (G-protein-activated inward rectifier K+ channels → K+ efflux → hyperpolarization → ↓heart rate [vagal M2]); Gαq: activates PLCβ → IP3 + DAG (see above); Gα12/13: activates RhoGEF → RhoA → ROCK → actin cytoskeleton + MLC phosphorylation → contraction/migration; examples: thrombin PAR-1, LPA, S1P, thromboxane TP; Gβγ signaling: PI3Kγ (in leukocytes → chemotaxis), PLCβ (some isoforms), AC (type II, IV stimulated by Gβγ), GIRK (Kir3.x), N-type Ca2+ channel inhibition. cAMP → PKA → targets: phosphorylase kinase (↑glycogenolysis), PFK-2/FBPase-2 (↓glycolysis/↑GNG in liver), HSL (↑lipolysis), CREB (↑gene transcription), L-type Ca2+ channel (↑Ca2+ in heart → ↑contractility), phospholamban (↓SERCA inhibition → ↑SR Ca2+ reuptake → ↑relaxation), troponin I (↓Ca2+ sensitivity → ↑relaxation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme catalase decomposes hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) to water and oxygen. In which subcellular compartment is catalase predominantly located?
options: Mitochondria: mitochondria contain MnSOD (SOD2: O2⁻ → H2O2) and glutathione peroxidase (GPx) for H2O2 detoxification; mitochondria do NOT contain significant catalase (catalase is peroxisomal)

Peroxisomes: catalase (CAT gene) is predominantly located in PEROXISOMES; catalase: 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2 (dismutation); catalase is a heme-containing enzyme (4 heme groups per tetramer); peroxisomes generate H2O2 from: β-oxidation of VLCFA (ACOX1 → FADH2 → directly reduces O2 → H2O2 [unlike mitochondrial FAO where FADH2 → ETF → CoQ → ETC]; peroxisomal FAO generates H2O2 as a byproduct, NOT FADH2 for ETC); also: D-amino acid oxidase, urate oxidase (in some species), and other peroxisomal oxidases generate H2O2; catalase detoxifies this H2O2 within the peroxisome → prevents H2O2 leakage → protects cell; peroxisome import: catalase (and most peroxisomal matrix proteins) have PTS1 signal (C-terminal -SKL tripeptide) recognized by PEX5 receptor → imported into peroxisome; ROS defense hierarchy: O2⁻ → [SOD1/Cu-Zn-SOD (cytoplasm) or SOD2/MnSOD (mitochondria) or SOD3/EC-SOD (extracellular)] → H2O2 → [catalase (peroxisomes) or GPx (cytoplasm/mitochondria, requires GSH → GSSG → [GR, NADPH] → GSH) or peroxiredoxins (Prx, thioredoxin system)] → H2O
Lysosomes: lysosomes contain acid hydrolases for macromolecule degradation (cathepsins, lipases, glycosidases, nucleases); lysosomes do NOT contain catalase as a primary enzyme
Endoplasmic reticulum: ER contains CYP450 enzymes (generate ROS as byproduct) and PDI (protein disulfide isomerase) but catalase is NOT primarily located in the ER
explanation: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) defense: Sources of ROS: mitochondrial ETC (Complex I [FMN site] + Complex III [Qo site] → O2⁻ leak; estimated 0.1-2% of O2 consumed → O2⁻); NADPH oxidase (NOX1-5, DUOX1-2: NOX2 in phagocytes → respiratory burst; NOX4 in kidney/endothelium → constitutive H2O2); xanthine oxidase (XO: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid + H2O2 + O2⁻; important in ischemia-reperfusion: ischemia converts XDH → XO → reperfusion + O2 → massive ROS burst); CYP450 (uncoupled CYP → O2⁻); peroxisomal oxidases. Antioxidant enzymes: SOD: O2⁻ + O2⁻ + 2H+ → H2O2 + O2; catalase: 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2; GPx (1-8, selenoproteins except GPx5): H2O2 + 2GSH → 2H2O + GSSG; also: GPx4 (phospholipid hydroperoxide GPx → reduces lipid hydroperoxides in membranes → prevents ferroptosis; GPx4 loss → ferroptosis [iron-dependent oxidative cell death; distinct from apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis]; RSL3 [GPx4 inhibitor] + erastin [system xc⁻ inhibitor → ↓cystine import → ↓GSH] → ferroptosis inducers in cancer research); GR (glutathione reductase): GSSG + NADPH → 2GSH + NADP+; thioredoxin system: TrxR (thioredoxin reductase, selenoprotein) + Trx (thioredoxin) + NADPH → reduces oxidized proteins + peroxiredoxins. Non-enzymatic antioxidants: vitamin C (ascorbate), vitamin E (α-tocopherol: lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes → prevents lipid peroxidation), GSH, uric acid, bilirubin, coenzyme Q10.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is caused by a defect in which DNA repair pathway?
options: Base excision repair (BER): BER repairs small, non-helix-distorting base modifications — oxidized bases (8-oxoG → OGG1), deaminated bases (uracil in DNA → UNG/UDG), alkylated bases (3-meA → MPG/AAG); BER steps: DNA glycosylase (recognizes+removes damaged base → AP site [abasic]) → APE1 (AP endonuclease → nicks 5' to AP site) → Pol β (gap-filling, single-nucleotide; short-patch BER) → Ligase IIIα/XRCC1 (seals nick); long-patch BER: Pol δ/ε + FEN1 + Ligase I; BER defects are NOT the cause of XP

Nucleotide excision repair (NER): XP is caused by defects in NER; NER repairs BULKY, HELIX-DISTORTING lesions — UV-induced pyrimidine dimers (CPDs [cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers] + 6-4 photoproducts) and bulky chemical adducts (benzo[a]pyrene-DNA adducts, cisplatin intrastrand crosslinks); TWO sub-pathways: GG-NER (global genome NER: XPC-RAD23B + UV-DDB [DDB1/DDB2=XPE] recognize damage genome-wide) and TC-NER (transcription-coupled NER: CSA [ERCC8] + CSB [ERCC6] recognize RNA Pol II stalled at lesion on transcribed strand); both converge: TFIIH (contains XPB [helicase 3'→5'] + XPD [helicase 5'→3']) unwinds DNA around lesion (~25-30 nt bubble) → XPA (damage verification) + RPA (ssDNA binding/stabilization) → dual incision: XPF-ERCC1 (5' incision) + XPG (3' incision) → removes ~24-32 nt oligonucleotide containing damage → Pol δ/ε/κ + RFC + PCNA fill gap → Ligase I or Ligase IIIα/XRCC1 seals; XP complementation groups: XPA through XPG (7 groups) + XP-V (variant: defective Pol η [POLH gene] → cannot perform translesion synthesis past CPDs → uses error-prone polymerases instead → ↑UV mutagenesis); XP clinical: extreme UV sensitivity → ↑sunburns → ↑skin cancers (BCC, SCC, melanoma; 10,000-fold ↑ risk) → must avoid ALL UV exposure; ↑internal cancers; ~25% have neurodegeneration (especially XPA, XPD, XPB mutations affecting transcription); Cockayne syndrome (CS): defective TC-NER (CSA or CSB mutations) → UV sensitivity + growth failure + neurodegeneration + cachectic dwarfism; NO ↑cancer risk (distinguishes CS from XP); trichothiodystrophy (TTD): TFIIH mutations (XPD most common) → brittle hair (↓sulfur-rich matrix proteins: tiger-tail pattern on polarized light microscopy) + ichthyosis + photosensitivity + neurodegeneration

Mismatch repair (MMR): MMR corrects replication errors — base-base mismatches and insertion-deletion loops (IDLs); MMR proteins: MSH2-MSH6 (MutSα: recognizes single base mismatches + small IDLs) or MSH2-MSH3 (MutSβ: recognizes larger IDLs) → recruit MLH1-PMS2 (MutLα) → EXO1 (excision) → Pol δ (resynthesis) → Ligase I (ligation); MMR defects → Lynch syndrome (HNPCC: AD mutations in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 → ↑colorectal cancer [right-sided], endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract cancers; microsatellite instability [MSI-H]); NOT the cause of XP

Homologous recombination (HR): HR repairs DSBs in S/G2 phase using sister chromatid as template; key proteins: MRN complex (MRE11-RAD50-NBS1) → ATM activation + end resection → RPA coats ssDNA → BRCA2 loads RAD51 → RAD51 filament → strand invasion → D-loop → synthesis → resolution/dissolution; BRCA1 (ubiquitin ligase, promotes HR over NHEJ) + BRCA2 (RAD51 loader); BRCA1/2 mutations → hereditary breast-ovarian cancer (HBOC); HR defects are NOT the cause of XP
explanation: DNA repair pathways summary: (1) Direct reversal: MGMT (O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase) → removes alkyl groups from O6-meG (single-use, suicidal enzyme; MGMT promoter methylation → loss of MGMT → ↑sensitivity to alkylating agents [temozolomide] in GBM → better prognosis/response); photolyases (not in humans; use light to directly reverse CPDs); (2) BER: small non-distorting lesions; (3) NER: bulky helix-distorting lesions; (4) MMR: replication errors; (5) HR: DSBs in S/G2 (error-free); (6) NHEJ: DSBs in G1 (error-prone; Ku70/Ku80 + DNA-PKcs + Artemis + Pol μ/λ + Ligase IV/XRCC4); (7) Fanconi anemia pathway: interstrand crosslinks (ICLs; 22 FA genes [FANCA-FANCW]; FANCD1=BRCA2, FANCN=PALB2, FANCS=BRCA1); (8) Translesion synthesis (TLS): damage tolerance (not repair); specialized low-fidelity polymerases (Pol η, ι, κ, REV1, Pol ζ) bypass lesions; Pol η (XP-V) correctly inserts AA opposite TT-CPD.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is caused by a complete deficiency of which enzyme?
options: Heme oxygenase: heme oxygenase (HO-1, HO-2) catalyzes the first step of heme degradation: heme → biliverdin + CO + Fe2+; NOT the enzyme deficient in Crigler-Najjar
Biliverdin reductase: biliverdin reductase converts biliverdin → bilirubin (unconjugated, indirect); NOT the enzyme deficient in Crigler-Najjar

UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1): Crigler-Najjar type I (CN-I): COMPLETE absence of UGT1A1 activity → cannot conjugate bilirubin → severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from birth (>20-25 mg/dL); bilirubin is lipophilic → crosses BBB → KERNICTERUS (bilirubin encephalopathy → basal ganglia, hippocampus, cranial nerve nuclei damage → opisthotonus, seizures, sensorineural hearing loss, death); CN-I does NOT respond to phenobarbital (because there is ZERO enzyme to induce); treatment: phototherapy (blue light 420-470 nm → photoisomerization of bilirubin → lumirubin [water-soluble] → excreted in bile without conjugation; phototherapy is needed 12-16 hrs/day lifelong) + ultimately LIVER TRANSPLANTATION (only definitive cure); gene therapy under investigation; Crigler-Najjar type II (CN-II, Arias syndrome): PARTIAL UGT1A1 deficiency (enzyme activity ~10-30% of normal) → moderate unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (6-20 mg/dL); RESPONDS to phenobarbital (induces residual UGT1A1 → ↓bilirubin by ~25-30%); kernicterus is rare but possible; Gilbert syndrome: mild UGT1A1 deficiency (enzyme activity ~30% of normal, typically due to (TA)7 repeat in promoter [UGT1A1*28, normally (TA)6] → ↓transcription); benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (1-4 mg/dL); exacerbated by fasting, stress, illness, menstruation; prevalence ~5-10% of population; no treatment needed

Conjugated bilirubin transporter (MRP2/ABCC2): MRP2 deficiency → Dubin-Johnson syndrome → conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia; dark liver (melanin-like pigment); NOT the enzyme deficient in Crigler-Najjar (which involves unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia)
explanation: Bilirubin metabolism pathway: (1) Heme degradation (in reticuloendothelial system [spleen/liver macrophages]): Hb → globin (recycled) + heme → [HO-1, rate-limiting, NADPH + O2] → biliverdin (green) + CO + Fe2+ → [biliverdin reductase, NADPH] → bilirubin (unconjugated/indirect, yellow; lipophilic, neurotoxic); (2) Transport: unconjugated bilirubin (UCB) binds albumin in blood → transported to liver; (3) Hepatic uptake: sinusoidal membrane: OATP1B1/1B3 (organic anion transporting polypeptide) + ligandin (GST, intracellular binding protein) → delivers to SER; (4) Conjugation: UGT1A1 (SER) → bilirubin mono- and diglucuronide (conjugated/direct; water-soluble, non-toxic); (5) Excretion: MRP2 (ABCC2, canalicular membrane) → bile → intestine; (6) Intestinal: conjugated bilirubin → [bacterial β-glucuronidases] → unconjugated bilirubin → [bacterial reductases] → urobilinogen (colorless); urobilinogen: 80% → stercobilinogen → stercobilin (brown; gives stool color); 20% → enterohepatic circulation → kidney → urobilinogen → urobilin (yellow; gives urine color). Hyperbilirubinemia syndromes: UNCONJUGATED: Gilbert (mild, common), CN-II (moderate, phenobarbital-responsive), CN-I (severe, no response); CONJUGATED: Dubin-Johnson (MRP2/ABCC2 deficiency; dark liver pigment; ↑urinary coproporphyrin I [normally III>I]), Rotor (defective hepatic storage of conjugated bilirubin [OATP1B1+OATP1B3 mutations]; NO liver pigment; ↑total urinary coproporphyrin with normal I:III ratio).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Sphingomyelinase cleaves sphingomyelin to generate ceramide and phosphocholine. Deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase causes which lysosomal storage disease?
options: Gaucher disease: Gaucher disease (type I, II, III) is caused by deficiency of GLUCOCEREBROSIDASE (acid β-glucosidase, GBA1 gene) → ↑glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) accumulation; Gaucher cells (lipid-laden macrophages with wrinkled-tissue-paper cytoplasm); NOT caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency

Niemann-Pick disease type A/B: Niemann-Pick type A and type B are caused by deficiency of ACID SPHINGOMYELINASE (ASM, encoded by SMPD1 gene [sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1]); ASM normally cleaves sphingomyelin → ceramide + phosphocholine in lysosomes; ASM deficiency → sphingomyelin accumulation in lysosomes (especially in reticuloendothelial cells: macrophages, hepatocytes, neurons); NPA (type A, infantile neurovisceral): severe, <3% residual ASM; hepatosplenomegaly + cherry-red spot (macula) + neurodegeneration → death by age 3; Niemann-Pick cells: lipid-laden macrophages with foamy/vacuolated cytoplasm ('sea-blue histiocytes' on bone marrow); NPB (type B, chronic visceral): milder, 5-10% residual ASM; hepatosplenomegaly + pulmonary infiltrates + ↑lipids; NO neurological involvement; survival to adulthood; treatment: olipudase alfa (recombinant ASM, ERT; approved 2022 for NPB); NOTE: Niemann-Pick type C (NPC) is a DIFFERENT disease — NOT ASM deficiency; NPC: NPC1 (95%) or NPC2 mutations → defective intracellular cholesterol trafficking → unesterified cholesterol accumulation in late endosomes/lysosomes → vertical supranuclear gaze palsy + ataxia + dystonia + hepatosplenomegaly + cataplexy/gelastic seizures; NPC treatment: miglustat (substrate reduction therapy, iminosugar; inhibits glucosylceramide synthase)
Fabry disease: Fabry disease is caused by deficiency of α-GALACTOSIDASE A (GLA gene, X-linked) → ↑globotriaosylceramide (Gb3, ceramide trihexoside) accumulation; NOT sphingomyelinase deficiency

Krabbe disease: Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy) is caused by deficiency of GALACTOCEREBROSIDE β-GALACTOSIDASE (GALC gene) → ↑galactosylceramide + ↑psychosine (galactosylsphingosine, toxic to oligodendrocytes) → demyelination; globoid cells = multinucleated macrophages; NOT sphingomyelinase deficiency
explanation: Sphingolipid metabolism and lysosomal storage diseases: Sphingolipid synthesis: Serine + palmitoyl-CoA → [SPT, serine palmitoyltransferase, PLP] → 3-ketosphingosine → sphinganine → dihydroceramide → [desaturase] → CERAMIDE (central hub); Ceramide → sphingomyelin (+ phosphocholine from PC, via SMS), glucosylceramide (GlcCer, via GCS), galactosylceramide (GalCer), ceramide-1-phosphate, sphingosine (→ S1P via SphK1/2); Lysosomal degradation (reverse order, each step requires specific acid hydrolase; deficiency → specific LSD): GM1 ganglioside → [β-galactosidase → GM1 gangliosidosis]; GM2 → [Hex A (α+β subunits) → Tay-Sachs (α deficiency, HEXA); Hex A+B → Sandhoff (β deficiency, HEXB); GM2 activator deficiency → AB variant]; Globoside → [Hex A] → Fabry is NOT here; Gb3 → [α-gal A → Fabry]; GlcCer → [GBA1 → Gaucher]; GalCer → [GALC → Krabbe]; Sphingomyelin → [ASM → Niemann-Pick A/B]; Ceramide → [acid ceramidase → Farber]; Sulfatide → [arylsulfatase A → MLD (metachromatic leukodystrophy)].

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hepcidin, the master regulator of iron homeostasis, exerts its effect by binding to and inducing degradation of which iron transporter?
options: Transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1): TfR1 mediates cellular iron uptake by binding diferric transferrin (Tf-Fe2) → receptor-mediated endocytosis → acidification releases Fe3+ → DMT1 exports Fe2+ to cytoplasm → Tf-TfR1 recycled; TfR1 is NOT the direct target of hepcidin

Ferroportin (FPN1/SLC40A1): Hepcidin (HAMP gene, liver-derived 25-aa peptide) is the MASTER REGULATOR of systemic iron homeostasis; hepcidin binds FERROPORTIN (FPN1, SLC40A1) → induces FPN1 internalization + lysosomal degradation → ↓iron export from cells (enterocytes [↓dietary iron absorption], macrophages [↓iron recycling from senescent RBCs], hepatocytes [↓iron release from stores]) → ↓plasma iron; hepcidin regulation: ↑hepcidin (↑iron stores [via BMP6-SMAD pathway: ↑iron → ↑BMP6 → BMP6 + HJV [hemojuvelin, co-receptor] → BMPR → SMAD1/5/8 → SMAD4 → ↑HAMP transcription]; ↑inflammation [IL-6 → JAK2-STAT3 → ↑HAMP]; ↑transferrin saturation [HFE + TfR2 sense diferric Tf → ↑HAMP]); ↓hepcidin (↑erythropoiesis [erythroferrone (ERFE, from erythroblasts) → suppresses BMP-SMAD → ↓HAMP]; iron deficiency; hypoxia [HIF → ↑ERFE, ↓HAMP]); hereditary hemochromatosis (HH): ↓hepcidin → unregulated iron absorption → iron overload: HFE-related HH (type 1, most common, C282Y homozygous → HFE cannot sense Tf saturation → ↓hepcidin → ↑iron absorption; AR; liver [cirrhosis, HCC], heart [cardiomyopathy], pancreas [bronze diabetes], joints [arthropathy], skin [bronze]); juvenile HH (type 2A: HJV mutations; type 2B: HAMP mutations → severe, early onset); type 3: TfR2 mutations; type 4 (ferroportin disease): FPN1 mutations (AD; can be loss-of-function [↓iron export → macrophage iron loading, low Tf-sat] or gain-of-function [hepcidin-resistant FPN → iron overload similar to classic HH]); treatment: phlebotomy (first-line) or iron chelation (deferoxamine IV/SC, deferasirox PO, deferiprone PO)

DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1): DMT1 (SLC11A2) transports Fe2+ across the apical membrane of enterocytes (dietary iron absorption) and out of endosomes (after Tf-TfR1 endocytosis); DMT1 is NOT the direct target of hepcidin

Ferritin: ferritin is the intracellular iron storage protein (24-subunit shell: H-chain [ferroxidase: Fe2+ → Fe3+] + L-chain [nucleation of ferrihydrite core]; stores up to ~4,500 Fe3+ atoms); serum ferritin reflects total body iron stores; ferritin is NOT an iron transporter and is NOT the target of hepcidin
explanation: Iron metabolism — complete: Dietary iron: heme iron (Fe2+ in heme, from meat; absorbed via HCP1 [heme carrier protein 1] → heme oxygenase releases Fe2+; more bioavailable) + non-heme iron (Fe3+ → reduced to Fe2+ by DcytB [duodenal cytochrome b, ferrireductase] → DMT1 [Fe2+ transporter] → enterocyte); Enterocyte: Fe2+ stored as ferritin or exported via FPN1 (basolateral) → hephaestin (ferroxidase: Fe2+ → Fe3+) → Fe3+ binds transferrin in plasma; Plasma: transferrin (Tf): 2 Fe3+ binding sites; Tf-saturation normally 20-45%; TIBC reflects transferrin level; TfR1: ubiquitous, ↑in iron deficiency (via IRE-IRP system); TfR2: liver-specific, senses Tf-saturation → regulates hepcidin; IRE-IRP system: iron regulatory elements (IREs) are stem-loop structures in mRNAs; IRP1/IRP2 bind IREs when iron is LOW → 5'-IRE binding → ↓translation (ferritin↓, FPN1↓); 3'-IRE binding → ↑mRNA stability (TfR1↑, DMT1↑); when iron is HIGH: IRP1 → cytoplasmic aconitase (gains 4Fe-4S cluster); IRP2 → ubiquitinated by FBXL5 → degraded → IREs unoccupied → ↑ferritin/FPN1 translation, ↓TfR1/DMT1 stability.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed step of fatty acid synthesis?
options: Fatty acid synthase (FAS): FAS (FASN gene) is the large multifunctional enzyme (2 identical 270-kDa subunits in head-to-tail homodimer) that catalyzes the actual synthesis of palmitate from acetyl-CoA + malonyl-CoA + NADPH; but FAS catalyzes downstream elongation steps, NOT the committed step

Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC): ACC (ACC1/ACCα for lipogenesis, ACC2/ACCβ for malonyl-CoA regulation of CPT I) catalyzes the COMMITTED (rate-limiting) step of fatty acid synthesis: acetyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → malonyl-CoA + ADP + Pi; ACC is a BIOTIN-dependent carboxylase (biotin covalently attached to ε-amino of Lys residue); requires Mn2+; mechanism: (1) biotin carboxylase (BC) domain: bicarbonate + ATP → CO2 transferred to biotin → carboxybiotin; (2) carboxyltransferase (CT) domain: CO2 from carboxybiotin → acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA; ACC regulation: ACTIVATION: citrate (allosteric activator → promotes ACC polymerization into active filaments); insulin (→ PP2A dephosphorylation → active ACC; also insulin → SREBP-1c → ↑ACC transcription); fed state; INHIBITION: palmitoyl-CoA (product feedback, allosteric → promotes depolymerization); AMPK phosphorylation (Ser79 on ACC1 → inactive; fasting/exercise → ↑AMP:ATP → ↑AMPK → ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↓FA synthesis + ↑CPT I activity [malonyl-CoA is CPT I inhibitor] → ↑FAO); glucagon/epinephrine → PKA → ↑AMPK → ↓ACC; malonyl-CoA dual role: (1) substrate for FAS in cytoplasm (lipogenesis); (2) allosteric inhibitor of CPT I on OMM (↓FAO); this ensures FA synthesis and FA oxidation do not occur simultaneously

ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY): ACLY cleaves citrate → acetyl-CoA + OAA in cytoplasm (provides cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA for FA synthesis; citrate shuttle: mitochondrial acetyl-CoA + OAA → [citrate synthase] → citrate → exported by CTP [citrate transport protein] → cytoplasmic citrate → [ACLY] → acetyl-CoA + OAA); ACLY is important for lipogenesis but is NOT the committed step
Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase: malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MCD) degrades malonyl-CoA → acetyl-CoA + CO2; it OPPOSES ACC; NOT the committed step of FA synthesis
explanation: Fatty acid synthesis — complete: Location: cytoplasm (liver, adipose, lactating mammary); Source of carbons: acetyl-CoA (from pyruvate [PDC], amino acids, citrate shuttle); Source of NADPH: pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD + 6PGD) + malic enzyme (malate → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH); citrate shuttle also generates NADPH (OAA → malate [MDH, NADH] → pyruvate [ME1, NADPH]); Steps: (1) ACC: acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (committed step); (2) FAS: 7 malonyl-CoA + 1 acetyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H+ → palmitate (16:0) + 7 CO2 + 8 CoA + 14 NADP+ + 6 H2O; FAS activities (7 enzymatic + 1 ACP): AT (acetyltransferase), MT (malonyltransferase), KS (β-ketoacyl synthase = condensing enzyme), KR (β-ketoacyl reductase, NADPH), DH (dehydratase), ER (enoyl reductase, NADPH), TE (thioesterase: releases palmitate); each cycle adds 2C from malonyl-CoA; 7 cycles → C16 (palmitoyl released by TE); FAS equation stoichiometry: 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 ATP + 14 NADPH → palmitate + 8 CoA + 7 ADP + 7 Pi + 14 NADP+ + 6 H2O; further modifications: elongation (ER → ELOVL enzymes; palmitate → stearate [18:0] → etc.) + desaturation (Δ9 desaturase [SCD1]: stearate → oleate [18:1 n-9]; also Δ5 [FADS1], Δ6 [FADS2] desaturases for PUFA modification); humans CANNOT introduce double bonds beyond Δ9 → linoleic acid (18:2 n-6) and α-linolenic acid (18:3 n-3) are ESSENTIAL fatty acids.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which glycosaminoglycan (GAG) is unique because it is NOT sulfated and is NOT attached to a core protein?
options: Heparan sulfate: heparan sulfate is a SULFATED GAG (N-sulfated, 2-O-sulfated, 6-O-sulfated GlcNAc/GlcA/IdoA); found attached to core proteins (syndecans, glypicans) as proteoglycans; defective degradation: MPS types (MPS I [Hurler/Scheie: α-L-iduronidase], MPS II [Hunter: iduronate-2-sulfatase, X-linked], MPS IIIA-D [Sanfilippo])

Chondroitin sulfate: chondroitin sulfate is a SULFATED GAG (4-O or 6-O sulfated GalNAc); attached to core proteins (aggrecan in cartilage); defective degradation: MPS IVA (Morquio A: galactose-6-sulfatase) involves keratan sulfate but CS is also affected in some MPSs

Hyaluronic acid (hyaluronan): Hyaluronic acid (HA) is the ONLY GAG that is: (1) NOT SULFATED (no sulfate esters); (2) NOT covalently attached to a core protein (it is a free GAG, not a proteoglycan); (3) NOT synthesized in the Golgi (synthesized at the inner surface of the plasma membrane by hyaluronan synthases [HAS1, HAS2, HAS3] → extruded directly into the ECM); (4) the LARGEST GAG (can reach 10^7 Da; repeat disaccharide: GlcNAc-β1,4-GlcA-β1,3-; hundreds to thousands of repeats); HA functions: (a) structural: vitreous humor, synovial fluid (viscosity/lubrication), umbilical cord (Wharton's jelly), cartilage ECM; (b) water retention: extremely hydrophilic → creates hydrated gel → resists compression; (c) signaling: HA fragments (low MW) are pro-inflammatory via TLR2/4 + CD44; high MW HA is anti-inflammatory; (d) cell migration: CD44 + RHAMM (HA receptors) → cell migration (important in embryogenesis, wound healing, and cancer metastasis); degradation: hyaluronidases (HYAL1, HYAL2) → HA fragments → lysosomal degradation; clinical uses: viscosupplementation (intra-articular HA for OA); dermal fillers (cross-linked HA); ophthalmic surgery; dissolved by hyaluronidase (spreading factor; used to enhance drug diffusion in subcutaneous injections)

Dermatan sulfate: dermatan sulfate is a SULFATED GAG (contains IdoA + 4-O-sulfated GalNAc); attached to core proteins (decorin, biglycan); defective degradation: MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy: arylsulfatase B/N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase)
explanation: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) — summary: All GAGs are unbranched polysaccharides of repeating disaccharide units (amino sugar + uronic acid [except keratan sulfate: Gal instead of uronic acid]). SULFATED GAGs (all attached to core protein → proteoglycans, synthesized in Golgi): Chondroitin sulfate (GlcA + GalNAc-4S or -6S; aggrecan); Dermatan sulfate (IdoA + GalNAc-4S; decorin); Heparan sulfate (GlcA/IdoA + GlcNAc with N-/O-sulfation; syndecan, glypican); Heparin (highly sulfated form of HS; IdoA-2S + GlcNS-6S; mast cell granules; anticoagulant → enhances AT-III); Keratan sulfate (Gal + GlcNAc-6S; NO uronic acid; cornea [KS I], cartilage [KS II]); NON-SULFATED, FREE: Hyaluronic acid (GlcA + GlcNAc; NOT attached to protein; synthesized at PM; largest GAG). Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS): lysosomal enzyme deficiencies → GAG accumulation: MPS I (Hurler [severe] / Scheie [mild]): α-L-iduronidase → ↑HS+DS; MPS II (Hunter): iduronate-2-sulfatase → ↑HS+DS [X-linked, ONLY X-linked MPS]; MPS III (Sanfilippo A-D): 4 different enzymes → ↑HS; MPS IV (Morquio A/B): galactose-6-sulfatase / β-galactosidase → ↑KS; MPS VI (Maroteaux-Lamy): arylsulfatase B → ↑DS; MPS VII (Sly): β-glucuronidase → ↑HS+DS+CS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the Warburg effect observed in cancer cells, what is the predominant fate of glucose even in the presence of adequate oxygen?
options: Complete oxidation via TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation: this is the normal aerobic metabolism in most differentiated cells (glucose → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → TCA → NADH/FADH2 → ETC → ~30-36 ATP); cancer cells with the Warburg effect do NOT primarily use this pathway despite adequate O2

Conversion to lactate (aerobic glycolysis): The WARBURG EFFECT (aerobic glycolysis): cancer cells preferentially convert glucose to LACTATE even in the presence of sufficient O2 (aerobic glycolysis), rather than oxidizing pyruvate via TCA/OXPHOS; Otto Warburg (1924): observed that tumor slices produce large amounts of lactate even with ample O2; mechanism: cancer cells upregulate glucose uptake (↑GLUT1 via HIF-1α, Myc) + ↑glycolytic enzymes + PKM2 (pyruvate kinase M2 splice isoform: less active → slows glycolysis → diverts intermediates to biosynthetic pathways [nucleotides, amino acids, lipids, NADPH via PPP]) + ↑LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase A: pyruvate → lactate + NAD+ regeneration → sustains rapid glycolysis); advantages for cancer: (1) rapid ATP production (glycolysis is faster than OXPHOS even though less efficient per glucose); (2) biosynthetic precursors (glycolytic intermediates → PPP [NADPH + ribose-5-P], serine synthesis [3PG → Ser → one-carbon metabolism], lipid synthesis [citrate export]); (3) lactate acidifies TME → immune evasion + invasion; (4) ↓ROS (↓mitochondrial OXPHOS → ↓ROS; also ↑PPP → ↑NADPH → ↑GSH → ROS scavenging); PET-CT: exploits Warburg effect: 18F-FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) → taken up by ↑GLUT1 → phosphorylated by hexokinase II → trapped (no further metabolism) → ↑signal = metabolically active tumor; oncometabolites: IDH1/2 mutations (glioma, AML) → neomorphic activity: α-KG → [mutant IDH1/2] → D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG, oncometabolite) → competitive inhibitor of α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (TET2 [DNA demethylation → ↓5hmC → hypermethylation], JmjC [histone demethylases → histone hypermethylation], PHD [prolyl hydroxylases → HIF stabilization]) → epigenetic dysregulation → differentiation block → oncogenesis

Conversion to glycogen for storage: glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis) is an insulin-stimulated storage pathway in liver/muscle; cancer cells generally do NOT store glucose as glycogen — they metabolize it rapidly

Conversion to fatty acids via de novo lipogenesis: while cancer cells DO have increased de novo lipogenesis (↑FASN, ↑ACC, ↑ACLY), the PRIMARY immediate fate of glucose in the Warburg effect is conversion to lactate; some glucose carbons are diverted to FAS via citrate, but lactate production is the hallmark
explanation: Cancer metabolism beyond Warburg: Glutamine addiction: many cancers are glutamine-dependent (Myc → ↑SLC1A5 [glutamine transporter] + ↑GLS [glutaminase]); Gln → Glu → α-KG (anaplerosis to replenish TCA cycle, especially when citrate is diverted to lipogenesis); Gln also provides nitrogen for nucleotide + amino acid synthesis + GSH; mTORC1 sensing of Gln; one-carbon metabolism: Serine synthesis pathway (3PG → [PHGDH] → 3-PHP → [PSAT1] → 3-PS → [PSPH] → Ser); Ser → [SHMT1/2] → Gly + CH2-THF (one-carbon unit for: dTMP synthesis [TS], purine synthesis, methionine cycle → SAM → methylation); SHMT2 (mitochondrial) is frequently upregulated in cancer; autophagy: cancer cells use autophagy for survival under nutrient stress (recycling); ferroptosis: emerging cancer vulnerability — GPx4 loss → lipid peroxidation → cell death; erastin (blocks cystine import → ↓GSH → ↓GPx4) and RSL3 (directly inhibits GPx4) induce ferroptosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biotinidase deficiency impairs the recycling of which vitamin?
options: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): B12 recycling involves intrinsic factor, TC-II, lysosomal release, and intracellular conversion to MeCbl/AdoCbl; biotinidase is not involved in B12 metabolism

Biotin (vitamin B7): Biotinidase (BTD gene) is essential for BIOTIN RECYCLING; biotin is covalently attached to carboxylases (via holocarboxylase synthetase [HCS]): PC (pyruvate carboxylase), ACC (acetyl-CoA carboxylase), PCC (propionyl-CoA carboxylase), MCC (3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase); when these enzymes are degraded, biocytin (biotin-lysine) is released; BIOTINIDASE cleaves biocytin → free biotin + lysine → biotin is recycled for reuse; biotinidase ALSO liberates biotin from dietary protein-bound biotin (biocytin in food); biotinidase deficiency (AR): ↓biotin recycling + ↓dietary biotin absorption → functional biotin deficiency → ↓all 4 carboxylase activities (multiple carboxylase deficiency, LATE-ONSET type; onset weeks-years); clinical: seizures + hypotonia + dermatitis (periorificial) + alopecia + lactic acidosis + metabolic acidosis + organic aciduria (↑3-methylcrotonylglycine, ↑methylcitrate, ↑3-HP, ↑lactate); also: sensorineural hearing loss + optic atrophy (can be irreversible if treatment delayed); treatment: FREE BIOTIN supplementation (5-20 mg/day orally; dramatic response, prevents all symptoms if started early); vs. HCS deficiency (holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency → multiple carboxylase deficiency, EARLY-ONSET/neonatal type; same enzyme deficiencies but presents earlier [neonatal]; also treated with biotin but may require higher doses); newborn screening: biotinidase activity measured in dried blood spots (DBS) → included in NBS panel in most countries
Folate (vitamin B9): folate recycling involves dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR: DHF → THF) + one-carbon metabolism enzymes; biotinidase is not involved in folate metabolism
Thiamine (vitamin B1): thiamine is converted to TPP by thiamine pyrophosphokinase; biotinidase is not involved in thiamine metabolism
explanation: Biotin-dependent carboxylases — mnemonic 'PAMM' or 'APMC': (1) Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → OAA (gluconeogenesis anaplerosis; mitochondrial matrix; deficiency → lactic acidosis + ↓GNG); (2) Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC1/2): acetyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → malonyl-CoA (FA synthesis committed step; cytoplasm); (3) Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC): propionyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → D-methylmalonyl-CoA (→ L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, AdoCbl] → succinyl-CoA; odd-chain FA, Val, Ile, Met, Thr, cholesterol side chain catabolism; mitochondrial; deficiency → propionic acidemia); (4) 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCC): 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA (leucine catabolism; mitochondrial; deficiency → 3-MCC deficiency → most common organic acidemia on NBS but usually benign). Multiple carboxylase deficiency: all 4 carboxylases affected; two causes: (1) biotinidase deficiency (late-onset, treated with biotin); (2) HCS deficiency (early/neonatal onset, treated with biotin). Dietary biotin sources: egg yolk, liver, nuts, legumes; raw egg white contains AVIDIN (glycoprotein that binds biotin with extremely high affinity [Kd ~10^-15 M, one of strongest non-covalent interactions in nature] → biotin deficiency if eating raw eggs chronically); cooking denatures avidin → no longer binds biotin.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the immediate precursor of all pyrimidine nucleotides synthesized de novo?
options: Inosine monophosphate (IMP): IMP is the first nucleotide formed in de novo PURINE synthesis (not pyrimidine); IMP → AMP (via adenylosuccinate [ADSS + ADSL]) or GMP (via XMP [IMPDH + GMPS]); de novo purine synthesis: ribose-5-P → [PRPS, PRPP synthetase] → PRPP → [amidophosphoribosyltransferase/GPAT, committed step, inhibited by AMP+GMP] → PRA → 10 steps → IMP

Uridine monophosphate (UMP): UMP is the FIRST PYRIMIDINE NUCLEOTIDE formed in de novo pyrimidine synthesis and serves as the immediate precursor from which ALL other pyrimidine nucleotides are derived; de novo pyrimidine synthesis pathway: (1) Gln + CO2 + 2 ATP → [CPS II, cytoplasmic, committed step; activated by ATP + PRPP, inhibited by UTP] → carbamoyl phosphate (NOTE: CPS II is cytoplasmic for pyrimidines; CPS I is mitochondrial for urea cycle); (2) carbamoyl phosphate + Asp → [ATCase/aspartate transcarbamoylase/ATCase-DHOase domain of CAD] → N-carbamoylaspartate (carbamoyl-Asp); (3) → [DHOase, dihydroorotase/CAD] → dihydroorotate (DHO); in humans: CPS II + ATCase + DHOase are a SINGLE trifunctional enzyme = CAD (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase + aspartate transcarbamoylase + dihydroorotase); (4) DHO → [DHODH, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, IMM, uses CoQ as electron acceptor; inhibited by LEFLUNOMIDE (→ teriflunomide, active metabolite → anti-inflammatory for RA/MS)] → orotate; (5) orotate + PRPP → [OPRT, orotate phosphoribosyltransferase] → OMP (orotidine-5'-monophosphate); (6) OMP → [OMPDC/OMP decarboxylase] → UMP; OPRT + OMPDC = UMP synthase (bifunctional enzyme); UMP synthase deficiency → orotic aciduria type I (↑orotic acid in urine + megaloblastic anemia resistant to B12/folate; treated with URIDINE supplementation → ↓orotic acid [via feedback inhibition of CPS II by UTP]); FROM UMP: UMP → UTP → CTP [CTP synthase: UTP + Gln → CTP]; UMP → dUMP → [thymidylate synthase + CH2-THF → DHF] → dTMP → dTDP → dTTP; RNR (ribonucleotide reductase) converts NDP → dNDP

Orotidine monophosphate (OMP): OMP is an intermediate in de novo pyrimidine synthesis (orotate + PRPP → OMP → [OMPDC] → UMP); OMP is a precursor TO UMP, but UMP itself is the first completed pyrimidine nucleotide from which all others derive
Carbamoyl phosphate: carbamoyl phosphate is the product of the committed step (CPS II) but it is an early intermediate, not a nucleotide; it still needs to go through multiple steps → UMP
explanation: Pyrimidine vs purine synthesis comparison: PYRIMIDINE de novo: ring built FIRST (as free base: orotate) → then attached to ribose (PRPP → OMP → UMP); CPS II (cytoplasmic, Gln as N donor; in CAD multifunctional enzyme); key steps: CAD (CPS II + ATCase + DHOase) → DHODH (mitochondrial IM) → UMP synthase (OPRT + OMPDC); regulation: CPS II (+: ATP, PRPP; -: UTP); end products: UTP, CTP, dTTP; salvage: uridine/cytidine kinases, thymidine kinase (TK1/TK2); drugs: 5-FU (→ 5-FdUMP → inhibits TS), methotrexate (↓DHFR → ↓THF → ↓CH2-THF → ↓TS), leflunomide (↓DHODH), hydroxyurea (↓RNR). PURINE de novo: ring built ON RIBOSE-5-P (PRPP); atoms from: Gln (N3, N9), Gly (C4, C5, N7), Asp (N1), CO2 (C6), N10-formyl-THF (C2, C8); committed step: GPAT/amidoPRT; 10 steps → IMP; IMP → AMP or GMP; regulation: GPAT (+: PRPP; -: AMP, GMP, IMP); salvage: HGPRT (hypoxanthine/guanine → IMP/GMP; deficiency → Lesch-Nyhan [HGPRT complete deficiency → ↑PRPP → ↑de novo purine synthesis → ↑uric acid → gout + self-mutilation + neurological dysfunction; X-linked]), APRT (adenine → AMP); degradation: AMP → IMP → inosine → hypoxanthine → [XO] → xanthine → [XO] → uric acid; GMP → guanosine → guanine → [guanase] → xanthine → uric acid.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which RNA polymerase transcribes messenger RNA (mRNA) in eukaryotes?
options: RNA Polymerase I (Pol I): Pol I transcribes rRNA (45S pre-rRNA → 28S + 18S + 5.8S rRNA) in the NUCLEOLUS; Pol I is NOT inhibited by α-amanitin (from Amanita phalloides); Pol I produces ~80% of total cellular RNA (rRNA is most abundant RNA); Pol I promoter: UBF + SL1/TIF-IB → upstream binding → Pol I recruitment

RNA Polymerase II (Pol II): Pol II transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes), plus snRNA (U1-U5 except U6), miRNA, most lncRNA, and some snoRNA; Pol II is the MOST STUDIED eukaryotic RNA polymerase; Pol II has a unique C-terminal domain (CTD) on its largest subunit (RPB1): consists of 52 repeats (human) of heptapeptide YSPTSPS; CTD phosphorylation coordinates transcription stages: unphosphorylated CTD → binds Mediator → PIC (pre-initiation complex) assembly; Ser5 phosphorylation (by TFIIH/CDK7 [CAK]) → promoter clearance + recruits capping enzymes (5' cap: 7-methylguanosine); Ser2 phosphorylation (by P-TEFb/CDK9) → productive elongation + recruits splicing factors + polyadenylation complex (3' poly-A: CPSF + CstF + PAP); Pol II is VERY SENSITIVE to α-amanitin (inhibited at low concentrations ~10 ng/mL); general transcription factors: TFIID (TBP + TAFs → binds TATA box [~-25 to -30] or Inr/DPE), TFIIA (stabilizes TFIID), TFIIB (recruits Pol II, determines start site), TFIIF (escorts Pol II to promoter), TFIIE (recruits TFIIH), TFIIH (helicase [XPB 3'→5', XPD 5'→3'] → melts DNA + CDK7 kinase → CTD Ser5 phosphorylation); Mediator complex: integrates signals from enhancers/activators/repressors → modulates Pol II activity

RNA Polymerase III (Pol III): Pol III transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL RNA (SRP RNA); Pol III is inhibited by α-amanitin at HIGH concentrations (~100 μg/mL); Pol III promoters: internal (type 1: 5S rRNA [box A + box C]; type 2: tRNA [box A + box B; TFIIIC → TFIIIB → Pol III]) or external (type 3: U6 snRNA)
RNA Polymerase IV: RNA Pol IV and Pol V exist in PLANTS (for RNA-directed DNA methylation / siRNA production); they do NOT exist in animals; this is a distractor
explanation: Eukaryotic RNA polymerases — summary + α-amanitin sensitivity: Pol I: nucleolar; rRNA (45S → 28S/18S/5.8S); NOT sensitive to α-amanitin; Pol II: nucleoplasmic; mRNA, snRNA (except U6), miRNA, lncRNA; VERY sensitive (low dose); Pol III: nucleoplasmic; tRNA, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL RNA; MODERATELY sensitive (high dose); Mitochondrial RNA polymerase (POLRMT): single-subunit (related to T7 phage RNAP); transcribes mitochondrial DNA (heavy + light strand polycistronic transcripts → processed by tRNA punctuation model [RNase P + ELAC2]); NOT sensitive to α-amanitin; sensitive to rifampicin is a MYTH (rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNAP [β subunit], not mitochondrial RNAP); α-Amanitin: bicyclic octapeptide from Amanita phalloides (death cap mushroom); binds Pol II bridge helix → prevents translocation → stalls transcription; ingestion: latent period 6-12 hrs → GI phase (severe gastroenteritis) → apparent recovery → hepatotoxic phase (acute liver failure day 3-5) → renal failure → death; treatment: supportive + NAC + penicillin G + silibinin (milk thistle extract, competitive inhibitor of OATP1B3 hepatocyte uptake of amanitin) + liver transplant if needed.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which epigenetic modification at CpG dinucleotides is catalyzed by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) and is associated with transcriptional silencing?
options: Histone H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3): H3K4me3 is a histone modification (not DNA methylation); H3K4me3 marks ACTIVE promoters (deposited by MLL/COMPASS family SET-domain methyltransferases); associated with open chromatin/euchromatin

5-Methylcytosine (5mC): DNMTs (DNA methyltransferases) catalyze the transfer of a methyl group from SAM to the C5 position of CYTOSINE in CpG dinucleotides → 5-methylcytosine (5mC); 5mC → TRANSCRIPTIONAL SILENCING: (a) directly impedes transcription factor binding (methylated CpG in promoter → ↓TF access); (b) recruits methyl-CpG binding proteins (MeCP2, MBD1-4) → recruit HDACs + chromatin remodeling complexes (NuRD/Mi-2) → histone deacetylation + chromatin compaction → ↓transcription; DNMTs: DNMT1 (maintenance methyltransferase: preferentially methylates HEMI-methylated CpG sites [after replication, new strand is unmethylated] → restores full methylation → preserves methylation pattern through cell division; recruited to replication fork by UHRF1/NP95 [recognizes hemi-methylated CpG via SRA domain]); DNMT3A + DNMT3B (de novo methyltransferases: establish NEW methylation patterns [embryogenesis, differentiation]; DNMT3L is catalytically inactive but stimulates DNMT3A/B); CpG islands: ~70% of promoters contain CpG islands (CG-rich regions, 200+ bp, observed/expected CpG ratio >0.6); most CpG islands are UNMETHYLATED in normal cells → genes transcriptionally competent; cancer: global DNA HYPOmethylation (→ genome instability, reactivation of transposons, oncogene activation) + promoter-specific HYPERmethylation of tumor suppressors (RB1, p16/CDKN2A, MLH1, BRCA1, VHL → silencing); 5-azacytidine/decitabine (DNMT inhibitors → ↓DNA methylation → reactivate silenced tumor suppressors; used in MDS/AML); TET enzymes (TET1/2/3): 5mC → [TET, Fe2+, α-KG, O2] → 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) → 5-formylcytosine (5fC) → 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC) → [TDG + BER] → unmethylated C (active DNA demethylation pathway); TET2 mutations in AML/MDS → ↓5hmC → hypermethylation; D-2-HG (from IDH1/2 mutations) inhibits TET → similar hypermethylation

N6-methyladenine (6mA): N6-methyladenine is a DNA modification found primarily in PROKARYOTES (restriction-modification systems: methylated DNA is 'self', unmethylated is 'foreign' → cleaved by restriction enzymes); also Dam methylase (GATC: adenine methylation) in E. coli → regulates replication initiation (hemimethylated oriC), MMR (MutH recognizes unmethylated GATC on new strand → nicks new strand); 6mA has been detected in eukaryotes but its role is minor compared to 5mC

Histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3): H3K27me3 is a histone modification catalyzed by PRC2 (EZH2 methyltransferase); it marks REPRESSED chromatin (Polycomb-mediated silencing); it is NOT DNA methylation
explanation: Histone modifications — summary: ACTIVATING marks: H3K4me3 (active promoters; writers: MLL/SET1; readers: PHD fingers, chromodomains); H3K36me3 (active gene bodies; writer: SETD2; prevents cryptic intragenic transcription); H3K79me2/3 (active transcription; writer: DOT1L [non-SET domain]; DOT1L inhibitors in MLL-rearranged leukemia); H3/H4 acetylation (open chromatin; writers: HATs [CBP/p300, GCN5, PCAF, Tip60]; readers: bromodomains; erasers: HDACs [class I-IV]); REPRESSIVE marks: H3K9me2/3 (heterochromatin, constitutive silencing; writer: SUV39H1/2; reader: HP1 [chromodomain]); H3K27me3 (Polycomb-mediated facultative heterochromatin; writer: PRC2/EZH2; reader: PRC1 chromodomain; EZH2 inhibitor: tazemetostat → EZH2-mutant FL/epithelioid sarcoma); H4K20me3 (pericentromeric heterochromatin); Bivalent chromatin: H3K4me3 + H3K27me3 at SAME promoter in ESCs → gene poised for activation or silencing upon differentiation; resolves to one mark during lineage commitment.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Cystinuria is caused by defective renal and intestinal transport of which group of amino acids?
options: Dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, arginine, lysine): Cystinuria (SLC3A1 [type A] or SLC7A9 [type B] mutations → defective rBAT/b0,+AT heterodimeric transporter) → impaired reabsorption of DIBASIC amino acids in the proximal tubule (S1-S3) and intestinal absorption: Cystine (disulfide of two cysteines) + Ornithine + Lysine + Arginine (mnemonic: COLA); cystine is the LEAST soluble amino acid → precipitates in urine (especially at pH <7) → CYSTINE KIDNEY STONES (hexagonal crystals on urinanalysis — pathognomonic; positive cyanide-nitroprusside test [purple color]); cystinuria is one of the most common inborn errors of amino acid transport (1:7,000); AR; clinical: recurrent nephrolithiasis from childhood (cystine stones are radio-opaque but less dense than calcium stones; staghorn calculi possible); treatment: (1) ↑fluid intake (maintain urine output >3 L/day → ↓cystine concentration below solubility threshold of ~250 mg/L); (2) urine alkalinization (K-citrate/Na-bicarb → pH >7.0-7.5 → ↑cystine solubility; cystine solubility doubles from pH 7 to pH 8); (3) D-penicillamine or tiopronin (thiol drugs: form mixed disulfide with cysteine [penicillamine-cysteine] → more soluble than cystine [50x] → ↑excretion; side effects of D-pen: nephrotic syndrome, pancytopenia, autoimmune; tiopronin preferred — fewer side effects); (4) captopril (thiol group → similar but weaker effect); NOTE: cystinuria is NOT cystinosis (cystinosis: CTNS/cystinosin mutations → defective lysosomal cystine transport → cystine accumulates IN lysosomes → Fanconi syndrome + renal failure + corneal crystals; treated with CYSTEAMINE [enters lysosome → reacts with cystine → cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide → exits via lysine transporter])

Aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan): defective transport of aromatic amino acids is NOT cystinuria; Hartnup disease involves neutral amino acids (including aromatic) but not cystinuria

Branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine): BCAAs have their own transporters; their defective catabolism → MSUD (not a transport defect); cystinuria involves dibasic amino acids, not BCAAs
Acidic amino acids (glutamate, aspartate): dicarboxylic aminoaciduria (rare) involves defective transport of acidic amino acids; cystinuria involves dibasic amino acids
explanation: Amino acid transport disorders: (1) Cystinuria (SLC3A1/SLC7A9 → b0,+AT/rBAT): ↓dibasic AA reabsorption (COLA) → cystine stones; (2) Hartnup disease (SLC6A19 → B0AT1): ↓neutral AA (including Trp) reabsorption → ↓Trp → ↓niacin synthesis → pellagra-like symptoms (photosensitive rash, cerebellar ataxia, psychiatric); triggered by poor diet/stress; treated with nicotinamide + high-protein diet; (3) Lysinuric protein intolerance (LPI; SLC7A7 → y+LAT1): ↓dibasic AA (Lys, Arg, Orn) efflux from cells → ↓Orn + ↓Arg → impaired urea cycle → hyperammonemia + growth failure + osteoporosis + protein aversion; (4) Iminoglycinuria (SLC36A2 → PAT2): benign ↑urinary Pro, OH-Pro, Gly; (5) Blue diaper syndrome: ↓Trp absorption → unabsorbed Trp → bacterial metabolism → indole → indicanuria → blue diaper (indigo).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which tumor marker is most useful for monitoring hepatocellular carcinoma and is also elevated in certain germ cell tumors?
options: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA): CEA is a glycoprotein tumor marker primarily associated with COLORECTAL CANCER (also ↑ in pancreatic, gastric, breast, lung); used for monitoring recurrence/treatment response, not initial diagnosis; CEA is NOT the primary marker for HCC

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP): AFP (alpha-1-fetoprotein): 70-kDa glycoprotein, major FETAL serum protein (synthesized by fetal liver + yolk sac; analogous to albumin in adults); AFP normally declines after birth (adult normal: <10-20 ng/mL); ↑AFP clinical significance: (1) HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA (HCC): AFP >400 ng/mL is highly suggestive of HCC in the setting of cirrhosis; used for surveillance (AFP + ultrasound every 6 months in cirrhotic patients) and monitoring treatment response; AFP-L3 (lens culinaris agglutinin-reactive fraction of AFP) → more specific for HCC (↑AFP-L3% suggests HCC over benign liver disease); (2) GERM CELL TUMORS: AFP ↑ in yolk sac tumors (endodermal sinus tumors; most common testicular tumor in children <3 years; Schiller-Duval bodies) + mixed GCTs with yolk sac component; also ↑ in embryonal carcinoma (variable) + hepatoid variant; AFP is NOT produced by pure seminomas or pure choriocarcinomas (β-hCG is the marker for choriocarcinoma); GCT markers: AFP (yolk sac), β-hCG (choriocarcinoma, also ↑ in some seminomas [syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells]), LDH (bulk/prognosis, all GCTs); (3) PREGNANCY: AFP is measured in 2nd trimester maternal serum screening (quad screen: AFP + β-hCG + inhibin A + uE3): ↑AFP → open neural tube defects (anencephaly, spina bifida), abdominal wall defects (omphalocele, gastroschisis), multiple gestation; ↓AFP → Down syndrome (trisomy 21: ↓AFP + ↑β-hCG + ↑inhibin A + ↓uE3); (4) Benign: ↑AFP in hepatitis, cirrhosis (usually <400), pregnancy (physiologic)
CA-125: CA-125 is the tumor marker for OVARIAN CANCER (especially epithelial serous carcinoma); also ↑ in endometriosis, PID, pregnancy, peritoneal disease; NOT the primary marker for HCC
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA): PSA is a serine protease produced by prostate epithelium; ↑PSA in prostate cancer, BPH, prostatitis; NOT related to HCC
explanation: Major tumor markers — exam-relevant: AFP: HCC + yolk sac tumors + NTDs (prenatal); CEA: colorectal cancer monitoring (also ↑ pancreatic, gastric, breast); CA-125: ovarian cancer (epithelial); CA 19-9: pancreatic cancer (also biliary); CA 15-3 / CA 27-29: breast cancer monitoring; PSA: prostate cancer (also BPH); β-hCG: choriocarcinoma + pregnancy monitoring; LDH: non-specific (lymphoma, GCTs, tissue damage); calcitonin: medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC; C-cells → calcitonin; RET mutations → MEN2A/2B); thyroglobulin: differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary/follicular; monitoring post-thyroidectomy); chromogranin A: neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid, pheochromocytoma, neuroblastoma); NSE (neuron-specific enolase): SCLC, neuroblastoma; S-100: melanoma; HE4 (WFDC2): ovarian cancer (with CA-125 in ROMA algorithm); 5-HIAA (urine): carcinoid syndrome (serotonin → [MAO] → 5-HIAA); VMA/HVA (urine): neuroblastoma + pheochromocytoma (catecholamine metabolites).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is the rate-limiting enzyme of which metabolic pathway?
options: Glycolysis: the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis is phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1: F6P + ATP → F1,6BP + ADP; activated by AMP, F2,6BP; inhibited by ATP, citrate); G6PD is NOT part of glycolysis

Pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt): G6PD catalyzes the FIRST and RATE-LIMITING step of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP/HMP shunt): G6P + NADP+ → [G6PD] → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH; then: 6-phosphogluconolactone → [lactonase] → 6-phosphogluconate → [6PGD, 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, also NADP+ → NADPH + CO2] → ribulose-5-P; total OXIDATIVE phase: 1 G6P → ribulose-5-P + 2 NADPH + CO2; NON-OXIDATIVE phase: ribulose-5-P → [isomerase] → ribose-5-phosphate (for nucleotide synthesis) or → [epimerase] → xylulose-5-P; transketolase (TK, TPP-dependent) + transaldolase (TA) → interconvert C3/C4/C5/C6/C7 sugars → link PPP to glycolysis (G3P, F6P); PPP functions: (1) NADPH production (for: reductive biosynthesis [fatty acid synthesis, cholesterol synthesis], glutathione reduction [GSSG → GSH by GR], CYP450 reactions, respiratory burst [NADPH oxidase → O2⁻], NO synthesis [NOS]); (2) Ribose-5-P for nucleotide/nucleic acid synthesis; G6PD deficiency (X-linked): most common enzymopathy (~400 million affected worldwide); ↓NADPH → ↓GSH → RBCs vulnerable to oxidative stress → oxidized Hb → Heinz bodies (denatured Hb aggregates → attach to RBC membrane → removed by splenic macrophages → bite cells) → hemolytic anemia; triggers: fava beans (favism: vicine/convicine → divicine/isouramil → generate ROS), infections, drugs (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase); G6PD variants: A- (African, mild, 10-60% activity), Mediterranean (severe, <10% activity), Canton (Asian)
Gluconeogenesis: rate-limiting enzyme is fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase-1: F1,6BP → F6P; bypasses PFK-1); G6PD is NOT part of gluconeogenesis
Glycogen synthesis: rate-limiting enzyme is glycogen synthase (GS: UDP-glucose + glycogen primer → α-1,4-glycosidic bond); G6PD is NOT involved
explanation: Pentose phosphate pathway — clinical correlations: Tissues with high PPP activity: RBCs (NADPH for GSH → no mitochondria → PPP is only NADPH source), liver (NADPH for FA synthesis + CYP450 + bile acid synthesis), adipose (NADPH for FA synthesis), adrenal cortex (NADPH for steroid synthesis), lactating mammary gland, gonads; PPP regulation: G6PD regulated by NADP+/NADPH ratio: ↑NADP+ (↓NADPH consumption) → ↑G6PD activity → ↑NADPH; this is demand-driven — when NADPH is consumed (reductive synthesis, oxidative stress), NADP+ rises → drives PPP; Wernicke-Korsakoff and PPP: transketolase (non-oxidative phase) requires TPP (thiamine); ↓thiamine → ↓TK → impaired PPP non-oxidative phase → ↓recycling of pentose phosphates → accumulation; this is the basis of the TK activity assay (erythrocyte TK + TPP effect → measures thiamine status); TPP effect >25% suggests thiamine deficiency.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency leads to accumulation of deoxyguanosine and primarily affects which cell lineage?
