options: T cells: PNP deficiency → accumulation of deoxyguanosine (and deoxyinosine) → dGuo taken up by T cells → phosphorylated to dGTP by deoxycytidine kinase (dCK) and dGuo kinase → ↑dGTP in T cells → inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (RNR, allosteric inhibition at substrate specificity site) → ↓dATP/dCTP/dTTP → DNA synthesis blockade → T-cell apoptosis (T cells are particularly sensitive because they have high dCK/dGK activity → accumulate dGTP more than other cells); PNP deficiency: AR, PNP gene; PNP normally: inosine → [PNP] → hypoxanthine + ribose-1-P; guanosine → [PNP] → guanine + ribose-1-P; deoxyinosine → [PNP] → hypoxanthine + dR-1-P; deoxyguanosine → [PNP] → guanine + dR-1-P; deficiency → ↑inosine, ↑guanosine, ↑dGuo, ↑dIno → ↑dGTP (in T cells) → ↓T cells (SCID-like T-cell immunodeficiency, B cells relatively spared initially); clinical: recurrent infections (viral, opportunistic), autoimmunity (2/3 of patients → autoimmune hemolytic anemia, SLE-like), neurological dysfunction (↓uric acid [since PNP feeds into xanthine → uric acid; ↓PNP → ↓uric acid → hypouricemia is a clue]); compare with ADA deficiency: ↑dATP → kills BOTH T and B cells → SCID (T-B-NK-); PNP deficiency: T-B+NK- or T-low immunodeficiency

B cells: PNP deficiency primarily affects T CELLS, not B cells; B-cell numbers are initially preserved (though may decline over time as T-cell help is lost); compare: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton: BTK mutations → arrested B-cell development at pre-B stage → ↓all Ig classes, ↓B cells, normal T cells)

Neutrophils: PNP deficiency does NOT primarily affect neutrophils; neutropenia can occur in some purine metabolism disorders but is not the hallmark of PNP deficiency; severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann: HAX1 mutations → ↓neutrophils; ELANE mutations → cyclic neutropenia)

Red blood cells: while dGTP accumulates in RBCs too, the primary clinical impact of PNP deficiency is on T-cell immunity, not erythropoiesis; ADA deficiency can affect RBCs (↑dATP in RBCs used as diagnostic marker) but the clinical phenotype is immunodeficiency
explanation: Purine metabolism immunodeficiency — ADA vs PNP: ADA (adenosine deaminase) deficiency: ↑adenosine + ↑deoxyadenosine → ↑dATP → inhibits RNR (more broadly) → kills T + B + NK cells → T-B-NK- SCID (most severe combined immunodeficiency; ~15-20% of all SCID); ↑dATP in RBCs (diagnostic); ↑AdoHcy (S-adenosylhomocysteine: adenosine inhibits SAH hydrolase → ↑SAH → inhibits SAM-dependent methylation → may contribute to toxicity); treatment: PEG-ADA (enzyme replacement), HSCT, gene therapy (first successful human gene therapy: ADA-SCID [1990 trial; more recent lentiviral GT: Strimvelis → approved EU 2016]). PNP deficiency: ↑dGuo → ↑dGTP → selective T-cell toxicity → T-cell immunodeficiency (T low, B initially normal); ↓uric acid (hypouricemia — KEY diagnostic clue; because PNP is needed to produce xanthine → uric acid); autoimmunity common. Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency): ↑PRPP → ↑de novo purine synthesis → ↑uric acid → gout + nephrolithiasis + self-mutilation (lip/finger biting) + intellectual disability + dystonia; X-linked; ↑uric acid (HYPERuricemia — opposite of PNP deficiency).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In DNA replication, which enzyme removes RNA primers and fills the resulting gaps with DNA?
options: DNA polymerase α-primase: Pol α-primase initiates DNA synthesis: primase synthesizes short RNA primer (~8-12 nt) → Pol α extends with ~20-30 nt of DNA → primer-template junction → handed off to Pol ε (leading) or Pol δ (lagging); Pol α has NO 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading) activity; it does NOT remove RNA primers

DNA polymerase I (in E. coli) / RNase H1 + FEN1 + DNA polymerase δ (in eukaryotes): In E. coli: DNA Pol I has 5'→3' exonuclease activity → removes RNA primers ahead of it + fills gaps with DNA simultaneously (nick translation); In EUKARYOTES: RNA primer removal is more complex: RNase H1 (degrades RNA in RNA-DNA hybrid, leaving 1 ribonucleotide at 5' end that RNase H cannot remove) → FEN1 (flap endonuclease 1: removes the remaining RNA [+ any displaced DNA flap created during Pol δ strand displacement synthesis]) → DNA Pol δ (fills the gap with DNA) → DNA Ligase I (seals the nick between Okazaki fragments); alternatively: Pol δ strand displacement → creates 5' flap → FEN1 cleaves flap → ligation; Dna2 helicase/nuclease may assist with long flaps; POINT: the question is testing primer removal; in eukaryotes the functional equivalent involves RNase H1 + FEN1 + Pol δ working together; Pol δ performs the gap-filling synthesis; in prokaryotes Pol I performs both removal and gap-filling

DNA polymerase ε: Pol ε is the primary LEADING STRAND polymerase (high processivity with PCNA, 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading); Pol ε does NOT remove RNA primers (that function is on the lagging strand where Pol δ + RNase H1 + FEN1 operate)
DNA ligase I: Ligase I seals nicks (joins 3'-OH to 5'-phosphate) between Okazaki fragments after gap filling; ligase does NOT remove RNA primers or fill gaps — it only seals the final nick
explanation: DNA replication — eukaryotic overview: Origins of replication: ORC (origin recognition complex) + Cdc6 + Cdt1 → load MCM2-7 (replicative helicase, 3'→5', minichromosome maintenance; loaded in G1 [licensing]; activated in S by CDK + DDK → CMG complex [Cdc45-MCM-GINS]); Replication fork: Helicase (CMG/MCM): unwinds dsDNA; SSB (RPA): stabilizes ssDNA; Topoisomerase (Top I ahead of fork: relieves positive supercoiling; Top II also contributes; Top II [= gyrase in bacteria → target of fluoroquinolones]); Primase (part of Pol α-primase): RNA primer; Leading strand: Pol ε (continuous, 3'→5' exonuclease [proofreading]); Lagging strand: Pol α (primer+short extension) → Pol δ (extends Okazaki fragments, ~100-200 nt; proofreading; processivity enhanced by PCNA [sliding clamp, loaded by RFC]); Primer removal: RNase H1 + FEN1 + Pol δ gap-filling → Ligase I seals; Telomeres: telomerase (TERT [reverse transcriptase] + TERC [RNA template]) extends 3' overhang → Pol α-primase fills lagging strand; telomerase active in stem cells, germ cells, ~90% of cancers → replicative immortality; drugs: imetelstat (telomerase inhibitor, for MF/MDS).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In collagen biosynthesis, what is the role of lysyl oxidase?
options: Hydroxylation of proline residues: prolyl hydroxylase (P4H: prolyl-4-hydroxylase; also P3H: prolyl-3-hydroxylase) hydroxylates proline → hydroxyproline (4-Hyp mainly); requires Fe2+, α-KG, O2, ASCORBATE (vitamin C); hydroxyproline stabilizes collagen triple helix via hydrogen bonding; ↓vitamin C → ↓hydroxyproline → unstable helix → SCURVY; this is NOT the role of lysyl oxidase

Hydroxylation of lysine residues: lysyl hydroxylase (PLOD1/2/3: procollagen-lysine, 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase) hydroxylates lysine → hydroxylysine; requires same cofactors as prolyl hydroxylase (Fe2+, α-KG, O2, ascorbate); hydroxylysine serves as attachment site for galactose and glucosylgalactose (O-linked glycosylation of collagen); this is NOT lysyl oxidase

Cross-linking of collagen fibrils in the extracellular space: LYSYL OXIDASE (LOX, copper-dependent amine oxidase): catalyzes the oxidative deamination of ε-amino groups of LYSINE and HYDROXYLYSINE residues in collagen (and elastin) → converts to ALLYSINE (α-aminoadipic-δ-semialdehyde); allysine residues spontaneously undergo condensation reactions with other allysine or hydroxylysine residues to form COVALENT CROSS-LINKS (aldol condensation → aldol cross-link; Schiff base → dehydro-lysinonorleucine; etc.; mature cross-links: pyridinoline [PYD] + deoxypyridinoline [DPD] → measured in urine as bone resorption markers); LOX is EXTRACELLULAR (secreted as pro-LOX → cleaved by BMP-1/procollagen C-proteinase → active LOX); LOX requires COPPER as cofactor (Cu2+ at active site + lysyl tyrosylquinone [LTQ] cofactor); LOX also cross-links ELASTIN (desmosine + isodesmosine cross-links → unique to elastin; formed from 4 lysine residues [3 allysine + 1 lysine] → measured as elastin degradation markers); clinical: ↓LOX → ↓cross-linking → weak connective tissue: (a) COPPER DEFICIENCY (Menkes disease: ATP7A mutations → ↓Cu absorption → ↓LOX + ↓ceruloplasmin + ↓cytochrome c oxidase + ↓dopamine β-hydroxylase → kinky hair [pili torti] + neurodegeneration + connective tissue laxity + hypothermia); (b) LATHYRISM: β-aminopropionitrile (BAPN, from Lathyrus sativus sweet peas) → irreversibly inhibits LOX → ↓cross-linking → aortic aneurysms, skeletal deformities; (c) LOX inhibition by homocysteine may contribute to vascular disease in homocystinuria; (d) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type V (rare, ↓LOX → skin hyperextensibility)

Cleavage of N- and C-terminal propeptides: procollagen N-proteinase (ADAMTS-2) cleaves N-propeptide + procollagen C-proteinase (BMP-1/tolloid) cleaves C-propeptide → converts procollagen to tropocollagen → self-assembly into fibrils; ADAMTS-2 deficiency → Ehlers-Danlos dermatosparaxis type (type VIIC); PICP and PINP (procollagen type I C-/N-terminal propeptide) → serum markers of bone FORMATION; this is NOT the role of lysyl oxidase
explanation: Collagen biosynthesis — complete steps: INTRACELLULAR: (1) Translation of pre-procollagen (signal peptide → RER); (2) Signal peptide cleavage → procollagen α-chain; (3) Hydroxylation: prolyl hydroxylase (4-Hyp [most common modified AA in collagen] + 3-Hyp) + lysyl hydroxylase (5-Hyl); requires Fe2+, α-KG, O2, ascorbate; (4) O-linked glycosylation of hydroxylysine (galactose ± glucose); (5) Triple helix formation: C→N direction; registration peptides (C-propeptide) align chains; Gly must be at every 3rd position (Gly-X-Y repeat; X often Pro, Y often Hyp); proline + hydroxyproline provide rigidity (imino acid ring restricts rotation); (6) Quality control: only properly folded triple helix passes ER QC → Golgi → secretory vesicles; misfolded → ER retention → UPR → degraded (this is why dominant-negative OI mutations [structural] are more severe than null mutations [quantitative]). EXTRACELLULAR: (7) Propeptide cleavage: ADAMTS-2 (N) + BMP-1 (C) → tropocollagen; (8) Self-assembly: tropocollagen → staggered quarter-stagger array → fibril (67 nm D-period banding on EM); (9) Covalent cross-linking: LOX (Cu-dependent) → allysine → cross-links; MATURE cross-links increase with age → tissue stiffening.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme deficiency causes non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (glycine encephalopathy)?
options: Glycine cleavage system (GCS): Non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH / glycine encephalopathy): AR disorder caused by defects in the GLYCINE CLEAVAGE SYSTEM (GCS, also called glycine decarboxylase complex); GCS is a mitochondrial multienzyme complex: P-protein (GLDC gene, pyridoxal phosphate-dependent glycine decarboxylase; most commonly mutated in NKH ~80%), T-protein (AMT gene, aminomethyltransferase; transfers one-carbon unit to THF → CH2-THF), H-protein (GCSH gene, lipoamide-containing hydrogen carrier), L-protein (DLD gene, dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase; same as E3 component shared with PDC, OGDH, BCKDH — DLD mutations → combined deficiency of all these complexes); GCS normally: Gly → CO2 + NH3 + CH2-THF (provides one-carbon units); NKH: ↑glycine in plasma AND CSF (CSF:plasma glycine ratio >0.08 — key diagnostic ratio; normally <0.02); glycine is an excitatory co-agonist at the NMDA receptor (binds glycine site/GluN1 subunit → required for NMDA receptor activation along with glutamate); ↑↑glycine → NMDA receptor overactivation → excitotoxicity → seizures + encephalopathy; also glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in brainstem/spinal cord (glycine receptors → Cl- influx → inhibition); neonatal NKH: lethargy, hypotonia, myoclonic seizures, apnea, hiccups (diaphragmatic myoclonus), burst-suppression on EEG, death or severe disability; treatment: limited efficacy — Na-benzoate (↓plasma glycine via hippurate conjugation), NMDA receptor antagonists (dextromethorphan, ketamine — limited benefit), anticonvulsants; prognosis: poor for severe neonatal form

Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT): SHMT (SHMT1 cytoplasmic, SHMT2 mitochondrial) catalyzes: Ser + THF ⇌ Gly + CH2-THF (reversible); SHMT deficiency is extremely rare and does NOT cause the classic NKH phenotype

Glycine transaminase: glycine can be transaminated to glyoxylate → oxalate; deficiency of alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT, peroxisomal, liver) → primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1: ↑oxalate → calcium oxalate kidney stones → nephrocalcinosis → ESRD; treated with lumasiran [siRNA targeting glycolate oxidase → ↓oxalate]); this is NOT NKH
D-amino acid oxidase: DAAO metabolizes D-amino acids (including D-serine, an NMDA receptor co-agonist); DAAO is not deficient in NKH
explanation: Glycine metabolism — complete: Sources: diet, serine (SHMT: Ser ⇌ Gly + CH2-THF), threonine (threonine dehydrogenase in some species), collagen degradation (Gly is 33% of collagen); Fates: (1) GCS (major degradation pathway in liver, brain; mitochondrial → CO2 + NH3 + CH2-THF); (2) SHMT (reversible: Gly → Ser); (3) conjugation with benzoate → hippurate (GLYAT); (4) conjugation with bile acids (glycocholic acid); (5) heme synthesis (Gly + succinyl-CoA → [ALAS, PLP] → δ-ALA); (6) purine synthesis (Gly contributes C4, C5, N7 of purine ring); (7) glutathione (GSH = γ-Glu-Cys-Gly; Gly is one of 3 amino acids); (8) creatine (Gly + Arg → [AGAT] → GAA); (9) collagen (every 3rd residue is Gly); (10) porphyrin/heme via ALA; (11) inhibitory neurotransmitter (brainstem/spinal cord: glycine receptors [GlyR, ligand-gated Cl- channels]; strychnine blocks GlyR → loss of inhibition → convulsions/muscle spasms); (12) excitatory co-agonist at NMDA receptor (GluN1 subunit glycine-binding site).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis. In which subcellular compartment does this reaction occur?
options: Mitochondrial matrix: CPS I (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) is mitochondrial and functions in the UREA CYCLE (NH3 + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate; activated by NAG [N-acetylglutamate]; CPS I deficiency → hyperammonemia, most severe UCD); CPS I is NOT CPS II

Cytoplasm (cytosol): CPS II is CYTOPLASMIC (cytosolic); CPS II: Gln + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate + Glu + 2 ADP + Pi (uses GLUTAMINE as nitrogen source, not free NH3 like CPS I; does NOT require NAG); CPS II is part of the trifunctional enzyme CAD (CPS II + ATCase + DHOase) in humans; CAD is cytoplasmic → entire early pyrimidine synthesis occurs in the cytoplasm (until DHODH, which is on the inner mitochondrial membrane); CPS II regulation: ACTIVATED by ATP + PRPP (↑purine synthesis → ↑PRPP → ↑CPS II → coordinate ↑pyrimidine synthesis; phosphorylation by MAPK → ↑CPS II activity [growth factor signaling → ↑nucleotide synthesis for proliferation]); INHIBITED by UTP (end-product feedback inhibition); KEY DISTINCTION: CPS I (mitochondrial, urea cycle, uses NH3, requires NAG) vs CPS II (cytoplasmic, pyrimidine synthesis, uses Gln, does NOT require NAG, part of CAD); this is a VERY frequently tested comparison
Peroxisomes: peroxisomes are involved in VLCFA β-oxidation, plasmalogen synthesis, bile acid synthesis, and H2O2 metabolism; CPS II is not peroxisomal
Endoplasmic reticulum: the ER is involved in protein synthesis/folding, lipid synthesis, Ca2+ storage, drug metabolism (CYP450); CPS II is not ER-localized
explanation: CPS I vs CPS II — critical comparison for exams: Feature | CPS I | CPS II: Location: mitochondrial matrix | cytoplasm; Pathway: urea cycle | de novo pyrimidine synthesis; N source: free NH3 (ammonia) | Gln (glutamine amide N); Activator: NAG (N-acetylglutamate, allosteric, obligate) | ATP, PRPP; Inhibitor: none (regulated mainly by NAG availability) | UTP (end-product); Associated enzyme complex: none (monofunctional) | CAD (trifunctional: CPS II + ATCase + DHOase); Deficiency: CPS I deficiency → hyperammonemia (most severe UCD; presents in neonatal period with lethargy, vomiting, cerebral edema) | CPS II deficiency → extremely rare; Product: carbamoyl phosphate → [OTC] → citrulline (urea cycle) | carbamoyl phosphate → [ATCase] → carbamoyl-aspartate (pyrimidine synthesis); NAG: synthesized by NAGS (N-acetylglutamate synthase; Arg is activator); NAGS deficiency → hyperammonemia (treated with N-carbamylglutamate [Carbaglu], a NAG analogue that directly activates CPS I).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which cardiac biomarker is most specific for myocardial injury and remains elevated for the longest duration after acute myocardial infarction?
options: Creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB): CK-MB is the cardiac-specific isoform of creatine kinase; rises 4-6 hrs, peaks 12-24 hrs, normalizes 48-72 hrs after MI; CK-MB was previously the gold standard but has been REPLACED by troponins for MI diagnosis; CK-MB is still useful for detecting REINFARCTION (because it normalizes faster than troponin; a re-elevation of CK-MB after initial decline suggests new injury)

Cardiac troponin I or T (cTnI/cTnT): Cardiac troponins are the MOST SPECIFIC and SENSITIVE biomarkers for myocardial injury and are the gold standard for MI diagnosis; cTnI and cTnT are structural proteins of the cardiac sarcomere thin filament (troponin complex: TnI [inhibitory, prevents actin-myosin interaction], TnC [Ca2+-binding], TnT [binds tropomyosin]); cardiac-specific isoforms (cTnI [TNNI3] and cTnT [TNNT2]) differ from skeletal muscle isoforms → detected by specific antibodies; kinetics: rise 3-6 hrs (hs-cTn [high-sensitivity] detects within 1-3 hrs), peak 12-24 hrs, REMAIN ELEVATED 7-14 DAYS (cTnI: 7-10 days; cTnT: 10-14 days; longest duration of all cardiac biomarkers); high-sensitivity troponin (hs-cTn): 4th generation assays detect very low levels → enables earlier diagnosis + better rule-out (0/1h or 0/3h algorithms); ↑troponin = myocardial injury (not necessarily MI; type 1 MI: plaque rupture + thrombus; type 2 MI: supply-demand mismatch [tachycardia, anemia, hypotension]; non-MI troponin elevation: myocarditis, PE, heart failure, sepsis, renal failure, takotsubo, cardiac contusion)

Myoglobin: myoglobin is the EARLIEST biomarker to rise after MI (1-3 hrs), peaks 6-10 hrs, normalizes 12-24 hrs; highly SENSITIVE but NOT SPECIFIC (also elevated in skeletal muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure); no longer routinely used since hs-cTn is available

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): LDH rises 24-48 hrs, peaks 3-6 days, normalizes 8-14 days after MI; LDH1 (HHHH) > LDH2 (HHHM) → flipped ratio is suggestive of MI; BUT LDH is very non-specific (elevated in hemolysis, liver disease, lymphoma, many other conditions); LDH is no longer used for MI diagnosis
explanation: Cardiac biomarker timeline after acute MI: Myoglobin: rise 1-3h → peak 6-10h → normal 12-24h (fastest rise, not specific); CK-MB: rise 4-6h → peak 12-24h → normal 48-72h (useful for reinfarction detection); Troponin (conventional): rise 3-6h → peak 12-24h → normal 7-14 days (most specific, longest elevation); hs-Troponin: rise 1-3h → same peak/duration (earliest specific marker); BNP/NT-proBNP: NOT injury markers — they are markers of myocardial WALL STRESS / VOLUME OVERLOAD; BNP (brain natriuretic peptide, actually from ventricular cardiomyocytes): proBNP → [corin/furin] → BNP (active, 32 aa, short half-life ~20 min) + NT-proBNP (inactive, longer half-life ~120 min, renally cleared → ↑in CKD); BNP/NT-proBNP used for: HF diagnosis (↑BNP >100 pg/mL or ↑NT-proBNP age-stratified cutoffs), HF prognosis, monitoring treatment response, dyspnea differentiation (HF vs pulmonary); CRP/hs-CRP: inflammatory marker, not myocardial-specific; ↑hs-CRP is a cardiovascular RISK marker (chronic low-grade inflammation → ↑atherosclerosis risk).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) requires a thermostable DNA polymerase. Taq polymerase, originally isolated from which organism, is most commonly used?
options: Escherichia coli: E. coli DNA Pol I (Klenow fragment) was used in early molecular biology but is NOT thermostable (denatures at high temperatures used in PCR); E. coli grows at 37°C (mesophilic)

Thermus aquaticus: Taq polymerase is isolated from THERMUS AQUATICUS, a thermophilic bacterium discovered in hot springs of Yellowstone National Park (by Thomas Brock, 1969); Taq DNA polymerase: optimal activity at 72°C, stable at 95°C (denaturation temperature in PCR); 5'→3' polymerase activity + 5'→3' exonuclease activity; LACKS 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading) activity → error rate ~1 in 10^4 nucleotides; adds dA overhang (terminal transferase activity → 3'-dA) → allows TA cloning; PCR (Kary Mullis, 1983, Nobel Prize 1993): 3 steps per cycle: (1) Denaturation (94-95°C → separate dsDNA → ssDNA templates); (2) Annealing (50-65°C → primers bind complementary sequences); (3) Extension (72°C → Taq synthesizes new strand from primer); ~25-35 cycles → 2^n amplification (exponential); PCR components: template DNA, 2 primers (forward + reverse), dNTPs (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP), Taq polymerase, Mg2+ (cofactor), buffer; PCR variants: RT-PCR (reverse transcription PCR: RNA → cDNA [reverse transcriptase] → PCR; detects RNA [gene expression, RNA viruses]); qPCR/real-time PCR (quantitative: fluorescent probes [TaqMan] or dyes [SYBR Green] → amplification monitored in real time → Ct value inversely proportional to template amount); nested PCR (two rounds with inner primers → ↑specificity); multiplex PCR (multiple primer pairs → detect multiple targets simultaneously); digital PCR (absolute quantification without standard curve)

Thermococcus litoralis: Vent polymerase is from Thermococcus litoralis (has 3'→5' proofreading → higher fidelity than Taq; used when high accuracy is needed); but Taq is the MOST COMMONLY used PCR polymerase (question asks about Taq specifically)

Pyrococcus furiosus: Pfu polymerase is from Pyrococcus furiosus (highest fidelity commercial polymerase; strong 3'→5' proofreading; but slower and more expensive than Taq); Pfu is NOT the source of Taq
explanation: Molecular biology techniques — exam-relevant: PCR: exponential amplification of specific DNA (see above); Southern blot (Edwin Southern): DNA → restriction enzyme digestion → agarose gel electrophoresis → transfer to membrane → hybridize with labeled DNA PROBE → detect specific DNA sequences; used for: gene rearrangements, RFLP, CGG repeat expansions (fragile X); Northern blot: RNA on membrane → hybridize with DNA/RNA probe → detect mRNA expression; Western blot: proteins → SDS-PAGE → transfer to membrane → antibody detection; confirmatory test for HIV (detect anti-HIV antibodies); ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay): antibody-based detection; sandwich ELISA (most common): capture Ab + antigen + detection Ab-enzyme → substrate → color; used for: HIV screening (4th gen: p24 antigen + anti-HIV Ab), HBsAg, pregnancy test (hCG); FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization): fluorescent DNA probe → hybridize to chromosomes/cells → detect chromosome abnormalities (translocations, aneuploidies, gene amplification [HER2]); Sanger sequencing: dideoxy chain termination (ddNTPs → terminate DNA synthesis → fragments of all lengths → separate by capillary electrophoresis → read sequence); NGS (next-gen sequencing): massively parallel sequencing → whole genome/exome/transcriptome; CRISPR-Cas9: guide RNA (sgRNA) → Cas9 endonuclease → site-specific DSB → gene editing (NHEJ [knockout] or HDR [knock-in]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which lipoprotein is responsible for transporting dietary (exogenous) triglycerides from the intestine to peripheral tissues?
options: VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein): VLDL transports ENDOGENOUS triglycerides (synthesized in the LIVER) to peripheral tissues; VLDL is assembled in hepatocytes: ApoB-100 (full-length; synthesized on RER → lipidated by MTP [microsomal triglyceride transfer protein] → nascent VLDL → Golgi → secretion); VLDL → [LPL] → IDL → [hepatic lipase/HTGL + further LPL] → LDL; VLDL carries endogenous TG, NOT dietary TG

Chylomicrons: Chylomicrons (CM) transport DIETARY (exogenous) triglycerides from the INTESTINE to peripheral tissues; chylomicron assembly: dietary lipids (TG, cholesterol, fat-soluble vitamins) absorbed by enterocytes → re-esterified in SER → packaged with ApoB-48 (truncated form of ApoB; B-48 is 48% of full ApoB-100; intestine-specific; produced by ApoB mRNA editing [APOBEC1: C→U editing at codon 2153 → UAA stop codon → truncated protein → ApoB-48]); MTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) loads lipids onto ApoB-48 → nascent chylomicron → secreted into LYMPH (lacteals) → thoracic duct → bloodstream (left subclavian vein); in plasma: nascent CM acquires ApoC-II (activator of LPL) + ApoE (hepatic receptor ligand) from HDL; LPL (lipoprotein lipase, on capillary endothelium of adipose/muscle/heart; requires ApoC-II as cofactor; requires GPIHBP1 for endothelial anchoring): hydrolyzes TG → FA + glycerol → FA taken up by tissues; chylomicron remnant (depleted of TG, enriched in cholesterol esters + ApoE) → taken up by LIVER via LRP1 (LDL receptor-related protein 1) + LDLR (both recognize ApoE); LPL deficiency (familial chylomicronemia, type I hyperlipoproteinemia): ↑↑chylomicrons → ↑↑TG → eruptive xanthomas + lipemia retinalis + hepatosplenomegaly + pancreatitis; also caused by ApoC-II deficiency

LDL (low-density lipoprotein): LDL transports CHOLESTEROL (cholesterol esters) to peripheral tissues (and back to liver); LDL is the end product of VLDL metabolism (VLDL → IDL → LDL); LDL contains ApoB-100 (one per particle); LDL uptake: LDLR (LDL receptor) → receptor-mediated endocytosis → endosome → lysosomal hydrolysis → free cholesterol → regulatory effects: ↓HMG-CoA reductase, ↓LDLR transcription (↓SREBP-2), ↑ACAT (cholesterol esterification for storage); LDL does NOT transport dietary TG

HDL (high-density lipoprotein): HDL mediates REVERSE CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT (peripheral cholesterol → liver); nascent HDL (discoidal, from liver/intestine: ApoA-I); ABCA1 (ATP-binding cassette A1) on macrophages/peripheral cells → effluxes free cholesterol to nascent HDL; LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase, activated by ApoA-I) → esterifies cholesterol → CE moves to core → spherical mature HDL; CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein): transfers CE from HDL → VLDL/LDL in exchange for TG; HDL delivers CE to liver via SR-B1 (scavenger receptor class B type 1, selective uptake); HDL does NOT transport dietary TG
explanation: Lipoprotein summary — exam table: Lipoprotein | Major lipid | Apo | Origin | Density: Chylomicron: dietary TG | B-48, C-II, E | intestine | lowest (<0.95); VLDL: endogenous TG | B-100, C-II, E | liver | 0.95-1.006; IDL: TG+CE | B-100, E | VLDL remnant | 1.006-1.019; LDL: CE (cholesterol) | B-100 | IDL remnant | 1.019-1.063; HDL: CE (reverse transport) | A-I, A-II | liver/intestine | 1.063-1.21; Lp(a): CE + Apo(a) | B-100 + Apo(a) | liver | ~LDL; Lp(a) is an independent CV risk factor (Apo(a) is structurally similar to plasminogen → may inhibit fibrinolysis → ↑thrombosis; also ↑atherosclerosis); genetically determined (KIV-2 repeats); elevated in ~20% of population; difficult to lower with statins (niacin has modest effect; PCSK9 inhibitors ↓Lp(a) ~25-30%; antisense oligonucleotides [pelacarsen/olpasiran targeting Apo(a) mRNA] in clinical trials).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the electron transport chain, which complex directly reduces molecular oxygen to water?
options: Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase): Complex I transfers electrons from NADH → FMN → Fe-S clusters → CoQ (ubiquinone → ubiquinol); pumps 4 H+ across IMM; does NOT reduce O2

Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex): Complex III transfers electrons from CoQH2 → cytochrome c via the Q-cycle (CoQH2 → Rieske Fe-S → cyt c1 → cyt c); pumps 4 H+ per pair of electrons (Q-cycle); does NOT reduce O2; inhibited by antimycin A (Qi site) and myxothiazol/stigmatellin (Qo site)

Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase, COX) is the TERMINAL oxidase of the ETC that DIRECTLY REDUCES O2 → H2O; 4 cyt c (reduced) + O2 + 8 H+(matrix) → 4 cyt c (oxidized) + 2 H2O + 4 H+(IMS); electron transfer within Complex IV: cyt c → CuA (binuclear copper center) → heme a → heme a3-CuB (binuclear center: site of O2 binding and reduction); pumps 2 H+ per electron (total 4 H+ for 2 electrons, or 8 H+ for 4 electrons to reduce one O2); contains 13 subunits (3 mitochondrial-encoded: COX I [heme a + heme a3-CuB], COX II [CuA], COX III; 10 nuclear-encoded); inhibitors: CYANIDE (CN⁻: binds Fe3+ of heme a3 → blocks electron transfer to O2; most potent ETC inhibitor; treatment: hydroxocobalamin [binds CN → cyanocobalamin] or nitrites [induce methemoglobin → MetHb-Fe3+ binds CN → cyanmethemoglobin] + thiosulfate [rhodanese: CN + thiosulfate → thiocyanate → renally excreted]); CARBON MONOXIDE (CO: binds reduced heme a3-Fe2+ [and Hb]; cherry-red appearance; treatment: 100% O2 or hyperbaric O2); HYDROGEN SULFIDE (H2S: similar to CN, binds heme a3); AZIDE (N3⁻: similar to CN)

Complex V (ATP synthase): Complex V (F1F0-ATP synthase) uses the proton gradient to synthesize ATP (chemiosmotic coupling; Peter Mitchell, 1961, Nobel 1978): H+ flow through Fo (membrane-embedded, c-ring rotates) → drives rotation of γ-subunit → conformational changes in F1 (α3β3 hexamer, catalytic β-subunits) → ADP + Pi → ATP (binding change mechanism: Paul Boyer + John Walker, Nobel 1997); Complex V does NOT reduce O2 — it synthesizes ATP
explanation: Electron transport chain — complete: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase): NADH → CoQ; 4 H+ pumped; inhibitors: rotenone, barbiturates, piericidin A; 45 subunits (7 mtDNA-encoded: ND1-6, ND4L); Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase, SDH): succinate → fumarate (TCA cycle) + FADH2 → CoQ; NO H+ pumped; only complex entirely nuclear-encoded (4 subunits: SDHA-D); SDH mutations → paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma (SDH tumor suppressor); inhibitor: malonate (competitive with succinate); CoQ (ubiquinone): mobile lipid-soluble electron carrier in IMM; accepts electrons from Complex I, II, ETF-QO (from FAO), DHODH (pyrimidine synthesis), G3P shuttle; Complex III (cyt bc1): CoQH2 → cyt c; Q-cycle; 2 H+ pumped (effective: 4 H+ per 2e⁻ considering Q-cycle); inhibitors: antimycin A (Qi), myxothiazol (Qo); Cyt c: small mobile protein on IMS face of IMM; also: released during apoptosis → apoptosome formation (cyt c + Apaf-1 + caspase-9); Complex IV (COX): cyt c → O2; reduces O2 → H2O; 2 H+ pumped per e⁻; inhibitors: CN⁻, CO, H2S, azide; Complex V (ATP synthase): H+ gradient → ATP; inhibitor: oligomycin (blocks Fo H+ channel → ↓ATP synthesis + ↓O2 consumption [tightly coupled]); Total H+ pumped per NADH: 4+4+2 = 10 H+ → ~2.5 ATP (10/4 = 2.5; ~4 H+ needed per ATP through Complex V including Pi transport); per FADH2: 0+4+2 = 6 H+ → ~1.5 ATP; Uncouplers: dissipate H+ gradient without ATP synthesis → ↑O2 consumption + ↑heat: 2,4-DNP, FCCP, thermogenin (UCP1 in BAT: cold → SNS → β3-AR → ↑UCP1 → non-shivering thermogenesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is decarboxylated to form histamine, a biogenic amine involved in allergic and inflammatory responses?
options: Histidine: Histidine → [histidine decarboxylase (HDC), PLP-dependent] → HISTAMINE + CO2; histamine: biogenic amine stored in mast cells (+ basophils) in granules (complexed with heparin proteoglycan); released by IgE-mediated degranulation (type I hypersensitivity: allergen crosslinks IgE on FcεRI → mast cell degranulation → histamine release); also: enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells in stomach (histamine → H2 receptors → parietal cells → H+/K+-ATPase → gastric acid secretion); histaminergic neurons in TMN (tuberomammillary nucleus → wakefulness); histamine receptors: H1 (Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG → smooth muscle contraction [bronchoconstriction], ↑vascular permeability, pruritus, nasal congestion; H1 antihistamines: 1st gen [diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine — cross BBB → sedation, anticholinergic]; 2nd gen [cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine — don't cross BBB, non-sedating]); H2 (Gs → AC → cAMP → gastric acid secretion; H2 blockers: ranitidine [withdrawn], famotidine → ↓acid); H3 (Gi → presynaptic autoreceptor in CNS → ↓histamine release; antagonists promote wakefulness); H4 (Gi → chemotaxis of eosinophils, mast cells → immune regulation)
Tryptophan: Trp is decarboxylated to form SEROTONIN (5-HT): Trp → [TPH, BH4] → 5-HTP → [AADC/DDC, PLP] → serotonin; Trp is NOT decarboxylated to histamine

Glutamate: Glu is decarboxylated to form GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid): Glu → [GAD, glutamic acid decarboxylase, PLP] → GABA; GAD67 (GAD1) and GAD65 (GAD2); anti-GAD antibodies: stiff-person syndrome, T1DM; Glu is NOT decarboxylated to histamine

Tyrosine: Tyr is hydroxylated (not decarboxylated in the first step) in catecholamine synthesis: Tyr → [TH, BH4] → L-DOPA → [AADC, PLP] → dopamine → [DBH, Cu, ascorbate] → NE → [PNMT, SAM] → epinephrine; Tyr is NOT the precursor of histamine
explanation: Biogenic amines from amino acid decarboxylation (PLP-dependent): His → [HDC] → histamine; Trp → [TPH → AADC] → serotonin (5-HT → [MAO] → 5-HIAA); Glu → [GAD65/67] → GABA (major inhibitory NT; ↑by benzodiazepines, barbiturates, vigabatrin; Huntington: ↓GABA in striatum); Tyr → [TH → AADC] → dopamine (→ [DBH] → NE → [PNMT] → Epi); DOPA → [AADC] → dopamine (also a decarboxylation); Cys → [CDO → CSAD] → taurine (bile acid conjugation, antioxidant, osmoregulation); Ser → [SDC] → ethanolamine (→ phosphatidylethanolamine → PE); Orn → [ODC, PLP] → putrescine (polyamine: putrescine → [SpdS, dcSAM] → spermidine → [SpmS] → spermine; functions: DNA stabilization, cell proliferation; DFMO [eflornithine/difluoromethylornithine] = irreversible ODC inhibitor → used in African trypanosomiasis [T.b. gambiense] and hirsutism cream); SAM → [SAMDC] → dcSAM (decarboxylated SAM, aminopropyl donor for polyamine synthesis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which form of vitamin D is measured in serum to assess a patient's vitamin D status?
options: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (calcitriol): calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D3) is the ACTIVE form of vitamin D but is NOT the best marker of vitamin D status because: (a) very short half-life (4-6 hrs); (b) tightly regulated by PTH, Ca2+, PO4 (↑PTH → ↑1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol even when stores are depleted); (c) can be NORMAL or even ELEVATED in vitamin D deficiency (secondary hyperparathyroidism ↑PTH → ↑CYP27B1 → ↑calcitriol despite low stores); calcitriol is measured in specific situations: suspected 1α-hydroxylase deficiency (VDDR type I), granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis: activated macrophages express CYP27B1 → ↑calcitriol → hypercalcemia)

25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol): 25-OH-D (calcidiol, 25-hydroxycholecalciferol) is the BEST marker of vitamin D status because: (a) long half-life (2-3 weeks) → reflects body stores; (b) major circulating form (bound to VDBP [vitamin D-binding protein/GC-globulin]); (c) NOT tightly regulated (reflects input from skin synthesis + dietary intake); vitamin D metabolism: skin: 7-dehydrocholesterol → [UVB 290-315 nm] → previtamin D3 → [thermal isomerization] → cholecalciferol (D3); dietary: D3 (animal: fish, egg yolk, liver) or D2 (ergocalciferol, plant/fungal); LIVER: D3 → [CYP2R1, 25-hydroxylase, ER] → 25-OH-D3 (calcidiol); KIDNEY: 25-OH-D3 → [CYP27B1, 1α-hydroxylase, mitochondria, proximal tubule] → 1,25-(OH)2D3 (calcitriol, active); regulation of CYP27B1: ↑PTH → ↑activity; ↓Ca2+ → ↑activity (indirect via ↑PTH); ↓PO4 → ↑activity; ↑FGF23 (from osteocytes) → ↓activity; calcitriol actions: VDR (nuclear receptor → heterodimerizes with RXR → VDRE [vitamin D response elements]): ↑intestinal Ca2+ absorption (↑TRPV6, ↑calbindin-D9k, ↑PMCA1b), ↑intestinal PO4 absorption, ↑renal Ca2+ reabsorption, ↑osteoclast differentiation (via RANKL on osteoblasts → RANK on osteoclast precursors), immune modulation (↓Th1/Th17, ↑Treg, ↑cathelicidin [antimicrobial peptide]); deficiency: rickets (children: craniotabes, rachitic rosary, Harrison groove, bowing of legs), osteomalacia (adults: bone pain, proximal myopathy, Looser zones [pseudofractures])

Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol): cholecalciferol is the parent compound produced in skin or from diet; it is rapidly hydroxylated in liver → 25-OH-D; measuring D3 itself does not reflect total body stores accurately

7-dehydrocholesterol (provitamin D3): 7-DHC is the cholesterol precursor in skin that is converted to previtamin D3 by UVB; it is NOT measured to assess vitamin D status; ↑7-DHC is seen in Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (DHCR7 deficiency → ↓cholesterol synthesis + ↑7-DHC → multiple congenital anomalies, 2-3 toe syndactyly, intellectual disability, genital anomalies in males)
explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins — D metabolism summary: Sources: D3 (cholecalciferol): skin (UVB + 7-DHC) + animal diet; D2 (ergocalciferol): plant/fungal diet + supplements; Activation: 2 hydroxylations: (1) liver 25-hydroxylase (CYP2R1) → 25-OH-D (measured clinically, t½ 2-3 wk); (2) kidney 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) → 1,25-(OH)2D (active, t½ 4-6 hr); Inactivation: CYP24A1 (24-hydroxylase): 25-OH-D → 24,25-(OH)2D and 1,25-(OH)2D → 1,24,25-(OH)3D (both inactive → degradation); FGF23 and calcitriol ↑CYP24A1 → negative feedback; Disorders: VDDR type I (CYP27B1 mutations → ↓calcitriol; ↓Ca, ↓PO4, ↑PTH, ↑ALP, ↓1,25-D but normal/↑25-OH-D; treat with calcitriol); VDDR type II (VDR mutations → end-organ resistance; ↑1,25-D, ↑PTH; often with alopecia [VDR important for hair follicle cycling]; treat with high-dose IV Ca2+); X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH: PHEX mutations → ↑FGF23 → ↓CYP27B1 + ↑CYP24A1 + ↓renal PO4 reabsorption → ↓PO4, normal Ca, inappropriately normal/↓1,25-D; treat with burosumab [anti-FGF23 Ab]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is responsible for adding the poly-A tail to mRNA during post-transcriptional processing?
options: RNA Polymerase II: Pol II transcribes the pre-mRNA but does NOT add the poly-A tail; however, Pol II CTD (Ser2-phosphorylated) recruits the 3' processing machinery (CPSF + CstF); the poly-A signal (AAUAAA) in pre-mRNA is recognized by CPSF → cleavage → then PAP adds the tail

Poly(A) polymerase (PAP): PAP (poly(A) polymerase, PAPOLA gene) is a template-INDEPENDENT RNA polymerase that adds the poly-A tail (~200-250 adenylate residues) to the 3' end of mRNA after cleavage; 3' end processing steps: (1) CPSF (cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor) recognizes AAUAAA hexamer in pre-mRNA (most conserved polyadenylation signal, ~10-30 nt upstream of cleavage site); (2) CstF (cleavage stimulation factor) recognizes GU-rich or U-rich downstream element; (3) CFI/CFII (cleavage factors) + CPSF → endonucleolytic cleavage between AAUAAA and GU-rich element (usually after a CA dinucleotide); (4) PAP adds poly-A tail (template-independent; uses ATP → AMP polymerization on 3'-OH); (5) PABPN1 (nuclear poly-A binding protein) binds the growing tail → stimulates PAP processivity + determines tail length (~250 A); in cytoplasm: PABPC1 (cytoplasmic PABP) binds poly-A → protects from deadenylases + interacts with eIF4G → circularization of mRNA (eIF4E [cap] + eIF4G + PABPC1 [poly-A] → closed-loop → enhances translation); poly-A tail functions: (1) ↑mRNA stability (protects 3' end from exonucleases); (2) ↑translation efficiency (PABPC1-eIF4G interaction → ribosome recycling); (3) nuclear export (PABPN1 aids mRNP assembly for export via NXF1/NXT1); deadenylation: first step of mRNA decay → CCR4-NOT complex (major deadenylase) or PARN → shortening of poly-A → decapping (DCP1/DCP2) → 5'→3' degradation (XRN1) OR 3'→5' degradation (exosome)

Terminal transferase (TdT): TdT (DNTT gene) is a template-independent DNA polymerase that adds random nucleotides to 3' ends of DNA during V(D)J recombination (junctional diversity, N-nucleotide addition); TdT is NOT an RNA polymerase and does NOT add poly-A tails to mRNA; TdT is a marker of immature lymphocytes (pre-B and pre-T cells; positive in ALL [acute lymphoblastic leukemia])

Guanylyltransferase: guanylyltransferase adds the GMP cap to the 5' end of mRNA (not the 3' poly-A tail); 5' capping: (1) RNA triphosphatase removes γ-phosphate → 5' diphosphate; (2) guanylyltransferase adds GMP via 5'-5' triphosphate linkage → G(5')ppp(5')N; (3) methyltransferase (cap methyltransferase) methylates N7 of guanine → m7G cap (Cap 0); (4) further methylation at 2'-OH of first and second nucleotides → Cap 1, Cap 2; cap functions: ↑stability (protection from 5' exonucleases), ↑translation (eIF4E recognizes m7G cap), ↑splicing of first intron, ↑nuclear export
explanation: mRNA processing — complete: Pre-mRNA undergoes 3 processing steps in the nucleus: (1) 5' CAPPING: co-transcriptional (added when ~20-30 nt transcribed); m7GpppN cap → recognized by CBC (cap-binding complex: CBP20/80) in nucleus → eIF4E in cytoplasm; (2) SPLICING: removal of introns + ligation of exons by spliceosome (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNPs + >150 proteins); U1 recognizes 5' splice site (GU), U2 recognizes branch point (A), U6 catalyzes transesterification (ribozyme); step 1: 2'-OH of branch point A attacks 5' splice site → lariat intermediate; step 2: 3'-OH of upstream exon attacks 3' splice site (AG) → exons ligated + lariat released; alternative splicing: same gene → different mRNA → different protein isoforms (>95% of human multi-exon genes); (3) 3' POLYADENYLATION: AAUAAA → CPSF/CstF → cleavage → PAP → poly-A tail; AFTER processing: mature mRNA → nuclear export (NPC: NXF1-NXT1/TAP-p15 pathway; CBC replaced by eIF4E) → cytoplasmic translation or storage (P-bodies, stress granules).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Myoadenylate deaminase deficiency affects which metabolic cycle in skeletal muscle that helps regenerate ATP during intense exercise?
options: Cori cycle: the Cori cycle (liver-muscle glucose-lactate cycle) involves: muscle glycolysis → lactate → blood → liver → GNG → glucose → blood → muscle; AMP deaminase is not part of the Cori cycle

Purine nucleotide cycle: Myoadenylate deaminase (AMP deaminase, AMPD1) catalyzes: AMP → IMP + NH3 (deamination); this is the first step of the PURINE NUCLEOTIDE CYCLE (PNC) in skeletal muscle: (1) AMP → [AMPD1] → IMP + NH3; (2) IMP + Asp + GTP → [ADSS, adenylosuccinate synthetase] → adenylosuccinate + GDP + Pi; (3) adenylosuccinate → [ADSL, adenylosuccinate lyase] → AMP + fumarate; NET REACTION: Asp → fumarate + NH3 (the purine ring is recycled — AMP → IMP → AMP — while generating fumarate [enters TCA → OAA → anaplerosis or GNG] and NH3); PNC functions in exercising muscle: (1) maintains high ATP:AMP ratio (removing AMP → ↓AMP → shifts adenylate kinase equilibrium: 2 ADP → ATP + AMP → toward ATP; if AMP accumulates → adenylate kinase runs backward → ↓ATP generation); (2) provides fumarate for TCA cycle anaplerosis (↑TCA flux → ↑aerobic ATP); (3) generates NH3 (buffer? may contribute to exercise hyperventilation; ↑serum NH3 during intense exercise); AMPD1 deficiency: most common inherited muscle enzyme deficiency (~2% of population are homozygous; AMPD1 c.34C>T, p.Gln12Ter, founder mutation); most homozygotes are ASYMPTOMATIC (may be benign polymorphism with reduced penetrance); symptomatic: exercise-induced myalgia + fatigue + cramps + ↑CK; ischemic forearm exercise test: NORMAL lactate rise but ↓ammonia (NH3) rise (in normal test: both lactate and NH3 should increase; ↓NH3 alone = AMPD1 deficiency; ↓lactate alone = GSD type V [McArdle] or similar glycogenolytic defect where muscle glycogen cannot be broken down → ↓lactate + normal/↑NH3)
TCA cycle: the TCA cycle (Krebs cycle) generates NADH/FADH2/GTP; AMP deaminase is not a TCA enzyme; however, the PNC does feed fumarate INTO the TCA → anaplerotic link

Urea cycle: the urea cycle operates in the liver to dispose of ammonia as urea; AMP deaminase/PNC is in skeletal muscle; while the PNC shares ADSS and ADSL with the urea cycle's aspartate-argininosuccinate-fumarate segment (homologous reactions), myoadenylate deaminase is NOT part of the hepatic urea cycle
explanation: Purine nucleotide cycle vs urea cycle — shared enzymology: PNC (muscle): AMP → [AMPD] → IMP → [ADSS, Asp + GTP] → S-AMP → [ADSL] → AMP + fumarate; Urea cycle (liver): citrulline + Asp + ATP → [ASS] → argininosuccinate → [ASL] → Arg + fumarate; ADSS/ASS and ADSL/ASL catalyze analogous reactions (condensation of amino with fumarate-containing compound, then lyase releases fumarate); this is an example of convergent biochemical logic in two different pathways. Ischemic forearm exercise test (grip test): patient exercises forearm with cuff occluding blood flow → measure venous lactate + NH3 before/after: Normal: ↑lactate (from anaerobic glycolysis) + ↑NH3 (from PNC); McArdle (GSD V, myophosphorylase deficiency): ↓lactate (can't break down glycogen) + ↑NH3 (PNC intact); AMPD1 deficiency: ↑lactate (glycolysis intact) + ↓NH3 (PNC blocked); BOTH ↓: possible combined or other myopathy.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which immunoglobulin class is present in highest concentration in serum?
options: IgA: IgA is the most abundant immunoglobulin in SECRETIONS (mucosal immunity: saliva, tears, breast milk, GI/respiratory secretions; secretory IgA [sIgA] is dimeric + J-chain + secretory component [from pIgR cleavage]); serum IgA is monomeric and is the 2nd most abundant serum Ig (~200-300 mg/dL); IgA deficiency: most common primary immunodeficiency (~1:500); most asymptomatic; ↑risk sinopulmonary infections, GI infections, autoimmune diseases; anaphylaxis risk with blood products containing IgA (anti-IgA antibodies in IgA-deficient patients)

IgG: IgG is present in the HIGHEST CONCENTRATION in SERUM (~800-1800 mg/dL, ~75-80% of total serum Ig); IgG has 4 subclasses: IgG1 (65%, most abundant), IgG2 (25%, polysaccharide antigens), IgG3 (7%, strongest complement activation, shortest half-life ~7 days), IgG4 (4%, does not activate complement, associated with chronic antigen exposure + IgG4-related disease); IgG functions: (1) opsonization (Fc receptors on phagocytes: FcγRI [CD64], FcγRIIA/B [CD32], FcγRIIIA [CD16]); (2) complement activation (classical pathway: IgG1>IgG3>>IgG2; NOT IgG4); (3) ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity: NK cells [CD16/FcγRIIIA] + IgG-coated target cell → NK cell degranulation → perforin/granzyme → target lysis); (4) neonatal immunity (IgG is the ONLY Ig that crosses the placenta [FcRn/neonatal Fc receptor → active transport across syncytiotrophoblast → fetal circulation; provides passive immunity for first ~6 months of life]); (5) longest half-life (~21 days for IgG1/2/4; maintained by FcRn recycling [endothelial/epithelial cells internalize IgG → acidic endosome → IgG binds FcRn at pH 6 → recycled to surface → released at pH 7.4 → ↑half-life; IgG that doesn't bind FcRn → lysosomal degradation])

IgM: IgM is the first Ig produced in a primary immune response (and first expressed on naive B cell surface as BCR); serum IgM is PENTAMERIC (5 monomers + J-chain) → 10 antigen-binding sites → high avidity → excellent complement activation (classical pathway: single IgM pentamer suffices to activate C1q); IgM does NOT cross placenta; serum concentration ~60-280 mg/dL (3rd most abundant)

IgE: IgE has the LOWEST serum concentration (~0.002 mg/dL) but plays crucial roles in: type I hypersensitivity (allergic reactions: IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells/basophils → allergen crosslinks IgE → degranulation → histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins); anti-parasitic immunity (eosinophils: FcεRII [CD23]); IgE is elevated in: atopic diseases (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema, food allergy), parasitic infections (helminths), ABPA, hyper-IgE syndrome (Job syndrome: STAT3 AD mutations → ↑IgE + eosinophilia + cold abscesses + coarse facies + retained primary teeth)
explanation: Immunoglobulin classes — serum concentration ranking: IgG >> IgA > IgM > IgD > IgE; IgG: ~75-80% of serum Ig, crosses placenta, longest t½, opsonization + complement + ADCC; IgA: most abundant in secretions, dimeric sIgA (J-chain + secretory component), mucosal defense; IgM: pentameric, first response, best complement activator, does not cross placenta; IgD: minimal serum levels, co-expressed with IgM on naive B cells (BCR), function unclear; IgE: lowest serum, allergy + anti-helminth, binds FcεRI on mast cells/basophils; Class switching (isotype switching): occurs in germinal centers; requires: (1) CD40L (CD154 on T helper cells) + CD40 (on B cells) → activates AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase); (2) cytokines direct switch: IL-4 → IgG1/IgE; IL-5 → IgA; IFN-γ → IgG2a/3; TGF-β → IgA/IgG2b; AID (AICDA gene) → cytosine deamination in switch regions → U:G mismatches → repair → DSBs → NHEJ → switch recombination → new constant region (Cγ/Cα/Cε) replaces Cμ+Cδ; AID also mediates somatic hypermutation (SHM: point mutations in variable regions → affinity maturation in GC [selection by FDC-presented antigen]); AID deficiency (hyper-IgM syndrome type 2, AR): ↑IgM, ↓IgG/IgA/IgE, absent SHM+CSR; compare X-linked hyper-IgM (type 1): CD40L/CD154 (TNFSF5) deficiency → same Ig pattern + absent GC formation + ↑opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the primary site for de novo cholesterol synthesis in the body?
options: Adrenal cortex: the adrenal cortex is a major consumer of cholesterol (for steroid hormone synthesis: cortisol, aldosterone, DHEA/androgens) but is NOT the primary site of de novo cholesterol synthesis; adrenal glands mainly take up cholesterol from LDL via LDLR + from HDL via SR-B1

Liver: The LIVER is the primary site of de novo cholesterol synthesis, accounting for ~60-80% of total endogenous cholesterol; cholesterol synthesis pathway (mevalonate pathway): acetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → [thiolase] → acetoacetyl-CoA → [HMG-CoA synthase, cytoplasmic] → HMG-CoA → [HMG-CoA REDUCTASE (HMGCR), rate-limiting, ER membrane, NADPH-dependent] → mevalonate → → → → → cholesterol (total ~30 enzymatic steps); HMGCR regulation: TRANSCRIPTIONAL: SREBP-2 (sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2): when cholesterol is LOW → SCAP escorts SREBP-2 from ER → Golgi → S1P + S2P proteases cleave → active nSREBP-2 → nucleus → SRE → ↑HMGCR + ↑LDLR transcription; when cholesterol is HIGH → SCAP binds Insig (insulin-induced gene) → retains SREBP in ER → ↓HMGCR + ↓LDLR; POST-TRANSLATIONAL: ↑sterols → Insig binds HMGCR → ubiquitination → proteasomal degradation (sterol-accelerated degradation); PHOSPHORYLATION: AMPK phosphorylates HMGCR → INACTIVE (↓cholesterol synthesis when energy is low); STATINS: competitive inhibitors of HMGCR (lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin; most effective LDL-lowering drugs; ↓HMGCR → ↓intracellular cholesterol → ↑SREBP-2 → ↑LDLR expression → ↑hepatic LDL uptake → ↓plasma LDL; also ↓isoprenoid synthesis → pleiotropic effects)

Small intestine: the intestine contributes to cholesterol synthesis (~15%) and is important for cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1 transporter: ezetimibe inhibits NPC1L1 → ↓cholesterol absorption), but it is NOT the PRIMARY site of de novo synthesis
Adipose tissue: adipose tissue has minimal cholesterol synthetic capacity; it primarily stores triglycerides; NOT a major site of cholesterol synthesis
explanation: Cholesterol metabolism overview: Daily cholesterol: ~1000 mg synthesized (mainly liver) + ~300-500 mg dietary intake; ~500 mg excreted as bile acids + ~600 mg excreted as biliary cholesterol + neutral sterols; Mevalonate pathway intermediates (beyond cholesterol): farnesyl-PP → squalene → cholesterol; but also: farnesyl-PP → geranylgeranyl-PP → protein prenylation (Ras, Rho GTPases → cell signaling; statins ↓prenylation → anti-inflammatory/antithrombotic pleiotropic effects); isopentenyl-PP → tRNA modification; farnesyl-PP → dolichol (N-linked glycosylation), ubiquinone (CoQ10, ETC); Bile acid synthesis (major cholesterol elimination pathway): cholesterol → [CYP7A1, rate-limiting, liver microsomes] → 7α-hydroxycholesterol → → → primary bile acids: cholic acid (CA) + chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA); conjugated with glycine or taurine → bile salts; bacteria: CA → deoxycholic acid (DCA, secondary); CDCA → lithocholic acid (LCA, secondary) + ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA, tertiary; used therapeutically in PBC, gallstone dissolution); FXR (farnesoid X receptor): bile acids are FXR ligands → FXR activation → ↓CYP7A1 (negative feedback) + ↑FGF19 (from ileum → portal blood → liver → ↓CYP7A1) + ↑BSEP (bile salt export pump) → bile acid homeostasis; obeticholic acid (OCA): FXR agonist used in PBC.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme deficiency is responsible for acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)?
options: ALA dehydratase (ALAD / porphobilinogen synthase): ALAD deficiency → ALAD porphyria (ADP, extremely rare; autosomal recessive); ↑ALA in urine; NOT AIP

Porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD / hydroxymethylbilane synthase, HMBS): AIP is caused by deficiency of PORPHOBILINOGEN DEAMINASE (PBGD, also called HMB synthase / HMBS; gene: HMBS, chromosome 11q23.3); autosomal DOMINANT with low penetrance (~10-20% of carriers have clinical attacks); AIP: most common ACUTE porphyria; ACUTE NEUROVISCERAL ATTACKS (NO skin involvement — distinguishes AIP from variegate porphyria [VP] and hereditary coproporphyria [HCP] which have both acute + cutaneous features): (1) severe abdominal pain (colicky, poorly localized; often misdiagnosed as surgical abdomen); (2) neuropsychiatric: anxiety, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, insomnia; (3) autonomic neuropathy: tachycardia, hypertension, vomiting, constipation; (4) motor neuropathy (proximal > distal; can → respiratory paralysis); (5) hyponatremia (SIADH → ↓Na+; most common electrolyte abnormality); (6) dark/red urine on standing (PBG polymerizes → porphobilin → dark pigment); diagnosis: ↑↑PBG (porphobilinogen) + ↑ALA in urine during attack (PBG is the KEY diagnostic test — ↑PBG >5x ULN; Watson-Schwartz test or Hoesch test for qualitative PBG; quantitative urine PBG is gold standard); triggers: drugs (barbiturates, sulfonamides, carbamazepine, OCPs, alcohol — induce hepatic CYP450 → ↑demand for heme → ↑ALA synthase 1 [ALAS1] → ↑ALA/PBG); fasting/caloric restriction, stress, menstruation (progesterone → CYP450 induction), infection; treatment: IV HEMIN (Panhematin/heme arginate → heme → negative feedback → ↓ALAS1 → ↓ALA/PBG production; definitive treatment); IV glucose (10% dextrose → ↓ALAS1 via glucose effect; mild attacks); givosiran (siRNA targeting ALAS1 mRNA in hepatocytes → ↓ALAS1 → ↓ALA/PBG; FDA 2019; GalNAc-conjugated for hepatocyte targeting via ASGPR; monthly SC injection; transforms management of recurrent AIP attacks); avoid triggers; liver transplant (curative but reserved for severe refractory cases)

Uroporphyrinogen III synthase: UROS deficiency → congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP, Günther disease; AR; severe cutaneous photosensitivity from childhood, red-brown teeth [erythrodontia] fluorescing under Wood's lamp, hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly); NOT AIP

Ferrochelatase: ferrochelatase deficiency → erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP; AD; ↑free protoporphyrin in RBCs → acute photosensitivity [burning, stinging in sunlight, NO blisters unlike other cutaneous porphyrias]; hepatobiliary disease in ~5%); NOT AIP
explanation: Heme synthesis pathway + porphyrias: Location: first step (ALAS) and last 3 steps (coproporphyrinogen oxidase, protoporphyrinogen oxidase, ferrochelatase) in MITOCHONDRIA; middle 4 steps in CYTOPLASM; Pathway: Gly + succinyl-CoA → [ALAS, PLP, rate-limiting] → δ-ALA → [ALAD] → PBG → [PBGD/HMBS] → HMB → [UROS] → uroporphyrinogen III → [UROD] → coproporphyrinogen III → [CPOX] → protoporphyrinogen IX → [PPOX] → protoporphyrin IX → [ferrochelatase, Fe2+] → HEME; ALAS isoforms: ALAS1 (housekeeping, liver; regulated by heme [negative feedback], drugs, fasting); ALAS2 (erythroid; regulated by iron [IRE in 5'UTR → IRP binding when iron low → ↓translation]); ALAS2 mutations → X-linked sideroblastic anemia (↓heme in erythroblasts → ↓hemoglobin + ring sideroblasts [iron-laden mitochondria around nucleus on Prussian blue stain]; treated with pyridoxine [B6, PLP is ALAS cofactor]); Porphyria classification: ACUTE (neurovisceral, ↑ALA±PBG): ADP (ALAD), AIP (PBGD), HCP (CPOX), VP (PPOX); CUTANEOUS (photosensitivity, ↑porphyrins): CEP (UROS), PCT (UROD — most common porphyria overall; ↑uroporphyrin; blistering photosensitivity [sun-exposed skin → vesicles/bullae → scarring]; associated with hepatitis C, alcohol, iron overload, estrogen; treatment: phlebotomy + low-dose hydroxychloroquine), EPP (ferrochelatase), XLP (ALAS2 gain-of-function); BOTH acute + cutaneous: HCP, VP.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Michaelis constant (Km) of an enzyme for its substrate represents which of the following?
options: The maximum velocity of the enzyme-catalyzed reaction: Vmax (maximum velocity) is achieved when ALL enzyme molecules are bound to substrate ([S] >> Km); Vmax = kcat × [E]total; Vmax is NOT Km

The substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax: Km (Michaelis constant) = the substrate concentration [S] at which v = Vmax/2 (half-maximal velocity); Michaelis-Menten equation: v = (Vmax × [S]) / (Km + [S]); when [S] = Km: v = Vmax × Km / (Km + Km) = Vmax/2; Km reflects the AFFINITY of the enzyme for its substrate: LOW Km → HIGH affinity (enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at low [S] → binds substrate tightly); HIGH Km → LOW affinity (needs high [S] to reach half-maximal velocity); Km is an intrinsic property of the enzyme-substrate pair (independent of [E]); Km has units of CONCENTRATION (moles/L); clinical relevance: glucokinase (GK, hexokinase IV, liver/β-cells): Km for glucose ~10 mM (high Km → acts as glucose sensor; activity proportional to blood glucose over physiological range 4-10 mM → regulates insulin secretion [β-cells] and hepatic glucose metabolism); hexokinase I-III (most tissues): Km ~0.1 mM (low Km → saturated at normal glucose → constitutive; ensures basal glucose phosphorylation); GK activators (GKAs, e.g., dorzagliatin): ↓Km of GK → ↑GK activity at lower glucose → ↑insulin secretion → investigational T2DM drugs; Lineweaver-Burk plot (double reciprocal): 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax; x-intercept = -1/Km; y-intercept = 1/Vmax; slope = Km/Vmax

The activation energy of the reaction: activation energy (Ea) is the energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction to proceed; enzymes LOWER Ea (by stabilizing the transition state → ↓Ea → ↑reaction rate); Ea is NOT Km

The equilibrium constant of the enzyme-substrate complex: Kd (dissociation constant) of the ES complex relates to Km but they are not identical; Km = (k-1 + kcat)/k1 ≈ Kd only when kcat << k-1 (rapid equilibrium assumption); Keq of the overall reaction is NOT Km
explanation: Enzyme kinetics — exam essentials: Michaelis-Menten: v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]); assumes steady-state ([ES] constant); Vmax = kcat[E]t (kcat = turnover number = molecules of substrate converted per enzyme molecule per second); Catalytic efficiency = kcat/Km (higher = better enzyme; diffusion-limited enzymes [catalytic perfection]: kcat/Km ≈ 10^8-10^9 M⁻¹s⁻¹; examples: carbonic anhydrase, triosephosphate isomerase, acetylcholinesterase); Enzyme inhibition: COMPETITIVE: inhibitor competes with substrate for active site (structural analog); ↑Km (apparent), Vmax unchanged; can be overcome by ↑[S]; L-B plot: lines intersect on y-axis (same 1/Vmax); example: malonate vs succinate (SDH), statins vs HMG-CoA (HMGCR), methotrexate vs DHF (DHFR); UNCOMPETITIVE: inhibitor binds only ES complex (not free E); ↓Km AND ↓Vmax (both decrease proportionally → Vmax/Km ratio unchanged); L-B plot: parallel lines; example: lithium inhibiting IMPase (uncompetitive at some concentrations); NONCOMPETITIVE (mixed when Ki ≠ Ki'): inhibitor binds E or ES at allosteric site; Km unchanged, ↓Vmax; L-B plot: lines intersect on x-axis (pure noncompetitive) or left of y-axis (mixed); example: heavy metals (Pb, Hg → bind -SH groups); IRREVERSIBLE: covalent modification of enzyme → permanent inactivation; example: aspirin (acetylates COX Ser530), organophosphates (phosphorylate AChE Ser), DFP, sarin; Allosteric regulation: sigmoidal kinetics (cooperative); effectors shift curve left (activators, ↑affinity) or right (inhibitors, ↓affinity); do NOT follow Michaelis-Menten.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which post-translational modification targets misfolded or damaged intracellular proteins for proteasomal degradation?
options: Phosphorylation: phosphorylation (by kinases, on Ser/Thr/Tyr residues) regulates protein activity, localization, and interactions; phosphorylation can mark proteins for degradation in some pathways (e.g., phosphodegrons recognized by SCF E3 ligases), but it is NOT the primary tag for proteasomal targeting

Ubiquitination: UBIQUITIN (Ub, 76-aa, 8.5-kDa, highly conserved protein) is covalently attached to target proteins via an isopeptide bond between Ub C-terminal Gly76 and target protein Lys ε-amino group; polyubiquitin chain (≥4 Ub linked via K48) is the canonical signal for 26S PROTEASOMAL DEGRADATION; ubiquitination cascade (ubiquitin-proteasome system, UPS): E1 (ubiquitin-activating enzyme: Ub + ATP → Ub-AMP → E1~Ub thioester; 2 E1s in humans), E2 (ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme: E1 → E2~Ub; ~40 E2s), E3 (ubiquitin ligase: determines SUBSTRATE SPECIFICITY; transfers Ub from E2 → substrate; ~600-700 E3s in humans); E3 types: RING (really interesting new gene: scaffold → E2 transfers Ub directly to substrate; e.g., SCF, APC/C, MDM2, VHL), HECT (homologous to E6AP C-terminus: E2 → E3~Ub thioester → substrate; e.g., E6AP/UBE3A → Angelman syndrome), RBR (RING-between-RING: hybrid mechanism; e.g., Parkin [PARK2: Parkin is an RBR E3 ligase for mitophagy; Parkin mutations → AR juvenile Parkinsonism]); 26S proteasome: 20S core (barrel: α7β7β7α7; β1 [caspase-like], β2 [trypsin-like], β5 [chymotrypsin-like] → proteolytic activities) + 19S regulatory cap (recognizes polyUb, deubiquitinates, unfolds, threads substrate into 20S); proteasome inhibitors: bortezomib (boronic acid → inhibits β5 chymotrypsin-like activity → ↑misfolded proteins → ER stress → apoptosis; used in multiple myeloma; ↓NF-κB [IκB not degraded → NF-κB stays cytoplasmic → ↓survival signals]), carfilzomib, ixazomib

Glycosylation: N-linked (Asn-X-Ser/Thr; ER/Golgi) and O-linked (Ser/Thr; Golgi) glycosylation are important for protein folding, stability, and function; glycosylation does NOT directly tag proteins for proteasomal degradation (though N-glycan trimming is part of ER quality control [calnexin/calreticulin cycle] and ERAD [ER-associated degradation] involves retrotranslocation + ubiquitination)

Acetylation: acetylation (by HATs on histone lysines; also non-histone proteins like p53, tubulin) regulates gene expression and protein function; acetylation does NOT directly tag proteins for proteasomal degradation
explanation: Protein degradation pathways: (1) Ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS): short-lived, regulatory, misfolded cytoplasmic/nuclear proteins; K48-polyUb → 26S proteasome → peptides → amino acids; (2) Lysosomal degradation (autophagy): long-lived proteins, organelles, aggregates; macroautophagy: isolation membrane (phagophore → autophagosome [LC3-II marker] → fuses with lysosome → autolysosome → degradation; ATG genes [Beclin-1, ATG5, ATG7, LC3/ATG8]; mTORC1 inhibits autophagy [↓ULK1 complex]; AMPK/starvation → ↓mTORC1 → ↑autophagy); microautophagy (lysosome directly engulfs cytoplasm); CMA (chaperone-mediated autophagy: KFERQ motif → Hsc70 → LAMP-2A receptor → unfold → translocate into lysosome); (3) Calpains: Ca2+-dependent cysteine proteases; cytoplasmic; muscle protein turnover, signal transduction; (4) Caspases: cysteine-aspartate proteases; apoptosis (initiator: casp-8 [extrinsic], casp-9 [intrinsic] → executioner: casp-3, casp-7 → PARP cleavage, lamin cleavage, DNA fragmentation [via CAD/ICAD]); N-end rule: N-terminal amino acid determines protein half-life (destabilizing N-terminal residues [Arg, Lys, Phe, Leu, Trp, Tyr, His, Ile] → recognized by N-recognins [UBR1 E3] → ubiquitination → degradation); Met (stabilizing) → most proteins start with Met; Ubiquitin chain linkages beyond K48: K63 (signaling, DNA repair, NF-κB activation, NOT degradation); K11 (ERAD, cell cycle); M1/linear (NF-κB, generated by LUBAC).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which vitamin serves as a cofactor for the enzyme-catalyzed carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X?
options: Vitamin A (retinol): vitamin A functions in vision (retinal: 11-cis-retinal + opsin → rhodopsin; light → all-trans-retinal → signal), cell differentiation (retinoic acid [RA]: RAR/RXR nuclear receptors), immune function, reproduction; vitamin A is NOT involved in γ-carboxylation of clotting factors

Vitamin K: Vitamin K (phylloquinone [K1, dietary: green leafy vegetables] + menaquinones [K2, bacterial synthesis in gut + fermented foods]); vitamin K is the essential cofactor for γ-GLUTAMYL CARBOXYLASE (GGCX): converts Glu residues → γ-carboxyglutamate (Gla) residues in vitamin K-dependent proteins; Gla residues bind Ca2+ ions → anchor these proteins to phospholipid membranes (phosphatidylserine on activated platelet surface) → essential for function; vitamin K-dependent CLOTTING FACTORS: II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X (procoagulant) + Protein C, Protein S (anticoagulant) + Protein Z; mnemonic for procoagulant factors: '1972' (factors 10, 9, 7, 2); vitamin K cycle: vitamin K (reduced, KH2 [hydroquinone]) → [GGCX: carboxylates Glu → Gla while oxidizing KH2 → vitamin K epoxide (KO)] → [VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1): reduces KO → vitamin K quinone → KH2; WARFARIN inhibits VKORC1 → ↓KH2 → ↓γ-carboxylation → ↓functional clotting factors → anticoagulation]; vitamin K deficiency: ↑PT/INR (factor VII has shortest half-life ~6 hrs → PT prolonged first; then aPTT as IX, X, II decline); causes: newborns (low stores, sterile gut, low breast milk K1 → hemorrhagic disease of newborn [VKDB] → prevented by vitamin K injection at birth), malabsorption (fat-soluble), antibiotics (↓gut bacteria → ↓K2), warfarin; treatment: vitamin K (phytonadione) IV/SC/PO; for severe bleeding: FFP or PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate: contains II, VII, IX, X)

Vitamin E (α-tocopherol): vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant (chain-breaking in membranes → prevents lipid peroxidation → protects PUFA in cell membranes); deficiency: hemolytic anemia (premature infants), spinocerebellar ataxia (chronic malabsorption → neurological: posterior column + cerebellum); vitamin E is NOT involved in clotting factor carboxylation

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid): vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylases (collagen synthesis), dopamine β-hydroxylase (NE synthesis), and various dioxygenases; also an antioxidant; vitamin C is NOT involved in γ-carboxylation of clotting factors
explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins — ADEK summary: A (retinol/retinal/retinoic acid): vision, cell differentiation, immune; deficiency: night blindness → xerophthalmia → Bitot spots → keratomalacia; toxicity: teratogenic (isotretinoin/Accutane), pseudotumor cerebri, hepatotoxicity; D (cholecalciferol): Ca/PO4 homeostasis (see vitamin D question); deficiency: rickets/osteomalacia; toxicity: hypercalcemia; E (α-tocopherol): antioxidant (lipid-soluble, membranes); deficiency: hemolytic anemia, spinocerebellar degeneration; toxicity: ↑bleeding (high-dose antagonizes vitamin K); K (phylloquinone/menaquinone): γ-carboxylation of Gla proteins (clotting factors + osteocalcin + MGP); deficiency: bleeding (↑PT/INR); VKDB in newborns; warfarin antagonist (vitamin K reverses warfarin anticoagulation, but takes 12-24 hrs for new protein synthesis; for immediate reversal: PCC or FFP); also: vitamin K-dependent osteocalcin (bone Gla protein, BGP): secreted by osteoblasts → binds Ca2+ in bone matrix; undercarboxylated osteocalcin → marker of vitamin K insufficiency; MGP (matrix Gla protein): inhibits vascular calcification → K deficiency may → ↑arterial calcification.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion?
options: Sickle cell disease: SCD is caused by a POINT MUTATION (missense: GAG → GTG in codon 6 of HBB gene → Glu → Val at position 6 of β-globin → HbS; under deoxygenation → HbS polymerizes → sickling); NOT a trinucleotide repeat

Huntington disease: Huntington disease (HD) is caused by an expanded CAG TRINUCLEOTIDE REPEAT in exon 1 of the HTT gene (huntingtin, chromosome 4p16.3); normal: 6-35 CAG repeats; HD: ≥40 repeats (36-39 = reduced penetrance); CAG codes for glutamine (Gln) → polyglutamine (polyQ) tract expansion → mutant huntingtin protein → toxic gain-of-function → selective neurodegeneration (medium spiny neurons of the CAUDATE NUCLEUS [neostriatum] → progressive loss → caudate atrophy visible on MRI); clinical: onset typically 30-50 years; chorea (involuntary, irregular, non-patterned movements) → progressively severe → rigidity, dystonia, bradykinesia (Westphal variant: juvenile onset [>60 repeats, usually paternal anticipation] → rigidity, seizures, rapid course); psychiatric: depression (high suicide rate), personality changes, psychosis; cognitive decline → dementia; ANTICIPATION: successive generations → ↑repeat length (especially paternal transmission: CAG expansion during spermatogenesis) → earlier onset + more severe disease; autosomal DOMINANT; treatment: tetrabenazine/deutetrabenazine/valbenazine (VMAT2 inhibitors: ↓dopamine release → ↓chorea); other trinucleotide repeat diseases: Fragile X (CGG repeat in FMR1 5'UTR → methylation → silencing; most common inherited cause of intellectual disability; X-linked); Friedreich ataxia (GAA repeat in FRN/FXN intron 1 → ↓frataxin → ↓Fe-S cluster assembly → mitochondrial iron overload → spinocerebellar degeneration + hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; AR — unique because GAA expansion causes loss of function, not toxic gain; and it's AR, not AD); myotonic dystrophy type 1 (CTG repeat in DMPK 3'UTR → RNA gain-of-function → MBNL1 sequestration → aberrant splicing; AD + anticipation; myotonia + distal weakness + cataracts + cardiac conduction defects + insulin resistance); spinobulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease: CAG repeat in androgen receptor [AR] gene; X-linked → males; lower motor neuron + bulbar weakness + gynecomastia + androgen insensitivity)
Cystic fibrosis: CF is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene (most common: ΔF508, deletion of phenylalanine at position 508 → misfolding → ERAD → ↓CFTR at PM); NOT a trinucleotide repeat
Phenylketonuria: PKU is caused by mutations in the PAH gene (>1000 different mutations: missense, nonsense, splice site, deletions); NOT a trinucleotide repeat expansion
explanation: Trinucleotide repeat expansion diseases — complete list for exams: CODING region repeats (polyglutamine/polyQ, CAG → Gln; typically AD, toxic gain-of-function, protein aggregation): Huntington (HTT, CAG ≥40, caudate atrophy, chorea), SBMA/Kennedy (AR, CAG ≥38, X-linked, LMN+bulbar), SCA1/2/3/6/7/17 (various genes, cerebellar ataxia), DRPLA (ATN1, CAG); NON-CODING region repeats (various mechanisms): Fragile X (FMR1, 5'UTR CGG >200 → methylation → silencing; intellectual disability, macro-orchidism, long face, large ears; premutation 55-200 → FXTAS [fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia in older males] + FXPOI [premature ovarian insufficiency in females]); Friedreich ataxia (FXN, intron 1 GAA >66 → ↓transcription → ↓frataxin; AR); Myotonic dystrophy 1 (DMPK, 3'UTR CTG >50 → RNA toxic gain; AD); Myotonic dystrophy 2 (CNBP/ZNF9, intron 1 CCTG; AD; milder than DM1); SCA8 (ATXN8OS, CTG/CAG); SCA10 (ATXN10, ATTCT); SCA12 (PPP2R2B, CAG 5'UTR); C9orf72 (GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat in intron 1 → most common genetic cause of ALS and FTD; dipeptide repeat proteins → aggregation + RNA foci).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is the primary nitrogen carrier from peripheral tissues (especially muscle) to the liver for urea synthesis?
options: Glutamate: glutamate is the major intracellular amino acid and the direct nitrogen donor in many transamination reactions; however, Glu does NOT circulate significantly in blood as a nitrogen carrier from muscle to liver (glutamate is largely retained intracellularly and metabolized locally)

Alanine: Alanine is the PRIMARY nitrogen carrier from MUSCLE to LIVER via the GLUCOSE-ALANINE CYCLE (Cahill cycle): In muscle: amino acid catabolism → amino groups transferred to α-KG → [aminotransferases, PLP] → glutamate; glutamate + pyruvate → [ALT/GPT, alanine aminotransferase] → alanine + α-KG; alanine released into blood → travels to liver; In liver: alanine + α-KG → [ALT] → pyruvate + glutamate; pyruvate → [gluconeogenesis] → glucose → blood → muscle (for glycolysis → pyruvate → repeat); glutamate → [GDH or aminotransferases] → NH4+ → urea cycle → urea → kidneys → excretion; NET EFFECT: muscle exports nitrogen (as alanine) and receives glucose from liver; this prevents muscle from having to release toxic free NH3; alanine is the most abundant amino acid released by muscle; ALT (alanine aminotransferase, GPT): high ALT activity in LIVER → serum ALT is a sensitive marker of HEPATOCELLULAR damage (more specific than AST for liver); ALT ratio: ALT > AST in most liver diseases; AST > ALT (>2:1) in alcoholic hepatitis (AST/ALT [De Ritis ratio] >2 → alcoholic; reason: alcohol depletes PLP [needed for ALT more than AST] + mitochondrial damage releases mitochondrial AST [mAST]); glutamine: second major nitrogen carrier → transports NH3 from brain, muscle → kidney (glutaminase → Glu + NH4+ → NH4+ excreted → acid-base regulation) and liver (glutaminase → NH4+ → urea cycle)

Aspartate: aspartate contributes nitrogen to the urea cycle (Asp + citrulline → argininosuccinate; Asp provides one of the two nitrogen atoms in urea), but Asp is NOT the primary nitrogen carrier from muscle to liver in the blood
Lysine: lysine is a purely ketogenic amino acid and is NOT a nitrogen carrier between tissues; lysine cannot undergo transamination (ε-amino group is not a substrate for standard aminotransferases)
explanation: Inter-organ amino acid/nitrogen transport: (1) Glucose-alanine cycle (muscle → liver): muscle exports alanine (carries amino N from muscle protein catabolism) → liver converts to glucose (GNG) + ammonia (→ urea); (2) Glutamine shuttle: muscle/brain/other tissues: Glu + NH4+ → [glutamine synthetase, GS] → Gln; Gln travels in blood to: KIDNEY: glutaminase → Glu + NH4+ → NH4+ excreted in urine (acid-base: ↑glutaminase in metabolic acidosis → ↑NH4+ excretion → ↑H+ elimination; NH3 is new HCO3- generation → corrects acidosis); LIVER (periportal): glutaminase → Glu + NH4+ → urea cycle; GUT: glutamine is the preferred fuel of enterocytes (not glucose); (3) BCAA shuttle: liver → exports BCAAs (Leu, Ile, Val) to muscle/brain (liver lacks BCAT for initial transamination → releases BCAAs intact); muscle has BCAT + BCKDH → catabolizes BCAAs for energy; in cirrhosis: ↓hepatic urea cycle → ↑NH3; ↑↑BCAAs consumed by muscle to detoxify NH3 → ↓plasma BCAA:AAA ratio (↑aromatic amino acids [Phe, Tyr, Trp → not cleared by diseased liver] → cross BBB → false neurotransmitters [octopamine from Tyr] → hepatic encephalopathy); BCAA supplementation in cirrhosis → may help normalize ratio.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the function of ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q10) in the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
options: Transfers electrons from Complex III to Complex IV: this function is performed by CYTOCHROME C (small peripheral membrane protein on IMS face of IMM; shuttles electrons from Complex III [cyt c1] to Complex IV [CuA]; also: released during apoptosis → apoptosome); NOT CoQ10

Serves as a mobile electron carrier between Complex I/II and Complex III: Ubiquinone (CoQ10, Coenzyme Q10): lipid-soluble mobile electron carrier in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM); CoQ shuttles electrons FROM Complex I (NADH → CoQ) and Complex II (FADH2 → CoQ) and other dehydrogenases [ETF-QO from fatty acid β-oxidation, DHODH from pyrimidine synthesis, mitochondrial G3P dehydrogenase from glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle] TO Complex III (CoQH2 → Q-cycle → cyt c); CoQ exists in 3 redox states: ubiquinone (Q, fully oxidized) → semiquinone (Q•⁻, radical intermediate) → ubiquinol (QH2, fully reduced); CoQ is also an important ANTIOXIDANT in membranes (reduced form QH2 prevents lipid peroxidation); CoQ10 supplementation: used in mitochondrial diseases (primary CoQ10 deficiency → steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, cerebellar ataxia, encephalomyopathy), statin-associated myopathy (statins ↓mevalonate pathway → ↓CoQ10 synthesis [CoQ shares mevalonate/isoprenoid pathway with cholesterol]; evidence for CoQ10 supplementation in statin myopathy is mixed), heart failure (some benefit in severe CHF; Q-SYMBIO trial)
Acts as the final electron acceptor in the ETC: MOLECULAR OXYGEN (O2) is the final electron acceptor (Complex IV reduces O2 → H2O); CoQ is NOT the final electron acceptor

Pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane: CoQ itself does NOT directly pump protons; the proton pumping is performed by Complex I (4 H+), Complex III (4 H+ via Q-cycle), and Complex IV (2 H+ per e⁻); CoQ is a mobile carrier, not a proton pump; however, CoQ participates in the Q-cycle within Complex III which results in H+ translocation
explanation: Mobile electron carriers in ETC: CoQ (ubiquinone/CoQ10): lipid-soluble in IMM; connects Complex I + II + other dehydrogenases → Complex III; isoprenoid tail (10 isoprene units in humans → CoQ10); synthesized via mevalonate pathway (shared with cholesterol → statins may ↓CoQ10); Cytochrome c: water-soluble peripheral protein on IMS face; connects Complex III → Complex IV; also key role in intrinsic apoptosis (released from IMS when MOMP [mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization] occurs via BAX/BAK pores [activated when pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins (BIM, BID, BAD, PUMA, NOXA) overwhelm anti-apoptotic BCL-2/BCL-XL/MCL-1] → cyt c + Apaf-1 + dATP → apoptosome [heptameric wheel] → caspase-9 activation → caspase-3/7 → apoptosis); venetoclax (BCL-2 inhibitor) → promotes apoptosis in CLL/AML by freeing pro-apoptotic proteins → MOMP → cyt c release.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: What is the biochemical basis of the cyanide-nitroprusside test used to screen for cystinuria?
options: Detects elevated urinary uric acid: the cyanide-nitroprusside test does NOT measure uric acid; uric acid is measured by enzymatic assay (uricase) or colorimetric methods

Reacts with the disulfide bond of cystine to produce a purple color: The cyanide-nitroprusside (Brand) test: sodium cyanide REDUCES the DISULFIDE BOND of cystine (cystine = two cysteine molecules linked by -S-S-): cystine + CN⁻ → 2 cysteine (free -SH groups); then sodium nitroprusside [Na2Fe(CN)5NO] reacts with free SULFHYDRYL (-SH) groups → PURPLE/MAGENTA color (nitroprusside reacts with thiol groups); positive test: urine cystine >75 mg/L (above normal); this is a qualitative SCREENING test for cystinuria; confirmatory: 24-hour urine amino acid quantification (ion-exchange chromatography or LC-MS/MS) → ↑cystine + ↑ornithine + ↑lysine + ↑arginine (COLA); stone analysis: hexagonal crystals on urine microscopy are PATHOGNOMONIC for cystine stones (only substance that forms hexagonal crystals in urine); cystine stones: slightly radio-opaque (less dense than calcium stones on CT, can be missed on plain X-ray; 'ground-glass' appearance), resistant to ESWL (hard stones); NOTE: the nitroprusside reaction also detects homocysteine (homocystinuria screening: silver-nitroprusside test [modified version]; homocysteine also has free -SH after reduction)
