Detects glucose in urine via enzymatic oxidation: this describes the glucose oxidase urine dipstick test (glucosuria screening); NOT the cyanide-nitroprusside test
Measures ammonia levels in urine: urinary ammonia is measured by direct ion-selective electrode or enzymatic methods; NOT by cyanide-nitroprusside
explanation: Urine screening tests — biochemistry exam: Cyanide-nitroprusside (Brand test): cystinuria screening (reduces disulfide → free -SH → reacts with nitroprusside → purple); Ferric chloride test (FeCl3): screens for various metabolites in urine — PKU (musty odor, green/blue-green color with FeCl3), MSUD (burnt sugar odor), alkaptonuria (transient blue → turns black); largely replaced by tandem MS/MS newborn screening; Dinitrophenylhydrazine (DNPH) test: detects α-keto acids in urine → positive in MSUD (↑α-ketoisocaproic acid, α-keto-β-methylvaleric acid, α-ketoisovaleric acid); Ninhydrin test: reacts with free amino groups → purple/blue (Ruhemann's purple); used to detect amino acids generally (not specific); Benedict's test / Clinitest: detects REDUCING sugars in urine (glucose, galactose, fructose, lactose); copper sulfate reduction → color change; glucose dipstick (glucose oxidase) is specific for glucose only — so a positive Clinitest + negative dipstick → non-glucose reducing substance (galactose in galactosemia, fructose in hereditary fructose intolerance); Sodium nitroprusside (separate from cyanide-nitroprusside): detects ketone bodies (acetoacetate) in urine → positive in DKA; does NOT detect β-hydroxybutyrate (which is the predominant ketone in DKA; measured by blood β-HB assay).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid disorder is characterized by lens subluxation (ectopia lentis), marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, and thromboembolism?
options: Homocystinuria (classical, CBS deficiency): Classical homocystinuria: deficiency of CYSTATHIONINE β-SYNTHASE (CBS, PLP-dependent); CBS normally catalyzes: homocysteine + serine → cystathionine (first step of transsulfuration pathway; cystathionine → [cystathionase/CTH, PLP] → cysteine + α-ketobutyrate); CBS deficiency → ↑↑homocysteine (plasma + urine) + ↑methionine (because remethylation of Hcy → Met continues, and Hcy cannot go forward through transsulfuration); clinical tetrad: (1) ECTOPIA LENTIS (lens subluxation, typically DOWNWARD/inferonasal; vs Marfan: upward/superotemporal); mechanism: homocysteine disrupts fibrillin-1 cross-linking in zonular fibers (Cys residues in fibrillin form disulfide bonds → homocysteine interferes → ↓zonule integrity → lens subluxation); (2) MARFANOID HABITUS (tall, thin, arachnodactyly, pectus; similar to Marfan syndrome but different cause); (3) OSTEOPOROSIS (Hcy interferes with collagen cross-linking → ↓bone quality; also ↓osteoblast function); (4) THROMBOEMBOLISM (arterial + venous; leading cause of death in homocystinuria; Hcy damages endothelium → ↑TF expression + ↓thrombomodulin + ↓protein C activation + ↑platelet adhesion + ↓fibrinolysis; also ↑Hcy → ↑oxidative stress → endothelial dysfunction); also: intellectual disability (if untreated), seizures, psychiatric symptoms; AR, CBS gene (21q22.3); diagnosis: ↑plasma total homocysteine (tHcy >100 μmol/L; normal <15), ↑methionine, ↓cysteine; urine: ↑homocystine (disulfide of 2 Hcy → detected by cyanide-nitroprusside test, same as cystinuria screening); treatment: (a) PYRIDOXINE (B6) trial: ~50% of patients are B6-responsive (↑PLP → ↑residual CBS activity → ↓Hcy; milder mutations, often I278T); (b) methionine-restricted diet + cysteine supplementation; (c) BETAINE (trimethylglycine): alternative methyl donor → betaine + Hcy → [BHMT, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase] → Met + DMG (dimethylglycine); ↓Hcy but ↑Met; (d) folate + B12 supplementation (↑remethylation pathway)
Maple syrup urine disease: MSUD is caused by BCKDH complex deficiency → ↑BCAAs (Leu, Ile, Val) + ↑BCKAs; sweet/burnt sugar odor; encephalopathy; does NOT cause lens subluxation or marfanoid habitus
Phenylketonuria: PKU (PAH deficiency) → ↑Phe → intellectual disability, seizures, eczema, musty odor, fair coloring; does NOT cause lens subluxation, marfanoid habitus, or thromboembolism
Alkaptonuria: alkaptonuria (HGD deficiency) → ↑homogentisic acid → dark urine, ochronosis, arthropathy; does NOT cause lens subluxation or marfanoid habitus
explanation: Methionine-homocysteine metabolism — complete: Met → [MAT, methionine adenosyltransferase] → SAM (S-adenosylmethionine; universal methyl donor → >100 methyltransferase reactions: DNA methylation [DNMTs], histone methylation, creatine [GAMT], PE→PC [PEMT], NE→Epi [PNMT], norepinephrine synthesis, polyamine [dcSAM]); SAM → [methyltransferases] → SAH (S-adenosylhomocysteine); SAH → [SAHH, SAH hydrolase; reversible, favors synthesis → product removal drives forward] → Hcy + adenosine; Hcy has TWO fates: (1) REMETHYLATION → Met: (a) MS (methionine synthase, MTR gene): Hcy + CH3-THF → [MS, requires MeCbl/B12] → Met + THF; (b) BHMT (liver/kidney only): Hcy + betaine → Met + DMG; (2) TRANSSULFURATION → Cys: Hcy + Ser → [CBS, PLP/B6] → cystathionine → [CTH, PLP] → Cys + α-KB; Cys → GSH, taurine, SO4²⁻; Hyperhomocysteinemia causes: genetic (CBS def → classical HCU; MTHFR C677T homozygosity → mild ↑Hcy [thermolabile variant, ~10% population]; Cbl deficiency [dietary/malabsorption] → ↓MeCbl → ↓MS; folate deficiency → ↓CH3-THF → ↓MS); nutritional (↓B6, ↓B12, ↓folate); renal failure; hypothyroidism; drugs (methotrexate → ↓folate; phenytoin; nitrous oxide → oxidizes Cbl → inactivates MS); cardiovascular risk: mild-moderate ↑Hcy is an independent CV risk factor (endothelial dysfunction + thrombosis); lowering Hcy with folate+B12 has NOT reduced CV events in major trials (HOPE-2, VITATOPS) → Hcy may be a marker not a causal target.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which glycogen storage disease is characterized by exercise intolerance with myalgia and a 'second wind' phenomenon?
options: GSD type I (von Gierke): G6Pase deficiency (type Ia) or G6P translocase deficiency (type Ib) → hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia; affects LIVER (not muscle exercise intolerance); 'doll-like facies' (fat cheeks from hyperlipidemia)

GSD type V (McArdle disease): McArdle disease (GSD V): MYOPHOSPHORYLASE deficiency (muscle-specific glycogen phosphorylase, PYGM gene); AR; muscle glycogen cannot be broken down → exercise intolerance + myalgia + muscle cramps + rhabdomyolysis (↑CK, myoglobinuria → risk of acute kidney injury); SECOND WIND PHENOMENON: after ~10 minutes of exercise, symptoms improve because: (a) ↑blood flow → ↑delivery of blood-borne fuels (free fatty acids, blood glucose); (b) ↑fatty acid oxidation becomes primary energy source; (c) hepatic glucose output ↑ → muscle takes up and uses blood glucose via hexokinase (bypasses glycogen phosphorylase block); patients learn to 'pace through' the initial cramp → can continue exercise at moderate intensity; diagnosis: (1) ischemic forearm exercise test: ↓lactate rise (no glycogenolysis → no pyruvate → no lactate) + normal ↑ammonia (PNC intact); NON-ischemic (aerobic) forearm test now preferred (lower risk of compartment syndrome); (2) ↑CK at baseline; (3) muscle biopsy: subsarcolemmal glycogen accumulation + absent myophosphorylase (PAS-positive, phosphorylase histochemistry negative); (4) genetic testing: PYGM mutations (p.Arg50Ter [R50X, formerly R49X] most common in Caucasians); treatment: moderate aerobic exercise training (improves exercise capacity; NOT bed rest), pre-exercise oral sucrose (provides exogenous glucose → can bypass block), avoid intense isometric exercise; vitamin B6 (PLP is GP cofactor; limited evidence)

GSD type II (Pompe disease): acid α-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency → glycogen accumulates in LYSOSOMES (not cytoplasmic); infantile: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + hypotonia + macroglossia → death <2 yrs; late-onset: progressive limb-girdle + respiratory myopathy; ERT: alglucosidase alfa (Myozyme/Lumizyme); does NOT have 'second wind'

GSD type III (Cori-Forbes): debranching enzyme deficiency → limit dextrin accumulates; hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia (milder than GSD I) + myopathy (type IIIa); can have exercise intolerance but 'second wind' is CLASSIC for McArdle
explanation: Glycogen storage diseases — muscle vs liver: LIVER GSDs (hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia): GSD I (G6Pase/von Gierke): severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricemia + hyperlipidemia; GSD III (debrancher/Cori): milder hypoglycemia + ↑CK (myopathy in IIIa); GSD IV (brancher/Andersen): hepatosplenomegaly → cirrhosis → liver failure (abnormal glycogen with fewer branch points → amylopectin-like → hepatotoxic); GSD VI (liver phosphorylase/Hers): mild hepatomegaly + ketotic hypoglycemia; GSD IX (phosphorylase kinase): most common GSD; mild hepatomegaly, often X-linked (PHKA2); MUSCLE GSDs (exercise intolerance ± rhabdomyolysis): GSD V (myophosphorylase/McArdle): myalgia + cramps + second wind + rhabdomyolysis; GSD VII (PFK-M/Tarui): similar to McArdle but NO second wind with glucose (because PFK block is downstream of glucose entry; exogenous glucose → ↑G6P → ↑F6P but cannot pass PFK → no benefit; actually may WORSEN because ↑G6P inhibits hexokinase → ↓blood glucose utilization → 'out of wind' phenomenon); also: hemolytic anemia (RBC PFK partly from M-subunit); BOTH liver + muscle: GSD III (IIIa), GSD IX (some subtypes).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The enzyme telomerase adds repetitive nucleotide sequences to chromosome ends. Which component of telomerase serves as the template for this extension?
options: TERT (telomerase reverse transcriptase): TERT is the CATALYTIC subunit (reverse transcriptase activity: synthesizes DNA from RNA template); TERT is essential for telomerase function but it is NOT the template — it is the enzyme

TERC (telomerase RNA component): TERC (also called TR or hTR) is the RNA component that serves as the TEMPLATE for telomere extension; human TERC contains the template sequence 3'-CAAUCCCAAUC-5' (which templates the synthesis of TTAGGG repeats on the 3' overhang of telomeric DNA); telomere structure: human telomeres consist of 5-15 kb of tandem TTAGGG repeats (G-rich strand: 3' overhang extends ~150-200 nt beyond the C-rich strand); the 3' overhang folds back and invades the duplex → T-loop + D-loop (protects chromosome end from being recognized as DSB → prevents DDR activation); Shelterin complex (6 proteins): TRF1 + TRF2 (bind dsTTAGGG), POT1 (binds ss 3' overhang), TIN2 + TPP1 + RAP1; shelterin protects telomeres and regulates telomerase access; telomerase mechanism: TERC template hybridizes to 3' overhang → TERT extends DNA (reverse transcription: RNA template → DNA) → adds TTAGGG repeats → translocation → repeat; after TERT extends the G-rich strand, DNA Pol α-primase fills in the C-rich strand (conventional lagging strand synthesis); telomere shortening: occurs with each cell division (end replication problem: RNA primer at 5' end of lagging strand cannot be replaced → progressive shortening ~50-100 bp per division → Hayflick limit → replicative senescence or crisis → apoptosis/senescence); telomerase expression: active in germ cells, stem cells, ~90% of cancers (replicative immortality; hallmark of cancer); most somatic cells lack telomerase activity; ALT (alternative lengthening of telomeres): homologous recombination-based mechanism in ~10% of cancers (especially sarcomas, astrocytomas) → telomere maintenance without telomerase

Dyskerin (DKC1): dyskerin is a telomerase-associated protein (pseudouridine synthase; stabilizes TERC by binding its H/ACA box motif); DKC1 mutations → dyskeratosis congenita (X-linked form: DKC1; also AD: TERC or TERT; AR: NOP10, NHP2, WRAP53); short telomeres → bone marrow failure + abnormal skin pigmentation + nail dystrophy + oral leukoplakia + pulmonary fibrosis + ↑cancer risk

Shelterin/TRF2: TRF2 (telomeric repeat-binding factor 2) is a shelterin component that binds double-stranded TTAGGG → protects telomeres + prevents ATM-mediated DDR; TRF2 is NOT a component of telomerase itself
explanation: Telomere biology and disease — clinical: Telomeropathies (short telomere syndromes): dyskeratosis congenita (DKC), aplastic anemia, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), liver cirrhosis; genes: DKC1 (X-linked), TERC/TERT (AD), RTEL1, TINF2, CTC1, PARN, POT1; telomere length measurement: flow-FISH (gold standard for clinical), Southern blot (TRF analysis), qPCR (T/S ratio); Cancer: ↑telomerase → replicative immortality (hallmark); TERT promoter mutations (C228T, C250T → create ETS binding site → ↑TERT transcription; common in melanoma, GBM, bladder, thyroid [follicular], hepatocellular carcinoma); TERT amplification in neuroblastoma (poor prognosis); telomerase inhibitors: imetelstat (GRN163L; oligonucleotide complementary to TERC template → blocks telomerase; FDA 2024 for lower-risk MDS with transfusion-dependent anemia); Anti-aging: telomerase activators (TA-65, TAT2) → marketed as supplements but unproven clinical benefit; concern about ↑cancer risk with telomerase activation in somatic cells.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) is the most potent allosteric activator of which glycolytic enzyme?
options: Hexokinase: hexokinase (HK I-III, low Km) is inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate (G6P feedback inhibition); glucokinase (HK IV, high Km liver/β-cell) is NOT inhibited by G6P but regulated by GKRP (glucokinase regulatory protein: sequesters GK in nucleus when F6P is high; releases when glucose↑ or F1P↑); F2,6BP does NOT activate hexokinase

Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1): PFK-1 (6-phosphofructo-1-kinase): catalyzes F6P + ATP → F1,6BP + ADP; the COMMITTED STEP (rate-limiting, irreversible) of glycolysis; F2,6BP is the MOST POTENT allosteric ACTIVATOR of PFK-1 (↑PFK-1 activity even when ATP and citrate [inhibitors] are high → overrides inhibitory signals → ↑glycolytic flux); F2,6BP is synthesized/degraded by the BIFUNCTIONAL ENZYME PFK-2/FBPase-2 (6-phosphofructo-2-kinase / fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase): PFK-2 activity (kinase): F6P + ATP → F2,6BP (↑F2,6BP → ↑glycolysis); FBPase-2 activity (phosphatase): F2,6BP → F6P + Pi (↓F2,6BP → ↓glycolysis); LIVER isoform regulation (PFKFB1): GLUCAGON (fasting) → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates bifunctional enzyme → ↓PFK-2 + ↑FBPase-2 → ↓F2,6BP → ↓PFK-1 → ↓glycolysis + ↑gluconeogenesis; INSULIN (fed) → PP2A dephosphorylates → ↑PFK-2 + ↓FBPase-2 → ↑F2,6BP → ↑PFK-1 → ↑glycolysis; this is how glucagon shifts liver from glycolysis → gluconeogenesis and insulin does the opposite; OTHER PFK-1 regulators: activators (AMP, ADP, F2,6BP, Pi); inhibitors (ATP [at allosteric site], citrate, H+); note: ATP is both a substrate (at catalytic site) AND an inhibitor (at allosteric site → sigmoidal kinetics)

Pyruvate kinase: PK (catalyzes PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP; last step of glycolysis) is activated by F1,6BP (feed-forward activation: upstream glycolytic intermediate promotes final step); PK is inhibited by ATP, alanine, and phosphorylation by PKA (glucagon → PKA → phospho-PK → less active → ↓pyruvate → ↓glycolysis in liver); F2,6BP does NOT directly activate PK

Aldolase: aldolase cleaves F1,6BP → G3P + DHAP; aldolase is NOT allosterically regulated by F2,6BP; aldolase B deficiency → hereditary fructose intolerance (↑F1P in liver → traps Pi → ↓ATP → liver failure + hypoglycemia)
explanation: Glycolysis regulation — the 3 irreversible steps: (1) HEXOKINASE/GLUCOKINASE: glucose → G6P; HK: low Km, product-inhibited by G6P; GK (liver/β-cell): high Km, NOT inhibited by G6P, regulated by GKRP + glucose; (2) PFK-1 (committed step, most important regulatory point): F6P → F1,6BP; KEY activator: F2,6BP (most potent); other activators: AMP, ADP, Pi; inhibitors: ATP (allosteric), citrate, H+; (3) PYRUVATE KINASE: PEP → pyruvate; activator: F1,6BP (feed-forward); inhibitors: ATP, Ala, phosphorylation (glucagon/PKA in liver → ↓PK); Gluconeogenesis bypass enzymes (4 reactions bypass the 3 irreversible glycolytic steps + one equilibrium shift): (1) Pyruvate carboxylase (PC): pyruvate → OAA (mito, biotin, activated by acetyl-CoA); (2) PEPCK: OAA → PEP (cytoplasm in humans; GTP-dependent; ↑transcription by glucagon/cortisol [CREB, FOXO1], ↓by insulin [FOXO1 phosphorylation → nuclear exclusion]); (3) FBPase-1: F1,6BP → F6P (inhibited by F2,6BP + AMP; glucagon ↓F2,6BP → ↑FBPase-1 → ↑GNG); (4) G6Pase: G6P → glucose (ER membrane, liver + kidney + intestine ONLY; NOT in muscle → muscle cannot release free glucose → muscle glycogen is for LOCAL use only).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which RNA modification at the 5' end of eukaryotic mRNA is essential for ribosome recognition and translation initiation?
options: Poly-A tail: the poly-A tail is at the 3' end (not 5' end); it enhances stability and translation (PABPC1 → eIF4G interaction), but it is NOT the 5' modification recognized by the ribosome

7-methylguanosine (m7G) cap: The 5' m7G cap (7-methylguanosine cap) is essential for ribosome recognition and cap-dependent translation initiation; cap structure: m7G(5')ppp(5')N (7-methylguanosine linked by 5'-5' triphosphate bridge to first transcribed nucleotide); cap addition: co-transcriptional (when transcript ~20-30 nt; by Pol II CTD-associated capping enzymes); cap recognized by: eIF4E (eukaryotic initiation factor 4E) → eIF4E is part of eIF4F complex (eIF4E [cap-binding] + eIF4A [RNA helicase, unwinds 5'UTR secondary structure] + eIF4G [scaffold: bridges eIF4E on cap + PABPC1 on poly-A → mRNA circularization; also recruits eIF3 → 43S PIC]); cap-dependent translation: 43S PIC (40S ribosomal subunit + eIF1/1A/3/5 + Met-tRNAi-eIF2-GTP ternary complex) → recruited to 5' cap via eIF4F-eIF3 interaction → SCANNING (5'→3' along 5'UTR) → encounters AUG start codon (Kozak consensus: gcc(A/G)ccAUGG; A/G at -3 and G at +4 are most important) → base-pairing with Met-tRNAi anticodon → eIF2-GTP hydrolysis → 48S complex → 60S joining (eIF5B-GTP) → 80S ribosome → elongation; regulation of cap-dependent translation: mTORC1 → phosphorylates 4E-BP1 → releases eIF4E → ↑translation; rapamycin → ↓mTORC1 → ↓4E-BP1 phosphorylation → 4E-BP1 sequesters eIF4E → ↓cap-dependent translation; some mRNAs use IRES (internal ribosome entry site) for cap-INDEPENDENT translation (viral: HCV, poliovirus; cellular: under stress [Myc, VEGF, p53 IRES])

N6-methyladenosine (m6A): m6A is the most abundant internal modification of mRNA (installed by METTL3/METTL14 [writers], removed by FTO/ALKBH5 [erasers], read by YTHDF1/2/3 [readers]); m6A regulates mRNA stability, splicing, translation, and localization; m6A is an INTERNAL modification, NOT the 5' cap
Pseudouridine (Ψ): pseudouridine is the most abundant modified nucleotide in rRNA and tRNA (C5-glycosidic bond instead of normal N1); also found in mRNA; it is NOT the 5' cap modification
explanation: Translation — initiation in eukaryotes (detailed): 1. eIF2 + GTP + Met-tRNAi → ternary complex (TC); eIF2 regulation: eIF2α PHOSPHORYLATION (Ser51) → ↓TC formation → ↓global translation (integrated stress response, ISR); kinases: HRI (heme deficiency), GCN2 (amino acid deprivation), PERK (ER stress/UPR), PKR (dsRNA/viral infection); all 4 kinases → P-eIF2α → paradoxically ↑translation of ATF4 (uORF-mediated: ATF4 mRNA has upstream ORFs that normally prevent ATF4 translation; under stress, reduced TC availability → ribosomes skip uORFs → translate ATF4 → stress response gene activation); 2. 43S PIC: TC + 40S + eIF1/1A/3/5; 3. mRNA activation: eIF4F (eIF4E+4A+4G) binds cap → recruits 43S via eIF4G-eIF3; 4. Scanning: 43S scans 5'→3' → AUG recognition → 48S; 5. 60S joining: eIF5B-GTP → 80S → start elongation; Elongation: aminoacyl-tRNA + eEF1A-GTP → A-site → peptide bond (28S rRNA ribozyme activity = peptidyl transferase) → translocation (eEF2-GTP → moves ribosome one codon 5'→3'); eEF2 target: DIPHTHERIA TOXIN (DT) ADP-ribosylates eEF2 (modifies diphthamide residue → inactivates eEF2 → ↓translocation → ↓protein synthesis → cell death; Pseudomonas exotoxin A has same mechanism); Termination: stop codon (UAA/UAG/UGA) → eRF1 (recognizes stop) + eRF3-GTP → peptide release → ribosome recycling.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome is caused by deficiency of which enzyme in the cholesterol synthesis pathway?
options: HMG-CoA reductase: HMGCR deficiency would be lethal (mevalonate pathway block → no cholesterol, no isoprenoids); statins are competitive inhibitors that ↓HMGCR but do not eliminate activity; HMGCR deficiency is NOT the cause of SLO syndrome

7-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR7): Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS): AR, caused by deficiency of DHCR7 (7-dehydrocholesterol reductase, the FINAL enzyme in the Kandutsch-Russell pathway of cholesterol synthesis); DHCR7 normally: 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC) → [DHCR7, NADPH] → cholesterol; DHCR7 deficiency → ↑7-DHC (and ↑8-DHC) + ↓cholesterol; clinical features (due to ↓cholesterol during embryogenesis → impaired Hedgehog signaling [Shh requires cholesterol for processing and signaling] + impaired membrane/lipid raft formation): (1) intellectual disability, (2) 2-3 toe SYNDACTYLY (Y-shaped; most characteristic finding), (3) microcephaly, (4) ptosis, (5) anteverted nares (short nose), (6) micrognathia, (7) cleft palate (in severe cases), (8) genital anomalies in males (hypospadias, ambiguous genitalia, cryptorchidism; ↓cholesterol → ↓testosterone synthesis → undervirilization), (9) cardiac defects (AVSD, VSD), (10) growth retardation, (11) behavioral: autism spectrum, self-injurious behavior; diagnosis: ↑7-DHC in plasma (elevated 7-DHC:cholesterol ratio; can be measured by GC-MS); ↓plasma cholesterol (but can be normal in mild cases); genetic: DHCR7 mutations; treatment: dietary cholesterol supplementation (egg yolks, high-cholesterol diet; exogenous cholesterol does NOT cross BBB well → limited neurological benefit); simvastatin paradox: some studies show ↓7-DHC with statin (↓upstream synthesis) but controversial; early diagnosis + cholesterol supplementation may improve growth and behavior but cannot reverse structural malformations

Squalene synthase: squalene synthase (FDFT1) catalyzes: 2 farnesyl-PP → squalene (first committed step to sterol pathway after the branch point); deficiency would be extremely rare/lethal; NOT the cause of SLOS
Lanosterol synthase: lanosterol synthase (LSS/OSC) cyclizes squalene 2,3-epoxide → lanosterol; deficiency is extremely rare; NOT the cause of SLOS
explanation: Cholesterol synthesis pathway — key steps from mevalonate: Mevalonate → [MK] → mevalonate-5-P → [PMK] → mevalonate-5-PP → [MDD] → isopentenyl-PP (IPP, 5C 'isoprene unit') ⇌ dimethylallyl-PP (DMAPP); IPP + DMAPP → [FPP synthase] → geranyl-PP (10C) → farnesyl-PP (15C); BRANCH POINT at farnesyl-PP: (a) → squalene → → lanosterol → → 7-DHC → [DHCR7] → cholesterol (Kandutsch-Russell pathway; SLOS = DHCR7 def); alternatively: → desmosterol → [DHCR24] → cholesterol (Bloch pathway); (b) → geranylgeranyl-PP (20C) → protein prenylation; (c) → dolichol (N-glycosylation); (d) → ubiquinone/CoQ10 (ETC); (e) → heme A (CIV); Inborn errors of cholesterol synthesis: SLOS (DHCR7, most common); desmosterolosis (DHCR24, extremely rare); lathosterolosis (SC5D); mevalonic aciduria (MVK, mevalonate kinase deficiency → ↑mevalonic acid + autoinflammatory [hyper-IgD syndrome/HIDS]); CHILD syndrome (NSDHL, X-linked dominant); congenital hemidysplasia with ichthyosiform erythroderma and limb defects.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which coenzyme, derived from pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), is essential for the transfer of acyl groups in fatty acid synthesis and oxidation?
options: NAD+ (from niacin/B3): NAD+ transfers hydride ions (electrons) in redox reactions; NAD+ is NOT an acyl group carrier; NAD+ is derived from niacin (B3), not pantothenic acid

Coenzyme A (CoA): CoA (coenzyme A) is derived from PANTOTHENIC ACID (vitamin B5); CoA structure: pantothenic acid + β-mercaptoethylamine (cysteamine) + 3'-phospho-ADP; the reactive group is the terminal THIOL (-SH) of the cysteamine moiety → forms THIOESTER bonds with acyl groups (R-CO~S-CoA; high-energy bond: ΔG°' of hydrolysis ~ -31 kJ/mol → drives acyl transfer reactions); CoA-dependent reactions: (1) PDC: pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (E2 component: dihydrolipoyl transacetylase transfers acetyl from lipoamide to CoA-SH); (2) fatty acid β-oxidation: generates acetyl-CoA (+ FADH2 + NADH per cycle); (3) TCA cycle: acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate (citrate synthase); succinyl-CoA → succinate + GTP (SCS); α-KG → succinyl-CoA (OGDH); (4) fatty acid synthesis: acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (ACC); malonyl-CoA transferred to ACP (acyl carrier protein of FAS — ACP also contains a phosphopantetheine arm derived from pantothenic acid via CoA → 4'-phosphopantetheine transferred to Ser of ACP); (5) HMG-CoA synthesis (cholesterol + ketone body pathways); (6) amino acid catabolism (propionyl-CoA from odd-chain FA, Val, Ile, Met, Thr, cholesterol side chain → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA); (7) bile acid conjugation (cholyl-CoA + glycine/taurine); (8) drug acetylation (acetyl-CoA + drug → NAT1/NAT2 → acetylated drug; isoniazid, sulfonamides; slow/fast acetylator status: NAT2 polymorphisms)
FAD (from riboflavin/B2): FAD transfers electrons in redox reactions (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase in β-oxidation, SDH in TCA, etc.); FAD is NOT an acyl group carrier; derived from riboflavin (B2)

Thiamine pyrophosphate (from thiamine/B1): TPP transfers aldehyde/acyl groups in α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes and transketolase; TPP is derived from thiamine (B1), not pantothenic acid; TPP carries activated aldehyde, not free acyl groups for synthesis/oxidation
explanation: Pantothenic acid (B5) → CoA + ACP: Pantothenic acid is ubiquitous in food ('pantos' = everywhere; deficiency is RARE: experimentally induced → 'burning feet syndrome'); CoA synthesis: pantothenate → [pantothenate kinase, PANK] → 4'-phosphopantothenate → + cysteine → [PPCS] → 4'-phosphopantothenoylcysteine → [PPCDC, decarboxylation] → 4'-phosphopantetheine → [PPAT, + ATP] → dephospho-CoA → [DPCK] → CoA; PANK (pantothenate kinase): rate-limiting step; PANK2 mutations → pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN, formerly Hallervorden-Spatz disease; NBIA = neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1; 'eye of the tiger' sign on MRI [central hyperintensity surrounded by hypointensity in globus pallidus due to iron deposition]; progressive dystonia + parkinsonism + cognitive decline; AR); CoA thioester bond energy: drives condensation reactions; acetyl-CoA: central metabolic intermediate linking carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism; 'common currency of activated acetic acid.'

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the function of signal recognition particle (SRP) in protein targeting?
options: Facilitates nuclear import of proteins with nuclear localization signals: nuclear import is mediated by importin α/β recognizing NLS (classical: monopartite [PKKKRKV, SV40 large T antigen] or bipartite) → importin-cargo → NPC → Ran-GTP dissociates complex in nucleus; SRP is NOT involved in nuclear import

Targets ribosome-nascent chain complex to the ER membrane for co-translational translocation: SRP (signal recognition particle): targets secretory/membrane proteins to the ER; components: 7SL RNA (SRP RNA, ~300 nt, Pol III transcript) + 6 protein subunits (SRP9/14 [translation arrest], SRP54 [signal sequence binding + GTPase], SRP19/68/72); mechanism: (1) ribosome translates mRNA → N-terminal SIGNAL PEPTIDE emerges (~16-30 aa: positively charged N-region + hydrophobic H-region + polar C-region with signal peptidase cleavage site); (2) SRP54 (methionine-rich M-domain) recognizes and binds the hydrophobic signal peptide; (3) SRP binding causes TRANSLATION PAUSE (SRP9/14 interact with ribosome → slows elongation → prevents misfolding of ER-destined protein in cytoplasm); (4) SRP-ribosome-nascent chain (RNC) complex docks at ER membrane via SRP RECEPTOR (SR, composed of SRα [GTPase] + SRβ [GTPase]; on ER membrane); (5) GTP-dependent handoff: SRP54-GTP + SRα-GTP → mutual GTP hydrolysis → SRP releases → signal peptide inserted into SEC61 TRANSLOCON (protein-conducting channel: Sec61α [pore-forming] + Sec61β + Sec61γ); (6) translation resumes → nascent polypeptide threaded through Sec61 into ER lumen (co-translational translocation); (7) signal peptidase (SP, lumenal) cleaves signal peptide → mature N-terminus; (8) BiP/GRP78 (Hsp70 chaperone in ER lumen) assists folding

Degrades misfolded proteins in the proteasome: proteasomal degradation involves ubiquitin-proteasome system (E1-E2-E3 → polyUb → 26S proteasome); SRP is NOT involved in proteasomal degradation; ERAD (ER-associated degradation) involves retrotranslocation from ER → cytoplasmic ubiquitination → proteasome

Chaperones nascent proteins in the mitochondrial matrix: mitochondrial protein import uses TOM complex (outer membrane) + TIM23/TIM22 (inner membrane) + mitochondrial Hsp70 (mtHsp70/mortalin) in matrix; MTS (matrix targeting sequence: amphipathic α-helix, positively charged); SRP is for ER targeting, NOT mitochondrial
explanation: Protein targeting/sorting — summary: ER (secretory pathway): signal peptide → SRP → Sec61 translocon → co-translational; OR post-translational (Sec62/63 + BiP for small proteins); ER → Golgi (COPII vesicles) → Golgi processing (glycan trimming/addition) → trans-Golgi sorting: constitutive secretion (default), regulated secretion (secretory granules, stimulus-dependent: insulin from β-cells), lysosomal targeting (M6P tag: GlcNAc-phosphotransferase adds M6P to lysosomal enzymes → M6P receptor → clathrin-coated vesicles → late endosome/lysosome; I-cell disease [mucolipidosis II]: GlcNAc-phosphotransferase deficiency → enzymes lack M6P → secreted instead of targeted to lysosomes → inclusion bodies in cells + ↑serum lysosomal enzymes); Mitochondria: N-terminal MTS → TOM/TIM complexes → matrix; requires ΔΨm (membrane potential) + ATP + mtHsp70; Peroxisomes: PTS1 (C-terminal SKL) → PEX5; PTS2 (N-terminal) → PEX7; PEX gene mutations → Zellweger spectrum disorders; Nucleus: NLS → importin → NPC; NES → exportin/CRM1 → NPC; Ran-GTP gradient drives directionality.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme is deficient in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked disorder characterized by hyperuricemia, self-mutilation, and neurological dysfunction?
options: Adenosine deaminase (ADA): ADA deficiency → SCID (T-B-NK-); ↑dATP → lymphotoxicity; NOT Lesch-Nyhan

Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT/HPRT1): Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: X-LINKED RECESSIVE; caused by COMPLETE deficiency of HGPRT (HPRT1 gene, Xq26-q27); HGPRT is a purine SALVAGE enzyme: hypoxanthine + PRPP → [HGPRT] → IMP + PPi; guanine + PRPP → [HGPRT] → GMP + PPi; HGPRT deficiency → cannot salvage hypoxanthine/guanine → (a) ↑PRPP accumulation (substrate not consumed) → ↑de novo purine synthesis (PRPP activates GPAT/amidophosphoribosyltransferase) → ↑purine production → ↑degradation → ↑uric acid (SEVERE HYPERURICEMIA); (b) ↓IMP/GMP from salvage → less feedback inhibition → further ↑de novo synthesis; clinical: (1) HYPERURICEMIA → gouty arthritis, uric acid nephrolithiasis, nephropathy (even in childhood); (2) SELF-MUTILATION (compulsive self-injurious behavior: lip/finger biting, head banging; unique to complete HGPRT deficiency; mechanism unclear — may involve dopaminergic dysfunction in basal ganglia [↓dopamine in caudate/putamen; possibly ↓GTP → ↓BH4 synthesis → ↓TH → ↓dopamine]); (3) neurological: choreoathetosis, dystonia, spasticity, intellectual disability; (4) megaloblastic features possible; X-linked → virtually all patients are MALE; heterozygous females are carriers (may have ↑uric acid); PARTIAL HGPRT deficiency → Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome (hyperuricemia + gout WITHOUT self-mutilation or severe neurological features); treatment: ALLOPURINOL (xanthine oxidase inhibitor → ↓uric acid; treats hyperuricemia but does NOT improve neurological symptoms); febuxostat (alternative XOI); hydration + alkalinization → prevent urate stones; behavioral management + physical restraints for self-injury; NO effective treatment for neurological symptoms
Xanthine oxidase (XO): XO deficiency → xanthinuria (↓uric acid → HYPOuricemia + xanthine stones; benign); XO is the TARGET of allopurinol treatment, not the deficient enzyme in Lesch-Nyhan

APRT (adenine phosphoribosyltransferase): APRT deficiency → adenine → 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (2,8-DHA) stones (radiolucent; often misdiagnosed as uric acid stones); treated with allopurinol (↓XO → ↓DHA formation); NOT Lesch-Nyhan
explanation: Purine metabolism disorders — uric acid spectrum: ↑Uric acid: (1) Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT complete def → ↑↑UA + neuro + self-mutilation); (2) Kelley-Seegmiller (partial HGPRT → gout, no neuro); (3) PRPS superactivity (↑PRPP synthetase → ↑PRPP → ↑de novo purines → ↑UA + gout + sensorineural deafness; X-linked gain-of-function); (4) Gout (primary: multifactorial ↓renal urate excretion [90%] or ↑production; secondary: tumor lysis syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, Lesch-Nyhan, PRPS); treatment: acute gout (colchicine [↓microtubule polymerization → ↓neutrophil migration], NSAIDs, corticosteroids); chronic: allopurinol/febuxostat (XOI → ↓UA production); uricosurics (probenecid: blocks URAT1 → ↑renal UA excretion); pegloticase (PEGylated uricase → uric acid → allantoin [soluble]; for refractory tophaceous gout); rasburicase (recombinant uricase; for tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis); ↓Uric acid: PNP deficiency (↓T-cells, hypouricemia); XO deficiency (xanthinuria, hypouricemia); HGPRT deficiency does NOT cause hypouricemia — it causes HYPERuricemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of the urea cycle?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I): CPS I catalyzes the RATE-LIMITING step of the urea cycle: NH3 + CO2 + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate + 2 ADP + Pi; CPS I is located in the MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX; CPS I REQUIRES N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an obligate allosteric activator (NAG binds CPS I → conformational change → active); NAG synthesis: NAGS (N-acetylglutamate synthase): Glu + acetyl-CoA → NAG; NAGS is activated by ARGININE (Arg is a urea cycle intermediate → when Arg↑ → ↑NAGS → ↑NAG → ↑CPS I → ↑urea cycle flux; positive feed-forward regulation); CPS I deficiency: most SEVERE urea cycle disorder → neonatal hyperammonemia (NH3 >1000 μmol/L; normal <35; onset within first 24-72 hrs of life → lethargy → poor feeding → vomiting → seizures → cerebral edema → coma → death if untreated); treatment of acute hyperammonemia: (1) STOP protein intake; (2) IV glucose + lipids (prevent catabolism → ↓endogenous NH3 production); (3) IV sodium benzoate + sodium phenylacetate (Ammonul) → alternate pathway nitrogen excretion; (4) IV arginine HCl (for all UCD except arginase deficiency → provides ornithine → pulls cycle forward; in CPS I/OTC def: Arg becomes essential because it cannot be made); (5) hemodialysis if NH3 >500 or rising despite medical treatment; (6) long-term: dietary protein restriction + Na-phenylbutyrate (Buphenyl) or glycerol phenylbutyrate (Ravicti) + L-citrulline/L-arginine supplementation; (7) liver transplantation (definitive cure for hepatic UCDs)

Ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC): OTC catalyzes the SECOND step (carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline + Pi; mitochondrial); OTC is NOT the rate-limiting step; OTC deficiency is the MOST COMMON UCD (X-linked; males: severe neonatal; females: variable, may present later with partial deficiency); diagnostic clue: ↑orotic acid in urine (accumulated carbamoyl phosphate → cytoplasm → enters pyrimidine pathway → → → orotic acid; distinguishes OTC from CPS I deficiency which has LOW orotic acid)
Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS): ASS catalyzes citrulline + Asp + ATP → argininosuccinate + AMP + PPi (cytoplasm); ASS deficiency → citrullinemia type I (↑↑citrulline in blood → diagnostic)

Arginase (ARG1): arginase catalyzes the final step: Arg → ornithine + urea (cytoplasm, liver); arginase deficiency → hyperargininemia (↑Arg; mildest UCD; progressive spastic diplegia, NOT acute hyperammonemia typically)
explanation: Urea cycle — complete: Location: 2 mitochondrial steps + 3 cytoplasmic steps in LIVER (periportal hepatocytes); Steps: (1) CPS I (mito): NH3 + CO2 + 2ATP → CP (rate-limiting, requires NAG); (2) OTC (mito): CP + Orn → Cit; (3) ASS (cyto): Cit + Asp + ATP → ASA; (4) ASL (cyto): ASA → Arg + fumarate; (5) Arginase (cyto): Arg → Orn + urea; NET: NH3 + CO2 + Asp + 3 ATP → urea + fumarate + 2 ADP + AMP + 2 Pi + PPi (4 high-energy phosphate bonds consumed: 2 ATP→2ADP [CPS I] + ATP→AMP+PPi [ASS, equivalent of 2 ATP]); Nitrogen sources in urea: N1 from free NH3 (via CPS I); N2 from aspartate (via ASS → ASA → ASL releases fumarate); fumarate from ASL → malate → OAA → Asp (aspartate-fumarate shuttle links urea cycle to TCA); UCD diagnosis: NH3↑, amino acid profile: CPS I def (↓Cit, ↓orotic acid); OTC def (↓Cit, ↑orotic acid); ASS def (↑↑Cit); ASL def (↑ASA + ↑Cit); Arginase def (↑↑Arg); NAGS def (↓NAG → ↓CPS I activity; treated with N-carbamylglutamate [Carbaglu, synthetic NAG analog → directly activates CPS I; only UCD with specific pharmacological cure besides liver transplant]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which serum enzyme is most specific for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
options: Amylase: serum amylase rises early in acute pancreatitis (within 6-12 hrs, peaks 48 hrs, normalizes 3-5 days); however, amylase is NOT specific — also elevated in: salivary gland disease (parotitis, mumps), bowel obstruction/perforation, mesenteric ischemia, renal failure (↓clearance), macroamylasemia, ectopic pregnancy, DKA; isoforms: P-type (pancreatic) and S-type (salivary); P-amylase is more specific but still not as specific as lipase

Lipase: Serum LIPASE is the MOST SPECIFIC (and now preferred) enzyme for diagnosing acute pancreatitis; lipase rises within 4-8 hrs, peaks 24-48 hrs, remains elevated for 8-14 DAYS (longer than amylase → useful in delayed presentations); lipase >3x upper limit of normal is diagnostic criterion for acute pancreatitis (along with characteristic abdominal pain and/or imaging findings [CT/MRI]; 2 of 3 criteria needed → revised Atlanta classification); lipase is more specific than amylase because: (a) lipase is predominantly pancreatic (less salivary/non-pancreatic sources); (b) lipase stays elevated longer (better for late presentations); (c) fewer false positives; lipase CAN be elevated in: renal failure (↓clearance), bowel obstruction, peritonitis, some malignancies; but overall more specific than amylase; most guidelines now recommend lipase ALONE (not both amylase + lipase; amylase adds little diagnostic value when lipase is available)

ALT (alanine aminotransferase): ALT is specific for HEPATOCELLULAR injury (liver; ALT > AST in most liver diseases; AST > ALT [De Ritis >2] in alcoholic hepatitis); ALT↑ in pancreatitis may suggest BILIARY etiology (gallstone pancreatitis: gallstone → CBD obstruction → ↑ALT/AST + ↑bilirubin + ↑ALP; ALT >150 U/L has ~95% PPV for gallstone pancreatitis); but ALT is NOT specific for pancreatitis itself

Creatine kinase (CK): CK is specific for MUSCLE injury (↑CK-MM in rhabdomyolysis/myopathy, ↑CK-MB in MI [now replaced by troponin], ↑CK-BB in brain injury [rare clinical use]); CK is NOT specific for pancreatitis
explanation: Diagnostic enzymology — organ-specific enzymes: LIVER: ALT (GPT, most specific for hepatocellular), AST (GOT, also in heart/muscle), ALP (cholestasis/bone; isoforms: liver, bone, placental, intestinal; ↑ALP + ↑GGT → hepatobiliary; ↑ALP + normal GGT → bone [Paget's, osteomalacia, bone mets]; 5'-nucleotidase also confirms hepatic ALP), GGT (most sensitive for cholestasis; ↑↑ in alcoholism [enzyme induction]; GGT alone is NOT specific for liver); PANCREAS: lipase (most specific), amylase (less specific, rises/falls faster); HEART: troponin I/T (most specific for myocardial injury), CK-MB (reinfarction detection); BONE: ALP (bone isoform), TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase, 5b: osteoclast activity → bone resorption marker); PROSTATE: PSA (kallikrein-like serine protease); MUSCLE: CK (MM), aldolase, LDH; Enzyme patterns: obstructive jaundice: ↑↑ALP + ↑↑GGT + ↑direct bilirubin + mild ↑AST/ALT; hepatocellular: ↑↑AST/ALT + mild ↑ALP + ↑indirect/direct bilirubin; alcoholic hepatitis: AST:ALT > 2:1 (B6 depletion → ↓ALT preferentially + mAST release from damaged mitochondria).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: What is the primary metabolic fuel for the brain under normal fed conditions?
options: Fatty acids: the brain CANNOT use fatty acids as fuel because: (a) fatty acids bound to albumin cannot efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB); (b) β-oxidation occurs in mitochondria → generates NADH/FADH2 → ETC → ATP, but this pathway is minimal in the brain under normal conditions; the brain relies on glucose as its primary fuel

Glucose: Under normal fed conditions, GLUCOSE is the primary (nearly exclusive) fuel for the brain; brain glucose consumption: ~120 g/day (~5 g/hr); brain accounts for ~20% of total body oxygen consumption and ~25% of glucose utilization despite being only ~2% of body weight; brain glucose uptake is insulin-INDEPENDENT (GLUT1: BBB endothelial cells [constitutive, high affinity]; GLUT3: neurons [highest affinity GLUT, Km ~1.4 mM → ensures glucose uptake even at low blood glucose]); glucose → glycolysis → pyruvate → PDC → acetyl-CoA → TCA → OXPHOS → CO2 + H2O + ATP; the brain has minimal glycogen stores (~0.1% of liver) → completely dependent on continuous blood glucose supply → hypoglycemia is immediately dangerous (neuroglycopenia: confusion, seizures, coma, death); during PROLONGED STARVATION (>2-3 days): liver produces KETONE BODIES (β-hydroxybutyrate + acetoacetate from hepatic fatty acid β-oxidation → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate → β-OHB by BDH1/NADH; ketones cross BBB via MCT1/MCT2 transporters) → brain adapts to use ketone bodies for ~60-75% of energy needs (↓glucose requirement to ~40 g/day → ↓muscle protein catabolism for gluconeogenesis → protein-sparing effect; this adaptation is critical for survival during prolonged fasting)

Ketone bodies: ketone bodies become an important brain fuel during prolonged STARVATION or uncontrolled diabetes (DKA), but under NORMAL FED conditions the primary fuel is glucose; ketone body utilization requires adaptation (↑MCT expression, ↑succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid-CoA transferase [SCOT/thiolase in brain])

Amino acids: amino acids are NOT a primary fuel for the brain under normal conditions; however, glutamate and glutamine are important for neurotransmitter pools (glutamate → excitatory NT; GABA → inhibitory NT; glutamate-glutamine cycle between neurons and astrocytes)
explanation: Fuel utilization by organ — exam table: BRAIN: fed → glucose (GLUT1/3, insulin-independent); fasted/starvation → glucose + ketone bodies (adaptation over days); CANNOT use FA; MUSCLE: fed → glucose (GLUT4, insulin-dependent) + FA; fasted → FA (primary) + ketone bodies; intense exercise → glucose (glycogen → glycolysis → lactate), then FA (endurance); rest → FA (70-80% of resting muscle energy); LIVER: fed → glucose (GK), amino acids, FA; fasted → FA (β-oxidation for energy; also → ketogenesis for export); liver does NOT use ketone bodies (lacks SCOT; or has low SCOT → ketones exported to peripheral tissues); HEART: FA (60-70% of cardiac energy at rest; β-oxidation is primary fuel); also glucose, lactate, ketone bodies; heart is metabolically flexible; ADIPOSE: fed → glucose (GLUT4) → glycolysis → G3P (for TG esterification) + FA synthesis; fasted → lipolysis (HSL → FA + glycerol → exported); RBC: glucose ONLY (no mitochondria → anaerobic glycolysis → lactate; GLUT1; also PPP → NADPH → GSH); KIDNEY: glutamine (cortex: gluconeogenesis from glutamine; important in acidosis → NH4+ excretion); also FA, ketone bodies, lactate, glucose.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following mutations in hemoglobin results in increased oxygen affinity?
options: HbS (Glu6Val on β-globin): HbS has DECREASED oxygen affinity (right-shifted O2-Hb dissociation curve under deoxygenated conditions → ↑O2 release to tissues; however, the primary pathology is polymerization of deoxy-HbS → sickling, not affinity change); HbS does NOT have increased O2 affinity

HbC (Glu6Lys on β-globin): HbC forms intracellular crystals (not polymers like HbS); HbC has near-normal oxygen affinity; HbCC → mild hemolytic anemia + target cells + splenomegaly; does NOT significantly ↑O2 affinity

Hb Chesapeake (Arg92Leu on α-globin): Hb Chesapeake has INCREASED oxygen affinity (left-shifted O2-Hb dissociation curve); Arg92 of α-globin (Argα92 = α1β2 interface) normally participates in the T→R conformational transition (salt bridges stabilize T-state/deoxy); Leu substitution disrupts T-state stabilization → favors R-state (oxy) → ↑O2 affinity → ↓O2 release to tissues → tissue hypoxia → ↑EPO → secondary ERYTHROCYTOSIS (polycythemia); HIGH-AFFINITY hemoglobin variants are an important cause of FAMILIAL ERYTHROCYTOSIS (autosomal dominant; distinguished from polycythemia vera [JAK2V617F, primary] by: normal JAK2, low/normal EPO in PV but NORMAL/HIGH EPO in high-affinity Hb + left-shifted P50); P50: partial pressure of O2 at which Hb is 50% saturated; normal P50 ~26.6 mmHg; ↓P50 = ↑affinity (left shift); ↑P50 = ↓affinity (right shift); other high-affinity Hb variants: Hb Yakima, Hb Kempsey, Hb Rainier; treatment: usually none needed (compensated by erythrocytosis); phlebotomy only if symptomatic hyperviscosity

HbH (β4 tetramers): HbH forms when α-globin is severely deficient (α-thalassemia: 3 α-gene deletions → HbH disease); HbH (β4) has very HIGH oxygen affinity (does NOT release O2 effectively → functionally useless; ↓P50 ~13 mmHg); however, this is a THALASSEMIA consequence, not a point mutation; HbH is unstable → precipitates → Heinz bodies → hemolysis; technically HbH does have ↑affinity but the question asks about a point mutation — Hb Chesapeake is the classic single amino acid substitution answer
explanation: Hemoglobin — oxygen binding and allosteric regulation: Hb structure: α2β2 tetramer; each subunit has heme (protoporphyrin IX + Fe2+); cooperative binding (sigmoidal O2-Hb dissociation curve); T-state (taut/deoxy): low O2 affinity; R-state (relaxed/oxy): high O2 affinity; Bohr effect: ↑CO2 + ↑H+ → ↓O2 affinity (right shift) → ↑O2 release in tissues (CO2 from tissue metabolism → ↑H+ [carbonic anhydrase: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3⁻] → H+ binds His146β → stabilizes T-state → ↓affinity); 2,3-BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, from RBC glycolysis via Rapoport-Luebering shunt): binds central cavity of deoxy-Hb (between β-chains) → stabilizes T-state → ↓O2 affinity → ↑O2 delivery; RIGHT SHIFT (↓affinity, ↑O2 release): ↑CO2, ↑H+ (↓pH), ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG; LEFT SHIFT (↑affinity, ↓O2 release): ↓CO2, ↓H+ (↑pH), ↓temperature, ↓2,3-BPG, CO (carboxyhemoglobin: CO binds heme Fe2+ with 250x affinity of O2 → left shift + ↓O2 carrying capacity), HbF (fetal Hb: α2γ2; γ-chains bind 2,3-BPG less well → ↑O2 affinity → facilitates O2 transfer from maternal to fetal blood), MetHb (Fe3+ → cannot bind O2; induced by nitrites, dapsone, benzocaine; treatment: methylene blue [↓by NADPH-MetHb reductase → leucomethylene blue → reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which transport mechanism is responsible for glucose uptake in the small intestinal enterocytes across the apical (brush border) membrane?
options: GLUT2 (facilitated diffusion): GLUT2 is present on the BASOLATERAL membrane of enterocytes → facilitates glucose exit from enterocyte into portal blood (facilitated diffusion, down concentration gradient); GLUT2 may transiently appear on the apical membrane at high luminal glucose concentrations, but SGLT1 is the PRIMARY apical transporter; GLUT2 is also the glucose transporter in liver (bidirectional: uptake in fed state, release in fasting; low affinity/high capacity → acts as glucose sensor) and pancreatic β-cells (rodents; humans use GLUT1 more)

SGLT1 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 1): SGLT1 (SLC5A1) is the PRIMARY glucose (and galactose) transporter on the APICAL (brush border/luminal) membrane of small intestinal enterocytes; SGLT1 is a SECONDARY ACTIVE TRANSPORTER (Na+-glucose symporter): couples the transport of 2 Na+ ions (down electrochemical gradient, maintained by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase [primary active transport: 3Na+ out, 2K+ in, 1 ATP]) with 1 glucose molecule (against concentration gradient → INTO enterocyte); SGLT1 transports: glucose AND galactose (both are substrates; fructose is NOT — fructose uses GLUT5 on apical membrane via facilitated diffusion); SGLT1 deficiency → glucose-galactose malabsorption (AR; neonatal osmotic diarrhea with glucose/galactose-containing feeds; fructose tolerance is normal → fructose-based formula as treatment); after apical uptake: glucose exits basolaterally via GLUT2 → portal blood; oral rehydration solution (ORS): exploits SGLT1 → Na+ + glucose in ORS → SGLT1 cotransport → drives water absorption by osmotic gradient → treats dehydration in diarrheal illness (WHO-ORS: reduced osmolarity; greatest medical advance — saves millions of lives from cholera/rotavirus/infectious diarrhea); SGLT2 (SLC5A2): kidney PCT (S1 segment) → reabsorbs ~90% of filtered glucose; SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins: empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) → block renal glucose reabsorption → glycosuria → ↓blood glucose + ↓weight + CV benefit (EMPA-REG, DAPA-HF) + renal protection (DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY)

GLUT4 (insulin-dependent facilitated diffusion): GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent glucose transporter in MUSCLE and ADIPOSE tissue; NOT present in intestinal enterocytes; insulin → Akt → AS160 → Rab10 → GLUT4 vesicle translocation to PM → ↑glucose uptake

GLUT1 (facilitated diffusion): GLUT1 is a constitutive, high-affinity glucose transporter in RBCs, BBB endothelium, and most tissues; GLUT1 is NOT the primary apical glucose transporter in intestinal enterocytes; GLUT1 deficiency syndrome (De Vivo disease): impaired glucose transport across BBB → seizures, microcephaly, developmental delay; treated with ketogenic diet (ketone bodies bypass need for glucose transport across BBB)
explanation: Glucose transporters — complete: GLUT family (SLC2A, facilitated diffusion, down gradient, no energy): GLUT1 (ubiquitous, BBB, RBC; Km ~1 mM); GLUT2 (liver, β-cell [rodent], kidney PCT basolateral, intestine basolateral; Km ~15-20 mM; low affinity/high capacity → glucose sensor); GLUT3 (neurons; Km ~1.4 mM; highest affinity → ensures neuronal glucose supply); GLUT4 (muscle, adipose; insulin-dependent vesicular translocation; Km ~5 mM); GLUT5 (intestine apical; FRUCTOSE transporter specifically; also in spermatozoa); SGLT family (SLC5A, secondary active transport, Na+-coupled, against gradient): SGLT1 (intestine apical + kidney PCT S3: 2Na+:1 glucose/galactose); SGLT2 (kidney PCT S1/S2: 1Na+:1 glucose; reabsorbs 90% filtered glucose; SGLT2i: gliflozins → glycosuria + natriuresis → CV + renal benefit independent of glucose lowering → now used in HFrEF, HFpEF, CKD regardless of diabetes status).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acids has an imidazole side chain that acts as a buffer at physiological pH?
options: Lysine: Lys has an ε-amino group (pKa ~10.5) → protonated at physiological pH (positive charge); Lys is NOT an effective buffer at pH 7.4 (pKa too far from 7.4; Henderson-Hasselbalch: buffer capacity is optimal within ±1 pH unit of pKa)

Histidine: Histidine has an IMIDAZOLE side chain (pKa ~6.0 for the imidazolium/imidazole equilibrium); this pKa is the CLOSEST to physiological pH (7.4) among all amino acid side chains → histidine can ACT AS A BUFFER near physiological pH; at pH 7.4: ~10% protonated (imidazolium, +charge) / ~90% deprotonated (imidazole, neutral) → can accept or donate protons; this buffering capacity is exploited in: (1) HEMOGLOBIN: His residues contribute to the buffering capacity of blood (Hb has 38 His residues per tetramer → major non-bicarbonate buffer in blood); His146β (C-terminal of β-chain): key residue in Bohr effect (deoxygenation → His146β forms salt bridge with Asp94β → ↑pKa of His146 → accepts H+ → stabilizes T-state → ↓O2 affinity; protonation of His146 consumes H+ → buffers blood in tissues where CO2/H+ are produced); (2) CARBONIC ANHYDRASE: His residues in active site coordinate Zn2+ and participate in proton shuttle (His64 acts as proton shuttle: transfers H+ from Zn-bound water to bulk solvent → regenerates active Zn-OH for next catalytic cycle; fastest known enzyme: kcat ~10^6 s⁻¹); (3) HISTIDINE acts as both proton donor and acceptor in many enzyme active sites (acid-base catalysis: serine protease catalytic triad [Ser-His-Asp: His57 in chymotrypsin acts as general base → abstracts proton from Ser195 -OH → nucleophilic Ser attacks peptide bond])
Glutamate: Glu has a carboxyl side chain (pKa ~4.1) → deprotonated (negative charge) at pH 7.4; Glu is NOT an effective buffer at pH 7.4 (pKa too far below)

Cysteine: Cys has a thiol side chain (pKa ~8.3) → mostly protonated at pH 7.4; Cys is a moderate buffer above physiological pH but not at pH 7.4; the most important amino acid buffer AT physiological pH is histidine due to its pKa ~6.0 being closest to 7.4
explanation: Amino acid side chain pKa values (exam-critical): Asp (β-COOH): ~3.65; Glu (γ-COOH): ~4.25; His (imidazole): ~6.0 (closest to physiological pH → best buffer); Cys (-SH): ~8.3; Tyr (-OH phenol): ~10.1; Lys (ε-NH3+): ~10.5; Arg (guanidinium): ~12.5 (almost always protonated → strongest base among amino acids); at pH 7.4: Asp⁻, Glu⁻ (negative), His (mostly neutral, ~10% positive), Cys-SH (mostly protonated/neutral), Tyr-OH (neutral), Lys⁺ (positive), Arg⁺ (positive); Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); buffer capacity is maximal at pH = pKa (equal amounts of acid and conjugate base); effective buffering range: pKa ± 1.0 pH unit; isoelectric point (pI): pH at which net charge = 0; for amino acids with non-ionizable R: pI = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2; for acidic R (Asp, Glu): pI = (pKa1 + pKaR)/2; for basic R (Lys, Arg, His): pI = (pKa2 + pKaR)/2; electrophoresis/chromatography separation is based on charge at given pH → depends on pI and pKa values.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which metabolic pathway converts glucose to fructose via sorbitol as an intermediate, and is clinically significant in diabetic complications?
options: Pentose phosphate pathway: PPP converts G6P → 6PG → ribulose-5-P (oxidative phase: NADPH) → various sugars (non-oxidative phase); PPP does NOT produce sorbitol or fructose from glucose via a sorbitol intermediate

Polyol pathway (sorbitol pathway): The POLYOL PATHWAY (sorbitol/aldose reductase pathway): glucose → [ALDOSE REDUCTASE (AR, AKR1B1), NADPH → NADP+] → SORBITOL → [SORBITOL DEHYDROGENASE (SDH), NAD+ → NADH] → FRUCTOSE; under normal glucose levels: minimal flux through polyol pathway (~3% of glucose); in HYPERGLYCEMIA (diabetes): ↑intracellular glucose → ↑flux through polyol pathway → ↑SORBITOL accumulation (sorbitol is an osmotically active polyol that does NOT easily cross cell membranes → trapped inside cells); consequences: (1) OSMOTIC STRESS: ↑intracellular sorbitol → water influx → cell swelling → damage (especially in lens → diabetic CATARACTS [sugar cataracts; also: galactitol accumulation in galactosemia → same mechanism]; Schwann cells → neuropathy); (2) ↓NADPH: aldose reductase consumes NADPH → ↓NADPH available for glutathione reductase (GSSG + NADPH → GSH) → ↓GSH → ↑oxidative stress; (3) ↑NADH (from SDH) → pseudohypoxia (↑NADH/NAD+ ratio → mimics hypoxic conditions → ↑reductive stress); diabetic complications involving polyol pathway: diabetic neuropathy (Schwann cells, peripheral nerves), diabetic retinopathy (pericytes, endothelial cells), diabetic nephropathy, diabetic cataracts; aldose reductase inhibitors (ARIs: epalrestat [approved in Japan/India for diabetic neuropathy]; ranirestat, fidarestat, sorbinil [withdrawn: hypersensitivity] — clinical trials have shown mixed results in Western populations); OTHER hyperglycemia damage mechanisms: (a) AGE (advanced glycation end-products): glucose non-enzymatically reacts with amino groups (Schiff base → Amadori product [HbA1c is an Amadori product: glucose + N-terminal Val of β-globin] → AGEs [CML, pentosidine] → RAGE receptor → NF-κB → inflammation); (b) PKC activation (↑DAG → ↑PKC → vascular dysfunction); (c) hexosamine pathway (↑F6P → ↑glucosamine → ↑UDP-GlcNAc → O-GlcNAcylation → altered gene expression)
Glycogenesis: glycogenesis converts glucose → glycogen (G6P → G1P → UDP-glucose → glycogen [via glycogen synthase + branching enzyme]); it does NOT produce sorbitol or fructose

Glucuronic acid pathway: the glucuronic acid pathway (uronic acid pathway): glucose → G6P → G1P → UDP-glucose → UDP-glucuronate (for conjugation reactions: bilirubin, drugs, steroids); in some species (not humans): → L-gulonate → L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C); humans lack L-gulonolactone oxidase → cannot synthesize vitamin C → essential vitamin; this pathway does NOT produce sorbitol
explanation: Diabetic complications — biochemical mechanisms (Brownlee unifying hypothesis): All 4 pathways are driven by MITOCHONDRIAL SUPEROXIDE OVERPRODUCTION: hyperglycemia → ↑glucose → ↑glycolysis → ↑NADH/FADH2 → ↑ETC flux → ↑superoxide (O2⁻) at Complex I/III → O2⁻ activates PARP → PARP depletes NAD+ → ↓GAPDH activity → upstream glycolytic intermediates accumulate → shunted into 4 damaging pathways: (1) ↑Polyol pathway (↑glucose → ↑sorbitol); (2) ↑AGE pathway (↑methylglyoxal/G3P → AGEs); (3) ↑PKC pathway (↑DHAP → ↑G3P → ↑DAG → ↑PKC); (4) ↑Hexosamine pathway (↑F6P → ↑glucosamine-6-P → ↑UDP-GlcNAc → O-GlcNAcylation); HbA1c: glycated hemoglobin; non-enzymatic glycation of β-globin N-terminal valine; reflects average blood glucose over ~2-3 months (RBC lifespan ~120 days); normal: <5.7%; prediabetes: 5.7-6.4%; diabetes: ≥6.5%; target: <7.0% for most diabetic patients; falsely ↓ in: hemolytic anemia, blood loss, hemoglobin variants, CKD+EPO; falsely ↑ in: iron deficiency, splenectomy, ↑RBC lifespan.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the role of PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen) in DNA replication?
options: Unwinds double-stranded DNA ahead of the replication fork: DNA unwinding is performed by MCM2-7 helicase (replicative helicase; part of CMG complex [Cdc45-MCM-GINS]; 3'→5' unwinding); PCNA does NOT unwind DNA

Acts as a sliding clamp that enhances processivity of DNA polymerases δ and ε: PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen): HOMOTRIMERIC ring-shaped SLIDING CLAMP that encircles dsDNA and tethers DNA polymerases (Pol δ and Pol ε) to the template → dramatically ↑PROCESSIVITY (ability to synthesize long stretches without dissociating); PCNA loading: RFC (replication factor C, clamp loader): uses ATP hydrolysis to open PCNA ring → loads it onto primer-template junction → PCNA closes around DNA → recruits Pol δ (lagging strand) or Pol ε (leading strand) via PIP box (PCNA-interacting peptide motif); PCNA also serves as a PLATFORM for many DNA replication and repair proteins: FEN1 (Okazaki fragment maturation), DNA ligase I, CAF-1 (chromatin assembly factor → nucleosome assembly behind fork), MMR proteins (MSH3/6, MLH1), TLS polymerases (Pol η, REV1 via monoubiquitinated PCNA [K164ub → recruits TLS pols for lesion bypass; RAD6/RAD18 E2/E3 → Ub-PCNA]); PCNA in cell cycle: ↑expression in S-phase → used as proliferation marker (immunohistochemistry: Ki-67 is more commonly used, but PCNA is also valid); PCNA in repair: NER (gap-filling by Pol δ/ε requires PCNA); BER (long-patch BER: Pol δ + PCNA); MMR (PCNA recruits MutSα/MutLα); in prokaryotes: β-clamp (homodimer, not homotrimer) + γ-complex (clamp loader) serve analogous function to PCNA + RFC
Synthesizes RNA primers for DNA replication: RNA primer synthesis is performed by PRIMASE (DnaG in bacteria; DNA Pol α-primase in eukaryotes); PCNA does NOT synthesize RNA primers

Joins Okazaki fragments by ligating DNA: Okazaki fragment ligation is performed by DNA LIGASE I (in eukaryotes) or DNA ligase (LigA in bacteria); ligase seals the nick between adjacent Okazaki fragments after primer removal and gap-filling; PCNA recruits Ligase I but does not perform ligation itself
explanation: Processivity factors in DNA replication — sliding clamps: PROKARYOTIC: β-clamp (dnaN gene product): HOMODIMER ring → tethers Pol III to DNA → processivity from ~10 nt to >50,000 nt; loaded by γ-complex (clamp loader, ATP-dependent); EUKARYOTIC: PCNA (homotrimer ring): tethers Pol δ/ε → ↑processivity; loaded by RFC (5-subunit clamp loader, ATP-dependent); Crystal structure: donut-shaped ring with inner diameter ~34 Å → fits dsDNA (~20 Å) through the central channel; PCNA slides along DNA → polymerase attached via PIP box → synthesizes DNA without falling off; PCNA modifications: K164 ubiquitination (mono-Ub → TLS; poly-Ub [K63-linked] → template switching/error-free tolerance); K164 SUMOylation → recruits Srs2 helicase → prevents unwanted recombination at stalled forks; PCNA as drug target: peptide/small molecule PIP-box mimetics can compete with protein-PCNA interactions → potential cancer therapy (disrupt replication/repair); T2AA (T2 amino alcohol) inhibits PCNA interactions → ↑sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which lipoprotein particle directly delivers cholesterol to cells via the LDL receptor (LDLR)?
options: HDL: HDL delivers cholesterol to the liver via SR-B1 (selective uptake; reverse cholesterol transport); HDL does NOT use the LDL receptor for cellular cholesterol delivery

LDL (low-density lipoprotein): LDL is the primary carrier of cholesterol to peripheral cells via LDLR (LDL receptor); LDL contains one molecule of ApoB-100 per particle; LDLR binds ApoB-100 on LDL → receptor-mediated endocytosis (clathrin-coated pits → coated vesicle → endosome [acidification → LDL dissociates from LDLR → LDLR recycled to surface; PCSK9 binds LDLR → targets it for lysosomal degradation instead of recycling → ↓surface LDLR → ↑plasma LDL; PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab → monoclonal Ab against PCSK9 → ↓PCSK9 → ↑LDLR recycling → ↑LDL clearance → ↓LDL-C by 50-60%; inclisiran: siRNA against PCSK9 mRNA → ↓PCSK9 synthesis → ↓LDL-C; SC every 6 months]) → lysosomal hydrolysis of LDL components → free cholesterol + amino acids + fatty acids; intracellular cholesterol regulatory responses: (1) ↓HMG-CoA reductase (↓endogenous cholesterol synthesis); (2) ↓LDLR transcription (↓SREBP-2 processing); (3) ↑ACAT (acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferase → esterifies excess cholesterol → cholesterol esters stored in lipid droplets); familial hypercholesterolemia (FH): LDLR mutations (most common) or ApoB-100 mutations (FDB: familial defective ApoB) or PCSK9 gain-of-function mutations → ↓LDL clearance → ↑↑LDL → premature atherosclerosis + tendon xanthomas + arcus cornealis; heterozygous FH: ~1:250 (LDL-C 300-500 mg/dL); homozygous FH: ~1:300,000 (LDL-C 600-1000 mg/dL → MI in childhood → requires LDL apheresis + aggressive therapy [statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9i, lomitapide (MTP inhibitor), evinacumab (anti-ANGPTL3)]); Goldstein & Brown: Nobel Prize 1985 for discovery of LDLR pathway

Chylomicron: chylomicrons deliver dietary TG to tissues (via LPL) and their remnants are cleared by the liver via LRP1/LDLR (recognizing ApoE); chylomicrons are NOT the primary source of cholesterol delivery to peripheral cells (that role is LDL)

VLDL: VLDL primarily delivers endogenous TG to peripheral tissues (via LPL → IDL → LDL); VLDL remnants (IDL) can be taken up by LDLR (via ApoE), but the primary cholesterol-delivering particle to peripheral cells is LDL
explanation: LDL receptor pathway — Goldstein & Brown: (1) LDL binds LDLR (ApoB-100 domain binds LDLR ligand-binding domain); (2) Receptor-mediated endocytosis via clathrin-coated pits (adaptor: AP2 → clathrin assembly → invagination → dynamin → scission → coated vesicle); (3) Uncoating → endosome (early → late/CURL); (4) Acidification (H+-ATPase → pH ~5.5): LDL dissociates from LDLR; (5) LDLR recycles to surface (vs PCSK9 → lysosomal degradation); (6) LDL → lysosome → acid lipase (LAL) hydrolyzes CE → free cholesterol + FA; LAL deficiency → Wolman disease (infantile, severe: hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal calcification, death <6 months) or CESD (cholesteryl ester storage disease, milder: hepatomegaly, ↑LDL, premature atherosclerosis); (7) Free cholesterol regulates: ↓SREBP-2 processing → ↓HMGCR + ↓LDLR transcription; ↑ACAT → CE storage; ↓SCAP-SREBP transport (Insig retention in ER when sterols present). Statin mechanism (complete): competitive inhibitor of HMGCR → ↓intracellular cholesterol → ↑SREBP-2 → ↑LDLR expression → ↑hepatic LDL uptake → ↓plasma LDL-C (20-55% reduction depending on statin/dose); pleiotropic effects (via ↓isoprenoids): ↓Rho/Ras prenylation → anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic, improved endothelial function.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) converts ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates. Which radical is essential for RNR catalytic activity?
options: Hydroxyl radical: hydroxyl radical (OH•) is a highly reactive ROS formed by Fenton reaction (Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + OH• + OH⁻); it is NOT the radical involved in RNR catalysis; hydroxyl radical causes indiscriminate oxidative damage to DNA/proteins/lipids

Tyrosyl radical: RNR (ribonucleotide reductase) class Ia (the major human RNR): contains a di-iron center in the R2 subunit that generates a stable TYROSYL RADICAL (Tyr122•) → this radical is transferred via a long-range radical transfer pathway (~35 Å) through aromatic residues to the active site Cys in the R1 subunit → generates a thiyl radical (Cys439•) → initiates substrate reduction (NDP → dNDP); RNR catalyzes: NDP + NADPH → dNDP + NADP+ + H2O (reducing equivalents: thioredoxin/glutaredoxin system → NADPH); RNR reduces the 2'-OH of ribose → 2'-H (deoxyribose); R1 subunit (RRM1): catalytic site + allosteric sites (activity site + specificity site); R2 subunit (RRM2 or p53R2/RRM2B): generates and stores the tyrosyl radical; R2 has a DIFERRIC-TYROSYL RADICAL center (Fe-O-Fe cluster + Tyr122•); allosteric regulation of RNR (critical for balanced dNTP pools): ACTIVITY SITE (on R1): ATP → activates; dATP → INHIBITS (overall shut-down; this is why dATP accumulation in ADA deficiency is toxic → kills lymphocytes by blocking RNR → ↓dNTP synthesis → ↓DNA synthesis); SPECIFICITY SITE (on R1): determines which NDP substrate is reduced → ensures balanced dNTP pools: ATP/dATP bound → reduces CDP/UDP; dTTP bound → reduces GDP; dGTP bound → reduces ADP
Superoxide radical: superoxide (O2•⁻) is produced by mitochondrial ETC, NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase; detoxified by SOD → H2O2; superoxide is NOT the radical in RNR

Nitric oxide radical: NO• is produced by NOS (eNOS, nNOS, iNOS) from arginine; NO activates sGC → cGMP; NO is NOT involved in RNR catalysis (though NO can inhibit RNR by quenching the tyrosyl radical → this is one mechanism of macrophage cytostasis against tumor cells/pathogens)
explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase — clinical significance: RNR is a TARGET for anticancer drugs: hydroxyurea (HU): free radical scavenger → quenches tyrosyl radical on R2 → inactivates RNR → ↓dNTP → S-phase arrest; used in: CML, polycythemia vera, sickle cell disease (↑HbF by unknown mechanism → ↓sickling); gemcitabine (2',2'-difluorodeoxycytidine): dFdCDP is a mechanism-based inhibitor of RNR R1 (binds active site → irreversible inactivation); also incorporated into DNA as dFdCTP → chain termination; used in: pancreatic cancer, NSCLC, bladder, breast; clofarabine: purine nucleoside analog → triphosphate inhibits RNR + DNA polymerase; used in: pediatric ALL (relapsed/refractory); RNR and dNTP pool imbalance: dATP excess: ADA deficiency → ↑dATP → RNR activity site inhibition → ↓all dNTPs → lymphocyte death (SCID); dGTP excess: PNP deficiency → ↑dGTP → RNR specificity site dysregulation → ↓T-cells; Balanced dNTP pools are essential for high-fidelity DNA replication; imbalanced pools → ↑mutagenesis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following enzymes requires selenium as an essential component?
options: Catalase: catalase is a heme-containing enzyme (Fe in heme); decomposes H2O2 → H2O + O2 in peroxisomes; selenium is NOT required

Glutathione peroxidase (GPx): GPx (glutathione peroxidase) is a SELENOPROTEIN — contains selenocysteine (Sec, the 21st amino acid, UGA codon [normally a stop codon → recoded by SECIS element in 3'UTR of selenoprotein mRNAs + special tRNASec + elongation factor eEFSec]); GPx catalyzes: H2O2 + 2 GSH → 2 H2O + GSSG (reduces H2O2 using glutathione); OR: ROOH + 2 GSH → ROH + H2O + GSSG (reduces lipid hydroperoxides); GPx family: GPx1 (cytoplasmic, most abundant), GPx2 (GI), GPx3 (plasma/secreted), GPx4 (phospholipid hydroperoxide GPx → unique: reduces lipid hydroperoxides in membranes → prevents FERROPTOSIS; GPx4 loss → ferroptosis → iron-dependent oxidative cell death), GPx5 (epididymis, NOT a selenoprotein), GPx6 (olfactory), GPx7/8 (ER); other selenoproteins: thioredoxin reductases (TrxR1/2/3: reduce oxidized thioredoxin; NADPH → TrxR → Trx-SH → reduce proteins, peroxiredoxins, ribonucleotide reductase); iodothyronine deiodinases (DIO1/2/3: T4 → T3 conversion [DIO1/2] or T4 → rT3/T3 → T2 [DIO3]; DIO1/2 activating, DIO3 inactivating); selenoprotein P (SELENOP: major selenium transport protein in plasma; also antioxidant); selenium deficiency: Keshan disease (endemic cardiomyopathy in Se-deficient regions of China → dilated CMP; associated with Coxsackievirus B3 → virus becomes more virulent in Se-deficient host); Kashin-Beck disease (osteoarthropathy; Se + iodine deficiency + mycotoxins)
Superoxide dismutase (SOD): SOD1 (Cu/Zn-SOD, cytoplasmic), SOD2 (Mn-SOD, mitochondrial), SOD3 (EC-SOD, extracellular Cu/Zn); SOD uses copper, zinc, or manganese — NOT selenium
Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV): Complex IV contains copper (CuA, CuB) and iron (heme a, heme a3); selenium is NOT a component of Complex IV
explanation: Trace minerals and metalloenzymes: SELENIUM: selenoproteins (GPx, TrxR, DIO, SelP; 25 human selenoproteins); ZINC: >300 enzymes (carbonic anhydrase, alcohol dehydrogenase, carboxypeptidase A/B, alkaline phosphatase, collagenase/MMPs, superoxide dismutase [Cu/Zn-SOD1], δ-ALA dehydratase, RNA polymerase, zinc finger transcription factors, thymulin); Zn deficiency: acrodermatitis enteropathica (SLC39A4/ZIP4 mutations → Zn malabsorption → periorificial/acral dermatitis + diarrhea + alopecia + immune dysfunction; acquired form with malnutrition/alcoholism); COPPER: ceruloplasmin (ferroxidase: Fe2+ → Fe3+ → binds transferrin → iron mobilization), lysyl oxidase (collagen/elastin cross-linking), cytochrome c oxidase (CIV), SOD1 (Cu/Zn-SOD), dopamine β-hydroxylase (DA → NE), tyrosinase (melanin synthesis); Cu disorders: Wilson (ATP7B mutations → Cu accumulation in liver/brain/cornea → hepatitis/cirrhosis + neuropsychiatric [basal ganglia] + Kayser-Fleischer rings + ↓ceruloplasmin; treated with penicillamine, trientine, zinc), Menkes (ATP7A mutations → Cu malabsorption → ↓Cu → kinky hair, neurodegeneration, connective tissue defects); IRON: heme proteins, Fe-S clusters (Complex I/II/III, aconitase), non-heme iron enzymes (prolyl hydroxylase, PHDs, TET, JmjC); MANGANESE: SOD2 (MnSOD), arginase, pyruvate carboxylase; MOLYBDENUM: xanthine oxidase, aldehyde oxidase, sulfite oxidase (molybdenum cofactor deficiency → ↑sulfite + ↓uric acid → seizures, lens dislocation).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: N-linked glycosylation of proteins occurs on which amino acid residue and in which cellular compartment does it begin?
options: Serine/threonine residues in the Golgi apparatus: O-linked glycosylation occurs on Ser/Thr residues and begins in the GOLGI (GalNAc addition by ppGalNAcT); O-linked is NOT N-linked

Asparagine residues in the endoplasmic reticulum: N-linked glycosylation occurs on ASPARAGINE (Asn) residues within the consensus sequence Asn-X-Ser/Thr (where X = any amino acid EXCEPT proline); N-linked glycosylation BEGINS in the ER: the oligosaccharide (Glc3Man9GlcNAc2, 14-sugar precursor) is pre-assembled on DOLICHOL phosphate (lipid carrier in the ER membrane; dolichol is synthesized from farnesyl-PP via the mevalonate pathway); assembly: cytoplasmic face of ER → first 7 sugars added (2 GlcNAc + 5 Man) → flipped to lumenal face by flippase → remaining 4 Man + 3 Glc added; OLIGOSACCHARYLTRANSFERASE (OST): transfers the entire 14-sugar block en bloc from dolichol-PP to the amide nitrogen of Asn side chain (N-glycosidic bond; co-translational: occurs as the nascent polypeptide enters the ER lumen through Sec61 translocon); ER processing: glucosidase I (removes terminal Glc) → glucosidase II (removes 2nd + 3rd Glc) → calnexin/calreticulin cycle (quality control: monoglucosylated glycoprotein binds calnexin [membrane-bound] or calreticulin [soluble] → proper folding; if misfolded → UGGT [UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase] re-adds Glc → re-enters calnexin/calreticulin cycle; if terminally misfolded → ER-mannosidase trims Man → ERAD [retrotranslocation → ubiquitination → proteasome]); Golgi processing: further trimming (mannosidases) and addition (GlcNAc transferases, galactosyltransferases, sialyltransferases, fucosyltransferases) → three types of N-glycans: (a) HIGH-MANNOSE (5-9 mannose; e.g., lysosomal enzymes [before M6P tagging]); (b) COMPLEX (GlcNAc, Gal, sialic acid, fucose branches; e.g., immunoglobulins, transferrin); (c) HYBRID (features of both)
Lysine residues in the endoplasmic reticulum: lysine residues can be hydroxylated (hydroxylysine in collagen) or acetylated/methylated (histones), but N-linked glycosylation does NOT occur on lysine
Asparagine residues in the Golgi apparatus: while Golgi MODIFIES N-glycans (trimming, branching), N-linked glycosylation BEGINS (the initial en bloc transfer) in the ER, not the Golgi
explanation: Glycosylation defects — CDG (congenital disorders of glycosylation): >150 types; most common: PMM2-CDG (CDG-Ia): phosphomannomutase 2 deficiency → ↓Man-6-P → GDP-mannose → ↓N-glycosylation; clinical: intellectual disability, cerebellar hypoplasia, inverted nipples, fat pads, strabismus, coagulopathy (↓AT-III, ↓protein C/S [glycoproteins!]); diagnosis: transferrin isoelectric focusing (IEF) → abnormal pattern (↓tetrasialotransferrin, ↑disialotransferrin + asialotransferrin); I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II): GlcNAc-phosphotransferase deficiency → lysosomal enzymes lack M6P tag → secreted instead of targeted to lysosomes → intracellular inclusion bodies (undigested substrates) + ↑serum lysosomal enzymes; clinical: similar to Hurler but NO mucopolysacchariduria (not MPS); coarse facies, skeletal dysplasia, growth failure; severe, early death; Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): acquired PIGA mutation in HSC → ↓GPI-anchor synthesis → loss of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55 [DAF] + CD59 [MIRL]) from RBC surface → complement-mediated hemolysis (↓CD55 → ↓decay acceleration → ↑C3/C5 convertase activity; ↓CD59 → ↓MAC regulation → ↑MAC [C5b-9] insertion → lysis); treatment: eculizumab/ravulizumab (anti-C5 → blocks terminal complement → ↓hemolysis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme of the TCA cycle?
options: Citrate synthase: citrate synthase catalyzes the first step (acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate + CoA); while important, citrate synthase is NOT the rate-limiting step of the TCA cycle; it is regulated by substrate availability (OAA, acetyl-CoA) and product inhibition (citrate, succinyl-CoA, NADH)

Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH): IDH3 (NAD+-dependent, mitochondrial; the TCA cycle enzyme) is the RATE-LIMITING enzyme of the TCA cycle; IDH3 catalyzes: isocitrate + NAD+ → α-ketoglutarate + CO2 + NADH (first oxidative decarboxylation in TCA); IDH3 regulation: ACTIVATED by ADP (↑ADP = energy needed → ↑TCA flux), Ca2+ (↑Ca2+ in exercise/muscle contraction → ↑TCA); INHIBITED by ATP (↑ATP = energy sufficient → ↓TCA), NADH (product inhibition); NOTE: IDH has 3 isoforms: IDH1 (cytoplasmic, NADP+-dependent), IDH2 (mitochondrial, NADP+-dependent), IDH3 (mitochondrial, NAD+-dependent = the TCA cycle enzyme); IDH1 and IDH2 mutations are found in cancers (glioma, AML, cholangiocarcinoma, chondrosarcoma): gain-of-function/NEOMORPHIC mutations → convert α-KG → D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG, oncometabolite) → inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases (TET2 → DNA hypermethylation, JmjC histone demethylases → histone hypermethylation, PHDs → HIF stabilization) → epigenetic dysregulation → differentiation block; IDH inhibitors: ivosidenib (IDH1 inhibitor, for IDH1-mutant AML/cholangiocarcinoma), enasidenib (IDH2 inhibitor, for IDH2-mutant AML), vorasidenib (dual IDH1/2 inhibitor, for IDH-mutant low-grade glioma)
Malate dehydrogenase: MDH catalyzes: malate + NAD+ → OAA + NADH (last step of TCA); not rate-limiting; regulated by product inhibition (NADH, OAA)

Succinate dehydrogenase (SDH/Complex II): SDH catalyzes: succinate + FAD → fumarate + FADH2; SDH is the only TCA enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (dual role: TCA + ETC Complex II); not rate-limiting; SDH mutations → paraganglioma, pheochromocytoma, GIST, renal cell carcinoma (succinate accumulation → inhibits PHD → HIF stabilization → pseudohypoxia → VEGF/angiogenesis)
explanation: TCA cycle — complete: Location: mitochondrial matrix (except SDH: inner mitochondrial membrane); 8 reactions: (1) Citrate synthase: acetyl-CoA + OAA → citrate; (2) Aconitase: citrate → isocitrate (via cis-aconitate; contains Fe4S4 cluster; aconitase is IRP1 in cytoplasm when Fe is low); (3) IDH3: isocitrate → α-KG + CO2 + NADH (RATE-LIMITING); (4) α-KGDH (OGDH): α-KG → succinyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH (TPP, lipoamide, CoA, FAD, NAD+; structurally similar to PDC/BCKDH); (5) SCS (succinyl-CoA synthetase): succinyl-CoA → succinate + GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation; GTP → GDP + Pi → NDP kinase → ATP); (6) SDH: succinate → fumarate + FADH2 (linked to ETC Complex II → CoQ); (7) Fumarase: fumarate → malate; (8) MDH: malate → OAA + NADH; NET per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH + 1 FADH2 + 1 GTP + 2 CO2; per glucose: ×2 (2 acetyl-CoA from 1 glucose); TCA cycle is AMPHIBOLIC: catabolic (oxidizes acetyl-CoA → CO2 + reducing equivalents) AND anabolic (provides biosynthetic precursors: citrate → FA synthesis [citrate shuttle]; α-KG → Glu → amino acids; succinyl-CoA → heme [ALA synthase]; OAA → Asp → purines, pyrimidines, Asn; OAA → PEP → GNG; malate → pyruvate [malic enzyme → NADPH]); anaplerotic reactions replenish TCA intermediates: PC (pyruvate → OAA, most important), glutaminolysis (Gln → Glu → α-KG), BCAA catabolism (→ succinyl-CoA), odd-chain FA (→ propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of methotrexate as an anticancer drug?
options: Inhibits DNA polymerase: DNA polymerase inhibitors include cytarabine (Ara-C, incorporated into DNA → chain termination; used in AML), aphidicolin (research tool); methotrexate does NOT directly inhibit DNA polymerase
