Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR): Methotrexate (MTX) is a structural analog of FOLIC ACID that competitively inhibits DIHYDROFOLATE REDUCTASE (DHFR); DHFR catalyzes: DHF (dihydrofolate) + NADPH → THF (tetrahydrofolate) + NADP+ (regenerates THF from DHF produced during thymidylate synthase reaction); thymidylate synthase (TS): dUMP + CH2-THF → dTMP + DHF (CH2-THF provides the methyl group; THF is oxidized to DHF in the process); MTX → ↓DHFR → ↓THF → ↓CH2-THF → ↓dTMP synthesis → ↓DNA synthesis (S-phase arrest → cell death); MTX also ↓purine synthesis (THF derivatives [N10-formyl-THF] required for purine ring carbons C2 and C8); uses: ALL (high-dose MTX + leucovorin rescue), breast cancer, osteosarcoma, choriocarcinoma, rheumatoid arthritis (low-dose, anti-inflammatory: ↑adenosine via AICAR accumulation → anti-inflammatory; folate-independent mechanism), ectopic pregnancy, psoriasis; leucovorin (folinic acid, N5-formyl-THF): bypasses DHFR block → provides THF directly → rescues normal cells (leucovorin rescue: given 24-36 hrs after high-dose MTX to prevent toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells [GI mucosa, bone marrow]); MTX toxicity: myelosuppression (pancytopenia), mucositis, hepatotoxicity (fibrosis/cirrhosis with chronic use), pneumonitis, nephrotoxicity (crystallizes in renal tubules at high doses → alkalinize urine + hydration); glucarpidase (carboxypeptidase G2): cleaves MTX → inactive metabolites → rescue therapy for delayed MTX clearance

Inhibits topoisomerase I: topoisomerase I inhibitors include irinotecan/topotecan (camptothecin analogs → stabilize Top1-DNA cleavage complex → DNA breaks → cell death; irinotecan: colorectal cancer; SN-38 is active metabolite [by carboxylesterase]; UGT1A1 polymorphism [Gilbert-like] → ↓SN-38 glucuronidation → ↑toxicity [diarrhea, neutropenia]); methotrexate does NOT inhibit Top1
Alkylates DNA: alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide, nitrogen mustards, cisplatin, temozolomide) covalently modify DNA bases → cross-links → replication block; methotrexate is NOT an alkylating agent
explanation: Antimetabolites in cancer therapy — folate antagonists and nucleotide analogs: FOLATE ANTAGONISTS: methotrexate (↓DHFR → ↓THF → ↓dTMP + ↓purines); pemetrexed (multi-targeted antifolate: ↓TS, ↓DHFR, ↓GARFT [glycinamide ribonucleotide formyltransferase, purine synthesis]; used in mesothelioma, NSCLC non-squamous); pralatrexate (↓DHFR; used in PTCL); PYRIMIDINE ANALOGS: 5-fluorouracil (5-FU → 5-FdUMP → inhibits TS [forms covalent ternary complex with TS + CH2-THF → suicide inhibition]; used in colorectal, breast, head/neck; toxicity: DPD deficiency [DPYD polymorphisms] → ↓5-FU catabolism → severe mucositis + myelosuppression → FATAL toxicity; DPD testing now recommended before 5-FU/capecitabine); capecitabine (oral prodrug → 5-FU; activated by thymidine phosphorylase [TP] in tumor → some tumor selectivity); cytarabine (Ara-C → Ara-CTP → DNA polymerase inhibition + DNA incorporation → chain termination; AML standard); gemcitabine (dFdC → dFdCTP → DNA incorporation + ↓RNR; pancreatic, NSCLC, bladder); PURINE ANALOGS: 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP → 6-thio-IMP → ↓de novo purine synthesis; ALL maintenance; metabolized by XO [↓dose with allopurinol!] + TPMT [TPMT polymorphisms → ↓metabolism → toxicity; genotype before starting]); azathioprine (prodrug → 6-MP; immunosuppression); fludarabine (F-Ara-A → ↓RNR + ↓DNA pol + ↓DNA repair; CLL, transplant conditioning).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: What is the function of carnitine in fatty acid metabolism?
options: Activates fatty acids by forming acyl-CoA: fatty acid activation (FA + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi) is catalyzed by ACYL-CoA SYNTHETASE (thiokinase/fatty acid:CoA ligase) on the outer mitochondrial membrane; this is NOT the function of carnitine

Transports long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane: CARNITINE (β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylammonium butyrate): essential for transport of long-chain acyl groups (C12-C20) across the INNER mitochondrial membrane (IMM); the carnitine shuttle: long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the IMM (impermeable to CoA); CARNITINE SHUTTLE mechanism: (1) CPT I (carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, on OUTER surface of OMM): acyl-CoA + carnitine → acylcarnitine + CoA; CPT I is the RATE-LIMITING step of fatty acid β-oxidation; CPT I is INHIBITED by MALONYL-CoA (product of ACC; fed state: insulin → ↑ACC → ↑malonyl-CoA → ↓CPT I → ↓FAO; fasting: glucagon → AMPK → ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT I → ↑FAO; this reciprocal regulation ensures FA synthesis and FAO don't occur simultaneously); CPT I isoforms: CPT Ia (liver; more sensitive to malonyl-CoA inhibition), CPT Ib (muscle/heart; less sensitive); (2) CACT (carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase, IMM): exchanges acylcarnitine (in) for free carnitine (out) across IMM; (3) CPT II (on INNER surface of IMM): acylcarnitine + CoA → acyl-CoA + carnitine (regenerates acyl-CoA inside matrix for β-oxidation); carnitine synthesis: Lys (trimethylated by SAM → trimethyllysine) → → → → butyrobetaine → [BBOX1, butyrobetaine hydroxylase, requires ascorbate, Fe2+, α-KG] → L-carnitine; synthesis mainly in liver/kidney; other tissues rely on blood carnitine (uptake via OCTN2/SLC22A5 transporter); PRIMARY CARNITINE DEFICIENCY (SLC22A5/OCTN2 mutations, AR): ↓carnitine uptake → ↓plasma + tissue carnitine → ↓FAO → hypoketotic hypoglycemia + cardiomyopathy (dilated CMP) + skeletal myopathy + Reye-like episodes; treatment: high-dose oral L-carnitine (dramatic response); CPT I deficiency: ↓FAO → hypoketotic hypoglycemia; liver involvement primarily; CPT II deficiency: most common inherited disorder of FAO in adults → exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis + myoglobinuria (adult myopathic form); severe neonatal/infantile forms exist
Provides NADPH for fatty acid synthesis: NADPH for FA synthesis comes from PPP (G6PD, 6PGD) and malic enzyme; NOT from carnitine

Serves as an electron carrier in β-oxidation: electron carriers in β-oxidation are FAD (bound to acyl-CoA dehydrogenase → FADH2 → ETF → ETF-QO → CoQ) and NAD+ (→ NADH in 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase step); carnitine is NOT an electron carrier
explanation: Fatty acid β-oxidation — complete: Location: mitochondrial matrix (long-chain; medium/short-chain can enter without carnitine shuttle); Activation: cytoplasm: FA + CoA + ATP → [ACS] → acyl-CoA (consumed 2 ATP equivalents: ATP → AMP + PPi; PPi → 2Pi); Transport: carnitine shuttle (CPT I → CACT → CPT II); β-oxidation cycle (4 steps per round): (1) Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FAD → FADH2 → ETF → CoQ → ETC): VLCAD (C14-C20), LCAD (C12-C18), MCAD (C6-C12), SCAD (C4-C6); MCAD deficiency (ACADM gene, most common FAO disorder ~1:15,000): hypoketotic hypoglycemia + ↑dicarboxylic acids + ↑acylcarnitines (C6-C10, esp. C8 octanoylcarnitine on NBS) + Reye-like episodes; fatal if undiagnosed; treatment: avoid fasting + emergency glucose; (2) Enoyl-CoA hydratase (hydration); (3) 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (NAD+ → NADH); (4) β-ketothiolase (thiolysis: + CoA → acetyl-CoA + shortened acyl-CoA); Each round: removes 2C as acetyl-CoA + generates 1 FADH2 + 1 NADH; Palmitate (C16): 7 rounds → 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH2 + 7 NADH; ATP yield: 8 × 10 (TCA+ETC from acetyl-CoA) + 7 × 1.5 (FADH2) + 7 × 2.5 (NADH) − 2 (activation) = 80 + 10.5 + 17.5 − 2 = 106 ATP (net).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which protein acts as the major oxygen-storage molecule in skeletal muscle?
options: Hemoglobin: hemoglobin (Hb, α2β2) is the oxygen TRANSPORT protein in RED BLOOD CELLS (each RBC ~270 million Hb molecules; each Hb binds 4 O2); Hb delivers O2 from lungs to tissues; Hb is NOT the muscle oxygen storage protein

Myoglobin: MYOGLOBIN (Mb) is a MONOMERIC heme protein (single polypeptide + 1 heme → binds 1 O2) that functions as the oxygen STORAGE molecule in SKELETAL and CARDIAC MUSCLE; Mb has a HIGHER oxygen affinity than Hb (Mb P50 ~2.8 mmHg vs Hb P50 ~26.6 mmHg) → Mb O2-dissociation curve is HYPERBOLIC (not sigmoidal; no cooperative binding because it's a monomer → no allosteric T↔R transition); Mb's high affinity means it: (1) readily accepts O2 released by Hb in muscle capillaries; (2) stores O2 intracellularly for use during intense exercise when blood O2 delivery is temporarily insufficient; (3) facilitates O2 diffusion within muscle cells (acts as O2 shuttle from sarcolemma to mitochondria); Mb is present in higher concentrations in: slow-twitch (type I) oxidative muscle fibers (red muscle; aerobic/endurance), cardiac muscle, diving mammals (whale/seal myoglobin: extraordinary O2 storage for prolonged dives); Mb is released into blood when muscle cells are damaged → MYOGLOBINURIA (dark brown/red urine; Mb is small [17 kDa] → freely filtered by kidneys → can cause acute tubular necrosis [ATN] → AKI; particularly in RHABDOMYOLYSIS: causes include crush injury, statins, seizures, extreme exercise, hyperthermia, toxins; treatment: aggressive IV fluids + urine alkalinization [NaHCO3] + mannitol [osmotic diuresis]; monitor CK [>>myoglobin for diagnosis])
Transferrin: transferrin is the iron TRANSPORT protein in blood (carries Fe3+ → delivers to tissues via TfR1); transferrin is NOT an oxygen storage protein
Ceruloplasmin: ceruloplasmin is a copper-containing ferroxidase in blood (Fe2+ → Fe3+ for transferrin binding; also carries ~90% of plasma copper); NOT an oxygen storage protein
explanation: Myoglobin vs Hemoglobin comparison: Feature | Myoglobin | Hemoglobin: Subunits: monomer (1 heme) | tetramer (α2β2, 4 hemes); O2-binding curve: hyperbolic | sigmoidal (cooperative); P50: ~2.8 mmHg | ~26.6 mmHg; Affinity: very high | lower (adjustable); Cooperativity: none | positive (Hill coefficient n ~2.8); Bohr effect: none (no allosteric) | yes (H+, CO2 → right shift); 2,3-BPG effect: none | yes (stabilizes T-state → ↓affinity); Function: O2 storage in muscle | O2 transport in RBCs; Location: skeletal + cardiac muscle | RBCs; MW: ~17 kDa | ~64 kDa; Clinical: myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis marker) | hemoglobinopathies (SCD, thalassemias); structure: 8 α-helices (A-H) forming a hydrophobic pocket for heme; His93 (F8, proximal His: coordinates Fe2+ directly) + His64 (E7, distal His: does NOT coordinate Fe; instead H-bonds to bound O2 → stabilizes O2 binding + discriminates against CO [distal His forces CO to bind at an angle → ↓CO affinity → ↓CO poisoning; without distal His, CO affinity would be ~25,000× > O2; with it, ~250×]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI) is caused by deficiency of which enzyme?
options: Fructokinase: fructokinase (ketohexokinase) deficiency → essential fructosuria (benign condition: fructose appears in urine; no symptoms; autosomal recessive; fructose detected by Clinitest [reducing sugar] but NOT by glucose oxidase dipstick)

Aldolase B: HFI is caused by deficiency of ALDOLASE B (fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase B, liver/kidney/intestine isoform); aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate (F1P) → DHAP + glyceraldehyde; in HFI: fructokinase is INTACT → fructose → [fructokinase, ATP] → F1P (rapidly); but aldolase B is deficient → F1P ACCUMULATES intracellularly; F1P trapping: (1) sequesters inorganic phosphate (Pi) → ↓ATP regeneration (Pi depletion → ↓oxidative phosphorylation) → ↓ATP → cell injury; (2) ↓Pi → loss of allosteric activation of glycogen phosphorylase → ↓glycogenolysis → HYPOGLYCEMIA; (3) ↓ATP → ↑AMP → ↑AMP deaminase → ↑IMP → ↑degradation → ↑uric acid → HYPERURICEMIA; (4) ↑F1P inhibits gluconeogenesis (inhibits aldolase-mediated steps) and glycogenolysis → further ↓glucose; (5) hepatotoxicity (↓ATP → cell death → ↑AST/ALT → progressive liver damage → cirrhosis if chronic exposure); clinical: presents when fructose/sucrose/sorbitol is introduced to diet (weaning from breast milk to complementary foods containing fruits, table sugar, honey); vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycemia, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, jaundice; severe: liver failure, proximal renal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi-like); patients develop natural AVERSION to sweets (protective); diagnosis: molecular (ALDOB gene: A149P most common in Europeans) or enzymatic (liver biopsy, rarely needed now); fructose challenge test (IV fructose → ↓glucose + ↓Pi + ↑urate; DANGEROUS — avoid); treatment: STRICT avoidance of fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol (lifelong); excellent prognosis with dietary restriction

Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase: F1,6BPase deficiency → impaired gluconeogenesis → fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis (F1,6BP → F6P is a GNG step bypassing PFK-1); triggered by fasting, NOT by fructose ingestion per se; this is a GNG disorder, NOT HFI
Phosphofructokinase: PFK deficiency → GSD VII (Tarui disease) when PFK-M (muscle isoform) is affected → exercise intolerance; hepatic PFK deficiency is a different entity; NOT HFI
explanation: Fructose metabolism — complete: Dietary fructose (fruits, honey, HFCS, sucrose [glucose+fructose]): absorbed by GLUT5 (apical, intestine) → GLUT2 (basolateral) → portal blood → LIVER (primary site of fructose metabolism); LIVER pathway: fructose → [fructokinase/KHK, ATP → ADP] → F1P → [aldolase B] → DHAP + glyceraldehyde; glyceraldehyde → [triose kinase] → G3P; DHAP + G3P → glycolysis (→ pyruvate → acetyl-CoA → TCA or FA synthesis) or gluconeogenesis (→ G6P → glucose); KEY POINT: fructose BYPASSES PFK-1 (the rate-limiting glycolytic step) → rapid, unregulated metabolism → rapid ATP depletion (fructokinase rapidly phosphorylates fructose → depletes ATP) + rapid generation of glycolytic intermediates → diverted to lipogenesis (↑TG synthesis → NAFLD, hypertriglyceridemia); fructose and metabolic syndrome: excessive fructose consumption → ↑hepatic lipogenesis (↑SREBP-1c, ↑DNL), ↑VLDL secretion (↑TG), ↑uric acid (ATP → AMP → IMP → uric acid), insulin resistance, NAFLD; this is why HFCS overconsumption is implicated in metabolic syndrome/obesity epidemic.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acids has a guanidinium group in its side chain, making it the most basic amino acid?
options: Histidine: His has an imidazole group (pKa ~6.0); while it acts as a buffer at physiological pH, His is NOT the most basic amino acid

Arginine: Arginine has a GUANIDINIUM group (–NH–C(=NH)–NH2) in its side chain; pKa ~12.5 → the MOST BASIC amino acid (virtually always protonated/positively charged at physiological pH); the guanidinium group can form up to 5 hydrogen bonds (3 NH groups + delocalized positive charge) → extremely good at interacting with negatively charged molecules (DNA phosphate backbone, carboxylate groups of Asp/Glu, phospholipid headgroups); Arg residues are important in: (1) enzyme active sites (binding anionic substrates; e.g., arginase binds Arg substrate; kinases use Arg to position phosphate groups); (2) DNA-binding proteins (histones: Arg-rich histones [especially H3, H4] bind DNA phosphate backbone; Arg methylation [by PRMTs: protein arginine methyltransferases] → epigenetic regulation); (3) nuclear localization signals (NLS: classical monopartite NLS like SV40 large T: PKKKRKV contains basic Lys+Arg; Arg-rich NLS common); (4) antimicrobial peptides (Arg-rich → cationic → bind bacterial anionic membranes); Arg metabolism: see earlier arginine hub question (NO, creatine, urea cycle, polyamines)

Lysine: Lys has an ε-amino group (pKa ~10.5); positively charged at pH 7.4; Lys is basic but NOT as basic as Arg (pKa 10.5 < 12.5); Lys is important for: ε-amino modifications (acetylation [HATs/HDACs on histones], methylation [KMTs: mono/di/trimethylation], ubiquitination [K48/K63-linked], SUMOylation, hydroxylation [hydroxylysine in collagen])
Glutamine: Gln has an amide side chain (–CH2CH2CONH2); pKa not applicable (amide does not ionize at physiological pH); Gln is NEUTRAL, not basic
explanation: Amino acid side chain chemistry — charged residues at pH 7.4: POSITIVELY CHARGED (basic): Arg (guanidinium, pKa 12.5 — always +), Lys (ε-amino, pKa 10.5 — always +), His (imidazole, pKa 6.0 — ~10% +); NEGATIVELY CHARGED (acidic): Asp (β-carboxyl, pKa 3.65 — always −), Glu (γ-carboxyl, pKa 4.25 — always −); POLAR UNCHARGED: Ser, Thr (hydroxyl), Asn, Gln (amide), Cys (thiol, pKa 8.3), Tyr (phenol, pKa 10.1); NONPOLAR: Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro, Phe, Trp, Met, Gly (simplest); SPECIAL: Pro (imino acid, cyclic → introduces kinks/rigidity in polypeptide; cis-trans isomerization by peptidyl-prolyl isomerases [PPIases: cyclophilin → target of cyclosporine; FKBP → target of tacrolimus/FK506]); Cys (thiol → disulfide bonds [S-S] in oxidizing environments [ER lumen, extracellular]; PDI catalyzes disulfide formation/isomerization in ER; reducing agents: DTT, β-mercaptoethanol break S-S bonds → denature proteins); Gly (smallest, most flexible → found in tight turns, collagen [every 3rd position]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the biochemical defect in galactosemia that leads to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate?
options: Galactokinase deficiency: galactokinase (GALK1) deficiency → galactose cannot be phosphorylated → ↑free galactose in blood → galactose enters lens → [aldose reductase] → GALACTITOL (sugar alcohol, osmotically active, cannot exit lens → swelling → CATARACTS); galactokinase deficiency causes cataracts ONLY (no liver disease, no intellectual disability); ↑galactose in blood and urine (galactosemia + galactosuria); galactitol accumulation; does NOT cause Gal-1-P accumulation (because galactokinase is the enzyme that MAKES Gal-1-P)

Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) deficiency: CLASSIC GALACTOSEMIA: deficiency of GALT (galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase); GALT normally catalyzes: Gal-1-P + UDP-glucose → glucose-1-P + UDP-galactose (Leloir pathway); GALT deficiency → ↑↑Gal-1-P (galactose-1-phosphate accumulates because galactokinase is functional: galactose → [GALK] → Gal-1-P → blocked here → ↑Gal-1-P); Gal-1-P toxicity: liver (hepatomegaly, jaundice, coagulopathy, cirrhosis → liver failure), brain (intellectual disability, speech dyspraxia), kidneys (proximal tubular dysfunction → aminoaciduria, galactosuria), eyes (cataracts: galactitol from alternative pathway: galactose → [aldose reductase] → galactitol); ovarian failure (↓FSH receptor? mechanism unclear; affects females even with early treatment → primary ovarian insufficiency); E. coli sepsis (newborns with galactosemia are predisposed to E. coli sepsis; mechanism: Gal-1-P may inhibit neutrophil function or galactose impairs bacterial defense); presents in neonatal period when milk feeding (lactose = glucose + galactose) begins → vomiting, poor feeding, jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts, E. coli sepsis; diagnosis: NBS (↑total galactose on Beutler test [GALT activity in RBCs] → confirmatory: ↑Gal-1-P in RBCs + ↓GALT activity + ↑urine reducing substance [galactose: positive Clinitest, negative glucose oxidase]); GALT gene: Q188R most common in Caucasians (classic, severe); N314D (Duarte variant, mild, ~50% activity in compound heterozygotes → usually benign); treatment: STRICT lactose-free + galactose-free diet (lifelong; soy-based formula in infancy); despite early treatment: long-term complications persist (speech/language deficits, learning difficulties, ovarian failure) → endogenous galactose production (from UDP-galactose via epimerase → cannot be eliminated by diet)

UDP-galactose-4-epimerase deficiency: GALE (UDP-galactose-4-epimerase) deficiency → epimerase-deficiency galactosemia; ranges from benign (RBC-only: ↑Gal-1-P in RBCs only, asymptomatic) to severe (generalized: mimics classic galactosemia); GALE converts UDP-galactose ⇌ UDP-glucose; rare; NOT the classic galactosemia causing Gal-1-P accumulation

Lactase deficiency: lactase (β-galactosidase, intestinal brush border) cleaves lactose → glucose + galactose; lactase deficiency → lactose intolerance (osmotic diarrhea, bloating, gas); does NOT cause galactose-1-phosphate accumulation (the problem is in the intestine, not intracellular galactose metabolism)
explanation: Galactose metabolism (Leloir pathway): Dietary lactose → [lactase, intestinal brush border] → glucose + galactose → absorbed → portal blood → liver; Galactose → [GALK, galactokinase, ATP] → Gal-1-P → [GALT, + UDP-glucose] → Glc-1-P + UDP-galactose; UDP-galactose → [GALE, UDP-galactose-4-epimerase] ⇌ UDP-glucose (regenerated for GALT reaction); Glc-1-P → [phosphoglucomutase] → G6P → glycolysis or glycogenesis; UDP-galactose is also used for: glycoprotein synthesis (galactosyltransferases in Golgi → add Gal to glycoproteins/glycolipids), lactose synthesis (mammary gland: UDP-galactose + glucose → [lactose synthase = galactosyltransferase + α-lactalbumin modifier] → lactose); Disorders: GALK def → cataracts only (galactitol); GALT def → classic galactosemia (Gal-1-P toxicity → liver, brain, eyes, ovaries, E. coli sepsis); GALE def → variable (benign to severe); NBS: all 50 US states screen for galactosemia.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the structure of a nucleoside?
options: Base + phosphate group: a base + phosphate (without sugar) is NOT a standard biochemical entity; nucleotides have all three components

Base + pentose sugar: A NUCLEOSIDE = nitrogenous BASE + pentose SUGAR (ribose or deoxyribose) linked by an N-glycosidic bond (β-N9-glycosidic for purines [N9 of purine ring to C1' of sugar]; β-N1-glycosidic for pyrimidines [N1 of pyrimidine ring to C1' of sugar]); nucleoside naming: adenine → adenosine (A); guanine → guanosine (G); cytosine → cytidine (C); uracil → uridine (U); thymine → thymidine (T, deoxy by default); deoxy-: deoxyadenosine (dA), deoxyguanosine (dG), deoxycytidine (dC); a NUCLEOTIDE = nucleoside + phosphate group(s) (mono/di/triphosphate at 5' position): adenosine 5'-monophosphate (AMP), ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP, dTMP, etc.; nucleotides are linked in DNA/RNA by 3'-5' phosphodiester bonds (phosphate connects 3'-OH of one nucleotide to 5'-OH of next); bases: PURINES (Adenine, Guanine: two-ring fused structure [pyrimidine ring fused to imidazole ring]; 'PURe As Gold'); PYRIMIDINES (Cytosine, Uracil [RNA], Thymine [DNA]: single 6-membered ring; 'CUT the PY'); base pairing (Watson-Crick): A=T (2 H-bonds; A=U in RNA), G≡C (3 H-bonds; GC base pairs are stronger → ↑Tm [melting temperature] of DNA with higher GC content); Chargaff's rules: A=T, G=C (in dsDNA; %A=%T, %G=%C; %A+%G = %T+%C → purines = pyrimidines)
Base + pentose sugar + phosphate group: this describes a NUCLEOTIDE, not a nucleoside; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate
Phosphate + pentose sugar: sugar-phosphate (without base) is the backbone of nucleic acids but is NOT called a nucleoside
explanation: Nucleic acid structure — DNA vs RNA: DNA: deoxyribose sugar + A,G,C,T bases + phosphodiester backbone; double-stranded (antiparallel: 5'→3' / 3'→5'); B-form (right-handed, major/minor grooves, 10 bp/turn, 3.4 nm pitch); other forms: A-DNA (right-handed, wider, RNA-DNA hybrids), Z-DNA (left-handed, zigzag, found in GC-rich regions, possible regulatory role). RNA: ribose sugar (2'-OH) + A,G,C,U bases; mostly single-stranded (but extensive secondary structure: stem-loops, hairpins, pseudoknots, bulges); types: mRNA (~5% of total RNA), rRNA (~80%, most abundant), tRNA (~15%), snRNA (spliceosome), snoRNA (rRNA modification), miRNA (gene silencing: ~22 nt, RISC complex → mRNA degradation or translational repression), siRNA (RNAi: exogenous dsRNA → Dicer → siRNA → RISC → mRNA cleavage), lncRNA (>200 nt, diverse regulatory functions: XIST [X-inactivation], HOTAIR [chromatin remodeling]), piRNA (transposon silencing in germ cells); ribozymes: catalytic RNA (self-splicing introns [Group I: Tetrahymena; Group II: mitochondrial/chloroplast], RNase P [tRNA processing], peptidyl transferase [28S rRNA in ribosome; protein synthesis is fundamentally an RNA-catalyzed reaction → supports RNA world hypothesis], hammerhead ribozyme, HDV ribozyme).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires which vitamin as a cofactor?
options: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6): PLP (pyridoxal 5'-phosphate) is cofactor for transaminases, decarboxylases, ALA synthase, CBS, cystathionase, glycogen phosphorylase; PLP is NOT the cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin): Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MCM, also called MUT, mitochondrial) requires ADENOSYLCOBALAMIN (AdoCbl, one of the two active forms of vitamin B12) as cofactor; MCM catalyzes: L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (isomerization; intramolecular rearrangement: carbon skeleton rearrangement requiring AdoCbl's Co-C bond homolysis → radical mechanism); MCM is critical for catabolism of: odd-chain fatty acids, valine, isoleucine, methionine, threonine, cholesterol side chain → all produce propionyl-CoA → [PCC, biotin] → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → [racemase] → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, AdoCbl] → succinyl-CoA → TCA; MCM deficiency (MUT gene mutations) → methylmalonic acidemia (MMA): ↑methylmalonic acid in blood/urine + metabolic acidosis + hyperammonemia + ketosis; severe neonatal form (mut0: no residual activity) vs milder (mut-: some activity, may respond to B12); B12 deficiency also → ↑MMA (because ↓AdoCbl → ↓MCM → ↑MMA; this is why MMA is a specific marker of B12 deficiency [unlike homocysteine which is elevated in both B12 and folate deficiency]); the OTHER B12-dependent enzyme: methionine synthase (MS/MTR): Hcy + CH3-THF → [MS, MeCbl] → Met + THF; MS requires methylcobalamin (MeCbl); B12 deficiency → ↓MeCbl → ↓MS → ↑Hcy + ↓THF → 'methylfolate trap' (folate trapped as CH3-THF → ↓THF → ↓CH2-THF → ↓dTMP → megaloblastic anemia [same mechanism as folate deficiency]); B12 deficiency also → subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord (↓MeCbl → ↓SAM → ↓myelin methylation → demyelination of posterior columns + lateral corticospinal tracts → loss of proprioception/vibration + spastic paraparesis)

Biotin (vitamin B7): biotin is cofactor for carboxylases (PC, ACC, PCC, MCC); PCC (propionyl-CoA carboxylase) acts UPSTREAM of MCM in the same pathway (propionyl-CoA → D-methylmalonyl-CoA); biotin is NOT the MCM cofactor
Thiamine (vitamin B1): TPP is cofactor for α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes (PDC, OGDH, BCKDH) and transketolase; thiamine is NOT the MCM cofactor
explanation: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) — complete: Structure: corrin ring (similar to porphyrin but with cobalt [Co] instead of iron); unique among vitamins (contains metal + is synthesized only by microorganisms); Sources: animal products (meat, fish, dairy, eggs); NOT in plants → vegans at risk; Absorption (complex): dietary B12 (bound to protein) → [pepsin + HCl in stomach] → free B12 → binds HAPTOCORRIN (R-protein/TCI, from saliva + gastric juice) → duodenum: pancreatic proteases degrade haptocorrin → B12 released → binds INTRINSIC FACTOR (IF, from gastric parietal cells) → IF-B12 complex → travels to terminal ILEUM → binds CUBILIN receptor (+ amnionless [AMN] → cubam complex) on ileal enterocytes → receptor-mediated endocytosis → B12 released → binds TRANSCOBALAMIN II (TCII, plasma transport protein; delivers B12 to tissues via TCII receptor [CD320] → endocytosis → lysosomal release → converted to: AdoCbl [mitochondria, for MCM] or MeCbl [cytoplasm, for MS]); Deficiency causes: pernicious anemia (autoimmune → anti-parietal cell Ab + anti-IF Ab → ↓IF → ↓B12 absorption; most common cause in developed countries), gastric surgery (gastrectomy → ↓IF), terminal ileum disease (Crohn's, surgical resection → ↓cubam), bacterial overgrowth (compete for B12), Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm, consumes B12), vegan diet, drugs (metformin, PPIs [↓acid → ↓B12 release from food proteins; long-term use]); Diagnosis: ↓serum B12, ↑MMA (specific), ↑Hcy (non-specific), ↑homocysteine; CBC: macrocytic anemia (MCV >100), hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes or any 6-lobe; pathognomonic for megaloblastic anemia), pancytopenia (severe); peripheral smear: macro-ovalocytes, Howell-Jolly bodies (if spleen dysfunction); Treatment: IM/SC hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin injections (bypass absorption defect); high-dose oral B12 (1-2 mg/day) can treat pernicious anemia via passive diffusion (~1% absorption regardless of IF).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is a competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase (SDH/Complex II)?
options: Rotenone: rotenone inhibits Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase); blocks electron transfer from Fe-S clusters to CoQ; NOT an SDH inhibitor; rotenone is used as a pesticide/piscicide; rotenone exposure → parkinsonism in animal models (↓Complex I → mitochondrial dysfunction → dopaminergic neuron death)

Malonate: MALONATE (malonic acid, OOC-CH2-COO⁻) is a COMPETITIVE inhibitor of SDH (Complex II); malonate is a structural ANALOG of SUCCINATE (OOC-CH2-CH2-COO⁻; succinate has 4 carbons, malonate has 3 → similar dicarboxylate structure → competes for the active site); SDH normally: succinate + FAD → fumarate + FADH2 (the only TCA cycle step directly linked to ETC); malonate binds the active site of SDH but CANNOT be oxidized (no β-hydrogens to remove → no dehydrogenation possible) → blocks succinate binding → ↓SDH activity → ↓fumarate production → ↓FADH2 → ↓ETC flux at Complex II; competitive inhibition: can be overcome by ↑[succinate]; malonate is a CLASSIC example of competitive inhibition in biochemistry textbooks; Lineweaver-Burk: malonate ↑apparent Km for succinate but Vmax is unchanged (intersect on y-axis)

Antimycin A: antimycin A inhibits Complex III (cytochrome bc1); binds Qi site → blocks electron transfer from cytochrome bL to CoQ at the matrix side of the Q-cycle → ↓CoQH2 oxidation → stalls ETC at Complex III; NOT an SDH inhibitor

Oligomycin: oligomycin inhibits Complex V (ATP synthase); blocks the Fo proton channel → ↓H+ flow → ↓ATP synthesis; also ↓O2 consumption (because proton gradient builds up → cannot be dissipated → backs up ETC → ↓electron flow → ↓O2 reduction); NOT an SDH inhibitor
explanation: ETC inhibitors — complete list for exams: Complex I inhibitors: rotenone (plant toxin), barbiturates (amobarbital), piericidin A, MPP+ (1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium; MPTP → [MAO-B] → MPP+ → taken up by DAT into dopaminergic neurons → ↓Complex I → parkinsonism; basis of MPTP model of PD); Complex II inhibitor: malonate (competitive with succinate); Complex III inhibitors: antimycin A (Qi site), myxothiazol/stigmatellin (Qo site); Complex IV inhibitors: cyanide (CN⁻, binds Fe3+ of heme a3), carbon monoxide (CO, binds Fe2+), hydrogen sulfide (H2S), azide (N3⁻); Complex V (ATP synthase) inhibitor: oligomycin (blocks Fo H+ channel); UNCOUPLERS (dissipate proton gradient → ↑O2 consumption without ATP synthesis → heat): 2,4-DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol; weak acid → protonated in IMS → crosses IMM → deprotonated in matrix → shuttles H+ → ↓ΔpH; historical weight-loss agent → hyperthermia → deaths), FCCP (carbonyl cyanide-p-trifluoromethoxyphenylhydrazone; research tool), thermogenin/UCP1 (brown adipose tissue → non-shivering thermogenesis); ATP/ADP translocase inhibitor: atractyloside (blocks ANT → ↓ADP import → ↓ATP synthesis + ↓ATP export); bongkrekic acid (also inhibits ANT but locks it in m-state [matrix-facing]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the role of chaperones in protein folding?
options: Chaperones directly catalyze peptide bond formation: peptide bond formation is catalyzed by the ribosome (peptidyl transferase activity of 28S rRNA in the large subunit); chaperones do NOT form peptide bonds

Chaperones prevent aggregation of unfolded proteins and assist proper folding without being part of the final structure: MOLECULAR CHAPERONES are proteins that assist the folding of other proteins (client proteins) by: (1) preventing AGGREGATION of unfolded/partially folded polypeptides (expose hydrophobic surfaces → tend to aggregate non-specifically; chaperones shield these surfaces); (2) providing a protected environment for folding (chaperonins: sequester client in a cage → fold in isolation); (3) unfolding misfolded proteins for another attempt at correct folding; CHAPERONES DO NOT PROVIDE STERIC INFORMATION for folding (the final fold is determined by the amino acid sequence → Anfinsen's dogma [Christian Anfinsen, Nobel 1972: RNase A refolding experiment → the primary sequence contains all information needed for 3D structure]); chaperones are NOT part of the final folded structure (they transiently associate → release correctly folded protein); Major chaperone families: HSP70 (heat shock protein 70 kDa: DnaK in bacteria, Hsc70/Hsp70 in eukaryotes; binds exposed hydrophobic patches on nascent/unfolded proteins; ATP-dependent: ATP-bound → low affinity [lid open]; ADP-bound → high affinity [lid closed, holds client]; co-chaperones: Hsp40/DnaJ [J-domain → stimulates ATPase] + NEF [nucleotide exchange factor: GrpE/BAG → releases ADP → rebinds ATP → releases client]); HSP60 (chaperonin: GroEL/GroES in bacteria [Anfinsen cage: GroEL = 2 stacked heptameric rings; client enters cavity → GroES cap seals → folding in protected chamber → ATP-driven cycle → release after ~10 sec]; TRiC/CCT in eukaryotes [8-subunit ring × 2; folds actin, tubulin, and many other proteins]); HSP90 (eukaryotic; folds signaling proteins: steroid hormone receptors, kinases [Src, Raf, CDK4], p53; geldanamycin/17-AAG → HSP90 inhibitors → client degradation → anticancer); small HSPs (αB-crystallin in lens → prevents protein aggregation → cataract prevention; mutations → myopathy or cataracts); HSP100/ClpB (disaggregases in bacteria/yeast: unfold + dissolve aggregates)

Chaperones cleave misfolded proteins into smaller fragments: protein cleavage for degradation is performed by proteasomes (ubiquitin-proteasome system) or lysosomal proteases; chaperones assist FOLDING, not cleavage; however, chaperones do participate in targeting misfolded proteins for degradation (e.g., Hsp70 → CHIP E3 ligase → ubiquitination → proteasome; this is a triage function)
Chaperones determine the amino acid sequence of proteins: the amino acid sequence is determined by mRNA (genetic code → translation); chaperones cannot alter the primary sequence
explanation: Protein folding and misfolding — disease connections: CHAPERONOPATHIES: ↓chaperone function → protein aggregation diseases; Prion diseases (CJD, BSE, kuru, FFI, GSS): PrPc (normal, α-helix-rich) → PrPSc (misfolded, β-sheet-rich, protease-resistant) → templates further misfolding → amyloid fibrils → spongiform neurodegeneration; infectious protein (no nucleic acid); Alzheimer's disease: Aβ peptide (from APP cleavage by β-secretase [BACE1] + γ-secretase [presenilin]) → amyloid plaques; tau hyperphosphorylation → neurofibrillary tangles; Parkinson's disease: α-synuclein misfolding → Lewy bodies; Huntington's: polyQ expansion in huntingtin → aggregation; ALS: SOD1 mutations (some) → misfolded aggregates; Amyloidosis: various proteins form amyloid fibrils (β-pleated sheet, Congo red birefringence [apple-green under polarized light], thioflavin T fluorescence); AA amyloid (serum amyloid A → chronic inflammation → reactive amyloidosis); AL amyloid (immunoglobulin light chains → primary amyloidosis / multiple myeloma); ATTR (transthyretin → familial amyloid polyneuropathy + cardiomyopathy; treatment: tafamidis [TTR stabilizer], patisiran/vutrisiran [siRNA targeting TTR mRNA], inotersen [ASO targeting TTR]); ER stress + UPR: ↑unfolded proteins in ER → UPR sensors (IRE1α → XBP1 splicing → ↑ERAD + ↑lipid synthesis; PERK → eIF2α phosphorylation → ↓global translation + ↑ATF4; ATF6 → Golgi processing → ↑chaperone [BiP/GRP78] transcription); prolonged UPR → CHOP → apoptosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which sugar is found in RNA but NOT in DNA?
options: Deoxyribose: 2'-DEOXYribose (2-deoxy-D-ribose) is the sugar in DNA (DNA = deoxyribonucleic acid); the 2'-position has an H instead of OH → this makes DNA more stable (↓susceptibility to alkaline hydrolysis; RNA's 2'-OH can participate in intramolecular nucleophilic attack on the phosphodiester bond → RNA is more labile)

Ribose: RIBOSE (D-ribose) is the sugar in RNA (RNA = ribonucleic acid); ribose has a hydroxyl group (-OH) at the 2' position (C2'); this 2'-OH: (1) makes RNA more susceptible to hydrolysis (2'-OH → nucleophilic attack → 2',3'-cyclic phosphate → strand cleavage; this is why RNA is less stable than DNA → DNA was selected as the genetic material for long-term storage); (2) affects secondary structure (2'-OH → additional hydrogen bonding → A-form helix [RNA and RNA-DNA hybrids adopt A-form]; DNA: B-form); (3) is modified in some contexts: 2'-O-methylation (abundant in rRNA/snRNA; protects from RNase; contributes to SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine stability [mRNA vaccines use N1-methylpseudouridine + 2'-O-methylation + 5' cap → ↑stability + ↓innate immune recognition]); DNA synthesis: ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) converts ribonucleoside diphosphates (NDPs) → deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates (dNDPs) by reducing the 2'-OH → 2'-H; this is the only pathway for deoxyribonucleotide synthesis → RNR is essential for DNA replication

Glucose: glucose is a hexose (6-carbon sugar) found in glycolysis, glycogen, etc.; glucose is NOT a component of nucleic acids (nucleic acids contain pentoses: ribose or deoxyribose, both 5-carbon sugars)
Fructose: fructose is a hexose/ketose sugar metabolized by fructokinase → aldolase B pathway; fructose is NOT a component of nucleic acids
explanation: DNA vs RNA — structural differences: Feature | DNA | RNA: Sugar: 2'-deoxyribose | ribose (2'-OH); Bases: A,G,C,T (thymine has methyl group) | A,G,C,U (uracil lacks methyl); Strands: double-stranded (usually) | single-stranded (usually); Helix: B-form (right-handed, 10 bp/turn) | A-form (when dsRNA or RNA-DNA hybrid); Stability: very stable (↓2'-OH, ↓hydrolysis) | less stable (2'-OH → ↑hydrolysis); Function: genetic information storage | protein synthesis (mRNA), structural/catalytic (rRNA), adapter (tRNA), regulatory (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA); Location: nucleus (chromosomes), mitochondria | cytoplasm (translation), nucleus (transcription, splicing), nucleolus (rRNA); Thymine vs Uracil: Thymine (5-methyluracil) in DNA: the methyl group at C5 distinguishes it from uracil; why DNA uses T not U: cytosine → [spontaneous deamination] → uracil; if DNA used U, this would be MUTAGENIC (U:G mismatch after C deamination would be indistinguishable from normal U:A → not repaired → C:G → T:A transition); by using THYMINE, any uracil found in DNA is recognized as an error → excised by URACIL-DNA GLYCOSYLASE (UNG) via BER → maintains genomic integrity; this is a key evolutionary advantage of using T in DNA.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following enzymes is deficient in essential fructosuria?
options: Aldolase B: aldolase B deficiency → hereditary fructose intolerance (HFI); NOT essential fructosuria

Fructokinase: ESSENTIAL FRUCTOSURIA is caused by deficiency of FRUCTOKINASE (ketohexokinase/KHK); fructokinase normally phosphorylates fructose → fructose-1-phosphate (F1P) in liver; when fructokinase is deficient: fructose CANNOT be phosphorylated → fructose accumulates in blood (fructosemia) and is excreted in urine (fructosuria); this is a BENIGN condition — no symptoms, no organ damage, no dietary restriction needed; fructose simply appears in urine after fructose-containing meals; detected incidentally: urine reducing substance positive (Clinitest/Benedict's) but glucose oxidase dipstick negative (because fructose is NOT glucose); autosomal recessive; prevalence ~1:130,000; distinguished from HFI: no hypoglycemia, no liver damage, no vomiting, no aversion to sweets
Phosphofructokinase: PFK deficiency → GSD VII (Tarui disease, muscle form) or hemolytic anemia (erythrocyte form); NOT essential fructosuria
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase: F1,6BPase deficiency → impaired gluconeogenesis → fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis; NOT essential fructosuria
explanation: Fructose metabolism disorders comparison: (1) ESSENTIAL FRUCTOSURIA: enzyme = fructokinase; substrate accumulates = fructose; presentation = benign, asymptomatic, fructose in urine; treatment = none needed; (2) HEREDITARY FRUCTOSE INTOLERANCE (HFI): enzyme = aldolase B; substrate accumulates = fructose-1-phosphate (F1P); presentation = hypoglycemia, vomiting, hepatomegaly, liver failure, failure to thrive, aversion to sweets; onset when fructose/sucrose introduced to diet; treatment = strict fructose/sucrose/sorbitol avoidance; (3) FRUCTOSE-1,6-BISPHOSPHATASE DEFICIENCY: enzyme = F1,6BPase; pathway affected = gluconeogenesis; presentation = fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis (NOT triggered by fructose ingestion specifically, but by fasting); treatment = avoid prolonged fasting; KEY DISTINGUISHING POINT: essential fructosuria = benign; HFI = dangerous (F1P toxicity); F1,6BPase def = GNG defect (fasting hypoglycemia).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate the pH of a buffer solution. Which of the following correctly states this equation?
options: pH = pKa + log([HA]/[A⁻]): this is INVERTED; the correct equation has [A⁻] (conjugate base) in the numerator and [HA] (weak acid) in the denominator

pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]): The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) where [A⁻] = concentration of conjugate base (deprotonated form) and [HA] = concentration of weak acid (protonated form); derived from Ka equilibrium: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻; Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; take -log of both sides: pKa = pH - log([A⁻]/[HA]); rearrange: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); KEY APPLICATIONS: (1) when [A⁻] = [HA] → log(1) = 0 → pH = pKa (buffer is most effective at pH = pKa ± 1); (2) bicarbonate buffer system: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻]/[0.03 × PCO₂]); normal: pH = 6.1 + log(24/1.2) = 6.1 + log(20) = 6.1 + 1.3 = 7.4; ratio 20:1 (HCO₃⁻:CO₂) → pH 7.4; (3) metabolic acidosis: ↓HCO₃⁻ → ↓ratio → ↓pH; respiratory compensation: hyperventilation → ↓PCO₂ → partially restores ratio; (4) respiratory acidosis: ↑PCO₂ → ↓ratio → ↓pH; metabolic compensation: ↑HCO₃⁻ reabsorption (kidneys) → partially restores ratio
pH = pKa × log([A⁻]/[HA]): the relationship is ADDITIVE (pKa + log), not multiplicative
pH = pKa − log([A⁻]/[HA]): the correct equation uses + log, not − log; pH = pKa − log([A⁻]/[HA]) would give pH < pKa when base predominates, which is incorrect
explanation: Buffer systems in human physiology: (1) BICARBONATE buffer (most important extracellular): CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ [carbonic anhydrase] ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; open system (CO₂ exhaled by lungs, HCO₃⁻ regulated by kidneys) → very effective despite pKa 6.1 being far from pH 7.4; Henderson-Hasselbalch for bicarb: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO₃⁻]/[0.03×PCO₂]); normal values: HCO₃⁻ = 24 mEq/L, PCO₂ = 40 mmHg → pH 7.4; (2) PHOSPHATE buffer (important intracellular + urine): H₂PO₄⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + HPO₄²⁻; pKa = 6.8 (close to intracellular pH ~7.0 → effective intracellular buffer); in urine: titratable acidity (H⁺ secreted by kidneys combines with HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻ → excreted); (3) PROTEIN buffers (hemoglobin, albumin, intracellular proteins): His residues (imidazole pKa ~6.0-7.0) → buffer at physiological pH; HEMOGLOBIN: most important intracellular blood buffer; deoxyhemoglobin is a better buffer than oxyhemoglobin (↓O₂ → ↑His buffering capacity → Haldane effect: deoxyHb binds more H⁺ and CO₂ in tissues); (4) AMMONIA buffer (renal): NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ → excreted in urine; important for acid excretion, especially in chronic acidosis (↑glutaminase → ↑NH₃ production in proximal tubule).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis?
options: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC): ACC catalyzes acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA; rate-limiting step of FATTY ACID synthesis, NOT cholesterol synthesis
Thiolase: thiolase (acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase) catalyzes 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA; this is an early step in cholesterol synthesis but NOT rate-limiting

HMG-CoA synthase: HMG-CoA synthase catalyzes acetoacetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA; this occurs in both cholesterol synthesis (cytoplasmic isoform) and ketogenesis (mitochondrial isoform); NOT the rate-limiting step

HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR): HMG-CoA REDUCTASE is the RATE-LIMITING enzyme of cholesterol synthesis; catalyzes: HMG-CoA + 2 NADPH → mevalonate + CoA; located in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane; Regulation (multilevel): (1) TRANSCRIPTIONAL: SREBP-2 (sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2) → when cholesterol is LOW: SREBP-2 in ER membrane → SCAP escorts SREBP-2 to Golgi → S1P/S2P proteases cleave → active N-terminal fragment → nucleus → binds SRE (sterol regulatory element) → ↑HMGCR gene transcription; when cholesterol is HIGH: cholesterol binds SCAP → conformational change → INSIG retains SCAP-SREBP-2 in ER → ↓HMGCR transcription; (2) DEGRADATION: high cholesterol → Insig-mediated ubiquitination → proteasomal degradation of HMGCR (sterol-accelerated degradation); (3) PHOSPHORYLATION: AMPK phosphorylates HMGCR → INACTIVE (energy-depleted state → ↓cholesterol synthesis); insulin → ↑phosphatase → dephosphorylation → ACTIVE; (4) PHARMACOLOGICAL: STATINS (lovastatin, simvastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, etc.) are competitive inhibitors of HMGCR → ↓cholesterol synthesis → ↑LDLR expression (compensatory) → ↓LDL-C; statins are first-line therapy for hypercholesterolemia; side effects: myopathy (↑CK), rhabdomyolysis (rare), hepatotoxicity, ↑diabetes risk
explanation: Cholesterol synthesis pathway (mevalonate pathway): All 27 carbons of cholesterol come from acetyl-CoA; pathway occurs in CYTOPLASM + ER; Steps: (1) 2 acetyl-CoA → [thiolase] → acetoacetyl-CoA; (2) acetoacetyl-CoA + acetyl-CoA → [HMG-CoA synthase, cytoplasmic] → HMG-CoA; (3) HMG-CoA → [HMGCR, RATE-LIMITING, 2 NADPH] → mevalonate; (4) mevalonate → [3 kinases + 1 decarboxylase] → isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP, 5C isoprene unit); (5) 6 IPP → [condensation: geranyl-PP → farnesyl-PP → squalene [squalene synthase, first committed step of sterol synthesis] → squalene-2,3-epoxide → lanosterol [first sterol] → [19 more steps] → cholesterol; Cholesterol functions: (1) membrane fluidity (inserts between phospholipids → ↓fluidity at high temp, ↑fluidity at low temp → 'fluidity buffer'); (2) precursor: bile acids (primary: cholic + chenodeoxycholic → 7α-hydroxylase rate-limiting), steroid hormones (glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, androgens, estrogens, progestins), vitamin D (7-dehydrocholesterol → [UV-B skin] → cholecalciferol); (3) lipid raft formation; (4) Hedgehog signaling (cholesterol modification of Hedgehog protein required for signaling).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is converted to serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine)?
options: Tyrosine: Tyr → [TH: tyrosine hydroxylase, BH4] → L-DOPA → [AADC] → dopamine → [DβH] → norepinephrine → [PNMT] → epinephrine; Tyr is precursor for catecholamines + melanin + thyroid hormones; NOT serotonin

Tryptophan: TRYPTOPHAN is the precursor of SEROTONIN (5-HT, 5-hydroxytryptamine); Pathway: Trp → [tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH), cofactor BH4] → 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) → [aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC), cofactor PLP] → SEROTONIN (5-HT); TPH is rate-limiting; two isoforms: TPH1 (peripheral: gut enterochromaffin cells, pineal gland) and TPH2 (brain: raphe nuclei); Serotonin functions: (1) CNS: mood, sleep, appetite, cognition, memory (↓5-HT → depression; SSRIs ↑synaptic 5-HT → antidepressant effect); (2) GI: 90% of body serotonin is in gut enterochromaffin cells → regulates motility, secretion (5-HT₃ antagonists [ondansetron] → antiemetic; 5-HT₄ agonists → prokinetic); (3) platelets: 5-HT stored in dense granules → released upon activation → vasoconstriction + platelet aggregation; (4) carcinoid syndrome: neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid) → ↑↑5-HT secretion → flushing, diarrhea, bronchoconstriction, right-sided heart disease (5-HT → fibrosis of tricuspid/pulmonic valves); urine 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, serotonin metabolite by MAO) is elevated → diagnostic marker; Serotonin → melatonin: 5-HT → [AANAT: aralkylamine N-acetyltransferase] → N-acetylserotonin → [HIOMT: hydroxyindole O-methyltransferase] → MELATONIN (pineal gland; circadian rhythm regulation; ↑darkness → ↑melatonin)
Histidine: His → [histidine decarboxylase, PLP] → histamine; NOT serotonin
Glutamate: Glu → [GAD: glutamic acid decarboxylase, PLP] → GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid); NOT serotonin
explanation: Biogenic amines from amino acids — comprehensive: (1) Trp → serotonin (5-HT) → melatonin; also: Trp → [IDO/TDO] → N-formylkynurenine → kynurenine pathway → NAD⁺ (niacin synthesis; this is why niacin deficiency [pellagra] worsens with Trp depletion; carcinoid tumors divert Trp to 5-HT → ↓NAD⁺ synthesis → pellagra-like symptoms); (2) Tyr → catecholamines (DA, NE, Epi); also: Tyr → [tyrosinase] → DOPA → melanin (melanocytes; albinism: tyrosinase deficiency); Tyr → thyroid hormones (T3/T4: Tyr residues in thyroglobulin iodinated by TPO → MIT/DIT → coupling → T3/T4); (3) His → histamine (allergic reactions, gastric acid secretion [ECL cells → parietal cells via H2 receptors]); (4) Glu → GABA (major inhibitory NT; GAD requires PLP → pyridoxine deficiency → ↓GABA → seizures in infants); (5) Arg → NO (nitric oxide; NOS: neuronal/endothelial/inducible); (6) Gly: itself is an inhibitory NT (spinal cord, brainstem); strychnine blocks glycine receptors → hyperexcitability → convulsions.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following thalassemias results from deletion of all four alpha-globin genes?
options: Alpha-thalassemia trait: α-thal trait = deletion of 2 α-globin genes (either cis [--/αα, common in Southeast Asians] or trans [-α/-α, common in Africans]); mild microcytic anemia; Hb electrophoresis may show ↓Hb A₂ or be normal; NOT lethal

Hemoglobin H disease: Hb H disease = deletion of 3 α-globin genes (--/-α); ↓↓α chains → excess β chains tetramerize → Hb H (β₄); Hb H: unstable (precipitates → Heinz bodies → hemolysis), high O₂ affinity (poor tissue O₂ delivery); moderate-to-severe hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, jaundice; compatible with life (though transfusion-dependent in severe cases); NOT the 4-gene deletion

Hydrops fetalis (Hb Bart's): HYDROPS FETALIS = deletion of ALL 4 α-globin genes (--/--); NO α-globin production at all; in fetal life: excess γ chains form Hb Bart's (γ₄); Hb Bart's has EXTREMELY HIGH O₂ affinity → does NOT release O₂ to tissues → severe tissue hypoxia → massive edema (hydrops), heart failure, death; incompatible with extrauterine life → stillbirth or death shortly after birth; also endangers mother (preeclampsia, hemorrhage); almost exclusively seen in Southeast Asian populations (where cis deletion [--/αα] is common → both parents carriers → 25% chance of --/-- offspring); α-globin genes: 4 copies on chromosome 16 (2 per allele: α1 and α2 on each chromosome 16); deletion spectrum: 1 gene deleted → silent carrier (α-/αα; asymptomatic, normal CBC); 2 deleted → α-thal trait (mild microcytosis); 3 deleted → Hb H disease; 4 deleted → hydrops fetalis

Beta-thalassemia major: β-thal major (Cooley anemia) = homozygous β⁰ or β⁰/β⁺ → severe ↓ or absent β-globin → excess α chains precipitate → ineffective erythropoiesis + hemolysis; presents at 6-12 months (when HbF → HbA switch occurs); transfusion-dependent; this involves BETA-globin genes on chromosome 11, NOT alpha-globin
explanation: Thalassemias overview: α-THALASSEMIA: gene deletions on chr 16; 4 genes total; clinical severity proportional to number deleted: 1 → silent carrier; 2 → trait (mild anemia); 3 → Hb H (β₄, moderate-severe); 4 → hydrops fetalis (γ₄/Hb Bart's, lethal); β-THALASSEMIA: point mutations on chr 11; β⁺ (reduced) or β⁰ (absent); β-thal minor (heterozygous): mild microcytic anemia, ↑Hb A₂ (α₂δ₂ >3.5%), ↑Hb F slightly; target cells; β-thal major (homozygous/compound): severe anemia (6-12 mo), hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary hematopoiesis), skeletal deformities (marrow expansion → crew-cut skull on X-ray, chipmunk facies), iron overload (from transfusions + ↑absorption) → hemochromatosis (cardiac, hepatic, endocrine); treatment: chronic transfusions + iron chelation (deferoxamine IV/SC, deferasirox PO, deferiprone PO) ± splenectomy; curative: allogeneic HSCT; gene therapy (betibeglogene autotemcel/Zynteglo: lentiviral β-globin gene transfer; exagamglogene autotemcel/Casgevy: CRISPR-based, edits BCL11A erythroid enhancer → ↑HbF); HbF inducers: hydroxyurea (↑γ-globin → ↑HbF → reduces sickling in SCD and ameliorates β-thal intermedia/major).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following statements about microRNAs (miRNAs) is correct?
options: miRNAs are long non-coding RNAs greater than 200 nucleotides: miRNAs are SHORT (~18-25 nucleotides, typically ~22 nt); lncRNAs are >200 nt by definition; completely different classes of non-coding RNA

miRNAs are small (~22 nt) non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally by binding to the 3'-UTR of target mRNAs: miRNAs are small (~22 nucleotides) SINGLE-STRANDED non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression POST-TRANSCRIPTIONALLY; mechanism: (1) BIOGENESIS: miRNA gene → [RNA Pol II] → pri-miRNA (primary transcript, has hairpin structure, may be polycistronic) → [Drosha + DGCR8 (Microprocessor complex), in NUCLEUS] → pre-miRNA (~70 nt hairpin/stem-loop) → [Exportin-5 + Ran-GTP] → CYTOPLASM → [Dicer (RNase III enzyme)] → miRNA duplex (~22 bp) → one strand (guide strand) loaded into RISC (RNA-induced silencing complex, core protein: AGO2/Argonaute) → mature miRNA-RISC complex; (2) SILENCING: miRNA-RISC binds complementary sequence in 3'-UTR (untranslated region) of target mRNA; seed sequence (nt 2-8 of miRNA) is critical for target recognition; IMPERFECT complementarity (partial match) → translational REPRESSION (↓protein without mRNA degradation) + mRNA destabilization (deadenylation → decapping → 5'-3' degradation); PERFECT complementarity (rare in animals, common in plants) → mRNA CLEAVAGE (AGO2 slicer activity); (3) BIOLOGICAL ROLES: one miRNA can target hundreds of mRNAs → regulate entire pathways; involved in development, differentiation, apoptosis, metabolism, immunity; (4) DISEASE: oncomiRs (miR-21, miR-155: ↑ in cancers → suppress tumor suppressors); tumor suppressor miRNAs (let-7, miR-15a/16-1: ↓ in cancers → fail to suppress oncogenes; miR-15a/16-1 deletion → CLL); circulating miRNAs: potential biomarkers (stable in blood; miR-122 ↑ in liver injury, miR-208 ↑ in MI)

miRNAs encode small proteins called micropeptides: miRNAs are NON-CODING RNAs — they do NOT encode proteins or peptides; some lncRNAs and 'non-coding' transcripts have been found to encode micropeptides, but miRNAs do not (they are too short to encode even the smallest peptide)

miRNAs function primarily in the nucleus to modify histone proteins: miRNAs function primarily in the CYTOPLASM (RISC-mediated mRNA silencing); some miRNAs have been found in the nucleus with possible roles in transcriptional regulation, but the canonical and primary function is cytoplasmic post-transcriptional gene silencing
explanation: RNA interference (RNAi) — siRNA vs miRNA: siRNA: exogenous dsRNA (viral, transfected, or from transposons) → [Dicer] → siRNA duplex (~21-23 bp with 2-nt 3' overhangs) → RISC (AGO2) → PERFECT complementarity to target mRNA → mRNA CLEAVAGE (endonucleolytic cut by AGO2 slicer); used as research tool (gene knockdown) and therapeutics (patisiran: siRNA targeting TTR mRNA for hereditary ATTR amyloidosis; givosiran: siRNA targeting ALAS1 for acute hepatic porphyria; inclisiran: siRNA targeting PCSK9 mRNA for hypercholesterolemia); miRNA: endogenous, genomically encoded; IMPERFECT complementarity → translational repression primarily; one miRNA → many targets (regulation of entire gene networks); piRNA: PIWI-interacting RNA; 24-31 nt; germ cells; silence transposons; associated with PIWI proteins (not AGO); biogenesis: Dicer-INDEPENDENT (unlike miRNA/siRNA); ping-pong amplification cycle; protect genome integrity in germline.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Elastin, the protein responsible for tissue elasticity, is rich in which of the following amino acids?
options: Hydroxyproline: hydroxyproline (Hyp) is characteristic of COLLAGEN (formed by prolyl hydroxylase, requires vitamin C); elastin has SOME proline but much less Hyp than collagen; Hyp is used as a marker for collagen turnover (urinary Hyp)

Glycine and proline, with unique desmosine cross-links: ELASTIN is the major elastic fiber protein (lungs, aorta/large arteries, skin, ligamentum nuchae, vocal cords); composition: (1) RICH in GLYCINE (~33%), PROLINE (~10-13%), ALANINE, VALINE — hydrophobic amino acids predominate (elastin is very hydrophobic → allows random coil structure essential for elasticity); (2) UNIQUE cross-links: DESMOSINE and ISODESMOSINE — formed from 4 LYSINE residues (condensation of 3 allysine [Lys oxidized by lysyl oxidase → allysine] + 1 unmodified Lys → desmosine/isodesmosine; pyridinium cross-links unique to elastin); these cross-links are covalent and highly stable → make elastin one of the most durable proteins (half-life ~70 years; elastin you make in childhood lasts your lifetime → cumulative damage = aging/emphysema); (3) TROPOELASTIN: soluble precursor secreted by smooth muscle cells/fibroblasts → cross-linked extracellularly by LYSYL OXIDASE (LOX, copper-dependent, requires O₂ → Cu deficiency [Menkes disease: ATP7A mutation → ↓Cu absorption → ↓LOX → ↓elastin/collagen cross-links → vascular fragility, kinky hair, neurodegeneration] and lathyrism [BAPN inhibits LOX → ↓cross-links → aortic rupture, joint hypermobility]); elastin degradation: ELASTASE (neutrophil elastase/NE, MMP-12); α₁-antitrypsin (α₁-AT/SERPINA1) is the major inhibitor of NE; α₁-AT deficiency → ↑unchecked elastase activity → ↓elastin in alveolar walls → EMPHYSEMA (panacinar, lower lobes; PiZZ genotype most severe) + liver disease (misfolded α₁-AT → ER accumulation in hepatocytes → PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules → cirrhosis)

Hydroxylysine: Hyl is found primarily in COLLAGEN (formed by lysyl hydroxylase → Hyl → O-linked glycosylation [galactose, glucosylgalactose] unique to collagen); elastin has Lys but not significant Hyl

Cysteine: elastin has very few Cys residues (almost none); Cys-rich proteins include keratins (hair: α-keratin, many disulfide bonds → strength + rigidity) and metallothioneins (Cys-rich → bind heavy metals)
explanation: Extracellular matrix proteins: (1) COLLAGENS: most abundant protein in body; triple helix (Gly-X-Y repeat; X often Pro, Y often Hyp); 28+ types; Type I: bone, skin, tendon (most abundant overall; mutations → OI); Type II: cartilage, vitreous humor; Type III: reticulin (skin, blood vessels, uterus; ↓ in Ehlers-Danlos type IV/vascular type: COL3A1 mutations → arterial/organ rupture); Type IV: basement membrane (non-fibrillar, forms mesh; α5 chain target of anti-GBM Ab → Goodpasture syndrome); (2) ELASTIN: elastic fibers; Gly/Pro/Ala/Val-rich; desmosine cross-links from Lys; random coil → stretch + recoil; α₁-AT protects; Marfan syndrome: FIBRILLIN-1 (FBN1) mutation → ↓microfibrils (scaffold for elastin deposition + TGF-β sequestration) → ↑TGF-β signaling → aortic root dilation/dissection, lens subluxation (upward: zonules contain fibrillin), tall stature/arachnodactyly/pectus; (3) PROTEOGLYCANS: core protein + GAG chains (heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate, keratan sulfate, dermatan sulfate); aggrecan (cartilage: aggregates with hyaluronic acid via link protein → compressive resistance); (4) GLYCOPROTEINS: fibronectin (cell adhesion: RGD motif binds integrins), laminin (basement membrane: binds type IV collagen + integrins + entactin/nidogen).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is a feature of kwashiorkor that distinguishes it from marasmus?
options: Severe muscle wasting: muscle wasting is more characteristic of MARASMUS (total caloric deficit → body uses fat AND protein stores → emaciated appearance, 'skin and bones'); kwashiorkor patients may actually have relatively preserved subcutaneous fat (because the primary deficit is PROTEIN, not total calories)

Edema: EDEMA is the hallmark feature distinguishing KWASHIORKOR from marasmus; kwashiorkor = PROTEIN deficiency (with relatively adequate caloric/carbohydrate intake); ↓protein intake → ↓hepatic albumin synthesis → ↓serum albumin (HYPOALBUMINEMIA) → ↓plasma oncotic pressure → fluid shifts from intravascular to interstitial space → EDEMA (pitting, dependent, starts in feet/legs → ascites → generalized); other features of kwashiorkor: (1) FATTY LIVER (↓apolipoprotein B synthesis → ↓VLDL secretion → TG accumulates in hepatocytes → hepatomegaly + steatosis); (2) SKIN CHANGES: 'flaky paint' dermatosis (hypopigmented/depigmented patches that peel, especially in areas of friction → resembles old paint peeling), 'enamel paint' (dark, shiny, desquamating skin); (3) HAIR CHANGES: sparse, thin, depigmented (hypopigmentation: reddish-brown, 'flag sign' = alternating bands of normal and depigmented hair reflecting periods of adequate vs inadequate nutrition); (4) moon face (edematous); (5) APATHY, irritability, anorexia; (6) IMMUNODEFICIENCY (↓cell-mediated immunity → ↑infections → ↑mortality); (7) growth retardation; biochemistry: ↓albumin, ↓transferrin, ↓prealbumin (transthyretin: shortest half-life ~2 days → best marker of acute nutritional status change), ↓retinol-binding protein

Loss of subcutaneous fat: loss of subcutaneous fat is characteristic of MARASMUS (total calorie deficit → fat stores depleted first [lipolysis → FFAs → β-oxidation → energy]); in kwashiorkor, subcutaneous fat may be relatively preserved

Decreased total calorie intake: marasmus = total calorie deficiency (protein + carbohydrate + fat all inadequate → global starvation); kwashiorkor = predominantly PROTEIN deficiency with relatively adequate calorie/carbohydrate intake; though in practice, overlap exists (marasmic-kwashiorkor: combined)
explanation: Protein-energy malnutrition: MARASMUS: total caloric deficiency → severe wasting (muscle + fat); emaciated ('skin and bones'), alert/hungry, NO edema, weight <60% expected; adaptation: ↑cortisol, ↑GH → ↑lipolysis + gluconeogenesis; albumin relatively preserved initially (catabolism of visceral proteins is slower than somatic); KWASHIORKOR: protein deficiency (calorie intake may be adequate from carbohydrates); EDEMA (hypoalbuminemia), fatty liver (↓VLDL), skin/hair changes, moon face, apathy; albumin very low (<2.5 g/dL); weight 60-80% expected (but edema masks actual weight loss → 'well-nourished appearance' is deceptive); MARASMIC-KWASHIORKOR: combined features; worst prognosis; REFEEDING SYNDROME: critical risk when refeeding malnourished patients; mechanism: prolonged starvation → ↓insulin, ↑glucagon → fat/protein catabolism → intracellular depletion of phosphate, Mg²⁺, K⁺, thiamine (used in low amounts during starvation); upon refeeding (especially high carbohydrate) → insulin surge → drives glucose + K⁺ + PO₄ + Mg²⁺ INTO cells → severe HYPOPHOSPHATEMIA (↓ATP, ↓2,3-BPG → tissue hypoxia, cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, seizures); also hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia; thiamine depletion → Wernicke's if glucose given without thiamine; PREVENTION: start low ('start low, go slow'), monitor electrolytes, supplement PO₄/K⁺/Mg²⁺/thiamine BEFORE refeeding.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the first sterol intermediate in cholesterol biosynthesis?
options: Squalene: squalene (C₃₀) is a linear triterpene formed from 2 farnesyl-PP → [squalene synthase] → squalene; squalene is NOT a sterol (it lacks the four-ring steroid nucleus); squalene → [squalene epoxidase/monooxygenase, NADPH + O₂] → squalene-2,3-epoxide → [oxidosqualene cyclase/lanosterol synthase] → LANOSTEROL

Lanosterol: LANOSTEROL (C₃₀) is the FIRST STEROL (first four-ring steroid nucleus compound) formed in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway; lanosterol is formed by cyclization of squalene-2,3-epoxide by oxidosqualene cyclase (lanosterol synthase); lanosterol then undergoes 19 further enzymatic steps to become cholesterol (C₂₇): removal of 3 methyl groups (at C₄, C₄, C₁₄), reduction of double bond in side chain, isomerization of Δ8 → Δ5 double bond; key intermediates: lanosterol → 14α-demethyllanosterol → zymosterol → desmosterol → cholesterol (Bloch pathway) or → lathosterol → 7-dehydrocholesterol → cholesterol (Kandutsch-Russell pathway); 7-dehydrocholesterol is also the precursor for vitamin D₃ synthesis in skin; pharmacological target: azole antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole) inhibit lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51) in FUNGI → block ergosterol synthesis (fungal 'cholesterol' equivalent) → ↓ergosterol → fungal membrane disruption
Mevalonate: mevalonate (C₆) is formed by HMG-CoA reductase (rate-limiting step); mevalonate is an early intermediate — NOT a sterol (no ring structure)
Isopentenyl pyrophosphate: IPP (C₅) is the basic 5-carbon isoprenoid unit; formed from mevalonate by kinases + decarboxylase; IPP is a building block, not a sterol
explanation: Cholesterol synthesis landmarks: Acetyl-CoA (C₂) → acetoacetyl-CoA (C₄) → HMG-CoA (C₆) → [HMGCR, rate-limiting] → mevalonate (C₆) → IPP (C₅, active isoprene) → DMAPP (C₅) → GPP (C₁₀) → FPP (C₁₅, farnesyl-PP; branch point: FPP → protein prenylation [farnesylation of Ras], dolichol, ubiquinone/CoQ₁₀, heme A) → squalene (C₃₀, first committed sterol precursor step [squalene synthase]) → squalene-2,3-epoxide → LANOSTEROL (C₃₀, first sterol) → 19 steps → cholesterol (C₂₇); mevalonate pathway products beyond cholesterol: (1) dolichol (glycoprotein N-linked glycosylation in ER), (2) ubiquinone/CoQ₁₀ (ETC mobile electron carrier), (3) isopentenyl-tRNA (tRNA modification), (4) farnesyl/geranylgeranyl groups (protein prenylation: Ras → membrane anchoring; statin side effect: ↓prenylation may contribute to muscle toxicity), (5) heme A (cytochrome c oxidase prosthetic group).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine?
options: Tyrosine hydroxylase: tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) catalyzes Tyr → L-DOPA (the rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis); TH requires BH4 as cofactor; located in adrenal medulla and catecholaminergic neurons; NOT the Phe → Tyr enzyme

Phenylalanine hydroxylase: PHENYLALANINE HYDROXYLASE (PAH) catalyzes: Phe + O₂ + BH4 → Tyr + H₂O + quinonoid-BH2; PAH is a mixed-function oxidase (monooxygenase: one atom of O₂ incorporated into Tyr [as -OH], other reduced to H₂O); requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor (BH4 is regenerated by dihydrobiopterin reductase [DHPR/QDPR]: q-BH2 + NADH → BH4); PAH is expressed in LIVER (primarily) and kidney; PAH deficiency → PHENYLKETONURIA (PKU): ↑Phe in blood (>1200 μmol/L in classic PKU) → Phe becomes essential (Tyr becomes conditionally essential since it cannot be made from Phe); consequences of ↑Phe: (1) intellectual disability (↑Phe → competes with other LNAA [large neutral amino acids: Trp, Tyr] at LAT1 transporter across BBB → ↓brain Trp/Tyr → ↓serotonin/catecholamines → neurodevelopmental impairment; + direct Phe toxicity: ↓myelin synthesis, ↑oxidative stress); (2) musty/mousy odor (phenylacetic acid: Phe → [transamination] → phenylpyruvate → [decarboxylation] → phenylacetate → excreted in urine/sweat); (3) fair skin/hair/eyes (↓Tyr → ↓melanin synthesis); (4) eczema; (5) seizures; NBS: ↑Phe on blood spot (Guthrie test historically, now tandem MS/MS); treatment: Phe-restricted diet (lifelong), Tyr supplementation, BH4 (sapropterin: for BH4-responsive PAH mutations, typically milder/moderate PKU), LNAA supplementation, pegvaliase (PEGylated phenylalanine ammonia lyase → converts Phe → trans-cinnamic acid + NH₃; for adults with ↑Phe despite diet)
Tryptophan hydroxylase: tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) catalyzes Trp → 5-HTP (serotonin synthesis); requires BH4; NOT Phe → Tyr
Phenylalanine decarboxylase: this enzyme name is not standard; aromatic amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) decarboxylates DOPA → dopamine and 5-HTP → serotonin; does NOT hydroxylate Phe → Tyr
explanation: BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin)-dependent hydroxylases — the three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases: (1) Phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH): Phe → Tyr (liver); deficiency → PKU; (2) Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH): Tyr → L-DOPA (adrenal medulla, catecholaminergic neurons); rate-limiting in catecholamine synthesis; (3) Tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH): Trp → 5-HTP (gut [TPH1], brain [TPH2]); rate-limiting in serotonin synthesis; ALL THREE require BH4 as electron donor; BH4 synthesis: GTP → [GTP cyclohydrolase I/GTPCH, rate-limiting] → dihydroneopterin triphosphate → [PTPS: 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase] → 6-PTP → [sepiapterin reductase] → BH4; BH4 recycling: q-BH2 → [DHPR: dihydropteridine reductase, NADH] → BH4; BH4 deficiency (GTPCH, PTPS, or DHPR deficiency) → 'malignant/atypical hyperphenylalaninemia': ↑Phe PLUS ↓catecholamines + ↓serotonin → severe neurological disease even with Phe-restricted diet (because the neurotransmitter deficit is the bigger problem); treatment: BH4 + L-DOPA + 5-HTP + carbidopa; NBS: must distinguish PAH-deficiency PKU from BH4-deficiency PKU (measure pterins + DHPR activity in blood spot); NOS (nitric oxide synthase) also requires BH4 as cofactor (BH4 → eNOS coupling; ↓BH4 → eNOS uncoupling → ↑superoxide instead of NO → endothelial dysfunction → atherosclerosis).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a cofactor for all of the following enzymes EXCEPT:
options: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex: PDC uses TPP (thiamine/B₁); PDC: pyruvate + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH; 5 cofactors: TPP (B₁), lipoic acid, CoA (pantothenate/B₅), FAD (riboflavin/B₂), NAD⁺ (niacin/B₃) → mnemonic: 'Tender Loving Care For Nancy' or 'The Lovely Coenzyme FAD-NAD'

α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase: OGDH uses TPP; OGDH: α-KG + CoA + NAD⁺ → succinyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH; same 5 cofactors as PDC (TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺); both PDC and OGDH are α-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes with identical cofactor requirements

Transketolase: transketolase uses TPP; catalyzes transfer of 2-carbon units in the pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative branch): (1) Xu5P + R5P → S7P + G3P; (2) Xu5P + E4P → F6P + G3P; transketolase activity in erythrocytes (before and after TPP addition) is used clinically to assess thiamine status; ↓transketolase activity with ↑TPP effect (>25% activation by exogenous TPP) → thiamine deficiency

Pyruvate carboxylase: PYRUVATE CARBOXYLASE (PC) uses BIOTIN (vitamin B₇/H) as cofactor, NOT TPP; PC: pyruvate + CO₂ + ATP → oxaloacetate (anaplerotic reaction replenishing TCA cycle; also first step of gluconeogenesis); PC is activated by acetyl-CoA (allosteric activator: ↑acetyl-CoA during β-oxidation signals need for ↑OAA to accept acetyl-CoA into TCA); biotin carboxylases (all use biotin + ATP + CO₂): PC, ACC, PCC, MCC (mnemonic: 'PAPM carboxylases')
explanation: Thiamine (vitamin B₁) — complete: Active form: TPP (thiamine pyrophosphate); Enzymes requiring TPP: (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC), (2) α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (OGDH), (3) Branched-chain α-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKDH; deficient in MSUD), (4) Transketolase (PPP), (5) Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1; — these are all α-keto acid dehydrogenases (except transketolase); Deficiency: (1) WET beriberi: high-output cardiac failure (↓ATP from ↓PDC → ↓aerobic metabolism → peripheral vasodilation → ↑CO to compensate → heart failure; dilated cardiomyopathy); (2) DRY beriberi: peripheral neuropathy (symmetric, distal, sensorimotor; ↓myelin? ↓ATP in nerves); (3) WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY: confusion, ophthalmoplegia (CN III/VI palsy, nystagmus), ataxia (cerebellar); triad often incomplete; thiamine-sensitive brain regions: mammillary bodies (most vulnerable → hemorrhagic necrosis), thalamus (medial dorsal nucleus), periaqueductal gray, cerebellum; (4) KORSAKOFF SYNDROME: chronic/irreversible; anterograde + retrograde amnesia, confabulation; mammillary body atrophy; often follows untreated Wernicke; WERNICKE-KORSAKOFF: mostly in alcoholics (↓intake + ↓absorption + ↓hepatic activation → ↓TPP; alcohol directly inhibits thiamine transporter); TREATMENT: IV thiamine BEFORE glucose (glucose metabolism requires TPP → giving glucose without thiamine → ↑pyruvate → ↑lactate + ↓ATP → worsens Wernicke); Sources: whole grains, pork, legumes; destroyed by heat/alkali/sulfites; polished white rice → beriberi (historically in Asian countries).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In steroid hormone biosynthesis, which enzyme catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step, converting cholesterol to pregnenolone?
options: CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase): CYP17A1 has dual activities: 17α-hydroxylase (pregnenolone → 17-OH-pregnenolone; progesterone → 17-OH-progesterone) AND 17,20-lyase (17-OH-pregnenolone → DHEA; 17-OH-progesterone → androstenedione); found in adrenal cortex (zona fasciculata/reticularis) + gonads; deficiency → ↑mineralocorticoids + corticosterone → hypertension + hypokalemia + ↓sex steroids → ambiguous genitalia in males (46,XY DSD), primary amenorrhea in females; NOT the first step

Cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme (CYP11A1/P450scc): CYP11A1 (also called P450scc [side-chain cleavage] or desmolase) is the enzyme that catalyzes the FIRST and RATE-LIMITING step: cholesterol → pregnenolone + isocaproaldehyde; this occurs in the INNER MITOCHONDRIAL MEMBRANE of steroidogenic cells (adrenal cortex, gonads, placenta); the reaction involves: (1) 20α-hydroxylation, (2) 22-hydroxylation, (3) oxidative cleavage of C20-C22 bond → removes 6-carbon side chain; requires: molecular O₂ + NADPH (electron transfer: NADPH → adrenodoxin reductase [FAD] → adrenodoxin [Fe-S protein] → CYP11A1); REGULATION: the rate-limiting step is actually the TRANSPORT of cholesterol from the OUTER to INNER mitochondrial membrane by StAR (steroidogenic acute regulatory protein); StAR is induced by ACTH (via cAMP/PKA) in adrenal cortex and LH in gonads → acute regulation of steroidogenesis; StAR mutations → lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia (most severe CAH: ↓ALL steroid hormones; lipid-laden adrenals; 46,XY → female phenotype due to ↓androgens)

CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase): CYP21A2 catalyzes: progesterone → 11-deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid pathway); 17-OH-progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol (glucocorticoid pathway); located in adrenal ER; most common CAH cause (90-95%): 21-hydroxylase deficiency → ↓cortisol + ↓aldosterone → ↑ACTH → adrenal hyperplasia + ↑17-OHP → ↑androgen shunt → virilization (46,XX ambiguous genitalia), salt-wasting (classic severe) or simple virilizing (classic) or late-onset (non-classic: hirsutism, acne, infertility); NOT the first step

CYP11B1 (11β-hydroxylase): CYP11B1 catalyzes: 11-deoxycortisol → CORTISOL; 11-deoxycorticosterone → corticosterone; located in adrenal mitochondria; 11β-hydroxylase deficiency → 2nd most common CAH (~5-8%): ↑11-deoxycortisol + ↑11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC: potent mineralocorticoid → HYPERTENSION + hypokalemia; distinguishes from 21-OHase def which has salt-wasting) + ↑androgens → virilization; NOT the first step
explanation: Steroid hormone synthesis zones (adrenal cortex: 'GFR = salt, sugar, sex'): ZONA GLOMERULOSA (outermost): mineralocorticoids → ALDOSTERONE; pathway: cholesterol → pregnenolone → progesterone → 11-DOC → corticosterone → [CYP11B2/aldosterone synthase: 18-hydroxylation + 18-oxidation] → aldosterone; regulated by: RAAS (angiotensin II), K⁺, ACTH (minor); ZONA FASCICULATA (middle, widest): glucocorticoids → CORTISOL; pathway: cholesterol → pregnenolone → 17-OH-pregnenolone → 17-OH-progesterone → 11-deoxycortisol → [CYP11B1] → cortisol; regulated by: ACTH (HPA axis); ZONA RETICULARIS (innermost): androgens → DHEA, DHEA-S, androstenedione; pathway: 17-OH-pregnenolone → [CYP17A1 17,20-lyase] → DHEA → DHEA-S (most abundant circulating steroid; sulfated by SULT2A1); regulated by: ACTH; ADRENAL MEDULLA: catecholamines (Epi > NE); chromaffin cells; from Tyr; regulated by: sympathetic nervous system + cortisol (from fasciculata → induces PNMT → NE → Epi).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acids serves as the major fuel for rapidly dividing cells such as enterocytes, lymphocytes, and tumor cells?
options: Alanine: Ala is primarily a glucogenic amino acid involved in the glucose-alanine cycle (muscle → liver); Ala is NOT the primary fuel for rapidly dividing cells

Glutamine: GLUTAMINE is the most abundant free amino acid in plasma and the primary fuel for rapidly dividing cells; enterocytes (small intestinal epithelium): Gln is the major energy substrate (more than glucose); Gln → [glutaminase] → Glu + NH₃; Glu → α-KG → TCA → energy; also: Gln → citrulline (intestinal CPS I → carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline → released to blood → taken up by kidney → converted to arginine → 'intestinal-renal axis' of arginine synthesis); lymphocytes/immune cells: Gln is essential for proliferation (↑Gln utilization during immune activation; ↓Gln → immunosuppression; rationale for glutamine supplementation in critically ill/burn patients [controversial but widely used]); tumor cells: glutamine addiction (many cancers upregulate glutaminase → ↑Gln → Glu → α-KG anaplerosis for TCA → biosynthetic intermediates + energy; also: Gln → nitrogen donor for purine/pyrimidine synthesis + amino acid synthesis [transamination] + glutathione [via Glu → Gly + Glu + Cys → GSH] + NADPH [via malic enzyme: malate → pyruvate + NADPH]); CB-839 (telaglenastat): glutaminase inhibitor in clinical trials for cancer; KIDNEY: Gln → [glutaminase] → Glu → NH₃; renal ammoniagenesis is critical for acid-base balance (NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ → excreted → net acid excretion); ↑in chronic metabolic acidosis

Leucine: Leu is the most potent amino acid activator of mTORC1 (→ ↑protein synthesis, ↑cell growth); Leu is important for muscle protein synthesis signaling; Leu is also a ketogenic amino acid (→ acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA); but Leu is NOT the primary fuel for enterocytes/lymphocytes/tumor cells
Aspartate: Asp is involved in the urea cycle (aspartate + citrulline → argininosuccinate), malate-aspartate shuttle, and purine synthesis; but Asp is NOT the major fuel for rapidly dividing cells
explanation: Glutamine metabolism — inter-organ relationships: MUSCLE: largest Gln pool; synthesizes Gln from Glu + NH₃ by glutamine synthetase (GS); releases Gln into blood (serves as non-toxic NH₃ carrier from muscle/brain to liver/kidney); GUT: major Gln consumer; enterocytes use Gln as primary fuel; produces citrulline + alanine + NH₃; LIVER: dual role — periportal hepatocytes: glutaminase → Glu + NH₃ → NH₃ enters urea cycle; perivenous hepatocytes: GS → Gln synthesis (scavenges remaining NH₃ that escaped urea cycle → safety net); KIDNEY: glutaminase → NH₃ production for acid-base regulation; ↑in acidosis (↑glutaminase expression → ↑NH₃ → ↑NH₄⁺ excretion → ↑net acid excretion); BRAIN: Glu (excitatory NT) released → taken up by astrocytes → [GS] → Gln → transported back to neurons → [glutaminase] → Glu (glutamate-glutamine cycle); this is critical because: (1) removes Glu from synapse (terminates signal, prevents excitotoxicity); (2) recycles Glu without losing carbon/nitrogen; hepatic encephalopathy: ↑NH₃ → astrocyte GS overloaded → ↑Gln osmotic effect → astrocyte swelling → cerebral edema.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the enzyme responsible for adding the poly-A tail to mRNA in eukaryotes?
options: DNA polymerase: DNA polymerase synthesizes DNA, not RNA; cannot add poly-A tail to mRNA

RNA polymerase II: RNA Pol II transcribes pre-mRNA (and also snRNA, miRNA genes); however, Pol II does NOT add the poly-A tail; Pol II transcribes through the polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA) → CPSF (cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor) + CstF (cleavage stimulation factor) recognize AAUAAA + downstream GU-rich element → cleavage → then PAP adds poly-A
