Poly-A polymerase (PAP): POLY-A POLYMERASE (PAP) adds the poly-A tail (approximately 200-250 adenosine residues) to the 3' end of pre-mRNA; process: (1) transcription by RNA Pol II proceeds past the polyadenylation signal (AAUAAA, the hexanucleotide signal ~10-30 nt upstream of cleavage site); (2) CPSF binds AAUAAA; CstF binds GU-rich/U-rich downstream element; (3) endonucleolytic CLEAVAGE (by CPSF-73) at the poly-A site (10-30 nt downstream of AAUAAA); (4) PAP adds ~200-250 A residues using ATP as substrate (template-INDEPENDENT; no DNA template needed); (5) PABPN1 (poly-A binding protein nuclear 1) binds nascent poly-A tail → stimulates PAP processivity and controls tail length (~250 A); functions of poly-A tail: (1) ↑mRNA STABILITY (protects 3' end from exonuclease degradation; PABPC1 [cytoplasmic PABP] binds poly-A → shields from deadenylases; mRNA decay often begins with deadenylation → decapping → 5'→3' degradation by XRN1); (2) ↑TRANSLATION EFFICIENCY (PABPC1 interacts with eIF4G [bound to eIF4E at 5' cap] → circularizes mRNA → ↑ribosome recycling → ↑translation); (3) EXPORT from nucleus (PABPN1 → facilitates mRNA export through nuclear pore); NOT all mRNAs are polyadenylated: replication-dependent HISTONE mRNAs end in a stem-loop (no poly-A tail; processed by U7 snRNP + SLBP)
Primase: primase (DnaG in bacteria; part of DNA pol α/primase complex in eukaryotes) synthesizes short RNA primers for DNA replication; does NOT add poly-A tail
explanation: mRNA processing in eukaryotes — the three co-/post-transcriptional modifications: (1) 5' CAPPING: occurs co-transcriptionally (when nascent mRNA is ~20-30 nt); mechanism: RNA triphosphatase removes terminal γ-phosphate → guanylyltransferase adds GMP (5'-5' triphosphate linkage, inverted) → cap methyltransferase adds methyl group to N7 of guanine → m7GpppN (Cap-0); further methylation: 2'-O-methylation of first nucleotide (Cap-1) and second (Cap-2); functions: ↑stability (protects from 5' exonucleases), ↑translation initiation (recognized by eIF4E), ↑splicing of first intron, ↑nuclear export, recognition as 'self' (2'-O-methylation distinguishes host mRNA from viral RNA → innate immune evasion; used in mRNA vaccine design); (2) SPLICING: removal of introns + joining of exons; spliceosome (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 snRNPs); mechanism: (a) U1 snRNP binds 5' splice site (GU); U2 binds branch point (A); (b) U4/U5/U6 join → U6 displaces U1 at 5' SS; (c) first transesterification: 2'-OH of branch-point A attacks 5' SS → lariat intermediate; (d) second transesterification: 3' OH of upstream exon attacks 3' SS (AG) → exons joined + lariat intron released → debranched + degraded; alternative splicing: ↑proteome diversity; (3) 3' POLYADENYLATION: CPSF/CstF → cleavage → PAP → poly-A tail.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: In the urea cycle, which reaction occurs in the cytoplasm and combines citrulline with aspartate?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I: CPS I: NH₃ + CO₂ + 2 ATP → carbamoyl phosphate; occurs in MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX; rate-limiting step of urea cycle; does NOT combine citrulline with aspartate

Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC): OTC: carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline + Pi; occurs in MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX; citrulline exits mitochondria via ORNT1 transporter; does NOT combine citrulline with aspartate

Argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1): ASS1 catalyzes: citrulline + aspartate + ATP → argininosuccinate + AMP + PPi; this is the CYTOPLASMIC reaction that combines citrulline with aspartate; ASS1 links the urea cycle to the aspartate shuttle from the TCA cycle (OAA → aspartate via aspartate aminotransferase/GOT); the fumarate released later (by argininosuccinate lyase) feeds back into TCA cycle → the 'Krebs bicycle' (urea cycle and TCA cycle interconnected via aspartate/fumarate); ASS1 deficiency → citrullinemia type I: ↑↑citrulline in blood (massively elevated; highest citrulline levels of any urea cycle disorder) + ↑orotic acid (because ↑carbamoyl phosphate overflows into pyrimidine pathway: CP → [OTC overflow not relevant; actually CPS II is cytoplasmic — but the excess mitochondrial CP → ↑cytoplasmic CP contribution); hyperammonemia; NBS: ↑citrulline on tandem MS; treatment: nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate → hippurate pathway; sodium phenylbutyrate → phenylacetate → phenylacetylglutamine) + Arg supplementation + dietary protein restriction

Arginase: arginase: arginine → urea + ornithine; occurs in cytoplasm; final step of urea cycle; does NOT combine citrulline with aspartate; arginase deficiency → argininemia (↑Arg, spastic diplegia, relatively mild hyperammonemia)
explanation: Urea cycle — complete: MITOCHONDRIAL steps (2): (1) CPS I: NH₃ + CO₂ + 2ATP → carbamoyl phosphate (rate-limiting; activated by NAG [N-acetylglutamate, made by NAGS from Glu + acetyl-CoA]); (2) OTC: carbamoyl phosphate + ornithine → citrulline (exits to cytoplasm); CYTOPLASMIC steps (3): (3) ASS1: citrulline + aspartate + ATP → argininosuccinate; (4) ASL: argininosuccinate → arginine + fumarate; (5) arginase: arginine → ornithine (re-enters mitochondria) + UREA (excreted by kidneys); Net: NH₃ + CO₂ + aspartate + 3 ATP → urea + fumarate + 2 ADP + AMP + 4 Pi; UREA has TWO nitrogens: one from free NH₃ (via CPS I → carbamoyl phosphate) and one from ASPARTATE (via ASS1); UCD (urea cycle disorders): all → hyperammonemia; proximal defects (CPS I, OTC, NAGS) → ↓citrulline; OTC deficiency (X-linked, most common UCD) → ↑orotic acid (↑carbamoyl phosphate overflows to pyrimidine synthesis: CP + aspartate → [ATCase/CPS II pathway] → orotic acid); distal defects (ASS1, ASL, arginase) → ↑citrulline (ASS1) or ↑argininosuccinate (ASL) or ↑arginine (arginase).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) is caused by deficiency of iduronate-2-sulfatase and shows X-linked recessive inheritance?
options: MPS I (Hurler syndrome): MPS I = α-L-iduronidase deficiency; autosomal recessive; accumulation of dermatan sulfate + heparan sulfate; spectrum: Hurler (severe: coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, intellectual disability, skeletal dysplasia, death by ~10 yr), Hurler-Scheie (intermediate), Scheie (mild: corneal clouding, joint stiffness, normal intelligence); treatment: ERT (laronidase/Aldurazyme) + HSCT for severe form

Hunter syndrome (MPS II): HUNTER SYNDROME (MPS II) is caused by deficiency of IDURONATE-2-SULFATASE (IDS/I2S); it is the ONLY MPS with X-LINKED RECESSIVE inheritance (all other MPS types are autosomal recessive); accumulates dermatan sulfate + heparan sulfate (same as MPS I); clinical: similar to Hurler BUT: (1) NO corneal clouding (key distinguishing feature from MPS I; 'Hunters can see their prey'); (2) X-linked → almost exclusively males; (3) severe form: intellectual disability, coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal dysplasia (dysostosis multiplex), pebbly ivory-colored skin lesions (distinctive), aggressive behavior, death in teens; mild form: normal intelligence, survival to adulthood; IDS gene on Xq28; treatment: ERT (idursulfase/Elaprase); HSCT less effective for CNS disease in MPS II

MPS III (Sanfilippo syndrome): MPS III = 4 subtypes (A-D), each with a different enzyme deficiency (all involved in heparan sulfate degradation); autosomal recessive; primarily CNS disease (behavioral problems, intellectual decline, minimal somatic features); NOT X-linked

MPS IV (Morquio syndrome): MPS IV = keratan sulfate accumulation; Type A: N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase deficiency; Type B: β-galactosidase deficiency; autosomal recessive; severe skeletal dysplasia (short trunk dwarfism, odontoid hypoplasia → atlantoaxial instability, corneal clouding); normal intelligence; NOT X-linked
explanation: Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS) — summary: All are lysosomal storage diseases with defective GAG degradation → GAG accumulation → progressive multisystem disease; MPS I: α-L-iduronidase; DS+HS; AR; Hurler/Scheie; corneal clouding; MPS II: iduronate-2-sulfatase; DS+HS; X-LINKED (only one); Hunter; no corneal clouding; MPS III: various (A-D); HS only; AR; Sanfilippo; severe CNS, mild somatic; MPS IV: various; KS; AR; Morquio; severe skeletal, normal IQ; MPS VI: arylsulfatase B; DS; AR; Maroteaux-Lamy; like Hurler but normal IQ; MPS VII: β-glucuronidase; DS+HS+CS; AR; Sly; hydrops fetalis in severe form; Diagnosis: ↑urinary GAGs (screening) → specific enzyme assay in leukocytes/fibroblasts → genetic confirmation; Treatment: ERT available for MPS I, II, IVA, VI, VII; HSCT for severe MPS I (can cross BBB → some CNS benefit); gene therapy in trials.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of methemoglobinemia?
options: Iron in hemoglobin is in the Fe³⁺ (ferric) state, rendering it unable to bind oxygen: METHEMOGLOBINEMIA: hemoglobin iron is oxidized from Fe²⁺ (ferrous, normal) to Fe³⁺ (FERRIC) state → METHEMOGLOBIN (MetHb); Fe³⁺ CANNOT bind O₂ → that subunit is non-functional; additionally, the remaining Fe²⁺ subunits in the same tetramer have INCREASED O₂ affinity (left-shifted ODC) → poor O₂ release to tissues; result: FUNCTIONAL ANEMIA (↓O₂ delivery) despite normal Hb concentration and normal PaO₂ on ABG; clinical: CYANOSIS (MetHb >1.5 g/dL; ~10% MetHb; earlier than deoxyhemoglobin-based cyanosis which needs ~5 g/dL deoxyHb); chocolate-brown colored blood (does NOT turn red on exposure to O₂ — key bedside test); pulse oximetry reads ~85% regardless of actual SaO₂ (because pulse ox measures absorbance ratio at 660/940 nm; MetHb absorbs equally at both → ratio approaches 1.0 → reads ~85%); PaO₂ on ABG is NORMAL (O₂ dissolved in plasma is unaffected; the problem is Hb binding); causes: (1) congenital: cytochrome b5 reductase (diaphorase I/CYB5R3) deficiency (AR; type I: RBC only → cyanosis, benign; type II: all tissues → cyanosis + neurological deterioration); Hb M variants (AD; amino acid substitutions near heme → stabilize Fe³⁺); (2) acquired (much more common): oxidizing drugs/chemicals: DAPSONE (most common drug cause), nitrites/nitrates, local anesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine → topical/spray → rapid onset MetHb), sulfonamides, phenazopyridine, chloroquine, nitric oxide (therapeutic → MetHb at high doses); treatment: METHYLENE BLUE (methylthioninium chloride) 1-2 mg/kg IV; mechanism: methylene blue → [NADPH-MetHb reductase (diaphorase II), requires NADPH from PPP/G6PD] → leukomethylene blue (reduced) → donates electrons to MetHb → reduces Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺; CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency (↓NADPH → methylene blue cannot be reduced → ineffective + may worsen; methylene blue itself can cause oxidative hemolysis in G6PD def); alternatives in G6PD def: ascorbic acid (slow, weak), exchange transfusion, hyperbaric O₂

Iron is in the Fe²⁺ (ferrous) state with increased oxygen affinity: Fe²⁺ is the NORMAL functional state of Hb iron; while MetHb does cause ↑O₂ affinity in remaining functional subunits, the defining feature is that the oxidized Fe³⁺ heme CANNOT bind O₂ at all

Hemoglobin has an abnormal amino acid substitution like in sickle cell disease: sickle cell disease (HbS) involves a specific point mutation (β6 Glu→Val); methemoglobinemia involves OXIDATION of iron, not necessarily a structural mutation (though Hb M variants exist, acquired causes are much more common)

Hemoglobin is unstable and precipitates as Heinz bodies: Heinz bodies are denatured/precipitated globin chains seen in G6PD deficiency (oxidative stress → Hb denaturation) and unstable Hb variants; MetHb does not typically form Heinz bodies (unless concurrent oxidative hemolysis)
explanation: Hemoglobin oxygen binding — allosteric regulation: Normal Hb: T-state (tense, deoxy, low O₂ affinity) ⇌ R-state (relaxed, oxy, high O₂ affinity); cooperative binding → sigmoidal O₂ dissociation curve (ODC); P50 = PO₂ at 50% saturation (~26.6 mmHg); RIGHT SHIFT (↓O₂ affinity, ↑P50, ↑O₂ release to tissues): ↑CO₂ (Bohr effect: CO₂ → ↑H⁺ → protonation of His residues → stabilize T-state), ↑H⁺ (↓pH), ↑2,3-BPG (binds β-chain cavity in T-state → ↓R-state transition; ↑2,3-BPG in: anemia, high altitude, chronic hypoxia → adaptive: ↑O₂ delivery), ↑temperature; LEFT SHIFT (↑O₂ affinity, ↓P50, ↓O₂ release): ↓CO₂, ↓H⁺ (↑pH), ↓2,3-BPG, ↓temperature, CO binding (HbCO: CO affinity ~240× > O₂; CO on one subunit → remaining subunits ↑↑O₂ affinity → ↓↓O₂ release → tissue hypoxia; cherry-red skin; treatment: 100% O₂ ± hyperbaric), MetHb (↑O₂ affinity of remaining Fe²⁺ subunits), HbF (↓2,3-BPG binding because γ-chains lack His 143 → cannot bind 2,3-BPG as well → ↑O₂ affinity → facilitates O₂ transfer across placenta from maternal HbA).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the function of the signal recognition particle (SRP)?
options: SRP degrades misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum: protein degradation in the ER is handled by ERAD (ER-associated degradation: misfolded protein → retrotranslocated to cytoplasm → ubiquitinated → proteasome); SRP does NOT degrade proteins

SRP targets ribosome-nascent chain complexes to the ER membrane by recognizing the signal peptide: The SIGNAL RECOGNITION PARTICLE (SRP) is a ribonucleoprotein complex (6 proteins + 7SL RNA [7S RNA, ~300 nt]) that mediates co-translational protein targeting to the ER; mechanism: (1) ribosome begins translating mRNA in cytoplasm; (2) the N-terminal SIGNAL PEPTIDE (typically ~16-30 aa: hydrophobic core [~8-12 hydrophobic residues] flanked by a positively charged N-region and a polar C-region with the signal peptidase cleavage site) emerges from the ribosomal exit tunnel; (3) SRP (specifically SRP54 subunit/Ffh in bacteria) recognizes and binds the signal peptide → TRANSLATION PAUSE (SRP binding slows/arrests elongation → prevents premature folding of the nascent protein in cytoplasm); (4) SRP-ribosome-nascent chain complex → docks to SRP RECEPTOR (SR; heterodimer: SRα [docking subunit] + SRβ [membrane anchor]) on ER membrane; both SRP54 and SRα are GTPases → GTP binding promotes interaction, GTP hydrolysis releases SRP for recycling; (5) ribosome transferred to SEC61 TRANSLOCON (heterotrimeric channel: Sec61α [channel-forming], β, γ) → translation resumes → nascent polypeptide threaded through translocon into ER lumen (co-translational translocation); (6) SIGNAL PEPTIDASE (ER luminal side) cleaves signal peptide → removed; mature protein folds in ER lumen with help of BiP/GRP78 (Hsp70 family chaperone) + PDI (disulfide bond formation) + calnexin/calreticulin (glycoprotein folding quality control); proteins that use SRP pathway: secreted proteins, membrane proteins, lysosomal enzymes, ER-resident proteins
SRP removes introns from pre-mRNA: intron removal (splicing) is performed by the spliceosome (snRNPs: U1, U2, U4, U5, U6); SRP is a completely different complex involved in protein targeting

SRP catalyzes the formation of disulfide bonds in the ER lumen: disulfide bond formation is catalyzed by PDI (protein disulfide isomerase) and Ero1 (ER oxidoreductin 1); SRP does NOT form disulfide bonds
explanation: Protein sorting and targeting: (1) ER targeting (co-translational, SRP-dependent): signal peptide → SRP → SR → Sec61 translocon → ER lumen; for secreted, membrane, lysosomal proteins; (2) MITOCHONDRIAL targeting (post-translational): N-terminal amphipathic helix (presequence: positively charged, forms α-helix) → recognized by TOM (translocase of outer membrane) → TIM23 (inner membrane; for matrix proteins) or TIM22 (for inner membrane carriers); requires ΔΨ (membrane potential) + mtHsp70 (pulling motor); presequence cleaved by MPP (mitochondrial processing peptidase); (3) NUCLEAR targeting: NLS (nuclear localization signal: basic amino acid-rich, e.g., PKKKRKV of SV40) → importin α/β → nuclear pore complex (NPC) → nucleus; NES (nuclear export signal) → exportin/CRM1 → cytoplasm; Ran-GTP/GDP gradient drives directionality (Ran-GTP in nucleus → releases cargo from importin; Ran-GDP in cytoplasm); (4) PEROXISOMAL targeting: PTS1 (C-terminal SKL tripeptide, most common) → Pex5 receptor; PTS2 (N-terminal nonapeptide) → Pex7; peroxisomal biogenesis disorders: Zellweger syndrome (PEX gene mutations → ↓peroxisomes → ↑VLCFA, ↑phytanic acid, ↑pipecolic acid; craniofacial dysmorphia, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, seizures; fatal in infancy); (5) LYSOSOMAL targeting: mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) signal → M6P receptor in Golgi → clathrin-coated vesicles → late endosome → lysosome; I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II): GlcNAc-phosphotransferase deficiency → ↓M6P tagging → lysosomal enzymes secreted extracellularly instead of targeting to lysosomes → ↑serum lysosomal enzymes + inclusion bodies in cells.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following fatty acids is an essential omega-3 (ω-3) fatty acid that must be obtained from the diet?
options: Oleic acid: oleic acid (18:1 ω-9, cis-Δ9) is a monounsaturated fatty acid (MUFA); NOT essential — synthesized from stearic acid (18:0) by Δ9-desaturase (stearoyl-CoA desaturase/SCD1); abundant in olive oil; ω-9: double bond at C9 from methyl end

Alpha-linolenic acid (ALA): ALPHA-LINOLENIC ACID (ALA, 18:3 ω-3, all-cis Δ9,12,15) is an ESSENTIAL ω-3 fatty acid; humans LACK Δ12-desaturase and Δ15-desaturase → cannot introduce double bonds beyond Δ9 → cannot synthesize ω-3 or ω-6 fatty acids de novo → MUST obtain from diet; ALA (ω-3) and linoleic acid (LA, ω-6) are the two essential fatty acids; ALA sources: flaxseed oil, chia seeds, walnuts, canola oil, soybean oil; ALA can be converted (inefficiently, <5%) to longer-chain ω-3: ALA (18:3) → [Δ6-desaturase] → stearidonic acid (18:4) → [elongase] → 20:4 ω-3 → [Δ5-desaturase] → EPA (20:5 ω-3, eicosapentaenoic acid) → [elongase] → DPA (22:5 ω-3) → [elongase + Δ6-desaturase + β-oxidation: Sprecher pathway] → DHA (22:6 ω-3, docosahexaenoic acid); EPA: precursor to 3-series prostaglandins (PGI₃: antithrombotic; TXA₃: weak prothrombotic) + 5-series leukotrienes (LTB₅: weak chemotactic) → anti-inflammatory compared to ω-6-derived eicosanoids; also: resolvins (from EPA: E-series resolvins), protectins/neuroprotectin D1 (from DHA), maresins (from DHA) → specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs) → actively resolve inflammation; DHA: critical for brain (neuronal membranes: ~40% of brain PUFA), retina (photoreceptor outer segments: ~60% of retinal PUFA), and fetal development; fish oil supplements provide preformed EPA + DHA

Arachidonic acid: arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4 ω-6, all-cis Δ5,8,11,14) is a conditionally essential ω-6 fatty acid; can be synthesized from linoleic acid (LA, 18:2 ω-6: LA → [Δ6-desaturase] → GLA [18:3 ω-6] → [elongase] → DGLA [20:3 ω-6] → [Δ5-desaturase] → AA [20:4 ω-6]); AA is the major precursor for eicosanoids via COX (→ PGH₂ → prostaglandins, thromboxanes) and LOX (→ leukotrienes) pathways; NOT an ω-3 fatty acid
Palmitic acid: palmitic acid (16:0) is a saturated fatty acid; the primary product of de novo fatty acid synthesis (FAS); NOT essential, NOT unsaturated
explanation: Essential fatty acids and eicosanoid synthesis: ESSENTIAL FAs: linoleic acid (LA, 18:2 ω-6; sources: vegetable oils [sunflower, safflower, corn, soybean]) and α-linolenic acid (ALA, 18:3 ω-3; sources: flaxseed, chia, walnuts); essential because humans lack Δ12 and Δ15 desaturases; ω-6 PATHWAY: LA → GLA → DGLA → AA (20:4 ω-6); AA → COX-1/COX-2 → PGH₂ → PGE₂/PGI₂ [prostacyclin]/TXA₂ [thromboxane]; AA → 5-LOX → LTA₄ → LTB₄ (neutrophil chemotaxis) / LTC₄/LTD₄/LTE₄ (SRS-A: bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability → asthma); AA → 15-LOX → lipoxins (anti-inflammatory → resolution); PHARMACOLOGY: NSAIDs inhibit COX (aspirin: irreversible acetylation of COX-1 Ser530; low-dose → ↓TXA₂ [platelets, no COX resynthesis] → antiplatelet; higher dose → ↓PGI₂ + PGE₂ → anti-inflammatory + antipyretic + analgesic); COX-2 selective (celecoxib): ↓GI toxicity but ↑CV risk (↓PGI₂ without ↓TXA₂ → prothrombotic imbalance); corticosteroids: ↑lipocortin/annexin A1 → ↓PLA₂ → ↓AA release → ↓ALL eicosanoids + leukotrienes; zileuton: 5-LOX inhibitor; montelukast: CysLT₁ receptor antagonist (asthma).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following best describes the Cori cycle?
options: Cycling of glucose and amino acids between liver and muscle: the glucose-ALANINE cycle (Cahill cycle) involves Ala transfer from muscle to liver (muscle: pyruvate + amino group → [ALT] → Ala → blood → liver: Ala → [ALT] → pyruvate → gluconeogenesis → glucose; + NH₃ → urea cycle); this is NOT the Cori cycle

Cycling of glucose and lactate between liver and muscle: The CORI CYCLE (named after Carl and Gerty Cori, Nobel 1947): (1) MUSCLE (especially during anaerobic exercise/O₂ debt): glucose → [glycolysis] → pyruvate → [LDH] → LACTATE + NAD⁺ (regenerates NAD⁺ to sustain glycolysis when O₂ limited); (2) lactate released from muscle into BLOOD; (3) LIVER takes up lactate → [LDH] → pyruvate → [GLUCONEOGENESIS] → glucose; (4) glucose released back to BLOOD → returns to muscle; NET EFFECT: energy burden shifted from muscle to liver; muscle: anaerobic glycolysis (2 ATP per glucose); liver: gluconeogenesis (costs 6 ATP equivalents per glucose); so the Cori cycle is energy-expensive overall (costs 4 ATP per cycle net; the 6 ATP of GNG minus 2 ATP of glycolysis); this is sustainable because liver has abundant mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation (using fatty acid β-oxidation → ATP → fuels GNG); clinical relevance: (1) exercise physiology (lactate from sprinting muscles → liver → glucose recycling); (2) RBC metabolism (RBCs: obligate glycolysis → lactate → liver); (3) cancer (Warburg effect: tumor glycolysis → ↑lactate → liver GNG → glucose → tumor → CORI CYCLE in cancer cachexia: tumor causes ↑metabolic futile cycling → contributes to weight loss/wasting)

Cycling of ketone bodies between liver and brain: ketone body production (ketogenesis: liver mitochondria: acetyl-CoA → acetoacetate + β-hydroxybutyrate) and utilization (brain, heart, muscle: β-OHB → acetoacetate → acetoacetyl-CoA → acetyl-CoA → TCA) is ketone body metabolism, NOT the Cori cycle
Cycling of urea between liver and kidney: urea synthesized in liver → blood → kidney → excreted in urine; NOT the Cori cycle
explanation: Metabolic cycles connecting organs: (1) CORI CYCLE: muscle lactate → liver glucose (glucose-lactate cycle); (2) GLUCOSE-ALANINE CYCLE (CAHILL CYCLE): muscle Ala → liver glucose + urea; purpose: transports NH₃ from muscle to liver in non-toxic form (as Ala) + provides gluconeogenic substrate; (3) GAMMA-GLUTAMYL CYCLE: extracellular glutathione (GSH) → [γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT), on cell surface] → γ-glutamyl-amino acid + cysteinylglycine → intracellular: γ-glutamyl-amino acid → [γ-glutamyl cyclotransferase] → 5-oxoproline + amino acid; 5-oxoproline → [5-oxoprolinase, ATP] → glutamate; GSH resynthesized from Glu + Cys + Gly by γ-GCS + GSH synthetase; function: amino acid transport across membranes (especially kidney, intestine); GGT: elevated in biliary obstruction, alcoholic liver disease (induced by alcohol); clinical: 5-oxoprolinase deficiency → 5-oxoprolinuria (metabolic acidosis with ↑anion gap from 5-oxoproline/pyroglutamic acid; also seen with chronic acetaminophen use → ↓GSH → ↑5-oxoproline).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which immunoglobulin is the first to be produced in a primary immune response?
options: IgG: IgG is the most abundant serum Ig (~75-80%); it is the predominant Ig in the SECONDARY (anamnestic) immune response (class switching: IgM → IgG); IgG does increase in primary response but LATER (after class switching, ~2 weeks); IgG: crosses placenta (only Ig that does; via neonatal FcRn receptor → passive immunity to fetus/newborn), opsonization (Fc binds FcγR on phagocytes), complement activation (classical pathway: IgG1, IgG3 > IgG2; IgG4 does NOT activate complement), ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity: NK cells bind via FcγRIIIa/CD16), longest half-life (~23 days for IgG1)

IgM: IgM is the FIRST immunoglobulin produced in a PRIMARY immune response; IgM is also the first Ig expressed on B cell surface during B cell development (surface IgM = BCR on naive B cells); serum IgM is a PENTAMER (5 monomers joined by J chain + disulfide bonds → 10 antigen-binding sites [highest VALENCY] → excellent at agglutination and complement activation); IgM is the most efficient complement activator (just ONE IgM pentamer can activate C1q → classical pathway; needs 2 IgG molecules in close proximity for same); IgM is confined to INTRAVASCULAR space (too large [~900 kDa] to cross into tissues easily); IgM → IgG/IgA/IgE class switching occurs later (driven by T cell help: CD40L-CD40 interaction + cytokines [IL-4 → IgE; IL-5 → IgA; IFN-γ → IgG1/IgG3 in humans]); class switch recombination (CSR) changes constant region (CH) but NOT variable region → same antigen specificity, different effector function; AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase) is essential for CSR + somatic hypermutation; AID deficiency → hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (AR; ↑IgM, ↓IgG/IgA/IgE); CD40L deficiency → hyper-IgM syndrome type 1 (X-linked; most common; ↑IgM + ↓IgG/IgA/IgE + opportunistic infections [Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium])

IgA: IgA is the predominant Ig in MUCOSAL secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk [colostrum], GI/respiratory secretions); secretory IgA (sIgA): dimer (2 monomers + J chain + secretory component [from poly-Ig receptor on epithelial cells; protects from proteolysis]); IgA does NOT activate complement via classical pathway (can activate via alternative/lectin); IgA is NOT the first Ig in primary response

IgE: IgE is the least abundant serum Ig; involved in type I hypersensitivity (allergic reactions: IgE → FcεRI on mast cells/basophils → cross-linking by allergen → degranulation → histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins) and anti-helminth immunity; IgE is NOT the first Ig in primary response
explanation: Immunoglobulin classes — summary: IgG: 75-80% serum; monomer; crosses placenta; opsonization, complement (classical), ADCC; 4 subclasses; longest t½; secondary response; IgM: 5-10%; pentamer (J chain); first in primary response; best complement activator; intravascular; BCR on naive B cells; IgA: 10-15% serum; major mucosal Ig; dimer in secretions (secretory piece); breast milk (passive immunity to neonate GI); IgA nephropathy (Berger disease: mesangial IgA deposits); IgE: <0.01%; monomer; type I hypersensitivity (allergy/anaphylaxis); anti-helminth; binds FcεRI (mast cells/basophils); omalizumab (anti-IgE mAb for severe asthma); IgD: <1%; monomer; co-expressed with IgM on naive B cells (BCR); function mostly unknown (may activate basophils/innate immunity); B cell development: pro-B (no Ig) → pre-B (cytoplasmic μ heavy chain + surrogate light chain) → immature B (surface IgM) → mature naive B (surface IgM + IgD) → activation by antigen + T cell help → plasma cells (secrete Ab) or memory B cells; negative selection: immature B cells with self-reactive BCR → receptor editing (change light chain) or clonal deletion (apoptosis) or anergy → central tolerance.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is caused by a defect in which DNA repair mechanism?
options: Mismatch repair (MMR): MMR corrects base-base mismatches and insertion/deletion loops that escape proofreading during replication; key proteins: MSH2/MSH6 (MutSα: recognizes mismatches) or MSH2/MSH3 (MutSβ: recognizes larger loops); MLH1/PMS2 (MutLα: endonuclease); then exonuclease digestion + resynthesis; defective MMR → Lynch syndrome (HNPCC: hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer; AD; ↑CRC [right-sided], endometrial, ovarian, urinary tract cancers; microsatellite instability [MSI-H]; immunohistochemistry: loss of MMR protein expression); NOT the repair mechanism defective in XP

Nucleotide excision repair (NER): XERODERMA PIGMENTOSUM is caused by defects in NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR (NER); NER repairs BULKY, HELIX-DISTORTING lesions: UV-induced thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers [CPDs] and 6-4 photoproducts [6-4 PPs]) and bulky chemical adducts (benzo[a]pyrene, cisplatin-DNA crosslinks); two sub-pathways: (1) GG-NER (global genome NER): scans entire genome; damage recognized by XPC-RAD23B complex (senses helix distortion); (2) TC-NER (transcription-coupled NER): repairs lesions on actively transcribed strand; damage recognized when RNA Pol II stalls at lesion → CSA (ERCC8) + CSB (ERCC6) recruited; subsequent steps shared: TFIIH complex (contains XPB [helicase, 3'→5'] + XPD [helicase, 5'→3']) → unwinds ~30 nt around lesion → XPA (verifies damage) + RPA (stabilizes ssDNA) → XPF-ERCC1 (endonuclease, cuts 5' side) + XPG (endonuclease, cuts 3' side) → excises ~24-32 nt oligonucleotide containing damage → DNA Pol δ/ε + PCNA fill gap → ligase seals; XP: 8 complementation groups (XPA-XPG + XP variant [XPV: DNA pol η deficiency → cannot perform translesion synthesis past CPDs]); clinical: extreme sun sensitivity (sunburn with minimal exposure), pigmentary changes (freckle-like), >1000-fold ↑ risk of skin cancers (BCC, SCC, melanoma) in sun-exposed areas, ↑internal cancers; neurodegeneration (some subtypes: XPA, XPD); ~30% have neurological involvement; DeSanctis-Cacchione syndrome: XP + severe neurodegeneration + dwarfism + gonadal hypoplasia

Base excision repair (BER): BER repairs small, non-helix-distorting lesions: oxidized bases (8-oxoguanine → OGG1 glycosylase), deaminated bases (uracil from cytosine deamination → UNG/uracil-DNA glycosylase), alkylated bases, AP sites (abasic); mechanism: DNA glycosylase recognizes + removes damaged base (cleaves N-glycosidic bond → AP site) → APE1 (AP endonuclease) → nicks backbone → DNA Pol β fills 1-nt gap (short-patch) or Pol δ/ε fills 2-10 nt (long-patch) → ligase seals; NOT defective in XP

Homologous recombination: HR repairs DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) using sister chromatid as template (S/G2 phase); MRN complex → ATM → end resection → RPA → BRCA2 loads RAD51 → strand invasion → D-loop → repair; BRCA1/BRCA2 deficiency → ↓HR → ↑breast/ovarian cancer; NOT defective in XP
explanation: DNA repair mechanisms — comprehensive: (1) DIRECT REVERSAL: O6-methylguanine → [MGMT/AGT: O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase → removes methyl group; suicide enzyme — irreversibly inactivated after one use]; photoreactivation (not in humans; bacteria/plants: photolyase + visible light → directly reverses CPDs); (2) BER: small base lesions (oxidation, deamination, alkylation); glycosylases → AP site → APE1 → Pol β → ligase; (3) NER: bulky lesions (UV dimers, chemical adducts); XPC/CSA/CSB → TFIIH → XPA/RPA → XPF+XPG → Pol δ/ε → ligase; defective in XP, Cockayne syndrome (CSA/CSB: TC-NER defect → growth failure, photosensitivity [no cancer], neurodegeneration), trichothiodystrophy (XPD/TFIIH: brittle hair [tiger-tail under polarized light], ichthyosis, photosensitivity, short stature); (4) MMR: replication errors; MutSα/β → MutLα → exonuclease → resynthesis; defective in Lynch syndrome; (5) HR: DSBs in S/G2; error-free; BRCA1/2, RAD51; (6) NHEJ: DSBs in G1; error-prone (may lose nucleotides); Ku70/Ku80 → DNA-PKcs → Artemis → XRCC4/Ligase IV; defective: SCID (Artemis mutations); (7) Translesion synthesis (TLS): specialized polymerases (Pol η, ι, κ, ζ, Rev1) bypass lesions; error-prone but allows replication to continue; XP variant: Pol η deficiency.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which coenzyme is specifically required by aminotransferases (transaminases)?
options: NAD⁺: NAD⁺ (niacin/B₃ derivative) is a coenzyme for dehydrogenases (LDH, MDH, PDC, OGDH, etc.); NOT specifically required by aminotransferases

Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP): PYRIDOXAL 5'-PHOSPHATE (PLP), the active form of vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine), is the coenzyme specifically required by AMINOTRANSFERASES (transaminases); mechanism: PLP binds to a Lys residue in the enzyme active site via a Schiff base (internal aldimine: PLP-Lys); substrate amino acid displaces Lys → external aldimine (PLP-amino acid Schiff base) → α-amino group transferred to PLP → pyridoxamine phosphate (PMP) + α-keto acid; PMP then transfers amino group to a different α-keto acid → new amino acid + PLP regenerated (ping-pong/double displacement mechanism); KEY TRANSAMINASES: (1) ALT (alanine aminotransferase/GPT): Ala + α-KG ⇌ pyruvate + Glu; primarily in LIVER cytoplasm → most specific liver enzyme; ALT > AST → hepatocellular disease (hepatitis, NAFLD); (2) AST (aspartate aminotransferase/GOT): Asp + α-KG ⇌ OAA + Glu; in liver (cytoplasm + mitochondria), heart, muscle, RBCs; AST > ALT → alcoholic hepatitis (De Ritis ratio >2; alcohol damages mitochondria → releases mitochondrial AST + ↓ALT synthesis due to B₆ deficiency in alcoholics), cirrhosis, muscle injury, MI; Both ALT and AST use α-KETOGLUTARATE as amino group acceptor → produce GLUTAMATE (Glu is the 'amino group collector'); Glu then → [GDH: glutamate dehydrogenase, NAD⁺/NADP⁺] → α-KG + NH₃ (oxidative deamination; this is how amino groups ultimately enter the urea cycle as free NH₃)

FAD: FAD (riboflavin/B₂ derivative) is a coenzyme for oxidases and dehydrogenases (succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, xanthine oxidase, MTHFR, etc.); NOT specifically for aminotransferases
Thiamine pyrophosphate: TPP (thiamine/B₁) is coenzyme for α-keto acid dehydrogenases and transketolase; NOT for aminotransferases
explanation: PLP (vitamin B₆)-dependent enzymes — comprehensive list: (1) AMINOTRANSFERASES (ALT, AST, and many others): amino group transfer; (2) DECARBOXYLASES: AADC (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase: DOPA→DA, 5-HTP→5-HT), GAD (glutamate→GABA), histidine decarboxylase (His→histamine), ODC uses PLP (ornithine→putrescine for polyamine synthesis); (3) ALA SYNTHASE (δ-aminolevulinate synthase): rate-limiting step of heme synthesis (succinyl-CoA + glycine → ALA); (4) CYSTATHIONINE β-SYNTHASE (CBS): Hcy + Ser → cystathionine (transsulfuration); deficiency → homocystinuria; (5) CYSTATHIONASE: cystathionine → Cys + α-ketobutyrate; (6) SERINE HYDROXYMETHYLTRANSFERASE (SHMT): Ser ⇌ Gly + CH₂-THF; (7) GLYCOGEN PHOSPHORYLASE: glycogenolysis (glycogen → G1P); PLP as acid-base catalyst; (8) SPHINGOSINE SYNTHESIS: serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT): palmitoyl-CoA + Ser → 3-ketosphinganine; B₆ DEFICIENCY: peripheral neuropathy (↓sphingomyelin?), microcytic sideroblastic anemia (↓ALA synthase → ↓heme → ↓Hb + iron accumulation in mitochondria → ringed sideroblasts), seizures in infants (↓GAD → ↓GABA → excitotoxicity), dermatitis, glossitis; caused by: isoniazid (INH: reacts with PLP → depleted; always co-prescribe pyridoxine with INH), oral contraceptives, alcohol, penicillamine.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following conditions is caused by a trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene?
options: Huntington disease: HD is caused by CAG repeat expansion in the HUNTINGTIN (HTT) gene on chromosome 4p16.3; >36 repeats → polyglutamine expansion → protein aggregation → caudate/putamen degeneration → chorea + psychiatric symptoms + dementia; anticipation (↑repeat length in successive generations, especially paternal)

Fragile X syndrome: FRAGILE X SYNDROME is caused by CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the 5'-UTR of the FMR1 (Fragile X Mental Retardation 1) gene on Xq27.3; normal: 5-44 repeats; premutation: 55-200 repeats (carriers: females may be asymptomatic or mildly affected; males: FXTAS [Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome, >50 years: cerebellar ataxia, intention tremor, parkinsonism, cognitive decline; RNA toxic gain-of-function: ↑FMR1 mRNA but ↓FMRP]; females with premutation: FXPOI [premature ovarian insufficiency, ~20%]); FULL MUTATION: >200 repeats → HYPERMETHYLATION of CGG repeats and FMR1 promoter → transcriptional SILENCING → ↓↓ or absent FMRP (Fragile X Mental Retardation Protein); FMRP function: RNA-binding protein that regulates synaptic translation (FMRP → represses translation of ~800 mRNAs at synapses → when absent: ↑unregulated translation → ↑mGluR5 signaling → immature dendritic spines [long, thin] → impaired synaptic plasticity → intellectual disability); clinical: MOST COMMON INHERITED cause of intellectual disability (Down syndrome is most common overall but is usually de novo, not inherited); males (full mutation): moderate-to-severe ID, long face, prominent ears, large jaw (macrognathia), macroorchidism (post-pubertal; ↑testicular volume, may be >25 mL; mechanism unclear), ADHD, autism spectrum (30%), joint hypermobility, mitral valve prolapse; females (full mutation): ~50% have some cognitive impairment (variable due to X-inactivation); GENETICS: X-linked dominant with reduced penetrance in females; premutation → full mutation ONLY during MATERNAL transmission (oogenesis: CGG expansion → >200; sperm: premutation contracts or stays stable → father cannot transmit full mutation); anticipation: ↑repeats across generations; Sherman paradox: grandfather (premutation carrier, unaffected) → daughter (premutation carrier, usually unaffected) → grandson (full mutation, affected); diagnosis: Southern blot or PCR for CGG repeat number + methylation analysis

Myotonic dystrophy type 1: DM1 is caused by CTG repeat expansion in the 3'-UTR of the DMPK gene on chr 19q13.3; RNA toxic gain-of-function (expanded CUG repeats → MBNL1 sequestration → aberrant splicing); anticipation; most common adult muscular dystrophy; myotonia + distal weakness + cataracts + cardiac conduction defects + insulin resistance; NOT FMR1

Friedreich ataxia: FA is caused by GAA repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN (frataxin) gene on chr 9q21; autosomal RECESSIVE (only trinucleotide repeat disorder that is AR); ↓frataxin → ↓iron-sulfur cluster assembly → ↓ETC function + ↑mitochondrial iron → oxidative damage; progressive ataxia (cerebellar + sensory), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (common cause of death), diabetes, scoliosis, pes cavus; NOT FMR1
explanation: Trinucleotide repeat disorders — high-yield: CODING (polyglutamine, CAG): Huntington (HTT, chr 4, caudate), spinobulbar muscular atrophy/Kennedy (AR gene, X-linked, androgen receptor polyQ), spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA1-3,6,7,17: various genes); polyQ → protein aggregation → neurodegeneration; anticipation (paternal in HD: spermatogenesis favors expansion); NON-CODING: Fragile X (CGG in 5'UTR of FMR1, X; methylation → silencing; maternal transmission for full), myotonic dystrophy 1 (CTG in 3'UTR of DMPK, chr 19; RNA toxicity; MBNL1 sequestered → aberrant splicing of ClC-1 → myotonia, insulin receptor → insulin resistance, cardiac troponin T → cardiomyopathy; congenital form: severe, maternal), myotonic dystrophy 2 (CCTG in CNBP/ZNF9, chr 3), Friedreich ataxia (GAA in intron 1 of FXN, chr 9; AR ONLY trinucleotide repeat that is recessive; frataxin ↓ → Fe-S cluster deficit → mitochondrial dysfunction); ANTICIPATION: tendency for repeat length to increase across generations → earlier onset + more severe disease; genetic mechanism: DNA polymerase slippage during replication → loop-out → expansion.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following enzymes is inhibited by fluoride, as seen when sodium fluoride is added to blood collection tubes to prevent glycolysis?
options: Hexokinase: hexokinase (HK) catalyzes glucose + ATP → G6P + ADP (first step of glycolysis); HK is inhibited by its product G6P (feedback inhibition); fluoride does NOT directly inhibit hexokinase

Enolase: ENOLASE is the enzyme inhibited by FLUORIDE; enolase catalyzes: 2-phosphoglycerate (2-PG) → phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) + H₂O (penultimate step of glycolysis); fluoride inhibits enolase by forming a magnesium-fluorophosphate complex (Mg²⁺-F⁻-PO₄³⁻) that binds the active site and blocks the dehydration reaction; this is why SODIUM FLUORIDE (NaF) is added to blood collection tubes (gray-top tubes) for glucose measurement: NaF inhibits enolase → blocks glycolysis in the blood sample → prevents glucose consumption by RBCs/WBCs → glucose level remains stable; without NaF, blood glucose decreases ~5-7% per hour at room temperature (RBCs and WBCs continue glycolysis ex vivo → ↓glucose → falsely low result); NaF tubes also contain potassium oxalate (anticoagulant); note: NaF takes ~1-2 hours to fully inhibit glycolysis (not immediate) → for most accurate glucose, process sample promptly or use NaF tube + refrigerate; other enolase facts: enolase isoforms are tissue-specific biomarkers: NSE (neuron-specific enolase, γγ): ↑ in small cell lung cancer (SCLC), neuroblastoma, neuroendocrine tumors; also ↑ after neuronal injury (stroke, TBI)
Phosphofructokinase-1: PFK-1 catalyzes F6P + ATP → F1,6BP + ADP (committed/rate-limiting step of glycolysis); PFK-1 is regulated by many allosteric effectors but NOT directly inhibited by fluoride

Pyruvate kinase: PK catalyzes PEP + ADP → pyruvate + ATP (last step of glycolysis); PK is regulated allosterically (activated by F1,6BP [feed-forward activation]) but NOT the target of fluoride inhibition
explanation: Glycolysis — all 10 steps with key regulatory points: (1) Glucose → [HK/GK] → G6P (irreversible; HK: low Km, inhibited by G6P; GK: high Km, NOT inhibited by G6P → liver/pancreatic β-cells); (2) G6P → [PGI] → F6P; (3) F6P → [PFK-1, RATE-LIMITING] → F1,6BP (irreversible; allosteric: ↑ by AMP, F2,6BP [most potent activator], ↓ by ATP, citrate); (4) F1,6BP → [aldolase] → DHAP + G3P; (5) DHAP → [TPI] → G3P; (6) G3P → [G3PDH, NAD⁺] → 1,3-BPG (substrate-level phosphorylation setup); (7) 1,3-BPG → [PGK] → 3-PG + ATP; (8) 3-PG → [PGM] → 2-PG; (9) 2-PG → [ENOLASE, inhibited by fluoride] → PEP; (10) PEP → [PK] → pyruvate + ATP (irreversible; activated by F1,6BP; inhibited by ATP, Ala; PK deficiency → chronic hemolytic anemia [↓ATP in RBCs → ↓Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → crenated cells → splenic sequestration → hemolysis; echinocytes]); NET: glucose + 2 NAD⁺ + 2 ADP + 2 Pi → 2 pyruvate + 2 NADH + 2 ATP + 2 H₂O; 3 irreversible steps (HK, PFK-1, PK) are bypassed in gluconeogenesis by different enzymes (G6Pase, F1,6BPase, PEP carboxykinase + PC).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the most common inherited hypercoagulable state (thrombophilia)?
options: Antithrombin III deficiency: AT-III deficiency → ↓heparin cofactor → ↓inhibition of thrombin + FXa → ↑thrombosis; autosomal dominant; prevalence ~1:2000-5000; important but NOT the most common inherited thrombophilia

Factor V Leiden: FACTOR V LEIDEN is the MOST COMMON inherited thrombophilia; prevalence: ~5% of Caucasians (heterozygous); caused by a point mutation in the F5 gene: Arg506Gln (R506Q) → substitution at the APC cleavage site; MECHANISM: Activated Protein C (APC) normally cleaves and inactivates Factor Va (at Arg506, Arg306, Arg679) → this is a natural anticoagulant mechanism; Factor V Leiden: Arg506→Gln → APC CANNOT cleave at this site → Factor Va remains active longer → ↑thrombin generation → ↑risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE: DVT, PE); this is called APC RESISTANCE (the screening test: measure clotting time with and without added APC; FVL → less prolongation of aPTT when APC is added → ratio <2); heterozygotes: 3-8× ↑VTE risk; homozygotes: 50-80× ↑VTE risk; FVL increases risk of VENOUS thrombosis (DVT/PE) but NOT arterial thrombosis (MI/stroke); risk is synergistic with other factors: oral contraceptives (OCPs × FVL heterozygous = ~35× ↑VTE risk; this is why some advocate screening before OCP use in populations with high FVL prevalence), pregnancy, surgery, immobilization, obesity; diagnosis: APC resistance assay (functional) → confirmatory: factor V Leiden mutation by PCR; treatment: anticoagulation for acute VTE (same as general population: heparin → warfarin/DOACs); prophylaxis: situational (during high-risk periods)

Protein C deficiency: Protein C deficiency → ↓APC → ↓inactivation of FVa/FVIIIa → ↑thrombosis; AD; prevalence ~1:200-500 (but low penetrance → many asymptomatic); homozygous → neonatal purpura fulminans (massive DIC-like thrombosis, often fatal); warfarin-induced skin necrosis: protein C has shortest t½ among vitamin K-dependent factors (~8h) → early warfarin treatment drops protein C faster than procoagulant factors → transient hypercoagulable state → microthrombi in skin → necrosis (especially in protein C-deficient patients); prevent by bridging with heparin; NOT the most common thrombophilia
Prothrombin G20210A mutation: prothrombin gene mutation (F2 G20210A) → ↑prothrombin levels → ↑thrombin → ↑VTE; 2nd most common inherited thrombophilia (~2% Caucasians); but LESS common than FVL
explanation: Coagulation and anticoagulant pathways — natural anticoagulants: (1) ANTITHROMBIN III (AT-III/SERPINC1): serine protease inhibitor (serpin); inhibits thrombin (IIa), FXa, IXa, XIa, XIIa; action GREATLY enhanced by HEPARIN (heparin binds AT → conformational change → ↑1000-fold inhibition; unfractionated heparin [UFH]: enhances anti-IIa + anti-Xa; LMWH [enoxaparin, dalteparin]: primarily anti-Xa [shorter chains cannot bridge AT to thrombin for anti-IIa]); (2) PROTEIN C / PROTEIN S pathway: thrombin binds THROMBOMODULIN (endothelial surface) → thrombin-TM complex activates PROTEIN C → APC (activated protein C); APC + PROTEIN S (cofactor) → cleaves and inactivates FVa + FVIIIa; protein C + S are vitamin K-dependent (like II, VII, IX, X → 'factors 1972' or '2, 7, 9, 10'); (3) TFPI (tissue factor pathway inhibitor): inhibits TF-FVIIa complex + FXa; released from endothelium by heparin; Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist → ↓γ-carboxylation of Glu residues → ↓functional II, VII, IX, X, protein C, protein S; monitored by PT/INR (extrinsic pathway most sensitive because FVII has shortest t½ ~6h); DOACs: rivaroxaban/apixaban (direct FXa inhibitors), dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor); no routine monitoring needed.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the primary buffer system in the intracellular fluid?
options: Bicarbonate buffer system: the bicarbonate/CO₂ system is the most important EXTRACELLULAR (blood/plasma) buffer; CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; effective because it is an open system (lungs regulate CO₂, kidneys regulate HCO₃⁻); the bicarbonate system is not the primary intracellular buffer (intracellular CO₂ is relatively low and bicarbonate is less abundant intracellularly)

Phosphate buffer system: The PHOSPHATE buffer system (H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻) is the primary INTRACELLULAR buffer; pKa = 6.8 → very close to intracellular pH (~7.0-7.2) → operates at maximum buffering capacity (a buffer is most effective within ±1 pH unit of its pKa); intracellular phosphate concentration is relatively high (~75 mM total Pi in cells vs ~1 mM in plasma) → significant buffering capacity; in addition to inorganic phosphate, organic phosphates (ATP, ADP, glucose-6-phosphate, 2,3-BPG) contribute to intracellular buffering; the phosphate buffer is also important in URINE: renal tubular H⁺ secretion → H⁺ + HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻ → this is the 'TITRATABLE ACIDITY' component of urinary acid excretion; in plasma/ECF: phosphate buffer has limited importance because plasma [Pi] is low (~1 mM) → low buffering capacity; so phosphate = excellent intracellular + urinary buffer; bicarbonate = excellent extracellular buffer

Hemoglobin buffer: hemoglobin is an important buffer IN RED BLOOD CELLS specifically (not a general intracellular buffer); deoxyHb is a better buffer than oxyHb (imidazole groups of His residues: ↓O₂ → ↑pKa → ↑proton buffering capacity); Hb buffers ~60-70% of H⁺ produced from CO₂ in RBCs
Ammonia buffer: NH₃/NH₄⁺ (pKa 9.2) acts as a buffer primarily in the KIDNEY (renal ammoniagenesis → NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ → excreted); not the primary intracellular buffer in most cells
explanation: Acid-base physiology — integrated: pH = -log[H⁺]; normal arterial pH: 7.35-7.45; [H⁺] ~40 nmol/L (tightly regulated; even small deviations → enzyme dysfunction); BUFFER SYSTEMS: (1) bicarbonate/CO₂ (primary ECF; open system; controlled by lungs + kidneys); (2) phosphate (primary ICF; also urinary titratable acidity); (3) proteins (hemoglobin in RBCs; albumin in plasma; intracellular proteins); RESPIRATORY REGULATION: chemoreceptors (central: medullary, sense ↑PCO₂ via ↑H⁺ in CSF [CO₂ crosses BBB → CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺]; peripheral: carotid body [CN IX], aortic body [CN X], sense ↓PO₂ [primary], ↑PCO₂, ↓pH) → adjust ventilation; response time: MINUTES; RENAL REGULATION: (1) HCO₃⁻ reabsorption (proximal tubule: 80-85%; Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger [NHE3] → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O [carbonic anhydrase IV, luminal] → CO₂ enters cell → CA II → H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ [basolateral NBC1] + H⁺ [recycled]); (2) H⁺ secretion (intercalated cells type A: H⁺-ATPase [apical] + H⁺/K⁺-ATPase → secrete H⁺; Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger [AE1, basolateral] → new HCO₃⁻ to blood); (3) titratable acidity (H⁺ + HPO₄²⁻ → H₂PO₄⁻); (4) ammoniagenesis (Gln → NH₃ + Glu; NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ → excreted; ↑in chronic acidosis); response time: DAYS.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the action of insulin on glycogen metabolism?
options: Insulin activates glycogen phosphorylase, promoting glycogenolysis: glycogen phosphorylase (GP) is ACTIVATED by glucagon/epinephrine (via cAMP → PKA → phosphorylase kinase → GP-a [active, phosphorylated]); INSULIN does the OPPOSITE — insulin ↓GP activity

Insulin activates protein phosphatase 1, which dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase: INSULIN promotes GLYCOGENESIS (glycogen synthesis) by activating PROTEIN PHOSPHATASE 1 (PP1); mechanism: insulin signaling → IR (insulin receptor tyrosine kinase) → IRS → PI3K → PIP₃ → Akt/PKB → (1) Akt phosphorylates + INACTIVATES GSK3 (glycogen synthase kinase 3; GSK3 normally phosphorylates GS → inactive GS-b); ↓GSK3 → ↓GS phosphorylation; (2) insulin also activates PP1 → PP1 dephosphorylates: (a) glycogen synthase (GS-b [inactive, phosphorylated] → GS-a [active, dephosphorylated]) → ↑glycogen synthesis; (b) glycogen phosphorylase (GP-a [active] → GP-b [inactive]) → ↓glycogenolysis; (c) phosphorylase kinase (active → inactive) → ↓GP activation; NET EFFECT: insulin → ↑glycogen synthesis + ↓glycogenolysis → ↓blood glucose; this is the FED STATE: abundant glucose → ↑insulin → glucose stored as glycogen (liver + muscle); PP1 is targeted to glycogen by a targeting subunit (GM in muscle, GL in liver) → ensures PP1 acts specifically on glycogen-associated enzymes

Insulin activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP levels: GLUCAGON (not insulin) activates adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA; insulin actually DECREASES cAMP by activating phosphodiesterase 3B (PDE3B) → ↓cAMP (opposes glucagon signaling)

Insulin phosphorylates glycogen synthase, activating it: PHOSPHORYLATION of glycogen synthase INACTIVATES it (GS-b = phosphorylated = inactive); insulin promotes DEPHOSPHORYLATION (via PP1) → GS-a = active; this is a common exam trick — phosphorylation ≠ activation for all enzymes (glycolytic/anabolic enzymes are generally active when dephosphorylated [fed state]; glycogenolytic/catabolic enzymes are active when phosphorylated [fasting/fight-or-flight])
explanation: Reciprocal regulation of glycogen metabolism: FED STATE (insulin): ↑insulin → ↑PP1 → dephosphorylation → GS ACTIVE (GS-a) + GP INACTIVE (GP-b) → NET: glycogen SYNTHESIS; also: ↑insulin → ↓GSK3 → ↓GS phosphorylation (reinforces); ↑insulin → ↑PDE3B → ↓cAMP → ↓PKA → ↓phosphorylase kinase → ↓GP; FASTING/STRESS (glucagon [liver] / epinephrine [muscle+liver]): glucagon → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA → (1) phosphorylase kinase (phosphorylated → active) → GP-b → GP-a (phosphorylated → ACTIVE) → glycogenolysis; (2) GS-a → GS-b (phosphorylated → INACTIVE) → ↓glycogen synthesis; NET: glycogen BREAKDOWN; epinephrine in muscle: also acts via α₁-receptors → PLC → IP₃ → ↑Ca²⁺ → Ca²⁺-calmodulin directly activates phosphorylase kinase (even without PKA phosphorylation) → GP activation; this is why epinephrine works faster/differently in muscle vs liver; KEY CONCEPT: phosphorylation generally activates catabolic pathways (glycogenolysis, lipolysis) and inactivates anabolic pathways (glycogenesis, lipogenesis, glycolysis at PFK-2/PK) → this is the 'cAMP cascade' coordinating the fasting response.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which vitamin deficiency causes scurvy, characterized by defective collagen synthesis?
options: Vitamin A: vitamin A (retinol) deficiency → night blindness (↓rhodopsin), xerophthalmia (corneal keratinization → Bitot spots → keratomalacia → blindness), squamous metaplasia, ↑infections, poor growth; NOT scurvy

Vitamin C: VITAMIN C (ASCORBIC ACID) deficiency → SCURVY; mechanism: vitamin C is an essential cofactor for PROLYL HYDROXYLASE and LYSYL HYDROXYLASE (α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases; require Fe²⁺, O₂, α-KG, ascorbate); prolyl hydroxylase: Pro → Hyp (4-hydroxyproline; stabilizes collagen triple helix via interchain H-bonds); lysyl hydroxylase: Lys → Hyl (hydroxylysine; site for O-linked glycosylation + cross-linking in collagen); without vitamin C → ↓hydroxylation of Pro and Lys → ↓collagen stability → defective/weak collagen → SCURVY; clinical: (1) BLEEDING: gingival hemorrhage (swollen, spongy, bleeding gums → teeth loosening), petechiae, perifollicular hemorrhages (pathognomonic: hemorrhage around hair follicles on skin → 'corkscrew hairs' [coiled hair due to defective collagen in hair follicles]); ecchymoses, subperiosteal hemorrhages (bone pain in children → pseudoparalysis); (2) POOR WOUND HEALING (collagen synthesis is critical for wound repair); (3) BONE ABNORMALITIES in children (↓osteoid matrix → subperiosteal hemorrhage, costochondral beading [scorbutic rosary]); (4) ANEMIA: multifactorial (↓iron absorption [vitamin C enhances non-heme Fe³⁺ → Fe²⁺ reduction → ↑absorption; deficiency → ↓Fe absorption → iron deficiency anemia]; also: ↓folate metabolism [vitamin C helps maintain THF]; bleeding → iron loss); other vitamin C functions: (1) antioxidant (scavenges ROS; regenerates vitamin E from tocopheroxyl radical); (2) cofactor for dopamine β-hydroxylase (DA → NE); (3) cofactor for carnitine synthesis (trimethyllysine → hydroxytrimethyllysine); (4) enhances iron absorption; sources: citrus fruits, berries, bell peppers, broccoli, tomatoes; RDA: 90 mg/day (men), 75 mg (women); scurvy at <10 mg/day for weeks; historically: sailors, pirates; now: elderly, alcoholics, psychiatric patients, food faddists
Vitamin D: vitamin D deficiency → rickets (children: defective bone mineralization → bowing, rachitic rosary) / osteomalacia (adults: bone pain, muscle weakness); NOT scurvy

Vitamin E: vitamin E (α-tocopherol) deficiency → hemolytic anemia (↓antioxidant protection of RBC membranes → lipid peroxidation → hemolysis), spinocerebellar degeneration (ataxia, peripheral neuropathy; similar to Friedreich ataxia), retinitis pigmentosa; seen in fat malabsorption (cystic fibrosis, abetalipoproteinemia) or premature infants; NOT scurvy
explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) — deficiency + toxicity summary: Vitamin A: deficiency → night blindness, xerophthalmia, ↑infection; toxicity → pseudotumor cerebri (↑ICP), hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity (isotretinoin → pregnancy category X → NTDs, craniofacial/cardiac defects); Vitamin D: deficiency → rickets/osteomalacia; toxicity → hypercalcemia → metastatic calcification, kidney stones, polyuria, confusion; Vitamin E: deficiency → hemolytic anemia, ataxia; toxicity → rare; may ↑bleeding (antagonizes vitamin K); Vitamin K: deficiency → bleeding (↓factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C, protein S → ↑PT/INR); HDN (hemorrhagic disease of newborn: neonates have ↓K → prophylactic IM vitamin K at birth); toxicity → hemolytic anemia in G6PD-deficient neonates (menadione/K₃; phytonadione/K₁ is safe); Water-soluble vitamins (B complex + C): generally nontoxic (excess excreted in urine); exceptions: B₆ (megadose → peripheral sensory neuropathy; paradoxical: deficiency AND excess both cause neuropathy), B₃ (niacin flush: prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation → flushing, pruritus; hepatotoxicity at high doses).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following porphyrias presents with acute neurovisceral attacks and is caused by deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD)?
options: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT): PCT is the MOST COMMON porphyria; caused by ↓uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD); primarily CUTANEOUS (photosensitivity: blistering fragile skin on sun-exposed areas [hands, forearms, face], hypertrichosis, hyperpigmentation, skin thickening); triggered by: iron overload, alcohol, HCV, estrogens, HIV; PCT is NOT an acute neurovisceral porphyria (no abdominal pain/neuropsychiatric attacks); ↑uroporphyrin in urine (pink-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp); treatment: phlebotomy (↓iron) ± hydroxychloroquine (↑urinary porphyrin excretion)

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP): AIP is caused by deficiency of PORPHOBILINOGEN DEAMINASE (PBGD, also called hydroxymethylbilane synthase/HMBS; the 3rd enzyme in heme synthesis pathway); autosomal dominant (low penetrance: ~10-20% of mutation carriers develop symptoms); ACUTE NEUROVISCERAL ATTACKS: (1) severe abdominal pain (colicky; often misdiagnosed as surgical abdomen → unnecessary laparotomies; pain is NEUROPATHIC, not structural → no peritoneal signs); (2) neuropsychiatric symptoms (anxiety, confusion, hallucinations, seizures, depression, insomnia); (3) autonomic neuropathy (tachycardia, hypertension, nausea/vomiting, constipation); (4) motor neuropathy (ascending weakness, can mimic Guillain-Barré; respiratory failure in severe cases); (5) HYPONATREMIA (SIADH → ↑ADH → dilutional hyponatremia → seizures); AIP is ACUTE only — NO cutaneous manifestations (no photosensitivity; the accumulating porphyrin precursors [ALA, PBG] are NOT photosensitizing because they lack the conjugated ring system); triggers: drugs (barbiturates, sulfonamides, griseofulvin, rifampin, phenytoin, alcohol → all ↑hepatic CYP450 → ↑heme demand → ↑ALA synthase → ↑ALA/PBG), fasting/dieting (↓glucose → ↓heme synthesis repression → ↑ALAS1), menstrual cycle (progesterone → ↑ALAS1; attacks more common in luteal phase → 'cyclical attacks' in women), stress, infection; diagnosis: ↑↑PBG in urine (Watson-Schwartz test or Hoesch test: Ehrlich's aldehyde reagent → cherry-red color with PBG; ↑ALA also); urine may turn PORT-WINE/DARK on standing (PBG polymerizes to porphobilin → dark pigment; exposure to light accelerates); confirmatory: ↓PBGD activity in RBCs + HMBS gene mutation; treatment: ACUTE: IV hemin (Panhematin/heme arginate → replenishes heme pool → negative feedback on ALAS1 → ↓ALA/PBG production) + IV glucose (10% dextrose → ↓ALAS1; less effective than hemin; 'glucose effect'); avoid triggers; givosiran (siRNA targeting ALAS1 mRNA → ↓ALAS1 → ↓ALA/PBG; FDA approved 2019 for prevention of recurrent attacks)

Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP): EPP = ferrochelatase deficiency (last enzyme: protoporphyrin IX + Fe²⁺ → heme); ↑free protoporphyrin IX in erythrocytes/plasma → PAINFUL PHOTOSENSITIVITY (burning, tingling on sun exposure within minutes; non-blistering initially; differs from PCT); may develop hepatic protoporphyrin accumulation → liver damage; NOT an acute neurovisceral porphyria

Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP): CEP (Günther disease) = uroporphyrinogen III synthase deficiency; extremely rare; ↑uroporphyrinogen I + coproporphyrinogen I → severe PHOTOSENSITIVITY (mutilating skin lesions from infancy), hemolytic anemia, red teeth (erythrodontia: porphyrins deposit in teeth → fluoresce under UV), red urine (from birth); NOT an acute neurovisceral porphyria
explanation: Heme synthesis pathway — all 8 enzymes: MITOCHONDRIAL steps: (1) ALA SYNTHASE (ALAS; rate-limiting): succinyl-CoA + glycine → [PLP cofactor] → ALA (δ-aminolevulinic acid); ALAS1 (liver, housekeeping; induced by ↓heme [negative feedback], drugs/CYP450 inducers, fasting; repressed by heme, glucose); ALAS2 (erythroid; regulated by iron [IRE-IRP system] + erythropoietin); ALA exits mitochondria. CYTOPLASMIC steps: (2) ALA DEHYDRATASE (ALAD/porphobilinogen synthase): 2 ALA → PBG; inhibited by LEAD (Pb²⁺ → ↓ALAD + ↓ferrochelatase → ↑ALA + ↑FEP [free erythrocyte protoporphyrin]; lead poisoning: microcytic anemia, basophilic stippling, encephalopathy, wrist/foot drop, lead lines on gums/bones, abdominal colic); (3) PBGD (porphobilinogen deaminase): 4 PBG → hydroxymethylbilane (HMB); deficient in AIP; (4) UROPORPHYRINOGEN III SYNTHASE: HMB → uroporphyrinogen III; deficient in CEP; (5) UROPORPHYRINOGEN DECARBOXYLASE (UROD): uroporphyrinogen III → coproporphyrinogen III; deficient in PCT. Coproporphyrinogen III enters mitochondria: (6) COPROPORPHYRINOGEN OXIDASE: coproporphyrinogen III → protoporphyrinogen IX; deficient in hereditary coproporphyria (HCP); (7) PROTOPORPHYRINOGEN OXIDASE: protoporphyrinogen IX → protoporphyrin IX; deficient in variegate porphyria (VP); (8) FERROCHELATASE: protoporphyrin IX + Fe²⁺ → HEME; deficient in EPP; inhibited by lead. Classification: ACUTE porphyrias (neurovisceral: AIP [most common acute], HCP, VP, ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria); CUTANEOUS porphyrias (photosensitivity: PCT [most common overall], CEP, EPP); HCP + VP = mixed (acute + cutaneous).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the synthesis of cGMP from GTP in response to nitric oxide (NO)?
options: Adenylyl cyclase: adenylyl cyclase converts ATP → cAMP (NOT cGMP); activated by Gαs-coupled receptors (β-adrenergic, glucagon, ACTH, PTH, TSH, D1); inhibited by Gαi (muscarinic M2, α2-adrenergic, D2); cAMP → PKA; this is a different second messenger pathway

Soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC): SOLUBLE GUANYLYL CYCLASE (sGC) synthesizes cGMP from GTP in response to nitric oxide (NO); mechanism: NO (a gas molecule, lipophilic → freely diffuses across membranes) → enters target cell → binds to the HEME group in sGC (sGC contains a prosthetic heme [Fe²⁺] → NO binds Fe²⁺ → conformational change → ↑catalytic activity ~200-fold) → GTP → cGMP; cGMP → activates PKG (protein kinase G/cGMP-dependent protein kinase) → (1) VASCULAR SMOOTH MUSCLE RELAXATION: PKG → ↓intracellular Ca²⁺ (↑Ca²⁺-ATPase [SERCA/PMCA], ↑K⁺ channels → hyperpolarization → ↓Ca²⁺ influx, ↓IP₃ receptor sensitivity) → ↓MLCK activity → ↓myosin phosphorylation → RELAXATION → VASODILATION; (2) ↓platelet aggregation (NO from endothelium → platelet sGC → ↑cGMP → PKG → ↓activation); (3) smooth muscle relaxation in other tissues (GI, airways, corpus cavernosum [penile erection: parasympathetic → ACh → endothelial eNOS → NO → sGC → cGMP → SM relaxation → erection]); cGMP is degraded by PDE5 (phosphodiesterase 5); SILDENAFIL/tadalafil/vardenafil: PDE5 inhibitors → ↓cGMP degradation → ↑cGMP → ↑vasodilation; used for erectile dysfunction + pulmonary arterial hypertension; CONTRAINDICATED with nitrates (additive hypotension → shock); riociguat: sGC stimulator (directly stimulates sGC + sensitizes to NO; for pulmonary hypertension)

Phospholipase C: PLC cleaves PIP₂ → IP₃ + DAG; activated by Gαq-coupled receptors (α1, M1/M3, H1, V1, AT1, endothelin); this produces IP₃ (→ Ca²⁺ release from ER) and DAG (→ PKC); NOT involved in cGMP synthesis
Phosphodiesterase 5: PDE5 DEGRADES cGMP (cGMP → 5'-GMP); it is the opposite of synthesis; PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) ↑cGMP levels by ↓degradation
explanation: NO (nitric oxide) signaling — complete: NO synthesis: L-arginine + O₂ + NADPH → [NOS: nitric oxide synthase] → NO + L-citrulline; NOS requires: BH4, FAD, FMN, heme, calmodulin; three isoforms: (1) nNOS/NOS1 (neuronal): constitutive, Ca²⁺/CaM-dependent; neurotransmission (retrograde signaling: post-synaptic → pre-synaptic); (2) eNOS/NOS3 (endothelial): constitutive, Ca²⁺/CaM-dependent; vasodilation, anti-platelet, anti-atherogenic; activated by: shear stress, ACh, bradykinin, estrogen; myristoylated + palmitoylated → membrane-anchored in caveolae; (3) iNOS/NOS2 (inducible): Ca²⁺-INDEPENDENT; induced by cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-1β) + LPS in macrophages → produces LARGE amounts of NO → antimicrobial (kills intracellular pathogens: Mycobacteria, Leishmania) but also contributes to tissue damage in sepsis (↓↓SVR → distributive shock → refractory hypotension; treatment: vasopressors; methylene blue used as rescue → inhibits sGC → ↑SVR); NO → sGC → cGMP → PKG → vasodilation; also: NO reacts with superoxide → peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) → powerful oxidant → protein nitration (nitrotyrosine marker of oxidative/nitrosative stress) → tissue damage; Clinical: nitroglycerin/isosorbide dinitrate → NO donors → vasodilation (primarily venodilation → ↓preload → ↓angina; in heart failure: ↓preload + afterload).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following enzymes converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I?
options: Renin: RENIN (also called angiotensinogenase) is an aspartyl protease produced by the JUXTAGLOMERULAR (JG) CELLS of the afferent arteriole in the kidney; renin cleaves ANGIOTENSINOGEN (a 452-amino acid α₂-globulin continuously produced by the LIVER) → ANGIOTENSIN I (a 10-amino acid peptide; inactive); this is the RATE-LIMITING step of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS); RENIN RELEASE is stimulated by: (1) ↓renal perfusion pressure (↓BP → baroreceptors in afferent arteriole → ↑renin); (2) ↓NaCl delivery to macula densa (↓GFR → ↓NaCl at macula densa → ↑renin via tubuloglomerular feedback); (3) sympathetic stimulation (β₁-adrenergic receptors on JG cells → ↑cAMP → ↑renin); RENIN RELEASE is inhibited by: ↑BP, ↑NaCl at macula densa, angiotensin II (negative feedback), ANP/BNP; downstream: AngI → [ACE, in pulmonary endothelium] → AngII (8 aa, active); AngII actions: (1) vasoconstriction (AT1 receptors on vascular SM → ↑SVR → ↑BP); (2) aldosterone secretion (adrenal zona glomerulosa → ↑Na⁺/H₂O reabsorption → ↑blood volume); (3) ADH secretion (posterior pituitary → ↑H₂O reabsorption); (4) ↑thirst (subfornical organ); (5) ↑proximal tubular Na⁺ reabsorption (↑NHE3); (6) ↑cardiac/vascular remodeling (fibrosis, hypertrophy → pathological in heart failure); PHARMACOLOGY: ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril, ramipril): ↓AngII + ↑bradykinin (ACE = kininase II → normally degrades bradykinin; ↑BK → vasodilation → cough [dry, non-productive; most common side effect ~10-15%], angioedema [rare, serious]); ARBs (losartan, valsartan): block AT1 receptor → no cough/angioedema (don't affect bradykinin); direct renin inhibitor (aliskiren): blocks renin → ↓AngI production

ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme): ACE converts AngI → AngII (the next step AFTER renin); ACE is located primarily on PULMONARY endothelial cells (lungs are a major site of AngI → AngII conversion); ACE is also identical to kininase II (degrades bradykinin); ACE does NOT convert angiotensinogen → AngI

Angiotensin II receptor: AT1/AT2 are receptors for angiotensin II; they do not catalyze any enzymatic conversion; AT1: most cardiovascular effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone, remodeling); AT2: vasodilation, anti-proliferative (less clearly defined role)

Chymase: chymase (mast cell protease) is an alternative AngI → AngII converting enzyme in tissues (heart, blood vessels); ACE-independent AngII generation; may explain why ACE inhibitors don't completely block AngII; chymase does NOT convert angiotensinogen → AngI
explanation: RAAS — complete pathway and pharmacology: Angiotensinogen (liver, constitutive) → [RENIN, JG cells, rate-limiting] → AngI (10 aa, inactive) → [ACE, pulmonary endothelium + others] → AngII (8 aa, active) → AT1/AT2 receptors; AngII → aldosterone (adrenal glomerulosa: ↑CYP11B2/aldosterone synthase); aldosterone → MR (mineralocorticoid receptor, nuclear) in principal cells of collecting duct → ↑ENaC (↑Na⁺ reabsorption) + ↑ROMK (↑K⁺ secretion) + ↑Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase + ↑SGK1; net: ↑Na⁺/H₂O retention, ↑K⁺ excretion, ↑H⁺ excretion → ↑BP + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis (in excess: Conn syndrome/primary hyperaldosteronism); MR antagonists: spironolactone (non-selective: also anti-androgen → gynecomastia), eplerenone (selective MR antagonist); used in heart failure (↓mortality: RALES/EMPHASIS-HF trials), resistant hypertension, Conn syndrome.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Hartnup disease is caused by a defect in the intestinal and renal transport of which group of amino acids?
options: Basic amino acids (Lys, Arg, Orn): defective transport of dibasic amino acids (Lys, Arg, Orn, cystine [Cys-Cys dimer]) → CYSTINURIA (not Hartnup); cystinuria: defect in rBAT/b⁰,⁺AT transporter (SLC3A1/SLC7A9) → ↑urinary cystine → cystine kidney stones (hexagonal crystals; cyanide-nitroprusside test positive); Lys/Arg/Orn also lost but don't form stones

Neutral amino acids: HARTNUP DISEASE: autosomal recessive defect in the B⁰AT1 (SLC6A19) transporter → impaired absorption of NEUTRAL (monoamino-monocarboxylic) amino acids in the intestinal brush border AND renal proximal tubule; affected amino acids: Ala, Ser, Thr, Val, Leu, Ile, Phe, Tyr, Trp, His, Gln, Asn (all neutral AAs); most clinically significant: ↓TRYPTOPHAN absorption → ↓Trp → ↓NAD⁺ synthesis via kynurenine pathway → PELLAGRA-LIKE symptoms (the 4 D's: Dermatitis [photosensitive, on sun-exposed areas], Diarrhea, Dementia [neuropsychiatric: confusion, hallucinations], and potentially Death if untreated); also: ↓Trp → ↓serotonin + ↓melatonin (may contribute to mood/neurological symptoms); presentation: intermittent; often precipitated by poor diet (low protein), stress, sunlight, illness; many patients are asymptomatic (if adequate dietary protein → enough AA absorption from alternative pathways [dipeptide/tripeptide transporters: PEPT1/SLC15A1 — these are INTACT in Hartnup → di/tripeptides absorbed normally → this is why high-protein diet helps]); diagnosis: ↑neutral aminoaciduria (generalized) on urine amino acid chromatography; plasma amino acids may be low-normal; treatment: high-protein diet + nicotinamide (niacinamide) supplementation (bypasses the Trp → NAD⁺ pathway deficit); prognosis: generally good with treatment; tends to improve with age
Acidic amino acids (Asp, Glu): dicarboxylic aminoaciduria is a rare, benign condition with ↑urinary Asp + Glu; NOT Hartnup disease
Imino acids (Pro, Hyp) and glycine: iminoglycinuria = impaired transport of Pro, Hyp, and Gly → ↑urinary excretion; benign condition; NOT Hartnup disease
explanation: Amino acid transport disorders — comparison: (1) CYSTINURIA: rBAT/b⁰,⁺AT (SLC3A1/SLC7A9) defect → ↑urinary COLA (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine); cystine stones (hexagonal crystals, radiopaque); cyanide-nitroprusside test +; treatment: ↑fluids + urine alkalinization (pH >7.5 → ↑cystine solubility) + D-penicillamine or tiopronin (form soluble mixed disulfides with Cys) + ↓Met diet (Met → Cys precursor); (2) HARTNUP: B⁰AT1/SLC6A19 defect → ↑urinary neutral AAs; pellagra-like (↓Trp → ↓NAD⁺); treatment: nicotinamide + high-protein diet; (3) CYSTINOSIS: NOT a transport disorder — it's a lysosomal storage disease; CTNS gene → cystinosin deficiency → ↓cystine efflux from lysosomes → cystine crystal accumulation in cells (kidney [Fanconi syndrome → renal failure], eyes [corneal cystine crystals → photophobia], thyroid, CNS, muscle); treatment: cysteamine (enters lysosome → reacts with cystine → cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide → exits via lysine transporter); DO NOT confuse cystinuria (↑urinary cystine excretion, stones) with cystinosis (lysosomal cystine storage, Fanconi syndrome).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of metformin at the molecular level?
options: Metformin directly stimulates insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells: direct insulin secretagogues include sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride: bind SUR1 → close K_ATP channels → depolarization → Ca²⁺ influx → insulin exocytosis) and meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide: same mechanism, different binding site); metformin does NOT stimulate insulin secretion → does NOT cause hypoglycemia as monotherapy

Metformin activates AMPK, leading to decreased hepatic glucose production: METFORMIN's primary molecular mechanism involves ACTIVATION of AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase); AMPK is the cell's master energy sensor; when AMP:ATP ratio is high (energy-depleted state) → AMPK is activated → switches on catabolic pathways (FA oxidation, glucose uptake) and switches off anabolic pathways (lipogenesis, gluconeogenesis, protein synthesis); how metformin activates AMPK: (1) inhibits mitochondrial Complex I (mildly) → ↓ATP production → ↑AMP:ATP ratio → ↑AMPK; (2) may also inhibit mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (mGPD) → ↓cytoplasmic NAD⁺ regeneration → ↓hepatic lactate → glucose conversion (↓gluconeogenesis); effects of AMPK activation: (a) LIVER (primary target): ↓gluconeogenesis (↓PEPCK, ↓G6Pase transcription; this is the main glucose-lowering mechanism of metformin — ↓hepatic glucose output); ↓lipogenesis (↓SREBP-1c, ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT-I → ↑β-oxidation → ↓hepatic steatosis); (b) MUSCLE: ↑GLUT4 translocation → ↑glucose uptake (insulin-sensitizing effect); ↑FA oxidation; (c) ADIPOSE: ↑FA oxidation, ↓lipogenesis; (d) GUT: ↑anaerobic glucose metabolism → ↑lactate (→ rare but serious: LACTIC ACIDOSIS, especially in renal failure [↓metformin clearance] → contraindicated if eGFR <30); also ↑GLP-1 secretion; clinical: first-line drug for type 2 DM; weight-neutral or slight weight loss; no hypoglycemia as monotherapy; ↓cardiovascular events (UKPDS); side effects: GI (nausea, diarrhea, metallic taste — dose-related, improve with time/XR formulation), B₁₂ deficiency (↓B₁₂ absorption in terminal ileum; check periodically), lactic acidosis (rare)

Metformin inhibits DPP-4, increasing incretin levels: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, etc.) inhibit dipeptidyl peptidase-4 → ↓GLP-1/GIP degradation → ↑incretins → ↑insulin + ↓glucagon (glucose-dependent); metformin is NOT a DPP-4 inhibitor

Metformin activates PPARγ, promoting adipogenesis: PPARγ agonists are the THIAZOLIDINEDIONES (TZDs: pioglitazone, rosiglitazone); PPARγ (nuclear receptor) → promotes adipocyte differentiation + lipogenesis → ↑subcutaneous fat storage → ↓FFAs → ↑insulin sensitivity; side effects: weight gain, edema, heart failure exacerbation, fractures; metformin does NOT act via PPARγ
explanation: AMPK — the metabolic master switch: STRUCTURE: heterotrimer (α catalytic + β [glycogen-binding] + γ [AMP/ATP-sensing]); ACTIVATION: ↑AMP/ADP:ATP ratio (allosteric: AMP binds γ → conformational change → protects from dephosphorylation; phosphorylation: LKB1 [constitutive → main upstream kinase; LKB1 = tumor suppressor → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome when mutated] + CaMKKβ [↑Ca²⁺]); EFFECTS when AMPK is active (low energy state): ↑catabolic: ↑glucose uptake (↑GLUT4 translocation), ↑glycolysis (↑PFK-2 → ↑F2,6BP → ↑PFK-1), ↑FA oxidation (↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT-I), ↑autophagy (↑ULK1); ↓anabolic: ↓gluconeogenesis (↓PEPCK/G6Pase), ↓FA synthesis (↓ACC, ↓FAS via ↓SREBP-1c), ↓cholesterol synthesis (↓HMGCR by phosphorylation → inactive), ↓protein synthesis (↓mTORC1 via ↑TSC2 phosphorylation), ↓glycogen synthesis (↓GS); AMPK activators: metformin, AICAR (research), exercise (↑AMP:ATP in muscle), calorie restriction; AMPK as drug target: metformin (T2DM), salicylate (anti-inflammatory via AMPK?); AMPK and cancer: tumor suppressor role (↓mTORC1 → ↓growth; LKB1-AMPK pathway); metformin associated with ↓cancer risk in epidemiological studies.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Biotin deficiency can be caused by excessive consumption of which of the following?
options: Cooked egg yolks: cooked eggs are safe; cooking denatures avidin (see below) → no biotin binding; egg yolk is actually a good SOURCE of biotin

Raw egg whites: RAW EGG WHITES contain AVIDIN, a glycoprotein that has extremely high affinity for BIOTIN (Kd ~10⁻¹⁵ M; one of the strongest non-covalent interactions in nature); avidin binds dietary biotin in the GI tract → prevents absorption → biotin deficiency; avidin is a tetrameric protein (4 subunits, each binding one biotin) → can sequester up to 4 biotin molecules; COOKING denatures avidin → ↓biotin binding → cooked eggs are safe; clinical: 'egg white injury' — consuming large quantities of raw egg whites → biotin deficiency; biotin deficiency symptoms: dermatitis (perioral, seborrheic), alopecia, glossitis, conjunctivitis, neurological symptoms (depression, lethargy, hallucinations, paresthesias, hypotonia in infants), lactic acidosis + organic aciduria (↓PC → ↓OAA → ↑lactate; ↓PCC → ↑propionic acid; ↓MCC → ↑3-methylcrotonylglycine); other causes of biotin deficiency: (1) biotinidase deficiency (AR; biotinidase normally recycles biotin from biocytin [biotin-lysine] released during protein turnover → biotinidase cleaves biocytin → free biotin + lysine; deficiency → ↓biotin recycling → progressive biotin deficiency → dermatitis, alopecia, seizures, developmental delay, hearing loss, optic atrophy; NBS: newborn screening in most US states; treatment: lifelong oral biotin supplementation → excellent response); (2) holocarboxylase synthetase (HCS) deficiency (attaches biotin to apocarboxylases; presents earlier [neonatal] with severe metabolic acidosis + organic aciduria; also responds to biotin); (3) prolonged parenteral nutrition without biotin supplementation; (4) anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital → ↑biotin catabolism)

Raw fish: raw fish contains THIAMINASE → degrades thiamine (vitamin B₁) → thiamine deficiency (beriberi); this is a risk factor in populations consuming large amounts of raw fish (Japanese cuisine → haff disease? No — thiaminase → B₁ deficiency); NOT biotin deficiency

Corn-based diet: corn-based diet without nixtamalization → niacin (B₃) deficiency → pellagra; corn contains niacin in bound form (niacytin) that is not bioavailable unless treated with alkali (nixtamalization: lime-water treatment used in Mexican cuisine); corn is also low in tryptophan (Trp → NAD⁺); NOT biotin deficiency
explanation: Biotin (vitamin B₇/H) — complete: Active form: biocytin (biotin covalently attached to ε-amino group of Lys in carboxylase enzymes by holocarboxylase synthetase [HCS]); Enzymes requiring biotin (all are ATP-dependent carboxylases, transfer CO₂ to substrates): (1) PYRUVATE CARBOXYLASE (PC): pyruvate → OAA (anaplerosis + first step of GNG); (2) ACETYL-CoA CARBOXYLASE (ACC): acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (committed step of FA synthesis); ACC1 (cytoplasmic, lipogenic) and ACC2 (mitochondrial outer membrane, regulates CPT-I); (3) PROPIONYL-CoA CARBOXYLASE (PCC): propionyl-CoA → D-methylmalonyl-CoA (odd-chain FA, Val, Ile, Met, Thr catabolism); (4) 3-METHYLCROTONYL-CoA CARBOXYLASE (MCC): Leu catabolism; (5) Sometimes: acetyl-CoA carboxylase β (ACC2); Mnemonic for biotin carboxylases: 'PAPM' (Pyruvate, Acetyl-CoA, Propionyl-CoA, Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylases); biotin-avidin interaction: used extensively in laboratory techniques (streptavidin [from Streptomyces avidinii]-biotin system: attach biotin to antibodies/DNA probes → streptavidin-conjugated fluorophore/enzyme detects → ELISA, immunohistochemistry, Western blot, FISH, pull-down assays); biotinylation = adding biotin tags to molecules for detection/purification.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which plasma protein has the longest half-life and is most useful for assessing long-term protein nutritional status?
options: Prealbumin (transthyretin): prealbumin/transthyretin (TTR) has a SHORT half-life (~2 days) → reflects ACUTE/SHORT-TERM changes in nutritional status; useful for monitoring response to nutritional therapy over days; ↓in acute inflammation (negative acute-phase protein); TTR also transports thyroxine (T₄) + retinol-binding protein (RBP)-retinol complex
