Albumin: ALBUMIN has the LONGEST half-life of commonly measured plasma proteins (~20 DAYS / 3 weeks) → best reflects LONG-TERM (chronic) protein nutritional status; albumin is synthesized exclusively by the liver (~12-15 g/day); serum albumin: normal 3.5-5.0 g/dL; ↓albumin (hypoalbuminemia): causes: (1) ↓synthesis: malnutrition/PEM (kwashiorkor > marasmus), chronic liver disease (cirrhosis); (2) ↑loss: nephrotic syndrome (↑urinary protein > 3.5 g/day; albuminuria → edema, hyperlipidemia, lipiduria), protein-losing enteropathy, burns (↑capillary permeability → protein loss); (3) ↑catabolism: sepsis, inflammation, surgery; (4) dilution: volume overload; albumin is a NEGATIVE acute-phase protein (↓during acute inflammation → IL-6/TNF-α → liver shifts to producing positive acute-phase proteins [CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin, haptoglobin, ceruloplasmin, SAA, complement] at the expense of albumin → so ↓albumin in inflammation reflects inflammatory state, NOT necessarily malnutrition); this limits albumin's specificity for nutritional assessment in hospitalized patients; functions of albumin: (1) maintains plasma ONCOTIC PRESSURE (~80% of plasma colloid osmotic pressure); (2) TRANSPORT: drugs (warfarin, phenytoin, diazepam, aspirin bind to albumin → only free/unbound fraction is pharmacologically active; hypoalbuminemia → ↑free drug → ↑effect/toxicity), fatty acids (FFA bound to albumin in blood), bilirubin (unconjugated bilirubin bound to albumin → prevents kernicterus in neonates), Ca²⁺ (~40% of serum Ca bound to albumin; hypoalbuminemia → ↓total Ca but normal ionized Ca → corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × [4.0 - albumin]), hormones, metals

Retinol-binding protein (RBP): RBP has the SHORTEST half-life (~12 hours) of commonly measured nutritional proteins → reflects very acute changes; ↓rapidly in malnutrition, liver disease; filtered by kidneys (↑in renal failure → less useful)

Transferrin: transferrin half-life ~8-10 days → intermediate; reflects medium-term nutritional status; also: transferrin ↑ in iron deficiency (compensatory → ↑TIBC); ↓in chronic disease, malnutrition, liver disease; less reliable than albumin for long-term nutritional assessment
explanation: Nutritional assessment proteins ranked by half-life: Albumin (~20 days) → long-term; Transferrin (~8-10 days) → medium-term; Prealbumin/TTR (~2 days) → short-term; RBP (~12 hours) → very short-term; all are negative acute-phase proteins (↓in inflammation); prealbumin is most commonly used clinically for monitoring nutritional repletion (quick turnaround reflects response to feeding within days); ACUTE-PHASE RESPONSE: liver reprioritizes protein synthesis during inflammation; POSITIVE acute-phase proteins (↑): CRP (most used clinically; massive increase [up to 1000×]; half-life ~19h → rises within 6-8h, peaks 48h; used for: monitoring infection/inflammation, cardiovascular risk [hs-CRP]; synthesized in liver in response to IL-6); fibrinogen (↑ → ↑ESR [rouleaux formation → faster sedimentation]; also ↑ESR in: anemia, pregnancy, infection, malignancy); ferritin (↑ → note: ferritin is acute-phase → ↑in inflammation even when iron stores are low → confounds iron deficiency diagnosis in sick patients → use transferrin saturation, soluble transferrin receptor [sTfR], or sTfR/log ferritin index); haptoglobin (↑ → but ↓ in hemolysis [binds free Hb] → haptoglobin ↓ in hemolysis overrides acute-phase ↑); ceruloplasmin (↑ → carries copper; ↓ in Wilson disease); serum amyloid A (SAA: ↑ massively; precursor of AA amyloid in chronic inflammation → reactive amyloidosis); NEGATIVE acute-phase proteins (↓): albumin, transferrin, prealbumin, RBP.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following describes the Bohr effect?
options: Increased oxygen affinity of hemoglobin at high pH: high pH (alkaline conditions) → LEFT shift of ODC → ↑O₂ affinity → this is the OPPOSITE direction of the Bohr effect; while it's true that pH affects O₂ affinity, the 'Bohr effect' specifically refers to how ↑CO₂/↓pH DECREASES O₂ affinity (facilitates O₂ unloading in tissues)

The decrease in oxygen affinity of hemoglobin in the presence of increased CO₂ and decreased pH: The BOHR EFFECT (Christian Bohr, 1904; father of Niels Bohr) describes the decrease in hemoglobin's oxygen affinity when CO₂ concentration increases and/or pH decreases → RIGHT SHIFT of the oxygen dissociation curve → facilitates O₂ UNLOADING in metabolically active tissues; mechanism: in tissues: ↑metabolic activity → ↑CO₂ production → CO₂ diffuses into RBCs → (1) CO₂ + H₂O → [carbonic anhydrase, CA-II in RBCs] → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ exits RBC via AE1/Band 3 (Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger → chloride shift: Cl⁻ enters, HCO₃⁻ exits → maintains electroneutrality); H⁺ produced → binds to specific residues on deoxyHb (His146 on β-chains [most important] + His122 on α-chains → salt bridges → stabilize T-state → ↓O₂ affinity → O₂ released to tissues); (2) CO₂ can also directly bind to N-terminal amino groups of Hb → carbaminohemoglobin (HbNHCOO⁻; accounts for ~10-15% of CO₂ transport; CO₂ binds better to deoxyHb → promotes O₂ release); IN LUNGS: reverse occurs → ↑O₂ (inhaled) → ↑oxyHb → releases H⁺ + CO₂ → CO₂ exhaled; ↓H⁺ → ↑pH → ↑O₂ affinity → ↑O₂ loading; the HALDANE EFFECT is the converse: oxygenation status affects CO₂/H⁺ binding; oxyHb is a WEAKER acid (binds fewer H⁺) than deoxyHb → in lungs: O₂ binding → releases H⁺ + CO₂ → CO₂ exhaled; in tissues: O₂ release → deoxyHb picks up H⁺ + CO₂ → transported to lungs; Bohr + Haldane effects work together to optimize gas exchange

Binding of 2,3-BPG to hemoglobin in the fetal circulation: 2,3-BPG binding to adult HbA (in the β-chain central cavity) → ↓O₂ affinity (right shift); HbF (α₂γ₂) binds 2,3-BPG less well (γ-chains lack His143 → weaker 2,3-BPG binding → HbF has ↑O₂ affinity → facilitates O₂ transfer from maternal to fetal blood); while 2,3-BPG is important, this is NOT the Bohr effect (the Bohr effect specifically involves CO₂/H⁺)

Cooperative binding of oxygen to hemoglobin subunits: cooperative binding (positive cooperativity: binding of first O₂ → conformational change → ↑affinity for subsequent O₂ → sigmoidal ODC; T→R transition; MWC model [concerted] and KNF model [sequential]) is the COOPERATIVE EFFECT, not the Bohr effect
explanation: Hemoglobin — gas transport summary: O₂ transport: 98.5% bound to Hb (each Hb binds 4 O₂; O₂-carrying capacity: 1.34 mL O₂/g Hb × 15 g Hb/dL → ~20 mL O₂/dL blood [CaO₂]); 1.5% dissolved (PaO₂ × 0.003 mL O₂/dL per mmHg); CO₂ transport: 70% as HCO₃⁻ (CA-II in RBCs → chloride shift); 20-25% as carbaminoHb (CO₂ bound to N-terminal of Hb); 5-10% dissolved (PCO₂ × 0.07); KEY RELATIONSHIPS: Bohr effect: ↑CO₂/↑H⁺ → ↓O₂ affinity (right shift); Haldane effect: ↑O₂ → ↓CO₂/H⁺ binding; both optimize tissue O₂ delivery and lung CO₂ excretion; O₂ dissociation curve (ODC): sigmoidal (cooperative binding); right shift (↑P50, ↓affinity, ↑unloading): ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑temp; left shift (↓P50, ↑affinity, ↓unloading): ↓CO₂, ↓H⁺, ↓2,3-BPG, ↓temp, CO, MetHb, HbF; myoglobin: HYPERBOLIC curve (no cooperativity; single subunit; very high O₂ affinity → P50 ~2-3 mmHg; functions as O₂ STORAGE in muscle → releases O₂ only at very low PO₂ [during intense exercise when tissue PO₂ drops critically low]).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the most abundant extracellular cation?
options: Potassium (K⁺): K⁺ is the most abundant INTRACELLULAR cation (~150 mEq/L inside cells vs ~4.0 mEq/L in ECF); K⁺ gradient maintained by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in); K⁺ is critical for resting membrane potential (Vm ≈ -70 to -90 mV; determined largely by K⁺ equilibrium potential [Nernst equation: EK = -61 log([K⁺]i/[K⁺]o) ≈ -90 mV]); hypokalemia → ↑resting membrane potential (more negative → hyperpolarization → initially harder to depolarize; but also → ↓K⁺ conductance → delayed repolarization → ↑risk of arrhythmias [U waves, T wave flattening, ST depression → severe: VF]); hyperkalemia → ↓resting membrane potential (less negative → initially easier to depolarize → peaked T waves → then ↑K⁺ → sustained depolarization → Na⁺ channel inactivation → ↓conduction → widened QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole)

Sodium (Na⁺): SODIUM (Na⁺) is the most abundant EXTRACELLULAR cation; normal serum [Na⁺]: 135-145 mEq/L (ECF); intracellular: ~10-15 mEq/L; Na⁺ is the primary determinant of ECF OSMOLALITY (serum osmolality ≈ 2[Na⁺] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; normal ~275-295 mOsm/kg; since Na⁺ is by far the largest contributor → Na⁺ essentially determines ECF osmolality); Na⁺ gradient (maintained by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) drives numerous secondary active transport processes: SGLT1/SGLT2 (Na⁺-glucose cotransport; intestine/kidney), NHE3 (Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger; proximal tubule → H⁺ secretion + Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ reabsorption), Na⁺-amino acid cotransporters, Na⁺-bile salt cotransporters (NTCP in liver); hyponatremia: [Na⁺] <135 mEq/L → most common electrolyte disorder; ↓osmolality → water shifts into cells → cerebral edema (headache, confusion, seizures, coma, brain herniation if acute/severe); causes: SIADH (↑ADH → ↑water retention → dilutional ↓Na⁺), heart failure, cirrhosis, hypothyroidism, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, thiazides, ecstasy/MDMA); treatment: depends on volume status and chronicity; fluid restriction (SIADH); hypertonic saline for severe/symptomatic (correct slowly: ≤10-12 mEq/L per 24h → risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome/central pontine myelinolysis [ODS/CPM] if corrected too fast)

Calcium (Ca²⁺): total serum Ca: ~8.5-10.5 mg/dL; but only ~50% is ionized (free, physiologically active); 40% bound to albumin, 10% complexed with anions (citrate, PO₄); Ca²⁺ is important but NOT the most abundant extracellular cation

Magnesium (Mg²⁺): serum Mg: ~1.5-2.5 mg/dL; Mg is the 2nd most abundant INTRACELLULAR cation (after K⁺); required for >300 enzymatic reactions (kinases, ATPases; Mg-ATP is the true substrate for kinases); ↓Mg → refractory hypokalemia + hypocalcemia (Mg required for K⁺ channels, PTH secretion/action)
explanation: Electrolyte distribution — ICF vs ECF: Most abundant INTRACELLULAR cation: K⁺ (~150 mEq/L); most abundant EXTRACELLULAR cation: Na⁺ (~140 mEq/L); most abundant INTRACELLULAR anion: phosphate (organic: ATP, ADP, etc.; inorganic: HPO₄²⁻); most abundant EXTRACELLULAR anion: Cl⁻ (~100 mEq/L) and HCO₃⁻ (~24 mEq/L); Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: electrogenic pump (3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in per ATP); consumes ~30-40% of cellular ATP at rest; cardiac glycosides (digoxin/digitalis): inhibit Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑intracellular Na⁺ → ↓Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) activity (less Na⁺ gradient to drive Ca²⁺ efflux) → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ → ↑cardiac contractility (positive inotropy; used in heart failure + atrial fibrillation); digoxin toxicity → hyperkalemia (↓K⁺ uptake) + arrhythmias (enhanced automaticity + ↓conduction); treatment: digoxin-specific Fab fragments (Digibind/DigiFab); Anion gap: AG = [Na⁺] - ([Cl⁻] + [HCO₃⁻]); normal ~12 ± 4 (or 8-12 with newer ion-selective electrodes); ↑AG metabolic acidosis (MUDPILES: Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, INH/Iron, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates; or GOLDMARK: Glycols, Oxoproline, L-lactate, D-lactate, Methanol, ASA, Renal failure, Ketoacidosis); non-AG (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis: diarrhea (↓HCO₃⁻ loss), RTA, saline infusion.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 endonuclease to a specific genomic locus. Which of the following best describes the requirement for Cas9 to cleave DNA at the target site?
options: The target DNA must contain a poly-A sequence: poly-A sequences are related to mRNA polyadenylation; there is no poly-A requirement for CRISPR-Cas9 targeting

The target DNA sequence must be adjacent to a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM): CRISPR-Cas9 requires a PROTOSPACER ADJACENT MOTIF (PAM) sequence adjacent to the target DNA site; for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9, the most commonly used): PAM = 5'-NGG-3' (where N = any nucleotide); the PAM must be on the NON-TARGET strand (the strand NOT complementary to the guide RNA), immediately 3' of the protospacer (the 20-nt target sequence); CRISPR mechanism: (1) guide RNA (gRNA): either crRNA + tracrRNA (natural) or single guide RNA (sgRNA, engineered fusion); the sgRNA has a ~20-nt spacer sequence complementary to the target DNA; (2) Cas9-sgRNA complex scans genomic DNA for PAM sequences (PAM recognition is the first step — Cas9 'reads' PAM on dsDNA without unwinding); (3) upon PAM recognition → local DNA unwinding → sgRNA hybridizes with the complementary target strand (R-loop formation); if ≥~12-nt match at the PAM-proximal 'seed' region → full R-loop → (4) Cas9 cleaves BOTH strands: RuvC domain cuts non-target strand, HNH domain cuts target strand → blunt-ended DSB ~3 bp upstream of PAM; (5) DSB repair by cell: (a) NHEJ (non-homologous end joining): error-prone → insertions/deletions (indels) → frameshift → gene KNOCKOUT; (b) HDR (homology-directed repair): if a repair template (donor DNA with homology arms) is provided → precise gene EDITING (knock-in, correction); HDR efficiency is lower (mainly S/G2 phase); variants: Cas9 nickase (D10A or H840A: one catalytic domain inactivated → nicks one strand → paired nickases for ↑specificity); dCas9 (dead Cas9: both catalytic domains inactivated → no cutting → used for CRISPRi [repression: dCas9-KRAB] or CRISPRa [activation: dCas9-VP64/p65/Rta]); base editors (dCas9/nickase fused to deaminase → C→T or A→G editing without DSB); prime editing (nickase-Cas9 fused to reverse transcriptase + pegRNA → precise edits without DSB or donor template)

The guide RNA must be at least 100 nucleotides long: the spacer (targeting) portion of the guide RNA is ~20 nucleotides, not 100; the full sgRNA including the scaffold is ~100 nt total, but the targeting specificity comes from the 20-nt spacer

Cas9 requires a zinc finger domain to recognize the target: zinc finger domains are part of ZINC FINGER NUCLEASES (ZFNs), an older gene editing technology; Cas9 uses guide RNA for target recognition, NOT zinc finger domains; ZFNs and TALENs (transcription activator-like effector nucleases) are protein-based targeting systems (each ZF recognizes ~3 bp; each TALE repeat recognizes 1 bp); CRISPR-Cas9 revolutionized gene editing because RNA-based targeting is much easier to design than engineering new protein domains
explanation: Gene editing technologies — comparison: (1) CRISPR-Cas9: RNA-guided; easiest to design (change 20-nt guide sequence); most widely used; PAM requirement limits some targets; off-target effects (mitigated by high-fidelity Cas9 variants: eSpCas9, HiFi-Cas9; truncated gRNAs; paired nickases); delivery: viral (AAV, lentivirus) or non-viral (lipid nanoparticles [LNPs], electroporation, RNP [ribonucleoprotein: Cas9 protein + sgRNA → transient, ↓off-target]); (2) ZFNs: protein-based (zinc finger arrays → each finger ~3 bp); fused to FokI nuclease (dimerizes → DSB); harder to engineer; first clinical gene editing trials; (3) TALENs: protein-based (TALE repeats → each repeat = 1 bp, RVD code: NI=A, HD=C, NG=T, NN=G/A); fused to FokI; easier than ZFNs but still protein engineering; CLINICAL APPLICATIONS: sickle cell disease/β-thalassemia (Casgevy/exagamglogene autotemcel: CRISPR edits BCL11A enhancer in patient's HSCs → ↑HbF → first FDA-approved CRISPR therapy, Dec 2023); transthyretin amyloidosis (NTLA-2001: in vivo CRISPR → LNP delivery to liver → knockout TTR; clinical trials); cancer (CAR-T cell engineering: CRISPR knockout of TRAC/PD-1 → allogeneic/enhanced CAR-T); hereditary angioedema (in vivo liver editing of KLKB1); sickle cell (also Lyfgenia: lentiviral gene addition, not CRISPR).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the site of fatty acid synthesis in the cell?
options: Mitochondrial matrix: the mitochondrial matrix is the site of FATTY ACID β-OXIDATION (catabolism: FA → acetyl-CoA); FA synthesis and degradation occur in DIFFERENT compartments → allows independent regulation; the mitochondrial matrix also houses the TCA cycle, urea cycle (CPS I, OTC), and PDC/BCKDH/OGDH

Cytoplasm (cytosol): FATTY ACID SYNTHESIS occurs in the CYTOPLASM (cytosol); the key enzyme is FATTY ACID SYNTHASE (FAS/FASN), a large multifunctional enzyme (mammalian FAS: homodimer, each subunit ~270 kDa with 7 catalytic domains + ACP [acyl carrier protein] domain); FAS catalyzes: acetyl-CoA + 7 malonyl-CoA + 14 NADPH + 14 H⁺ → palmitate (16:0) + 7 CO₂ + 8 CoA + 14 NADP⁺ + 6 H₂O; the building block is MALONYL-CoA (3C; made from acetyl-CoA by ACC [acetyl-CoA carboxylase, rate-limiting, biotin-dependent]); each elongation cycle adds 2 carbons (from malonyl-CoA → the CO₂ added by ACC is released → net 2C addition); 7 cycles → 16C (palmitate); NADPH sources for FA synthesis: (1) pentose phosphate pathway (PPP; G6PD + 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase → provide majority of NADPH); (2) malic enzyme (malate → pyruvate + CO₂ + NADPH; part of the citrate shuttle); (3) NADP⁺-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (cytoplasmic); acetyl-CoA for FA synthesis: originates from mitochondrial PDC (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA); acetyl-CoA cannot cross IMM → CITRATE SHUTTLE: acetyl-CoA + OAA → [citrate synthase, mito] → citrate → exits mito via citrate transporter → [ATP-citrate lyase, cytoplasm] → acetyl-CoA + OAA; OAA → [MDH] → malate → [malic enzyme] → pyruvate + NADPH → pyruvate returns to mito

Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: SER is involved in FA ELONGATION (beyond C16; elongases: ELOVL family → add 2C units using malonyl-CoA + NADPH) and DESATURATION (Δ9-desaturase/SCD1: stearate → oleate; Δ5, Δ6-desaturases: essential FA conversions); also: steroid synthesis, drug metabolism (CYP450), Ca²⁺ storage; SER is NOT the primary site of de novo FA synthesis (that's cytoplasm)

Peroxisomes: peroxisomes perform β-oxidation of VERY LONG CHAIN fatty acids (>C22; VLCFAs: shortened to medium-chain → transferred to mitochondria for complete oxidation) and α-oxidation (branched-chain FAs: phytanic acid → [α-hydroxylase] → pristanic acid → β-oxidation; Refsum disease: phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency → ↑phytanic acid); peroxisomes also synthesize plasmalogens (ether phospholipids: abundant in myelin, cardiac tissue); NOT the site of de novo FA synthesis
explanation: Fatty acid synthesis vs β-oxidation — comparison: SYNTHESIS: location = cytoplasm; carrier = ACP (acyl carrier protein on FAS); acyl unit = malonyl-CoA (3C → net 2C per cycle); reductant = NADPH; direction = C2 → C16 (builds up); rate-limiting enzyme = ACC (acetyl-CoA carboxylase); activator = citrate, insulin; inhibitor = palmitoyl-CoA (product feedback), AMPK phosphorylation, glucagon/epinephrine; product = palmitate (16:0); β-OXIDATION: location = mitochondrial matrix; carrier = CoA (acyl-CoA); acyl unit = acetyl-CoA (2C released per cycle); oxidant = FAD + NAD⁺; direction = removes 2C per cycle; rate-limiting = CPT-I (carnitine shuttle); activator = glucagon/epinephrine (↓malonyl-CoA); inhibitor = malonyl-CoA (made by ACC → blocks CPT-I → when FA synthesis is active, β-oxidation is inhibited and vice versa → reciprocal regulation); ENERGY: one palmitate (16:0) → 8 acetyl-CoA (7 cycles of β-ox) → 7 FADH₂ + 7 NADH + 8 acetyl-CoA (→ TCA: 8 × [3 NADH + FADH₂ + GTP]); total ~106 ATP (or 129 by older count) - 2 ATP (activation: acyl-CoA synthetase uses ATP → AMP + PPi = 2 ATP equivalents) = ~104 net ATP per palmitate.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which lipoprotein is responsible for reverse cholesterol transport, carrying cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver?
options: LDL (low-density lipoprotein): LDL delivers cholesterol TO peripheral tissues (LDL = 'bad cholesterol'); LDL is formed from IDL (VLDL remnants) after hepatic lipase removes more TG; LDL is the major carrier of cholesterol in blood (~70% of plasma cholesterol); LDL → binds LDLR on cells → receptor-mediated endocytosis → lysosomal degradation → free cholesterol released; ↑LDL → atherosclerosis (subendothelial LDL → oxidized by ROS → oxLDL → scavenger receptor uptake by macrophages [SR-A, CD36] → foam cells → fatty streak → atherosclerotic plaque)

HDL (high-density lipoprotein): HDL mediates REVERSE CHOLESTEROL TRANSPORT (RCT), the process of transporting excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver for excretion as bile acids/biliary cholesterol; HDL = 'good cholesterol' → ↑HDL is cardioprotective; mechanism: (1) nascent HDL (discoidal, phospholipid-poor): secreted by liver and intestine as apoA-I (the major HDL apolipoprotein); (2) apoA-I interacts with ABCA1 (ATP-binding cassette transporter A1) on peripheral cells (macrophages, other cells) → ABCA1 effluxes free cholesterol + phospholipids → loaded onto nascent HDL; (3) LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase, activated by apoA-I) on HDL surface → esterifies free cholesterol → cholesteryl ester (hydrophobic) → moves to HDL core → HDL becomes spherical (mature HDL₃ → HDL₂ as more CE accumulates); (4) mature HDL delivers CE to liver via: (a) SR-B1 (scavenger receptor class B type 1): selective CE uptake without particle endocytosis (HDL docks → CE transferred → HDL released for recycling); (b) CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein): transfers CE from HDL to VLDL/LDL in exchange for TG → CE eventually reaches liver via LDLR (indirect pathway; CETP inhibitors were developed to ↑HDL but clinical trials largely failed [torcetrapib: ↑CV events; dalcetrapib: no benefit; anacetrapib: modest benefit but shelved; obicetrapib: in trials]); Tangier disease: ABCA1 deficiency (AR) → ↓HDL (near-zero) + ↓cholesterol efflux → cholesterol accumulates in macrophages → orange tonsils (pathognomonic: enlarged, orange-yellow from CE-laden macrophages), hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, premature atherosclerosis; familial LCAT deficiency → ↓CE formation → corneal opacities (fish-eye disease), hemolytic anemia (abnormal RBC membranes), proteinuria/renal failure

VLDL (very low-density lipoprotein): VLDL is synthesized by the LIVER; carries endogenous TG to peripheral tissues; apoB-100 is the structural apolipoprotein; VLDL → [LPL] → IDL → [hepatic lipase] → LDL; ↑VLDL in metabolic syndrome, diabetes, alcohol excess → hypertriglyceridemia

Chylomicrons: chylomicrons carry dietary (exogenous) TG from intestine to tissues; largest and least dense lipoprotein; apoB-48 (truncated apoB from intestinal mRNA editing [APOBEC-1: introduces stop codon at position 2153 → 48% of full apoB]); chylomicrons → [LPL, activated by apoCII] → chylomicron remnants → taken up by liver (remnant receptor: LRP1 + LDLR); ↑chylomicrons → type I hyperlipoproteinemia (LPL or apoCII deficiency → severe hypertriglyceridemia → eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis, lipemia retinalis, creamy supernatant on standing)
explanation: Lipoprotein metabolism overview: EXOGENOUS pathway: dietary fat → intestinal absorption → chylomicrons (apoB-48) → [LPL in capillaries, apoCII cofactor] → FFA to tissues + chylomicron remnants → liver (LRP1); ENDOGENOUS pathway: liver synthesizes VLDL (apoB-100, carries endogenous TG) → [LPL] → IDL → [hepatic lipase] → LDL (primarily carries cholesterol; apoB-100); LDL → LDLR on cells → internalized; REVERSE transport: HDL (apoA-I) → ABCA1/ABCG1 pick up cholesterol from cells → LCAT esterifies → CE in HDL core → SR-B1 (liver) or CETP transfer; Apolipoproteins: apoB-100 (VLDL, IDL, LDL; LDLR ligand), apoB-48 (chylomicrons), apoA-I (HDL; LCAT activator), apoC-II (activates LPL), apoC-III (inhibits LPL → ↑TG), apoE (remnant receptor ligand; apoE genotypes: ε2 → ↓LDLR binding → type III hyperlipoproteinemia [ε2/ε2 + trigger]; ε3 = wild type; ε4 → ↑Alzheimer risk [↑Aβ accumulation] + ↑CV risk); Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH): LDLR mutations (most common) or apoB-100 mutations (FDB: familial defective apoB) or PCSK9 gain-of-function → ↓LDL clearance → ↑↑LDL → premature atherosclerosis; heterozygous FH: LDL 300-500 mg/dL; homozygous: >600 → MI in childhood; treatment: high-intensity statins + ezetimibe + PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab: mAbs → ↓PCSK9 → ↑LDLR → ↓LDL up to 60%).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following enzymes catalyzes the committed step of the pentose phosphate pathway?
options: 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase: 6PGDH catalyzes the second oxidative step: 6-phosphogluconate → ribulose-5-phosphate + CO₂ + NADPH; this is the second NADPH-generating step but NOT the committed/rate-limiting step

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD): G6PD catalyzes the FIRST and COMMITTED (rate-limiting) step of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP): glucose-6-phosphate + NADP⁺ → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH; this is irreversible and commits G6P to the oxidative branch of the PPP; REGULATION: ↑ by NADP⁺ (substrate; when NADPH is consumed → ↑NADP⁺ → ↑G6PD activity → ↑NADPH regeneration); ↓ by NADPH (product inhibition; high NADPH → ↓need for PPP); G6PD DEFICIENCY: most common human enzymopathy (~400 million people worldwide; X-linked recessive; high prevalence in malaria-endemic regions → heterozygous females have survival advantage against P. falciparum [↓parasite growth in G6PD-deficient RBCs]); ↓G6PD → ↓NADPH in RBCs → ↓reduced glutathione (GSH; NADPH → [glutathione reductase] → GSH; GSH → [glutathione peroxidase] → neutralizes H₂O₂/ROS) → ↑oxidative stress → Hb denaturation → HEINZ BODIES (precipitated denatured Hb; stain with crystal violet/methyl violet; Heinz bodies are removed by splenic macrophages → 'bite cells' on peripheral smear) → hemolysis (intravascular + extravascular); episodic hemolytic crises triggered by: oxidative stress → infections (most common trigger), drugs (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue [paradox: treatment for MetHb but contraindicated in G6PD def]), fava beans (favism: divicine/isouramil → ROS); neonatal jaundice (G6PD def is an important cause of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia → kernicterus if untreated); diagnosis: ↓G6PD enzyme activity in RBCs (quantitative assay); NOTE: test during non-acute phase (during hemolysis, old deficient RBCs are destroyed → remaining young RBCs + reticulocytes have higher G6PD → false normal; retest 2-3 months later)

Transketolase: transketolase is an enzyme in the NON-OXIDATIVE branch of the PPP (transfers 2C units: Xu5P + R5P → S7P + G3P; Xu5P + E4P → F6P + G3P); requires TPP (thiamine); transketolase is NOT the committed step
Transaldolase: transaldolase transfers 3C units in the non-oxidative PPP branch (S7P + G3P → E4P + F6P); NOT the committed step
explanation: Pentose phosphate pathway — complete: Two branches: OXIDATIVE (irreversible, generates NADPH + R5P): (1) G6P → [G6PD, NADP⁺] → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH; (2) 6-PGL → [lactonase] → 6-phosphogluconate; (3) 6-PG → [6-PGDH, NADP⁺] → ribulose-5-phosphate + CO₂ + NADPH; per G6P: 2 NADPH + 1 CO₂ + ribulose-5P; NON-OXIDATIVE (reversible, interconverts sugars): ribulose-5P → [isomerase] → ribose-5P (for nucleotide synthesis: purines, pyrimidines, NAD⁺, FAD, CoA, RNA, DNA); OR ribulose-5P → [epimerase] → xylulose-5P; then transketolase + transaldolase rearrange C₃/C₄/C₅/C₆/C₇ sugars → ultimately: F6P + G3P (feed back into glycolysis); PPP functions: (1) NADPH production (lipogenesis [fatty acid + cholesterol synthesis], reductive biosynthesis, glutathione reduction [antioxidant defense], CYP450 reactions [drug metabolism, steroid synthesis], respiratory burst [NADPH oxidase in phagocytes: NADPH + O₂ → O₂⁻ (superoxide) → H₂O₂ → HOCl [MPO] → killing of engulfed bacteria; CGD (chronic granulomatous disease): NADPH oxidase (gp91phox/CYBB most common, X-linked) deficiency → ↓superoxide → ↓killing of CATALASE-POSITIVE organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia, Nocardia, Serratia → 'PLACESS'; catalase-negative organisms [Strep] survive because they produce H₂O₂ themselves → host MPO can use it; catalase-positive organisms degrade H₂O₂ → nothing for MPO to use)]); (2) ribose-5-phosphate (nucleotide synthesis); tissues with high PPP activity: liver (lipogenesis), adipose (lipogenesis), adrenal cortex (steroid synthesis), RBCs (NADPH → GSH → antioxidant; RBCs have NO mitochondria → PPP is the ONLY source of NADPH), lactating mammary gland, gonads.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following amino acids is a precursor for both nitric oxide (NO) and creatine?
options: Glutamine: Gln is a nitrogen donor for purine/pyrimidine synthesis, fuel for enterocytes/immune cells, and participates in acid-base balance (renal ammoniagenesis); Gln is NOT a direct precursor for NO or creatine (though Gln → Glu → various; the direct NO precursor is Arg)

Arginine: ARGININE is a remarkably versatile amino acid that serves as the precursor for both NO and creatine (and several other important metabolites); (1) NO synthesis: Arg → [NOS: nitric oxide synthase, requires BH4/NADPH/FAD/FMN/heme/CaM] → NO + citrulline; the guanidinium group of Arg is the nitrogen source for NO; (2) CREATINE synthesis (two steps, two organs): Step 1 — KIDNEY: Arg + Gly → [AGAT: arginine-glycine amidinotransferase, rate-limiting] → guanidinoacetate (GAA) + ornithine; Step 2 — LIVER: GAA → [GAMT: guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase, requires SAM] → CREATINE; creatine → transported to MUSCLE + BRAIN → phosphorylated by CREATINE KINASE (CK): creatine + ATP → phosphocreatine (PCr) + ADP; PCr serves as rapid ATP buffer (PCr + ADP → [CK] → ATP + creatine; Lohmann reaction); PCr → spontaneous non-enzymatic cyclization → CREATININE (constant rate proportional to muscle mass → excreted by kidneys → serum creatinine used to estimate GFR); (3) UREA CYCLE: Arg → [arginase] → ornithine + urea; (4) POLYAMINES: Arg → ornithine → [ODC] → putrescine → spermidine → spermine (cell growth/proliferation); (5) AGMATINE: Arg → [ADC: arginine decarboxylase] → agmatine (neuromodulator, imidazoline receptor agonist); Arg is a conditionally essential amino acid (essential in neonates, growth, severe illness/trauma → ↑demand exceeds endogenous synthesis [mainly from citrulline in kidney])

Methionine: Met is the precursor for SAM (S-adenosylmethionine → universal methyl donor), homocysteine, and cysteine (transsulfuration); Met/SAM are involved in creatine synthesis (GAMT uses SAM → actually creatine synthesis is the LARGEST consumer of SAM → ~40% of all SAM-derived methyl groups go to creatine synthesis), but Met is NOT the direct precursor/substrate — Arg provides the guanidinium group
Histidine: His → histamine (histidine decarboxylase, PLP); His is NOT a precursor for NO or creatine
explanation: Arginine metabolism hub: Arg is at the crossroads of multiple pathways: (1) NOS → NO + citrulline (vasodilation, neurotransmission, immunity); (2) AGAT → GAA → GAMT → creatine (energy buffer; SAM is consumed by GAMT); (3) Arginase → ornithine + urea (nitrogen disposal); (4) ODC → putrescine → spermidine → spermine (polyamines: DNA stabilization, cell proliferation; elevated in rapidly growing cells/tumors; ODC inhibitor: DFMO/eflornithine → used for African trypanosomiasis [T. brucei gambiense] and as anti-cancer adjunct); (5) ADC → agmatine; competition between NOS and arginase for Arg substrate is clinically relevant: in asthma, ↑arginase in airways → ↓Arg for NOS → ↓NO (bronchodilator) → bronchoconstriction; in wound healing: M1 macrophages → iNOS → NO (antimicrobial); M2 macrophages → arginase → ornithine → proline (collagen synthesis for tissue repair) + polyamines (cell proliferation); this M1/M2 polarization and Arg metabolism is a key concept in immunometabolism.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which amino acid is required for the synthesis of heme, serving as one of the two substrates for ALA synthase?
options: Glutamate: Glu is NOT a substrate for ALA synthase (ALAS); Glu is important in amino acid metabolism (transamination, GDH) but not directly in heme synthesis

Glycine: GLYCINE is one of the two substrates for δ-AMINOLEVULINIC ACID SYNTHASE (ALAS), the first and rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis; reaction: SUCCINYL-CoA (from TCA cycle) + GLYCINE → [ALAS, cofactor PLP] → δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) + CO₂ + CoA; this reaction occurs in the MITOCHONDRIAL MATRIX; ALAS has two isoforms: ALAS1 (ubiquitous/housekeeping, liver-predominant; regulated by heme [negative feedback: heme represses ALAS1 transcription + blocks mitochondrial import of ALAS1 precursor protein] + drugs/CYP450 inducers [↑heme demand → ↑ALAS1] + glucose [↓ALAS1; 'glucose effect']) and ALAS2 (erythroid-specific; regulated by IRON via IRE-IRP system: ALAS2 mRNA has 5'-IRE → when iron is LOW, IRP binds IRE → blocks translation → ↓ALAS2 → ↓heme synthesis [appropriately, since no iron to insert]; when iron is HIGH, iron binds IRP → IRP dissociates → translation proceeds → ↑ALAS2 → ↑heme); sideroblastic anemia: can be caused by ALAS2 mutations (X-linked sideroblastic anemia) → ↓ALA → ↓heme → iron accumulates in mitochondria (cannot be incorporated into protoporphyrin) → ringed sideroblasts (Prussian blue stain of bone marrow: iron-laden mitochondria around the nucleus → perinuclear ring); also caused by B₆ deficiency (PLP is ALAS cofactor → ↓ALAS activity → same result), isoniazid (depletes PLP), copper deficiency, lead poisoning (↓ALAD + ↓ferrochelatase), myelodysplastic syndromes
Alanine: Ala is the major amino acid in the glucose-alanine cycle; NOT a substrate for ALAS

Serine: Ser is involved in one-carbon metabolism (Ser → [SHMT, PLP] → Gly + CH₂-THF) and sphingolipid synthesis (SPT: palmitoyl-CoA + Ser → sphinganine); while Ser can be converted to Gly (which then enters heme synthesis), Ser itself is NOT the direct substrate for ALAS
explanation: Heme degradation pathway (equally high-yield): OLD RBCs (120-day lifespan) → phagocytosed by reticuloendothelial system (splenic macrophages > Kupffer cells/liver > bone marrow macrophages) → Hb released → heme + globin (globin → amino acids recycled; iron → stored [ferritin] or transported [transferrin] → reused); HEME → [HEME OXYGENASE: rate-limiting; cleaves α-methene bridge; requires O₂ + NADPH] → BILIVERDIN (green; CO released → exhaled; iron released → transferrin) → [BILIVERDIN REDUCTASE, NADPH] → BILIRUBIN (yellow; unconjugated/indirect bilirubin [UCB]; UCB is lipophilic → toxic to brain [kernicterus in neonates]; transported bound to ALBUMIN in blood → liver); LIVER: UCB → [UGT1A1: UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1] → bilirubin diglucuronide (conjugated/direct bilirubin [CB]; water-soluble; excreted in bile → intestine); INTESTINE: CB → [bacterial β-glucuronidases] → unconjugated bilirubin → [bacterial enzymes] → UROBILINOGEN (colorless); most urobilinogen → STERCOBILINOGEN → oxidized to STERCOBILIN (brown: gives feces color); some urobilinogen → reabsorbed (enterohepatic circulation) → kidney → UROBILIN (yellow: gives urine color); Jaundice: serum bilirubin >2.5 mg/dL → yellow discoloration of skin/sclera/mucous membranes; types: (1) prehepatic/hemolytic: ↑UCB (↑RBC destruction > liver conjugation capacity); (2) hepatic: ↑UCB or CB depending on cause (Gilbert: ↓UGT1A1 activity → mild ↑UCB; Crigler-Najjar: ↓↓UGT1A1 → severe ↑UCB; hepatitis: ↑both); (3) posthepatic/obstructive: ↑CB (bile duct obstruction → ↓bile flow → CB refluxes to blood; pale/clay-colored stools [no stercobilin]; dark urine [↑CB excreted in urine]; ↑ALP/GGT).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is used as an antidote for acetaminophen overdose. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: NAC directly inhibits CYP2E1, preventing formation of NAPQI: NAC does NOT directly inhibit CYP450 enzymes; the toxic metabolite NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) is formed by CYP2E1 (and CYP1A2, CYP3A4) regardless of NAC; NAC works AFTER NAPQI is already formed

NAC replenishes glutathione (GSH) stores, allowing detoxification of the toxic metabolite NAPQI: N-ACETYLCYSTEINE (NAC) is the antidote for ACETAMINOPHEN (paracetamol/APAP) overdose; mechanism: NAC serves as a precursor for GLUTATHIONE (GSH) synthesis; NAC → deacetylated → L-cysteine (the RATE-LIMITING substrate for GSH synthesis: γ-GCS catalyzes Glu + Cys → γ-Glu-Cys → [GSH synthetase] → γ-Glu-Cys-Gly = GSH); in normal APAP metabolism: ~90% of APAP → glucuronidation (UGT) + sulfation (SULT) → nontoxic metabolites → renal excretion; ~5-10% → CYP2E1 → NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine; highly reactive electrophilic metabolite); normally: NAPQI + GSH → [glutathione-S-transferase] → mercapturic acid conjugate → nontoxic → excreted; in OVERDOSE: glucuronidation/sulfation pathways saturated → more APAP shunted to CYP2E1 → ↑↑NAPQI production → GSH stores DEPLETED (when GSH < ~30% of normal → NAPQI cannot be conjugated) → free NAPQI → covalently binds hepatocyte proteins (mitochondrial proteins especially) → oxidative stress + mitochondrial dysfunction → hepatocyte NECROSIS → acute liver failure (zone 3/centrilobular necrosis: CYP2E1 is highest in zone 3 → most NAPQI generated here → most damage); clinical: toxic dose >150 mg/kg or >7.5-10 g in adults; timeline: 0-24h: nausea, vomiting (may be asymptomatic); 24-72h: rising AST/ALT (massive ↑, can be >10,000; AST > ALT early; ALT > AST later), RUQ pain, ↑PT/INR; 72-96h: peak liver injury → hepatic failure (↑bilirubin, coagulopathy, encephalopathy, renal failure, lactic acidosis); >96h: recovery (if survive) or death; diagnosis: serum APAP level at 4h (plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram → above treatment line → treat); NAC protocol: most effective within 8h (>95% prevention of hepatotoxicity); still beneficial up to 24-72h+ (also has anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, and direct mitochondrial protective effects beyond GSH replenishment); IV NAC (21h protocol or modified 2-bag protocol) or oral (72h Rumack protocol)

NAC chelates acetaminophen in the GI tract, preventing absorption: NAC is NOT a chelator of acetaminophen; NAC works at the metabolic level (GSH replenishment), not by binding/neutralizing the parent drug in the GI tract; activated charcoal (not NAC) can adsorb APAP if given within 1-2h of ingestion
NAC enhances renal excretion of acetaminophen: NAC does NOT significantly enhance renal excretion of APAP; the therapeutic mechanism is GSH replenishment for NAPQI detoxification
explanation: Glutathione (GSH) — comprehensive: Structure: γ-Glu-Cys-Gly (tripeptide; note unusual γ-peptide bond between Glu γ-carboxyl and Cys α-amino); synthesis: (1) γ-GCS (γ-glutamylcysteine synthetase/glutamate-cysteine ligase): Glu + Cys + ATP → γ-Glu-Cys (RATE-LIMITING; feedback inhibited by GSH; Cys availability is rate-limiting); (2) GSH synthetase: γ-Glu-Cys + Gly + ATP → GSH; Functions: (1) ANTIOXIDANT: GSH + H₂O₂ → [GPx, selenium-dependent] → GSSG + H₂O; 2 GSH → GSSG (oxidized); GSSG → [glutathione reductase, NADPH] → 2 GSH (recycled; this is why NADPH from PPP is critical for maintaining GSH); (2) DETOXIFICATION: GSH + electrophiles → [GST: glutathione-S-transferase] → conjugates → mercapturic acid → excreted (NAPQI, aflatoxin epoxide, etc.); (3) AMINO ACID TRANSPORT: γ-glutamyl cycle (GGT on cell surface); (4) LEUKOTRIENE synthesis: LTA₄ + GSH → [LTC₄ synthase] → LTC₄ (cysteinyl leukotriene); (5) maintains protein thiol groups in reduced state (prevents oxidative damage to enzymes); (6) reduces dehydroascorbate → ascorbate (vitamin C recycling); GSH/GSSG ratio: normally >100:1 (highly reduced); ↓ratio = oxidative stress marker.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the enzyme deficient in Tay-Sachs disease?
options: Sphingomyelinase: sphingomyelinase (acid SMase) deficiency → Niemann-Pick disease type A/B; accumulates sphingomyelin in reticuloendothelial cells; type A: fatal infantile (hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spot, neurodegeneration); type B: chronic visceral (no CNS involvement, hepatosplenomegaly); NOT Tay-Sachs

Hexosaminidase A: TAY-SACHS DISEASE is caused by deficiency of HEXOSAMINIDASE A (HEX A; α-subunit encoded by HEXA gene on chromosome 15); HEX A cleaves the terminal N-acetylgalactosamine residue from GM2 ganglioside; deficiency → GM2 GANGLIOSIDE accumulation in NEURONS (gangliosides are particularly abundant in neuronal membranes); clinical: infantile form (most common): normal at birth → developmental regression beginning at ~3-6 months; exaggerated startle response (hyperacusis); progressive neurodegeneration (loss of motor skills, seizures, blindness); CHERRY-RED SPOT on fundoscopy (pathognomonic: fovea centralis appears red because it lacks ganglion cells → underlying choroidal vasculature visible; surrounding macula is pale/white due to GM2-laden ganglion cells); macrocephaly (megalencephaly: ↑brain volume from GM2 storage); NO HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY (distinguishes from Niemann-Pick: in Tay-Sachs, storage is primarily neuronal, NOT reticuloendothelial); death by age 3-5 years; diagnosis: ↓HEX A enzyme activity in serum/leukocytes + HEXA gene mutation analysis; carrier screening: ↓HEX A activity (carrier has ~50% normal activity; important in Ashkenazi Jewish population [carrier frequency ~1:30] → preconception screening recommended); Sandhoff disease: deficiency of BOTH HEX A and HEX B (β-subunit encoded by HEXB gene); clinically similar to Tay-Sachs BUT with visceral involvement (hepatosplenomegaly) because HEX B processes additional substrates in visceral organs; also has cherry-red spot

β-Glucocerebrosidase: β-glucocerebrosidase (GBA1/acid β-glucosidase) deficiency → Gaucher disease; accumulates glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) in macrophages → Gaucher cells ('crumpled tissue paper' appearance); type 1 (non-neuronopathic, most common): hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises (avascular necrosis, Erlenmeyer flask deformity), pancytopenia; NO CNS involvement; treatment: ERT (imiglucerase, velaglucerase) or SRT (eliglustat, miglustat); NOT Tay-Sachs

α-Galactosidase A: α-galactosidase A deficiency → Fabry disease; X-linked recessive; accumulates globotriasoylceramide (Gb3/GL-3) in vascular endothelium, kidneys, heart, nerves; painful acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, corneal opacities (cornea verticillata), progressive renal failure, cardiomyopathy, stroke; NOT Tay-Sachs
explanation: Sphingolipid metabolism and storage diseases — overview: Sphingolipid backbone: ceramide (sphingosine + fatty acid); add different head groups → different sphingolipids: (1) sphingomyelin (ceramide + phosphocholine); (2) cerebrosides (ceramide + single sugar: galactose [galactocerebroside, in myelin] or glucose [glucocerebroside]); (3) gangliosides (ceramide + oligosaccharide containing sialic acid/NANA): GM1 → GM2 → GM3 etc. (numbered by number of sialic acid residues and complexity); Degradation: lysosomal hydrolases sequentially remove sugar/sialic acid residues; each enzyme deficiency → specific LSD: Tay-Sachs (HEX A → GM2); Sandhoff (HEX A+B → GM2 + other); Gaucher (GBA → glucocerebroside); Fabry (α-Gal A → Gb3, X-linked); Niemann-Pick A/B (SMase → sphingomyelin); Krabbe (galactocerebroside β-galactosidase/GALC → galactocerebroside + psychosine; globoid cells in brain); Metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A/ARSA → sulfatide → metachromatic staining with toluidine blue/cresyl violet); Farber (acid ceramidase → ceramide; painful subcutaneous nodules, hoarse cry).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the mechanism by which carbon monoxide (CO) causes toxicity?
options: CO inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) of the electron transport chain only: while CO does inhibit cytochrome c oxidase (binds to Fe²⁺ of heme a₃, similar to cyanide), this is NOT the primary mechanism of CO toxicity; the dominant mechanism is Hb binding

CO binds hemoglobin with much higher affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin, and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left: CO has approximately 200-250× HIGHER AFFINITY for hemoglobin than O₂; CO binds to the same Fe²⁺ in heme as O₂ → forms carboxyhemoglobin (HbCO); effects: (1) DIRECT DISPLACEMENT: CO occupies O₂-binding sites → ↓available Hb for O₂ transport → functional anemia; (2) LEFT SHIFT of ODC: CO binding to one subunit → conformational change in remaining subunits → ↑O₂ affinity → remaining oxygenated subunits hold onto O₂ more tightly → ↓O₂ release to tissues → this is actually MORE harmful than the simple displacement (the left shift means even the O₂ that IS bound cannot be effectively delivered); (3) Cytochrome oxidase inhibition (secondary): CO binds heme a₃ in Complex IV → ↓oxidative phosphorylation → cellular hypoxia; (4) Myoglobin binding: CO binds cardiac/skeletal myoglobin → ↓O₂ storage in muscle → cardiac dysfunction; clinical: cherry-red skin (HbCO is bright red; often only seen post-mortem; living patients may appear pale/cyanotic); headache (earliest symptom), confusion, syncope, seizures, coma, MI (cardiac is very sensitive), death; pulse oximetry reads FALSELY NORMAL or HIGH (pulse ox cannot distinguish HbCO from HbO₂ → both absorb similarly at 660 nm → SpO₂ appears normal despite severe hypoxia); PaO₂ on ABG is NORMAL (dissolved O₂ unaffected); diagnosis: CO-oximetry (multi-wavelength → measures HbCO directly); HbCO levels: <3% normal (non-smokers), <10% smokers; >20% → symptoms; >60% → coma/death; treatment: 100% O₂ via NRB mask (↓CO half-life from ~5h on room air to ~60-90 min on 100% O₂; displaces CO from Hb by mass action); hyperbaric O₂ (↓t½ to ~20-30 min; ↑dissolved O₂ → bypasses Hb → direct tissue oxygenation; indicated for: syncope/LOC, HbCO >25%, pregnancy, cardiac ischemia, persistent neuro symptoms)

CO causes methemoglobinemia by oxidizing Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺: methemoglobinemia involves oxidation of Hb iron Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺; CO does NOT oxidize Hb iron — CO BINDS to Fe²⁺ (keeping it in ferrous state, similar to O₂ binding); methemoglobin-forming agents include dapsone, nitrites, benzocaine, etc.

CO directly denatures hemoglobin protein structure: CO does not denature Hb; it binds reversibly (albeit with very high affinity) to the heme iron; Hb structural denaturation occurs with oxidative agents → Heinz bodies (seen in G6PD deficiency, unstable Hb variants)
explanation: Toxic gases and hemoglobin — comparison: CO (carbon monoxide): binds Fe²⁺ (like O₂); 200-250× affinity > O₂; HbCO → cherry-red; left-shifts ODC; pulse ox falsely normal; treatment: 100% O₂, HBO; sources: incomplete combustion (car exhaust, house fires, gas heaters, charcoal grills); CN⁻ (cyanide): binds Fe³⁺ of cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) → blocks ETC → cells cannot use O₂ → cytotoxic/histotoxic hypoxia (↑venous O₂ [O₂ not extracted by tissues]; bright red venous blood; ↑lactate [anaerobic metabolism despite adequate O₂ delivery]); sources: house fires (burning plastics/nylon → HCN), nitroprusside, amygdalin (bitter almonds, apricot pits); bitter almond smell; treatment: hydroxocobalamin (binds CN → cyanocobalamin → excreted; preferred first-line) or cyanide antidote kit (amyl nitrite → sodium nitrite [induces MetHb → MetHb binds CN preferentially → cyanmetHb] + sodium thiosulfate [rhodanese converts CN → thiocyanate → renal excretion]); H₂S (hydrogen sulfide): also inhibits Complex IV (binds Fe³⁺); 'rotten egg' smell; sources: sewers, volcanic gas, industrial; treatment: similar to cyanide (nitrites + supportive).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the function of ubiquitin in the proteasome pathway?
options: Ubiquitin acts as a chaperone to fold misfolded proteins: chaperones (Hsp70, Hsp90, chaperonins) fold proteins; ubiquitin does NOT fold proteins — it TAGS proteins for degradation

Ubiquitin is a small protein that tags target proteins for degradation by the 26S proteasome through covalent attachment: UBIQUITIN is a highly conserved 76-amino acid protein (~8.5 kDa) that is covalently attached to target proteins as a signal for degradation by the 26S PROTEASOME; ubiquitination process (E1-E2-E3 cascade): (1) E1 (ubiquitin-activating enzyme; only 2 in humans: UBA1, UBA6): ubiquitin + ATP → E1~Ub thioester (activates Ub); (2) E2 (ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme; ~40 in humans): E1~Ub → E2~Ub (transfers Ub); (3) E3 (ubiquitin ligase; ~600-700 in humans → confer SUBSTRATE SPECIFICITY): E2~Ub + target protein → Ub covalently attached to target Lys residue (isopeptide bond between Ub C-terminal Gly76 and ε-amino group of target Lys); POLYUBIQUITINATION: multiple rounds → polyubiquitin chain; K48-linked polyubiquitin (chains linked through Lys48 of ubiquitin) → canonical degradation signal → recognized by 26S proteasome; K63-linked polyubiquitin → non-degradative signals (NF-κB activation, DNA repair, endosomal sorting); 26S PROTEASOME: 20S core (barrel-shaped, 4 stacked rings [α₇β₇β₇α₇]; proteolytic activity in β-subunits [β1: caspase-like, β2: trypsin-like, β5: chymotrypsin-like]) + 19S regulatory cap (recognizes polyUb chain, deubiquitinates [DUBs recycle Ub], unfolds substrate, feeds into 20S core → ATP-dependent); products: short peptides (8-25 aa; some presented by MHC class I → immune surveillance); proteasome inhibitors: bortezomib/carfilzomib/ixazomib → used in multiple myeloma (↓NF-κB → ↑apoptosis of myeloma cells; ↓degradation of pro-apoptotic proteins)
Ubiquitin directly degrades proteins by proteolytic cleavage: ubiquitin has NO protease activity; it is a TAG/signal — the actual proteolysis is performed by the 26S proteasome

Ubiquitin is a large enzyme complex that cleaves peptide bonds: ubiquitin is SMALL (76 aa) and has NO enzymatic activity; the proteasome is the large enzyme complex (~2.5 MDa) that cleaves peptide bonds
explanation: Protein degradation pathways: (1) UBIQUITIN-PROTEASOME SYSTEM (UPS): cytoplasmic/nuclear; selective (specific proteins tagged by E3 ligases → polyUb → 26S proteasome); degrades: regulatory proteins (cyclins → cell cycle; IκB → NF-κB activation; p53 → Mdm2 E3 ligase; HIF-1α → VHL E3 ligase [↓O₂ → ↓VHL → ↑HIF → angiogenesis; VHL mutations → clear cell renal cell carcinoma]), misfolded ER proteins (ERAD: retrotranslocation → cytoplasmic Ub → proteasome), short-lived proteins, damaged proteins; (2) LYSOSOMAL DEGRADATION: (a) autophagy (macroautophagy: double-membrane autophagosome engulfs cytoplasmic content → fuses with lysosome → degradation; induced by: starvation, mTOR inhibition [rapamycin], AMPK activation; ATG genes; microautophagy: direct lysosomal invagination; chaperone-mediated autophagy [CMA]: KFERQ-motif proteins → Hsc70 → LAMP-2A receptor → lysosomal import); (b) endocytosis/phagocytosis → lysosomal digestion; lysosomal enzymes: acid hydrolases (pH ~4.5-5; acid phosphatase, cathepsins, lipases, glycosidases, nucleases); M6P targeting to lysosomes; (3) CALPAINS: cytoplasmic Ca²⁺-dependent cysteine proteases; involved in: muscle protein turnover, cell migration, apoptosis; (4) CASPASES: cysteine-aspartate proteases; initiator (caspase-8, -9, -10) and effector (caspase-3, -6, -7) → apoptosis.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which vitamin serves as a cofactor for glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), the enzyme that synthesizes GABA?
options: Thiamine (B₁): TPP is cofactor for α-keto acid dehydrogenases (PDC, OGDH, BCKDH) and transketolase; NOT for GAD
Riboflavin (B₂): FAD/FMN are cofactors for oxidoreductases (succinate dehydrogenase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, MTHFR, xanthine oxidase, etc.); NOT for GAD

Pyridoxine (B₆): PYRIDOXAL 5'-PHOSPHATE (PLP), the active form of vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine), is the cofactor for GLUTAMATE DECARBOXYLASE (GAD); GAD catalyzes: glutamate → GABA (γ-aminobutyric acid) + CO₂; GABA is the major INHIBITORY neurotransmitter in the brain; two GAD isoforms: GAD65 (synaptic vesicle-associated; synthesizes GABA for neurotransmission) and GAD67 (cytoplasmic; synthesizes GABA for metabolic functions); PLP deficiency → ↓GAD activity → ↓GABA → loss of inhibitory neurotransmission → SEIZURES (particularly in infants: pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy → neonatal/infantile seizures refractory to standard anticonvulsants → responsive to pyridoxine/PLP supplementation; caused by ALDH7A1 mutation [antiquitin deficiency] → accumulates α-aminoadipic semialdehyde/piperideine-6-carboxylate [P6C] → P6C inactivates PLP by Knoevenagel condensation → functional PLP deficiency → ↓GAD + ↓other PLP enzymes → seizures); INH (isoniazid) overdose → seizures: INH inhibits pyridoxine phosphokinase (↓PLP) + directly reacts with PLP → ↓GABA → seizures; treatment: IV pyridoxine (gram-for-gram replacement: 1g B₆ per 1g INH ingested); autoimmune: anti-GAD65 antibodies → stiff-person syndrome (↓GABA → continuous motor neuron firing → severe muscle stiffness/spasms; associated with T1DM [GAD65 is also expressed in pancreatic β-cells → autoimmune target in T1DM]; treatment: diazepam [GABA-A agonist], IVIG, immunosuppression)
Cobalamin (B₁₂): B₁₂ (AdoCbl/MeCbl) is cofactor for MCM and methionine synthase; NOT for GAD
explanation: GABA metabolism and clinical connections: Synthesis: Glu → [GAD, PLP] → GABA (brain; GAD is present in GABAergic neurons); Degradation: GABA → [GABA transaminase/GABA-T, PLP] → succinic semialdehyde → [SSADH] → succinate → TCA cycle; this is the 'GABA shunt' (bypasses α-KG → succinyl-CoA step of TCA in neurons); vigabatrin: irreversible inhibitor of GABA-T → ↑GABA → anticonvulsant (used for infantile spasms/West syndrome); side effect: irreversible concentric visual field constriction; GABA receptors: GABA-A: ionotropic (ligand-gated Cl⁻ channel; fast inhibition; binding sites for: benzodiazepines [↑frequency of Cl⁻ channel opening], barbiturates [↑duration of Cl⁻ channel opening], alcohol, neurosteroids, propofol; benzodiazepine site = between α and γ subunits; z-drugs [zolpidem] bind α₁-selective; flumazenil: BZD antagonist); GABA-B: metabotropic (G-protein coupled; Gi → ↓cAMP; also activates K⁺ channels [hyperpolarization] and inhibits Ca²⁺ channels [↓NT release]; slow, prolonged inhibition; baclofen: GABA-B agonist → muscle relaxant/antispastic).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Allopurinol, used in the treatment of gout, inhibits which enzyme?
options: Adenosine deaminase: ADA converts adenosine → inosine (purine degradation); ADA deficiency → SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency; ↑dATP → toxic to lymphocytes → ↓T + ↓B + ↓NK cells); allopurinol does NOT inhibit ADA

Xanthine oxidase: ALLOPURINOL inhibits XANTHINE OXIDASE (XO); XO catalyzes the last two steps of purine catabolism: (1) hypoxanthine → xanthine; (2) xanthine → URIC ACID (+ H₂O₂/superoxide); allopurinol is a structural ANALOG of hypoxanthine (differs by one atom: allopurinol has N at position 1 of the pyrazolo ring vs C in hypoxanthine); allopurinol is a SUICIDE INHIBITOR: XO oxidizes allopurinol → OXYPURINOL (alloxanthine) → oxypurinol binds tightly to the reduced form of XO (Mo⁴⁺) → inactivates it (mechanism-based inhibition → the enzyme processes the drug into an inhibitor); result: ↓uric acid production → ↓serum urate → ↓urate crystal deposition → ↓gouty arthritis flares (long-term); allopurinol is used for: chronic gout prophylaxis (NOT acute attack → can worsen acute gout by mobilizing crystals; start with colchicine/NSAID cover), tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis (↑purine release from dying cells → ↑uric acid → urate nephropathy; rasburicase [recombinant urate oxidase] preferred for high-risk TLS → converts uric acid → allantoin [highly soluble]; humans lack urate oxidase naturally → uric acid is the end product of purine catabolism in humans); FEBUXOSTAT: non-purine selective XO inhibitor (does NOT require XO activation → not a suicide inhibitor; more potent; for allopurinol-intolerant patients; concern: possible ↑CV mortality [CARES trial]); allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome: severe (SJS/TEN, DRESS); associated with HLA-B*5801 allele (common in Southeast Asians, African Americans → screen before starting in high-risk populations)

HGPRT: HGPRT (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) is a SALVAGE pathway enzyme (hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP; guanine + PRPP → GMP); HGPRT deficiency → Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (X-linked; ↑↑uric acid + severe neurological: self-mutilation [lip/finger biting], intellectual disability, choreoathetosis, dystonia, spasticity); allopurinol ↓uric acid in Lesch-Nyhan but does NOT treat neurological symptoms (the neurological problems are due to dopamine pathway dysfunction from ↓purine salvage, not uric acid); allopurinol does NOT inhibit HGPRT

Phosphoribosylpyrophosphate (PRPP) synthetase: PRPP synthetase makes PRPP (ribose-5P + ATP → PRPP + AMP); PRPP is used in purine/pyrimidine de novo synthesis and salvage pathways; PRPP synthetase superactivity (gain-of-function, X-linked) → ↑PRPP → ↑purine synthesis → ↑uric acid → gout; allopurinol does NOT inhibit PRPP synthetase
explanation: Purine metabolism — catabolism and gout: Purine catabolism: AMP → [AMP deaminase] → IMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → inosine → [PNP: purine nucleoside phosphorylase] → hypoxanthine → [XO] → xanthine → [XO] → URIC ACID; GMP → [5'-nucleotidase] → guanosine → [PNP] → guanine → [guanine deaminase] → xanthine → [XO] → uric acid; Uric acid: end product of purine catabolism in humans (we lack urate oxidase/uricase → cannot convert uric acid → allantoin; most other mammals have uricase → lower urate levels); normal serum urate: <7 mg/dL; GOUT: ↑urate → monosodium urate (MSU) crystal deposition in joints → inflammatory arthritis; acute: sudden onset, extremely painful, usually 1st MTP (podagra); MSU crystals: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent under polarized light (bright yellow when parallel to slow axis of compensator); NLRP3 inflammasome activation → IL-1β → intense inflammation → neutrophil recruitment; treatment acute: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine (inhibits microtubule polymerization → ↓neutrophil migration; binds tubulin; also ↓NLRP3 inflammasome), corticosteroids, IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab); chronic prophylaxis: allopurinol/febuxostat (XO inhibitors → ↓urate production), probenecid (uricosuric → ↑renal urate excretion; blocks URAT1 transporter), lesinurad (URAT1 inhibitor), pegloticase (PEGylated uricase → converts urate → allantoin; for refractory gout).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the function of carnitine in fatty acid metabolism?
options: Carnitine activates fatty acids by forming acyl-CoA: fatty acid activation (FA + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi) is performed by ACYL-CoA SYNTHETASE (fatty acid thiokinase) on the outer mitochondrial membrane; carnitine is NOT involved in activation

Carnitine transports long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane for β-oxidation: CARNITINE (β-hydroxy-γ-trimethylaminobutyric acid) is essential for transporting LONG-CHAIN fatty acyl groups (≥C14) across the INNER MITOCHONDRIAL MEMBRANE (IMM), which is impermeable to CoA and acyl-CoA; the CARNITINE SHUTTLE: (1) acyl-CoA (outer membrane) + carnitine → [CPT-I (carnitine palmitoyltransferase I), outer face of IMM] → acylcarnitine + CoA; CPT-I is the RATE-LIMITING step of β-oxidation; (2) acylcarnitine → [CACT: carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase, IMM] → crosses IMM (exchanges acylcarnitine in for free carnitine out); (3) acylcarnitine → [CPT-II, inner face of IMM] → acyl-CoA + carnitine (acyl-CoA now in matrix → enters β-oxidation spiral); CPT-I is inhibited by MALONYL-CoA (product of ACC; ↑malonyl-CoA during FA synthesis → ↓CPT-I → ↓β-oxidation → prevents futile cycle of simultaneous FA synthesis and degradation); carnitine deficiency: primary (SLC22A5/OCTN2 transporter mutations → ↓carnitine uptake → systemic carnitine deficiency: hypoketotic hypoglycemia [↓β-oxidation → ↓ketogenesis + ↓GNG substrates], cardiomyopathy [heart relies heavily on FA oxidation], skeletal myopathy, ↑CK; treated with oral L-carnitine supplementation → dramatic improvement); secondary (organic acidemias → acylcarnitine esters accumulate and are excreted → carnitine depletion; also: valproic acid [↓carnitine], hemodialysis [carnitine lost], certain renal conditions); carnitine sources: meat (especially red meat; 'carnitine' from Latin 'caro' = flesh), dairy; endogenous synthesis from lysine + methionine (requires vitamin C, iron, B₆, niacin)
Carnitine is a cofactor for citrate synthase in the TCA cycle: citrate synthase catalyzes OAA + acetyl-CoA → citrate; it does NOT require carnitine; citrate synthase is in the mitochondrial matrix
Carnitine serves as an electron carrier in the respiratory chain: electron carriers in the ETC include NADH, FADH₂, CoQ (ubiquinone), and cytochrome c; carnitine is NOT an electron carrier
explanation: Fatty acid β-oxidation — complete: Location: mitochondrial matrix; substrates: activated fatty acids (acyl-CoA); process: 4-step cycle repeated → each cycle removes 2C as acetyl-CoA: (1) acyl-CoA → [acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, FAD → FADH₂] → trans-Δ²-enoyl-CoA (introduction of trans double bond between C2-C3); acyl-CoA dehydrogenases: VLCAD (C14-C20), LCAD (C12-C18), MCAD (C6-C12; MCAD deficiency: most common inherited β-oxidation defect; presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia during fasting/illness in infancy; ↑C8-acylcarnitine on NBS; ↑dicarboxylic acids in urine; risk of sudden death; treatment: avoid fasting, frequent feeding, IV glucose during illness), SCAD (C4-C6); (2) trans-Δ²-enoyl-CoA → [enoyl-CoA hydratase] → L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA (hydration); (3) L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA → [L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase, NAD⁺ → NADH] → 3-ketoacyl-CoA; (4) 3-ketoacyl-CoA → [thiolase/β-ketothiolase, CoASH] → acetyl-CoA + acyl-CoA(n-2) (thiolytic cleavage); cycle repeats; palmitate (C16): 7 cycles → 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH₂ + 7 NADH; energy: ~106 ATP; odd-chain FA: final product is propionyl-CoA (C3) → [PCC, biotin] → methylmalonyl-CoA → [MCM, B₁₂] → succinyl-CoA → TCA; unsaturated FA: require additional enzymes (enoyl-CoA isomerase for cis bonds; 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase for polyunsaturated).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following is the primary energy source for the brain during prolonged starvation?
options: Glucose: glucose is the primary brain fuel under FED conditions (brain consumes ~120 g glucose/day; obligate glucose user normally); however during PROLONGED starvation (>2-3 days), glucose availability ↓ markedly (hepatic glycogen depleted by 24-48h; gluconeogenesis from amino acids is limited by the need to preserve muscle protein) → brain ADAPTS to use an alternative fuel

Ketone bodies: During PROLONGED STARVATION (>2-3 days), KETONE BODIES (β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) become the PRIMARY energy source for the brain, supplying 60-70% of cerebral energy needs; ketone body production (KETOGENESIS): occurs in LIVER mitochondria; pathway: fatty acid β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA (exceeds TCA capacity because OAA is diverted to gluconeogenesis) → acetyl-CoA → [thiolase] → acetoacetyl-CoA → [HMG-CoA synthase, RATE-LIMITING for ketogenesis] → HMG-CoA → [HMG-CoA lyase] → acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA; acetoacetate → [β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, NADH] → β-hydroxybutyrate (β-OHB; most abundant ketone in blood; β-OHB:AcAc ratio increases during starvation as NADH:NAD⁺ rises); acetoacetate → [spontaneous decarboxylation] → acetone (volatile → exhaled → fruity breath odor in DKA); BRAIN UTILIZATION: β-OHB → [β-OHB dehydrogenase] → AcAc → [succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase/thiophorase/SCOT → transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA] → acetoacetyl-CoA → [thiolase] → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA → ATP; KEY: liver CANNOT use ketone bodies (liver lacks SCOT/thiophorase → this ensures ketones produced by liver are exported for peripheral use); PROTEIN-SPARING EFFECT: ↑ketone use by brain → ↓glucose requirement → ↓need for gluconeogenic amino acids → ↓muscle proteolysis → preserves lean mass during prolonged starvation (survival advantage)

Fatty acids: free fatty acids (FFAs) are a major fuel for many tissues during fasting (muscle, heart, liver); however, fatty acids CANNOT cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) efficiently — FFAs are bound to albumin in plasma and are too hydrophobic/large for significant BBB transport; the liver converts FFAs to ketone bodies (small, water-soluble → readily cross BBB) → this is why ketones, not FFAs, fuel the brain

Amino acids: amino acids contribute to gluconeogenesis (Ala from muscle → liver → glucose) but are NOT a primary direct brain fuel; excessive proteolysis for GNG would be fatal (loss of essential muscle including respiratory/cardiac muscle); the protein-sparing effect of ketones reduces amino acid use
explanation: Starvation metabolism — timeline: HOURS 0-4 (fed/absorptive): intestinal absorption → ↑glucose → ↑insulin → glycogenesis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis; brain uses glucose; HOURS 4-16 (post-absorptive): ↓glucose → ↓insulin + ↑glucagon → hepatic glycogenolysis → maintains blood glucose; HOURS 16-48 (early fasting): glycogen depleted → ↑gluconeogenesis (liver: from Ala, lactate, glycerol); ↑lipolysis (adipose: HSL activated by ↑glucagon/↑epinephrine/↓insulin → FFAs + glycerol); FFAs → liver β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA → early ketogenesis; muscle uses FFAs; brain still primarily glucose; DAYS 2-3+ (prolonged starvation): ↑↑ketogenesis; ketones rise → brain adapts → uses ketones for 60-70% energy; ↓GNG demand → ↓muscle proteolysis (protein-sparing); adipose lipolysis → FFAs fuel most tissues; WEEKS (late starvation): fat stores become depleted → forced ↑proteolysis → muscle wasting → immune suppression → organ failure → death; survival depends on initial fat stores (~160,000 kcal in adipose for average person → sustains ~60-70 days).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following correctly describes a Lineweaver-Burk plot?
options: It plots 1/[S] on the y-axis and 1/V on the x-axis: this is INVERTED; the correct Lineweaver-Burk plot has 1/V on the y-axis and 1/[S] on the x-axis

It is a double-reciprocal plot of 1/V versus 1/[S], where the y-intercept equals 1/Vmax and the x-intercept equals -1/Km: The LINEWEAVER-BURK PLOT (double-reciprocal plot) is a graphical representation of the Michaelis-Menten equation in linearized form; derived by taking the reciprocal of both sides of V = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]): 1/V = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax; this is a straight line (y = mx + b) where: x-axis = 1/[S]; y-axis = 1/V; SLOPE = Km/Vmax; Y-INTERCEPT = 1/Vmax (when 1/[S] = 0 → [S] = ∞ → V = Vmax); X-INTERCEPT = -1/Km (when 1/V = 0); uses: determining Km and Vmax from experimental data; distinguishing types of inhibition: COMPETITIVE: ↑apparent Km (inhibitor competes for active site → need more substrate to reach ½Vmax), Vmax UNCHANGED (at infinite [S], substrate outcompetes inhibitor); Lineweaver-Burk: different slopes, SAME y-intercept (1/Vmax unchanged), different x-intercept; UNCOMPETITIVE: inhibitor binds ONLY to ES complex → ↓apparent Km AND ↓Vmax by same factor; LB: parallel lines (same slope, different y- and x-intercepts); NONCOMPETITIVE (pure): inhibitor binds E or ES equally; ↓Vmax (some enzyme always inactive), Km UNCHANGED; LB: different slopes, SAME x-intercept (-1/Km), different y-intercept; MIXED: binds E and ES with different affinities; both Km and Vmax affected; lines intersect left of y-axis
It plots V versus [S] on a logarithmic scale: a V vs log[S] plot is a different representation (often used in pharmacology for dose-response curves); NOT a Lineweaver-Burk plot

It is a plot of V versus [S] that produces a sigmoidal curve: a V vs [S] plot producing a sigmoidal curve represents cooperative/allosteric kinetics (e.g., hemoglobin O₂ binding, ATCase, PFK-1); this is NOT a Lineweaver-Burk plot (which is a double-reciprocal linearization)
explanation: Enzyme kinetics — key concepts: Michaelis-Menten: V = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Km = substrate concentration at which V = ½Vmax; reflects enzyme's affinity for substrate (LOW Km = HIGH affinity); Vmax = maximum velocity (all enzyme saturated; proportional to [E]total × kcat); kcat (turnover number) = Vmax/[E]total = reactions per enzyme per second; catalytic efficiency = kcat/Km (higher = more efficient; limited by diffusion ~10⁸-10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ = 'diffusion-limited' or 'catalytically perfect' enzymes: carbonic anhydrase, triose phosphate isomerase, acetylcholinesterase); INHIBITION: Reversible: competitive (↑Km, same Vmax; overcome by ↑[S]; e.g., malonate vs succinate for SDH; statins vs HMG-CoA for HMGCR; methotrexate vs DHF for DHFR), uncompetitive (↓both Km and Vmax; binds ES; rare for single-substrate but common for multi-substrate), noncompetitive (↓Vmax, same Km; binds allosteric site on E or ES equally), mixed (changes both; binds E and ES with different Kd's); Irreversible: covalent modification → permanent inactivation; e.g., aspirin (acetylates COX Ser530), organophosphates (phosphorylate AChE Ser), DFMO (ODC), allopurinol → oxypurinol (suicide/mechanism-based); Allosteric enzymes: do NOT follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics → sigmoidal V vs [S] curves; positive cooperativity (Hill coefficient n > 1); no Lineweaver-Burk linearization applicable.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Which of the following conditions is associated with a deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase?
options: McArdle disease (GSD V): McArdle disease = glycogen phosphorylase (muscle isoform/PYGM) deficiency; exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, myoglobinuria after intense exercise, second wind phenomenon (hepatic glucose mobilization + FA oxidation takes over); NO hypoglycemia (liver glycogenolysis is intact)

Von Gierke disease (GSD I): VON GIERKE DISEASE (GSD Ia) = GLUCOSE-6-PHOSPHATASE (G6Pase) deficiency; G6Pase catalyzes the final step of both gluconeogenesis AND glycogenolysis: G6P → glucose + Pi (in the ER lumen of hepatocytes); this is the step that allows liver to RELEASE FREE GLUCOSE into blood; deficiency → G6P TRAPPED in liver → cannot be released → SEVERE FASTING HYPOGLYCEMIA (most prominent feature; the liver makes G6P via glycogenolysis and GNG but cannot convert it to free glucose); accumulated G6P → shunted to alternative pathways → ↑glycogen storage (G6P → G1P → UDP-glucose → glycogen: HEPATOMEGALY from massive glycogen + fat accumulation), ↑glycolysis (G6P → F6P → ... → pyruvate → LACTATE: LACTIC ACIDOSIS), ↑PPP (G6P → PPP → ribose → purines → degradation → HYPERURICEMIA → gout), ↑lipogenesis (acetyl-CoA from excess pyruvate → ↑FA synthesis → HYPERTRIGLYCERIDEMIA + ↑VLDL); clinical: presents in infancy with severe hypoglycemia (seizures), hepatomegaly (massive; kidneys also enlarged [nephromegaly: glycogen deposition]), 'doll-like' facies (fat cheeks from hyperlipidemia), growth retardation, bleeding tendency (platelet dysfunction from hyperlipidemia); labs: hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia; diagnosis: liver biopsy (↑glycogen, ↓G6Pase activity) → now usually genetic (G6PC gene); treatment: frequent feeds/continuous overnight feeds (nasogastric cornstarch infusion → slow glucose release → prevents hypoglycemia); raw CORNSTARCH (uncooked: slowly digested → sustained glucose release; given every 4-6h during day + overnight); avoid fructose/galactose (→ G6P but cannot be released → worsen lactic acidosis); liver transplant for severe cases; GSD Ib: G6P translocase (SLC37A4) deficiency → G6P cannot enter ER for G6Pase to act → same metabolic features + NEUTROPENIA + neutrophil dysfunction (↑infections); treated with G-CSF + empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor, reduces intracellular G6P in neutrophils → ↓neutrophil dysfunction)

Pompe disease (GSD II): Pompe = acid α-glucosidase (GAA/acid maltase) deficiency; lysosomal glycogen accumulation; infantile: massive cardiomegaly (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), hypotonia ('floppy baby'), macroglossia, hepatomegaly; death by ~1 year without treatment; late-onset: progressive proximal myopathy, respiratory insufficiency; treatment: ERT (alglucosidase alfa/Lumizyme); NOT associated with G6Pase deficiency

Cori disease (GSD III): Cori = glycogen debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase + 4-α-glucanotransferase) deficiency; accumulates abnormal glycogen with short outer branches (limit dextrin); milder hepatomegaly + hypoglycemia than GSD I (because GNG is intact → fasting hypoglycemia less severe); myopathy in type IIIa
explanation: Glycogen storage diseases — high-yield comparison: GSD 0 (glycogen synthase deficiency): ↓glycogen; fasting hypoglycemia + postprandial hyperglycemia/lactic acidemia; GSD I (von Gierke, G6Pase): severe hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hyperuricemia + hyperlipidemia + hepatomegaly; GSD II (Pompe, acid maltase): LYSOSOMAL; cardiomegaly (infantile), myopathy; only GSD with lysosomal accumulation; GSD III (Cori/Forbes, debranching enzyme): milder GSD I-like; limit dextrin; hepatomegaly + myopathy; GSD IV (Andersen, branching enzyme): abnormal glycogen (amylopectin-like, long unbranched chains) → cirrhosis → liver failure in childhood; GSD V (McArdle, muscle phosphorylase): exercise intolerance, myoglobinuria, second wind, no hypoglycemia; GSD VI (Hers, liver phosphorylase): mild hepatomegaly + mild hypoglycemia; benign; GSD VII (Tarui, PFK-M): exercise intolerance like McArdle but also hemolytic anemia (↓PFK in RBCs); KEY DIFFERENTIATORS: hepatomegaly → I, III, IV, VI; hypoglycemia → I (severe), III (moderate), VI (mild), 0; myopathy → II (all), III (a), V, VII; cardiomegaly → II.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Wilson disease is caused by mutation in which gene, leading to defective copper transport?
options: ATP7A: ATP7A encodes a copper-transporting ATPase expressed in INTESTINAL enterocytes; ATP7A mutations → MENKES DISEASE (X-linked recessive; ↓copper absorption from intestine → systemic copper deficiency; kinky/steely hair [pili torti: hair shaft twisted 180°; trichorrhexis nodosa], neurodegeneration, connective tissue defects [↓lysyl oxidase: ↓collagen/elastin cross-links → vascular fragility, bladder diverticula], hypothermia, seizures; low serum copper + low ceruloplasmin; fatal in early childhood; treatment: subcutaneous copper histidine [limited efficacy; bypasses intestinal defect]); ATP7A is NOT Wilson disease

ATP7B: WILSON DISEASE (hepatolenticular degeneration) is caused by mutations in ATP7B, encoding a copper-transporting ATPase expressed primarily in HEPATOCYTES; ATP7B functions: (1) in trans-Golgi: loads copper onto APOLCERULOPLASMIN → secreted as CERULOPLASMIN (holoceruloplasmin; ceruloplasmin carries ~95% of serum copper; also has ferroxidase activity: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ → loaded onto transferrin); (2) at canalicular membrane: excretes excess copper into BILE (the major excretory pathway for copper); ATP7B deficiency → ↓copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin (→ ↓serum ceruloplasmin → apoCP is rapidly degraded) + ↓biliary copper excretion → COPPER ACCUMULATES: first in liver (hepatocytes → oxidative damage → hepatitis → cirrhosis → liver failure); then overflows to blood → deposits in: BRAIN (basal ganglia [lenticular nucleus: putamen + globus pallidus] → neuropsychiatric symptoms: dysarthria, dystonia, tremor, rigidity, choreoathetosis, behavioral/psychiatric changes), EYES (Descemet's membrane of cornea → KAYSER-FLEISCHER RINGS [golden-brown/green-brown rings at corneal periphery; pathognomonic when present with neuropsychiatric disease; seen on slit-lamp; due to copper deposition]; also sunflower cataracts), KIDNEYS (proximal tubular dysfunction → Fanconi-like), RBCs (copper → oxidative hemolysis → Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia); presents age 5-40; autosomal recessive (AR); diagnosis: ↓ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), ↑24h urinary copper (>100 μg/day), ↑hepatic copper on liver biopsy (>250 μg/g dry weight), KF rings, ATP7B mutations; treatment: D-PENICILLAMINE (copper chelator: forms soluble complexes → ↑urinary copper excretion; side effects: hypersensitivity, SLE-like, nephrotoxicity, bone marrow suppression) or TRIENTINE (alternative chelator; fewer side effects), ZINC (↑intestinal metallothionein → metallothionein binds dietary copper → ↓absorption → used for maintenance/presymptomatic), dietary copper restriction (avoid liver, shellfish, mushrooms, chocolate, nuts); liver transplant for fulminant hepatic failure (curative: new liver has functional ATP7B)

SLC40A1: SLC40A1 encodes FERROPORTIN (the only known iron exporter on basolateral membrane of enterocytes + macrophages; hepcidin binds ferroportin → internalization + degradation → ↓iron export → ↓serum iron); ferroportin disease (SLC40A1 mutations) → rare iron overload disorder; NOT related to copper/Wilson disease

CP: CP encodes CERULOPLASMIN; aceruloplasminemia = CP gene mutations → absent ceruloplasmin → ↓ferroxidase activity → iron accumulation (brain, liver, pancreas → neurodegeneration, DM, retinal degeneration); ↓serum iron + ↓ferritin paradoxically because ceruloplasmin's ferroxidase is needed for iron export; this is an IRON disorder, not a copper transport disorder; in Wilson disease, ceruloplasmin is ↓ but the genetic defect is in ATP7B, not CP
explanation: Copper metabolism: Dietary copper → absorbed in duodenum/jejunum (via CTR1/SLC31A1 on apical membrane) → inside enterocyte: copper binds metallochaperones (ATOX1 → delivers Cu to ATP7A [Golgi/basolateral] or ATP7B [in liver]) → basolateral export → portal blood (bound to albumin, amino acids [histidine], transcuprein) → LIVER (major site of Cu metabolism); in hepatocyte: Cu → ATP7B → (1) Golgi: Cu loaded onto apoceruloplasmin → holoceruloplasmin secreted to blood; (2) bile canaliculus: excess Cu excreted in bile (primary excretion route; ~80% of daily Cu excretion is biliary); ceruloplasmin (CP): 132 kDa glycoprotein; carries 6 Cu atoms; ferroxidase activity (converts Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ for transferrin loading; this is why ceruloplasmin deficiency → iron accumulation [aceruloplasminemia]); CP is also a positive acute-phase protein (↑in inflammation, pregnancy, OCP use → can mask Wilson disease by normalizing CP levels); daily Cu requirement: ~0.9 mg; excess → toxicity (Cu generates ROS via Fenton-like chemistry: Cu⁺ + H₂O₂ → Cu²⁺ + OH⁻ + OH• → oxidative damage to lipids, proteins, DNA); Cu enzymes: ceruloplasmin (ferroxidase), cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV: Cu_A + Cu_B), SOD1 (Cu/Zn-SOD: superoxide dismutase), tyrosinase (melanin synthesis), lysyl oxidase (collagen/elastin cross-links), dopamine β-hydroxylase (DA → NE).

subject: Biochemistry
stem: Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) is a component of which of the following coenzymes?
options: NAD⁺ and NADP⁺: NAD⁺/NADP⁺ are derived from NIACIN (vitamin B₃/nicotinic acid/nicotinamide); NAD⁺ = nicotinamide + ADP-ribose; NOT from riboflavin

FAD and FMN: RIBOFLAVIN (vitamin B₂) is the precursor of two coenzymes: FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide); riboflavin → [riboflavin kinase, ATP] → FMN → [FAD synthetase/FMN adenylyltransferase, ATP] → FAD; FMN and FAD are FLAVIN coenzymes (contain the isoalloxazine ring system that undergoes reversible oxidation-reduction: accepts 2 H atoms [2e⁻ + 2H⁺]); enzymes that use FAD/FMN are called FLAVOPROTEINS; key FAD-dependent enzymes: succinate dehydrogenase (Complex II: succinate → fumarate + FADH₂), acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (β-oxidation: first step), dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3 component of PDC/OGDH/BCKDH complexes), glutathione reductase (GSSG + NADPH → 2 GSH; FAD-dependent), xanthine oxidase (hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid), MTHFR (5,10-CH₂-THF → 5-CH₃-THF; FAD-dependent; MTHFR C677T variant → ↓activity → ↑Hcy if folate intake is low), monoamine oxidase (MAO: oxidative deamination of catecholamines/serotonin; MAO-A: NE/5-HT/DA; MAO-B: DA/phenylethylamine); key FMN-dependent: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase: NADH → FMN → Fe-S clusters → CoQ), L-amino acid oxidase; riboflavin deficiency: cheilosis (fissures at corners of mouth/angular stomatitis), glossitis (magenta tongue), corneal vascularization, seborrheic dermatitis, normocytic anemia; sources: dairy (milk is a major source → why milk in glass bottles loses B₂ [riboflavin is photosensitive → destroyed by UV light/sunlight → opaque containers preferred]), eggs, lean meats, green vegetables
Coenzyme A and ACP: CoA and ACP contain PANTOTHENIC ACID (vitamin B₅); CoA = pantothenate + cysteine + ADP; pantothenate is NOT riboflavin
